title: The lake the Yelamu knew first
place: East shore of Lake Merced, near today's SF State campus (approximate)
hook: Long before anyone named it for Our Lady of Mercy, Yelamu families gathered tule reeds here and camped in the dunes above the surf.
story: For thousands of years, Yelamu groups of Ramaytush-speaking people hunted, fished and harvested tule reeds at Lake Merced. The tule became clothing and boats, and mussels and native Olympia oysters fed people camping in the high dunes west of the lake [1]. Archaeologists have found tools and other signs of Yelamu people on the lake's east side and where Fort Funston is today, and two names in the Mission Dolores registers, "Mitline" and "Opurome," may be connected with these camps [1]. Of the roughly 50 places in the city where Indian artifacts have turned up, Gary Kamiya counts a couple of sites by Lake Merced and the "sparse remains of bones" found on the SF State campus [2]. The Yelamu numbered perhaps 200 people, moving seasonally between village sites [1]. In the fall of 1774 Fernando Rivera y Moncada's expedition camped just northeast of the lake, and in 1775 Father Francisco Palóu named it La Laguna de Nuestra Señora de la Merced, after the feast day on which he left [1]. About a decade after the Spanish arrived, the last local Yelamu had been baptized into Mission Dolores. Nobody recorded what they called the lake [1].

title: A brush shelter by the lake of sorrows
place: Camp and Albion Streets (California Historical Landmark 327-1)
hook: San Francisco's first Catholic mass was said not at the famous adobe, but under brushwood on the shore of a lake that may never have been a lake.
story: Mission Dolores did not start where the white adobe stands. On June 29, 1776, Father Francisco Palóu, travelling with the Anza expedition, had a shelter of brushwood put up at the edge of a lagoon the Spanish called the Lago de los Dolores, and offered the first mass there [1]. The site had been scouted that March by the missionary Pedro Font, and the mission took its popular name from a nearby creek, the Arroyo de Nuestra Señora de los Dolores [2]. Wikipedia's infobox records the Ohlone place name as Chutchui [2]. A log-and-thatch mission was dedicated on October 9, 1776, once the needed church papers arrived; the adobe church a few blocks west came in 1791 [1][2]. Some sources place that first chapel near today's Camp and Albion streets, where a state plaque went up on June 29, 1995 [1][2]. The famous lagoon is slippery history. FoundSF argues it was probably only a seasonal, tidal pool, and that its reputation as a year-round lake comes largely from a map published in 1912 [3]. Either way, the water is long gone under the Mission's alleys.

title: A mud-walled square on a windy slope
place: Site of the original Spanish Presidio, east of Pershing Square
hook: San Francisco's first European settlement was a small square of mud walls, and within two years a single rainstorm had nearly washed it away.
story: In June 1776 about 193 colonists and soldiers, most of them of mixed Spanish and Indigenous descent, reached the bay with Lieutenant José Joaquín Moraga after a long march from Sonora, driving a herd of around 1,000 animals [1]. The site Anza had marked, on the cliff where Fort Point now stands, was too exposed, so the fort was built about a mile southeast, where there was more shelter and fresh water [2]. It was a square of oak and mud, and it was dedicated on September 17, 1776 [2]. Two years later a violent rainstorm almost destroyed it, and the settlers had to rebuild with a commandant's house, barracks and a chapel [2]. The Presidio was the northernmost outpost of Spain's empire on the coast. It usually got at most one supply ship a year, and women and children often outnumbered the soldiers, who were regularly sent off on guard duty elsewhere [1]. Nothing of the square survives above ground. A boulder by the sidewalk just east of Pershing Square roughly marks its northwest corner, and the whole square measured about 300 feet on each side [3].

title: Lilies in the tent at Mountain Lake
place: Mountain Lake, south edge of the Presidio
hook: Before there was a San Francisco, a Spanish captain pitched camp beside a small lake, and two local men walked in carrying firewood.
story: In late March 1776 Juan Bautista de Anza, who had led colonists hundreds of miles north from today's Mexico, camped beside a lake he described as 'of very fine water near the mouth of the port of San Francisco' [1]. He liked the running water, firewood and pasture, but grumbled that there was no timber 'even for barracks' [1]. From here Anza and his chaplain, Father Pedro Font, rode out to scout sites for the future presidio and mission [1][2]. The land they saw was not empty wilderness. Two Yelamu men, members of the small Ohlone-speaking people who lived on the peninsula, visited the camp and brought firewood, the first recorded exchange of gifts between the newcomers and the locals [3]. Their burning of the land kept the mesa open and full of flowers. Font wrote that there were so many lilies by the lake 'that I had them almost inside my tent' [3]. The lake was later drawn down: in 1897 its water irrigated the Presidio's new golf course [2]. A 1957 plaque on the park side of the shore marks the camp, dated March 27, 1776 [1].

title: Oaks and Springs in a Sheltered Hollow
place: Hayes Valley (around Hayes and Buchanan streets)
hook: Most of the peninsula was shifting sand. Hayes Valley was different: a shallow hollow of coast live oaks and natural springs, in Yelamu Ohlone territory.
story:
Before Spanish settlers arrived in 1776, most of the northern San Francisco peninsula was shifting sand dunes and coastal sage scrub. The planners' historic context statement for this area describes Hayes Valley as different: "a shallow hollow containing groves of coast live oaks and natural springs" [1][2]. Shelter and fresh water made it attractive.

The land lay within the territory of the Yelamu, a group of the Ohlone people. The same report says the nearest known Ohlone village was Chutchui, on Mission Creek and probably not far from Mission Dolores. Its people moved with the seasons to another village, Sitlintac, to gather shellfish on the tidal flats of what is now Mission Bay [1]. Ohlone life centred on extended families and seasonal camps, with acorns among the most important foods [1].

No major prehistoric site has been recorded in the Market and Octavia plan area, which takes in the eastern edge of this map. The land was heavily disturbed long before archaeologists took an interest. The report still concludes that, with abundant water and food nearby, prehistoric deposits probably remain intact under parts of the area [1].

The dunes came back into the story later. In the 1850s, fog, wind and shifting sand defeated Thomas Hayes's attempts to farm the valley [1][2].

title: Sea Lions, Springs and a Spanish Cross
place: Lands End bluffs above Mile Rock Beach
hook: For centuries the Yelamu came to these cliffs to hunt sea lions and gather shellfish. Then, in the 1770s, strangers planted a cross on the precipice.
story: Long before golf courses and museums, the Yelamu, the Ohlone people of the northern San Francisco peninsula, came to Lands End in seasonal camps. Hillside springs gave fresh water, brush gave shelter, and the shore gave otters, sea lions, sea birds, shellfish and birds' eggs. They played stick games here and told tribal stories [1]. The Yelamu lived in five known inland villages, Chutchui, Sitlintac, Amuctac, Tubsinte and Petlenuc, and spoke the language now called Ramaytush. Shell middens along today's trail still mark campsites perhaps a thousand years old [2]. On December 4, 1774, the Spanish officer Fernando Rivera y Moncada led a party up Point Lobos and stopped on the cliff edge, near today's Fort Miley or Legion of Honor, to gaze at the Golden Gate. Before heading back to Monterey he raised a cross as a beacon for later expeditions [3]. Those parties came: Spanish settlement began in 1776 and ended the Yelamu's traditional life at Lands End, and many were forced into the missions [1][2]. Ohlone people still live in their ancestral homelands, reviving languages, songs, basketry and plant knowledge [2].

title: Springs and Shellmounds Above the Cove
place: Sutro Baths Upper Trail, Lands End
hook: Long before Sutro's glass palace, Yelamu Ohlone families camped above this cove, drinking from hillside springs that still trickle down into the ruins.
story: Before there was a Cliff House, a toll road or a single numbered avenue, this windy headland belonged to the Yelamu, a tribal group of the Ramaytush Ohlone, the people of the western side of the bay [2]. Their main villages lay near Mission Creek, Visitacion Valley and today's Crissy Field, but Lands End was a seasonal camp [2]. Here they found fresh water from hillside springs, brush and trees for shelters, and a shore rich in otters, sea lions and sea birds; they also played stick games and told stories [1]. Some of those springs still run just below the Lands End Lookout, down into the old Sutro Baths pools, and a shellmound, or midden, of shells, bones and seeds survives beside the Sutro Baths Upper Trail [2]. The National Park Service notes that Spanish settlement of San Francisco, which began in 1776, ended the Yelamu's traditional life here [1]. Under Mexican rule the coast became part of a land grant, Rancho Punta de Lobos [1]. The next time crowds came to this cove, they would arrive by toll road to gawk at the sea lions.

title: The Cove of the Weepers empties
place: Former open water of Mission Bay (today's UCSF campus)
hook: The Spanish named this bay for three people they saw weeping on its shore. Within a year, its Ohlone hunters had vanished from the water.
story: In August 1775 a Spanish pilot, Juan Bautista Aguirre, paddled a redwood dugout into this shallow cove. Later accounts agree he saw three Native people on the shore, weeping, and called it Ensenada de los Llorones, the Cove of the Weepers [1][2]. The people who used it were Yelamu Ohlone. Historians writing for the city's Planning Department suggest families from Chutchui, a village on Mission Creek, came down seasonally to a bayside camp called Sitlintac to gather shellfish, though no one knows exactly where it stood [2][3]. In the summer of 1776 settlers arrived to found Mission Dolores at the head of the creek. Father Francisco Palou wrote that the local people brought mussels and wild seeds as gifts. Then on August 12 he recorded that Salsonas from a village near San Mateo had defeated them, burned their huts and forced them to flee on their rafts. For months afterward, he noted, no Indians came to hunt ducks on Mission Bay or to trade [1]. The first converts came only the following spring, and mission life proved deadly. A visitor in 1826 found only about 260 of a thousand converts left [1]. All of this was water then.

title: The mission road hiding under Chenery Street
place: Chenery Street's curve near Arlington Street (route of the old San Jose Road)
hook: Chenery Street's odd bend may be a ghost of the road between the missions, possibly the route Anza's expedition took south in 1776.
story:
In 1776, after choosing the sites for the Presidio and Mission Dolores, Juan Bautista de Anza's party marched "three leagues south, southwest and west, rounded the hills" towards the arroyo Father Palou had named San Bruno. Local historians think that was the first recorded European passage through the Bernal Gap, the dip between Fairmount and Bernal hills [1].

Long before that, Yelamu Ohlone people probably followed Islais Creek up into Glen Canyon to hunt and gather. The Glen Park Neighborhoods History Project suggests that today's Alms Road may be what is left of one of their trails [2].

In 1856 a survey of José de Jesús Noé's Rancho San Miguel marked a "San Jose Road Used in 1850-52" and a "Large Rock" near a branch of Islais Creek. Evelyn Rose and Amy O'Hair laid that map over a modern street grid. Their overlay suggests that the old road became the curve of Chenery and Arlington streets, while the other "San Jose Road" follows Wilder Street. Travellers tangled around Diamond and Chenery to get across the creeks [1]. The authors call this a preliminary finding, still being checked. If it holds, some of Glen Park's oldest streets once carried traffic between the missions [1].

title: A feast day, a fog and a rock
place: Delta Street near Visitacion Avenue (the 'Indian Rock' backyard)
hook: Somewhere behind a fence on Delta Street sits a lump of chert that neighbours say served as an altar in 1777.
story: Long before the Spanish came, this sheltered valley by the bay held two Yelamu Ohlone settlements, Amuctac and Tubsinte [1]. The valley's Spanish name has an exact date. On July 2, 1777, friars and soldiers on their way to the new Presidio stopped here. It was the feast of the Visitation of the Virgin Mary, so they named the valley after it [1]. The story the valley tells about itself goes further. According to tradition, the party got lost in thick fog on the road north, spent the night in the hills, and at dawn looked down on a valley with the bay at its feet [2]. Then they said a thanksgiving Mass, using a large rock as the altar [2]. Local historians call that rock 'Indian Rock'. It still sits fenced inside the backyard of an ordinary city lot on Delta Street near Visitacion Avenue [1][2]. Historian Woody LaBounty notes that the valley's naming story carries 'all associated subtexts of colonialism' [1]. Afterwards the Spanish turned the land into grazing for Mission Dolores and Presidio livestock [1][2]. The city's planning department also dates the name to 1777, when a Franciscan priest called the basin 'La Visitacion' [3].

title: A valley named on a feast day
place: South slope of McLaren Park, above Visitacion Valley (Philosopher's Way origins marker)
hook: The valley below McLaren Park's southern slopes has an exact birthday, a sacred rock in a backyard, and a spelling locals will defend to the end.
story: Look south from McLaren Park's southern slopes and you see a valley whose name has an exact birthday. Before the Spanish came, this sheltered valley by the bay was home to two Yelamu villages, Amuctac and Tubsinte [1]. On July 2, 1777, friars and soldiers heading for the new Presidio stopped here. It was the Catholic feast of the Visitation, so they named the valley for it, and it is still Visitacion with a 'c' [1]. Tradition says they held mass on a chert outcrop. That rock now sits fenced inside a backyard on Delta Street [1]. The Spanish used the valley to graze Mission Dolores cattle. Later the hills that became the park were part of the Mexican land grant Rancho Cañada de Guadalupe la Visitación y Rodeo Viejo. The sources disagree on when. The city's 1983 park master plan says Governor Alvarado made the grant in 1840, while SF Heritage says the valley went to American trader Jacob Leese in the 1830s [1][2]. Today a stone 'musing station' on Philosopher's Way, overlooking the old Brisbane Lagoon, tells walkers this origin story [3].

title: From Chamis to Viridiana
place: Mission Dolores cemetery, 16th and Dolores
hook: In 1814 a padre wrote that everyone who had seen the missionaries arrive was now dead. The cemetery holds about 5,000 unmarked Native graves.
story: On June 24, 1777, a 20-year-old Ohlone man named Chamis became the first adult Native person baptised at Mission Dolores. He was renamed Francisco Moraga, after his godfather, the soldier José Joaquín Moraga. The next year he married Paszém, the first Native wedding at the mission [1]. Thousands followed Chamis into the mission, and mission life was harsh. In the summer of 1795 about 280 people fled at once, complaining of too much work, too much punishment and too much hunger [1]. Measles, smallpox, diphtheria and syphilis killed people again and again. More than 5,000 Native people had died at the mission by the time Mexico took over [2]. On July 22, 1814, Padre Ramón Abella wrote in the burial register: "Today I buried Viridiana, the last of the adults who witnessed the founding of the mission… of those who have been born since that time, rare are those who live" [1]. By 1842 only eight Native Christians still lived there [1][2]. The garden cemetery beside the church holds the unmarked graves of about 5,000 Ohlone, Miwok and other Native people [2].

title: The church Ohlone hands built
place: Mission Dolores adobe church, 3321 16th St at Dolores
hook: San Francisco's oldest building was raised from tens of thousands of mud bricks by Ohlone workers, and its ceiling still carries their designs.
story: The squat white church at 16th and Dolores is the oldest intact building in San Francisco, and it was built by Ohlone labour. Foundation stones went down in 1783 and the adobe walls rose from 1788; one account counts some 26,000 bricks made by that year, another says Ohlone workers made 36,000 [1][2]. The church was dedicated on August 2, 1791 [1]. Its walls are four feet thick, and ten feet thick on the side facing Dolores Street. The mud is thought to have come from the banks of Dolores Creek, near today's Dolores and Dorland streets [1]. Redwood beams hold up a ceiling painted with traditional Ohlone designs in vegetable dyes [2]. Roof tiles were laid in 1794 and 1795, and many of the originals are still up there [1]. Three bells brought up from Mexico in the 1790s hang in the façade. The middle one still sits in its wooden stocks, lashed with rawhide [1]. The main altar came by ship from Mexico in 1796. In 1936 federal surveyors called the interior "a most extraordinary piece of Spanish Baroque decorative art, possibly without equal in North America outside of Mexico" [1].

title: A British captain's report, and a castle
place: Site of the Castillo de San Joaquín (now Fort Point)
hook: After a British captain reported how weak San Francisco's defences were, Spain rushed to build an adobe fort on the white cliffs of the Golden Gate.
story: In 1792 Captain George Vancouver of HMS Discovery visited the Presidio and reported that it was poorly supplied and poorly fortified. When Spanish officials learned what he had written, they ordered new forts built [1]. On La Punta de Cantil Blanco, the point where white bluffs overlook the two-mile-wide strait, soldiers built a brick-faced adobe fort with 15 gun openings. It was finished in December 1794 and named the Castillo de San Joaquín [2]. Fear of a British attack brought six bronze guns up the coast on the royal frigate Aranzazu [2]. The castle never lived up to its name. It was staffed only now and then, usually by soldiers from the Presidio, and rain and shifting sand kept wearing down its adobe [2]. When the Americans began Fort Point in the 1850s, they levelled the cliff it stood on, and nothing of it remains [2]. Its guns survived, though. Cast in Lima, Peru, in the 1600s, they are among the oldest cannon in North America, and two of them stand today in Pershing Square [3].

title: Five cannons on the dune point
place: Black Point, Upper Fort Mason
hook: Two decades after the Presidio was founded, Spanish soldiers hauled cannons onto a sandy bluff to guard the anchorage. Within ten years they had walked away.
story: Long before it was Fort Mason, the headland at the north end of today's Van Ness Avenue was a sandy promontory the Spanish called Punta Medanos, 'dune point', and later Punta de San José [1]. In 1797 soldiers from the Presidio of San Francisco built an artillery battery here, armed with five eight-pounder cannons, to give extra protection to the Yerba Buena anchorage around the corner [2]. Even the Park Service can't settle on its name: one of its publications calls it the Bateria de Yerba Buena, another the Batteria San Jose [2][3]. Either way it did not last. The post was only briefly occupied and had been abandoned by 1806 [1]. After 1849 the Americans renamed the bluff Black Point, after the dark California bay laurels that grew on it [1]. The strategic logic outlived Spain: the promontory commanded both the cove and the passage toward Alcatraz, and Mexico and then the United States also saw it as a place for guns [2]. Walk out to the tip of Black Point today and you are on what is described as the last remaining stretch of original shoreline in San Francisco east of the Golden Gate Bridge [1].

title: The Russian count and the commandant's daughter
place: Presidio Officers' Club (surviving Spanish-era adobe walls)
hook: A starving Russian crew sailed into the Golden Gate for food. Their leader left engaged to a 15-year-old Californio, and the story became a legend.
story: In the winter of 1805–06 the Russian colony at Sitka, Alaska, was starving and sick with scurvy. Nikolai Rezanov sailed south on the Juno to buy food from the Spanish, whose crown forbade giving aid to Russians [1][3]. The ship reached the Golden Gate in late March 1806 [1][2]. The ship's doctor, Georg von Langsdorff, could talk to the Mission priest only in Latin, their one shared language [2]. At the Presidio, which Langsdorff thought had 'the look of a German farmstead', the commandant's family served the Russians dinner on silver plates [2]. There Rezanov met Concepción Argüello, the commandant's daughter, then 15 [1][3]. They became engaged, though his interest was at first driven by practical considerations: he needed Spanish help [3]. Rezanov died in Siberia in 1807 on his way home [3]. By one account she did not learn of his death until 1808. She never married and later became a Dominican nun [3]. Bret Harte made the story a ballad [3]. Adobe walls from the 1790s Presidio survive inside today's Officers' Club [4].

title: Juana Briones, healer of Tennessee Hollow
place: El Polín Spring, Tennessee Hollow
hook: In a spring-fed valley below the fort, a soldier's daughter learned herbal medicine, nursed sailors and quietly hid deserters in her attic.
story: By the 1820s the Presidio community had spread out beyond its walls. Families including Marcos Briones and the Miramontes built farmsteads in the small creek valley around El Polín Spring, beside the trail to the Mission [1]. Juana Briones came here as a girl after her mother died in 1812. Her mother and grandparents had come north with Anza in 1776, and from Native neighbours she had learned a deep knowledge of healing herbs [2]. In 1820 she married Apolinario Miranda, a Presidio cavalryman, and the couple had eleven children [2]. She nursed sick sailors and turned her attic into a hiding place for sailors who had deserted their ships, then arranged their passage to her brother's ranch across the bay [2]. It is said that Russian sailors built a timber house nearby for her [1]. When the Presidio was temporarily abandoned in 1835, and her husband had become abusive, she moved to the foot of today's Telegraph Hill. There she became one of the first settlers of Yerba Buena, holding land in her own name [1][3]. Stanford archaeologists have since dug at the Briones house site here [2].

title: A lake sold for a hundred cattle
place: Rancho Laguna de la Merced, around Lake Merced
hook: In 1837 the whole of Lake Merced and its 2,200 acres changed hands for 100 cattle and $25 worth of goods.
story: Before anyone owned it, Lake Merced belonged to the Yelamu, who cut its tule reeds for boats and clothing and camped in the dunes to the west [1]. After the Franciscan missions were secularized, the Mexican governor José Castro granted about 2,200 acres around the lake to José Antonio Galindo in September 1835 [2][3]. The land was described at the time as worthless, and Galindo ran cattle on it for less than two years [3]. He then sold the entire rancho to Francisco de Haro, the first alcalde of the little port of Yerba Buena, for 100 cattle and goods worth $25 [2][3]. De Haro built a house at the south end of the lake but mostly lived nearer town, until his twin sons were killed during the Bear Flag Revolt of 1846. Grieving, he retired to Lake Merced and died there in 1849 [2][3]. His heirs would spend some fifteen years in American courts trying to prove the family owned what it had bought for a small herd [2].

title: A Governor's Coffin and a Herd of Goats
place: Hillsides of Yerba Buena ("Goat") Island
hook: Mexican California handed the island to a sea captain as payment for carrying a dead governor. Then came the goats, and a name that stuck for a century.
story:
In September 1835 the acting governor of Mexican California gave Captain Gorham H. Nye a certificate saying he owned "Wood Island", a league from the pueblo of Yerba Buena. According to the paper, it was his payment for carrying the body of Governor José Figueroa from Monterey to Santa Barbara [1]. The Navy's later history doubts that Nye ever used the island. It says he let the merchant Nathan Spear run it instead [2].

Nye had brought goats from the Sandwich Islands (Hawaii), and in late 1836 or early 1837 Spear turned a flock loose on the island. A Mr. Fuller trapped and butchered them for passing ships, and he also sold the island's oak for firewood until the hills were bare [2]. Locals called it Spear's Island or, more lastingly, Goat Island [2][3]. The last goat, a scrawny one-horned billy called "Lonesome Billy", died soon after 1900 aged 30-plus. His stuffed head hung in the training station's offices until it went missing around 1931 [2]. The U.S. Geographic Board made "Goat Island" official in 1895 (one lighthouse history says 1912 [4]) and restored Yerba Buena in 1931 [2][3].

title: Juana Briones's dairy on Washington Square
place: Northwest corner of Washington Square (Filbert & Powell)
hook: Decades before Washington Square had a name, a mestiza healer who had fled her abusive husband ran cattle and sold milk to sailors on this ground.
story: Juana Briones was born in 1802 at Villa de Branciforte, today's Santa Cruz, a mestiza of Spanish and Native heritage whose family came to California with the Anza expedition [1][2]. She married a Presidio soldier, Apolinario Miranda, who turned abusive. In the mid-1830s, with help from a bishop and the mayor, she moved her children to the western foot of Loma Alta, the hill we now call Telegraph Hill [1]. She could neither read nor write, yet she put up an adobe, held the title in her own name, and was one of the first three settlers of Yerba Buena. Her corral and dairy sat on what is now Washington Square [2][3]. She sold milk and vegetables to ships' crews, worked as a nurse and midwife, and was known to hide sailors who had deserted their ships [1][3]. The shore below was called La Playa de Juana Briones [1]. She later won a court fight over her land titles and died in Mayfield, near Palo Alto, in 1889 [2]. It took almost eight years of campaigning before a state plaque honouring her went up in the square in 1997 [3].

title: A rancho its owner never lived on
place: South bank of Islais Creek, near Quint St and Jerrold Ave
hook: All of today's Bayview once belonged to one Californio soldier who ran cattle here, built a corral, and lost it all to a mortgage held by William Tecumseh Sherman.
story: In 1839 the salt-marsh corner of southeastern San Francisco became Rancho Rincon de las Salinas y Potrero Viejo, 'the corner of the salty marsh' and 'the old pasture' [2]. Its grantee, José Cornelio Bernal, was baptized at Mission Dolores in 1796, served as a Presidio soldier and married Maria Carmen Cibrian in 1819 [1]. He had been running cattle here since at least the mid-1830s; an earlier petition was rejected because the land was claimed as pueblo commons [1]. The rancho's hand-drawn diseño shows a corral in the gap between Mt. St. Joseph and Candlestick Hill, and freshwater springs, aguajitos, along the south bank of Islais Creek, whose name comes from an Ohlone word for the islay cherry [1][3]. As far as historians know, Bernal never lived here; his home was an adobe near today's Duncan Street [1]. The land did not stay in the family. Like many Californios, the Bernals borrowed to defend their title, and in 1859 a large piece was foreclosed by the mortgage holder, General William Tecumseh Sherman, and auctioned for $1,500 [1][2]. Sources differ on which governor signed the 1839 grant.

title: The Corner of the Salt Marsh
place: Crocker-Amazon hills, once Rancho Rincón de las Salinas
hook: Before any street had a name, the Excelsior was cattle range on a Mexican rancho whose owner was better known at the tavern than the courthouse.
story: Every house in the Excelsior sits on land that was once part of Rancho Rincón de las Salinas y Potrero Viejo, 'the corner of the salt marsh and the old pasture.' The grant covered some 4,446 acres of today's Bernal Heights, Excelsior, Crocker-Amazon and Outer Mission, with a second piece around Hunters Point [1]. It went to José Cornelio Bernal, a presidio soldier from a family that had come north with the Anza expedition. Sources disagree on the details: one gives the grant as 1839, another says his first petition was refused because the land was common grazing ground and was only confirmed in 1840 [1][2]. Bernal kept cattle and sheep, and the local justice of the peace called him up several times in two years for drunken brawls and stabbings at John Vioget's tavern in Yerba Buena [2]. He died in 1842. His widow, Carmen Sibrian de Bernal, and their son won a U.S. patent in 1857, but the family gradually sold off the land. In 1859 William Tecumseh Sherman foreclosed on a mortgage, and by the 1860s the old pasture had been cut into small lots for immigrant farmers and dairymen [1][3].

title: The rancho that shrank to twenty-five acres
place: Bernal Hill (heart of the old Rancho Rincon de las Salinas y Potrero Viejo)
hook: A Mexican land grant once gave one family about a fifth of today's San Francisco. The last scrap was lost in 1917.
story:
On 10 October 1839 the Mexican government granted José Cornelio Bernal a square league of land, the Rancho Rincon de las Salinas y Potrero Viejo [1]. Bernal's father had come north with the Anza expedition in 1776, and the family ran cattle on the grant [2]. The "old pasture" of Potrero Viejo took in the hill that still carries their name, and its northern edge ran along Precita Creek [3]. According to the Chronicle's 1926 account, riding right round the boundary took a whole day [1].

It all slipped away. The paper said the first big piece went in 1859, when a mortgage held by William T. Sherman, the banker who later became a Union general, was foreclosed. The sheriff sold a huge tract for $1,500 [1]. More land went piece by piece, until a grandson, also named José Cornelio Bernal, was left with about 25 acres of vegetable gardens near today's Onondaga Avenue. That land was foreclosed in 1917, and with it the last San Francisco land held under an original grant passed out of the grantees' families [1][2]. He died in Oakland in November 1926, and his funeral mass was said at Mission Dolores, where the Bernals had worshipped for three generations [1].

title: The twins who owned a pasture
place: Potrero Hill (Rancho Potrero Nuevo)
hook: Before any streets, Potrero Hill was a cattle pasture granted to two teenage brothers. Neither lived to see what became of it.
story: Long before it had a single street, Potrero Hill was a pasture. From the late 1700s Mission Dolores grazed its cattle here. The name stuck: potrero means pasture, and Potrero Nuevo means "new pasture" [1]. Mission Creek, the bay and Islais Creek hemmed the land in so well that it needed little fencing [2]. Under Mexican rule the rancho went to Francisco and Ramón de Haro, teenage twin sons of Francisco de Haro, first alcalde of Yerba Buena. Sources disagree on whether the grant was made in 1841 or 1844 [1][3]. In June 1846, during the American conquest, the twins and their relative José de los Reyes Berreyesa were shot dead near San Rafael by Kit Carson on the orders of John C. Frémont [3]. Their father took over the land, and early accounts say he died of grief in 1849 [4]. Then the family's claim fell apart. In 1867 the courts ruled that the de Haros had only ever held a licence to run cattle, not title [3]. Squatters, speculators and "land sharks" with forged Spanish grants fought over the hill [4]. The family's name survives on De Haro Street.

title: Don José's rancho above the valley
place: Grand View Avenue between 22nd and Elizabeth streets (approximate early Noé homesite)
hook: The whole neighbourhood was once one man's cattle range, and historians still argue over where he actually lived.
story:
José de Jesús Noé was born in Puebla, Mexico, in 1805 and came north in 1834 with the Híjar-Padrés colony, bringing his wife Guadalupe Garduño and their baby son Miguel [1]. In 1845 he petitioned the governor of Alta California for one square league of land west of Mission Dolores. He said his herds of cattle and horses had grown too big for his old pasture [2]. The grant, Rancho San Miguel, came to about 4,443 acres. It covered today's Noe Valley, the Castro, Glen Park and Diamond Heights. For part of 1846 Noé served as alcalde of Yerba Buena [1].

Where he lived on all that land is less clear. Historian Mae Silver placed his homestead near 23rd and Guerrero, and an earlier homesite off Grand View between 22nd and Elizabeth [3]. The Noe Valley Voice has written that he reportedly ran the rancho from a Grand View homestead [4]. The Gold Rush and the American conquest ended the rancho way of life, and Noé began selling in 1852. The 1862 city directory lists him simply as "farmer, dwelling on old San Jose Road" [1].

title: Noé's square league of cattle country
place: Western edge of old Rancho San Miguel near Junipero Serra Blvd and St. Francis Circle
hook: Nearly every garden suburb west of Twin Peaks sits on one Mexican land grant, handed to a Yerba Buena official in 1845 and fought over for fifty years.
story: In 1845 Governor Pío Pico granted Rancho San Miguel to José de Jesús Noé, a Puebla-born official who had come to California in 1834 and served as alcalde of the little bay-side settlement [1][2]. The grant covered 4,443 acres, running roughly from today's Junipero Serra Boulevard east to San Jose Avenue and taking in the city's highest hill, now Mount Davidson [2]. After Noé's wife died in 1848, he began selling. John Horner, 'California's First Farmer', paid $200,000 for much of it (sources date the sale to 1852 or 1854) and then lost everything in the financial panic of the 1850s [1][2][3]. The land passed through the hands of bankers such as François Pioche until Adolph Sutro bought about 1,200 acres in 1880 [2][3]. In 1895 Noé's sons sued, claiming their mother's half had been sold illegally. They lost [1]. Decades later the park activist Madie Brown tracked down the original title, and a copy went into the time capsule under the Mount Davidson cross [3].

title: The breasts of the maiden, and a rancho
place: South Twin Peak (Noe Peak), Twin Peaks summit
hook: Before they were 'Twin Peaks', Spanish maps gave these hills a blunter name, and a Mexican alcalde claimed them as the tip of a 4,400-acre ranch.
story:
Twin Peaks served for centuries as an Ohlone lookout, local historian Devin Smith writes [3]. The Spanish who fortified the Presidio in 1776 were less poetic. Their maps named the hills "Los Pechos de la Choca", the breasts of the Indian maiden. Other writers spell it "Chola" [2]. Much later, writers retold a supposed Native legend in which a quarrelling husband and wife were split apart by a bolt of lightning. The Chronicle's gardening columnist passed it on in 2004 as something told by "chroniclers of Indian legend", and nobody can confirm it [2].

The paper trail starts with José de Jesús Noé, a Mexican official who served as alcalde of Yerba Buena. He petitioned Governor Pío Pico for Rancho San Miguel in 1845. Historian Mae Silver says the grant came through in 1846, while other accounts date it to 1845 [1][4]. The ranch covered one Spanish league, about 4,444 acres or a sixth of today's San Francisco. Its northern boundary cut across Mount Sutro, and the grassy peaks sat near its top [1]. Noé sold the land in 1852 but still had to prove his claim to the Americans. His United States patent finally came in 1857, five years after he had sold the ranch [1].

title: The road that fenced Noe's rancho
place: San Jose Avenue through Mission Terrace (old San Jose Road, edge of Rancho San Miguel)
hook: Before there were lots or streetcars, San Jose Avenue was the property line of a Mexican cattle ranch that covered one-sixth of San Francisco.
story: Traffic on San Jose Avenue follows a much older line. Part of the modern avenue traces the colonial El Camino Real, the road that tied Mission Dolores to the missions and farms further down the peninsula [1]. In 1845 José de Jesús Noe asked Governor Pío Pico for a square league of land next to the ranchos of Francisco de Haro and José Bernal. The historic context statement dates the grant to December 1845, while historian Mae Silver puts it in 1846 [1][2]. Rancho San Miguel ran across Mount Davidson and Merced Heights, and its eastern border was almost exactly this road [1][2]. One account credits Noe with up to 2,000 cattle and 200 horses [1]. He was acting alcalde, or mayor, of Yerba Buena when the Americans took over in 1846. American rule soon undid the rancho. Noe began selling land to speculators such as John Horner in 1852, and the United States did not confirm his title until late 1856 [1]. Houses on the east side of the avenue stand just outside the old grant, and the land to the west was once Noe's.

title: The tailor who owned the hills
place: Rancho San Miguel lands, upper Eureka Valley near Castro and 20th
hook: Before there was a Castro there was a rancho: some four thousand acres granted to a Mexican tailor who became San Francisco's last Mexican alcalde.
story: José de Jesús Noé arrived in California from Puebla in 1834 with the Híjar-Padrés colony. The colony's records list his trade as "tailor" [1]. In 1845 he was granted Rancho San Miguel, about four thousand acres running from Twin Peaks down into what became Eureka and Noe valleys [1][2]. In 1846 the occupying Americans kept him on as alcalde, and his term saw Yerba Buena renamed San Francisco [1]. He was the last Californio to hold the office [1]. Under the American system he had to prove his title. He filed his claim in 1852 but was not confirmed until 1857. By then he had already sold much of the rancho, starting in 1854 with a big sale to John M. Horner [1]. Horner laid out a street grid with Castro Street as its western edge [2]. Noé died in 1862 and was buried at Mission Dolores [1]. In 1895 his heirs sued to recover their mother's half of the rancho, and they lost [1]. Horner's grid sat mostly empty until cable cars arrived in the late 1880s [2].

title: Where Rancho San Miguel Ran Out
place: Junipero Serra Blvd near Sargent St (old rancho line)
hook: The odd diagonal kinks in Ocean View's western streets trace a line drawn in 1845, when a Mexican governor granted José de Jesús Noé a cattle ranch.
story: Before any streets, the valley between Mount Davidson and Merced Heights may have been a Native route to Lake Merced, where early Spanish accounts mention tule reed boats; no permanent Ohlone settlement has been found here [1]. In 1845 José de Jesús Noé petitioned Governor Pío Pico for vacant land beside the ranchos of Francisco de Haro and José Bernal, and that December was granted part of it as Rancho San Miguel, whose southern third later became the OMI [1][2]. One account credits Noé with up to 2,000 cattle and 200 horses, though no evidence of grazing in this corner has been found; when the Americans seized Yerba Buena in July 1846, he was its acting alcalde [1]. The United States did not validate his claim until late 1856 [1]. The rancho's edge still shapes the map. When the City Land Association laid out western Ocean View around 1868-70, its boundary ran down today's Junipero Serra Boulevard from Holloway, due south to Sargent Street, then slanted southeast along the old rancho line toward Ralston and Ramsell [1]. That western line marked the grant's southwest corner [3], so the slanting lots here are a Mexican-era survey hiding in plain sight.

title: Seventy Marines and a Borrowed Flagpole
place: Portsmouth Square (the old Mexican plaza)
hook: Before Chinatown, before the Gold Rush, this sloping square was the dusty plaza of Mexican Yerba Buena — until one July morning in 1846.
story: In July 1846 the open ground now called Portsmouth Square was the plaza of Mexican Yerba Buena, beside an adobe custom house. On July 9, Captain John B. Montgomery of the sloop USS Portsmouth marched about 70 marines and sailors to the plaza, hauled down the Mexican flag and raised the Stars and Stripes near the custom house [1][2]. The museum's chronology records that he had already taken formal possession the day before and appointed Lt. Washington Allen Bartlett, a fluent Spanish speaker, as the first American alcalde [2]. Three days later Montgomery led the town's first public Protestant service [2]. The square still carries the name of his ship, and Montgomery Street carries his own [1]. Within two years this same patch of earth would host the town's first public schoolhouse, erected in 1847 at its southwest corner, and later the crowd that heard Sam Brannan announce gold [1]. The state plaque recording all this is, as one landmark chronicler grumbled, 'half hidden by a shrub' on a lower tier of the park [1].

title: The captain who built Yerba Buena's waterfront
place: Leidesdorff's warehouse, California & Leidesdorff streets
hook: Before the Gold Rush, the shoreline here belonged to a mixed-race ship captain from St. Croix who became the town's treasurer, vice consul and richest man.
story: When the schooner Julia Ann dropped anchor at Yerba Buena in 1841, its master was William Alexander Leidesdorff, born on St. Croix in the Danish West Indies to a Danish merchant father and a creole mother [1][2]. The village then held only about thirty families. Leidesdorff built a warehouse on what was then the waterfront, at today's California and Leidesdorff streets, and put up the City Hotel near Clay and Kearny [2]. He launched the first steamboat on the bay, became a Mexican citizen in 1844 and received a 35,000-acre grant on the American River [1]. In 1845 Consul Thomas Larkin made him U.S. vice consul, and in July 1846 he hosted what is described as the first reading of the Declaration of Independence in California, on his veranda [1]. Under American rule he sat on the town council and the first school board, and served as city treasurer [1][2]. He died in May 1848, aged 38, just as gold was reported on his ranch; his estate later sold for more than $1.4 million [1]. The alley beside his old warehouse still carries his name [2].

title: The Newspaper That Ignored the Gold Rush
place: 743 Washington Street (site of the California Star)
hook: The first newspaper in San Francisco renamed the town — then buried the biggest story in its history.
story: The building at 743 Washington Street stands, according to FoundSF, on the site of Sam Brannan's California Star, San Francisco's first newspaper [1]. Brannan had brought the press with him from New York, and the first issue appeared on January 9, 1847, with Dr. E.B. Jones as editor [2]. Weeks later, on January 30, the alcalde's order renaming Yerba Buena as the Town of San Francisco was published in its pages [2]. The Star's most famous moment was a miss. On March 25, 1848 it carried a news item about the discovery of gold, and the town barely stirred [2]. It took Brannan himself, waving gold dust in the plaza in May, to set off the fever — after which the Star reported whole towns emptying for the diggings [2]. The site kept its knack for communication: Chinatown began its own telephone service in 1887, and a new Chinese Telephone Exchange opened here in the fall of 1901, its operators memorising subscribers by name and address rather than by number [1].

title: A town shuts down for Leidesdorff
place: Mission Dolores, front entrance, 16th and Dolores
hook: In May 1848 the flags dropped to half-mast and the schools closed. San Francisco was burying its most prominent Black citizen at the mission.
story: William Alexander Leidesdorff was born in 1810 on St. Croix in the Danish West Indies, and his ancestry was African Caribbean and European [1]. He sailed into Yerba Buena in 1841 as master of the schooner Julia Ann. The village then had only about thirty Mexican and European families [1]. He soon became one of its busiest men. He built a waterfront warehouse and the City Hotel, and he launched the first steamboat on the bay [1][2]. He also served as U.S. vice-consul and later as city treasurer, a councilman and a member of the school committee [2]. FoundSF calls him San Francisco's most prominent early Black citizen [2]. He died of "brain fever" on May 18, 1848, aged 38. On the day of his burial the flags flew at half-mast, businesses closed and the schools shut. He was laid to rest near the front entrance of Mission Dolores [1]. One mission history puts the grave inside the church and gives a March date [3]. The same history says most of the town's roughly 400 people came [3]. The gold rush soon multiplied the value of his land. He had died without a will, and his estate became a long controversy [1].

title: "Side-wheel steamer!": the hill that talked
place: Summit of Telegraph Hill (Coit Tower site)
hook: The whole Gold Rush town watched one pole on this hilltop, and knew its signals so well that a single gesture could stop a play.
story: In 1849 George Sweeny and Theodore Baugh put up a two-storey lookout on top of the hill then called Loma Alta, which commanded a view of the Golden Gate [1][2]. A tall pole with movable arms told the town below what kind of ship was coming in, whether a sailing vessel or one of the Pacific Mail side-wheelers [3]. The nomination form credits the semaphore to Lieutenant John K. Deur and dates it to 1850 [2]. Merchants and newspapers paid for the early warning. The side-wheel signal meant mail from home. Men came out of their shops to look up the line of Montgomery Street, then went off for a celebratory drink [4]. One night at the American Theatre, an actor playing Master Walter in "The Hunchback", dressed all in black, threw up his arms and cried "What does this mean?" A voice from the gallery roared "Side-wheel steamer!" and the play stopped for several minutes of laughter [4]. On 22 September 1853 an electric telegraph to Point Lobos opened here, the first in California, and it gave the hill its name [1][3]. A storm destroyed the station in 1870 [2].

title: Happy Valley, the tent city that turned deadly
place: Happy Valley, Mission Street between First and Second
hook: In 1849 about a thousand gold-seekers pitched tents along Mission Street and named the spot for its sunshine. By winter, the name had become a grim joke.
story: South of Market's first known settlement was a canvas town strung along Mission Street from First to Third in 1849 [1]. Perhaps a thousand would-be miners lived there, and they called it Happy Valley for its sunshine, its shelter from the prevailing wind, its scrub oaks and spring water [1]. One lodging house, the Isthmus House, is said to have sheltered James and Peter Donahue, later founders of the Union Iron Works, along with the future Comstock silver kings Flood, Fair, Mackay and O'Brien [1]. By the winter of 1849–50 the cheerful name had turned ironic: dysentery and cholera swept the camp [1]. Getting there was hard work too; the road to Mission Dolores was so sandy that hauling hay cost a fortune, until a plank toll road opened along Mission Street in 1850 [1]. Real houses followed, some shipped in pieces around Cape Horn: merchant W.D.M. Howard put up several of the 25 houses he imported from Boston [1]. East of First Street, the Donahues opened a blacksmith shop and foundry in 1849–50 that grew into Union Iron Works, the start of the district's heavy industry [1][2].

title: Laundry day at Washerwoman's Lagoon
place: Approximate site of Washerwoman's Lagoon, near Octavia and Greenwich
hook: Gold Rush miners shipped their dirty shirts to Hawaii and China. Then someone opened a laundry beside a freshwater pond out past Russian Hill.
story: In Gold Rush San Francisco a clean shirt was a luxury. You couldn't get anyone to do your washing, and anyone who would charged several times what the clothes were worth, so some people sent their laundry to Hawaii, or even China [1]. The answer turned out to be a freshwater lagoon below the heights, where the Marina now stands, almost three miles from the old plaza [1]. Several Chinese entrepreneurs set up a laundry on its banks, and a man named Pratt started a bigger one that eventually became the Occidental Laundry [1]. Thrifty housewives made a Sunday outing of it. They brought the family, a picnic lunch and wheelbarrows or dump carts of washing, scrubbed and rinsed on the shore, hung everything on the chaparral to dry, and carried it home to iron that night [1]. The name stuck: Washerwoman's Lagoon. The pond had an older history too. Writers on FoundSF argue that the 'laguna de manantial' (spring-fed lagoon) Juan Bautista de Anza noted in 1776 was this same pond, then called Laguna Pequeña [2]. A handful of old buildings in Blackstone Court, off Franklin and Lombard, still sit on the trail that once curved around the lagoon between the Presidio and Yerba Buena [3].

title: The Mutineers Buried on Goat Island
place: Former Yerba Buena Island cemetery, near Treasure Island Rd
hook: Gold fever drove two sailors to throw their officer into the bay. The Navy hanged them from the yardarm and rowed their coffins here.
story:
In 1849, merchant sailors in San Francisco earned $130 to $150 a month, and Navy crews were deserting to the goldfields [1]. On the night of 13 September, the gig of the survey schooner Ewing was rowing back from a wharf near today's Sansome Street. Oarsman John Black jumped on Passed Midshipman William Gibson, and one of the crew shouted, "Damn him, throw overboard, that's the quickest way!" The five-man crew left Gibson half-drowned in the tide and pulled for the mines [1]. In George Davidson's account, an English ship's master grabbed him by the hair as he swept past [1].

The deserters were caught near the mouth of the San Joaquin River, muddy and swollen with mosquito bites. A court-martial condemned all five. Three were spared, but the two Blacks, who confessed they had planned it alone, were hanged at 11 a.m. on 23 October 1849: John on the Ewing, Peter on the frigate Savannah [1]. The Ewing's log records both bodies being sent to Yerba Buena Island for burial. These were the island's first graves [1][2]. A chaplain later told a strange story: a lawyer came looking for two Scottish brothers using the name Black, heirs to £20,000. Gibson doubted the pair were even brothers [1][2].

title: The Quarryman the Army Evicted
place: Dowling's wharf site, west side of East Cove
hook: Thomas Dowling spent 17 years quarrying stone, building boats and burying a son here. Then ten soldiers rowed over and threw him off.
story:
Thomas Dowling arrived on Yerba Buena Island in 1849 [1][2]. He opened a quarry that supplied building stone to San Francisco and ballast to ships, built a boatway and a small plank wharf, and even filled in about two acres of bay [1][2]. His neighbour Jennings put up a barn, a windmill, a forge and oyster beds [2]. The island held grief too. A Dowling son playing on a stone scow was swept overboard and drowned, and he was buried on the hilltop [2].

Ownership was a tangle of Mexican paper, squatters' rights and city ordinances. By 1864 Dowling had bought Captain Nye's old certificate, and the Navy history says the retired captain was living with him at the time [1][2]. The dispute with a rival occupant, J. Pelter, got so bad it nearly came to pistols [2]. On 12 October 1866 the President ordered the Army to take the island, and a detachment of ten soldiers "ejected therefrom by force the said Thomas H. Dowling" [1]. The commanding officer later bought six of Dowling's hogs for $40 and turned his house into the post hospital [2]. Congress weighed Dowling's claim in 1871, but the Navy history says no claimant was ever compensated [1][2].

title: The garrison that ran off to the mines
place: Main Post parade ground
hook: In the summer of 1849 one company of U.S. soldiers shrank from 57 men to 15. Even the men sent after the deserters joined them.
story: When the New York Volunteers took over the Presidio in 1847, they moved into the old Spanish adobes. One visiting officer called them 'not much more than unsightly mud enclosures' [1]. Then gold was found. Company M of the 3rd Artillery arrived in May 1849 with 57 men [1]. Every one of them knew he could earn more in a single day at the diggings than in months in the Army. By the end of August, only 15 were left at the post [1]. Captain Keyes, who commanded from 1849 to 1858, spent much of his time on desertions and on squatters. Once he sent an officer and a squad after some runaways, and when the squad caught up with them it deserted too [1]. The Gold Rush also made the Presidio matter more. As San Francisco suddenly grew, President Millard Fillmore set the land aside for military use in November 1850 [2]. The Army kept it for the next 144 years [2].

title: An Arctic bog where Seventh Street runs
place: Seventh Street between Folsom and Harrison (site of Behr's lone madrone)
hook: Before the grid, a German doctor botanized a hidden bog near Mission Street that he called an "Arctic oasis", home to a plant later lost from the region.
story: Hans Hermann Behr, a Berlin-trained doctor and naturalist, reached San Francisco by September 1850 and stayed for the rest of his life [2]. In 1896 he published "Botanical Reminiscences", a record of the South of Market landscape he had walked in the 1850s [1][2]. He described sand ridges covered in shrubs, and between them swamp, bog and salt flat, crossed by winding tidal creeks [1]. A deep, boggy branch crossed the line of Mission Street. An arm of this swamp, "inaccessible, even to cows", ran along Howard Street as far as Fifth, where it ended in a thicket of wax myrtle, ceanothus and ferns [1]. At the center of the bog, water trickled beneath a carpet of the floating fern Azolla, among sedges, bog orchids and buckbean. Behr called it "a kind of Arctic oasis amidst a vegetation of California type" [1]. It was the only local home of a marsh sandwort, Arenaria palustris, which he listed as extinct. He also remembered a single straggling madrone on a ridge where Seventh Street now runs between Harrison and Folsom [1].

title: Cows, tulips and the Valley of Windmills
place: Schwerin Street near Geneva Avenue, heart of the old Schwerin dairy lands
hook: A German baker bought hundreds of acres here, grazed dairy cows where the Cow Palace parking lot is now, and grew tulips.
story: After the American takeover, the huge Mexican-era rancho was cut up, and the valley's rich soil went to nurseries, dairies and vegetable farms [1]. One of the earliest buyers was Henry Schwerin, a German baker. Neighbourhood historians say he arrived in 1850 and bought several hundred acres near today's Geneva Avenue [2]. Henry and his wife Ottilia held land on both sides of the county line from the 1850s to the early 1900s. They ran a dairy and a tulip nursery near where the Cow Palace now stands [1]. The Grapevine history puts his cows on today's Cow Palace parking lot and says his flowers went to the San Francisco Flower Mart [2]. Schwerin Street runs roughly where his buildings stood [2]. Smaller dairies filled most of the valley down to Candlestick Cove. Italian families such as the Rossis and Sechinis grew vegetables for downtown markets [1]. They pumped irrigation water with windmills, and the windmills gave the area its first nickname: the 'Valley of the Windmills' [1][2]. Greenhouses run by families such as the Gattis and Restanis filled whole blocks well into the 20th century [1].

title: Hunter's Folly: a paper city on the bay
place: Near Oakdale Ave and Fitch St, site of the Hunters' lodging house
hook: In 1850 three brothers from the East Coast tried to build a rival city called South San Francisco. It left behind empty shacks, $15,000 of debts and their surname.
story: During the Gold Rush, Robert and Philip Hunter, soon joined by their brother John, took on a speculative plan to sell lots on Bernal's rancho [1][2]. They platted an entire new city, 'South San Francisco', filed in November 1850, with a grid of 340-foot blocks that ignored hills and creeks. To attract buyers they put up houses, a flagpole and a large sign at the tip of the peninsula [1]. Hardly anyone came. An 1854 Sacramento Union clipping titled 'Hunters Folly' reported that 'little has been done since' [1]. A French traveller who met the Hunter who ran a stage-road inn in 1850 described a courteous Yankee who spoke French and had been 'ruined and re-established three times'. Of the new city, he wrote, nothing remained 'but some uninhabited shacks and fifteen thousand dollars in unpaid bills' [1]. The brothers stayed, farming and dairying near today's Oakdale Avenue and Fitch Street [2][3]. They also sold spring water: from 1855 the Independent Water Company paid $50 a month for it, and ships anchored nearby filled their casks before sailing out the Golden Gate [2]. The family left in 1874, but the point still carries their name [1]. Early sources disagree about who started the venture.

title: The Bernals' last corner of their rancho
place: Near Alemany Boulevard and Ocean Avenue (site of Carmen Bernal's adobe and the family's last 25 acres, along old Ocean House Road, now Onondaga Avenue)
hook: A Californio family's adobe stood by Islais Creek for half a century, and the last scrap of their Mexican land grant was a vegetable patch here.
story: By the early 1850s, Carmen Cibrián de Bernal had built an adobe house in a sheltered pocket at the south-west corner of her family's land grant. She was the wife of José Cornelio Bernal, original claimant of the Rancho de las Salinas. The spot is close to where Alemany Boulevard now meets Ocean Avenue [1]. Two more houses, possibly adobe, soon went up nearby, perhaps for relatives. This 'Bernal Reservation' may have been the only homes near here in the early 1850s. The adobe, the two houses and outbuildings, including an adobe oven, stayed in use until 1900 and perhaps as late as 1915 [1]. By then the grant had shrunk to almost nothing. When his grandson and namesake died in 1926, the Chronicle reported that by 1908 this last owner under the grant had only about 25 acres left. They lay 'west of Mission road in the little valley crossed by the Ocean House road, now Onondaga avenue', and were planted as vegetable gardens [2]. That land was lost to foreclosure in 1917. It was the last piece of San Francisco still held by the families of the original grantees [2]. A 1990s study for a fire-main project flagged the ground around it as the area's one site of historical archaeological concern [1].

title: The Californio who married a Mormon outcast
place: Site of the Valencia family adobe, near Notre Dame, 347 Dolores St at 16th
hook: In 1850 a Californio farmer of the Valencia clan married a 16-year-old whose father had been cast out of his church. Perhaps the only match of its kind.
story: When the ship Brooklyn sailed in on July 31, 1846, carrying about 230 Mormons, one family was already in disgrace. On the voyage, Sam Brannan had excommunicated Ambrose Todd Moses [1][2]. Shut out of the Mormon camp at Yerba Buena, the Moses family walked three miles to Dolores, a hamlet of about 100 Californios around the crumbling mission. There, according to historian Richard Bullock, the father built a lean-to against an old wall [1]. The neighbours were the Sanchez, de Haro, Bernal and Valencia clans. José Manuel Valencia had come with Anza in 1776. His grandson Candelario, a former Presidio sergeant, lived in an adobe near today's Notre Dame convent with his wife, Paula Sanchez, and their 13 children [1]. Valencia Street is named for the family [1][3]. On October 29, 1850, Candelario's son Eustaquio, 20, married Ann Frances Moses, 16. The wedding was reportedly held at the mission [1]. Gary Kamiya argues that a Californio man marrying an Anglo woman was almost unheard of at the time [1]. Ann died young. Her tombstone in the mission cemetery reads "Ann F. Moses, wife of E. Valencia," born March 3, 1834, died February 5, 1859 [2].

title: The Fishermen's Camp in the Cove
place: China Beach cove, below the end of Sea Cliff Avenue
hook: Long before the mansions, the little cove below Sea Cliff was a camp for Chinese fishermen who, tradition says, anchored their boats right here.
story: The sheltered cove between Baker Beach and Lands End is named for the people remembered as its first users in the American era. Chinese immigrants began arriving in California in 1849. When the Foreign Miners Tax of 1850 forced many of them out of the goldfields, a number came back to the Bay and became fishermen [1]. Local memory holds that some of them anchored their junks in this cove and camped on the sand. The Parks Conservancy calls that a legend, and the National Park Service describes a monument to the Chinese fishermen "who camped and anchored in the cove" [2][3]. Their work was no sideline. By the 1880s, the Conservancy says, Chinese fishermen made up half of all fishing crews. Anti-Chinese laws then pushed their share down to about 20 percent by the end of the century [1]. A stone marker at the trailhead, given in 1981 by Henry and Diana Chung, thanks them for efforts that "helped establish one of the area's most important industries and traditions" [1].

title: The Graveyard Beneath Civic Center
place: Site of Yerba Buena Cemetery (UN Plaza / Main Library area)
hook: Before City Hall, before the library, this sandy triangle was where Gold Rush San Francisco buried its dead. Not all of them left.
story: When Gold Rush San Francisco needed somewhere to bury its dead, it chose sand hills on the far edge of town. Yerba Buena Cemetery opened in 1850 near today's Eighth and Market streets [1]. Among those laid in its sandy ground was Edward W. McGaughey, an Indiana congressman who caught 'Panama fever' aboard the steamer Winifred Scott on his way west and died in the city on August 6, 1852. Back in Washington his career had run curiously parallel to Abraham Lincoln's: both were lone Whigs in their state delegations, and both were offered territorial governorships by President Taylor [2]. By the late 1850s the graveyard had been abandoned [1]. Around 1870, as the city cleared the ground for a grand new City Hall, remains were moved west to the new Golden Gate Cemetery in the Richmond dunes, by some estimates about 3,000 of them, McGaughey included [2][3]. Not everyone left. When crews dug foundations for the new Main Library in the 1990s, an anthropologist on site found no whole skeletons, but a steady trickle of rib and fibula fragments, finger bones and teeth. Each night the wind shifted the sand, and 'you'd return and see new exposed bones' [4].

title: The Oldest House and Its Rival Origin Stories
place: Abner Phelps House, 1111 Oak Street
hook: San Francisco's oldest house has at least three birth stories: shipped from New Orleans, framed from Maine lumber, or built from California redwood.
story:
At 1111 Oak Street stands a Gothic Revival cottage that its 1971 National Register nomination calls "generally considered to be the oldest unaltered residence in San Francisco", dating from 1850-51 [1]. The same nomination admits that "accounts vary as to its date and builder" [1].

The earliest published account, from 1934, said John Middleton & Sons built it in 1850 from lumber framed into sections and shipped "round the Horn from Maine, there being no sawmills here at the time" [1][2]. In 1961 Abner Phelps's great-granddaughter told another story. The house had been bought in New Orleans and shipped around the Horn to ease the homesickness of his bride, Augusta Roussell [1]. The raised foundation and veranda do recall Louisiana cottages [1]. A 1907 San Francisco Call interview with the family agreed that it "was built in Louisiana and came around the Horn all ready to be put up" [3]. Then a 1970s analysis of the wood by UC Berkeley scientists suggested California redwood [3].

The Junior League book Here Today states with certainty that Phelps, a Mexican War colonel and lawyer, lived there in 1851, well outside a city whose limits did not reach Divisadero until 1854 [1]. When it sold in 2024, the Chronicle still called it "widely believed to be the city's oldest house" [4].

title: The Playhouse That Became City Hall
place: Kearny Street facing Portsmouth Square
hook: Tom Maguire built his playhouse three times in one year. Then the city bought it — and the public was furious.
story: Gold Rush San Francisco wanted entertainment, and Tom Maguire gave it to them. On October 30, 1850 his Jenny Lind Theatre opened above his Parker House on the plaza [1]. Fire was the city's other constant. The Parker House burned, and a rebuilt Jenny Lind reopened on the site in June 1851 [1]. Days later, on June 22, the sixth great fire tore through 14 blocks and destroyed City Hall and the Jenny Lind again [1]. Undeterred, Maguire opened a third Jenny Lind on the same Kearny Street site on October 4, 1851 [1]. Then the city came shopping. On June 1, 1852, citizens gathered in Portsmouth Square for an 'indignation meeting' protesting the City Council's plan to buy the theatre as a city hall [2]. The protest failed: on October 20, 1852 the Town Council purchased the Jenny Lind for that purpose [3]. San Francisco's government thus spent its early years governing from a converted gold-rush playhouse, looking out over the plaza where the town had begun.

title: The street named for Bloody Island's captain
place: Lyon Street at Geary Boulevard (east edge of City Center)
hook: Lyon Street honours an army officer. A 1912 history said he 'punished the Indians of Clear Lake.' Pomo descendants tell it as a massacre.
story: In his 1912 history of the city, Zoeth Eldredge explained where Lyon Street's name came from: Nathaniel Lyon, captain of C Troop, 1st Dragoons. Eldredge wrote that Lyon "punished the Indians of Clear Lake for murder", which he dated to 1849. He also recorded that Lyon became a general and was killed at Wilson's Creek, Missouri, on August 10, 1861 [1]. What happened at Clear Lake, on May 15, 1850, is now known as the Bloody Island Massacre. Two ranchers, Andrew Kelsey and Charles Stone, had enslaved and starved Pomo people, and in the end the Pomo killed them. U.S. soldiers under Lyon and Lt. J.W. Davidson then fell on Pomo families gathered to fish and collect plants at the island of Bonopoti [2][3]. The Daily Alta first reported "the work of butchery," in which neither sex nor age was spared. Three days later, after an army officer objected, it printed a new version describing a fight and calling the massacre of women and children "wholly unfounded" [2]. Estimates of the dead run from about 60 to 200 or more [2][3]. A six-year-old, Lucy Moore, survived by hiding underwater and breathing through a reed. She lived to 110 [2]. A state landmark calling it a massacre went up in 2005 [3].

title: When the Mayor Welcomed the 'China Boys'
place: Portsmouth Square
hook: Before exclusion laws and plague ropes, San Francisco's first mayor held a public ceremony here to welcome Chinese newcomers.
story: It is easy to forget that San Francisco's relationship with its Chinese residents began, officially at least, with a welcome. On August 28, 1850, Mayor John W. Geary welcomed new Chinese residents to the city in a ceremony in Portsmouth Square, the town's civic heart [1]. Histories drawn from Judy Yung and others say Geary welcomed about 300 'China Boys' [2]. The warmth did not last. That same year the state had imposed a $20-a-month Foreign Miners Tax [1], and by 1854 the Daily Alta California, which had earlier supported Chinese immigrants, was warning that the city was filling up 'with these people' [2]. The plaza where the ceremony took place became, over the next half-century, the front porch of Chinatown, the district growing up the slope of Dupont Street behind it. It remains Chinatown's main open space today.

title: A Homestead With a Duck-Hunting Lake
place: Abner Phelps House, 1111 Oak Street
hook: Abner Phelps rode his horse to a downtown law office from a 160-acre homestead with its own lake. As the grid closed in, his family kept moving the house.
story:
In the 1850s the Phelps house stood in the middle of a 160-acre homestead at the foot of Buena Vista Hill. Part of today's Panhandle belonged to it [1]. Abner Phelps kept a law office in the Montgomery Block downtown. The National Register nomination says he made "a long dusty journey to town daily by horseback", when Divisadero was "no more than a path" [1].

A 1907 San Francisco Call profile, quoted by SFGATE, described a ranch lake, 100 feet deep, "for the boys who were devoted to swimming and duck-hunting" [2]. The Call said it flooded in heavy rain. After one flood, a neighbour's piano and a barrel of his whiskey "were found out in the Mission" [2].

When Divisadero was graded in the 1890s, the house was repositioned, and in 1904 it was moved back to the middle of the block so the family could build stores on Divisadero [1][3]. SFGATE reports that two Phelps sisters ran a haberdashery there. The house could only be reached by a 75-foot alley, and Phelps's son Walter told the Call: "It has cost us more than building a new house, but we like to keep the old place" [2]. His brother George lived there until he died in 1940. The house was turned to face Oak Street in 1977 [2].

title: Alleys named for ships, not madams
place: Natoma Street between Fifth and Sixth streets
hook: Jessie, Minna, Natoma, Clementina: the old story says these alleys were named for Gold Rush madams. A historian went through the 1850s newspapers and found ships.
story: The narrow alleys between South of Market's big streets carry names that sound like women's: Jessie, Annie, Minna, Clementina, and their "sisters" Tehama and Natoma. A popular tale says they honor Gold Rush prostitutes or madams, and at least one bar on these streets uses the story in its marketing [1]. Historian LisaRuth Elliott doubts it. Very few early San Francisco streets were named for women, she notes, and a book from 1912 said the alley names had no meaning at all [1]. Searching the Daily Alta California, the Sacramento Daily Union and other papers of the time, she found ships instead. A Peruvian brig named Annie cleared the port in May 1851, a ship called Jessie arrived that March, the steamboat Tehama made her first voyage in June 1850, and the Californian wrote up a Bremen whaler called Clementine, with an untrustworthy crew, in November 1847 [1]. Natoma was also the name of a gold digging on the American River [1]. Minna Street appears in December 1850 advertisements as "the first street below Mission", so new that it needed directions [1]. Elliott offers the ship idea as a theory, not a proof. Others say Jessie Street honors Jessie Benton Frémont, wife of the explorer John C. Frémont, and the photographer Mark Ellinger calls the prostitute legends apocryphal [1][2].

title: The pile that sank out of sight
place: Mission Street at Seventh Street, where the Mission Plank Road crossed the swamp
hook: Builders of the toll road to Mission Dolores drove a 40-foot pile into the swamp at Seventh Street. With one blow of the hammer it disappeared.
story: Today's Mission Street began as the Mission Plank Road, a toll road of wooden planks that opened in 1851 and ran three and a quarter miles from the town to Mission Dolores [1]. The obvious route would have followed Market Street, but an 80-foot sand hill stood in the way between Second and Third streets [1]. The worst trouble came where the road crossed the line of Seventh Street. The historian John S. Hittell, writing in 1878, said the contractor planned a bridge on pilings. The first pile, forty feet long, "at the first blow of the pile driver sank out of sight." A second pile driven on top of it disappeared too, and there was no firm bottom within eighty feet [1]. So the builders laid cribs of logs on the peat instead. The bridge shook whenever heavy teams crossed and slowly sank until its middle was about five feet below the original level [1]. The road cost $96,000 [1]. Hittell thought these "swamps" were partly underground lakes 40 to 80 feet deep under a crust of peat. The botanist Hans Behr also remembered a deep, boggy branch crossing Mission Street [2].

title: When North Beach actually had a beach
place: Water Street, between Mason and Taylor
hook: A one-block alley called Water Street is the last clue to a sandy cove where waves once broke, four blocks from today's shore.
story: Around 1851 Fritz Wikersheim, a Frenchman with gold fever, climbed Telegraph Hill and sketched what lay to the west. He drew a pretty, shed-lined cove on the bay between Point San Jose and North Point [1]. That was the real North Beach, a stretch of sand running from a bright dune bluff called White Point, near today's Hyde Street, east to Meiggs' Wharf [1]. The street names still carry clues: Bay, Beach, and the one-block Water Street just south of Francisco, where water once really did lap along the line [1]. In the early 1850s the shore was remote, a place for a city dump, a prison and asylum ship, a convent, a 'Home for Inebriates' and a cemetery. Hold-ups were so common that one paper asked, 'Do the police ever visit this quarter?' [1] Industry followed. A lead smelter went up on White Point in 1867, and Montgomery Avenue was cut through to reach the shore [1]. By 1887 fill had pushed the cove past Bay Street, and the 1900 fishing wharf filled the rest [1][2].

title: Racehorses where Treat Avenue runs
place: Pioneer Race Course site, 24th Street between Folsom and Bryant
hook: Before the grid reached here, Gold Rush San Franciscans rode out the new plank road to bet on horses around a track spanning several of today's blocks.
story: In the early 1850s the Mission was where San Francisco went to misbehave. By 1851 the buildings around the old mission held a brewery, saloons, a gambling den and a dance hall. The Mission Plank Road opened that year as a toll road along today's Mission Street, at 25 cents for a rider and a dollar for a four-horse team, and it made the trip from town easy [1]. In 1852 the Pioneer Race Track opened on land bounded by Mission, Bryant, 24th and Army (now Cesar Chavez) streets [1]. The blogger Burrito Justice, who has pored over the old maps, notes that the course belonged to George Treat, the name still on Treat Avenue. The ground lay just above the stone wall marking the northern boundary of the Bernal family's rancho [2]. An 1864 subdivision map of the race course still shows grandstands near 24th Street between Howard (now South Van Ness) and Folsom [2]. By then the track's days were numbered. In 1868 a baseball ground was built in the middle of it [2], and houses soon followed.

title: The Sea Goddess on the Top Floor
place: Tin How Temple, 125 Waverly Place
hook: Gold Rush sailors and miners prayed to the goddess of the sea here — and her image survived the fire that levelled everything around it.
story: Climb the narrow stairs at 125 Waverly Place and you reach one of the oldest Chinese temples still operating in the United States. The Tin How Temple is dedicated to Mazu, the sea goddess known in Cantonese as Tin How, 'Empress of Heaven', guardian of fishermen, seafarers and women in distress [1][2]. For immigrants who had just survived a Pacific crossing, the choice made sense. The temple was reportedly founded around 1852 or 1853 at this very location by Day Ju, described as one of the first Chinese people to arrive in San Francisco; the sources hedge on the details [1]. When the 1906 fire destroyed the building, the image of the goddess, the temple bell and part of the altar were saved, and the Sue Hing Benevolent Association reopened the temple in 1910 on the top floor of a new four-storey building [1]. Its presence shaped the map: the Chinese name for Waverly Place means 'Tin How Temple Street' [1]. FoundSF observes that Chinese worshippers have been communing with the deities here since the 1850s [2].

title: The night the lake ran to sea
place: Dune barrier between Lake Merced and the ocean (near today's zoo)
hook: In November 1852 San Franciscans heard that Lake Merced was pouring through a fissure into the Pacific and might soon be empty.
story: Lake Merced began, some three thousand years ago, as a lagoon with a channel to the Pacific. Into the nineteenth century a tail of the lake still wound from its northwest corner, across what is now the zoo, to Ocean Beach, and big storms or earthquakes sometimes broke the sand barrier open [1]. In late November 1852, after a reported earthquake, fissures opened between the lake and the ocean and the lake's water rushed out to sea. The Chronicle's informant said the water "was still rushing out with great force, and that he had no doubt but that it would soon be emptied" [1]. Accounts say the lake dropped around thirty feet [1]. The lake survived, refilled by springs. Modern geologists are not sure the quake was to blame: the U.S. Geological Survey notes that heavy rain overtopping or seeping through the natural embankment could equally explain the break [2]. The escape route was finally closed for good in 1895, when the Spring Valley Water Company built a 78-foot earthen dam across the gap [1].

title: When the smelt turned the water silver
place: Old mouth of Mission Creek, near Division and Henry Adams streets
hook: Before landfill, hunters here could shoot more ducks in an hour than a horse could carry home.
story: The 1852 U.S. Coast Survey map shows what this place was before the city swallowed it: a tidal lagoon of more than 500 acres, including salt marshes that reached inland toward Folsom and Mission streets. Mission Creek wound in from the Mission and met the bay close to today's Division Street [1][2]. The water was so shallow that much of it was less than a foot deep, and it sheltered an astounding array of wildlife [2]. In one old-timer's phrase, "the smelt turned the water silver," and the fish drew egrets, herons, ospreys and gulls. Hawks and owls hunted mice and rabbits in the upper marsh [3]. In Gold Rush days the marshes were the favourite ground of duck hunters, who could count on bagging more birds in an hour than they could carry home on horseback [4]. Within fifty years steam shovels, garbage and earthquake rubble had filled nearly all of it. Only the narrow Mission Creek channel survives, a thin sliver of the vanished bay [1].
