title: A Toll Road, a Roadhouse and a Rope
place: Cliff House, 1090 Point Lobos Ave
hook: On July 4, 1863, a plain clapboard bar opened on the cliff. Three years later a woman walked a tightrope from it to Seal Rocks.
story: The Cliff House was born as a real-estate play. Speculator Charles C. Butler built it alongside the new Point Lobos Toll Road, backed by State Senator John P. Buckley, an officer of the road company [1]. It opened on July 4, 1863, with the well-known host Captain Junius G. Foster in charge. Despite being called a hotel, it served only food and drink, and the real draw was the view of the sea lions on the rocks below [1]. Omnibuses left Kearny and Clay streets for the seals at 50 cents a ride, and drivers paid a toll near today's Masonic Avenue [2]. Early-morning carriage rides out for breakfast became the fashion; Mark Twain made the trip in 1864 and wrote a grumpy, funny account [1]. When the view wasn't enough, Foster booked balloon ascensions and acrobats. On June 24, 1866, Miss Rosa Celeste walked a 400-foot rope from the cliff to Seal Rocks, 100 feet above the surf and without guide wires, while five thousand people watched [1]. Presidents Grant and Hayes later came to dine [1].

title: A college built on gold dust
place: Site of St. Mary's College, College Avenue at Mission Street
hook: The college now in Moraga began on a windswept Bernal slope, paid for partly with gold dust from Sierra miners.
story:
Archbishop Joseph Alemany wanted an affordable college for the children of miners, mechanics and farmers. The cornerstone was laid on 3 August 1862 [1]. He bought 60 acres of the old Bernal rancho from Jesus Bernal for $1,600 [2]. To pay for the building he sent the Irish priest James Croke on a two-year fundraising trip to farmers, merchants and Sierra gold miners. Croke came back with cash and gold dust worth $37,166.50 [3]. According to a lecture published by the college, one early donor was the celebrated Mary Ellen Pleasant [4].

St. Mary's College opened in 1863 as a college for boys. It struggled, and in 1868 nine mostly Irish Christian Brothers sailed from New York to take it over. It awarded its first bachelor's degrees in 1872 [3]. An 1875 photograph shows the walled campus facing Mission Road, with two baseball diamonds beside it [3]. In 1889 the college left its "cold, windswept campus" for Oakland, and later moved to Moraga [2][3]. The Bernal site became a parish and then a truck farm [2]. The south-west corner of Bernal is still called College Hill, and a 1962 marker stands at the west end of College Avenue [2].

title: Lake Geneva, a spring that fed Islais Creek
place: Block bounded by Geneva, Niagara, Delano and Cayuga avenues (approximate site of 'Lake Geneva')
hook: An 1863 map shows a spring-fed 'Lake Geneva' near today's Cayuga Avenue. It was one source of a creek that ran all the way to the bay.
story: Before the house lots, this corner of the city had its own lake. A spring-fed pond marked as 'Lake Geneva' on some maps sat roughly on the block now bounded by Geneva, Niagara, Delano and Cayuga avenues. The city's 1863 'West End Map #1' is one of those maps [1]. The pond was one of the sources of Islais Creek, which ran east through the valley and emptied into a wide tidal estuary at today's Islais Creek Channel [1]. According to stories passed down by local historians, travellers on the old road stopped at the spring to water their animals, although no written record from the colonial era confirms this [1]. The creek did not survive the city. Its valley was put into culverts and covered by San Jose Avenue and Alemany Boulevard, and later by Interstate 280 [2]. People still point to what is left. FoundSF notes that the headwaters of one branch of Islais Creek run somewhere deep beneath nearby Cayuga Park, under the BART tracks [3].

title: The first train left from 25th Street
place: Valencia Street station site, 25th and Valencia Streets
hook: Four hundred passengers, two locomotives and a speech about angels: the Peninsula railroad began at a depot in the Mission, not downtown.
story: The railroad that grew into today's Peninsula line began in the Mission. At about 10:30 on the morning of October 17, 1863, the first San Francisco and San Jose Railroad excursion left the Mission station, near 25th and Valencia. Two locomotives pulled six passenger cars, two baggage cars and a freight car, carrying about 400 people to the end of the line at Mayfield [1][2]. The company had been one of the first railroads to hire Chinese labourers [1]. Its hardest job was the cut through Bernal Hill, blasted in 1862 with "heavy and continuous assaults of powder" [1]. The line reached San Jose on January 16, 1864, and turned an eight-hour trip by steamboat and stagecoach into about three and a half hours [1]. The Valencia Street depot got a proper station building in 1866. It stayed a stop as the tracks were pushed closer to downtown, until most regular service ended in 1903 [2]. The tracks cut diagonally across the neighbourhood, crossing Mission Street between 24th and 25th. After the line was abandoned, the right of way became housing and, in one strip, the little park called Juri Commons [3].

title: Two blocks of middle-class time travel
place: Liberty Street between Valencia and Guerrero (Liberty Street Historic District)
hook: Gilders, Mint workers, box-makers and a judge built side by side on Liberty Street, leaving every Victorian style in one short walk.
story: Liberty Street sits on the eastern edge of the old Rancho San Miguel, which José de Jesús Noé received in 1845. He sold it in 1854 to John M. Horner, who laid out "Horner's Addition" and sold it block by block. Horner's 1863 map shows just one building here [1]. The oldest house on the National Register's list is the Marshall Doane House at 45 Liberty, dated 1863. Beside it is the Siamese Twin House of 1879 at 20-26 Liberty [1]. Over the next half-century, 51 houses went up on the two blocks between Valencia and Guerrero, in every style of the day: early Italianate, Stick, Eastlake, Queen Anne and Classical Revival [1]. No famous architects worked here, and only thirteen of the houses have known designers [1]. The owners were solidly middle class: foremen, attorneys, two U.S. Mint employees, two gilders, carriage makers, sailors and the partners in a box factory [1]. Around the corner, coal-yard partner Marsden Kershaw built his house at 845 Guerrero in 1871, one of the district's earliest [2]. Liberty Street still keeps more of that 19th-century feeling than almost any street in the city [3].

title: A Toll Road Through the Sand Hills
place: Route of the Central Macadamized Road, near 17th Avenue & Kirkham Street
hook: For thirty years the only road across the Inner Sunset was a private toll road that ignored the street grid.
story: Until the early 1880s the Inner Sunset was sand hills crossed by a single road. It was called the Central Macadamized Road, and also the Central Road, the Central Toll Road or the Central Ocean Road. It was a private business owned by ten proprietors. Two of them, William Bryan and James Reilly, also owned the Central Homestead Association, which claimed much of the land it crossed. Engineer L. H. Shortt surveyed the route, and in November 1864 the owners advertised for contractors [1]. The road started at Fulton and Divisadero, beside the Sans Souci resort. It ran past the Masonic Cemetery, through the dunes south of the future park, and on to the Ocean House near Lake Merced [1]. Historian Lorri Ungaretti traced it zigzagging north between 17th and 18th Avenues from R Street to K Street, then turning east toward town [2]. Hardly anyone lived along it, so the tolls could not have been the point. Historian William Kostura suggests the road helped support the owners' land claims and raise the value of their lots [1]. Early directories gave addresses such as 'on Central Road two miles from the toll gate.' As the official streets were graded in the 1890s, the diagonal road faded from the land and from the maps [1].

title: A racetrack built on a marsh
place: Former Bay View Park racecourse, around Yosemite Slough
hook: The Bayview got its name from a horse track built on tidal marsh, apparently because the soggy ground was thought to put a spring in the horses' step.
story: In the 1860s the mining millionaire George Hearst and other investors built Bay View Park, a racetrack with a hotel and stables, on a low tidal marsh south of the Hunters Point peninsula [1]. The 1864 city directory described it: 'The ground is reclaimed and protected from the tide by a breakwater or bulkhead. A large and spacious hotel, with stables and outhouses attached, has been added.' It also mentioned 'a beautiful shell road' about three miles long, expected to cost around $30,000 [1]. Historians think the shells were most likely dug from nearby Ohlone shellmounds [1]. The site was not chosen to sell real estate. Its springy marsh was thought to make the horses faster, and an 1869 drawing shows Yosemite Slough still running through the middle of the oval [1]. Weekend crowds rode out from the city, as they did to other tracks at the edge of town. The track did not last. By the early 1880s the hotel had burned, the tides had broken through the dikes, and by the 1883 Coast Survey map the course was gone [1]. Only its name survived. 'Bay View' spread to the flats and then to the whole district [1], and decades later land offered to the city was still described as the old racetrack site [2].

title: Colonel Hayes's Pleasure Garden
place: Near Hayes and Laguna streets
hook: To sell lots in a sandy hollow, Tom Hayes built a day-trip resort with a concert hall, gymnasium, shooting gallery and bar.
story:
Thomas Hayes was an Irish-born politician who sailed for San Francisco in January 1849 with two of his brothers. He got a 160-acre tract through a preemption deed, in effect a squatter's claim, and the Van Ness Ordinance confirmed it in 1855 [1]. A 1928 Chronicle writer called him "a rather picturesque but shrewd figure in early San Francisco politics and in state military affairs" [2].

Farming failed in the fog, wind and sand, so Hayes started selling his land for homes instead [1][3]. To bring buyers out, he opened what planners describe as a "come-on" attraction: Hayes Park, near today's Hayes and Laguna streets, with a picnic ground, restaurant and bar [3]. Sources give different opening dates. The city's context statement says around 1856, and other accounts say the early 1860s [1].

By 1864 the San Francisco Directory was advertising Hayes' Park, Pavilion and Garden as a "suburban resort" with a garden, concert hall, gymnasium and shooting gallery [2]. Townspeople made a day or half-day trip of it. A photograph of Hayes Valley taken that year shows the semicircular pavilion in the distance, with the Protestant Orphan Asylum in one corner [2].

title: Lakeville, a suburb only on maps
place: East side of Lake Merced (projected 'Lakeville' tract)
hook: In 1864 a speculator carved the east shore of Lake Merced into suburban lots. For twenty years 'Lakeville' existed only on maps.
story: By the 1860s San Francisco speculators were eyeing every open acre, and in 1864 land auctioneer John Middleton tried to sell lots of 160 by 200 feet on the eastern side of Lake Merced for a new suburb he called "Lakeville" [1]. It was a colossal failure, in a district so remote that even its roadhouses struggled against the distance, the weather and competition from resorts closer to town [1]. Lakeville never got beyond paper, yet it kept appearing on maps of the city for the next twenty years; George Goddard's 1869 map shows the projected suburb on the east shore alongside the Lake House, Ocean House and racetrack [1]. By 1875, after land schemes, roadhouses and racing had all come and gone, the best business around the lake turned out to be growing potatoes [1]. The east shore stayed farmland until the twentieth century, when the Spring Valley Water Company began selling its holdings and developers took options on the cultivated fields [2]. Large-scale housing finally reached the east shore with Parkmerced, which opened in 1952 [3].

title: Steam trains and a lonely Elkton stop
place: Site of Southern Pacific's Elkton station, just south of Ocean Avenue beside today's Balboa Park BART
hook: Long before BART, trains stopped here, at a quiet station called Elkton that served cabbage farmers and a reform school.
story: The first railroad from San Francisco to San Jose came through here in the early 1860s. Wikipedia gives October 1863 for the start of service through the city, and the historic context statement says the San Jose line was complete in 1864 [1][2]. The single track ran out of the Mission, through the Bernal Cut, and south along what is now the I-280 corridor [1]. Farmers were already ploughing wild iris meadows in 1862 because they expected the railroad to arrive [1]. There was a stop called Elkton about 300 feet south of Ocean Avenue, close to where BART's Balboa Park station is now [2]. It handled mostly farm freight, but it also served the Industrial School on the hill [2]. The railroad did less for the area than people had hoped. In 1884 a one-way ticket from Fourth and Townsend to Ocean View cost 15 cents, three times a cable car fare, and farmers kept driving their wagons to market [1]. After Southern Pacific opened its Bayshore Cutoff in 1907, this line was left with a few local trains [2]. Its right-of-way later became the route of the freeway and BART.

title: Sunday picnics among the Masonic tombs
place: Former Masonic Cemetery, now USF's lower campus
hook: Before Golden Gate Park, San Franciscans went for their Sunday air among the tombs. USF's campus still turns up the occasional casket.
story: The cemeteries around Lone Mountain were meant for the living as much as the dead. Lone Mountain Cemetery, opened in 1854, was modelled on the grand garden cemeteries of the East, a sign that the raw young city could match the country's great metropolises [1]. The Masons laid out their own lavishly landscaped cemetery for members here, opened in 1864 [1][2]. Sources disagree on its size: 38 acres in one account, 30 in another [1][3]. Families made Sunday outings of it, because surveying for Golden Gate Park did not begin until August 1870 [2]. Once the park opened, it took over the cemeteries' role as a place to stroll, and the neighbours began asking for the graves to go [1]. The Masonic Cemetery closed in 1931, and about 19,900 bodies were moved to Woodlawn Cemetery in Colma [3]. Its land became the lower campus of the University of San Francisco. Not every trace left. In 2011 construction workers digging for USF's new science centre uncovered 25 mostly empty caskets, and a skull tumbled out of a shovel [3].

title: Tar Flat and the 200-foot shot tower
place: First and Howard streets (gas works and Selby Shot Tower)
hook: At First and Howard a gasworks dumped tar into the bay and a 200-foot tower rained molten lead. Mothers brought coughing children to breathe the fumes.
story: East of First Street, the land being filled in from the bay became San Francisco's first industrial zone, with foundries, machine shops and boiler works [1]. Its landmark was a 200-foot tower raised in 1864 at First and Howard by the Selby Smelting and Lead Company for making bullets and shot; it worked until the 1906 earthquake [1]. Across the corner stood the Donahue brothers' gas works, which distilled coal and brought gas lighting to the city in early 1854 [2]. The early technology was crude, and the sludge was dumped into the open water at Fremont Street [2]. It killed the shellfish, and the smell gave the neighbourhood its name, Tar Flat [2]. Workers' families on nearby Mission Street lived in the thick of it, and some mothers carried sick children into the plant, believing the fumes would cure whooping cough [2]. The gas company absorbed its rivals and in 1905 re-incorporated as Pacific Gas and Electric [2]. Tar Flat came back in the 1980s: a layer of still-hazardous tar three to five feet thick stopped work on a new tower at Beale and Howard until it was removed [2].

title: The Union's preacher, buried at Geary
place: Sarcophagus of Thomas Starr King, First Unitarian Church, 1187 Franklin Street at Geary
hook: One of the few graves San Francisco never moved belongs to the preacher who campaigned for the Union and raised a fortune for wounded soldiers.
story: Thomas Starr King came west in 1860 to lead First Unitarian, then a congregation deep in debt on Stockton Street. He cleared the debt and raised money for a larger church at 133 Geary Street near Union Square, finished by January 1864 [1]. When the Civil War began he toured California speaking for the Union and campaigned with his friend Leland Stanford. Lincoln allegedly credited him with keeping California in the Union [1]. He also raised more than $1.5 million for the U.S. Sanitary Commission. His plaque calls it the forerunner of the American Red Cross [1][2]. Worn out by constant travel, he died of diphtheria and pneumonia on 4 March 1864, aged 39. Around 20,000 people attended his funeral, and Bret Harte gave a eulogy [1]. He was entombed in a sarcophagus beside the church. In 1889 the congregation moved to Percy & Hamilton's rough granite Romanesque church at Franklin and Geary, and the tomb moved with it [1][3]. Most of the city's burials were later removed, but his sarcophagus still sits in the corner of the lot near O'Farrell Street [1].

title: The first streets that bent to the hills
place: Laidley Street on the curving slope of Fairmount Hill
hook: San Francisco usually laid its grid straight over hills. In 1864 the Fairmount Tract went on sale with streets that curved around the slopes instead.
story:
San Francisco's early surveyors ran their grid right over the hills. John Horner's addition laid a gridiron that suited the flats but not the hilly ground of the future Fairmount [1]. In December 1862 a group of Gold Rush pioneers announced the Pacific Railroad Homestead Association. They included Richard Chenery as president and James Laidley as vice president. They planned up to 600 lots on 120 to 130 acres beside the new San Francisco-San Jose Railroad [1].

The Civil War seems to have delayed things. On 27 February 1864 the scheme came back as "Fairmount," sold through the agents Cobb & Sinton. Its streets curved to follow the ground. The Glen Park Neighborhoods History Project argues this predates Corbett Heights, usually called the city's first terrain-following neighbourhood, by five years [1]. Advertisements boasted that the land was "laid out so as to avoid the heavy grading which has proven so great a charge on city property" [1]. At the first auction on 19 March 1864, $57,000 worth of lots sold. The rest of the sale was put off a week while General H. A. Cobb got over a cold [1].

Street names honour the founders: Chenery, Laidley, Bemis, Whitney [1]. By 1868, according to FoundSF, people in the area included carriage makers, stablers, bankers, painters and building-trades workers [2].

title: The ironclad that sank before it sailed
place: Third and King streets, site of the Camanche's 1864 launch
hook: The Pacific coast's only Union ironclad arrived in pieces, sank at the wharf within days, and had to be fished off the bottom before anyone could build it.
story: In the middle of the Civil War, a Passaic-class monitor named Camanche was prefabricated in Jersey City by Secor Brothers, taken apart and shipped around Cape Horn to San Francisco in the sailing ship Aquila [1]. The Aquila reached San Francisco on November 10, 1863. Four days later, after storm damage and a collision with another ship, she sank at her wharf in 30 feet of water with the dismantled ironclad aboard [1][2]. The parts were salvaged from the wreck [1][2]. Mechanics from Peter Donahue's Union Iron Works then put the monitor together at Third and King, on the old Steamboat Point shipbuilding shore, on the site of one of John North's earlier yards. Her turret armour was eleven inches thick [3]. The Camanche was launched on November 14, 1864, a year to the day after the Aquila went down [1][2]. For more than a year she was the only U.S. ironclad on the Pacific coast. She spent most of her career laid up at Mare Island and trained the California Naval Militia in 1896-97 [1][2]. Sold in 1899, she was stripped and spent decades hauling coal around the bay as a collier [1].

title: The railroad that cut the valley diagonally
place: Dolores Street at 27th Street, where the Southern Pacific bridge crossed
hook: Wonder why some Noe Valley houses are shaped like slices of pie? A steam railroad ran diagonally through the neighbourhood for nearly 80 years.
story:
In January 1864 the first train on the San Francisco–San Jose line left the city. It blew smoke across open cattle land on its way south. The route followed the flattest ground it could find. It ran down Harrison Street, angled west across the Mission, and curved southwest near today's Cesar Chavez and Dolores. Then it cut diagonally across lower Noe Valley to Duncan Street and ran south to 30th [1].

Photos show the line's bridge over Dolores at 27th Street as late as 1929. Another bridge is visible behind houses at 29th and Dolores around 1902 [2]. After the 1906 earthquake, a photographer on Valley Street near Dolores caught St. Paul's rising behind the old railroad bridge [3].

The line lost importance in 1907, when a new bayshore route opened on filled marshland. It became a branch line and finally faded out in 1942 [1]. The city grew around the tracks, and you can still trace the route today. Look for the odd triangular houses built to fit the right-of-way along its old path [1].

title: A blacksmith's manor on a country road
place: Casebolt House, 2727 Pierce Street between Vallejo and Green (Landmark No. 51)
hook: When Henry Casebolt built this Italianate manor, Pierce Street was a dirt road running down to Washerwoman's Lagoon. He went on to rethink the city's streetcars.
story:
Henry Casebolt was a blacksmith from Virginia, born in 1816. He came to California in the early 1850s with his wife and eleven children. The landmark report says 1851 and an 1895 trade journal says 1852 [1][2]. In 1865 he built this Italianate manor house. Pierce Street was then a country road through Cow Hollow down to Washerwoman's Lagoon [1][2].

Casebolt turned from blacksmithing to transit. He helped incorporate the Front Street, Mission Street & Ocean Railway Company, chartered in 1873, which was the forerunner of the Sutter Street Railway [2]. After the Clay Street cable line proved itself, he planned and engineered the conversion of the Sutter Street line to cable, and patented a number of devices along the way [2]. Not all his ideas caught on. His "balloon car" never became popular, and he and a partner, Montgomery Howe, went broke trying to finance an East Bay transit system, including an experimental car on a steep Piedmont hill [2].

The sources disagree here too: the landmark report has Casebolt selling the house in 1893, while the 1895 journal dates his death to September 23, 1892 [1][2]. It is still a private home [1].

title: A mile of timber over the bay
place: Long Bridge landing, Third (Kentucky) and Mariposa streets
hook: To reach the Potrero you once needed a boat. Then the city built a bridge a mile long straight across Mission Bay's mudflats.
story: Before 1865, getting to the Potrero meant a slow trip around the edge of Mission Bay or a boat from the foot of Third Street [1]. Then the city built a bridge straight across the water. The first pilings went in off Steamboat Point in February 1865, and by 1867 the timber trestle had reached land near today's Mariposa Street [2]. It was about a mile long, and people called it Long Bridge or the Mission Bay Bridge [1]. Taking the road on south along Kentucky Street (now Third) meant blasting through a ridge of serpentine rock that joined Potrero Point to the hill. More than 100,000 cubic yards of rock were removed, the first big reshaping of Potrero Hill [2]. Within months, horsecars of the Potrero and Bayview Railroad were running across, linking downtown with Potrero Point for the first time [2]. The bridge was also a place for fun. Hobbs Wharf, off the bridge, was a favourite spot for Sunday smelt fishing, where hundreds of rented bamboo poles stuck out a yard apart [2]. Land speculation came next, and factories and workers' cottages followed [3]. Once the railroads filled in Mission Bay in the early 1900s, the bridge was closed [3].

title: A one-room school on the Ocean House Road
place: Commodore Sloat Elementary School, Ocean Avenue at Junipero Serra Boulevard (site of the 1865 Ocean House School)
hook: For nearly fifty years, one teacher and one stove served children from second to tenth grade at a remote outpost. Later, a future Broadway star found her calling here.
story: In 1865 San Francisco opened a school in a rented building on the Ocean House Road, today's Ocean Avenue, near what is now Junipero Serra Boulevard. It was, as the Western Neighborhoods Project puts it, a remote outpost of education: one room, one teacher, one stove, and anywhere from 12 to 67 pupils sharing a handful of desks. Mixed classes from second to tenth grade learned together there for almost fifty years [1]. The old road, lined with scattered bars and roadhouses, ran right past the schoolhouse [2]. Around 1911 the school grew slightly and became the first Paul Revere School. After the Twin Peaks Tunnel opened in 1918 and houses began to replace Sutro's forest, the district planned a large modern building named for Commodore John Sloat. It was finished in 1922 and almost completely rebuilt in the 1970s [1]. One of its pupils was Carol Channing. At seven, nominated for class secretary, she stood frozen on the auditorium stage, knees shaking. Then, she later told the Chronicle, she thought: "I'll do what I do best. I'll turn into somebody else." She did an impression of the principal, Miss Berard, and was hooked on the stage for life [3].

title: Long Bridge: a causeway across the bay
place: Third Street, along the route of the vanished Long Bridge
hook: Third Street was once a wooden bridge over open water, crowded on Sundays with smelt fishermen, rowers and thirsty day-trippers.
story: In February 1865 pile drivers began hammering a causeway into Mission Bay. Long Bridge ran out along the line of Fourth Street, turned south near today's Third Street, and by 1867 reached the Potrero, later carrying horsecars all the way to the Bay View racetrack near Hunters Point [1][2]. It was sold as rapid transit for workers, but on Sundays it became the South of Market crowd's playground. Smelt fishing from the rails was so popular that elbow room was scarce. At Hobbs Wharf, off the bridge, hundreds of long bamboo poles, many rented from booths on the wharf, jutted out a yard apart [1]. Rowing clubs built boathouses on pilings, boats could be hired to row out to Mission Rock, and saltwater bathhouses stood right over the bay. James Gallandett and G.W. Purdy opened a Half-Way House beside the San Francisco Yacht Club's clubhouse [1][3]. The bridge also had a lasting effect. It sealed off most of the western bay, with only a narrow drawbridge for shallow scows at high tide, and the stagnant lagoon behind it was steadily filled in [1][2]. No trace survives, but Fourth and Third streets still follow its route [2].

title: The butchers' house that moved uphill
place: Sylvester House, 1556 Revere Ave
hook: One of the Bayview's oldest houses was built by a local carpenter, lived in by a family of cattle dealers, and moved to a new street in 1913.
story: The Italianate house at 1556 Revere Avenue is among the finest of the Bayview's surviving Victorian houses [3]. It was built by Stephen L. Piper, a well-known carpenter and house builder in what was then called South San Francisco. He lived near the old Bay View Park in the 1860s and 1870s [1]. The city's landmark report dates the house by its style to between 1865 and 1870; FoundSF gives 1865 [1][2]. From 1884 to 1900 it was home to the Sylvester family. Daniel and John Sylvester appear in 1879 as wholesale butchers and cattle dealers on First Avenue South, in the Butchers' Reservation the state had set aside in 1870 [1]. Their house then stood on the south side of Sumatra Street, now Quesada Avenue, between Savannah and Platte streets [1]. In 1913 it was moved to Revere. Its new basement was built from the stables that had stood on the old Quesada lot [1]. Today it is San Francisco Landmark No. 61 [1][3].

title: Where the milkmen stopped for a drink
place: Former Five Mile House, 3556–3564 San Bruno Avenue
hook: At the top of the climb out of the valley, dairy workers dragging milk wagons to the city stopped for a drink.
story: By 1865 a Five Mile House was pouring drinks on the San Bruno Toll Road, today's San Bruno Avenue [1]. It stood at the top of the ridge out of Visitacion Valley, facing Bayview Hill. Its regulars were the dairy workers listed in directories as 'milk dealers'. They stopped for a drink after hauling their wagons up the hill in the morning, and again on the way back to the ranches with empty cans [1]. The toll road carried mostly these milkers from dairies in the valley, Brisbane and South San Francisco [2]. It was so narrow that one wagon had to pull into the deep grass to let another pass [2]. The original building burned in 1896. Its replacement still stands in the middle of the 3500 block, hidden behind later storefronts [1]. Despite the name, none of the valley's mile houses was really five, six or seven miles from Portsmouth Square [1]. Old-timers remembered the Five Mile House for another reason. Its corner at Wilde and San Bruno avenues was the start of the streetcar line to Market Street [2]. The business moved a block away just before World War II and may have lasted into the late 1980s [1].

title: A Whiskey Palace on the Old Shoreline
place: Hotaling Building, 451 Jackson Street
hook: Anson Hotaling's iron-shuttered warehouse once looked out on the Bay. Forty years later, God allegedly spared it.
story: Around 1866, pioneer liquor merchant Anson Parsons Hotaling put up an Italianate building at Jackson Street and what is now Hotaling Place, then the northern edge of the Montgomery Street business district and on the Bay shoreline [2]. Hotaling had sailed from New York in 1852 and built a fortune in real estate, trade and mining [2]. Its cast-iron front and iron shutters were the fireproofing technology of the day [1]. Hotaling & Co. imported Kentucky whiskies and blended its own bourbons, notably Cutter and Old Kirk, and Hotaling bought neighbouring buildings to warehouse the stock [1][2]. When he died in 1900, the Call guessed his estate at seven to ten million dollars [2]. The building became famous in 1906. Employees reportedly rolled thousands of barrels to the empty customhouse construction site, and the warehouse survived [2]. When clergymen called the disaster divine punishment, Charles Field replied in verse: 'If, as they say, God spanked the town / For being over-frisky, / Why did He burn His churches down / And spare Hotaling's whiskey?' [1]

title: A zoo, museum and circus behind a hotel
place: Woodward's Gardens site, 1700 Mission St at Duboce (California Historical Landmark 454)
hook: The strait-laced hotelier who banned women from his hotel built the city's favourite playground, with sea lions, an aquarium and a tunnel under 14th Street.
story: Robert B. Woodward made his money at the What Cheer House, a hotel that served no liquor. According to an 1897 Chronicle piece, it did not allow women either: men made the beds [1]. With that fortune he bought John C. Frémont's former estate between 13th and 15th, Mission and Valencia. On May 1, 1866, he opened it to the public as Woodward's Gardens [1][2]. For a quarter (children a dime), visitors got a museum in his old house, with a 97-pound gold nugget among its specimens. There were also conservatories, an art gallery, ponds full of seals and sea lions, and a tunnel under 14th Street to the zoo [1][3]. In 1876 a guide called its aquarium the largest in the country. Its pavilion could seat 6,000 [3]. Woodward's granddaughter remembered the tightrope walker Blondin cooking an omelette high above the crowd [1]. On May 11, 1886, some 10,000 union men marched here for what FoundSF calls the city's first Labor Day celebration [4]. After Woodward died in 1879 the gardens faded. They closed in 1891, and much of the collection later went to Adolph Sutro [1][2].

title: Dutch Charley's Squatter Headquarters
place: Block bounded by Divisadero, Fulton, Scott and McAllister streets
hook: Twice banished by vigilantes, fire chief Dutch Charley Duane ran a squatter operation from a cottage just west of Alamo Square, and killed a man over land.
story:
Charles P. "Dutch Charley" Duane was a Gold Rush fireman, political enforcer and brawler. He was chief engineer of the volunteer fire department from 1853 to 1855 [1]. The Vigilance Committees banished him from the city in 1851 and again in 1856, threatening death if he came back. He returned early in 1860 anyway [2].

In a 1918 series, journalist Edward Morphy described how Charlie and his brother Jack built a little one-story cottage in the middle of the block bounded by Divisadero, Fulton, Scott and McAllister. From there, Morphy wrote, they hired "desperadoes" to defend "various properties [they] unlawfully preempted from being taken over or built upon by their legitimate owners" [3].

Colonel William G. Ross lived nearby, on the block bounded by Divisadero, McAllister, Broderick and today's Golden Gate Avenue [3]. On May 23, 1866, Duane shot Ross dead in a dispute over who owned a piece of land. He was tried in the 12th District Court and acquitted on October 31, 1866 [1]. The Parks Alliance's history of Alamo Square calls Duane "a known killer and tenacious squatter" and says the city finally ousted him from the land in 1868 [4]. He died in San Francisco on May 13, 1887 [1].

title: A whaling captain's ship-shaped house
place: Adams House, 300 Pennsylvania Avenue
hook: A New Bedford whaling captain let his lumber age for two years, then built a house on the hill as carefully as he would build a ship.
story: Captain Charles Adams sailed into San Francisco Bay in 1850 from New Bedford, Massachusetts. He was looking for a base for his whaling fleet, and he chose Potrero Hill for its springs and sunshine [1]. He bought about thirteen acres around Eighteenth Street and Pennsylvania, at a time when the bay came to within a block of the site [1]. Adams took his time. The lumber for his house lay on the ground for two years so it could season, and the house was built rather like a ship. Its attic was one huge room shaped like an upturned keel, and it held two water tanks. Water came from a spring and a well, and pipes running past the fireplaces warmed it for the bath [1]. The house dates from 1867 [2]. Across the street, on land Adams sold, pharmacist Clayton French Richards built an Italianate house around 1865. Part of his fortune came from "Dr. Le Richau's Golden Pills", a patent medicine sold for "seminal weakness" [3]. The two houses were among the first on the hill with bay windows [1][3]. In 1906 the Adams well supplied water to earthquake refugees. In 1907 the Richards family rented their house to Union Iron Works as a hospital for $125 a month [1][3].

title: Ten Dollars a Month for a Homestead
place: Broad St near Capitol Ave (Railroad Homestead Association tract)
hook: Ocean View began as a shareholder scheme: $10 a month bought a stake in 150 railside acres, and newspapers warned of lonely wives trudging through mud.
story: An 1861 state law let homestead associations pool members' monthly dues to buy a large tract, then divide it into lots once it was paid off [1]. The Railroad Homestead Association incorporated on November 1, 1864, after buying 150 acres through attorney Levi Parsons for $60,000; investors paid $20 to join and $10 a month [1]. Its name advertised the San Francisco-San Jose railroad on the tract's eastern edge, an answer to the common complaint that homestead lands were remote [1]. Sceptics were unmoved. 'How will his wife enjoy the solitude of the charming residence, three, four, five or six miles from town?' the Daily Evening Bulletin asked in 1862. 'In stormy weather how will he like to foot it through the mire to work?' [1] When payments were complete, A.E. McGregor platted the east half of today's Ocean View, and on April 15, 1867, the map was filed and lots distributed the same day [1]. Broad Street was drawn wider than its neighbours, perhaps for commerce, and some original 200-foot-wide lots survive on Broad between Capitol and Plymouth [1]. Many members were speculators; by the mid-1870s lots resold for less than half the share price [1]. A 1993 local history instead dates the association's first real success to 1883 [2].

title: The Sugar King's first cubes
place: California Sugar Refinery site, Eighth and Brannan streets
hook: A German grocer who learned sugar-making on a New York night shift opened a refinery at Eighth and Brannan and sold Californians their first sugar cubes.
story: Claus Spreckels left Hanover in 1848 with one thaler in his pocket [1]. He ran a grocery and then a brewery in San Francisco, and then turned to sugar. To learn the trade he worked a night shift in a New York refinery, and later spent months as a workman in a beet-sugar plant in Magdeburg [1][2]. In April 1867 he opened the California Sugar Refinery at Eighth and Brannan streets, this time keeping full control of the company [1]. The plant started at about 9,000 tons a year. Spreckels sped it up with machines patented in his own name and enlarged the buildings four times [2]. He also brought granulated and cube sugar, already known in Europe, to American shoppers. Until then grocers mostly sold hard sugarloaves that had to be broken up with special tools [1][2]. By 1869 overwork had given him a breakdown, and he spent 18 months recovering in Europe [1]. By 1880 he had a near-monopoly on sugar in California. In 1881 he moved production to a huge new refinery at Potrero Point [1][2].

title: The almshouse where the poor grew dinner
place: Laguna Honda Hospital, 375 Laguna Honda Blvd (site of the 1860s Almshouse)
hook: Not everyone struck gold. On a spring-fed lagoon behind Twin Peaks, the city built a home for the broke, the sick and the old, and made them farm it.
story:
Many who came for the Gold Rush were left with nothing. The city's answer was an almshouse on ranch land west of Twin Peaks, beside a deep, spring-fed lagoon called Laguna Honda. Sources date its founding to 1866 or 1867 [1][2]. The residents were poor, sick or destitute, and they grew their own food, raised livestock on 87 acres, and made their own clothes. By 1870, 500 people lived there. A smallpox epidemic in 1868 brought a small hospital, later used as an asylum [1][2]. Over the hill, the hog rancher Thomas Mahoney refreshed his herd's bloodlines by now and then trading a pig with the Alms House [3].

After 1906 the almshouse sheltered earthquake victims who had never thought of themselves as poor, and Theodore Roosevelt dedicated a 1,000-bed pavilion for them in 1909 [1][2]. In the 1920s, under Mayor James 'Sunny Jim' Rolph, the Spanish Revival buildings that still crown the hill went up. In the 1930s the place became a teaching centre for the University of California's medical school and gained its WPA murals. Even so, the old poorhouse only became an accredited hospital in 1963 [1].

title: The mayor's smelter on the cove
place: Selby smelter site, eastern shore of Black Point Cove near Beach and Larkin streets
hook: For eighteen years a lead smelter owned by a future mayor smoked on the shore of today's Aquatic Park, until it packed up for the other side of the bay.
story: Thomas Henry Selby was 29 when the Gold Rush drew him from New York to San Francisco, where he became a merchant. He built the Selby Shot Tower and founded the Selby Smelting Works [2]. In 1867 he put up a large smelter on the eastern shore of Black Point Cove, today's Aquatic Park. With the water company's pump station and the woolen mill beside it, the shoreline took on a decidedly industrial character [1]. The army, which had fortified Black Point in 1863, decided in 1869 to evict these 'squatting' industries. Opposition was fierce, and on July 1, 1870, Congress shrank the military reservation, leaving the cove to the private speculators who occupied it [1]. By then Selby was mayor, serving from December 1869 to December 1871 as the city's first Republican mayor [2]. The works loomed over the swimmers: in August 1875 the banker William Ralston took his last swim off the end of Larkin Street 'in the shadow of the Selby Lead Smelting Works' [3]. Selby himself had died of pneumonia that June [2]. In 1885 the company closed the smelter, saying it needed rail service, deep-water frontage and room to grow, and within the year it had moved to the eastern shore of the bay [1].

title: The squatters' hill that became a park
place: Buena Vista Park, Haight St at Buena Vista Ave West
hook: San Francisco's oldest official park began as a sandy, oak-studded hill the city had to buy back from squatters.
story: Long before the Haight had houses, the city reserved the steep hill above it. In 1867 San Francisco's Committee on Outside Lands set aside the slope as "Hill Park", and Wikipedia calls it the oldest official park in the city [1][2]. (A walking-tour text dates the reservation to 1868 [3].) The hill wasn't empty. The city paid squatters $88,250 to give up their claims to the hilltop [1]. It was also one of the few places in town with native trees. The great dunes that once covered about a third of San Francisco had climbed right over this hill. Over centuries, plants steadied the sand until coast live oaks could grow, and the park's northern slopes still hold one of the city's largest remnant stands of oak woodland [4]. The park was dedicated as Buena Vista Park in 1894. Superintendent John McLaren then oversaw planting eucalyptus, cypress, pine, Australian tea trees and small redwoods alongside the old oaks and toyon. During Adolph Sutro's term as mayor (1894 to 1898), schoolchildren planted seedlings there on Arbor Day [1]. Sources even disagree on the hill's height: 569, 575 or 589 feet [1][2][3].

title: A dry dock carved from green rock
place: Site of Drydock No. 1, Hunters Point Shipyard
hook: San Francisco's richest men cut a ship-sized trench into the serpentine tip of Hunters Point and lined its mouth with granite hauled from the Sierra foothills.
story: Hunters Point was made of green serpentine, a rock that is easy to dig but lets no water through, and it had deep water right at its tip [2]. That made it a natural place for a graving dock, where a ship floats in, the gate closes and the water is pumped out [2]. In 1866 engineer A. W. von Schmidt got 30 acres at the end of the peninsula and brought in the banker William Ralston as partner [1]. The California Dry Dock Company that followed also included Lloyd Tevis and the wheat baron Isaac Friedlander [2]. Workers cut the dock into the bedrock and lined it with timber, and set massive granite blocks from Rocklin at its mouth [2]. Sources differ on its length, 400 or 462 feet, and on whether it was finished in 1867 or 1868 [1][2]. The Alta California admired the new sheds and stables, which gave 'the appearance of active life in striking contrast with the unbroken stillness' of the bare hills, and predicted 1,500 jobs [1]. In November 1868 the Chronicle described the docking of the Pacific Mail side-wheeler Colorado [3]. The dock was obliterated in 1916 to make room for a bigger one, though some of its granite may still lie under the piers [2].

title: America's first dynamite factory, in a canyon
place: Glen Canyon Park ball fields (approximate site of the Giant Powder Company works)
hook: Alfred Nobel personally licensed a factory in Glen Canyon, and it made dynamite before his US patent was even granted. Then it blew up.
story:
In 1867 Alfred Nobel licensed his new explosive to Julius Bandmann of San Francisco, and in August Bandmann incorporated the Giant Powder Company [1][2]. Nitroglycerin had to be stored far from people, so the company leased land in the empty "outlands" of a gorge people then called Rock Canyon or Rock Gulch. Today it is Glen Canyon [1]. The factory began turning out dynamite in March 1868, two months before Nobel's American patent was granted [1].

It ran smoothly for 15 months. Then at about 6:45 pm on 26 November 1869 an explosion tore through the one-acre works, killing the chemist and his teamster and injuring nine others [1][2]. Giant moved out to the sand dunes of the future Sunset District, where another blast in 1879 killed four people [1].

No one is sure exactly where the Glen Canyon factory stood. A 1927 history of the explosives industry put it west of Burnside Avenue between Chenery and Bosworth streets, which would put it roughly on today's ball field [1]. The site became California Historical Landmark No. 1002 in 1991, but its plaque was not put up until 2018 [3].

title: The Artillery Post Soldiers Hated
place: Site of Army Post parade ground, East Cove
hook: Fear of a Confederate raider in the fog put soldiers on the island. They got a parade ground, a bakery, a fire and a transfer out.
story:
During the Civil War, planners worried that a Confederate warship could slip past Fort Point and Alcatraz on a foggy night. The Navy first proposed garrisoning Yerba Buena Island in 1861 [1]. The guns were never built, but the soldiers came anyway. After a first small detachment in early 1867, 125 men arrived to set up an artillery post and depot on the island's only flat ground, at the east cove [1][2].

They built it the Army way, around a square parade ground: a two-wing barracks for 150 men, mess hall, laundresses' quarters, bakery, sutler's store, guard house and wharf. The hospital was Thomas Dowling's old house [2]. The Fourth Artillery held the post from 1871 to 1879 [1][2]. The barracks burned in 1875, and the Navy's historians report that most of the men hated island life [2]. In 1879 General McDowell ordered them back to the Presidio, which was a relief to the garrison [2]. Two of the post's buildings are known to survive. They were moved and rebuilt on Angel Island [1]. The Army kept title all the same, and around 1881 Barnacle Bill was living here as caretaker of the empty post [2].

title: The Mission Creek gunboat war
place: Block 40, near Seventh and Berry streets
hook: Sixty men fought with pistols, knives and a cannon-armed scow over a patch of mud that was half underwater.
story: California's Tidelands Act of 1868 let a settler buy a water lot if he was in "bona fide actual possession" of it on January 1, 1868. Around Mission Creek that phrase was read as a licence to grab. Rival claimants, some with titles going back to 1846 or to the notorious water-lot sales of the 1850s, moved in with pile drivers and a scow schooner armed with a cannon, promptly nicknamed the "Mission Creek Gunboat" [1]. On November 19, 1868, the Alta California reported a 3 a.m. raid in which men demanded possession of the ground and a man named Baxter was seriously wounded. A week later police were guarding the pile driver and the gunboat and letting no one aboard, for fear of a riot [1]. Some sixty men fought over Block 40, which was then partly salt marsh and partly open water. Several were badly hurt, and nobody was killed [1][2]. The two accounts place the block slightly differently, but both put it between Seventh and Eighth streets near Berry. The battles over title dragged on in the courts into the late 1870s [1].

title: The day Butchertown opened for business
place: Butchers' Reservation, Third St and Arthur Ave
hook: Pushed out of the city, San Francisco's butchers built a meat town on stilts over Islais Creek, where the tide carried their waste away.
story: In 1867 the state granted about 80 acres of mostly underwater land south of Islais Creek to the Wholesale Butchers' Association, and city law soon made it the only place where slaughtering was allowed [1][2]. On September 14, 1868, 'a numerous concourse' watched the first slaughterhouse open. It was a 50-by-30-foot shed with pens for up to 75 cattle [1]. By 1877 all eighteen of the city's slaughterhouses had moved here, along with tanneries, glue works, fertilizer plants and wool pulleries [2]. That year the Bulletin counted about 325 cattle, 650 hogs and 1,000 sheep killed every day. Horns went to comb makers, hooves to glue and blood to the sugar refineries at Potrero Point, and about 400 men earned $60 to $250 a month [1]. Most of the killing floors stood on pilings over the creek so the tide could carry off the offal [2]. Around 50 vaqueros, about half of them Spanish-speaking Californios, drove cattle from the Second Street wharf out to the pens [1]. Getting the meat back to town was hard: in 1870 the Bulletin complained the only road was 'cut up and ungraded' [3].

title: The mill that rolled the West's iron
place: Former Pacific Rolling Mills, north shore of Potrero Point near the foot of 20th Street
hook: Before Pier 70 built warships, a roaring mill here turned out the rails, beams and cable-car tracks of a growing West, worked by Irish and Scottish hands.
story:
Pacific Rolling Mills was organized on May 10, 1866, by William Alvord, John Bensley and D.O. Mills. They took a state grant of submerged land and about twenty acres on the north shore of Potrero Point, near the foot of what is now 20th Street [1]. The mill started up in July 1868. VerPlanck calls its first product rolled steel, the first on the West Coast. Olmsted says it rolled its first bar of iron [1][2].

The output was enormous. It made rails, I-beams for bridges and houses, ship shafts, chains, bolts and whole iron bridges, and it rolled the rails for San Francisco's streetcars and cable cars. By 1880 it ran day and night with 450 men, paying more than East Coast mills did. Irish immigrants "headed for the big mills the moment they arrived in town," and Scottish iron moulders made up much of the crew [2]. Many lived on Irish Hill next door. One was James Dixon, who married Katherine in 1883 and went on to put up a building on 18th Street that still stands [3].

In the mid-1890s the plant became Risdon Iron & Locomotive Works, and it built gold dredges. Bethlehem Steel bought it in 1911 and folded it into the shipyard [1].

title: The private company that drank the lake
place: Spring Valley 'City Pumps', east side of South Lake near Brotherhood Way
hook: For sixty years a private monopoly pumped Lake Merced into San Francisco's taps, and the city bought it back for almost $40 million.
story: In 1868 the Spring Valley Water Works, already San Francisco's monopoly supplier, bought the water rights to Lake Merced for $150,000 [1][2]. From the 1870s it bought up almost 3,000 acres of surrounding watershed [2]. Its first pumps, on the north shore, were running by 1 October 1877 and could push 3.5 million gallons a day through 16,000 feet of iron pipe [2]. In 1877 the company drew 295 million gallons from the lake; by 1902 almost 1.8 billion gallons of Lake Merced water came out of city taps each year [2]. In 1891 it built City Pumps on the east side of South Lake, just west of where Brotherhood Way now meets Lake Merced Boulevard, and the station still moves city water today [2]. Spring Valley became the largest privately owned water utility in the country and a favourite target of reformers, and the city was often behind on its bills [2]. After years of lawsuits and failed bonds, voters approved buying it in 1928. On 2 March 1930 the treasurer handed over a check for $39,962,606.51, and 454 employees became city workers [2].

title: Baseball's first pros crush the Eagles
place: Recreation Grounds site, Folsom Street near 25th
hook: The Cincinnati Red Stockings rode the brand-new transcontinental railroad to the Mission and ran up scores like 76-5.
story: San Francisco baseball began in the Mission. FoundSF dates California's first official game to February 22, 1860 [1]. Burrito Justice places it at 16th and Harrison, beside Mission Creek, where the Eagles won after the Red Rovers refused to finish [2]. In 1868 a proper ground went up at Folsom and 25th, in the middle of the old Pioneer Race Course (one FoundSF caption puts it at Folsom and Cesar Chavez instead). A researcher of early baseball dates its first game to November 26, 1868 [2]. FoundSF credits the Hatton brothers with building the "Recreation Grounds" [1]. In September 1869 the Cincinnati Red Stockings, the famous team of the day, arrived on one of the first transcontinental trains [1][2]. According to a 1924 Call Bulletin history, they beat the Eagles 35-4, then 58-4, then 66-4. They also beat the Pacifics 54-4 and the Atlantics 76-5 [1][2]. One family historian says some published scores contain typos [2]. The grandstand did not last long: one researcher reports that an arsonist burned it two weeks after Cincinnati left [2]. Seven houses that stood behind the stands, on the 2900 block of Folsom, are still there [2].

title: Harvard, Yale and a Street Once Called Berlin
place: Brussels Street at Dwight Street
hook: The Portola's street grid was drawn in 1869 for a city that hadn't arrived yet. It survives almost unchanged, apart from one street that stopped being called Berlin.
story: In 1869 a Homestead Association filed a plan with the city's Department of Streets and Maps. It laid out the Portola's blocks and streets almost exactly as they are today [1]. There were only a few changes. Berlin Street became Brussels, and College Street was renamed Colby [1]. Many of the names honour colleges and universities, which suits a hill called University Mound: Harvard, Oxford, Cambridge, Yale, Amherst, Princeton and Dartmouth [2]. The map ran well ahead of the people, though. In the early 1900s the district was still mostly farmland and its few streets were unpaved. Cattle grazed on the hills, flower greenhouses stood west of Charter Oak Avenue, and truck gardens ran east toward the bay [1]. A photograph from about 1920 looks north between Brussels and Goettingen from roughly Dwight Street toward Bernal Heights [3]. Goettingen kept its old name. The valley picked up nicknames of its own, 'Little Jerusalem' and 'The Flat', which have long since been dropped [1].

title: Noe Valley's little house on the prairie
place: 39 Chattanooga Street, between 22nd and 23rd streets
hook: A sagging cottage with a cowboy-movie false front turned out to be older than the grading of its own street. Its discovery set off a four-year fight.
story: In 2002 builder John Williams, who lived on Elizabeth Street, paid $681,000 for a 986-square-foot, two-bedroom cottage at 39 Chattanooga Street. He told neighbours he would tear it down and put up a much larger two-unit building [1]. His demolition request triggered a historical review, and it landed with city planner Moses Corrette, who had once lived around the corner. The clues were in the bones. The house has a central entrance and hallway, typical of the 1850s and 1860s, and its ground floor sits well below the sidewalk, which suggests it was built before Chattanooga Street was graded in the 1870s. It appears on an 1869 U.S. Coast Survey map but not on one from 1857 [1]. Corrette noted that fewer than 50 of the city's 70,000 buildings date from those decades [1]. Playwright Charlie Varon, who lived next door, called it Noe Valley's "Little House on the Prairie," and neighbours and preservationists banded together as Save 39 Chattanooga [1][2]. Williams dropped the demolition and drew about half a dozen alternatives. But in 2006, after some $120,000 in carrying costs, he sold. "Life's too short," he said. The buyer paid $902,000 for the dilapidated cottage, well over the asking price [2].

title: Stevedores' cottages on the Filbert Steps
place: 228 Filbert St, Filbert Steps at Napier Lane
hook: Along a wooden boardwalk cut into a cliff, the dock workers of the 1850s and 60s left the best-preserved Gold Rush-era street in the city.
story: Telegraph Hill's steep east face overlooked the busiest docks in the city, so the men who worked them built shacks and small Gothic Revival houses here [1][2]. The best of them still line the Filbert Steps and Napier Lane, one of the last wooden boardwalks in San Francisco [1]. 224 Filbert went up in 1859 for James Callaghan, a waterfront labourer who later became a warehouse foreman [1]. In 1857 a teamster and a labourer from the Greenwich Dock warehouse, the Clark brothers, built the cottage at 10 Napier [1]. The standout is 228 Filbert, a 'Carpenter Gothic' house built in 1869 by Phillip Brown, a seaman who became a stevedore. The basement looks as if it was meant for a shop. But Brown had ruled that his wife would not be a shopkeeper, so the family ate dinner down there [1]. Neighbours called it 'the Captain's House' only because a Captain Laughton spent so much time on its porch [1]. There were no streets for carts, just steps, boardwalks and hidden footpaths, and the city later made these a protected historic district [2].

title: The Farmhouse That Lived on India Avenue
place: 400 Peru Avenue (originally 400 India Avenue)
hook: The Excelsior's streets were named for the world's nations. Then China, Japan and India quietly disappeared from the map.
story: The Excelsior's map was drawn in 1869 by a homestead association. It laid out a grid of streets named for the world's countries and capitals, from Persia and Russia to Madrid and Naples, long before there were many houses to line them [1]. A walking-tour historian told the Excelsior branch library that the developers were men in international trade [2]. But not every nation kept its place. Under the anti-Asian pressure of the Chinese Exclusion era, China, Japan and India avenues were renamed, and today they are Excelsior, Avalon and Peru [2][3]. The house at 400 Peru Avenue, at Naples Street, began life as 400 India Avenue. It is a simple Italianate farmhouse with a centre gable and bracketed windows. SF Heritage suggests it may date to the 1870s, and the 1915 Sanborn fire map shows a rear wing that once led to a large barn [4]. In 2013 Supervisor John Avalos introduced a resolution to add the original names, 'China,' 'Japan' and 'India,' back onto the street signs above the current ones [3].

title: The Railroad That Wanted the Whole Island
place: Yerba Buena Shoals (today's Treasure Island)
hook: Leland Stanford planned to flatten Goat Island, fill the shoals and run the transcontinental railroad out to the middle of the bay.
story:
Here's a San Francisco fear from the 1860s: the transcontinental railroad would end somewhere else. Around the end of the 1860s, Leland Stanford's Central Pacific tried to get Goat Island from the federal government. The plan was to level it, fill the surrounding shoals and run a causeway across to the Contra Costa shore, making the island the line's western terminus [1]. San Franciscans saw a trap in it: a railroad port in mid-bay could make the city itself unnecessary. Remarks by Stanford, the Navy's historians note, suggested they were right [1]. The railroad won in Sacramento. San Francisco won in Washington, and only intense opposition from the city blocked the transfer [1][2].

It was a hollow victory, because the Central Pacific simply built its terminus in Oakland [1]. The fight still had a long afterlife. It started the first serious debate about a bridge across the bay and about filling the Yerba Buena shoals [1]. The 1861 city directory had already imagined an artificial island here, built with earth dug from Yerba Buena itself [1]. In the mid-1930s, dredged fill made that idea real as Treasure Island, right where you're standing [3].

title: The day they sliced Rincon Hill in half
place: Second Street cut at Harrison Street, Rincon Hill
hook: One landowner's scheme dug a canyon through San Francisco's most fashionable hill, and within a few years the rich had packed up for Nob Hill.
story: In the 1850s and 1860s Rincon Hill was one of the city's most fashionable addresses [1][3]. Then John Middleton, who owned a lot at Second and Bryant, decided a level road to the Pacific Mail wharves would make him richer [1]. He got himself elected to the State Assembly and pushed through a bill letting the supervisors change street grades [1]. Residents protested that the hill was home to the city's finest houses; supporters answered that a few wealthy people should not stop progress [1]. The Board fell one vote short, but in February 1869 the California Supreme Court ordered the cut, with the rubble to fill South Beach [1]. The crest at Harrison came down 87 feet [1]. The job took 500 men and 250 horse teams over a year, ran at least $100,000 over budget, and left a $90,000 wooden bridge across the gap that the press called atrocious [1]. The sand kept slipping, wrecking houses along the edge [2]. Land values collapsed and the wealthy moved north; Robert Louis Stevenson later called the hill 'a new slum' of sandy cliffs and solitary old houses [3].

title: When the hilltop spoke Scots
place: Scotch Hill, 522 Connecticut Street
hook: Ironworkers from the Clyde made the top of Potrero Hill their own. They built a church with their own hands and gave the hill its name.
story: The top of Potrero Hill once had a Scottish accent. From 1865, workers from the Clyde valley in Scotland came to work in the shipyards and later at Union Iron Works. They settled along Mississippi, Texas and Connecticut streets, an area its residents called Scotch Hill [1]. Many were skilled iron moulders at the Pacific Rolling Mills on the waterfront below, which rolled its first iron in 1868 [3]. In 1869 a congregation of seventeen Scottish ironworkers from the mill built a small church on Tennessee Street. It burned in 1877, and they rebuilt on Mississippi Street, closer to the Scottish homes on Connecticut [2]. That was Olivet Presbyterian. A 1964 neighbourhood study dates the church to 1868 instead and says it burned more than once [1]. A Mr. Rintoul, who arrived in 1893, was still living in the same house at 522 Connecticut Street decades later. He remembered the hill as "mostly pastureland", with a few houses "all of them belonged to Scottish families." To visit a relative on De Haro Street he crossed "Chilit Pass", the dip near Carolina Street that separated Scotch Hill from the higher hill to the west [1].

title: A Potter's Field at the Continent's Edge
place: Golden Gate Cemetery site, Lincoln Park Golf Course
hook: The golf fairways cover what was the city's cemetery for the poor, the unclaimed and the immigrant, laid out in dozens of separate sections.
story: In 1868 the city set aside this windswept headland for a municipal burial ground, the Golden Gate or City Cemetery, and the first interment was recorded in July 1870 [1]. While the grand Lone Mountain cemeteries mostly served the well-off, this one served the working class, immigrants and the indigent [2]. It was carved into sections for the Chinese Six Companies, French, German, Italian, Russian, Jewish, Greek Orthodox, Japanese and Chinese Christian communities, for the Knights of Pythias, the Grand Army of the Republic, the Colored I.O.O.F. and the Ladies' Seamen's Friend Society, and a Potter's Field for those who died with nothing [1]. Bodies moved from the old Yerba Buena Cemetery were reburied here too [2]. By 1887 there were over 11,000 interments, more than 4,000 of them Chinese. By 1893 there were 18,000, and over 11,000 of those lay in Potter's Field [1]. Adolph Sutro and other prominent citizens called the place an eyesore. The city banned burials in 1901 and in 1909 ordered the cemetery moved to Colma [1]. Many of the dead never left. A Seamen's monument and a Chinese tomb or gateway still stand among the tees [1][2].

title: A hill of paper streets and generals
place: Banks Street, east of Cortland (one of Bernal's 'general' streets)
hook: Bernal's street grid was drawn over a bare cattle hill, and more than a dozen of its streets are named after generals.
story:
Long before anyone lived here, the hill was a real-estate product. In 1859 surveyor Milo Hoadley cut the slopes into hundreds of narrow lots for the "Precita Valley Lands" auction. On his map a neat grid ran straight over the top of Bernal Hill. More than 400 parcels sold, at an average of $84, mostly to speculators who never meant to build [1].

The names came next. Journalist Lynn Ludlow counts more than a dozen generals from the nation's first century on Bernal's street signs, including Gates, Moultrie, Appleton, Wool, Anderson, Putnam, Banks and Prentiss. He suggests they were picked around 1868 or 1869, when Civil War commanders were fresh in people's minds, because they appear on the city's official map of 1870 [2]. Two battles got streets too: Bennington (renamed from Scott Street in 1882) and Lundys Lane [2]. The Thanksgiving story gave the east slope Mayflower, Brewster, Bradford, Massasoit and Samoset. Old Hickory Avenue, named for Andrew Jackson, soon became Ogden [2]. Ludlow admits most of the reasons were never written down, and the 1906 fire burned many city records [2]. So even the streets' origins are partly guesswork.

title: An English castle brewing ale on India Basin
place: Albion Brewery ('Albion Castle'), 881 Innes Ave
hook: A failed fur trader from Sussex found a spring under Hunters Point, cut tunnels into the hill and built a Norman-style stone castle to brew English ale.
story: John Hamlin Burnell, from East Hoathly in Sussex, came to San Francisco by way of British Columbia after failing in the fur trade [1][3]. He wanted to brew ales and porters 'in the English tradition', and for that he needed plenty of fresh water. He found it in a natural spring on the north slope of Hunters Point ridge, near today's Innes Avenue and Griffith Street [1][3]. In 1870 he founded the Albion Ale and Porter Brewery, cutting tunnels about 200 to 300 feet into the hillside [1][2]. Above them rose a rough stone building with a three-story tower modelled on English Norman castles [1]. Nobody agrees on where the stone came from. One account says ships' ballast limestone, another says 'float rock' quarried from the nearby hills [1][3]. The landmark report says the hops came from Scotland and the casks and bottles from England [1]. It also says the brewery was never very profitable, though it supported the family [1]. After Burnell died in 1890, his widow, brother and nephews kept it going until 1919, when Mrs. Burnell died and Prohibition arrived [1][3]. The castle is Landmark No. 60 [2].

title: The Street Grids That Never Met
place: Orizaba Ave between Randolph St and Broad St
hook: Ride the M line down Orizaba and you feel it: a jog where two nineteenth-century land schemes refused to line up.
story: West of the Railroad Homestead tract, the City Land Association formed in 1868 and offered lots for just $90, payable at $4 a month without interest [1]. It promised streetcars, a few ready-built houses and side-by-side lots for relatives, and in April 1870 it allocated 2,400 lots to 1,130 subscribers [1]. City Surveyor William P. Humphries dropped a rectilinear grid straight over the slopes and peak of Merced Heights, creating steep streets, some impassable to traffic [1]. His east-west streets also failed to line up with the neighbouring tract at Orizaba Avenue, leaving dead-ends and a dip connecting Randolph and Broad Streets [1]. Why the two grids never met is unknown [2]. Several names from the 1870 map survive, including Shields, Vernon, Victoria and Bright, while others changed: Ford became Byxbee, Walnut became Ralston and State became Ramsell [3]. The mismatch outlived everyone who drew it. When the Municipal Railway opened the M-Ocean View in 1925, its tracks ran along Randolph, turned down Orizaba and onto Broad [1]. A 1927 photograph looking south down Orizaba past Farallones shows the same bend riders still take today [4].

title: The Synagogue That Let Families Sit Together
place: Congregation Sherith Israel's synagogue, Post and Taylor streets
hook: On Post Street, a Gold Rush congregation of Polish Jews built a Gothic synagogue and slowly began to change how it worshipped.
story: San Francisco's Jewish pioneers split along lines of origin. Jews from Germany and Central Europe founded Congregation Emanu-El, and Jews from Prussian Poland and Eastern Europe founded Congregation Sherith Israel, the 'loyal remnant of Israel', in 1851 [1][2]. By the end of the 1850s Jews were perhaps six percent of the city's population, briefly a higher share than in New York [1]. In 1870 Sherith Israel moved into a Gothic-style synagogue at Post and Taylor streets, its home for more than three decades [1]. The congregation had been Orthodox in the Polish style, and here it began to move toward Reform. The Post Street sanctuary was built for mixed seating. Over years of discussion and struggle, head coverings became optional, Friday evening services began, a choir was introduced and a new prayerbook was chosen [1]. A Prussian-Polish tailor worked near the synagogue, and his son Toby Rosenthal became the most important visual artist to come out of pioneer San Francisco [2]. By the 1890s the congregation had outgrown Post Street. It bought land at California and Webster in 1902 and hired Albert Pissis to design a domed temple there. The new temple was finished in 1905 and was the congregation's fifth home in less than fifty years [1][2].

title: The island that became a pier
place: Pier 50, site of the former Mission Rock
hook: A 25-foot rock in the bay became a drydock, then a grain terminal, and was finally burned and buried under Pier 50.
story: Early charts show Mission Rock standing alone in the water off the mouth of Mission Bay. It was the largest of three small peaks on a submerged ridge, rising about twenty-five feet, and ships used it as a landmark [1][2]. In 1870 H.B. Tichenor, whose marine railway near Steamboat Point had served the city's shipbuilders since the 1850s, sold his ways to the railroad interests and turned his attention to the rock. He secured a tidelands grant around it and built a drydock, expanding a fraction of an acre into about four acres [1]. By 1884 the rock carried warehouses and served as an extended wharf. It became a grain terminal, and an 1897 photograph shows men working cargo there with Yerba Buena Island faint in the distance [1][2]. Holiday rowers on Long Bridge could rent boats to row out to it [3]. The island kept growing until January 1946, when the obsolete grain terminal was deliberately set on fire so the Port could extend Pier 50 over it. Pier 50 swallowed it, the farthest reach of Mission Bay's landfill [4].

title: The keeper's cottage by the reservoir
place: College Hill Reservoir keeper's cottage site, 336 Elsie Street
hook: A naked bather with a beribboned wand, a drowning and a firefighter's rescue: a century of drama at Bernal's open reservoir.
story: The Spring Valley Water Company built College Hill Reservoir at the edge of Holly Park in 1870, and a keeper's cottage went up beside it at 336 Elsie Street in 1871 [1]. For years the water lay open to the sky, as photos from 1913 show [2]. It drew people in. One December morning in 1877 Mrs. Peter Brickley of Cherubusco Street walked up to the reservoir wearing nothing but a wand tipped with coloured ribbons. She bathed first in a trough and then in the reservoir itself. The keeper's elderly father tried to fend her off with a garden rake, She was taken to the City Prison, and neighbours drank well water for a few days [1]. In April 1892 the keeper, Thomas Quinlan, found his wife Caroline floating near the shore [1][3]. In January 1916 Edward Ford, a relief firefighter at the Holly Park station, jumped in and wrestled out Agnes Graham, who was trying to drown herself [1]. In 1968 the Junior League named the farmhouse-like cottage one of four architecturally significant buildings in Bernal. After it fell into disrepair, the Public Utilities Commission tore it down in 1971 [1].

title: The last cow in the Western Addition
place: Ortman-Shumate House, 1901 Scott St at Pine
hook: A German grocer bought a huge lot in 1870. His family held on for more than a century, and so, for a while, did the family cow.
story:
On 25 February 1870, John Frederic Ortman bought this unusually large lot at Scott and Pine [1]. He was born in Germany in 1829, came to California in 1851, and started out as a grocery clerk before running his own grocery business. A few years after moving here he retired, and the 1876 city directory lists him simply as a "Capitalist" [1].

Before 1890 Ortman owned the whole block frontage from California to Pine, and in the 1890s he built houses for his two daughters when they married [1]. The family also kept a cow. When Emerson School took a neighbouring lot for its new concrete building in the 1920s, the Shumate cow lost its pasture. The city's landmark report calls it "one of the last, if not the very last" privately owned cow in the Western Addition [1].

The Italianate house stayed with the builder's descendants. When it became Landmark No. 98 in 1977, Dr. Albert Shumate, the first president of the city's Landmarks Preservation Advisory Board, was still living here [1][2].

title: The poorhouse that grew its own food
place: Laguna Honda Hospital grounds (the old Almshouse farm), off Laguna Honda Boulevard
hook: In 1870 the city's poorhouse west of Twin Peaks fed more than 500 people from its own 87-acre farm, with vegetables left over to sell in town.
story: In 1866 San Francisco put up a four-storey wooden building on the old Rancho San Miguel, west of Twin Peaks, for people the Gold Rush had left broke, sick or alone. It was called the Almshouse. Nearby a spring fed a deep lagoon, a laguna honda, the name the place still carries [1]. The Almshouse was expected to feed itself. Residents worked 87 acres of farmland and kept livestock. By 1870 the farm fed more than 500 men, women and children and still produced a surplus, carted three miles into town to sell. Residents made their own clothes and their own shoes [1]. In 1872 the administrator reported that the food, clothing and cleanliness were "equal, if not superior" to any such place in the United States or Europe. By 1890 the residents came from some forty nations [1]. The farm had neighbours too. Around 1910, a man who grew up there later recalled, Louis Lagomarsino, whose family grew vegetables from today's West Portal toward the State College site, drove a horse-drawn wagon of produce to the institution every day [2]. Work stayed part of life here. After the Second World War residents wove on looms in a "rug room" known for its products, and the programme grew into an occupational therapy department in 1953 [1].

title: A hospital for 'all creeds and color'
place: Esmeralda and Prospect Avenues, first home of St. Luke's Hospital
hook: St. Luke's Hospital started with room for twenty patients in a cluster of buildings on the west slope of Bernal Hill.
story: San Francisco's hospitals in 1871 mostly served their own: the French, the Germans, the Italians, the Catholics. That year the Protestant Episcopal Church opened St. Luke's in a group of buildings around Esmeralda and Prospect avenues, on the west side of Bernal Hill, with room for 20 patients [1]. From the start its founders planned for it to be "open to the sick of all nations and denominations… people of all creeds and color" [1]. The managers raised money across the city, and in 1874 they bought a two-acre lot at Valencia and Army (now Cesar Chavez) streets. The first permanent building went up there in 1874–75, and by 1878 D. O. Mills and James R. Keane had paid for two more buildings [1]. A later summary dates the move off the hill to the 1880s, so sources differ on exactly when the hilltop cottages closed [2]. St. Luke's joined California Pacific Medical Center in 2007 [2], and a new hospital has since risen on Valencia Street [1].

title: Bret Harte's hill of Sindbad
place: Lone Mountain's western (seaward) slope, above the old cemetery grounds
hook: To Bret Harte, the graveyard hill was Sindbad's magnetic mountain, pulling every ship in the bay onto its rocks sooner or later.
story: In the 1850s and 1860s San Franciscans buried their dead around Lone Mountain. The first cemetery here opened in 1854 as Lone Mountain Cemetery and was renamed Laurel Hill in 1867 [1]. Bret Harte gave the hill two poems in his 1871 collection East and West [2]. "Lone Mountain," subtitled "Cemetery, San Francisco," makes it the magnetic mountain of the Sindbad tales: "This is that hill of awe / That Persian Sindbad saw, / The mount magnetic." Scattered along its seaward base lie "the wrecks prophetic." Every ship on the bay, the argosies blown by every idle breeze and the little shallops "launched on yon shining bay," drifts toward it in the end. The poem closes with the poor porter of the tales: "Here come alike the same, / Hindbad and Sindbad" [2]. In "The Two Ships" the speaker stands on the summit: "As I stand by the cross on the lone mountain's crest, / Looking over the ultimate sea." One ship spreads its white wings and sails away; another lies at rest in the mountain's gloom, "the ship that is waiting for me" [2]. The cross he stood by was real. A Chronicle writer in 1918 recalled that it could be seen from every part of the burial grounds below [3].

title: Leveling Flyshacker Valley by Hand
place: The Panhandle (then 'The Avenue'), between Baker and Stanyan
hook: Before there was a park there was a sandy hollow, a 24-year-old surveyor, and a hundred men moving 273,000 cubic yards of sand.
story: In August 1870, visitors to the Masonic Cemetery could look downhill into sandy "Flyshacker Valley" and watch a survey party staking out San Francisco's new park [1]. The surveyor was William Hammond Hall, just 24, who had won the contract for $4,860 and delivered the survey and a preliminary plan in six months [2]. Work began at the city end. By May 1871 crews were leveling the thirty-acre strip then called The Avenue, today's Panhandle [1]. It looks like a billiard table now, but hills had to be cut and hollows filled: 273,000 cubic yards of sand, moved mostly by men, horses and hand tools, with a steam shovel for the big cuts [1]. More than a hundred men worked the valley at a time. Next came a seventy-foot macadam drive from Baker to Stanyan, the grand approach to the park proper, plus fences, because roaming dairy cows were devouring the new plantings [1]. Hall was named superintendent on August 14, 1871 [2][3], and he laid out curving drives deliberately, to slow fast buggy drivers and shelter visitors from the wind [3].
