title: The abolitionist poet in the Masonic ground
place: Former Masonic Cemetery, now USF's lower campus near Fulton Street (grave site not recorded)
hook: A barber whose anti-slavery poems ran in Frederick Douglass's paper came west, led California's Black Masons, and was buried in the cemetery that became USF.
story: James Monroe Whitfield was born in Exeter, New Hampshire, in 1822 and made his living as a barber [1][2]. Living in Buffalo, he wrote anti-slavery poems that appeared in the North Star, Frederick Douglass' Paper and The Liberator, and he worked with Martin Delany on proposals for Black Americans to emigrate [1]. His 1853 book was America and Other Poems [3]. After two years in Central America he settled in San Francisco around 1860 and kept cutting hair, with spells in Portland, in Idaho and in Nevada. In Elko in 1869 he and three other Black men sat on a jury, a first for that state [1]. From 1864 to 1869 he was Grand Master of the Prince Hall Masons in California [1]. On New Year's Day 1867 he read a poem at Platt's Hall for the fourth anniversary of the Emancipation Proclamation, printed at the Elevator office and dedicated to P. A. Bell. It opens with two ships nearing America "with different intent": one carried the Pilgrims, the other enslaved Africans [3]. He died of heart disease on April 23, 1871, aged 49, and was buried in San Francisco's Masonic Cemetery, ground that later became part of the University of San Francisco campus [1][2][4].

title: Pay the toll, then on to the races
place: Near where Market Street, Corbett Avenue and Portola Drive meet
hook: Portola Drive began life as a private macadam toll road carrying gamblers over the shoulder of Twin Peaks to the Ocean Avenue racetracks.
story:
Long before Portola Drive became a busy boulevard, the route around the southern flank of Twin Peaks was a private business. On an 1872 map it is the "Mission and Ocean Beach Macadamized Road", owned by an attorney named William Fitch. Fitch made it a toll road [1]. His toll gate stood near the junction of what are now Market Street, Grandview Avenue and Corbett Avenue. From there the road ran on to the Ingleside and Ocean House racetracks on Ocean Avenue, which gave it what Mae Silver calls a "racy past" [1].

The land around it passed to Adolph Sutro, who bought up much of old Rancho San Miguel. Around the turn of the century the road took the name Corbett Road [1]. Farmers hauled milk and vegetables along it, and lumber came down from Sutro's forest [1]. A city photograph from May 10, 1910, labels it "Corbett Road (now Portola Drive)" near Twin Peaks Boulevard [2]. In 1912 the Residential Development Company, which had taken over Sutro's land, deeded the road to the city. A 1914 ordinance created Portola Drive [1]. In 1929 the road was widened east from Twin Peaks Boulevard, making it easy to drive to the new homes going up west of the Peaks [3].

title: The City Hall That Took a Quarter-Century
place: Site of the 1870s-1906 City Hall (today's Main Library, 100 Larkin St)
hook: Promised in five or six years for $1.5 million, San Francisco's City Hall took decades, cost millions and still smelled.
story: In 1870 the city graded the old Yerba Buena Cemetery square, bounded by Market, Larkin and McAllister streets, for what its promoters meant to be the handsomest municipal building in the United States [1][2]. The plans came from Augustus Laver, known for his work on the New York capitol at Albany. The estimate was about a million and a half dollars and five or six years [2]. On February 22, 1872, Masonic Grand Master Leonidas E. Pratt dedicated the cornerstone with a ceremonial trowel [3]. Then things went wrong. To save money, the commission sold the lots fronting Market Street, leaving the hall on a back street. It swapped Laver's clock tower for a dome and cut his mansard roof, leaving what historian John P. Young called 'a squatty appearance' [2]. Voters dreaded debt, so the hall was paid for piecemeal out of taxes; Young wrote that the city 'chose to have their money wasted rather than stolen' [2]. It went through seven chief architects and cost about six million dollars. Sources give its completion as 1895 or 1897 [1][3]. Occupants complained of floors that did not line up, smoky rooms and a constant stink [3]. The 1906 earthquake wrecked it [3].

title: The Emperor Orders a Bridge via Goat Island
place: Yerba Buena Tunnel, Bay Bridge crossing of the island
hook: In 1872 a penniless self-proclaimed emperor decreed a bridge from Oakland to Goat Island. Sixty-four years later, the Bay Bridge took his route.
story:
Joshua Norton was a failed rice speculator who had declared himself Norton I, Emperor of the United States. On 23 March 1872 his proclamation in the Pacific Appeal ordered "that a suspension bridge be built from Oakland Point to Goat Island, and thence to Telegraph Hill; provided such bridge can be built without injury to the navigable waters of the Bay" [1]. That September, annoyed that nothing had happened, he ordered a survey to see whether a bridge or a tunnel would be better. According to the Museum of the City of San Francisco's chronology, he also ordered the arrest of the Board of Supervisors [1][2].

City Guides notes that the bridge was "somewhat delayed" [3]. When the San Francisco-Oakland Bay Bridge finally opened in 1936, it crossed the bay by way of Goat Island, as Norton had specified, boring straight through its rocky middle [3][4]. That tunnel has never been officially named. For its 90th anniversary in 2026, the Emperor Norton Trust and State Senator Scott Wiener proposed Senate Concurrent Resolution 193 to call it the Emperor Norton Tunnel [4].

title: The Park's First Family, Beside a Dynamite Works
place: Site of the Quigley house, triangle west of Kezar Stadium near Lincoln Way
hook: The park's first laborer raised his family in a house with no plumbing, 250 yards from a factory where nitroglycerin kept exploding.
story: Patrick Quigley was born in County Roscommon in 1829, fled the Irish famine, mined gold in Mariposa County and ran the Oak Springs House there. In May 1872 he became Golden Gate Park's first officially appointed laborer, a foreman at $80 a month [1]. The work site was far from town, so the Quigleys got a house on a two-acre triangle west of today's Kezar Stadium, beside an old toll road. It had no indoor plumbing, and water came from a well [1]. Their nearest neighbor, 250 yards south, was the California Powder Works. On June 21, 1872, 1,500 pounds of nitroglycerin exploded there, leaving a crater fifty feet across. More blasts followed in December 1872 and June 1877 [1]. Five Quigley children were born in the park, and three of them died in infancy [1]. Park jobs were precarious too. Hall resigned in 1876 after his salary was cut in half [2], and in 1882 commissioners debated firing Quigley. Hall had praised him as "the oldest employee on the force." Quigley kept working for forty years and died in his park home in November 1912 [1].

title: The Semi-Annual Explosion
place: Likely site of the California Powder Works, near 2nd Ave & Irving St
hook: Before houses, the Inner Sunset's sand hills made nitroglycerin. The factory blew up so often that the Chronicle joked about its 'semi-annual explosion.'
story: In the 1870s the empty dunes south of the young Golden Gate Park looked like the perfect place to make dynamite: nobody lived there. The California Powder Works took a 120-acre parcel called the Byfield Tract. No map shows exactly where the works stood, but the area around today's 2nd Avenue and Irving Street is the likeliest site [1]. On June 21, 1872, at 6:15 p.m., between 1,500 and 2,000 pounds of glycerin went up, rattling windows across the city and leaving a crater 12 feet deep and 50 feet wide. The workers had gone home an hour earlier [1]. Six months later, on December 21, came what the Chronicle called 'the semi-annual explosion.' Two men were killed, and one body was found 600 feet away. Laguna Honda School on 7th Avenue, opened that fall with 38 pupils, lost windows and plaster, but it was closed for Christmas [1]. The last blast, on the hottest day of 1877, wrecked nearby saloons and threw a butcher, Herman Gertsheim, off his wagon and astride a fence. The powder makers soon moved to the East Bay, where one company town became Hercules [1][2].

title: The dairyman's cottage that outlasted everything
place: 657 Chenery Street (Tietz house)
hook: Set back from Chenery Street as if it predates the street itself, a tiny gabled cottage built by a dairyman in 1872 is Glen Park's oldest known building.
story:
Walk down Chenery Street past Bird & Beckett and you might miss the little gable-roofed cottage at number 657. It sits about twenty feet back from the sidewalk. Architectural historian Christopher VerPlanck found that it was built in 1872 by a dairyman named William Tietz, which makes it the oldest known residence in Glen Park [1]. Back then there were no graded roads here, and many early farmhouses didn't line up with the streets that were laid out later, in the 1890s. That may explain the odd setback [1].

The name turns up again in a photograph in the San Francisco Public Library, reproduced on FoundSF. It shows Elise Beneke Tietz with a cow in Glen Canyon around 1909 [2]. The caption doesn't say how she was related to William, but it shows that cows were still grazing the canyon decades after he built his house.

In 2025 the city's SF Survey flagged the house as a potential historic resource. It called the building a Folk Victorian structure and Glen Park's oldest. The survey also found the whole Glen Park Center commercial district eligible as a historic district [3]. The farmhouse is now surrounded by the village that grew up around it.

title: A Spilled Feed Bag Tames the Dunes
place: West end of the park near Ocean Beach
hook: Newspapers called it a white elephant where grass needed four posts to stop it blowing away. Then some spilled horse feed sprouted.
story: In the 1870s most people thought the park's western two-thirds was hopeless. In 1873 the Santa Rosa Press-Democrat called it "a dreary waste of shifting sand hills where a blade of grass cannot be raised without four posts to keep it from blowing away" [2]. That year William Hammond Hall began reclaiming the sand at the west end [3]. Lupine alone could not root fast enough to hold the blowing sand near the beach. Then, as park historian Christopher Pollock tells it, barley spilled from a horse's feed bag and sprouted. Hall broadcast barley across the dunes, but it lived only a couple of months [1]. What worked was sea bent grass mixed with yellow lupine, covered with topsoil, manure and organic matter [1]. By 1873 the drifting sand at the beach had been tamed and backed by a fence of boards and posts woven with brush, about 100 feet from the shore [1]. Fertilizer turned political. After the park barred heavy wagons in 1873, the Street Department retaliated by withholding its horse-manure sweepings, and the feud lasted until the mid-1890s [2].

title: Copper rivets on Battery Street
place: Levi Strauss & Co., 14–16 Battery Street
hook: A Reno tailor couldn't afford a patent, so he wrote to his cloth supplier on Battery Street. Their 1873 partnership gave the world blue jeans.
story: Levi Strauss, born Loeb Strauss in Bavaria in 1829, reached San Francisco in 1853 to open a West Coast branch of his brothers' New York dry goods firm [1][2]. By 1866 his wholesale house filled 14–16 Battery Street [1]. One of his customers was Jacob Davis, a Latvian-Jewish tailor in Reno who bought denim by the bolt [2]. When a customer kept tearing his work pants, Davis reinforced the pocket corners and fly with copper rivets. He couldn't afford the patent, so in 1872 he wrote to Strauss proposing they share it [1][2]. On May 20, 1873, the two received U.S. patent 139,121 [2]. Demand for the riveted 'waist overalls' was enormous [1]. The patent expired in 1890, the year the company began numbering its lots and gave the famous overalls the number 501; nobody knows why, because the firm's records burned in 1906 [2]. Strauss insisted employees call him Levi. He was a charter member of the Board of Trade, a member of Temple Emanu-El, and in 1897 he funded 28 scholarships at UC Berkeley [1].

title: Four A.M. on Clay Street
place: Clay & Kearny, eastern terminus of the Clay Street Hill Railroad
hook: Horses slipping to their deaths on a wet hill gave Andrew Hallidie an idea that would travel from Edinburgh to Melbourne.
story: Andrew Smith Hallidie, whose father held a British patent for wire rope, said his idea came in 1869 after watching horses struggle to haul a horsecar up wet cobblestones on Jackson Street; as the story goes, they slipped and were dragged to their deaths [1]. His Clay Street Hill Railroad began building in May 1873 and had to run by August 1 under its franchise [1]. Just when it first ran is disputed: the Cable Car Museum says Hallidie tested the car at 4 a.m. on August 2, a day late, while the city's landmark report gives August 1 [1][3]. Wikipedia repeats a tale that the hired gripman looked down from Jones Street and refused, so Hallidie took the grip himself [2]. Regular service began on September 1, 1873, climbing 348 feet in six blocks from Kearny Street [1][2]. Within a year it carried 3,000 passengers a day [2], and by the 1880s cable lines ran in cities from Edinburgh to Melbourne [3]. The marker for the line's eastern terminus stands in Portsmouth Square [2].

title: Gold fever on Bernal Hill
place: Bernal Hill summit
hook: "Gold! Gold! Gold!" shouted a German well-digger in 1873. Within a day hundreds were climbing Bernal Hill to see.
story:
In late summer 1873, Henry Housler was digging a well on Bernal Heights. At about fifteen feet down, he believed, he saw the colour of gold. According to the report the Chronicle printed on 2 September, he swore his wife and daughter to secrecy for two weeks. When the news got out, a reporter hurried out and found neighbours already planning to stake claims across the entire Heights. Hundreds of people came that day to look at the samples [1].

The rock told a different story. Claims were marked out and ledges cut open, but the samples turned out to be copper and iron sulphides, with "no gold in the rock." SFGATE's review of the archives says people rushed to stake claims on land that was already occupied, which was illegal. A geological study found the ore was the same stone that makes up much of the peninsula. Scientists suspected someone had planted a little gold to cheat buyers, and land prices rose for a while [1].

The fever came back. In May 1876 Victor Ressayre filed notice of a gold-quartz ledge, which he called the "Eureka Lode and Paris Milling and Mining Company" [1]. Local lore still tells of an 1876 mini gold rush set off by con artists salting the hilltop [2].

title: Moving day for 300 orphans
place: Mount St. Joseph orphanage hilltop, Silver Terrace (near Revere Ave and Quint St)
hook: In one day in 1873, about 300 children moved from downtown to a hilltop orphanage in the countryside, in borrowed carriages and carts.
story: The Daughters of Charity reached San Francisco in 1852 and started caring for orphans in an 'old brown house' at Market and Montgomery streets [1]. In 1858 the sisters incorporated as the Roman Catholic Orphan Asylum, perhaps the first group of women in California to form a corporation, so their property could not be taken over by the Church [1]. As downtown grew around them, they bought land in rural South San Francisco. It was 52 acres, according to the district's historic context statement [2]. They opened an infant asylum there first, then began a large orphanage in 1869 [1][2]. In 1873 about 300 orphans moved out in a single day. A streetcar company carried children and sisters door to door, and ordinary San Franciscans lent carriages and carts for the furniture [1]. The Market Street lot where they had lived later became the site of the Palace Hotel [1]. The big Second Empire-style building on the summit took its popular name from the hill, Mt. St. Joseph, and in 1888 a Call reporter admired the orphanage crowning it [2]. It survived the 1906 earthquake but burned in 1910 [1][2].

title: Old Thad and the Great Race
place: Southern edge of the Ocean Course racetrack site, along Eucalyptus Drive
hook: Where quiet Lakeshore streets now curve, a California horse ran sixteen miles against Eastern rivals while the whole city bet on him.
story: The Ocean Course, on 100 acres leased from the Green family, opened on 23 May 1865 before 8,000 fans, then a record crowd for California [1]. Mark Twain tried to go, but could only rent "part of a horse" for $240, and declined [2]. Its last hurrah came on 15 November 1873: the "Great Race" between California-raised Thad Stevens and Eastern horses, for $20,000 in gold [3]. The Chronicle estimated $150,000 had been bet in the week before [3]. Coachmen charged up to $40 for a one-way ride along the single dirt road [3]. The race was four heats of four miles each. Joe Daniels of Michigan took the first heat, True Blue the second, and in the third True Blue broke a fetlock [3]. "Old Thad" won the deciding heat by ten lengths [1]. Men threw their hats in the air and ladies waved handkerchiefs [1]. Accounts of the crowd vary, from about 20,000 to a remembered 40,000 [2][3]. The trip home, the Chronicle noted, produced many drunken smash-ups [3]. The track closed soon after, and the Gellert brothers' Lakeshore Park homes now cover it [3].

title: Rowers at the foot of Third Street
place: Third and Berry streets, site of the 1884 South End clubhouse
hook: San Francisco's famous Aquatic Park swimmers began here, as a working men's rowing club on Mission Bay.
story: The South End Boat Club was founded in 1873 at the end of Third Street. It was only the third rowing club in San Francisco, and it existed to beat the others [1]. In the 1880s, at the height of the rowing craze, thousands of spectators lined the shore to watch races, betting large sums, and the best oarsmen became celebrities. The clubs were mostly made up of working men. Rowing was second only to horse racing in popularity and even outdrew baseball [1]. In 1884 the club put up a clubhouse at Third and Berry streets, designed by Adolph C. Lutgens for $2,000. Boats were stored downstairs, and the ground floor doubled as a dance hall. A panorama of Channel Street from about 1885 shows its peaked roof among the lumber wharves [1][2]. Renamed the South End Rowing Club in 1891, it added handball, boxing and Ladies' Days. Industry kept pushing it out. A new boathouse at the foot of Sixteenth Street followed in 1903, and in 1908 it was floated by barge to Black Point Cove. Its descendant still swims at Aquatic Park [1][3].

title: The Shortest Tender Run on the Coast
place: 12th District Lighthouse Depot (now Coast Guard Base), east of the light
hook: From this little wharf, steamers carried paychecks, mail and a dreaded inspector to every lighthouse on the Pacific coast.
story:
In 1873 the Lighthouse Service moved its Pacific district depot from Mare Island to Yerba Buena's southeast shore [1][2]. It grew into storehouses, a paint shop, a machine shop, a dock and two houses for the men who worked there. Every one of the district's 28 lighthouses was supplied through here, and buoys were hauled in to be refurbished and stacked on the wharf [3]. Tenders such as the Shubrick, Manzanita and Madrono steamed out to remote stations with paychecks, mail and food. They also brought the notoriously strict inspector, which made the tender's arrival a mixed blessing for keepers [1].

The depot's own lighthouse got what keepers called "the shortest tender run": a trip of a couple of hundred yards around the point. A steam winch hoisted up the coal, and food was carried up the "goat trail" [1]. Island life had its gentler days too. On 21 August 1892, the San Francisco Call reported "the first wedding in Goat Island's history" [4]. Charles McCarthy, keeper of the Oakland mole light, married Mrs. Jennie Lewis at the home of Captain Linne, the Goat Island station-keeper [4]. The depot survives today as the Coast Guard base [2].

title: The city wanted a park; it got guns
place: Battery East, bluff above Fort Point
hook: In 1870 San Franciscans lobbied Congress to hand the Presidio over for parks and homes. The Army answered by digging giant earthen gun pits on the bluffs.
story: The Civil War showed that brick forts like Fort Point could be battered to pieces by modern guns, so after the war the Army switched to low batteries built of packed earth [1]. In 1870 San Franciscans started a campaign to have the Presidio given to the city for parks, homes and businesses, and California's senators introduced bills to do it [2]. A board of Army engineers replied that large earthen batteries were already planned for the ocean and bay sides of the reservation, and that these would need land behind them for defence against an attack overland. The transfer idea died [2]. Work began on the bluffs behind Fort Point in 1872. By 1873 West Battery was finished and armed with twelve 15-inch Rodman cannon. Battery East was started the same year, joined to its twin by a covered path [1]. In 1898, during the Spanish-American War, 8-inch rifled guns were mounted at Battery East [1]. West Battery was mostly destroyed when newer concrete batteries went up in the 1890s. Battery East's earthworks and brick-lined powder magazines survive, looking out on one of the best views in the city [1].

title: The park with too many birthdays
place: Holly Park, Holly Park Circle
hook: Was Holly Park a millionaire's gift, a court decision or a Victorian improvement project? Its histories don't agree.
story:
Holly Park is a round hilltop park on the Bernal slope, and one of the oldest parks in the city. Its early history is a tangle. A San Francisco Parks Alliance history says silver king James Fair bought the 7.5-acre parcel from the Bernal rancho in 1862 and gave it to the city [1]. Molly Martin's essay repeats the 1862 Fair story [4]. Yet the same Parks Alliance account also has the circle road opening in 1874 and the district not being developed until 1887 [1].

The newspapers tell another version. Searching the Chronicle archive, SFGATE found the moment in 1873 when a court ruled that Holly Park was public ground [2]. An 1875 photograph shows only a fenced circle on open grassland, with the new College Hill Reservoir, built in 1870, nearby on the slope [3][4]. Bernalwood dates the park "we know and love" to the 1890s [3]. The Parks Alliance says the area had about 200 houses by 1889, and that in April 1929 the Playground Commission asked for the shrubs to be cleared for basketball and tennis courts [1]. The name may come from the hollyleaf (Islais) cherry that once grew along nearby Islais Creek [4].

title: Beer Town on the edge of the park
place: Fulton Street at 9th Avenue (site of the Jockey Club beer garden, NE corner)
hook: For forty years, five blocks of Fulton Street facing Golden Gate Park were 'Beer Town'. In 1894 seven saloons stood side by side on half a block.
story: In 1874 James Dickey, a horseman who called himself 'Colonel' without any military rank, opened a roadhouse at 'D' Street (today's Fulton) and Sixth Avenue for the crowd at the Bay District Race Track. His cook, Wong, was famous for biscuits, bacon and eggs [1]. Cable and steam lines soon ended their runs nearby. In October 1893 the Examiner complained that the park was getting 'an unsavory frame around it' [1]. Nobody listened. When the Midwinter Fair opened in the park in 1894, the saloons multiplied, and the city directory lists seven of them packed into half a block of Seventh Avenue [1]. The Richmond's improvement clubs wanted a quiet district of homes, and they never liked the strip. In September 1906 the Call printed the names and addresses of women in three 'disreputable houses' on Fulton, and the Richmond Banner cheered the campaign [1]. Then a long streetcar strike in 1907 kept visitors away and emptied the strip [1]. The last piece of it was the old Jockey Club, moved from the racetrack to the northeast corner of Ninth and Fulton. It served as a beer garden for more than twenty years and was pulled down in 1914 [1]. Today no bars or restaurants are allowed along the park side of Fulton [1][2].

title: Named for the teacher who won equal pay
place: Former Clement / Kate Kennedy School, Noe and 30th streets
hook: An Irish famine refugee found she earned $22.50 a month less than the men. She changed California law, sued the school board and won. A school here took her name.
story:
Neighbours researching Upper Noe history in 1959 recorded that one of the area's first schools, a small wooden building called the Clement School at Noe and 30th streets, had become the Kate Kennedy School [3]. Kate Kennedy was born in Ireland in 1827 and left during the potato famine. She arrived in San Francisco in 1856 [1][2] and was hired as a teacher in 1858 [2]. As principal of the North Cosmopolitan Grammar School she was paid at the lower primary-school rate: $180 a month instead of $202.50, a gap of $22.50 [2]. She took on the Board of Education. Her test case produced a state law requiring equal pay for women teachers holding the same certificates as men, which FoundSF dates to 1874 [1][2]. FoundSF's historian calls her the first woman to receive equal pay for equal work under law [2].

In 1886 she ran for state superintendent of schools on the Labor ticket, at a time when women couldn't vote. The board then transferred her to a remote two-teacher school, nearly halving her pay, and dismissed her without a hearing. She sued, won at the California Supreme Court in 1890 and collected $5,700.75 in back pay. The ruling helped establish teacher tenure [1][2].

title: The fortress that held gold
place: Old United States Mint, 88 Fifth Street at Mission
hook: The 'Granite Lady' at Fifth and Mission is mostly sandstone, and its foundations were designed to stop robbers tunnelling into the vaults.
story: The first San Francisco mint, which opened on Commercial Street in 1854, was soon outgrown [1]. By 1869 the Treasury had bought a new site at Fifth and Mission. Its architect, Alfred B. Mullett, designed a sober Greek Revival building with a pedimented portico, set around an enclosed central courtyard [1][2]. Three schooners carried sandstone from Newcastle Island in British Columbia for the upper walls and the six great portico columns. Rocklin granite was used for the basement [1]. The cornerstone was laid on May 26, 1870, and the building was finished in 1874 at a cost of about $2 million [1][2]. Its concrete and granite foundation was designed to stop anyone tunnelling into the vaults [2]. The nickname "Granite Lady" is a misnomer, since most of the building is sandstone, and the name only caught on as a marketing term in the 1970s [2]. FoundSF records that Ambrose Bierce, back from England in 1875 and unable to live on freelance writing, took a job at the Mint [3]. The building made coins here until 1937 [1].

title: The racetrack under the Avenues
place: Bay District Racing Track site, 3rd Ave between Anza & Balboa
hook: Before the flats and bay windows, a one-mile racetrack filled these blocks. It once offered the biggest purse in America, and neighbours fought it for twenty years.
story: In August 1873 a group of the city's richest men leased 60 acres between First Avenue (today's Arguello), Fulton Street, Fifth Avenue and Point Lobos Road (today's Geary) for a one-mile track. The Bay District Racing Track opened in September 1874. On November 14 it ran a 'Great Race' with a $25,000 purse, the largest yet offered in America. The local favourite, 'Old Thad', lost to the Eastern mare Katie Pease, and the Chronicle's headline read 'THAD'S WATERLOO' [1]. Money trouble after the silver crash left the track without racing for three years. In 1890 Thomas Williams, then 30, brought it back with thoroughbreds and, from 1893, racing five days a week for months on end [1]. By then houses had crept up to its fence. Residents petitioned to reopen the streets the track had closed, and they complained about 'Beer Town', the saloons facing it on Fulton Street and Fifth Avenue [1]. The track closed on May 27, 1896. Two years later its empty ground became an army camp, and from 1902 builder Fernando Nelson covered it with homes [2].

title: A child star's gift to Market Street
place: Lotta's Fountain, Market, Geary and Kearny streets
hook: Lotta Crabtree started out dancing for miners at eight. In 1875 California's favourite entertainer gave the city a cast-iron drinking fountain.
story: Lotta Crabtree arrived in San Francisco in 1853, aged six, when women and children were still rare in the city [2]. Coached as a child by the notorious dancer Lola Montez, she began dancing for miners at Rabbit Creek at eight, then toured saloons and gambling halls across Northern California with her mother [2]. Her song, dance and comedy made her California's favourite entertainer and eventually very rich; she never married and left a fortune of four million dollars [2]. In 1875 she gave the city a cast-iron drinking fountain, dedicated on September 9 at the meeting of Market, Kearny and Geary [1]. Not everyone loved it: in 1947 Samuel Dickson called it 'the ugliest monument in the city' [2]. After 1906 it became a meeting point for survivors, and on Christmas Eve 1910 the soprano Luisa Tetrazzini sang there to a vast crowd [1][2]. A bronze column was added in 1916, and the 1999 restoration shortened the fountain back to its 1875 look and painted it gold-brown [1].

title: Cows, wells and a ranch on the hill
place: Charles Dow house, 1745 20th Street
hook: Victorian Potrero Hill had dairy herds, a 300-foot well and a ranch whose hired hands looked after cattle from the hilltop down to Army Street.
story: Well into the Victorian era, Potrero Hill was farmland. In 1875 a farmer named Charles Dow built a house at what is now 20th and Wisconsin streets. A photograph from that year looks from the spot out across the open water of Mission Bay toward Yerba Buena Island [1]. It is one of the oldest buildings on the hill and still stands at 1745 20th Street. Palms now hide it, and designer Larry Masnada remade it in the 1980s [1][2]. A few blocks west, an Englishman named Charlie Hawe ran a dairy from a farmhouse built in 1889 on the northwest corner of Connecticut and 20th. Next to it was a well 300 feet deep. A large cattle barn stood across 20th Street, and water troughs sat on the northeast corner [3]. Around 1900 a dapper man with a goatee, known only as Ramond, lived in a big white house at Wisconsin and 20th. Beside it was a row of identical cottages for the hired hands who looked after cattle grazing from the hilltop down toward Army Street. People called it Ramond's and Hawe's Ranch [3]. Ramond's daughter-in-law sold the house around 1925. The deep well had to be filled in before an apartment building could go up [3].

title: The Little Wooden Light Midway Across
place: Yerba Buena Lighthouse, southeast point
hook: California's only freestanding wooden lighthouse tower got a second-hand lens from Oregon. The keeper's daughters sailed to school.
story:
No island in the bay had more traffic passing it than Yerba Buena. Ferries crossed between San Francisco and the railroad terminus at Oakland, carrying millions of passengers a year [1]. A fog bell borrowed from Point Conception came first, struck by clockwork [1][2]. Then, on 1 October 1875, a steam whistle and a light went into service in a short octagonal tower with 1875 over its door [2]. The dates are muddled: the National Register form says the tower was finished in 1873 but had to wait for its lens [1].

That lens was second-hand, a fifth-order Fresnel from the closed Yaquina Bay Lighthouse in Oregon [1][2]. The Navy's historians called it the weakest lighthouse the government ran, visible for 12 miles [3]. The station is also unusual: it is the only freestanding wooden lighthouse tower in California, in ornate Eastlake style, with the keepers' Gothic house 80 yards uphill [1]. The cliff below was painted white to help mark the island [2]. With no school on the island, the keeper's three daughters sailed their own sloop across the bay to classes in San Francisco every day [3].

title: The Spanish Church and Little Mexico's ruins
place: Our Lady of Guadalupe Church, 906 Broadway
hook: Consuls from seven countries helped build the 'mother church' of Spanish-speaking San Francisco. After 1906, families made tortillas inside its burned walls.
story: In the early 1870s Spanish-speaking businessmen, most of them Mexican, began raising money for a church of their own. Consuls from Chile, Peru, Nicaragua, Spain, Costa Rica, Colombia and Bolivia joined in, and a Basque hotel owner, Juan Miguel Aguirre, gave a large gift [1]. On August 15, 1875 the cornerstone was laid after a procession that included the Mexican militia clubs the Juarez Guards and Laredo Guards [1]. For five years only the basement stood. The wooden church was dedicated in March 1880, and newspapers called it the "Spanish Church" [1]. The 1906 fire left only its masonry walls. Mexican families who had lost their homes moved inside them. In January 1907 the Sunday Call ran a story headlined "Little Mexico in the Ruins of a Church," with photographs of residents making tortillas, cooking on outdoor stoves and hanging out laundry [1]. The church was rebuilt in 1912 by Shea and Lofquist, probably the first church in San Francisco made of reinforced concrete [2]. Through the rebuilding, at least a third of the city's Mexicans lived nearby, in what came to be called "Barrio Guadalupe." From 1924, parishioners serenaded the Virgin with Las Mañanitas, the Mexican birthday song, every December 12 [1].

title: The bank run that ended in the bay
place: Bank of California, California and Sansome streets
hook: At 2:35 on an August afternoon in 1875 the West's grandest bank ran out of money. The next day its founder went for a swim.
story: William Ralston opened the Bank of California on July 4, 1864, in a building of Angel Island stone at California and Sansome, with Darius Ogden Mills as president and himself as cashier [1]. Fed by Comstock silver, Ralston's 'Bank Crowd' became the richest capitalists in the West, and Montgomery Street became the Wall Street of the West [2]. Ralston poured money into mills, water rights, real estate and the vast Palace Hotel, and he blurred the line between the bank's money and his own [2]. On August 26, 1875, rumours set off a run. At 2:35 p.m., its vaults empty, the bank shut its doors [2]. The next day the directors found he owed the bank nearly five million dollars, close to its whole capital. They forced his resignation and had him sign his assets over to William Sharon [2]. Ralston left for his daily swim in the bay and drowned [1][2]. Fifty thousand people followed his funeral. Whether his death was an accident is still argued; the historian H.H. Bancroft scrawled in a margin that it was suicide [2]. The reorganised bank reopened on October 2, 1875 [2].

title: The banker's last swim
place: Neptune Bath-house site, foot of Larkin St at Black Point Cove
hook: The day after his Bank of California collapsed, San Francisco's greatest financier went for his usual dip in the bay off Larkin Street, and never came out alive.
story: In the 1870s Black Point Cove, now Aquatic Park, was a working-class bathing beach squeezed between a woolen mill and a lead smelter. The first formal bathhouse, Joseph Dunkley's 'Sea Baths', later known as the Neptune Bath-house, was a jumble of frame shacks at the foot of a sand cliff, reached by stairs from Beach Street. Swimmers took their towels and suits from a line strung along a rickety wharf [1]. The Neptune's most famous regular was William Chapman Ralston, founder of the Bank of California and the builder behind the Palace Hotel [2]. In August 1875 his financial empire collapsed and the bank closed its doors. On August 27 he went for his daily swim off the end of Larkin Street, in the shadow of the Selby smelter [3]. He was pulled from the water dead [1]. A coroner's jury ruled that he had overexerted himself and died of a pulmonary embolism, but many at the time believed he had chosen his favourite pastime as a way to die. Accounts still differ between a stroke and suicide [1][2]. About 50,000 people are said to have watched his funeral procession [2].

title: The designer who disowned his houses
place: 151 and 168 Delmar Street
hook: Two Delmar Street houses wear a style named after an English tastemaker, who called what Americans did with his ideas "extravagant and bizarre".
story: Walk down one block of Delmar Street and you pass fifty years of San Francisco house fashion, all in wood [1]. The oldest style here is Eastlake, seen at 151 and 168 Delmar. It was most popular from about 1875 to 1890. Builders took the tall lines, flat fronts and cornices of the earlier Italianates and the square bays and jigsaw trim of the Sticks, then added showier carved panels and mouldings made possible by new machinery [1]. The name came from English designer Charles Eastlake, whose book Hints on Household Taste inspired it. He was not pleased. "I feel greatly flattered by the popularity which my books have attained in America," he wrote, "but I regret that their author's name should be associated there with a taste in architecture and industrial arts with which I have no real sympathy and which by all accounts seems to be extravagant and bizarre" [1]. American builders, especially in California, kept going anyway, trading flat-cut gingerbread for lathe-turned spindles. The style later blended with Italianate and Second Empire into what became known as the "San Francisco Style" [2]. The Queen Annes further down the block came next, from about 1890 [1].

title: Trotters Racing Down Point Lobos Road
place: Geary Blvd (old Point Lobos Road) west of 23rd Ave
hook: Before houses, today's Geary Boulevard was a toll road through sand, with a half-mile racetrack for San Francisco's fastest horses laid along it.
story: Geary Boulevard began life as the Point Lobos Road, a private toll road opened in the early 1860s that was, for years, the fashionable drive out of the city [1]. Drivers paid at a toll house near today's Masonic Avenue, received a ticket and dropped it at a second gate before the road ran downhill to the Cliff House [1]. Around 1875 ('about twenty years ago', wrote the San Francisco Call in 1895), the road's operators tried to make the trip more exciting by building a straightaway half-mile speed track on the north side of the road, starting at the line of 23rd Avenue [1]. Some of the best horses of the day, including Norfolk and Lodi, were run there. Nearby, horseman Jim Eoff opened an Agricultural Park race track, which did not succeed [1]. The Western Neighborhoods Project describes the area of that era as foggy sand and scrub with roadhouses, racetracks and dairymen [2]. As the city crept west, the toll gates came down, streetcars replaced omnibuses, and in 1895 the dissolved road company auctioned its last 160 Richmond District lots [1].

title: Where the bay's hay boats were born
place: Shipwright's Cottage, 900 Innes Ave
hook: Immigrant shipwrights on India Basin built the flat-bottomed scows that carried Northern California's hay. The last surviving one was built in a family's front yard.
story: Before trucks, much of Northern California's cargo moved by water in scow schooners, boxy shallow-draft boats that could reach farms up the sloughs of the Delta [1]. As the district's historic context statement puts it, the nineteenth century moved on hay the way the twentieth moved on gasoline [1]. Many of the scows were built on India Basin. Johnson J. Dircks, a Dutch-born builder, set up a yard at today's Evans Avenue and Lane Street in 1868. William Stone moved to Innes Avenue in 1871, and Dircks set up next door in 1876 [1]. The builders were mostly German, Danish, English and Dutch, and they lived among their boat sheds and taught the trade to their sons [1]. The Italianate cottage at 900 Innes, built around 1875, was the Dircks family home and is now a city landmark [1][3][4]. Fred Siemer, who had come from Germany in 1865, built a scow named Adelia after his daughter. In 1891 he built a second, in his son-in-law James Peterson's front yard, and named it Alma after Peterson's daughter [2]. Alma is the last of about 400 bay scows, preserved by the Maritime Park and still sailing [2]. FoundSF credits the 900 Innes yard with building her [4].

title: A wedding gift paid for in sealskins
place: Lilienthal-Pratt House, 1818-1824 California St
hook: This Italianate mansion was a father's wedding present. The money behind it came from fur seals on remote Alaskan islands.
story:
In 1876 Louis Sloss built this Italianate house, with Stick-style touches, as a wedding present for his daughter Estelle and her husband, Ernest L. Lilienthal [1]. The Slosses lived nearby, and their friends the Wormsers built the house next door [1].

Sloss had started out dealing in mining stocks, and he saw an opportunity in Alaska. After the United States bought the territory from Russia in 1867, he and his partners bought out the old Russian-American Company, and in 1868 they reorganised it as the Alaska Commercial Company [2]. The firm won a federal concession to harvest seal skins on two Alaskan islands, and the landmark report says that concession "netted him a large fortune" [1]. So one of Pacific Heights' finest Victorians was built on the fur trade of the far north.

In 1907 the Lilienthals sold the house to Orville C. Pratt Jr., whose family ran a large ranch near Chico. His widow Emily lived here until 1953. In 1955 the Bransten family bought it, which kept together a row of four Victorian mansions and their gardens [1].

title: Jack London is born near Third and Brannan
place: Jack London birthplace plaque, 601 Third Street at Brannan
hook: The author of The Call of the Wild was born South of Market to a spiritualist music teacher. A plaque on a bank now marks the spot.
story: John Griffith Chaney, later Jack London, was born near Third and Brannan streets on January 12, 1876 [1]. His mother, Flora Wellman, worked in San Francisco as a music teacher and spiritualist. Biographers believe his father was the astrologer William Chaney. According to Flora's account in the Chronicle of June 4, 1875, Chaney demanded that she have an abortion. When she refused he disowned the child, and she shot herself but survived [1]. After the birth she sent the baby to be nursed by a neighbor, Virginia "Jennie" Prentiss, who had been born into slavery. London later called her his main source of love as a child [1]. Late in 1876 Flora married John London, a partly disabled Civil War veteran [1]. The family kept moving in search of cheaper rent. They lived in Bernal Heights, then in a two-story house at 920 Natoma Street, then in a flat on Folsom Street, before crossing the bay to Oakland [2]. The birthplace house burned in 1906, and the California Historical Society placed a plaque at the site in 1953 [1]. It reads: "To mark the birthplace of the noted author, Jack London, January 12, 1876" [2].

title: Lumber, fine groceries and a 1957 rescue
place: Talbot-Dutton House, 1782 Pacific Avenue (Landmark No. 57)
hook: A lumberman's family built it, a fine-foods grocer enlarged it, and by the Second World War it was flats. Two men rescued it with the help of old family photographs.
story:
The Talbot-Dutton House looks like a two-story Italianate townhouse from Pacific Avenue. Because of the slope, though, it has three stories at the back. Its elaborate portico shelters an entry floored with marble mosaic [1]. It was built in 1876 [1].

Its first family was in the lumber business. The landmark resolution says that William Chaloner Talbot sailed to California in 1850 aboard the schooner Oriental with a cargo of lumber. He formed Pope and Talbot with his brother-in-law Andrew J. Pope [1]. Another history of the firm names Andrew Jackson Pope and Frederic Talbot, both from East Machias, Maine, as its founders in 1849, and says their Port Gamble sawmill ran for 142 years [2]. Henry Dutton married Mary Talbot in 1869, and the couple lived here until they died [1].

In 1905 Jacob Goldberg, a founder of the fine-foods firm Goldberg-Bowen, bought the house and enlarged it. By the Second World War it had been cut up into apartments [1]. In 1957 Paul D. Hardman and A. Warren Kopp bought it. Using early photographs lent by the original family, they rebuilt the portico and found period mantels and light fixtures [1].

title: Pop Blanken's resort for boxers
place: Site of the Six Mile House, Bayshore Boulevard between Visitacion and Sunnydale avenues
hook: Famous prizefighters trained at a country roadhouse on the San Bruno Road. The house served clam chowder, shooting and bowling.
story: Henry 'Pop' Blanken's Six Mile House took up most of the block of today's Bayshore Boulevard between Visitacion and Sunnydale avenues [1]. It had shade trees, gardens, bowling alleys, trap shooting and training rooms for boxers [1]. A Six Mile House appears on maps as early as 1861, but Blanken's 1915 obituary says his version opened on the Fourth of July, 1876 [1]. Blanken started across the road at the Overland Mail House, where long-distance mail carriers changed horses. At the Six Mile House travellers could stay an hour or a weekend for drinks, lodging and clam chowder [1]. Valley historians say its real fame came from the fighters who trained there: Jim Jeffries, Jack Johnson, 'Gentleman Jim' Corbett and Sam Langford [2]. On October 25, 1909, the single-track Visitacion Valley streetcar line opened from Geneva and Mission to the Six Mile House [3]. Riders later called its cars the 'galloping goose' [3]. The old building came down in 1938 for a garage and gas station [1][2]. Blanken Avenue, across the boulevard, still carries Pop's name [1].

title: Silk ribbons in a farm valley
place: San Bruno Road (Bayshore Boulevard) near Sunnydale Avenue, opposite the Six Mile House
hook: Among the dairies and cabbage fields, a silk mill backed by a famous banker turned out thousands of dollars of ribbon every week.
story: In the 1870s, when the valley was still mostly fields, the Union Pacific Silk Manufacturing Company opened a factory on the San Bruno Road, across from the Six Mile House roadhouse [1]. The valley's own history dates it to 1876. It names the banker and investor W. C. Ralston as the organiser and puts the company's capital at $250,000 [2]. Every week, that account says, the factory turned out about $6,000 worth of silk ribbons [2]. Within a few years the company moved to larger premises in South San Francisco [2]. Heritage lists a 'ribbon factory' among the valley's 19th-century industries, along with a fertilizer plant, breweries and quarries that shipped their goods by rail over the bay fill [3]. The Pacific Coal and Fertilizer Company, running by 1890 near the water's edge, got a blunter nickname from residents: 'the bone yard' [2][1]. Around the same time, a brewery on today's Bayshore Boulevard was selling pitchers of beer for five cents [2]. The exact site of the silk works has not been pinned down, so this marker shows only the stretch of road it faced.

title: Terrific Street, heart of the Barbary Coast
place: Pacific Ave between Kearny and Montgomery (557 Pacific)
hook: One block of Pacific Street was so notorious that the city nicknamed it Terrific Street, and a man made his living by letting strangers beat him.
story: In the mid-1860s San Franciscans started calling the district of dives and dance halls along Pacific Street the Barbary Coast, after the pirate coast of North Africa [1]. Its worst block, Pacific between Kearny and Montgomery, got the name Terrific Street [1]. In 1876 Benjamin Lloyd described it as 'the haunt of the low and the vile of every kind', crowded with concert saloons, gambling dens and opium dens [1]. 'Pretty waiter girls' earned $15 to $25 a week, and crimps and runners prowled for sailors to shanghai [1]. Its most famous oddity was Leon Borchardt, known as Oofty Goofty. He first appeared in 1884 as a caged 'Wild Man of Borneo' covered in tar and horsehair, and later earned his living by letting paying customers hit him [2]. The later tale that he could feel no pain came from Herbert Asbury's 1933 book. Oofty himself told the Examiner he wore a leather pad in the seat of his trousers [2]. The 1906 earthquake and fire all but wiped out the old district, but dance halls like the Hippodrome at 557 Pacific carried the Barbary Coast name into the new century [1].

title: The Chinese vault pelted with stones
place: Former Lone Mountain/Laurel Hill Cemetery, near Wood St (exact site of the Chinese burial grounds not recorded)
hook: In 1876 a guidebook writer found the Chinese burial ground the most fascinating corner of the city's grandest cemetery, and the one most often smeared with mud.
story:
Benjamin E. Lloyd's 1876 guide Lights and Shades in San Francisco walked readers through Lone Mountain Cemetery, the burial ground that became Laurel Hill. To a stranger, he wrote, the Chinese vault and burial grounds were "perhaps more attractive than any other feature" of the cemetery [1].

He described a wooden vault topped with an "oriental steeple" hung with wooden bells. In front stood a trough of earth full of burnt tapers and joss sticks. Each Chinese company's plot had its own board or picket fence, with a canopy over the entrance bearing the company's name. Inside were low graves, a rough brick furnace, a cheap table and plain wooden headboards [1].

Lloyd also recorded something uglier. The vaults and tombs were "bespattered with mud and filth, battered with stones, and sometimes defaced in a most irreverent manner". He added: "The animosity that many persons bear to the living, seems to extend even beyond the grave" [1]. Historian Greg Gaar ties the vandalism to the "Chinese must go!" movement of the 1870s [2]. Nothing of these plots survives. Between 1939 and 1941 the cemetery was emptied and built over [2].

title: The King of the Bernal Heights Hoodlums
place: Bernal Heights east slope, 1870s gang territory
hook: In the 1870s there were no police beyond 26th Street, and a teenage gang with a self-styled king ruled the hill.
story:
In August 1876 a man named Richard Brown came before the Police Court on eight misdemeanour charges. He was known as "The Chicken No. 2" and "The King of the Bernal Heights Hoodlums." The Chronicle said he cross-examined the witnesses "in a manner that would do credit to the most notorious Police Court shyster" and got one charge thrown out [1]. That October police rounded up 27 members of the Bernal Heights and Mission gang, aged 16 to 22. Among other things, they had been harassing the women teachers at the Fairmount School [1].

Jail did not hold them for long. In February 1877 Brown and two friends raided the Five-mile House, a roadside bar run by an invalid named John Bracken, and made off with a demijohn of whisky [1]. That December, masked men pretending to be police broke into the home of Patrick Haight and beat him and his wife. After two of them were identified, gang members came back and cut the throat of the Haights' cow [1][2]. The paper noted there were "no policemen beyond Twenty-sixth Street." One resident cut gun ports in his walls and slept with a shotgun at the head of his bed [1].

title: A Horsecar Man Reinvents the Grip
place: Sutter & Polk streets, site of the Sutter Street Railway powerhouse
hook: The cable-car grip used on California Street today traces back to a horsecar operator who decided to grab the cable from the side.
story: Henry Casebolt had run horsecar lines through the 1860s, and by 1876 they were losing money. His answer was cable [1]. On January 27, 1877, his Sutter Street Railroad opened, running cable cars along Sutter from Market Street west to Larkin [1]. Most of it copied Andrew Hallidie's Clay Street system, with one important exception: Casebolt's grip seized the moving cable from the side rather than from below, and the gripman worked a lever instead of Hallidie's hollow-screw device [1]. The side grip caught on; the California Street line would later use one too [2]. The route was nearly flat, and ridership rose by 962,000 in the first year [1]. In late 1878 the company opened a crosstown line running from its powerhouse at Larkin and Bush south to Hayes Street [1]. Casebolt sold out in 1883 to real estate broker Robert F. Morrow, who pulled all the lines into a single powerhouse at Sutter and Polk [1]. By 1891 the system ran about six miles of track. In 1902 it was merged into the United Railroads of San Francisco [1][2].

title: An ironworks owner's country house
place: Axford House, 1190 Noe Street at 25th Street
hook: Before the rows of Victorians came, an English ironworker built a farmhouse here with its own well and a hay lift. It still stands.
story:
In 1877 Noe Valley was still close to open country. William Axford, born in England in 1837, built a Stick-style house and carriage house on the corner of Noe and 25th [1]. He owned the Mission Iron Works, which the city's landmark report says began as a cottage industry run from the property itself [1].

The house was one of the first in the neighbourhood. Like many early homes here, it had its own water supply, because city water did not reach it until 1905. The carriage house still has a hay lift in its gable, and there is a garden behind an iron fence. The landmark report says that together they show the area's early rural scale. Later, denser housing grew up around them [1].

That housing came quickly after the Castro Street cable car started running in 1886 [1]. Over time the carriage house became a home, and a new wing now links it to the main house. San Francisco made the complex City Landmark No. 133 in 1981 [1][2].

title: Burning Barrels Outside Crocker's Door
place: In front of the Crocker mansion, California & Taylor streets (now Grace Cathedral)
hook: On an October night in 1877, thousands of unemployed men climbed Nob Hill by torchlight to threaten the railroad kings in their own front yards.
story: By 1877 Denis Kearney, an Irish-born drayman who owned five wagons, had become the loudest voice of San Francisco's jobless [3]. His Workingmen's Party of California blamed two targets at once: the railroad millionaires and the Chinese workers they employed, under the slogan "The Chinese Must Go" [1]. On October 29, 1877, several thousand marchers surged up Nob Hill to the front of Charles Crocker's new mansion [1]. Burning lime barrels lit the scene; one account says armed men waited inside to guard Crocker's art collection [2]. Kearney roared that "the Central Pacific Railroad men are thieves," gave the railroad three months to discharge its Chinese workers, and promised that if Crocker did not remove the spite fence around his neighbour's house by November 29, he would lead the workingmen up to tear it down and give Crocker "the worst beating with the sticks that a man ever got" [1]. Within days Kearney was arrested; he was released before Thanksgiving, and the march on the fence never came [1][2]. (FoundSF's spite-fence essay dates the rally to 1878, but the newspaper it is quoted from is from November 1877.)

title: Lucky Baldwin's Palace of Bay Windows
place: Site of the Baldwin Hotel and Theatre (today's Flood Building, 870 Market St)
hook: A lucky Comstock gambler built a hotel-theatre of crimson satin and gold at Powell and Market. It was shaken by gunfire and scandal, and it burned in 1898.
story: Elias 'Lucky' Baldwin made a fortune on the Comstock and in property, then built a hotel and theatre that filled the block at Powell and Market, running up Powell to Ellis [1][2]. Sumner Bugbee designed it in the Second Empire style, with countless bay windows and a dome over the corner [1][2]. Historian John P. Young says the theatre opened in March 1876 and the hotel the following February. Other accounts put both a year earlier [1][2]. In 1877 the visiting writer Mrs. Frank Leslie called the theatre 'a perfect little gem, fitted up like a bonbonniere in crimson satin and gold' [1]. Its stock company, run by the veteran manager Maguire with much help from a young David Belasco, put on a new play every week, and James O'Neill was one of its actors [2]. The hotel had its own drama. In 1883 Verona Baldwin, who said Baldwin had raped her, shot and wounded him inside it [3]. Young warned that so much wood made the building very vulnerable to fire [2]. In 1898 a fire that started in the theatre's scene lofts destroyed it. Two people died, and Baldwin was rescued from his rooms [1][2][3]. The Flood Building went up on the site and opened in 1904 as the city's largest building [4].

title: One flat-front Victorian, fifty residents
place: 411 30th Street, between Church and Sanchez
hook: A birthday present grew into a 310-page biography of one Upper Noe house, starring a jazz pianist, a cellar winery and a $360 coat of stucco.
story: In 1996 Christian Ard set out to write his father-in-law, Neil Mosher, a history of Mosher's house as a birthday present. He thought it would take five months. It took more than two years and filled 310 pages [1]. The two-storey flat-front Victorian at 411 30th Street went up in 1877, probably built by contractor John Nelson and his teenage son Fernando. Fernando had arrived from New York at 16 and went on to become one of San Francisco's most prolific builders [1][2]. The first known residents were Irish seaman John Higgins, his wife Julia and their seven children. Carpenter William Cavanaugh, who built streetcars for the Market Street Railway, split the house into two flats. From 1903 to 1905 the downstairs flat was home to the Ellis family, whose teenage son Frankie taught piano. He later played in Art Hickman's band and led the orchestras at the St. Francis Hotel and the Cliff House [1][3]. In 1921 bootblack Frank Fazzio and his wife Josephine bought the house. Every year two tons of Napa grapes arrived by rail for Frank's cellar wine. Josephine didn't drink, but she could judge a grape's sugar by taste, and she salted olives while he worked [1]. After Frank died, a contractor stripped off the Victorian ornament and stuccoed the front for $360 [1].

title: Speeches on the Sand Lot
place: The 'sand lot' beside City Hall (today's UN Plaza, Market St)
hook: On an empty lot beside a half-built City Hall, jobless crowds gathered in 1877 and a new political party took shape, built on anti-Chinese hate.
story: The Market Street lots sold off by the City Hall commission sat empty for years, and in hard times they filled with people. In the summer of 1877, as a depression dragged on, jobless crowds gathered on the 'sand lot' beside the half-built hall [1][2]. On September 7, Denis Kearney, an Irish-born organiser from County Cork, announced at Dashaway Hall on Post Street that he would speak on the sand lot that Sunday. The papers printed the notice, and a large crowd came [2][3]. Kearney soon drew crowds of up to 2,000, sometimes speaking for two hours. He attacked the press, capitalists and politicians, and above all Chinese immigrants, with the slogan 'The Chinese must go!' [3]. His Workingmen's Party of California won 51 of 152 delegate seats at the 1878 state constitutional convention, and it helped write a constitution that took voting rights away from Chinese Californians [4]. Not every sandlot voice was Kearney's. Anna Smith, a New York-born widow and former Civil War nurse who had cooked, scrubbed and ironed her way west, was a regular speaker. She liked to end by saying she wanted 'something to keep her jaws going and give her tongue a rest' [1].

title: The Undertaker Who Wouldn't Sell
place: Sacramento & Taylor streets, NE corner of the Crocker block (now Grace Cathedral)
hook: The richest men in California bought the whole block. One German undertaker refused, so Charles Crocker walled his house inside a forty-foot fence.
story: Nicholas Yung, a German immigrant who had come to America in 1848, was an undertaker. In 1855 he and his wife bought a corner lot atop what was then the steep, lonely California Street Hill and built a modest house with views of the Golden Gate and the bay [1]. Two decades later railroad baron Charles Crocker bought up the rest of the block for a palace of his own. Yung would not sell. Crocker raised his offer, reportedly doubling it, and Yung still said no [1]. So Crocker's workmen built a three-sided wooden fence about forty feet high around the little house, cutting off its sun and view; the family said it felt like living at the bottom of a well [1]. Newspapers called it "Crocker's Crime," and sightseers rode up the hill to stare at it [1]. In October 1877 the agitator Denis Kearney publicly gave Crocker a deadline to take down "the fence around Jung's house" [2]. It stayed. According to FoundSF, it came down only when the Yung property finally passed to Crocker [1]. Grace Cathedral stands on the block today.

title: The pick-handle battle at the Pacific Mail docks
place: Pacific Mail Steamship docks, First and Brannan streets
hook: In July 1877 an anti-Chinese mob set out to burn the docks where Chinese immigrants landed. A citizens' militia armed with pick handles stood in the way.
story: From the late 1860s the Pacific Mail Steamship Company's docks off South Beach, between First and Second streets, were where most Chinese immigrants first set foot in California [1][2]. In 1867 the line had opened the world's first regular trans-Pacific steamship service, to Yokohama with links to Hong Kong and Shanghai [2]. In July 1877, amid unemployment, three days of anti-Chinese rioting swept the city, burning laundries [3]. Rumours spread that rioters would torch the Pacific Mail docks to stop further Chinese immigration [3]. A Committee of Safety chaired by William T. Coleman, the old vigilance leader, armed volunteers with clubs, and on July 25 police and this 'pick-handle brigade' guarded the wharves [3]. Rioters set fire to a nearby lumberyard instead; one account places it at the Beale Street wharf, another suggests Mission Creek [2][3]. Mobs tried to stop firemen, and in the fighting four men were killed [1][3]. One of the pick-handle men was a drayman named Denis Kearney, who was drawn into politics by those July days and went on to lead the anti-Chinese Workingmen's agitation [1][3]. The 1867 Oriental Warehouse near First and Brannan is the complex's only survivor [4].

title: The school where the janitor carried water
place: Dolores Huerta Elementary (former Fairmount School), 65 Chenery Street near Randall
hook: In 1875 Fairmount's 170 pupils were crammed into a two-room wooden schoolhouse and rented rooms, and the janitor hauled drinking water on his head from blocks away.
story: Fairmount School first opened in September 1864 for children of the new Fairmount Tract, making it one of the oldest schools in San Francisco [1]. By the end of 1875 it was a scandal. About 170 pupils were squeezed into a wooden building with two small rooms and some rented space, and the library held 33 books. One complaint said the janitor had to "carry water on his head, like the ancients, a distance of several blocks, providing the neighbors will let him have it" [1]. In 1876 Supervisor Henry Haight declared it "high time to give the suburban primary schools some of the necessaries." Within a month the Board of Education agreed to seek plans. In December 1877 a two-storey, eight-room school by architect Charles Geddes was dedicated on Chenery near Randall, praised for its ventilation, for desks arranged so light fell over the pupils' left shoulders, and for lockable toilet rooms that kept "prowling thieves" from the children's hats and shawls [1]. It soon overflowed too: by 1891 one class had 74 pupils. The streetcar company even blamed Fairmount pupils for sliding down the Chenery Street rails on boards [2]. A brick school replaced it in 1917, a new building came in 1977, and in 2018 the school was renamed for Dolores Huerta [1].

title: Where Modern Dance Was Born
place: Isadora Duncan's birthplace, 501 Taylor Street at Geary
hook: A plaque at Taylor and Geary marks where Isadora Duncan was born, the barefoot rebel who 'liberated the dance'.
story: Angela Isadora Duncan was born in San Francisco, the youngest of four children. Her birth date is usually given as May 26, 1877, though some sources say May 27, 1878 [1]. The plaque at 501 Taylor Street, put up by the Daughters of California Pioneers, gives 1878 and says 'America's Genius of the Dance was born on this site' [2]. Her father, Joseph Charles Duncan, was a banker, mining engineer and art lover. Soon after she was born, the family's bank collapsed and he was charged [1]. Her parents divorced, and her mother took the children to Oakland, where she earned a living as a seamstress and piano teacher [1]. The family moved from one poor apartment to another. In the evenings her mother played Beethoven, Schumann and Chopin or read Shakespeare, Shelley and Keats aloud. Duncan later called that her 'real education' [3]. She left school at about ten, and she and her siblings taught dance to local children for money [1]. She took her freeform, corset-free dancing to London in 1898 and then across Europe, and became one of the founders of modern dance [1][3]. A later admirer, Mignon Garland, got the city to rename the block's Adelaide Place as Isadora Duncan Lane [1].

title: Ocean View's Oldest Houses Hide in Plain Sight
place: 215 Randolph Street
hook: A Stick-style house on Randolph Street may date from about 1878, when Ocean View was a homestead scheme with more lots than people.
story: Ocean View was mapped in the 1860s and 1870 by homestead associations, but it filled slowly. By 1900 it still had only about 200 buildings [1]. A few from that thin early period survive. The OMI historic context statement singles out 215 Randolph Street, a Stick-style house built around 1878, as an example of pre-1906 Ocean View [1]. The authors think the district's oldest surviving buildings date from the 1870s and may be tied to the homestead associations or the vanished railroad station. They add that no survey of the area's buildings has been done to confirm it [1]. The statement also points to four Victorians on Broad Street that got Spring Valley water service in the 1890s, and to 222 Plymouth Avenue, built in 1904 [1]. Western Neighborhoods Project historian David Gallagher called 222 Plymouth 'kind of a farmhouse that sits on the corner', behind a fence at Plymouth and Broad [2]. Woody LaBounty suggested why such houses survive: in overlooked neighbourhoods that 'haven't become trendy', old buildings are rarely restored or renovated away [2]. Because pre-1906 buildings are so rare in Ocean View, the context statement argues they deserve extra consideration even when altered [1].

title: Stanford's Railroad Up His Own Hill
place: California Street at Jones, crest of the California Street cable line
hook: Leland Stanford built a cable line up California Street, past his own mansion, and had to pay his rival $30,000 for the privilege.
story: Nob Hill was a brutal climb for horses. Leland Stanford, the Central Pacific's president, was building his mansion near California and Powell, and he joined Mark Hopkins and other businessmen to form the California Street Cable Railroad [1][3]. Stanford won a franchise in 1876 and handed the job to Henry Root, one of his railroad engineers. Despite his efforts to get around Andrew Hallidie's cable-car patents, Stanford was forced to pay Hallidie $30,000 in licensing fees, "to his great chagrin" [1]. Work began on July 5, 1877; within five months 1.7 miles of track ran from Kearny Street up over Nob Hill "past Nabob palaces" to Fillmore Street [1]. After delays the line opened on April 10, 1878, and carried more than 11,000 riders that day [1]. Stanford sold out in 1884 to banker Antoine Borel, and the company later moved its powerhouse to California and Hyde [1]. Unlike most rival lines, California Street stayed on cable: the grades were too steep for electric trolleys. The city bought it in January 1952, and it still runs [1][2].

title: The Clipper That Keeps Resurfacing
place: Ocean Beach at the foot of Noriega Street (King Philip wreck site)
hook: Built in Maine in 1856, the clipper King Philip ran aground here in 1878. Every few decades, when the sand is scoured low, her ribs come back into view.
story: King Philip was launched in Alna, Maine, in 1856. She was a medium clipper of about 1,194 tons, named for the Wampanoag leader Metacomet, whom the English called King Philip [1]. It was a hard-luck career: there were at least two mutinies, and both times the sailors set the ship on fire. By her old age she was hauling lumber, grain and even guano [1][2]. On January 25, 1878, she left San Francisco in ballast behind a tug. Nearby, the collier Western Shore had an accident that killed its captain, and the tug went off to help. King Philip dropped anchor, but in heavy seas it would not hold, and she drove onto Ocean Beach. Nobody died, but the ship was a total loss [2]. The next day businessman John Molloy bought the wreck at auction for $1,050. He salvaged the metal fastenings, masts and sails, then blew up the hulk with black powder [2]. The lower hull stayed buried at the tide line, and sand pushed onto the beach around 1910, when the Great Highway was built, covered it further [1]. The timbers came back into view in the 1980s and in 2007. In November 2010 the Ocean Beach Bulletin reported the hull's outline showing again at low tide off Noriega Street [3].

title: The West's first free kindergarten
place: Stillman Street (formerly Silver Street) between Third and Fourth streets
hook: In 1878 a young teacher who would later write Rebecca of Sunnybrook Farm opened a free class for Tar Flat's poorest children. A thousand people came to watch.
story: Kindergartens were a new idea in the 1870s: fewer than a dozen existed in the United States before 1870 [2]. In San Francisco, Judge Solomon Heydenfeldt and the merchant Samuel Levy, inspired by lectures from the New York reformer Felix Adler, formed the Public Kindergarten Society with $130 in pledges and went looking for a teacher [2]. They found Kate Wiggin, a young New Englander trained at Emma Marwedel's kindergarten school [2]. As Kate Douglas Wiggin she would later write Rebecca of Sunnybrook Farm [1]. She wanted to plant a kindergarten "in some dreary, poverty-stricken place in a large city, a place swarming with unmothered, undefended, under-nourished child-life" [1]. In September 1878 ("toward the end of 1878", in another account) she opened the Silver Street Free Kindergarten on a small alley between Third and Fourth streets, today's Stillman Street. The city's planning history calls it the first free kindergarten in the West [1][2]. Free kindergartens served working families whose mothers had no other childcare [1]. In the first year and a half, about a thousand educators, writers, society people and curious visitors came to watch the Tar Flat class [2]. More followed: the western South of Market eventually had at least four kindergartens, on Ninth, Harrison and Folsom streets and at Thirteenth and Treat. None survive [1].

title: 'Dere's de Author': Stevenson's Hungry Winter
place: 608 Bush Street, Robert Louis Stevenson's lodging
hook: Before Treasure Island, a sick, broke Robert Louis Stevenson split kindling on a Bush Street windowsill and cut his dinner budget to 25 cents.
story: Robert Louis Stevenson had followed Fanny Osbourne, the married American he loved, from Europe to Monterey and then to San Francisco [2]. Through the winter of 1879–80 his letters home were headed "608 Bush Street" [1]. On December 26, 1879, he wrote that for four days he had spoken to no one but "my landlady or landlord or to restaurant waiters" [1]. In January he described his routine for his friend Sidney Colvin. Each morning a "slender gentleman in an ulster" left No. 608, walked down Powell for a ten-cent coffee and roll, then split kindling on the windowsill, since harder blows elsewhere might "knock the entire shanty" down. His landlady's youngest child would announce, "Dere's de author" [1]. By January 26 he was dropping "from a 50 cent. to a 25 cent. dinner" [1]. Fanny introduced her gaunt, chain-smoking fiancé, in his worn velvet jacket, to her friend Dora Norton Williams, who became a lifelong friend [2]. (That account gives the address as 680 Bush; the letters say 608.) Stevenson married Fanny in May 1880 [3].

title: A Dead Millionaire's Greenhouse Kit
place: Conservatory of Flowers, 100 John F. Kennedy Drive
hook: The park's oldest building was meant for a San Jose estate, until its eccentric buyer died and the crates of glass needed a new home.
story: The glass palace above Conservatory Valley was meant for San Jose. The eccentric millionaire James Lick bought the materials, believed to be a kit from the greenhouse makers Lord & Burnham, for his estate. He died in 1876 before it was built [1]. The crates passed through his estate, and in 1877 a group of 27 prominent San Franciscans bought them and gave them to the park. The group included Leland Stanford, Charles Crocker, Claus Spreckels and former mayor William Alvord [1][2]. It went up in 1878 and opened in April 1879 [1][3]. Its frame is wood, not iron. Materials analysis suggests California redwood, cut into short arch pieces and glazed with panes that overlap like shingles [1]. Early visitors came to see a giant water lily, Victoria regia, then said to be the only specimen in the United States [1]. Disaster struck early: an 1883 fire badly damaged the central Palm Room, and its dome was rebuilt [1]. Today it is North America's oldest public wood-and-glass conservatory [4], and one of only three San Francisco buildings that are city, state and national landmarks at once [3].

title: A teetotal dentist's fountain gets banished
place: Benjamin Franklin statue, centre of Washington Square
hook: The spigots were labelled Vichy and Cal. Seltzer, but only city water ever ran. San Francisco mocked the fountain, then sent it into exile here.
story: Henry Cogswell was a millionaire dentist and '49er who made most of his money in real estate [1]. When the city cut Montgomery Avenue (now Columbus) diagonally through North Beach in the 1870s, it took a corner off Washington Square [1][2]. The new avenue also split one of Cogswell's lots and left him a triangle only 12 feet long on its longest side. He put a temperance drinking fountain on it, crowned with Benjamin Franklin and unveiled in May 1879. The taps were marked Vichy and Cal. Seltzer, but they only ever ran city water [1]. The Chronicle called it 'that grey granite tombstone'. Cogswell rented out booths and a podium around it and promised one fountain for every 100 saloons in the city [1]. Sources disagree about where Franklin first stood. The Semaphore puts him at Kearny and Columbus, while the city's landmark report says Market Street [1][3]. Both agree the statue was moved in 1904 to Washington Square, which the Chronicle dismissed as the place 'where mostly the children of San Francisco's Latin Quarter play' [1][3]. It still stands there today, and a time capsule lies beneath it [2].

title: Paderewski in the piano man's parlor
place: Leander Sherman House, 2160 Green Street
hook: A clock-shop apprentice who arrived at 14 built a San Francisco music empire, then built a house whose whole west wing was a concert hall.
story: Leander Sherman came to San Francisco from Boston in 1861, when he was 14. He apprenticed in a clock shop and then clerked at A. A. Rosenberg's music store, and in 1870 he bought the business [2]. With Clement Clay as partner it became Sherman, Clay and Co., in time one of the oldest commercial firms in the West [2]. In 1879 Sherman built himself a house on Green Street between Fillmore and Webster [1]. What made it famous was the music room. As Roger Olmsted and T. H. Watkins described it in their 1968 book Here Today, 'a huge, three-story music and reception room forms the entire west wing of the house.' Under its skylight was a platform where 'such music greats as Paderewski performed.' From a balcony in the corner, singers such as Madame Schumann-Heink entertained, and earlier Lotta Crabtree, who lived next door to the west [1]. The Chronicle's Carl Nolte summed it up simply: Sherman 'built a mansion that came with a concert hall. Famous artists, Paderewski among them, played there' [2]. Sherman died in 1926. His company stayed in family hands until 1960; in 2013, after 142 years in San Francisco, it sold its flagship Mission Street store to Steinway & Sons [2]. The house is San Francisco Landmark No. 49 [1].

title: The Day the Dunes Exploded
place: Approximate site of the Giant Powder Works packing house, 22nd Avenue between Kirkham & Lawton
hook: In 1879 a dynamite packing house near today's 22nd Avenue blew up with five workers inside. People felt the blast from the Cliff House to the waterfront.
story: The Sunset's first big industry was one nobody wanted as a neighbor. In 1869 an explosion wrecked the Giant Powder Company's works on San Jose Road, so the company moved out to the empty sand south of Golden Gate Park. It set up on about 25 fenced acres off the Powder House Road, near today's 19th Avenue [1]. The two sources draw the tract a little differently: the Western Neighborhoods Project puts it between Kirkham and Moraga, while the Parkside context statement says between K (Kirkham) and N (Noriega) Streets, from 19th to 23rd Avenues, as early as 1871 [1][2]. At 2 p.m. on January 15, 1879, the packing house blew up. It was a 30-by-60-foot building standing roughly at 22nd Avenue between Kirkham and Lawton, holding 6,000 pounds of powder and five workers. Nothing of the building, its contents or the men was found, and nine other buildings were destroyed [1]. The shock was felt from the Cliff House to the waterfront. Glass broke as far away as 16th Street, and in a schoolhouse on McAllister Street, more than two miles off, students were thrown from their desks [1]. Nearby saloons were damaged too [2]. Indignant editorials followed. Within a year the powder makers had left for the East Bay, and Giant rebuilt in Berkeley [1].
