title: The West Coast's first observatory
place: Lafayette Park, near Octavia and Clay Streets (site of George Davidson's observatory)
hook: In 1879 a surveyor who never went to college set up a telescope at Octavia and Clay, and helped talk James Lick into building an observatory of his own.
story:
George Davidson sailed into San Francisco Bay in June 1850 aboard the Tennessee, a young assistant with the U.S. Coast Survey. His job was to fix the latitude and longitude of the coast's bays and headlands and to choose sites for lighthouses [1]. He only ever attended one school, Philadelphia's Central High School, yet in 1870 he became professor of astronomy and geodesy at the University of California [1].

In 1879 he built what is described as the West Coast's first observatory, in Lafayette Park. The historian Bancroft noted that "Professor Davidson of San Francisco has a 6.4 inch object glass in a portable observatory at the corner of Octavia and Clay Streets" [1]. By then Davidson had led the U.S. expedition to observe the 1874 transit of Venus, and in 1882 he took a party to New Mexico to watch the next one [2]. His enthusiasm helped persuade James Lick to pay for an observatory on Mount Hamilton [1].

He published 260 papers. In 1886 the supervisors asked him to study the city's sewers, and he reported that they were the worst he had seen anywhere but one [1]. When he died in 1911, the city renamed its highest peak Mount Davidson [1][2].

title: Cable, horse and steam to the Presidio
place: Union and Steiner Streets, where cable cars met the steam line
hook: One early line along Union Street used three kinds of power on one trip. One stormy night in 1904, a cable train was swept right off its tracks.
story: The Presidio & Ferries Railroad, organised in 1878 with cable-car pioneer Andrew Hallidie as its president, ran mostly along Union Street, roughly two miles [1]. It combined three kinds of early transit. A horsecar carried riders from the Ferry Building to Columbus and Montgomery. A cable line climbed over Russian Hill and ran west on Union to Steiner Street. At Steiner a steam train took over for the run to the Presidio [1][2]. Sources disagree on the opening date: the Cable Car Museum gives October 23, 1880, while other accounts say December 1881 [1][2]. The cable was extended along Union and Baker in 1892 [2]. The line is probably the only one in the city to lose a car to the rain. During severe storms in the autumn of 1904, a cable train was washed off its tracks near Baker and Union around midnight [1]. The 1906 earthquake damaged it worse than any other cable line, so it was converted to small electric cars [1]. When its franchise ran out in 1913 the city took it over, and it became the E Union streetcar ahead of the 1915 fair. Its descendant, the 41 Union trolleybus, was suspended in 2020 [1][2].

title: Elias Wolfe's saloon, hall and village centre
place: Plymouth Avenue and Sickles Avenue, the old Ocean View station plaza (site of Wolfe's Hall)
hook: Ocean View ran its lectures, dances and political rallies from a roadhouse bar next to the railway tracks.
story: Around 1880 Elias Wolfe moved to Ocean View, a village of homestead lots next to the railroad station, and opened a roadhouse and meeting hall on the corner of Plymouth Avenue and Sickles Street [1]. The streets met the station like the spokes of a wheel. Residents built a fountain in the plaza, useful for looking at and for watering tied-up horses [2]. The Diamond Saloon, the Tell House, Pellegrini's Bayview Bazaar, Pesce's Grocery and Canada's Barber Shop stood around it [2]. Wolfe's served drinks and food downstairs and had a hall upstairs [1]. It hosted lectures, dances, rallies and the meetings of the improvement clubs that lobbied City Hall for water, a fire station and a school [1]. Wolfe helped start the area's first school. When the new Sheridan School was dedicated in 1910, he was named one of the neighbourhood's 'honored settlers' [1]. His first building burned in 1891. The rebuilt hall and bar stayed open for years after he died in the 1910s, until freeway construction cleared Wolfe's, the Tell House and the Diamond Saloon [1].

title: He sold to miners instead of digging
place: Stadtmuller House, 819 Eddy Street between Van Ness and Franklin
hook: A Nevada storekeeper made his money selling to silver miners, then built one of Eddy Street's showpiece Italianates.
story:
Frederick D. Stadtmuller made his money in Silver City, Nevada. He owned a chain of stores there, Stadtmuller & Co., and a timber business [1]. As NoeHill puts it, he sold things to the miners 'rather than grubbing around in the dirt' [2]. He moved to San Francisco in 1879 and went into California wines and brandies with the firm of Walter, Schilling & Co. One of his partners was Claus Schilling, brother of the spice maker A. Schilling [1].

In 1880 the architect P. R. Schmidt designed him this Italianate house on Eddy Street. It has two-storey bay windows, carved and panelled entrance doors, and a portico on fluted Corinthian columns under a carved balustrade [1]. The street was then a prosperous one [2]. The family kept the house until 1951. It then became a rooming house, as many large old homes did [1][2]. In 1963 Mr. and Mrs. Peter R. Loebs bought it and restored it as a single-family home. They kept its original woodwork and onyx and marble fireplaces [1].

title: Survivors From the Hillside Farm Days
place: 699 Paris Street at Italy Avenue
hook: On a little hill below McLaren Park, a house from the 1880s still stands. Neighbours saved it in 1990.
story: Before the building booms, the slope below McLaren Park was farm country, and a few houses from those years are still there. 699 Paris Street has stood at the corner of Italy Avenue since the 1880s. It sits on the top of a small hill in an open yard, 'recalling the agrarian character of early settlement,' as a 1990 preservation note put it [1]. That year the owner planned to knock it down and split the fifty-foot lot for two new homes. The Neighbors of the Excelsior asked for a review, the Landmarks Board recommended keeping the house, and the Planning Commission saved it. In the compromise, one new house went up at the back of the lot, at 225 Italy Avenue in 1991 [1]. Nearby, the Frank R. Smith house of about 1890, with its 'eyebrow' window hoods, spent almost a century at 503 Vienna Street beside the family's corner grocery before it was moved around the corner to 750 Persia Avenue in the 1980s. And 291 Munich Street, a brick cottage built in 1908, is what historian Hannah Simonson calls 'an exceedingly rare example of Richardsonian Romanesque residential architecture' [2].

title: Swiss cows, then asphalt, beside Geneva Avenue
place: West side of San Jose Avenue at Geneva Avenue (block of the Furrers' Eureka Dairy, between San Jose, Niagara, Tara and Geneva)
hook: Swiss dairymen gave Geneva Avenue its name. Within a generation their pasture had become a railway paint shop and an asphalt plant.
story: French Swiss families settled along Islais Creek, perhaps by the late 1850s, and gave Geneva Avenue and Geneva Lake their names, says the city's archaeological review [1]. The 1880 census and city directory list 17 farmers or dairymen living along the Ocean House Road and the old San Jose Road [2]. In the 1880s (or about 1876, by another page of the same report) the brothers Ambrose and Frank Furrer started the Eureka Dairy on the block bounded by San José Road, Niagara Avenue, Tara Street and Geneva Avenue. Their farmhouse was at 2224 San José Road [1]. By 1900 the dairy seems to have passed to Fred Furrer, who had arrived in 1886 aged 22 and married Emma, also from Switzerland [1]. By 1915 most of the dairy land had gone to the Southern Pacific for a railway car paint shop, and part had been leased or sold to the Blanchard & Brown Asphaltum Plant. The old farmhouse still stood, renumbered 2332 San Jose Avenue [1]. By then two asphalt plants worked nearby, the Moore Boode Gravel Co. was on Geneva, and a Spring Valley lumber yard filled the block across San Jose Avenue [1]. Even in 1930, Italian-born labourers living nearby still worked small truck farms [2].

title: The Emperor's surprisingly small funeral
place: Former Masonic Cemetery, centre of the grounds (now USF's lower campus)
hook: Ten thousand people filed past Emperor Norton's coffin downtown. Only three carriages followed it out to the Masonic Cemetery, where about thirty people watched him buried.
story: Joshua Norton, self-proclaimed Emperor of the United States and Protector of Mexico, collapsed and died at California and Dupont streets on the night of January 8, 1880 [1]. He had five or six dollars in small change on him and nothing else of value. He would have had a pauper's funeral if members of the Pacific Club had not raised a fund for a rosewood casket [2]. On January 10 he lay in state at the undertakers at 16 O'Farrell Street, and the Chronicle estimated that 10,000 people came to look, "from capitalists to the pauper, the clergyman to the pickpocket" [2][3]. A legend later grew of a cortege two miles long. The Chronicle actually reported just three carriages, with nobody from the crowd following on foot [3]. Some people rode the streetcar out to the Masonic Cemetery. There, in a little square formed by four graves near the superintendent's house, about thirty people watched him committed to the earth, with no stone or board to mark the spot [3]. When the cemetery was cleared his remains were dug up in 1932. On June 30, 1934, members of the Pacific-Union Club gave him a grander reburial at Woodlawn in Colma [1][3].

title: The cable line that crowned Russian Hill
place: Union Street hill between Larkin and Polk, on the Presidio & Ferries cable line
hook: In 1880 the first cable line to take on Russian Hill hauled its cars along Union Street from a powerhouse on the summit, and rounded the first cable-car corner.
story: The Presidio & Ferries Railroad, organised in 1878, was the first cable line to take on Russian Hill. Andrew Hallidie had been president of its predecessor company [1]. It opened on October 23, 1880 [1][2]. A horsecar from the Ferry Building met the cable at Montgomery Street (now Columbus Avenue). The cable ran out Columbus and turned west along Union to Steiner, where a steam train carried on to the Presidio: three kinds of transport on one ride [1]. The powerhouse stood at the line's highest point, at Union and Sharp Place near Leavenworth, on the summit of the hill. That eased the strain on the cables but made hauling fuel uphill harder [1]. It was the first cable line to go around a corner, at Columbus and Union [2]. In November 1885 a car climbing the steep hill between Larkin and Polk 'broke its grip and started back down the hill at a rapid rate' [2]. In 1904 a storm swept a train off its tracks at Baker and Union [1]. The 1906 earthquake twisted the Union Street rails, and the line took the worst damage of any cable road. It was rebuilt as an electric line [1][2]. The city took it over in 1913, and its descendant is the 41 Union trolleybus line, suspended since 2020 [1][3].

title: The millionaire who planted a mountain
place: Western slope of Mount Davidson (then 'Blue Mountain'), Mount Davidson Park
hook: The dark eucalyptus woods on Mount Davidson are no wilderness. They are what survives of a forest one man planted on treeless, windswept hills.
story: When Adolph Sutro bought about 1,200 acres of the old Rancho San Miguel in 1880, using money from his famous Comstock tunnel, the hills were mostly bunchgrass and scrub [2]. Over the next two decades he covered them with pine, cypress and, above all, blue gum eucalyptus. The planting spread across the hill then called Blue Mountain (now Mount Davidson), the future Forest Hill and St. Francis Wood, and all the way south to Ocean Avenue [1]. At California's first Arbor Day in 1886, held on Yerba Buena Island, he called trees 'the children of my old age, that will live long after I am laid to rest' [2]. He was right. In 1910, twelve years after Sutro's death, the appraiser A. S. Baldwin walked the estate and reported a forest 'in many places almost impenetrable' [3]. Developers soon cut most of it down for residence parks, but on Mount Davidson the trees Sutro planted are still standing [3][4].

title: The powerhouse that pulled Geary Street
place: Geary Street cable powerhouse site, NW corner of Geary & Buchanan
hook: A carpenter died building it. For 32 years it hauled cable under Geary. Then the city took the line over and started Muni.
story: In August 1879 a carpenter named Michael Rochfort was killed by a falling derrick while building an engine house at Geary and Buchanan for the new Geary Street cable road [1]. The line opened on 16 February 1880. From a two-storey wooden powerhouse on the northwest corner, a cable ran under Geary out toward Central (now Presidio) Avenue, and steam dummies sometimes carried riders further west [1][2]. By the 1900s Progressive reformers wanted the city to own its utilities, and riders were fed up with the slow little cars, which the Western Neighborhoods Project puts at six miles an hour [3]. Voters approved a city-run line on Geary in 1909 [1]. When the private franchise was not renewed, the last cable car left the Market Street turntable at 12:32 a.m. on 6 May 1912. Gripman F. Brainerd and conductor F. Stanley were aboard, and workmen were already ripping out cable behind them [1]. On 28 December 1912 Mayor James Rolph opened the city's electric A and B Geary lines, the first pieces of what became Muni [2][3].

title: Where the cable ran out at 'Cemetery'
place: California Street at Presidio Avenue (formerly Central Avenue, nicknamed 'Cemetery')
hook: In 1880 two cable car lines ended at Central Avenue, a stop riders called "Cemetery." From there, smoky steam trains carried them on west.
story: Presidio Avenue used to be called Central Avenue, and riders knew the stop as "Cemetery" [1]. The California Street Cable Railroad began running cable cars from Kearny Street to Central Avenue on May 30, 1879. Its franchise ran on to First Avenue (today's Arguello), and for that last stretch it was allowed to use steam. So the company leased a Southern Pacific locomotive and one car, and they started running from Cemetery Avenue on February 6, 1880. The steam train probably lasted until about 1884. After that a one-horse car took over [1]. A few blocks south, the Geary Street, Park & Ocean Railroad opened on February 16, 1880. Its cable passengers also changed at Central Avenue, onto four Baldwin steam dummies that ran on to Golden Gate Park [1]. The spot was a gateway even before the cable. An 1860s photograph shows a tollhouse on Point Lobos Road, now Geary, near Presidio Avenue, with Calvary Cemetery's graves behind it [2]. By 1890 the Point Lobos Improvement Club was calling the steam dummy a "noisy, sooty and smoky nuisance." Full cable service on the Geary line, from Market Street to Golden Gate Park, opened on August 7, 1892 [1].

title: A sugar king's refinery on the shore
place: Former California (later Western) Sugar Refinery, east end of 23rd Street
hook: For seventy years, raw sugar went in at the end of 23rd Street and refined sugar came out, and a tenth of Dogpatch lived off the work.
story:
In 1881 the sugar baron Claus Spreckels bought a five-block site on the south shore of Potrero Point, east of Louisiana Street; both powder companies had sold him their plants [1]. There he built the California Sugar Refinery. Its big brick melt, wash and char houses were designed that year by a New York architect named Hepworth [1]. Station A, a power station at the east end of 23rd Street built between 1902 and 1905, fed the industries around it. The Potrero View says Spreckels built it for his factory; by 1905 it was part of the mergers that formed Pacific Gas and Electric [2].

The American Sugar Refining Company bought the plant in 1891 and renamed it the Western Sugar Refinery. It employed about 1,000 men. It stayed one of Dogpatch's top five employers into the early 1950s and gave work to 10 to 15 percent of the neighbourhood's residents [1]. A 1919 photograph shows sugar workers behind the factory on 23rd Street [3].

The end came quickly. California & Hawaiian Sugar bought the refinery in 1949, judged it too old to modernise, and in 1951 demolished the buildings and sold the machinery for scrap [1]. Station A is the last of the power station's brick buildings, saved largely through the efforts of the Potrero Hill Archives Project [2].

title: The Atherton women of California Street
place: Atherton House, 1990 California St at Octavia
hook: A strong-willed Chilean widow, a restless young novelist, a husband who never came home and, later, a woman with fifty cats.
story:
Dominga de Goñi Atherton was a Chilean widow whose husband, Faxon Atherton, had made his fortune in Valparaíso and then bought a large estate in San Mateo County. In 1881 she built this eccentric Queen Anne and Stick-Eastlake house at California and Octavia [1][2]. Her son George and his wife Gertrude moved in with her. Gertrude found life under her mother-in-law stifling and began to build an independent life. Her first serial story appeared in The Argonaut in 1882 under the pen name "Asmodeus" [3].

In 1887 George sailed for Chile and died at sea [2][3]. House lore has it that his body came home preserved in a barrel of rum [2]. Left to support herself, Gertrude published her first novel in 1888 and went on to a long career as a writer [3].

After Dominga died in 1890 the house was sold [1]. In 1923 the architect Charles J. Rousseau divided it into 13 apartments, and his widow Carrie lived here with fifty cats until 1974 [1]. Ghost-hunters say the house is haunted, which may be the most Pacific Heights ending of all [2].

title: The brigantine Tahiti's grim last voyage
place: Mission Creek channel near Seventh Street, head of the old shipyards
hook: America's most prolific wooden shipbuilder launched a handsome South Seas trader here. Ten years later it was found floating upside down.
story: Before he moved to Benicia, Matthew Turner built ships on Mission Creek. Turner, an Ohio-born sea captain, built more sailing vessels than any other American shipbuilder, over 270 in all [1]. A modern tally of his hulls lists dozens launched at "Mission Creek, Channel Street" between the mid-1870s and early 1880s. They included a San Francisco bar pilots' schooner, Alaska Commercial Company traders and fast brigantines for the Hawaiian sugar trade of Claus and John D. Spreckels [2][3]. On August 18, 1881, he launched the 290-ton half-brigantine Tahiti for Turner & Rundle, his trading partnership with Captain Richard Rundle [1][2]. The yard was cramped and the creek was busy, yet big, graceful ships slid off the ways at its head [3]. In 1891 the Tahiti fell into what Vanished Waters calls "evil hands": Captain W.H. Ferguson used her for "blackbirding", recruiting coffee-plantation labour by legal and illegal means. She was later found bottom-up near Manzanillo, "with no sign of life, nor were any bodies seen floating around." Turner blamed the captain for failing to keep her water casks filled [3].

title: The heiress, the silver king and the brother
place: Theodore F. Payne House, 1409 Sutter Street between Franklin and Gough
hook: A Comstock millionaire died, a supposedly dead brother turned up to claim his share, and the niece's windfall helped build this turreted house.
story:
Theodore Payne reached San Francisco in 1849 with nothing. He had lost everything when his steamship sank before it arrived [1]. His son Theodore F. Payne married Mary Pauline O'Brien, whose unmarried uncle, William S. O'Brien, was one of the Comstock 'Silver Kings'. In 1877 O'Brien heard that his brother Patrick had died and left a wife and daughter destitute. He brought them west from Brooklyn [1]. O'Brien himself died on 2 May 1878, and news of his death was published all over the country. Then Patrick, very much alive, appeared to claim a share. To prevent a lawsuit over the will, the other heirs paid father and daughter over $600,000. With the $800,000 O'Brien had left her, Mary Pauline received more than twice as much as any other heir [1].

William Curlett designed the house, finished around 1881. It has an octagonal turret and about 16,000 square feet across four floors. The bathrooms were built into the house rather than added onto a porch, and the tubs and basins had hot and cold running water [1][2]. It is the last of the large houses that once lined this block of Sutter [2].

title: Where sailors never sailed away again
place: Marine Hospital cemetery, behind the former hospital near 15th Avenue and Lake Street
hook: Behind an old hospital lie hundreds of merchant seamen, most of them young and foreign, in graves later buried under 16 feet of fill.
story: In 1875 a new Marine Hospital opened on land the Treasury Department leased at the Presidio. It cared for merchant seamen, and later for Coast Guardsmen and others [1][2]. In 1881 the records of the Marine Hospital Service first mention a cemetery in a little valley beside it, and burials went on until at least 1912 [1]. These were San Francisco's great years as a port. Sailors of the day, as one account puts it, were outcasts with no families who worked long hours in brutal conditions [1]. Most of the dead were young, many in their 20s, and most died of respiratory diseases like tuberculosis [1]. About 80 percent were foreign-born [1]. In 1896 the San Francisco Call described the graveyard as 'a valley dreary with stunted growths and hummocks of half-tamed sand dunes', resting place of men 'who sailed into the port of San Francisco and never sailed away again' [1]. Estimates of the number of graves run from 200 to 800 [1]. In the 1950s the wooden headstones vanished under about 16 feet of debris, with a parking lot and a tennis court on top, and the cemetery was forgotten [1][3].

title: The Forty-Niner Who Wanted the Park
place: Nightingale House, 201 Buchanan Street
hook: John Nightingale, Forty-Niner and pioneer booster, tried to claim part of Alamo Square in court. He lost, and built himself a picturesque villa instead.
story:
The city's title to Alamo Square was fought over in court for years. Hoodline, drawing on historian Joe Pecora and on Anne Bloomfield's 1983 research for the historic district, lists several claimants besides the Duane brothers. They included captain of detectives Isaiah W. Less, City Hall saloon keeper Michael Keeney and real estate man John Nightingale [1]. San Francisco's municipal reports record a ruling against Nightingale after he took the city to court. In 1918 journalist Edward Morphy credited a line of city attorneys with saving the park from such claims [1].

Losing did not slow Nightingale down. He was a Forty-Niner, real estate dealer and property manager, and served as president of the Society of California Pioneers [2]. He built speculative housing in Hayes Valley [3]. In 1882 he took a large lot on the west side of Buchanan Street between Laussat and Waller and built a Stick/Eastlake villa designed by John Marquis [3]. Its large lot and picturesque shape set it apart from the row houses around it [3].

The Landmarks Board noted that this "cottage" is all that remains of Nightingale's extensive holdings in the area [2]. It is now San Francisco City Landmark No. 47 [2][3].

title: The lane once called "Japan Street"
place: Cottage Row, off Bush Street between Webster and Fillmore (Bush Street–Cottage Row Historic District)
hook: Built for working families and renters in the 1870s and 1880s, this lane of Italianate cottages survived the bulldozers of redevelopment. In the 1930s it was nicknamed "Japan Street".
story:
In September 1874 the Real Estate Associates, San Francisco's biggest home builder of the 1870s, bought the block west of what is now Cottage Row for $25,250. The company divided it into 23 lots, built houses on them and sold them in 1875 [1]. The firm aimed at working people, with easy credit and plenty of advertising [1]. Next door, the developer Col. Charles L. Taylor put up 2101–2107 Bush in 1874. In 1882 he added 2109–2111 Bush and the six two-story houses of 1–6 Cottage Row, which he rented out for about a dozen years [1].

In the 1930s the lane was nicknamed "Japan Street", because its houses were owned by Japanese immigrants and Japanese Americans. The small park on the row, once the site of a house, was created around 1942 [1].

After the war the Redevelopment Agency bulldozed much of the Western Addition around it. From 1966 to 1976, though, the agency's residential rehabilitation chief, Enid Sales, saved more than 350 Victorians with low-cost loans and free architectural help. Cottage Row and 2101–2125 Bush are among the houses her program restored [2].

title: Where Stanford's medical school was born
place: Cooper Medical College site, Sacramento & Webster Sts
hook: For 77 years, Stanford trained its doctors on this corner of Pacific Heights, not in Palo Alto.
story:
In 1858 Dr. Elias Samuel Cooper founded the first medical school on the West Coast, in a building on Mission Street [1]. When he died in 1862 the school faded. His nephew, Levi Cooper Lane, revived it in 1870, and in 1882 he gave it a new building at Webster and Sacramento streets, renamed Cooper Medical College [1]. Lane went on to add a hospital, a nursing school and the endowed Lane Medical Library [1].

Dr. Charles Ellinwood, a Civil War surgeon who founded the Marine Hospital in the Presidio, taught physiology here and later became the college's president [2]. In 1908 Cooper Medical College was given to Stanford University, and it became Stanford's medical department. The school did not move to the Palo Alto campus until 1959 [1].

The original building, described as a "Dickensian Gothic structure," was torn down around 1970 [2]. Albert Pissis's Classical Revival library of 1912 still stands at 2395 Sacramento, and it is now city Landmark No. 115 [3].

title: A bear cub loose on Sacramento Street
place: Sacramento and Webster Streets
hook: At two in the morning a patrolman met a young bear near Sacramento and Webster. His pistol misfired, and the bear slipped away into the scrub.
story:
In January 1883 this corner was not yet the Pacific Heights of mansions and boutiques. On January 20 the Daily Alta California reported that "residents of the Western Addition are excited over the pranks of a young bear" [1].

At about two o'clock the previous morning, Patrolman Russell spotted the animal near Sacramento and Webster streets. The paper said the bear "escaped being shot on account of the officer's pistol missing fire." It then went over a fence and "disappeared in the chaparral." Sergeant Fleming took a squad of officers out to hunt for the cub, but they could not find it [1]. The report does not say what became of it.

Photographs taken from the slopes of what is now Lafayette Park around 1860 and 1870 show how open this country still was [2]. By 1883, as FoundSF's editors put it, "enough chaparral remained to hide a small bear" [1].

title: A cable car to the dunes' edge
place: Haight and Stanyan streets, park entrance
hook: In 1883 a railroad baron's cable line reached the sand at Stanyan, and steam trains carried the weekend crowds on to the ocean.
story: Until 1883 the Haight was mostly isolated farms and acres of sand dunes. Then the Haight Street cable line was finished, linking the east end of Golden Gate Park with Market Street and downtown [1]. It belonged to Leland Stanford and his associates, who had bought the Market Street Railroad in 1882 and switched it to cable [2]. At Stanyan, riders could go further. Grading for the Park and Ocean Railroad began on October 5, 1883. This steam extension of the Haight cable line ran around the southern edge of the park to the beach, and needed a short tunnel under the park drive that was built in three weeks. Service began on December 1, and papers said thousands rode to the beach on its first Sunday [3]. The 1983 National Register nomination for a nearby hotel puts its terminal just inside the park between Haight and Waller, and calls it the first public service to the beach [4]. The line joined the Market Street Railway in 1894 and was electrified around 1899 or 1900 (sources differ) [2][3]. One of its steam locomotives, Southern Pacific No. 20, was preserved at Travel Town Museum in 1954 [3].

title: Gaslights Still Burning on Haight Street
place: 188-198 Haight Street
hook: Two Victorian houses and a barn stayed in one family for a century, with working gaslights, a copper bathtub and Army blankets from 1906.
story: At 188 and 198 Haight Street stand two single-family houses and a barn, built in 1883 and 1889 and kept by the same family for about a century, until 1983 [1]. One is Italianate with a mansard roof and Eastlake detail, and the other is fully Eastlake [1]. The real surprise is inside. The landmark record calls the interiors a virtual time capsule of late-19th-century life. The upstairs bedrooms still have working gaslights, and the kitchen and baths keep their original fixtures, including a copper bathtub, along with the original carpets, wallpaper and custom-made furniture [1]. Only partial electrification was ever added [1]. The houses also hold a memory of 1906. At 2:00 a.m. on April 19, as the fire spread west, the Lagan family was ordered to leave, and the flames were stopped two blocks to the east [1]. Soldiers from the Presidio then slept in the barn, and the landmark record says blankets marked 'U.S. Army' are still there [1]. The complex became city Landmark No. 164 on November 6, 1983, the same year the family's ownership ended [1][2].

title: Layman's Folly: a castle on the summit
place: Pioneer Park, summit of Telegraph Hill
hook: For twenty years a wooden German castle crowned Telegraph Hill, reached by its own cable railway. Locals had a name for both.
story: After the telegraph station blew down in 1870, twenty-two merchants and civic-minded San Franciscans bought the hilltop in 1876 to keep it open, and named it Pioneer Park [1]. Frederick O. Layman had a more commercial idea. In 1883 he built a wooden castle up here in the German style, meant to be an observatory and restaurant, along with a cable car line to carry customers up the slope [2][3]. The cable line stopped running in 1887. Residents called both the castle and the railway 'Layman's Folly' [2][3]. The castle survived another sixteen years and burned on 25 July 1903 [2]. The fire may have left a mark. Julius Roz and his architect Louis Mastropasqua both arrived from Italy in 1902, and records suggest Layman's castle helped inspire Julius' Castle, the turreted restaurant they built lower on the hill at Greenwich and Montgomery two decades later [2].

title: Planting a forest on the dunes
place: Presidio forest, southern ridges
hook: The Presidio's famous forest is not natural. An Army major designed it in 1883 to make the base look larger and the government mightier.
story: The Presidio of the 1870s was bare dune and grassland [1]. In March 1883 Major W. A. Jones proposed planting trees across it, with Golden Gate Park as his model [1]. His aims were frankly theatrical. He wanted to 'crown the ridges' and cover the sand and marsh with a forest that would 'appear immensely larger than it really is'. He also ringed the entrances with dense woods to 'accentuate the idea of the power of the Government' [1]. The first mass planting came on California's first Arbor Day in 1886, after Jones had been transferred, and Adolph Sutro donated 3,000 trees [1]. By 1892 the Army claimed 329,975 trees planted [1]. Not everyone was pleased. That year the post commander, Colonel William Graham, complained that the trees used up training ground and that the thickets hid 'tramps' [1]. In 1895 a real-estate journal called the eucalyptus along the southern boundary an eyesore that blocked 'the finest view in the country' [1]. By 1902 Jones himself was urging heavy thinning, and suggested the Army 'leave the sand dune just as it is' [1]. The planting was part of an 1880s drive to beautify the post [2].

title: The Letters That Shamed a Railroad
place: Site of the Colton (later Huntington) house, California & Taylor (now Huntington Park)
hook: A railroad lawyer's Nob Hill house held a stack of private letters. After he died, a lawsuit made them public.
story: David Colton, the Central Pacific's chief counsel, built a relatively restrained house across Taylor Street from Charles Crocker's mansion [1]. He was mocked as the "Half" in the railroad's "Big Four and a Half" [2]. Sources disagree on who was first to build on the hilltop: one credits Colton with the first railroad mansion [2], while FoundSF says Leland Stanford led the way in 1876. Colton died in October 1878 [2]. His files held a long run of private letters from Collis Huntington, the partner who spent most of his time in Washington looking after the railroad's interests. When litigation opened those files in 1883, the letters became a public embarrassment. They described lobbying, payoffs and bribes to officials in frank, profane detail [3]. They did not prove that money actually changed hands, but they showed how the Big Four did business [3]. Huntington later bought the Colton house and rarely used it [1]. After it burned in 1906, his widow Arabella gave the land to the city in 1915, and it is now Huntington Park [4].

title: The wallpaper man's house keeps its wallpaper
place: Frank G. Edwards House, 1366 Guerrero St
hook: A forty-niner turned paper-hanger built a house on Guerrero in 1883, and the paper he chose is still on the parlour walls.
story: Frank G. Edwards had lived in New York, St. Louis and New Orleans before he arrived in San Francisco in 1852 on the clipper Eureka [1]. He spent two years looking for gold, then went to work as a paper-hanger. In 1859 he opened his own firm selling wallpaper and imported furniture [1]. He also joined the Mechanics' Institute, the Vigilance Committee of 1856, Pennsylvania Fire Company No. 12 and the Dashaway temperance society [1]. In 1883 Edwards had architect Joseph Gosling design a ten-room, flat-front Italianate house, built by the carpenter Florence Crowley. It was one of the first buildings on its block, set back behind a brick retaining wall on a lot that once ran nearly 170 feet along Guerrero [1][2]. Front yards were unusual in this crowded neighbourhood [1]. The inside is rarer still. The original wallpaper survives, along with the marble fireplaces, a gold-leaf moulding and the mahogany bookcases [1][2]. San Francisco Architectural Heritage holds a preservation easement on the house. At the time of writing it was the only one of its more than 50 easements that also protected interior features [2].

title: Whale oil and corset stays at 16th Street
place: Arctic Oil Works, Illinois Street between 16th and 17th streets
hook: Before petroleum, San Francisco's streets and machines ran on whales, and they were boiled down right here at the bay's edge.
story: In 1883 the Arctic Oil Works opened on Illinois Street between 16th and 17th streets, at the edge of the bay. It refined oil from whales, seals and elephant seals. Before electricity, and before the petroleum industry took off in the 1890s, that oil lit streetlamps and lubricated factory machinery [1]. Steam schooners tied up at the works' T-shaped pier, with Mission Rock visible just offshore [1][2]. Nothing was wasted. An 1890 drawing shows baleen, the bristly plates from whales' jaws, drying in the yard along 16th Street. It would be cut into stays for corsets, collars and umbrellas, and into buggy whips [1][2]. The works also has an unexpected place in architectural history. Ernest L. Ransome, the pioneer of reinforced concrete, is credited with a building here in 1884, which an architecture guide called the first reinforced-concrete building of its kind in the United States [3].

title: Yellow Cars and Green Cars to the Park
place: McAllister cable powerhouse block (McAllister, Central, Fulton and Masonic)
hook: In the 1880s, bright yellow cable cars on McAllister and green ones on Hayes turned a windy fringe into a place where the wealthy wanted to live.
story:
Cable traction reached the Western Addition in 1883. That year the old horse-drawn Market Street Railway became the Market Street Cable Railway [1][2]. Its McAllister Street line opened in late 1883. It ran from the Ferry Building out Market and McAllister to Central Avenue, then crossed its own powerhouse block on a private right of way and continued out Fulton to Golden Gate Park [2]. The powerhouse and car barn filled most of the block bounded by Fulton, McAllister, Masonic and Central [1].

On May 26, 1886, a Hayes Street line followed. It had its own powerhouse and a 33-car barn very near the McAllister plant [1][2]. Each line had its own colour, so riders could spot their car on crowded Market Street. McAllister cars were bright yellow, Hayes cars green and Haight Street cars red [1].

The effect on the neighbourhood was fast. Historian Joe Pecora writes that the 1880s building boom around Alamo Square "coincided with the arrival of the cable and horse cars down Hayes and McAllister Streets" [3]. The Planning Department credits the cable car with drawing the wealthy to the park's views and weather [4]. The McAllister powerhouse later served as a streetcar barn until 1948 [2].

title: A Catalog Obelisk for Forgotten Sailors
place: Seamen's Memorial, Lincoln Park Golf Course (15th green), below the Legion of Honor parking lot
hook: In the middle of a golf green stands a tall Victorian obelisk for sailors buried here. The man who paid for it may have ordered it from a catalog.
story: In 1884 Rebecca Lambert, a sea captain's widow, asked Henry Cogswell to pay for a monument over the plot where the Ladies' Seamen's Friend Society buried sailors, on a hill looking out to the Golden Gate [1][3]. Cogswell was a millionaire dentist, a '49er and a champion of temperance. San Francisco already knew him for the temperance fountains he gave the city, topped with a figure that looked suspiciously like him. In 1894 a gang of young journalists lassoed one at Market and Drumm and pulled it down [1]. Accounts of the size differ. Lenhart describes a 15-foot iron monument; historian John Martini calls it a bronze column about seventeen feet tall [1][2]. It has maritime motifs on every side. Martini found a maker's mark and learned it was a catalog item, with side panels you could swap to suit whoever you were mourning [2]. Merchant sailors were among the most exploited workers of the 19th-century port, and many died with nothing [2]. The city's landmark report sees the obelisk as Victorian 'sentimentality, melancholy, romanticism, and didactic moralism' [3]. The graves were never all moved [3]. Today it stands on the 15th green, and along with the Chinese funerary shrine it is one of the only visible traces of the old cemetery [1][4].

title: Hay scows and a city of horses
place: Former Hay Wharf, north side of Channel Street between Second and Third streets
hook: Before cars, San Francisco ran on horses, and their feed came up Mission Creek by the scow-load, with sailors' pipes starting fires on the pier.
story: A horse-drawn city needed mountains of hay. It came by water, in flat-bottomed scow schooners that could slide over mudflats on the tide to load bales along creeks and sloughs from Petaluma to Sacramento and Milpitas [1][2]. Nobody wanted the hay men as neighbours. 'The hay dealers make a warehouse of wharves, landing their hay and keeping it there until it is peddled off,' the San Francisco Call complained in 1876. The supervisors had promised the China Basin area to the harbor commission for the hay dealers, then reneged [1]. By 1884 they finally had their own wharf, angling into Channel Street from Pope & Talbot's lumber yard between Second and Third. A dozen or more scows could be seen tied up there at once, two or three abreast [1][2]. One scow, the 65-foot Annie L., built in 1900 by Emil Munder, brought in more than 350 bales at a time [1]. In a single week in 1896 three fires broke out on the hay wharf, blamed on scow men knocking out their pipes [1]. Kiel-born seaman Fred Klebingat, who arrived on the waterfront in 1909, remembered cheap restaurants and saloons at the foot of Third Street. That year a scow out of control pushed its bowsprit through his cabin porthole and then backed out again [1].

title: Is it a disgrace to be born Chinese?
place: Spring Valley School, 1451 Jackson St
hook: In 1884 a principal on Jackson Street turned away eight-year-old Mamie Tape. Her parents sued and won, and the city still kept her out.
story: Spring Valley, founded in 1852, bills itself as the oldest school in California and the only one of seven schools founded in Gold Rush days still operating [1]. In September 1884 Joseph and Mary Tape tried to enroll their eldest daughter, eight-year-old Mamie, at its primary school [2][3]. Both parents had come from China as children. Joseph ran a delivery business, Mary had been raised in a home for destitute girls, and the family lived among white neighbours at Black Point, in today's Cow Hollow [2]. Principal Jennie Hurley refused, citing the school board's policy against Chinese pupils [2]. The Tapes sued, and in March 1885 the California Supreme Court agreed that state law opened public schools to "all children" [2][3]. The board simply pushed a new state law through allowing separate schools for Chinese children, with Superintendent Andrew Moulder warning that classes would be "inundated with Mongolians" [2]. When the Tapes tried again, Hurley pleaded crowding and missing vaccination papers. Mary wrote to the Alta California: "Is it a disgrace to be born a Chinese? Didn't God make us all!!!" [2]. Five days later the Chinese Primary School opened in Chinatown, and Mamie was enrolled there. She never attended Spring Valley [2].

title: James Lick's Promise to Women
place: Lick Old Ladies Home, later University Mound Ladies Home, 350 University Street
hook: One of California's richest men left $100,000 for elderly women with no means. It was twice what he first planned, because a friend's wife asked him to double it.
story: When James Lick died in 1876, his fortune was conservatively put at $3 million. His will paid $700,000 for the Lick Observatory, and $100,000 for a San Francisco home for 'aged and needy ladies' [1]. The idea came from Mary Staples. Her husband, David J. Staples, helped Lick draft the will. According to the historian (and later mayor) Edward Robeson Taylor, Lick asked her whether she had any request. She proposed a home for aged women, and Lick set aside $50,000, then doubled it when she asked [1][2]. Trustees bought the empty three-storey college on University Mound, with 25 acres, and incorporated in November 1884 [1]. A $300 payment bought care for life, but only women in reasonably good health were admitted [1]. The residents kept cows, pigs and chickens, grew hay and vegetables, and rode a horse and carriage to the nearest cable-car line [1]. By 1888 the May Day bazaar drew carriage after carriage of visitors. They bought the ladies' crocheted tidies and picked 'golden eschscholtzias', California poppies [1]. The home kept going for 130 years and closed in 2014 [2].

title: The house that named a district
place: Site of George Turner Marsh's 'Richmond House', SE corner 12th Ave & Clement St
hook: An Australian-born dealer in Japanese art kept carrier pigeons, sent messages home by bird, and named his sand-dune estate after a suburb of Melbourne. The whole neighbourhood took the name.
story: George Turner Marsh was born near Melbourne in 1857. At 15, on his family's voyage to America, he begged to be left behind in Yokohama, and he stayed there until 1876. Back in San Francisco he opened what was probably the first Asian-art gallery in the United States [1]. He married Lucy Whiteside in 1880, and the couple built a home in the foggy 'Outside Lands'. It grew into a big estate at the southeast corner of 12th Avenue and Clement Street, with an ornamental stream, orchard and stables. The Newsom Brothers built a large house there in late 1886 [1]. Marsh rode to work downtown carrying pigeons. In the afternoon he sent one home to tell Lucy when he would be back and whether guests were coming for dinner [1]. He called the estate 'Richmond House', after the Melbourne suburb where he was born. In 1884 local property owners, tired of 'Outside Lands', chose 'Richmond' for the growing area, and in 1890 the supervisors made it official [1]. Some later accounts credit booster George R. Fletcher with the idea instead [1][2]. A 1917 ordinance renamed it 'Park-Presidio', but the new name never caught on. The city officially restored 'Richmond' in 2009 [1][2].

title: The smell of malt on Chestnut Street
place: Bauer & Schweitzer malt house, 530-550 Chestnut St
hook: German brewers made beer on this block from the 1860s on, and the malting went on long enough to supply Anchor Steam.
story: In the 1860s nearly everyone in San Francisco's beer trade was German, and small breweries sprang up wherever Germans settled [1]. The 500 block of Chestnut was home to brewers and maltsters from at least 1867, when the Lyon Brewery set up there [2]. Sources give different dates for the next step. The city's landmark resolution says John Bauer and Joseph Schweitzer replaced the brewery with the Empire Malt House in 1884, while a Telegraph Hill Dwellers history says Bauer took over the premises in 1878 [1][2]. Freight cars came up a spur from Jefferson Street to be loaded [1]. In 1906 the plant was fitted with malting equipment based on French designs from the 1860s, and then the earthquake and fire almost destroyed it [2]. Bauer's son George, a Navy militia captain, called up 800 sailors to patrol the waterfront during the disaster [1]. The concrete plant rebuilt in 1908 kept malting until 1981. By then it was the last barrel-malting works west of the Mississippi, and one of its customers had been Anchor Brewing [1][2].

title: A Reservoir Burnham Wanted as a Mirror
place: University Mound Reservoir, North Basin (University and Bacon streets)
hook: Since 1885 a reservoir has sat on top of the Portola's hill. San Francisco's most famous planner wanted to turn it into the centrepiece of a park.
story: In 1885 the Spring Valley Water Company finished a reservoir basin on top of University Mound. The federal dam inventory still lists the North Basin with that completion year [1]. A 44-inch pipe fed it with water from Crystal Springs Reservoir in San Mateo County [2]. In 1905 Daniel Burnham's plan for San Francisco saw beauty in the site. He proposed a 218-acre 'University Mound Park' with 'luxuriant vegetation' and wrote: 'Advantage should be taken of the reservoir, which could be used in vista as a mirror for the park'. Like his proposed Hunter's Point Park, it was to be laid out with level contour roadways and terraces [3]. In September 1913 city photographer Horace Chaffee recorded the reservoir's buildings and photographed cracks in its slope [4].

title: A Row-House Builder Builds for Himself
place: 280 Divisadero Street (Charles L. Hinkel House)
hook: The Hinkels built rows of Italianate houses from Pacific Heights to Eureka Valley. For his own home, Charles Lewis Hinkel took a double lot and went big.
story: The Hinkel family built houses for four generations. Charles E. Hinkel, a German immigrant, set up as a residential builder in San Francisco. His son Charles Lewis Hinkel (1847–1908) carried on the trade, and later his three sons and a grandson did too. Rows of Hinkel-built Italianates still stand from Pacific Heights through the Western Addition to Eureka Valley [1]. Hoodline reports that the Hinkel brothers bought up lots, built well-made homes and sold them to middle- and upper-class buyers, and together put up hundreds of houses [2]. In 1885 Charles Lewis built his own house at 280 Divisadero, between Haight and Page, as one of the earliest buildings on the street [1][2]. He used a 50-by-137.5-foot lot, twice the standard 25-by-100, which left room for landscaping and a carriage house. The house rises four storeys in a transitional Second Empire style, finished even on its side and rear walls [1][2]. Hard times came later: a 4-inch concrete slab was poured over the hardwood floors, but brass speaking tubes linking the carriage house, kitchen and laundry still worked [2]. The house became a city landmark in 1988 [3].

title: A hospital run by and for women
place: 3700 California Street (former Children's Hospital, later CPMC California Campus)
hook: Refused by the city's medical society, three women doctors started their own dispensary. It grew into a hospital on California Street with its own nursing school.
story:
In 1875 Drs. Charlotte Blake Brown, Sara E. Brown and Martha E. Bucknell opened the Pacific Dispensary for Women and Children at 520 Taylor Street [1][2]. Women doctors treated women and children there, with care free and only medicine charged for [2]. Charlotte Blake Brown had been turned down by the San Francisco Medical Society because she was a woman [2]. In 1880 the dispensary opened the first training school for nurses west of the Rockies [1].

In 1885 it was reincorporated as the Hospital for Children and Training School for Nurses. Its stated purposes included "the advancement of women in medicine" [1]. It then moved to 3700 California Street. One account dates the move to 1885, another to 1887 [3][4]. The 1906 earthquake badly damaged the building, and a new one opened on the same site in 1911 [3]. The hospital became an important centre for polio treatment, with the first Drinker respirator, or "iron lung", in the western United States [3].

By its centennial in 1975, Children's Hospital had grown to 362 beds [1]. In 1991 Children's Hospital merged with Presbyterian Hospital, and the combined institution became California Pacific Medical Center [4].

title: A sailors' declaration from a lumber pile
place: Folsom Street Wharf, foot of Folsom Street
hook: Sailors could be drugged, shanghaied and treated as virtual slaves at sea. In 1885 they climbed onto a lumber pile here and declared their independence.
story: In the 1880s San Francisco was the busiest port on the West Coast, and supplying sailors was a racket run by boarding-house keepers called crimps [1]. A seaman who went on a binge could wake up at sea, signed aboard by a crimp who pocketed his wages [1]. At sea the captain's power was near absolute; as late as 1897 the U.S. Supreme Court ruled sailors outside the Thirteenth Amendment's ban on involuntary servitude [1]. The radical lawyer Burnette Haskell harangued sailors from a soapbox on the waterfront between Howard and Harrison, and on March 6, 1885, from a lumber pile on the Folsom Street Wharf, the Coast Seamen's Union was founded with a 'Sailors' Declaration of Independence' [1][2]. A dour Norwegian, Andrew Furuseth, joined that June and led the union from 1887 [2][3]. In 1891 it merged with the steamship sailors to form the Sailors' Union of the Pacific, which still exists [2][3]. Furuseth's long campaign produced the Seamen's Act of 1915 [3]. In 1901 he told striking sailors, 'There is no other way of having peace except by fighting for it' [4].

title: Line Upon Line of Collapsing Headboards
place: Former potter's field, high ground of Lincoln Park near the Legion of Honor
hook: Reporters came out to the paupers' graves and found no trees, no grass, only numbered boards leaning in the wind. Then the new neighbours wanted the dead gone.
story: Every so often a newspaper sent a reporter out to the City Cemetery. As historian John Martini sums up their stories, some sections were well tended, especially the Serbian and Jewish plots. The potter's field was different. At least 11,000 of the city's poor lay there, on the high ground where the Legion of Honor stands now. There was no tree and no grass, just row after row of faded, collapsing headboards, with paper and rubbish blowing between them [1]. Many indigent graves had a numbered wooden marker instead of a name [2]. Then the city came closer. Railroads reached the ocean, and one line ran around Lands End just below the cemetery. That was good for families visiting their dead. For anyone building a house nearby, it was bad for property values. Early in the 1880s, Martini says, the Richmond Association took up the cry that the cemetery had to go [1]. There were also stories of homeless people living at the cemetery's edge, who ate the food left after Chinese funerals [1]. The city banned new burials in 1898 [2], but thousands of the poor were never moved [2].

title: The King of the Potrero
place: Irish Hill, east of Illinois Street between 20th and 22nd
hook: A saloon-keeper who controlled jobs at the shipyard, two rival brothers, streets of blue mud and a pistol shot that missed.
story: Irish Hill was a rough little neighbourhood of boarding houses and saloons on a rise 90 feet above the shipyards east of Illinois Street. You reached it by climbing 98 steps [1][2]. Its unofficial ruler was Frank McManus. He had fled the Irish famine, arrived in 1865 and, so the rumour went, won the Union Hotel in a card game. The papers called him the "King of the Potrero". Anyone who wanted a job at Union Iron Works had to go through McManus, board at his hotel and drink at his saloon [1]. In 1885 the brothers Thomas and John Welsh opened two rival hotel-saloons, one right behind the Union Hotel. They were Democrats; McManus was a Republican. The feud that followed was fought with fists, knives, clubs and arson, in streets that turned to blue mud when it rained. It became known as the Blue Mud Wars [1]. In the final battle, in 1892, McManus fired a gun at Thomas Welsh at point-blank range and missed [1]. In 1894 his brother Cornelius was stabbed to death in a bar fight at the Union Hotel, and Frank drank himself to death, dying at 57 [1]. Saturday nights also brought bare-knuckle fights, held outside Gately's San Quentin House or Mike Boyles' Steam Beer Dump, depending on the account [1][2].

title: The Milliner's House That Moved Around the Corner
place: 1153 Oak Street
hook: Sarah Mish, a downtown milliner since 1854, had her $15,000 Stick-Eastlake house moved off its Divisadero corner and onto Oak Street.
story: From 1854 Sarah Mish ran a dressmaking and millinery business downtown, moving between premises on Kearny, Geary, Market and Dupont Streets, and she also sold wholesale along the coast [1]. Her husband Phenes imported dry goods and was president of Congregation Sherith Israel from 1881 to 1885 [1]. In 1885 the couple built a Stick-Eastlake house on the corner of Oak and Divisadero, designed by McDougall and Son at a cost of $15,000, and the city directory listed them at 407 Divisadero [1]. Phenes died in 1895. In 1897 Sarah had the house moved onto another lot she owned on Oak Street, at a cost of $1,700, and shops and flats went up on the old corner. Some later accounts date the move to 1889 [1][2]. Sarah died on January 2, 1916, and her heirs sold the house in 1928 [1]. It became a rooming house, then as many as 14 apartments, and part of it housed a dance school in 1930 [1][2]. Along the way it lost its mansard roof, and it was damaged by a fire in the 1950s [1]. The city made it Landmark No. 62 in 1974 [3]. The next year the Preservation Group restored it, fitting fifty new windows and restoring its 14-foot ceilings [1].

title: The last farm in Cow Hollow
place: Abraham House, 30 Blackstone Court (off Franklin near Lombard)
hook: Behind a Lombard Street hotel hides a gated alley on a trail older than the street grid, where a nurseryman grew plants until 1947.
story: Just off Franklin near Lombard, behind a hotel, a gated blind alley called Blackstone Court runs at an odd angle to the street grid. It follows an early trail that led from town toward the Presidio around the north end of Washerwoman's Lagoon, which was drained and filled long ago [1][2]. In 1885 Charles Abraham built a house at No. 30 and enlarged it in 1905. He also founded the Western Nursery, which operated on most of the block from 1885 to 1947. It was the last agricultural business in a district that had taken its name from dairy cows [1][2]. Next door, the building at 9-11 Blackstone Court appears to date from the 1850s and may have been moved here. It is first documented on the site in 1893. Before 1899 the Favilla family from North Beach raised it a story. They were very early Italian American residents of what became the Marina [1]. FoundSF credits the nursery with saving the court: Abraham's business held the land, and when postwar housing demand shrank the parcel, the five surviving buildings were kept and designated a historic district in 1987 [2]. An Australian peppermint tree and a Monterey cypress appear to date from the nursery [1]. The court is private property and closed to casual visitors [1].

title: A ferry captain's farmhouse
place: Leale House, 2475 Pacific Ave
hook: A captain who logged over a million miles on 18-minute bay crossings retired to an old dairy farmhouse, and built himself a ship's cabin in the garden.
story:
Set back from Pacific Avenue among the mansions is one of the oldest houses in San Francisco. It was probably built around 1853 as the main house of a dairy farm, though historians disagree about exactly when it went up [1][2].

From the 1880s until 1964 it belonged to the family of Captain John Leale. Sources disagree on the date: NoeHill says he bought it in 1883, while the Bloomfields date the family's ownership from 1886 [1][2]. Leale spent 34 years as a San Francisco Bay ferry captain. In his memoir, Recollections of a Tule Sailor, he counted more than 125,000 round trips and over a million miles, on crossings scheduled to take 18 minutes [2]. His daughter Marian remembered him as "punctilious, spartan, commanding" [2].

The family added the porch, bay windows and rear extension between 1899 and 1913 [2]. In retirement the captain entertained friends at the back of the garden in a replica ship's cabin made from parts salvaged from old vessels, porthole included [1][2]. The farmhouse remains, surrounded by the city that grew up around it.

title: Brownstone, Bronze and a Full-Time Polisher
place: James C. Flood Mansion (Pacific-Union Club), 1000 California Street
hook: A silver king shipped his walls from Connecticut and hired a servant just to polish the fence. That stone later outlasted the 1906 fire.
story: James C. Flood was one of the "Silver Kings" who struck it rich on the Comstock Lode, and in 1886 he finished a townhouse on Nob Hill that outshone its neighbours [1][3]. Historians William Issel and Robert Cherny call it the most ostentatious house on the hill: it cost $1.5 million, was built of brownstone brought from Connecticut, and was ringed by a $30,000 bronze fence that needed a full-time servant just to keep it polished [1]. The house filled a whole block bounded by California, Cushman, Mason and Sacramento streets, and has been called the first brownstone west of the Mississippi [3]. Its neighbours were Crockers, Hopkinses, Stanfords and Huntingtons; as a 1968 Junior League survey put it, the hill's householders "may well have represented the majority interest" in California [1]. In 1906 its stone walls made it the only great Nob Hill house to survive the fire, and the Pacific-Union Club bought the shell and had Willis Polk rebuild it [2]. It is still the club's home. NoeHill notes drily that it is "decidedly not open to the public. Not ever." [2]

title: California's First Arbor Day on a Bald Island
place: Summit of Yerba Buena Island, Signal Rd
hook: Goats and woodcutters had stripped the island bare. A poet rallied the city to plant a forest here in the shape of a cross.
story:
Picture Yerba Buena Island with no eucalyptus. After decades of goat grazing and oak cutting it was almost bare. The National Register calls it "a barren wasteland" [1][2]. The poet Joaquin Miller campaigned to replant it, along with the Presidio and Black Point. The island was his main focus, and the planting was laid out as a Greek cross centred on the summit [2]. One newspaper said it was to remind people "that we all have some cross to bear" [2].

The planting became California's first Arbor Day. The National Register and City Guides date it to 27 November 1886 [1][3]. The Navy's study says 5 March 1887 [2]. Ex-Governor Perkins, General Howard and Adolph Sutro were there. The elderly General Mariano Vallejo was to give the main address but could not climb the hill in time, so someone else read his speech. He did reach the top in time to plant a tree [2]. The summit trees died from exposure and later a fire, but some of the lower plantings are thought to survive in today's forest [2].

title: Crusader panels on Mansion Row
place: Stone House, 1348 South Van Ness Ave (formerly 2818 Howard St)
hook: Before it was South Van Ness, lower Howard Street was a row of mansions, with frescoed ceilings, a legendary Japanese bird and a lawyer's diamond.
story: In the 1880s, well-off San Franciscans built grand houses along Howard Street in the Mission. The city's landmarks board called it "Mansion Row" [2]. City Architect Charles Havens designed his own French Second Empire house and carriage house at what is now 1381 South Van Ness in 1884 [2]. Two years later, attorney Frank M. Stone commissioned architect Seth Babson to design a Stick and Queen Anne house across the street, on a lot with rare front and side yards [1]. The 1887 book Artistic Homes of California described brass panels in the hall showing a Crusader's departure and return. It also described a drawing-room ceiling painted as a sunburst, with a "peacock-plumaged" bird flying into the rays [1]. Stone had sailed out of Boston as a supercargo before arriving in 1874 to study law [1]. After he won a conviction in a Chinatown hatchet-murder case, the victim's Fong family collected money across California and gave him a solitaire diamond [1]. When the house became a landmark in 1975, almost all of the described interior, including the frescoes, survived [1]. Howard Street's lower stretch was renamed South Van Ness in 1939 [1].

title: A goddess on the city's centre
place: Mount Olympus, Upper Terrace
hook: Adolph Sutro put a 12-foot Goddess of Liberty on Mount Olympus. A sci-fi novelist hid a time-travel sleeping chamber in her base.
story: On Thanksgiving Day, November 24, 1887, a crowd climbed Mount Olympus, the hill then said to mark San Francisco's geographic centre [1][2]. The land belonged to Adolph Sutro. He had ordered a copy of a work by the Belgian artist Antoine Wiertz: a 12-foot Goddess of Liberty with a torch in one raised hand and a sword in the other, standing over a man said to represent evil. It was called the Triumph of Light [1]. The mayor and supervisors came, along with the Presidio band and the pupils of the Sanchez Street school. Judge Solomon Hedenfeldt declared that "liberty is not license, is not anarchy." Poet Ella S. Cummins read verses ending "let there be light and liberty." Sutro made the schoolchildren the statue's permanent custodians and deeded the hilltop plot to the city [1]. That same year, Presidio officer Alvarado M. Fuller published a science-fiction novel, A.D. 2000. Its hero sleeps from the 1880s into the 2000s in a chamber inside the new statue's base [1]. By 1954 the city's Art Commission called the battered statue "beyond repair". It was removed and never replaced, so only the empty pedestal remains [1][2].

title: First Mass in a dance hall
place: Star of the Sea Church, 4420 Geary Blvd (parish began at 9th Ave & Geary)
hook: The Richmond's Irish dairy families had nowhere to worship. So on Easter Sunday 1887 they held Mass upstairs in Farrell's Dance Hall.
story: In the 1880s the land along Point Lobos Road was sand, fog and dairy ranches. Locals nicknamed it 'Pneumonia Gulch', and many of the ranchers were Irish [1]. Catholic families made the long trip to Old St. Mary's, or to the Holy Cross cemetery chapel on Eddy Street. In 1886, forty-one families decided they were 'strong enough' to support a church of their own [1]. The first Mass was said on Easter Sunday 1887 on the second floor of Farrell's Dance Hall at Ninth Avenue and Geary. Within a year the congregation had built a 500-seat wooden church for $10,000 [1]. The original Star of the Sea faced Eighth Avenue, behind the site of today's church. In the 1890s it was the only church near Point Lobos Avenue [2]. It became a full parish in 1894 under Father John P. Coyle, the first San Francisco-born man ordained a Catholic priest. Coyle led it through the 1906 earthquake and the growth that followed [1]. His successor, Father Philip O'Ryan from County Tipperary, opened the parish school with the Sisters of St. Joseph in 1909, with 137 children [1]. The present church dates from 1914 [1].

title: Free house plans in the Saturday paper
place: Pelton Cottages, 1002–1014 Tennessee Street (backing onto 903–915 Minnesota)
hook: An architect printed free cottage plans in a working man's newspaper. Thirteen of the little houses still stand in two back-to-back rows in Dogpatch.
story:
Between 1880 and 1883 the "well-known" young architect John Cotter Pelton Jr. published a series called "Cheap Dwellings" in the San Francisco Evening Bulletin, a paper read by laborers and immigrants. It printed floor plans, materials lists and cost estimates for cottages a worker could build on a 20-foot lot. The four-room version came to $854.25 [1]. The Bulletin said every Saturday edition carrying a plan sold out [2]. Architectural historian Christopher VerPlanck calls it the first and only known case of a California architect publishing free workers' house plans in a daily paper [1].

In 1887 the contractor Rees Davis used the four-room design to build two rows back to back, on Tennessee and Minnesota streets near 22nd [1]. Thirteen survive, the largest group of Pelton cottages left, though VerPlanck counted sixteen Pelton-based houses in Dogpatch. They were part of the case for its 2002 historic-district status [1][2][3].

The houses are full of small histories. In 1897 Mr. and Mrs. Peter Hamilton held their tin wedding party at 1010 Tennessee with a piper, Daniel Beaton, among the guests. In 1932 a later owner, Bartolomeo Lazzareschi, was the surprise witness who sealed a murder case [1].

title: Graves leased only until the year 2000
place: Former Calvary Cemetery, western slope of Lone Mountain near Parker Avenue (site of the pauper ground)
hook: In 1887 a Calvary plot cost 60 cents a square foot, and the deed let you stay only until the year 2000. Paupers, suicides and priests each had their ground.
story: Archbishop Joseph Alemany opened Calvary Cemetery in 1860 on a tract that took in Lone Mountain itself. Its first burial, that November, was John Riley, a pauper [1][2]. By 1887 it was the most populous cemetery in San Francisco. Within seventeen years of opening it had taken 23,500 bodies, and the Morning Call described headstones "as thick as standing corn", with three or four funeral processions climbing to the gate on most days [2]. The paper also explained the business side. The Archbishop, the cemetery's sole owner, sold lots at 60 cents a square foot: $10 bought enough ground for a baby, and a small single lot cost about $15 [2]. The deed let a family occupy the lot only until the year 2000, though some deeds promised the right to renew for 300 years more. "There will be very little left of the Calvary graves in A.D. 2000," the reporter predicted [2]. The poor lay in the valley on the western slope under short wooden crosses. Suicides and unbaptised children went into a patch of unconsecrated ground, and priests into a heart-shaped plot called The Heart [2]. The prediction came true early. Removals began in 1938, and by the late 1940s the graves had gone to Colma [3].

title: Ivory cable cars over Castro hill
place: Market and Castro streets
hook: The Castro began as a cable-car suburb, where little steam trains gave way to ivory cars that climbed Castro hill.
story: In the early 1880s you reached empty Eureka Valley by steam dummy, a tiny locomotive in a box pulling one passenger trailer. It ran out Market from Valencia to Castro [1][2]. To push Market through, crews dynamited the hill beside today's Mint at Duboce [1]. In the late 1880s the Southern Pacific-backed Market Street Cable Railway replaced the dummy with a cable line from the Ferry Building up Market and over the Castro Street hill to 26th Street. Sources give its opening as 1886 or 1887 [1][3]. Each Market Street line had its own colour so riders downtown could spot their car. Castro's were ivory, Valencia's blue and Haight's red [1]. The 9-mph ride downtown set off a building boom. Victorian rows went up within walking distance of the stops [1]. Irish, German, British and Scandinavian tradesmen filled the new cottages and flats [3]. After 1906 electric streetcars took over Market, but the hill south of 18th Street was too steep for them. The "Castro Cable" kept running there until April 5, 1941 [2].

title: The Last Powerhouse Still Pulling
place: Cable Car Barn & Powerhouse, 1201 Mason Street at Washington
hook: San Francisco once had about fourteen cable car barns and powerhouses. This brick hulk on Mason Street is the only survivor.
story: Stand on the museum deck at Washington and Mason and you can watch huge winding wheels pull the cables that still run beneath the city's streets [2]. The barn and powerhouse were built between 1885 and 1887, near the site of the original spring and reservoir of the Spring Valley Water Company, which helped supply the city in the 1850s [1]. It first held the cars and machinery of the Powell Street Railway, which merged into the Ferries and Cliff House Railway in 1887 [1]. Some fourteen cable car barns and powerhouses once served San Francisco's lines, and this is the only one left [1]. Until 1906 its engines were driven by steam boilers [1]. The great fire destroyed much of the original three-storey building. It was rebuilt with two storeys and a similar look, and its engines were converted to electric motors [1]. The round chimney on the Washington Street side is a leftover from the steam era [1]. Today the building houses the Cable Car Museum, including grip car No. 8 from Hallidie's Clay Street line [2][3].

title: The Night the Dynamite Ship Blew
place: Cove below the Cliff House (Parallel Point)
hook: An abandoned schooner packed with forty tons of dynamite drifted onto the rocks below the Cliff House. At 12:30 a.m., it was felt in Sacramento.
story: The schooner Parallel left a San Francisco wharf on Wednesday, January 12, 1887, bound for Oregon and illegally packed with a cargo that included forty tons of dynamite powder [1]. Three days of bad weather left her no farther than Lands End. On Saturday evening, caught in a heavy swell, the crew rowed for safety without sending any warning [1]. The empty ship drifted onto a rock in the cove below the Cliff House. Adolph Sutro and other locals went down to help but found no one aboard and went home to wait for morning [2]. Just after midnight on Sunday, January 16, the cargo exploded. The blast was felt as far away as Sacramento, Vacaville and San Jose; the crew watched from Point Bonita across the Gate [1]. The Cliff House lost a wing and most of its windows [3]. Seal Rock House, Sutro Heights and nearby cottages were hit by debris [1]. Nobody died. The next day a crowd estimated as high as 80,000 came hunting relics, and by morning a hand-painted 'Bar Open' sign was up [1]. The bluff became known as Parallel Point [2].

title: The little cable car over the hill
place: Castro Street at 26th Street, site of the cable car turntable
hook: Electric streetcars couldn't climb the Castro hill, so Noe Valley kept its own cable car for 35 years after the rest of Market Street's cable network was gone.
story:
The hill between Eureka and Noe valleys kept Noe Valley out of easy reach until the Market Street Cable Railway brought its line over it. The line ran down Castro to 26th Street. Sources give different opening dates: the city's Axford House report says 1886, and the Noe Valley Voice says 1887 [1][2]. Once it arrived, farmland on the valley floor became rows of Victorians [2].

After the 1906 earthquake, faster electric streetcars replaced the cable lines on Market Street. Castro between 18th and 26th was the exception. It was too steep for electric cars, so it stayed a small cable shuttle. Noe Valley riders took it over the hill to catch streetcars downtown [3].

At 26th Street the cars were turned on a turntable, sometimes with help from local boys. Children called the small cars "Dinkies" [3][4]. The Castro cable made its last run on 5 April 1941, and a bus replaced it [3].

title: Twenty thousand fans at Stanyan Street
place: Site of Haight Street Grounds, Stanyan, Waller, Shrader and Frederick
hook: The blocks across Stanyan from Kezar were once one of San Francisco's earliest ballparks, where the California League drew crowds by the thousand.
story: The ordinary blocks between Stanyan, Waller, Shrader and Frederick were once one of San Francisco's earliest baseball parks. The Haight Street Grounds were built for the California League, and 10,000 fans came to the opening game between the Haverlys and the Pioneers on April 3, 1887. An 1895 newspaper gives the opening as March 24 [1]. The grounds' record crowd is given as 22,000 on November 25, 1889 [1], but a National Register report on the block says crowds of up to 7,000 [2]. This was the league of the moment. In 1888 the Examiner published "Casey at the Bat", and its "Mudville" was a common jab at Stockton, one of the league's four teams [3]. Next door, Harry Heagerty's two-story saloon sat in the curve of the ballpark, right by the ticket office, on the 1892 Sanborn map [2]. The California League folded in 1893. In March 1895 the Call reported that the grounds would be sold for building lots, and the last game was played on March 10, 1895 [1]. The site was to be carved into house lots [1].

title: A Playground for Children and Their Mothers
place: Children's Quarters and Sharon Building, off Bowling Green Drive
hook: Long before playgrounds were ordinary, Victorian San Francisco built a sandstone canteen, swings and a carousel just for children.
story: William Hammond Hall designed a "Children's Quarters" for the park. When John McLaren arrived as Hall's assistant in 1887, landscaping it was one of his first jobs [1]. The centerpiece was designed by the architects George W. Percy and Frederick F. Hamilton: a sandstone building in the Richardsonian Romanesque style that served as a canteen for children and the mothers who brought them [2]. The park's chronology records the plans being accepted in 1887 and the playground dedicated in 1888, with the first carousel in 1889 (it also lists the Sharon Building as completed in 1890) [3]. The playground is often described as the first public children's playground in the United States. It was funded by a bequest from William Sharon, whose name the building still carries [4]. Over the years the quarters offered more than swings. At various times donkeys and goats gave children rides, and chickens lived in an imitation barnyard [1]. The Sharon Building was damaged in 1906 and by fire in 1974, restored both times, and now houses the Sharon Art Studio [2].

title: First Block Ever Cut Up
place: The 'Buckingham Block', 7th–8th Aves between Irving & Judah
hook: A cigar dealer turned developer is often credited with naming the Sunset. The newspapers of 1888 tell a different story.
story: In October 1886 the Richardson Tract, 30 full blocks of dunes south of the park, sold for between $625 and $1,450 a block, and speculators took notice. A year later blocks were worth ten times as much [1]. In April 1888 Buckingham and Company advertised lots on the block bounded by 7th and 8th Avenues and I and J streets (today's Irving and Judah) as the 'First Block Ever Cut Up In This Locality.' $650 bought a lot [2]. Aurelius Buckingham, a former clothing clerk and cigar dealer, is often credited with naming the Sunset. Researcher Angus Macfarlane found no evidence of it: the papers simply called this 'the Buckingham Block' [2]. The name 'Sunset' first appeared in print in February 1889, when Wendell Easton's firm, Easton, Eldridge & Co., suggested 'Sunset Heights' for the Byfield Tract and then auctioned blocks under that name [2]. Easton's advertisement described the sun as it 'dips itself gracefully into its evening bath in the placid Pacific' and 'throws its last kisses' on 'these, the truly Sunset Heights' [1]. Hardly anyone lived here. The 1890 voter register lists only 57 men in today's Sunset and Parkside [1].

title: Five Cents to Ride the Cliffs
place: Lands End Coastal Trail (old Cliff Line railbed)
hook: The city's most scenic railroad clung to the cliffs here, and a five-cent fare let anyone ride it. Then came a fare war, and the landslides.
story: The trail that hikers follow around Lands End was once a railroad bed. In 1888, after two years of construction by Adolph Sutro, a steam line nicknamed 'the Cliff Line' began running along the curving bluffs above the Golden Gate. It was hailed as the city's most scenic railroad. Its inner end was near California Street and Presidio Avenue and its outer end at 48th and Point Lobos avenues. Its five-cent fare, with a free transfer to the cable cars, put the ocean within reach of people of every income [1]. After Southern Pacific took control, it scrapped the transfers in 1894, which doubled the fare downtown to ten cents. Sutro answered by building his own electric railroad. By late 1894 the fare was back to a nickel [1]. A shed-like waiting room went up beside the tracks for walkers heading down to the beach below Lands End [2]. In 1902 Thomas Edison's company filmed a panorama of the Golden Gate from a moving train on the line [3]. The line was electrified in 1905 as the #1 California streetcar. Landslides plagued the cliffs, and in 1925 one closed the Cliff Line [1].
