title: The farmhouse that moved twice
place: 11 Piedmont Street
hook: The Haight's oldest building is said to have been hauled across the city to a pig farm, then moved again up a hill away from the sand fleas.
story: Tucked away on little Piedmont Street, 11 Piedmont is described as the oldest building in the Haight, and it wasn't built here [1]. According to the neighbourhood's architectural walking tour, Peter Schadt sold the Lange family land bounded by Cole, Carl, Stanyan and Grattan streets in 1870, and the Langes ran a pig farm there. When they moved from Divisadero and Sutter to the farm, they brought everything with them, including the family house. In 1888 the house moved again, to its present spot. It was lived in by a Lange daughter, who reportedly chose the site to escape the sand fleas of the flats below. Her parents built a new house that still stands at the southeast corner of Carl and Stanyan [1]. This was still farm country. Photographs of Cole Valley from around 1890 to 1892 show cows grazing below Mount Sutro and a pond at about Parnassus and Cole [2]. A 1956 student history of the district describes ranchers fencing off five to ten acre plots here to raise cattle, sheep, pigs and chickens for the city [3]. Treat the family details as local tradition: the tour text is the only source found for them.

title: The opera house that perhaps never staged opera
place: South San Francisco (Bayview) Opera House, 4705 Third St
hook: The city's oldest surviving theatre opened in 1888 in a district known mainly for slaughterhouses. David Belasco's name is written in the dressing rooms.
story: The South San Francisco Opera House opened on October 24, 1888, with a performance of John W. Sherman's 'Phantasma' [1]. It was designed by Henry Geilfuss, a prolific architect of the city's Victorian era, and is often called the oldest surviving theatre in San Francisco [2]. Beside it stood a Masonic Hall, and lodges and fraternal groups met there from about 1890 to 1930 [3]. In a district most of the city knew only for Butchertown, the pair became the neighbourhood's main place for dances, plays and meetings [3]. Around 1890 residents held a party there to celebrate a new cable-car line to Railroad Avenue, though maps of the time do not show it [1]. Its curtains and backdrops came from well-known theatres downtown, including the old California Theatre [3]. Famous actors played here: David Belasco's name is written in the dressing rooms below the stage, and Pawnee Bill's Wild West Show also came [3]. The name may be grander than the programme. The city's 1968 landmark description says no opera was ever performed here, but FoundSF says it hosted several [3][4]. It survived 1906 and became City Landmark No. 8 [2][3].

title: The steam schooners of Berry Street
place: Alexander Hay's shipyard, Fifth and Berry streets
hook: Fifty-six caulkers and shipwrights paused on the hull of the Ajax for a rare photograph of shipbuilding on Mission Creek.
story: In the late 1880s, amid the lumber schooners and hay scows crowding Channel Street, shipwrights built a new kind of vessel. Alexander Hay ran two yards on the creek, one at Fifth and Berry with its launching ways into the water and another between Sixth and Seventh streets, beside the yard of Boole and Beaton [1]. In 1887 and 1888 alone Hay turned out steam schooners with names like Alcazar, Navarro, Point Arena, Pasadena and Mendocino. A clipping from 1887 describes the Pasadena: 150 feet long, built of Oregon pine with eastern oak posts, able to carry 400,000 feet of lumber, cost $45,000 [1]. These steam-powered lumber carriers could keep to a contract schedule winter and summer. The twenty-three launched by Hay and Boole in those two years carried as much lumber as an armada of sailing ships [1]. In 1888, fifty-six men at Boole and Beaton's yard stopped work on the wooden collier Ajax to pose for one of the few photographs known of shipbuilding on the creek [1]. After 1900 the builders moved closer to the forests, and the yards vanished [1][2].

title: A Quarter-Million Trees Behind the Reservoir
place: Site of Adolph Sutro's tree nursery, behind Laguna Honda Reservoir (1000 Clarendon Ave)
hook: The dark eucalyptus forest on Mount Sutro began as seedlings in a nursery beside a reservoir. By 1889 it held 250,000 trees.
story: In 1880 the silver millionaire Adolph Sutro bought the remains of Rancho San Miguel, including the bare hill he named Mount Parnassus (today's Mount Sutro). Soon afterwards he took up tree planting with a passion [1]. With the poet Joaquin Miller he organised California's first Arbor Day on November 26, 1886, when thousands of children planted trees he had donated on Yerba Buena Island [1]. On his own land he built a nursery behind the Laguna Honda reservoir, at what is now 1000 Clarendon Avenue, to find out which plants could hold the sand [1]. On June 24, 1889, his son-in-law George Merritt reported: 'the nursery has 250,000 trees, 50,000 for sale this year according to Flanagan.' Alonzo Flanagan, the ranch superintendent, had started out as a gardener there [1]. Accounts of who did the planting differ. Some say schoolchildren, and one rumour blames day-hired unemployed men for planting too close together. Sutro's accounts show paid nurserymen and labourers [1]. Blue gum eucalyptus, Monterey pine and cypress spread over the hills [2]. Sutro meant the eucalyptus as fast-growing shelter for other trees, but it smothered them, and the forest still divides opinion [1][2].

title: Dumpville, the village built on garbage
place: South side of Channel Street between Sixth and Seventh streets
hook: Three hundred garbage wagons a day rolled down Sixth Street, and a shantytown of scavengers lived off what they dumped.
story: From around 1878 until 1895, San Francisco's city dump was the edge of Mission Bay itself. The Chronicle estimated in 1889 that at least 300 teams a day passed down Sixth Street to a dumping ground covering some twenty acres on the south side of Channel Street, between Sixth and Seventh. As fast as garbage filled the water, the new land was graded with clay and sand and leased or sold for building [1][2]. Around its edges grew "Dumpville," a settlement of shanties made of wood and tin. Its residents sifted every load with pitchforks, shovels and sticks. The Chronicle wrote that rags, old bottles, scraps of iron, old sacks, bricks, oyster shells and even half-decayed fruit "all were prized" [1][3]. The police raided it from time to time. In 1895, after a bottle collector was murdered, reportedly for straying outside his assigned dump, officers burned the shanties and drove the scavengers out. The Call's headline read "Dumpville Is No More" [2][4]. The Army of Heaven Mission, which had been helping Dumpville's people, later opened a soup kitchen and free sleeping barn nearby on Mission Creek [1][2].

title: Fake Stalactites and a Concrete First
place: Alvord Lake Bridge, near Haight and Stanyan
hook: The walk from Haight Street into the park passes through a fake cave, and under America's first reinforced concrete bridge.
story: In 1881 park commissioner and former mayor William Alvord gave $200 for a lily pond near the Haight Street entrance. The shallow basin was the park's first man-made lake [1], and the park's chronology dates its construction to 1882 [2]. In 1889, beside it, Ernest L. Ransome built something more important: a single-arch underpass considered the first reinforced concrete bridge in the United States [3][4]. Ransome set square, cold-twisted steel bars, his own patented invention, along the underside of the arch, bent to follow its curve [3]. To dress up the new material, the outside was scored and hammered to look like sandstone. The ceiling of the passage was sculpted with concrete "stalactites," like a cave [4]. Ransome later left San Francisco, frustrated that local builders ignored concrete [4]. He was proved right in 1906, when the bridge and many of his concrete buildings came through the earthquake undamaged [3]. The American Society of Civil Engineers made it a landmark in 1969 [4]. Visitors from the Haight still walk through Ransome's grotto into the park.

title: Hearst's grizzly goes on show
place: Woodward's Gardens zoological section, Mission St south of 14th (today's Armory, 1800 Mission)
hook: A newspaper stunt brought one of California's last wild grizzlies to the city, and 20,000 people lined up to stare at him.
story: In 1889 William Randolph Hearst sent his San Francisco Examiner reporter Allen Kelly to bring back a live California grizzly. Kelly searched for about five months before a bear was trapped in the Ventura County backcountry [1][2]. "He bit and tore at the logs," Kelly wrote of the captive [1]. The bear, named Monarch, arrived in San Francisco by train. The Examiner reported that 20,000 people came to see him on November 10, 1889, and afterwards called itself the "Monarch of the Dailies" [1]. Where exactly they saw him is disputed. The Monarch Bear Institute says Golden Gate Park turned the gift down, so Hearst put the bear on show at Woodward's Gardens [2], and Wikipedia agrees [3]. A 2011 Chronicle account places his cage near Eighth and Brannan instead [1]. Either way, the stunt did not last. Monarch spent the rest of his 22 years in captivity, most of them in a cage in Golden Gate Park, and died in May 1911 [1]. His stuffed body, now at the California Academy of Sciences, was used as the model for the bear on the state flag in 1955 [1].

title: Sutro's tree factory behind Laguna Honda
place: Site of Adolph Sutro's tree nursery, behind Laguna Honda Reservoir near the 1000 block of Clarendon Avenue
hook: In 1889 a nursery here held 250,000 young trees. Adolph Sutro was turning the bare hills west of Twin Peaks into a forest, and it nearly burned.
story: The hills west of Twin Peaks were once open grass and sand. From 1880 the silver millionaire Adolph Sutro, later the city's mayor, bought land here. His largest holding was part of the old Rancho San Miguel, running from near today's UCSF up over Twin Peaks and on south [1]. Sutro set out to cover it with trees. Behind the Laguna Honda reservoir, at what historian Richard Brandi gives as 1000 Clarendon Street, he built a nursery to test which plants best held the sand. On June 24, 1889 his son-in-law George Merritt reported that it held 250,000 trees, 50,000 of them for sale [1]. Eucalyptus came to dominate the resulting Sutro Forest [2]. Some said Sutro planted to cut his taxes, but Brandi argues the nursery and its caretakers cost more than any tax break [1]. The woods drew picnickers, hunters and tramps, and fire. On October 8, 1899 a blaze burned 60 acres and threatened the Almshouse and the Affiliated Colleges before 70 firemen and hundreds of volunteers put it out. One engine needed five horses to climb the slope [1]. Not everyone admired the planting. The naturalist James Roof later said Sutro "perverted" the native Franciscan flora, but "did leave Twin Peaks alone because it was a symbol of the city" [3].

title: The Engine House at Oak and Broderick
place: Oak and Broderick streets
hook: In 1889 a powerhouse at Oak and Broderick began pulling cables under two new lines to Golden Gate Park. Within six years both had been converted.
story:
The Omnibus Railroad started in 1861 as a horse-car company. In 1889 it went into cable [1]. Two of its new lines met at Oak and Broderick streets, where the company built a powerhouse to drive their cables [1].

The Oak Street line opened in late 1889. It ran from Howard up 10th Street to Fell, jogged along Fell and Franklin, then ran straight out Oak Street and Stanyan to the Haight Street entrance of Golden Gate Park [1][2]. The Ellis Street line came out Ellis to Broderick, turned south to Oak and joined the same route to the park [1]. The cars gripped the cable from below with an Eppelsheimer bottom grip [1]. A photograph taken between 1889 and early 1894 shows Oak Street car No. 6 at the Stanyan terminal while crowds wait at the park gate [1].

Cable-car historian Joe Thompson argues that the company "made the wrong choice" in picking cable over electricity, since only the Oak Street line had significant hills [1]. The Market Street Railway took over the Omnibus company on August 13, 1893, and the Oak and Ellis lines were converted in late 1895 [1]. By 1890 cable cars ran on Market, Hayes, Oak and Haight streets, and planners say such lines "ushered in waves of new construction" [2].

title: The Many Lives of the 'Russian Embassy'
place: 1198 Fulton Street (Westerfeld House), at Scott
hook: A candy maker's mansion that became a Russian émigré club, a home for jazz musicians, and the place where Kenneth Anger filmed an occult movie.
story: In 1889 the German-born confectioner William Westerfeld had Henry Geilfuss build him a towered Stick-style Italian villa at Fulton and Scott [1][2]. Six years later the house passed to John Mahony of the Mahony Brothers building firm, who added a garage for his Stanley Steamer [1][2]. Mahony died in 1918, and about a decade later the house became a community centre for Russian émigrés. The ballroom turned into the Dark Eyes nightclub and the house picked up a nickname, the "Russian Embassy" [2][1]. After the club closed in the late 1930s, the apartments carved out of the house were rented for about two decades to African American jazz musicians [2][3]. In 1965 Charles Fracchia bought it and leased it to the filmmaker Kenneth Anger, who shot parts of "Invocation of My Demon Brother" there [2][4]. Anton LaVey came to the house often, and Tom Wolfe described it in 1968 as "a great shambling old Gothic house, a freaking decayed giant" [2][4]. Jim Siegel bought the house in 1986 and restored its Victorian interiors [4].

title: The Toxicologist's Corner Drugstore
place: 500–502 Divisadero Street (Theodore Green Apothecary), at Fell
hook: Behind the owl-eyed oval windows at Divisadero and Fell, a pharmacist who later ran the coroner's poison tests counselled students and did target practice.
story: Samuel Newsom, the Queen Anne architect best known for the Carson Mansion in Eureka, designed this corner pharmacy in 1889. It is one of the few unaltered 19th-century storefronts left in San Francisco, and it became a city landmark in 1986 [1][4]. The business opened as Theodore Green and Son, and by 1896 the son, Frank T. Green, ran it [2]. Green was born in Nevada County in 1863 and graduated from the California College of Pharmacy in 1880. He rose to professor of pharmaceutical chemistry and was dean from 1909 to 1927. Along the way he worked as a toxicologist for the San Francisco coroner's office and counted John Muir as a friend [3]. Former students remembered him breaking off a lecture to shout "OPEN THE WINDOWS!" [2]. A trade journal described the shop as a "little laboratory" where he examined precious stones or practised with his revolver [2]. Green's Pharmacy stayed in business for decades. When a Burger King tried to take the corner, neighbours fought it off, and Madrone opened in the space in 2004. The tiled "Green's Pharmacy" doorway is still there [2].

title: The butcher shop that wouldn't die
place: Drewes Bros. Meats, 1706 Church Street, near 29th
hook: In 1998 the Examiner ran Drewes Meats' obituary on its front page. Eleven days later, two young butchers were pounding chicken behind the counter again.
story:
Drewes has been selling meat on outer Church Street since about 1888 or 1889. By 2011 it was one of the street's oldest businesses [1][2]. Daniel Murphy remembered his mother sending him there in 1946, aged ten, with a five-dollar bill in a leather pouch and a note for "Mr. Dietz" asking for two pounds of lamb for a stew, at 50 cents a pound. He spent an hour treating half the kids on Duncan Street to penny candy, and when he finally reached the counter the five-dollar bill was gone [2].

In October 1998 the shop nearly died. Staff first noticed business slipping in 1991, during the filming of Sister Act at St. Paul's. Muni medians then cut parking, and his tendonitis made butchering painful. Owner Dave McCarroll closed the doors on October 15. The next day the Examiner's front page announced that Drewes had ended its 109-year run [1]. Workers Josh and Isaac Epple, aged 26 and 24, called themselves "the Drewes Brothers" and reopened the shop eleven days later. Its fate rested with Phil Tomasello, who had worked there as a butcher for 40 years and owned the building. "We're going to take it slow," he said [1]. The name stuck. In 2011 the shop was still trading as Drewes Bros. Meats [2].

title: Windmills, celery and the city's best farmland
place: Garden Tract market gardens, near Paul Ave
hook: In the 1880s the sheltered southern Bayview grew the city's vegetables. Newspapers watched Italian and Portuguese newcomers take over from Chinese growers.
story: Sheltered from the fog, with good soil and water from artesian springs, the southern Bayview came to be seen as the best farmland in San Francisco [1]. Market gardeners pumped water with windmills and grew broccoli, asparagus, celery, carrots, radishes, leeks and potatoes for the city's produce market [1]. In 1888 a Call reporter on a 'flying trip' south passed 'a Sahara of sand dotted with here and there a dairy-house' before 'entering Italian market gardens on the left, stocked with luxuriant vegetables' [1]. A year later, on November 17, 1889, the Chronicle reported that Italian and Portuguese immigrants were pushing Chinese growers out of the market-garden and dairy business along the San Bruno Road and in the Bayview Tract. 'Where once the Chinese were the commonest sight with their vegetable baskets swung on poles ... now they have been crowded out by the Italians and the Portuguese,' it wrote [1]. Many gardeners lived in 'light shanties' on their plots, next to their stores of seeds and root crops [1]. By the early 1900s Italian farmers dominated local farming [2], and the Bayview was long remembered as an Italian and Maltese enclave [3]. A few greenhouses survived into the 21st century [1].

title: A Church in a Cow Pasture
place: Broad St near Plymouth Ave
hook: Ocean View's Catholics heard Mass upstairs from a bar for 27 years, while seventeen Protestants founded their church in a tent among the cows.
story: Nineteenth-century Ocean View was a village of farm hands and railroad workers, split roughly half Catholic and half Protestant [1]. With no church of their own, Catholics gathered each Sunday from 1872 for Mass upstairs from the bar of the Tell House, a roadhouse beside the railroad station [1][2]. The Tell House was a true neighbourhood hub; decades later it was still a drinking spot and a boarding house where German was spoken, lodging Swiss and German immigrants [2]. The Protestants started smaller. In 1889 the Rev. Lincoln Wirt began a Sunday school in a store on Plymouth, and four people attended regularly [1]. In July 1890 seventeen residents declared themselves a church and met in a tent in someone's cow pasture until 1895, when they built the Ocean View Congregational Church on Broad Street [1]. The Catholics finally got a small church on Broad in 1899, christened St. Michael's [1]. It soon anchored local families such as the Gdovins of Plymouth Avenue, who worshipped there in the 1890s and 1900s [3]. The Congregational church survives as Pilgrim Community Congregational Church on Randolph Street [1].

title: A miser's gift: free hot baths
place: James Lick Baths, 165 Tenth Street
hook: James Lick once begged bones from butchers. His fortune paid for a bathhouse where working people could soak in a hot tub for free.
story: James Lick was famous for being a miser. In 1847, FoundSF recounts, he was the town's lowest bum, begging bones from butchers, while the sand lots he had bought were about to make him rich [1]. Before his death in 1876 he gave nearly all his money away: to the observatory on Mount Hamilton, to the California Academy of Sciences, and to free public baths for the poor. "Tell them to wash and be clean," he is remembered as saying [1]. In 1890 the Lick estate opened the baths at 165 Tenth Street. At the time many working-class San Franciscans had no indoor plumbing [2][3]. The men's wing had forty bathtubs in private changing rooms and the women's wing had twenty. The baths pumped water from their own wells, heated it in boilers and stored it in 10,000-gallon tanks in the tower, so each bather could mix hot and cold at the tap [2]. The building was damaged in 1906, repaired, and used as a bathhouse until 1919. For decades after that it was the People's Laundry [2][3]. It became a San Francisco landmark in 2004 [2].

title: Eighteen Hundred Men and a Road
place: Middle Drive West, built by relief workers
hook: In the hard spring of 1890, the jobless of San Francisco dug a road through the sand dunes for $1.50 a day.
story: Hard times hit San Francisco in early 1890, and a charitable relief fund decided to put jobless men to work in Golden Gate Park at $1.50 a day. Their job was to cut a rough road through the sand, from today's Transverse and Overlook drives west toward what is now JFK Drive and Bernice Rodgers Way [1]. On March 11, 150 men were at work. Two days later there were 600, and by March 25 there were 1,800, all with shovels and wheelbarrows [1]. By mid-April the 1.5-mile road was roughed out, and donors had pledged more than $31,000, roughly twenty thousand days of work [1]. Foreman Patrick Quigley's crews then graded and surfaced it. The route survives as Overlook Drive, Middle Drive West and part of MLK Drive [1], and the park's chronology records Middle Drive being built in 1890 [2]. It happened again in the depression of 1894. A citizens' relief committee sent up to 2,800 men into the park at a dollar a day, on ten-day work tickets. The first ticket went to Jerry Sullivan, a San Franciscan of 21 years with a wife and six children, described as "utterly without means and hungry" [3].

title: Houses in ostrich-leather plaster
place: Albert Wilford Houses, 2121 and 2127 Vallejo Street
hook: A Swedish-born carpenter who once ran a saloon borrowed ideas from a millionaire's mansion and dressed two Vallejo Street houses in plaster that looks like ostrich skin.
story: Albert Wilford was born in Stockholm in 1843 and came to the United States in 1866 [1]. San Francisco directories list him as a carpenter, then a builder, and in 1880 as running a liquor saloon [1]. In 1889 and 1890 he built twelve houses on one Pacific Heights block, facing Webster, Buchanan and Vallejo Streets [1]. The best survivors are the twin houses at 2121 and 2127 Vallejo, perched high above the sidewalk with views over the bay [1][2]. Their oddest feature is a broad band of plaster set with small rocks and scored between them. The National Register nomination calls it a large-scale imitation of ostrich-skin leather, and it has not been documented on any other house [1][2]. The nomination suggests Wilford took the idea from the pebbled-plaster gables of William H. Crocker's 1888 mansion on California Street. That house had become a kind of 'builder's poster' for San Francisco rowhouse designers [1]. Wilford signed for the water connections on June 24, 1890, and had both houses sold by early December [1]. One buyer quickly resold his house to Richard M. Tobin, later president of the Hibernia Bank, who rented it out [1].

title: How Lakeview Lost and Found Its Name
place: Lakeview Avenue near Plymouth Avenue, crest of the ridge
hook: Adolph Sutro named a tract 'Lakeview' in 1890. The name vanished, then decades later reappeared a hill away, and nobody agrees why.
story: In 1890 Adolph Sutro subdivided his land south of the old Ocean Road, which he liked to call 'Grand Ocean Boulevard'. He named the tract 'Lakeview' [1][2]. Its grid, from Ashton to Harold Avenue and from Ocean Avenue up to Lakeview Avenue, is still the Ingleside's street plan [1]. Sutro turned down the name 'Ingleside City', but it won anyway. Locals named the area after Cornelius Stagg's Ingleside Inn, and after the Ingleside Racetrack opened in 1895, 'Lakeview' survived only on some official maps [1][2]. Then the name came back somewhere else. According to the OMI context statement, the African American community revived 'Lakeview', and many residents still use it for Ocean View, south of the ridge [2]. Sources disagree about the origin. Woody LaBounty of the Western Neighborhoods Project thought residents took it, perhaps in the 1960s, from Lakeview Avenue along the crest of the hill [3]. Wikipedia's Oceanview article says instead that it recalls the vanished Lake Geneva to the east, not Lake Merced [4]. Either way, a developer's 1890 label now belongs to a neighbourhood Sutro never planned.

title: The Olympians' Track on Lincoln Way
place: Former Olympic Club grounds, Lincoln Way to Irving St between 7th & 8th Aves
hook: A whole Inner Sunset block was once an athletic ground, then a rival Japanese Tea Garden, before anyone built houses on it.
story: The Olympic Club was founded in 1860 and always had a downtown clubhouse. Its members still needed somewhere outdoors to run and jump. In 1889 the club leased an entire block of dunes from owner John T. Doyle, bounded by Lincoln Way, Irving Street and 7th and 8th Avenues. Winter rains delayed the work, so athletes began training there in April 1890 and the grounds formally opened at the end of May [1]. There was an oval track, a grandstand, a clubhouse, a handball court, dressing rooms, a lunchroom and a horse shed, all inside a high board fence [1]. Photographs published that year show the entry gate on Lincoln Way with Mount Sutro behind [2]. The Olympians left after 1900. In 1902 Doyle leased the block to a Japanese company, which kept some of the club buildings, replaced the track and grandstand with gardens and opened a Japanese Tea Garden to compete with the one across the street in Golden Gate Park [1]. By 1909 the land had become too valuable for gardens. Doyle's estate negotiated an end to the lease. Builder Eugene Hallett put up eighteen houses on the 7th Avenue side during 1909–1913, and in 1911–1912 the McKillop Brothers lined 8th Avenue with flats [1].

title: The dredging king's tower on Guerrero
place: John McMullen House, 827 Guerrero St
hook: The man who dredged harbours from Oakland to Manila dressed up his plain Mission house with a round tower and a horseshoe-arch door.
story: John McMullen came to San Francisco from Connecticut in 1876 as a carpenter. By 1877 he had founded the San Francisco Bridge Company, the first of several contracting and dredging firms [1]. His companies dredged Oakland Harbor and Boston Harbor, and cut the tidal canal between Oakland and San Leandro Bay. They built forty-seven bridges for the Canadian Pacific Railway, the Hunters Point drydock, piers at Fort Mason, and harbour works in Manila Bay [1]. When he died, his obituary said "McMullen's history is the history of contracting in the West" [2]. His house at 827 Guerrero shows that rise. It started in 1881 as a Stick-style house on a standard 25-by-100-foot lot [1]. The noted architect Samuel Newsom then widened it and added a round tower, a horseshoe-arched entry and shingled walls in the latest Queen Anne fashion [1][2]. The National Register nomination dates that makeover to 1890. The city's landmark summary ties it to 1881 and to McMullen's growing wealth [1][2]. Later owners kept adding: a bigger kitchen in 1892 and a butler's pantry in 1904 [1].

title: The plan to banish Chinatown to Hunters Point
place: Hunters Point ridge
hook: In 1890 San Francisco passed a law ordering every Chinese resident out of Chinatown. The place picked for them was remote Hunters Point.
story: In 1890 Supervisor Bingham introduced an order that required all Chinese residents to leave the part of the city where they lived. They could leave San Francisco altogether or move to one designated district [1][2]. The district was Hunters Point, then a thinly settled peninsula of boatyards, shrimp camps and pasture far from downtown [1]. Order No. 2190, known as the 'Bingham Ordinance', was enforced, and Chinese residents were arrested for breaking it [2]. Lee Sing and others challenged their arrests in federal court. Attorney Thomas D. Riordan argued for them, and the court's opinion turned on the Fourteenth Amendment. Judge Lorenzo Sawyer ruled on August 25, 1890 [2], and the ordinance was struck down [1]. The idea kept coming back. In October 1900, John Partridge of the California Geographical Society proposed a Chinese homestead association that would buy land at Hunters Point and build an 'Oriental City'. It never won the support of Chinese San Franciscans [1]. After Chinatown burned in 1906, some San Franciscans again pushed to move it to Hunters Point [3].

title: Two young women start a settlement house
place: TEL HI Neighborhood Center, 660 Lombard St (its home since the 1950s)
hook: In 1890 two Sunday-school teachers aged 21 and 25 started classes for immigrant children on Telegraph Hill. The centre they founded is still working in North Beach.
story: In 1890 Elizabeth Ashe, 21, and Alice Griffith, 25, were teaching Sunday school at Grace Cathedral when they got to know children from Telegraph Hill. Irish, Italian, German and Latin American families lived there in tiny flats without plumbing or heat, and epidemics hit harder than almost anywhere in the city [1]. Jane Addams had just opened Hull House in Chicago, and like her the two women wanted to work directly with the poor. They founded what became the Telegraph Hill Neighborhood Center, San Francisco's first settlement house [1]. It began with a boys' club and sewing classes. A house near the crest of Vallejo Street provided two nurses for local families and ran an evening club for girls who worked in the canneries [2]. Italian neighbours, suspicious at first, began bringing gifts of fruit and vegetables [2]. The centre later ran a day care for cannery workers' children and a clinic with an operating room, and it helped start the West Coast's first school nurse programme [1]. Griffith spent years badgering officials to stop the quarrying that was eating away the hill [2]. After 1906 Bernard Maybeck designed a new centre on Stockton Street, and in the 1950s it moved here to Lombard Street [1].

title: A Castle for the View
place: Summit of Strawberry Hill, Stow Lake
hook: A landowner's gift put a mock castle on the park's highest hill, and opened the door to naming park features after donors.
story: In April 1886 the park cut a road to the top of Strawberry Hill for a planned reservoir. The view proved so popular [2] that Thomas U. Sweeny gave $8,000 for a lookout. On September 9, 1891, a castle-like observatory of red-tinted concrete was dedicated on the summit [1][3]. It was less an observatory than a walled windbreak: carriages drove straight into its circular court. A glassed-in second story was added in 1892, and a plaque read "Park Panorama, Gift of Thos. U. Sweeny, 1891" [1]. Historian Woody LaBounty calls it perhaps the first park gift that required the donor's name to be attached. Ray Clary wrote that accepting it reversed the park's ban on "personal advertisement and self-aggrandizement" [1]. Hall, who wanted a park free of monuments, was offended [1]. Soon Huntington Falls poured from a pool in front of the observatory into the new Stow Lake [1]. Sweeny could see his gift from home near today's 7th Avenue and Judah until he died in 1900. The 1906 earthquake wrecked it, and Hall is quoted seeing the hand of "a Higher Power" [1].

title: An agnostic's gift to Cow Hollow
place: Episcopal Church of St. Mary the Virgin, 2325 Union Street at Steiner
hook: Frank Pixley told a young priest he hated all religions. He still gave him land for a church, and his ashes lie beneath its floor.
story: In August 1888 Florence Gay started a Sunday school for five children in a Cow Hollow home, in a pasture where dairy cows grazed among the chaparral [2]. In 1890 the mission got a priest, the Cambridge-educated Anglo-Catholic William Bolton, whom Bishop Ingraham Kip seemed glad to send to the frontier [1][2]. Bolton needed land. The obvious owner was Frank Pixley, former state attorney general and publisher of the Argonaut. His family estate filled the wooded block bounded by Union, Steiner, Green and Fillmore, and he called himself 'an agnostic with a touch of atheism' [1]. Bolton's memoirs record the answer: 'I hate your —– religion and all religions and you ask me for land to spread it... but I like your pluck in tackling that Hell's job in Cow Hollow.' Pixley said he would speak to his wife. His wife, Amelia, probably had a lot to do with what happened next [1]. St. Mary the Virgin became San Francisco's ninth Episcopal parish in April 1891 and held its first services in the new church on October 4, 1891. The Pixleys also gave the altar painting [2]. He died in 1895 and Amelia three years later. Their cremated remains lie in the crypt beneath St. Mary's floor [1].

title: Ben Harrison and Sarah Bernhardt, Bison
place: Bison Paddock, off John F. Kennedy Drive
hook: With American bison nearly wiped out, San Francisco brought a bull from Wyoming, named him after the president, and found him a mate.
story: By 1890, one estimate holds, only about 800 American bison survived of the 50 million that had roamed the plains in 1800 [1]. San Francisco decided to help. Pushed by Superintendent John McLaren, the city brought a bull from Wyoming to Golden Gate Park in 1891 and named him Ben Harrison, after the sitting president [1]. The park's master-plan chronology dates the purchase to 1890 [2]. Ben was soon joined by a cow named Sarah Bernhardt, after the famous actress, and the pair started a herd [1]. Later arrivals had names like Grover Cleveland and Bill McKinley, and some bison came from Yellowstone. By 1918 there were 30 in the herd [1]. They shared the park with a changing menagerie that at various times included elk, deer, moose, antelope and bears [3]. The bison moved to their present paddock in the western park around 1900 [2]. Their descendants still graze there, and the herd has produced about 500 calves [1].

title: Fourteen sea lions in the drinking water
place: North Lake, Lake Merced
hook: To fix an algae problem they added carp. To fix the carp they added sea lions. Then came a fish from New York.
story: In the 1890s algae blooms were fouling Lake Merced, then part of San Francisco's drinking supply [1]. Carp had been put in the lake, and one account says they were meant to eat the algae. As bottom feeders they churned up the lakebed instead, leaving the water muddy [1][2]. The Spring Valley Water Company tried nets and hooks and considered black powder. In 1891 it brought in fourteen sea lions [1]. "Our seals [...] are destroying them by the thousands," said company president Charles Webb Howard [1]. One newspaper, as the Western Neighborhoods Project retells it, began its story with the news that fourteen sea lions were now swimming in the drinking water [2]. The sea lions did kill carp, but took one large bite from each fish's midsection and left the rest. Rotting half-carp drew gulls, whose droppings fouled the water further [1][2]. Next, 100,000 fry of muskellunge, a predatory pike from New York State, arrived by special train car [1]. By 1896 the lake was found to be essentially fish-free, the sea lions were removed, and pumping for the city was increased [1].

title: Hawaii's last king dies at the Palace
place: Palace Hotel, Market and New Montgomery streets
hook: Hawaii's 'Merrie Monarch' came to San Francisco for his health and checked into the grandest hotel in the West. He went home aboard a warship, in a coffin.
story: When it opened in October 1875, William Ralston's Palace Hotel was the largest hotel in the western United States: 755 rooms, 120 feet high, with a skylit Grand Court where carriages drove in beneath seven storeys of white balconies [1]. Guests rode redwood-panelled hydraulic 'rising rooms' and could summon staff with an electric call button [1]. In December 1890 King Kalākaua of Hawaii arrived aboard the USS Charleston and took a suite there [1][2]. His health was already failing. After a stroke in Santa Barbara he was rushed back to the Palace and put in the care of the Pacific Fleet's surgeon, George Woods [2]. Against advice, on January 14 he went to his initiation into the Shriners, propped up with a tonic of Vin Mariani, and was back in his suite within the hour [2]. Two days before his death he fell into a coma. He died at 2:35 p.m. on January 20, 1891; Navy officials gave the cause as Bright's disease [2]. The Charleston carried his body home, and Honolulu learned of his death only when the ship arrived on January 29. His sister Liliʻuokalani became queen that day [2].

title: Joost's trolleys and the water war
place: Miller-Joost House, 3224 Market St
hook: Behind a retaining wall on Market Street hides the oldest house on Twin Peaks. Its owner ran the city's first electric streetcars and feuded for life with Nobby Clarke.
story: Most drivers on upper Market Street miss 3224. The Market Street cut left a high retaining wall in front of what may be the oldest house on Twin Peaks, parts of it perhaps from 1867 [1]. It is named for two German immigrants, Adam Miller and Behrend Joost, who married Miller's daughter in 1874 [1]. Joost arrived around 1850 and built grocery stores and property holdings with his brother [1]. In 1891 the brothers organised the San Francisco and San Mateo Railroad, the city's first taste of electric trolleys [1]. By 1892 one of its lines ran along 18th Street out to Douglass, nearly to his door [1][2]. It lost money and was sold at foreclosure in 1896 [1]. Joost also founded a water company to sell Twin Peaks spring water to his neighbours [1]. That business set off a lifelong feud with his downhill neighbour Nobby Clarke. In neighbourhood lore they even came to blows on 18th Street [3].

title: The Army Takes the Graveyard
place: Fort Miley (now the SF VA Medical Center grounds)
hook: To guard the Golden Gate, the federal government went to court to seize part of the city cemetery, then mounted 12-inch guns among the graves.
story: In the early 1890s the Army wanted the cemetery headland for new guns to guard San Francisco Bay. On June 9, 1891, the U.S. district attorney, the city's district attorney and the city and county attorney met Mayor Sanderson to talk over condemning the City Cemetery for fortifications. The federal attorney was already drafting the papers [1]. Adolph Sutro and other prominent citizens backed condemnation. The city, though, asked too much for the whole 200 acres, so the government took only 54 [2]. The National Register nomination dates the condemnation to 1893 [3]. On top of the 350-foot headland the Army built Battery James Chester: two 12-inch rifles on 'disappearing' carriages, finished in 1901, with a third gun added in 1903. In the east a mortar battery of sixteen 12-inch mortars was finished in August 1901 [3]. The guns were designed for duels with enemy warships and covered all three channels into the bay. Wooden barracks and quarters stood on the parade ground between the batteries [3]. Those buildings were torn down in 1934 for the Veterans Administration hospital that stands there today. The concrete batteries still edge its grounds [3].

title: The Church That Moved Twice
place: Old St. Patrick's Church / Holy Cross Parish Hall, 1820 Eddy St
hook: The city's oldest wooden church started out on Market Street, where the Palace Hotel now stands. It was carted across town twice before it came to rest on Eddy Street.
story: The plain Classical Revival building on the north side of Eddy between Scott and Divisadero began life downtown, as St. Patrick's Church in Happy Valley on Market Street [1]. Its exact age is disputed. The parish historian Luke Carroll dated it to 1854 and said it was brought around the Horn in a sailing vessel. The Historic American Buildings Survey argued that it more likely dated to 1851, and another account gives 1852 [1][2]. The Palace Hotel was going up on its site, so in 1873 the church was moved to Eddy Street between Octavia and Laguna and reconsecrated as St. John the Baptist. From 1885 to 1891 Archbishop Riordan used it as his pro-cathedral [1]. When St. Mary's Cathedral opened on Van Ness in 1891, the little church moved again, this time to Eddy near Divisadero. It was rededicated on May 24, 1891 as the first home of Holy Cross Parish [1][2]. Holy Cross laid the cornerstone of a larger church next door on April 3, 1898 and dedicated it on August 13, 1899, under pastor Rev. John McGinty. The old building became the parish hall [2]. It was named San Francisco Landmark No. 6 in 1968 and is considered the oldest frame church building in the city [3][4].

title: The Coal Rush Under Lands End
place: Lands End cliffs below the old railway, east of Lands End point (approximate)
hook: In March 1891 an old miner swore there were thousands of tons of coal under the cliffs. Adolph Sutro sent men to tunnel into the bluff.
story: On March 28, 1891, the Chronicle told San Franciscans that coal had been found in the city. A 'grizzly old miner' named Charles Jackson had found a vein of bituminous coal, six to eight feet wide, hugging the coast near Baker Beach. 'Do try to buy up that land,' he urged H.H. Lynch, superintendent of the Cliff House railway. 'There is a fortune in it.' But the land belonged to Adolph Sutro [1]. Within days Sutro had fifteen to twenty men at work about a quarter mile beyond the railway's Baker Beach station. They drove a tunnel into the bluff below the track [2]. Jackson was convinced the vein ran under the Golden Gate to Marin. He went prospecting on the Marin shore and came back claiming good bituminous coal thirty feet down [2][3]. Not everyone believed him. A State Mining Bureau official told the Morning Call he had little faith in the find. He guessed it was prehistoric driftwood and seaweed slowly carbonized where the sea once beat against a rocky ridge [4]. The mine was never developed. Its tunnel, half washed away and reached only through a sea cave, still shows veins of coal [1].

title: The Mine Shed That Stopped a Bridge
place: Torpedo Assembly Building (Building 262), East Point
hook: The Army needed a rust-proof home for its underwater mines. It hired a concrete pioneer, and his shed still sits in the Bay Bridge's shadow.
story:
In 1884 the Army sent a shipment of buoyant "torpedoes" (underwater mines) to San Francisco and stored them on foggy Alcatraz. They rusted within months [1]. Lieutenant Colonel George Mendell wanted a storehouse on sheltered Yerba Buena Island, but by the time Congress paid for it in 1889, brick prices had jumped by more than 30 percent [1]. So he turned to Ernest L. Ransome, a Bay Area pioneer of reinforced concrete who had patented his twisted iron reinforcing bars in 1884 [1].

The shed was finished in 1891. It measured 158 by 72 feet, with 24-foot walls and room for more than 1,100 mines [1]. In 1893 it held 579 [1]. Its walls were cast in molds to look like masonry, then bush-hammered to resemble quarry-cut stone. They still carry the mark of Ransome's patent No. 405,800 [1]. In the 1930s the Navy wanted it razed for the Bay Bridge, but the Army refused to give it up without a replacement [2]. It survives under the bridge's eastern approach as the only Army building left on the island, a rare early reinforced-concrete building [1][2].

title: The President Who Wouldn't Pose Twice
place: Sutro Heights parapet
hook: Benjamin Harrison came to Adolph Sutro's clifftop garden, stared silently at the Golden Gate, endured one photo, and sat down to a very long, very wet lunch.
story: Adolph Sutro turned a clifftop cottage into Sutro Heights, a garden of more than twenty acres with flower beds, hedge mazes, a conservatory and over 200 concrete copies of classical statues imported from Belgium, tended by a staff of 17 [2]. Anyone could stroll it, and guests from Oscar Wilde to presidents breakfasted there [4]. On April 27, 1891, President Benjamin Harrison arrived. The Morning Call reported that he stood silently gazing at the Golden Gate, seeing it for the first time, until Sutro's hired photographer pointed a camera at him. Hands in overcoat pockets, hat pulled down, the president allowed exactly one shot and walked off [1]. Lunch ran nearly two hours: oysters, caviar, sweetbreads, roast duck, and wines including an 1872 Chateau Lafitte and 1825 cognac. The Postmaster-General turned his glass upside down [1]. Then Sutro rose and gave Harrison a photolithograph of a 1602 letter from the navigator Sebastián Vizcaíno at Monterey, which Sutro said he had found in the archives at Seville [1]. The National Park Service dates the public garden to 1885; Sutro bought the cottage in 1881 [2][3].

title: Twelve Residents on Silver Avenue
place: Jewish Home, 302 Silver Avenue
hook: In farm country at Silver and Mission, San Francisco's Jewish community opened a home for its elders in 1891. It has been caring for them ever since.
story: In 1871 the Pacific Hebrew Orphan Asylum and Home Society was incorporated 'to found and maintain an asylum for orphan children' and 'to establish and support a Home for aged and infirm Israelites' [1]. In 1872 the society bought land at Silver Avenue and Mission Street, then open country at the southern edge of the city. There it put up a rambling two-storey wooden Victorian building, which opened its doors in 1891 to twelve residents [1]. A San Francisco Public Library photograph of the building is labelled simply 'Old Silver Ave. home' [2]. In 1923 the wooden house gave way to a red-brick building with Roman columns, designed by the architect Samuel Lightner Hyman. It has a formal symmetrical plan: a central pavilion with a giant portico, linked to identical wings [1]. The site grew to almost nine acres and the institution kept its purpose. More than 125 years later it is still a senior home, now called the San Francisco Campus for Jewish Living, and it is one of the Excelsior's oldest institutions [1][2].

title: Two-and-twenty let-gos on the Hyde Street Grip
place: Hyde and Union streets, where Hyde Street cars dropped the rope to cross the Union Street cable
hook: San Francisco's last new cable line crossed so many older ones that its gripmen let go of the rope 22 times a trip. Gelett Burgess put it in verse.
story: On February 9, 1891, the California Street Cable Railroad opened its O'Farrell, Jones and Hyde line, 2.5 miles from Market Street over Russian Hill to Beach Street. It was the last new cable line built in the city [1]. Coming last meant giving way at every crossing: its cars used a bottom grip and had to drop the rope 22 times on a round trip, at nine crossings, the powerhouse and the end of the line. At Union Street they had to let go to cross the older Presidio & Ferries cable [2]. The poet Gelett Burgess, of 'The Purple Cow' fame, caught the gripman's job in 'The Ballad of the Hyde Street Grip', published in 1901: 'Two-and-twenty "let-go's" every double trip / It takes a bit of doing on the Hyde Street Grip!' And: 'Drop your rope at Union—never make a slip' [1]. Cal Cable stopped on July 31, 1951, after Lloyd's of London cancelled its insurance when an injured waitress won a $140,000 judgment [1]. Muni reopened it in 1952, but the last O'Farrell, Jones and Hyde car went into the barn on May 15, 1954 [1][2]. In 1957 its Hyde Street leg was joined to a cut-back Powell line to create today's Powell–Hyde route, whose descent of about 21 percent is the steepest in the system [1][3].

title: A Roadhouse in the Eucalyptus
place: Trocadero Clubhouse, Sigmund Stern Grove (near 19th Ave & Sloat Blvd)
hook: Squatters turned blowing sand into a sheltered grove and put a gingerbread inn in it. In 1907 San Francisco's political boss was arrested hiding there.
story: The Greene family arrived during the Mexican-American War and squatted on land that includes today's Stern Grove. They grew barley and potatoes and planted bunch grass and eucalyptus to hold the sand, and those trees are still there [1]. The Stern Grove Festival dates the homestead to 1847 and says a nephew, George, planted the first eucalyptus [3]. In 1892 the family built the Trocadero Inn. It is a two-story wood-frame roadhouse with steep dormers, a stick-work porch, a paneled bar and a massive stone fireplace. The sources disagree about which Greene built it: the Parkside context statement names George, the festival names Alfred [1][3]. The Greenes leased it to operators including Hiram Cook, and under Cook it had a deer park, a boating pavilion and a beer garden [1]. It was a good place to hide. In 1907, as the graft trials began, political boss Abe Ruef was arrested at the Trocadero [1]. George Greene closed the inn in 1916 because he feared trouble with bootleggers under Prohibition [2]. In 1931 Rosalie Stern paid $50,000 for the land as a memorial to her late husband, Sigmund, and gave it to the city. The old inn still stands in the grove [2][3].

title: A silver baron's wall in the bay
place: Former Harbor View lagoon, roughly Divisadero to Webster between Bay Street and Marina Boulevard
hook: Before there was a Marina, a Comstock millionaire bought up the underwater lots and started walling off the bay. The dunes of Cow Hollow went in behind it.
story: In the 19th century the future Marina was called Harbor View. It was a semi-rural corner of truck farms, fishermen's shacks and industrial plants, much of it underwater or marsh, and cut off from the city by big sand dunes [1][2]. In the early 1890s the 'Silver Baron' James G. Fair began buying the submerged water lots. By 1893 he controlled all but five of the 49 blocks between Chestnut, Baker and Webster Streets and the bay [1]. In 1892 he began a seawall along the northern edge of his holdings, the first step in filling the 'land' for industrial sites [1][2]. The next year the city took over the job and hired Warren & Malley to finish the wall and fill and grade the streets. The fill came from dunes at Fort Mason and from a large dune that separated Harbor View from Cow Hollow [1]. An oval lagoon was left, roughly between Divisadero, Webster, Bay and today's Marina Boulevard [1]. Fair's heirs welcomed the 1915 exposition, which filled the rest for free. In 1912, dredges pumped more than 1.3 million cubic yards of bay mud into the 70-acre lagoon over 146 days [1].

title: Nobby Clarke's Folly
place: Alfred E. Clarke Mansion, 250 Douglass St at Caselli
hook: A police clerk who somehow saved $200,000 built a towered castle on a bare hillside. His wife refused to move in.
story: Alfred Clarke came from Ireland as a cabin boy in 1850. He tried the gold fields, worked as a stevedore and joined the police in 1856 [1][2]. He rose to clerk to the chief of police and ran a side business lending money to patrolmen. By the time he resigned in 1887 he was said to have saved some $200,000, by what Wikipedia calls "dubious means" [1][2][3]. He studied law and sued the city again and again, earning a name as the police department's own Emperor Norton [2]. In 1892 he finished a four-storey, multi-towered Baroque Queen Anne mansion at the head of Eureka Valley. It had bands of scalloped shingles and cost a reputed $100,000 [1][3]. Neighbours called it "Clarke's Folly" [1]. His wife would not leave Nob Hill for the empty hills, and the depression of the 1890s ruined him. He lost the house in 1896 [3]. By 1904 it was a hospital that boasted it was "Sheltered from the Cold West Wind" [1]. Clarke died in 1902, aged 69 [2].

title: San Francisco's first electric streetcar comes to Chenery
place: Chenery Street, Fairmount (route of the San Francisco-San Mateo electric railway)
hook: Behrend Joost spent his Panama Canal money on the city's first electric railway. Suddenly downtown was fifteen minutes away, not a long walk to a horsecar.
story:
Behrend Joost had made a fortune investing in the French attempt to dig the Panama Canal. By April 1892 his San Francisco-San Mateo Railroad, the first electric road in the city, was running along Chenery Street, south on Diamond over Islais Creek, and on towards San Mateo County [1]. Before that, anyone going downtown had to walk to Cortland and Mission to catch a horse-drawn car. According to one neighbourhood history, an 8 am car could get you to the Ferry Building in 15 minutes for a five-cent fare [2].

Joost built a trestle to carry Diamond Street over the creek. A little "toonerville trolley" also ran along Bosworth. On Sundays another car took picnickers west along Chenery [2]. He bought 200 acres he called Sunnyside and put 2,250 lots on sale, then the largest development the city had seen. Sales were slow, and Joost ended up in lawsuits accusing him of mismanaging both the railroad and his land company. He sold the line at a loss to James D. Spreckels, son of the sugar magnate [1]. His tracks set the pattern for the whole district, though. Streetcars would bring the crowds, and after 1906, the settlers [2].

title: Taming a Primeval Forest of Rocks
place: Alamo Square
hook: For decades the city's reserved square was bare rock. In 1892 the city spent $25,333 grading the hill, and in 1896 it added the masonry wall.
story:
Saving Alamo Square from squatters did not make it a park. In 1918 journalist Edward Morphy recalled that the block stayed "a primeval forest of rocks at the top of hill" for decades [1]. The rock is still there. In 2018 historian Joel Pomerantz pointed to serpentinite bedrock showing in an open lot at 804 Steiner, part of a ridge of that rock [2].

The work finally began in 1892. According to Hoodline, the park was "graded and tamed" that year at a cost of $25,333 [1]. The Parks Alliance history says crews graded and landscaped the rocky hill, laid out the curving paths, and built stairways and a masonry wall [3]. Hoodline dates the wall to 1896 and credits it to the California Concrete Company [1].

Houses were rising around the park at the same time. Across Steiner Street, the row of Queen Anne houses now called the Painted Ladies went up between 1892 and 1895, facing a view that Planning calls probably the most photographed view of Victorians in the world [4]. The trailside watering hole of the early 1800s had become a landscaped park at the centre of a new neighbourhood.

title: The Bank San Franciscans Called 'The Paragon'
place: Hibernia Bank, 1 Jones Street at McAllister and Market
hook: Irish miners' savings paid for a domed temple on Market Street, and in 1892 a poll of artists named it the most beautiful building in town.
story: The Hibernia Savings and Loan Society opened in April 1859 in a small office at Jackson and Montgomery. Many of its first depositors were Irish miners who brought in unminted gold from the diggings, and it came to be called 'the people's bank' [1]. When it needed a bigger headquarters, its directors took a chance on a little-known architect, Albert Pissis, to design a building on the corner of McAllister, Jones and Market [1][2]. Finished in 1892, the domed Beaux-Arts bank was an instant hit, and San Franciscans called it 'The Paragon' [1][2]. That September the San Francisco Call asked twenty local artists which building in the city was the most artistic. Fourteen named the Hibernia, the Mills Building got four votes, and the paper declared it 'The Most Artistic Building in Town' [1][2]. The landmark writer NoeHill calls it the oldest 'temple' bank in San Francisco and one of the best [3]. Architect and Engineer later wrote that the bank 'marked an epoch in San Francisco architecture' and put Pissis at the front of his profession [1]. It survived the 1906 fire with damage, and it reopened on May 25, 1906 to lines of depositors five blocks long [1][2].

title: The Builder Who Lived Next Door
place: 710–720 Steiner Street (Postcard Row)
hook: The world's most photographed row of Victorians began as one contractor's gamble: build three houses on spec, see if they sell, then finish the block.
story: Between 1892 and 1896, the contractor Matthew Kavanaugh developed the 700 block of Steiner Street, the uphill row facing Alamo Square that the world now calls Postcard Row [1][2]. He started with his own house on the corner at Grove Street in 1892. It is the biggest of the group and breaks the pattern of the other six [1][3]. According to a 2010 article quoted by SFGATE, once Kavanaugh's own place was done he built the three matching houses at the far end on spec. When those sold for around $8,000 apiece, he finished the strip in 1896 [1]. The result, 710 to 720 Steiner, is a matching run of houses, also nicknamed the Seven Sisters, with downtown rising behind them [1][4]. They started out as a builder's speculation, not as monuments. More than a century later the Alamo Square Neighborhood Association still credits Kavanaugh as their builder, and the row still houses locals [4].

title: The Opera Impresario's Chateau
place: 1057 Steiner Street (Chateau Tivoli), at Golden Gate Avenue
hook: A lumber baron built it and an opera-house owner gave it her theatre's name. By the 1970s the towered house on Steiner rang with New Age drumming.
story: In 1892 the architect William H. Armitage designed a towered house at Steiner and Golden Gate for the lumber baron Daniel B. Jackson [1]. Jackson also built three apartment buildings next door on Golden Gate Avenue. All four were painted alike so they read as one huge facade, and together they were known as the Seattle Block [1]. Jackson later sold the house to Ernestine Kreling, founder and owner of the Tivoli Opera House on Eddy Street, and the house still carries the Tivoli name [1]. By the 1970s the house had become a New Age centre, "bringing drum beats and chanting to its halls" [1]. In 1985 Rodney Karr and William Gersbach began a long restoration. They put on a new slate roof in stripe and diamond patterns, stripped many layers of paint and hung hand-printed Bradbury & Bradbury wallpaper [1]. The pair ran Chateau Tivoli and later restored the Hinkel House on Divisadero too, repainting it in "empire colors" such as aubergine, turquoise, mustard and teal [2].

title: The Schoolhouse Next to the Roadhouse
place: Laguna Honda School (now Independence High School), 1350 7th Ave
hook: Fever-breeding ponds chased the Sunset's first school down the hill. It landed beside a saloon, and the saloonkeeper became its janitress.
story: Laguna Honda School began in 1869 in a rented room. From 1872 it had a two-room wooden building between 7th and 8th Avenues, Kirkham and Lawton Streets. In 1879 the Inner Sunset had only about fourteen households, so many of its pupils came from the reservoir, the Almshouse and nearby dairies [1]. In 1892 the reservoir overflowed and left two stagnant ponds by the school. They were blamed for malaria and typhoid among the children, so that July the building was moved to 7th Avenue between Irving and Judah for $2,000 [1]. The new neighbour was Elizabeth Chadwick's Park View Road House, where, the Chronicle wrote, travellers 'make merry over foaming milk punches.' 'Chaddy' got herself appointed the school's janitress at $20 a month while still running the saloon. She was removed, so she had her daughter appointed instead [1]. A brick school was being built on the lot when the earthquake of April 18, 1906 did $24,000 of damage. A 1906 photograph shows the ruins, with the old wooden school behind them [1][2]. The rebuilt school, designed by Will D. Shea, was dedicated in May 1909 [1]. The building is now Independence High School.

title: The first Big Game, minus a football
place: Haight Street Grounds, near Stanyan and Waller
hook: Stanford's student manager, the future President Herbert Hoover, printed too few tickets, and nobody remembered to bring the ball.
story: The Stanford–Cal rivalry began on a Haight Street ballfield. On March 19, 1892, the two teams met at the Haight Street Grounds for the first Big Game [1][2]. Stanford had opened only the previous October. Its team, captained and coached in all but name by transfer student John Whittemore, was playing its first season against a Cal side that had played for ten years [1]. Stanford's student manager was the future president Herbert Hoover. Hoover had 10,000 tickets printed, and one account says 20,000 people came. The two managers ended up collecting cash in pots, bowls and anything else they could find [1][3]. Then, as kickoff neared, both teams realised that no one had brought a ball. A sporting-goods store owner in the crowd was sent off on horseback to fetch one, and the game started an hour late. Stanford used trick plays to score the first three touchdowns, then held on to win 14–10 [1]. The grounds hosted the first four Big Games, through November 1894. The December 1892 rematch ended in a 10–10 tie [2][4].

title: The powerhouse behind SF's first electric streetcar
place: Site of the Sunnyside Powerhouse, 117-159 Monterey Blvd (block of Monterey, Circular and Baden)
hook: Years before most San Francisco homes had electricity, a coal-fired plant on Sunnyside Avenue was burning 25 tons a day to push streetcars along overhead wires.
story: In April 1892 the first car of the San Francisco and San Mateo Electric Railway ran down its tracks. It was the city's first electric streetcar line, running from Steuart Street out to Holy Cross Cemetery in San Mateo County for a nickel [1][2]. Its power came from a big powerhouse on a flatiron-shaped block of Sunnyside Avenue (now Monterey Boulevard), which burned about 25 tons of coal a day and also housed the car barn [1]. The backer was Behrend Joost, a millionaire land speculator selling lots in his new Sunnyside tract. His engineer, J. W. Hartzell, had crews work all night to string overhead wires before the Supervisors could ban them [1]. Workers liked Hartzell so much that they gave him a diamond ring at Christmas 1891. Joost was another matter. He ignored his engineer's advice, which led to injuries and deaths on the line, and held back wages for months [1]. Hartzell quit ten weeks after opening day. The powerhouse went offline in December 1900, was pulled down in the 1910s, and houses went up on the block around 1940 [1].

title: Warships built at the foot of the hill
place: Union Iron Works Machine Shop, 20th Street, Pier 70
hook: Dewey's flagship at Manila Bay and the battleship whose dash around South America helped get the Panama Canal built were both launched here.
story: In 1883 Irving M. Scott moved Union Iron Works from First and Mission streets to 32 acres of deep-water frontage at Potrero Point. He spent about $2 million on brick shops, including the machine shop that still stands on 20th Street [1]. Scott then went after Navy contracts, competing head to head with the big East Coast yards. When the Navy asked for bids on Cruiser No. 6 in 1890, Union Iron Works was the only bidder. Her keel was laid in June 1891, and on November 5, 1892 she was launched as the Olympia [2]. On May 1, 1898, as Commodore George Dewey's flagship at Manila Bay, she received his order, "You may fire when you are ready, Gridley", and fired the first shell of the battle [2]. The yard also built the battleship Oregon, launched on October 26, 1893. In 1898 the Oregon steamed some 14,000 nautical miles around South America in 66 days to join the fleet off Cuba. The voyage got so much press coverage that it added to public pressure for a Panama Canal [3]. Between 1884 and 1902 the yard built 75 vessels [4]. Olympia survives as a museum ship in Philadelphia, the oldest steel American warship still afloat [2].

title: A Widow's Castle Becomes an Art School
place: Site of the Hopkins mansion and Mark Hopkins Institute of Art, California & Mason (now the Mark Hopkins hotel)
hook: Mark Hopkins never lived to see his towering mansion. His widow's second husband gave it away to art students.
story: Mark Hopkins, one of the railroad Big Four, was persuaded by his wife and first cousin, Mary Frances Sherwood Hopkins, to build a San Francisco estate to rival his partners' [3]. The house, furnished by the decorators Herter Brothers, was completed in 1880, two years after Hopkins died [3]. Novelist Gertrude Atherton said it "looked as if several architects had been employed, and they had fought one another to a finish" [4]. In 1887 the widow married Edward Francis Searles, and when she died in 1891 the bulk of her fortune passed to him [3]. In February 1893 Searles donated the mansion to the University of California, in trust for the San Francisco Art Association, for "instruction in and illustration of the fine arts, music and literature"; the state plaque calls it San Francisco's first cultural center [1]. As the Mark Hopkins Institute of Art it housed the California School of Design and the association's collection, turning a railroad fortune's showpiece into a school [2]. The 1906 fire destroyed it [3], and in 1926 the school, later called the San Francisco Art Institute, moved to Chestnut Street on Russian Hill [2].

title: Chocolate, mustard and a clock tower
place: Ghirardelli Square, 900 North Point St
hook: An Italian confectioner who once sold sweets to miners bought an old woolen mill and turned the waterfront into a chocolate factory. It came through 1906 almost untouched.
story: Domenico Ghirardelli was born in Rapallo, Italy, in 1817 and trained as a candy maker. He ran a confectionery in Lima, Peru, next door to James Lick, who took 600 pounds of Ghirardelli's chocolate with him to San Francisco in 1847 [1][2]. Ghirardelli followed during the Gold Rush and sold sweets and supplies to miners in the Sierra foothills. Fire destroyed his first San Francisco store in 1851, and he started over [1]. In 1893 his company bought the old Pioneer Woolen Mill block at the foot of Russian Hill and moved its works there. Domenico died the next year while visiting Rapallo [1]. In 1900 the company built the Cocoa Building and sold off its coffee and spice lines to concentrate on chocolate and mustard. Every building survived the 1906 earthquake and fire, and business stopped for only a few days [1]. About a decade later came the Power House, an apartment building and the Clock Tower, modelled on the Château de Blois in France. In 1923 the Cocoa Building gained two storeys and the fifteen-foot sign that still greets anyone sailing the bay [1].

title: Fifty-Four Hours on Duty from Oak Street
place: 1152 Oak Street
hook: From this Victorian station, now the city's oldest fire department-owned firehouse, Engine Company 21 fought the 1906 Hayes Valley fires for 54 hours straight.
story: Behind its Victorian facade, 1152 Oak Street is the oldest firehouse still owned by the San Francisco Fire Department [1]. Henrikson & Mahoney designed it and R. Doyle & Sons built it in 1893. The architects also designed two near-twin stations: one survives on Washington Street, and the other, on Folsom Street, was demolished [2]. The Oak Street house opened just before the California Midwinter International Exposition of 1894 began nearby in Golden Gate Park [1]. When the city burned in April 1906, its crew, Engine Company 21, 'sought out and fought the Hayes Valley conflagrations, remaining on-duty for 54 hours' [1]. The horses went in 1915 when the department switched to motors, Truck Company 6 moved out in 1916, and Engine 21 left in 1958 for its current station a few blocks north on Grove Street [1]. A giant blue whale was painted on the western wall from the 1970s until the early 2000s [1]. The building's identity has always been a little muddled. The '27' painted on it is, as Hoodline put it, 'a goof' [1], and the city's official landmark list names it 'Old Firehouse, Engine Company No. 2 and Truck No. 6'. It became Landmark No. 89 in 1977 [3].

title: First firehouse with a three-horse team
place: Old Engine Company No. 23, 3022 Washington St
hook: In the horse-drawn era, this plain wooden firehouse sent out the city's first three-horse hitch, racing to fires from the Richmond to the bay.
story:
In June 1893 the city approved plans for three new firehouses by Henriksen and Mahoney. The architect Bernhardt E. Henriksen was praised in 1884 as "the pioneer native born architect" [1]. This one, on Washington Street between Broderick and Baker, is now one of only two of the three still standing [1].

Engine Company No. 23 was organised in 1894. A 1902 report lists its equipment: a third-class La France engine and a Graves hose wagon carrying 750 feet of two-inch hose. Its crew answered alarms across the Richmond District and the whole area west of Laguna, between Geary and the bay. It was the first house in the Fire Department to use a three-horse hitch [1]. The horses were replaced by engines in 1915 [1].

The building stayed a firehouse until 1963. Then John Dickinson bought it and turned it into a studio and home, and by 1970 many of its missing exterior details had been restored [1]. The city lists it as Landmark No. 93 [2].

title: Salt Water Piped to Post Street
place: First permanent Olympic Club clubhouse, Post Street near Mason
hook: America's oldest athletic club started in a backyard gym. By 1893 it had a downtown palace with a pool of real seawater, and a world boxing champion on staff.
story: The Olympic Club began in the Broadway backyard of Charles and Arthur Nahl, German-born artist brothers who were keen gymnasts. In 1860, 23 charter members met at a nearby firehouse and formed what became America's oldest athletic club [1]. Mark Twain went to the club often and wrote to his mother that he felt 'like a new man. I sleep better, I have a healthier appetite and my intellect is leaner' [1]. As membership grew, the club bought land at Post and Mason and hired architect Henry A. Schultz [1]. The first permanent clubhouse opened on Post Street on January 2, 1893 [2]. Its natatorium was filled with salt water piped all the way from Ocean Beach [1]. Its most famous member was James J. Corbett, who joined in 1884, won the world heavyweight title in 1892 and later coached boxing at the club for many years [2]. It is said that Baron Pierre de Coubertin, founder of the modern Olympic Games, came to inspect the facilities in 1893 [1]. The club sent its first athletes to the Olympic Games in 1904 [1]. The clubhouse burned in the 1906 fire, and members paid for a new one that opened in 1912 [1][2].

title: The Bar That Outlived the Fair
place: Little Shamrock, 807 Lincoln Way
hook: Opened for the workers building the 1894 Midwinter Fair, the Little Shamrock is the oldest bar in the Outside Lands after the Cliff House.
story: In October 1893, with the Midwinter Fair rising across the road in Golden Gate Park, Julia Herzo (later Quigley) opened the Little Shamrock at 807 H Street, now Lincoln Way [1]. Columnist Frank Dunnigan says it was built to serve the many Irish labourers working on the fair [2]. Herzo also ran saloons near the racetracks in the Richmond and the Ingleside. When those tracks closed she shut those saloons and kept this one [1]. After the fair, her customers were men who worked in the park and graded the Sunset's sand hills. In the free-lunch tradition, they got slices of ham [1]. Not everyone welcomed it. In 1897 a neighbour petitioned the supervisors not to renew the licences of three local saloons, the Shamrock among them. A newspaper reported that forty women property owners agreed but were afraid to sign. All three stayed open [1]. The building gained a second storey in 1900 and a new front in 1924. As far as is known, the 1893 wooden frame is still inside [1]. Herzo's son Tony started tending bar in 1907. In 1948 he said 'not one customer in fifty wears skirts' [1]. Today the bar is known for board games, sofas and Irish coffee [2].

title: The Confederate scout's rental on Richland
place: 386 Richland Avenue
hook: The man who built this odd little rental had once stolen thousands of Union cattle and escaped a spy's gallows.
story:
In the 1890s George David Shadburne signed for water service to a new 825-square-foot house at 386 Richland Avenue. According to the water company's record, service began on 1 August 1893 and he paid $10 in gold coin. A clerk first charged for two cows, then rubbed them out [1]. Shadburne never lived there. He was a combative downtown lawyer from Texas who had come to San Francisco in 1868, and he rented the house to poorer tenants [1].

His earlier life was darker. As one of Wade Hampton's Confederate "Iron Scouts" he had spied behind Union lines in Virginia [1]. In September 1864 he reported a lightly guarded herd of about 3,000 cattle near Grant's headquarters, which led to the famous Beefsteak Raid [2]. Martin calls him a captain, while the Wikipedia account calls him a sergeant [1][2]. Captured in 1865 and charged as a spy, he escaped [1]. An 1858 appraisal of his Louisiana property lists 20 enslaved people [1].

Much later, electrician Molly Martin and her lesbian collective bought the building in 1980. When she opened the walls she found an 1893 racing form used as insulation, and signs that several separate buildings had been joined together [1].

title: The Neighbour Who Sold Spring Water
place: 72 Majestic Avenue, Columbia Heights (site of George Wilson's private water works)
hook: The private water company wouldn't lay mains up to this hilltop tract, so a resident tapped a spring in his yard and charged his neighbours for water.
story:
In 1893 Easton, Eldridge & Co. auctioned off "Columbia Heights", a wedge of lots on the east slope of Merced Heights above San Jose Avenue [1][2]. It promised "perfect natural drainage and perpetual sunshine," lots from $145 and "200 per cent profit" within a year. Only 68 of the 391 lots sold [1]. There was no gas, electricity or sewer, and the street grades were not set. Buyers were told "pure water can be had by boring 14 feet" [1][2]. On January 5, 1895, a storm blew one of the first houses over: "Household furniture was scattered in all directions" [1].

After the 1906 earthquake brothers Thomas and Christopher Rivers bought the unsold lots, built houses and advertised hard. Their sales office still stands, altered, at 15 Lakeview Avenue [1]. In July 1907 they complained to the Board of Supervisors that neighbours' cows kept trespassing [1].

The Spring Valley Water Company decided the ridge was not worth new mains. So for years a resident named George Wilson ran his own utility. He tapped a spring on his Majestic Avenue land and piped water to neighbours for a fee, until city pressure made Spring Valley buy him out. The 1915 Sanborn map shows his water works behind 72 Majestic Avenue [1].

title: The gasworks by the cove
place: San Francisco Gas Light Company building, 3640 Buchanan Street
hook: Before the mansions and the Marina Safeway, this shore made the city's gas from coal shipped to its own wharf. One brick building survives.
story: Before the world's fair, the shoreline where the Marina now stands was not all dunes and marsh. Most of the sand hills had been levelled, and a jumble of wharves and industrial plants stretched from about Laguna Street to Steiner Street [1]. Among them was the San Francisco Gas Light Company, which made gas for heating and lighting out of coal and petroleum delivered to its own wharf nearby [2]. In 1893 the company put up a Romanesque Revival brick building on Buchanan Street between Bay and North Point. According to Susan Cerny's architectural guidebook, it was designed by the company's own president, Joseph B. Crockett [2]. Pacific Gas & Electric closed the plant in the 1950s, and the building is now offices. It is the only industrial building left in the neighbourhood [2]. The industry also left its name on the water. The little basin west of Fort Mason still appears on the Park Service's map as Gas House Cove [3].

title: The house that walked downhill
place: 23rd Street between Church and Chattanooga (3780–3784 23rd St)
hook: In 1893 a crew jacked up a whole family home and slid it down the slope to face another street. Its walls held through 1906, though the fireplace did not.
story:
Noe Valley illustrator Florence Holub arrived from Idaho in 1925 at age six. Her family stayed with the Haglunds, part of the neighbourhood's Swede-Finn colony, while her mother looked for a place to live. From their window Florence watched a grand Victorian across 23rd Street [1][2].

Years later a schoolmate whose family had lived there told her its story. The house was built in 1869 facing Church Street. It had a stable and a windmill with a water tower, fed from a well on 24th Street. In 1893, grading for a new streetcar line forced a move. Using jacks, blocks and timbers, a crew lowered the house down the slope and set it on a new foundation facing 23rd [1].

Nicholas Schneider and Mary Pracy Schneider raised six children there. Their sons Nicholas and George went on to found Schneider Brothers, fur dealers on Post Street [1]. The house survived 1906, but its fireplace broke apart. The bricks fell into the garden and missed the parlour where the family had gathered [2]. Holub's two columns give the address as 3780 and 3784 23rd Street.

title: The spy and the Great Western
place: San Francisco National Cemetery
hook: Among thousands of soldiers lie two remarkable women: a Union spy once sentenced to hang, and a six-foot camp follower called 'the Great Western'.
story: In 1884 the old post cemetery became the San Francisco National Cemetery, the first national cemetery on the West Coast [1]. It also took in the dead of army posts closing elsewhere in the West [2]. One was Sarah Bowman, a six-foot innkeeper and camp follower famous as 'the Great Western' and the 'Heroine of Fort Brown' in the Mexican War. A Texas Ranger said she could 'whip any man, fair fight or foul' [2]. She died at Fort Yuma in 1866, was buried with military honours, and was moved here in 1890 when that fort closed [2]. Three years later came Pauline Cushman, an actress who had spied for the Union. The Confederates caught her with papers hidden in her shoes and sentenced her to hang, but Union troops arrived first [3]. Lincoln made her an honorary major [3]. Her last years were spent in a San Francisco boarding house, working as a seamstress and charwoman and in pain from arthritis. On December 2, 1893, she died of a morphine overdose [3]. Union veterans of the Grand Army of the Republic arranged her funeral with full military honours, and she lies in the Officers' Circle [3].
