title: The stockyard by Seculovich's kitchen
place: Mission Street at Fair Avenue
hook: Cows on Mission Street, manure by the kitchen door, and a neighbour who wouldn't stop complaining until the Board of Health listened.
story: In 1893 the law allowed no more than two cows on a city lot, but the district it covered was loosely drawn [1]. On Mission Street at Fair Avenue, roughly where Taqueria Cancun is today, Salomon's stockyard held cows, horses and goats among piles of manure. It had 200 feet of frontage on Mission Street [1]. Right next door lived Peter Seculovich, a former locksmith turned property owner, whose yard was full of flowers and fruit trees. The back of Salomon's cow stables sat a few feet from his kitchen door [1][2]. Seculovich was president of the new Mission Street and Precita Valley Improvement Club, and it voted to help the authorities remove the yard. The Board of Health had Salomon arrested three times [1][2]. "It is all spitework," Salomon told the Call, "caused by this man Seculovich" [1]. Seculovich had already become famous for putting a price of $250 on each cherry tree the city wanted for a street widening. That autumn the club gave him a gold-headed cane [2].

title: Vegetables watered by Pacific Heights
place: Former Chinese vegetable gardens north of Chestnut, near Steiner Street
hook: In 1893 the city engineer noted, quite matter-of-factly, that sewage from the mansions uphill was watering Chinese vegetable gardens on the flats.
story: Late 19th-century San Francisco still had farms inside the city, and some of them were watered with sewage [1]. On the flats that later became the Marina, farmers used wastewater running downhill from the mansions of Pacific Heights [1]. An 1893 report by the city engineer put it plainly: 'The sewage of the Steiner Street sewer, and to some extent that of the Pierce Street, is being utilized during the spring and summer months for the irrigation of Chinese vegetable gardens . . . north of Chestnut Street' [1]. A photograph from the 1890s in the San Francisco History Center shows more Chinese vegetable gardens farther east, below Pacific Heights at about today's Union and Gough streets [2]. The same stretch was drawing the attention of health officials. On a tour with a reporter, health officer Dr. Keeney showed off the Franklin Street sewer, pouring out 'in a turbid, foul stream' and falling about thirty feet into a gully within a hundred yards of a public school [2]. Not long after, the gardens and marsh north of Chestnut were filled and levelled for the 1915 world's fair, and then covered by the houses of the Marina [3].

title: A Fair's Japanese Village Takes Root
place: Japanese Tea Garden, 75 Hagiwara Tea Garden Drive
hook: Built as an exotic fair exhibit, the Japanese Village became a permanent garden and home to a Japanese immigrant family for decades.
story: For the 1894 fair, George Turner Marsh, an Australian-born dealer in Japanese goods, designed a Japanese Village and Tea Garden built by Japanese craftsmen. It had a grand gateway, a tea room of thatch and wood, a three-story theater for a troupe of Japanese jugglers, and ponds, bridges and bonsai [1]. A guidebook promised a single step from "Western civilization" into the "semi-barbaric" Land of the Mikado [1]. Marsh also supplied jinrikishas for the fairgrounds and hoped Japanese men would pull them. None would, and in the end they were pulled by white men in face paint and Japanese costume [1]. The garden was so popular that park commissioners bought it from Marsh when the fair closed [1]. From 1895 until his death in 1925, its caretaker was Makoto Hagiwara, an immigrant from Yamanashi who turned the exhibit into a permanent garden and, by tradition, introduced the modern fortune cookie there [2]. The garden was enlarged in 1902 [3]. During World War II his descendants were forced out and interned, and the Hagiwara house in the garden was demolished [2][3].

title: Alice Toklas Keeps House on O'Farrell
place: Levinsky family home, 922 O'Farrell Street (between Polk and Van Ness)
hook: Before Paris and Gertrude Stein, Alice B. Toklas was a San Francisco girl keeping house for a family of men and quietly planning her escape.
story: Alice Babette Toklas was born in San Francisco on April 30, 1877, to Ferdinand and Emma Levinsky Toklas. Both sides of the family came from Polish Jewish immigrants [1]. Her grandfather Louis Levinsky arrived as a forty-niner. He found dry goods more profitable than gold, first in Jackson and then in San Francisco [1]. An 1894 city block book lists his home at 922 O'Farrell Street, where his teenage granddaughter lived [2]. The Toklases had moved to Seattle in 1890 but came back when Alice's mother fell ill [2]. Emma died in March 1897, weeks before Alice turned twenty. For the next decade Alice kept house for her father, her brother and assorted male relatives [1]. She was good enough at the piano to think about a concert career [1]. Her friend Harriet Lane Levy later wrote a memoir of their shared San Francisco girlhood called '920 O'Farrell Street' (1947) [1]. Toklas knew she was attracted to women friends and did not expect to marry, and she wanted to get away [1]. After the 1906 earthquake Michael and Sarah Stein told her about their life in Paris. She sailed in 1907 and met Gertrude Stein the day after she arrived [1][2]. The block of Myrtle Street nearby is now Alice B. Toklas Place [2].

title: From 'slimy ooze' to Precita Park
place: Precita Park (then Bernal Park), Folsom Street and Precita Avenue
hook: Neighbours were so fed up with their swampy 'park' that they told the city to hand it over as a fish hatchery.
story:
On Milo Hoadley's 1859 auction map, the hollow at the foot of Bernal's north slope was marked as a public square, "Precita Place." In reality it was where Precita Creek overflowed. In dry months it was a garbage pit. In wet months it was a swamp full of frogs and sewage [1]. Waste from tanneries, run-off from slaughterhouses and sewage from the county hospital all ended up there. When the streets around it were graded, parts of the pit sat 30 feet below the sidewalk [1].

In 1894 the supervisors named it "Bernal Park," but that did not turn it into one. Grocer John T. Graham of Precita and Alabama called it "one of the worst cesspools I ever saw." His Precita Valley Improvement Club petitioned the city to fill it in, or else give it to the Fish Commissioners because the winter rains would make it a fine hatchery [1]. The pit was filled in 1899. In 1901 park superintendent John McLaren put in pipes, grass and trees. When neighbours asked for benches, logs were dumped on the site instead [1]. By the 1920s Bernal Park had a formal border of Blackwood acacias [2]. It was later renamed Precita Park.

title: Human Exhibits and the Color Line
place: Midwinter Fair grounds, east of the Music Concourse
hook: At the 1894 fair, people were exhibits, a baby was born in a plaster igloo, and San Franciscans of color fought over their place.
story: Behind the Midwinter Fair's promise of "a living and moving encyclopaedia" of the world were real people on display [2]. The Esquimaux Village covered three acres, with igloos made of plaster, sled dogs and Inuit families from Labrador and Alaska. Francisca Tehama Deer was born there on February 10, 1894, and died in early April. All five children born to Inuit performers at the Chicago and San Francisco fairs died as infants [2]. Historian Mae Silver notes that Black San Franciscans, kept out of white trade unions, had no part in building the fair. When organizers declared May 2 "Colored Americans Day," some Black residents objected to the "needless drawing of the colored line" [1]. Asian San Franciscans had to fight harder than other groups to get their own days. On Japanese Day (June 9) and Chinese Day (June 17), many Japanese and Chinese visitors rode in jinrikishas pulled by white men dressed as Japanese. The Chronicle sneered, but historian Barbara Berglund suggests the sight briefly upended the racial order [2].

title: James Lick's $100,000 Bronze History Lesson
place: Original site of the Pioneer Monument, Marshall Square (Hyde, Grove and Market)
hook: A Gold Rush millionaire's will ordered a bronze history of California for City Hall. Its heroic version of the past has caused trouble ever since.
story: James Lick, a Pennsylvania-born former piano builder who got rich on Gold Rush real estate, left a trust with an unusual clause: erect 'at the City Hall' a group of bronze statuary 'well worth one hundred thousand dollars' showing the history of California [1]. In September 1890 the Lick trustees picked sculptor Frank Happersberger's model from four artists and 28 design entries [1]. Ground was broken in May 1894 at Marshall Square, near Hyde and Grove, right in front of the unfinished City Hall. The cornerstone was laid on September 10, 1894, with the Society of California Pioneers and the Native Sons of the Golden West [1]. Some accounts give November 29 as the dedication date [1]. Minerva and a grizzly bear stand on top, above medallions of Drake, Sutter, Frémont, Serra and Lick. Around the base are Commerce, Plenty, the miners of 'In '49' and 'Early Days', which shows a fallen Native American at the feet of a missionary and a vaquero [1][2]. The monument's placement was pointed: a planner later remarked that it was 'plopped' onto the sand lots where workers had held their rallies [3]. It was moved one block in 1991 and 'Early Days' was removed in 2018 [1][2].

title: Oaks older than the park
place: Coast live oak grove, north slope of Buena Vista Park
hook: Under the eucalyptus planted by John McLaren is something much older: one of San Francisco's last native oak woodlands, growing where sand dunes once poured over the hill.
story:
Before the city existed, the great sand dunes that covered about a third of San Francisco climbed right up and over this hill. Hundreds of years ago, pioneering plants held the sand in place and the soil got rich enough for coast live oaks to grow [1]. When the city set the hill aside in the 1860s, one reason was that it had native trees and shrubs, which were rare in San Francisco [3].

After it was dedicated as Buena Vista Park in 1894, John McLaren had the hill planted with eucalyptus, cypress, pine, Australian tea trees and small redwoods around the few native live oaks and toyons already there. During Adolph Sutro's term as mayor, schoolchildren planted seedlings on Arbor Day [2]. The newcomers now tower over the park, but the old grove survived. The city describes it as one of its few remaining coast live oak groves, on the park's northern side [4]. Along with stands in Golden Gate Park and by Lobos Creek, it is among the largest left in San Francisco [1]. Today park staff and the Friends of Buena Vista Park pull ivy and plant natives around the oaks [1].

title: Ocean Water Piped Four Miles Downtown
place: Site of the Lurline Baths, Bush & Larkin streets
hook: San Franciscans once swam in real Pacific seawater at Bush and Larkin, and Thomas Edison's camera caught them flying down the slide.
story: Bay water near downtown was fouled by sewage and factory waste, so in 1892 a group headed by John D. Spreckels formed the Olympic Salt Water Company to bring "pure ocean water for bathing purposes" into the city [1]. They laid an intake 600 feet offshore south of the Cliff House, a pump across the Great Highway, and nearly four miles of iron pipe along today's Geary Boulevard to a reservoir in Laurel Heights. From there, gravity carried the sea downhill [1]. The company's own Lurline Baths opened in 1894 at the corner of Bush and Larkin, with public baths and a swimming pool [1][3]. In August 1897 Edison cameraman Frederick Blechynden filmed there. His 20-second film shows the pool's toboggan slide, bathers going down "some sitting, others lying down, head first or feet first" [2]. The film survives at the Library of Congress. The company also tried selling salt water for firefighting and street washing, without success [1]. The baths and their seawater supply lasted until 1936 [1][3].

title: Shooting the Chenery Chute
place: Chenery Street hill between 30th and Randall streets
hook: Overloaded cars full of mourners came down Chenery Street hill 'like toboggans'. The railway blamed its motormen's inexperience, and schoolboys on the rails.
story: When Behrend Joost's electric railway opened in 1892, its cars swung south onto Chenery at 30th Street and climbed a very steep grade to Randall [1]. The first accident came six weeks into service, and most that followed had the same script: cars overloaded with passengers returning from the cemeteries, people with "barely a foothold" hanging onto the ends, and a car that turned "unmanageable" on the way down or rounded the 30th Street curve "with a heavy list to starboard." Some cars left the tracks and crashed. There were many injuries; three in 1894 were life-threatening [1]. Management said the operators needed more practice, and blamed Fairmount School children for using the track as a toboggan run, sliding down on boards until the rails were too smooth for brakes to hold. Newspapers began calling it the "Chenery street slide" [1]. A 2001 neighbourhood history tells a grimmer version, of brakes failing near Roanoke Street and cars leaping the tracks at Diamond, "frequently killing passengers," until the Municipal Railway took over the line in 1916 [2]. The grade was later reduced, but in 1927 three young men died when their speeding touring car fishtailed at the Natick curve into a 26-line streetcar. Police called Chenery "one of the worst death traps in San Francisco" [1].

title: Sutro's Secondhand Amusement Park
place: Merrie Way, above Sutro Baths
hook: That windswept parking lot above the Sutro Baths ruins once held a Ferris-style wheel, a mirror maze and a room that swung around its riders.
story: Adolph Sutro could never pass up a bargain [1]. When the 1894 Midwinter Fair in Golden Gate Park sold off its attractions, he bought several and rebuilt them on a cleared strip just east of his baths [1]. The centrepiece was the 100-foot 'Firth Wheel', whose 16 carriages carried riders on 20-minute trips high above the baths. Across the midway stood the Mystic Maze, a house of mirrors, and the Haunted Swing: visitors sat on a gently rocking glider while the whole furnished room, mounted on gimbals, swung the other way, creating the illusion that the room was spinning around them. It was reported to be very unsettling [1]. By 1898 there was also a small 'Scenic Railway' coaster and chowder stands made from recycled fair kiosks [1][2]. The name Merrie Way came later. But the fun did not last. Sutro died in 1898, and by 1900 insurance maps marked every attraction closed or not in operation [1]. A 1910 photo shows the weather-beaten wheel above a deserted midway; after 1923 only cleared land remained [1].

title: The Electric Tower That Wouldn't Fall
place: Music Concourse, site of the Midwinter Fair's Grand Court
hook: The Midwinter Fair's 266-foot tower of light outstayed its welcome, so the park foreman came back with thirty pounds of dynamite.
story: The Midwinter Fair was the answer of Chronicle publisher Michael H. de Young to a national depression: a California world's fair that opened on January 27, 1894, on 200 acres east of the new Stow Lake [1]. Its symbol, rising over the Grand Court (today's Music Concourse), was the Bonet Electric Tower, 266 feet of iron and steel [2]. Designed by Leopold Bonet, it carried about 3,200 colored lights and a searchlight that swept the park [3]. More than two million people visited before the fair closed six months later [1]. McLaren had fought to keep the fair out. It left the park in a "deplorable state," and repairs took sixty men and twelve teams several months [2]. Eighteen months after closing, the tower still stood. On January 11, 1896, a dynamite charge failed to bring it down. The next morning foreman Patrick Quigley came back with more. "Now don't be at all sparing with that stuff, Quigley," McLaren told him. Quigley packed thirty pounds into the footings, pushed the crowd back and gave the signal [2]. The fair's Fine Arts Building lived on as the first de Young Museum [1].

title: A German church a block from dynamite
place: St. Mark's Lutheran Church, 1135 O'Farrell Street at Franklin
hook: In 1906 soldiers blew up buildings a block away and its cross melted in the heat. St. Mark's survived, and it took in the homeless.
story:
St. Mark's dates its founding to 1849, when German immigrants were arriving in Gold Rush San Francisco [1]. The congregation dedicated this church on Cathedral Hill on 10 March 1895. It was designed by the German-American architect Henry Geilfuss in a mix of Romanesque and Gothic styles [1][2]. The city's landmark listing calls it the oldest Lutheran church in the West [2].

The 1906 earthquake weakened the east tower. Then the fire came west. Dynamite was set off a block away, at O'Farrell and Van Ness, to make a firebreak. The heat of the fire was fierce enough to melt the church's cross [1]. The landmark record credits the Van Ness dynamiting with saving the building [2]. The fire stopped just short of the church, and St. Mark's immediately became a refuge for families left homeless by the disaster [1].

The church's Victorian neighbours did not last. Decades later redevelopment cleared hundreds of Western Addition homes, and the round Carillon Tower apartments rose behind it [2]. The 1895 church is still there.

title: A Kyoto tea room shipped to Sutter Street
place: Hokka Nichi Bei Kai (Japanese American Association of Northern California), 1759 Sutter Street
hook: A club founded in the 1890s to help Issei find their feet in America now keeps a tea room that Kyoto built, took apart and shipped across the Pacific.
story: Nichi Bei Kai, the Japanese American Association, began in the late 1800s. Its own history gives the year as 1895 [2]. It helped Japanese immigrants adjust to life in America and keep up their culture, and it worked to build goodwill between the two countries [1][2]. In 2000 it merged with the Japanese Speaking Society of America to become Hokka Nichi Bei Kai. Today it teaches Japanese language, classical dance, ikebana, shamisen, sumi-e and tea ceremony [1]. Its three-storey building on Sutter Street holds a treasure. It is an authentic tea room, a chashitsu, given by the City of Kyoto. It was built in Japan, taken apart, shipped to America and put back together on this site [1][2]. The association calls it the finest tea ceremony facility outside Japan, and it runs Japanese speech contests for children every spring and adults every autumn [2]. The city's surveys can't agree on when the building went up. One credits it to Mitsuru Tada & Associates in 1972, another dates it to 1980 [2].

title: A Saloon on the Road to the Races
place: 4447-4449 Mission Street
hook: One of the Excelsior's oldest buildings served beer to farmhands and Sunday crowds heading for the Ingleside racetrack.
story: Between Avalon and Excelsior avenues, 4447-4449 Mission Street is a little Victorian storefront from the 1890s, with its second-floor porch and panelled bulkheads still in place. It began as a saloon for the district's farm labourers and for the Sunday crowds heading out to the Ingleside Racetrack [1]. Two other survivors from about the turn of the century stand farther south at 4716 and 4722 Mission, with carved wooden cornices and bracketed arched windows. They appear in a city photograph of May 1915 [2]. Mission Street soon filled in. Guadalupe Hall at 4555 Mission, built in 1909, was the Excelsior's earliest social venue. For a time it was the only hall in the southern part of the city, hosting weddings, dinners and meetings of the Native Sons and Daughters of the Golden West [3]. In 1910 Central Drug Store opened on the corner of Santa Rosa Avenue at 4494 Mission. It is the oldest business in the Excelsior still operating [1].

title: A Seaside Town Built from Old Streetcars
place: Site of early Carville, La Playa between Irving and Judah Streets
hook: Horsecars sold off for $20 became beach shacks, clubhouses and even a church. By 1908 'Carville' reportedly had 2,000 residents.
story: When cable and electric lines made horsecars obsolete, the Market Street Railway advertised the old cars for $20, or $10 without seats [1]. Out at the Park and Ocean railroad's beach terminus, Colonel Charles Dailey, a Civil War veteran and a friend of Adolph Sutro, rented three cars from Sutro for $5 a month. He opened one as a coffee saloon, and in 1896 a Bulletin reporter called the little cluster 'Beachside' [1]. It became known as Carville. A women's bicycle club, the Falcons, napped on the upholstered seats of their clubhouse car. Musicians coming off late shifts in the city's cafés named their car 'La Boheme' and took dips in the icy surf between rounds [1]. By 1901 a reported fifty families lived in about 100 cars [1]. After 1906, refugees and more surplus cable cars made the settlement bigger. The Overland Monthly put its 1908 population at 2,000, with stores, restaurants and an Episcopal church, St. Andrew's-by-the-Sea, built from streetcars [2]. Neighbors in ordinary houses called the area Oceanside and saw the cars as an embarrassment. On July 4, 1913, Oceanside Improvement Club president Alexander Russell burned the Falcons' old car with $10 worth of fireworks. The slogan: 'Make clean today by sweeping and burning up the debris of yesterday' [1][2].

title: A Venetian palace for the Lovers of Peace
place: Bush Street Temple (Ohabai Shalome), 1881 Bush St
hook: Wood made to look like Sienese marble, minarets and Venetian arches: San Francisco's third Jewish congregation built itself a palace on Bush Street.
story:
On 15 September 1895, exactly thirty years after it consecrated its first temple on Mason Street, Congregation Ohabai Shalome ("Lovers of Peace") dedicated this new home on Bush Street [1]. The architect, Moses J. Lyon, borrowed from Venice. A loggia of seven arches with delicate tracery recalls the Ca' d'Oro or the Doge's Palace, and the wooden front was painted to imitate Sienese marble. There were seats for a thousand people. Tall minarets once rose from the towers, and Judaic symbols, including the tablets of the Ten Commandments, filled the space between them [1].

The congregation was one of the most conservative in the city [2]. Many of its neighbours were Jewish merchant families, most of them of German background. A census study of the 1700 block of Bush in 1900 found cigar importers, clothing wholesalers, clerks and Rabbi Jacob Nieto of Sherith Israel living a block away [2]. The temple later became a centre for Zionist causes [1].

As membership waned, the building was sold in 1934 to a group of Japanese Soto Zen Buddhists. It later housed the early San Francisco Zen Center, before becoming part of a senior home [1].

title: A church built like a forest
place: Swedenborgian Church, 2107 Lyon St at Washington
hook: Bark-covered madrone trunks hold up the roof, and the chairs were made without a single nail. It was a manifesto of California's Arts and Crafts movement.
story:
The Reverend Joseph Worcester came to San Francisco from Boston in 1867 to lead a congregation of followers of the mystic Emanuel Swedenborg. At first they worshipped in Druids Hall on Sutter Street [1]. In 1894 Worcester began planning a church of his own at Lyon and Washington, working with a remarkable group of friends [1][2].

The painter Bruce Porter sketched an Italian village church he had seen near Verona. A young draughtsman in A. Page Brown's office, Bernard Maybeck, drew up the plans [1]. The church, finished in 1895, brings nature indoors. Massive madrone logs, their bark still on, support a heavy tile roof. The maple chairs were made by hand without nails, and their seats were woven from tule rushes gathered in the Sacramento River Delta. Even the walled garden was planted with symbolic meaning [1].

It is considered one of California's earliest pure Arts and Crafts buildings [2]. In 2004 it was named a National Historic Landmark [1][2], and it is still in use as a church.

title: A stone palazzo in a city of wood
place: George W. Gibbs House, 2622 Jackson Street (Landmark No. 203)
hook: The Examiner called it San Francisco's first classical house. Its owner died two months after moving in, and it later became Japan's consulate.
story:
George W. Gibbs was one of the leading iron and steel producers on the West Coast. For his house on Jackson Street, the young architect Willis Polk borrowed from the Italian Renaissance: its massing recalls a Tuscan villa, its details come from Raphael's Palazzo Pandolfini in Florence, and its round portico echoes the Temple of Vesta at Tivoli [1]. The Examiner called it "the first classical residence in San Francisco" [1][2]. It was one of the city's earliest houses built entirely of stone, in gray Oregon sandstone under a glazed tile roof. In a city built of wood, it stood for grandeur and permanence [1][2]. (Sources date it to 1894 or 1895.)

Gibbs died only two months after he moved in. His widow Augusta lived there until her death in 1918 [2]. The house then became the Japanese Consulate, until the outbreak of the Second World War. After that it was the local Red Cross headquarters, and from the late 1940s it belonged to the San Francisco Music and Arts Institute [2]. In 1994 it was University High School's Decorator Showcase house. A little-known caretaker's cottage by Polk still stands behind it, toward Pacific Avenue [2].

title: Alice Eastwood's Wildflower Walk on the Tracks
place: Lands End Coastal Trail (old Cliff Line railbed) between 32nd Avenue and Lands End
hook: In the 1890s a great botanist walked the Lands End railway line noting sand verbenas and cow-parsnip. Since 2004, volunteers have been planting natives back.
story: Alice Eastwood worked for more than six decades at the California Academy of Sciences. In the late 1890s she compiled a valuable record of San Francisco's native plants [1]. In 1945, in the journal Leaflets of Western Botany, she described the city's lost wildflower gardens [1]. Another attractive excursion, she remembered, followed the railroad that 'once went to Sutro Heights via Lands End'. Apart from the wild currant, which was abundant in spring, she wrote that this stretch 'was better for summer and fall'. Pink and yellow sand verbenas grew along it, with San Francisco willow-herb, Angelica hendersonii, cow-parsnip, goldenrod, lizard leaf, Baccharis and the heather-leaved Ericameria [1]. The landscape did not stay that way. Grading, planting and building over the next 150 years crowded out coastal scrub, prairie, dune and streamside plants. Non-native species moved in [2]. Since 2004 the Golden Gate National Parks Conservancy has worked with hundreds of volunteers to bring natives back to Lands End: arroyo willow, seaside daisy, California poppy, dune grass, salt rush, coyote brush and red alder [2]. Seaside daisy, which Eastwood still found in the city's dunes in 1945, is on that list [1][2].

title: Lo Mo and the Mission Home Raids
place: Presbyterian Mission Home, 920 Sacramento Street
hook: Brothel owners called her the White Devil. The girls she hid called her Lo Mo. On her first day, someone planted dynamite.
story: The Presbyterian Church opened the Occidental Mission Home at 920 Sacramento Street in the 1870s (the landmark report says 1873, FoundSF 1874) as a refuge for Chinese girls and women trafficked into prostitution and forced labour [1][2]. Exclusion laws had left Chinatown with far more men than women, and many women arrived sold or indentured [1][2]. In April 1895 a 25-year-old Donaldina Cameron came to teach sewing [2]. Dynamite was reportedly found around the building on her first day [2]. When superintendent Margaret Culbertson died in 1897, Cameron took charge [2]. She led night raids on brothels with policemen carrying axes and sledgehammers, then fought in court for guardianship of the women she freed, relying on Chinese aides such as Tien Wu [1][2]. More than 800 women and girls are recorded as living at the home between 1874 and 1909 [2]. FoundSF also notes the paternalism: residents were expected to pray daily and adapt to Western ways, and Cameron never learned Chinese [2]. In 1906 firefighters dynamited the home in a failed attempt to make a firebreak. It was rebuilt in 1908 from its salvaged bricks and is now Cameron House [1].

title: Named for the Sunset Outside the Hall
place: Site of La Grande Hall, SE corner of 9th Ave & Lincoln Way (then H St)
hook: Stranded when their streetcar was cut off, angry neighbours met at 9th and H in 1895. A sunset outside the window gave the district its name.
story: In 1893, as the Midwinter Fair rose in Golden Gate Park, a $6,000 building went up on the southeast corner of 9th Avenue and H Street (today's Lincoln Way). It had seven shops, a rooming house and a meeting hall, and it was the first large commercial building south of the park [1]. One morning in August 1895 the Metropolitan streetcar line suddenly stopped running west of Cole and Waller streets, stranding residents. The Call suspected that Southern Pacific wanted to spoil Adolph Sutro's offer of land on Mount Parnassus for the new Affiliated Colleges [1]. At the end of August the people who actually lived and worked here met at La Grande Hall and elected W. H. Jones president. They were not the absentee speculators of the older South Side Improvement Club. One member, Gus Fox, had just watched a magnificent sunset outside, and he proposed the name 'Sunset District Improvement Club' [1]. On September 1, 1895, 'Sunset' appeared in print as the district's name for the first time [1]. Popular accounts credit Aurelius Buckingham or the fair's newspaper nickname, 'Sunset City,' but Macfarlane's research in the papers does not support either [2][3].

title: Ten cents to shoot the Chutes
place: Haight Street Chutes, Haight, Cole, Waller and Clayton
hook: A boat on rails dropped off a tower into an artificial lake on Haight Street, and daredevils kept trying to top each other.
story: On November 2, 1895, a tall wooden tower on Haight Street, on the block bounded by Cole, Waller and Clayton, opened as the city's newest thrill [1][2]. "Shoot the Chutes" was based on Paul Boyton's Chicago water chute. Cars hauled riders to the top, where a boat was launched about every fifteen seconds down a roughly 300-foot ramp into a man-made lake. The boat's nose often shot up, and sometimes it flipped. That was part of the fun [2]. Accounts put the tower at 60 or 70 feet [1][2]. One claimed the boat hit the water at 60 miles an hour, faster than almost anyone had ever travelled [1]. Admission was 10 cents. On November 19, 1896, 13,634 people paid it [1]. The showmen kept trying to top each other. Professor Markesburg parachuted while hanging by his teeth, and a rival did it by his toes. A "Man Fish" ate, drank and smoked underwater. Antonio Pirri rode a bicycle down the chute into the lake, and Albert Richards dove 60 feet into two feet of water [1]. The park sat on land leased from the estate of John Baird. It was run by Charles Ackerman, an attorney for the Southern Pacific, whose Market Street Railway held the lease [2].

title: The $24 million suit against a neighbourhood
place: 24th and Noe streets, in the former Rancho San Miguel
hook: In 1895 Noé's heirs threatened to sue more than 7,000 landowners, even though Noé himself had told his sons never to go to court.
story:
In March 1862, knowing he was dying, José de Jesús Noé wrote his will. It divided what remained of Rancho San Miguel among his children. It also advised his sons to settle any quarrels through "friendly arbitration" and avoid legal proceedings [1].

Thirty-three years later his heirs went the other way. On 13 August 1895 the San Francisco Call reported a coming suit for about $24 million in property. It would cover the whole old rancho, and more than 7,000 defendants would be served, among them the City, the Southern Pacific, the Stanford and Crocker estates and Adolph Sutro [2]. The plaintiffs were Noé's son Miguel and two grandchildren. They argued that when Noé's wife died in 1848, Mexican law had passed her share to the children. If so, the sale to Horner five years later was invalid [2].

The next day's Call carried the headline "Land-Owners Laugh at the Twenty-Four Million Dollar Suit" [2]. The suit failed. By then, as the Noe Valley Voice notes, the land was mostly covered with Victorian houses [3].

title: The Demon of the Belfry
place: Emmanuel Baptist Church site, Bartlett Street near 21st (exact address unconfirmed)
hook: On the eve of Easter 1895, women decorating a Mission church found one murdered parishioner in a cupboard. Another was in the belfry.
story: On April 3, 1895, witnesses saw Theodore Durrant, a 23-year-old medical student and assistant Sunday-school superintendent, ride a streetcar to the 21st Street stop with Blanche Lamont, a 20-year-old former schoolteacher from Montana [1][2]. They walked into Emmanuel Baptist Church on Bartlett Street. She was never seen alive again [2]. That afternoon the organist met a pale, shaken Durrant coming down from the belfry. Durrant said he had been checking a gas leak, but the organist later realised he had smelled no gas [2]. Nine days later, on Good Friday, Durrant was seen arguing outside the church with another parishioner, Minnie Williams [1][2]. The next morning, women preparing for Easter opened a cupboard and found her body. Police then searched the belfry and found Lamont [1][2]. Durrant was arrested with his Signal Corps unit [1]. He was tried for Lamont's murder in what newspapers called the "crime of the century." More than a thousand people were called as possible jurors, and the jury took five minutes to convict [2]. He was hanged at San Quentin on January 7, 1898, still saying he was innocent [1][2].

title: The French hospital built to stop contagion
place: French Hospital site, Geary Blvd between 5th & 6th Aves
hook: A mutual-aid society started by homesick French gold-seekers built a hospital out in the dunes. Each kind of disease got its own building, so patients could not infect one another.
story: The French Hospital began in December 1851 as La Société Française de Bienfaisance Mutuelle. Led by journalist Étienne Derbec, it set out to help French immigrants who came back from the mines sick, broke and unable to speak English. Its first home was a rented wooden house with 20 beds [1]. The society soon ran on dues-paying membership and moved several times. In the late 1880s it paid $48,000 for a full block on Point Lobos Road between Fifth and Sixth Avenues, surrounded by open land [1]. The chosen design, by M.G. Morin-Goustiaux working with M. Mooser, was unusual for its time. It separated diseases by type into pavilions set apart from one another, to stop contagion spreading from ward to ward [1]. The cornerstone was laid on February 25, 1894. A year later the 170-bed hospital opened with courts and gardens and one of the first nursing schools at a private hospital in the city [1]. The hospital moved to Point Lobos Road in 1895 [2]. A new building replaced it in 1963, and the site is now Kaiser Permanente's French Campus [2].

title: The Genoese corner of the hill
place: DeMartini House, 1809 Taylor St at Macondray Lane
hook: Macondray Lane marked the highest reach of North Beach's Italians: home to a banker's adviser, a waiter turned painter and a glass-maker.
story: Around 1900 the upper end of Macondray Lane was as far up Russian Hill as San Francisco's Italian community reached, and the Italians there were mostly from the Genoa area [1]. The grandest house belonged to Luigi DeMartini. He had come to America as an infant in 1856 and built a business supplying confectioners. In 1895 he commissioned the prominent firm of William Mooser and Son to design his Queen Anne house at 1809 Taylor Street. A. P. Giannini is said to have sought his advice when founding the Bank of Italy, later Bank of America, and persuaded him to invest early. His family stayed in the house for some 70 years, and it survived the 1906 fire [1]. Down the lane at 15–17 Macondray lived Giuseppe Cadenasso, who had risen from waiter at Coppa's, a bohemian restaurant, to landscape painter and head of art at Mills College. The National Register gives his birth year as 1858, other sources 1854 [1][2]. At number 68, Charles Bovone, who had arrived in 1884, made the curved glass for San Francisco's bay windows, including the one on his own 1908 house [1].

title: The House Built for a Jockey
place: 280 Byxbee St
hook: On Byxbee Street stands a cottage whose front door is just 5 feet 9 inches tall, possibly the last home of the Ingleside Racetrack's jockeys.
story: When the Ingleside Racetrack opened just to the north in 1895, it brought hostlers, trainers, jockeys and other track workers to cottages on the Merced Heights slope south of the track [1]. The 1900 census of the neighbouring Lakeview tract listed occupations such as hostlers, saddlers and jockeys alongside farmers and saloon keepers [2]. Some of those cottages can still be found on the blocks between Holloway Avenue and Garfield Street, from Beverly to Ramsell [1]. The best-known candidate is 280 Byxbee, on a street called Ford on the 1870 map [1]. In 2002-03 its owner, Jim Wessel, showed a 13-year-old history enthusiast, Sean Hall, the evidence: his research indicated the front of the house was a jockey house, with the back added later; the front door is only 5 feet 9 inches tall, the roof was later raised, and newspapers from 1921 turned up as insulation [3]. A story passed down with the house says the track's owner once knocked himself out on the low ceiling and, revived with a glass of water thrown by a jockey's wife, said he would like his next drink 'in a glass' [3]. That tale is folklore; the tiny door is real.

title: The Photographer Who Hid His Camera
place: Ross Alley, between Washington and Jackson
hook: A German tutor with a hidden camera made the only known photographs of Chinatown before it burned.
story: Arnold Genthe arrived in San Francisco from Germany in 1895 to work as a tutor and taught himself photography [1]. He became fascinated by Chinatown. As FoundSF describes it, he regularly came down Nob Hill to walk the length of Dupont Street and its alleys with his camera [2]. Many residents disliked being photographed, so Genthe sometimes hid his camera. He also cropped or erased signs of Western culture from his pictures [1]. Ross Alley, which he photographed from Jackson Street around 1898, was one of the lanes where elite 'parlor houses' flourished [3][4]. By the turn of the century he had around 200 glass negatives and lantern slides [2]. About 200 of his Chinatown pictures survive, and they are the only known photographs of the district before the 1906 fire destroyed it [1]. They are beautiful and complicated records, full of real faces in a streetscape the photographer made more exotic than it was.

title: The city's oldest schoolhouse
place: Irving M. Scott School, 1060 Tennessee Street
hook: Named for a shipyard boss, this 1895 schoolhouse is the oldest left in San Francisco. Its pupils once escorted a president to a battleship.
story: The oldest surviving public schoolhouse in San Francisco stands at 1060 Tennessee Street, among the old workers' cottages of Dogpatch [1]. Classes on the Potrero started in 1865 in a building at 20th and Kentucky (now Third) streets. In 1877 an eight-room Potrero School was built on Minnesota Street between 21st and 22nd [2]. In 1895 an addition went up on Tennessee Street. A 1964 neighbourhood history says it held the first woodshop and homemaking lab in the city [2]. The school took the name of Irving M. Scott, the head of Union Iron Works, where many pupils' fathers worked [2][3]. That connection brought the school its big day. Scott was a close friend of President William McKinley, and when McKinley came to the shipyard for the battleship Ohio, a group of Scott School boys escorted him [2][3]. The accounts differ on the occasion. One says it was the keel-laying in 1899, another says it was the launch. Ohio's keel was laid on April 22, 1899, and she was launched on May 18, 1901 [3][2][4]. The schoolhouse was made a San Francisco landmark and is also on the National Register of Historic Places [1].

title: The creek that Butchertown choked
place: Heart of Butchertown, Evans Ave near Islais Creek
hook: By 1895 a city inspector said the smell from Islais Creek's mudflats was beyond description, and the harbor engineer claimed a man could step across it.
story: For decades, the slaughterhouses built out over Islais Creek on pilings dumped offal straight into the water and waited for the tide to take it away [1][3]. In 1889 the Chronicle defended the butchers, writing that 'there is not a cleaner place in the manufacturing portion of San Francisco.' That December the city attorney drafted an ordinance to shrink Butchertown, but it apparently never took effect [1]. In 1890 a fire started at 1:30 a.m. in the Horn & Chapman stables and did $20,000 of damage [1]. In October 1895 Health Inspector Lovelace came to look. 'At low tide,' he reported, 'the stench which arise from the mud flats exposed to the sun's rays ... is beyond the possibility of description.' He asked the city to end the dumping and build sewers [1]. The creek was also filling with silt. Local property owners pushed to reopen it to boats, but the state harbor board's chief engineer scoffed that 'Islais Creek can be stepped across by any active man' [2]. In 1900 a neighbourhood club petitioned for dredging so boats could again reach what is now Oakdale Avenue and Quint Street [1].

title: The laundry girl of Francisco Street
place: De Bretteville family flat, 1000 block of Francisco St
hook: Before she was the grande dame of San Francisco, Alma de Bretteville was pulled out of school at 14 to carry rich people's laundry across the city.
story: Alma de Bretteville was born in 1881 on a struggling farm in the dunes near Lake Merced, the fifth of six children of Danish immigrants [1][2]. Her father, Viggo, boasted of descent from French nobility and, her biographers say, used it as an excuse not to work [1][2]. It was her mother, Mathilde, who kept the family going. When the farm failed they moved to a flat on Francisco Street on Russian Hill, which Mathilde turned into a combination Danish bakery, laundry and massage parlour [1][2]. At 14 Alma was made to quit school and work full time delivering laundry, often to the mansions of the rich, whose lives she came to admire [1][2]. A 1901 Examiner item placed the family at 1024 Francisco Street [1]. She took night classes at the Mark Hopkins Art Institute and paid for them by modelling [2]. The popular story that she posed for the Dewey Monument in Union Square is disputed, since a 1902 article names another model [1]. But the chairman of the monument's committee, sugar heir Adolph Spreckels, 24 years her senior, courted her for five years. They married in 1908, and she later persuaded him to give the city the Legion of Honor [1][2].

title: The mayor who stopped the races
place: Urbano Drive, laid out on the oval of the Ingleside Racetrack
hook: Urbano Drive curves for a reason. It follows the oval of San Francisco's last horse track, where a mayor once shut down a race day just before the final race.
story: On Thanksgiving Day 1895 the Pacific Coast Jockey Club opened the Ingleside Racetrack off the dusty Ocean Road. It had a grand clubhouse, a special Southern Pacific spur to the gates and six inches of groomed loam laid over the sand [2]. About 12,000 people came in the rain, though a Cal-Stanford football game the same day drew even more [1]. Fog was a problem, and in 1898 it hid most of the races from the crowd [2]. Betting was the bigger fight. In March 1899 the Supervisors banned wagering and Mayor James Phelan signed the ban, which ended racing [1]. In February 1901 the board voted 11-7 to allow 36 racing days, and 8,000 fans turned up on March 16. But Phelan had quietly vetoed the ordinance. As the races began he telephoned the police chief, and officers arrived just before the last race [1]. Racing came back under Tom Williams in 1902, and the last race was run on December 30, 1905 [1][2]. When the land was built over, Urbano Drive was laid along the old oval [2][3].

title: Two streetcars on one cable
place: Top of Fillmore Street hill at Broadway, upper end of the Fillmore Counterbalance
hook: For 46 years, a streetcar going down Fillmore Street's cliff from Broadway pulled another one up. It was a funicular found nowhere else in San Francisco.
story:
North of Broadway, Fillmore Street drops so steeply toward Cow Hollow that the streetcars needed help. When the first electric line on Fillmore opened in the summer of 1895 (July by Muni's account, August 5 by another [1][3]), it ran from 16th and Folsom to the hilltop at Fillmore and Broadway [1]. To get over the edge, engineers combined streetcar and cable technology in a way used on no other line in hilly San Francisco [1].

The cars had no grips. Instead, a car hooked onto an underground cable that ran around a pulley. As a northbound car descended from Broadway, its weight pulled a southbound car up from Green Street [1]. In his memoir Marina Memories, Walter de Vecchi remembered the two blocks as "two massive Kilamanjaros" of dirt, grass and cobblestone. Carefully synchronized bell signals told both motormen exactly when to start, so the descending car could pull the other uphill [2]. The line was later extended north to Bay Street [1].

In 1941 shuttle buses replaced the counterbalance cars, and in 1948 the rest of the line was converted to trolley buses. The route is still the 22 Fillmore [1].

title: Two streetcars on one rope
place: Fillmore Street hill between Broadway and Green
hook: On Fillmore's steepest blocks, every car going down the hill hauled another one up. San Francisco used this trick nowhere else.
story: The Fillmore Street line crossed a brutally steep hill: grades on its three steepest blocks ran from 14.5 to 25.5 percent [1]. In 1895 the Market Street Railway solved the problem with a counterbalance. A looping underground cable ran around sheaves in brick vaults beneath the street [1][2]. Small electric streetcars hooked onto it through a slot, so the weight of a car going down the hill helped pull another car up [1][2]. When the system was tested with two cars on August 5, 1895, it was called 'a perfect success from the start' [1]. The cars were the smallest in San Francisco, single-truck 'dinkies'. A railway official said a car going downhill without the cable could not have been stopped by its own brakes, because the wheels would skid faster than they could roll [1]. Walter de Vecchi remembered the hill as 'two massive Kilamanjaros, mixtures of dirt, grass and cobblestone', with bell signals timing each pair of runs [3]. A tunnel under Fillmore was proposed for the 1915 fair but cancelled [1]. In 1941 shuttle buses replaced the counterbalance cars [2].

title: A Country Road Inside the City
place: Clarendon Avenue, once the Almshouse Road
hook: In 1896 a newspaper writer walked a dirt road over the hills to the Almshouse and felt he was in the Sierra, not San Francisco.
story: On November 8, 1896, the San Francisco Call printed an anonymous writer's account of a walk along 'the Almshouse Road.' This dirt track left the top of Stanyan Street and wound over the hills to the city Almshouse, where Laguna Honda Hospital now stands. Most of it survives as today's Clarendon Avenue [1]. 'What other city in the world the size of San Francisco can boast of a country road within its limits?' the writer asked. It had no sidewalks and no lamp-posts. In the canyon beyond the first cut, 'one might as well be in the depths of the Sierras,' with a brook tumbling over the rocks [1][2]. Near the Almshouse the road was lined with pretty houses, 'ponds and reservoirs,' crowing roosters, bellowing cows and 'the sound of the woodsman's ax' [1]. Past the gate ran a 500-foot avenue of eucalyptus whose branches met overhead. Elderly inmates sat in the sun on fresh-cut logs, wearing clothes 'out of fashion over half a century.' Further on, gardeners sang among rows of vegetables [1]. When Rex Bell retraced the walk in 2011, he found a four-lane road, but also a forest where the city still feels far away [1].

title: A country road hidden inside the city
place: Clarendon Avenue, the old Almshouse Road, between Mount Sutro and the Sutro Tower hill
hook: In 1896 a newspaper writer walked today's Clarendon Avenue and swore he might as well be in the Sierra.
story:
On Sunday, November 8, 1896, the San Francisco Call printed an unsigned piece that dared readers to name another big city with "a country road within its limits" [1]. The writer set off where Stanyan Street turned to dirt and followed the Almshouse Road. It was named for the city's poorhouse, where Laguna Honda Hospital stands today [1][2]. Past a cut in the hill the pavement gave out. He wrote that he dropped "into a canyon" where "all sight of the big City is lost ... one might as well be in the depths of the Sierras." He heard a brook tumbling over rocks, the woodsman's axe, roosters and cows. Near the almshouse, elderly inmates sat on logs in the sun, dressed in clothes "out of fashion over half a century" [1].

In July 2011, Western Neighborhoods Project writer Rex Bell retraced the walk with the article in hand. He worked out that the canyon road is now Clarendon Avenue, running between Mount Sutro and the hill where Sutro Tower stands [1]. The creek still runs, just underground [1]. The almshouse opened in the 1860s. It housed the poor, sick and disabled on 87 acres, and its residents grew their own food and kept dairy cows [2].

title: A gold mine's fortune in brick and stone
place: Bourn Mansion, 2550 Webster Street between Pacific and Broadway (Landmark No. 38)
hook: The man who owned the Empire Mine and the city's water company asked a young Willis Polk for a town house. Nothing like it was being built in San Francisco.
story:
William Bourn made his fortune from the Empire Mine near Grass Valley, and he headed the Spring Valley Water Company [1]. He hired the young architect Willis Polk to design a town house at 2550 Webster Street [1][2].

Polk gave him something in what one historian calls the Carolingian style, a masterpiece of the bricklayer's and stonemason's crafts, with fine carving and fittings such as its bronze lantern. "Nothing like it was being built in the city in 1897," James B. Alexander wrote [1]. Both sources date the house to 1896, though the landmark text also says Bourn commissioned it in 1897 [1][2].

The commission was the start of a long partnership. Polk went on to design the offices and main residence at the Empire Mine and much of Bourn's estate at Filoli in Woodside [1][2]. Decades later television audiences knew Filoli as the Carrington mansion in Dynasty [2]. After 1906 it was Bourn who arranged for the burned-out Flood mansion on Nob Hill to be rebuilt as the Pacific-Union Club [2]. A history of the neighborhood around 1900 lists Bourn among its magnates, alongside M. H. de Young and William Whittier, a partner in the West Coast's largest paint company [3].

title: Frogs' Legs From the Village Pond
place: Old Ocean View village centre near Sagamore Street and Plymouth Avenue (pond site approximate)
hook: Before houses filled Ocean View, a pond in the middle of the village supplied San Francisco's French colony with frogs' legs.
story: Ocean View began as a scatter of homes around a railroad stop that locals first called San Miguel [1][2]. In April 1896, a Call article on 'Ocean View Progress' paused over one old feature that still sat in the centre of the settlement: a pond that 'has in the past supplied the French colony with frogs' legs' [1]. The paper said the 'nice, fat batrachians' had made San Miguel the favourite haunt of 'the unfortunate frog-catcher, Jennie Bonnet'. It recalled that she had been shot through a window about twenty years earlier while sharing a bottle of wine with a companion, and that the house where she died still stood [1]. The same article boasted that Ocean View was 'the choicest of sections about the City for the growth of wild flowers' [1]. More than a century later, Western Neighborhoods Project historians described a brackish pond where people caught frogs to sell to French restaurants downtown. David Gallagher suggested it might have fed the arroyo that now runs along Brotherhood Way; that is a guess, not a documented fact [3]. It was a different pond from 'Lake Geneva', the spring-fed source of Islais Creek farther east near Geneva Avenue [2][3].

title: Ocean View's Firehouse Since 1896
place: Former Engine Company No. 33 firehouse, 117 Broad Street
hook: For 78 years Ocean View's firefighters answered calls from a wooden firehouse on Broad Street. It is still standing and could become a city landmark.
story:
Early Ocean View was a village of farm hands and railroad workers. Its improvement clubs lobbied City Hall for fire stations, water service and a public school [1]. On April 8, 1896, the Fire Department organized Engine Company No. 33 there and housed it at 117 Broad Street [2].

The 1906 disaster brought no fire and little recorded damage to the OMI, but it did damage the company's two-storey wood-frame firehouse, to the tune of $500 [1][2]. The engine company stayed on Broad Street for another 68 years. On May 11, 1974, it moved into a new station at 8 Capitol Avenue. It left again in 2003, sharing Engine 15's quarters at 1000 Ocean Avenue while its station was earthquake-retrofitted, and came home on September 10, 2004 [2].

The old Broad Street firehouse survived. Restored, it became the base for riding tours on an antique fire engine [3]. In 2026 the Planning Department named the "decommissioned Ocean View firehouse" among buildings in the greater Ingleside that it considered worthy of landmark designation [4].

title: Seven Pools Under 100,000 Panes of Glass
place: Sutro Baths ruins
hook: Adolph Sutro built a glass palace where the tide filled seven pools, 10,000 swimmers could splash at once, and Egyptian mummies watched from the lobby.
story: Adolph Sutro began planning public baths in 1888, offering a $500 prize for the design, won by architects C. J. Colley and Emil S. Lemme [1]. After years of engineering, a long fight with the Southern Pacific over railway access and more than a million dollars, Sutro Baths officially opened on March 14, 1896 [1]. A classical portal led into a glass enclosure roofed with 100,000 panes over seven pools, one of cold seawater and the rest heated to different temperatures [1][2]. At high tide the ocean itself could fill the 1.7 million gallons needed in about an hour. The baths could hold 10,000 people and rented out 20,000 bathing suits and 40,000 towels [2]. Swimmers entered by slides, trapezes, flying rings and diving platforms [1]. Jerry Flamm remembered the favourite dare: dive into the hot pool, then race to the ice-cold one [1]. The lobby held stuffed animals, art and Egyptian mummies [2]. In 1913 and 1914 Duke Kahanamoku set world records there [1]. Sutro wanted cheap, healthy recreation for thousands, but the baths never made steady money [2].

title: The Boss Gardener's Stone House
place: McLaren Lodge, 501 Stanyan Street
hook: John McLaren lived at the park's front door for 47 years, hiding statues he disliked behind shrubs and outlasting every retirement rule.
story: In 1896 the park built a lodge of basalt and sandstone at its Stanyan Street entrance. Architect Edward R. Swain designed it with eighteen-inch walls to hold the Park Commission's offices and a home for the superintendent [1][2]. That superintendent was John McLaren, a Scottish gardener who grew up on a farm near Stirling and trained at Edinburgh's Royal Botanic Garden. He became Hall's assistant in 1887 and superintendent in 1890 [3]. He started with 40 gardeners and eventually led 400. When he came to inspect, workers muttered "Wild game is coming" [3]. McLaren disliked statues, which he called "stookies," and when a new one arrived he would reportedly say, "Aye, then, we'll plant it oot!" and hide it behind dense shrubs [3]. He refused to retire. When he reached 70 in 1916, the supervisors let him stay in charge for life [3]. He lived in the lodge for 47 years [1]. When he died in 1943, aged 96, he lay in state at City Hall, and his funeral procession passed through the park [3].

title: The Emporium lights up Market Street
place: The Emporium, 835 Market Street
hook: San Francisco's great department store started as a co-op of small shops in a widow's building, and its young electrician put up the city's first moving electric sign.
story: The Emporium was founded in 1896 by Adolph Feist as a co-operative of individually owned shops. It was housed in the leased Parrott Building, owned by Abby Parrott, the wealthy widow of a Gold Rush banker [1]. The store at 835 Market Street, between Fourth and Fifth, was designed by Albert Pissis, one of the first Americans trained at the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris [1]. In 1897 the Golden Rule Bazaar, founded on Kearny Street in 1871, merged into the new Emporium Company run by the German-born merchant Frederick W. Dohrmann [1]. John James Marshall, a young Liverpool-born electrician, worked at the Emporium for three years around the turn of the century. His daughter recalled that he designed what was described as the first moving electric sign in the city, over the store entrance [2]. He later passed a three-day civil service exam to become electrician of the Mint around the corner and switch it from steam to electricity [2]. The Emporium survived the 1906 earthquake but burned in the fire that followed. It was rebuilt in 1908 [1].

title: The Hermit of Lynn's Beach
place: Lands End Beach (Mile Rock Beach)
hook: A ruined machinist made a sea cave his home, cooking beef stew behind a driftwood breakwater and selling mussels to picnickers.
story: In September 1896 the Call went to meet the man who lived in a cleft in the rocks below Lands End station, a spot the paper called the extreme western limit of the United States [1]. Edward Lynn had named the little cove 'Lynn's Beach' and cut a path down to it from the railway [1][2]. He had built a bulkhead of stray planks against the spring tides. Inside stood a stove with a tall pipe, where he was cooking beef and onions. A striped blanket hung across the cave mouth, hiding a barrel table and a bed of planks [1]. His only company was a cat and an old black hen [1]. Lynn said he had been a machinist for seventeen years before bad investments took his savings and his house, and then his wife died [1][2]. About a dozen years earlier, he said, he had come out to this wilderness, first renting a cabin from Adolph Sutro for $1 a month. 'I gather mussels and sell them,' he explained, and picnickers handed him their leftovers. 'I have soured on society' [2]. By late 1898 the Chronicle reported that he had vanished and no one knew what became of him. By 1903 a Chinese man, Ny Pum Chun, known as 'Old Tom', was living in the same cave [2].

title: Wyatt Earp's Worst Night in the Ring
place: Site of the Mechanics' Pavilion (today's Bill Graham Civic Auditorium, 99 Grove St)
hook: The hero of the O.K. Corral stepped into a San Francisco boxing ring as referee, with a revolver in his pocket, and never lived down what happened next.
story: The Mechanics' Pavilion, built beside City Hall in 1882, was San Francisco's first major indoor arena and seated nearly 11,000 [1]. On December 2, 1896, it hosted the most anticipated prizefight in America, Bob Fitzsimmons against Tom Sharkey [2]. The two camps could not agree on a referee, so on the day of the fight they settled on Wyatt Earp, then 48 and working in horse racing [2][3]. Before the bell, Police Captain George Wittman noticed a bulge in Earp's coat and took a revolver off him. As the Examiner put it, 'For the first time in the history of the prize ring in California, it was necessary to disarm the referee' [3]. Fitzsimmons controlled the fight until the eighth round, when Sharkey went down clutching his groin. Earp called a foul and awarded the fight and its $10,000 purse to Sharkey [2][3]. The hall erupted in boos. Accounts of the crowd range from 10,000 to 15,000 [2][3]. For weeks the Call mocked Earp as a gunslinger, and he paid a $50 fine for carrying a concealed weapon [2]. In 1905 a doctor who had treated Sharkey said the fight had been fixed. Whether Earp knew is still unclear [2].

title: A Maltese Poultryman's Roadhouse
place: Site of Roberts-at-the-Beach, 2200 block of Great Highway between Rivera & Santiago
hook: Sent to the beach for the sea air, Dominic Roberts bought a roadhouse on the dunes in 1897. His son made it 'the Most Unusual Place in the West.'
story: Dominic Roberts came to San Francisco from Malta in the late 1860s and ran a poultry business for 30 years. The family story is that a doctor told him to get some sea air. He moved his large family, ten children, out to the Great Highway between Rivera and Santiago Streets, next to a roadhouse called the Sea Breeze Resort. In 1897 he sold the poultry business, bought the Sea Breeze and renamed it Roberts-at-the-Beach [1]. The Parkside context statement notes that it first appears in city directories in 1901–02 [2]. Dominic died in 1910, and his eldest son, Richard 'Shorty' Roberts, turned the place into a hangout for newspapermen, entertainers, boxers and racing fans. It had a four-sided stone fireplace, big marine paintings, and a 'Fireplace Broiler' where meals were cooked in plain sight [1]. Prohibition was the real test. Roberts stopped selling liquor but let guests bring their own. Then Police Captain Charles Goff raided one weekend, and in August 1925 he announced that 'the carefully secreted hip flask is to disappear from San Francisco cafes' [1]. Roberts survived the dry years all the same, 'though no one was remembered to have gone thirsty' [2]. The roadhouse closed in the 1960s [1][2].

title: Big Game, falling roof
place: Recreation Park site, Eighth, Harrison, Gordon and Ringold streets
hook: Fifteen thousand fans crammed into a new ballpark on Eighth Street for Stanford versus Cal. In the final seconds, the roof full of freeloading boys gave way.
story: Recreation Park opened in September 1897 on the block bounded by Eighth, Harrison, Gordon and Ringold streets. It hosted baseball and football [1]. One of its first big events was that November's Stanford–California game, held on Thanksgiving Day [1][2]. Contractor J. C. Weir had built the stands and was alarmed by what he saw. About 15,000 fans were packed into space he thought was fit for 10,000. Crowds of freeloaders, mostly boys, had climbed the outside fence onto roofs meant only to keep off the rain. Weir later said nobody listened to his warnings [2]. With seconds left in a Stanford rout, a section of roofing over the grandstand collapsed. Spectators pulled jagged beams off trapped fans, but only one victim was hospitalized, a 10-year-old boy thrown from the roof [2][3]. "That many people were not killed or maimed for life is simply miraculous," one witness told the Examiner [2]. The same mix of overflowing crowds and unsupervised boys caused a deadly factory-roof collapse at the 1900 game [2][3]. From 1903 the park was the first home of the San Francisco Seals, until the 1906 fire [1].

title: John Harris Buys a Ticket to Swim
place: Sutro Baths entrance, Point Lobos Ave
hook: On the Fourth of July, 1897, a Black San Franciscan paid his quarter at Sutro Baths and was refused the water. So he sued Adolph Sutro.
story: On July 4, 1897, John Harris came to Sutro Baths with some white friends and bought a 25-cent ticket for admission, a bathing suit and a changing room. Staff refused him because he was Black. On July 11 he tried again and was turned away again [1]. Harris sued Adolph Sutro for $5,000 per refusal under the Dibble Bill, a new California civil rights law that took effect on April 29, 1897 and banned discrimination by bathhouses and other public businesses [1]. The baths' superintendent openly defended the policy: Black patrons could watch but not swim, because white customers would leave. He predicted the case would never come to trial [1]. The Assembly Club, a Black social organisation, offered to help pay for test cases like it [1]. On February 17, 1898, the Chronicle reported the result: the judge instructed the jury that it had to find for Harris. The jury awarded the minimum, $50 for each refusal. Because the verdict was under $300 Harris had to pay costs, so he gained little money [1]. The National Park Service now calls it an early civil rights victory [2].

title: Lions roaring over Waller Street
place: Chutes Theatre and zoo, Haight Street between Cole and Clayton
hook: Vaudeville for 3,000, a zoo of lions and orangutans, a camera obscura and Little Egypt's dance, until a family trust ran out.
story: The Chutes soon became much more than a water slide. In 1896 a Casino building went up beside the tower for vaudeville and roller skating. On June 27, 1897, it became the 3,000-seat Chutes Theatre [1]. By March 1898 the adverts promised a zoo, with lions, bears, jaguars, leopards, kangaroos, monkeys, orangutans, a tiger, an alligator and a hyena, and they listed the carnivores' feeding times. Animals that died were stuffed for the Chutes Museum [1]. Neighbours could hear the lions roaring at night [2]. That August a camera obscura opened in a Japanese-style structure on top of the tower. A "Scenic Railway" ran nearly a mile around the grounds and through an 800-foot tunnel of lighted dioramas [1]. The dancer Little Egypt caused the biggest stir in 1899 with her "hootchy kootchy" dance. At Christmas 1901, a giant tree held a present for every child in the audience [2]. It couldn't last. The land belonged to the estate of John Baird, which was held in trust. When the trust began distributing the estate in 1901, the lease ended. The Chutes announced it had outgrown Haight Street, closed on March 16, 1902, and reopened near Fulton Street and Tenth Avenue [1][2].

title: The Mansion at the Edge of the Dunes
place: 301 Lyon Street (Clunie House), at Fell
hook: When Congressman Thomas Clunie built his turreted mansion in 1897, only sand dunes lay between it and the Pacific. Seventy years later, R. Crumb painted "Keep on Truckin'" upstairs.
story: Architect William Curlett designed 301 Lyon in 1897 for Thomas Jefferson Clunie, a lawyer, state senator, congressman and real estate speculator [1][2]. The house stood at what was then the western edge of the city, with nothing but dunes between it and the ocean [2]. Clunie spared no expense and even put in a telephone [1][2]. The city made it Landmark No. 128 in 1981 [3]. Curlett stacked a concrete-block base, a brick first floor and wooden upper storeys, and capped the corner bay with an open belvedere, one of only two left in San Francisco [1]. From 1945 the house changed hands quickly and served as a nursing home, a boarding house and then apartments [2]. By the 1967 Summer of Love as many as 40 "flower children" lived there, among them the cartoonist R. Crumb, who painted his "Keep on Truckin'" cartoon on a top-floor wall [2]. "Word got around that it was a good place to crash," the Examiner's Walter Blum wrote in 1976 [2]. In 1973 Theta Seminars bought the house for rebirthing sessions [1]. It later became a bed-and-breakfast, and its owners told the New York Times in 1992, "We found lots of pills in the walls" [2].

title: Three saloons on one creekside corner
place: 701-703 Chenery Street at Diamond (Haack's saloon and hall, later Glen Park Cleaners)
hook: Before Glen Park had sewers, it had beer. By 1907 three saloons faced each other across Diamond and Chenery, and one of them came with a community hall.
story: In the 1890s the spot where today's Diamond and Chenery streets meet, beside Islais Creek on the road south, was a place for travellers to rest and have "a good stiff drink" [1]. In 1897 Walter Haack built a saloon, residence and community hall there, the building at 701-703 Chenery that later housed Glen Park Cleaners and is now a yoga studio [1]. A 2001 survey called it the oldest surviving commercial building in Glen Park, though it dated the building to the early 1890s, when it came with a large tank house and stables [2]. That September the San Francisco Call printed a picture of Haack being held up in his Gum Tree Saloon [3]. Within ten years the crossing had three saloons on opposite corners, kept by Haack, August Straub and Anton Dissmeyer [1][3]. Dissmeyer's Enterprise Steam Beer Saloon opened in a new building at 702 Chenery, just north of the old creek trestle, and still stands, much altered, where Glen Park Cafe later traded [2][3]. Straub was more than a barkeeper. In 1907 he and Theodore Pinther organised the Glen Park Improvement Association, the first San Francisco neighbourhood association open to both men and women [4]. In the 1910s and 1920s his Straub's Refreshment Parlor traded at 673 Chenery [2].

title: 'Give Us Light in the Sunset District'
place: Start of the 1898 intercepting sewer, 8th Avenue & Judah Street
hook: Tired of floods, fever ponds and pitch-black streets, Sunset residents lobbied, sang, and finally walked to their victory party by miners' lanterns.
story: In the 1890s, winter rain running off Mount Sutro overflowed a waste pond at 7th Avenue and Lawton Street, where FoundSF places a natural lake filled in during the early 1900s [1][2]. It flooded lots, cut gullies and left stagnant pools that were blamed for fever at the school [1]. Mayor Adolph Sutro, who owned the Byfield Tract, wanted street surveys to wait until grass had grown to hold the sand. The new Sunset District Improvement Club replied that small owners 'have grown tired of waiting for the grass to grow' [1]. In March 1896 the city hired its engineer to survey grades and sewers. In June residents threw a party for the supervisors, and fifteen young women sang 'Give Us Light in the Sunset District.' The club's president that year was Julius Frankel, who kept a dairy at 12th Avenue and Lawton [1]. In March 1898 the city hired a contractor to build an intercepting sewer from 8th and Judah to 10th Avenue, north to Lincoln Way and west to 14th, where it emptied into the sand [1]. Streetlights took longer. On July 11, 1898, residents walked to their victory party through what the Call called 'Egyptian' darkness, carrying '49er lanterns. In August Mayor Phelan vetoed eleven arc lamps planned for the Sunset [1].

title: 114 years of nuts, bolts and advice
place: Former Tuggey's Hardware, 3885 24th Street, near Sanchez
hook: The sign said 1900 because two zeroes were cheaper to paint. For more than a century, Tuggey's sold Noe Valley the parts nobody else stocked.
story:
The hardware store at 3885 24th Street opened in 1898 as Sawyer's Hardware. About a year later William Tuggey bought it and put his own name on it. He passed it to his son Gene [2][3]. Why did the sign say 1900? "Purely cost," the last owner explained. "It was cheaper to go with two zeroes than '98" [3]. An earlier Voice profile, working back from the store's age in 1997, put the founding a few years earlier [1].

Gene Tuggey hired a neighbourhood boy from Sanchez Street, Bob Giovannoli, as a delivery boy. After Bob came home from the Army in World War II, Gene shut the front door one day and took him to the bank to buy the business, in 1957 [2]. Bob's son Denny took over in 1976. He once spent 20 minutes sketching an ancient plumbing part for a first-time customer. Even Home Depot sent people to him for obscure pieces, and he still kept catalogues for parts that had vanished around Prohibition [1].

Tuggey's closed on July 16, 2012, after 114 years, beaten by online shopping and big-box stores with free parking. Giovannoli turned down restaurants and leased the building to a medical practice [3].

title: A Seville tower at the foot of Market
place: Ferry Building, foot of Market Street
hook: Before the bridges, transcontinental rail passengers finished their journey by ferry and stepped off here, beneath a tower modelled on a Spanish cathedral's.
story: The foot of Market Street had been a ferry landing long before the grand terminal: a wooden depot stood on the site from 1875 [1]. In 1892 the architect A. Page Brown drew up a Beaux-Arts replacement, and it opened on July 13, 1898 [1]. It was the biggest project the city had yet undertaken [1]. Its 245-foot clock tower, with four dials 22 feet across, may have been inspired by the Giralda bell tower of Seville's cathedral [1][2]. Behind the arcades ran a 660-foot Great Nave [1]. Because the transcontinental railroads ended in Oakland, travellers from the East finished their journey by ferry and landed here, while commuters from the East Bay and Marin poured through daily [1]. Until the bridges opened in the 1930s it was the second-busiest transit terminal in the world, after London's Charing Cross [1]. Its solid construction carried it through both the 1906 and 1989 earthquakes with little damage [1]. Market Street itself had a rough start: the surveyor Jasper O'Farrell, who laid it out unusually wide in 1847, reportedly had to flee a lynch mob on the Sausalito ferry [2].

title: A Stone From Tara in a Fillmore Cornerstone
place: Sacred Heart Church, 554 Fillmore Street at Fell
hook: The 'most Irish parish west of Chicago' sealed rock from Ireland's Hill of Tara into its church. The building now hosts roller skating.
story: Founded in 1885, Sacred Heart was the first Catholic parish in western San Francisco, and it was later remembered as 'the most Irish parish west of Chicago' [1]. Its first pastor, Father James Flood, who was no relation to the Comstock millionaire, started out in a derelict Methodist chapel at Linden and Buchanan Streets. In 1886 he bought land at Fillmore and Fell [1]. Architect Thomas J. Welsh designed a wooden church there in 1887, and then, with his partner John Carey, the present brick Romanesque Revival church, his only surviving church in that style [1]. On September 7, 1897 the parish laid the cornerstone and filled it with ancient coins, rock from Tara Hill in Ireland, moss from the roof of St. Columbkille's Abbey, minerals from El Dorado County mines and copies of the day's newspapers [1]. Money ran short. Archbishop Riordan dedicated the church on September 25, 1898, with a temporary wooden wall where the transepts now stand [1]. The complex came through 1906 unharmed, and the finished church was rededicated in 1909 [1]. Damage from the 1989 earthquake and the cost of a retrofit led the Archdiocese to close the church at the end of 2004 [1][3]. The Church of 8 Wheels now runs roller skating inside, and the complex became Landmark No. 316 in 2024 [1][2].

title: A soldiers' hospital on Jordan's sandlots
place: Jordan Park (blocks between Geary Blvd, California St, Palm Ave and Commonwealth Ave)
hook: Before Jordan Park had lawns and wide streets, it had rows of tents, a crowded field hospital and volunteer soldiers waiting for ships to the Philippines.
story: In May 1898, with the Spanish-American War under way, volunteer regiments poured into San Francisco on their way to the Philippines. Thousands camped in the Richmond at Camp Merritt [1]. When the number of soldiers there neared 7,000, the Army spread onto James Clark Jordan's land next door, today's Jordan Park. On May 28 the division hospital moved here. Troops from Montana, North Dakota, South Dakota and Iowa pitched tents on the blocks between Geary Boulevard, California Street, Palm Avenue and Commonwealth Avenue [1]. Sand, fog, thin cotton blankets and poor sanitation made men sick. On July 11 more than 150 soldiers crowded the field hospital, a number of them with pneumonia. Ten men died that summer of measles, typhoid and other diseases. Joseph I. Markey of the 51st Iowa wrote that he hoped "the guilty will not go unpunished" [1]. By August the Army had moved the remaining troops back to the Presidio [1]. Jordan had bought these blocks in 1891. Between 1900 and 1920 he developed them into a district of wide streets and large houses set on spacious lots with lawns and gardens [2].

title: Bernal's war on the poundmen
place: Cortland Avenue, home of the 1890s goat-owning grocers
hook: When the city pound came for Bernal's goats and cows, the whole hill came out throwing stones.
story:
In 1894 the Chronicle called Bernal Heights "this paradise of the agile goat and the speckled hen" [1]. Irish settlers grazed livestock on the open slopes, and the city poundmen made their money by seizing loose animals and charging fees to sell or return them [2]. According to local lore, one day the poundmen took the cow of the Widow O'Brien, a hard-working woman who had raised two daughters on her own and was much respected on the hill. As the book Hills of San Francisco tells it, "every man, boy, and dog on the hill" turned out, roughed up the poundmen and chased them off. The book says they never came back [2].

The newspapers record a real fight in September 1898. Frank Tyrrell, chief deputy keeper of the city pound, was rounding up wild goats when he took the pet goat of Cortland Avenue grocer Gottlieb Katz. When Katz protested, Tyrrell hit him with a pistol. Tyrrell later complained that "the whole neighborhood rose up against him and battered his party with stones" [1]. Around 1906 a Katz family grocery, run by Ernestine and Annie Katz, is listed at 806 Cortland. The sources do not say whether they were related to Gottlieb [3].

title: Electric streetcars for mourners on San Jose Avenue
place: San Jose Avenue at the county line, route of the San Francisco & San Mateo line to the Colma cemeteries
hook: San Francisco's first electric streetcar line soon had a sombre extra job. It carried coffins and mourners down San Jose Avenue to the cemeteries.
story: The San Francisco & San Mateo Railway opened in 1892 as the city's first electric streetcar line. It ran from Steuart and Market streets, through the Mission and Glen Park, then down San Jose Avenue to the cemeteries in Colma [1]. Accounts disagree on the opening day. The SFMTA gives April 27, 1892, and Mae Silver's essay on the founder, Behrend Joost, describes a festive first run on August 27, 1892, with some 400 guests [1][2]. Joost's venture never made much money, and he sold out in 1896 to the Spreckels brothers, who added a branch to Holy Cross Cemetery [1][2]. At the county line the tracks left the city for the burial grounds, and a photograph published by FoundSF shows the line's first electric funeral train in 1898 [3]. The line's later owner, United Railroads, ran coffins and mourners straight to the cemeteries on spur tracks [4]. After 1906 the main San Mateo service was moved to Mission Street, and San Jose Avenue kept a local line [1].
