title: Elk, balloons and a fake Havana castle
place: Sussex Street near Swiss Avenue (approximate site of 'Morro Castle', Glen Park and the Mission Zoo)
hook: A real-estate man built a zoo to sell house lots. Up to 10,000 people came each week, and the neighbourhood took its name from the park.
story:
Around 1897 the estate agent A. S. Baldwin had a problem. He wanted to sell house lots in a far-off valley of dairy ranches. His answer was to make people come and see it. He put in seal ponds and a bear pit, fenced a herd of elk behind an eight-foot fence, and built "Morro Castle" to hold an aviary, a tea house and a children's playground [1]. The castle was a miniature of the fortress at the mouth of Havana harbour, where the USS Maine had exploded in 1898, and it stood roughly where Swiss Avenue meets Sussex Street today [2][3].

The resort was called Glen Park, and the whole district later took the name. It drew 8,000 to 10,000 visitors a week, and Baldwin's advertisements claimed 41,287 people on "Dewey day" [1]. Crowds watched balloon ascensions and tightrope walkers crossing the canyon [3][4].

The lots hardly sold, though. Maybe buyers didn't like the idea of thousands of picnickers tramping past their front doors. Baldwin had sold out by 1903 [1]. He went on to build park-like developments such as Westwood Park and St. Francis Wood, where ownership was restricted to wealthier white buyers [2].

title: Gold mining in Sutro's forest
place: 800 block of Darien Way, Mount Davidson Manor (mine shafts marked on a 1910 Sutro estate map)
hook: For seventeen years two hermits dug gold-mine shafts inside San Francisco's city limits, and chased off anyone who came near with clubs.
story: In May 1898 a dying 73-year-old named Nelson Hundley Shoots told a San Francisco Call reporter something surprising. For about seventeen years he had been mining for gold in the rocky hills of Adolph Sutro's eucalyptus forest [1]. He had built a cabin there around 1880 and later taken on a partner, James Demott. The pair were known to 'snarl like wild beasts at any curious trespassers' and drive them off with clubs [1]. Visiting the camp, the reporter counted at least 300 feet of shafts, one of them about 125 feet deep, and some 1,400 feet of tunnels [1]. Nobody ever saw any gold. Still, the two paid their way, lost big at the Ingleside track, and once paid $8,000 in damages after Shoots sued the Spring Valley water company over a broken pipe flooding his mine, and lost [1]. Shoots admitted he may not have 'made a cent' and said he mined 'to have something to do and have a home of his own' [1]. He died on June 1, 1898. A 1910 estate map puts the shafts under today's Darien Way, in what was then Sutro's forest [1][2].

title: Newspaper Row's race for the sky
place: Call Building (Central Tower), Third and Market streets
hook: Two feuding newspaper barons fought over the corner of Third and Market by building ever-taller towers. The winner was visible from San Jose.
story: The newspaper wars of the 1880s and 1890s were personal. The Chronicle's founders, Charles and M.H. de Young, traded insults and bullets with rivals: in 1880 the mayor's son shot Charles dead inside the Chronicle's offices, and in 1884 Adolph Spreckels, enraged by Chronicle attacks on his family's sugar company, shot M.H. de Young, who survived [3][4]. In 1889–90 M.H. de Young built a steel-framed tower with a clock at Market, Third and Kearny, often called San Francisco's first skyscraper [1][2]. The Spreckels family answered. After buying the Call in 1895, Claus Spreckels broke ground that September across Market on a 75-by-70-foot lot [1][5]. His Call Building rose 315 feet to the lantern atop its dome, the tallest building west of Chicago, and it was exempt from the height limit passed that very summer [1][5]. Papers crowed about how it would tower over the Chronicle [5]. Its opening light show could be seen from San Jose, and 'CS' monograms were stamped on its doorknobs [1]. It survived 1906 but lost its dome to a 1938 'modernisation', and today it's the plain Central Tower [5]. (Sources give the Chronicle Building as anywhere from 160 to 218 feet tall.)

title: Seven thousand soldiers on the sand
place: Camp Merritt plaque, 695 2nd Ave at Cabrillo St
hook: In the summer of 1898 the old racetrack became a tent city of volunteers bound for the Philippines. Saloons sprang up, measles spread, and ten men never left.
story: After Dewey's victory at Manila Bay in May 1898, volunteers from Pennsylvania to Oregon poured into San Francisco to sail for the Philippines. The Presidio was short of water, so from May 18 white tents went up on the empty Bay District track, between today's Geary, Fulton, Arguello and Sixth Avenue [1]. The camp was named Camp Merritt, though General Wesley Merritt himself stayed at the Palace Hotel [1]. The Richmond Banner called the neighbourhood 'the liveliest part of the city'. It also warned mothers against letting daughters visit the camp without chaperones [1]. Thirteen new 'groggeries' opened, including 'The Maine' on First Avenue, before the city stopped issuing liquor licences [1]. Sand, fog, thin blankets and poor sanitation took their toll. Ten men died of measles, typhoid and other diseases [1]. The number of men is disputed: Western Neighborhoods Project says close to 7,000 camped in the Richmond, while the California State Military Museum gives 18,000 [1][2]. The camp was cleared by August 1898 [1]. In 1952, seven veterans unveiled a plaque at 695 Second Avenue. It went missing and was put back up in 2008 [1].

title: Sutro's Gift on Mount Parnassus
place: Affiliated Colleges (now UCSF), Parnassus Avenue
hook: Before UCSF, the city's medical schools were scattered around downtown. Then Mayor Sutro gave them 13 acres of sandy hillside, with strings attached.
story: For decades the University of California's professional schools in San Francisco were scattered. Hugh Toland's medical college in North Beach opened in 1864 with eight students and was deeded to the UC Regents in 1873. Pharmacy was on Market and later Fulton Street, and dentistry moved to the Donohoe Building [1]. After years of lobbying, the Legislature approved $250,000 for a new campus. In 1895 Mayor Adolph Sutro settled the question of where by donating 13 acres on the slopes of Mount Parnassus [1]. The gift came with a condition: the land had to be used for professional medical education. Decades later that condition helped keep the medical school in San Francisco when Rockefeller money was offered to move it to Berkeley [2]. The Medical Department moved in by October 1898, and Pharmacy followed a few months later. The buildings held an auditorium, lecture halls, laboratories, a dissection room and a library [1]. They stood alone on the hillside at the end of the streetcar line, on what was then the far western edge of the city [3]. Today's UCSF grew from these buildings.

title: Tent cities for a war across the Pacific
place: Tennessee Hollow, east of Funston Avenue
hook: In 1898 volunteers from Tennessee, Utah, Iowa and beyond pitched tents in a Presidio ravine, waiting for ships to take them to the Philippines.
story: Eleven days after the United States declared war on Spain in April 1898, Commodore Dewey defeated the Spanish fleet in Manila Bay. President McKinley then ordered an army sent to take Manila, and the Presidio, beside the West Coast's finest harbour, became its staging ground [1]. The first overseas units, the 1st California and 2nd Oregon infantry, left in May 1898 [1]. Volunteers from Washington, Montana, Iowa, Wyoming, Kansas, Tennessee and Utah followed [1]. The 1st Tennessee and 1st Utah pitched their tents in this valley, then an open ravine with few trees and no houses, which is how it came to be called Tennessee Hollow [1]. Nearby Camp Merriam, by the Lombard Gate, housed the first volunteers shipped out [1]. The camps were crowded, and disease spread in the damp tents [1][2]. One historian notes that some soldiers were killed by careless gunfire before they ever reached the Philippines [2]. Between 1898 and 1900 about 80,000 men passed through the post [1]. Filipino nationalists expected independence. Instead the United States kept the islands, and a far longer war began in 1899 [1][2].

title: Tessie Wall Opens a 'Boarding-House'
place: 211 O'Farrell Street, Tessie Wall's first house
hook: The woman who would be crowned 'Queen of the Tenderloin' opened her first brothel here in 1898 and swore she'd never leave Powell Street.
story: Teresa Susan Donohue, better known as Tessie Wall, was born in 1869. She worked as a dance-hall girl and had a reputation as a hard drinker; the story goes that she once outdrank the boxer John L. Sullivan [1]. In 1898 she opened her first brothel at 211 O'Farrell Street, calling it a 'boarding-house'. It shows up that way in the 1900 census [1]. She became the most successful madam in early 20th-century San Francisco [1]. WPA writers who covered the district in the 1930s remembered her 'red plush and gilt bagnio' near Powell and O'Farrell and called her the 'Queen of the Tenderloin' [2]. Her husband, the gambler and political boss Frank Daroux, once suggested they move to a house in San Mateo. Her reported answer: 'San Mateo! Why I'd rather be an electric light pole on Powell Street than own all of the county' [2]. The 1906 fire destroyed her first house. She reopened farther along the same street at 337 O'Farrell and married Daroux that year [1]. When he tried to divorce her in 1917, she tried to kill him [1]. In the 1920s she was the unofficial queen of the annual policemen's balls at the Civic Auditorium [1].

title: The Cook Who Won Birthright Citizenship
place: 751 Sacramento Street (Wong Kim Ark's birthplace)
hook: Born above a Chinatown shop, a restaurant cook was refused entry to his own country, and took his case to the Supreme Court.
story: Wong Kim Ark was born in San Francisco at 751 Sacramento Street, the address of the Quong Sing store run by his merchant parents [2]. The Supreme Court record gives his birth year as 1873, though other documents suggest dates as early as 1868 [1][2]. His parents were subjects of the Chinese emperor who lived in San Francisco and, in 1890, went back to China [1]. Wong made his life in San Francisco as a cook [2]. In August 1895, returning from a visit to China on the steamship Coptic, he was refused permission to land by the collector of customs, who argued that under the Chinese Exclusion Act he was not a citizen [1][2]. Wong went to court. On March 28, 1898 the Supreme Court ruled 6–2 in United States v. Wong Kim Ark, in an opinion by Justice Horace Gray, that a child born on American soil to parents living here is a citizen under the Fourteenth Amendment [1][2]. The principle of birthright citizenship for children of immigrants still rests on the case of a cook from Sacramento Street.

title: The farmers' church on Santa Rosa Avenue
place: Corpus Christi Church, 62 Santa Rosa Avenue (at Alemany Boulevard)
hook: Italian vegetable growers here faced a trip of nearly three and a half hours to mass in North Beach. In 1898 they got a church of their own.
story: Long before the Excelsior filled up with stucco houses, the land around here was worked by Italian truck farmers, the giardinieri, who came from Liguria, Tuscany and elsewhere. They grew lettuce, cabbage and artichokes for the Colombo produce market downtown [1]. Going to mass meant a journey of almost three and a half hours to Saints Peter and Paul in North Beach [2]. In 1898 an Italian national church, Corpus Christi, was founded at what is now the corner of Alemany Boulevard and Santa Rosa Avenue [1]. A 2010 post on the Excelsior library's blog describes it as an offshoot of Sts. Peter & Paul [3]. Local historian Walter Jebe Sr. recorded that the first Gothic Revival church cost $7,000 and served a small flock of Italian, Swiss and German farmers. (One account dates that building to the 1880s rather than 1898.) [2] In 1952 the parish replaced it with a modern church and school by the architect Mario Ciampi. LIFE magazine photographed its front wall of coloured glass panes in 1955. Those panes were later swapped for the amber glass you see today, supposedly because a pastor didn't like them [2]. Later, when Filipino families settled in the Excelsior, Corpus Christi saw a revival of its own [4].

title: The mystery albums of Tenth Avenue
place: 447–453 10th Ave (originally 425 & 427 Tenth Ave), near Geary
hook: Two family albums, rescued from a Los Angeles prop-shop sale, turned out to show the Richmond of 1898 from one electrical engineer's front porch.
story: In 2011 Craig Bryan of Northridge wrote to the San Francisco Museum and Historical Society about two photo albums he had found in the corner of a prop-shop liquidation sale in Los Angeles. Richmond historian John Freeman took up the puzzle [1]. One picture showed uniformed men crowding Point Lobos Avenue (today's Geary) at Sixth Avenue beside the old French Hospital, a flag draped over a facade: Freeman dated it to the Fourth of July, 1898, when Camp Merritt's volunteers were camped nearby [1]. Others showed two identical houses and a porch view of windmills and the original Star of the Sea church; old Sanborn maps matched them to 425 and 427 Tenth Avenue [1]. The albums named only two children, Marian (born 1891) and George (born 1893). Bryan's search of the 1898 city directory turned up George P. Low, publisher of the Journal of Electricity, and the 1900 census showed him with children Marian and George [1]. Low had supervised the electrical system of the 1894 Midwinter Fair; his journal, launched in July 1895 and co-edited with F. A. C. Perrine, even ran an article, copyrighted in Low's name, on photographing the fair at night by electric light [1][2]. The houses survive, disguised by 1911 and 1913 remodels as flats at 447–453 Tenth Avenue [1].

title: The palace of ashes that outlived its cemetery
place: San Francisco Columbarium, 1 Loraine Court
hook: Built as the jewel of the Odd Fellows Cemetery, the copper-domed Columbarium was left stranded when the graves went to Colma, then rescued by a painter.
story: When it opened in 1898, the copper-domed Columbarium was the showpiece of the Odd Fellows Cemetery, approached by a grand flight of steps up from Geary Boulevard [1]. An 1899 Odd Fellows publication called it "without exception the most beautiful and elaborate building in the world, used exclusively as a repository for the ashes of the dead." Its ground-floor rooms are named for the mythological winds [1]. Then the city turned against its dead. The cemetery was cleared, the crematorium beside the Columbarium was demolished along with the mausoleums, and once cremation was outlawed in the city the building had no way to earn its keep [2]. In 1972 the Examiner found a lone part-time caretaker, Claude Fuller, waiting for the phone to ring among tin cans of ashes and old pigeon feathers [2]. The Neptune Society of Northern California bought and restored it in 1980, and it became a city landmark in 1996 [2]. Emmitt Watson came to paint the outside and stayed on as the whole crew: gardener, caretaker and tour guide. He called the small niches "apartments" and the big ones "condos", and his neighbours called him the Mayor of Loraine Court [3].

title: Upstairs at the Poodle Dog
place: The Poodle Dog restaurant, 151 Mason Street at Eddy
hook: Twenty-three courses downstairs, private 'love nooks' upstairs: the Poodle Dog was the Tenderloin's most famous and most discreet restaurant.
story: San Francisco's Poodle Dog restaurants went back to the Gold Rush. Historians still argue about the name: a proprietor's pet, a begging stray adopted for luck, or 'Poulet d'Or', which customers couldn't pronounce [1]. By the 1890s the Poodle Dog stood for luxury, with a 17-page menu, dinners of up to 23 courses, a huge wine cellar and a reputation as a 'five-storied dome of pleasure' [1]. Around 1898 (some say 1895) it moved to 151 Mason Street at Eddy [1]. At noon, bankers, judges, politicians, poets and journalists met over lunch, and it was said that the fate of many big business deals was settled at those tables [1]. In the evening the private upstairs dining rooms and 'love nooks' gave the city's nightlife a Parisian air. They also gave it a reputation as a discreet meeting place for powerful men and their mistresses, with scandals that reached as high as the mayor [1]. WPA writers in the 1930s remembered Mason Street as the district's 'White Way', lit up by cabarets, saloons and 'the later Poodle Dog' [2]. The 1906 fire ended the Mason Street years. Prohibition closed the restaurant in 1922, because its owners felt a French restaurant without wine wasn't worth running [1].

title: A Giant Dentist on Polk Street
place: Polk Street near California, the 'accommodation street' of McTeague
hook: Frank Norris set his great naturalist novel among Polk Street's butcher boys and car conductors, and he drew its murder from a real San Francisco case.
story: In 1899 Frank Norris published McTeague, the tale of a slow-witted, enormous dentist whose marriage decays into greed and murder [2]. Norris began it at Harvard in 1895 and wrote most of it in 1897. Its central killing is believed to be based on the 1893 murder of Sarah Collins, killed by her husband after she refused him money [2]. He planted it firmly on Polk Street, which he called "an 'accommodation street' of small shops in the residence quarter of the town" [1]. McTeague's "Dental Parlors" serve "butcher boys, shop girls, drug clerks, and car conductors". On Sundays he eats at the "car conductors' coffee-joint on Polk Street," carries steam beer home from Joe Frenna's saloon, and naps in his operating chair beneath a canary in a gilt cage [1]. From his bay window he watches the well-dressed ladies "from the great avenue a block above Polk Street" doing their morning marketing, and at night he hears how "at one o'clock the cable stopped" [1]. Erich von Stroheim filmed the book as Greed in 1924 [2].

title: Bones Beneath the Navy's Barracks
place: East Cove, Yerba Buena Island (now Coast Guard base)
hook: When sailors dug the foundations for a new naval school in 1899, the island gave up its oldest residents, and a legend of giants was born.
story:
Long before goats or guns, the gentle beach at Yerba Buena Island's east cove was a place people came back to. The earliest descriptions of the island depict a fishing village there, with ceremonial huts and cremation pits; early newspapers called the people the Tuchayunes [1]. Costanoan (Ohlone) paddlers crossing the bay are said to have stopped to gather acorns on the island's oak-covered slopes [2]. William Bernard, later known as "Barnacle Bill", landed in 1849 and described the village, its temescal (sweathouse) and its burial pits [1].

In 1899, crews levelling ground for the Naval Training Station's barracks dug into graves northeast of the beach. Newspapers reported skeletons of men over 6 feet 6 and a woman over 6 feet, buried sitting with their knees drawn up. That was enough to start a local legend about a race of giants [1]. More remains turned up in the early 1900s under the summit signal tower, and in 1933 during Bay Bridge excavations, when UC Berkeley anthropologist E. W. Gifford was called in to remove them [1]. The Navy's own historians put it bluntly: the island's Native graveyards "were destroyed by the military and by bridge construction" [1].

title: Boy Sailors of the Goat Island Station
place: Site of Naval Training Station barracks, North Gate Rd
hook: Teenage apprentices climbed the masthead every afternoon. Some tried to escape to Oakland by paddling across the bay on a log.
story:
In March 1899 Captain Henry Glass sailed the Civil War veteran USS Pensacola to Yerba Buena Island and anchored her in the cove. The ship served as headquarters and dormitory for the Pacific coast's first Naval Training Station while its buildings went up [1][2]. The barracks, finished in January 1900, housed 500 and had the largest drill hall on the Pacific coast. Apprentices slung their hammocks in the gallery above it [2].

Recruits were 15 to 17, had to avoid profanity, and earned $9 a month [2]. The day ran from 6 a.m. reveille to 9 p.m. taps, with knotting, splicing, signalling and gun drills, and every afternoon every boy went "over the masthead" [2]. Not all of them stayed. In July 1901 a paper reported a "mania for deserting" and described boys being hauled ashore from stolen launches. Six of them had decided "bread and water was better than paddling across to Oakland on a log on a cold night" [2]. The station was one of only four in the country [2][3]. It became so overcrowded during World War I that the Navy moved training to San Diego, and it closed in 1923 [2][3].

title: Digging for Klondike gold, he found a coffin
place: Golden Gate Avenue at Stanyan Street
hook: In August 1899 a seven-year-old playing gold miners at Golden Gate and Stanyan dug up bones, coffin wood, a shroud and a pair of boots.
story: On August 14, 1899, seven-year-old Willie Elsie of 2722 Golden Gate Avenue was "playing Klondike" with some boys his own age where Golden Gate Avenue met Stanyan Street, digging for gold [1]. They didn't find nuggets. They found human bones and pieces of a coffin, then scraps of a shroud and a pair of boots [1]. The finds went to the Morgue, but there was no inquest or autopsy. The Morning Call explained that the site had been a cemetery many years before, "and when the bodies were exhumed some were forgotten" [1]. Which cemetery is not certain. The Western Neighborhoods Project says a Greek cemetery once lay close to this intersection, reached through the Odd Fellows grounds. Its bodies were moved to the Golden Gate Cemetery, it adds, possibly without much care [2]. The Odd Fellows Cemetery itself lay just to the north, between Turk Street and Geary, and the Masonic Cemetery began a block east at Parker Avenue [2][3]. The corner is now the western edge of USF's campus, and builders there have kept finding what the movers missed: human remains turned up during work on the Gleeson Library, Hayes-Healy Hall and the Lo Schiavo science centre [3].

title: Mary Ellen Pleasant's house at Octavia and Bush
place: Mary Ellen Pleasant Memorial Park, Octavia St at Bush
hook: The eucalyptus trees on Octavia are all that remain of the mansion of a Black entrepreneur and abolitionist whom the city's gossip papers turned into a villain.
story:
Mary Ellen Pleasant arrived in San Francisco in 1852 and became one of its most remarkable figures [1]. She helped fugitives escape slavery, invested in mining and banking alongside her partner Thomas Bell, and in 1866 was thrown off a streetcar with two other Black women [2]. Her lawsuit, Pleasant v. North Beach & Mission Railroad, reached the California Supreme Court, which ruled segregation on streetcars unlawful, although it overturned her $500 in damages [2][3].

For the last two decades of her life she lived in a 30-room mansion at Bush and Octavia, which she had paid to build [2]. After Bell died in 1892, his widow Teresa accused Pleasant of stealing from the estate. In 1899 Pleasant left the house for a six-room apartment on Webster Street [2]. She died in 1904, having lost most of her fortune [1].

Newspapers spread lurid tales of "Mammy" Pleasant and voodoo. Historians such as Lynn Hudson have since shown how much of that story came from gossip sheets [1]. The eucalyptus trees she planted still stand here as Mary Ellen Pleasant Memorial Park, said to be the smallest park in the city [2].

title: Mrs. Stevenson's house at Hyde and Lombard
place: Fanny Stevenson house site, Hyde and Lombard streets
hook: Robert Louis Stevenson's widow came back to San Francisco wealthy, hired Willis Polk to build her a Russian Hill house, and took in a young admirer.
story: Fanny Van de Grift Osbourne married Robert Louis Stevenson in a San Francisco parlour in May 1880. The only witnesses were the minister's wife and Fanny's friend Dora Norton Williams, a painter [1]. After Stevenson died in Samoa in 1894, Fanny came back. In 1895 she and her daughter Isobel spent six months on a lower floor of Dora's Willis Polk house at the summit of Russian Hill. There Fanny fell in with the hill's bohemian circle, including Gelett Burgess, editor of the little magazine The Lark [1]. The two widows went to séances hoping to reach their husbands, though Fanny, visiting mediums on her own, wrote to Dora that she had seen "many tricks that could hardly deceive a child" [1]. In 1899 a now wealthy Fanny hired Polk to design a home of her own at Hyde and Lombard [1]. The writers Anne and Arthur Bloomfield later listed a house "that belonged to Mrs. Robert Louis Stevenson" among the things that gave Russian Hill its "Upper Bohemian" flavour [2]. Burgess kept her company for a time. Then she took in Ned Field, a young newspaperman 38 years younger, as her secretary, protégé and, by some accounts, lover [1][3]. After Fanny died in 1914, Field married her daughter Isobel [3].

title: Seventy Firemen Against Sutro's Forest
place: Sutro Forest on Mount Sutro, above the Affiliated Colleges
hook: In 1899 flames tore through Sutro's young eucalyptus forest. The hill was so steep that one fire engine needed five horses to reach the fire.
story: Within a few years of planting, Sutro's forest was a fire hazard and a magnet for trespassers. The Chronicle complained that 'the woods are overrun with picnickers, hunters and tramps' [1]. On October 8, 1899, a 'great' fire burned sixty acres and threatened both the new Affiliated Colleges and the Almshouse. Seventy firemen and hundreds of volunteers finally put it out [1]. The slopes were so steep that one engine needed five horses instead of the usual three, and the animals were 'white with foam and apparently ready to drop in their tracks' [1]. Of at least seven fires recorded in the forest since the late 1800s, it was the largest [2]. Sutro had died in 1898, and on June 10, 1901, his estate hired John Brickwedel as a ranger to keep people out. Harold Wollenberg, who grew up at the Almshouse, where his father was superintendent, remembered him as 'a gruff, mean guy' who had a small apple orchard and chased apple-stealing children with a shotgun. 'It was all posted No Trespassing' [1]. Sutro's estate was worth $3 million, but only $473.50 of it was cash [1].

title: Ten Saloons on a Racetrack Road
place: Ocean Ave, south side between Ashton and Harold Aves
hook: The fire-insurance maps of 1899 show fifteen buildings on this stretch of Ocean Avenue. Ten of them were saloons.
story: Ocean Avenue began as the Ocean House Road, the route to Lake Merced's roadhouses, mentioned in newspapers as early as 1853 [1]. Its first buildings chased weekend traffic, and business boomed after the Pacific Jockey Club's Ingleside Racetrack opened on Thanksgiving Day, November 28, 1895; estimates of the rain-soaked opening crowd range from over 10,000 to 12,000 [1][2]. That December the Market Street Railway extended its Mission Street electric line out Ocean Avenue, a job that took six days [1]. The Sanborn fire-insurance maps of 1899-1900 show fifteen structures on Ocean between Ashton and Harold Avenues; ten were saloons [1]. In Adolph Sutro's struggling Lakeview subdivision south of the road, which had just 223 residents in 1900, about one in ten were bartenders, saloonkeepers and their families [1]. City Hall set the rhythm: supervisors banned betting on horse and dog races in March 1899, and racing at Ingleside stopped on March 15 [2]. Even after the track closed for good, a relief report on the refugees housed there after 1906 worried about their access to 'five saloons at the gate' [1]. Only later did the gambling dens give way to pharmacies, grocers and five-and-ten stores [3].

title: The Firehouse That Hosted Halloween
place: Old Engine 22 firehouse (City Landmark No. 29), 1348 10th Ave
hook: Before Engine 22 even moved in, the Inner Sunset's first firehouse hosted a Halloween party. Seventy years later a children's charity bought it at auction.
story: A fire station was on the Sunset District Improvement Club's wish list, and by the end of the 1890s it had one [1]. The first firehouse in the Inner Sunset, at 1348 10th Avenue between Irving and Judah, was designed by Charles R. Wilson. The contractor was C. F. Sheibley [1][2]. NoeHill dates it to 1898 and William Kostura to 1899 [1][2]. It first housed Chemical Company No. 2, and the fire museum records Engine Company 22 moving in from Post Street in 1900 [2][3]. It became a neighbourhood room too. In 1899 the Sunset Literary, Musical and Social Club held a Halloween party in the new building [1]. Its firemen were locals too: stoker and driver Eugene Crummey lived around the corner at 1351 11th Avenue, and Jeremiah Mahoney served as a hoseman [1]. On December 17, 1962, Engine 22 moved to a new station at 1290 16th Avenue [3]. The old house stood empty for years. The city auctioned it in 1969 to the Oakes Children's Center, which spent two years raising money to rehabilitate it [1]. In 1970 it became City Landmark No. 29. Most later alterations have since been reversed, and it is one of about seven 19th-century firehouses left in San Francisco [1].

title: The Gray brothers blast Corona Heights
place: Corona Heights, above Museum Way
hook: The bare red rock above the Castro isn't natural. It is what's left of a quarry and brickworks run by two of the city's most hated businessmen.
story: Corona Heights looks raw for a reason. In the 1890s George and Harry Gray opened a quarry and brick factory on its south slope, above farmland in Eureka Valley [1][2]. By 1899 they had carved away tons of rock and fired tens of thousands of bricks. Photographs show a blasted, bare landscape [1][2]. The brothers also quarried Telegraph Hill and Billy Goat Hill above Noe Valley, and they were notorious. On Telegraph Hill they blasted on through lawsuits and angry mass meetings while falling rock injured neighbours [2][3]. Many of their Corona Heights bricks are said to have gone into cable-car track beds and later been judged substandard [2]. The kilns reportedly exploded and collapsed in the 1906 earthquake [4]. Sources disagree on whether quarrying stopped then or went on until George Gray was killed by a former worker over unpaid wages in 1914 [2][3][4]. The streets cut for the quarry wagons later became home sites, and the hilltop became a park [2].

title: The homeopaths build a college at Maple Street
place: Corner of Sacramento and Maple Streets (site of Hahnemann Hospital College; hospital later on California Street)
hook: A contractor who refused to take a dollar, a 2,000-book library and women on the faculty: San Francisco's homeopathic medical school finally got its own home in 1899.
story: San Francisco's homeopathic doctors ran their own medical college, named for Samuel Hahnemann, the founder of homeopathy. Early in 1895 its trustees picked a lot at the corner of Sacramento and Maple Streets [1]. Doctors from Oakland to Carson, Nevada chipped in, and the college raised just over $10,000. The contractor, George Lang, was a keen homeopath and refused to take a single dollar for himself [1]. The cornerstone went down on February 4, 1899, and the building was dedicated on July 25 with Mayor Phelan among the speakers. It was a colonial-style building of four floors, and gold letters over the porch read "Hahnemann Hospital College." Inside were a chemistry laboratory, a museum and more than 2,000 volumes collected by Samuel Lilienthal and his son James [1]. Women were on the faculty: Florence N. Ward was professor of obstetrics, and her husband, the dean James W. Ward, taught diseases of women [1]. The cornerstone of a Hahnemann Hospital was laid on May 31, 1905 [1]. It stood on California Street next to Children's Hospital and was damaged in the 1906 earthquake. In 1970 it was renamed Marshall Hale Hospital and later became part of California Pacific Medical Center [2].

title: The hospital born from a sick camp
place: Former U.S. Army General Hospital (later Letterman), near the Lombard Gate
hook: Volunteers fell ill in muddy tent camps faster than the small post hospital could cope. The Army's answer became the first general hospital to employ the new Army Nurse Corps.
story: In 1898 the soldiers waiting to sail for the Philippines got sick in their tent camps faster than the small Presidio hospital could treat them [1]. The Army set up a tent hospital at Camp Merritt, just south of the Presidio, and then a general field hospital in the brand-new brick barracks on Montgomery Street [1][2]. Colonel Johnson V. D. Middleton, the department's chief surgeon, pushed for a proper general hospital [1]. San Francisco architect W. H. Wilcox designed a 300-bed hospital of ten wards arranged around a central green and joined by covered corridors. It was built between 1899 and 1902, close to the troop camps near the Lombard Gate and to the docks where patients came off the ships [1][2]. It had up-to-date equipment, including an intercom telephone system and early X-ray machines [1]. In 1901 it became the first Army general hospital to employ women of the newly created Army Nurse Corps [1]. Even before it was finished, it was treating soldiers back from the Philippines [1]. In 1911 it was renamed for Jonathan Letterman, the Union Army's medical director [1].

title: The shrimp camps and the 15,000-pound bonfire
place: Chinese shrimp camp site, Evans Ave and Ingalls St by the bay
hook: Chinese fishermen turned the bay's tiny shrimp into an export business. In 1899 health officials burned their catch, and later admitted it was probably safe.
story: From the early 1870s, Chinese fishermen built camps of plank wharves and weathered shacks along the Hunters Point shore [1]. In 1882 the historian John Hittell described camps of 12 to 40 men under a manager. They set funnel-shaped nets 30 feet long in the tidal current, and 200 men in 40 boats landed about a ton and a half of shrimp a day [1]. Most of the catch was sun-dried for export to China, and the shells were ground up for fertilizer [3]. By 1895 the shrimp harvest, almost all of it Chinese, was second in value only to oysters among the region's fisheries [2]. White competitors and officials kept up the pressure. An 1880 state ban on Chinese shrimping was overturned in federal court [3]. Then came the scare over 'Butchertown shrimp', said to be tainted by slaughterhouse waste. In 1899 the city's health officer arrived at the Hunters Point camp with the city chemist, police and inspectors, condemned 15,000 pounds of shrimp and set it on fire. Months later the Board of Health admitted the shrimp had not been germ-ridden after all [2]. Worse followed: a closed season in 1901 and a ban on exports in 1905 [3].

title: A Commandant's Mansion, Later Nimitz's Last Home
place: Quarters 1 (Nimitz House), 1 Whiting Way
hook: The Navy built its commandant a Classical Revival house in the style of fashionable Bay Area mansions. Sixty-six years later, a famous admiral died in it.
story:
Navy base housing was usually plain. Quarters 1 is not. It was completed in January 1900 for the commandant of the new Naval Training Station [1][2]. The National Register describes it as an unusual Navy example of Classical Revival, the style fashionable in private Bay Area homes of the 1890s [1]. It has a symmetrical front, balconies on carved brackets, and Ionic columns framing the hall and staircase [1]. Uphill from the drill hall, a row of matching officers' houses followed along the curving road. The nominations disagree on dates: one says the six were built in 1900, the other says 1901-1905 [1][3].

From its porch, a lawn sweeps down toward the bay. In 1916, according to its National Register nomination, the house became the residence of the commander of the Naval Base, San Francisco [1]. It is best known now for a later occupant. Fleet Admiral Chester Nimitz, who commanded the Pacific Fleet in World War II, lived here from 1963 and died in the house on 20 February 1966 [1][3]. That's why it is still called the Nimitz House.

title: A Death in the Globe Hotel Basement
place: Site of the Globe Hotel, Grant Avenue & Jackson Street
hook: One man's death in a Chinatown basement led to Chinatown being sealed off within a day — and to years of official denial.
story: Wong Chut King, a 41-year-old lumber-yard owner who had lived in San Francisco for 16 years, lived in the basement of the Globe Hotel at what is now Grant and Jackson [3]. When his body was examined on March 6, 1900, doctors found swollen lymph glands, and the city bacteriologist thought he saw plague bacilli under the microscope [3]. The next day the city quarantined Chinatown. White people were allowed to leave, while Chinese residents, estimated at 20,000 to 35,000, were trapped inside the cordon [1][2][3]. The quarantine was lifted on March 9, but residents then faced forced house-to-house inspections, fumigation and an experimental vaccine made from plague cells, which many feared was poison [1][2]. Business leaders, newspapers and Governor Henry Gage denied the outbreak to protect trade. The Call headlined 'Plague Fake Part of a Plot to Plunder' [1]. Federal quarantine officer Joseph Kinyoun, who insisted it was plague, was vilified and transferred out of the city [1][2]. The last case was recorded on February 19, 1904, after 121 documented cases [1].

title: A Sugar King's Gift of Free Music
place: Spreckels Temple of Music (Bandshell), Music Concourse
hook: On Admission Day 1900, a German-born sugar magnate handed 75,000 people a sandstone bandshell and a promise: music 'rendered free to all.'
story: Sunday crowds had outgrown the park's bandstands (the first went up in 1882, a bigger one in 1888). So in 1895 talk began of something grander [1]. Adolph B. Spreckels, president of the Park Commission, persuaded his father, the sugar magnate Claus Spreckels, to pay. Claus put in $75,000 of the $78,810 cost [1]. Architects Reid & Reid designed a 70-foot coffered shell faced in Colusa sandstone, with room for 100 musicians. It stands at the west end of the Music Concourse, the sunken bowl first dug for the 1894 fair [1][2]. It was dedicated on Admission Day, September 9, 1900, the fiftieth anniversary of statehood, before about 75,000 people [1]. Spreckels spoke of his gratitude as an immigrant and said he chose a music stand because music was uplifting and should be "rendered free to all" [1]. The concourse and bandshell were designed as one landscape, with pedestrian tunnels and London plane trees [3]. The 1906 earthquake brought down much of its sandstone, but it was repaired and still draws crowds of thousands [1].

title: A parish for Eureka Valley
place: Most Holy Redeemer Church, 100 Diamond St
hook: In 1900 the new cable-car suburb got its own Catholic parish, founded for Irish, Italian and German families. It later became a refuge in the AIDS years.
story: By 1900 the Castro cable line had filled Eureka Valley with working families. Most were Irish, German and Scandinavian tradesmen, clerks and builders, living in new cottages and flats [2]. In November 1900 a new Catholic parish, Most Holy Redeemer, was established on Diamond Street. It was meant for what the parish describes as a largely Irish, Italian and German population [1]. The church was first dedicated on Christmas Day 1901 [1]. A rectory, school and convent followed [1]. The founding is a milestone in neighbourhood timelines [3]. Eureka Valley remained a working-class Irish neighbourhood until the 1960s [2]. Its story took a remarkable turn much later. In the 1980s the parish started an AIDS support group, and its old convent became Coming Home Hospice for people dying of AIDS [1].

title: Bones Shipped Home as 'Fish'
place: Chinese funerary structure, Lincoln Park Golf Course
hook: A concrete shrine by the first fairway marks the cemetery's Chinese section. In 1900 a newspaper exposé claimed the dead were leaving it disguised as fish bones.
story: Many Chinese immigrants believed their remains must finally rest in Chinese soil. So the Chinese dead were buried here only for a time. Once the flesh was gone, the bones were exhumed, cleaned and shipped across the Pacific. The city charged $10 for each set [1][2]. In April 1900 the Call reported that many cases of 'fish bones' were leaving on Pacific Mail steamers, while only about half a dozen permits to ship human remains had been bought. Health officials suspected the label was a way to dodge the fee [3]. Kamiya writes that white officials who took a cut helped the scheme along [2]. The Call noted that burial in the City Cemetery had been banned for more than two years. In March 1898 the Chinese companies had bought five acres near Colma for a new graveyard [3]. The old section left other marks. Mourners set out roast pig and sweets for the spirits, and the writer Charles Caldwell Dobie recalled 'ghoul-like hoboes' who feasted on them [2]. Near the first fairway stands a concrete structure with Chinese writing on top. It is described as a gateway, tomb or shrine, and it survives from the Chinese burial ground [1][4].

title: Death's Crossing at Sickles and San Jose
place: San Jose Avenue at Sickles Avenue, Ocean View's railroad crossing
hook: Steam trains and electric streetcars met at street level here, and the collisions were frequent enough that Ocean View named the crossing after death.
story: At the Ocean View station, Southern Pacific's steam line crossed San Jose Avenue at street level, right where the electric streetcars ran [1]. Residents called the junction of Sickles Avenue and San Jose Avenue 'Death's Crossing' because the collisions there were frequent and often fatal [1]. On May 30, 1900, the Chronicle reported an 'Accident at Death's Crossing' in which a locomotive smashed an electric car. In 1903 the paper reported another Ocean View resident struck by a train [1]. Mission District residents, tired of smoke, soot and dangerous crossings, wanted the tracks removed altogether. Ocean View fought to keep its trains. In 1900 the village had only about 200 buildings, and the railroad was its main link to the rest of the city, even though fares were too high for many working families [1]. A 1926 photograph shows Southern Pacific tracks still running down San Jose Avenue at Sickles [2]. That right-of-way is now under Interstate 280 [2].

title: Dr. Shumate's first corner drugstore
place: Site of the first Shumate's Pharmacy, corner of Divisadero and Sutter streets
hook: A night-school pharmacist opened one drugstore at Divisadero and Sutter. The earthquake spared it, and by 1933 San Francisco had around thirty Shumate's on its corners.
story: Thomas Shumate was born in St. Louis in 1871 and came to California for his health. He clerked in a drugstore, earned a pharmacist's licence at night school, then bought a pharmacy so he could pay his way through medical school, minding the counter at night after classes [2]. In 1900 the state licensed his business, and his first pharmacy opened at the corner of Divisadero and Sutter, three blocks from the corner house at Pine and Scott that later became the family home [1][2]. The 1906 earthquake and fire made him. "His store was not touched," his son Dr. Albert Shumate said in a 1978 oral history, while established drugstores downtown burned and some never came back. Divisadero, like Fillmore, suddenly became a centre of the city [1]. The chain spread from corner to corner. A 1933 city directory listed 30 Shumate's pharmacies, run from an office at 1640 Divisadero; another account puts the peak at 28 [1][2]. Shumate also served as a police commissioner from 1912 to 1937 and bred saddle horses in Sunnyvale [2]. Every store has since closed. A few doorways elsewhere in the city still spell out "Shumate's" in black-and-white tile [1].

title: Fresh Eggs from Sunset Ranch Every Day
place: Carl Larsen's chicken ranch, 16th–17th Aves between Moraga & Noriega
hook: Every morning a horse-drawn wagon carried eggs from a chicken ranch in the dunes to a famous downtown café. Once a year the ranch threw a party.
story: Carl Larsen was born in Odense, Denmark, in 1844. He came to San Francisco as a carpenter and in 1879 opened the Tivoli Café on Eddy Street downtown [1]. From 1888 he bought up the Sunset's dunes, and by 1910 he owned fourteen whole city blocks plus lots adding up to about nine more [1]. On one square block, bounded by Moraga and Noriega streets and 16th and 17th Avenues, he ran a chicken ranch. Each morning a horse-drawn wagon took its eggs to the Tivoli, probably along the Central Ocean Road that zigzagged through the sand behind the ranch. The café's ads promised 'Fresh eggs from Sunset Ranch EVERY DAY' [1][2]. Every Easter the ranch threw a neighbourhood party with open bars and tables of food. Some reports say the parties got out of hand and ended in 1913 [1]. Remembered as the 'Gentle Dane,' Larsen later gave the city land on Golden Gate Heights and two blocks for Larsen Park on 19th Avenue [1][2]. He died in 1928. A handwritten 1909 will leaving more than $500,000 for a museum in Golden Gate Park was found with his signature cut off, and a judge declared it invalid in 1931 [1].

title: Genoese gardeners on Sutro's flatlands
place: West Portal Avenue near Vicente Street (Sutro's farm leases between Portola, Kensington, Taraval and Wawona)
hook: Before West Portal had a shopping street, Italian families grew vegetables here and drove them by wagon to the market downtown, three to four hours each way.
story: Adolph Sutro covered most of his Rancho San Miguel with trees, but the flat land that became West Portal he rented to Italian vegetable farmers [1][2]. Many early Italian immigrants came from the farm country around Genoa. Once they realized they wouldn't strike it rich in the gold fields, they saw money in feeding the boomtown instead [1]. Four families, the Aratas, Bottinis, DeMartinis and Lagomarsinos, farmed Sutro's land between today's Portola Drive, Kensington Way, Taraval Street and Wawona Street for decades spanning two centuries. Early each morning they loaded their wagons and made the three-to-four-hour trip to the Colombo Market on Davis Street, the city's produce exchange [1]. An old-timer named Wollenberg remembered Louis Lagomarsino coming every day with a horse-drawn wagon loaded with vegetables for the Relief Home, today's Laguna Honda Hospital [1]. Just south, around today's St. Francis Circle, Giuseppe Merlo's family farmed until 1915, when the land was sold for development. They found work cutting down trees to build Forest Hill [1]. After the tunnel opened, Fernando Nelson turned the fields into West Portal [2].

title: Neighbours versus the dynamite brothers
place: Douglass Playground, Douglass and 26th streets (former Gray Brothers quarry)
hook: The rock walls in Douglass Playground were cut by quarrymen who went on blasting while their neighbours' windows broke.
story:
George and Harry Gray were San Francisco's most notorious quarrymen. In 1895 a judge ordered them to stop blasting on Telegraph Hill after a rockslide from their blasting crushed a duplex there. They moved their operation to a new quarry near 26th and Douglass in Noe Valley [1].

The complaints followed them. In November 1899 local residents sued over flying rock, broken windows, cracked plaster, and broken sewer pipes spilling onto the street. On 25 May 1900 about 40 residents, "most of them ladies," went to the Board of Supervisors to protest that the blasting was still going on [1]. The Grays had political friends. Supervisors warned that "1,500 men would be thrown out of work" if the quarry closed and promised to inspect the site. They never did [1].

The brothers were hated across the city for careless blasting and poor-quality products, and they sometimes failed to pay their workers [2]. Quarrying in Noe Valley went on until 1914 [2][3]. The sheer rock walls on the west side of Douglass Playground are what remains [1].

title: Pansy Hill, Poppy Hill, Kite Hill
place: Merced Heights ridge, rocky outcrop at Shields St and Orizaba Ave
hook: Before houses climbed Merced Heights, San Franciscans came out to pick wildflowers on a bald, rocky ridge they named for its blooms.
story: Merced Heights is a 500-foot ridge of Franciscan sandstone that rises and falls three times, with peaks near Thrift and Summit Streets, at Shields and Orizaba, and at Shields and Vernon, today's Brooks Park [1]. It held scrub and grassland: bunchgrass, blue-eyed grass, Douglas iris, pink currant and golden yarrow, plus blue-blossom ceanothus, now gone locally and likely the source of Mount Davidson's early name, 'Blue Mountain' [1]. A century ago the ridge looked almost bald, splashed each spring with poppies and pansies, and locals called its western knoll 'Pansy Hill', 'Poppy Hill' or 'Kite Hill' [1][2]. The area was known for seasonal wildflowers, and early-1900s postcards show picking parties at Ingleside [1]. Botanist Alice Eastwood, remembering the 1890s, wrote that 'on the hills back of Ingleside, then known as Sunset Heights,' a great many flowers could be found, and that near Lake Merced they grew so thick it was impossible to avoid stepping on them [3]. Until the 1930s only a handful of homes stood on the central ridge, left to wildflower gatherers and picnickers among the rocks [1]. Several dozen native plant species still survive on Brooks Park's outcrops [4].

title: The brickworks that shook Corbett's windows
place: Site of the Simons-Fout quarry, between Corbett Avenue and Graystone Terrace
hook: Thirty thousand bricks a day, a 100-foot iron chimney and explosions next door that broke neighbours' windows, until the matter ended up in court.
story:
In May 1900 Edward Simons, Charles E. Fout and three partners from Los Angeles incorporated a brick company. They bought a slope on the east side of Twin Peaks that the 1900 insurance map simply labelled 'steep'. By 1905 it wasn't steep any more [1]. Their quarry sat between Corbett Road and Lincoln Road (today's Graystone and Villa Terraces). Crushers turned blue rock and red chert into macadam and concrete, and the company planned to level the land 'for real estate purposes' [1].

The brick plant straddled Iron Alley. It was a wood and corrugated-iron shed 300 feet long, with a 100-foot iron chimney and a coal-fired Hoffman kiln. According to the State Mining Bureau, its stiff-mud machine averaged 30,000 bricks a day. A fire levelled the plant in October 1902, and it was rebuilt [1]. Horse teams hauled the bricks away, most likely down Corbett [1][2].

After 1906, cottages and flats filled the area around the pit during the housing shortage. In 1911 a lawsuit, Pacific States Supply Company v. the City and County of San Francisco, dealt with explosions and noise at the plant that disturbed neighbours, broke windows and created hazards. That year the company was sold. The quarry was closed by 1911, and the brickyard had shut for good by 1918 [1].

title: The fishing fleet moves to Taylor Street
place: Fisherman's Wharf, foot of Taylor St at Jefferson
hook: Orange-brown lateen sails, Sicilian crews, and in 1900 an order that moved the fishermen from the foot of Telegraph Hill to a new wharf.
story: By the 1880s San Franciscans had developed a taste for Dungeness crab. Fishermen landed nearly 2.9 million pounds in 1882, and the catch reached a record 3.7 million pounds in 1899 [1]. The bay was full of feluccas with orange-brown lateen sails, worked by Italian immigrants [2]. By 1900 the fishermen were mostly Sicilian, and about half of all fishermen and oystermen in the city were Italian [2]. The fish trade had centred on docks at the foot of Filbert, Vallejo and Union streets, the spot people called 'Italy harbor' [2][3]. As ocean shipping grew those berths were needed, so in 1900 the state set aside the shore from the foot of Taylor to Leavenworth for commercial fishing boats. Land was filled out to Jefferson Street [3][4]. Fishermen sold parts of their catch straight from their boats to housewives, some set up stalls, and over time those stalls turned into the restaurants of today's Fisherman's Wharf [3]. By 1903 there were already too few crabs in the bay, and the state brought in a minimum size and a closed season [1].

title: The servant with no name in the record
place: Laidlaw-Stanford House, 3232 Jackson Street
hook: In 1900 a senator's nephew lived on Jackson Street with his wife, daughter and two servants. One has a name. The other is just 'a Japanese man (age 24).'
story:
Dr. Horace Laidlaw, a physician and druggist who worked on Sacramento Street, had this Classical Revival house built in 1897 for $3,500. He never lived in it [1]. He rented it to Jerome B. Stanford, nephew of Senator Leland Stanford, who had brought him to California as a small child in 1856. Jerome was at various times a mining engineer, merchant, stockbroker and editor [1].

The 1900 census found Stanford, 52, living here with his wife Clara, 31, their daughter Helen, 3, and two servants. The house's history, drawn from that census, names one, Selma Gaffe, 43. The other appears only as "a Japanese man (age 24)" [1].

Other big households nearby relied on live-in staff too. In 1910 the Koshlands on Washington Street had seven live-in servants from Finland, Germany, Sweden and Japan, and only one was a U.S. citizen. The Platts on Locust Street had a Swedish maid, Ellen Loeser, 26 [1]. Helen Salz, on Clay Street, later remembered her big dinner parties "in the days when servants were easier to get" [2].

Others worked the streets. A rag, bottle and sack cart came round, the milkman delivered three or four times a week, and vegetable trucks, driven mostly by Chinese, sold fresh produce. Children played kick-the-can in the road [1].

title: The zoo groundskeeper who learned to fly
place: Whitney Street (then Palmer Street) near Randall, Fairmount Heights, Maloney's home in 1900
hook: In the 1900 census a 21-year-old from Palmer Street gave his job as "Aeronaut." Five years later he was gliding over Santa Clara from about 4,000 feet.
story:
In the 1900 census, 21-year-old Daniel John Maloney was living on Palmer Street, now Whitney Street, near Randall. He gave his occupation as "Aeronaut" [1]. He had been a groundskeeper at Glen Park and the Mission Zoo, where he watched balloonists go up and come down again on canvas parachutes. One day a booked performer didn't show, and Maloney volunteered to go instead. On his fourth flight at Glen Park he lost his grip 40 feet up and broke a rib. The week before, his balloon had caught fire [1].

By 1904 he was working as test pilot for Professor John J. Montgomery of Santa Clara College. Maloney suggested lifting Montgomery's glider under a balloon and cutting it loose high up [1]. On 29 April 1905 he let go at about 4,000 feet above Santa Clara College, while crowds watched from below [2]. It was among the first high-altitude glides by anyone [1].

On 18 July 1905 a balloon rope fouled the glider on the way up. After Maloney released, the craft broke apart and he was killed [1][2]. Montgomery himself died in a gliding crash in 1911 [1].

title: A brick castle for the streetcars
place: Geneva Office Building (Geneva Car Barn), 2301 San Jose Avenue at Geneva Avenue
hook: In 1901 an electric railway built a red-brick office with a round turret among dirt roads and fields. It still shows cracks from 1906.
story: In 1901 the San Francisco & San Mateo Electric Railway built its new headquarters on the southeast corner of Geneva and San Jose avenues [1][2]. It was a Romanesque red-brick office building with a round corner turret, beside the company's car barn and powerhouse. The architects were James and Merritt Reid, who also designed the Cliff House and the Fairmont Hotel [2]. Most of the land around it was still dirt roads and fields [2]. The top floor had a large social hall where the company held entertainments for its workers [1]. The railway was soon absorbed into United Railroads, and the Geneva barn went on to house more cars than any other barn in the city during the electric-streetcar era [3]. The load-bearing masonry came through the 1906 earthquake with only minor damage, and the marks can still be seen on the north wall [1][2]. The city made the building Landmark No. 180 in 1985 [1]. The 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake put it out of service, and neighbours later stopped a plan to demolish it for parking [3].

title: Cows, Clams and Rock Fights at the Creek
place: Northern edge of the Portola, former Islais Creek marsh (near today's Alemany and Bayshore interchange)
hook: Where freeway ramps now tangle, Portola and Bernal Heights kids once lined up on opposite banks of a muddy creek and pelted each other with rocks.
story: On June 28, 1901, a Spring Valley Water Company photographer pointed his camera south across Islais Creek toward what would become the Portola. His picture shows cows grazing in the marsh and the pipeline to University Mound being worked on. Interstate 280 and Alemany Boulevard now cross the scene [1]. Residents born around 1907 later described the creek for local historian Chris Ortiz. It was the boundary between Bernal Heights and the Portola, and youngsters from the two neighbourhoods settled their disputes by throwing rocks at each other across the mudhole, though their parents warned them to stay away [2]. The creek drained into bay marshland just past the old Clam House on Bayshore Boulevard, where one boy's mother sent him to buy freshly dug clams [2]. The San Bruno Avenue streetcar gave a rough ride over the wetland because its tracks kept sinking [2]. By July 1915 the city had built a fill to carry San Bruno across the creek [3].

title: The dynamite fortune that froze the Haight
place: Baird estate lands, Page to Waller between Masonic and Shrader
hook: For two decades much of the heart of the Haight couldn't be sold, because a gunpowder magnate's will had locked it in trust.
story: Why did an amusement park sit on prime land on Haight Street in the 1890s? Blame a will. John H. Baird, president of the California Powder Works, one of the dynamite makers out in the Sunset District, had acquired much of the land from Masonic to Shrader and from Page to Waller [1][2]. He died in 1880, and his will put property into a trust that could not be sold until a son came of age. One account says the youngest child, and the National Register nomination for a Haight and Ashbury house names the eldest son, Joseph [1][2]. An 1894 plot book shows the Baird holdings [2]. The Chutes were built on the trust's land under a lease [1]. Then, in 1901, the heir turned 21. The Chronicle reported the estate being distributed, the lease ended and the Chutes left [1]. Lots began to sell that same year, among them a corner lot at Haight and Ashbury bought by Richard Doolan [2]. As the NR nomination puts it, much of Haight-Ashbury was built in the first years of the twentieth century [2].

title: The music teacher's house over the Presidio wall
place: Julian Waybur House, 3232 Pacific Avenue (wedge block against the Presidio wall)
hook: A music teacher famous for his kindness to children and the poor built an unpainted shingle box that hangs out over the Presidio's stone wall.
story:
Between the Presidio Avenue and Arguello gates, the Presidio's rough stone wall cuts across Pacific Avenue at an angle. It leaves a narrow wedge of a block, where shingled houses step down the hill, each narrower than the one above [1][2]. The Julian Waybur House, designed by Ernest Coxhead and finished around 1901, sits on the wall at one end and hangs out over it at the other [1].

Waybur was born Julius Rehn Weber in Philadelphia in 1855 and left school at fourteen to work in a music store [1]. He taught for 23 years at Mills Seminary and created the music extension division of the University of California, and pushed for a music department at the San Francisco Public Library. He was best known for his work with young musicians, especially children and the poor. "To bring beauty into the homes of rich and poor alike - these were his ambitions," his friend Redfern Mason wrote after his death in 1925 [1]. The house had a piano room behind pocket doors for his lessons [1].

The land came from his wife Margaret's family. Her brother, the artist Bruce Porter, built next door, and Coxhead designed both houses together in the plain, natural "simple home" style [1].

title: A church faced with the city's curbstones
place: St. Brigid Church, 2151 Van Ness Avenue at Broadway (Landmark No. 252)
hook: The face of this Irish parish church on Van Ness is built from San Francisco curbstones. George Moscone received his sacraments here and stayed a parishioner all his life.
story:
Around 1870 an earlier St. Brigid's church stood on the hillside at Broadway and Van Ness, above the gardens of the E. Willard Burr estate [2]. The present church, finished in 1902, is Richardsonian Romanesque, designed by Shea & Shea with Henry A. Minton. Its façade uses an unusual material: San Francisco curbstones and crossing stones [1].

St. Brigid's survived the 1906 earthquake and reopened only seven months after the disaster to serve as a refuge [1]. It also came through the 1989 quake. Inside it collected treasures: a pipe organ built for the church by Italy's Fratelli Ruffatti, stained glass from the Harry Clarke Studios in Dublin, and statues by the Irish sculptor Seamus Murphy [1].

The city calls the church an anchor for the Marina, Pacific Heights and Russian Hill, and it has long mattered to San Francisco's Irish community. Mayor George Moscone received his sacraments here, went to St. Brigid School and remained a parishioner all his life [1]. In February 2005 the Board of Supervisors began designating it a city landmark. It became Landmark No. 252 [1].

title: A church rebuilt from a million bricks
place: Calvary Presbyterian Church, 2501-2515 Fillmore St at Jackson
hook: Calvary took its Union Square church apart and rebuilt it on Fillmore, bricks, pews and all. Four years later it was sheltering congregations and even a courtroom.
story:
Calvary Presbyterian was founded on 23 July 1854. Its first church on Bush Street, between Montgomery and Sansome, was then the largest Protestant church on the West Coast. As business crowded in, the congregation moved in 1869 to Powell and Geary on Union Square [1].

At the turn of the century it moved west again, to Fillmore and Jackson, and it brought its old church along. About one million bricks from the Union Square building went into the new church, with all the pews, the metal balcony supports and much of the woodwork [1]. The first service was held on Thanksgiving Day 1902, and the church was dedicated on 7 February 1904 [1].

The move proved timely. After the 1906 earthquake and fire destroyed downtown, St. Luke's Episcopal, Old First Presbyterian and Temple Emanu-El all held services here, and a temporary Superior Court courtroom ran in the basement [1]. The city's landmark report notes that the church's interior of around 1900 has seen "almost no unsympathetic change" [2].

title: A library on a benefactor's lot
place: Eureka Valley/Harvey Milk Memorial Library site, 16th St near Noe
hook: The library where the Castro now borrows books opened in 1902 as the McCreery Branch, on land one man gave and a building he paid for.
story: On January 2, 1902, the young streetcar suburb of Eureka Valley got the second branch library in the whole San Francisco system [1]. It was called the McCreery Branch after Andrew McCreery, who donated the land and paid for the building [1]. The neoclassical branch served the neighbourhood for more than half a century. It was damaged in the 1957 Daly City earthquake and pulled down. A new branch opened on the same site on December 20, 1961 [1]. By then Eureka Valley was changing. In 1981 the Library Commission renamed the branch to honour Harvey Milk, the first openly gay man elected to public office in California [1]. Wikipedia's neighbourhood history also records the 1902 opening [2]. In 2006 the stretch of 16th Street beside it became José Sarria Court [1].

title: A wild garden that turned trousers orange
place: Former wildflower fields southeast of Lake Merced, near today's Brotherhood Way (approximate)
hook: In 1902 a Chronicle writer sent city readers on a streetcar-and-tramp pilgrimage to fields of poppies, buttercups and Johnny-jump-ups beside Lake Merced.
story: On 13 April 1902, the San Francisco Chronicle's Sunday supplement printed Lillian E. Purdy's guide to what she called the natural garden of San Francisco [1]. To reach it, she wrote, take the San Mateo cars to Ocean View, walk south along the railroad track for about half a mile, then cut across the field toward the ocean. Ahead lay "patches of gold, blue, rich, deep red and cream," and beyond the green hills, Lake Merced and a bit of ocean [1]. She listed poppies, buttercups, baby-blue-eyes, wild wallflowers and popcorn flowers, and whole fields sprinkled with wild pansies, which she said grew like that nowhere else in the city. The baby-blue-eyes on the lake's slopes, she wrote, were considered the finest in the state [1]. FoundSF's editor, Pete Holloran, points out that some of her prose was lifted, uncredited, from Mary Elizabeth Parsons's 1897 guide, and that botanist James Roof remembered the flowers being so thick that walking through them turned his pants orange with pollen [1]. Those grasslands south and east of the lake have largely disappeared under asphalt [1]. What survives is protected: the city has designated 395 acres around the lake as Natural Areas, home to dune tansy and California pipevine [2].

title: An inventor's glass octagon on Sunnyside Avenue
place: Sunnyside Conservatory, 236 Monterey Blvd
hook: This octagonal redwood greenhouse was built by an English inventor of gold-mining machines, whose house next door had an observatory with a rotating roof window.
story: William Augustus Merralls came to America from Chatham, Kent, in 1869 at seventeen. He won his first patent, a gold separator, in 1888 and went on to register more than twenty, for everything from ore mills to refrigerators to car starters [1]. His Merralls Mill Company on First Street sold rock-crushing machinery to mines across the West [1]. In 1897 he and his wife Lizzie bought a house at 258 Sunnyside Avenue (now Monterey Boulevard) and then bought up the lots beside it [1][2]. On that land rose an octagonal redwood-and-glass conservatory for his exotic plants. The 1905 Sanborn map also shows a chicken coop and an observatory whose roof window turned a full 360 degrees [1]. The build date is disputed. NoeHill's summary of the 1975 landmark resolution gives 1897, though the resolution itself says only 'around the turn of the century' and admits that 'very little is known' of the owners. A plaque on the fence says 1898. Local historian Amy O'Hair argues for mid-1902, after the Merralls owned all the land [1][2]. Merralls died in 1914 when a Southern Pacific train struck him in Alameda [1].

title: Fifty horses on a gambler's street
place: Cora Street, Visitacion Valley
hook: In 1902 a family built a house on weekends on a two-block road named, it was said, for a notorious Gold Rush gambler. Soon it held fifty horses.
story: In 1902 Joseph Edelmann and Dorothy's uncles built a house in the valley on weekends. Dorothy's grandmother, Katherine Bergold, had bought seven $50 parcels along what soon became Cora Street [1]. With the grandmother's house nearby, the property kept up to 50 horses and was known in the family as 'the farm'. 'We never had a Christmas or New Years with less than 50 people,' Dorothy, later Mrs. Frandsen, remembered [1]. She went to one of the valley's first elementary schools, a shack at the foot of Cora Street, sitting on a wooden bucket [1]. Grapevine columnist Len Appiano wrote that the two-block street was named 'for a controversial Gold Rush gambler' [1]. The city's best-known gambler named Cora was Charles Cora. In 1856 the Vigilance Committee hanged him before a crowd of about 20,000 [3]. Neighbouring streets honour early officials. Appiano wrote that Burr Avenue is named for Ephraim Burr, the mayor who presided when city and county were consolidated in the 1850s, and Garrison Avenue for Mayor Cornelius Garrison, a shipbuilder elected six months after he arrived [2]. Streets could change names too: Delta Street was once Cowden Street [4].

title: Harnessing the Ocean Wind for Water
place: Dutch (North) Windmill, northwest corner of the park
hook: Tired of paying a private water company, the park built a Dutch windmill on the dunes, run best, an engineer said, by a sailor.
story: A park built on sand needs endless water, and the private Spring Valley Water Company charged for it. Before the windmill, the park spent $4,800 a year on water [2]. John McLaren and Adolph Spreckels came up with a Dutch-style windmill near the ocean, where the westerly winds blow hardest. Alpheus Bull Jr. designed it [1][2]. Sources disagree on when it was finished (1902 or 1903) and on the cost ($18,160 or $25,000) [1][2]. It stands 75 feet tall and pumped up to 30,000 gallons of well water an hour for irrigation [2]. A 1914 engineering account describes arms 102 feet from tip to tip, a 12-ton revolving cap turned by a small helper windmill, and water that had been filtered through the sand hills, with "no taint whatsoever" of the nearby sea. It added that "a sailor is better operator of the Dutch windmill than an engineer" [3]. A caretaker and his wife moved into a new cottage and grew vegetables for the park's animals [1]. Its neighbor was the 1878 U.S. Life-Saving Station, whose surfmen rescued people from the Ocean Beach surf [4].

title: Teeing Off Among the Tombstones
place: Lincoln Park Golf Course
hook: While the dead still lay beneath the turf, golfers laid out three holes on the cemetery hill. By 1917 there were eighteen.
story: Golf was new to the West Coast at the turn of the century. The Presidio got one of California's first courses in 1895. In 1902 golf enthusiasts laid out a three-hole course here, on part of the old city cemetery [1][2]. In 1909, once the city had ordered the cemetery moved, the Board of Supervisors gave about 150 acres to the Park Commission. The commission named the land Lincoln Park in honor of Abraham Lincoln [3]. The course kept growing and reached a full 18 holes in 1917 [2][4]. Graves were supposed to be moved to Colma, but many were not [3]. A photograph from 1914, in the course's early years, shows the Chinese funerary structure already standing among the golfers. Stone grave markers from the Chinese section still sit near the first and 13th fairways [4][5]. Today Lincoln Park is the city's oldest municipal golf course: a short par-68 layout on the cliffs, with the Golden Gate Bridge as a backdrop that private clubs would envy [2].

title: The Big Game in the backyards
place: Site of the Richmond Grounds, block of California & Lake Sts, 7th & 8th Aves
hook: In 1902 Cal and Stanford played the Big Game on a sand lot in the Richmond, and one runner crossed what are now the backyards of 7th Avenue.
story: In 1902 the Cal–Stanford 'Big Game' suddenly had nowhere to play. Stanford alumnus Dave Brown leased the sandy block between California and Lake Streets and Seventh and Eighth Avenues. Carpenters built stands for about 11,500 people in less than a month, and wagons dumped clay and loam onto the sand [1][2]. Neighbours feared the grounds would draw 'undesirable resorts'. The Board of Supervisors' Streets Committee let the field stay only until January 1904 [1]. On November 8, 1902, every streetcar and steam train was packed. People watched from rooftops and from the Presidio hillside for free [2]. Cal's Bobby Sherman, a last-minute replacement, misjudged a punt and fumbled it twice before finally grabbing it on his own 10-yard line. Then he ran 100 yards, cutting through what are now the backyards on the odd side of the 100 block of Seventh Avenue, to score at the California Street end [2]. Cal won 16–0. The 1903 game ended in a 6–6 tie and a brawl over the ball [2]. It was the last Big Game played in San Francisco. Dismantling of the grandstands began almost at once [2].

title: The Last Building of Old Fort Miley
place: Fort Miley ordnance storehouse area, trail east of the VA Medical Center
hook: Barracks, stables and an officers' club once ringed a parade ground here. One plain storehouse outlived them all, and even it was moved.
story: The Army built its first two buildings on the Point Lobos reservation in 1898, during the Spanish-American War. They housed a small Signal Corps detachment. Its job is now long forgotten, though it may have been to watch for enemy ships [1]. Once the gun batteries went in, the Army built a parade ground between them, with a complex of frame barracks and quarters to standard plans. The horseshoe-shaped ground opened to the north toward the Golden Gate. Most of the complex went up between 1902 and 1906 [1]. One of those buildings was an ordnance storehouse, built in 1902 [2]. In the early 1930s the parade ground was chosen for the new Veterans Administration hospital. In 1934 almost all the old army buildings around it were pulled down [1][3]. The storehouse was the exception. It is the only Fort Miley building from before 1934, though it no longer stands on its original site [1]. The state military museum's history says it was moved southeast and became a ranger office [2]. The Park Service's World War II guide calls it a maintenance building [3]. A resurfaced trail east of the hospital passes the area [1].

title: The Proud Park Bums of Big Rec
place: Big Rec ball fields, opposite Seventh Avenue
hook: Unemployed men started a pickup baseball game in the 1890s, called themselves the Park Bums, and cursed badly enough to alarm the commissioners.
story: The park's chronology records a ball ground first discussed in 1885 and laid out in Recreation Valley, the "Big Rec," in 1893 [2]. Around then, according to a 1937 Chronicle account, a group of perpetually unemployed men began choosing up sides on the lawn opposite Seventh Avenue. They became the Golden Gate Park Bums [1]. They wore the insult proudly. Men with jobs were later allowed to play on Sundays, but weekday games were kept for the unemployed [1]. The Bums had no officers and no membership list. A newcomer showed up every Sunday with a glove and waited, sometimes for weeks, to be picked [1]. Full uniforms were for fops. A longtime third baseman called Old Jeff played in corduroy pants, a vest and a derby hat [1]. Not everyone was charmed. Park Commission minutes from 1902 record complaints about "profane and obscene language indulged in by the ball players in the park on Sundays and weekdays in the presence of ladies and children," and ask for more police patrols [1]. That same year the city added handball courts at the Big Rec grounds [2].

title: The Substation That Restarted the Streetcars
place: 1190 Fillmore Street, at Turk
hook: This brick powerhouse helped electrify San Francisco's streetcars and got the Fillmore line running soon after 1906. It has now stood empty for nearly fifty years.
story: The brick and sandstone substation at Fillmore and Turk went up in 1902, when San Francisco's street railways were switching from horse cars to electricity [1]. It came through the 1906 earthquake and fire, and the Fillmore Street line was one of the first back in service afterwards [1]. For three-quarters of a century it fed power to United Railroads, the Market Street Railway and finally Muni [2]. In 1978 it was declared surplus and shut, and on April 23, 1979 it became city Landmark No. 105 [2][4]. Since then it has mostly waited. The Redevelopment Agency took it over, and in 2009 redevelopment funds were diverted to bail out the nearby Yoshi's jazz club. When the agency was dissolved, the building went back to the City [2]. In August 2021 Public Works ordered emergency repairs after cracks in its unreinforced masonry were found to pose 'a significant collapse hazard to pedestrians, bicyclists, and motorists below' [2]. A seismic retrofit estimated at $2-3 million in 2003 was put at $20-30 million by 2024. A 2008 call for proposals drew only two bids, and both were rejected [3]. Neighbours have proposed a history museum, a shelter behind the preserved facade, and a 'Maya Angelou Still I Rise Center' [3].

title: The builder with plans on an index card
place: Fernando Nelson homes, 4th-5th Aves between Balboa & Cabrillo
hook: Fernando Nelson carried his two house plans on a single index card and collected mortgage payments at the door. Hundreds of Inner Richmond homes are his.
story: In 1902 Fernando Nelson bought land on the old Bay District track, already graded and served by new water and sewer lines [1]. He built only when a buyer had signed up. His two floor plans, A and B, were printed on either side of an index card he carried in his pocket [1]. He often put the plumbing at the back so that a house could later be split into flats, and he often carried the buyer's mortgage himself, calling in person each month for the cash [1]. Look for his 'donuts', a row of jigsawed redwood circles above the front door [1]. After the 1906 quake the army took his lumber. By November the Richmond Banner reported he was building on the whole block between Fourth and Fifth Avenues, B and C Streets (now Balboa and Cabrillo), with houses 'sold before being built' [1]. In 1909 the Banner claimed he had put up a house every working day for six years. John Freeman's count is 246 buildings [1]. Nelson also set a San Francisco to Los Angeles driving record in November 1906 [1]. His family left the Richmond by 1916 [1].

title: The hill saved by a smallpox scare
place: Bayview Hill (Bayview Park) summit
hook: The city bought Bayview Hill for a quarantine hospital. A neighbouring landowner gave away land to stop it, and the hill became a park instead.
story: In the late 1890s the Bay View Land Company planned luxury homes on the rocky hill above Candlestick Point. The plan failed because the hill was too far from downtown [1][2]. In 1902 the city bought the hilltop for a 'pest house', a hospital to isolate people with contagious diseases. Even that plan ran into the same distance problem: getting there would need a new road [3]. The owners of the neighbouring land feared a quarantine hospital would drag down the value of their land [1]. The usual story says the railroad baron Charles Crocker gave the city his part of the hill on condition that the pest house be dropped [1][2]. But Crocker had died in 1888, so the donation must have come from the Crocker Land Company [3]. In 1905 Daniel Burnham's city plan marked the hill as a future 'Visitacion Park', and it was dedicated as parkland in 1915 [1][3]. Because no one built on it, the hill still has some of the city's richest native grassland, remnant oaks and islay cherry, and rare plants such as San Francisco Chinese houses that grow nowhere else in the city [1].
