title: Widow Richardson's house on Cortland
place: 440-448 Cortland Avenue (Bernal Meats)
hook: A dockworker's widow with nine children ran a coal yard and a boarding house. Her son opened the butcher shop that anchored Cortland Avenue.
story:
In 1887 Clement Richardson, a roustabout on the docks, and his wife Bridget moved their six children into a house at 440 Cortland Avenue. Three more children were born there. Clement was killed in an accident in 1897. Bridget, then 44 with eight children still at home, kept the family going by running a coal yard at 3501 Mission Street and taking in boarders [1]. In 1902 her son George opened Bernal Meats at 448 Cortland. His younger brother Walter later joined him, and the shop did well for about 25 years [1][2].

It was a busy spot. After the 1906 earthquake new families poured onto the hill, with more than 600 houses built in the year after the disaster [3]. Cortland's grocers, bakers, barbers and butchers grew with them [2]. In the 1920s Dora Munsil kept a hardware and notions shop next door at 450, and her father John ran Post Office Station No. 31 from a nook at the back [2]. A 1909 photograph shows bunting on the house for the Portola Festival, the celebration of the city's recovery [1]. In 1925 a new building replaced both older ones. Good Life Grocery now stands on the site [1][2].

title: A School Beneath the Grocery Store
place: Site of the 1908 Oceanside Primary School, 43rd Avenue between Irving and Judah Streets
hook: The beach settlement's first classroom met under a grocery on 48th Avenue. It grew into Francis Scott Key School.
story: By 1903 families were living among the streetcar houses and cottages near Ocean Beach, and the neighborhood called Oceanside started its first school. The Oceanside Primary School met beneath a grocery store on 48th Avenue [1]. In 1908 the city built a big new Oceanside Primary School on 43rd Avenue between Irving and Judah, two stories and a basement under wooden shingles. It was demolished and rebuilt in 1913 and renamed Francis Scott Key School [1]. A half-timbered annex, its first story clad in 12-inch redwood planks, went up at 1351 42nd Avenue in the late 1910s or early 1920s, and it still stands [1]. Mothers ran things too. Ottie Fulmore, wife of a marine engineer, lived at 1247-49 46th Avenue from 1904. In 1947 a newspaper remembered her as the first president of the school's Parent-Teacher Association, originally called the 'Mother's Congress' [2]. Val Golding grew up across the street from the school at 3822 Kirkham. On his 11th birthday, December 8, 1941, a soldier knocked while the candles burned and ordered the lights down. Within days city crews painted the seaward side of every streetlight globe brown [3].

title: A battleship dwarfed in a new dock
place: Drydock No. 2, Hunters Point Shipyard
hook: In January 1903 the battleship Ohio floated into a brand-new 750-foot dock at Hunters Point. 'Big Battleship Ohio Seems Lost,' ran the headline.
story: After the Spanish-American War the Navy expanded its Pacific squadrons, and the San Francisco Dry Dock Company expected more Navy repair work [2]. Its 1868 dock was now too small for modern ships [1]. The company hired Howard C. Holmes, who gave up his job as chief engineer of the State Board of Harbor Commissioners, to design a bigger one [1]. Work began on January 9, 1901, cutting a second basin into the serpentine of Hunters Point at a slight angle to the first. It was 750 feet long, among the largest docks in the world [1]. Union Iron Works built its floating steel gate and launched it in August 1902, while two copies were being built for the Russian government [1]. At the end of January 1903 the battleship Ohio was the first ship docked. Engineers, company president W. F. Babcock and about 100 guests watched the dock drain in two hours as workers scraped marine growth off the hull [1]. The 388-foot Ohio 'Seems Lost', the Call's headline said, and the paper called the dock 'a monument to mechanical skill' [1]. Its brick Neoclassical powerhouse survives [1].

title: A house on the most famous corner
place: 557 Ashbury St / 1500 Haight St, northwest corner
hook: Long before hippies made Haight and Ashbury world-famous, a bookkeeper-turned-lawyer built a family home on the corner, then jacked it up to fit shops underneath.
story: The corner building whose façade reads "Haight" and "Ashbury" started life as a family home. By 1903 Richard P. Doolan had bought a 32.5-by-100-foot corner lot carved from the Baird estate, and that year he built a two-storey Colonial Revival house at 557 Ashbury Street [1]. Doolan had worked his way up as a clerk and bookkeeper, a Custom House assistant appraiser and a lawyer, and in 1903 he was a financial agent downtown. The house was designed by Frank T. Doolan, presumably his brother, an architectural draftsman whose own career the nomination calls undistinguished [1]. The contractor was Charles J. U. Koenig [1]. The original house sat about six feet above the ground, with a deep recessed entry. The nomination explains that after 1906 it became clear this stretch of Haight would go commercial. So in 1907 Doolan had the whole house raised and shopfronts built beneath it [1][2]. The corner has more storefronts than any other property on the strip. Its later fame as the hippie movement's "ground zero" belongs to another era [2].

title: Captain Young escorts the President
place: Presidio Golf Course (the 1903 'Presidio Golf Links')
hook: In May 1903 Black cavalrymen from the Presidio escorted Theodore Roosevelt through San Francisco, led by the only Black troop commander in the regular Army.
story: In October 1902 the 3rd Squadron of the 9th Cavalry, one of the Black regiments known as the Buffalo Soldiers, arrived at the Presidio [1]. Commanding Troop I was Captain Charles Young. The son of formerly enslaved parents, he was the third African American to graduate from West Point and the only Black troop commander in the regular Army [1][2]. Off duty the men played baseball and mixed with San Francisco's small, close-knit Black community [1]. When President Theodore Roosevelt visited on May 12–14, 1903, Troops I and M rode alongside his carriages as escort and guard of honour. The San Francisco Call praised them as 'crack military organizations' [1]. Many had last seen Roosevelt at San Juan Hill in 1898, and he had since angered them by belittling Black soldiers in Scribner's magazine [1]. A photograph shows the honour guard at the Presidio Golf Links [1]. Six days later Young led the two troops on a 16-day, 323-mile ride to Sequoia National Park. There he became acting superintendent, the first Black officer to hold the post, and his men built more road in one season than in the three before [3].

title: Dynamite versus the women of Telegraph Hill
place: Gray Brothers quarry site, Sansome & Green
hook: Quarrymen blasted away a third of the hill while houses slid off the cliff. A group of determined women spent 13 years fighting back.
story: In 1887 George and Harry Gray began blasting the east face of Telegraph Hill for their paving business. The National Register nomination says they removed about a third of the hill [1]. Their quarry at Sansome and Green ran for about 20 years [2][3]. Irish and Italian families living on the hill sometimes watched their small homes tumble down the cliff after a blast, and some threw rocks at the quarry crews [2]. On Calhoun Terrace there were seven houses on the east side in 1880. By 1899 all of them had been destroyed [4]. The fight back was led by women, most of them from other parts of the city. Alice Griffith, Elizabeth Ashe and eight others formed the Willing Circle in 1890 and opened a settlement house near the crest of Vallejo Street, with two nurses for the neighbourhood [2]. Griffith went after officials, found lawyers to take on the Grays and got the press involved. The Sailors' Union paper backed the cause as well [2]. In October 1903 a court revoked the blasting permits and stopped the rock crushers [2]. Even so, the Grays went on digging, bribing and ignoring orders for years afterwards [2][3].

title: Hogs on the Disputed Dunes
place: Near 14th Avenue & Judah Street
hook: While lawyers fought over who owned these dunes for forty years, the people living on them kept pigs, cows and geese.
story: For almost forty years nobody could say for sure who owned the blocks around 12th to 16th Avenues between Irving and Lawton. In 1868 the McGrath family moved onto the land as squatters. They later leased it from one claimant, outlasted court orders meant for someone else, and stopped paying rent [1]. From 1892 to 1908 they sublet it to a Mahoney family of blacksmiths and labourers. In 1894 a reporter described their 'very old' house with cows, geese, chickens and dogs. That year William McGrath put up a big sign warning buyers that anyone buying there would waste their money. The lawyer in charge of the suit had forgotten its details [1]. In March 1903 the Chronicle ran a feature on farms inside the city limits. Among them was Thomas Mahoney's seventeen-pig hog ranch near 14th Avenue and Judah Street. His original stock came off an English ship in 1866. Twice pushed west by the growing city, he settled here in 1891, sometimes traded hogs with the Almshouse over the hill, and fed his herd on refuse he collected in the Western Addition [2]. Whether he belonged to the subletting Mahoneys isn't known. In April 1908 a judge finally ruled for 200 to 300 claimants, and a reporter predicted a building boom [1].

title: The Dark Side of Sutro's Forest
place: Sutro Forest on Mount Sutro, behind the Affiliated Colleges (now UCSF)
hook: Mushroom pickers, a forest keeper and passing strangers kept making the same discovery in Adolph Sutro's eucalyptus woods above Parnassus.
story:
Adolph Sutro planted his eucalyptus on the bare hills above the Inner Sunset to give the city a forest [2]. Around 1900 its dense, lonely groves became the scene of one suicide after another, reported mostly in the San Francisco Call [1].

In December 1899 the forest keeper reported a man's body a few feet from a path behind the Affiliated Colleges. He had a bicycle pump in his pocket and a packet marked "poison." A postcard in his pocket named him Frank Parker; a friend later identified him as Grant Bell, a bicycle repairer from San Jose [1]. In November 1903, two mushroom gatherers from Stanyan Street found remains midway between the colleges and the Almshouse. The dead man was a member of the Marine Firemen's Union whose name had been scraped off his union certificate. Across it was scrawled an unsigned note: "If you want to bury me, I'm thankful to you" [1].

In April 1904 two men found Thomas Murnane, 52, in a tall eucalyptus. Once a wealthy businessman, he had ended up in the Almshouse. He had vanished in February, the day after telling a fellow inmate that his last child had died and he was tired of a life of poverty [1].

title: The quiet Fleishhacker brother
place: Mortimer Fleishhacker Sr. house, 2418 Pacific Avenue
hook: The son of a paper-box maker ran a power company that rivaled PG&E, then sat as a UC regent for thirty years, despite never finishing high school.
story:
Behind the dark Flemish-bond brick of 2418 Pacific lived Mortimer Fleishhacker Sr. He was the son of Aaron Fleishhacker, who ran a modest paper-box business, and he became his father's partner in 1892 [1][3]. With his younger brother Herbert, he is said to have built a business empire on a 1,000 percent profit from buying and reselling an Oregon paper mill that Herbert came across on his sales route [1].

In 1903 the brothers organized the American River Electric Company, an early hydroelectric venture. For a dozen years Mortimer was president of the Great Western Power Company, a serious rival to PG&E until it was bought out in 1930 [1]. Herbert, who lived at the St. Francis Hotel and gave his name to the Fleishhacker Zoo and Pool, went into banking, and the brothers worked together there for three decades [1][3]. Mortimer was the quieter one. His schooling ended in high school, yet he was a University of California regent for thirty years [1].

His son Mortimer Jr. grew up here. In 1936 he had William Wurster design a modern house down the street at 2600 Pacific, and from 1955 to 1970 he was president of KQED [2].

title: A Gilded Undersea Ballroom, Hidden Between Floors
place: 1536 La Playa, former Breakers / Crest / Mendel's roadhouse facing Great Highway
hook: Behind a plain stucco apartment front, gilded plaster carp, seahorses and turtles from a 1904 roadhouse still swim in a hidden crawlspace.
story: From 1904 to about 1940, a roadhouse near the beach end of La Playa went by three names in turn: the Breakers, the Crest and finally Mendel's [1]. Guests ate, drank and danced under a make-believe sea. Plaster-and-wire carp hung lamp chains from their open mouths, among seahorses, starfish, crabs and a turtle about to snap up a school of fish, all gilded and touched with iridescent blue-green [1]. In the carriage house next door, customers left their horses, bicycles, motorcycles and cars. According to stories handed down, the upper floors held card rooms, beds for sleeping it off, and cribs for working girls [1]. In 1911 some 75 riders of the San Francisco Motorcycle Club lined up for a photo in front of its balconied, towered facade [1]. In the 1920s Mendel's was one of the big Ocean Beach roadhouses with bands and fine dining [2]. World War II seems to have ended the roadhouse days. The building was reportedly used for offices, cut into apartments, and given a beige stucco front in the early 1970s [1]. In January 2013, historian Woody LaBounty and friends climbed through a ceiling hatch and found the decorations still there between the floors. Most had been sprayed gray with fire retardant, but where the spray missed, the gold still shone [1].

title: A Palace for the Archbishop
place: 1000 Fulton Street (Archbishop's Mansion), at Steiner
hook: Built for San Francisco's archbishop in 1904, the mansion on Alamo Square later housed nuns, a boys' home, a psychiatric clinic, an opera-themed inn and a startup incubator.
story: In 1904 a Second Empire mansion went up facing the northeast corner of Alamo Square as the home of Patrick Riordan, second archbishop of San Francisco [1][2]. Architect Frank Shea gave it a mahogany staircase under a stained-glass dome, ornate fireplaces and French doors [3]. The Alamo Square Neighborhood Association calls it a symbol of the Catholic Church's prominence in the city's life at the time [2]. The house came through the 1906 earthquake and went on to host a Pope and later archbishops [3]. Over the decades it has also housed a convent, an orphanage, a psychiatric hospital, a rehab centre and a bed-and-breakfast [3]. It sold for $7 million in 2012, and in 2018 the co-living company Roam turned it into rooms for "modern nomads" [3]. By early 2023 it housed HF0, a live-in startup incubator, and the archbishop's house had become a tech "hacker house" [4].

title: A Petit Trianon for Menuhin and Stravinsky
place: Koshland House, 3800 Washington Street at Maple Street
hook: A wool fortune built a copy of a Versailles chateau on Washington Street, opened it with a Marie Antoinette costume ball, then filled it with the world's great musicians.
story:
Marcus Koshland, whose family firm S. Koshland & Sons was one of America's leading wool companies, built 3800 Washington Street between 1902 and 1904 [1]. Architect Franklin S. Van Trees gave its front a nearly exact copy of the Petit Trianon at Versailles, in Colusa sandstone [1]. The house was opened with a Marie Antoinette costume ball [2]. Two years later the 1906 earthquake brought down much of the cornice and all four front columns, which were soon replaced [1].

Inside, a basement ballroom lined with mirrors had small stages at each end for concerts [1]. Marcus's wife, Corinne Schweitzer Koshland, loved music. She helped establish the San Francisco Symphony and Opera, and served on the Symphony's early board [1]. The National Register nomination lists musicians who played at the house or stayed there: Isaac Stern, Leonard Bernstein, Jascha Heifetz, Pierre Monteux, Igor Stravinsky and the child prodigy Yehudi Menuhin, whose education she helped to pay for [1]. The artist Bruce Porter designed its art-glass windows, one of them marked "Salve" (welcome) and dated 1904 [1]. The city made the house Landmark #95 in 1977 [1][2].

title: A Saloon Bank for the 'Little Fellow'
place: Columbus Avenue & Washington Street (site of the first Bank of Italy)
hook: The world's largest bank started in a converted saloon at the edge of Chinatown and North Beach, lending to immigrants others ignored.
story: Amadeo Pietro Giannini, the son of Italian immigrants, made his money as a produce broker. He then became a director of Columbus Savings & Loan, but fell out with the other directors, who did not share his wish to serve the city's growing immigrant population [1]. So he quit and started his own bank. The Bank of Italy opened on October 17, 1904, in a converted saloon in the Jackson Square neighbourhood, as an institution for the 'little fellow' [1][2]. First-day deposits came to $8,780, and within a year they topped $700,000 [1]. The original building is gone. The Colombo Building of 1909 now stands on the site, at the gore corner where Columbus Avenue meets Washington and Montgomery (the city's landmark file dates the building to 1912) [2][3]. After the 1906 earthquake, Giannini reportedly hauled his bank's cash to San Mateo under a load of garbage and was soon making loans from a plank across two barrels [1]. His bank was renamed Bank of America in 1930 and by 1945 was the largest commercial bank in the world [2].

title: A Windmill Feud on Sadowa Street
place: 131 Sadowa Street
hook: In 1904 Ocean View's water came from backyard windmills. One owner turned off a neighbour's supply over a broken window.
story: In 1900 Ocean View had only about 200 buildings. A typical lot held a small house with a windmill or water tank beside it [1]. Some residents drew water from a neighbour's pump, which could go badly wrong. In September 1904 Andrew Douglas of 131 Sadowa Street and William Wells of 137 Sadowa came before Police Judge Mogan on a charge of disturbing the peace. Patrolmen King and Cronin had needed five minutes to pull the two men apart [2]. According to the testimony, Douglas owned a windmill pump that supplied several Sadowa Street homes. Small boys had broken a window in the house where Wells lived, which belonged to Douglas's mother-in-law, Mrs. Condon. Each side said the other should pay for the glass, so Douglas cut off the Wells family's water [2]. Wells said it was 'the principle of the thing'. The judge told the men they reminded him of 'the obstinate characters in a New England rural drama', and dismissed the case [2]. A 1905 advertisement for a new cottage at 272 Sadowa listed a barn, stables, chicken houses, 'windmill, tank' [3]. Water mains came in the 1920s. No Ocean View windmill is known to survive [1].

title: Burnham's hilltop drawing office
place: A spur of Twin Peaks (exact site unknown)
hook: To redesign San Francisco, America's star planner asked for one thing: a cabin on Twin Peaks with the whole city at his feet.
story:
In 1904 the Association for the Improvement and Adornment of San Francisco, a group of civic boosters, invited Daniel Burnham to plan the city's future. Burnham had already planned Washington, Cleveland, Chicago and Manila. He agreed to work unpaid, and the association covered expenses and his staff's salaries [1]. He made one request, a bungalow "on a spur of Twin Peaks", and Willis Polk designed it. There, at a spot "selected to command the panorama of the city and to permit uninterrupted study," work began on September 20, 1904 [1][2]. His assistant was Edward H. Bennett [1].

The plan that came out of the cabin in September 1905 was huge. Historian Robert Cherny notes that it assumed two million future residents and set aside a third of the city as parks. New diagonal avenues and circles were borrowed from L'Enfant's Washington and from Paris. Burnham devoted less than two pages to the economy and said little about housing [3]. It even included a grand staircase from the Castro to the summit [3]. Seven months after the report came out, the 1906 earthquake and fire struck. Most of the plan was buried as the city rushed to rebuild [4].

title: From saloon to park-side hotel
place: Stanyan Park Hotel (built as Park View Hotel), 750 Stanyan St
hook: The park banned business, so the saloons crowded onto Stanyan Street. One Irish saloon keeper's bet became the park's oldest surviving hotel.
story: Golden Gate Park's first superintendent, William Hammond Hall, banned commercial business inside the park. The result, when street railways reached the park's edge, was a row of saloons along Stanyan Street [1]. Around 1883, when the steam train to the beach began running from just inside the park, Harry P. Heagerty, an Irish immigrant who had arrived in 1876, opened a liquor business on the southeast corner of Stanyan and Waller. His two-storey saloon and small boarding house sat right beside the Haight Street Grounds ticket office [1]. When the ballpark closed, Heagerty looked for new trade. In 1904 and 1905 he built a real hotel, one of a dozen serving the park and seven on Stanyan Street alone [1]. To compete, he hired the firm of Martens & Coffey, who gave him the costliest of their many buildings in the neighbourhood, at $28,000, with a round corner bay and a metal-covered dome [1]. It was the Park View Hotel on the 1905 Sanborn map, and later the Hotel Golden Gate, the Hotel Roamer and the Stadium Hotel. Today it is the Stanyan Park Hotel, the oldest surviving hotel on the park's border [1][2].

title: Shoot the Chutes on Fulton Street
place: Site of the Chutes amusement park, 10th Ave & Fulton St
hook: Boats that bounced and flipped, a zoo, a mirror maze and the Avenues' first moving pictures, all for a dime, just across from Golden Gate Park.
story: Early in the 1900s the Chutes amusement park sat just off D Street, now Fulton Street, at Tenth Avenue [1]. Its main ride sent boats down a steep flume into a pool. 'There was no safety device on those old Shoot-the-Chutes and those boats would literally go flying,' one man told the Western Neighborhoods Project. 'They flipped over all the time!' [1] The Chutes also showed some of the first films in the Avenues, before Fisher's opened on Clement Street in 1907. A Chronicle ad from March 21, 1904 promised moving pictures of boxers Britt and Young Corbett in training, a 'Cabaret de la Mort', 'animals from all climes in the zoo', a mystic mirror maze and a trip down the flume. Admission was 10 cents, or 5 cents for children [1]. The park did not last. In May 1910 builder Fernando Nelson bought the whole block and a half it had covered, on the east side of Tenth Avenue and between Cabrillo and Fulton from Tenth to Eleventh [2]. Over the next few years the Nelsons covered it with homes, including a half-timbered house at the northeast corner of Tenth and Fulton [2].

title: The gun that ducks after every shot
place: Battery Chamberlin, north end of Baker Beach
hook: At Baker Beach, a 1904 battery hid its six-inch guns behind concrete. After each shot the recoil swung them down out of sight to be reloaded.
story: By 1905 the Army had built twelve reinforced-concrete gun batteries along the San Francisco headlands to strengthen the bay's defences [1]. They were part of the Endicott programme, which put seventeen batteries on the western Presidio between 1891 and 1946 [2]. Battery Chamberlin was finished in 1904 above the north end of Baker Beach. It was named for Captain Lowell A. Chamberlin, who had served with distinction in the Civil War [3]. Its four six-inch rifles sat on 'disappearing' carriages. For firing, a gun rose above the parapet. Its recoil swung it back down, out of sight from the sea, where the crew could reload it in cover [3]. The job was to guard the underwater minefields laid outside the Golden Gate in wartime. The guns could reach 7.5 miles, and trained crews fired two rounds a minute [3]. The original guns were taken away in 1917 for the First World War [3]. Today a matching 1905 gun on a working disappearing carriage sits in one of the emplacements. It is one of only a score or so of such guns left in the world that still operate, and it is demonstrated to visitors [3].

title: A Bitter Glass of Poland Water
place: Site of the Stanford mansion, 905 California Street (now the Stanford Court hotel)
hook: One January night the co-founder of Stanford University took a sip of mineral water in her Nob Hill bedroom, and it tasted of strychnine.
story: Leland Stanford built one of Nob Hill's first great mansions in 1876 [3]. In 1905 his widow, Jane, still used it. On the evening of January 14, 1905, she drank from a bottle of Poland Spring water that a servant set in her room every night [1]. It tasted bitter, so she made herself vomit and called her secretary and maid, who agreed it tasted "queer" [1]. Weeks later a chemist reported enough strychnine in the bottle to kill [1]. Private detectives she hired called it an accident [2]. Unsettled, and doubting university president David Starr Jordan, the 76-year-old sailed for Hawaii on February 15 [1]. On February 28 at the Moana Hotel in Honolulu she took bicarbonate of soda prepared by her secretary, Bertha Berner, and woke crying, "I think I have been poisoned again!" [1]. She died that night. A coroner's jury found strychnine poisoning; Jordan hired another doctor and announced heart failure [1]. In 2003 Stanford neurologist Robert Cutler concluded she was murdered, but no culprit has ever been named [1][2].

title: A Hindu temple among the sand lots
place: Old Vedanta Temple, Webster and Filbert Streets
hook: In 1905 a monk from India bought a lot among Cow Hollow's sand lots and built what his society calls the first Hindu temple in the West.
story: Swami Vivekananda arrived in San Francisco on February 22, 1900, and that April his students founded the Vedanta Society [1]. Vivekananda arranged for a fellow disciple, Swami Trigunatita, to take over the work, and Trigunatita was always in a hurry [1][2]. In 1904 he and a committee found a lot on Webster Street, near the bay 'among sand lots', for $8,000 [1]. The cornerstone was laid on August 21, 1905, and the building was dedicated on January 7, 1906, three months before the earthquake [1]. The architect Joseph A. Leonard worked from the swami's ideas, and the third floor and towers were added in 1908 [2][3]. The swami called it 'a combination of a Hindu temple, a Christian church, a Mohammedan mosque, a Hindu Math or monastery, and an American residence' [2]. One tower copies a small Shiva temple at Dakshineswar, where Ramakrishna lived. Another is modelled on a European castle tower [2]. Neighbourhood kids found it spooky. Walter de Vecchi remembered its 'weird signs and magic symbols' [3]. Then, on December 27, 1914, a former student threw a bomb onto the pulpit during a Sunday service. The student was killed, and Trigunatita died of his injuries on January 10, 1915 [4].

title: A Parthenon planned between the peaks
place: Western slope below the peaks, near Marview Way (proposed Athenaeum site)
hook: Burnham wanted a marble Athenaeum, an artists' colony, a stadium like Delphi's and a colossal statue of 'San Francisco' on these slopes.
story:
Burnham's 1905 report gave Twin Peaks a starring role. It proposed that the city buy the peaks, and the land out to Lake Merced, for a park [1]. High on the western side he placed an "Athenaeum" of courts, terraces and colonnades, modelled on the sun-trapping walls of Hadrian's Villa and meant to hold "some few of the greatest works of art" [1]. Burnham called the spot "the moral and geographical center of the city." At its centre would stand "a colossal figure symbolical of San Francisco", looking down a glade towards the Laguna de la Merced [1]. Local historian Devin Smith describes the statue in the report's rendering as a 300-foot woman raising a torch towards the Pacific [2].

The report asked for more. It sketched an academy on the southeast slope where writers, scientists and artists could live and work, with a little Greek open-air theatre [1]. It proposed a maternity home in "surroundings of the most ideal character", and an enormous stadium in the hollow to the north, compared to the one at Delphi [1]. By night, lights would trace the forest glades from hill to hill [1]. None of it was built. The slopes filled instead with 1950s houses and 1960s apartments [2].

title: A Teenager's Wireless Phone in the Dunes
place: Approximate site of a McCarty Wireless Telephone Co. station, near 45th Avenue & Lawton Street
hook: In 1905 a 17-year-old sang 'Auld Lang Syne' over the air from the Cliff House. One of his company's stations was a shack half-buried in Sunset sand.
story: Francis J. McCarty left St. Ignatius College young and taught himself electricity. By 1902, when radio could otherwise send only Morse code, he and his brother were testing a homemade 'wireless telephone' across Stow Lake in Golden Gate Park [1][2]. Investors formed the McCarty Wireless Telephone Company. On September 2, 1905, reporters gathered at the Cliff House and dug trenches to make sure no hidden wires were buried there. Then they went to listen at a receiver about a mile down the beach, in the empty Cyclers' Rest. McCarty's voice first came through 'like the far hum of bees.' As he raised the power it grew clear enough to follow 'Auld Lang Syne' and 'Home Sweet Home' [1]. Wikipedia, citing the Call, dates the public demonstration to October [2]. One of the company's experimental stations was a shack in the Sunset dunes at about today's 45th Avenue and Lawton Street [1][3]. 'Frequently, we'd wake up in the morning and have to shovel our way out the front door through the sand that had drifted waist-high against it,' his brother Ignatius remembered [1]. After the 1906 earthquake the company moved to Oakland. There, on May 8, Francis was thrown from a horse-drawn cart, and he died three days later at 17 [2].

title: A dollar down, a dollar a week
place: Former Bay Shore Hotel, southwest corner of Bayshore Boulevard and Leland Avenue
hook: In 1905 you could buy a Visitacion Valley building lot for $125, paying a dollar down and a dollar a week. Leland Avenue grew up to serve the buyers.
story: In 1905 Visitacion Valley's farmland began turning into lots for sale. Charles A. Louis was sales agent for the Reis Tract, then the largest housing development in the valley [2]. It advertised 'the finest building sites' for as little as $125, with $1 down and $1 a week [2][3]. That same year, on May 18, 1905, residents formed the Visitacion Valley Improvement Club, which pushed community projects for years [2]. On the corner of the San Bruno Road and Leland Avenue stood the Bay Shore Hotel, built in the early 20th century [1]. Guest rooms with rounded and angled bay windows filled the second floor. W. A. McGahey ran a corner bar downstairs [1]. Real estate offices, hardware stores and the Read family's grocery lined the Leland Avenue side. The building anchored Leland as the valley's shopping street [1]. Next door, the local water works had its pumping station and office [2]. For its first decades Leland was paved for only three blocks and had wooden sidewalks [1]. The old hotel, now covered in stucco, still houses apartments and small businesses [1].

title: A dome that rode out the quake
place: Temple Sherith Israel, 2266 California St at Webster
hook: A Gold Rush congregation moved west in 1905. Seven months later the earthquake struck, and its great domed temple barely noticed.
story:
Congregation Sherith Israel was founded during the Gold Rush, and it is one of the oldest synagogues in the United States [1]. From 1868 it worshipped downtown at Post and Taylor, but like many of the city's Jewish families it moved west to the Western Addition [2]. Its rabbi, Jacob Nieto, lived on Bush Street [2].

For the new temple at California and Webster, the congregation hired Albert Pissis, who was trained at the École des Beaux-Arts. The cornerstone was laid on 22 February 1904, and the temple was consecrated on 24 September 1905 [3]. It blends Byzantine and Romanesque forms and rises 140 feet, under a dome 60 feet across. Its organ has 3,500 pipes [1].

Seven months later the 1906 earthquake struck. The temple suffered only modest damage, which was quickly repaired, while the fire destroyed downtown [1][3]. According to the congregation's history, the synagogue then became a principal site of the city's graft prosecution trials, in which political boss Abe Ruef and his allies faced corruption charges [3]. It came through the 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake undamaged as well [3].

title: A park in the sunny belt
place: Mission Park (today Mission Dolores Park), 19th and Dolores
hook: Developers wanted the empty graveyards cut into house lots. The Mission's neighbours voted to buy them for a park.
story: With the Jewish cemeteries emptied, developers wanted the land for building lots. The neighbours had other ideas. In 1897 ex-judge F. W. Van Reynegom of the Mission Improvement Union argued for a park there: "It would be a crime to permit these fifteen acres in the old cemeteries to be cut up into building lots… They are in the center of the Mission sunny belt. One may sit out doors there when the fog is over every other part of the peninsula" [1]. Mayor James D. Phelan backed the idea. Voters approved park bonds in December 1899, but a court challenge sank them on a technicality [1]. More than 1,000 southside property owners formed the Mission Park Association in 1903 [2]. That September, Item No. 12, a $293,000 bond to buy the cemeteries, passed 19,386 to 6,862 [1]. The city bought the land in February 1905 and promised the old owners it would always be a place of beauty [1]. Mission Park was barely laid out when the 1906 earthquake struck. It became a refugee camp [1][2].

title: A post office that's a palace
place: U.S. Courthouse and Post Office (James R. Browning Courthouse), Seventh and Mission streets
hook: Washington built its most lavish West Coast building more than a mile from downtown, among Irish and German workers' flats, and brought in Italian artisans to finish it.
story: By the 1870s San Francisco's federal courts and post office were squeezed into rented rooms around downtown [1]. In 1887 a site commission reported that the $350,000 Congress had set aside was not enough, and the budget went up to $1,250,000 [1]. The lot chosen was at Seventh and Mission, more than a mile from the business district, in a working-class neighborhood of Irish and German immigrants. Many people objected, but it was bought in 1891 [1][2]. Supervising Architect James Knox Taylor chose an Italian Renaissance palazzo design, and skilled artisans were brought from Italy to finish the interiors [1][2]. The walls were lined with Carrara and Yellow Siena marble from Italy and Red Numidian from North Africa, the vaulted ceilings with marble mosaics, and the rotundas topped with stained-glass domes. The bronze entry lanterns copy torch-holders made in 1489 for the Florentine banker Filippo Strozzi [1]. Work began in 1897. When the building opened in 1905 it was hailed as "a post office that's a palace" [1][2]. Within months it would face the 1906 earthquake and fire.

title: America's First Zen Master, on the Great Highway
place: Site of the Ocean Side House (later Tait's-at-the-Beach), Great Highway between Ulloa & Vicente
hook: In 1905 a Zen abbot from Kamakura spent nine months in a converted roadhouse out on the dunes, teaching a San Francisco household to meditate.
story: The Ocean Side House was the first building in what became the Outer Sunset. Attorney B.S. Brooks put it up as a roadhouse in the 1860s on the Great Highway between Ulloa and Vicente, so remote it was nicknamed Brooks' Folly [1][2]. After decades of struggling proprietors, it became the home of Alexander and Ida Russell; the sources say 1901 or 1902 [1][2]. Ida studied world religions and had studied in Japan with the Zen master Soyen Shaku [1]. Shaku, abbot of Engaku-ji in Kamakura, was the first Zen master to teach in the United States. In 1905 he came as the Russells' guest for nine months and taught the whole household Zen, and Ida Russell is called the first American to study koans [3]. His student Nyogen Senzaki soon joined him [3]. The lectures Shaku gave in the house may have been the first regular Buddhist teaching anywhere in the country [2]. The Russells filled the house with religious art and added a chapel and a Japanese garden. They also took in children with nowhere else to go, which set off rumors, and in 1910 an Examiner story called the place a 'House of Mystery' [1]. Ida died there in 1917 after a botched cosmetic treatment. From 1919 the building was Tait's-at-the-Beach, and it burned in 1940 [1][2].

title: Burnham's park that came first on paper
place: Northern ridge of McLaren Park (Burnham's proposed University Mound Park)
hook: Twenty years before anyone said 'McLaren Park', the architect of Chicago's World's Fair had already drawn a park on these hills.
story: Twenty years before McLaren Park existed, the Chicago architect Daniel Burnham more or less drew it. His 1905 Report on a Plan for San Francisco looked at the 'low range of hills' between Islais Creek and Visitacion Valley. It called them 'comparatively unbuilt upon' and said the steep slopes should be planted and terraced. It also set aside the eastern half of 'the University Mound and Excelsior Homesteads Hill' for a park [1]. Burnham named it University Mound Park and listed it at 218 acres. He pictured 'luxuriant vegetation', with the nearby reservoir 'used in vista as a mirror for the park' [1]. After the 1906 fire, the plan's supporters thought nothing stood in the way. Instead, newspapers mocked it as 'the cobweb plan', property owners threatened to sue, and it fell apart in City Hall politics [2]. The idea survived anyway. The city's 1983 master plan for McLaren Park traces the park's story back to Burnham, noting that his proposed hilltop parks sat roughly where McLaren and Bayview parks are today [3].

title: Burnham's temple for Bernal Hill
place: North face of Bernal Hill along the line of Shotwell Street
hook: The 1905 plan to remake San Francisco as a Paris by the Bay put a monumental building on Bernal Hill.
story: Daniel Burnham designed Chicago's 1893 White City, the model for the City Beautiful movement. Downtown business owners then hired him to make San Francisco majestic. His team worked out of a cottage on Twin Peaks and finished the plan in autumn 1905. According to legend, the printed copies reached City Hall on April 17, 1906, the day before the earthquake [1][2]. The map gave Bernal Hill a starring role. It would be the southern end of two grand promenades: a 'Mission Parkway' running east–west between 23rd and 24th streets, and a 'Mission Arcade' in place of today's South Van Ness Avenue [2]. A broad garden would run up the north face of the hill roughly along Shotwell Street, from Army Street (now Cesar Chavez) up to Stoneman, and a large neo-classical building would look out over the Mission. The plan never said what it would be for [2]. After the disaster, San Franciscans wanted to rebuild quickly and in a familiar way, and Burnham's Bernal never happened [1].

title: Craftsman cottages for working families
place: Howard and 26th Street Cottages, 3274-3294 26th St at South Van Ness
hook: The Arts and Crafts style was meant for suburban bungalows. On a Mission corner in 1905, someone used it for working-class row houses around a shared courtyard.
story: In 1905, the year before the earthquake, an unknown architect put up two eight-unit wood-frame buildings at Howard (now South Van Ness) and 26th Street, arranged around a carefully scaled courtyard [1]. San Francisco's landmarks board calls them the city's only example of attached Craftsman row housing [1]. That is unusual. Late-19th-century row houses here were almost always Italianate, Stick or Queen Anne. Few Craftsman houses of any kind were built in San Francisco before 1910 [1]. The Craftsman style was popular in Berkeley, and it was usually sold as a detached, single-storey house for a middle-class family in a leafy suburb [1]. These units were built for working families who needed to live close to the docks and factories [1]. By then the Mission had been growing for forty years. A railroad station had opened at 25th and Valencia in 1863, and horse cars carried baseball crowds to 26th and Folsom around 1870 [1][2]. The Planning Commission backed landmark status in 1993, and the cottages became San Francisco Landmark No. 206 in January 1994 [1][2].

title: Down to Seven Members, Then a Tower
place: Seventh Avenue Presbyterian Church, 1329 7th Avenue
hook: In 1903 this congregation had seven active members. Two years later it bet everything on a lot in the Inner Sunset's sand.
story:
The congregation began downtown in 1892 as Cumberland Presbyterian Church. It soon had 132 members, but by 1903 only seven were still active [1]. A new pastor revived it, and in 1905 the members bought land on 7th Avenue in the barely built Inner Sunset. The church there was finished in 1907, and the congregation has been on the same site ever since [1][2].

The neighbourhood filled in around it. By the 1920s there were more than 300 members, and the building was enlarged into its present form, dedicated in 1929. For decades a big neon cross with the church's name stuck out over the sidewalk, until it was taken down in the 1960s [1][2]. The church got through money trouble in the Depression, paid off its debts by the late 1950s and had more than 400 members, before suburban moves thinned the pews after 1975 [1].

Then came October 17, 1989. The Loma Prieta earthquake seriously damaged the church [1]. Nearby, an apartment building at the northwest corner of 7th Avenue and Judah was so badly damaged that it was torn down the next April, with the church tower looking on [2][3]. The church was repaired, and membership has grown back to more than 100 [1].

title: Great is Ross the architect
place: Site of the Albert Pike Memorial Scottish Rite Temple, 1859 Geary Boulevard
hook: The Freemasons' temple on Geary was the work of a Scottish architect who once carved his own praise over a doorway.
story:
In May 1904 the Chronicle printed a sketch of a proposed Masonic temple for the south side of Geary between Fillmore and Steiner. It was to be three storeys of yellow brick and terra cotta in a Romanesque Revival style, valued at $80,000. The building appears on the 1905 Sanborn fire-insurance map [1]. It was named the Albert Pike Memorial Scottish Rite Temple, after the lawyer, writer, soldier and famous Freemason Albert Pike [1].

Its architect was Thomas Ross, a Scot who came to the United States in 1883. He also designed the Sing Fat and Sing Chong buildings at California and Grant, which are credited with inspiring Chinatown's pagoda-style rebuilding after 1906 [1]. For the Shriners on Geary near Jones he built a Moorish temple, now the Alcazar Theater. According to Bridget Maley, writing in The New Fillmore, he placed an Arabic inscription over its entry: 'Great is Allah and Great is Ross the Architect' [1][2].

The 1906 earthquake left the Geary temple structurally damaged, and it was repaired. The Masons used it until the mid-1960s. In the 1970s it became the San Francisco home of Jim Jones's Peoples Temple [1].

title: Opera Every Night, and a Diva Discovered
place: Tivoli Opera House, Eddy and Mason streets
hook: A beer garden turned opera house staged opera every night of the year. In 1905 it gave an unknown Italian soprano her American debut.
story: The Tivoli started out in 1879 as a beer garden in a frame building among shrubs at Sutter and Stockton. It served beer and Gilbert and Sullivan, and that July it ran 'Pinafore' and 'Trial by Jury' for 81 nights in a row [1]. It later moved to an opera house on Eddy Street near Market and Powell. Historian John P. Young thought it was probably the first house in the United States to give opera every night of the year [1]. Patrons sat at tables with refreshments while they watched the show [2]. By the 1900s the Tivoli stood at the corner of Eddy and Mason [1]. In December 1904 its impresario, William H. 'Doc' Leahy, was in Mexico when he heard Luisa Tetrazzini sing Lucia, and he invited her to San Francisco [3]. On January 11, 1905, she made her American debut at the Tivoli as Gilda in 'Rigoletto' [3]. Young wrote that the audience at once 'voted her a star of the first magnitude' [1]. A 1912 survey of opera singers quoted a New York critic who wrote that 'San Franciscans acclaimed her a second Patti' before the East had heard of her [4]. She stayed loyal to the city that discovered her [1][3].

title: Reach the Beaches: A Railroad in a Trench
place: Alemany Boulevard beside Sagamore Street (old Ocean Shore Railroad cut)
hook: A grand electric railroad to Santa Cruz dug a trench through Ocean View. The trains are long gone, but the trench became Alemany Boulevard.
story: The Ocean Shore Railway was incorporated on May 18, 1905. It planned a 1,500-volt electric, double-track line between San Francisco and Santa Cruz, and construction began that September [1]. Its San Francisco route ran from 12th and Mission Streets through what is now Alemany Boulevard, partly alongside the Southern Pacific tracks through Ocean View [2]. A photograph dated April 3, 1906, shows a steam shovel mounted on a rail car, digging a cut under the United Railroads streetcar tracks near today's Alemany Boulevard and Sickles Avenue. The company's slogan invited city people to 'Reach the Beaches' [3]. The 1906 earthquake sent parts of the coastal roadbed and equipment into the Pacific. The line never reached Santa Cruz and ran as two separate pieces, the northern one ending at Tunitas Glen. The company filed for bankruptcy in 1909, and mainline service was abandoned in 1920 after a labour walkout [1]. The OMI context statement judges that it had 'minimal impact' on the neighbourhood [2]. Its right of way outlived it. A city photograph from February 1926 looks northwest up Sickles from Winnipeg Avenue across the below-grade Ocean Shore cut, captioned as the 'future route of Alemany Boulevard' [4].

title: Seattle beer bottled beside the graveyards
place: 2739-2741 Geary Boulevard (formerly 219 Point Lobos Avenue), near Masonic
hook: Among the florists and saloons facing the cemeteries, a teamster's family bottled beer inside their own Geary Boulevard house, which still stands.
story: On the south side of Geary near Masonic, a pair of 1880s Italianate houses has outlasted the three cemeteries that once hemmed in this corner, earlier "improvements" to Masonic and the 1950s Geary tunnel [1]. Around 1905 a photographer caught a delivery wagon out front lettered "Apollo Lager Beer / Seattle's Famous Brew. C. H. Dechent & Co. 219 Pt. Lobos Ave." Point Lobos Avenue was the old name of this stretch of Geary [2]. Charles Dechent Jr. had started out as a teamster. He and his wife Nettie bottled beer inside the middle house while raising Charles Wallace, Chester and Clarice, who probably appear by the wagon [1]. Charles Jr.'s father kept a nursery and flower shop up the hill, where the Muni offices stand now, selling arrangements to mourners bound for Calvary, Masonic and Laurel Hill cemeteries [1]. The children did well: Charles and Clarice went to Stanford [1]. The house was standing by 1889. In 2018 it held a café and apartments and was up for sale [1]. On the corner nearby, the old Pub restaurant (later Mo'z Café) kept a muraled Prohibition speakeasy in its basement [1].

title: The Danish church a queen helped fund
place: St. Francis Lutheran Church (built as St. Ansgar), 152 Church St
hook: San Francisco's Danes wrote to their queen for help building a church. She sent 500 kroner, and the cornerstone went down in 1905.
story: For years San Francisco's Danish Lutherans relied on pastors sent up from Fresno, where Danish settlement in California had begun [1]. Around 1900 the community was big enough to want its own church, so it wrote to Queen Louise of Denmark for help. She sent 500 kroner, which became the start of the building fund [1]. The cornerstone of St. Ansgar Church was laid on September 17, 1905, at 152 Church Street, between Market and Duboce [2]. It was red brick over a wooden frame with a wooden steeple, in a Danish Gothic style [1]. Next door stood the First Finnish Lutheran Church, founded in 1899 on Belcher Street [2]. The area was so Scandinavian and German that it eventually supported five Lutheran congregations. Each held services in its own language: Norwegian, Danish, Swedish, Finnish and German [1]. By spring 1906 only the ground-floor hall was finished. After the April earthquake it served as a Red Cross hospital and shelter [1][2]. In 1964 the Danes and Finns merged as St. Francis Lutheran [1].

title: The Last Steam Train to the Cliff
place: Former steam depot, 48th Ave and Point Lobos Ave
hook: Until 1905, San Franciscans rode a little steam train along the cliffs of Lands End to a depot at 48th Avenue. Thomas Edison's cameramen filmed it.
story: The Ferries and Cliff House steam line ran from California Street and Central Avenue (now Presidio Avenue) out California Street to 33rd Avenue, then swung north along the cliffs above the Golden Gate to a terminus above the Cliff House at 48th Avenue and Point Lobos [1]. It was built by the Powell Street cable railway to give it a route to the beach. Sources disagree on its opening, giving both 1886 and 1888 [1]. Its double-ended locomotives needed no turntables, and the route passed through two tunnels [1]. On January 11, 1902, a camera crew from Thomas Edison's company filmed the train on the coast [1]. From the depot, visitors walked downhill past souvenir stands to the Cliff House and Sutro Baths [2]. The last steam trains ran on May 17, 1905, the last steam-powered streetcar line in the city, when United Railroads rebuilt the route for electric streetcars [1][3]. The cliffs had the final word: after a landslide on February 7, 1925, the tracks along Lands End were abandoned [1].

title: The warehouse the 1906 fire skipped
place: Baker & Hamilton Building, 601 Townsend Street (Seventh and Townsend)
hook: It was built for a hardware firm founded by two of the railroad's Big Four. In 1906 the fire came down Townsend Street, then turned away.
story: The brick warehouse at Seventh and Townsend was built in 1904-05 for the Pacific Hardware and Steel Company. Mark Hopkins and Collis P. Huntington had founded the firm in Sacramento in the 1850s [1]. Sutton & Weeks designed it. Years later Charles Peter Weeks, working with W.P. Day, designed the Mark Hopkins and Huntington hotels on Nob Hill [1]. In April 1906 the fire came down Townsend Street, turned north and burned only the east side of Seventh. The warehouse survived, and the rebuilding boom made the company one of the biggest steel and hardware wholesalers in the West [1]. The new warehouse district grew up around it [1][2]. In 1918 the firm merged with Baker & Hamilton, a Gold Rush hardware house. Baker & Hamilton had built the 'Sweepstake' wooden-wheel plow, the first made on a large scale, and later the steel 'Eureka' [1][2]. Rail cars loaded along Townsend and wagons along King [1]. The business left in 1981 [1]. In 2000-01 the building was turned into offices, later used by Macromedia and then Adobe [1][3]. The rooftop sign still reads 'BAKER HAMILTON, SINCE 1849' [1].

title: Where the Southern Pacific turned its engines
place: Former Southern Pacific Mission Bay yard, rail crossing on 16th Street near Third
hook: The Southern Pacific once turned its locomotives on a roundhouse here. The last tracks across 16th Street survived until the children's hospital was nearly finished.
story: By 1938, an aerial photograph shows Mission Bay as largely a Southern Pacific railyard [1]. The yard's heart was a roundhouse, where engines could be switched from one track to another. A 1905 Sanborn map and a 1938 aerial photo put it near Mariposa and Third (then Kentucky) Street; photo captions on another page place it near Mariposa and Minnesota [1][2][3]. The 1905 Sanborn map shows it with a surprising amount of Mission Bay still under water nearby [2]. The roundhouse's workers often came from the Italian neighborhood on Potrero Hill. A 1942 photograph of the roundhouse crew shows Frank I. Alioto in the center of the second row [2]. Around 1943, Library of Congress photographer Ann Rosener photographed women taking over car and maintenance work in the company's San Francisco yards [2]. Aerial film from 1963 still shows the railyards spread across the flats, the roundhouse tracks running amid dozens of others [2]. In 2014, as the new UCSF Children's Hospital was finished, a few rails still crossed 16th Street toward the old roundhouse site. They are gone now [2]. Sources differ on the hospital's exact position: one says it stands on the roundhouse site, another that the roundhouse lay just west of it [1][2].

title: 'How Much Money Is in It for Us?'
place: 20th Avenue, route of the first Parkside streetcar (at Quintara Street)
hook: To get a streetcar out to its sand-dune suburb, the Parkside Realty Company paid Boss Abe Ruef $15,000 in cash, one month after the earthquake.
story: In 1905 a syndicate led by banker William H. Crocker quietly bought about 100 blocks of dunes south of Golden Gate Park and formed the Parkside Realty Company [2]. The company planned to sell to working families, and they could not get downtown without a streetcar, so everything hung on one [1]. Company president J.E. Green took the mayor and supervisors on a tour of the tract, then gave them lunch, speeches and plenty of wine. Supervisor Charles Boxton stood up and asked, 'How much money is in it for us?' [1][2]. The company got the message. Working through realtor Gus Umbsen, it agreed to 'employ' political boss Abe Ruef as its attorney for two years at $30,000. A month after the April 1906 earthquake, with the directors keen to sell to the newly homeless, Umbsen paid Ruef half of that in cash. The books recorded it as a payment for lots [1]. The Parkside deal was one of the first scandals the graft prosecutors uncovered. Company officers testified against Ruef in exchange for immunity, but the jury deadlocked 6 to 6 [1][2]. Meanwhile more than 1,000 Sunset property owners petitioned for the line whatever the scandal. A reform board granted the franchise in October 1907, and by mid-1908 streetcars ran south on 20th Avenue from Lincoln Way [1][2].

title: 'Only Caucasians' at Presidio Terrace
place: Presidio Terrace, off Arguello Blvd
hook: San Francisco's first master-planned enclave sold electric streetlights, buried wires and a promise in print that no one who wasn't white could live there.
story: In 1905, Baldwin & Howell began building Presidio Terrace off Arguello Boulevard. It had 36 large lots around one private oval street, with electric streetlights, underground utilities and roads laid out for cars, all rare at the time [1][2]. After the 1906 fire, well-off families rebuilt here, in houses designed by leading architects including George Applegarth, Albert Farr and Julia Morgan [1]. The developer's 1906 advertisement made its main selling point plain: 'There is only one spot in San Francisco where only Caucasians are permitted to buy or lease real estate or where they may reside. That place is Presidio Terrace.' Its headline read 'The Japs Have Invaded The Western Addition' [3]. That was the same year the school board ordered Asian children segregated [3]. The builder Fernando Nelson bought a double lot in 1909 and built No. 30 there in 1910 [4]. Rules like this were declared unenforceable nationwide in 1948, when the Supreme Court decided Shelley v. Kraemer [3]. The gate still stands at the entrance on Arguello [3].

title: A Full Reservoir, Cut Off From the Fire
place: University Mound Reservoir, where the Crystal Springs pipeline ended (University and Bacon streets)
hook: In 1906 the University Mound reservoir came through the earthquake almost unharmed. But the pipes leading out were cut, and its water couldn't reach the fire.
story:
In the 1880s the Spring Valley Water Company laid a 44-inch wrought-iron pipe from Crystal Springs Reservoir in San Mateo County to its new reservoir on University Mound [1]. On April 18, 1906, the earthquake broke the system in two places at once. To the south, the big pipe crossed three swamps on wooden bridges built on piles between San Bruno and San Francisco. The shaking threw sections of it four or five feet to the east and west [1]. Chief engineer Hermann Schussler later marvelled at one 800-foot length lying twisted into a 'snake-like' curve, yet showing hardly a strained seam [1].

On May 26, 1906, a reconstruction subcommittee reported that the reservoirs themselves had come through largely unharmed. But the mains leading out of College Hill and University Mound were 'completely severed', and the committee believed every serious break was in made ground. The breaks rapidly wasted the water stored in the city's reservoirs, and the districts where the main fires started were cut off completely [2]. Repair crews had to wait about ten days for scarce lumber. When it came, they rebuilt the pipe bridges with planks and flexible joints braced with wire cables made on the spot. At 7:10 a.m. on May 16, Crystal Springs water began flowing into University Mound again [1].

title: A Mortar Battery Split in Two
place: Mortar battery (Batteries Livingston and Springer), east side of Fort Miley
hook: Sixteen squat mortars were dug in here to guard the Golden Gate. By 1906 the pits were so crowded the Army pulled half of them out.
story: On November 27, 1899, work began at the new Point Lobos reservation on a battery for sixteen 12-inch mortars [1]. Nearby, Battery Chester's big rifles covered all three channels into the Golden Gate [1]. In 1900 the post was renamed Fort Miley, after Lieutenant Colonel John D. Miley, who had died in Manila the year before [1]. The state military museum's history says the mortars were finished in 1902 [2]. In December 1904 the Army named the battery for Colonel LaRhett Livingston of the 3rd Artillery, a Civil War veteran who had died in 1903 [2]. The four pits were too cramped for four mortars each. In 1906 the two forward guns in each pit were taken out and the battery was divided. The southern pits became Battery Anton Springer [2]. Captain Springer of the 1st Infantry had been killed in action near Lipa in the Philippines in 1901 [2]. So the fort and one of its batteries both carry the names of men who died in America's war in the Philippines. A fourth battery, Call, followed in 1914 [2]. The concrete remains of these early batteries still edge the hospital grounds [1].

title: A Mushroom City on the Park Lawns
place: Speedway Meadow, Golden Gate Park
hook: In April 1906 the city's grandest playground became its biggest bedroom, where a banker might sleep on the grass beside a laborer.
story: By noon on April 18, 1906, the wounded from Mechanics' Pavilion were being carried to Golden Gate Park as the 'Ham and Egg' fire spread [1]. The next morning, wrote editor Charles Sedgwick, 'the far-sighted ones' headed for the park: mothers with babies, old maids with dogs and parrots, children with toys and bags of popcorn, men with bedding and grub [2]. A 1906 account called the park 'the mecca of the destitute', a 'vast mushroom city' where disaster 'wiped out all social, financial and racial distinctions'. The grass was the only bed for many, the bread lines at the parks were longer even than the four-block queue at Fillmore and Turk, and one guest who fled the Palace Hotel paid $25 for a wagon to 'the Casino near Golden Gate Park' [3]. The long, straight Speedway Meadow, once a .9-mile road for racing horses, was used as a camp for a while [4]. The quake also twisted the Sweeney Observatory on Strawberry Hill beyond repair. By the new year the park camps had closed [4].

title: A Palace Post Office, Six Months Old
place: U.S. Post Office and Courthouse, Seventh and Mission streets
hook: San Francisco's lavish new post office had been open barely six months when the earthquake hit. Its staff saved it with wet sandbags and fire hoses.
story: Critics grumbled when the government chose Seventh and Mission, more than a mile from the business district in a working-class Irish and German neighborhood, for its new courthouse and post office [2]. It opened in 1905 to acclaim as "a post office that's a palace," finished in Italian and North African marble by artisans brought over from Italy [1][2]. Hardly six months later, on April 18, 1906, the earthquake threw walls into the middle of rooms. "In the main corridors the marble was split and cracked," said Burke, the assistant to the postmaster, "while the mosaics were shattered and had come rattling down upon the floor" [3]. Then came the fire. Employees on duty moved valuable records into the vaults, plugged the oil lines, rigged fire hoses and piled wet sandbags against the inner doors, and the flames were held to a few rooms [1]. With the Mint, it was one of the only buildings south of Market to survive [2]. Because of that stand, federal court records dating back to the 1850s still exist [1]. Repairs took until 1910, and the building now houses the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit [1][2].

title: A Teachers' College Among the Orphanage Ruins
place: Former Teachers College campus, Haight Street between Laguna and Buchanan
hook: After the 1906 earthquake, San Francisco State's forerunner set up in the damaged grounds of the West Coast's first orphanage and stayed for almost fifty years.
story: The block bounded by Haight, Laguna, Buchanan and Hermann Streets once belonged to the Protestant Orphan Asylum, founded in 1851 as the first orphanage on the West Coast [1]. Hayes Valley did not burn in 1906, but the earthquake badly damaged the asylum's masonry building [1]. The San Francisco State Normal School, founded on Nob Hill in 1899, spent a short time in Oakland and then moved into the orphanage's surviving outbuildings [1][2]. It was led by Frederic Burk, president until his death in 1924. Undeterred by what the nomination calls 'old, barren-looking' facilities, he set admission standards equal to the University of California's and introduced seminar classes and practice teaching [1]. State Architect George B. McDougall worked with Burk on a master plan, and between 1924 and 1935 the Spanish Colonial Revival campus of Richardson Hall, Woods Hall and the WPA-built Woods Hall Annex went up [1]. The Depression stopped the rest of the plan. In 1938 students protested the crumbling 'temporary' buildings, one of San Francisco State's earliest protests [1]. The college, renamed San Francisco State Teachers College in 1921, moved to Lake Merced in 1953-54, and UC Extension used the campus until 2003 [2]. The three surviving halls became city landmarks in 2007 [3].

title: A flag, soda siphons and a saved hilltop
place: House of the Flag, 1652-1656 Taylor Street
hook: As the 1906 fire climbed Russian Hill, a man dipped his biggest flag at the soldiers below. They ran up the hill and fought with seltzer bottles.
story: This shingled house was built in two stages: the lower part in 1864 for the civil engineer Angus McPherson, the upper part in 1903 for Eli T. Shepherd, a lawyer and former U.S. consul in China [2]. Neighbourhood legend says a sea captain built it with Georgia pine brought around the Horn [1]. In April 1906, with the fire closing in, the publisher Edward A. Dakin dipped his largest flag in salute before leaving the house [2]. NoeHill says the flag was raised and lowered three times. That caught the eye of a company of soldiers below, who charged up the hill [1]. They found a bathtub full of water, sand from a mansion being built nearby, and soda-water siphons to squirt into places they couldn't reach [1][2]. A photo caption of the day claimed the flag flew through the whole fire, but that is not what happened [1]. The house and its neighbours survived as an island in the burned city [2]. Two weeks after the fire, Frank "Pop" Demerest moved into a cistern on his family's lot at Broadway and Florence. As the "Hermit of Russian Hill" he offered cheap quarters to generations of bohemians; his compound survived until the mid-1950s [2].

title: A house jacked up twelve feet
place: Goodman Building (St. Beryl Hotel), 1117 Geary Street between Van Ness and Franklin
hook: Seven weeks after the fire, a ladies' tailor filed plans to lift his 1869 house into the air and slide five shops underneath.
story:
In 1869 Joseph Emeric, a French immigrant who had become a Contra Costa landowner and a wine importer, built a residence on the south side of Geary between Van Ness and Franklin. The arched window heads still carry the letter 'E' [1]. His son Henry, a state assemblyman, served as State Fish Commissioner in the 1890s [1]. After Henry's death his daughter sold the building to Abraham and Sarah Goodman, New Yorkers who ran a ladies' tailoring business. The Register nomination dates the sale to 28 December 1900; the city landmark summary says 1899 [1][2].

The fire of 1906 destroyed everything east of the building, from Van Ness to the waterfront [1]. On 6 June 1906 Goodman applied for a permit to raise the two-storey frame building 12 feet and put five stores underneath. His architect, Conrad Meussdorffer, turned the upper floors into a hotel and added a mansard fourth floor as a photographer's studio for H. Pierre Smith [1]. The St. Beryl Hotel was named after Beryl Goodfriend, its first proprietress. The couple's son Mervin put the cost at about $50,000. It was one small answer to the housing shortage after the fire [1].

title: A poet starts over on Macondray Lane
place: 17 Macondray Lane
hook: The fire of 1906 destroyed 3,000 of her books, letters from Mark Twain and her unfinished memoir. California's future poet laureate rebuilt her life a few steps away.
story: Ina Coolbrith had been one of the Overland Monthly's 'Golden Gate Trinity' with Bret Harte and Charles Warren Stoddard. She was California's first public librarian and ran a literary salon [1]. On the morning of April 18, 1906, she left her house on Taylor Street carrying a pet cat, expecting to return. Her boarder and her companion saved only another cat, a few bundles of letters and her scrapbook [2]. Joaquin Miller crossed the bay to help rescue her treasures, but soldiers turned him back. The fire consumed her 3,000 books, signed first editions, paintings by William Keith, letters from Whittier and Mark Twain, and a nearly finished manuscript that was part memoir and part literary history of early California. She never wrote it again [2]. From 1907 to 1909 she lived at 17 Macondray Lane, in the woodsy enclave that had lost much of its housing to the fire [1][3]. Friends raised money for a new home: Twain sent signed photographs to sell, and Gertrude Atherton made up the shortfall from her own pocket [2]. In 1915 Coolbrith was named California's first poet laureate [2].

title: A queen's kroner and a quake hospital
place: St. Francis Lutheran Church (built as St. Ansgar), 152 Church Street
hook: San Francisco's Danes wrote to their queen for help building a church. When the earthquake struck, its half-finished hall became a Red Cross hospital.
story: Around 1900, San Francisco's Danish community decided it was big enough for a church of its own. For years, Lutheran pastors had been sent up from Fresno to lead services. So the congregation wrote to Queen Louise of Denmark, and she sent 500 kroner, which started the building fund [1]. The cornerstone of St. Ansgar Church on Church Street, between Market and Duboce, was laid on September 17, 1905 [2]. The building was brick over a wooden frame, in a Danish Gothic style. By spring 1906 the ground-floor hall was in use, with the sanctuary above still unfinished [1]. Then came April 18. The earthquake damaged the sanctuary, but the main floor held, and the Red Cross used it as a hospital and shelter for the injured and homeless [1]. The neighbourhood around it was then mostly Scandinavian and German. For years it supported five Lutheran churches, worshipping in Norwegian, Danish, Swedish, Finnish and German [1]. As English replaced the old languages, the congregations merged. In 1964 the Danish and Finnish churches united as St. Francis Lutheran, a name the city's landmark report says no other Lutheran church in the world uses [1].

title: A rare tap after the earthquake
place: Dixon building, 1400 18th Street at Missouri (now Christopher's Books)
hook: After the 1906 earthquake, police had to hold back the crowd at one backyard gate on 18th Street, because the Dixons had running water.
story:
In the 1890s residents asked City Hall for a reservoir, a two-cow limit and a grander name, "Southern Heights." According to the Potrero Hill Archives Project, it took 30 years for water service to reach the neighbourhood [1]. The hill had wells and springs; one 1890 well near Connecticut and 20th was 300 feet deep. Thorburn Adams recalled that the spring and well beside his family's house at 18th and Pennsylvania supplied many 1906 refugees [2].

Katherine Dixon had married James Dixon, an Irish Hill man who worked at Pacific Rolling Mills, in 1883. The couple bought several properties. A 1902 application for water service at their lot at 1400 18th Street noted "No horse here now." In 1905 they put up the three-story building that stands on the corner today [1].

It was one of the few houses on the hill with piped water. After the earthquake and fire of April 1906, so many people gathered at the Dixons' backyard gate for water that police were called to control the crowd [1]. From 1919 to 1928 the ground floor was a branch of Wulzen's Pharmacy. Christopher's Books opened there in 1991 [1].

title: A refuge the earthquake built
place: Laguna Honda Hospital campus, where the Relief Home buildings and Clarendon Hall stood
hook: After 1906 the city's poorhouse became the Relief Home for people the earthquake left homeless. The hall built beside it stood for almost a century.
story: The 1906 earthquake and fire turned the Almshouse on the western slope of Twin Peaks into something new. It took in thousands of displaced San Franciscans, gathering earthquake victims from refugee camps scattered across the city, and became known as the Relief Home. A new pavilion-style building went up, able to hold 1,000 people [1]. In 1910 the city added Clarendon Hall. It housed 250 people and was the first building there meant specifically for long-term medical care [1]. Charles Wollenberg ran the institution from 1907 to 1943. His son Harold, born in 1906, remembered that "it was all forest around the Relief Home, planted by Adolph Sutro" [2]. Clarendon Hall came down in 2008 to make room for new buildings able to withstand a far stronger earthquake [1]. Victoria Sweet, a doctor at the hospital, watched it go. Workmen first stripped out windows, faucets, sinks, copper pipe and clay tiles. Then a machine she compared to a metal praying mantis worked its way around the century-old Edwardian building, taking bites out of the tiled roof. By the end of the day, she wrote, Clarendon Hall was rubble [3].

title: A tent city in Bernal Park
place: Bernal Park refugee camp (today's Precita Park), east end
hook: After the 1906 fire, the park at the foot of Bernal Hill filled with refugees. When it closed, many took their homes with them.
story:
After the earthquake and fire of April 1906, refugee camps went up in parks all over the city. In this neighbourhood they included Precita Park, then called Bernal Park, and Dolores Park [1]. A month after the disaster, the Chronicle reported that thousands of people were still camped at the Bernal Park relief station [2]. As winter came on, union carpenters built about 5,600 wooden cottages to Army designs. Residents paid a small rent and lived under camp rules [1][3].

The camp changed the neighbourhood. Factory hands, carpenters and teamsters who had been burned out of South of Market and the Mission found cheap lots on Bernal. A relief cottage hauled out of the camp made "a good instant starter home" [4]. By summer 1907 tenants had to buy their cottages and move them onto private lots, or be evicted [3]. A 1907 photograph shows the shacks leaving Bernal Park, and some were dragged straight up the hill [1][4].

title: Brooms and blankets on 20th Street
place: 20th Street near Guerrero (the 1906 fire line)
hook: After days of burning, the great fire of 1906 was stopped on 20th Street, mostly by neighbours with brooms, knapsacks and one working hydrant.
story:
In 1906 the fire burned its way down Valencia Street into the Mission. Young DeWitt Baldwin looked down Valencia from his family's wagon and saw the fire 'bursting on both sides meeting each other on the street' [1]. On April 21 it was finally stopped at 20th and Dolores. The work was done by about 3,000 volunteers and a few firemen, using knapsacks, brooms and a little water from a hydrant that still worked at 20th and Church [2].

With some 300 breaks in the city's mains, most hydrants were dry. This one kept flowing, probably because it drew on an underground spring. About 300 residents hauled fire engines up the 20th Street hill themselves, a climb too steep for the horses [3]. Historian Art Peterson credits that effort with saving a good piece of the Mission [3]. The 'little hydrant that could' sits a block west, at Church Street. It gets a coat of gold paint every April 18. The disaster also pushed City Engineer Marsden Mason to design the high-pressure auxiliary water system that San Francisco still relies on [3].

title: Camp 24: green cottages in a square
place: Columbia Square refugee camp site (today Victoria Manalo Draves Park), Folsom Street between Sixth and Seventh
hook: With South of Market burned flat, one small park became a village of 1,500 refugees living in rows of green two-room cottages.
story: The 1906 earthquake and fire destroyed most of South of Market's housing and left thousands of its residents homeless [1]. Many fled to makeshift camps in the unburned Mission and Potrero districts [1]. After the San Francisco Relief and Red Cross Funds Corporation was incorporated on July 20, 1906, it hired union carpenters to build thousands of small cottages before the rains came [1]. Open land was scarce in the district, so South of Market had just two official camps: South Park, Camp No. 28, and Columbia Square, Camp No. 24, a small park on the block bounded by Folsom, Sixth, Harrison and Seventh streets [1]. On September 29, 1906, Columbia Square became the second camp in the city to switch from tents to cottages. It housed 1,500 people in 605 two-room and 40 three-room cottages [1]. The cottages had cedar-shingle roofs, fir floors and redwood walls, and were painted green to blend into the parks [2]. When the camps began closing in August 1907, refugees hauled their cottages away to private lots, often joining two or more into a bigger house [2]. Only a handful are known to survive [2]. The square later became the site of the Bessie Carmichael School, and today it is Victoria Manalo Draves Park [3].

title: Camp No. 16: Cottages You Could Keep
place: Jefferson Square (Camp No. 16)
hook: The tents in Jefferson Square gave way to rows of little redwood cottages. Families who paid their rent could haul them away and keep them.
story: Jefferson Square became official Camp No. 16 on June 2, 1906. That month it held as many as 2,000 people [1]. With the rainy season coming, the relief corporation decided to replace the tents with separate wooden cottages. Construction began in the camps on September 10, 1906 [1]. Union carpenters built them in standard sizes, the smallest 10 by 14 feet, and 5,610 went up across the city [2]. Planners later described Camp No. 16 as a large camp holding 1,710 people in these mass-produced cottages [3]. The tents had been free, but the cottages were not. Relief officials charged a small rent, arguing that giving everything away "killed the self-respect of the efficient class" [1]. The lease worked as a purchase. A tenant who paid rent up to August 1, 1907 owned the cottage, but had to move it out of the square at their own expense [1]. The camp closed on August 23, 1907 [1]. Many cottages were dragged off on wagons to private lots, and a few are still standing somewhere in the city [2].

title: Camp No. 22: Tents on the Hill
place: Alamo Square (Hayes Street side)
hook: Alamo Square became an official refugee camp, with its tents propped up on wooden legs so they stood level on the slope.
story: In the first days after the fire, refugees camped wherever they found open ground, and Alamo Square was one of those places [2]. In July 1906 the Army took it over as an official camp, No. 22 [1]. The Relief Survey's records say it opened on July 9, 1906, and was fullest on October 1, with 857 people. It closed on March 13, 1907 [1]. The hill was a problem, because a tent pitched on a slope isn't much of a bed. A photograph shows the camp's answer: the tents were set on wooden undercarriages that held them level [3]. That summer tents in the official camps were given floors, and buildings with latrines, wash-houses and hot and cold running water went up [1]. Alamo Square was one of several camps nearby. Duboce Park, a few blocks south, was Camp No. 19, with up to 650 people until February 1907 [1][2]. Relief District IV, which covered the neighbourhood north of Market, housed 10,737 refugees in all [2].
