title: Two Cable Cars and a Horsecar, Upstairs
place: Lower Great Highway near Moraga Street (private home; exact address withheld)
hook: From the street it looks like an ordinary beach house. Upstairs, passenger benches, slatted ceilings and a sliding horsecar door survive from Carville.
story: Most of Carville's streetcar houses vanished. Some were shingled over, some burned, some were torn down. One is known to survive, on the Lower Great Highway near Moraga Street [1][2]. It was built for Minnie Collins, a notary public and photojournalist, out of two streetcars and a horse car [2]. Researcher James Heisterkamp later found permits showing that she had the cars set on a frame in 1908, and that they were probably raised to make a second story in 1921 [1]. The San Francisco News profiled Mrs. Collins and her house in 1947 [1]. Heisterkamp, a San Francisco State student, tracked the house down in 1994. He walked 47th Avenue, 48th Avenue and the Great Highway asking strangers about cable cars, until a young man pushing a bicycle pointed him to the house next door [1]. Inside, the front door opens into a room made of two cable cars placed side by side with their inner walls taken out. One wall still has the cars' wooden benches under the original tongue-and-groove ceiling. The bedroom and bath fill an intact horse car, with a sliding panel door between them [1]. Filmmaker Scott Anderson bought the house in the 1990s and told his tenant not to put any new nails in the walls [1].

title: 'Julius Caesar' Today at the Gem
place: Former Gem Theatre, 2542 San Bruno Avenue
hook: When the Portola was still mostly cattle and greenhouses, a storefront picture house on San Bruno Avenue hung out the bunting for 'Julius Caesar'.
story: The Portola was still mostly farmland in the early 1900s. Cattle grazed on its hills and its few streets were unpaved. Along San Bruno Avenue, though, a line of businesses was growing, and their owners often lived upstairs [1]. One of them was the Gem Theatre at 2542 San Bruno Avenue, between Felton and Burrows. A photograph from about 1909 shows it decorated with flags and bunting, with a sign that reads 'Special To-Day Julius Caesar' and children waiting at the door [2]. The collection that holds the photograph dates the Gem to 1909-1910, and notes that the building was still standing in 2018 [2]. A generation later the district had grown enough to support a bigger house, the Avenue Theatre, a block south, where children paid a dime for Saturday matinees in the 1920s [3].

title: A Nob Hill Doorway Beside a Lake
place: Portals of the Past, Lloyd Lake
hook: Six marble columns on the edge of Lloyd Lake are all that survived of a railroad boss's Nob Hill mansion.
story: Alban N. Towne, longtime president and general manager of the Southern Pacific, built his mansion at 1101 California Street in 1891 to designs by Arthur Page Brown. He enjoyed it only briefly, dying of a heart attack in 1895; his widow Caroline stayed on until the fire of 1906 consumed everything but the marble portico [1][2]. Arnold Genthe photographed the empty doorway by moonlight, later writing that the picture 'brought out its classic beauty', and Willard Worden's images of it framing the ruined City Hall helped make it an icon [1][3]. In 1909 Caroline Towne donated the portico in her husband's memory. Park historian Christopher Pollock credits Senator James D. Phelan with leading the move and architect Edgar A. Mathews with choosing the site [1]. The nickname came from a line found by poet Charles Kellogg Field: 'This is the portal of the past — from now on, once more forward' [1]. Set at the water's edge, it works like the follies of English landscape gardens: a ruin placed to be reflected in a lake [2].

title: Dynamite under cover of the Fourth
place: Gray Brothers quarry, east face of Telegraph Hill near Lombard & Montgomery
hook: Court orders couldn't stop the Gray Brothers blasting Telegraph Hill away. So in 1909 they timed the dynamite to the holiday fireworks.
story: For about twenty years George and Harry Gray blasted and crushed rock from the east face of Telegraph Hill for ship ballast and roadbeds. Their explosions undermined and destroyed houses on Vallejo, Green, Union, Calhoun, Montgomery and Greenwich streets [1]. Irish and Italian residents sometimes answered with barrages of rocks. The brothers ignored court orders or paid their way around them [2]. A campaign led by Alice Griffith and the Telegraph Hill Neighborhood Association got blasting permits revoked in 1903, but the quarry kept going [2]. In 1909, despite another court order, the Grays set off a blast on the Fourth of July, timed to be drowned out by the Presidio's celebration guns (or the fireworks, in another telling). Falling rock gave them away, and angry neighbours chased the crew off [1][2]. The end came from inside the business. Sicilian quarry worker Joseph Lococo, unpaid for months, shot and killed George Gray. Sources date it to 1914 or 1915, and one says the sum owed was just $17.50 [1][2]. Lococo was acquitted and the blasting stopped. The raw cliffs it left behind are still sending rock slides down on Lombard Street and Broadway [1].

title: Fire in the Keepers' Gothic House
place: Light station keepers' quarters, Hillcrest Rd
hook: A keeper heard timbers crackling above his kitchen. A passing Navy tug blew its whistle, and the island's sailor boys came running.
story:
Uphill from the lighthouse stands a Victorian Gothic house with steep cross-gables and a sweeping veranda. It was built as a duplex for the keeper's and assistant keeper's families, and it is one of only two such keepers' houses left in California [1]. On the afternoon of 17 July 1909, Assistant Keeper John Kofod was sitting in his kitchen when he heard burning timber and saw the roof and eaves above him on fire [2]. He alerted his wife and daughter and Keeper Herbert Luff's family downstairs. Aboard the approaching Navy tug Vigilant, Captain Lockyer saw the flames and sounded his whistle, which brought men running from the Naval Training Station. They dragged a hose from the tug's engines up the hill and fought the fire for an hour. The roof and several upper rooms were lost [2].

The house carried on. Kofod's daughter Anna married Walter Fanning, a radioman at the island's naval station, and their son was born in the dwelling [2]. On New Year's Eve, Kofod would take his grandchildren down to give three blasts on the fog whistle. The passing ferries answered [2]. Today a senior Coast Guard officer lives in the house [1].

title: How Irving, Judah, Kirkham and Lawton Won
place: Irving Street at 9th Avenue
hook: Why do four un-Spanish names break the alphabet of Spanish explorers south of the park? Blame a furious 1909 revolt over 'Spanish Town.'
story: Until 1909 the streets south of the park had letters: H, I, J, K, L and on. A commission appointed by Mayor Taylor was asked to end the city's street-name confusion, and the Post Office estimated that 500 letters a day went astray [1]. It proposed giving every numbered avenue and lettered street in the Richmond and Sunset an alphabetical Spanish name. First Avenue would become Arguello, Third Avenue Coronado, and so on [1][2]. On November 15 the supervisors voted 12 to 5 in favour, and the western districts erupted. Speakers warned that the avenues would be mocked as 'Spanish Town,' and the Richmond Banner denounced a 'miserable surrender of American names' [1]. After mass protest the commission gave the avenues their numbers back. The Sunset Improvement Club then asked for the names of Americans 'that reflect glory and luster upon our civilization' [1]. H Street became Lincoln Way. I, J, K and L became Irving (after Washington Irving), Judah (after railroad engineer Theodore Judah), and Kirkham and Lawton (both army generals). Irving and Judah were borrowed from a list meant for Bayview [1][2]. After L the fight ran out, and Moraga, Noriega and Ortega stayed Spanish [2].

title: Maybeck's Tudor wedding gift, braced for quakes
place: Roos House, 3500 Jackson Street at Locust Street
hook: Three years after 1906, a theatre magnate gave his daughter a half-timbered dream house, secretly braced with piles and bolts. A later earthquake cost it its garden.
story:
In 1909, nineteen-year-old Elizabeth Meyerfeld married Leon Roos of the Roos Brothers clothing firm. Her father Morris Meyerfeld, a partner in the Orpheum theatre circuit, asked Bernard Maybeck to design a house for the couple as a wedding present [1][2]. Elizabeth had travelled Europe with her father looking for talent, and she wanted something theatrical. Maybeck mixed Tudor half-timbering with Gothic details. At about 9,000 square feet it is the largest house he designed for a San Francisco client [1][2].

The house was built just three years after the 1906 earthquake and fire. Maybeck and Leon Roos cared a great deal about seismic safety. It stands on wooden piles driven into the hillside, unusual for a house. Maybeck's engineer, Herman Kower, worked out the loads on the basement columns and showed exactly how they were to be bolted to the foundation and tied to the floor above. The decoration hides all of this [2].

Earthquakes shaped the house again eight decades later. After the 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake, the back of the lot, once Maybeck's formal vegetable garden, was sold to pay for repairs [2]. When the house joined the National Register in 2009, its owner was Jane Roos LeRoux [2].

title: Nine Children Above the Grocery
place: 118 Sagamore St (Pesce's Market)
hook: Paul and Marie Pesce left Genoa in 1903, opened a grocery across from the train station in 1909, and raised nine children in the flat upstairs.
story: Ocean View's early farmers were mostly Italian immigrants from Genoa, working vegetable plots in the valleys below Merced Heights [2]. Paul and Marie Pesce came to San Francisco from Genoa in 1903, and in 1909 opened a grocery at 118 Sagamore Street, just across from the Southern Pacific station, the centre of a small community still isolated from the rest of the city [1]. The family lived in the flat over the store, where they raised all nine of their children, and every one of them worked in the shop at some point [1]. It sat at the old village crossroads; a 1926 city photograph of Sagamore shows a meat market, a couple of barber shops and 'Blue Ribbon' ice cream signs nearby [3]. Pesce's outlasted the station, the plaza fountain and the steam trains. When the OMI News profiled it in 1977, son Elmer, 68, still made the deliveries, bought the produce and lived upstairs, and a third-generation Pesce studying at San Francisco State said she learned more in the store than at school: 'This is life' [1]. Known for large Italian sandwiches and gooey pastries at the checkout, Pesce's Market closed in the 1980s [1].

title: Operators Who Knew Every Name
place: Chinese Telephone Exchange, 743 Washington Street
hook: Callers never gave a number. They asked for a person by name, and the operators, who memorised about 1,500 of them, put them straight through.
story: The pagoda at 743 Washington Street was built in 1909 as the second Chinese Telephone Exchange on the site [1]. Sources disagree about when Chinatown's phone service began, giving 1887 or 1898 [2][3]. What made it famous was the switchboard. Callers asked for people, not numbers. In 1901 the Examiner marvelled that the operators had nearly 1,500 names to remember, along with where each person lived, and warned that the work 'would drive an American operator insane' [1]. The first operators were men. Women became the chief operators in 1906, and the Examiner claimed they were preferred for their good tempers [2]. Operators had to handle the district's many languages and dialects, and more than 13,000 calls a day. The switchboard doubled as a job exchange: employers phoned in work and the operators knew whom to connect [2]. In 1943 the exchange's thirty workers joined the Telephone Traffic Employees Organization Local 120, fought their seven-day schedule and won $5,000 in back pay and overtime [2]. Dial phones ended the exchange in the 1940s [2]. Long before, the site had housed Sam Brannan's California Star, San Francisco's first newspaper [1].

title: Palou Avenue, because Paine was an 'infidel'
place: All Hallows Church, 1715 Oakdale Ave (by Palou Ave)
hook: Palou Avenue was meant to honour Thomas Paine. Then the parish priest of All Hallows stood up and objected.
story: In 1909 San Francisco set out to end decades of misdelivered mail by renaming the Bayview's numbered "avenues, South" [1]. The Street Names Commission picked a roster of American heroes, arranged alphabetically, and proposed Thomas Paine for Sixteenth Avenue South [1][2]. Father O'Sullivan of All Hallows parish exploded. "He was an infidel, and in South San Francisco we are all Christians," the Examiner quoted him [1]. A local improvement club suggested hiding Paine's name on some "out-of-the-way avenue on the hillside where nobody lived"; the commission refused to use it at all [1]. The priests also vetoed Belfast and Cromwell as insults to Irish Catholics, who O'Sullivan said made up three-quarters of the district, and objected to Wallace, a "Scotch hero" [1][2]. He vowed locals would keep using the old numbers anyway. At the final vote on 21 December 1909, the commission placated him: Sixteenth Avenue became Palou, after the Franciscan padre, while Carroll (for the only Catholic signer of the Declaration of Independence) and Bancroft replaced Cromwell and Belfast [1]. Those names, from Arthur to Yosemite, are still on the street signs [2].

title: Peaches, monastery stones and the waiting dead
place: Haslett Warehouse, 680 Beach St at Hyde
hook: Built to store canned fruit, this brick warehouse on Beach Street later held a Spanish monastery in numbered pieces and the dead awaiting passage home to China.
story: The California Fruit Canners Association, whose largest peach cannery stood across the street [3], commissioned this warehouse at the same time as the Cannery. It went up in 1907–1909 to designs by William S. Mooser Jr. [1]. Until 1936, peaches, asparagus, cherries and apricots came from the interior valleys by riverboat and ferry. Once canned, they were shuttled across the street on a short railroad line to be stored here. From 1916, after a merger created the California Packing Company, they carried the Del Monte label [1]. By 1936 canning had moved to the East Bay, and in 1948 the Haslett Warehouse Company bought the building [1]. Over the years it sheltered strange cargo. Some 10,000 stones of Santa María de Óvila, a Spanish monastery bought by William Randolph Hearst for a castle he never built, reached San Francisco in 1931 on eleven freighters and were stored here, running up fees of $15,000 a year [2]. (The landmark report calls it Italian and dates its stay 1930–1943 [1].) Shortly after the Second World War it served as a mortuary. The bodies of Chinese dead bound for burial in their homeland rested here until brokers decided there was a full cargo for China [1]. In 1963 the state bought the building for a railroad museum that never opened [1].

title: The Arctic Sloop Parked on the Sand
place: Site of the Gjøa and Amundsen monument, north of the Beach Chalet
hook: The first ship ever to sail the Northwest Passage spent 63 years in Golden Gate Park, guarded by a live-in caretaker and a barking seal.
story: Roald Amundsen's 69-foot sloop Gjøa finished the first voyage through the Northwest Passage in San Francisco in October 1906. Amundsen, to the dismay of the Norwegian community planning a grand welcome, slipped into the Bay Area by train ahead of his boat [1]. The Gjøa then languished at Mare Island until the Norwegian consul asked the Park Commission to take her [1]. On July 6, 1909, some 5,000 people watched her dragged by cables up onto Ocean Beach; some hung wet stockings on the cables. The Call predicted she would stand 'until her mighty timbers rot. That will be 200 years or more' [1]. Souvenir hunters carved initials into her hull, so the city fenced her, hired a caretaker who lived aboard (he appears in the 1910 census), and installed a fur seal in a tank that, the Call promised, would 'bark its bullet shaped head off' at pirates [1]. In 1929 a Norwegian granite shaft honouring Amundsen was added [2]. The sloop went home to Norway in 1972 [3].

title: The Chutes Come to Fillmore Street
place: Chutes Park, block of Fillmore, Turk, Webster & Eddy (entrance near 1226 Fillmore)
hook: In 1909 San Francisco's famous water-chute amusement park moved to Fillmore Street. Two years later a fire that began in a barber shop destroyed it.
story: After 1906 Fillmore had the crowds, and a showman moved in. On March 8, 1909, Irving Ackerman, son of the original Chutes owner, took a 13-year lease on the old Coney Island amusement park. It filled the block bounded by Fillmore, Webster, Eddy and Turk [1]. He spent $250,000 moving and enlarging the Chutes, and the new park opened on July 14, 1909 [1]. It had the famous water chute, a merry-go-round, a Circle Swing, a "Dante's Inferno" labyrinth, a human roulette wheel, a dance pavilion and an outdoor movie screen. There were daredevils, an elephant named Mike, a flea circus, and boxing exhibitions that included heavyweight champion Jack Johnson [1]. A fireproof Chutes Theatre opened on December 31, 1909 [2]. Some time after midnight on May 29, 1911, fire broke out in the Bondy brothers' barber shop. It killed three people, injured seven and wrecked most of the park [1]. The concrete theatre survived [1][2]. Ackerman did not rebuild the park. The theatre, turned to face Fillmore Street, reopened in 1915 as the Lyric under Ackerman and Harris [2].

title: The Richmond Refuses to Become Spanish Town
place: Cabrillo Street (formerly C Street)
hook: In 1909 the city voted to rename every numbered avenue in Spanish, from Arguello to Zamorano. The Richmond revolted within a week.
story: After the 1906 earthquake, the Post Office struggled with two sets of numbered streets. In 1909 a city commission proposed replacing the Richmond and Sunset's numbered avenues with Spanish names in alphabetical order, running from Arguello to Zamorano and then on to Spanish saints beyond 26th Avenue [1][2]. On November 15 the Board of Supervisors approved the changes 12 to 5 [1]. The avenues were furious. Speakers mocked the 'unpronounceable' names and the Richmond Banner warned the districts would be called 'the Spanish Town of San Francisco' [2]. The Richmond had the city's oldest continuously operating improvement club, and it mobilised fast [1][2]. At a packed Saturday meeting on November 20, the commission backed down. The Examiner claimed thirty-five thousand residents had 'arose en masse' [2]. The avenues kept their numbers; only First Avenue (Arguello) and 49th Avenue (La Playa, 'the beach') changed [2]. The Richmond's lettered streets went through several drafts before settling on explorers after all: A, B and C streets became Anza, Balboa and Cabrillo [1][2].

title: The brownstone that outlived the fire
place: Pacific-Union Club (Flood Mansion), 1000 California Street
hook: Every wooden palace on Nob Hill burned in 1906. The one real stone mansion survived as a scorched shell, and a gentlemen's club moved in.
story: When the silver king James Clair Flood built his Nob Hill mansion in the 1880s, he had brownstone cut in Connecticut and shipped around Cape Horn. His neighbours' palaces were wood, painted to look like stone [1]. The difference showed on April 19, 1906, when the fire reached the house. It destroyed the interior, but the stone shell stood [1]. Flood's unmarried daughter Cora, who had lived there until that year, sold the scorched building to the Pacific-Union Club in 1909 [1]. The club held an architectural competition. Albert Pissis, a member, won with a grand white stone building that would have made Nob Hill "a second Acropolis". It began to look too expensive, and the commission went to Willis Polk, the only contender who wanted to keep what was left of the mansion [1]. NoeHill says William Bourn, who sat on the building committee, secured the job for Polk [2]. In 1910 Polk added semicircular wings and a third floor, using brownstone from the same Connecticut quarry, and fitted out five dining rooms, a swimming pool and a squash court [1]. By the time of the mansion's 1960s landmark nomination, women had been allowed inside only once, for the 1952 Centennial Ball [1].

title: The busiest, smelliest creek on the waterfront
place: Mission Creek channel between Third and Fourth streets
hook: Sailors said two gulps of Mission Creek would kill you. It turned white lead paint black overnight, and ships still came in droves.
story: Fred Klebingat arrived on the south waterfront in 1909, a 20-year-old German seaman working as a donkeyman, running the steam winch on the schooner Annie E. Smale. He never forgot Mission Creek. "It was an open sewer, a cesspool," he recalled. Great gas bubbles broke the surface, men said you would not last two minutes if you fell in, and the water "would turn white lead paint black in one night" [1][2]. It was also, in his words, "the busiest place on the San Francisco waterfront." Steam schooners, sailing vessels and hay scows lined both banks, from Pope & Talbot's lumber yard to the hay wharf opposite, leaving barely room to tow a ship down the middle. Sailors had their own blunt name for it [1]. Scow schooners brought hay from as far as Sacramento and Milpitas to feed the city's horses. They were tied three abreast and tacked out through the crush. Once a runaway scow's bowsprit came straight through Klebingat's porthole and backed out again [1]. Idle seamen haunted the wharves hoping for a berth. As Klebingat put it, it was "not what you knew, but WHO you knew" [1].

title: The nuns' hospital that fled the fire
place: St. Mary's Hospital (now UCSF Health), 450 Stanyan St / 2200 Hayes St
hook: Eight Irish nuns started it in 1857. After the 1906 fire burned it out, St. Mary's rebuilt at the edge of Golden Gate Park.
story: The Sisters of Mercy reached San Francisco on December 8, 1854. There were eight of them, led by 25-year-old Mother Mary Baptist Russell, who had nursed cholera victims in Ireland [1]. They had been booked on the steamer Arctic, which was lost with everyone aboard, but it was overbooked, so they sailed on another ship [1]. Within a year they were nursing the city through a cholera outbreak. When the county would not repay what they had spent running the county hospital, the sisters opened their own St. Mary's Hospital in 1857 [1]. Sources differ on its first site: one says a Stockton Street building, another Rincon Hill at First and Bryant [1][2]. After the 1906 fire the hospital worked from temporary quarters at 2344 Sutter Street. By 1909 it had settled at 2200 Hayes Street, between Shrader and Stanyan [2]. From 1951 its nursing graduates earned bachelor's degrees from USF next door. A new building replaced the old one in 1972 at 450 Stanyan Street [2]. It is the oldest continuously operating hospital in San Francisco, and it joined UCSF in 2024, when it stopped being a Catholic hospital [1][2].

title: The reservoir built because the city burned
place: Twin Peaks Reservoir ('Summit Reservoir'), off Twin Peaks Boulevard
hook: Near the top of Twin Peaks, 10.5 million gallons of water are kept only for fighting fires. It was the city's answer to 1906.
story:
The 1906 earthquake broke the city's water mains, and San Franciscans blamed the failed water system for the destruction. Insurance rates soared, and in some areas coverage could not be had at any price [1]. Fire Department chief engineer Dennis T. Sullivan had proposed a separate firefighting water system back in 1903. In 1908 City Engineer Marsden Manson studied 250 cities around the world to design one [1]. Construction ran from 1909 to 1913 [1].

The Twin Peaks Reservoir is the backbone of what is now called the Emergency Firefighting Water System. It holds 10.5 million gallons in a tank built of six-inch reinforced-concrete slabs, set at 758 feet [1]. The tank is split in two, so a broken pipe can drain only half of it. The white fire hydrants with black tops, west of Twin Peaks, draw on it [1]. In a big fire downtown, commanders can bring the reservoir online by radio, which raises the pressure in the mains to 328 pounds per square inch [1]. A city photograph captioned "Twin Peaks Reservoir. General view of work" records its construction [1].

title: The revolt against 'Spanish Town'
place: Arguello Boulevard (formerly First Avenue) at Clement St
hook: In 1909 the city tried to swap the numbered avenues for Spanish names from Arguello to Zamorano. The Richmond fought back, and a pirate joke helped end it.
story: In November 1909 a Street Naming Commission, trying to sort out mail muddled after the quake, proposed replacing every numbered avenue in the Richmond and Sunset with Spanish names in alphabetical order: Arguello, then Coronado, De Soto and on to Zamorano for 26th Avenue. Spanish saints would follow after that [1]. The Board of Supervisors approved it 12 to 5. Speakers from the Avenues called the names 'unpronounceable', and some said the city was 'selling out' to the Spain the country had just beaten in the Philippines. They said the district would be mocked as 'Spanish Town' [1]. The Richmond's improvement club organised petitions, and the commission backed down at a meeting in Richmond Hall on November 20 [1]. At one hearing a lawyer objected to naming First Avenue 'St. Francis Boulevard' because St. Francis Drake had been 'one of the very worst pirates'. The chairman reminded him that St. Francis of Assisi was a priest, and the room broke into laughter [1]. The numbered avenues stayed, but First Avenue became Arguello, and the lettered streets became Anza, Balboa and Cabrillo [1][2].

title: Weddings upstairs, produce downstairs
place: Guadalupe Hall, 4555 Mission Street
hook: It was once the only social hall in the southern part of the city. For over a century it has served the Excelsior's changing crowds.
story: It doesn't look like much from the sidewalk, but 4555 Mission Street is the Excelsior's oldest social venue. Guadalupe Hall went up in 1909. For a time it was the only hall of its kind in the southern part of the city [1]. It hosted weddings, dinners, club meetings and the regular gatherings of the Native Sons and Daughters of the Golden West [1]. A photograph from about 1920 shows the words 'Guadalupe Hall' across the top of the building. The 1915 Sanborn fire-insurance map marks it as a 'Hall' and shows a garage and repair shop in the same building [1]. The people upstairs kept changing. In later years seniors from the Filipino community held dances in the hall, and today it is a Spanish-language church hall [1]. The ground floor now holds Casa Lucaz #3 Produce and Meats, which reflects the Mexican and Central American families who made the Excelsior a significant Latino neighbourhood after the Second World War [1][2].

title: Where Pullman porters could get a bed
place: New Pullman Hotel, 228-248 Townsend Street
hook: In the Jim Crow era, Black railroad workers often couldn't find a hotel that would take them. For about forty years this plain two-storey building on Townsend Street did.
story: Built in 1909, as South of Market rebuilt after the fire, this two-storey building had a hotel upstairs and six storefronts below [1]. The hotel changed names again and again: Bancroft Hotel, Hotel Carlo, Hotel Townsend, Dades Hotel, Eleanor Hotel, Aunt Mary's Hotel, New Townsend Hotel. From 1948 it was the New Pullman Hotel [1]. Pullman porters and maids, the African American workers who staffed the railroads' sleeping cars, often struggled to find lodging under Jim Crow. In San Francisco their main option was here [1]. City directories and census records show Black waiters, cooks, laborers, maids and porters living in the building from 1909 to about 1950. The first documented porter, Claude C. Waller, moved in in 1911 [1]. By the 1950s the building also held the Red Cap Café, Porter's Inn Liquors and the Galilee Mission Baptist Church. From 1950 the hotel was listed in the Negro Motorist Green Book, the guide to places that would serve Black travelers [1]. Lena's Luncheonette served downstairs from at least the 1960s until 1984, the year the hotel closed [1]. In 2018 the city made it a landmark. It is the only known San Francisco building strongly tied to the Pullman porters, whose union was the first all-Black union in the country [2].

title: A Diva Sings Free at Lotta's Fountain
place: Lotta's Fountain, Market, Kearny & Geary
hook: Blocked by a lawsuit, soprano Luisa Tetrazzini vowed to sing in the street if she had to. On Christmas Eve 1910, she did.
story: Luisa Tetrazzini had made her American debut at San Francisco's Tivoli in 1905 and gone on to conquer New York and London [1]. When impresario Oscar Hammerstein served her with an injunction in November 1910, she told reporters: "I will sing in San Francisco... If necessary, I will sing in the streets. I will sing at Lotta's Fountain" [1]. A judge let her tour go on, and she kept the promise anyway. On Christmas Eve 1910 a stage went up beside Lotta Crabtree's 1875 fountain, opposite the Chronicle's offices [1][2]. With no amplification, a crowd variously reported as up to 250,000 filled Market Street to Union Square; the historian who retold the story urges caution about the number [1]. Office workers hung telephone receivers out of windows so families at home could listen. Tetrazzini, in a gown sewn with 3,000 rhinestones, sang just two pieces, "The Last Rose of Summer" and the waltz from Romeo and Juliet. Men wept; she called the city "my home" [1]. In 1912 a plaque honouring the concert was placed on the fountain [1][2].

title: A Mayor's Fist at Sheridan School
place: 431 Capitol Ave (Sheridan School)
hook: At the cornerstone ceremony for Ocean View's new school in 1910, a speaker swore he would rather his right hand palsy than stay silent.
story: Ocean View's improvement clubs had long petitioned the city for services, a public school among them [1]. On February 20, 1910, a large crowd gathered at Capitol Avenue and Lobos Street for the cornerstone-laying of Sheridan Primary School [1][2]. Pupils sang 'America,' the Columbia Park boys' band played, and a speaker, likely Mayor P.H. McCarthy, raised his fist against the school board appointed by his predecessor: 'I would rather that my good right hand would palsy than fail to lift it against a subtle scheme to do redhot politics in the schools' [2]. The day also honoured the district's pioneers. Among the neighbourhood's 'honored settlers' at the dedication was Elias Wolfe, the roadhouse keeper who had helped start the area's first school decades earlier [1]. Sheridan opened to students in 1911 with special classrooms for 'manual training and domestic science' and one designated for 'delinquent pupils' [2]. A new building replaced it in 1975, yet the banner displayed onstage in 1910 is still shown at the school, and two buildings visible behind the 1910 crowd still stand [2].

title: A Saloonkeeper's Hall Becomes a Church
place: Site of Farley's Hall, west side of Brighton Avenue just south of Ocean Avenue
hook: Barney Farley ran a bar, staged boxing and illegal dog fights, and sold a cure-all elixir. Then his hall became the first home of a Catholic parish.
story:
Bernard Farley was one of Ingleside's early settlers. From the 1860s he farmed land near Ocean Avenue and today's Junipero Serra Boulevard. He also ran a small bar, staged boxing matches and illegal dog fights, and sold an elixir called "B. Farley's Wonderful Discovery" [1]. His hall was one of the first meeting places in the district.

After the 1906 earthquake, refugees came out to Ingleside. The old racetrack became a camp for elderly and infirm refugees, and 24 percent of the people who lived there had been born in Ireland [1]. Farley gave his hall to the refugees to use as a church [1]. The parish dates its first home to 1910, in "a Hall owned by Barney Farley on the west side of Brighton Avenue, just south of Ocean Avenue" [2]. It was named for St. Emydius, the patron saint against earthquakes, because so many of the first parishioners had lost their homes in 1906 [2].

By 1911 the congregation was meeting in three shacks joined together [1]. A Tudor Gothic church opened on DeMontfort Avenue (1913 in one account, 1914 in the parish's), and the congregation soon outgrew it. In 1928 it dedicated today's golden-domed, twin-towered church, which seats 800 [1][2].

title: A parish born in a 24th Street workshop
place: St. Philip the Apostle Church, 725 Diamond Street
hook: Upper Noe Valley's Catholics were tired of climbing hills and crossing creeks to get to Mass. So they started a church in an old workshop.
story:
In 1910 upper Noe Valley was a working-class, largely Irish neighbourhood with wooden sidewalks on 24th Street. It had no Catholic church of its own [1]. Every choice meant a long walk. Most Holy Redeemer was over the steep hill at 18th and Diamond. St. James was more than a mile downhill at 23rd and Guerrero. St. Paul's, at Church and 29th, was also about a mile from Diamond Street. "You had to cross three creeks to get to church," as one longtime parishioner puts it [1].

Archbishop Patrick Riordan approved a new parish, and the job of starting it went to Father John Cullen from County Cavan, Ireland. The first chapel was a converted workshop at 4296 24th Street. Cullen lived in a rented upper flat a few doors away, at 4262, for nearly two years [1].

The congregation soon outgrew the workshop. It opened a church on Elizabeth Street in 1914, then raised $71,000 for a Romanesque church at Diamond and Elizabeth, where the first Mass was held in 1925 [1]. Mae Silver's history notes that the Irish were the largest group in Noe and Eureka valleys from the start [2].

title: A secret airship in the racetrack gully
place: Former Ingleside Racetrack grounds, Ingleside Terraces (Urbano Drive area)
hook: Guards chased gawkers away while an inventor built an 8,000-pound flying machine on the abandoned Ingleside Racetrack, planning to fly it to Paris.
story: After the horses left, the empty Ingleside Racetrack had an odd tenant. In a gully out of sight of Ocean Avenue, Willis Grant Murray was building a $100,000 airship paid for by wealthy investors [1]. In December 1910 he gave a San Francisco Call reporter a long interview. The paper found the machine 'hardly nameable': part biplane, part dirigible, part helicopter, with three car engines driving 14-foot propellers, a deck for five crew and ten passengers, and aluminium boats for skids [1]. Murray planned to fly six days and nights without landing, cross the continent and perhaps go on to Paris. He called ordinary aeroplanes 'a plaything beside it' [1]. Then he hired watchmen to chase off the curious. By February 1912 Joseph Leonard's crews were grading the old track for Ingleside Terraces around him [1][2]. Murray was still trying to get the 176-foot machine off the ground, but high winds kept ripping its hydrogen bags and damaging the frame. The airship never flew, and Murray died in 1919 [1].

title: Before the Fillmore, the Majestic
place: Majestic Hall (later the Fillmore Auditorium), Geary & Fillmore
hook: The hall where Hendrix and the Dead later played began as a mother-and-daughters venture, and it kept a colour line for more than forty years.
story: Decades before the psychedelic posters, the corner of Geary and Fillmore held a dance hall built by women. According to the city's Japantown historic context statement, Emma Gates Butler and her daughters built the Majestic Hall at the southwest corner in 1910. It was designed by the well-known architects James W. and Merritt Reid, who in 1911 also designed a five-storey building across Fillmore Street [1]. Other accounts give 1912 and describe the first tenant as the Majestic Hall and Academy of Dancing [2]. It was part of the entertainment boom that followed the 1906 quake, when Fillmore Street briefly became the city's downtown [1]. For a neighbourhood that was fast becoming one of the most mixed in the West, the Majestic kept a colour line. The same report notes that it was segregated until the 1950s [1]. The building went on to become the Ambassador Dance Hall in 1936 and a roller rink from 1939 to 1952. In 1954 the Black promoter Charles Sullivan took the lease, renamed it the Fillmore Auditorium and opened its doors to everyone [2].

title: Farragut School, as Its Pupils Remembered It
place: Site of Farragut School, Holloway Avenue at Capitol Avenue
hook: Nobody photographed it much and nobody saved it. But the Ingleside's old grammar school lives on in the memories of the children who went there.
story:
Farragut School opened in 1910 on the corner of Holloway and Capitol avenues. It is long gone [1][2]. Ray Wilson, born in the mid-1940s, started kindergarten there with Miss Robinson. His mother watched from the window of their apartment at 210 Jules, a block away, to see him come out [3]. He called the building "dilapidated". The hallways "smelled like urine," even though three or four janitors worked there all day. His teacher Mrs. Preston was 76 or 78, he said, and had taught his sister years before [3]. After first grade he moved to West Portal Lutheran School.

Two decades later, in about 1969, Ella Driscoll's daughter started there. Then school busing sent her across town to Robert Louis Stevenson School in the Sunset. On the first day she was the only white child on the bus [4].

Al Harris remembered what came next. The school stood abandoned for a long time, and its alarm went off in the night. Then it was torn down, and the James Johnson Center and condominiums went up in its place. "The whole thing kind of went through a whole decline and rebirth," he said [2].

title: Frogs, watercress and whist above the coal yard
place: Leland Avenue, where the Bay Shore Hall stood above Anderson's Coal Yard
hook: Valley kids sold frogs and watercress to restaurants, slid down hills in cardboard boxes, and watched old ships being broken up on the bay.
story: In the valley's early decades, social life happened in halls. Clubs and service groups held whist parties, dances, minstrel shows and bazaars at the Bay Shore Hall above Anderson's Coal Yard on Leland Avenue, at the Fireman's Hall on Wilde Avenue, at the Alpine Hall on Raymond Avenue and in the gymnasium of the Six Mile House [1]. Children made their own fun. They hiked the hills, picnicked on the ridges and slid down the slippery spring grass in large cardboard cartons [1]. They waded and swam in the bay and watched old ships being taken apart at the 'ships' graveyard' at the Johnson-Brown wharf [1]. For pocket money they caught frogs and gathered watercress to sell to local restaurants, and peddled bouquets of wildflowers door to door [1]. They saved through a school program run by the Bank of Italy, later Bank of America, at a time when the valley had no other banking service [1]. Getting downtown was slow. By 1910 two streetcar lines served the valley, and the long waits while cars were switched on a single track earned it the nickname 'Hesitation Valley' [1][2].

title: From French laundry to Irish seisún
place: The Plough and Stars, 116 Clement St near 2nd Ave
hook: For more than sixty years 116 Clement was a French laundry. Then it became a home for Irish music and newly arrived Irish immigrants.
story: The little building at 116 Clement Street went up in 1905 and spent most of its life as a French laundry, a reminder of the French community that also built the French Hospital nearby on Geary [1]. Frank Mirandette, born to a Spanish mother and French father, had come from France in 1890, married fellow immigrant Francoise Gouber and run a laundry in Los Gatos before opening this one around 1910; his family lived next door at 114 [1]. Partner Calixte Lapuyade took it over as the Clement French Laundry, and by 1960 the Baylacq family, French laundrymen since 1906, ran it until 1974 [1]. On Friday, April 30, 1975, the space reopened as the Plough and Stars, named for Sean O'Casey's play about the 1916 Easter Rising [2]. Its first owner, Bob Heaney, also ran the Starry Plough in Berkeley; in 1981 Sean Heaney, part of a wave of Irish immigrants escaping Ireland's 1980s recession, took over [1][2]. It became a gathering place for newcomers seeking community, work contacts and familiar music, famous for its seisúns, informal sessions any musician can join [1]. The city named it a Legacy Business in 2018 [1].

title: Gymnasts, then Norwegians, on 18th Street
place: Mission Turn Hall (now the Women's Building), 3543 18th Street
hook: Long before its famous murals, the Women's Building was a German gymnastics hall, and after that a Norwegian lodge called Dovre Hall.
story:
Around 1900 the Irish and Germans were the Mission's biggest immigrant groups, and the Mission Turn Verein, a German gymnastics club, already had a hall on 18th Street near Valencia [1]. In 1910 architect August Reinhold Denke designed the Turners a new four-storey home at 3543 18th Street in the Mission Revival style [2][3].

For 25 years Mission Turn Hall was open to the whole mixed district. It ran after-school classes for children and put on a monthly exhibition followed by a social and a dance. It hosted weddings, receptions and parties [2]. The Native Sons and Daughters of the Golden West were tenants for fifty years [2]. In 1935 the Sons of Norway and the Daughters of Norway bought the building and renamed it Dovre Hall, after a mountain range in Norway [2][3]. It kept that name until 1978, when the San Francisco Women's Center bought it. It has been the Women's Building ever since [2][3].

title: Opening night at the Haight Theater
place: Haight Theater, 1700 Haight St at Cole St
hook: The mayor gave a speech and every one of its 1,310 seats sold. For half a century, kids spent whole Saturdays here for twenty cents.
story: On March 8, 1910, the Haight Theater opened at the northwest corner of Haight and Cole. It had one screen and 1,310 seats. The Ashbury Club sold out the first night, and Mayor Patrick Henry McCarthy gave a speech. The building cost $33,000. It showed films and vaudeville, with a system of lines and pulleys for shifting backdrops quickly, and the Haight orchestra often played live with the double features [1]. John Molloy grew up nearby. His father had pitched for the Hollywood Stars in 1926, and later gardened for Golden Gate Park's John McLaren and then drove for him. As a preteen, Molloy's favourite weekend treat was spending the whole day at the Haight Theater. Admission was 20 cents, and the 50 cents his father gave him covered everything else. His mother shopped on Haight Street, and at the GallenCamps shoe store he liked to use the X-ray machine to watch the bones of his feet wiggle [2]. By the 1950s, the suburbs and television were emptying neighbourhood movie houses [1]. The Haight closed as a cinema in 1964, after more than fifty years [3].

title: The Champion's Camp at Seal Rock House
place: Site of Seal Rock House, foot of Sutro Heights, Point Lobos Ave and Great Highway
hook: In June 1910, the first Black heavyweight champion made his headquarters at an Ocean Beach roadhouse, training for the most racially charged fight in American history.
story: In 1910 former champion James J. Jeffries came out of retirement to fight Jack Johnson, the first African American heavyweight champion of the world. Jeffries said he was fighting 'for the sole purpose of proving that a white man is better than a Negro' [3]. Before the bout, Johnson set up his headquarters at Seal Rock House, a roadhouse at the foot of Sutro Heights, and trained at the Ocean Beach Pavilion nearby [1]. A photo dated June 26, 1910 shows him with his trainers outside the roadhouse [1]. It was taken by Percy Dana, a boxing photographer nicknamed 'Pee Wee' because he was so small, whose studio went on to be principal photographer for the fight [2]. On July 4, 1910, in Reno, Johnson won in the fifteenth round. Race riots broke out across the country, and more than 20 people died [3]. Films of the fight were banned in many places, and in 1912 Congress banned carrying fight films across state lines, a ban not lifted until 1940. Dana's photographs were for years one of the few ways to see the fight [2].

title: The camp that became a Maybeck house
place: Power House, 1526 Masonic Avenue
hook: A lawyer's family burned out in 1906 fell for a hillside view, hired an unknown architect named Maybeck, and later got into a feud with relatives across the street.
story:
When the 1906 fire burned their downtown flat, the family of lawyer E. B. Power took refuge in the Masonic Cemetery and, by some accounts, then camped on open land at the edge of today's Cole Valley [2]. They liked the quiet and the view so much that they built there. In 1910 they hired Bernard Maybeck, then known mainly for his work in the East Bay, to design 1526 Masonic Avenue [1][2]. It already shows what made him famous: rough shingles against huge smooth beams, a pitched roof and deep eaves [1][3]. He went on to design the Palace of Fine Arts [1][3].

The neighbours had their own dramas. Relatives living across the street at 1524 Masonic fell out with the Powers and added a second-floor "spite wall" that blocked the bay view from their living room [1]. OpenSFHistory is more careful and calls it a "supposed" spite wall [2]. The family lived in the house into the 1940s [2]. In 2026 the Board of Supervisors started the process of making it a city landmark [3]. Sources disagree on the details: FoundSF and the city call the owner "Powers", a U.S. Attorney, while OpenSFHistory has E. B. Power, a state assistant attorney general [1][2][3].

title: The newspaper that told Issei to stay
place: Nichibei Shimbun (Japanese American News), Laguna Street
hook: A former laundry owner made his Laguna Street paper the leading Japanese-language newspaper in America, and used it to urge immigrants to put down roots.
story: Kyutaro Abiko arrived in San Francisco in 1885, worked menial jobs and put himself through school and into UC Berkeley. He briefly ran a restaurant and a laundry [1]. In 1897 he took over a small paper, and in 1899 a merger created the Nichibei Shimbun (Japanese American News) [1]. After the 1906 fire it was one of two Japanese newspapers anchoring the new Japantown. The Nichibei was on Laguna Street and its rival, Shin Sekai (New World), was on Geary [2][3]. By 1910 the Nichibei led the field, and by the 1920s it had around 25,000 readers across the West [1]. Abiko used its pages to urge laborers to commit to permanent settlement and stable family life. In 1906 he founded a land company whose Yamato Colony near Livingston sold 40-acre plots to Japanese farmers [1]. Shin Sekai was less assimilationist and closer to the Buddhist community, and the two papers feuded for years [3]. After the 1924 Immigration Act, Abiko added an English section aimed at the Nisei and sponsored their study tours of Japan [1].

title: Thirty Cows on Mission Street
place: Mission Street near Silver Avenue
hook: In 1910 a rancher was arrested for grazing thirty cattle near Mission and Silver. His accusers were his new suburban neighbours.
story: For decades the Excelsior fed San Francisco. Italian truck farmers, the giardinieri from Liguria and Tuscany, grew lettuce, cabbage and artichokes there for the Colombo produce market downtown, next to hog farmers and dairy ranchers [1]. In the 1890s the Excelsior Homestead and Sunnyside had sprawling dairies, and the milk trade was filthy. In 1895 the city hired James P. Dockery as its first Milk Inspector, who accused crooked dairies of having 'murdered infants.' A dairy ordinance finally passed in 1896 [2]. The same year the city first restricted hog ranches [1]. As late as 1910, about 1,200 Italian truck farmers still worked some 8,000 acres along the city's southern edge. But houses were spreading, and in 1910 the law limited each owner to two cows. That February a rancher was arrested for running thirty head of cattle near Mission Street and Silver Avenue. He was arrested at the request of a neighbourhood group, the Excelsior Progressive Association [1]. The farm district was becoming a neighbourhood, and the neighbours wanted the cows gone.

title: Fourteen years to build, debt-free
place: St. Paul's Catholic Church, 221 Valley Street at Church Street
hook: Noe Valley's twin-spired church took 14 years to build because the priest refused to borrow. Part of it is quarry granite and rubble from 1906.
story:
St. Paul's parish started in 1876. That year George Shadbourne asked Archbishop Alemany for a new parish and offered to help raise the money. A church for about 750 people opened in 1880 [1].

In 1897 Father Michael Connolly started a much larger English Gothic church designed by Frank T. Shea. Connolly acted as his own contractor, and nearly every able-bodied man in the parish worked on it. He refused to borrow and paid for the work as money came in from contests, raffles and bazaars, so construction took more than a decade [2]. The walls are granite from a quarry near 30th and Castro, with some curbstones and rubble from the 1906 earthquake [2]. Archbishop Riordan dedicated the church on 29 May 1911, free of debt [1][2]. Its two unequal slate-covered spires can be seen from almost anywhere in Noe Valley. The taller one is about 200 feet high [3].

Sources disagree about who filled the pews. FoundSF calls St. Paul's a bastion of the city's Irish Catholics, while a parish history in the Voice describes the area as a German immigrant stronghold [4][5].

title: Ingleside Heights: A Name Borrowed From Next Door
place: 146 Beverly Street
hook: When a fancy residence park rose on the old racetrack, the humble slope next door rebranded itself. A 1914 house still stands among 1940s neighbours.
story: For decades the west end of Merced Heights was open hillside, laid out on paper in 1870 by the City Land Association but reached by few roads [1]. In July 1911 the Call reported that owners in the City Land tract 'on the south of the Ingleside track' were about to start street work 'on an extensive scale'. It called the slope, overlooking Lake Merced and the ocean, 'one of the most sightly locations in the city' [2]. In 1912 the Ingleside Terraces residence park began rising on the old racetrack next door. Real estate salesmen and residents started calling the slope 'Ingleside Heights' [1]. The context statement, which ties the name to the builders of the post-war years, says it was presumably meant to add cachet, although the houses, materials and street plan matched other Merced Heights blocks [3]. Residents lobbied for basic services, including water, and in the 1920s builders began filling the blocks south of Holloway Avenue with Sunset-style stucco houses [1]. Most of the hill waited until after World War II. The context statement's example is 146 Beverly Street, built in 1914 and now surrounded by houses from the 1940s [3].

title: Ishi's Five Years on Parnassus
place: University Museum of Anthropology, Affiliated Colleges campus (now UCSF)
hook: The last known survivor of the Yahi people spent his final years in a museum on Parnassus. Thousands came to watch him make arrowheads.
story: In August 1911 a starving man walked out of the Butte County wilderness into Oroville. UC anthropologists Alfred Kroeber and T. T. Waterman identified him as the last survivor of a remnant Yahi band. On September 4, Waterman brought him to live on the Parnassus campus, and the world came to know him as Ishi [1]. When the Museum of Anthropology opened there that October, some 24,000 people came in six months to watch him make arrowheads and fire [1]. Surgeon Saxton Pope, who taught next door, wrote that Ishi could make fire from two sticks of buckeye in under two minutes and was employed 'in a small way as a janitor' [2]. Pope became his doctor and friend. Ishi taught him to make bows and to hunt 'Indian fashion,' and called him Ku wi, 'Medicine Man' [2]. Ishi had little resistance to disease, and on March 25, 1916, he died of tuberculosis in the UC Hospital [1]. Kroeber, away in New York, wrote 'Please shut down on it' about an autopsy, but his letter came too late. The brain was preserved and sent to the Smithsonian [1]. In 1999 the Smithsonian named the Redding Rancheria and Pit River tribe as his closest kin, and in 2000 his brain and ashes were returned to them for burial [1][3].

title: Lodge hall by night, saddle works by day
place: New Era Hall, 2117-2123 Market Street
hook: Seven months after the quake, a Swedish architect's hall gave homeless lodges a place to meet. Then, for four decades, it turned out cowboy saddles.
story: New Era Hall was finished seven months after the 1906 earthquake and fire. Its architect, August Nordin, used a Howe truss to span the big meeting rooms without columns, which also saved scarce building materials [1]. It arrived when San Francisco badly needed rooms. Lodges burned out of their halls, among them the Odd Fellows, the Knights of Pythias and the Woodmen of the World, met there [1]. The hall also helped shape the city. On April 18, 1910, the fourth anniversary of the quake, a convention of neighbourhood improvement clubs met at New Era Hall to push for a streetcar tunnel through Twin Peaks, the project that became the Twin Peaks Tunnel [2]. In 1911 the building took a surprising second career. From then until 1953 it housed the Visalia Stock Saddle Company, which the landmark application calls a pioneering Mexican-American business that made high-end saddles and contributed to the development of the western saddle [1]. None of Visalia's other factories survive. San Francisco had 72 social halls in 1907, and New Era Hall is one of only nine still standing [1].

title: Rube Goldberg's building for his father
place: R. L. Goldberg Building, 182-198 Gough Street
hook: The cartoonist whose name means 'needlessly complicated' built something quite simple on Gough Street: shops downstairs and a flat for his widowed dad upstairs.
story: Before his name became shorthand for absurdly complicated contraptions, Reuben Goldberg was a San Francisco boy, born here in 1883. His father, a city police and fire commissioner, steered him toward engineering. Rube graduated from UC Berkeley in 1904 and went to work as an engineer for the city's Water and Sewers Department [2]. He lasted six months, then quit to become a sports cartoonist at the San Francisco Chronicle [2]. In 1911 he commissioned a building at 182–198 Gough Street. Its ground-floor shops brought in rent, and upstairs were two apartments, one for himself and one for his widowed father, Max [1][2]. Goldberg spent most of his career in New York, where his drawings of machines that did simple jobs in hilariously roundabout ways made him famous. He won the Pulitzer Prize for political cartooning in 1948 [2]. He still made long visits to his San Francisco home and kept the building for the rest of his life [1]. The city later made it Landmark No. 268 for its close association with the man whose name now describes any device 'deliberately over-engineered to perform a simple task' [1].

title: The 25-Line and a Staged Accident
place: San Bruno Avenue at Woolsey Street
hook: In 1911 a streetcar company employee posed on San Bruno Avenue to act out how an accident had happened, and the company photographer took his picture.
story: San Bruno Avenue was still called San Bruno Road in March 1908. That month United Railroads photographer John Henry Mentz stood near Woolsey Street and photographed the road running south toward Bayview Hill [1]. The company's cameras came back to the Portola for less scenic reasons. On October 10, 1911, Mentz photographed 25-line car #961, a former Omnibus Railway car, on San Bruno near Felton. A company employee in the picture is shown acting out an accident, and the photograph is filed with accident report 4949 [2]. For Ruth Eshow Upton's family, who lived just beyond the Portola, the 25 was a lifeline. It started at Fifth and Market, ran along Bryant, swung over to Potrero and took San Bruno for the final stretch to the Five Mile House [3]. One rider remembered the trip into town as 'tedious and devoid of interest', which made it good for reading [3]. Old-timers told Chris Ortiz that the ride over the Islais Creek marsh was rough because the tracks kept sinking [4].

title: The Builder Who Came Before the Streets
place: Alonzo Harrington's Craftsman row, 1200 block of 42nd Avenue (1223 42nd Ave)
hook: Alonzo Harrington moved to the empty Sunset in 1892. His 1911 row of shingled houses on 42nd Avenue is still among the district's finest.
story: Alonzo Harrington started as a carpenter in San Francisco in 1886. In 1892 he moved to the Sunset, when it was almost empty, and he became one of its first important builders [1]. On the 1200 block of 42nd Avenue he built a row of fifteen houses in 1911. A neighborhood survey by SPEAK calls them some of the finest of the many Craftsman houses built in the Sunset in the 1910s. Each has its own composition and details. Eleven were still much as built in 2005, and two had been restored [1]. At 1223 there is a cross-gabled roof, wood shingles and heavy carved beam ends. At 1235 a front gable sweeps down in a 'ski-slope' curve, and the entry is a Tudor arch [1]. In January 1913 the Chronicle noted that 'A. Harrington, who has been building homes for more than twenty years in the Sunset district,' had more houses under construction on 42nd Avenue. He planted grass, palms and flowers in front of each one [2]. Survivors like these are rare. Of the 549 houses standing in the beachside Oceanside neighborhood in 1915, only about 50 or 60 kept high integrity by the 2000s [3].

title: The showpiece house that sold segregation
place: Leonard-Poole House, 90 Cedro Avenue, Ingleside Terraces (SF Landmark #213)
hook: The developer who built this Craftsman house wrote racial bans into every deed. Nearly half a century later, a Black civil-rights lawyer bought it.
story: Joseph A. Leonard bought the old Ingleside Racetrack for $2,500 an acre and in 1911 built himself a large Craftsman showpiece at 90 Cedro Avenue, where he lived until 1920 [1][2]. His Ingleside Terraces offered curving streets, pillars and landscaping, and also restrictions on who could live there [3]. A 1913 sales brochure promised 'ample protection against building abuses or objectionable occupation', and 'objectionable occupation' mainly meant minorities [1]. Tim Kelley's landmark report calls Leonard 'one of the first to use restrictive racial covenants as a real estate marketing tool' in San Francisco [2]. In 1957 Cecil F. Poole, a Harvard-trained lawyer, president of the San Francisco Urban League and assistant district attorney, became the first non-white owner in the Terraces. The house he bought was Leonard's own [1]. Someone burned a cross on his lawn. The Pooles stayed until the early 1980s, and Poole later became a federal judge [1][2]. In 2000 the city made the house Landmark #213, honouring both men. The report calls it 'particularly ironic' [2].

title: The world's fair that almost came here
place: Proposed 'Merced Park' exposition: Venetian zone and miniature Panama Canal on today's zoo site
hook: Before the 1915 world's fair went to the Marina, boosters drew up a Lake Merced version, with a miniature Panama Canal on the zoo site.
story: After San Francisco won the 1915 Panama-Pacific International Exposition, the city fought over where to put it. "There is hardly a section of San Francisco that has not many to do it reverence in asserting it to be the logical and only defensible place," the Chronicle wrote in March 1911 [1]. Harbor View, Golden Gate Park, the waterfront, the Bay View and Lake Merced all had boosters [1]. The Lake Merced Fair Site Association had civil engineer J. E. Pope draw up "Merced Park." Its midway was nicknamed "The Canal." Where the zoo now stands, a Venetian-themed zone held a Panama Canal in miniature. Grand courts and fountains filled the land south of Sloat Boulevard where Merced Manor and Lakeshore were later built, and a "Tropical Orchard" was planned for the foggy southwest corner [1]. It lost. Grading such a site would have been costly, few people lived nearby, and getting crowds out there depended on the Twin Peaks streetcar tunnel, which didn't open until 1918 [1]. By the time President Taft broke ground in October 1911, Lake Merced was out, and the fair went to the Marina [1].

title: Where the studio apartment may have been born
place: MacBeth (now Rossmoor) Apartments, 765 Geary Street
hook: One room, a bed that folds into the wall, a tiny kitchen. A 1911 Geary Street building may have been among America's first studio apartments.
story: After 1906, fire laws required brick or concrete buildings in the burned district. Building cost more, so owners built bigger, and the Uptown Tenderloin slowly filled with hotels and then apartment houses [1]. Many middle-class people still associated apartments with slum tenements. In 1907, architect Charles Peter Weeks predicted that "all of the down town hillside district will be covered with apartment houses" [1]. In 1911 he designed the MacBeth at 765 Geary Street: four stories of patterned brick with terra-cotta trim, an angel-head cornice and 48 small units [1]. Historian Eric Sandweiss, quoted in the National Register nomination, calls it "one of the first studio apartment buildings in San Francisco" and says it "may have been one of the first in the country as well" [1]. A studio was a single room for living and sleeping, with a wall bed that folded away by day and a small kitchen, which suited the clerks, stenographers and single people who filled the district [1]. The building was renamed the Rossmoor in 1937 and still carries that name over the door [1]. It is one of 409 contributing buildings in the 33-block historic district [2].

title: A Fort Built for Guns Soon Obsolete
place: Fort Winfield Scott parade ground, Ralston Ave
hook: In 1912 the Army carved a whole new fort out of the Presidio's windy west side to command the big guns guarding the Golden Gate.
story: On June 19, 1912, the Army created Fort Winfield Scott in the western part of the Presidio. It was a coast artillery post and the headquarters of the Artillery District of San Francisco [1][2]. The fort looked after seventeen concrete gun batteries of the Endicott era, built, armed and manned between 1891 and 1946 [1]. In 1922 Fort Scott became headquarters of the Coast Defenses of San Francisco, renamed Harbor Defenses of San Francisco in 1925. From here the Army commanded Forts Baker, Barry, Cronkhite, Miley and Funston. Only the Presidio itself and Fort Mason stayed outside its control [1]. The fort's families lived nearby. Enlisted family housing on Ruckman Road went up in 1921 [3]. After World War II, Fort Scott became a sub-post of the Presidio. Then, on June 1, 1946, the Army moved its Coast Artillery School here from Fort Monroe, Virginia. The move came too late: air power, amphibious warfare and nuclear weapons had made fixed coastal guns obsolete. The Army ended its Coast Artillery in 1950, and the school's stay was brief [1].

title: A Rancho Heiress Behind the Grocery Counter
place: 834 Irving Street (today's Blackthorn Tavern), near 10th Avenue
hook: The woman selling Acme Beer and jam on Irving Street was a Tanforan, daughter of a Mexican-era land grantee.
story:
834 Irving Street went up in 1907 as a corner grocery. In 1912 grocer William A. Rodgers and his wife Nelly bought it with a loan from the Bank of Italy. They lived around the corner at 1307 10th Avenue and sold Acme Beer and Sunlit jams [1].

Then things came apart. In 1916 Nelly went into partnership with August W. Peterson, who lived on 9th Avenue, and the shop became N. Rodgers & Co. In 1918 she sued William for divorce on grounds of desertion. In August 1919 the whole business, stock, Ford truck, meat slicer and all, was sold at auction [1].

Nelly had been born Catherine Nelly Tanforan on May 13, 1877. Her father, Toribio Tanforan, was a native of Chile (some said Peru) who held part of an 1836 Mexican land grant near Mission Dolores. The San Bruno racetrack, and the mall that replaced it, were named for him [1][2]. Orphaned at seven, she later lived with her siblings in the family's old cottages on Dolores Street until her death in 1953 [1].

The storefront carried on: a sheet-metal shop, Billings Dime Store, then a line of bars (Ole's, The Scene, the Golden Grommet), and today the Blackthorn [1].

title: A widow's gift, a pond and 6,000 guests
place: Jackson Playground, 17th and Arkansas streets
hook: The land was given on one condition: it must always be a park. Neighbours filled in its pond, and in 1912 the mayor opened it to cheering crowds.
story: When Potrero Nuevo was surveyed in 1856, three plots were set aside for public parks: the future Franklin Square, McKinley Square and Jackson Playground [1]. According to a 2017 Potrero View history, the Jackson site at 17th and Arkansas was deeded to the city around 1870 by Diana Chatham, widow of a miller named Roland Chatham, on condition that it always be used as a park [1]. A 1964 account credits "a Mr. Chatham" with the gift but agrees on the condition [2]. The land was not always dry. At times Mission Bay's water reached it, and neighbours filled in a large pond on the site, then raised money for a playground and clubhouse [1]. In a photograph from October 1909, taken from 17th and Carolina, the site is still empty beside the huge wooden Queen Lily Soap factory [4]. In 1912 Mayor James Rolph opened the playground in front of about 6,000 people. In its early days, pupils from two Excelsior District elementary schools used it as an "amusement area" [1]. Photographs from September 1912 and about 1920 show children and girls at play there [3].

title: Alma's château on Washington Street
place: Spreckels Mansion, 2080 Washington St
hook: The daughter of poor Danish immigrants married a sugar heir and got a French Baroque palace, but she insisted the Victorians on the site be saved, not torn down.
story:
Alma de Bretteville was born in San Francisco in 1881, the fifth of six children of Danish immigrants [2]. Adolph Spreckels, heir to his father Claus's sugar empire, courted her for five years. They married on 11 May 1908, when he was 24 years older than she was [1][2]. (The popular story that she posed for the Dewey Monument in Union Square is disputed. An article from 1902 names a different model [2].)

For their home, Adolph bought and combined several lots on Washington Street with views of the bay and the Golden Gate. George Applegarth, trained at the École des Beaux-Arts, designed the French Baroque mansion, which was completed in 1912 [1][2]. Alma refused to let the existing houses be demolished. Six Victorians on Jackson Street and two on Washington were moved instead [1].

She went on to collect Rodin and had Applegarth design the California Palace of the Legion of Honor. It opened on 11 November 1924, six months after Adolph's death [1][2]. Alma lived in the mansion until she died in 1968 [1].

title: America's first big city-owned streetcars
place: Geary Blvd at Arguello Blvd (old cable car barn)
hook: Frustrated by a slow private cable line, the city refused to renew its franchise and built its own railway on Geary. Muni was born here in December 1912.
story: In the late 1800s the Geary Street, Park & Ocean Railroad ran cable cars out Geary to the Richmond on a franchise renewed each year. They kept a carbarn at Geary and Arguello, and its brickwork survives inside a later building [1]. The small cars ran at about six miles an hour. Progressive reformers wanted public ownership of utilities, and voters approved a bond for a city streetcar line in 1909, partly out of anger at the private United Railroads [1][2]. When the franchise ran out, the last cable car ran on May 5, 1912. Crews dug the cable machinery out of Geary and strung trolley wires overhead [1]. On December 28, 1912, Mayor James Rolph opened the Municipal Railway's first lines, the A and B, both on Geary [1]. SFMTA calls it the first major publicly owned, land-based transit agency in the United States [2]. The A turned at Tenth Avenue for Golden Gate Park, and the B went on towards the beach. A later C line turned at Second Avenue to reach California Street [1].

title: Barred from the Y, they built their own
place: Japanese YWCA / Issei Women's Building, 1830 Sutter Street
hook: Shut out of the city's YWCA, Issei women founded the nation's first independent Japanese YWCA, then raised money for a building the law barred them from owning.
story: In 1912 Japanese women were kept out of the facilities at San Francisco's main YWCA by segregationist policies. Issei women answered by founding the first independent Japanese YWCA in the United States [1]. Many of the women it served were newly arrived "picture brides" who had married men they knew only from photographs and letters. Its leading founder, Yonako (Yona) Abiko, aimed it at community, stability and job training [2]. The Y taught flower arranging and tea ceremony and organised concerts and socials [2]. After a short stay on Gough Street it moved to 1826 Sutter in the 1920s [3]. In 1928 Abiko launched a fundraising campaign for a building of its own on the site [2]. California's Alien Land Laws, passed in 1913 and 1920, meant Issei women could not own the building their own money paid for. So the San Francisco YWCA agreed to hold title in trust for the Nikkei community [1][2]. The Julia Morgan-designed building opened in 1932. The city's landmark report says it appears to be the only building in the United States purpose-built by and for Issei women [1].

title: City Hall Moves Into a Future Hotel
place: Hotel Whitcomb (temporary City Hall), 1231 Market Street
hook: For three years San Francisco was governed from a building designed to become a hotel. The words "City Hall" still show faintly above its entrance.
story: The 1906 earthquake wrecked San Francisco's grand City Hall, and for years the city rented offices wherever it could, including five floors of the Hewes Building on Sixth Street [1]. In October 1910 Mayor P. H. McCarthy and the supervisors accepted an offer from the Whitcomb estate, whose trustee James Otis proposed a seven-story building on Market between Eighth and Ninth streets that "may eventually be used as a hotel" [1]. The architects had to draw two sets of plans, one superimposing the city offices on the future hotel [2]. The reinforced-concrete building cost $600,000, and the city paid $5,250 a month in rent [1]. From 1912 to 1915 it housed the county clerk, tax collector and assessor on the first floor, the supervisors, fire commissioners and Board of Education on the second, and even a Central Emergency Hospital [1]. Once the new Civic Center was built, the building reopened in 1917 as the Hotel Whitcomb [2]. A publication of the day told of an elderly woman who arrived with a tax bill and six silver dollars, only to be escorted across Market Street to the new City Hall [1]. The faded words "City Hall" can still be made out over the door [1].

title: Climbing Sutro's fence to find St. Francis Wood
place: St. Francis Boulevard, spine of St. Francis Wood
hook: Five Berkeley developers climbed a wooden fence one March morning in 1912, saw poppies and the Farallones, and decided to build a model suburb.
story: On a sunny March morning in 1912, Duncan McDuffie and four partners from Berkeley climbed the wooden fence along Junipero Serra Boulevard that marked the edge of the Sutro estate. They walked up a wood road towards Mount Davidson [1]. He later remembered ground 'carpeted with California poppies, cowslips, buttercups, wild pansies, babyblue eyes and iris', and a view past Sloat Boulevard to the jagged Farallones [1]. They bought 175 acres [2]. The Olmsted Brothers laid out curving streets, and John Galen Howard designed the main gate, the first fountain, the lampposts and the brick-diamond sidewalks. Sales opened on October 12, 1912, with the then-novel promise of underground utilities [2]. Then the First World War stopped sales almost entirely from 1914 to 1919. In 1915, McDuffie said, total sales came to $5,000, and only the banks kept the company afloat [1]. The founding covenants also barred certain ethnic groups, a clause the homes association now calls 'discriminatory and inexcusable' [2]. The German planner Werner Hegemann later called it America's most distinguished residential suburb [1].

title: Eighteen stools and a lucky Danish swan
place: Swan Oyster Depot, 1517 Polk Street
hook: Fire destroyed the Lausten brothers' oyster shop in 1906. Six years later they tried again on Polk Street, and named it after Denmark's bird of good fortune.
story: Before 1906, a group of Danish brothers named Lausten ran a nearby seafood shop called the Cable Oyster Shop. Accounts differ on exactly when it opened, but it was around the turn of the century [1]. The fire that followed the earthquake destroyed it [1]. In 1912 the Laustens rebuilt and opened a new shop on Polk Street. This time they wanted some luck, so they named it after the swan, Denmark's national bird and a Danish symbol of good fortune [1]. The Chronicle reports that its vintage stools date from 1912 [1], and the counter still seats just 18 [2]. After the Second World War the Sancimino family bought the business. One Chronicle piece gives the year as 1946, another as 1947 [1][2]. Sal Sancimino's sons and grandsons have worked the counter ever since, cracking crab and steaming whole lobsters to order [2]. The Chronicle calls the place "perfectly preserved in its timeless glory" [1]. Swan later won a James Beard Award as an American Classic [2].

title: Forty Years in a House in the Park
place: Former Quigley home, triangle west of Kezar Stadium (Kezar Dr, Lincoln Way, Arguello)
hook: Everyone knows McLaren. Almost no one remembers Patrick Quigley, the laborer who helped build the park and raised a family inside it.
story: Patrick Quigley joined the park workforce in 1872 at $80 a month and collected nearly five hundred paychecks over a forty-year career, bridging the eras of William Hammond Hall and John McLaren [1]. The commission gave his family a house on a two-acre triangle west of today's Kezar Stadium, bounded by Kezar Drive, Lincoln Way and the line of Arguello Boulevard, and the Quigleys lived there for four decades [1]. Several Quigley men worked in the park; another son, George, became a pharmacist nearby, which historian Angus Macfarlane jokes made him the Haight-Ashbury's first 'drug dealer' [1]. The park also took its toll: in June 1907 son Charles was killed by a hit-and-run driver near the park police station [1]. Then came 1912. Joseph, a park employee, died in April; his mother Mary soon after; son James in early November. On November 14, 1912, Patrick died at home aged 83, still on the payroll, and the commission granted his heirs an unprecedented full month's pay [1]. The empty house burned in a 1914 arson fire [1]. Nearby, the park nursery site later became Kezar Stadium [2].

title: Muni's first car house, cut by a cemetery
place: Presidio Division (Geary Car House), 949 Presidio Avenue at Geary Boulevard
hook: America's first big-city public transit system was run for nearly a century from a car barn with one corner lopped off, because a graveyard was in the way.
story: In 1912 the new Municipal Railway built its Geary Car House at Geary and Presidio Avenue. It was a reinforced-concrete building on bedrock, with streetcar shops, storage tracks, a three-storey office tower and an Art Deco relief over the bronze doors at 949 Presidio Avenue [1]. Its neighbours were the dead: Laurel Hill Cemetery lay to the north and Calvary Cemetery across Geary. The building's northeast corner had to be cut at an odd angle to fit the edge of Laurel Hill, and the clipped corner can still be seen beside the bus-yard entrance [2]. The cemeteries also blocked streets. Bush and Post dead-ended at Laurel Hill, and business owners had to settle for a short jog linking Bush with Masonic [3]. After Laurel Hill's graves went to Colma, Muni dug a trolley-bus yard in the late 1940s right on top of the old cemetery ground, and the building became Presidio Division [1][2]. The streetcar bays along Geary were once used to store the city's voting machines. The building was Muni's headquarters until the early 2000s. It is now Muni's oldest bus yard, and SFMTA plans to rebuild it [1].

title: Piers for an Army across the Pacific
place: Lower Fort Mason piers (today Fort Mason Center)
hook: Starting in 1912 the Army built three piers and a tunnel under the bluff here, turning an old gun post into the supply door to its Pacific outposts.
story: By the early 20th century the U.S. Army was building new posts in Hawaii, the Philippines and other Pacific islands, and most of the supplies for them went through San Francisco [1]. In 1912 the Army began building piers and sheds at the foot of Fort Mason to store supplies and to serve as the home base for the ships of the Army Transport Service [1]. By 1915 three piers and their warehouses were finished, and the Fort Mason Tunnel had been driven under the upper post to link the docks with the State Belt Railroad on the Embarcadero [1][2]. The old harbour-defence post had become a logistics and transport hub [1][2]. The Army ferry General Frank M. Coxe made as many as eight scheduled runs a day to the processing centre at Fort McDowell on Angel Island [1]. Photos from the 1920s show four big Army transports tied up beside the warehouses [2]. Its biggest years were still ahead. The Park Service describes the Port of Embarkation as built in 1915, though it was formally designated under that name on May 6, 1932 [1][2]. In the Second World War it shipped out two-thirds of all the troops sent to the Pacific [1]. The piers and sheds are now Fort Mason Center [3].
