title: Puerto Rico's club on Athens Street
place: 596 Athens Street, near Russia Avenue (early home of Club Puertorriqueño)
hook: San Francisco's Puerto Rican club began at an Excelsior corner bar, founded by immigrants who had been recruited for Hawaii's sugar plantations and stayed here instead.
story: Club Puertorriqueño de San Francisco was founded in 1912 so that Puerto Rico would be represented at the Panama-Pacific International Exposition of 1915. Its founders were Puerto Rican immigrants who had been recruited to work on Hawaii's sugar plantations. Some of them got as far as San Francisco, decided not to go on, and built a Puerto Rican community in the Bay Area instead [2]. In its early years the club met at a bar on the corner of Athens Street and Russia Avenue, near the home of its first president, Raymond Milan [1]. It later bought a building on Athens Street as its headquarters. The 1957 city directory still lists 'Club Puertorriqueno' at 596 Athens, and the club stayed there until it moved to the Mission in the 1970s [1]. Back then the Excelsior's mix included Italian, Maltese, German, Ukrainian and Irish families [1]. Irma Iris Vargas joined the club in 1974, when she was 18. Her Puerto Rican-born parents had joined in 1953, and when the club turned 50 in 1962 her father was vice president [2]. The club, which bills itself as the oldest Latinx organisation in the United States, now meets at 3249a Mission Street [2].

title: Steam Beer Beside a Vanished Lake
place: Eagle Brewing Company, 5050 Mission Street at Seneca Avenue
hook: Painted signs read MALT, HOPS, STEAM BEER AND PORTER. The Excelsior once had its own brewery, with its name spelled out in hedges.
story: A 1916 photograph looking down Mission Street near Seneca shows a big building covered in painted words: 'MALT,' 'HOPS,' 'STEAM BEER AND PORTER.' The front lawn had letters cut into topiary hedges [1]. This was the Eagle Brewing Company. It started in 1899 on Guerrero Street and moved to Harrison Street, where fire destroyed the brewery in 1911. From 1912 the company brewed at 5050 Mission Street [1]. Its building, designed by C. A. Meussdorffer, had a grand, vaguely Mission-style front. Behind it was a three-storey wooden plant with a 40-foot brick oil-fired oven and an iron smokestack 20 feet above the roof, plus a barn and its own electric plant, close to the railway on today's Alemany Boulevard [1]. SF Heritage says Prohibition shut it in 1918. The cross street was then called Mohawk, and an 1873 map shows a small 'Lake Geneva' nearby, one of the city's vanished waters [1]. Industry was coming to Mission Street. From about 1914 to 1923 the Green Valley Macaroni Factory made pasta at 4736 Mission [2].

title: Steam Beer Rises Again on Folsom Street
place: Jackson Brewing Company, 1489 Folsom Street at 11th Street
hook: The Jackson Brewing Company's new brewery was half-built when the 1906 earthquake wrecked it. The family rebuilt, brewed for a few years, then Prohibition arrived.
story: The Jackson Brewing Company was older than most of San Francisco. Irish-born Thomas Green and Jacob Lynn started it around 1858-59 near the waterfront, and German immigrants William A. Frederick and Joseph Behrens bought it about 1867 [1][2]. After Frederick died around 1885, his Irish-born widow Mary ran the business with two employees, and their son William Jr. later became president [1]. In 1905 the company began a big brick brewery at Folsom and 11th streets. The 1906 earthquake and fire wrecked it while it was still under construction; only a fragment of a ground floor and an arched carriage entrance were salvaged [1][2]. In 1912 engineer James T. Ludlow designed Romanesque Revival replacements, and by 1913 fire-insurance surveyors noted 110 barrels of steam beer per brew; by 1919, 279 [1]. Then Prohibition effectively ended the brewing, and when repeal came in 1933 the brewery never reopened [1]. The family held the property until 1947 [2]. When daughter Mary Louise Frederick died in 1942, she left the bulk of a $300,000 fortune to charity [1]. The brick complex survives and joined the National Register in 1993 [2].

title: The 850-Foot Lighthouse That Never Rose
place: Heights of Lincoln Park, near the Legion of Honor
hook: The first plans for the 1915 world's fair put an 850-foot tower on these cemetery heights, honouring the pioneers. It would have been a lighthouse, too.
story: After the 1906 earthquake and fire, San Francisco rebuilt fast. Many people regretted that the city had missed its chance to carry out Daniel Burnham's grand 1905 plan [1]. The first plans for the Panama-Pacific International Exposition read, as historian Gray Brechin puts it, like an atonement for the hasty rebuilding. Instead of one fairground, the exposition would turn the whole city into a fair with permanent improvements. There would be centres in Golden Gate Park, Lincoln Park, Harbor View, on Telegraph Hill and along the waterfront, linked by lit, planted boulevards [1]. The boldest piece was for this headland. A permanent tower 850 feet high would rise on the heights of Lincoln Park. It would honour the 'heroic pioneers' and double as an immense lighthouse at the Golden Gate [1]. In 1912 the citywide plan was dropped because of its enormous cost. The fair shrank to 635 acres at Harbor View and in the Presidio [1]. At the time the ground here was the old City Cemetery, only recently handed to the park commissioners and named Lincoln Park in 1909 [2]. Lincoln Park got a piece of the fair all the same. After the exposition, a permanent copy of its French Pavilion went up here as the Legion of Honor [3].

title: The Firehouse That Went Dark in 1918
place: Former Engine Company 43, 724 Brazil Avenue
hook: The Excelsior got its own horse-drawn fire company in 1912. Six years later the company was disbanded, and it stayed shut for seven years.
story: The firehouse at 724 Brazil Avenue went up in 1911, when horses still pulled the engines. Like other firehouses of the time it had a tall tower for hanging wet hoses to dry [1]. Engine Company 43 was organised in 1912 and moved in, giving the growing district a company of its own [2]. The fire department's historical records show the company disbanded on August 15, 1918, and not reorganised at the same Brazil Avenue quarters until 1925. For seven years the Excelsior's firehouse had no company [2]. The records do not say why. Once revived, Engine 43 stayed on Brazil Avenue until 1970, when it moved to new quarters at 720 Moscow Street [2]. The city auctioned the old firehouse in 1976 and it became a private home. It had a moment of fame when it was featured in the 2001 film 'The Princess Diaries' [1].

title: The House That Walked to Funston
place: 1322 Funston Avenue (moved from 831 Irving St)
hook: A family bought an old photo and gasped: it showed their Funston Avenue home standing on Irving Street.
story: Around 1990 Michael Farfan and his father were looking through Greg Gaar's vintage photographs when they found their own house. The family had rented 1322 Funston Avenue in 1965 and later bought it. In the photo the house stood alone and stately on Irving Street, with the future UCSF in the distance. Gaar guessed the spot was the south side of Irving between 9th and 10th Avenues, around 1915. Farfan's own research dated the house to 1900; he guessed it was moved between 1915 and 1935, and never found out who built it [1]. Historian William Kostura's research fills in the story. He dates it to 1902, built at 831 Irving Street for Ermina Cox, mother of the builder Ed Cox, and moved to Funston Avenue in 1912, earlier than Gaar's photo date suggests [2]. Ed Cox and his brother Levitt became the most prolific builders in the Inner Sunset's history. During 1906–1916 they put up 101 known houses and four apartment buildings, mostly Craftsman rows, and about 75 of those houses still stand [2]. It was not the only house to move. In 1913 the O'Brien house of 1889 was rolled around the corner to 627–633 Irving and raised over an auto repair shop [2].

title: The Playground That Made a Hall of Famer
place: Excelsior Playground, Russia Avenue and Madrid Street
hook: The Excelsior Playground opened in July 1912. One block away lived a boy who would become one of baseball's greatest shortstops.
story: On July 30, 1912, a crowd gathered between Madrid and Edinburgh streets to dedicate the Excelsior Playground. The photographer labelled it 'No. 3 Excelsior Homestead Play Grounds,' with the houses of Russia Avenue behind [1][2]. San Francisco's playgrounds then had directors who organised teams and games against other playgrounds, and this one was a block from the house of a young Joe Cronin [3]. His Irish-born father had moved the family to the Excelsior after the 1906 fire. Joe played soccer, ran track and won the boys' city tennis championship in 1920, but baseball was his first love [3]. In 1922 he and Wally Berger helped Mission High win the city baseball championship. After Mission High burned he moved to Sacred Heart, which won the citywide prep title in his senior year, 1924 [3]. That autumn he turned down the hometown Seals for a better offer from a Pittsburgh Pirates scout. He went on to star as a shortstop and manager and was elected to the Baseball Hall of Fame in 1956 [3][4].

title: The Streetcar to the Stars
place: Summit terminus of the old 6-line, 9th Ave & Pacheco St
hook: In 1912 a brass band rode a streetcar all the way from the Ferry Building to a sandy hilltop, where 4,000 people danced until sunset.
story: On Sunday, June 16, 1912, two streetcars draped in bunting and full of dignitaries left the Ferry Building. A band rode along and played the whole way to the sandy heights at 9th Avenue and Pacheco Street [1]. The day before, United Railroads had begun running its Hayes and Masonic line up 9th Avenue to Pacheco [1]. At the mostly empty summit the Upper Sunset Improvement Club put up a grandstand, tents and a giant American flag, and served free food. A reported 4,000 people stayed for speeches and danced 'until sunset' [1]. Bob Fisher, a longtime Sunset Heights resident, said the neighbours had paid for the extension and nicknamed it the 'streetcar to the stars.' Rail historian Walter Rice also heard that developers paid. That was common at the time, and Forest Hill went on sale just as the line opened [1]. In 1916 it was renamed the 6 Haight and Masonic, running from the Ferry Building via Haight, Parnassus and Judah to 9th and Pacheco [1][2]. A 1939 photo caption calls the hill the highest rail location the city ever had. The last streetcars climbed here on July 3, 1948 [1].

title: The Waller Street firehouse that guarded the Sunset
place: Hose Company #30 Firehouse, 1757 Waller St
hook: From a granite-and-wood firehouse near Stanyan Street, one ladder company answered alarms across the whole Sunset District, all the way to the Pacific.
story: In 1895 the city built a two-storey Italianate firehouse on Waller Street, between Stanyan and Shrader, for Engine Company No. 30. The western neighbourhoods were still thinly settled then. The Haight was growing mainly because Golden Gate Park drew weekend crowds [1]. The building's busiest years came after the earthquake, as houses spread over the sand dunes to the west. From 1912 to 1956 it was home to Truck Company No. 12. The city's landmark ordinance says its district covered the entire Sunset, out to the Pacific Ocean [1]. Engine 30 was disbanded in 1918, and Chemical Company No. 5 moved in. The building served as a firehouse until 1959 [1]. Look up at the front today and the old tenants are still listed. The moulded panels are lettered "Chemical 5," "S.F.F.D." and "Truck 12," above carriage doors and arched windows [1]. The city calls it one of San Francisco's earliest surviving firehouses and a rare intact pre-1900 non-residential building in the neighbourhood. The Board of Supervisors made it a city landmark in 2026 [1][2].

title: The district attorney's house on Green Street
place: Charles and Ethel Fickert house, 1060 Green St (Paris Block)
hook: In 1912 District Attorney Charles Fickert built a house on Russian Hill's Paris Block. Four years later his office sent an innocent labour leader toward execution.
story: The 1000 block of Green Street, the "Paris Block", lost the houses on its north side in the 1906 fire, and they were rebuilt in 1912–13 [1]. One of the new houses, 1060 Green, was designed by Edward T. Foulkes for Charles M. Fickert, a former Stanford football guard and coach who became district attorney in 1910 [1][2]. The National Register nomination is blunt: history gives him "an unsavory reputation" as the DA who had the city's graft trials dismissed and who framed the evidence against Tom Mooney [1]. After a bomb exploded at the Preparedness Day parade on July 22, 1916, Fickert's office charged the labour militant Mooney and Warren Billings. A photograph placing Tom and Rena Mooney on the Eilers Building on Market Street, a mile away, at the moment they were said to be planting the bomb was in the prosecutors' hands but never shown at trial [3]. Witnesses later said Fickert coached them to lie [2]. Mooney's death sentence was commuted after President Wilson intervened, but he was not pardoned until January 1939 [3]. Fickert lost the office in 1920, and he brawled with critics including the editor Fremont Older [2]. In 1935 his wife Ethel divorced him, citing drinking and gambling, and was awarded the house on Green Street [2].

title: The people's railroad rolls down Geary
place: Geary Street between Laguna and Webster, on the original Municipal Railway line
hook: After a bribery scandal and a bloody strike, voters bought a streetcar line of their own. Mayor Rolph took the controls on its first run.
story:
By 1902 one company, United Railroads, controlled nearly all of San Francisco's streetcar lines. In 1907 the graft prosecution revealed that the company had paid to secure the supervisors' consent. The same year it violently broke the carmen's strike, which earned it the lasting hostility of organized labour [1]. In December 1909, after three failed attempts, voters approved bonds by a three-to-one margin to buy the independent Geary Street cable line, electrify it and extend it down Market Street [1][2]. The Geary cable ran for the last time on 5 May 1912 [2].

Construction had crawled under Mayor P. H. McCarthy. His successor, James Rolph, brought in the traction expert Bion J. Arnold and moved to contract building. The remaining 3.5 miles of track were finished in less than six months [1]. The builder W. L. Holman had delivered only 10 of the 43 cars ordered [3]. Rolph drove the first car himself and told the crowd: 'It is in reality the people's road, built by the people and with the people's money' [2]. The sources give the opening date as 28 December or 30 December 1912 [2][3]. Supporters called it the nation's first municipally owned streetcar line [1].

title: The tunnel Fillmore Street almost got
place: Planned south portal of the Fillmore Street Tunnel, Fillmore Street just south of Sutter
hook: In 1912 the city voted to bore a streetcar tunnel from Sutter Street under Pacific Heights to the World's Fair. Then one merchant got his tax bill.
story: Fillmore merchants had a problem. "Proud as we are of Fillmore Street, it is today a cul-de-sac with a wall at each end," one of their brochures complained [1]. With the 1915 Panama-Pacific Exposition rising on the bay shore, the Fillmore Street Improvement Association campaigned for a tunnel. Transit expert Bion J. Arnold endorsed a route under the hill from Sutter to Filbert Street [1]. On 23 April 1912 the city adopted the plan: a bore 4,332 feet long with a gentle 2 percent grade for streetcars, cars and pedestrians, starting from a portal at Fillmore and Sutter [1][2]. Property owners would pay through an assessment district. Heiress Virginia Vanderbilt, who owned 22 blocks of the future Marina, refused to meet the delegation sent to New York to ask her to contribute [1]. In September 1913 the association's own vice chairman, Samuel Adelstein, received a bill of $2,309.50 for his Fillmore Street lot between Post and Geary. He thought it unfair and went overnight from the tunnel's leading champion to its chief opponent. Within days the supervisors voted to postpone the project indefinitely, blaming high assessments and the risk it would not be finished before the fair opened [1]. Fairgoers came by the new Stockton Street Tunnel instead, or rode the Fillmore Street streetcar over the hill [1].

title: The urologist's brick jewel box
place: Dr. Martin Krotoszyner Medical Offices and Residence, 995-999 Sutter Street at Hyde
hook: A German philology student turned ship's surgeon brought the cystoscope to San Francisco, then built one of downtown's finest doctor's office buildings.
story: Martin Krotoszyner was born in Ostrowo, Germany, in 1861 and, fluent in Greek and Latin, began studying philology in Berlin to become a teacher. After three semesters he switched to medicine [1]. With his medical degree in hand he answered an advertisement for a ship's surgeon and reached New York in March 1888 [1]. He filled in for a young doctor in Arizona, found frontier life not to his liking, and moved on to Los Angeles, which was just as hot. That autumn he came to San Francisco, where he had relatives, and set up at 43 Sixth Street [1]. After six months of specialist study in Germany in 1893, he is credited with bringing the cystoscope to San Francisco, demonstrating it in 1894 [1]. He became chief urologist at the French Hospital and later at the German (Franklin) Hospital, and at the Polyclinic he "trained many of the best known urologists in San Francisco" [1]. In 1911–12 the architect Herman Barth designed this combined office and home for him on the southeast corner of Sutter and Hyde, with a richly mottled brick front [1][2]. The ground floor held his office, reception and examining rooms. The family lived upstairs, staying on after his death in 1918 until 1938 [1]. It is thought the finest of its kind downtown [2].

title: A Suburb Laid Out by a Park Ranger
place: El Camino del Mar at 25th Avenue, gateway to Sea Cliff
hook: The man who curved Sea Cliff's streets was also running America's national parks at the time, and he believed the landscape architect's best skill was knowing what not to do.
story: Sea Cliff was planned as a residence park, an exclusive enclave set among the Richmond District's working-class cottages and sand dunes. The John Brickell Company, working with several other firms, started it in 1913 [1]. The streets were laid out by the landscape architect Mark Daniels. In 1914 he was hired as landscape engineer at Yosemite, and within months he had been promoted to general superintendent of all the national parks [2]. In his spare time he was laying out Sea Cliff and Crocker-Amazon [3]. Daniels later shaped the 17-Mile Drive at Pebble Beach and helped plan Bel-Air [2][3]. His creed, published in 1915, was that the landscape architect's art "consists more in knowing what not to do than what to do" [2]. By June 1924 the magazine The Home Designer was running a whole feature on "Homes in Sea Cliff", with interiors of Harry B. Allen's house. It reported that a newly finished Sea Cliff house had been chosen and furnished as the city's show home for the national Better Homes campaign [4].

title: A firehouse that waited for engines
place: Fire Station 44, 1298 Girard Street at Wilde Avenue
hook: The city finished this brick firehouse in 1913, then left it empty for two years while the horses gave way to motor engines.
story: Before the city firehouse opened, the valley relied on its own Volunteer Hose Company. Its Fireman's Hall on Wilde Avenue doubled as a place for dances and even housed a kindergarten for a while [2]. Then in 1913 the city put up Station 44 at Girard Street and Wilde Avenue, designed by architect John Reid Jr. [1]. Firefighters did not move in until 1915. The department was waiting for delivery of modern motor-driven equipment, because horses were finally on their way out [1]. The building has a brick front, careful cornice work and three recessed balconies that remind Heritage's Woody LaBounty of an Italian villa. Its historic integrity is very high [1]. A 1976 city survey was lukewarm about it. The Planning Department lists its status as 'unknown', although a similar Reid firehouse at 100 Hoffman Street in wealthier Noe Valley is recognised as a historic resource [1]. Heritage calls it the oldest firehouse still in active service. In 2021, still without landmark status, it was one of the group's three 'easy' landmark candidates for a neighbourhood that had no city landmarks at all [1].

title: A giant sundial unveiled at night
place: Ingleside Terraces Sundial, Entrada Court
hook: Billed as the world's biggest sundial, this 28-foot gnomon was unveiled after dark, by children dressed as sylphs, to sell houses.
story: On October 10, 1913, some 1,500 people gathered on a new cul-de-sac in Ingleside Terraces to unveil a sundial. It was promoted as the biggest in the world, and they did it at night [1]. The date was chosen to mark the day the Atlantic and Pacific first met in the Panama Canal and to celebrate the coming Twin Peaks Tunnel [1]. The developer Joseph Leonard narrated. City Engineer Michael O'Shaughnessy was there and the Coast Artillery Band played [1]. Schoolchildren dressed as sylphs unveiled each part: a 28-foot gnomon, a 34-foot clock face in Roman numerals, a lit reflecting pool with fountain, and four columns and urns for 'the four ages of man and nature's four seasons'. A baby rode in a pram 'drawn by a stork'. Then fifty couples danced into the night [1]. It was a sales gimmick, a Beaux-Arts ornament meant to draw buyers to the new residence park [2][3]. A popular story later claimed the sundial was left over from the racetrack. It wasn't [1].

title: A seamstress on Taylor Street finds the stage
place: Modotti family flat, 1952 Taylor St
hook: In 1913 a teenage factory worker from Udine moved into a flat on Russian Hill's north-east slope. Within five years Italian San Francisco was applauding Tina Modotti.
story: Tina Modotti was born in Udine, in north-east Italy, in 1896 and as a girl worked in a textile factory to help feed her family [1][2]. Her father, Giuseppe, a machinist and socialist, had gone ahead to San Francisco's Italian quarter [1]. In 1913 she crossed the Atlantic alone to join him, at 16 by one account and 17 by another [1][2]. Home was a first-floor, two-bedroom flat at 1952 Taylor Street on the north-east slope of Russian Hill, whose bay window caught a glimpse of the bay [1]. Giuseppe had a machine shop on Montgomery Avenue, where he later designed a popular ravioli machine. Tina joined her sister Mercedes as a seamstress at I. Magnin and was soon modelling its newest designs at the downtown store [1]. She acted in the neighbourhood's amateur Italian theatres, and in 1917 she made her professional debut with the Città di Firenze company. The paper L'Italia wrote that the evening would "always leave in her all of that freshness of a soul in love with her art" [1]. In 1918 she left for Los Angeles and the movies with the poet and painter Roubaix de l'Abrie Richey [1][2]. She went on to become one of the great photographers of 1920s Mexico [1][2].

title: A suffragist's nickelodeon and the King of Bs
place: 2780 Diamond Street (site of the Glenodeon / Diamond Theatre, demolished)
hook: A woman ran Glen Park's first picture house in a trade run by men. Its last manager was a teenager who went on to make 'The Fly'.
story:
In 1913 Glen Park got its own nickelodeon, the Glenodeon, on Diamond Street just north of Chenery. Its proprietor was Caroline Evers, a Canadian-born suffragist and the first president of the Glen Park Outdoor Art League. Almost all theatre owners were men at the time [1]. Along with silent serials the little hall held political meetings. In 1915 Mayor "Sunny Jim" Rolph and City Engineer Michael O'Shaughnessy came to argue for the water bond tied to the Hetch Hetchy project [1]. Evers renamed the theatre the Diamond in 1917, and in 1920 she personally welcomed cowboy star Tom Mix to a convention of theatre owners [1].

She left the business around 1926. The theatre reopened in 1927 and closed for good in 1929, the year talking pictures arrived [2]. A teenage orphan named Bob Lippert later said he had run a movie house at Diamond and Chenery. Historians think he was probably running the Diamond in those last years [2]. Lippert went on to own a chain of more than a hundred theatres and to finance more than 300 films, among them I Shot Jesse James and The Fly. He became known as the "King of the Bs" [2][3].

title: Brick Gates on a Grid
place: Windsor Terrace, 8th Avenue at Lawton Street
hook: The developers of Sea Cliff gave a block and a half of the Inner Sunset its own ceremonial gates.
story: Once streetcars climbed 9th Avenue to Pacheco Street, the hilly southern blocks of the Inner Sunset began to fill with larger houses [1]. In 1913 the developers Allen and Company, who were building Sea Cliff at about the same time, laid out Windsor Terrace. It covers both sides of 8th Avenue and the east side of 9th Avenue between Lawton and Moraga Streets [1]. Early in 1914 the Chronicle called it 'City's Newest Park' [1]. Like other San Francisco residence parks it announced itself with ceremonial gates, here of brick. Unlike most of them, it kept the city's rectangular street grid instead of curving its streets [1]. A 1939 photograph of a 6-line streetcar at 9th and Lawton has one of the pillars in the frame [2]. Allen and Company built the first sixteen houses in 1913–1915, hiring architects Albert Farr, Dolliver and Swain, and H. R. Schulze. Farr's 1635 8th Avenue is Arts and Crafts [1]. The rest came slowly, as individual owners commissioned Harold Stoner, J. C. Hladik and others through the 1920s and 1930s. The result is a group of freestanding, mostly stucco houses, a little larger than their neighbours, in Arts and Crafts, Spanish Colonial, Classical and Tudor dress [1].

title: De Young's Dunes Become Nelson's Villas
place: Fernando Nelson's house, 2701 Lincoln Way at 28th Avenue (Parkway Terrace)
hook: In 1913 a builder bought newspaper baron M.H. de Young's empty dunes along Lincoln Way. He added stone benches and put his name on the sewer covers.
story: On February 27, 1913, the Chronicle reported 'the largest deal of its kind in the history of San Francisco.' Builder Fernando Nelson had bought four blocks between Lincoln Way and Irving Street, from 27th to 33rd Avenue, from M.H. de Young, who had held them empty since buying from Adolph Sutro in 1897. Nelson bought a fifth block from Lyon & Hoag, at nearly $45,000 a block [1]. The Lincoln Way streetcar made the land attractive. The Chronicle had just reported that new homes were going up fast facing the park [2]. Nelson graded the dunes and set the houses on raised berms, with garages dug in at street level. He put the wires in back yards, widened the avenues slightly mid-block, and placed rounded stone benches where each avenue meets Lincoln Way. Sewer covers in the sidewalks still carry his name [1]. His own Italian villa at 2701 Lincoln Way had solid mahogany rooms and a rooftop pergola facing the ocean. His wife Julia died after surgery in October 1916, soon after they moved in [1]. Over 60-plus years Nelson built about 4,000 houses. In 2015 the San Fran Dhammaram Temple restored the neglected villa as a home for its Buddhist nuns [1].

title: Dish Night at 'The Flea Bag'
place: Former Alta / New Potrero Theater, 312 Connecticut Street
hook: The hilltop picture house showed The Perils of Pauline, gave free china to the ladies, and later housed the Grateful Dead at work on an album.
story:
The brick building with black columns at 312 Connecticut Street, just up from 18th Street, opened in 1913 as the Alta Theater. It showed silent films, among them the 1914 serial The Perils of Pauline. When it converted to sound in 1929 it was renamed the New Potrero Theater, and it served as the neighbourhood's movie house until 1963 [1].

Locals had their own names for it, first "The Nick" and later "The Flea Bag." They also remembered Dish Night, when china was handed out "Free to the Ladies." In 1937 a film of St. Teresa's Church's saint's-day procession was made to be shown only at this theater [1][2].

In 1968 the Grateful Dead used it while working on their album Anthem of the Sun [1], which Warner Bros. released that July [3]. In 1973 it appeared in an episode of The Streets of San Francisco. In 1993 the San Francisco Gurdjieff Society bought it for $280,000 [1]. The ticket booth, marquee and sloping floor are long gone [1].

title: Free ambulances from Stanyan Street
place: Park Emergency Hospital, 811 Stanyan St
hook: For decades, a hurt San Franciscan could be stitched up or driven off in an ambulance for free. One of the stations stood at the edge of the park.
story: The single-storey Park Emergency Aid Station went up on Stanyan Street near Beulah in 1902. It was part of a system that later ran five aid stations and 14 ambulances, all free of charge and backed by San Francisco General Hospital [1][2]. A 1920s photograph shows a horse-drawn ambulance parked out front, with its driver and attendant [1]. The city was early to motorise. The historian Ryan Bell, in The Ambulance: A History, wrote that San Francisco had one of the first automobile ambulances in the nation in 1913 and "never looked back." By 1932 the emergency ambulances were answering five calls a day. The stations were placed so an ambulance could reach any call within six minutes [1]. The system drew national magazine coverage. In 1964 the Examiner called it the "only one of its kind in the U.S." [1] Most cases at the aid stations were cuts, bites and specks in the eye. But the crews also worked through the bloodshed of the 1934 waterfront strike and the V-J Day riot of 1945 [1]. Park station stopped treating patients in 1978 and stayed an ambulance station until 1991. Today it is city Landmark No. 201 [2].

title: Garages in the Basement, Park at the Door
place: 15th Avenue between Lincoln Way & Irving St
hook: In 1913 the Chronicle watched sand dunes along Lincoln Way turn into rows of Craftsman homes, each with a garage tucked into the basement.
story: On January 18, 1913, the Chronicle reported that no part of San Francisco was growing faster than the Sunset's first tier of blocks between Lincoln Way, 'formerly H street,' and Irving Street [1]. Builders had arrived only a year earlier. Now, 'instead of sand dunes there are rows of very attractive homes,' priced from $5,000 to $10,000 and many already occupied by 'delighted owners' [1]. Most were two stories and a basement, 'with garages in the basements.' The majority followed Craftsman ideals, and some were Italian Renaissance [1]. The Sunset Home Realty Company was building a row on 15th Avenue between Lincoln Way and 'I street,' which the paper still called by its letter three years after the renaming, with 'each house' in 'a different style.' The McKillop brothers were putting up houses on 8th Avenue near Lincoln [1]. United Railroads was relaying heavy rail on Lincoln Way for beach traffic, and the city was about to pave the park side of the street [1]. The paper said buyers had turned into 'boosters' for the Sunset and the park [1]. Most of the district was still sand, though, and full development of its blocks would take until after World War II [2].

title: Mrs. Davis's club for Glen Park's children
place: Surrey Street between Diamond and Castro streets
hook: In 1913 a Black evangelist from Surrey Street told reformers she had started a club for Glen Park's boys and girls. Then she vanished from the record.
story: Mamie F. Davis was born in California in June 1875. In 1900 she was a 24-year-old waitress living with her widowed mother, Annie, a Louisiana-born seamstress who ran a boarding house on Minna Street [1]. By 1913 the city directory listed Mrs. Davis on Surrey Street between Diamond and Castro [1], a street where, after the earthquake, Umbsden Realty sold small cottages to working-class buyers; a row of six identical ones survives [2]. In February 1912 the new Colored Women's Nonpartisan League, formed to study politics, was the only club to enrol en masse at a St. Francis Hotel registration. That October Davis spoke to the League on social education, and to the California League for the Protection of Motherhood in favour of pensions for working mothers. In December she represented the Nonpartisan League at the convention of the California Federation of Women's Clubs [1]. In March 1913, described in the press as a "negro evangelist," she told the Juvenile Protective Association that she had set up a neighbourhood club for boys and girls in Glen Park, and asked for help to open a reading room. After that she disappears from public records [1]. Glen Park's history project calls her the first African American woman in San Francisco linked to a women's club that it has yet identified [1].

title: Ostriches in the Fog at 47th Avenue
place: Site of the Golden Gate Ostrich Farm, north side of Balboa Street between 46th and 47th Avenues
hook: In 1913 investors bet that African ostriches could turn a profit on the windy dunes by Sutro Heights. Then Paris changed its hats.
story:
Ostrich plumes were the height of fashion, and ads promised ostrich farms were a sure thing. The Golden Gate Ostrich Farm incorporated in late November 1912 and asked permission to open on the north side of Balboa Street between 46th and 47th Avenues. The Sutro heirs protested about the smell. They lost, and the farm opened on March 1, 1913, where the show was the plucking of its prize bird, "William Jennings Bryant" [1].

But it sat two steep blocks from the nearest streetcar stop. When the city's new Geary line reached Cabrillo Street and the Great Highway on June 25, 1913, the farm leased a lot facing the end of the tracks and moved its fences there by August [1].

When war broke out in 1914, Paris hats turned to plain turbans and feather sales plummeted; one paper said a whole ostrich was now worth about what one feather used to fetch. The farm let its one-year lease lapse in August 1915 and "loaned" its 20 birds to Golden Gate Park. By 1916 park staff were boiling the eggs and feeding them to the peacocks [1]. It lasted five months on Balboa and a year by the beach. Across Cabrillo, Looff's carousel was going up: the Call announced it in October 1913, though FoundSF dates it to 1912 [1][2].

title: The 'Exposition Church' at Green and Steiner
place: St. Vincent de Paul Church, 2320 Green Street at Steiner
hook: A Catholic parish that began in a Fillmore Street hall finished its church just in time for the world's fair, and crowds filled the pews.
story: Archbishop Patrick Riordan formed the parish of St. Vincent de Paul on August 24, 1901. On September 22 an Irish priest, Father Martin P. Ryan, said its first Mass in a hall near Fillmore and Greenwich [1][2]. The next year the parish built a rectory and a small one-story church at Green and Steiner. Both came through the 1906 earthquake [1][2]. In June 1902 the Call announced a grander 'sacred edifice of great beauty' in Northern Italian Romanesque style, but it proved too ambitious for a young parish [1]. Work on the present church, designed by Shea and Lofquist around the earlier building, started in 1911, and it opened with a celebration Mass on October 26, 1913 [1]. Father Ryan had reportedly spent time in Switzerland and liked Swiss buildings, so he asked the architects to take their cue from them [1]. The timing was lucky: the Panama-Pacific Exposition opened on the bay 16 months later. Locals and visitors crowded in, the Mass schedule was expanded for the length of the fair, and it became known as the 'Exposition Church' [1]. A parish school was added next door in 1924 [1].

title: The 'unsafe' school that was never demolished
place: Old Lowell High School, now City College John Adams Campus, 1860 Hayes Street at Masonic
hook: For fifty years the city's top public high school filled this brick block. Students left in 1962 believing it would be torn down. It never was.
story: In January 1913 Lowell High School, the city's college-preparatory public school, moved into a full block of brick buildings bounded by Hayes, Masonic, Ashbury and Grove [1][2]. Students had to be recommended to get in. They came from all over the city by cable car, streetcar and trolley bus [1]. For half a century its halls turned out politicians, artists and business people: Cyril Magnin (1918), Governor Pat Brown (1923), William Hewlett (1930), Carol Channing (1938), the painter Richard Diebenkorn (1939) and Justice Stephen Breyer (1955) [1]. In 1952 the school began looking for a new site near Lake Merced, and it moved there in 1962 [2]. Students were told the old campus was seismically unsafe and would be demolished. It wasn't. The brick buildings survived and became part of City College [1]. On May 19, 2012, the class of 1962, the last to spend four years here, borrowed the building back for its 50th reunion and filed into the third-floor auditorium as if for an assembly. "It still smells exactly the same," said art dealer Ed Russell. "Polished linoleum" [1].

title: The Irish Parish That Rebuilt in Stone
place: St. Joseph's Church, 1401 Howard Street at 10th Street
hook: Fire erased St. Joseph's parish at Tenth and Howard in 1906. The Romanesque church its people raised afterward outlived the neighborhood that built it.
story: St. Joseph's parish had stood at Tenth and Howard since Archbishop Joseph Alemany dedicated its first church on December 8, 1861. By 1906 it served more than 3,000 families, mostly Irish, and the Young Men's Institute, later a national Catholic organization, had been founded there in 1883 [1]. The fire after the April 1906 earthquake destroyed the church and both parish schools. Within months the parish put up a plain hall to serve as church and school at once, and a rectory beside it [1][2]. In April 1913 the cornerstone was laid for a permanent church designed by John J. Foley: a Romanesque Revival basilica with gilded column capitals, rose windows and stained glass imported from Europe, completed the following year [1]. But many of the Irish families who fled the fire never came back, and the blocks around the new church turned industrial [1]. Over the decades the congregation became one of newer immigrants from Latin America, the Pacific Islands and the Philippines. By 1979 most parishioners were Filipino, and St. Joseph's was called the largest Filipino parish in the United States [1][2].

title: The railroad that saved the Palace
place: Belt Railroad line at Marina Boulevard and Laguna Street, beside Fort Mason
hook: Freight tracks laid to build the 1915 fair ended up as a bargaining chip. The Army swapped the Palace of Fine Arts for the right to run trains.
story: In 1913 the state's Board of Harbor Commissioners laid out a Belt Railroad extension from Fort Mason to the exposition site [1]. A railroad tunnel under Fort Mason, which the Park Service dates to the World War I years, carried the line from the downtown waterfront [1][2]. Large amounts of building materials were hauled from the downtown port to the Esplanade, today's Marina Boulevard. The line was not used during the fair itself [1]. The Army saw a use for it afterwards. In 1915 it asked to extend the Belt Line from Fort Mason to the general warehouses in the Presidio. To seal the deal it offered the city the Palace of Fine Arts, the last exposition building still standing on federal land, in exchange for the right to run and maintain a spur track [1]. The swap was ratified in 1927, and the Palace and its grounds have been the city's ever since [1]. The tracks went on to serve two world wars. Troops and supplies moved along them between the Presidio and the Port of Embarkation at Fort Mason. Hospital trains carried wounded men from ships at Fort Mason to Letterman Army Hospital [1]. The Belt Railroad, once 67 miles long, shut down in 1993 [1][2].

title: $17.50 and a shot at the quarry
place: Castro Street near 29th, below the Gray Brothers quarry
hook: A sick, starving quarryman asked a millionaire for $17.50 in back pay. What happened next shut the quarry down, and a jury let him go.
story:
The Gray Brothers quarry above 29th and Castro produced gravel for Noe Valley's roads [1]. Some of its granite went into the walls of St. Paul's Church [2].

On 10 November 1914 Joseph Lococo, a 36-year-old Sicilian immigrant, went to find George Gray at the quarry. He wanted $17.50 in unpaid wages. According to FoundSF, Lococo was sick and had not eaten in two days. His wife and two babies were going hungry, and they were about to be evicted from their home on Arkansas Street. Gray, by then a millionaire, laughed and told him to leave. Lococo shot him dead [3].

Lococo was acquitted, on grounds of temporary insanity according to FoundSF. Both FoundSF and local historian Greg Gaar describe cheering in the courtroom [1][3]. The company went bankrupt and the quarry closed. The scarred hillside became a place for picnics and children's games. Today part of it is Billy Goat Hill [1][3].

title: A Moorish fortress over a buried creek
place: San Francisco Armory, 1800 Mission Street
hook: After 1906 the state built a castle for the National Guard on the site of an old amusement park. For decades its drill floor was the city's boxing capital.
story:
The 1906 disaster wrecked the old armory, and the National Guard ended up in a temporary wooden shed on Van Ness [1][2]. In 1909 Captain Herman G. Stundt lobbied Governor James Gillett for a new armory. On April 20 the governor signed a $420,000 appropriation, as long as San Franciscans raised $100,000 for the land [1]. By the end of the year they had managed only $60,000. The money finally came in after the Real Estate Board pointed out how many construction contracts the project would bring [1].

Woollett & Woollett designed a brick 'Spanish or Moorish fortress'. It went up between September 1912 and June 1914 on part of the old Woodward's Gardens, with Mission Creek still running through the basement [1][2]. Its drill court is said to be the largest unsupported enclosed space in the city [1]. A balcony was added in 1925 for boxing bleachers. From the 1920s to the 1940s, at least two prizefights a week earned the building the nickname 'the Madison Square Garden of the West' [1][2]. It also served as a base for the Guard during the 1934 General Strike [2].

title: A railroad under the point to the fair
place: Belt Line tracks at the north end of Van Ness Avenue, by the Fort Mason Tunnel's east portal
hook: To reach the 1915 world's fair, a waterfront railroad crossed Black Point Cove on a trestle and bored under Fort Mason. The tunnel is still waiting for trains.
story: In 1913 backers of the coming Panama-Pacific International Exposition wanted the waterfront Belt Line Railroad to reach their fairground west of Black Point. They won permission to run it across Black Point Cove, today's Aquatic Park, on an elevated trestle, and to cut a tunnel through Black Point itself. The tailings were dumped beside the trestle [1]. The single-track tunnel opened to trains in 1914. Its east portal is near the north end of Van Ness Avenue, its west portal on Marina Boulevard at Laguna Street. It carried goods and passengers to the fair, and the army used it to build its port of embarkation at Fort Mason [2]. In 1921 the trestle was moved closer inland [1]. The state-owned Belt Railroad, begun in 1889, eventually ran 67 miles of track linking the docks to the big railroads [3]. Part of Dirty Harry was filmed on either side of the tunnel in 1971 [2], and in November 1975 the American Freedom Train's locomotive, Southern Pacific No. 4449, stood on display at Aquatic Park near the foot of Hyde Street [3]. Service ended in 1993 [2][3]. In 2012 the National Park Service released a final environmental report on running Muni's F-line streetcars through the tunnel; in 2017 the cost was put at $60 million [2].

title: A widower's gift: Mount Zion on Post
place: Mount Zion Hospital, Hellman Building, 2200 Post Street
hook: When Esther Hellman died, her grieving husband gave $100,000 so San Francisco's Jewish hospital could rise again in the Western Addition. It is still treating patients.
story: Mount Zion was incorporated as a Jewish hospital in 1887 and opened ten years later at Sutter and Hyde, according to J. The Jewish News Weekly [1]. Historians William Issel and Robert Cherny place its first building on Sutter near Scott and date it to 1898 [2]. The Mount Zion Ladies' Auxiliary Society was central to the hospital, especially under Esther Hellman, wife of the banker Isaias Hellman [1]. When she died in 1908 he gave $100,000 for a new hospital in the Western Addition to be named after her. A UCSF librarian later remarked that it was remarkable the money was raised at all while the city was "in such a demolished state" [1]. Ground was broken in December 1911 and the cornerstone laid in 1912. The Hellman Building at 2200 Post opened in 1914 with room for 160 patients, and private wards cost $3 a day [1]. Issel and Cherny date the new building to 1913 [2]. It was part of a Jewish Western Addition that included synagogues, a Hebrew school and Sinai Memorial Chapel [2]. The building still stands and is now part of UCSF [1].

title: Gracie Allen's age, solved by a yearbook
place: 4th Avenue, Inner Richmond (Allen family home, 1910)
hook: Gracie Allen joked that the 1906 earthquake had destroyed her birth certificate. A Richmond schoolbook bought at an auction helped settle how old she was.
story: Comedian Gracie Allen, George Burns's partner, never gave her age straight. The joke went that the 1906 earthquake had destroyed her birth certificate, and Burns claimed he didn't know how old she was either [1][2]. Birth years given for her range from 1895 to 1906 [1][2]. Historian John Freeman went to Star of the Sea Grammar School in the late 1940s and had heard she was a former student. He won a Star of the Sea yearbook at auction. Its high-school class of 20 had four boys and one Grace Cecelia Allen [1]. The 1910 census showed her family living on Fourth Avenue in the Richmond District. That census wasn't much help on dates: in ten years, family members had aged only three to nine years [1]. Freeman compared her face with a 1914 Chronicle photo of her dancing and went back to the hard-to-read 1900 census. He concluded she was born on July 26, 1895, and graduated from Star of the Sea High School on June 19, 1914, a month before she turned 19 [1]. The Chronicle's list of famous Bay Area graduates also gives her as Star of the Sea, class of 1914 [3].

title: Icicle Field: the Seals' season in the fog
place: Site of Ewing Field, now Ewing Terrace (Masonic Ave & Anza St)
hook: The San Francisco Seals moved to a new ballpark at the foot of Lone Mountain in 1914. They lasted one season. The fog stayed.
story: On May 16, 1914, 18,000 people filled Ewing Field, the Seals' new ballpark at Masonic Avenue and Anza Street. Owner J. Cal Ewing had lost his lease in the Mission, and the foot of Lone Mountain was the only big enough site left [1]. Two boys from Grove Street without the 25-cent admission crawled under the centre-field fence: Scotty Sullivan, the future sportswriter, and Pat Brown, the future governor [1]. Once the sun dropped behind Lone Mountain the wind came up, and someone suggested "Icicle Field" as a better name. Writers in the unheated press box warmed their hands on cans of hot tamales, and on one wet June day Oakland's Elmer Zacher played centre field holding an umbrella [1]. After a single season the Seals went back to the Mission, though the park found a second life as the city's "pigskin palace" in the 1920s [2]. A 21-alarm fire on June 5, 1926 destroyed the grandstand and dozens of nearby homes [2]. In 1932 Boris Karloff played cricket here. The land was sold in 1938, demolition began on Halloween, and the first Ewing Terrace houses were advertised in July 1939 [2].

title: San Francisco's first Carnegie library
place: Richmond Branch Library, 351 9th Ave
hook: The steel magnate Andrew Carnegie's money built libraries across America. The first one San Francisco built with it went up in the Richmond, not downtown.
story: The Richmond got a library early. It was the fourth branch in the San Francisco Public Library system, opened in 1892 at 809 Point Lobos Avenue, now Geary, at Parker Avenue [1]. As the district grew after 1906, the city used a grant from Andrew Carnegie to build a proper branch on Ninth Avenue. It opened in 1914, the first library building in San Francisco paid for with Carnegie money [1]. Architects Bliss & Faville designed it in the Classical Revival style, in sandstone and reinforced concrete [2]. Six more Carnegie branches followed, in Chinatown, Golden Gate Valley, the Mission, Noe Valley, the Presidio and the Sunset, and all seven are still libraries [2]. The Richmond branch became San Francisco Landmark No. 247 after being nominated in December 2000 [1][2]. It reopened in 2009 after a seismic renovation, and today it carries the name of Senator Milton Marks [1].

title: Seventeen dollars and fifty cents
place: Gray Brothers quarry, Castro Street near 30th Street (Billy Goat Hill)
hook: A hungry quarryman asked his millionaire boss for $17.50 in back wages at the Castro Street pit. George Gray laughed at him. It was the last thing he did.
story: George and Harry Gray blasted rock out of San Francisco's hills for ships' ballast, paving and bay fill, and ignored the neighbours whose houses they damaged. After a judge banned their blasting on Telegraph Hill in 1895 they kept moving, and by the 1910s were quarrying at 29th and Castro streets, on today's Billy Goat Hill [1][2]. On 10 November 1914 Joseph Lococo, a 36-year-old Sicilian immigrant, came to that quarry to ask George Gray for $17.50 in back wages. According to one account he was ill, had not eaten for two days, had a wife and two babies who were starving, and was about to be evicted from his house on Arkansas Street. Gray, a millionaire by then, laughed in his face and told him to get out. Lococo pulled a gun and shot him dead [1]. He was acquitted by reason of insanity and, one account says, walked out of court cheered by 100 supporters [1]. The Grays' firm went bankrupt; Harry lived until 1937 [1]. It was not the first such killing: in 1909 the Grays' cashier, Carolyn Bush, had been shot dead by an unpaid worker who lost his temper [1]. The quarry left a scarred hillside above 30th and Castro [1].

title: The Lodge Where the Streetcar Turned
place: Former Parnassus Masonic Temple, 1407 9th Ave (SW corner of Judah)
hook: A classical temple built by Freemasons on a streetcar corner now houses a Taoist temple.
story: By 1914 the Inner Sunset was no longer a scatter of cottages in the dunes. Streetcars on the Parnassus line ran west along Judah Street and turned south up 9th Avenue toward Pacheco. Property owners had agreed to put up $20,000 to bring them [1]. That year the Parnassus Lodge of the Masons built itself a Classical Revival hall on the southwest corner of 9th and Judah, designed by architect Charles A. Haber [1]. A photograph from about 1924 shows the building being painted, with 'for rent' signs in its storefronts and a gas street lamp on the corner [2]. The Masons stayed for decades and were still meeting there in at least 1982. The ground floor has since been altered, but the building now serves as a Taoist temple, and the classical upper floors remain [1]. The corner is also a reminder of how transit shaped the neighbourhood. The Municipal Railway's N-Judah arrived in 1928 [1], and today it too swings around this corner, jogging one block along 9th Avenue to reach Judah [3].

title: The creek the tunnel buried
place: Wawona Street near 15th Avenue, below West Portal (line of the old creek ravine)
hook: A nameless creek once ran from Edgehill past West Portal toward Pine Lake. Its ravine was filled with Twin Peaks Tunnel rubble, but the water still finds its way.
story: A creek nobody seems to have named once drained this part of the west side. Western Neighborhoods Project historians think it started near Edgehill and ran down through what became West Portal toward Stern Grove and Pine Lake [2]. It cut a ravine along present-day Wawona, and the Merlo family's farm lay beside it. Between 1914 and 1917 the ravine was filled with 250,000 cubic yards of earth dug out of the Twin Peaks Tunnel. In 2002 a neighbor on the 200 block of Wawona said sinkholes still opened now and then [1]. When St. Francis Circle was being planned, landscape designers proposed looping the streetcar tracks around the creek so riders could look down on it. City Engineer M. M. O'Shaughnessy turned the idea down [2]. The water hasn't forgotten its old route. On February 14, 1938, after 18 days of rain, the low ground around Wawona and 15th Avenue flooded. Shortly before 2013 a broken water main in the same basin flooded houses about three feet deep [2]. A deep, still-wooded stretch of the old gully survives behind Arden Wood and Sloat Boulevard [2].

title: The fight to save Black Point Cove
place: Aquatic Park beach (Black Point Cove)
hook: Buried under 15,000 truckloads of earthquake rubble and split by a railway trestle, the cove was nearly filled in. Working-class swimmers refused to let it go.
story: Frederick Law Olmsted proposed a waterfront park at Black Point Cove in 1866, a 'sea-gate of the city', but industry and the army kept it from happening [1]. By the 1890s the German-speaking working men of the Dolphin, South End and Ariel rowing and swimming clubs, which began in the 1870s as turnvereins, had been pushed off the waterfront south of Market. By 1900 they had barged their clubhouses to the foot of Van Ness Avenue [1]. Then the cove was buried. After 1906 it was made a dump for the ruined city: 15,000 truckloads of broken brick, stone and burnt rubble covered the beach. In 1913 a Belt Line Railroad trestle was built across the cove for the coming Exposition, and the harbor commissioners pressed to fill it for factories [1]. The swimmers fought back. Voters turned down park bonds in 1909, and again in 1912, when a majority voted yes but fell short of the two-thirds required. On March 13, 1914, Supervisor McLaren's resolution to 'arrest this march of commercialism' passed and the fill permit was refused [1]. The park itself was only dedicated in 1939 [2].

title: The firehouse redrawn without horses
place: Engine Company No. 24, 100 Hoffman Avenue
hook: Halfway through its design, this brick firehouse lost its horse stalls. It was one of the first signs the city's fire department was switching to motor engines.
story:
In 1914 the city built a two-storey brick firehouse on Hoffman Avenue, high on the western slope of Noe Valley. It has an arched entry and a simple bracketed cornice [1]. The architect was John Reid Jr. Two years later he also designed the neighbourhood's Carnegie library [1][2].

What makes the building special is a change to the plans. Reid's first drawings were revised so the station would house motor-driven engines, with no stalls or other provision for horses. NoeHill describes the change as the beginning of the department's switch from horses to motors [1].

The firehouse is still in use. It was enlarged in 1997, and Engine 24 still answers calls from the Hoffman Avenue building, covering Noe Valley, Twin Peaks and parts of the Mission [1][3].

title: The forty-year fight over the dead
place: Former Odd Fellows Cemetery, now Angelo J. Rossi Playground (Arguello Blvd & Anza St)
hook: Twice San Franciscans voted to keep the Lone Mountain cemeteries. The living won anyway, and the headstones ended up in the Bay.
story: In 1895 Richmond District property owners began demanding that the Lone Mountain cemeteries go, calling them "blurs on our fair city's face" [1]. In 1900 Mayor James Phelan signed an ordinance banning burials in the city after August 1, 1901 [1]. Removal was harder. In November 1914 voters rejected it, 68,918 to 43,433 [1]. Defenders argued the graveyards were harmless: in a brief to the state Supreme Court, a lawyer for pioneer families pointed out that after the 1906 earthquake tens of thousands of people had lived in these cemeteries for months, drinking from their artesian wells [1]. Voters said no again in 1924, by a narrower 69,677 to 62,338. But a 1930 court ruling let the city remove the cemeteries one at a time [1]. The Odd Fellows cleared their ground, which is where this playground came from (a 1933 photograph shows the clearing), and sold the rest for houses [1][2]. When the Masons tried to reach families, nearly 15,000 of 20,000 bodies went unclaimed [1]. The city used many of the abandoned headstones in sea walls at Aquatic Park and the yacht harbour [1][3].

title: The one building the boss couldn't enter
place: San Francisco Labor Temple (Redstone Building), 2940 16th Street
hook: Bakers, cigar makers, bindery women and horseshoers all met in this plain red-brick temple on 16th Street, the headquarters of union San Francisco for half a century.
story:
The San Francisco Labor Council dedicated its Labor Temple at 16th and Capp on September 7, 1914. The dedication was led by P.H. McCarthy, former mayor and head of the Building Trades Council [1]. The red-brick building was plain on purpose, with none of the Gothic or Greek airs of the bosses' office towers. It was meant as a refuge: the one building in the city the boss could not enter [2]. Inside were pool tables, reading rooms, a ladies' parlour and medical care at prices workers could afford [2].

By May 1916, 54 unions held their meetings here. Among them were the bakers and bakery wagon drivers, bindery women, blacksmiths, butchers, cigar makers, coopers, horseshoers, milk wagon drivers, janitors, sail makers and tailors [1]. The Temple played a part in the 1917 streetcar strike and in the maritime strike that grew into the 1934 General Strike [1][2]. It was expanded in 1939 [2]. As unions grew richer they built their own halls, and in 1968 the building was sold and renamed the Redstone [2]. Today its lobby murals tell that history [1].

title: The street the neighbours built themselves
place: Vallejo Street Improvements, Vallejo Street at Jones
hook: The city owned the land, but it was the neighbours who hired Willis Polk to turn its steep crest into balustraded ramps and stairs.
story: Horatio Putnam Livermore (1837–1916) was the son of a Maine pioneer who reached California in 1850 and began damming the American River at Folsom. At the end of 1897 H.P. Livermore moved his family to the top of Vallejo Street [1]. The architect Willis Polk had already rented one of Livermore's houses before building his own nearby [1]. In 1912 Livermore began building nine houses. By the time he died four years later people called him the "Father of Russian Hill" [2]. For Florence and Jones streets he hired Charles F. Whittlesey, a former Santa Fe Railroad architect from Los Angeles, to design Pueblo- and Mission-style houses [2]. Then came the street itself. In 1914–15 Polk's firm built retaining walls, car ramps and a walk that zigzags down the slope. The City owned the land, but it was the neighbouring owners, organised by Livermore, who commissioned the work. It is one of the very few city-beautification plans Polk ever saw built [1]. Across the district, walls, steps and ramps tame grades of 16, 23 and 40 percent [2]. Livermore's son Norman had Polk design four more houses on Russian Hill Place in 1915 [1].

title: Twin towers that ships could see
place: St. Ignatius Church, Fulton St & Parker Ave
hook: After the 1906 fire destroyed their grand church, the Jesuits built again on a hilltop by the cemeteries. Its bell had survived the flames.
story: The 1906 fire destroyed the Jesuits' third St. Ignatius Church at Hayes and Van Ness, a building that had held 4,000 worshippers [1][2]. The Jesuits then acquired a small strip of land at Fulton Street and Parker Avenue [3]. It was former Masonic Cemetery land [1], and the new church was begun "as a Jesuit act of faith" [1]. Built between 1910 and 1914, the neo-Baroque church had a steel frame, fluted terra-cotta columns, walls of more than 250,000 pressed bricks and 128 clerestory windows [1]. Its twin towers could be seen by ships at sea. The 5,824-pound bell in its campanile had been saved from the ruined church on Hayes Street [1]. Finished in 1914 [3], it was the fifth St. Ignatius Church in the city [2]. In 1927 the college built next door and moved in, and three years later it was renamed the University of San Francisco [3]. The church came through the 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake undamaged [2]. Today it is illuminated in the evenings, glowing on its hill [1].

title: 27,000 Lines Behind a Brick Front
place: Former telephone exchange, 35 Russia Avenue at London Street
hook: A handsome brick apartment block off Mission Street hides its past in its doorway: the bell of the old telephone company.
story: In 1915 the Pacific Telephone and Telegraph Company built a telephone exchange on the northwest corner of Russia Avenue and London Street, just off Mission [1]. The brick building is in the Classical Revival style, solid and formal. Inside, some 27,000 phone lines were wired into switchboards [1]. The building is now apartments, known as the Randolph Apartments, and a 2014 photograph on FoundSF labels it the 'Randolph Exchange' [1][2]. The telephone company's bell logo, set in mosaic tile in the entry, still records what it used to be [1]. The corner also shows how the Excelsior grew. A few doors away is the Italian American Social Club at 25 Russia Avenue, whose members first met in a basement on Naples Street in 1928 [2][3].

title: A dome higher than the Capitol's
place: San Francisco City Hall, 1 Dr. Carlton B. Goodlett Place
hook: Six years after the old City Hall burned, San Francisco still had no plan to replace it. Then a new mayor won an 11-to-1 vote.
story: The 1906 earthquake and fire ruined the old City Hall, and a 1909 bond to replace it failed [1]. When James "Sunny Jim" Rolph became mayor in 1912, the city had no permanent City Hall, no plans for one, and no money to build one [1]. Rolph tied a March 1912 bond measure to the coming Panama-Pacific Exposition, promised jobs for local workers, and won by eleven to one [1]. John Bakewell and Arthur Brown Jr. won the design competition. Rolph broke ground in spring 1913 and dedicated the building in late December 1915 [1]. The building covers two full city blocks, and its dome rises 306 feet [2]. Rolph liked to tell visiting dignitaries that it was taller than the dome of the U.S. Capitol [1]. San Franciscans boasted that it was "built within the appropriation and, what is more, it was built without any scandal and without any graft." [1]. Around it, a library, an auditorium and later a state building completed a monumental "City Beautiful" civic centre [1].

title: A hilltop park won by dogged lobbying
place: Bayview Park, Bayview Hill
hook: For decades the Bayview had no public park at all. Its first one was a windy hilltop the city had once planned for a quarantine station.
story: Before 1915 the Bayview did not have a single public park; the homestead companies that carved up the district never set land aside [1]. In 1911 the Bay View Improvement Club begged the supervisors to buy a block for a playground; nothing happened, and both blocks filled with houses [1]. The breakthrough came on the steep summit of Bayview Hill. The city had bought the hilltop in 1902 for a quarantine facility, and Charles Crocker's estate, fearing for the value of its nearby land, offered land to kill the idea [2]. In December 1914 the city accepted 17 acres from the Bay View Land Company and the Crocker Estate Company on condition that eight acres of city land once earmarked for a hospital be added [1]. The improvements were minimal, an access drive and several hundred eucalyptus saplings, but about 500 people came to the May 1915 dedication, which ended with a City Band concert and dancing on the hill [1]. In the Depression, WPA crews returned: they laid 6,500 feet of road, planted 2,500 more trees and built walls and steps from the hill's own chert, work finished by 1938 [1][2][3]. Some of San Francisco's richest native grasslands survive among them [2].

title: A ruin built on purpose
place: Palace of Fine Arts, 3301 Lyon Street
hook: Bernard Maybeck designed a palace that was meant to look like it was already falling apart. Asked later what to do with it, he suggested letting it die.
story: Bernard Maybeck was fifty and known mostly for houses when he was chosen to design the Palace of Fine Arts for the 1915 exposition [1][2]. He built a melancholy fantasy. The exposition's historian Frank Morton Todd called it 'a cloister enclosing nothing, a colonnade without a roof, stairs that ended nowhere'. He said it was inspired by Arnold Böcklin's painting The Isle of the Dead, and its language of ruins echoes Piranesi's etchings [2]. Weeping maidens guarded caskets along the colonnade, deliberate overgrowth spilled from huge planter boxes, and everything was reflected in a dark, irregular lagoon [2]. Visitors loved it. Thomas Edison is quoted as saying, 'The architect of that building is a genius' [2]. It was the one building nobody had the heart to tear down [3]. But its plaster-like 'staff' was never meant to last, and by the 1940s chunks were falling off 'like leaves from autumn elms' [3]. Asked in old age what should be done, Maybeck suggested planting redwoods around the rotunda, so the columns would crumble as the trees grew and the palace would 'become its own cemetery' [2]. Instead, after financier Walter Johnson offered money that others matched, it was rebuilt in permanent materials in the 1960s [3].

title: A widow's gift, and the stolen turtles
place: Collis P. Huntington Park, California and Taylor streets
hook: Collis Huntington's mansion burned in 1906, and his widow gave the empty block to the city. Decades later it gained a Roman fountain, and eventually lost its turtles to thieves.
story: The railroad baron Collis P. Huntington's house stood on this Nob Hill block until the 1906 earthquake and fire. In 1915 his widow donated the land to the city, and it became a 1.3-acre neighbourhood park between California and Sacramento streets at Taylor [1]. Across California Street, the Crocker family's burned-out estate had been given to Grace Cathedral, whose front doors face the park [2]. The park's centrepiece arrived later. It is a copy of Rome's Fontana delle Tartarughe, the Fountain of the Turtles, designed by Giacomo della Porta and Taddeo Landini in 1583. The wife of the banker William H. Crocker found the copy at a villa outside Rome and bought it for her home in Hillsborough [2]. When that estate was sold, the Crocker heirs gave the fountain to San Francisco. The Board of Supervisors accepted it on October 4, 1954, and it was installed here in 1955 [2]. The turtles didn't stay put. Vandals stole them, and for the fountain's 1984 restoration new ones were cast from a similar fountain at the Ringling Bros. and Barnum & Bailey circus headquarters in Sarasota, Florida [2].

title: Carnegie's gift at 24th and Bartlett
place: Mission Branch Library, 300 Bartlett Street
hook: San Francisco's first branch library began in a Mission storefront in 1888. Andrew Carnegie's money later gave it an Italian Renaissance palace for about $51,000.
story:
The Mission Branch was the first branch of the San Francisco Public Library, opened in 1888 in a storefront two blocks from where it stands now [1]. The 1906 fire stopped four blocks to its north [1]. Nine years later the neighbourhood got a real building at 24th and Bartlett, paid for by the philanthropist Andrew Carnegie and designed by G. Albert Lansburgh [1][2]. The building and furnishings cost $50,877 [1].

The library says the branch opened in December 1915. The city's landmark listing dates the building to 1916 [1][2]. It was the second of seven Carnegie branches in San Francisco, and all seven still work as libraries. It was also Lansburgh's first Carnegie commission; he later designed the Chinatown, Presidio and Sunset branches [2]. Lansburgh also designed the grand El Capitan movie palace a few blocks away on Mission Street [3]. One boy who grew up in the postwar Mission remembered the high-arched branch as imposing, a place for 'serious readers only' [4].

title: Challah the Size of a Shop Window
place: Langendorf Bakery, 1160 McAllister St
hook: The 1906 fire burned out a Viennese baker south of Market. He started again on McAllister Street and built what neighbors considered the Fillmore's number one Jewish bakery.
story: Bernard Langendorf came to America from Vienna at sixteen. In 1895 he moved his small bakery from Chicago to San Francisco and opened Langendorf's Vienna Bakery on Folsom Street, baking rye bread said to follow an old Viennese formula [1]. The 1906 earthquake and fire destroyed it. Like many Jewish families burned out of South of Market, he moved west to the Fillmore and reopened at 878 McAllister near Laguna [1][2]. In 1915, with $400,000 raised from ten prominent San Franciscans, he built a larger plant at 1160 McAllister [1]. Neighbors remembered Langendorf's as the number one Jewish bakery in the district. During the High Holidays its windows held giant challahs, some filled with raisins and candied fruit and sprinkled with colored candy or poppy seeds [1]. By the early 1920s horse-drawn wagons and battery-powered white trucks carried its bread across the city. A 1917 film shows a parade of its horse-drawn wagons and delivery trucks, painted with the slogan "The Best of all Breads" [1][3]. Merchants and former employees remembered Bernard himself riding the No. 5 McAllister streetcar to the bank with a paper bag full of the day's cash [1].

title: Jewel City rises from the marsh
place: Marina Green, once the exposition's North Gardens
hook: San Francisco filled more than 600 acres of tidal marsh to throw itself a party. Nearly all of it came down within a year, except the lawn you picnic on.
story: To prove it had recovered from 1906, San Francisco held the Panama-Pacific International Exposition on the shallows and marshes then called Harbor View [1][2]. The city filled more than 600 acres of tidal marsh to create three miles of exhibition grounds [2]. From February 20 to December 4, 1915, the fair drew 18,876,438 visitors [1]. At its centre stood the 435-foot Tower of Jewels, hung with more than 102,000 mirror-backed cut-glass prisms branded 'Novagems' and lit at night by 54 searchlights [1]. The young Edmund Wilson wrote to a friend that it was so good it raised the question of why American architects couldn't build permanent buildings like it [3]. They didn't. The buildings were made of 'staff', a mix of plaster and fibre, and nearly all were pulled down after the fair closed [1]. Arches and towers fell in clouds of coloured plaster, showing the lath underneath [4]. What the fair left behind was the shoreline. The North Gardens became the Marina Green, and the yacht harbour stayed too [4]. The Column of Progress at the foot of Scott Street lasted into the 1920s, until so many cars had hit it that it was taken down [4].

title: Laura Ingalls Wilder's room with a view
place: Williams-Polk House, 1019 Vallejo Street
hook: Years before the Little House books, Laura Ingalls Wilder came to stay with her reporter daughter at the very top of Russian Hill.
story: Rose Wilder Lane came to San Francisco in 1908 and worked as a telegrapher at the Fairmont Hotel [2]. In early 1915 she took what she meant as a stopgap job at the San Francisco Bulletin, and soon her byline was running every day [2]. Around 1915–16 she rented rooms in the Williams side of a shingled duplex that Willis Polk built in 1892. The widowed painter Dora Norton Williams had paid for it by giving Polk's parents half the building and lot [1]. That year Rose's mother, Laura Ingalls Wilder, came to visit and see the Panama-Pacific Exposition. She was still learning to write; her Little House books would not start appearing until 1932 [1]. Her letters home to her husband Almanzo were published decades later as West From Home. She called the flat "a dandy little place to live with a fine view from the windows. It is up at the very top of a hill, with the bay in sight" [1]. She also described the stone stairs that climb inside the Theller retaining wall on Taylor Street, and found "the little artist girl" who illustrated her verses living nearby at 1637 Taylor [1]. Rose's diaries suggest she and her husband were separated that year, though her mother's letters don't say so [2].

title: Racing Cars on Pumped-Up Bay Mud
place: Crissy Field (site of the 1915 exposition raceway)
hook: Before it was an airfield, today's Crissy Field was a brand-new motor raceway on land that had been bay mud three years earlier.
story: To make room for the 1915 Panama-Pacific International Exposition, dredges pumped more than a million cubic yards of the bay onto the mudflats along the Marina and the Presidio shore. The job took 147 days [1]. The fair's planners won the Army's permission to use Presidio land, and a new raceway ran around what is now Crissy Field [1][2]. The weather did not cooperate. The Vanderbilt Cup, planned for February 22, the fair's second day, was rained out. The Grand Prix went ahead in the rain on February 27, more than 100 laps of a 3.9-mile course. Italian-born English driver Dario Resta won it in a Peugeot and took $3,000. When the Vanderbilt Cup finally ran on March 6, 77 laps and 300 miles, Resta won that too [2]. After the fair, Army aviators picked the site partly because the racetrack infield was already being used for flying. When the airfield opened in the early 1920s, the old track's outline could still be seen in the grass [3].

title: Racing the palaces in the pouring rain
place: Exposition grounds of the central Marina, where the 1915 race course looped the palaces
hook: In 1915 some of the era's star drivers raced 400 miles through the fairgrounds, over planks laid on a swamp, past bales of hay and a crowd of 65,000.
story: Heavy rain followed the exposition's February 1915 opening, and the part of its automobile course that ran around the dirt race track 'was a swamp' [1]. The fair bought 650,000 feet of lumber, and three shifts totaling 1,000 men planked the course day and night under searchlights from the Tower of Jewels [1]. On February 27 about 65,000 people watched the International Grand Prix in the rain. It was 400 miles: 104 laps of a 3.85-mile course. It circled the race track on planks that spurted muddy water, then wound around the Palaces of Varied Industries and of Mines, with right-angle turns lined with hay bales [2]. Thirty cars started, with Barney Oldfield, Ralph de Palma and Eddie Rickenbacker among the drivers [2]. Dario Resta, an Italian-born English driver in a French Peugeot, won in 7 hours, 7 minutes and 57 seconds, just over 56 miles an hour. The race finished after 6 p.m., in the dark [2]. A car went through the rail and a dog was killed, but nobody was hurt [2]. On March 6 Resta also won the postponed Vanderbilt Cup, even stopping to help when 'Wild Bob' Burman's car overturned [2]. The official history said it was the first time on record that one driver and car had won both races [2].

title: The Fire That Took Pershing's Family
place: Pershing Square flagpole, Main Post (site of the Pershing house)
hook: While General Pershing was on the Mexican border, fire swept his Presidio home. A flagpole now marks where the house stood.
story: General John J. Pershing was commander of the Presidio, but in 1915 he was away on the Mexican border. On August 27, 1915, fire broke out in the family's house on the Main Post [1][2]. His wife, Frances Warren Pershing, and their daughters Helen, 8, Anne, 7, and Mary Margaret, 3, died of smoke inhalation. Only his six-year-old son, Warren, survived [2]. Accounts differ on how it started. The Park Service says coal fell from an unattended dining-room fireplace [3]. Other accounts say a lacquered floor caught fire [2]. The post had no trained firefighters. Frances's father, Senator Francis Warren of Wyoming, pushed Congress for better fire protection, and San Francisco Fire Chief Thomas Murphy recommended a permanent company [3]. The Army built the Presidio Fire Station in 1917, the first on any U.S. Army post to house a permanent company of trained firefighters [3]. The house was never rebuilt. The flagpole at the centre of Pershing Square marks the spot. Beside it stand two bronze Spanish cannon, one cast in Lima in 1693 [1].

title: The Irish village that wasn't Irish enough
place: Site of the Shamrock Isle on the exposition's Joy Zone, now the Moscone Recreation Center ball fields (Chestnut, Bay, Laguna and Webster)
hook: The 1915 fair promised San Francisco's Irish the 'real Ireland.' They got an Englishman's concession, a fight with a firebrand priest, and a flop.
story: In March 1914 the Monitor, the archdiocese's newspaper, told its readers that at the coming exposition 'the real Ireland is to be properly represented' [1]. The Shamrock Isle went up on the Joy Zone, the fair's amusement strip, about where the Moscone Recreation Center's baseball diamond is now. Visitors entered through a replica of Drogheda's St. Laurence Gate, and the Chinese Village stood directly across the way [1]. The concession went to an Englishman, Kenneth Croft. Father Peter Yorke, the Mission District's 'labor priest,' smelled 'small graft' and predicted the return of the 'degrading stage Irishman' [1]. The fair's directors made Croft drop his first name for it, 'Donnybrook Fair,' and appointed six Irish American 'censors,' Archbishop Riordan among them, to oversee it [1]. None of it helped. By April admission was free, and by May a vaudeville act of triplets from Barnum and Bailey's circus had joined the Gaelic singing and dancing. In June Croft left town escorting recruits for the British army; he was arrested for violating American neutrality and later acquitted [1]. The official historian was dry: the village 'failed to reach any very altitudinous position in the financial world,' and the public 'did not seem especially interested in Irish singing and clog dancing' [2]. It had cost $100,000 and took in about $13,097 [1].
