title: The Mayor Who Toured the Sewer
place: Former sewage pumping station site, 48th Avenue and Fulton Street
hook: In 1915 Mayor Sunny Jim Rolph was photographed deep inside a new tunnel built to carry the Richmond's sewage beneath the neighbourhood to the ocean.
story:
As the dunes filled with houses after 1906, the city laid sewers ahead of the builders. Under a 1908 sewer bond it dug the Mile Rock Sewage Tunnel, beginning at a pumping station at 48th Avenue and Fulton Street. City photographer Horace Chaffee photographed the station's excavation on March 11, 1915, and on September 2 of that year Mayor James "Sunny Jim" Rolph posed inside the tunnel. It ran more than 4,200 feet, up to 300 feet below the streets, with walls about a foot thick, and emptied at Mile Rock Beach north of the Cliff House [1].

For decades the outfall did exactly what that implies. In wet weather, old outfalls around the city, Mile Rock among them, poured untreated sewage into the sea. Critics in the 1960s noted that Ocean Beach was often too polluted for swimming on more than 100 days a year [2]. The fix was a huge new system begun in the mid-1970s. By 1995, FoundSF reported, the Mile Rock and China Beach outfalls were no longer active, and waste went to the Southwest plant through the Richmond Transport, a big tunnel under Sutro Heights [2]. The old tunnel now carries only storm water in the heaviest rains [1].

title: The Road of the Sea Opens
place: El Camino del Mar at 26th Avenue
hook: In 1915 the World's Fair, the city and the Army paid for a clifftop boulevard through the land being sold as Sea Cliff.
story: Park superintendent John McLaren is credited with a 1909 or 1910 plan for a boulevard system through Lincoln Park. By 1912 the Panama-Pacific International Exposition's plans showed a coastal boulevard to Lincoln Park [1]. By the end of 1915 the John Brickell Company, working under the City Engineer, had finished the first stretch of El Camino del Mar, "The Road of the Sea", between the Presidio and Lincoln Park [1]. The Bureau of Engineering described 1,665 feet of boulevard "along the cliffs above Bakers Beach" into the Presidio near Lobos Creek. Its contract list says the road ran "through John Brickell Tract", the land then being sold as Sea Cliff [2]. The Exposition gave $56,000 for paving and the city $30,000 for rights of way. Because it would also serve as a military road between Fort Miley and the Presidio, the federal government put up $30,000 more. The Park Service history counts that money toward this section; the city engineers said it was for carrying the road on through the Presidio [1][2]. In September 1915 two ceremonies were held in Lincoln Park: one for the completion of the transcontinental Lincoln Highway, the other opening El Camino del Mar on September 26 [1]. Farther west, landslides later closed the Lincoln Park stretch to cars for good [1].

title: The Thinker's Nine Years in Golden Gate Park
place: Court of Honor, Legion of Honor (The Thinker)
hook: Before he settled into the Legion's courtyard, Rodin's Thinker spent nine years sitting on a rock in Golden Gate Park, in the fog near the Conservatory.
story: Rodin's Thinker is so much a part of the Legion of Honor that it seems it has always been there. It hasn't [1][2]. The cast first came to San Francisco for the 1915 Panama-Pacific International Exposition. It stood at the entrance court of the French Pavilion, just south of the Palace of Fine Arts [1]. A 1915 book on the exposition's sculpture called it a replica of the Thinker placed before the doors of the Panthéon in Paris [1]. Loie Fuller, the dancer who introduced Alma Spreckels to Rodin, had encouraged her to buy it [2]. When the fair closed in December 1915 there was no museum to take it. So the statue was set on a big rock near the Conservatory of Flowers in Golden Gate Park, and there it sat for about nine years [1]. The San Francisco Public Library puts it more gently: the Thinker 'did moonlight in Golden Gate Park for a spell' before the museum opened [2]. Only in 1924, when the Legion of Honor, a permanent copy of the French Pavilion, opened on Armistice Day, did it move to Lincoln Park [1][2]. It has presided over the Court of Honor ever since [2].

title: The lots de Young gave his daughters
place: Tobin House, 1969 California Street between Gough and Octavia (Landmark No. 260)
hook: The Chronicle's owner bought the lots next to his mansion and gave them to two daughters. For years they preferred the suburbs. Then Willis Polk built this.
story:
Michael H. de Young and his brother Charles founded the Daily Dramatic Chronicle, which became the Daily Morning Chronicle. By the 1870s the paper could make or break a politician [1]. De Young built the West Coast's first steel-frame skyscraper at Kearny and Market in 1889, led the 1894 Midwinter Fair, and built a family mansion on the crest of California Street in the Western Addition [1]. A history of the neighborhood around 1900 lists him among its residents, alongside mining and shipping magnates [2].

In 1911 he bought the two lots next to his estate, on the south side of California between Gough and Octavia. He gave the deeds to his daughters Helen, the wife of George Cameron, and Constance, the wife of Joseph O. Tobin, a Hibernia Bank executive. He offered to build them houses too. For years nothing happened, because both families preferred to live in towns south of the city [1].

The Tobin house finally went up in 1915, designed by Willis Polk in the medieval English manner he favored. Polk saw that restraint as a cure for what he considered the architectural chaos of San Francisco's 19th-century streets [1]. It is a city landmark and is listed on the National Register [1].

title: The man who owned the sky
place: Bay off the exposition grounds, Marina shoreline
hook: Fifty thousand people at the fair watched the world's greatest stunt pilot flip his new plane upside down above the bay. Then the wings broke.
story: Lincoln Beachey was born in San Francisco in 1887 [1]. As a boy, Radiolab reports, he hurtled down the steep Fillmore Street hill on a bicycle with no brakes [2]. He grew up to be America's most famous stunt pilot. He invented the figure eight and the vertical drop, and in one year 17 million people came out to watch him fly [2]. His 'dip of death' took him up to 5,000 feet, then down toward the ground in a full-speed dive with his hands outstretched [1]. For the Panama-Pacific International Exposition he flew a new monoplane, the Beachey-Eaton Taube, with an enclosed cockpit [1]. On March 14, 1915, with 50,000 people on the fairgrounds and perhaps 200,000 more on the hills, he looped and rolled the plane onto its back about 2,000 feet above the bay [1]. As he pulled out, the rear spars of the wings broke, and the plane fell into the water between two ships [1]. Navy men jumped in to help, but it took an hour and 45 minutes to bring up his body. The autopsy found he had survived the crash with only a broken leg. He drowned because he could not free himself from his harness. He was 28 [1].

title: Where America's First Coast Road Ends
place: Legion of Honor plaza and fountain (Lincoln Highway western terminus)
hook: A road that started in Times Square ran almost 3,400 miles to finish here, beside a new cliff-top boulevard that the landslides never stopped attacking.
story: In 1912 Carl Fisher of Indianapolis gathered friends from the auto industry and called for a 'coast-to-coast rock highway' finished in time for San Francisco's 1915 exposition. 'Let's build it,' he said, 'before we're too old to enjoy it!' [1]. The Lincoln Highway Association laid out a route of nearly 3,400 miles from New York. Its western terminus was dedicated in 1915 in Lincoln Park, where the Legion of Honor's plaza and fountain are now [2]. The same year, work began on El Camino del Mar, the parks superintendent's scenic boulevard from the Harbor View district to Ocean Beach. By the end of 1915 it reached from the Presidio to Lincoln Park. It was carried through the park to Sutro Heights in 1924 [2]. In 1925 new numbered federal routes broke the named highway into pieces. On September 1, 1928, Boy Scouts set out concrete markers along its length, each with a bronze Lincoln medallion. The NPS counts about 2,440 markers and the Federal Highway Administration about 3,000 [1][2]. One original marker survives at 32nd Avenue and El Camino del Mar. The road's first landslide came in 1928, and only fragments survive as trail [2].

title: A boarding house named for Dewey's flagship
place: Olympia Building, corner of 20th and Illinois streets
hook: Shipyard workers slept above a saloon named for a cruiser built across the street. Decades later, in the same spot, a nameless district was branded 'Dogpatch'.
story:
In 1916 John and Barbara Syme, immigrants from Scotland and Ireland, opened a three-story boarding house at the corner of 20th and Illinois streets for waterfront workers. They named it after the USS Olympia, Commodore George Dewey's flagship at Manila Bay in 1898, which had been built at Union Iron Works across the street [1][2]. It had a restaurant and saloon downstairs and rooms upstairs, and it filled with workers during both world wars [1].

After a fire gutted the upper floor, the Symes tore the wooden building down in 1971 and put up a plain cinderblock one in 1972. In 1992 the designer John Borg took the lease on a handshake with Bill Syme [1].

In the 1990s the area had no agreed name. Activists settled on "Dogpatch," a rarely used local name that old-timers said began as a 1940s insult, and Borg's ground-floor studio did the branding for free. Borg helped found the Dogpatch Neighborhood Association in 1998, and its first planning meetings were held in the Olympia. The original concept for Crane Cove Park was drawn up there, and volunteers gathered the history that helped win historic-district status [1]. In 2024 basketball star Steph Curry bought the building for $8.5 million, with plans to replace it [1].

title: A chemist's lab, a photographer's studio
place: Burr House, 1772 Vallejo Street
hook: Behind a mansard-roofed wedding present on Vallejo Street, a sugar chemist kept a laboratory and his daughter built a studio for painterly photographs.
story: The Italianate house at 1772 Vallejo, with its Second Empire mansard roof, was built for Edmund Burr, son of former mayor Ephraim Willard Burr. Local lore says it was a wedding present for Edmund and his bride, Anna Barnard [1][2]. The city landmark listing gives 1875 as the building date; the 2014 National Register nomination says 1878 is most likely [1][2]. Edmund had trained as a chemist in Germany. After perfecting a sugar-refining process he bought the Alameda Sugar Company in 1889, and he kept a chemical laboratory in the garden cottage [1]. His daughter Alice took the house in another direction. She graduated in 1916 from the Clarence White School of Photography in New York, where Dorothea Lange also studied, and her work belongs to the Pictorialist school [1]. That year architect Henry H. Gutterson designed an Arts and Crafts studio for her at the Green Street edge of the garden [1]. She tried bromoil, pigment and colour Autochrome processes, and photographed the city, nature and the family's own house [1]. Alice and her sister Marian lived there until they died, in 1968 and 1966, ending almost a century of Burr family life in the house [1].

title: A tin-can factory on a ballfield
place: Former American Can Company, now American Industrial Center, 2325 Third Street
hook: The last giant factory to reach Potrero Point was blasted out of serpentine on an old baseball field. Today some call it a horizontal skyscraper.
story:
By 1910 Potrero Point had almost no big industrial lots left. In early 1915 the American Can Company, the largest maker of tin cans in the United States, paid $172,000 for two square blocks bounded by Kentucky (now Third), 20th, Illinois and 22nd streets. The land had belonged to the Crocker Estate and was last used as a baseball field. The company blasted away the serpentine rock and put up an enormous concrete-frame plant, finished in June 1916 [1].

VerPlanck puts the workforce at 1,200. The Potrero View gives a peak of "upwards of 800" [1][2]. The plant made cans and also canned fruit, and it hired many women, who were reputedly better at the work. After the Second World War it was the largest employer in Dogpatch [1]. It closed in 1969 [2].

In 1975 Angelo Markoulis, who had come to America from Crete as a young man, bought the mostly empty complex. He divided it into about 40 workshops and warehouses. The tenants shifted with the times: almost 60 photographers in the 1980s, garment firms in the 1990s, and later a chocolatier and a butcher. One longtime tenant says the family turned down a chance to sell the whole complex to Google rather than displace its 200-plus businesses [2].

title: Andrew Carnegie's gift on Jersey Street
place: Noe Valley/Sally Brunn Branch Library, 451 Jersey Street
hook: Built with steel magnate Andrew Carnegie's money on the street Horner named for his home state, this 1916 library has lent books to Noe Valley for more than a century.
story:
Noe Valley had a branch library before it had this building. FoundSF says the branch was the seventh in the San Francisco Public Library system and that its first home was at 1308 Castro Street [1].

With a grant from Andrew Carnegie, the city then built a two-storey branch of brick and terra cotta on Jersey Street. It was finished on 17 September 1916 for $45,499, furnishings included [1]. The architect was John Reid Jr., who had designed the Hoffman Avenue firehouse two years earlier. It was the third of seven Carnegie branch libraries in San Francisco, and all seven are still libraries [2].

Neighbours have looked after it ever since. They added a deck and community garden in the 1970s. Later they sold 250 engraved bricks, and more than 400 households gave money during a 2006–08 seismic renovation [1][3]. The city made the building Landmark No. 259 [2].

title: Birth-control leaflets from a Stockton Street club
place: Gruppo Anarchico Volontà club room, 1602 Stockton St (near Union)
hook: In 1916 young Italian anarchists facing Washington Square printed 20,000 birth-control leaflets in Italian and signed them with their group's name and address.
story: In March 1916 The Blast, the anarchist paper Alexander Berkman published in San Francisco, sent a writer to a "dingy club room" at 1602 Stockton Street [1][2]. Its window read "GRUPPO ANARCHICO VOLONTÁ" in big red letters over a sketch of the sun rising behind mountains. Inside hung pictures of the Haymarket martyrs, Giordano Bruno and Francisco Ferrer, and radical newspapers were pegged with clothespins along a railing. The group had no officers, its door was never locked, and nobody knew how many members it had [1]. After a mass meeting protesting Emma Goldman's arrest, one young member brought back a handbill with contraceptive information. Members chipped in to print 20,000 copies in Italian, signed with its name and address, and one night ten members slipped 6,000 into mailboxes across the Italian quarter [1]. A policeman came calling, and member Joseph Macario, asked to explain, was jailed on the chief's order; attorney Charles Sferlazzo bailed him out [1]. "You know these things; you use them; why shouldn't I and the rest of us?" Macario had told the chief. On the night the writer visited, Berkman and the attorney Jack Margolis spoke to an overflowing hall, while police informers took notes at the back [1].

title: Bungalows for the family of average means
place: Miramar Avenue, the landscaped spine of Westwood Park
hook: 'When the tunnel is complete, to Westwood Park we will retreat,' promised a promotional coin. The bungalows were drawn up by one of the West's few women architects.
story: A. S. Baldwin had sold Sutro land to the builders of Forest Hill and St. Francis Wood. He then tried something new on 93 forested acres of Sutro land north of Ocean Avenue. His firm Baldwin & Howell broke ground in 1916 on 'a model home community for the family of average means' [1][2]. The residence-park touches stayed: Louis Christian Mullgardt's gateways, a median on Miramar Avenue, and oval loops laid out by engineer John M. Punnett. The houses, though, were modest bungalows picked from a catalogue, on lots starting at $3,000 [1]. A promotional coin carried a rhyme: 'When the tunnel is complete, To Westwood Park we will retreat' [1][2]. Charles Strothoff designed nearly 500 of the 650 houses [1]. Another hundred or so came from Ida F. McCain, whom the company once called head of its architecture department. In a 1920 ad she wrote, 'I am in good company' [1][2]. The 1920 census found about 450 residents, most commonly managers, salespeople and accountants. The deeds banned minority occupation [2]. The tract sold out by 1925 [2].

title: Double Roads and Red Brick Walls
place: Sea Cliff Avenue near 27th Avenue (Harry B. Allen listed at 290 Sea Cliff Avenue, late 1920s)
hook: Sea Cliff's split-level streets and brick retaining walls were an engineer's plan for a private, picturesque hillside. Its builder lived on the street he sold.
story: The old Baker Tract became Sea Cliff through a partnership between the John Brickell Company, the builder and developer Harry B. Allen, and the engineer William B. Hoag [1]. Lots first went on sale in 1913, and further subdivisions followed in 1916, 1923 and 1928 [1]. Buyers could hire their own architect, subject to the developer's approval, or have Allen & Company build a house for them. The result was remarkably consistent in scale, setbacks and materials, yet full of one-off designs by Willis Polk, Albert Farr, George W. Kelham, William Wurster and a long list of others [1]. To keep the hillside private and picturesque, Hoag designed double roadways with red brick retaining walls, landscaping and raised sidewalks, and he terraced the lots into the slope [1]. The neighbourhood was entered through columned gateways [2]. Allen lived in what he sold. A society blue book from the late 1920s lists Mr. and Mrs. Harry B. Allen at 290 Sea Cliff Avenue [3]. In 2013 city planners called Sea Cliff an excellent example of the restricted residence parks laid out west of Twin Peaks, and they treat it as a district eligible for the California Register [1][2].

title: Horsehair and Plaster on Islais Creek
place: Site of P. Biggins & Co. Hair Works, 2165 San Bruno Avenue (vanished address near Islais Creek)
hook: Where San Bruno Avenue crossed the Islais Creek marsh, a wholesale firm dealt in hair for plasterers and saddle makers.
story: San Bruno Avenue reached the Portola by crossing the Islais Creek marsh. In the 1910s city photographer Horace Chaffee kept coming back to record the work there. In July 1915 he photographed San Bruno running out across a new fill over the creek [1]. On September 29, 1916, he looked northwest toward Bernal Heights from Gaven Street. At the right of his picture is a sign for 'P. Biggins & Co, Hair Works' [2]. A few weeks later, on October 20, crews were laying streetcar tracks across the creek, and his photograph identifies the firm more fully. It was Patrick Biggins & Co., wholesale dealers in plastering and saddlers' hair, at 2165 San Bruno Avenue, right on the creek [3]. Old-timers remembered the streetcar ride over the creek as rough because the tracks were always sinking [4]. The address no longer appears on the city's address list.

title: Nickelodeon, Holiness Temple, then the Blue Church
place: 1596 Church Street at 28th Street (site of the Searchlight Theater)
hook: The royal-blue church at Church and 28th had been a movie house with nine or more names before it found religion. Its last years ended in court.
story:
In 1916 a nickelodeon opened at Church and 28th streets. A piano played along to the silent films [3]. It opened as the Searchlight and went on to be the Empress, the Lux, the De Lux, the Isis, the Princess, the Church, the Rita and finally the Del Mar. In the 1930s it showed German and Russian films [1]. In 1965 the Holiness Temple in Christ bought it, and the building became the royal-blue "Blue Church" of outer Church Street [1][2].

From 1996 the congregation, by then the non-denominational Church at San Francisco, was led by Rev. Joesiah Bell, a social-activist pastor. His food and clothing giveaways and his plans for a shelter for homeless women brought complaints from some neighbours. Bell called the harassment racist [1]. In 2006 the church agreed to hand the building to a developer in exchange for 40 percent of the profits from condos on the site. When the lease ran out, it refused to leave. A jury sided with the church in 2008, but appeal judges reversed the verdict in 2009 [2]. By then 15 to 20 people with nowhere else to go were living in a building with no kitchen or showers [2]. The old theatre was torn down soon after, and by 2011 gold-and-grey condos were planned for the corner [4].

title: The Bomb at Steuart and Market
place: Steuart Street just south of Market
hook: A suitcase bomb killed ten at a pro-war parade. The city convicted a labour organiser, though a photo placed him a mile away.
story: On Saturday, July 22, 1916, the Chamber of Commerce staged a huge Preparedness Day parade, reportedly with 51,329 marchers and 52 bands, to rally support for entering the war in Europe [1]. At 2:06 p.m., about half an hour in, a bomb hidden in a suitcase exploded on the west side of Steuart Street just south of Market, killing ten bystanders and wounding forty, the worst terrorist act in the city's history [1][2]. Suspicion fell at once on radical labour. Tom Mooney, a militant organiser, and Warren Billings were convicted on testimony later shown to be false, and a detective with long ties to utilities had coached witnesses [2]. A photograph taken at 2:01 p.m. showed Tom and Rena Mooney on the roof of the Eilers Building at 975 Market, a mile away; prosecutors had it but never showed it at trial [2]. Mooney was sentenced to death. After pressure from President Wilson his sentence was commuted to life, and Governor Culbert Olson pardoned him in January 1939. Sources differ on Billings: one says he was pardoned too, another that he was freed in 1942 [1][2]. The bomber was never identified [1].

title: The Burr sisters never left Vallejo Street
place: Burr House, 1772 Vallejo Street
hook: Two daughters of a Cow Hollow chemist grew up in a Vallejo Street house and never left it. One of them was a gifted photographer.
story: The house at 1772 Vallejo is traditionally called a wedding present from Ephraim Willard Burr, the 1850s mayor who started the first savings bank on the Pacific Coast, to his son Edmund and Anna Barnard, who married in 1875. Water records suggest it was finished around 1878 [1][2]. Edmund had trained as a chemist in Leipzig. He kept a laboratory in the garden cottage and took control of the Alameda Sugar Company in 1889 [1][2]. Two of the couple's three daughters stayed for good. Alice, born in 1883, finished the Clarence White School of Photography in New York in 1916; White's students included Dorothea Lange. That same year a small Arts and Crafts studio was built on the property just for her [1][2]. In it she tried bromoil prints and the early color Autochrome process, and she later filmed her travels in Africa with her sister Marian using a motion picture camera [2]. Alice was active in the League of Women Voters; Marian worked with the Red Cross [1][2]. Marian died in 1966 and Alice in 1968, ending almost a century of Burr family life in the house [1]. Her work had rarely been shown for decades when a 1998 traveling exhibition, seen at Wesleyan University, presented her as a Pictorialist rediscovered [3].

title: The Rooftop Photo That Proved an Alibi
place: Eilers Building, 975 Market Street (between Fifth and Sixth)
hook: At 2:01 p.m. a photographer caught Tom and Rena Mooney on a Market Street rooftop. Minutes later a bomb exploded a mile away, and Mooney was blamed.
story: On July 22, 1916, business leaders staged a huge Preparedness Day parade up Market Street to drum up support for entering the European war. At 2:06 p.m. a bomb exploded near Steuart Street, killing ten people and critically injuring 40 more [1]. District Attorney Charles Fickert charged militant labor organizer Tom Mooney, his wife Rena, Warren Billings and two others [1][3]. Yet a photograph by Wade Hamilton places Tom and Rena on the roof of the Eilers Building at 975 Market, between Fifth and Sixth streets, at 2:01 p.m., when prosecutors claimed they were planting the bomb a mile east [1]. A Market Street clock linked to the photographs is now preserved in Vallejo as the "Alibi Clock" [2]. Mooney was convicted anyway and sentenced to hang; Billings got life, and Rena was acquitted [2][3]. After protests around the world, Governor William Stephens commuted Mooney's sentence to life in 1918, and he became one of America's most famous political prisoners [2]. Governor Culbert Olson finally pardoned him in 1939, after more than two decades behind bars [1][2].

title: The fair's last column, felled by cars
place: Marina Boulevard at Cervantes Boulevard, former site of the Column of Progress
hook: After the 1915 fair closed, its towers came down in clouds of coloured plaster. One column held on by the waterfront until drivers kept crashing into it.
story: The Panama-Pacific International Exposition closed on December 4, 1915, with buglers playing 'Taps' from the Tower of Jewels as the lights went out [1]. Many people hoped to save it. Architect Willis Polk lobbied to keep the Palace of Fine Arts, the Palace of Horticulture, the gardens and the Avenue of Palms, and the Commonwealth Club passed a resolution urging preservation [2]. Speculators won instead. Arches and towers came down 'in clouds of colored plaster', showing the lath framework underneath. Small buildings were barged around the Bay Area [2]. Anything movable was sold, from furniture to sculpture, and the rest was demolished. The site was cleared by February 1917 [1]. Two things lingered. One was the Palace of Fine Arts. The other was the Column of Progress, topped by a sculpture called 'The Adventurous Bowman', which stood at the end of Scott Street, where Marina and Cervantes Boulevards now meet [1][2]. After one too many reckless motorists hit it, the column was pulled down in the mid-1920s [1][2].

title: 'Pay after the war': the railroad shop boom
place: Bayshore Boulevard near Sunnydale Avenue, facing the former Southern Pacific Bayshore yard
hook: In 1917 a downtown realtor promised that $70 cash for a lot facing the new Southern Pacific shops would soon be worth thousands.
story: In 1907 the Southern Pacific laid its 'Bayshore cutoff' across bay fill at the valley's edge. Soon afterwards it built an enormous rail yard and shop complex that cut the first valley streets off from the bay [1]. The Grapevine's Matthew Brady put the complex at $2,300,000 and 260 acres. Heritage says it sprawled over more than 200 acres [1][2]. It became the main maintenance centre for the company's Coast Division and employed hundreds of workers, many of whom lived in the valley [1]. Speculators moved in early. In 1917 J. W. Wright & Co. of 228 Montgomery Street advertised: 'Where S.P. shops are building – secure a business location now. Pay after the war if you want to' [2]. The ad promised that 'thousands of high-priced skilled artisans' would work at the shops. A $700 lot facing them, it said, would soon be 'worth thousands', and '$70 cash secures today a car-line business location' [2]. For decades the yards hemmed in the valley [3]. Before the century closed, though, train maintenance and storage had moved elsewhere, and the Southern Pacific was gone from the valley [1].

title: 'Such a club could never be a success'
place: Woman's Athletic Club (now Metropolitan Club), 640 Sutter Street
hook: A husband scoffed that women couldn't run a club. They built one anyway, with a seawater pool and the city's first indoor tennis court.
story: The idea came from Elizabeth Taylor Pillsbury, who had visited the new Woman's Athletic Club of Chicago. From 1912 she and a circle of friends spread it among their friends, and the club was incorporated in 1915 [1]. Its Sutter Street clubhouse by Bliss & Faville, modelled on a Florentine palazzo, opened in 1917. It was the first women's athletic club west of Chicago [1]. The club says it also had the city's first indoor tennis court [2]. Seawater for the pool was pumped in from Ocean Beach under contract with the Olympic Salt Water Company. The Olympic Club sent two huge baskets of American Beauty roses [1]. Not everyone was impressed. The club's historian recorded one member's husband saying "such a Club could never be a success run by women" [1]. Seven months in, the Examiner reported a row over a male "efficiency expert" brought in to cut a deficit. By autumn the treasurer said the club was paying its way [1]. The 1920 bulletin fined anyone "caught shampooing in the shower bath" a dollar [3]. In 1945 members hosted women at the United Nations conference [1]. In 1966 they voted 688 to 184 to become the Metropolitan Club [1].

title: A silent film sold the tunnel
place: Above the western stretch of the Twin Peaks Tunnel (the tunnel's line is approximate)
hook: In October 1917 San Franciscans could watch a real-estate film about the tunnel being dug under these hills, probably in a storefront. It ran for weeks.
story: Real-estate men had bet heavily on the Twin Peaks Tunnel. Advertisements promised that Sunset lots would "triple" in value once it was built, and in 1914 five big developers holding land west of the hills agreed to pay $924,000 in assessments, which assured the project could go ahead [1]. The firm of Baldwin and Howell, on Kearny Street, went further and commissioned a movie. The Pathescope film company shot "Twin Peaks Tunnel", documenting construction of what was then claimed to be the longest municipal tunnel in the world [2][3]. It shows the tunnel being dug, Sutro Forest being cleared, and the new West Portal, St. Francis Wood and Westwood Park neighbourhoods, along with officials, engineers, workers and ordinary citizens [2]. According to historian David Kiehn, newspaper advertisements show it was first screened on October 13, 1917, most likely in a San Francisco storefront, and it was popular enough to run continuously for weeks [2]. A National Film Preservation Foundation grant paid for its restoration, and the Niles Essanay Silent Film Museum holds the original 28mm copy and a 35mm preservation negative [2]. The silent film runs about 19 minutes and can be watched online [2][3].

title: An empire's enemies on Wood Street
place: Ghadar Memorial (Gadar Memorial Hall), 5 Wood Street
hook: On a short street above Geary, Indian revolutionaries ran their headquarters and printing press, working to overthrow British rule a world away.
story: The Ghadar Party was founded in San Francisco in 1913 to free India from British rule by force. Most of its members were South Asian workers on the West Coast [1][2]. Its weekly paper, Ghadar, first came out in November 1913. Its masthead called itself "an enemy of British rule" [1]. The party began at 436 Hill Street, active there from 1913 to 1917, and then moved its headquarters to 5 Wood Street [2]. The three-storey house there held a printing press and people living and working together, and it hosted public and secret meetings [2]. In August 1914 the party called on overseas Indians to go home and rise up, and some 8,000 were said to have gone. Because of strong British vigilance, most were captured on the way or when they arrived [2]. The Hindu-German Conspiracy Trial that followed in San Francisco broke up what was left of the leadership. In the courtroom one defendant, Ram Singh, shot the party leader Ram Chandra dead [1]. After independence the building passed to the Government of India, formally in 1952. Ground was broken in September 1974 and the memorial opened in March 1975 [2]. The consulate calls that work a restoration, but FoundSF says the present building went up after the original was demolished [1][2].

title: Guns on the dunes: Fort Funston
place: Fort Funston (former Lake Merced Military Reservation)
hook: The Army bought these dunes in 1900 and left them empty for seventeen years. World War I brought mortars from the Presidio.
story: In December 1900 the federal government acquired about 45 acres of the sandy ridge between Lake Merced and the Pacific as the Lake Merced Military Reservation [1][2]. The Army had sued the Spring Valley Water Company for the land and paid $42,162 [3]. The plan was two mortar batteries, but nothing was built [1][2]. When the United States entered World War I in 1917, construction finally began. Battery Howe got four 12-inch mortars and Battery Bruff two 5-inch guns, both taken from older batteries at Fort Winfield Scott by the Presidio [1][2]. That year the reservation was expanded by about 150 acres to the south, and wooden buildings went up for the garrison [1]. It was renamed for Major General Frederick Funston, who died in 1917. He had commanded the Army troops in San Francisco after the 1906 earthquake [1][3]. Peace came quickly: Battery Bruff was disarmed in 1920, and the fort sat largely inactive until 1936 [1][3].

title: Holed through, an eighth of an inch off
place: Above the Twin Peaks Tunnel beneath the western slope (the tunnel's line is approximate)
hook: On April 5, 1917, crews digging from opposite sides of Twin Peaks broke through to each other. Their bores were out of line by an eighth of an inch.
story: For decades the hills in the middle of San Francisco kept the west side nearly empty. From 1909 merchants, improvement clubs and real-estate men campaigned for a streetcar tunnel under Twin Peaks [1]. The city signed with Robert C. Storrie & Co. on November 2, 1914, for $3,372,000, and excavation began that December at both portals and at a station site at Laguna Honda [1]. The tunnel ran directly beneath the old Rancho San Miguel [2]. It was dangerous work. Inspector Ernest Dunden was killed in July 1915 when he fell onto live wires at the west portal, and several men died in the delayed explosion of a dynamite cap in February 1917 [1]. In August 1916 workers found a petrified redwood trunk 90 feet down; it is unclear whether anyone ever settled if redwoods once grew here or it was ancient driftwood [1]. On Thursday, April 5, 1917, came the drillers' cry: "Holed through!" The two bores met off by a mere eighth of an inch [1]. A driller named Sam Campbell squeezed through first. Four supervisors then rode muck cars to the opening and raced to get through; Joseph Lahaney won and muddied his suit [1]. Muni streetcars began carrying passengers through on February 3, 1918, and 21,000 people rode out through the tunnel the next Sunday [1].

title: Julia Morgan's school for college-bound girls
place: Former Miss Burke's School, 3065 Jackson Street (now San Francisco University High School)
hook: Katherine Delmar Burke wanted girls prepared for college, not finishing school. Her friend Julia Morgan, the first woman admitted to architecture at the École des Beaux-Arts, built the classrooms.
story:
In 1908 Katherine Delmar Burke opened Miss Burke's School. Instead of the usual finishing school for girls, she wanted one that prepared them for college [1]. It started at Steiner and Pacific, then moved to a house at 2310 Broderick [1].

As it grew, Burke turned to her friend Julia Morgan [1]. Morgan had been the first woman ever admitted to the architecture section of the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris [3]. Her building at 3065 Jackson Street dates from 1917, and the school moved in by 1918 [1][2][3]. Among its students was the future abstract painter Nell Sinton [4].

From 1929 Burke's began moving its younger grades to Sea Cliff. The high school stayed on Jackson Street until it closed in 1975. That year the building went to the new San Francisco University High School, which still uses Morgan's building as its "Upper Campus" [1][2].

Morgan also had a home in the neighborhood. She bought 2231 Divisadero in 1923 and the house next door in 1929. She took the upper story off the second house to let light into the first [3].

title: Market Street climbs over the mountain
place: Portola Drive where it leaves upper Market Street
hook: Upper Market Street and Portola Drive follow an old wagon road around Twin Peaks. Turning it into a boulevard took a motorcade, a tunnel and decades of widening.
story: The only early road over Twin Peaks wound up Corbett and down what is now Portola Drive. Today's upper Market Street and Portola closely follow it, though they are twice as wide [1]. The modern road came with the Twin Peaks Tunnel. On June 15, 1917 a City Hall delegation drove over the hill in a small fleet of automobiles on "the new Market Street extension called Portola Drive", then entered the tunnel's west portal and drove through to the east. It was the first and last time cars made that trip [2]. Historian Richard Brandi, though, dates the extension of Market southwest from 17th and Castro to the early 1920s, built along with the tunnel's east portal on a curve that followed the older road [1]. The road kept growing. City photographers recorded Portola being widened near Clipper Street in November 1929 [3]. In 1954 the San Francisco News reported plans to rebuild Portola from Woodside Avenue to Corbett Avenue as a straightened, six-lane divided highway [4]. In the late 1950s the stretch from Woodside west to St. Francis Circle was widened, and dozens of homes were moved to vacant lots, some as far away as Daly City [1].

title: No streetcars through the park
place: 10th Avenue & Fulton Street (end of the Municipal Railway A line)
hook: Richmond residents wanted a streetcar line straight through Golden Gate Park. The park commissioners fought it off, and in 1917 buses crossed the park instead.
story: From 1912, the city's new A streetcar ended at 10th Avenue and Fulton Street. Golden Gate Park lay ahead like a wall, and riders bound for the Sunset had to go east to Divisadero Street and double back [1]. The Richmond Banner had called for a line across the park since 1908 [1]. In 1913 the transit engineer Bion J. Arnold recommended a line from 10th and Fulton to 9th Avenue and Lincoln Way. In 1915 the supervisors approved a route with an underpass and an open trench behind the de Young, cutting into part of the Japanese Tea Garden [1]. Park Commission chairman William Metson fumed that 'the real estate men have put it over on the Board of Supervisors.' Rolph signed it, but after an eight-month stalemate with the park board he vetoed the call for construction bids, and on June 5, 1916, the supervisors failed to override him [1]. Instead, on September 1, 1917, Muni Route 1 started carrying passengers across the park, at first in rented buses. It lost about $80 a day at first [1]. Its route through the park survives in today's 44 O'Shaughnessy, and no streetcar tracks were ever laid across the park [1]. The A line itself had come out Geary and turned down Tenth Avenue to the park's edge [2].

title: Storefronts Dressed as Bungalows
place: 1524-1532 Ocean Avenue, beside Westwood Park
hook: To sell a new residence park, its developers built shops that looked like the houses and advertised them under a name that left out 'Ingleside'.
story: Ocean Avenue began as a muddy road of seasonal roadhouses and saloons. In the 1910s and 1920s, new residence parks north of it changed that: Westwood Park, Balboa Terrace, Westwood Highlands and St. Francis Wood [1]. Their developers helped build shops and community buildings to make their tracts more attractive [1]. Baldwin & Howell, the firm behind Westwood Park, called its 280-acre tract 'a typical Baldwin and Howell product' in the 'high class' tradition of its Presidio Terrace development [2]. In 1917, as the first Westwood Park houses were occupied, long buildings with several storefronts went up beside the tract. They were styled like the bungalows behind them, Craftsman with Colonial and Tudor touches. Examples survive at 1524 and 1532 Ocean Avenue and at 1700-1720 Ocean [1]. The firm's advertisements usually described the shops as being in the 'Westwood District'. The context statement suggests Baldwin & Howell may have wanted to avoid the working-class associations of the name Ingleside [1]. By 1950 every lot on Ocean Avenue from Plymouth to Fairfield was occupied [1].

title: Strikebreakers and the door to nowhere
place: Geneva Car Barn yard side, 2301 San Jose Avenue (the second-storey 'door to nowhere')
hook: High on the Geneva Car Barn's yard wall is a door that opens onto a sheer drop. It dates from a streetcar strike in 1917.
story: On the night of August 11, 1917, a hundred platform men walked off their United Railroads streetcars near Market and Valencia. They were demanding union recognition, $3.50 a day and an eight-hour day [1]. More than 1,600 of the company's roughly 1,800 workers soon joined them, and the city saw daily marches, mob attacks on cars and armed company men [1]. United Railroads brought in hundreds of strikebreakers and housed them in its carbarns, including 75 at the Geneva barn [1]. At Geneva, the company turned a second-floor window into a doorway and built a temporary wooden stairway down to the rail yard. Strikebreakers could sleep in the office building, then go down and start the streetcars without being seen by the strikers outside [2][3]. The company waited the strikers out, and the walkout was defeated by late November [1]. The stairway is gone, but the doorway is still there on the eastern wall, opening onto a drop to the yard below. It is known as the 'door to nowhere' [2].

title: Tallest Man in San Francisco, at 5'4"
place: San Francisco National Cemetery, Officers' Section
hook: The general who ran the city in the days after the 1906 fire came back to the Presidio in 1917, and the whole city stopped for two minutes.
story: Frederick Funston stood less than five and a half feet tall, but he loomed large over San Francisco [1]. On April 18, 1906, his superior was at a daughter's wedding in Chicago, so Funston had command at the Presidio. He called out the troops, took charge of relief and had buildings dynamited for firebreaks [2]. Critics said he overstepped his authority. His shoot-looters orders led to innocent people being shot, and his dynamiting often started new fires [3]. He went on to Veracruz and the Mexican border and was in line to lead American troops to France. Then, on February 19, 1917, he died of a heart attack in a San Antonio hotel, aged 51 [2]. San Francisco brought him home. Funston lay in state at the Alamo and then under the City Hall rotunda, the first person given that honour there. Presidio cannon fired a thirteen-gun salute and the city stopped for two minutes [2]. He was buried in full dress uniform in the Officers' Section, Section 68, Grave 3 [2][4]. The command he was expected to take went to his former subordinate, John J. Pershing [3].

title: The Shriners' Alhambra on Geary Street
place: Islam Temple, now the Alcazar Theatre, 650 Geary Street
hook: Between Jones and Leavenworth stands a Moorish palace of coloured terra cotta. It was built not for a mosque or a theatre, but for a men's fraternal lodge.
story: In 1917 the Shriners, formally the Ancient Arabic Order of the Nobles of the Mystic Shrine, opened a new home for their San Francisco chapter, Islam Temple, at 650 Geary Street [1]. Architect Thomas Patterson Ross gave them a building in an eclectic Moorish and Byzantine style, with Byzantine arches and filigree latticework. Most of the facade is ornate polychrome terra cotta above a granite base [1]. That June the trade journal Architect and Engineer praised it as "an adaptation from Alhambra, a building that stands as the highest mark of Arabian art and civilization" [1][2]. Wikipedia, citing SF City Guides, gives the cost as $150,000 [2]. The Shriners held meetings and ceremonies here from 1918 to 1970 [1]. The building then took its name from an older Alcazar Theatre. That theatre opened on O'Farrell Street in 1885 and burned in 1906, and the rebuilt Alcazar at 260 O'Farrell was razed for a parking lot, in March 1962 by Wikipedia's account and in 1963 by NoeHill's [1][3]. The Geary Street temple became a legitimate theatre called the Alcazar in 1976 [2]. It was gutted in 1982, named a San Francisco Landmark in 1989 and reopened in 1993 [2].

title: The streetcar that cuts through the park
place: J-Church right-of-way, west edge of Mission Dolores Park
hook: Church Street was too steep for a streetcar, so in 1917 Muni sent its trains off the road, through Dolores Park and behind people's backyards.
story: Riders on the J-Church notice it at once: heading south, the train leaves Church Street at 18th, runs along the west edge of Dolores Park, then weaves through private land around Liberty and 21st before rejoining Church at 22nd [1]. The detour exists because of the hill. When Bion J. Arnold planned the young Municipal Railway in 1912, he faced the steep climb over Dolores Heights. One of his ideas was a tunnel for cars and streetcars under the line of Chattanooga Street. That was one of at least fifteen proposals. The supervisors chose the cheaper private right-of-way around the steepest part of the hill [1]. Track-laying in the park was under way by May 1916 [1]. On August 11, 1917, Mayor 'Sunny Jim' Rolph drove the first car himself, as he liked to do, after being handed a union motorman's cap, card and button [1]. The grade through the park is still 9 percent, the steepest in the Muni Metro system [1]. That hill also saved the line. After the Second World War, when the city turned streetcar routes into bus routes, Church Street proved too steep, and the J kept its rails [1][2].

title: Three hundred women walk into church
place: Site of Central Methodist Church, O'Farrell and Leavenworth streets
hook: A preacher planned a mass meeting to wipe out Tenderloin vice. That morning, the women he was preaching against arrived first, and asked how they were supposed to live.
story: By January 1917 the Rev. Paul Smith of Central Methodist Church, at O'Farrell and Leavenworth, was waging a crusade against the cafes and parlor houses around his church. Newspapers joked that his fiery sermons sent more customers into the district than any madam could [1]. On the morning of January 25, 1917, hours before a planned mass meeting, Mrs. M. R. "Reggie" Gamble, who ran a parlor house on Mason Street, arrived with about 300 women dressed in their finest [1][2]. They asked Smith how they would support themselves once the houses closed. He suggested domestic work at $10 a week. They answered that a pair of shoes alone cost $10, and told him that three-quarters of them were mothers supporting children [1]. Gamble put the blame on the men who bought and profited from the trade. Smith promised to fight for a minimum wage law, but the women walked out unconvinced [1][2]. That afternoon he addressed a crowd of 7,000. By late January, according to a 1988 account in the Tenderloin Times, new laws had shut 208 cafes, dance halls and parlor houses, and February raids closed the brothels. Most of the women were left worse off than before [1][3].

title: When the Barbary Coast moved uptown
place: Mason Street near Eddy (Poodle Dog Restaurant and Hotel, 111 Mason, c. 1910)
hook: A French restaurant with a discreet back driveway. Each time police closed the Barbary Coast, its trade moved a few blocks west.
story: Prostitution was one of the first businesses to return to the Uptown Tenderloin after the fire. By autumn 1906 the District Attorney was already trying to shut it down [1]. By 1910 the Poodle Dog Restaurant and Hotel stood at 111 Mason Street, with dining downstairs, rooms upstairs, and a discreet driveway to a "female boarding house" at the back [1]. A WPA writer in the 1930s remembered Mason Street as the "White Way," lit by cabarets, the Poodle Dog and Billy Lyons' saloon, "the Bucket of Blood" [2]. The same account quotes madam Tessie Wall, who refused to move to San Mateo: "Why I'd rather be an electric light pole on Powell Street than own all of the county" [2]. Reformers kept pushing vice out of the Barbary Coast, and it kept landing here. Police ordered the Coast's dance halls closed in 1913. When the Red Light Abatement Act was finally enforced on February 14, 1917, prostitutes scattered, "especially" to the Uptown Tenderloin [1]. After another crackdown in 1921, "many of the clubs followed the parlors into the Tenderloin" [1].

title: Yiddish Lectures in a Painted Lady
place: 1057 Steiner St (now the Chateau Tivoli), at Golden Gate Ave
hook: A shipping magnate's colorful Victorian became a home for young Jewish immigrant women. Later it became a hall for Yiddish writers and radicals.
story: The colorful Victorian at the corner of Steiner and Golden Gate was built in 1892 for the shipping magnate Daniel B. Jackson [1]. After 1906, as the Jewish Fillmore filled in around it, the house took on two new lives. In 1917 it became the Emanu-El Sisterhood's Residence for Single Jewish Women [1][2][3]. The Sisterhood had been founded in 1894 by women of Temple Emanu-El. It offered job help and clubs for working girls, and the Steiner Street house was meant to ease newly arrived Eastern European immigrants into American life [1][4]. The residence stayed until 1923, when the Sisterhood moved into a new building designed by Julia Morgan on Page Street [2][3]. In 1929 the house became the Yiddish Cultural Center [2][3]. It was the district's hub for secular Jewish life: classes in Yiddish language and literature, and lectures by prominent Yiddish writers from around the world. It was, the New Fillmore notes, "also a center of radical politics" [1]. The center lasted into the 1960s [3]. The house, now the Chateau Tivoli, is one of the few buildings of the Jewish Fillmore still standing [1].

title: A new church rises beside the adobe
place: Mission Dolores Basilica, 16th & Dolores Streets
hook: The 1791 adobe came through the earthquake, but the big brick church beside it did not. What replaced it became the West's first basilica.
story: In 1876, for the mission's centennial, a large red-brick church was built next to the 1791 adobe at 16th and Dolores [1]. The 1906 earthquake wrecked it, and it was torn down. The adobe, also damaged, survived [1][2]. Firefighters kept the flames from both buildings by dynamiting the convent and School of Notre Dame across the street [2]. For years the parish worshipped in a hastily built wooden church behind the old mission [1]. The cornerstone of a new church was laid on September 7, 1913. America's entry into the First World War slowed the work, and the church was finished in 1918 and dedicated at Christmas [1][2]. In 1917, architect Willis Polk quietly strengthened the adobe with concrete-covered steel beams and roof trusses, an early earthquake retrofit [1]. In 1924 part of the old cemetery became a parking lot and schoolyard for parishioners who now came by car [1]. In 1926 the plain new church was redone with ornate Churrigueresque detail inspired by San Diego's 1915 exposition [1]. In 1952 Pope Pius XII made it a minor basilica, the first west of the Mississippi [1][2].

title: A school that began in a back yard
place: Presidio Hill School, 3839 Washington Street (behind the Salz home at 3838 Clay)
hook: Two Presidio Heights mothers didn't like the schools on offer. So one couple built a kindergarten in their back yard, and the husband bought the lot behind it.
story:
By 1917 Helen and Ansley Salz's children, at 3838 Clay Street, were nearing kindergarten age. The couple built a one-room schoolhouse in their back yard, hired a teacher with Larry and Flora Arnstein, who had two children of their own, and soon other parents' children came too [1]. When the children were ready for real school, Ansley bought the big lot behind the yard and built one [1].

The Presidio Open Air School opened in 1918, built on John Dewey's idea of learning by doing. The school's history counts 15 original pupils [2]. Its director Marion Turner, trained at Columbia, had the children govern their own playground affairs using Robert's Rules of Order [1].

Flora "Forgie" Arnstein taught there for many years, first music and dance and then poetry. Her classes produced the book Adventure into Poetry, later reprinted as Children Write Poetry. In it, a three-year-old says the sun "makes my eyes all out of breath" [1]. The school says she taught a young piano prodigy, Pierre Salinger, later John F. Kennedy's press secretary, to read, writing the words he asked for on cards [3].

Renamed Presidio Hill School, it is still there. The school says the Salz family donated the property; Helen recalled that Ansley sold it and gave the building to a new group of parents [1][3].

title: A subway stop paid for in house lots
place: Forest Hill (originally Laguna Honda) Muni Station, 390 Laguna Honda Boulevard
hook: A developer gave the city 21 building lots so its new suburb would get a subway stop. The station, deep under the hill, is now a city landmark.
story: In October 1912 the Newell-Murdoch Company, which was cutting Forest Hill out of Sutro's forest, deeded 21 building lots to the city free of charge for a station on the planned Twin Peaks Tunnel. Like other developers of the Sutro lands, it was betting that a quick commute downtown would set off a boom in sales [1]. Engineer Bion Arnold's original plan gave the stop simple classical portals rather than a large building [2]. What opened with the tunnel in 1918, under the name Laguna Honda Station, has a headhouse mixing Mission and Neoclassical styles. Its construction was overseen by City Engineer Michael O'Shaughnessy, who was also building the Hetch Hetchy water system [3]. The Western Neighborhoods Project calls it the oldest subway station in North America west of Chicago and Muni's deepest underground [2]. In the 1950s, at the height of the Cold War, someone proposed building a vault inside the station to protect city records from nuclear attack [2]. Renamed Forest Hill, it became San Francisco Landmark No. 231, recognized for its role in opening the West of Twin Peaks residence parks [3].

title: Big Guns Shipped East, Too Late for War
place: Battery Chester, West Fort Miley picnic area
hook: In 1918 the Army pulled two 12-inch barrels out of Fort Miley and sent them across the country for the war in Europe. The war ended first.
story: Battery Chester was Fort Miley's heavyweight. Its first two 12-inch rifles were mounted in 1901. They sat on Buffington-Crozier 'disappearing' carriages [1][3]. A third 12-inch gun went in on the south flank in 1903 [2]. On December 27, 1904, the Army named the emplacements for Major James Chester of the 3rd Artillery, a Civil War veteran who had died the year before [1][2]. Then came the First World War. The Army modified many coastal gun barrels and sent them overseas to help the war in Europe. In 1918 the barrels in Chester's emplacements #1 and #2 were lifted out and shipped to New York for modification [2]. The war ended before they could be used. Fort Miley got replacements from two other forts guarding the Golden Gate: Battery Spencer at Fort Baker and Battery Lancaster at Fort Winfield Scott [2]. The state military museum's table tells it differently, recording just one gun removed [1]. Those guns served until 1943, when they were scrapped [2]. Today the emplacement foundations and doors of Battery Chester are still there, and the old gun platform is a picnic area in the Golden Gate National Recreation Area [2].

title: Eight destroyers in one day
place: Bethlehem Steel Administration Building, 20th and Illinois streets
hook: On July 4, 1918, the shipyard launched eight warships in one day. That same summer, the last of Irish Hill's saloons and cottages were torn down.
story: In 1905 Charles M. Schwab stood on the steps of the Union Iron Works office on 20th Street as the only bidder at an auction, and bought the whole yard for Bethlehem Steel for $1 million [2]. By 1918, with America in the First World War, the yard was working flat out. According to the Dogpatch historic district study, it employed 10,000 people, and with Bethlehem's other Bay Area yards it made up the largest shipbuilding complex in the world [1]. In 1918 alone it built 18 submarines, ten of them for Britain, and 66 destroyers [1]. On July 4, 1918, eight destroyers went down the ways in a single day [1][2]. A new administration building had been finished in 1917 on the northeast corner of 20th and Illinois, and it still stands [1][3]. The boom finished off the neighbourhood next door. Bethlehem bought the Irish Hill lots on 20th Street for a new concrete foundry. Photographs from May 1918 show a saloon, a French laundry and another saloon facing Illinois Street, months away from demolition [3]. Accounts differ on the foundry's date and cost, and one says it was never built at all. What was left of Irish Hill became a parking lot next to a rocky stump [1][3].

title: Fiddles, cops and $2,600 on Sanchez
place: 1316 Sanchez Street, between 25th and 26th
hook: Agnes Farrell's Irish parents bought their Sanchez Street house outright for $2,600. The parties there were loud enough that police called at 2 a.m.
story:
Agnes Farrell was born South of Market to Irish immigrant parents. In 1918 the family moved to 1316 Sanchez Street, and after renting for years they scraped together $2,600 to buy it outright. They sold it in 1964 for $9,000 [1]. Her father had watched the 1906 fire from the top of the Noe Street hill [1].

In her memory, 1920s Noe Valley was a working-class mix of Irish and Italian families. Horse-drawn buggies still made their rounds, and a rags-and-bottles man came by once a week calling for empties. Every corner had a grocery, and the butcher handed children free slices of baloney. Kids played "hickey," skating with one foot in the gutter, and hitched rides on the produce truck until the driver threw potatoes at them [1]. A nickel streetcar ride took them to the Beach Chalet to watch hurling and Gaelic football. Back on Sanchez, the after-match parties went on until the police asked for quiet at 2 a.m. Next-door neighbour Bill O'Dwyer played the fiddle, and "When Irish Eyes Are Smiling" got more off-key as the night went on [1]. In 2008, aged 91, she was booked to share these stories on a panel at St. Paul's Parish Center for a festival on Noe Valley's Irish [2].

title: Holed through, off by an eighth
place: West portal of the Twin Peaks Tunnel, West Portal Avenue at Ulloa Street
hook: Drillers boring from opposite sides of Twin Peaks met almost perfectly. Ten months later Mayor Rolph drove the first streetcar out of the hill here.
story: Digging on the Twin Peaks Tunnel began on December 11, 1914, at three sites, including this western portal near Ulloa Street [1]. It cost lives. In July 1915 inspector Ernest Dunden slipped onto live wires at the west portal and was killed, and in February 1917 a delayed dynamite cap killed several more [1]. In August 1916, 90 feet down, workers found a petrified redwood trunk [1]. On April 5, 1917 came the drillers' shout of 'Holed through!' The two bores met out of line by just an eighth of an inch [1]. Four supervisors raced to be first through the gap, and Joseph Lahaney won with his suit covered in mud. On February 3, 1918, Mayor James Rolph drove the first official streetcar through the 2.27-mile bore himself. It stopped at Laguna Honda (now Forest Hill) station, some 70 feet below ground, and came out here to a huge crowd [1][2][3]. The next Sunday more than 21,000 people rode out just to look. The tunnel opened the west side to settlement [1].

title: Miss Friedman's forty-one years
place: Visitacion Valley Community Center, Raymond Avenue near Bayshore Boulevard
hook: A schoolteacher took charge of a new community centre in 1918 and ran it for 41 years. Local men built its gym by hand.
story: The valley's first school opened in September 1896. After a court session it was decided to keep the Spanish 'Visitacion' in its name, but the new sign arrived reading 'Visitation' [1][2]. One of its early teachers was Florence Friedman. In 1918 she left the classroom to become the first director of the new Visitacion Valley Community Center, and she led it for 41 years until she retired in 1959 [1][2]. Old newspaper clippings reprinted by the neighbourhood paper show how it grew [3]. A friend of the Center donated materials for a gymnasium and men's clubroom, on condition that the valley's men supply the labour. One clipping counted about 6,000 hours of work needed, a quota of eight hours for every man [3]. Architect Dorothy Wormser donated plans for a clubhouse on Raymond Avenue between Alpha Street and San Bruno Avenue, the road now called Bayshore Boulevard. It was to have a gym, an auditorium, a clinic and a domestic science room [3]. Women and girls who had never used a needle took dressmaking and millinery classes there [3]. Friedman lived in the valley until her death in 1984 [2].

title: Praying in masks on Van Ness
place: Site of the second St. Mary's Cathedral, Van Ness Avenue at O'Farrell Street (NW corner)
hook: In the autumn of 1918 San Francisco made masks the law, and worshippers gathered outdoors at the cathedral on Van Ness.
story:
Archbishop Patrick Riordan bought the corner of Van Ness Avenue and O'Farrell Street in 1883. He broke ground in 1885 and dedicated the new St. Mary's Cathedral in January 1891 [1]. Twenty-seven years later it faced a different kind of emergency.

The city's first case of Spanish flu was diagnosed on 23 September 1918 [2]. From 18 October the Board of Health closed theatres, schools and lodge meetings. According to the University of Michigan's influenza archive, it did not close churches but advised that services stop or be held in the open air [3]. A local account says churches were ordered shut, so the sources disagree [2]. From 25 October a city ordinance required everyone in public to wear a mask. On 27 October alone, police arrested 110 people for not wearing one [3].

A photograph from 1918 shows an outdoor service at the cathedral, with some worshippers in influenza masks [2]. By the time the epidemic ended in early 1919, the city had recorded almost 45,000 cases and more than 3,000 deaths [2]. The cathedral burned in 1962 and was replaced by the present cathedral on Cathedral Hill, completed in 1970 [1].

title: Roller skates checked at the Coliseum
place: Former Coliseum Theatre, 745 Clement Street at 9th Avenue
hook: Depression kids paid a dime, skated to 9th and Clement, and handed their skates to an usher for safekeeping before the Saturday matinee.
story: The Coliseum opened on November 22, 1918, with Mary Pickford in 'Johanna Enlists'. It was designed by the Reid Brothers, the firm behind the Fairmont Hotel and the Cliff House [1][2]. Remodelled in Art Deco style in 1931, it was badly damaged by fire in 1935 [1]. Pat French Swendsen remembered Depression Saturdays there. The matinee cost a dime, and boys scrubbed stoops to earn one. Kids skated to Ninth and Clement, bought candy-coated licorice from 'Nick the Greek' next door, and checked their skates in a 'skate vault' in return for a numbered disk [3]. The manager staged yelling contests between boys and girls. When the assistant manager threatened to stop the show over spitballs, some boy with a slingshot inevitably fired one at him [3]. In 1949 the new Coronet on Geary took over the Coliseum's action pictures. The Coliseum was left with re-runs and went dark around 1952. It reopened when the Coronet began showing 'Oklahoma!' in 1956 [4]. It closed for good on October 17, 1989. The auditorium was gutted in 2000, and condominiums were later built above a ground-floor drugstore [1].

title: Tent City and Influenza, 1918
place: Camp Paul Jones site, Lighthouse Reservation slopes
hook: World War I crammed 13,000 men onto a hilly island built for 500. Then the flu came, and the caskets went out by launch.
story:
When America entered World War I, Yerba Buena Island's training station exploded. It reached a peak of 13,000 men on an island with maybe 150 usable acres [1][2]. Rows of canvas tents on wooden floors spread across the slopes [2]. The Lighthouse Service gave up 1.5 acres of its reservation, where the Navy carved Camp Paul Jones into the hillside. By 1919 it had 806 tents, and a separate detention camp had 384 more [2].

In 1918 influenza swept the Bay Area and the island was quarantined for weeks. A young boat orderly who ferried caskets to San Francisco remembered that "funerals seemed an almost daily occurrence, sometimes with six to nine caskets". The first coffin of the day rode on a field gun and the rest followed on a truck [2]. Every recruit spent three weeks isolated in a hilltop tent camp. A separate camp for meningitis patients stood on the northwest point, next to the cemetery [2]. The crowding convinced the Navy to move training to San Diego. On 31 July 1923 the Goat Island station was officially closed, and only a "receiving ship" stayed behind [1][2].

title: The Library Carnegie's Man Grumbled About
place: Sunset Branch Library (City Landmark No. 239), 1305 18th Ave
hook: Andrew Carnegie paid for it, but his secretary objected to its 'wasted' loggia and its lofty ceiling.
story: Andrew Carnegie's money was controversial in labour-minded San Francisco. It took years to accept it, and even then none of the seven branch libraries built with $375,000 of his money carried his name [1]. The Sunset branch opened in 1918 [1][2]. G. Albert Lansburgh drew two plans. His octagonal scheme was judged 'quite impossible,' so a rectangular Classical Revival design went ahead [2]. Carnegie's secretary, James Bertram, still objected. He was offended by the 'wasted space' of the entrance loggia. Six months later, with construction under way, he grumbled that the ceiling was too high. Lansburgh wrote back that 'the proportions of the exterior could not be conveniently altered,' and Bertram gave in [1]. The loggia is still there: three tall arches with Corinthian columns, and names of authors, many of them Western, carved under the windows [2]. The children's room was on the main floor, as Carnegie's guidelines required [1]. A 1920 photograph, taken across 19th and Irving, shows the library almost alone at the edge of settlement, with Sutro Forest beyond [3]. Decades later, Frank Dunnigan, then a USF student, treated it as his home away from home, open 9 a.m. to 9 p.m. on weekdays [4].

title: The Marine-View Park off Lake Street
place: West Clay Park (West Clay Street), off Lake Street between 22nd and 24th Avenues
hook: Tucked between Lake Street and the Presidio, West Clay Park was sold as a "marine view residence park", and Ansel Adams's parents gave it as their address.
story: West Clay Park was once an address of its own. The 1918 San Francisco Blue Book gave it a section, "between Lake and San Francisco Bay" [2], and West Clay Street survives there today. It came out of the residence-park era, when developers sold big lots with building restrictions and views. The firm of Lyon & Hoag boasted about it in a brochure for its next tract, Lincoln Manor. "When a few years ago we put West Clay Park—at that time the newest marine view residence park—on the market," it said, "we told our buyers of the sure increase and all our predictions have been fulfilled" [1]. Lots at West Clay Park, the brochure added, now sold for $200 to $300 a front foot [1]. According to Wikipedia, Lincoln Manor's builder, the S. A. Born Building Company, also built in West Clay Park and Sea Cliff [3]. The Blue Book lists the park's residents house by house, from Mr. and Mrs. E. I. De Laveaga at No. 2 to Dr. and Mrs. B. Foulkes at No. 346. It also files one 24th Avenue household under the park's name: "Mr. and Mrs. Chas. H. Adams, 129 24th Ave., West Clay Park" [2]. That was the house where Ansel Adams grew up [4].

title: The Tyrrels, Fairmount's first Black family
place: Poole-Bell House, 196-198 Laidley Street at Fairmount Street
hook: Myths about the Laidley Street mansion claim Mary Ellen Pleasant and a trapdoor. The true story is a Guyanese-born City Hall clerk and his family.
story:
For decades the gothic house at Laidley and Fairmount was said to belong to Mary Ellen Pleasant, with a trapdoor for disposing of unwanted guests. Researchers have shown that Pleasant never lived there [1][2]. The house was built for the attorney John P. Poole, dated to 1887 by one researcher. His widow Annie sold it in 1906 to Teresa Bell, who had once shared a mansion with Pleasant [1][2].

In 1918 Bell moved out and rented the house to Bertram and Frances Tyrrel. They were the first African American family in the Glen Park-Fairmount district, and in the 1930 and 1940 censuses they were the only one [3]. Bertram, born in 1867 in Demerara, British Guiana, had served in the US Navy. He was one of 28 workers fired in 1896 when white unions pushed the Palace Hotel to get rid of its Black staff. He later rose from messenger to clerk at the Board of Public Works, an unusual promotion for a Black man then [3]. Frances was the daughter of Black pioneers who had come to California in the 1850s. She was Grand Secretary of her Eastern Star chapter [3]. They rented the house until 1921 and stayed in the district for three decades, finally settling on Chenery Street [3]. Bertram died in 1946 [3].

title: The cross the wind knocked down five times
place: Summit of Lone Mountain, now USF's Lone Mountain campus
hook: For decades a wooden cross topped Lone Mountain. In 1918 a writer predicted the hill's own funeral, and the roads that would bring it.
story: The Spanish called this hill El Divisadero, a place from which to look far [1]. In 1860 Archbishop Joseph Alemany bought the land for Calvary Cemetery, and the hill came with it. A year after the dedication a cross went up on the sandy summit [2]. On February 11, 1918, the Chronicle ran Walter J. Thompson's elegy for the hill. The cross could be seen from every corner of the surrounding cemeteries. Five times the wind threw it to the ground, and each time it was put back. Young visitors hacked their initials and dates into its soft wood with jack-knives [2]. But Thompson saw what was coming. The city had promised to extend Parker Avenue over the hill to the new St. Ignatius Church, and Turk Street would soon be cut through from Masonic to Parker. Contractors "who haven't an ounce of sentiment" said the clay hill would be easy to reshape [2]. Alice Brown Chittenden's 1910 watercolour still shows the cross above the shacks or tents of 1906 refugees [3]. The last wooden cross came down in 1930, and in 1932 work began on a college on the summit [4].

title: Under the mountain in seven minutes
place: Twin Peaks Tunnel east portal, Market & Castro Streets
hook: From a hole at the top of Market Street, crews dug more than two miles under Twin Peaks, opening up the whole southwest of the city.
story: By 1910, neighbourhood improvement clubs were holding conventions to push for a streetcar tunnel under Twin Peaks. They argued that thousands of acres of empty land on the far side would fill with homes [1]. The city hired Chicago consultant Bion J. Arnold. The property owners who stood to gain agreed to pay through assessment districts, with the undeveloped west side carrying most of the cost [1][2]. Digging began in December 1914, with the eastern end cut open from the top of Market Street near Castro [1][2]. The soft ground there meant the first blocks were built as concrete boxes in an open trench, one box for each track, with a small underground station at Eureka Street [2]. The work was deadly. An inspector was electrocuted in 1915, and several men died when a delayed dynamite charge went off in February 1917 [1]. On February 3, 1918, Mayor James Rolph took the controls of Muni car No. 117 for the first passenger run [2]. Contemporary reports called it the longest streetcar tunnel in the world, about 12,000 feet from end to end [3]. The trip took seven minutes, and new neighbourhoods such as West Portal, Forest Hill and St. Francis Wood grew up at the far end [2][4].

title: Willis Polk's Wall of Glass
place: Hallidie Building, 130 Sutter Street
hook: Decades before glass towers took over downtown, a seven-storey building on Sutter Street hung its whole face in glass.
story: Architect Willis Polk designed a modest seven-storey office block at 130 Sutter Street whose street front was not masonry at all but a sheer sheet of glass hung in front of the structure: a curtain wall [1][2]. It is often called one of the first glass curtain walls in the country, though a 1909 clothing building in Kansas City came earlier, and even the opening year is disputed: guidebooks give 1917 or 1918 [1][2]. The building was named for Andrew Smith Hallidie, the cable car pioneer, and Polk softened the glass with ornate iron fire escapes and sheet-metal cornices [2]. In 1971, when a bank was thinking of replacing it with a much taller tower, the Board of Supervisors made it City Landmark #37, and it was added to the National Register the same year [1][2]. The technique Polk tried here would come to dominate commercial architecture later in the century [1]. A two-year restoration finished in 2013, and the local chapter of the American Institute of Architects now occupies its ground floor [2].

title: Constantinople Cafe and Greek Town's Third Street
place: Greek Town, Third Street between Folsom and Harrison
hook: A century ago the cafes on Third Street were named Smyrna, Athens and Constantinople. This was Greek Town, until a bridge pushed it aside.
story: A city photograph from January 23, 1919, captures a row of Greek businesses on Third Street between Folsom and Harrison: Patris Photo Studio, the Constantinople Cafe, the Acropolis Bar and Grill and Apollo Bros. Cigars. Around 1920 the Athens Restaurant & Oyster House and the Smyrna Cafe stood nearby [1]. Greeks began arriving in San Francisco in the 1880s but came in far greater numbers after 1906, when workers were needed to rebuild the city. The 100 through 400 blocks of Third Street and adjoining side streets were overwhelmingly Greek-owned, according to Jim Lucas of the Greek Historical Society [1]. The Greek consulate sat at Mission and Third, the Greek American Hall at Second and Harrison, and the first Holy Trinity Greek Orthodox Church at 345 Seventh Street [1]. Community life was not always calm: in July 1908 a quarrel over parish elections and money turned violent at Holy Trinity, and a breakaway faction built its own church on Rincon Hill before the two sides reconciled in December 1909 [2]. Building the Bay Bridge in the 1930s displaced many Greeks, who moved their businesses elsewhere in the city [1][2].

title: Forest Hill's residents take over their suburb
place: Forest Hill Clubhouse (Bernard Maybeck), 381 Magellan Avenue
hook: Fed up with their developer's shoddy streets, Forest Hill's homeowners took over the whole tract in 1918. Then came a clubhouse by Bernard Maybeck.
story: Newell-Murdoch sold Forest Hill as 'sylvan solitude' carved from Sutro's forest. They hired landscape architect Mark Daniels, who gave it a grand staircase on Dewey Boulevard, and advertised every Saturday in the city papers [1]. They also cut down most of the trees they were selling, and they wrote strict rules about the design of homes and the race of the people who could live in them [1]. The first house was finished in February 1914. In October 1912 the company had given the city 21 lots for the Laguna Honda tunnel station, betting on a quick commute [1][2]. When the tunnel opened in 1918, war had stalled sales, and homeowners were fed up with streets and utilities that did not meet city standards. They formed the Forest Hill Association and took over the entire tract from the developer [1]. In 1919 the neighbourhood got a community clubhouse at 381 Magellan, designed by the renowned Bernard Maybeck [1][3]. A 1968 Junior League guide called its high, heavily beamed interior 'Maybeck at his best' [3].

title: The K Line's Dead End on Brighton
place: Brighton Avenue at Grafton Avenue (former K-Ingleside terminal)
hook: The city's streetcars had to pay a rival company to run on Ocean Avenue. For decades the K's terminal was a stub on a quiet side street.
story: The Municipal Railway opened its K line through the new Twin Peaks Tunnel on February 3, 1918. But Ocean Avenue already carried the cars of the privately owned United Railroads, successor to the Market Street Railway, which had built a line out Ocean Avenue in just six days in 1895 to serve the new Ingleside Racetrack [1]. That November the city signed the 'Parkside Agreements': Muni cars could use the company's Ocean Avenue track as far as Harold Avenue in exchange for cash and shared maintenance [1]. The K reached Miramar Avenue in February 1919. On May 18, 1919, it was pushed a few blocks further east to Brighton Avenue, then two blocks down Brighton to a stub-end terminal at Grafton Avenue [1]. Entering the 1920s, Ocean Avenue had two streetcar lines serving the fast-growing neighbourhoods [2]. A 1950 photograph in the OMI context statement shows a K car at Brighton and Grafton [2]. After Muni bought the private Market Street Railway, the old route 12 streetcar left Ocean Avenue in April 1945 [1]. On May 18, 1952, the Brighton Avenue trackage was abandoned and replaced by the Phelan Loop near City College, and the quiet side street lost its streetcars [1].

title: The Pilot Who Never Came Back
place: Crissy Field historic airfield buildings, Mason St
hook: Major Dana Crissy took off from the Presidio in a coast-to-coast race in 1919. He died the first day out, and the new airfield took his name.
story: Dana Crissy started out as a Presidio coast artilleryman fascinated by flying. By 1917 he had transferred to the Signal Corps' Aviation Section, and he rose to major and commander of Mather Field in Sacramento [1]. In October 1919 a new airfield at the Presidio hosted the Army's first Transcontinental Reliability and Endurance Test. Sixty-one planes took part, 46 flying west from Long Island and 15 flying east from here [1]. Only nine finished. Crissy and his observer, Sgt. 1st Class V. Thomas, were killed on the first day, trying to land their de Havilland DH-4 near Salt Lake City [1]. Wikipedia gives the date of the crash as October 8 [3]. His friend Col. Henry 'Hap' Arnold asked that the new field be named for him [1]. The Army accepted Crissy Field on June 24, 1921. The 91st Observation Squadron arrived that August [3]. Its pilots watched artillery practice, took aerial photographs and supported the Air Mail, and they flew the first aerial forest-fire patrols in the West [2]. Crissy is buried in the Presidio's national cemetery, in grave 98-5 of the Officers' Section [1].
