title: The church that was sawn in half
place: St. Teresa of Avila Church, 19th and Connecticut streets
hook: When its Irish neighbourhood disappeared, the parish sawed its church in two and hauled both halves up Potrero Hill.
story: In the 1860s, Catholics at Potrero Point heard Mass in the dining room of the Breslin Hotel on Irish Hill, said by priests who came from St. Peter's [1]. In 1880 Archbishop Patrick Riordan created a new parish named for St. Teresa of Ávila. Its first pastor, Father John Kenny, turned a warehouse into a church with three altars and a confessional [1]. The parish today remembers its beginnings in a Third Street boarding house [2]. In 1892 Father Patrick O'Connell built a proper church on the northeast corner of Tennessee and 19th streets. After 1906 he decided the growing Catholic population needed a school, and in 1912 the Sisters of the Presentation opened one with more than 100 pupils [1]. Then the neighbourhood started to disappear. Irish Hill was levelled during the First World War, the Irish Catholic population of Potrero Point fell sharply, and industry kept closing in [1]. So in 1924 movers cut the church in two and moved each half separately up the hill to the northeast corner of 19th and Connecticut streets [1][2]. The rebuilt church still stands there, and the parish is still small and close-knit [2].

title: Where the 'P.O. Kids' Grew Up
place: Edgewood Center (former S.F. Protestant Orphanage), 1801 Vicente Street at 29th Avenue
hook: San Francisco's first orphanage, founded by women in 1851, moved to the Parkside dunes in 1924, where children lived with 'cottage mothers.'
story: In 1851 a group of San Francisco women, most of them clergymen's wives, took in five children orphaned by an epidemic. Their society ran the San Francisco Protestant Orphan Asylum on Haight Street, and until 1958 its board was all women. It took only white Protestant children, and in its early years it turned away children of parents judged 'immoral' [1]. Experts were moving away from dormitories toward cottages that felt like family homes. In 1923 the orphanage bought ten acres on Vicente Street between 28th and 30th Avenues and hired Bliss & Faville. The model was the Pacific Hebrew Orphan Society's cottage campus, Homewood Terrace, on Ocean Avenue [1]. Edgewood opened in 1924. It had an administration building with twin staircases and six cottages, each for twenty children, two 'cottage mothers' and an assistant. The children went to Parkside School and called themselves 'P.O. kids' [1]. Few were really orphans. By 1944 only about six percent were, and the institution renamed itself Edgewood that year [1]. Later it dropped its race and religion rules and became a treatment center for children at risk. The cottages still stand among the pines [1][2].

title: A Hospital Opened With a Nine-Day Carnival
place: Chinese Hospital, 835 Jackson Street
hook: Chinatown celebrated its new hospital with a nine-day party that began on April 18, the anniversary of the earthquake, complete with beauty queens and a baby contest.
story: Chinatown's residents had long faced discrimination and limited access to public health care [1]. The community's answer began with the Tung Wah Dispensary, founded in 1899 and staffed by both Western-trained doctors and Chinese herbalists [1]. In 1923 fifteen community organisations formed the Chinese Hospital Association to build something bigger [1]. When its permit came before the Board of Supervisors, the Chronicle ran the headline 'Residents Protest Chinese Hospital', but the Health Committee recommended approval unanimously, in front of a large Chinese audience [2]. Money came from the Six Companies, the Chinese Chamber of Commerce, churches and a whole neighbourhood of donors [2]. The hospital already had patients, but it held off its formal opening so it could begin with a carnival on April 18, 1925, that ran for nine days. It drew 'automobiles by the score', a beauty contest for a festival queen and a baby popularity contest [2]. The Chronicle hailed 'one of the finest hospitals in San Francisco' [2]. Chinese Hospital at 835 Jackson Street called itself the first and only institution of its kind in the country [1].

title: A Streetcar Through Open Farmland
place: Randolph St near 19th Ave (M-Ocean View route)
hook: In 1925 the city ran a streetcar through half-empty farmland to Ocean View, rezoned the route for shops, and waited for customers who didn't come.
story: The Municipal Railway's M-Ocean View opened in 1925 as a shuttle from West Portal along 19th Avenue, Worcester (today's diagonal extension of 19th Avenue), Randolph, Orizaba and Broad Street to Plymouth Avenue [1]. When it opened, the tracks along the diagonal and Randolph ran through mostly open farmland; a March 1926 city photograph looking east on Randolph from Worcester shows a lone M car [2]. The city bet on growth. In 1925 and 1927 about 13.4 acres along Worcester and Randolph were rezoned from residential to commercial in anticipation of the line, but only a few scattered stores appeared because housing on Merced Heights grew slowly until after World War II [1]. Riders were scarce, too. Local historian Marsha Fontes wrote that the line lost $96,000 in its first six months and 'struggled along' before being discontinued until 1946 [3]. The context statement gives a slightly different timeline: partial service through the Twin Peaks Tunnel from 1927, buses replacing streetcars in 1939, and rails returning in 1944 [1]. Sporadic building did begin south of Ingleside Terraces in the late 1920s once the line arrived [1].

title: A clubhouse for mothers, boys over six barred
place: Mothers Building (Delia Fleishhacker Memorial Building), San Francisco Zoo near Sloat Blvd
hook: Two brothers built their late mother a memorial: a Tuscan-style lounge where mothers could rest. Boys over six were not allowed in.
story: At their mother Delia's memorial service, Herbert and Mortimer Fleishhacker looked for a fitting tribute. A friend suggested a "Mothers House" for the new playfield going up beside the great pool [1]. The brothers gave about $50,000 for the building and a large wading pool [1][2], and architect George W. Kelham designed a single-room building in the style of Tuscany around 1500, fronted by an arched loggia, with Corinthian columns and a frieze of playing cherubs [1]. It was meant to be the "finest of its kind in the United States": a lounge for mothers with small children, with restrooms and a small kitchen. Boys over the age of six were specifically excluded [1]. Matrons helped the mothers, and tea and picnic lunches were served [1]. When the playfield opened on Labor Day weekend in 1925, the Chronicle admired its walnut settles, Italian-tiled tables and hangings in "mulberry and thistle tones" [1]. In the 1930s New Deal artists added mosaics and huge murals of Noah's Ark [1]. The pool and playfield are gone, but the Mothers Building still stands at the zoo [1][3].

title: A golf course named for a dead president
place: Harding Park, 99 Harding Rd
hook: President Harding died at the Palace Hotel in 1923. Two years later San Francisco opened a public course on Lake Merced's peninsula in his name.
story: In 1923 the city leased about 170 acres of Spring Valley land between the north and south arms of Lake Merced for a municipal golf course [1]. That August, President Warren Harding, an avid golfer and a widely scorned leader, died at the Palace Hotel while visiting San Francisco [2]. The new course took his name. Willie Watson and Sam Whiting, who had built the courses at the neighbouring Olympic Club, agreed to design it for $300. Construction cost about $295,000 [2]. Harding Park opened on 18 July 1925, one of several big public recreation grounds the city acquired in the 1920s and '30s, a period when City Hall came to see its job as providing places for families to play [2][3]. The everyman course soon won national notice. It hosted the U.S. Amateur Public Links Championship in 1937 and 1956, and Byron Nelson won two events there in 1944 [2]. For many golfers who rode the bus across town, it was their first taste of a "real" course, with wide grass fairways lined by cypress [2].

title: Annie's Pink Cocktail on Parnassus
place: The Connell house, 311 Parnassus Avenue
hook: She weighed 77 pounds, argued politics with a cocktail tilted at 30 degrees and never spilled a drop. Her silent husband outwitted a paddy wagon.
story:
Annie Lynch Connell was born in County Cavan in 1848, the last of fourteen girls. At five she and four sisters were sent to America, at $10 a passage. She married Jim Connell at 35, honeymooned in San Francisco, fell for its "blessed fog" and refused to leave [1].

At 311 Parnassus she ruled a table of seven. Her grandson remembered her at 77 pounds, debating politics with a stemmed glass of her own pink cocktail. Five o'clock was cocktail time. She once talked a police officer into letting her keep flowers she had picked in Golden Gate Park. She also let in a friendly assessor because he said he was from Ireland, and he rewarded her with a whopping personal property tax bill [1].

Jim was big and quiet. After Annie died he rode downtown each day on a quarter: a dime for the round-trip streetcar, fifteen cents for silent movies. One evening he dozed off against a hydrant on Market Street, and police took him for a drunk. As the patrol wagon climbed Haight Street alongside the No. 6 streetcar he usually rode home, he convinced the officers he was no drunk and, with their permission, swung aboard [1][2]. At dinner, his grandson recalled, he spoke just four words: "Pass the Worcestershire Sauce."

title: Burying Islais Creek, the drawbridge commute
place: Third Street at Islais Creek
hook: The city once sold these marshes for $10 a lot. Filling them took a reclamation district, 475,000 tons of rock and a decade.
story: Islais Creek once spread into a square mile of marsh and mudflat. In 1861 the city practically gave the water lots away, for $10 to cover the deed and notary fee [1]. After 1906 boosters dreamed of a port here, and in 1909 the state spent $1 million in bonds buying back 173 acres [1][2]. Nothing much happened: by 1925 there were still 63 owners and 549 parcels of mud, and no one wanted to pay for the 2,200-foot seawall [1]. That year a state law launched the reclamation district that finally did the job [1][2]. The seawall alone swallowed 475,000 tons of rock from Potrero Hill and Bernal Heights; spoil from building Bayshore Boulevard went in too [1][2]. The work was declared finished in 1936, leaving only the Islais Creek Channel [1][2]. Crossing it was part of daily life. Ruth Eshow Upton, commuting downtown on the No. 16 streetcar from 1937, dreaded the Third Street drawbridge rising for a boat; her office elevator starter learned to ask whether the bridge had been up [3].

title: Feathers on Buchanan Street
place: Jefferson Market, 1002 Buchanan St
hook: Cages of squawking chickens were stacked on the sidewalk, and feathers hung in the air. This was where Jewish San Francisco came to buy its Sabbath bird.
story: In the 1920s and '30s, the Jefferson Market at 1002 Buchanan, owned by I. Goldstein, was the main place in San Francisco's Jewish community to buy a fresh chicken [1]. Jerry Flamm's account remembers a place that "bulged with screeching chickens". Cages were piled on the sidewalk, leaving only narrow aisles for passers-by, and a cloud of feathers hung in the air [1]. You picked your bird and a clerk carried it, flapping, to the back. There the shochet, the kosher slaughterer, killed it with a straight-edge razor and hung it to bleed. Then it was plucked, wrapped in newspaper and handed to you [1][2]. The Jefferson was one of four places in the district that sold kosher chickens, along with Sosnick's, Diller's and Shenson's [2]. They belonged to a dense little world. In the two blocks bounded by Fillmore, Buchanan, McAllister and Golden Gate there were two synagogues, three kosher restaurants, four Jewish bakeries, five kosher meat markets, at least three delicatessens and a Jewish liquor merchant [2][3]. On Saturday nights, after the Sabbath ended at sundown, shops reopened and stayed busy until eleven [1].

title: Fish, pills and midwives on Post Street
place: Uoki K. Sakai Fish Market, 1684 Post Street
hook: A fish market with nine children upstairs across the road, the city's first Japanese pharmacy and a maternity hospital: one block of 1920s Post Street held a whole community.
story: By 1925 the Uoki K. Sakai Fish Market had moved from its first home on Geary, near Nikkei hotels, groceries and the Benkyo-do confectionery, to 1684 Post Street. The Sakai family took a big house across the street at 1628 Post, with room upstairs for their nine children [1]. By the late 1920s the north side of this block, between Buchanan and Laguna, also held the Nippon Drugstore, Namiye Murayama's Kinmon Maternity Hospital and the Gosha-do Books and Stationery store [1]. A few doors down at 1609 Post, a Mrs. Misawa ran what the city's history calls the first Japanese pharmacy registered in San Francisco [1]. Hatsuro Aizawa, whose father managed Gosha-do for owner Shoroku Ono, later remembered it as a place where people browsed and played cards even when they had no money to spend [1]. None of this was secure. The Alien Land Law kept most Issei from owning the buildings they traded in, so businesses often moved [1]. The Nippon Drug building later housed the jazz club Jimbo's Bop City and was eventually moved around the corner to Fillmore Street [2].

title: From Gold Rush refuge to Julia Morgan home
place: The Heritage (San Francisco Ladies' Protection and Relief Society), 3400 Laguna Street
hook: A women's charity founded during the Gold Rush ran an orphanage for sixty years, then moved to former fairgrounds in a building by Julia Morgan.
story: The San Francisco Ladies' Protection and Relief Society was founded in 1853 [1]. Its mission was 'to render protection and assistance to strangers, to sick independent women and children,' and it began by helping women and families stranded by the Gold Rush [3]. For six decades it ran a children's home on Franklin Street that people affectionately called the 'Old Brown Ark.' After the 1906 earthquake 145 children were moved to tents in the Presidio [3]. In 1921 the state began placing orphans in foster homes. In 1922 the society changed course, deciding to care for elderly women and convalescents instead, and accepted a block of former exposition land bounded by Francisco, Bay, Laguna and Octavia from Kate F. Austin [3]. Julia Morgan designed the new home. It is reinforced concrete faced with brick and trimmed with terra cotta [2]. The society held its first meeting in the front parlor on March 3, 1925. The job came in $28,000 under its $150,000 budget [3]. Later benefactors included Edith and Lucy Allyne, sisters from Green and Gough, who were members and made a significant gift [4]. In 1957 residents of the Crocker Old People's Home moved in, and in 1959 the enlarged home was named The Heritage [3]. It came through the 1989 earthquake almost untouched [3].

title: Kezar: Where the 49ers Were Born
place: Kezar Stadium, Frederick and Stanyan
hook: A bequest honouring one woman's mother became the concrete bowl where San Francisco's first major-league team kicked off.
story: In 1922 the Park Commission accepted $100,000 from the estate of Mary A. Kezar for a memorial to her mother and relatives, added $200,000 of its own, and built a stadium on the old park nursery at the southeast corner [1][2]. Most of McLaren's first rhododendron dell was lost to it [2]. Kezar was dedicated on May 2, 1925, with a two-mile race [1], and the National Register says it was enlarged in 1928 to seat 65,000 [2]. Before the war, college football packed it: Cal's Wonder Teams, Stanford's Wow Boys, St. Mary's, Santa Clara and USF [3]. That convinced Tony Morabito the Bay Area was ready for pro football. After much lobbying he won a franchise, and his San Francisco 49ers played their first home game at Kezar, an exhibition, on September 1, 1946, beating the Chicago Rockets 34-14 before 45,000 fans [3]. The National Register says the 49ers stayed until 1969; another history dates their last Kezar game to January 3, 1971 [1][2]. The concrete stands came down in 1989 [2].

title: Seventy-Five Cents at Diller's
place: Diller's Strictly Kosher Restaurant, 1233 Golden Gate Ave
hook: Dinner at Diller's cost a bissel more than at Schindler's, but on weekend nights the kosher restaurant on Golden Gate Avenue was packed.
story: Among the kosher eateries along Golden Gate Avenue and McAllister Street, Diller's Strictly Kosher Restaurant was, in Jerry Flamm's words, "the biggest, the best, and the most popular" [1]. It stood on Golden Gate between Webster and Fillmore [1][2]. A dinner cost seventy-five cents, a "bissel" (a little) more than the fifty cents charged at Schindler's, and people agreed it was worth it [1]. On weekend nights the place was full. Families coming back from the popular Sunday picnics at San Mateo Park or at Alum Rock Park in San Jose often went straight to Diller's for dinner before going home [1]. Diller's also sold kosher chickens, one of four places in the district that did [2]. It stood in a two-block pocket bounded by Fillmore, Buchanan, McAllister and Golden Gate that held three kosher restaurants, four Jewish bakeries and five kosher meat markets [2][3]. The Jewish Fillmore grew up after the 1906 earthquake, when Jews burned out of South of Market moved west. It faded after World War II as families left for the Richmond, the Sunset and the suburbs [2]. Later redevelopment cleared many of these blocks [3].

title: Stall No. 8 and Rose Alioto
place: Alioto's, 8 Fisherman's Wharf, foot of Taylor St
hook: A Sicilian immigrant's fish stand became the first building on Fisherman's Wharf. After he died, his widow Rose turned it into a restaurant that lasted more than eighty years.
story: In 1925 Nunzio Alioto, a Sicilian immigrant, opened a fish stand at stall number 8 on Fisherman's Wharf [1][2]. The wharf was still young: the state had set aside the waterfront between Taylor and Leavenworth Streets for the fishing fleet only in 1900 [3]. In 1932, with business going well, Alioto put up the first building on the wharf and began selling fresh crab and shrimp cocktails over the counter [1][2]. He died the next year. His widow, Rose, took over with their three children, becoming, SFGATE says, the first businesswoman on Fisherman's Wharf [1][2]. In 1938 the family opened a full restaurant at Stall No. 8. "Alioto's mythology", as the Chronicle put it, credits Rose with creating cioppino at this point, cooking the fish stew for Italian day labourers [1]. The 1939 World's Fair made the wharf a tourist destination for the first time [1]. In 1957 a fire gutted the restaurant; one of the few things to survive was the wall of clamshells [1]. Alioto's closed in March 2020 and never reopened. In 2025 the Port announced it would be torn down for a public plaza looking over the fishing boats in the lagoon [2][4].

title: The Greenhouses of the Garden District
place: Woolsey Street below the University Mound reservoir, once lined with greenhouses
hook: Before the Portola filled with bungalows, glass roofs glittered across its slopes. Much of San Francisco's cut-flower crop was grown here.
story: For decades after 1900 the Portola stayed half rural, and it grew flowers. In the early 1900s greenhouses lined the west side of Charter Oak Avenue, a street now mostly buried under the 101 freeway, while truck gardens stretched east toward the bay [1]. The likely buyers of the cut flowers were the city's boarding houses, hotels, restaurants and well-off households [1]. The slopes around the reservoir held more than a dozen flower nurseries, University Mound Nursery among them [2]. A photograph taken from McLaren Park around 1925 shows houses and greenhouses side by side, with Woolsey Street in the foreground and the reservoir's south basin still unbuilt [3]. The Portola had more than 20 commercial farms and greenhouses at one time, and its nurserymen grew much of the city's flower crop. That earned it the nickname the Garden District [4].

title: The Night Irving Street Won Its Tunnel
place: Irving Street at 8th Avenue
hook: When the supervisors picked the Sunset's tunnel route, the neighbourhood threw a parade with four bands, fireworks and dancing in the street.
story: The Sunset spent years fighting for a city streetcar. In March 1921 more than 500 residents met at Laguna Honda School and founded the Sunset Transportation and Development Association. Realtor Frank Doelger was one of its officers throughout [1]. City Engineer M. M. O'Shaughnessy offered four tunnel routes. The Sunset wanted the Duboce Avenue route, the fastest to downtown and at $2,467,000 the most expensive. Mission and Eureka Valley residents wanted a route through their own neighbourhoods [1]. On April 14, 1925 the supervisors chose Duboce. The association then claimed 3,000 members [1]. On the night of April 25 a 'monster' parade with floats ran along Irving Street from Arguello to 25th Avenue. It was led by a Presidio military band, the Fire Department's 40-piece band, Polytechnic High's ROTC band, a Moose drill team and the California Grays. At 9:30 the crowd gathered at 8th and Irving for speeches, drills, dancing in the street and fireworks until midnight [1]. Court cases held up the tunnel. On October 21, 1928, Mayor James Rolph, in a motorman's cap, drove the first N-line car out of the Sunset Tunnel [1][2][3]. One reporter counted fourteen speeches by Rolph along the way [1].

title: The lost swimming cove at Egbert Avenue
place: Former cove at the foot of Egbert Avenue, near Gilman Avenue
hook: Bayview kids once swam in the bay every summer day, racing to a raft off an old wharf, until the 'Polluted Water' signs went up.
story: In the 1920s and '30s, summer in the Bayview meant swimming in the bay almost every day. Ruth Eshow Upton, who grew up on Le Conte Avenue, later listed the options: Hunters Point (too far, and the slaughterhouses fouled the air), rocky, windy Candlestick, Gilman, and her favourite, a sheltered strip of tawny sand at the foot of Egbert Avenue [1]. From her bedroom window she watched the tide on South Basin; only when it was coming in did her 4-foot-10 mother lead five children to the beach, past backyards where bocce balls clicked [1]. Off the cove stood the remains of an old wharf with a raft tied to a barnacled piling. "When you finally lost your fear of being in water over your head and swam all the way to the raft you had graduated from kid-hood," she wrote [1]. Lunch was cold kufta, Armenian meatballs, and golden cheorag rolls [1]. Around 1936 or 1937, "Polluted Water" signs went up [1]. In the same years New Deal crews were building Gilman Playground nearby [2]. Returning in the 1970s, Upton found the sand gone and oily, rainbow-coloured water [1].

title: The saloon dancer of Rocky Hill
place: States Street near Levant Street, Corona Heights
hook: Conceived in a refugee tent and named after a cow, Norma Ball grew up on Rocky Hill, and once set the whole hill on fire.
story: Norma Ball's family lived on States Street near Levant, on the slopes of the old quarry hill locals called Rocky Hill, now Corona Heights [1]. By her own account she began in the 1906 disaster. Her parents' home burned, they sheltered in a Golden Gate Park tent, and she was 'the result of the earthquake' [1][2]. Her German-born mother, the family said, named her after a favourite cow [1]. Her father, Lester Ball, owned saloons around the city. Newspaper records confirm he was a 'San Francisco saloon man' in 1906, and by 1917 he was advertising saloons, delis and restaurants for sale through the Eureka Investment Company [1]. Norma said she danced for coins from sailors and longshoremen in his bars. She also said she once accidentally started a fire that burned all the grass off Rocky Hill [1]. Her photo album, now on OpenSFHistory, shows her in 1925 with the Native Daughters of the Golden West Castro drill team, in costume with swords [1]. She started work as a legal secretary at 14 and lived to 99. At the 2006 quake centennial she told Mayor Gavin Newsom she was 'Cold. But I've got Gavin Newsom to warm me up' [2]. Historians note that not every tale can be proven [1].

title: The world's largest swimming tank
place: Site of Fleishhacker Pool, now the zoo parking lot, Sloat Blvd and Great Highway
hook: A thousand feet long, filled with six million gallons of seawater, and so big the lifeguards patrolled it in rowboats.
story: In 1922 San Francisco bought sixty acres of beach south of Sloat Boulevard from the Spring Valley Water Company. Park Commission president Herbert Fleishhacker had a vision: a giant pool, playfields and a zoo [1][2]. Work began in spring 1923. Engineer Earl Clements planned the pool, and Ward & Blohme designed the Mediterranean-style bathhouse, with lockers for 800 swimmers and a small hospital [1]. It opened on 23 April 1925, billed as the "world's largest swimming tank" [1]. It was a thousand feet long and held some six million gallons of seawater; sources give its width as 150 or 100 feet [1][2]. Twelve to twenty-four lifeguards watched over it, some in rowboats [1]. The water was supposedly heated to seventy degrees, but everyone remembers the cold. Almost 60,000 people still jumped in during its first two months [1]. Lifeguard Billy Nichols once asked Fleishhacker why he built it so big. Fleishhacker told him to swim the length and back, then asked, "Did anyone get in your way?" No. "That's why I did it" [1]. It closed in 1971 and was buried for a parking lot [1].

title: West Portal's movie house, by a bridge architect
place: Portal Theatre (later the Empire), 85 West Portal Avenue
hook: West Portal's movie theater opened the day after Christmas 1925. Its architect and his wife are credited with the Golden Gate Bridge's Moderne look.
story: The Portal Theatre opened at 85 West Portal Avenue on December 26, 1925, as the streetcar suburb filled in around the new Twin Peaks Tunnel [1]. Local architect Irving Morrow, of Morrow & Garren, drew up plans in 1923 for the theater and a block of shops. His first design had a more open entry courtyard, but much of the plan, including its Moorish style, was carried out [1]. Historian Richard Brandi calls it the one notable architectural exception on West Portal Avenue, an imposing Mediterranean-style movie house until much of its original detailing was stripped away in later years [2]. Morrow went on to become consulting architect for the Golden Gate Bridge, and he and his wife, Gertrude Comfort Morrow, are credited with the bridge's Moderne detailing [2]. The Portal was renamed the Empire when it reopened on October 1, 1936. In 1974 its single screen was split into three, and in the 21st century it was promoted as "CinéArts at the Empire" [1]. For generations it was the neighborhood's movie house, until it closed its doors [3].

title: Where every working musician paid dues
place: Musicians Union Hall (Local No. 6), 230 Jones Street
hook: Terra-cotta musical symbols still decorate a Jones Street facade. The union hall opened with six brass bands, and it ended with the union's archives thrown in a dumpster.
story: Local No. 6 of the American Federation of Musicians built its hall at 230 Jones Street in 1924. Sylvain Schnaittacher, then president of the local chapter of the American Institute of Architects, designed it with musical symbols worked into the second-floor arches [1]. The official opening on June 9, 1925, was dedicated by Mayor James Rolph Jr. and began with a morning parade down Market Street: six huge brass bands and fifty cars full of civic and union leaders. Balls, dinners and concerts followed for five days [1]. Inside were a ballroom and meeting hall, soundproof phone booths, and offices for the stage hands' and movie projectionists' unions. The top floor held a members' club with card rooms [1]. In the mid-20th century the Tenderloin's theatres, hotels, burlesque houses and clubs kept musicians working, and the union building on Jones Street was part of that world [2]. Local 6 reached a peak of 5,900 members in 1969 [1]. The union moved to Ninth Street in 1998. Photographer Mark Ellinger writes that the San Francisco Rescue Mission, which took over the Jones Street hall, sent the union's archives to the dump [1].

title: 'How Do You Dream?': The First Chinese Teacher
place: Commodore Stockton School (now Gordon J. Lau Elementary), Clay Street
hook: To get into teachers' college she said she would teach in China. Instead she became San Francisco's first Chinese American public school teacher.
story: Alice Fong Yu was born in Nevada County in 1905 and grew up in a family so poor that one napkin went from hands to stove to floor [1]. When she applied to San Francisco State Teachers College, principal Frederic Burk objected. She got in by telling him she planned to teach English in China [1]. When she looked for work, the school district quizzed her with questions like 'How do you dream?' and tried to trick her into speaking Chinese [1]. In 1926 she was hired at Commodore Stockton School, the renamed 'Oriental School' that Chinatown's children attended, becoming the first Chinese American woman in the city's public school system [1][2]. There was irony in her classroom: students there were barred from speaking Chinese at school or on the playground [2]. That year she told the Examiner that a Chinese child could not be a good American citizen 'unless he retains the fineness and restraint of his own race' [1]. She had already co-founded the Square and Circle Club in 1924, a women's service club that raised money for Chinatown causes [1]. Today a Chinese-immersion public school carries her name [1].

title: A 550-Acre Park on Paper
place: University Street at Mansell Street, the park's northeastern edge
hook: In 1926 San Francisco planned a park of 550 acres here and named it after John McLaren. Voters wouldn't pay for it, and the park ended up far smaller.
story:
In October 1926 the Board of Supervisors voted to take land by eminent domain for a large new public park south of Silver Avenue and east of La Grande Avenue. It was to be called Mission Park [1]. On November 29, 1926, they renamed it John McLaren Park, in thanks for the work of the city's long-serving park chief [1]. The plan was generous: 550 acres in the broad area between Alemany Boulevard, Bayshore Boulevard, Mission Street and the county line [1].

In 1927 appraisers valued every property inside the line. But the city attorney never began condemnation because there wasn't enough money, and on November 6, 1928, voters rejected a $2 million bond to buy and build the park [1]. After that the city bought land a piece at a time. The park shrank in stages to about 420 acres and then 361. Land inside the original line went to the School and Convent of the Good Shepherd, the Lick Home on University Street, two water department reservoirs, the Sunnydale housing project and Crocker Amazon Playground [1][2]. In 1946 the supervisors set the boundary at 318 acres, and the last purchases were made in 1958 [2].

title: A Byzantine dome rises on Lake Street
place: Temple Emanu-El, 2 Lake St at Arguello Blvd
hook: Twenty years after the fire gutted its Sutter Street temple, the West's oldest Jewish congregation built a domed temple at the edge of the Richmond.
story: Congregation Emanu-El grew out of the Gold Rush. Its founders were mostly Bavarian Jewish merchants, and it was chartered in 1851 [3]. Its twin-spired Sutter Street temple was destroyed in April 1906. At first members patched it up within its old walls on a budget 'not to exceed $75,000' [1]. Two decades after the quake, the congregation finished a new temple at Arguello Boulevard and Lake Street, on the edge of the Richmond [1]. The Jewish Daily Bulletin listed the design team: the late architect Schnaittacher, the firm of Bakewell & Brown, and consulting architects Bernard Maybeck and G. Albert Lansburgh [2]. The style was 'Levantine', which the congregation described as a 'fusion of the architectural styles of Asia Minor, Palestine and the Mediterranean world' [1]. A fountain in the atrium recalls the ritual washing of ancient Jerusalem [1]. NoeHill notes that the dome was influenced by Hagia Sophia [4]. The temple was dedicated over three days, April 16 to 18, 1926, and Mayor James Rolph was among the speakers [2]. The full group was expected to cost $1,250,000 [2].

title: A seaside railroad becomes Alemany Boulevard
place: Alemany Boulevard near Cayuga Park (route of the Ocean Shore Railroad and old Islais Creek)
hook: Alemany Boulevard follows the roadbed of a doomed railroad to Santa Cruz, laid in a creek valley that the city later buried.
story: The Ocean Shore Railway was incorporated in May 1905 to run south along the coast from a terminal at 12th and Mission streets toward Santa Cruz [1]. Inside the city, its tracks ran along the route of today's Alemany Boulevard, partly parallel to the Southern Pacific [2][3]. An old-timer later remembered a flag stop further west in Ocean View. You waved a flag, and if the engineer felt like it he stopped, or else he left you standing in his soot [3]. The 1906 earthquake threw parts of the coastal roadbed and construction equipment into the Pacific. Mainline service ended on July 31, 1920, after a labour walkout [1]. The empty right-of-way got a second life in 1926, when Alemany Boulevard was built on it for the growing car traffic [3]. The boulevard followed the valley of Islais Creek. A 1910 photo taken from the Mission Street viaduct already shows the 'proposed Alemany Boulevard' along the creek. By 1930 the creek was being culverted underneath it [4].

title: An Ice Rink at the Dunes' Edge
place: Site of the San Francisco Ice Arena, 1557 48th Avenue at Kirkham Street
hook: For 65 years San Franciscans skated a block from the ocean, until the country's oldest operating rink fell to the wrecking ball.
story: In September 1925 investors at the Burlingame Country Club were shown plans for an oval rink with no corners, better for fancy skating and the double turn waltz. It opened in March 1926 at 1557 48th Avenue. That July it staged the first hockey game seen in the city in ten years, and there was standing room only [1]. After general manager J.T. Ludlow died in 1929, his widow ran it briefly, then sold to Thomas and Lucinda 'Ma' Campbell. In 1938 the city refused to renew Lucinda's beer permit, since her customers were mostly minors. In 1946 she opened the ice to veterans from Bay Area military hospitals [1]. In 1959 two former Ice Follies stars, Hugh Hendrickson and Marlene Jackson, took over with her husband Joseph Thurston. That August Hendrickson was electrocuted in the brine room. He was 31. The Thurstons kept the rink going for three more decades. It hosted birthday parties and broomball after hours, and skaters like Peggy Fleming and Dorothy Hamill came out to the Sunset [1]. Seismic work and insurance costs finally beat it, even after Karen Wood gathered 1,200 signatures to save it. The rink came down on July 8, 1991. WNP says it was then the oldest operating arena in the country [1][2].

title: An art school moves up the hill
place: California School of Fine Arts (later SF Art Institute), 800 Chestnut St
hook: The West's oldest art school finally built itself a Spanish-style home with a bell tower on Russian Hill. Students soon swore the tower was haunted.
story: The school began in 1873, when the San Francisco Art Association founded the California School of Design [1]. Its first director was the painter Virgil Williams [2]. It had occupied rooms above a Pine Street market [2] and several sites on Nob Hill [1]. In 1916 it was renamed the California School of Fine Arts [1][3]. In 1926 it finally built a campus of its own at 800 Chestnut Street, in Spanish Colonial Revival style by the firm of Bakewell and Brown, with a courtyard and a tall bell tower [1][4]. The doors opened on January 15, 1927 [4]. Within a few years the Mexican muralist Diego Rivera came in 1930 to paint a fresco there, and over the decades the artists associated with the school came to include Ansel Adams, Dorothea Lange, Imogen Cunningham, Clyfford Still, Mark Rothko and Richard Diebenkorn [1]. The tower gained a reputation of its own. From the 1940s, students and staff reported footsteps, doors opening and closing, and tools switching themselves on. A night watchman living in the tower in 1947 described hearing an invisible visitor walk through his room [4].

title: Bank Night at the Roozie
place: Roosevelt Theatre (now Brava Theater), 2781 24th Street at York
hook: In the Depression the whole neighbourhood crowded the sidewalk at 24th and York to hear whose name came out of a glass drum. The jackpot once reached $610.
story:
The Roosevelt Theatre opened on September 22, 1926 with Norma Talmadge in 'Kiki'. It had 1,006 seats and was designed by the Reid Brothers [1]. Everyone called it 'the Roozie'. The novelist Dorothy Bryant grew up nearby and remembered it as the real centre of her 1930s neighbourhood. For less than a dollar a family of four got a double feature, cartoons and newsreels. On Saturdays children were handed a dime and left there from eleven until nearly five [2].

Wednesday was Dish Night, when every woman got a piece of pottery, so that 'you could walk into any home in the neighborhood and find us all eating from the same plates'. Monday was Bingo. Saturday was Bank Night: a child drew a card from a glass drum and the manager read the name aloud three times. The cash prize started at $10 and grew by $10 every week nobody claimed it. Once it reached $610 and the crowd filled the sidewalk and spilled round the corner [2]. Bryant never knew anyone who won [2]. The theatre was renamed York 24 in 1962 and is now the Brava Theater [1].

title: Dish night at the Flea House
place: Site of the Bay Shore Theatre, Bayshore Boulevard near Leland Avenue
hook: For 31 years the valley had one movie house. Everyone called it the 'Flea House', and you could furnish your kitchen just by going.
story: From 1926 until October 1957, Visitacion Valley had its own movie house, the 350-seat Bay Shore Theatre on Bayshore Boulevard near Leland Avenue [1]. Its advertising promised, 'We show only the best pictures ... Come and see!' [2] Locals called it the 'Flea House' [1]. It ran double features, and on the weekly 'dish night' patrons could collect a whole set of dinnerware just by attending [1]. In 2011, 87-year-old Mary Glidden Bertram remembered going every Saturday for the serials, which continued week to week 'like a soap opera on TV nowadays' [1]. Dawn Pyne Murayama took a part-time job there as the candy girl while she was a student at City College. Weekend matinees were busiest, she recalled, with parents dropping off children who 'had money to burn' on candy and popcorn. 'It's a wonder I don't have more fillings, as I ate more than my share' [1]. An OpenSFHistory photograph looking northwest across Bayshore, as a streetcar crew removes old tracks, shows the theatre in the background. The archive dates it November 1941; SF Heritage captions it 1943 [1][3]. The theatre has since been demolished [3].

title: Horse teams plant a park called Mission
place: Near Mansell Street and Visitacion Avenue, site of a 1927 tree-planting photograph
hook: It began as 'Mission Park', with dreams of a zoo and an 18-hole golf course. Then the voters said no.
story: In October 1926 the city approved a resolution to take land by eminent domain for a park south of Silver Avenue and east of La Grande Avenue. It was to cover 550 acres and be called Mission Park [1]. Within weeks the supervisors renamed it after John McLaren, the Golden Gate Park superintendent [1]. Its supporters imagined an 18-hole golf course, bridle trails, playing fields and possibly the city zoo, moved here [2]. A photograph dated February 1, 1927 shows the bare ridge near today's Mansell Street and Visitacion Avenue, with workers and horse teams that seem to be planting trees [3]. McLaren dedicated the park in 1927 and Boy Scouts planted trees [4]. But in November 1928 voters turned down a $2 million bond to buy and develop the land [1]. According to one park group, the campaign slogan was 'Our People Need This Breathing Space' and the measure failed by a few hundred votes [4]. After that the city bought land one lot at a time. It took until 1958 to finish [2].

title: Klansmen on a Shipwreck
place: Lyman Stewart wreck near Helmet Rock, Lands End
hook: In 1926 five men hung from ropes to paint 'KKK' on a wrecked tanker, and they dared the police to come and get them.
story: By the mid-1920s the wrecked tanker Lyman Stewart, stuck on the rocks below Lands End since 1922, had become a billboard. Someone painted 'Mother's Cakes & Cookies' across her hull. Just forward of it, in a photograph taken in April 1926, is a chillier message: 'KKK-S.F. #2' [1]. Historian John Martini found the story behind it. San Francisco police spotted five men dangling from ropes, painting 'KKK' in huge letters on the ship's side. Ordered down, they shouted back: 'Come out and get us, we're going to stay here until we finish this job.' Rather than climb the sheer steel hull, the officers waited, then arrested the men as they came down [1]. The five got 30-day sentences, not for hate but for breaking a city ordinance against 'advertising or signs of any description on private property' [1]. The Klan was then at its national peak. It claimed three million members, more than half of them in cities, and San Francisco was not immune [1]. Why 'S.F. #2'? No one knows whether the city had more than one Klan group [1]. The letters washed away with the ship [1][2].

title: Ninety Years of Farewells at 4840 Mission
place: Former Valente, Marini, Perata & Co. funeral home, 4840 Mission Street near France Avenue
hook: North Beach undertakers followed their customers out Mission Street after 1906. Their funeral home got a peach-to-crimson modern makeover and a very wordy neon sign.
story: The funeral directors Valente, Marini, Perata & Co. began in North Beach and were a cornerstone of the city's Italian community. Frank Dunnigan dates the firm to 1888; SF Heritage says its roots go back to 1889 [1][2]. In the two decades after the 1906 earthquake, many of its customers moved to the Excelsior. In 1926 Virgil Valente, Frank Marini and John B. Perata followed them to 4840 Mission Street, near France Avenue [1][2]. The architect John A. Porporato designed the building in the Spanish Colonial Revival style of the new houses around it, with stucco walls and a red tile roof. In 1959 it was remodelled in a Midcentury Modern look: a brick base and porcelain-enamel panels in peach, salmon and crimson. A wordy 1937 neon sign pointed mourners to the big parking lot [1]. As the neighbourhood changed, the firm served more Latino and Filipino families. It kept holding services for local parishes such as Corpus Christi and the Church of the Epiphany [2]. It closed quietly in July 2017, after nearly 130 years [2]. A historic evaluation found the building eligible for the California Register, but the site was sold for affordable housing, and the 2020 plans called for demolition [1][2].

title: Opening Night Starred a Famous Female Impersonator
place: Site of the Irving Theatre, 1300 block of Irving St (14th–15th Aves)
hook: The Inner Sunset's neighbourhood movie palace opened in 1926 with a comedy starring America's most famous female impersonator.
story: On June 10, 1926, the Irving Theatre opened on the north side of Irving Street between 14th and 15th Avenues. At night its big sign lit up the Inner Sunset [1]. The first film on its screen was 'Madame Behave!' [1], a silent comedy that had premiered the previous November. It starred Julian Eltinge as a young man who hides from a policeman by passing himself off as a woman, and it was sold as 'a Cousin to Charley's Aunt' [2]. Eltinge was one of the best-known performers of female roles of his day. Rather than playing women for laughs, his stage act gave the illusion of actually being one, and he took off his wig at the end to surprise the audience [3]. For the next 36 years the Irving was the neighbourhood's movie house. A June 1941 photo shows 'Topper Returns' on the marquee, a Safeway to its left and the Montrose Market to its right. In 1951 an ad promoted 'I Was a Communist for the FBI' [1]. The Irving closed on July 8, 1962, was torn down, and an apartment building now stands on the lot [1].

title: Stairs where 22nd Street gave up
place: 22nd Street stairs between Castro and Diamond, at Collingwood Street
hook: Too steep for a road, one block of 22nd Street became a staircase. Kids rode plywood down it, and neighbours turned it into a native-plant hillside.
story: On the map, 22nd Street runs straight over the hill between Castro and Diamond streets. On the ground, it was always too steep for that. In June 1920 a city Department of Public Works photographer recorded the corner of Collingwood and 22nd before grading [1]. In August 1926 another photographer caught the stairway climbing from Diamond Street, "not long after they were built." The sources differ on the age of the stairs: one says the hill was climbed by staircases well before 1920 [1][2]. Writer Chris Carlsson calls such stubs ghost streets, found mostly on hillsides too steep for traffic [2]. In the 1960s, Ed Ferris and his friends played on the flights and rode down them on pieces of plywood [2]. In 2012 the staircase, known as the Jungle Stairs, became a project of the city's Street Parks program. Artists, muralists, metalworkers, landscapers and neighbours, with city and institutional funders, have since worked on the hillside and the stairs on both sides of the hill [1]. They gave priority to plants native to the Franciscan bioregion, and yellow lupine now blooms beside the steps. A metal sign made by Brennan Cox of Groundworks marks the Collingwood exit [1].

title: The Architect and the Coffee Man Next Door
place: 98 Sea Cliff Avenue (George W. Kelham's home, c. 1918–1928)
hook: In the 1920s the man who planned the 1915 World's Fair lived at 98 Sea Cliff Avenue. Listed right beside him was a Hills Bros. coffee man.
story: George W. Kelham came to San Francisco in 1906 for the Palace Hotel job and never left [2]. He drew the master plan for the 1915 Panama-Pacific International Exposition. He went on to design the old Main Library, now the Asian Art Museum, the Federal Reserve Bank, the Russ Building and the Shell Building [1][2]. The Pacific Coast Architecture Database says that from about 1918 to 1928 he lived at 98 Sea Cliff Avenue with his wife, their son Bruce and a Norwegian-born servant, Gertrude Hall [1]. A society blue book from the late 1920s lists the Kelhams there. The entry just before theirs is Mr. and Mrs. R. W. Hills Jr., at No. 90, and the same book gives Hills's other address as 2 Harrison Street [3]. That was the Hills Bros. Coffee building. The firm had been founded by the brothers Austin H. and Reuben W. Hills, and in 1900 it was the first to pack roast coffee in vacuum cans [4]. The firm moved into 2 Harrison in 1926, and the building was Kelham's own design [1][4]. So the man next door went to work each day in a plant his neighbour had drawn. The records don't say whether they ever talked shop.

title: The Harding: Movies, Operetta, the Dead, a Church
place: Harding Theater, 616 Divisadero Street at Hayes
hook: One Divisadero movie palace has been a vaudeville house, a Gilbert and Sullivan stage, a Grateful Dead venue, a church and an arcade bar.
story: The Harding was built in 1926 for theatre owner Samuel H. Levin, whose chain also included the Balboa, Alexandria, Coliseum, Metro and Empire. It was designed by the Reid Brothers, James and Merritt Reid [1][2]. It seated 1,250 people and opened with Colleen Moore in 'Irene'. Cinema Treasures dates the opening to April 8, 1926, while another account says May [1][2]. In the 1920s it was a neighbourhood movie and vaudeville house, and it later ran as a single-screen cinema [2]. Then it began a long run of second lives. The Lamplighters, San Francisco's Gilbert and Sullivan company, performed there in the 1960s [1][2]. In the late 1960s and early '70s it was a music venue, and the Grateful Dead played on November 6 and 7, 1971 [1][2]. For about thirty years after that it was a church and community centre, until 2003 or 2004 according to different sources [1][2]. In 2008 a Planning Department historic resource evaluation concluded that the Harding was a landmark building [2]. In November 2017 it reopened as Emporium SF, an arcade and bar with pinball, games and billiards [1].

title: The Magician Who Came Home to Sea Cliff
place: 801 El Camino del Mar (Carter family address in the 1939 city directory)
hook: He made elephants vanish and toured the world with tons of props. Between tours, Carter the Great came home to a house above the Golden Gate.
story: Charles Joseph Carter was born in Pennsylvania in 1874 and was billed as a boy magician before he was eleven. As Carter the Great he spent decades circling the globe with a show that at one point weighed 31 tons [4]. The Western Neighborhoods Project says he always found his way back to San Francisco, where he made his home in Sea Cliff [1]. At Christmas 1926 he opened at the Capitol Theater downtown, starting what Billboard called his tenth world tour. The Chronicle's critic listed the tricks: live elephants disappeared, a young woman was "s-t-r-e-t-c-h-e-d", a condemned woman on the gallows turned out to be the executioner, and a blindfolded mind reader read names off slips of paper no one else had seen [2]. In 1936 Carter had a heart attack on the way to Bombay. He died there that February, and his son Larry took over the act [4]. The 1939 city directory lists Corinne M. Carter, "wid C J", at 801 El Camino del Mar [3]. His house is sometimes mistakenly called the "Houdini Mansion" [4].

title: The New Balboa Lights Up the Avenues
place: Balboa Theatre, 3630 Balboa St
hook: As the sand dunes filled with bungalows, a showman built an 800-seat neighbourhood movie palace on a street that barely escaped a different name.
story: By the mid-1920s the dunes of the Outer Richmond were filling with houses, and the new residents wanted movies close to home. Samuel H. Levin, whose San Francisco Theatres Inc. ran a chain of neighbourhood houses including the Alexandria and the Coliseum, opened the New Balboa Theatre near 38th Avenue with 800 seats [1][2]. Cinema Treasures gives the date as February 27, 1926, but Wikipedia cites an Examiner item dated June 27, 1926 announcing the opening 'tonight', so the exact day is uncertain [1][2]. It was designed by brothers James and Merritt Reid, whose credits included the Fairmont Hotel, the Spreckels Temple of Music in Golden Gate Park and the 1909 Cliff House about a mile away [1][3]. The theatre took its name from the explorer Vasco Núñez de Balboa, like the street itself, which got that name in 1909 after the Richmond fought off a plan to rename its avenues [2][4]. The Levin family ran the Balboa for almost 60 years, until February 2001, and in 1966 and 1967 it showed The Sound of Music for 92 weeks [1]. It is still showing films today, one of the last neighbourhood theatres in the city [1].

title: The diary in the attic
place: Santa Marina and Elsie Streets
hook: A boy's misspelled diary, found in a Bernal attic, records broken bones, a fall from the quarry and first love.
story:
Around 1995, a diary was found in the attic of a house at the corner of Santa Marina and Elsie streets. It belonged to Henry Behrenst, a boy whose family moved from Salt Lake City to "Frisco" in 1923. When he first saw a ferry boat he "thought it was a house" [1]. His entries, all in his own spelling, are a list of disasters. He almost drowned riding rafts at the foot of Army Street, and got burned by firecrackers. In February 1926 his father died. Then, on 3 November 1926, he "Fell off of the quarry on top of Bernal Heights." He thought he had sprained his collarbone, "but it was broken" [1][2]. Bernal's summit quarries were real enough: their scars on the south side of the hill show up in 1920s aerial photos [3].

In August 1930 Henry moved to Elsie Street and met "a very nice girl her name is Elizebeth Hird she is a blonde... in fact I love her." On New Year's Day 1931: "I got drunk and sit in Elizebeth steps 1 hr. in the rain" [1]. Decades later Elizabeth's daughters passed a copy of the diary to the History Project. Elizabeth had never known about Henry's heartbreak [1].

title: The push-button lock comes to Bayshore
place: Former Schlage Lock administration building, Bayshore Boulevard
hook: In 1926 a lock company moved beside the railroad tracks. It became the city's biggest manufacturer, and its office building is still locked.
story: In the mid-1920s the Schlage company bought its first 2.5 acres beside the Southern Pacific tracks from the Bodinson Manufacturing Company. It had finished a factory building by June 1925, and in 1926 took the name Schlage Lock Company [2]. That year it built an administration building designed by William P. Day, architect of the Mark Hopkins Hotel [1]. The complex grew to 12 acres of factory, distribution and office buildings [1]. Schlage perfected and popularised the push-button lock, with a spring button in the centre of the doorknob. Its locksets ended up on countless San Francisco doors [1]. During World War II the plant made shell casings, bomb tail fuses, aircraft parts and proximity fuses [1]. By the 1970s it was the largest manufacturer in San Francisco, with 1,600 workers, many living across Bayshore Boulevard in the valley [1]. The factory closed in 1999 [3]. Neighbours blocked a Home Depot on the site [1][3]. Day's office building survives as a welcome centre for the planned Baylands housing. When Woody LaBounty tried its door, it was, of course, locked [1].

title: Treadmills in the Alhambra's balcony
place: Alhambra Theatre, 2330 Polk St
hook: Russian Hill's Moorish movie palace survived a bomb, a cinder-block wall and television. Then it became a gym, with exercise bikes where the balcony seats used to be.
story: The Alhambra opened on Polk Street in 1926, a $500,000 picture palace with 1,625 seats, designed by Timothy Pflueger a few years after his Castro Theatre [1]. A Victorian mansion on the lot was moved to 2214 Clay Street to make way [3]. Its Moorish castle decor offered Russian Hill and Cow Hollow a nearer alternative to the grander Market Street theatres [3]. In October 1930 a pipe bomb was found in its ticket booth [2]. The Chronicle later reported that a janitor found the device, big enough to level the building, during a spate of theatre bombings [1]. Television thinned the crowds. In 1974 the auditorium was "twinned" with a cinder-block wall, which failed partly because the dome could not be soundproofed, and in 1988 the wall came down [2][3]. "Wag the Dog" was the last film shown before it closed in 1998 [1]. It became a gym in 2001. Treadmills and exercise bikes stand on the old balcony facing the big screen, which in 2011 was still showing films with subtitles [1][2]. One man working out there in 2011 had come from Granada in Spain, a few miles from the real Alhambra. "It has the magic of an old theater," he said [1].

title: Where the wild poppies grew
place: Wilde Avenue at Rutland Street (former Visitacion View Grocery, later KC Market)
hook: A 1926 sales booklet promised paved streets and 'beautiful bungalows' on the valley's sunny hillside. The same year, a hilltop grocer opened at Wilde and Rutland.
story: In 1926 the Visitacion Reis Tract Improvement Association published a booklet selling the valley's northern slopes. 'Where the wild poppies grew are paved streets, fire hydrants, high tension wires, and beautiful bungalows,' it boasted. It praised the tract's 'sunny southern exposure' and pointed buyers to the builders' ads [1]. Wilde Avenue was the tract's main paved street, and the booklet sold its transit links. At the Five Mile House, where Wilde met San Bruno Avenue and Third Street, residents could choose from three Market Street Railway lines [1]. Stucco subdivisions went on filling the hillsides around older farmhouses into the 1950s [3]. That same year, 1926, a store was built at the corner of Wilde Avenue and Rutland Street: the Visitacion View Grocery and Meat Market, phone RAndolph 4855 [2]. It became a lesson in how not to run a corner shop. The owner, Pete, refused a boy some carrots until his family's two-week-old tab was paid. Another day he yelled across the intersection at Parshall's mother, who was carrying groceries bought 'down the Valley'. Neither family went back [2]. Pete kept his business until retirement anyway, and the store, later the KC Market, lasted until 2008 [2].

title: A Consul's Son Falls for Baseball
place: Sea Cliff (the Laguerre family home; address not given in sources)
hook: A French diplomat's boy spent two years in Sea Cliff and fell for American sports. Decades later he turned Sports Illustrated into a giant.
story: In the summer of 1927 Léon Laguerre, a French diplomat, took a post at the French Consulate General in San Francisco. According to Wikipedia's account, which draws on Michael MacCambridge's history of the magazine, the family settled in Sea Cliff [3]. Their eldest, André, had already lived in England, France and Syria. Here he went to the Santa Monica School and St. Ignatius, became a baseball fan, and got his first newspaper job as a copyboy at the Chronicle. In 1929 he was sent back to England for school [3]. Sports Illustrated's 1960 profile of him listed the Chronicle among his first newspaper jobs [1]. That career ran through Dunkirk, where he was one of the last to be evacuated, and through service as press officer for de Gaulle's Free French [1]. When he joined the magazine as an assistant managing editor in 1956, some thought it radical to put a Frenchman on an American sports magazine. The magazine's own obituary answered that he had lived for years in San Francisco and was on familiar terms with American sports [2]. He became managing editor in 1960, and circulation more than doubled under him [2].

title: A cathedral for selling Packards
place: Earle C. Anthony Packard Showroom, 901 Van Ness Avenue at Ellis
hook: On Auto Row, Bernard Maybeck built a car showroom from Numidian marble and Persian lanterns and told his workmen to imagine a medieval cathedral.
story:
By the mid-1920s the new-car trade had settled along Van Ness Avenue [1]. Earle C. Anthony was, according to Wikipedia, the world's most prominent Packard dealer, selling one of every seven Packards between 1915 and 1957. He also founded the Los Angeles radio station KFI [2]. For his San Francisco showroom at Van Ness and Ellis he hired Bernard Maybeck, the architect of the Palace of Fine Arts [4]. Sources date the building to 1926 or 1927 [3][4].

The opening night drew Hollywood starlets and was broadcast on one of Anthony's radio stations [3]. His booklet 'A Saga of Transportation' described rose marble from Numidia and black marble from Belgium, travertine, scagliola, 'lanterns from a Persian Hareem', and Spanish and Gothic doorways, which together made 'an Aladdin's palace' [3]. The booklet also printed Maybeck's instructions to the builders: 'Imagine that no cars roar by on Van Ness Avenue and that no telephone will call you from your work. Believe yourselves, instead, working in the gloom of a cathedral of the Middle Ages' [3].

title: A medieval stone cottage to sell a suburb
place: 'Studio House of Stone', 400 Castenada Avenue, Forest Hill
hook: When Forest Hill's lots sat empty, a realty firm built a stone cottage straight out of the Middle Ages and invited the public in. It said thousands came.
story: Forest Hill's first developer, Newell-Murdoch, promised "a country home within the city," but sales stalled, and in 1918 the residents took over management of the tract [1][2]. Most of the homes built in the 1920s and 30s were sold by the Lang Realty Company [2], and it relied on gimmicks [1]. In 1926 Lang teamed up with the San Francisco Chronicle and home-furnishing companies on a "San Francisco Model Home" at 90 Lopez Avenue, supposedly for "educational purposes in better homecraft." The paper praised everything from the roof tiles to the Frigidaire, which "unlike an ice box" had "no drain pan to empty and no ice delivery to worry about" [1]. The next year Lang opened the "Studio House of Stone" at 400 Castenada Avenue. The company claimed thousands visited the free exhibit, "enthusiastic in their praise of the quaint, medieval atmosphere that pervades every room" [1]. The Western Neighborhoods Project calls it Forest Hill's most popular destination of 1927 [3]. When historian Woody LaBounty walked past in 2003, he found it looked "just as medieval and stoney today" [1].

title: A queen, a violin and an old gardener
place: Hilltops of the new park above Visitacion Valley (exact ceremony sites not recorded)
hook: Before it had a single path, McLaren Park had a queen, a parade of floats, and a flag raised by the 88-year-old gardener it was named for.
story: Long before it had paths or playgrounds, McLaren Park had a party. On May 1, 1927, a huge crowd gathered on the hill to celebrate the dedication of land for the new park. Homage was paid to Miss Elizabeth Stagnaro, who had been elected Queen of the Park by the people of San Francisco [1]. Anna Stuart Johnson, then 12, later told oral historians that she rode on one of the floats playing her violin. The Visitacion Valley Community Center entered its own float, full of cheering youngsters [1]. The park's namesake came in person later. After WPA crews built a view drive in the early 1930s, John McLaren dedicated the park in a flag-raising ceremony in 1934, hoisting a flag presented by the California Works Administration [2]. He was about 88. Born in Scotland in 1846, he had run Golden Gate Park since 1887 and famously loved trees and hated buildings, 'keep off the grass' signs and statues. He died in 1943 at 97 [2]. The sources don't agree on the date of the dedication: a park group's timeline puts McLaren's dedication celebration in 1927 [3].

title: Fifty-Cent Chicken on the Great Highway
place: Former Chick-ery restaurant, 2600 Great Highway (3655 Vicente Street), SE corner of Vicente
hook: Locals whisper that two odd buildings on the Great Highway were a speakeasy and a haunted house. They started out selling chicken dinners.
story: Two corner buildings frame the Great Highway block between Vicente Street and tiny Cutler Avenue. One mixes a Mission-style tile roof and rough wooden balconies with red brick and twin chimneys. The other has a long ocean-facing balcony and Art Deco trim. The stories about them are persistent: a Prohibition speakeasy, a brothel, a Schilling spice heir's retreat, a 'vicious ghost' [1]. Historian Woody LaBounty found something more ordinary. Both were built in 1927, well into Prohibition. Each was designed by an architect and cost more than $10,000, which would be a lot to spend on a conspicuous illegal business [1]. The real clue is the crowds. Cars were bringing San Franciscans to the beach in huge numbers: the Examiner counted 15,468 automobiles at Ocean Beach on a single Sunday in 1917 [1]. Fleishhacker Pool opened at the south end of the highway in 1925 and the zoo in 1929 [2]. Small eateries competed for those visitors. The brick building on the Vicente corner was the Chick-ery, a family place offering 50-cent chicken dinners. Directories list a man named Ulysses Ciati running a restaurant at the Cutler corner [1]. Neither lasted long into the Depression. Both are apartments now [1].

title: Homing In on a Beacon to Hawaii
place: Crissy Field west hangars
hook: In 1927 two Army lieutenants tested a radio beacon at Crissy Field before trying something no one had managed: flying from the mainland to Hawaii.
story: In 1925 two Navy flying boats took off from Crissy Field on the first attempt to fly from the mainland to Hawaii. The trip was supposed to take 26 hours. It took twelve days, and the crew of the one plane that got partway had to be rescued at sea [1]. Two years later the Army tried again, this time with radio. Lieutenants Lester Maitland and Albert Hegenberger flew their three-engine Fokker C-2, the Bird of Paradise, west from Ohio in June 1927. From 125 miles south of Crissy Field they picked up the Signal Corps beacon installed there [2]. Crissy's runway, about 3,000 feet long, was too short for the plane at full load. On June 27 they hopped across the bay to Oakland's new airport [2]. They took off from Oakland the next morning and landed at Wheeler Field on Oahu at 6:29 a.m. on June 29, after 25 hours and 50 minutes in the air. It was the first flight from the mainland to Hawaii [1][2]. The officers insisted it was no race, though Lindbergh's Atlantic flight and a $25,000 Dole prize had set off a rush of civilian rivals [2].

title: Sailors who wanted a club in town
place: St. Francis Yacht Club, on the Marina jetty
hook: In 1927, before the Golden Gate Bridge, some sailors refused to follow their club to Belvedere. They built a new one on the fair's leftover harbour.
story: The 1915 exposition left behind a small harbour east of the Presidio, and some sailors saw a use for it [1]. In early 1927 the San Francisco Yacht Club was moving its clubhouse from Sausalito to Belvedere. Before the Golden Gate Bridge, that meant a boat trip for every city member [1][2]. At a general meeting on February 5, 1927, Don Lee told his fellow members: 'if you say that you are going to build it here, you can build it here, because here is where your demand for a club is' [1]. The breakaway group incorporated the St. Francis Yacht Club on May 6, 1927, with former commodore John Punnett as its first commodore [1]. Their Mediterranean-style clubhouse, on land leased from the city on the fair's fill, is credited to Willis Polk; Polk died before the plans were finished, and his office completed them [1][2]. On December 21, 1976, the clubhouse caught fire during a party. One member was killed and seven were badly injured, and the western half had to be rebuilt [2]. The 1989 earthquake then damaged its foundations, and the club notes that little of Polk's building remains [1][2].

title: Tea, biscuits and a 2 a.m. raid
place: 31 Alta St, Telegraph Hill
hook: At 2 a.m. in 1927 police raided a 'tea party' in one of Telegraph Hill's oldest houses. The hostess insisted they had only been admiring a painting.
story: 31 Alta Street, with its double-decker balconies hanging over the street, is one of the oldest houses on Telegraph Hill. It was built by a sea captain, Richard Andrews; sources give 1852 or 1858 [1][2]. In the late 1920s a woman said to be a Russian noble, Myrtokleia Sawvelle, turned its brick basement kitchen and dining room into the Telegraph Hill Tavern, advertised as having "all the atmosphere of the Montmartre with a Marine view" [1][3]. Tea was served at two, dinner at six and supper after ten [1]. At 2 a.m. one night in February 1927 the neighbours had had enough. Police arrived, and the Black Maria took Myrtle and her guests to jail [1]. She told reporters they had been admiring Elwood Decker's new painting, "an esoteric blue damsel charging through a red fog". "We weren't even drinking anything but tea and I was making a pan full of biscuits for a little supper when the police came," she said [1]. It was Prohibition, though. According to historian David Myrick, her homemade brews later earned her 90 days in jail, where she was made jailhouse cook and became a heroine to the inmates [1]. In the 1950s the backyard hosted Silvio Catelli's Peach Blossom Festival [2].

title: Television's First Picture: A Straight Line
place: Farnsworth's lab, 202 Green Street
hook: In a plain loft below Telegraph Hill, a 21-year-old farm boy from Utah sent a single line across a room and invented electronic television.
story: Philo Taylor Farnsworth said he had worked out the principle of his image dissector as a teenager, inspired by the back-and-forth rows of a ploughed field [2]. Backed by San Francisco philanthropists, he set up a laboratory at 202 Green Street at the foot of Telegraph Hill [1][2]. On September 7, 1927, the 21-year-old and his assistants sent the first all-electronic television image from the camera tube to a receiver in another room. It was a straight line, lit from behind by an arc lamp through a glass slide [1][2]. His wife Pem later recalled him breaking the stunned silence: "There you are, electronic television!" [2]. When his backers asked when they would see dollars from the invention, the image he showed at a 1928 press demonstration was a dollar sign [2]. In 1929 he transmitted live human images, including a tiny picture of Pem with her eyes closed against the glare [2]. Farnsworth later won a patent interference case brought by RCA, and the state marked the Green Street site as California Historical Landmark 941, calling him "the Genius of Green Street" [1][2].

title: Ten-Cent Saturdays at the Avenue
place: Avenue Theatre, 2650 San Bruno Avenue
hook: One dime bought a newsreel, a cartoon, a comedy, a western and a cliffhanger. Three small sisters worked out how to keep paying the child's price until they were 16.
story: A photograph from July 15, 1927, shows the Avenue Theatre's marquee on San Bruno Avenue between Felton and Paul [1]. Ruth Eshow Upton, who grew up speaking Armenian [3], spent her Saturday afternoons there. You bought a ticket from a glass booth under the marquee. There was no lobby selling popcorn, and her mother called that sort of food 'junk' anyway [1]. A dime paid for a Pathé newsreel, a cartoon, a comedy, a western and one episode of a serial, and every so often a wheel was spun on stage for a prize, usually a Hershey bar [1]. At 12 the price went up to twenty cents. The Eshow girls were small for their age, so they lined up by height behind their little brother Haig, who handed the usher every ticket at once. They got in for a dime until they were 16 [1]. On Friday and Saturday nights there was vaudeville, and through the cigarette smoke Ruth watched a line of chorus girls high-kicking [1]. The Avenue later became a church [2].

title: The newspaper tree that named Christmas Tree Point
place: Christmas Tree Point, Twin Peaks
hook: A 120-foot fir was cut in half, stripped, trucked up Twin Peaks and rebuilt branch by branch, so the mayor could flip a switch.
story:
Christmas Tree Point got its name from a 1927 promotion by the San Francisco Examiner. The newspaper paid to put an enormous 'Forest Monarch' Christmas tree on the promontory, and city agencies joined in [1]. The Albion Lumber Company cut a 120-foot fir in Mendocino County. To move it, workers cut it in half and stripped off every branch, and trucks carried it up Twin Peaks in piles [1]. On the summit, city crews joined the trunk with an iron collar and drilled holes to put the branches back in. Park superintendent John McLaren added extra boughs, and the tree got 3,000 lights, giant metal candles, fake snow and thirty floodlights [1].

Shell Oil built a fifty-foot Santa Claus gateway. The Pioneer Auto Bus Company brought orphanage groups, children's clubs and the Municipal Band up for the lighting on December 19, 1927. At 7:30 p.m. Mayor James Rolph flipped the master switch: 'A sudden flare of light,' the Examiner wrote, 'and fairyland!' [1]. The tree could be seen from Marin to the East Bay. In 1928 a castle-like entrance and a shuttle bus greeted visitors [2]. The tree came back for a couple more years, until a campaign against cutting Christmas trees won out [1].

title: The parish that raffled off a house
place: 'Casa Emydio', 245 Brentwood Avenue, Monterey Heights
hook: To raise $130,000 for a new church, a pastor built and furnished a Spanish-style bungalow on Mount Davidson's slope, then raffled it off at a Civic Auditorium ball.
story: St. Emydius parish needed $130,000 to build its present church, and the pastor came up with an unusual way to raise it: raffle off a brand-new house [1]. The parish bought a lot at 245 Brentwood Avenue in Monterey Heights, a small neighborhood on the south slope of Mount Davidson, and built a Spanish-style bungalow called "Casa Emydio," complete with furniture [1]. Mayor James Rolph came to its dedication on September 18, 1927, and the drawing was held at a ball in the Civic Auditorium on December 15. The fundraiser was a notable success [1]. Monterey Heights was a well-heeled place to win a house. Its first custom homes, built in the 1920s, were as large and fine as those next door in St. Francis Wood. Harold G. Stoner designed many of them, including a Tudor at 225 Maywood in 1929. Building stopped during the Depression and only resumed in 1938 [1]. The Western Neighborhoods Project counts bootleggers and raffles among the neighborhood's stories, and a sign for a Chronicle model home stood on Monterey Boulevard in 1928 [2].

title: The patrician radical of Macondray Lane
place: Whitney cottage, 74 Macondray Lane
hook: The Supreme Court upheld her conviction for a speech. A governor pardoned her. Then Anita Whitney moved into a hidden cottage on Russian Hill and kept organising.
story: Charlotte Anita Whitney was the daughter of a patrician Oakland lawyer and a Wellesley graduate. She became in turn a social worker, a charter member of the NAACP, a suffrage organiser and a civil libertarian [1]. On November 28, 1919, after she spoke to the Oakland Civic Club for the new Communist Labor Party, she was arrested under California's Criminal Syndicalism Act [2]. On May 16, 1927, the U.S. Supreme Court unanimously upheld her conviction [3]. In a concurring opinion, Justice Louis Brandeis argued that only a 'clear and present danger' could justify restricting free speech, and the case itself was overruled in 1969 [2][3]. Governor C. C. Young decided that imprisoning her was 'unthinkable' and granted an unconditional pardon on June 20, 1927 [2]. That year Whitney moved into a small 1907 cottage at 74 Macondray Lane, a leafy pedestrian lane of artists and working people. She lived there until about 1945, working as a labour organiser and fundraiser for California's Communist Party [1].

title: Two Riders from a Woman Sculptor
place: Legion of Honor forecourt: El Cid and Joan of Arc statues
hook: The warrior on horseback facing the Golden Gate, and Joan of Arc nearby, came from one of the few women of her era trusted with giant public statues.
story: Two bronze riders stand at the Legion of Honor, and both are the work of Anna Hyatt Huntington. She was born in Cambridge, Massachusetts, in 1876, the daughter of the artist Audella Beebe and Alpheus Hyatt, who taught paleontology and zoology at Harvard and MIT and encouraged her interest in animal anatomy. Her first teacher, Henry Hudson Kitson, reportedly threw her out after she pointed out mistakes in the anatomy of his horses [1]. At a time when very few women made a living as artists, she became one of New York's most prominent sculptors. The Metropolitan Museum of Art ranks her among the foremost American women to take on large public commissions [1]. Her El Cid, modelled in 1927, shows the 11th-century Spanish warrior in the saddle. The Lincoln Park cast faces the Golden Gate [2][1]. Other casts stand in Seville, Valencia, New York, Buenos Aires and San Diego, where one was dedicated on July 5, 1930 [3][1]. Her Joan of Arc began in Manhattan at Riverside Drive and 93rd Street. It marked the 500th anniversary of Joan's birth, and its unveiling made Huntington famous around the world. A replica stands in front of the Legion of Honor [1]. She died in 1973 [1].

title: A Spanish Revival high school named for Balboa
place: Balboa High School, 1000 Cayuga Avenue
hook: Balboa High School was founded during San Francisco's biggest decade of school building and named for the Spanish explorer credited with discovering the Pacific.
story: Balboa High School was founded in 1928, at the end of the busiest decade of school building San Francisco had seen. Between 1920 and 1930 the district added 49 new school buildings [1][2]. It was named for Vasco Núñez de Balboa, the Spanish explorer who reached the Pacific, and its motto is 'First on the Pacific' [1][2]. The campus is in the Spanish Colonial Revival style, which became fashionable after San Diego's Panama-California Exposition of 1915. Its three buildings were designed by John Reid Jr., Hyman and Appleton, and Bakewell and Weihe [1]. The landmark report praises the design for suiting the city's hills and climate, with indoor and outdoor spaces that let pupils have fresh air and sunshine in the middle of the city [1]. Sources disagree on when the campus was finished. Wikipedia says construction was completed in 1931, and NoeHill's landmark page lists 1934 [1][2]. Balboa is Landmark No. 205 and the only San Francisco public school operating in a designated landmark [2]. Jerry Garcia later attended tenth grade there, in 1958 [1].

title: Babies, Then Pianos, in Mullgardt's Last Building
place: Former Infant Shelter / S.F. Conservatory of Music, 1201 Ortega Street at 19th Avenue (City Landmark No. 242)
hook: The last building by a celebrated San Francisco architect housed orphaned babies, then a conservatory of music. Its designer claimed Shakespeare was dictating plays to him.
story: The Infant Shelter traced its roots to the 1870s. In 1927 it planned a new orphanage at 19th Avenue and Ortega Street, and the building went up in 1928 and 1929 [1]. Heritage News calls it the last building by Louis Christian Mullgardt (WNP says one of his last), who had designed the Court of the Ages at the 1915 Panama-Pacific Exposition [1][3]. Mullgardt loved color, texture and applied art. On the Ortega Street side, the entry has ornamental brick, terra cotta columns and a sculpted frieze, probably carved by the architect himself, and the corner gables show a Mission Revival influence [1]. In a 1936 photo a sand-hauling streetcar works along Ortega near 21st Avenue with the shelter in the background [2]. Mullgardt's own end was sad. In 1935 he was found wandering the streets with a carpetbag of unfinished plays that he said William Shakespeare was dictating to him. In 1941 he was found incapacitated in a dreary residential hotel and taken to a pauper's ward, and he died the next year [1]. The orphanage lasted until the mid-1950s. In 1956 the San Francisco Conservatory of Music moved in and stayed fifty years before leaving for Oak Street in 2006 [1][4]. Today it houses the Lycée Français La Pérouse [1].
