title: City Hall's Architect Designs a Branch Bank
place: Former Hibernia Bank branch (El Chico market), 4600 Mission Street at Norton Street
hook: The man behind San Francisco City Hall's dome gave the Excelsior a Beaux-Arts banking hall. Today its high-ceilinged hall is a produce market.
story: In 1928 the Hibernia Bank opened a branch on the corner of Mission and Norton streets. It hired Arthur Brown Jr., principal architect of San Francisco City Hall, who designed it in the Beaux-Arts style [1]. The building has six grand windows, stately detailing and a high ceiling. It is the oldest bank building still standing in the Excelsior. Hibernia built branches in the same style at 18th and Castro streets, Valencia and 22nd streets, and Geary Boulevard and 10th Avenue [1]. The building outlived its days as a bank. Today it is El Chico, a Mexican produce and grocery store, where its stately detailing, six windows and high ceiling can still be appreciated [1]. Mission Local calls the former Hibernia 'grandiose and ornate' [1][2]. Just to the south stands a lesson in how quickly bank architecture changed. The US Bank building, put up in 1963, is what SF Heritage calls an excellent example of the Midcentury Modern New Formalist style [1]. The two banks show 35 years of the Excelsior's main street side by side.

title: Dreamland's floor that tilted
place: Dreamland Rink / New Dreamland Auditorium site, Steiner between Post & Sutter
hook: The old boxing barn closed on a knockout. Its $1 million replacement had a floor on hydraulic jacks that could lie flat for dances or tilt for opera.
story: For twenty years the Dreamland Rink, entered mid-block on the west side of Steiner, was the neighbourhood's big room. It held roller skating and boxing, and on the eve of the 1916 election Governor Hiram Johnson drew crowds so large that the theatre next door took the overflow [1]. By the 1920s, the city's Japantown report notes, Dreamland was also staging sumo wrestling [2]. The last event was a fight on 2 September 1927, when Ray Pelkey met Bert Colima. The Bulletin's Les Cohen quipped that the old rink and Pelkey "went out simultaneously" [1]. A new Dreamland Auditorium, designed by Ward & Blohme, went up across the rink and the old National Theatre lot. It opened in June 1928 [1][3]. The Examiner counted 8,500 seats for boxing and 4,500 for opera. The floor sat on hydraulic jacks so it could be level for dances or tilted for concerts [1]. The Examiner put the cost at $1.2 million. Wikipedia says $1 million, and opening dates vary between 26 and 29 June [1][3]. In 1939 the building was renamed Winterland [1].

title: Fifty years with nobody home
place: Ellinwood Residence, 2799 Pacific Avenue at Divisadero (Landmark No. 207)
hook: A 14-fireplace mansion on the crest of Pacific Heights stood empty from 1928 to 1978. Its stained-glass dome and a gift tree from Queen Victoria came through intact.
story:
The Ellinwood house went up in 1893–94. It was one of the first homes built on the crest around Pacific and Divisadero, after a cable car line up Pacific Avenue made the hilltop reachable [2]. The architect, J. Eugene Freeman, also designed Oakland's Dunsmuir House, and he gave this one a similar abundance of balustrades, climbing right up to a widow's walk [2]. Inside are 106 windows, 14 fireplaces and an interior dome of about 8,000 pieces of stained glass [1].

Its owner, Dr. Charles Ellinwood, was a Civil War surgeon, an early officer of the U.S. Public Health Service and a founder of the Marine Hospital in the Presidio [1]. Divisadero had once been the dividing line between the city and a much larger Presidio [1].

Then, from 1928 to 1978, nobody lived in the house at all. The city's landmark resolution calls this "a unique event", and it explains why so much of the original decoration survived [1]. The Bloomfields wrote that for many years it came as close as any house in their book to being a haunted house [2]. The garden kept three trees more than a century old. One of them was a gift from Queen Victoria [1].

title: It's-It Was Born in a Playland Pie Shop
place: Site of Playland-at-the-Beach food stands, Great Highway between Balboa and Cabrillo Streets
hook: Ice cream, two oatmeal cookies and a dip in chocolate. For more than 40 years it was a Playland treat.
story:
In 1928 George Whitney, the operator behind Playland-at-the-Beach, came up with a treat for his pie shop: a disc of vanilla ice cream pressed between two oatmeal cookies and dipped in melted chocolate, made to order [1].

Nobody knows for certain where the name came from. The company's president in 1998 said a woman who had worked at the pie shop told them it went back to the cow races held near Playland. A cow named It won one day, someone asked who had come in first, and the answer was "It's it." Whitney liked it [1].

Generations of San Franciscans grew up eating Playland It's-Its, along with meals at The Hot House [2]. It was sold there until the park was razed in the early 1970s. In 1974 a Burlingame company, Jamal's Enterprises, acquired the trademark. By 1998 its plant was turning out more than 3 million sandwiches a year, in chocolate, strawberry, mint and cappuccino as well as the original vanilla [1]. One couple, according to company lore, even had a wedding "cake" made of them [1].

title: Maybeck builds for the city's charity
place: Family Service Agency (Associated Charities) building, 1010 Gough Street at Eddy
hook: Bernard Maybeck designed a Mediterranean home for the Associated Charities. Across the street stood a mansion that would later appear in Vertigo.
story:
The Associated Charities of San Francisco dates to 1889 [1]. The kindergarten pioneer Sarah B. Cooper was one of its directors [2]. In 1928 Bernard Maybeck designed a Mediterranean-style headquarters for the organisation at Gough and Eddy. In 1938 it renamed itself the Family Service Agency, partly to escape the stigma attached to the word 'charity' [1].

When the building was new, most of its neighbours were fine Italianate row houses. Next door was the 1880 Hugo Rothschild House, which became a rooming house early in its life [1][3]. The corner was shared with St. Paulus Lutheran Church and the twenty-room mansion Henry F. Fortmann built in 1888 at 1007 Gough [1]. The Call reported that on 26 February 1901 Emma Fortmann married Dr. W. E. Stevens at the house [1]. The mansion was demolished in 1959, a year after it played the McKittrick Hotel in Alfred Hitchcock's Vertigo. Many websites wrongly call it the 'Portman' mansion [1]. The Rothschild house has since been restored as a single-family home [3].

title: Mission Street's 3,000-seat movie palace
place: El Capitan Theatre and Hotel, 2353 Mission Street
hook: The Cap had a doorman in a top hat, a curtain behind the curtain, and 3,000 seats. Today you can drive through its old lobby into a parking lot.
story:
Mission Street belonged to blue-collar San Francisco [4]. At its peak the district had about 15,000 theatre seats, more than anywhere in the city except mid-Market [1]. The grandest was the El Capitan, which opened in 1928 between 19th and 20th Streets. G. Albert Lansburgh designed it, with a Mexican Baroque façade and a Spanish Colonial Revival interior. With 3,000 seats it was once the second-biggest movie theatre in town [2]. A few blocks south, Timothy Pflueger gave the 1916 New Mission Theater its Art Deco look in 1932 [3].

Regulars called it 'the Cap'. One remembered a manager in a tuxedo and top hat with a huge handlebar moustache, and two stage curtains, the second rising straight up as the first parted. The previews promised films 'Coming Soon.....To YOUR El Capitan' [2]. A boy in the 1950s paid a quarter to see CinemaScope there [4]. The auditorium was torn down in 1961. The façade, marquee and hotel still stand, and cars now drive through the old lobby into a parking lot [2].

title: Movies Among the Sand Dunes
place: Former Parkside Theatre, 933 Taraval Street near 19th Avenue
hook: When the Parkside Theatre opened in December 1928, dunes came right up to its walls, and new patent-leather shoes walked home without their shine.
story: The streetcar made Taraval Street the Parkside's main street. The Municipal Railway's L-Taraval reached 20th and Taraval in September 1918, 33rd Avenue in April 1919 and 48th Avenue by January 1923, and shops popped up along the tracks [1]. Entertainment followed. The Parkside Theatre, at 933 Taraval near 19th Avenue, opened on December 28, 1928, with 'Red Lips,' starring Charles 'Buddy' Rogers [2]. (The Parkside context statement lumps the district's only movie house with its first two bank branches, which opened near 20th and Taraval in 1927 [1].) The neighborhood was still half empty. 'There were sand dunes on both sides of it,' Irene Sullivan Fay remembered. 'We had to walk quite a ways to get to the movies. I had these new black patent-leather shoes, and we came back and they were dull: all the shine was gone' [2]. From the mid-1930s to the mid-1960s its handsome facade anchored the Taraval shopping district. Then a 1965 Fox remodel added what theatre historian Jack Tillmany called an 'embarrassingly ugly marquee' [2]. It stopped running as a regular cinema in 1976, closed for good in July 1988, and the building now holds condominiums and a childcare center [1][2].

title: Old King Cole Above the Children's Fireplace
place: Pinehurst Lodge, 2685 30th Avenue
hook: Among the Parkside's stucco row houses stands a brick lodge the Junior League built for children waiting for foster homes, decorated with tiles of animals and ships.
story: In 1928 the San Francisco Junior League built Pinehurst as a home for poor children and orphans waiting for foster homes [1][2]. The architects were Ashley, Evers and Hayes. Their two-story brick building has a tile roof and a curved driveway, and it stands out on a big wooded lot among the Parkside's modest row houses. Three wings enclose a courtyard on the west side for gatherings [1]. The details were made for children. The recreation room walls have tiles of animals, ships and castles, and the fireplace in the visitors' room carries a frieze of Old King Cole [1]. The Ghirardelli family gave the salon in memory of their daughter Esperance. Its ceiling is inscribed in Latin with the verse from Corinthians that ends, 'the greatest of these is love' [1]. In 1929 the building won a 'city clubhouses' award at the Northern California Architectural Exhibition at the de Young Museum [1]. Pinehurst later served several social service agencies. The Salvation Army has owned it since 1946 [1], and WNP notes its long history of sheltering vulnerable women and children [3].

title: One corner, a century of shopkeepers
place: 186–198 Leland Avenue at Rutland Street
hook: A grocery where a boy earned his first dollar, then a Hawaiian restaurant, then a bakery: one Leland corner held a century of valley life.
story: The corner building at 198 Leland Avenue, at Rutland Street, began life as Dougherty's Grocery in the early 1900s [1][2]. Joe Luccini, born in the valley in 1913, earned his first dollar there in 1928; the Chronicle spelled it 'Dorharty's' [3]. He remembered when every family kept a vegetable garden and most raised chickens and rabbits [3]. In the 1980s the building was Paddy's Hawaiian Restaurant, and murals have covered its Rutland Street wall since then [1][2]. By 2000 it was home to the G&L Bakery [3], listed in 2002 as G & L Bakery & Restaurant [4]. With its two neighbours, the building forms an unusually intact row of early vernacular shops that SF Heritage said 'takes an observer right back to the neighborhood's earliest days' [1]. Luccini, a retired machinist, married his wife Emma in 1940. His sister lived across the street in a house 100 years old [3]. In 2021 the row was slated for demolition, which Heritage called 'a significant loss to the neighborhood and city' [1][2].

title: Sam Spade's apartment, and his creator's
place: 891 Post Street at Hyde
hook: Dashiell Hammett wrote The Maltese Falcon in a small apartment at Post and Hyde, then gave his detective Sam Spade the same address.
story: Dashiell Hammett came to San Francisco in 1921, a former Pinkerton detective sick with tuberculosis he had caught in the Army [1]. From 1926, on a nurse's advice, he lived apart from his wife and daughters so they wouldn't catch it, taking the ferry to see them in Fairfax on Sundays [1]. He was living at 891 Post Street, on the corner of Hyde, while he wrote his first three novels, and he put Sam Spade in the same building in The Maltese Falcon [2]. The Chronicle says he wrote the book at the kitchen table of his Post Street apartment in 1928. It was published on Valentine's Day 1930 [1]. No record shows which unit he rented. But Hammett scholars, reading the Falcon closely and comparing the building's layouts, think #401 is the likeliest home for both Hammett and Spade. It's a front corner flat with windows on Post and Hyde [2]. It has the small bathroom where Spade sits on the tub while Brigid O'Shaughnessy is made to strip [2]. Hammett left San Francisco in 1929 [1]. When the building was dedicated as a literary landmark, his daughter Jo toured the flat and told visitors his first name was said more like "Da-sheel" than "Dash-el" [2].

title: The Hardware Man Who Dug His Own Well
place: Ferrera Building, 4534-4540 Mission Street at Harrington
hook: Alfonso Ferrera arrived in 1909 unable to speak English. By 1928 his name was on a new building on Mission Street, and the building had its own well.
story: Alfonso Ferrera arrived in San Francisco in 1909, 'a poor Italian boy' who spoke no English. He worked in a restaurant for seven years and then started his own business in the Excelsior, where many Italian families were settling. He began with a 5-10-15 cent store at 4655 Mission Street, and in 1921 he took over McCall's hardware store on the corner of Harrington Street [1]. The 1920s building boom was good for business, with hundreds of new neighbours needing paint and building materials. Ferrera decided to build big. While his wife Irene ran the store in a temporary location down the block, he put up the steel-framed Ferrera Building. A special edition of the Excelsior News in August 1928 described its offices 'for professional men' and apartments with steam heat, Frigidaires and an elevator [1]. He also dug a well for the building's own water. His nephew, the historian Walter Jebe, wrote that 'until the city made him cap it, it was one of the last freshwater wells in San Francisco' [1]. An old-timer told another local historian that in droughts the store handed out its well water [2]. Ferrera Hardware served the Excelsior until 1992 [1][3].

title: Tunnelling under Buena Vista to the Sunset
place: Sunset Tunnel west portal, Carl St near Cole St
hook: For seven years politicians argued over how to reach the Sunset. Then crews blasted 4,232 feet through serpentine rock, and streetcars came out in Cole Valley.
story: Planners wanted a streetcar tunnel to the Sunset from 1913 on. The Twin Peaks Tunnel was built first, and the Supervisors did not fund a Sunset tunnel until September 1921. City Engineer M. M. O'Shaughnessy favoured a route from Duboce Avenue under the hill beside Buena Vista Park. The final route was approved only on April 6, 1925, after what one account called "protracted political discussion" [1]. Youdall Construction broke ground on June 10, 1926, and cut mostly through serpentine rock. The pilot drift broke through on March 11, 1927. The tunnel was finished on February 4, 1928, for $1,477,618, although a court order held up the rail work from October 1927 to May 1928 [1]. At the east end, the city took the southwest corner of Duboce Park for the entrance [2]. At the west end, a row of billboards lined the tunnel's construction fence near Clayton and Frederick streets [3]. On October 21, 1928, Mayor James Rolph opened the 4,232-foot tunnel. The new N line soon earned the second-highest fares of any streetcar line in the city. Along with the Twin Peaks Tunnel, it helped the Sunset fill with houses in the 1930s and 1940s [1].

title: Where the West's pipe organs were made
place: Schoenstein Organ Factory, 3101 20th Street
hook: In a Mission Revival factory on 20th Street, a Black Forest family built nearly every piece of the pipe organs that filled the West's churches, temples and civic halls.
story:
In 1868 two sons of the German organ builder Leo Schoenstein came to San Francisco to install an instrument in a beer garden near Portsmouth Square. One of them, Felix, stayed [1][2]. By 1877 he had his own business, installing mechanical orchestrions at the Cliff House and Woodward's Gardens and looking after organs in the Nob Hill mansions of Stanford and Hopkins [1]. Three of his ten children joined him, and in about 1909 the firm became Felix F. Schoenstein & Sons [1][2].

In 1928 the family built this factory on 20th Street, one of the few buildings anywhere designed just for organ-building [2]. Unlike many small builders, who assembled parts ordered from catalogues, Schoenstein made every component except the metal pipes in its own shops [1]. For most of its first century it was the largest organ builder in the West. It looked after instruments at Temple Emanu-El, Sherith Israel, the Legion of Honor and Civic Auditorium [1]. The family sold in 1977, and organs were built here until 2004, when the firm moved to Benicia [1][2].

title: A redwood hall for the Camp Fire Girls
place: Campfire Girls Building, 325 Arguello Boulevard
hook: On Arguello Boulevard, the Camp Fire Girls got a Craftsman meeting hall with a redwood-trussed ceiling like a cathedral. It is now a City Landmark.
story: In 1929 the Camp Fire Girls built a headquarters at 325 Arguello Boulevard, between California and Clement Streets. The city later called it a significant example of Bay Area Craftsman architecture [1]. Its architect, Henry Gutterson, gave it the irregular, picturesque shape typical of the style. Inside, redwood lines the walls and forms the trim and the beams of a trussed, cathedral-like vault over the central meeting hall [1]. Gutterson was born in Minnesota in 1884 and studied architecture at Berkeley under John Galen Howard. He then trained at the Ecole des Beaux-Arts in Paris and helped draw the Burnham Plan for San Francisco [2]. The city's landmark report adds that he studied with Bernard Maybeck and worked with him on the First Church of Christ, Scientist in Berkeley [1]. For about 40 years Gutterson was the supervising architect of St. Francis Wood, where he designed more than thirty houses and many of its fountains [1][2]. Historian Richard Brandi describes his work as woodsy and small in scale, sheathed in redwood, with the garden treated as an extension of the living room [2]. The city made the building Landmark No. 169 in 1984 [1][3].

title: A talkie on a moving streetcar
place: Haight Street at Masonic Avenue (route of the 6 Haight and Masonic line)
hook: In November 1929 a 6 Haight and Masonic streetcar became a moving cinema, showing Harold Lloyd's first talking picture as it looped around San Francisco.
story: In 1929 the silent comedy star Harold Lloyd spoke on screen for the first time, in Welcome Danger. He played a bumbling botanist, the son of a former police chief, who is called to San Francisco to fight crime [1]. The film opened at the Granada Theatre on November 8, 1929. Paramount also tried a publicity stunt: it showed the whole film, all twelve reels, on a moving car of the Market Street Railway's 6 Haight and Masonic line [1]. That was the line that carried Haight-Ashbury riders down Haight Street toward downtown [2]. The company magazine described the car. Seats were removed from the smoking section to make a projection room, and acoustic cloth lined the inside to keep out light and traffic noise. The audience sat in ten rows of leather seats. The car left Second and Market as the picture began and circled the city without stopping, arriving back just as it ended [1]. During a railroad scene, the car happened to pass the Third and Townsend depot, and "the sound of real locomotives traveled through the ventilators and mingled with those from the talkie." The riders could tell they were moving only when the lit screen rose or dipped on the hills [1].

title: An animal dealer becomes zoo director
place: San Francisco Zoo (originally Fleishhacker Zoo), 1 Zoo Rd
hook: San Francisco's zoo began in 1929 beside the giant pool, and its first director was the dealer who had sold it its animals.
story: Herbert Fleishhacker's 1920s plan for the beach south of Sloat Boulevard always included a zoo alongside the pool and playfields [1]. In 1929 it was established as the Herbert Fleishhacker Zoo, named after the banker and Park Commission president who founded it [2][3]. Its first director was George Bistany, a former wild-animal collector and importer. He got the job after delivering many of the zoo's first animals himself that year [2]. The early zoo shared the site with the pool, the playfield and the Mothers Building [1][2]. After Bistany died in 1935, zoologist Edmund Heller took over and oversaw the Works Progress Administration project that built most of the zoo. By 1940 it had cost about $3.5 million and included the Lion House, bear grottos and Monkey Island [2]. The architects wanted fireproof, permanent buildings of reinforced concrete, and decades later crews renovating the elephant yards found concrete poured seven feet deep [2]. At Fleishhacker's own suggestion, the name became the San Francisco Zoological Gardens in 1941 [2].

title: Minnie Vogel picks up the cleaver
place: 683 Chenery Street (Vogel Bros. Meat Co. building, later Chenery Park restaurant)
hook: Widowed in 1906 with six children, Minnie Vogel ran the family butcher shop herself. Her sons built a meat business and a Spanish-style market on Chenery.
story: German-born Herman Vogel opened his own butcher shop on San Bruno Road in 1892. When he died at 46 in late 1906, his wife Wilhelmina, known as Minnie, took over as butcher, a highly unusual job for a woman then, with six children to feed [1]. The family soon had a foothold in booming post-quake Glen Park. Herman's nephew August Vogel was a butcher living on Chenery by 1907, a director of the new Glen Park Volunteer Fire Company in 1908, and a partner in Henderson & Vogel at today's 683 Chenery [1]. Minnie's sons turned the trade into a small empire, with markets at Civic Center, on Fillmore and in the Mission. In 1928 the youngest, Adolph, took over the Chenery shop. In 1929, the year Vogel Bros. Meat Co. was incorporated with $200,000 in capital, he replaced the old building with the Spanish Colonial/Mediterranean Revival storefront that still stands [1]. The company was dissolved in 1947. Albert's Meats, a laundromat, Diamond Pizza and the Chenery Park restaurant followed [1]. The owners of a nearby liquor store remembered that even after the shabby 1970s laundromat became a pizzeria, one tiled wall still read "Vogel Bros. Meat Co." [2] In 2025 builders found the green and yellow mosaic behind drywall, but it could not be saved [1].

title: Ravioli from a garage on Chestnut
place: Lucca Delicatessen, 2120 Chestnut Street
hook: In 1929 a railroad man from Colorado opened an Italian deli in a garage on a half-empty Chestnut Street. The ravioli machine he imported still runs.
story: In 1929 Mike Bosco opened an Italian delicatessen at 2120 Chestnut Street with two partners, Maggiore Colona, a cook, and Italo Cencini. Bosco had grown up in Glenwood Springs, Colorado, working on the Denver & Rio Grande Railroad [1]. The Marina was still thinly settled then, with vacant lots along Chestnut. Landlords were turning the ground floors under their apartments into shops, and Lucca's started out as the parking garage beneath a six-unit building [1]. The partners put a kitchen in back and bought an Italian-built machine for ravioli and fresh pasta. The ravioli sold so well they began delivering it, and one of their first customers was the Fairmont Hotel [1]. That same 1930s machine still makes it, although the cutting and rolling are done by hand [1]. Italians were spreading from North Beach into the Marina. Bosco's grandson Paul remembered 'a small, tight-knit community, where everyone kind of knew everyone.' His maternal grandfather, one of the founders of Columbus Salame, lived just behind the deli [1]. Bosco bought out his partners in 1959, his son Ed became sole owner in 1968, and Ed's children Linda and Paul took it over [1]. Its customers have included Joe DiMaggio and Marilyn Monroe [1]. The 1920s black tiles and the old salami rack are still there [1].

title: The Neighbours Who Fought for the Cove
place: Head of the China Beach path, end of Sea Cliff Avenue
hook: In 1929 Sea Cliff's own developer filed plans to subdivide the little beach below it. A women's committee, PTAs and shopkeepers set out to stop it.
story: The Allen Company built Sea Cliff, and by the late 1920s it had its eye on the cove below. The National Park Service's history dates its plans to 1928. The city's Playground Commission says the owners filed a subdivision map of the China Beach area early in 1929 [1][2]. Neighbours organised fast. A women's committee led by Mrs. Annette L. Bachman, with Mrs. Herbert Gunn, Mrs. Charles Robinson, Mrs. W. S. Berry and Mrs. Paul Paige, pushed a city bond to buy the beach [1]. Their allies were a very San Francisco mix: the Garden Club, the Daughters of California Pioneers, the Galileo and Sutro parent-teacher associations, the Clement Street Merchants' Association, the Building Trades Council and disabled veterans [2]. In November 1929, after a campaign of less than a month, the measure lost by 3,948 votes out of 72,175 [2]. They kept going. James D. Phelan left $50,000 in his will, and the state matched it [2]. In 1933 California paid the Allen Company $160,000 for the six-acre beach, which officials called the only safe swimming spot on the city's shoreline [1][2].

title: The bank that became a bar
place: 540 Clement Street near 6th Avenue
hook: 540 Clement opened as a savings bank a month after the 1929 crash. It was robbed in 1932, and it has been a neighbourhood bar since 1936.
story: If the front of 540 Clement doesn't look like a bar, that's because it was built as a bank. The Park-Presidio office of Pacific States Savings and Loan opened here in 1929, one month after the stock market crash [1]. On December 23, 1932, the Examiner reported that robbers hit the Clement and Market Street branches at the same time and got away with $363 in all [1]. Pacific States began to fail the next year. By 1936 William and Ella Greely were serving beer at the address, and it has been a bar ever since. It has been the Five-Forty Club, Touchables 540 Club, Hak's, Max's 540 Club and O'Rourke's. Hak, the story goes, took the bank vault out piece by piece [1]. In 1966 a bartender here, Mike Chiechi, heard a customer telling a story. Twelve years earlier Chiechi had nearly drowned water-skiing, and he had been brought back with CPR. The customer was one of the off-duty officers who had saved him [1]. 'This is the only bar in town where the customer's never right,' a bartender told the Examiner in 1989. In 2020 former bartenders took it over as Rogues 540 [1].

title: The housewife who stopped the steam shovels
place: Mount Davidson Park, Dalewood Way entrance
hook: When subdividers started clearing Mount Davidson in 1926, a housewife got PTA children to mail wildflowers to the city's powerful, and saved the summit.
story: By 1926 houses were climbing Mount Davidson's slopes, and Mrs. Edmund N. 'Madie' Brown was, in her words, 'alarmed by the destruction' [1]. She took her case to the Commodore Sloat School PTA: 'The subdividers' axe and steam shovel are destroying in ruthless fashion the beauties of nature on our beloved Mt. Davidson' [1]. As chair of a new conservation committee, she gathered maps, histories and an appraisal. PTA mothers and children mailed wildflowers from the mountain to people of influence, and the city's women's clubs, with 15,000 members, voted their support [1]. Mayor 'Sunny Jim' Rolph and Supervisor Margaret Mary Morgan, the first woman on the board, joined in [1][2]. In 1927 the city set aside $15,000, but the deal dragged for two years. The developer August Lang had first offered 78 acres at $4,000 an acre, bundled with a reservoir he wanted built for his houses [2]. On December 20, 1929, John McLaren's 84th birthday, Mayor Rolph dedicated Mount Davidson Park [1][2]. Sources disagree on how much land was bought and when the summit was donated.

title: Wagner played with a whisk broom
place: Salz home, 3838 Clay Street
hook: At one Clay Street house, a small Isaac Stern played for Hadassah and Ansel Adams played Wagner with a whisk broom, then with an orange.
story:
Helen and Ansley Salz lived at 3838 Clay Street from 1914 to 1954 [1]. He was a tannery businessman and a fine amateur violinist whose collection of violins went to Israel and the University of California. She was a painter who had studied with Robert Henri, and co-founded the school behind their garden [1][2].

Their house was full of music. Helen remembered Isaac Stern giving what she believed was his first concert there, about 1929, when he was around ten, for the Jewish women's group Hadassah. Afterwards she rescued him from his admirers and sent him to play in the yard with the children [1].

At the Salzes' New Year's parties, the photographer Ansel Adams sat at the piano and played Wagner with a whisk broom, and later with an orange. There were skits and a big supper. At midnight one year the watercolourist Dong Kingman's wife asked when the bridge game would start. The Salzes had no cards in the house [1].

One private evening, only for musicians, the cellist Luigi Silva played Ernest Bloch's Schelomo. Bloch was so pleased that he rushed up and kissed him on both cheeks. Many people, Helen said, were insulted not to be asked [1].

In 1934 Helen Salz and Alexander Meiklejohn founded the Northern California branch of the ACLU [1].

title: Where San Francisco built and burned streetcars
place: Site of the Elkton Shops, between San Jose Avenue, Ocean Avenue, Geneva Avenue and the railroad (now Muni's Green Metro Center and Balboa Park BART)
hook: In 1929 more than two hundred men worked at the Elkton Shops, building new streetcars and burning old ones in the lower yard.
story: After the 1906 earthquake, United Railroads was expanding its streetcar network and quickly put up its main maintenance shops next to Southern Pacific's Elkton station [1][2]. The site ran between San Jose Avenue, the railroad, Ocean Avenue and Geneva Avenue, and the railroad itself brought in materials [2]. The complex had a main shop with sixteen tracks running inside, a separate paint shop, open storage and a first-aid hospital [1]. In 1929, a peak year, the Elkton Shops employed 226 men. They built 26 new car bodies and overhauled 316 cars, and they burned the bodies of scrapped cars in the lower yard [1]. The company rented about a dozen cottages and flats nearby to its own employees. In 1930, carmen, motormen, conductors and railroad workers still filled small boarding houses around San Jose and Navajo avenues [1]. The shops stayed open under Muni until May 30, 1977. They were cleared for the Curtis E. Green Metro Center, after part of the land had already been taken for Balboa Park BART [1].

title: A cattle baron's widow builds a church
place: Glide Memorial Church, 330 Ellis Street at Taylor
hook: Long before the famous choir and the Sunday crowds, Glide began as a quiet memorial from a Sacramento widow, whose foundation also ran a temperance hotel nearby.
story: In 1929 Lizzie Glide, a Methodist philanthropist, bought land at Ellis and Taylor and founded the Glide Foundation in memory of her husband, H. L. Glide, a Sacramento cattleman [2]. The church was designed by James W. Plachek and finished in 1930 in an Italian Renaissance style. It has an arcaded base, a corner tower with a cupola, a neon cross that revolves on top, and a cornerstone reading "Glide Memorial Evangelistic Center 1930" [1]. Two blocks away, the Glide Foundation owned the 16-story Hotel Californian on Taylor Street from 1935 [1]. It was run for decades as a temperance hotel [3]. Glide stayed conservative until the 1960s, and by then it had a large endowment but no programs [2]. That changed in 1962, when the foundation hired the Rev. Lewis Durham, who soon brought in Cecil Williams. The quiet memorial became one of the most famous liberal churches in the country [2].

title: A church hidden inside a skyscraper hotel
place: William Taylor Hotel and Temple Methodist Church (now McAllister Tower), 100 McAllister Street
hook: Four Methodist congregations pooled their money and put a 1,500-seat Gothic church inside a dry skyscraper hotel in the middle of the Tenderloin.
story: In 1930 San Franciscans got what TIME called a "brand new 30-story pyramidal skyscraper-church-hotel" at McAllister and Leavenworth [1]. The National Register counts 28 stories [2]. Four Methodist congregations had merged into Temple Methodist, led by Dr. Walter John Sherman, who spent ten years on the scheme [1]. The building cost $2,800,000. It had 500 guest rooms, 32 tower apartments and seven elevators that reached the roof in 30 seconds. Inside was a Gothic church seating 1,500 [1]. The hotel was named for William "California" Taylor, a Forty-Niner preacher. TIME says he set his Bible on an overturned whiskey barrel in Portsmouth Square and sang until the saloons emptied [1]. Timothy Pflueger's firm drew the Gothic-trimmed tower, and Lewis P. Hobart finished it [2][3]. The idea did not last. The hotel never turned a profit, and the church eventually left, losing its investment [3]. The building went on to be the Empire Hotel, federal offices and, from 1981, law-school housing [3].

title: A dance floor split by the county line
place: Sam's Lodge / A. Silvestri Co., 2629 Bayshore Blvd
hook: In the early 1930s a Swiss-born roadhouse owner painted the San Francisco–San Mateo county line down the middle of his dance floor. Then the fun began.
story: On the old Bayshore road, right where San Francisco ends, stands a fake log cabin. In the early 1930s Swiss-born Samuel Chappat turned a plain wooden building into Sam's Lodge, a roadhouse built directly on the San Francisco–San Mateo county line [1][2]. To make the point, Sam painted a yellow line down the middle of the dance floor [1]. What was legal in one county was illegal in the other, and the Chronicle's Carl Nolte records slot machines, after-hours drinking along a 40-foot bar, and police from both sides who didn't look too hard at nightlife on the edge [1]. The road outside had become U.S. 101, the busiest north–south highway in California [1]. After Sam sold, the cabin became a refined Chinese restaurant under the Chan family in the 1940s [2], then a Polynesian place with fire dancers, a stage for some of the city's first punk shows, and even a tropical-fish shop [1]. Since the 1960s it has been the showroom of A. Silvestri Co., the statuary firm [3]. In 2022 it was one of three finalists in San Francisco Heritage's vote to pick the valley's first landmark [2]. "We're the unsung heroes of San Francisco," Sandra Silvestri said [1].

title: A dime bought the whole Saturday
place: Avenue Theatre, 2650 San Bruno Avenue
hook: Newsreel, cartoon, comedy, cowboy picture and a cliffhanger serial, all for ten cents, until your mother came down the aisle hissing your name.
story: The Avenue opened on San Bruno Avenue on 20 July 1927 with Charles Murray in "McFadden's Flats" [1]. For neighbourhood kids of the 1920s and '30s it was the Saturday ritual. Ruth Eshow Upton, who grew up nearby, remembered a dime buying a Pathé newsreel with its crackling electric tower, a cartoon (Mickey Mouse, Betty Boop), a comedy, often Wheeler and Woolsey, a cowboy picture and one episode of a ten-part serial [2]. There was no popcorn lobby, and her mother considered such food "junk" anyway. The price doubled to 20 cents at age twelve, so the small-for-their-age Eshow girls lined up by height behind their little brother, who handed the usher all the tickets at once; they got in for a dime until 16 [2]. Any on-screen kiss set off bedlam. Once, staying for a second showing, Ruth spotted her mother searching the rows, hissing "Ruthie!", and was dragged home by the ear [2]. On Friday and Saturday nights there was vaudeville, chorus girls high-kicking through the cigarette haze [2]. Sources disagree on who built the house: 1920s trade papers quoted on Cinema Treasures name Ackerman & Harris, while a theatre history credits the four Levin brothers [1][3].

title: From railroad trench to freeway stub
place: San Jose Avenue in the Bernal Cut, between Fairmount and Bernal hills (beside Arlington Street)
hook: San Jose Avenue's sunken, freeway-like run past Glen Park began as an 1860s railroad trench. It is also what remains of a freeway stopped at Randall Street.
story:
In the summer of 1861 crews building the San Francisco-San Jose Railroad started cutting a trench through the gap between Fairmount and Bernal hills. It became known as the Bernal Cut [1]. The line opened in January 1864 with a Grand Celebration as "the first link of the Great Central Railway." Its local stop was the Four-mile House, near today's Randall Street [1]. By 1926 Southern Pacific trains still ran down the middle of what is now San Jose Avenue [2].

In the late 1920s the city widened the cut for cars. One architectural history dates the widening to 1928. Photographs record the opening day of the new Bernal Cut on 16 April 1930 [2][3]. The new road gave direct access from the Mission District to Glen Park and points south [3]. When the Southern Freeway, now I-280, was built in the 1960s, it followed the old railroad right-of-way [2][4].

A second freeway, the Mission Freeway, was planned to run overhead along Valencia Street. It was stopped at Randall Street. A 2003 city plan called the "freeway-like" stretch of San Jose Avenue that was left "an unneeded remnant of this misguided idea" [4].

title: Hollywood's lions on Hyde Street
place: Film exchanges, 245-259 Hyde Street ('Film Row')
hook: Carved lions and theatre masks on a Tenderloin block mark where MGM, Fox and United Artists once kept the reels for Market Street's movie palaces.
story: The Tenderloin once had its own small Hollywood. Just north of Market Street's movie palaces, studios and distributors ran "film exchanges," offices that stored and handled the films bound for the city's cinemas [1][2]. The earliest were in ordinary brick shops after 1906. From 1920 to 1922, investor Louis R. Lurie built a group of purpose-built exchanges on Golden Gate Avenue, Turk and Leavenworth, designed by Albert Schroepfer. One on Turk Street housed the Pathé Exchange in 1923 [1]. Around 1930 the Bell Brothers added two-story Moderne concrete exchanges on Hyde Street [1]. By 1937, 255-259 Hyde held 20th Century Fox, Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer, Loew's and United Artists, and its facade still carries cast lion heads for MGM and comedy and tragedy masks [1]. Next door, 245-251 Hyde housed Fox and RKO in 1932 [1]. Columbia Pictures was across the street at 230 Hyde from 1932 to 1937 [1]. Decades later 245 Hyde became Wally Heider's recording studio, used by the Grateful Dead and Jefferson Airplane [3].

title: Safety Patrol Boys and a Missing Pledge
place: Site of Portola Junior High (now Martin Luther King Jr. Middle School), Bacon Street at Goettingen
hook: At Portola Junior High, boys drilled as traffic patrols, pupils dug gardens, and one Bayview girl was left craving the end of a pledge nobody recited any more.
story: In the 1930s Portola Junior High School stood at Bacon and Goettingen, on the site of today's Martin Luther King Jr. Middle School. A photograph from the decade shows its Safety Patrol traffic boys marching in formation across the yard [1]. Another, captioned 'Burrows & Brussels', shows children and adults gardening at the school [1]. Pupils came from well beyond the Portola. Ruth Eshow Upton went to Bret Harte Grammar School on Third Street in the Bayview, then followed her classmates to Portola Junior High [2]. At Bret Harte, every morning ended with the Pledge of Allegiance and then a second pledge, 'I am a California Child'. When she moved up to the seventh grade at Portola she was surprised to find the class simply stopped after the national pledge. It left, she wrote, 'an unfinished feeling', like putting down an apple or cookie with one bite left and then not being able to find it [3]. Decades later she found the California pledge's full lyrics on the website of Johnson Park Elementary School in Marysville, though nobody there knew who wrote it [3].

title: San Francisco's Only Expressionist Schoolhouse
place: Roosevelt Middle School, 460 Arguello Boulevard
hook: Timothy Pflueger gave the Richmond a brick school in a style found nowhere else in San Francisco, and possibly nowhere else in America.
story: Between 1920 and 1930 San Francisco issued bonds to build fifty public schools, and one of the last was the most unusual [1]. Theodore Roosevelt Middle School, built in 1929 and 1930 at 460 Arguello, was designed by Timothy Pflueger in what the city's landmark report calls an idiosyncratic Dutch-German Expressionist style [1]. The report calls it the only example of that avant-garde style in San Francisco, and possibly the United States [1]. NoeHill calls it probably the most impressive example of the bricklayer's art in San Francisco [1]. Inside, the Depression left its mark in art. With money from the WPA Federal Art Project, Nelson Poole painted two 5-by-20-foot murals, 'Land' and 'Harvest', for the lobby [2]. George Wilson Walker's 5-by-25-foot oil 'Education' hangs above the entrance to the auditorium balcony [3]. The murals survive, well preserved, and helped earn the school designation as San Francisco Landmark No. 285, approved by the Board of Supervisors in March 2019 [1].

title: The $39,962,606.51 check for a lake
place: Shore of North Lake, Lake Merced (site of the March 9, 1930 dedication, approximate)
hook: After decades of lawsuits and failed bond votes, San Francisco finally wrote one enormous check and got its biggest lake back from a private monopoly.
story: By the 1910s the Spring Valley Water Company was the largest privately owned water utility in the United States, and an unpopular one with reformers, progressives and newspaper editors [1]. Over the years the city sued it several times over rates and over free water for fighting fires [2]. Lake Merced was part of its supply: in 1902 almost 1.8 billion gallons of lake water flowed from city taps [1]. After 1906 the city looked to Hetch Hetchy, but bond measures to buy Spring Valley failed in 1910, 1915 and 1921 [1]. Meanwhile the company sold land around the lake to golf clubs, and the city leased ground for Fleishhacker Pool, the future zoo and Harding Park [1]. Voters finally approved the purchase in 1928 [1]. On March 2, 1930, at a ceremony in City Hall, the city treasurer handed company president S. P. Eastman a check for $39,962,606.51. In return San Francisco received 62,500 acres of watershed, reservoirs, tunnels and pipes, and 454 Spring Valley employees became civil servants on the spot [1]. A week later, on March 9, a grander dedication was held on the shore of Lake Merced, with patriotic bunting, a speech by the mayor and a walk around lands that had long been fenced off [1].

title: The Day a Twister Spun a House
place: The 'Tornado House', 1896 46th Avenue near Ortega Street
hook: In February 1930 police rushed to an 'explosion' in the Outer Sunset. What they found was a house screwed sideways into the sand.
story: On February 24, 1930, a violent storm hit the Bay Area. It swept a deckhand off a tugboat at the Ferry Building, lightning set Oakland's city hall on fire, and hail and snow fell in the Mission. Then police got reports of an explosion near 46th Avenue and Ortega Street [1]. The block between 45th and 46th Avenues, Noriega and Ortega, still had just one house. Crews found it tilted in the dunes, ringed with broken lumber. It had not blown up. It looked as if it had been spun off its foundation and screwed down into the sand. Mrs. James C. Crampton of 2243 45th Avenue had watched a huge funnel go by: 'It seemed as if tons of sand were swirling round and round' [1]. The owner, John Voltz, was at work. Reporters and curious neighbors posed on the steeply tilted floors. A garage behind 1800 48th Avenue was wrecked too. The four daily papers weren't sure what to call it: 'freak squall,' 'freak storm,' 'a miniature twister' [1]. Voltz put his losses at $5,000 but didn't give up. His house, first built in 1911, was repaired where it stood, and it is still at 1896 46th Avenue, with a taller, angled upper floor [1][2].

title: The little girl in the bay window
place: Corner of 23rd and Castro streets
hook: A cable car conductor told his kids to be grateful, like the sickly girl who waved from a window at 23rd and Castro. Years later his son married her.
story:
In the 1930s the little Castro Street cable cars, which local children called "Dinkies," climbed over the hill from 18th Street to a turntable at 26th [1]. The line was phased out by 1941 [2]. One conductor, Bob Beban Sr., kept telling his family about a sad, sickly girl of four or five. She knelt in a big bay window at 23rd and Castro and waved at every car. He told his children to stop complaining about their vegetables and be grateful they were healthy [1].

Years later his wife, Marie, told this story to her daughter-in-law, Vivian. Vivian's eyes grew wide: "Mom, that little girl was me!" Just before her fifth birthday her appendix had burst. She spent six weeks in San Francisco General and had 13 operations. She was only allowed home once her mother bought an electric refrigerator to make ice packs. Her bed was set in the sunny front window of their corner flat, and she waved at the Dinkies. One man always smiled and rang the bell for her [1]. Her husband Bob was stunned: "You? I married the little girl in the window?" Bob Sr. had died of a heart attack at 48, so Vivian never got to reminisce with him [1].

title: A Communist Paints the Stock Exchange
place: Stock Exchange Tower (City Club), Sansome near Pine
hook: When Timothy Pflueger hired Diego Rivera to paint inside capitalism's West Coast citadel, just about everyone in San Francisco was angry.
story: In September 1930 architect Timothy Pflueger announced that Mexican muralist Diego Rivera, an avowed Communist, would paint a fresco in his new Stock Exchange tower [1]. Pflueger's firm had just remodelled the exchange at Pine and Sansome [3]. The painter Maynard Dixon called Rivera "the greatest living artist in the world" but said the exchange "could look the world over without finding a man more inappropriate" [1]. The Chronicle mocked up his satirical Capitalist Dinner panel on the Lunch Club staircase and asked whether the club's art would be "touched in pink" [1]. Rivera's 1931 fresco, Allegory of California, climbs the stairwell wall and runs across the ceiling [2]. Its giant goddess was modelled on tennis champion Helen Wills Moody, one hand holding fruit and wheat, the other scooping up earth to show miners at work. Around her are oil refineries, Matson and Dollar Line ships, gold dredges, James Marshall and Luther Burbank [2]. He pleased his patrons, but signed it in red paint beneath a redwood stump. A red-handed warning gauge may hint at his belief that capitalism would destroy itself [2]. The fresco remains inside a private club [1].

title: A Movie King with an Aviation Beacon
place: El Rey Theatre, 1970 Ocean Avenue at Victoria Street
hook: Timothy Pflueger crowned an Ocean Avenue movie palace with a tower meant to guide planes through the fog. Then came a church, a sci-fi dream and bankruptcy.
story:
In 1931 neighbourhood theatre mogul Samuel H. Levin spent $500,000 on an 1,830-seat picture palace at Ocean Avenue and Victoria Street, and the opening film was Maurice Chevalier's "The Smiling Lieutenant" [1]. Timothy Pflueger, who also designed the Castro Theatre, mixed the Spanish Colonial Revival style then popular in Ingleside Terraces and Balboa Terrace with streamlined Moderne. He named it El Rey, "The King" [1]. He meant the 146-foot tower to be a beacon in the foggy district, with green and red neon and a directional light charted by aviation authorities [1].

The last movie played in 1977 [2]. For some thirty years the Voice of Pentecost church used the building and painted a cross on the tower. The church mortgaged it to pay for upgrades and a science-fiction film the pastor described as "the Ten Commandments meets Star Wars." The film was never finished, the church went bankrupt, and the building was foreclosed on in 2015 [1]. The Board of Supervisors made it City Landmark No. 274 in 2017, and developers drew up plans for 42 condos [1]. Instead, in September 2025, an evangelical congregation, The Father's House SF, bought the long-empty theatre. That upset neighbours who had hoped for an arts or community centre [3].

title: A Russian Cathedral in an Episcopal Church
place: Old Holy Virgin Cathedral, 858–864 Fulton St
hook: Russians who had fled the Revolution bought a redwood Episcopal church on Fulton Street. For 34 years it was the cathedral of the Russian Orthodox Church Outside Russia's western diocese.
story: In 1927, as refugees from the Russian Revolution settled in San Francisco, a group of faithful led by Archbishop Apollinary (Koshevoi) formed a parish of the Russian Orthodox Church Outside Russia. They dedicated it to the icon of the Mother of God, "Joy of All Who Sorrow" [1]. At first they worshipped in a storefront on Sacramento Street. In 1931 they bought the former St. Stephen's Episcopal Church on Fulton Street between Webster and Fillmore [1][2]. It is a German Renaissance–style building of California redwood, dated to about 1880 [2]. They installed an iconostasis in front of the altar and carved icon shrines along the walls, and the building became the cathedral of the diocese [1]. Archbishop Tikhon (Troitsky) led the diocese from 1930 to 1962 [1]. After the communist victory in China, thousands of Orthodox refugees came to San Francisco in the early 1950s, many of them by way of the Philippines under the guidance of St. John of Shanghai and San Francisco. The cathedral was packed so tight that candles had to be passed hand to hand to reach the stands [1]. St. John became archbishop of San Francisco in 1963 and kept serving at Fulton Street until the new cathedral on Geary opened in 1965 [1][3]. The old building became City Landmark No. 28 in 1970 [1][2].

title: A curving pier built from leftovers
place: Foot of Van Ness Avenue, landward end of the Aquatic Park Municipal Pier
hook: Voters refused to pay for Aquatic Park, so the city built half a pier anyway, using salvaged timber, borrowed tools and a stockpile of old street cobblestones.
story: In 1923 the architects Bakewell, Brown and Bauer drew an ambitious plan for Black Point Cove: curving concrete piers arcing into the bay to enclose the water, at a cost of almost two million dollars [1]. A bond issue went to voters in November 1928 with ads urging, 'People Demand and Deserve A Safe Place to SWIM, ROW, FISH in the Heart of San Francisco.' Hoping it would pass, the supervisors set aside $100,000 for one enclosing pier. The bonds failed, but the money had been promised [1]. Van Ness Avenue was pushed out over landfill to the tip of Black Point, and on August 17, 1931, a crew began clearing the site beside a sign announcing 'Site of San Francisco's AQUATIC PARK.' Salvaged cribbing was piled at the foot of Van Ness. By December the Healy-Tibbetts company had the first half of the reinforced concrete pier in place [1]. Then the money ran out, and it sat half-built until 1933. While the city waited, workers with borrowed tools stockpiled granite cobblestones trucked in from resurfaced streets [1]. The WPA later built a stepped granite cobblestone seawall whose curve mirrors the pier's [1]. The curving Municipal Pier is now part of the Aquatic Park Historic District, a National Historic Landmark since 1987 [2].

title: Diego Rivera paints himself from behind
place: Diego Rivera Gallery, 800 Chestnut St
hook: The great Mexican muralist put himself at the center of his San Francisco fresco, and the most visible part of him is his backside.
story: In 1926 the California School of Fine Arts moved into a new Spanish Colonial Revival campus at 800 Chestnut Street, designed by Bakewell & Brown [1]. Mexican muralist Diego Rivera arrived in San Francisco in 1930 to paint a fresco there [1]. When the school's landmark case was prepared in 1977, the report noted that Rivera had asked for more wall space rather than a bigger fee [2]. Finished in 1931, "The Making of a Fresco Showing the Building of a City" is a painting about making a painting. It shows steel riveters and industrial workers building a city. Among the figures are school president William Gerstle and Coit Tower architect Arthur Brown Jr. Rivera also painted himself, seen from behind, so viewers get a good look at his broad backside [2]. It is one of only three Rivera murals in San Francisco [2]. The school was renamed the San Francisco Art Institute in 1961, and the campus became city landmark No. 85 [1]. Nine decades after Rivera painted it, the fresco would become the prize in a fight over the school's survival [2].

title: Football with skulls, then Latin from a platform
place: Former Masonic Cemetery grounds, USF's lower campus
hook: In the late 1920s, schoolboy Ray Pallas played football with skulls on the half-cleared Masonic Cemetery. By the 1960s he was St. Ignatius's last old-style Jesuit lecturer.
story: The Jesuits had campaigned for years to move the cemeteries out of their neighbourhood, and in the late 1920s the old Masonic Cemetery was still not empty. Ray Pallas, then a St. Ignatius student, remembered wandering the site in the late 1920s with friends and playing pick-up football games with disinterred skulls that lay strewn about as the land was cleared [1]. The clearing took years. In December 1931 the cemetery association reported that relatives had moved 5,600 bodies, mostly to Woodlawn in Colma, but 14,300 were still there. Of 5,000 letters sent to families, about 2,500 had come back undeliverable. Anyone left unclaimed would go to a special section at Woodlawn [2]. Pallas became a Jesuit. In the mid-1960s Father Pallas was teaching World History at St. Ignatius on Stanyan Street, the last Jesuit there who still insisted on a raised lecture platform at the front of his classroom [3]. He read aloud from up there, slipped Latin punchlines into his jokes to see who was keeping up, and was not above throwing out class clowns himself [3]. One of his 1932 classmates, the father of columnist Frank Dunnigan, warned his freshman son over dinner: "Don't let him offer you any cigarettes—he's the one who got me started smoking" [3].

title: Junior high sweethearts, married at 82
place: Aptos Middle School (formerly Aptos Junior High), 105 Aptos Avenue
hook: Carol Channing fell for the leader of the Aptos Junior High band in the early 1930s. Six decades later, they married.
story: Aptos Junior High was built in 1931 at 105 Aptos Avenue to serve the families filling the new West of Twin Peaks neighborhoods [1]. In 1932 the secretary of its seventh grade was Carol Channing, the only child of a newspaperman who became a leader in the Christian Science church [1][2]. When she ran for student-body vice president, she joined the school band because she needed it for her campaign song. "The leader of the school band was Harry Kullijian," she wrote in her 2002 memoir. "I was so in love with Harry I couldn't stop hugging him" [1]. A school plaque from 1936–37 carries both their names; each won the best all-around student award, in successive years. He was a class ahead of her. "That was something," she said, "to go with a guy a year ahead of you in school" [2]. Life pulled them apart. She became the star of "Hello, Dolly!" and they did not see each other for more than sixty years [2]. In May 2003, at 82, she married him [1][2]. In 2008 the couple came back to Aptos, where she pointed out her old home-room window [2].

title: Sunny Jim's rumoured 'pleasure den'
place: 3690 21st Street, near Sanchez, on Liberty Hill
hook: For decades neighbours whispered that a hilltop house on 21st Street was Mayor Rolph's Prohibition party pad. The records tell a duller, more interesting story.
story:
James "Sunny Jim" Rolph ran San Francisco for 19 years, from 1912 until he quit City Hall in January 1931 to become governor of California. He died in office in 1934 [2]. A rumour tied to him has clung to the house at 3690 21st Street, at the corner of Sanchez on the crest of Liberty Hill. The story went that it was an "entertainment hideout" where rich, well-connected men drank and met prostitutes during Prohibition [1].

FoundSF checked the paperwork. A Rolph-linked company, the Burlingame Corporation, did control the lot late in the Prohibition era. But the house wasn't built until 1931. City directories place James Rolph III, the governor's son, living there with his wife in 1932 and 1933. In 1933 it was sold to Francisco and Beatrice DiGrazia. One source claims DiGrazia was an eye surgeon who had operated on a relative of Mussolini, and that the grateful dictator sent over a lavish fountain [1]. The Rolph family owned the finished house for only about two years, and there's little reason to think it was ever a den of anything. It's simply a nice house with a great view that has fed salacious gossip for years [1].

title: Ten Cents to Sleep on a Rope
place: Site of the Standard Hotel, Seventh and Harrison streets
hook: In 1931 a sixteen-year-old who dreamed of going to sea ended up in a Seventh Street flophouse, sleeping upright with his elbows hooked over a clothesline.
story: After the 1929 crash, waves of men and boys on the move swelled South of Market's already large population of out-of-work transients [1]. One was Harlan Soeten, who arrived in 1931 at age 16, hoping to ship out as a sailor [1]. When his money ran out he landed in the Standard Hotel at Seventh and Harrison, a two-story flophouse where a guard buzzed people in and out. "At night they would string up clothesline over the benches and you could rent space for 10 cents a night to sleep, sitting on a bench with your elbows hooked over the rope," he remembered. Rooms cost 25 cents [1]. Soeten was picked out of a line to work at a city soup kitchen on Clara Alley run by a deputy sheriff, serving oatmeal, prunes and coffee in the morning and stew at 3 o'clock. By his memory, 4,000 men were fed at each meal, and he used six different soup kitchens himself [1]. The district had filled with cheap lodging houses for single working men after the 1906 rebuilding [2]. On the waterfront, it took the bloody 1934 strike to replace the daily shape-up with union hiring halls [1].

title: The Granada's tower and a final curtain
place: Former Granada Theatre, 4631 Mission St
hook: A plain 1922 movie house on Mission Street got a Spanish tower, a new name and 1,421 seats, then ended its run in tragedy.
story: The Excelsior Theatre opened in 1922 at Mission Street and Ocean Avenue, designed by G. Albert Lansburgh. In 1931 it was remodelled with a tall tower and reopened as the Granada, seating 1,421 [1][2]. About ten years later the whole building was given a sleek Streamline Moderne makeover, and that is the tower you still see rising over Mission Street today [1]. A 1939 photo shows a Market Street Railway streetcar passing its marquee, bringing passengers home from the zoo [2]. By the late 1970s the neighbourhood had changed. The Granada, run by the Lim family, joined the Apollo on Geneva Avenue in screening Filipino films for the Excelsior's growing Filipino community [3]. On October 5, 1981, the manager, Myla Lim, was murdered in a botched robbery attempt [2]. The theatre closed soon afterwards; the exact date is unrecorded, but it was perhaps November 1982 [2]. Today a Goodwill store fills the old lobby and a Walgreens takes up much of the rest of the building [1][2].

title: The goat head and the name change
place: Old Naval Training Station pier, east side of Yerba Buena Island
hook: When Goat Island officially became Yerba Buena Island again in 1931, the Navy marked the moment by kicking a sailor in a goat suit off the pier.
story:
For about a century the island in the middle of the bay had two names. Goats made "Goat Island" the popular one, and in 1895 the U.S. Geographic Board made it official [1]. Accounts differ on when the goats came. The Navy's history says Nathan Spear brought a herd around 1837; a City Guides history credits squatters after the Gold Rush [1][2].

The last goat anyone remembered was Lonesome Billy, a thin, one-horned billy who died just after 1900 at more than 30 years old. He was so cantankerous that, the Navy's historians note, there is no record of anyone mourning him. His stuffed, mounted head hung for years in the Goat Island Training Station's administration building [1].

Then the Native Daughters of the Golden West ran an intense campaign to bring back the old Spanish name, and in 1931 the same board reversed itself: Yerba Buena Island again [1]. According to the Navy's account, the change was not marked by throwing Billy's head into the bay. Instead Navy Radioman Jack Lowe put on a goat suit and Rear Admiral W. C. Cole kicked him off the end of the pier. Billy's head was lost around the same time [1]. "Goat Island" fell out of use by about 1940 [1].

title: Waiting for the banana boats, 1931
place: United Fruit wharf, south bank of Mission Creek between 3rd and 4th
hook: A 16-year-old hoping to ship out watched hungry longshoremen stand on Channel Street for hours, hoping a fog-delayed banana boat would bring a day's pay.
story: Harlan Soeten arrived in San Francisco in 1931, aged 16, hoping to ship out to sea. He roomed at the Coastline Hotel at Third and Townsend, opposite the depot, among longshoremen and railroad men, two of whom loaded United Fruit's banana boats on Mission Creek [1]. When his money ran out he slept in a flophouse and served oatmeal in a city soup kitchen that fed, as he remembered it, 4,000 men a meal [1]. He walked down to the creek in 1931 and 1932 to watch. The channel was too narrow for the big banana boats to turn, so tugs towed them in by the bow and out by the stern; conveyor belts carried the fruit into boxcars at the China Basin Building [1]. Early each morning men gathered for the 'shape-up'. If a ship due at 10 was held up by fog until noon, nobody was paid until noon [1]. Ending that system was the strikers' key demand in 1934 [1]. A 1932 photograph shows United Fruit shacks along the creek between Third and Fourth [1], and the company kept offices across the water from the China Basin Building [2]. Soeten never lost his love of ships: he went on to become curator of San Francisco's Maritime Museum [1].

title: Where the Giants first played in the West
place: Seals Stadium site, 16th and Bryant (now Potrero Center)
hook: Men begged for $3-a-day jobs building it. Joe DiMaggio hit in 61 straight games here. Then, in April 1958, major-league baseball arrived on the West Coast at 16th and Bryant.
story:
Seals Stadium opened on April 7, 1931, at the height of the Depression. Seals president 'Doc' Strub said workers jumped onto the running boards of his car to beg for a job at $3 a day [1]. The stadium had no roof, since fans liked the Mission sun, and some years a live seal lived in a tank under the grandstand [1]. Dorothy Bryant remembered it as one of the few entertainments her neighbourhood could afford, where 'local boys like Joe Dimaggio played' [2]. In 1933, playing for the Seals, DiMaggio hit safely in 61 straight games [1]. In 1950 the fans staged a 'Peanut Revolt' after peanut sales were stopped [1].

On April 15, 1958 the relocated Giants played the first major-league game on the West Coast here, beating the Los Angeles Dodgers 8–0 [1]. Pitcher Johnny Antonelli was less charmed by the wind: 'Worst ballpark in America' [1]. After the last game on September 20, 1959, the stadium was knocked down that November. Its light towers and many of its seats went to Tacoma. A shopping centre now covers the site [1][3].

title: A Spanish Gothic college crowns Lone Mountain
place: Lone Mountain campus (former San Francisco College for Women), 2800 Turk Blvd
hook: In 1930 the last cross came down from Lone Mountain's summit. Two years later the Religious of the Sacred Heart began building a women's college there.
story: The last of the wooden crosses that had topped Lone Mountain was torn down in 1930 [1]. In 1932 construction began at the top of the hill on a Spanish Gothic building for the San Francisco College for Women [1]. It was run by the Religious of the Sacred Heart, and it had begun as Sacred Heart Academy in Menlo Park in 1898 [2][3]. From Turk Street, three flights of garden stairs modelled on Rome's Spanish Steps climb to the main building [1][2]. In 1958 the Chronicle wrote that the hill gave "the impression ... of a place remote and apart from the city around it," and ran a photo of a nun in full habit on the roof, looking out at the Golden Gate Bridge [2]. The 1960s undermined all of that. In 1969 the school admitted men and renamed itself Lone Mountain College, but by then enrolment and alumnae giving were falling [2]. In 1978 the University of San Francisco, the Jesuit school down the hill, bought the 23-acre campus for $5.8 million [2]. The college's former chapel now houses USF's admissions office [2].

title: A cornerstone laid in the snow
place: Jewish Community Center of San Francisco, 3200 California Street at Presidio Avenue
hook: On the coldest day San Francisco had ever recorded, the governor laid the first stone of a Jewish centre that soon welcomed refugees from Hitler's Europe.
story:
On 11 December 1932 the city recorded its coldest temperature ever, 27 degrees, and snow was falling. That day Governor James Rolph Jr., Mayor Angelo Rossi and Lloyd W. Dinkelspiel laid the cornerstone of the Jewish Community Center at 3200 California Street [1]. Arthur Brown Jr. designed it with Hyman and Appleton in a Mediterranean style with Art Deco touches [1].

The centre traced its roots to the Young Men's Hebrew Association of the 1870s. Sources give the founding year as either 1874 or 1877 [1][2]. Louis Blumenthal ran it from the mid-1920s until his death in 1959, and Emma Loewy Blumenthal was associate director for 39 years [1][2]. By 1936, one in ten Jews in the San Francisco area was a member [1].

In 1938 refugees from Germany, Austria, Poland, Spain and Czechoslovakia began arriving. The centre gave them free membership and classes in English and citizenship [1][2]. In the war years it ran civil defence and Red Cross courses and childcare for mothers in war industries [1]. Radio host John Rothmann remembered that the city's first Holocaust commemorations were held here [1].

title: A war memorial that sings
place: War Memorial Opera House, 301 Van Ness Avenue
hook: A court ruling blocked San Francisco's opera house until a returning major had an idea: build it as a memorial to the war dead.
story: The 1906 fire destroyed San Francisco's theatres and opera houses. In 1911 and 1912 the Musical Association tried to build a new hall, but the state Supreme Court ruled that the city could not give land for what was essentially a private building [1]. The group met again in April 1918. That November Major Charles H. Kendrick came home from the First World War with an idea: combine the hall with a memorial to the war's veterans [1]. The Association bought land on Van Ness Avenue, where St. Ignatius Church and College had stood before 1906 [1]. Arthur Brown Jr. and G. Albert Lansburgh designed twin buildings, an Opera House and a Veterans Building, facing City Hall [1]. Foundation work began on January 28, 1931, and the cornerstones were laid on Armistice Day that year [1][2]. The Opera House opened on October 15, 1932, in the depths of the Depression, with Puccini's Tosca. Gaetano Merola conducted and Claudia Muzio sang the title role [1][2]. The nine performances sold out, and three more were added [2]. According to the city's landmark report, it was the first municipally owned opera house in the world [1].

title: Cows in the snow above Miraloma
place: Panorama Drive, Midtown Terrace (dairy pasture in 1932)
hook: When it snows in San Francisco, Twin Peaks gets it first. In 1932 the photographers found puzzled dairy cows standing in it.
story:
When snow falls on San Francisco it usually lands on Twin Peaks and the west side [2]. On December 11, 1932, after a rare snowfall, a photographer caught dairy cows grazing on the white slope where Panorama Drive now curves through Midtown Terrace. Miraloma Park lay below and Mount Davidson rose to the right [1]. It snowed several times that year, and newspapers said the city hadn't seen snow like it since 1887. At the Fleishhacker Zoo, animals were moved into a hospital heated to 70 degrees, except the polar bear, who stayed out and enjoyed himself [2].

Snow came again in late February and early March 1951. The Chronicle ran 'The snow on Twin Peaks' in giant letters above its masthead, and people carried skis up the hill. One photo caption admitted the snow wasn't as thick as the mud, though the skier said he had fun [2]. In 1976 snow dusted the hilltops and melted quickly, and a forecaster warned it wouldn't end the drought [2].

By then the cows were long gone. In 1953 the Standard Building Company began building Midtown Terrace on these slopes, and hundreds of houses went up where the herd had stood in the snow [1].

title: Julia Morgan's YWCA for Chinatown's Women
place: Chinese YWCA (now Chinese Historical Society of America), 965 Clay Street
hook: Chinatown's women commissioned Julia Morgan, and she gave them a building that blends Chinese and Tuscan styles and hides its true size.
story: The first Chinese YWCA in America was organised in San Francisco in 1916 [1]. By the early 1930s its members wanted a proper home. The YWCA's women's governing committee commissioned Julia Morgan, who had designed the rebuilt Cameron House mission nearby, to design and build it [2][4]. The building opened in 1932 [2]. Morgan mixed traditional Chinese and Tuscan elements, and from the Clay Street side the building is much larger than its modest Powell Street face suggests [3]. For half a century it was a social centre for Chinese American women, offering dance lessons, cultural programmes, cooking classes and youth activities [1]. By the 1980s it was out of date and fell short of building codes. Faced with the cost of retrofitting, the city handed it to the Chinese Historical Society of America [1], which opened its museum and learning centre there in 2001 [2]. The Powell Street portion now holds ninety-seven subsidised apartments for low-income elderly and disabled residents [3].

title: Quail and Quarries Above Quintara
place: 140 Quintara Street and the water-tank hill, Golden Gate Heights
hook: In the 1930s the top of Golden Gate Heights was still wild: quail, jackrabbits, a quarry used for target practice and a dare-worthy water tank.
story: City Engineer M. M. O'Shaughnessy signed off plans for Golden Gate Heights in 1926. They split streets into upper and lower levels and added retaining walls and stairways where slopes were too steep for cars [1]. Buyers were slow to come. Many of the higher lots between 12th and 15th Avenues were still empty into the 1960s [1]. In 1932 Dick Boyd's father paid $5,000 for a 1919 house at 140 Quintara Street, with a $37 monthly mortgage [2]. Quintara was cobblestone and ended in a one-lane dirt road, and there was no through traffic to the Sunset until about 1938 [2]. Across the street, a hill topped by a green water tank was home to brush rabbits, jackrabbits, skunks, quail, owls and hawks, among lupines and poppies. In the Depression, groups of men beat the bushes and drove the rabbits downhill to others waiting with clubs, because people needed food [2]. Below the tank was a rock quarry that adults used for target practice [2]. Neighbour Celita Bennett spent years asking the Planning Department to save the hilltop as a lookout. Within weeks of her death a development was approved, and the view went to about ten houses [2]. The Golden Gate Heights Neighbors Association formed in the 1970s to halt such development [3].

title: Radio's Favourite Family Lived Here, Sort Of
place: Sea Cliff Avenue (the fictional Barbour home had no real address)
hook: For 27 years, millions of Americans tuned in to a Sea Cliff family that never existed. Sightseeing buses even put their house on the route.
story: On April 29, 1932, radio listeners met the Barbours of Sea Cliff. Henry Barbour was a stockbroker (one account calls him the head of a bond house). With his wife Fanny he was raising five children: Paul, Hazel, the twins Clifford and Claudia, and Jack. Carlton E. Morse, who wrote, cast and directed every episode, set the show in a San Francisco neighbourhood he knew well. For years it went out from the San Francisco studios of KPO, NBC's West Coast flagship, before production moved to Los Angeles [2]. One Man's Family ran until 1959, making it the longest uninterrupted serial in American radio: 136 "books" and 3,256 chapters [2]. The writer James O. Clifford Sr. puts the audience at about 20 million. The Barbours seemed so real that sightseeing buses put their Sea Cliff home on the route, even though it didn't exist [1]. Herb Caen remembered that "Sunday night became sacred. We all ran home to hear it" [1]. It seems an odd hit for the Depression, a banker's family in the city's poshest enclave, but Michael Raffetto, who played Paul, said it gave "people hope and a goal" [1]. Morse himself lived in the redwoods off Skyline, near Woodside [1].

title: Skippers, Pirates, Bulldogs and Carlos Santana
place: James Lick Middle School, 1220 Noe Street
hook: An ivory Art Deco school rose on Noe Street in 1932. Its hallways have seen home-ec circle skirts, Beatles-haircut expulsions and a future guitar legend.
story: The big ivory-coloured Art Deco building at 1220 Noe Street was finished in 1932. A James Lick school had been on the site since at least the 1890s, when a grammar school stood at 25th and Castro, on what is now the upper yard [1]. The school is named for James Lick, the piano builder and land baron who was the richest man in California when he died in 1876 [1]. Alumni remember it well. Rose Shuck, a student in the late 1950s, still sang the Skippers' school song decades later. She remembered girls being kept out of shop class and made to sew circle skirts, and a 1956 earthquake that knocked a projector off a table mid-film [1]. Joe Cepeda, there in the early 1960s, recalled the first two boys who turned up with Beatles haircuts. Both were sent straight home with letters for their parents [1]. The most famous graduate is Carlos Santana, who lived in the Mission, finished at James Lick and left Mission High in 1965 [2]. When the building turned 75 in 2007, he came back to open the Santana Peace Garden at the front entrance [1]. The team names, by the way, went from Skippers in the 1950s to Pirates by the 1980s and Bulldogs in the 1990s [1].

title: The Henry Ford of Housing's Front Door
place: Doelger Building, 320 Judah St
hook: A $4,000 Art Deco office on Judah Street was mission control for the man who covered the Sunset's dunes with houses, two a day.
story: In January 1932 Henry Doelger, a builder who had quit school after eighth grade, hired architect Charles O. Clausen to design a headquarters at 320 Judah Street. It cost $4,000: a bold Art Deco front with miniature model houses displayed in cases beside the entrance [1]. It needed to be bold. From here Doelger ran the firm that the city's landmark report calls the largest home builder in the United States from 1934 to 1941, averaging two houses a day and employing 500 people. He borrowed Henry Ford's assembly-line methods, with specialised crews moving from house to house [1]. The office grew with the business: a raised roof and a neon 'Henry Doelger Homes' sign in 1936, and a Streamline Moderne wing in 1940 [1]. The same report doesn't flatter him. His childhood hotdog stand in Golden Gate Park reportedly fronted for homemade liquor, and by the late 1930s his Doelgerville deeds barred anyone but white buyers [1]. A longtime Inner Sunset pharmacist heard the rumour that Doelger kept his Prohibition liquor in a building at 9th and Irving [2]. His brother Frank ran a real estate office a few blocks away on Irving [3]. The building became a city landmark in 2013 [1].

title: The Rosy Dome Above Judah Street
place: St. Anne of the Sunset Church, 850 Judah St
hook: The 1906 quake flattened the Sunset's little wooden parish church. The domed church that replaced it in 1932 still anchors a parish that now prays in Cantonese too.
story: St. Anne's parish was founded in 1904. Its first church, a small wooden building, fell in the 1906 earthquake. Work on a new church began in 1930 and ended in 1932, when Archbishop John J. Mitty dedicated a Romanesque Revival building with a huge dome, two uneven towers and seats for 750. The frieze over the entrance, carved by Sister Justina Niemierski, tells the whole story of salvation [1]. For decades it was the landmark of the Inner Sunset. Photos of the streetcar graveyard a block north, around 1940, show the church and school behind the rows of dead cars, and one view of the yard was probably taken from the church itself [2]. Frank Dunnigan remembers his family going to the parish festival and the July novena to St. Anne. When he was at St. Ignatius in the late 1960s, more than half the students came from four Sunset parishes, St. Anne's among them [3]. The novena has run every year since 1908 [1]. The parish has changed along with the neighbourhood: Sunday's noon Mass is now in Chinese, and the parish runs a Chinese School [4].
