title: Methuselah Arrives by Steamship
place: Steinhart Aquarium, California Academy of Sciences, Music Concourse
hook: In 1938 an Australian lungfish moved into the Steinhart Aquarium. She is still there, and possibly the oldest aquarium fish on Earth.
story: After the 1906 fire destroyed its Market Street museum, the California Academy of Sciences moved to Golden Gate Park, dedicating a new museum on the Music Concourse in 1916 [1][2]. Steinhart Aquarium opened beside it on September 29, 1923 [2][3]. In 1938 an Australian lungfish arrived by sea. She was named Methuselah [3][4]. Lungfish breathe with both lungs and gills and are thought to be an evolutionary link between fish and amphibians [4]. In 1947 the Chronicle described them as creatures 'with green scales looking like fresh artichoke leaves' and a possible 'missing link' [4]. When the previous record-holder, a lungfish named Granddad at Chicago's Shedd Aquarium, died in 2017 aged 95, Methuselah was left as the oldest known aquarium fish. By 2022 she was thought to be about 90 [4]. Her keepers describe a mellow 'underwater puppy' who enjoys belly rubs and will only eat figs when they are fresh and in season [4].

title: The Elite, the Rex, the Plaza, the Vogue
place: Vogue Theatre, 3290 Sacramento Street
hook: A little neighbourhood cinema has gone through four names and more than a century. In 2007 it was feared lost; in 2025 it got its neon back.
story: The small cinema at 3290 Sacramento Street is one of the city's oldest. Sources disagree on when it opened. Cinema Treasures says it opened as the Elite Theatre in 1910. Its current operator says it was established in 1912 [1][3]. It was renamed the Rex in 1919 and was the Plaza by 1932. On July 1, 1938 it reopened as the Vogue, with Katharine Hepburn in Bringing Up Baby and Jack Holt in Under Suspicion. The Blumenfeld circuit ran it then. United Artists ran it later [1]. Cinema Treasures lists Simeon Charles Lee as architect, and its style as Streamline Moderne [1]. In 2007 the Vogue closed for a short while, and people feared it would be torn down. Instead a small non-profit bought it and volunteers reopened it [2]. Today the San Francisco Neighborhood Theater Foundation owns it and the non-profit CinemaSFBay runs it [3]. On December 3, 2025 Mayor Daniel Lurie cut the ribbon and lit its restored marquee. Neon Works had spent five months on it, replacing the transformers and reusing some of the original tubes. Afterwards everyone was invited to stay for a free screening of the 1936 film San Francisco [3][4].

title: The Klotovich boys and Kate's Charleston medal
place: Visitacion Valley Community Center, 50 Raymond Avenue
hook: Their mother feared football, so the siblings signed each other's permission slips. One brother scored in the Cotton Bowl; their sister won the Charleston.
story: The Klotovich children of Visitacion Valley loved sports, and their mother dreaded football. She feared the injuries. Yet every season, her daughter Kate Jasoni recalled, brothers Mike and Yotz were ready to play, cleared by permission forms their siblings had signed [1]. Mike had been a football great at Mission High, and both brothers excelled at St. Mary's College in Moraga [1][3]. On January 2, 1939, Mike ran for a touchdown as unranked St. Mary's beat unbeaten, 11th-ranked Texas Tech 20–13 in the Cotton Bowl [2]. He went on to play semi-pro for the San Francisco Clippers and then for the New York Giants in 1945 [3]. A younger brother, Tony, showed promise at baseball until a series of hand injuries ended his hopes [1]. Kate played baseball, basketball and tennis, but one of her fondest memories came in 1938 on the dance floor of the Visitacion Valley Community Center, where she won top honours in a Charleston contest. 'I still have the medal,' she told the Grapevine in 1987 [1]. When neighbourhood historians collected oral histories in 2003, Mike's name came up more than once. He died in April 2008, aged 90, remembered as modest as well as fast [3].

title: The Women Who Struck the Dollar Store
place: Strike meeting site, 720 Washington Street
hook: Chinatown's garment workers had been shut out of unions for generations. In 1938 more than a hundred of them walked out, and won.
story: In the 1930s the garment trade was Chinatown's largest employer, with low pay, long hours and poor light and ventilation [1]. Unions had long treated Chinese workers as 'unfair competition' [1]. That changed at the National Dollar Stores factory, owned by Joe Shoong. With help from organiser Jennie Matyas, workers formed Local 341 of the Chinese Ladies' Garment Workers' Union in November 1937 [2]. A union election on January 24, 1938, went their way, and an agreement followed the next day. Two weeks later the company announced it had sold the factory to its own foreman and manager, a move the workers saw as a ploy to break the union [2]. At 8 a.m. on February 26, 1938, they struck, picketing the factory and three National Dollar stores. White retail clerks refused to cross the lines and the stores closed for two weeks [2]. Strikers met at 720 Washington Street [1]. The strike lasted 13 weeks [3] and ended with a closed union shop, a 5% raise and a 40-hour week [1]. One striker recalled: 'The strike was the best thing that ever happened. It changed our lives' [2].

title: The neighbourhood flea pit that went international
place: Larkin Theatre (later the Century), 816 Larkin Street
hook: Ten-cent features changed every night. Then a new operator filled the little Larkin with films from abroad, and San Franciscans came across town to see them.
story: The Larkin opened in June 1914, the work of an entrepreneur named Joy B. Rothschild, and closed within weeks [1]. In early 1916 Charles and William Goodwin reopened it with new ventilation and a Wurlitzer organ. They changed the feature every night and charged 10 cents, so for $3 a month a regular could see thirty studio pictures [1]. Film historian Jack Tillmany calls it a "little known neighborhood flea pit" until 1938 [1]. That year Herbert Rosener, who had filled the Clay on Fillmore Street with imported, subtitled films, took over the Larkin and brought the same policy [1]. In January 1942 the Australian war film "40,000 Horsemen" premiered at the Larkin and the Clay on the same day [1]. After the war, audiences tired of films censored by Hollywood's Production Code came for foreign ones, and "Diabolique" ran 24 weeks [1]. The building is listed as a contributor to the Uptown Tenderloin Historic District. It is the Tenderloin's only surviving early movie theatre, though it later turned to adult films [1][2].

title: Two Women Paint Noah's Ark
place: Mother's Building, San Francisco Zoo
hook: Two artists who came to sketch the animals spent four and a half years painting the flood's aftermath across the walls of a mothers' lounge.
story: Herbert and Mortimer Fleishhacker gave $50,000 for a Mother's Building in memory of their own mother, and it opened in 1925 beside the giant Fleishhacker Pool as a refuge for mothers and small children [1][2][3]. In the Depression, two San Francisco artists who had been sketching animals at the zoo, Helen Forbes and Dorothy Puccinelli, won New Deal support to decorate it [2][3]. Given free choice of subject, they picked Noah's Ark, after the waters recede [2][3]. Working in egg tempera for four and a half years, they finished in 1938 [3]. Elephants, white pelicans and donkeys make their way across the drying land while Noah stands among deer, a theme of renewal for a city in hard times [3]. Hoodline has described them as the largest set of egg tempera murals in the West [3]. Advocates note that every mural here was painted by women, unlike Coit Tower [3]. Moisture from fog and sea has damaged the walls, and the building has long been closed to the public while supporters push for restoration [2][3].

title: Who Was Kelly of Kelly's Cove?
place: Kelly's Cove, Ocean Beach just south of the Cliff House, below Sutro Heights
hook: San Francisco surfing grew up on a patch of sand below the Cliff House. Nobody is sure whether it was named for a swimmer or a tire ad.
story:
Around 1900 the northern tip of Ocean Beach was just "Cliff House Beach," where visitors in bowler hats posed beside Seal Rocks. It also drew open-air exercise enthusiasts, often older men in homemade swimsuits [1].

Patrick Cunneen, a sixth-grader in the mid-1940s, remembers taking the 7 streetcar to Playland, then building driftwood bonfires at what everyone called Kelly's Cove. An old man he took to be Kelly had a roofless driftwood windbreak on the rocks and seemed to live there. In 1938 a Samuel Kelly, "well-known to beach habitues," did die on Ocean Beach after his daily swim. There is a rival theory: in the 1920s a Kelly Tire Company billboard stood against the Sutro Heights cliff just above the beach [1].

By the late 1940s and 1950s the cove belonged to swimmers in flippers and early surfers, who burned old car tires as a smoky beacon on foggy days [1]. Surfing was not yet welcome. Early surfers recalled police harassing and arresting board riders south of the Lurline pipeline pier at the foot of Balboa Street. Jim Gallagher said he bought one of the first two boards Jack O'Neill sold commercially, when O'Neill's shop was out by Sloat Boulevard [2].

title: A cinema named for the new bridge
place: Bridge Theatre, 3010 Geary Boulevard at Blake Street
hook: It opened in 1939 as a cut-price, late-run neighbourhood house, then spent over half a century as one of the city's great art cinemas.
story: Attilio A. Zerga built the New Bridge on Geary at Blake Street. It opened in July 1939 with Irene Dunne and Charles Boyer in Love Affair [1]. The theatre historian Jack Tillmany gives July 21, and Cinema Treasures July 22 [1][2]. The name honoured the Golden Gate Bridge, which had opened in 1937 [1]. Until the mid-1950s it was a cheap, late-run neighbourhood theatre. Films reached it after Market Street and the second-run houses, so Love Affair was three or four months old when it played here [1]. In the mid-1950s the Bridge became an exclusive first-run "art" house for prestige American and foreign films, and it did well at it for decades [1]. Cinema Treasures calls it one of the most successful venues for independent and foreign film in San Francisco. It had 399 seats [2]. Its last operator, Landmark Theatres, closed it on December 27, 2012 after The Perks of Being a Wallflower [1]. The building was renovated with its facade and blade sign kept, and it reopened as the San Francisco Baseball Academy [1].

title: A marble mansion given to the nuns
place: Flood Mansion, Convent of the Sacred Heart, 2222 Broadway
hook: In 1939 a widow gave away her marble mansion with its Golden Gate view. Within a year, 97 schoolgirls and 25 nuns had moved in.
story: In June 1939 the Society of the Sacred Heart learned that Maud Lee Flood wanted to give them her family home: a marble mansion on the Broadway ridge that looked out over the Bay and the newly finished Golden Gate Bridge [1]. Her husband had died and her children had grown up and left, and she wanted the house to have a purpose. So she handed it over to Reverend Mother Eleanor Deming [1]. The family drawing room became a chapel. At the start of 1940 about 25 nuns, seven lay teachers and 97 students moved in [1]. Mrs. Flood wrote that she was pleased the house of "happy and unforgettable memories" had become "a house of learning, refinement, and peace" [1]. The war changed the school too: many families wanted their sons and daughters in one school, so boys joined the lower grades [1]. When the Grant mansion next door came up for sale, the nuns had already slipped religious medals onto its grounds through the latticework. The family sold it to them for $150,000. The school gives 1950 as the year, while NoeHill says 1948 [1][2]. In 1956 the Society bought Hammond House on the other side, and Stuart Hall for Boys opened there with 42 boys [1].

title: A quarter to peek at the Nude Ranch
place: The Gayway, north end of the fairgrounds
hook: The fair borrowed Botticelli's Venus from Italy. For six months, a sideshow of cowgirls in G-strings outsold it.
story:
At the north end of the island, beside a 12,000-car parking lot, lay the Gayway, a 40-acre fun zone of thrill rides and shows [1]. Its sideshows included 82 little people in cowboy costumes and a racetrack where monkeys drove cars. The one everybody remembered was Sally Rand's Nude Ranch [2].

For a quarter, visitors could peek through glass panels at 20 'cowgirls' wearing only G-strings and boots as they tossed horseshoes, swung lariats and played badminton [2]. The museum's account adds pistol belts and donkeys [3]. About 65,000 people packed in during the first week. Meanwhile, most other Gayway shows lost money; about two-thirds of them went broke [2].

The fair also showed a celebrated collection of European masterpieces. When, after six months, the art exhibit finally took in more than the Nude Ranch, the exposition put out a press release about it [2].

Rand herself, the fan dancer who became famous at 1930s world's fairs, did not perform on the island. She owned the Music Box Theater on O'Farrell Street, which is still there today as the Great American Music Hall [4].

title: Chinatown builds China's pavilion
place: Chinese Village, Golden Gate International Exposition (approximate site)
hook: Invaded by Japan, China couldn't come to the fair. So San Francisco's Chinese community built its own village, complete with opera.
story:
The 1939 fair billed itself as a 'Pageant of the Pacific', but one great Pacific nation was missing. China, exhausted by the Japanese invasion, did not take part. Instead, Chinese residents of San Francisco built and ran a Chinese Village [1]. It was a pointed contrast. Japan had put up an expensive, elaborate pavilion, and historians later concluded its purpose was to project 'harmony' and deflect attention from Japan's atrocities in Asia [1].

The Chinese Village was designed by the landscape architect Mark Daniels, who had a long interest in Chinese garden design [2]. Performers from San Francisco's Chinatown staged classical Chinese opera there, and a photograph in the Bancroft Library shows the Village's opera troupe [3]. The Works Progress Administration's 1938 guide to the fair listed a 'Chinese City' among the showplaces planned for the Gayway fun zone [4].

The fair's gateway to China outlasted the peace. After Pearl Harbor, anti-Japanese feeling in the city ran so high that there was a serious proposal to turn Golden Gate Park's Japanese Tea Garden into a hamburger stand. Daniels wrote to the Examiner urging that it become a 'Chinese Tea Garden' instead [2].

title: Give 'Em the Pools!
place: Anglers' Lodge and Fly Casting Pools, west of the Polo Field
hook: Some members of this fishing club have never set foot in San Francisco. They join for the WPA casting pools, some of the finest anywhere.
story: The fly casters began with a small lodge and dock at Stow Lake. When they outgrew it, John McLaren himself picked a new site west of the Polo Field [1]. During the Depression, Works Progress Administration crews built a rustic lodge with fish-carved shutters overlooking concrete casting pools 450 feet by 185 feet [1][2]. Getting them wasn't easy. Club member Ralph Keating recalled 'real bumps in the road' until Herbert Fleishhacker settled a civic meeting by declaring: 'They are performing a public service. Give 'em the pools!' [1]. Keating also remembered meeting McLaren at Stow Lake as a ten-year-old [1]. The WPA handed the finished facility to the Park Commission on a Sunday afternoon in March 1939, and it has barely changed since [1]. Members still honour an old agreement to coach any novice who asks [1]. The records disagree on some dates: the National Register gives the lodge as 1936 and the club's founding as 1890, while the WPA history says 1894 [1][2].

title: Gutters paved with forgotten gravestones
place: Paths on the western and northern slopes of Buena Vista Park
hook: Look down at the rain gutters beside Buena Vista's paths. Some of the marble still carries names and dates carved for people buried long ago.
story: San Francisco ordered its cemeteries emptied in 1914, and the removals dragged on through the 1940s. Headstones went to Colma, though the remains were not always moved with them. Unclaimed stones were recycled into sea walls, landfill and park gutters [4]. In Buena Vista Park, Depression relief crews built retaining walls and drainage ditches out of broken marble slabs, and in places the inscriptions can still be read [1]. Clyde Healy's December 1939 report on the Works Progress Administration lists improvements to Buena Vista among its 70 park projects [2]. Sources disagree about where the stones came from. One points to the Odd Fellows Cemetery, cleared in the early 1930s [2]. The Encyclopedia of San Francisco says tombstones from Laurel Hill were broken up for the park's gutters once removal there was complete [3]. Others say only "Lone Mountain cemeteries" [1]. The hill was almost lost to development as well. In 1950 Supervisor Chester MacPhee proposed selling parts of the park, calling it "unused, unsightly" and in need of a policeman at all times. The Board tabled the idea indefinitely [1].

title: Joe DiMaggio's church, twice
place: Saints Peter and Paul Church, 666 Filbert St
hook: The Yankee Clipper married his first wife inside North Beach's Italian church. Fifteen years later he came back with Marilyn Monroe, but only for the photographs.
story: Joe DiMaggio was raised in a ground-floor flat on Taylor Street, the eighth of nine children of Sicilian parents [1]. In 1939, already a Yankees star, he married the actress Dorothy Arnold inside Saints Peter and Paul, the twin-spired church facing Washington Square that had long been the heart of North Beach's "Little Italy" [1][2][3]. That marriage lasted five years and produced a son, Joe Jr. [1]. On 14 January 1954 he married Marilyn Monroe. Because both were divorced, there was no church wedding: Judge Charles Peery married them at 1:45 p.m. in his City Hall chambers, and the couple then had to push through corridors full of press and some 300 well-wishers outside [1]. Afterwards they came to Saints Peter and Paul to pose for wedding photographs [2]. The Church was less sentimental. A spokesman for the archdiocese said DiMaggio had been automatically excommunicated for remarrying [1]. "San Francisco will be our headquarters," DiMaggio told reporters, but the couple spent most of their ten-month marriage in Los Angeles. When it ended, he said, "San Francisco has always been my home" [1].

title: Last drinks at Weepers' Corner
place: Top of the Mark, Mark Hopkins Hotel, 999 California Street
hook: Pacific-bound servicemen toasted their last night of liberty nineteen floors up. As their ships slipped out the Golden Gate, the women they left behind gathered at one window.
story: The Mark Hopkins Hotel opened on December 4, 1926, on the site of the railroad magnate Mark Hopkins' mansion, which burned in 1906 [1][2]. In 1939 the owner, George D. Smith, turned the 11-room penthouse on the 19th floor into a glass-walled cocktail lounge with a 360-degree view. NoeHill credits the design to Timothy Pflueger and dates it to 1936 [2][3]. The hotel's own history says Smith doubted anyone would ride 19 floors just for a drink. But the Top of the Mark was an instant hit when it opened on May 11, 1939, the year the Golden Gate International Exposition lit up Treasure Island [3]. According to the Chronicle columnist Herb Caen, the name came from Smith's friends. When Smith said he didn't know what to call the top of The Mark, they told him he had just named it [3]. During the Second World War it was a favourite last stop for Pacific-bound servicemen. Squadrons left a bottle with the bartender, and returning men signed the label and drank for free. Whoever finished the bottle bought the next one [2][3]. As the ships left the Golden Gate, wives and sweethearts gathered in the northwest corner to watch, and it became known as "Weepers' Corner" [3].

title: Mona's, where girls could be boys
place: Mona's 440 Club, 440 Broadway
hook: Waitresses in tuxedos, Gladys Bentley in a top hat, and a teenage Johnny Mathis learning his stagecraft: the story of San Francisco's first famous lesbian bar.
story: Mona Sargent and her husband Jimmie opened a bar at 451 Union Street soon after Prohibition ended. They moved to 140 Columbus in 1936, then to 440 Broadway. FoundSF dates that last move to 1939, and other accounts are earlier [1][2]. They had imagined a sawdust-floored bohemian hangout for writers and artists. Instead it became a club where women in men's clothes waited tables and sang [2]. Mona's is often called San Francisco's first lesbian bar. It advertised itself as the place "where girls can be boys", and its male impersonators became local celebrities [2]. The 440 had actually been opened by Charlie Murray, who brought Mona in as a partner. Men often had to front for lesbian-run bars [1]. Blues singer Gladys Bentley, famous for performing in a tuxedo and top hat, played there in the 1940s [1][2]. In the mid-1950s singer Ann Dee took over and renamed it Ann's 440. In 1955 she hired a 19-year-old Johnny Mathis two weeks into his professional career and coached his stage presence [1][3]. Mona went on with a new club, Mona's Candle Light, at 473 Broadway from 1948 to 1957 [1].

title: Motel Row on the Road to the Bridge
place: Marina Motel, 2576 Lombard Street
hook: Why does a stretch of a San Francisco street look like a 1940s highway town? Blame the Golden Gate Bridge, and one retired man's hunch.
story: Before the Golden Gate Bridge, Lombard Street through the Marina was a quiet two-lane road [1]. Once the bridge was planned as the longest suspension span in the world, Lombard became its main approach, and after the bridge opened in 1937 drivers poured through [1][2]. One man saw what was coming. Heidi Detjen says her grandfather, the son of a Gold Rush miner, came out of retirement after visiting a motor court. In 1939 he opened the Marina Motel at Lombard and Broderick, the first motor lodge on the street [1]. Motor lodges let guests park right outside their own door, which suited a country that had fallen for the car [1]. The city then widened Lombard to six lanes. To do it, buildings on the south side of the street were torn down, leaving empty lots, and that's when all these other motels appeared, Detjen says [1]. In the early days, she recalls, drivers came off the bridge and went from motel to motel looking for the best rate. The strip of roadside motels is still there today [1][2]. So is the Marina Motel, now run by the third generation of the same family, with the fourth getting involved [1].

title: Relief crews and ten thousand trees
place: Brazil Avenue entrance, start of the WPA view drive
hook: In the Depression, federal relief workers carved roads, bridle trails and a scenic drive into bare hills, and planted a forest.
story: The Depression finally brought workers to McLaren Park's empty hills. Money and labour from the Works Progress Administration built a scenic 'view drive' in the 1930s. It started at Brazil Avenue and ended just east of the twin water tanks off today's Mansell Street. The WPA also built equestrian trails on the south slopes [1]. The McLaren Park Collaborative's timeline says that by 1939 WPA workers had finished a long network of footpaths, hiking, fire and bridle trails, plus culverts, roads and the view drive. They had also planted more than 10,000 eucalyptus, cypress and pine trees [2]. For a while the park had a stable and riders on its trails. That didn't last. By 1983 the city's planners noted that horseback riding was no longer allowed, because without separate trails nobody could keep horses out of areas the public used [1]. The park's plant life has changed since. In 2004 a park worker told the Chronicle that invasive plants like eucalyptus, pampas grass, fennel and French broom worried him far more than human intruders [3].

title: San Francisco's first international airport
place: Hall of Transportation (Building 2), 300 California Ave
hook: For a few short years, passengers walked out of a Treasure Island hangar, down to a floating dock, and flew off across the Pacific.
story:
Treasure Island was built to be an airport. With federal aid, three permanent buildings went up alongside the fair: an administration building meant to be the terminal and two steel-and-concrete hangars, each 335 feet long and 78 feet high, that spent 1939 full of borrowed art [1][2]. This one, now Building 2, housed the fair's Hall of Transportation [2].

Pan American Airways moved its Clipper flying boats here from Alameda in 1938, making Treasure Island San Francisco's first international airport, the only time the island served its planned purpose [3]. During the fair, passengers and crew walked from Building 2 to a floating dock and boarded aircraft that took off and landed on the water of Clipper Cove [3]. It was luxury travel: the trip to Manila took five days, hopping between islands with overnight hotel stops, and a one-way ticket cost about $2,000 in 1935 [3].

War ended the dream. The airport was never built [2]. By 1943, Pan Am-operated 'Coronado' transports were loading wartime cargo at the Clipper Cove dock, and by the war's end the flying boats were obsolete [3].

title: The Avenue Club's Organist and All-American
place: The Ave Bar, 1607 Ocean Avenue
hook: A 1922 Ocean Avenue storefront went from fix-it shop to shoe repair to bar, run for a while by a Fox Theatre organist and later by an All-American football star.
story: The building at 1607 Ocean Avenue, near Capitol, dates from 1922. Its first known tenant was Crown Electrical and Plumbing, and from 1934 it housed Louis Nessier's Balboa Shoe Repair [1]. In 1938 it began selling alcohol as Horgan & Fex liquors. It first appears as the Avenue Club in 1939, ten years earlier than the date on its Legacy Business listing [1]. From 1944 Audrey and Mel Hertz ran it. Mel had been a popular theatre organist and in 1933 was house organist at the Fox Theatre on Market Street. He was declared bankrupt in 1932 [1]. In 1949 the bar passed to Johnny Schiechl, a Balboa High graduate named All-American center at Santa Clara for the 1939 season. He played for the Steelers, Lions and Bears, and for the 49ers in 1947. After a divorce and a nervous breakdown in 1950, he reportedly sold his share to his partner, Bob Wells [1]. In 1959 the owners, Jim and Hallie Emmett, made the papers when their Dalmatian Debbie, a "bar stool regular", went missing. She was found [1]. The bar entered the city's Legacy Business Registry in 2017 [1]. City records list The Ave Bar at the address under one owner from 2006 to 2024 [2].

title: The Mansion the WPA Tore Down
place: Sutro Heights Park, site of the Sutro residence and parapet
hook: Adolph Sutro's daughter lived on in his crumbling clifftop estate until 1938. Within months of her death, New Deal crews knocked the house down.
story: Sutro Heights passed to the city in 1920 on condition that it be 'forever held and maintained as a free public resort or park,' but Adolph Sutro's daughter, Dr. Emma Sutro Merritt, kept the right to live there [1]. Upkeep dwindled; in 1935 the San Francisco Garden Club found cypresses 'under the spell of some enchantment' and statues 'moss grown' [1]. Emma died in residence in 1938, while Works Progress Administration crews were already shoring up the western slope with artificial concrete cliffs [1]. The WPA then demolished the decaying house, the remains of the conservatory, the entrance gates and fences and the structures on the parapet, spending $90,994 on the 'improvements' [1]. Historian John Martini calls it an 'ill-advised WPA clean up'; Sutro's two Belgian lion statues, by Guillaume Geefs, survived at the vanished gate for another forty years [2]. During the Second World War the park was closed for security because it stood so close to Fort Miley, and concrete range-finding stations were built beside the parapet [1]. After 1977 the National Park Service retired the weather-worn lions to storage and installed cast copies [2].

title: The Palace for the People, padlocked
place: Aquatic Park Bathhouse (Maritime Museum), 900 Beach St
hook: The WPA built San Francisco a shining ship-shaped bathhouse for everyone. Days after it opened, the public was shown the door.
story: Between 1936 and 1939 the Works Progress Administration built a Streamline Moderne bathhouse on Black Point Cove, designed by William Mooser III to evoke a ship at port. It had lockers for 3,000 swimmers and showers switched on by photoelectric "eyes" [1]. Hilaire Hiler, just back from Paris, painted the lost continents of Atlantis and Mu across the lobby. Sargent Claude Johnson, the first Black artist on the West Coast to win national fame, carved the green slate frieze and designed the veranda mosaics [1][2]. At the dedication on January 22, 1939, the Chronicle called it "A Palace for the People." But just before opening, the city had leased it to Gordon Brothers Concessions, and it became the Aquatic Park Casino, an exclusive nightclub. Up went signs reading "Private – Keep Out," and schoolboys eating sack lunches on the veranda were ordered to leave [1]. Beniamino Bufano hauled his animal statues down to the beach: "I would rather have kids playing over my statues than to have drunks stumbling over them." Johnson walked away, and his mosaic is still unfinished. By the end of 1940 the concessionaires had been ousted amid lawsuits and the doors were padlocked [1].

title: The Swing Mikado's two-week run
place: Golden Gate International Exposition fairgrounds (central Treasure Island)
hook: An all-Black, swing-era Gilbert and Sullivan hit the island running. Two weeks later, politics shut it down.
story:
Among the fair's liveliest shows was The Swing Mikado, a production of the New Deal's Federal Theatre Project. It moved Gilbert and Sullivan's story from feudal Japan to a make-believe South Pacific island and set it to swing music with an all-Black cast [1][2]. It had played Chicago and New York before arriving on Treasure Island in 1939 [2].

It did not last. Political attacks on progressive New Deal programmes closed the show after only two weeks on the island [2]. It then did very well at the Geary Theater in San Francisco and toured the Western states. A few days after its sudden closure, Benny Goodman, 'the King of Swing', started a sold-out residency at the fair [2].

Black music kept a place on the island. A three-day 'Negro Music Festival' traced African American music from ancient Africa to swing [1]. When the fair closed in 1940, the ASCAP festival's afternoon concert included works by the Black composer William Grant Still. That evening W. C. Handy, 'the Father of the Blues', played 'St. Louis Blues'. Years later he remembered it as 'the greatest program of all-American music ever staged' [2].

title: The first NCAA tournament's western bracket
place: Site of the California Coliseum, northern fairgrounds (approximate)
hook: March Madness has a Treasure Island chapter. In 1939, Oregon's future champions won the West in a fair hall later dismantled and shipped to Mare Island.
story:
The very first NCAA men's basketball tournament, in March 1939, was a modest affair split into East and West. The NCAA's record book lists the Western Regional in San Francisco at the California Coliseum, a hall built in 1938 that seated 9,476 [1]. It was one of the new fair's buildings on Treasure Island, used for animal shows and indoor athletic contests [2].

On March 21, 1939, Oregon beat Oklahoma to win the West, after leading 21–14 at halftime. The record book counts that game as a national semifinal [1]. Six days later Oregon beat Ohio State 46–33 for the first national title [1]. The final was played elsewhere, but the champions' run went through the island. Oregon's 1939 players included Bobby Anet, Laddie Gale, John Dick and Slim Wintermute [1].

The Coliseum outlived the fair around it. Most exposition buildings were torn down for the naval base, but this one was carefully taken apart, moved to Mare Island Naval Shipyard and put back together. There it became the Field House, Building 523, and it was still standing in 1995 [2].

title: The goddess the Navy tore down
place: Site of the Court of Pacifica (today's Mersea restaurant parking lot)
hook: An 80-foot goddess of the Pacific once ruled this corner of the island. She did not survive the war; some of her stone companions did.
story:
The fair's theme, Pacific Unity, found its grandest expression in the Court of Pacifica, designed under Timothy Pflueger [1]. Presiding over it stood Ralph Stackpole's 80-foot 'Pacifica', the fair's goddess of the western ocean, conceived as a composite of peoples of the Pacific Rim [1][2]. At her feet the three-tiered Fountain of Western Waters was ringed by twenty oversized sculptures of Pacific peoples, dancing, making music, working and sleeping. Chronicle critic Alfred Frankenstein thought them the finest sculpture made for the fair [1].

Pacifica herself was demolished when the Navy took over the island for the war [2]. The fountain figures, cast in stone rather than the usual plaster, were built to last. Accounts of how many survive vary: the museum's sculpture exhibit says ten are in storage and four are lost, while six restored figures have stood flanking the doors of Building One [1][3]. The court itself lay where the Mersea restaurant's parking lot is now [3]. In 2013 an Oakland engineer, William Chamberlain, was raising money to build a new Pacifica, estimating the cost at up to $2 million [2].

title: The neighbors who won a bus line
place: Miraloma Park Improvement Club clubhouse, Del Vale Avenue off O'Shaughnessy Boulevard
hook: Miraloma Park had new houses but no transit. Its improvement club lobbied until the mayor himself drove the first bus up the hill, with a parade behind it.
story: Miraloma Park went up on the slopes of Mount Davidson with a business district planned for 2,000 families, but it had no convenient transit, so residents needed cars [1]. When the Miraloma Park Improvement Club formed in 1935, transportation was at the top of its list: members wanted a bus line to Forest Hill Station and the Twin Peaks Tunnel [1]. They got it on July 23, 1939, when Mayor Angelo Rossi drove the first bus over the route himself. The day was celebrated with a big parade of American Legionnaires, Boy Scouts and school bands in the Portola Drive business district [1][2]. The line ran from Forest Hill via Laguna Honda Boulevard, Portola Drive, Evelyn Way and Teresita Boulevard [2]. It began as the 7 Miraloma, was renumbered 36 in 1949, and renamed the 36 Teresita in 1980 [2]. In 1940, with half the homes finished, developers Meyer Brothers built the clubhouse they had promised, on land leased from the Water Department for $1 a year. It was dedicated on November 10, 1940 [1][2]. By July 1946 the combined Garden and Improvement Clubs had 1,000 members, which historian Rosalie Kuwatch called an unequaled record in San Francisco [1][2].

title: Thirty-five thousand pioneers evicted to Colma
place: Iris Avenue, Laurel Heights (houses built on the former Laurel Hill Cemetery)
hook: The city's 'silent city' of senators and founders held out for decades against Richmond District boosters. Then its tombstones ended up in park gutters and Marina breakwaters.
story:
By 1900, when the city stopped new burials, Laurel Hill held some of San Francisco's most famous dead, including the cable car pioneer Andrew Hallidie and several U.S. senators [1][2]. It had also become an obstacle. The Richmond Banner campaigned for almost twenty years to remove the cemeteries that blocked the way west. "This district of ours, beyond the land of the dead, wants to be firmly united to the rest of San Francisco," one editorial said in 1924 [1].

In 1914 the Board of Supervisors ordered all bodies out of the city. The Calvary, Masonic and Odd Fellows cemeteries gave in, but Laurel Hill's association held out until 1937, when the supervisors demanded that it be emptied at once [3]. Campaigners for a Pioneer Memorial Park lost [2]. Between 1939 and 1941 about 35,000 bodies were reburied, most at Cypress Lawn in Colma. NoeHill puts the number buried at 38,000 [1][2].

The headstones were not wasted. Some became sculptors' blocks, gutters in Buena Vista Park and breakwaters along the Marina shore [2]. Houses, flats and small apartment buildings rose on the slopes in the 1940s and 1950s [4].

title: Where Billy Rose's Aquacade swam
place: Site of Palace C-1 and the Aquacade, south-west fairgrounds (approximate)
hook: Esther Williams and Johnny Weissmuller swam here for the fair. A few years later, sailors shot baskets on a floor laid over the filled-in pool.
story:
Billy Rose's Aquacade, a water show, was one of the fair's star attractions. Its headliners were the swimmers Johnny Weissmuller and Esther Williams [1][2]. The Navy's building records place it at the east end of Palace C-1, one of the Homes and Gardens halls, in the 1939–40 fair years [1].

Singers wanted in too. Mel Lewis, 23, heard that bandleader Fred Waring, inventor of the Waring Blender, was auditioning a chorus for the Aquacade. Lewis sang "All the Things You Are" without looking at the music, but part of it was in harmony. "You don't read music, do you," Waring said, rather than asked. With a new show every week and the harmonies to be memorised, that ended it. Lewis went on to win a radio amateur hour instead [2].

What happened to the pool depends on who you ask. The Navy's 1995 history says the Aquacade became the base swimming pool [1]. The base newspaper told sailors in 1945 that if they played basketball in Gymnasium No. 1, they were "romping about on the spot where Billy Rose's Aquacade swam its way to fame." The pool, it said, was "of a tar and chicken wire construction," and had been filled in with a floor laid over it [3].

title: Where the elephant towers stood
place: Site of the Portals of the Pacific and Elephant Towers, west side of Treasure Island (approximate)
hook: The fair's gate was tested with a fan and chicken feathers. Six years later, sailors needed a newspaper guide to find where it had been.
story:
The fair's main entrance faced west, into the prevailing wind. Its gateway, the Portals of the Pacific, was guarded by the Elephant Towers, which blended Asian and Mayan motifs [1][2]. The portals were built as windbreaks to shelter the court behind them. While designing them, the engineer tested models with a fan and chicken feathers [2]. The fair was so big that visitors rode "Elephant Trains": small tractors dressed as elephants, each towing up to five cars. After the fair their costumes came off and they went to Mare Island Naval Shipyard, where they carried workers around during the war [2].

By February 1945 the fair was gone, and the Masthead ran a guide to the one under sailors' feet. The main entrance, it explained, had been between Barracks D and E, guarded by huge elephant towers "long since torn down." The Tower of the Sun's foundation now held the bandstand. The street in front of the Administration Building had been the Avenue of Palms, and it was "rumored that the brig now stands" on the old Gayway [3]. The Navy's own history, though, lists an "Elephant Gate Building" among the few structures spared when the palaces were razed in 1947 [2].

title: Who Cooked Dinner on El Camino del Mar
place: 625 El Camino del Mar (one of many households listing live-in staff)
hook: Leaf through the 1939 city directory and Sea Cliff's big houses fill with other names: the maids, cooks, nurses and a butler who worked there.
story: The city directories of the late 1930s listed domestic workers under their own names, with the houses where they worked. In the 1939 and 1940 editions, dozens of Sea Cliff entries on El Camino del Mar, Sea Cliff Avenue, Scenic Way and McLaren Avenue are for maids, cooks and nurses, often several at one house [1][2]. Nora O'Brien is listed as cook at 625 El Camino del Mar in both years. In 1940 the same house also had a maid, Kath, and a nurse, Eleanore Kawaite [1][2]. Bertha was the maid at 740 El Camino del Mar in both years [1][2]. Bridie McNulty was the nurse at 498 Sea Cliff Avenue in 1939. In 1940 the directory lists a butler, Oscar, at the same address [1][2]. Haru Shimuru was a maid at 190 Sea Cliff Avenue in 1939. Louise Saiki was a maid at 600 El Camino del Mar in 1940 [1][2]. Erika Chalfant cooked at 80 Scenic Way, where Mary was the nurse [1][2]. The scanned text is imperfect, so a search surely misses some.

title: A Zoo Poured in Concrete
place: San Francisco Zoo, Sloat Boulevard
hook: Depression-era builders wanted a zoo that could never burn. Decades later, renovators found concrete poured seven feet deep under the elephants.
story: Banker and parks commissioner Herbert Fleishhacker founded the zoo in 1929, and it carried his name until 1941, when at his suggestion it became the San Francisco Zoological Gardens [1][2]. Its first director, George Bistany, was an animal importer who got the job after delivering many of the first animals [1]. The zoo was largely built in the 1930s as a Works Progress Administration project, under zoologist Edmund Heller [1]. The rules were simple: it had to be fireproof, permanent and cheap to maintain, built only of reinforced concrete, with nothing blocking the view of the animals [1]. By 1940, at a cost of about $3.5 million, it had ten structures, including the Pachyderm and Lion Houses, an aviary, bear grottos and Monkey Island, with barless pits that were then considered innovative [1]. Monkey Island was demolished in 1995 [2]. Generations of west-side kids remember the Lion House at feeding time, when "hungry lions lunging for a dozen or so raw pot roasts" held them spellbound [3].

title: A dentist's vow, rung in 44 bells
place: Grace Cathedral, Singing (north) Tower, 1100 California Street
hook: In 1875 a lonely young immigrant knelt in a church with no bell tower and promised it chimes. Sixty-five years later, his bells rang out over Nob Hill.
story: When Nathaniel T. Coulson arrived in San Francisco in 1875, he found his way to Grace Church, which had no bell tower. As he knelt there, he later said, a thought came to him: "If ever I will have the money, this church will have its chimes" [1]. Coulson was a British-born dentist and realtor, and a Methodist. He spent his life savings on that promise, and in his last years he lived on a dollar a day [1]. His gift was a carillon of 44 bronze bells, cast by Gillett & Johnston in Croydon, England, in 1938, with a six-ton hour bell. He also paid for the "Singing Tower" to house them in Lewis Hobart's Gothic cathedral, which was then still being built [1][2]. One small bell is named Sympathy after Abigail Santo, a Sunday school organist in Cornwall. When other children refused to sit near the orphaned Coulson, he had seen her cry [1]. The tower wasn't finished in time, so the bells first rang at the Tower of the Sun during the 1939–40 exposition on Treasure Island. They rang from Nob Hill for the first time on Christmas Eve 1940 and were dedicated in 1943. At first they chimed every hour through the night, until neighbours who couldn't sleep complained [1].

title: Bufano's bear at the Sunnydale projects
place: Sunnydale community center, about 1654 Sunnydale Avenue
hook: Among the barracks-style blocks of Sunnydale stands a work by one of San Francisco's most famous sculptors: a growling bear above a woman's face.
story: Beniamino 'Benny' Bufano's rounded, whimsical animals turn up all over San Francisco. One of them is at the Sunnydale public housing development. It stands in front of the community center at 1654 Sunnydale Avenue [1]. The piece shows a bear above a human head. One writer calls it 'Bear over the Head of Peace' and dates it to about 1935–1940 [1]. A July 2009 Nob Hill Gazette survey, quoted in the Grapevine, called it 'Bear and Virgin'. It described 'the head of a growling black bear over a woman's head, symbolizing peace' [2]. That article counted three Bufano works in San Francisco public housing projects [2]. Bufano was born in Italy in 1886, one of sixteen children, and his family emigrated to New York when he was three. He came to San Francisco in 1915 to assist a sculptor working on the Panama-Pacific Exposition [2]. A legend claimed he had cut off a finger and mailed it to President Wilson to protest the First World War. His wife said he had lost two finger joints to an electric saw [2]. Either way, the legend fixed his reputation as a lifelong pacifist [2]. Oddly, that date is earlier than Sunnydale itself, which the same writer says was built in the 1940s to house military personnel and their families [1].

title: Cottages for Children Fleeing Europe
place: Former Homewood Terrace campus, Ocean Avenue between Faxon and Keystone
hook: On Ocean Avenue, a Jewish orphanage replaced dormitories with cottages. During the Second World War it took in children who had escaped the Holocaust.
story:
In 1921 the Pacific Hebrew Orphan Asylum, founded in 1872, left its building on Divisadero Street for a new campus on Ocean Avenue between Faxon and Keystone, and renamed itself Homewood Terrace [1][2]. Led by Dr. Samuel Langer, it housed children in a campus of cottages. Its own 1972 centennial history calls these "the first cottage type child care facilities in the United States" [1].

The same history says the agency grew most under director Benjamin Bonaparte, and that "during World War II, Homewood Terrace provided for many children brought from the European Holocaust." [1] Many alumni went on to careers in the professions and business, it adds [1].

In 1965, as fewer children needed institutional care, director Ralph Ross moved the children into seven ordinary houses in the Richmond District, where they lived with house counsellors [1]. The Ocean Avenue cottages took years to be torn down, and homes and shops now cover the site [1]. The agency merged with Jewish Family Service in 1977 to form today's Jewish Family and Children's Services [2].

title: Diego Rivera paints in public
place: Palace of Fine and Decorative Arts (Building 3), 600 California Ave
hook: In 1940, fairgoers could watch Diego Rivera paint Hitler, Frida Kahlo and a Detroit stamping press in wet plaster.
story:
In the fair's second season, organizers turned the Palace of Fine and Decorative Arts into a working studio called Art in Action. Sculptors, weavers, printmakers and potters worked while visitors watched [1]. At its centre was Diego Rivera [2]. The architect Timothy Pflueger, his friend and patron, had brought him back to San Francisco to paint a fresco in ten sections in front of the public. It was meant to go afterwards to a library Pflueger was designing for the new junior college [2][3].

The result is 22 feet high and 74 feet long [3]. Rivera called it The Marriage of the Artistic Expression of the North and of the South on this Continent; it is better known as Pan American Unity [3]. It includes Frida Kahlo, Charlie Chaplin and Paulette Goddard in The Great Dictator, and Hitler, Stalin and Mussolini in a war cloud. At its centre is a figure that merges an Aztec earth goddess with a Ford stamping press [2].

Then war intervened, Pflueger died in 1946 and the library was never built. The crated panels waited until 1961, when they were installed in a City College theatre lobby [2][3].

title: Frida and Diego try again on Calhoun Terrace
place: 42 Calhoun Terrace, Telegraph Hill
hook: Divorced, ill and shaken by Trotsky's murder, Frida Kahlo came to San Francisco in 1940 and moved in with Diego Rivera in a porthole-windowed flat on Telegraph Hill.
story: The apartment building at 38–50 Calhoun Terrace, with its telltale portholes, went up in 1937 in the Moderne style and steps down the hillside toward Sansome Street [1][2]. In 1940 flat 42 was the temporary home of Frida Kahlo and Diego Rivera [1][2]. By then they were divorced. Rivera had come north after Mexican authorities wanted to question him about an attempt on Leon Trotsky's life, and he was painting his huge Pan American Unity mural before crowds at the Golden Gate International Exposition on Treasure Island [3]. Kahlo followed after Trotsky was murdered and police held her for questioning. She was in pain and, says historian Celia Stahr, "in a terrible emotional state" [3]. Her friend and doctor Leo Eloesser prescribed a better diet, less drinking and reconciliation with Rivera. She stayed with him at 42 Calhoun before Eloesser admitted her to St. Luke's Hospital in the Mission [3]. Once she was stronger, the pair remarried at City Hall on Rivera's 54th birthday, and this time the Oakland Tribune called her "an artist in her own right" [3]. Next door stood Richard Neutra's brand-new Kahn House, built in 1939 [1][2].

title: Hearing Lions from 34th Avenue
place: Van Dyke family home, 1727 34th Avenue
hook: A dentist's son skied the dunes on barrel staves and fell asleep to lions roaring at the zoo. Later he rode some of the biggest waves on Earth.
story: In 1940 Fred Van Dyke's parents paid $6,000 for a new Henry Doelger house at 1727 34th Avenue. Only five houses stood on the block, and nothing but sand dunes lay between them and the beach. From the windows they could see Marin, the ocean and Lake Merced [1]. Fred, born in 1929 to a downtown dentist, said the neighborhood was like a ghost town at certain times of day. At night he could hear the surf, and the lions and elephants at the Fleishhacker Zoo. By day he saw rabbits, raccoons, hawks, snakes and now and then a deer [1]. He and his friends skied the dunes between 22nd and 30th Avenues on redwood barrel staves tied to their feet, an idea they got from a movie. After big windstorms, families were "sanded in" and sometimes waited three or four days for bulldozers to dig out their street. Getting groceries meant a walk through the dunes to 43rd Avenue [1]. Van Dyke learned to bodysurf on San Francisco beaches and first stood up on a board in 1950. In the mid-1950s he became one of the first California surfers to move permanently to Hawaii's North Shore and ride its giant winter waves [2].

title: Nine brothers and a union boss
place: 28 Bennington Street
hook: At 27 the ILWU's future first secretary-treasurer still shared a small Bernal house with his mother and eight brothers. He once had an affair with Katharine Graham.
story: In 1940 Eugene 'Pat' Paton, aged 27, was still living with his mother and eight of his brothers at 28 Bennington Street, a house that is 'not particularly large'. His brother Robert remembered: "Pray you get in the bed first," or there was no room [1]. He was one of twelve children; their father worked the killing floor in Butchertown. The brothers became firefighters, Muni conductors and Teamsters [1]. Pat became the chief organiser of the city's warehouse workers after the 1934 waterfront strike. He was president of ILWU Local 6 from 1938 to 1940 and then the union's first secretary-treasurer. Arbitrator Sam Kagel called him the best negotiator he ever met [1]. In 1938 he drank on the waterfront with Harry Bridges and a young labour reporter, Katharine Meyer, later Katharine Graham of the Washington Post. Paton was married, and the affair was brief, but she mentioned him in her memoirs [1]. He enlisted in 1943 and was promoted in the field at the Battle of the Bulge. He struggled with drink, and on March 22, 1951, aged 38, he jumped from the Golden Gate Bridge. Bridges gave the funeral oration [1].

title: Soccer got him out of a Nazi camp
place: Negoesco Stadium, USF (near Stanyan St & Golden Gate Ave)
hook: At 15 he punched a German soldier and was sent to a labour camp. Soccer with the guards helped him escape, and he became USF's legendary coach.
story: Steve Negoesco was born in New Jersey, the son of a sea captain, and was sent to Romania as a boy to live with an aunt and uncle [1][2]. At 15, after the Nazi occupation began, he beat up a German soldier who had hit him on his own street. The soldier said "Come with me" [1]. Negoesco packed two soccer balls first and his clothes second. He was sent to a camp at Immendorf in Germany, where prisoners rolled bomb casings between factory buildings on one meal a day, and his weight fell from 155 to 135 pounds [1]. The prisoners started playing soccer, and the young guards joined in. One guard told him that if he were going to run, he would go on a Friday, when the camp commander visited his girlfriend. Negoesco and three others left that Friday and made it by train to Vienna [1]. He played fullback for USF in the late 1940s and early 1950s, took over the soccer program in 1962 and coached it until 2000. His teams won national titles in 1966, 1975, 1976 and 1980 [2]. In 1982 the university named this field after him [2].

title: The Pontiac Dealer Who Lost to a Firehouse
place: Former Sunset Service / Mohawk station, SE corner 16th Ave & Irving St
hook: A brick gas station at 16th and Irving pumped gas, sold Pontiacs, and then lost a showroom lot to City Hall by eminent domain.
story: In 1926 Charles Kleinclaus opened a gas station on the southeast corner of 16th Avenue and Irving Street. The 1930 city directory lists him at the 'Sunset Service Station' [1]. To make room for it, the family moved its house around the corner onto 16th Avenue. His grandson Jack Goldsworthy grew up pumping gas and fixing flats there, and he remembered customers by their cars: a Hupmobile he kept going, a creamery owner's Buick convertible, the Furlong sisters' Roadmaster [1]. Pumps and tyres, Jack said, 'just wasn't enough'. So the family took on a small Pontiac agency. General Motors wanted a real showroom, so they bought the vacant lot across the street. Before the carpenters arrived, a man from City Hall said the city needed the corner for a firehouse. The city took the lot by eminent domain, and the car business ended [1]. The little brick office outlived all of them. Columnist Frank Dunnigan called it one of the city's last truly old gas stations and thought it dated from around World War I, earlier than the family's account [2]. Jack lived next door until he died in 2012, aged 86 [1].

title: The city's first public housing
place: Holly Courts, 100 Appleton Ave
hook: The architect of City Hall and Coit Tower also drew San Francisco's very first public housing, on a quiet slope beside Holly Park.
story:
San Francisco set up its housing authority in 1938, using money from the new federal Housing Act of 1937. Of the first projects it started, the most prominent was Holly Courts, on the southern slope of Bernal Heights between Holly Park and Mission Street [1]. The architect was Arthur Brown Jr., the man behind City Hall and Coit Tower. His plan put 118 homes facing the street, wrapped around inner courtyards and play spaces [1][2]. A photo from March 1940 shows it still under construction [1].

Like other early projects, it was meant for the 'deserving poor' of the Depression, who were mostly white. The city's housing projects stayed officially segregated until the NAACP won Banks v. San Francisco Housing Authority, which led to desegregation in 1954 [1]. Decades later the residents were running things themselves. Karen Huggins, president of the Holly Courts Resident Council, helped write the city's 2011 community-policing ordinance and pushed for broken lights and gates to be fixed. She told reluctant neighbours to get involved: 'You'll learn' [3]. In 2015 Mayor Ed Lee toured units in need of repair with Resident Board president Deborah Gibson [2].

title: The witch in the Wilde Avenue reservoir
place: Old reservoir site above Wilde Avenue, Mansell Street and Visitacion Avenue
hook: Flag signals sent the valley's water downhill. Twenty years later the kids of the 'Wilde Avenue gang' peered through the cracks and decided a witch lived inside.
story: Before it was a lookout, the hilltop above Wilde Avenue held Visitacion Valley's water. Betty Parshall of the Visitacion Valley History Project recorded how it worked. The Spring Valley Water pumping station stood at 31-33 Leland Avenue, and its reservoir sat at the top of the hill, just off today's Mansell Street. In the 1920s the station supervisor, Dan Condon, and a woman at the reservoir kept in touch with signal flags. When he signalled, she opened the gates so water could run down to the station. Another signal told her the station was full [1]. The flag story now appears on one of the Philosopher's Way plaques [2]. By the 1940s, Parshall wrote, the 'Wilde Avenue gang' had the run of the hill. They picked wildflowers, slid down the dry grass on cardboard sleds and played all kinds of games. The reservoir had a wooden roof, black with age and peaked along the top, 'like a huge old Gothic house that had sunk into the ground.' Parshall and her best friend, Marian Rado, peered through the cracks at the black water and half-believed a witch lived there [1]. Later the reservoir was drained and torn down. When the padlocked viewing tower went up in its place, Parshall joked that the witch had cursed the site [1].

title: Twelve Years of Lobbying for Lincoln High
place: Abraham Lincoln High School, 2162 24th Avenue
hook: Sunset teenagers once paid two streetcar fares to reach a high school across town. Their parents spent twelve years fighting for one of their own in the dunes.
story: Before 1940, teenagers from the fast-growing Sunset and Parkside had to ride across town to Commerce High in the Civic Center or Poly High by Kezar Stadium. In 1927 the Parkside District Improvement Club began campaigning for a local high school named for Abraham Lincoln [1]. "About 3000 children from our district right now have to pay two fares to get to the high schools they are compelled to attend," activist Ray Schiller told the Chronicle, "and the cars are so crowded they can't get on them" [1]. The city finally put an education bond on the ballot in 1938. Voters passed it after the club lobbied for it [1][2]. Lincoln was dedicated on September 22, 1940: a four-story concrete building by Fred H. Meyer, Martin Rist and Timothy Pflueger [1][2]. Tight budgets kept out the kind of elaborate frieze Pflueger had given Washington High [2]. It opened with 50 classrooms, and "temporary" bungalows stood in the upper yard for more than 50 years. The school song begins "High on a hilltop, 'Mid sand and sea" [1]. After Martin Luther King Jr. was assassinated in 1968, teachers Jackie Andersen and Yvonne Golden used the money raised for a memorial to buy his portrait for the library. It still hangs on the same wall [1].

title: Two hundred men, then the women
place: Italian American Social Club, 25 Russia Ave
hook: Founded in a Naples Street basement, this Art Deco club stayed men-only for nearly a century, though women had been running it for decades.
story: The club began in 1928 in the basement of a member's home on Naples Street. After a merger with the Alfieri Club in 1938, the members voted to build a hall of their own [1]. It was dedicated in 1940 just off Mission Street. Along its roofline runs Art Deco ornament in green, white and red, the colours of the Italian flag [1][2]. The members played cards, pool and bocce, and later the hall hosted wedding banquets and dinner dances [2]. Membership was a badge of honour. According to its current manager, the club once took only 200 members, all of whom had to be '100 percent Italian', and kept a waiting list [3]. That manager, Julie Clima, took over in 2005 as the first woman in the job. Her grandfather opened Joe's Fish Grotto up the street in 1946 [3]. As the old families moved to the Peninsula the waiting list disappeared, and in 2025 the club finally admitted women. About 30 joined in the first year [3]. It was added to the city's Legacy Business Registry in 2021 [2].

title: Underage dancing at the castle
place: The 'castle' complex, Bayshore Boulevard at Visitacion Avenue
hook: Teenagers danced at the bar in 'the castle' and ran out to the parking lot whenever the police showed up.
story: Where Visitacion Avenue meets Bayshore Boulevard, locals point to 'the castle' [1]. It is a complex of three buildings, built in the 1930s as income property by Austrian-born Joseph Rodiack: an apartment house, a space that held a series of restaurants and bars, and a small gas station [1]. The bars drew Schlage Lock workers, locals and anyone else after food, drink and entertainment. One proprietor was Raymond 'Babe' Baron, who ran Babe's Tower Inn [1]. Dawn Pyne Murayama remembered it from the 1940s: 'The castle was a bar that we went to. We weren't of age so when we needed to we would run out to the parking lot until the police were gone. We not only drank but danced too' [1]. The gas station once sold gas for 15½ cents a gallon, and later became a car wash [1]. In 2021 SF Heritage's Woody LaBounty named the complex one of his favourite buildings in the valley, though he suspected it might rank 'too high on the quirk factor' to win official landmark status [2].

title: When coal was king on Geary
place: Site of Richmond Coal Company, 3907 Geary Boulevard near 4th Avenue
hook: In the days of coal chutes and ice men, a coal yard stood beside the Richmond's oldest lumberyard on Geary, and coal went down chutes into basements along the avenues.
story: Into the middle of the 20th century, John and Louis Damele ran the Richmond Coal Company at 3907 Geary Boulevard. Next door, on the southeast corner of Fourth Avenue, stood Gillon Lumber [1]. Columnist Frank Dunnigan calls Gillon the oldest lumberyard in the Richmond District, founded in 1896 [2]. The coal man was one of many trades that came to the house. Deliveries went down coal chutes into basements. The milkman came, and the ice man carried blocks of ice in the years before refrigerators. The 'rags, bottles, sacks' man bought junk for recycling [1]. There was competition up the street. Longino F. Ginotti's coal company worked from a brick building at 4419 Geary and from another yard at 6045 Geary [1]. We know what the Damele shop looked like thanks to Luigi Damele. At a Richmond History Day in April 2008 he brought in a photograph of the family's shop, probably taken in the early 1940s [1]. Gillon Lumber stayed on its corner until a few years before 2008 [1].

title: Where San Francisco's Streetcars Went to Die
place: Former Market Street Railway 'Boneyard', Lincoln Way to Irving, Funston to 14th Ave
hook: For a few years a whole block beside Golden Gate Park was filled with dead streetcars, and one boy spent hours at their controls.
story: Around 1940 the whole block between Lincoln Way and Irving Street, from Funston to 14th Avenue, held rows of dead streetcars. Rail fan Val Golding called it 'a streetcar graveyard.' The Market Street Railway parked retired cars there in the open, where they rotted fast. A small shed handled the few 6, 7 and 17 runs sent out from the yard, which also staged the extra cars for football crowds at nearby Kezar Stadium [1]. Some of the most exotic cars in the fleet ended up there: second-hand cars from Williamsport and East St. Louis, and the five all-steel St. Louis 'Sedan' cars, the company's most modern. They stayed until 1941, when they went to be scrapped. As the company switched to buses, the tracks filled with the old cars it no longer needed [1]. Golding, still under his teens, went in and 'played motorman'. Most of the controls, he recalled, 'could be operated with a wrench' [1]. He also remembered the 7-line cars racing empty down Lincoln Way late at night [2]. Two large apartment buildings and a grocery store later replaced the yard [1]. Frank Dunnigan remembers the Park & Shop at Funston and its 'modern' apartments facing the park [3].

title: Where the Catholic dead gave way to shoppers
place: Geary Blvd & Masonic Ave (2675 Geary, former Calvary Cemetery corner)
hook: The big-box store at Geary and Masonic sits on the city's old Catholic burial ground, which held out longer than almost any other.
story: Calvary, the Catholic cemetery, was the giant of the Lone Mountain group. The archdiocese received 49 acres for it in 1860 [1], and by the time it left it held about 55,000 bodies [1][2]. The Church resisted removal, believing that the dead deserved a permanent home [2]. Its lawyer argued that selling the land would not even cover the cost of moving the graves. As a compromise, the archbishop offered to let the city cut roads through the cemetery so traffic could flow between the western neighbourhoods and downtown [1]. Once the city set its 1937 deadline, Calvary quickly gave in [1]. By 1940 its dead had been sent to Holy Cross Cemetery in Colma [2]. A photograph from June 26, 1946 shows the corner of Geary and Masonic scraped bare [3]. Housing, Kaiser's hospital and a big Sears store went up on the old burial ground [3]. Today the retail building at 2675 Geary is a Target, one of two in the city that stand on former cemeteries [2].

title: 18,500 workers, round the clock
place: Bethlehem Steel San Francisco Yard gate, 20th and Illinois Streets
hook: In May 1941 machinists picketed the shipyard gate at 20th and Illinois. Within months the same yard was running around the clock, building destroyers and patching up battleships.
story:
The old Union Iron Works at the foot of Potrero Hill had been Bethlehem Steel's shipyard since 1905 [1]. Through the 1930s its workers, many of whom lived in Dogpatch, went on strike for higher wages. A photograph from May 12, 1941 shows striking machinists outside the plant at 20th and Illinois Streets [1].

Once the US entered the war, the disputes were set aside. The yard employed 18,500 people on round-the-clock shifts [1]. Its slipways turned out Atlanta-class cruisers and dozens of destroyers, including Benson- and Fletcher-class ships [2]. Repair crews overhauled the aircraft carrier Essex and the battleships California, Maryland, Mississippi, Nevada and Pennsylvania [1].

The work remade the neighbourhood. Recruiters brought in Dust Bowl migrants from Oklahoma and Texas, African Americans from Louisiana, Texas and Arkansas, and Mexican workers. With no materials or land for new housing, families doubled and tripled up in Dogpatch's old flats and cottages [1]. By the 1950 census the Potrero Hill tract had 568 African American residents, almost all of them in Dogpatch or the Potrero View defense housing [1]. Shipbuilding ended with the war, and the yard fell back on repairs [2].

title: A Greek grocer's bet on a no-man's-land
place: Tower Market, Portola Drive at the top of Miraloma Park
hook: A Greek teenager who cleared 1906 earthquake rubble for $5 a day later gambled on a supermarket on the empty slopes of Twin Peaks. He opened it in wartime.
story: In 1905 fifteen-year-old Mark Pommon left the Greek island of Zakynthos to visit San Francisco, telling his father he would be back within a year. Six months later the 1906 earthquake struck, and he went to work clearing rubble for $5 a day. He stayed, worked in logging camps on the Mendocino coast, and in 1912 came back to the city and soon opened the first of several markets, at Eighth and Natoma. At Dudley's Market on Sixth Street he wore a suit to work every day [1]. His dream was a one-stop market, a novel idea when shoppers went to separate butchers, greengrocers and fishmongers. He bet the city would grow toward what was then a no-man's-land on the slopes of Twin Peaks [1]. Tower Market opened on Portola Drive in 1941 by one account [2], and the other history shows its debut in 1942 [1]. Either way, it was wartime: Pommon apologized to each customer for missing items and filled out forms with hundreds of their ration stamps so he could restock [1]. In 1954, with his son Dan in charge after Mark's death, the store welcomed the holidays with a 165-pound pumpkin pie, cut up for some 500 neighborhood children [1]. Mollie Stone's bought it in the mid-2000s; the two histories say 2005 and 2006 [1][2].

title: A Merry-Go-Round Retired From the Fair
place: Carousel, Koret Children's Quarter
hook: The park's carousel spent decades in Los Angeles and a season at a world's fair before it came to Golden Gate Park in 1941.
story: The carousel in the Children's Quarter was built in 1914 (some records say 1912) by the Herschell-Spillman Company of North Tonawanda, New York. It first ran in Lincoln Park in Los Angeles, then at the 1939 Golden Gate International Exposition on Treasure Island. The city bought it and installed it in Golden Gate Park in 1941 [1]. It joined a playground that had been there since about 1888, next to the sandstone Sharon Building, a Richardsonian Romanesque canteen for mothers and children that was badly damaged in 1906 and rebuilt to its original plans [1]. Pat French Swendsen remembered the scramble at the end of each ride, with children rushing for their favourite animals and 'barely three seconds' to climb off, the tall giraffes that didn't move, and the chariots that were 'a choice of last resort' for mothers with toddlers [2]. She also recalled elephant rides at two for a nickel and grizzly bears kept in pits near the playground [2]. The carousel was fully restored in 1984 [1].

title: A Seals pitcher from Mizpah Street
place: Mizpah Street, home of the Dunn family from 1924
hook: George Dunn grew up a block from Glen Canyon's ball field and pitched for the Seals. He died aboard the USS West Virginia on 7 December 1941.
story:
The Dunn family moved to Mizpah Street in 1924, one block from Glen Canyon. Their son George was born in 1917 [1]. He grew into a pitcher who could hit, and the Examiner wrote in 1936 that "this boy wins most of his games and does what most chuckers are not expected to do, pummel that horsehide" [1]. He trained with the San Francisco Seals. In 1938 he was at their Hanford camp when Joe DiMaggio turned up to get in shape. In 1939 he tried out in front of manager Lefty O'Doul [1]. In 1940 the Glen Park Athletic Club hired him to revive neighbourhood baseball on the canyon's field [1].

That November he joined the Navy. He trained as a radioman and was posted to the battleship USS West Virginia at Pearl Harbor. On 7 December 1941 torpedoes and bombs hit the ship, and Dunn was among more than 200 men killed on board. His body was found only months later, when the ship was raised [1]. In October 1947 his remains came home under the Golden Gate Bridge among 2,967 fallen service members, and he was buried at Golden Gate National Cemetery [1]. His signature survives in a Mizpah neighbour's school autograph book, dated May 1931 [1].

title: A Secret School in a Hangar
place: Building 640, Crissy Field (MIS Historic Learning Center)
hook: Five weeks before Pearl Harbor, sixty soldiers sat on orange crates in an old Crissy Field hangar and began to learn the Army's Japanese.
story: In 1941, as relations with Japan fell apart, the Army found it had hardly anyone who could read military Japanese. Officials grudgingly budgeted $2,000 for a language school under Lt. Col. John Weckerling [1]. The school's own survey found that of 3,700 Nisei (American-born children of Japanese immigrants), only about three percent were accomplished linguists [1]. Classes began on November 1, 1941, in Building 640, a small, abandoned hangar on Crissy Field [1][2][3]. It served as office, classroom and barracks all at once. Orange crates stood in for desks and chairs, and students worked from mimeographed sheets. The first class had 60 students: 58 Nisei and two white soldiers [1]. Head instructor John Aiso drove them hard. Lessons ran ten hours a day, and some students kept studying after 'lights out' by flashlight under their blankets, or in the latrine, the only room lit at night [1]. Forty-five graduated in May 1942 [1]. By then the Army was forcing their families out of the West Coast, and the school soon moved to Minnesota [1][2]. Its graduates served as translators and interpreters across the Pacific [1][2]. The hangar is now the MIS Historic Learning Center [2].

title: A Spanish Monastery in Crates
place: Monastery stones, San Francisco Botanical Garden (Strybing Arboretum)
hook: William Randolph Hearst bought a 12th-century Spanish monastery, shipped it to San Francisco, then sold it to the city for a token sum.
story: In 1930 William Randolph Hearst paid $97,000 for Santa María de Óvila, a Cistercian monastery near the Tagus River in Spain, planning to rebuild it as part of a vast new castle at Wyntoon [1]. Julia Morgan oversaw a year of dismantling. The numbered stones crossed the Atlantic on eleven freighters and then sat in the Haslett Warehouse for ten years at $1,000 a month [1]. As his money ran out, Hearst gave up. In August 1941 his friend Herbert Fleishhacker persuaded him to sell the stones to the city for $25,000, meant to be reassembled in Golden Gate Park as a museum of medieval art [1][2]. Soon after the crates arrived in the park, a fire burned them, damaging stones and their markings. A second fire in 1958 did more damage, and the museum was never built [1]. Gardeners reused the stones in walls around the botanical garden and the Tea Garden [1]. In 1994 museum trustees released many of the stones on indefinite loan to a Cistercian abbey at Vina, where the chapter house has been rebuilt [1].

title: A radio family's dream house, built for real
place: KGO Radio 'Dream House', 1 Cresta Vista Drive, Sherwood Forest
hook: Radio listeners heard a fictional family plan their dream home on the air. A developer built it for real on Mount Davidson, and 25,000 people toured it before Pearl Harbor.
story: To publicize its expansion of Sherwood Forest, high on Mount Davidson, Baldwin & Howell teamed up with KGO radio's popular fictional Edwards family: John and Edna and their children Jack, Sam and Florida [1][2]. As the family talked through the design of their dream home on the weekly broadcasts, the developer and the furniture company W&J Sloane built and furnished it to their specifications at 1 Cresta Vista Drive [1]. It had four bedrooms, a step-down living room, maid's quarters and an "all electric" General Electric kitchen with metal cabinets. It also had one of the first electronic security systems installed in a San Francisco home, and a machine-age stair railing that recalled an ocean liner [1]. The first open house, on October 12, 1941, drew several thousand people, along with representatives of GE, KGO and NBC, radio stars, and the Edwards family broadcasting on the air from the house [1]. It stayed open every Sunday that fall, and more than 25,000 people came through. The last open day was Sunday, December 7, 1941, the day Pearl Harbor was bombed. Then the house was sold [1][2].

title: Half the Navy's radio technicians
place: Site of Radio Materiel School A (Building 27), Treasure Island (approximate)
hook: The school opened in the rain with a blown-up boiler and no textbooks. By V-J Day it had trained more than half of the Navy's wartime radio technicians.
story:
The first technical school on the new naval station, the Radio Materiel School, opened in October 1941 with nine officers, nine chiefs and six hundred students [1]. Very little was ready. Its buildings were unfinished and the rainy season was in full swing. The heating plant blew up, so a donkey boiler was brought in. The books and equipment promised by Washington never came, and classes began with mimeographed pamphlets that officers had brought from Bellevue. After an entrance exam, the fifty highest scorers were told almost overnight that they would be teachers instead of students. Luckily several of them were electrical engineers [1].

The first class graduated in June 1942. The quota doubled from 100 men a month to 200, then settled at 400 [1]. By V-J Day the school had turned out more than ten thousand radio technicians, which the Navy's historians put at more than half of all those it trained in the war [1].

Students knew they had a good posting. "Radio technician is a 'good deal' because I like the work," F. R. Hicks, a seaman first class at the school, told the base newspaper in 1945. "Besides I can get college credits for the time I am spending in this Navy school" [2]. After the war the school became the island's Electronics Schools [1].

title: Hillside homes for wartime shipbuilders
place: Potrero Terrace and Annex, south slope (around 25th and Connecticut)
hook: Potrero Terrace opened in 1941 on terraces cut into the south slope. Its first homes went to shipyard families, and at first not one went to a Black family.
story:
When the San Francisco Housing Authority opened Potrero Terrace in 1941, its 469 units made it one of the city's first public housing projects [1]. Builders cut "benches" into the steep south slope, and the new streets followed the land rather than the city grid, which set the project apart from its neighbours [2]. Most of the first residents worked in the shipyards [2]. Of the Authority's first five projects, only Westside Courts in the Western Addition housed African Americans. Potrero Terrace, like the other three, had no Black tenants [1].

That changed after the war. In 1955 the Authority added Potrero Annex: 137 more units in 23 buildings, on land it described as "marginal land which perhaps otherwise would have laid undeveloped for many years" [2]. Over the decades its residents, some 1,300 at a time, included O.J. Simpson and the actor Danny Glover [2][3]. But unemployment rose and the complex's reputation sank. In 2017 BRIDGE Housing put violent crime there at five times the city average [2]. Under the city's HOPE SF rebuild, the first new building, at 1101 Connecticut, was finished in 2019. Excavators began tearing down the Annex in 2026 [2].

title: Hitler's captain on Jackson Street
place: Whittier Mansion, 2090 Jackson Street
hook: In the spring of 1941 a sandstone mansion on Jackson Street became Nazi Germany's San Francisco consulate. Its consul had been Hitler's commanding officer in the First World War.
story: William Franklin Whittier's Arizona sandstone mansion was built between 1894 and 1896 [2]. In April 1941 it passed in quick steps from the family to a title company, then to Herman Loeper on April 28, then to "Das Deutsches Reich" the next day [1]. The Chronicle later reported that the price was $44,000 [3]. The consul general was Fritz Wiedemann, whom a 1937 Chronicle headline had called "Hitler's War Captain" [3]. According to the federal architectural survey, he entertained elegantly while carrying out secret Nazi business, including trying to pressure German-Americans into "serving the party" [1]. Staff piled filing cabinets in the old dining room, and his family lived on the third floor [3]. In July 1941 he was ordered to leave. A stove near the furnace is thought to have been used to burn documents [1]. After a false start via Japan, the consular party flew to New York and sailed home via Portugal [1][3]. The US government seized the house, which stood shut through the war. In March 1950 it was auctioned [1]. It later housed Mortimer Adler's Institute for Philosophical Research and, from 1956, the California Historical Society [2].
