title: The Dentist Upstairs and the Nazi Prisoners
place: Dental office above the corner drugstore, NW corner of 9th Avenue and Irving Street
hook: A no-nonsense dentist drilled Inner Sunset teeth above the Rexall. His son spent 1945 testing Göring and Hess.
story:
Denis Quinn remembered the corner of 9th and Irving around 1959: a Rexall drugstore, known locally as K & K, with phone booths and a soda fountain. Upstairs was the office of George F. Kelley, DDS, a "no-nonsense" dentist whose motto was "Get in and get the work done!" Quinn believed Kelley's son had been chief psychiatrist at the Nuremberg trials [1].

The details fit. Douglas McGlashan Kelley, born in Truckee in 1912 and raised in San Francisco, was the son of George Kelley, a dentist [2][3]. In 1945 the Army made him chief psychiatrist for the captured Nazi leaders. Over five months he examined 22 of them, including Hermann Göring and Rudolf Hess, using Rorschach and IQ tests. His conclusion was that they had no special Nazi pathology [3].

The story ended badly. On New Year's Day 1958, Kelley, by then a Berkeley criminologist, drove into San Francisco to pick up his father, the dentist, to watch the Rose Bowl. Back home in Kensington, in front of his wife, his father and his three children, he swallowed potassium cyanide, the same poison Göring had used [2].

title: The Preacher Who Ran for City Hall
place: Third Baptist Church, 1399 McAllister Street
hook: Two decades before San Francisco seated a Black supervisor, a Baptist pastor ran three times, and in 1951 he won 36,000 votes.
story: Frederick Douglas Haynes was born in Talcott, West Virginia, in 1899 and orphaned as a child. He took the pulpit of Third Baptist in 1932, when, a 1953 profile said, most members were unemployed and "often the Sunday offering did not exceed thirty dollars" [1]. By his death in 1971 the church had more than 3,000 members [1]. In 1945 Haynes became the first African American to run for the San Francisco Board of Supervisors, and he ran again in 1947 and 1951 [1]. One campaign flyer read: "I have pledged myself to fight to my dying day to wipe out discrimination against minority races in the economical, political, and social life of our city, state, and nation" [1]. He never won, but his 36,000 votes in 1951, backed by the Union Labor Party, the CIO Council and the Fillmore Democratic Club, showed white politicians that Black voters counted [1][3]. The city context statement names him among the ministers who served as the community's main liaisons with the white power structure [2]. Terry Francois became the first Black supervisor in 1964, and in 1972 Haynes's widow, Charlie Mae, won a seat on the school board [1].

title: The atomic bomb's secret departure
place: Hunters Point Naval Shipyard, Drydock 4 area
hook: On July 16, 1945, a cruiser slipped out of Hunters Point carrying half the uranium-235 in America, and waited for word from the New Mexico desert.
story: On 15 July 1945 the heavy cruiser USS Indianapolis tied up at Hunters Point under extraordinary security: drydocks and berths were emptied, Marines stood guard with automatic weapons and planes circled overhead [1]. A crate the size of an automobile was craned aboard and stowed in the hangar. The real cargo came aboard in two heavy metal cylinders, one of them a dummy, in the luggage of two Manhattan Project officers, Major Robert Furman and Captain James Nolan, posing as artillery officers [1]. It held the uranium-235 projectile for "Little Boy," about half the U-235 then available in the country [1]. Crew members grew suspicious when the "artillerymen" could not answer basic gunnery questions [1]. The ship cast off early on 16 July but, according to the exhibit account, was held in the harbour until the Trinity test succeeded in New Mexico that morning [1]. It raced to Tinian and delivered the bomb components used on Hiroshima [1][2]. Four days later, on 30 July, a Japanese submarine sank the Indianapolis; of 1,195 men aboard, only 316 survived [1].

title: V-J Day and a ward of broken jaws
place: U.S. Naval Hospital, Treasure Island (site approximate)
hook: The base planned only a simple ceremony of thanksgiving for Japan's surrender. Instead, its hospital had its busiest day ever and had to open a whole ward for broken jaws.
story:
As Japan's surrender neared in August 1945, the island's commander sent round a memo. The base would mark V-J Day with nothing more than "a simple ceremony of thanksgiving," and routine would "proceed as on any other day" [1]. San Francisco had other ideas. When President Truman announced the surrender at 4 p.m. on August 14, thousands ran into the streets, and by evening the celebrations had turned into riots. When the "peace riots" ended on August 18, eleven people were dead and about a thousand injured [2].

For the naval hospital on Treasure Island, V-J Day was the busiest day in its history. Three complete surgical teams worked around the clock, and by the end of the night an entire ward had been set aside for patients with fractured jaws. The surgeons treated 125 cases that day and night. The Navy's historians added, with some pride, that not one of them was a corpsman [3].

The hospital was used to pressure. Commissioned in April 1942 with 500 beds, it admitted more than 17,500 patients in 1944 alone. All wounded servicemen flown in from fleet hospitals in the South and Central Pacific were sent here, and none were turned away [3].

title: A Giant Camera Left on the Patio
place: Camera Obscura (Giant Camera), 1096 Point Lobos Avenue
hook: Behind the Cliff House sits a building shaped like a Brownie camera. Step inside, and the Pacific slides across a table in the dark.
story: Floyd Jennings approached the Whitney brothers, owners of the Cliff House and Playland, with an idea older than photography: a darkened room where a rotating mirror and lenses throw a live, moving image of the outside world onto a horizontal table [1][2]. The National Register nomination dates his camera obscura to 1946; a Western Neighborhoods Project history says construction was finished by 1949 [1][2]. Around 1957, at George Whitney's suggestion, Jennings and his assistant Gene Tuttle widened the building so it looked like a Brownie camera, a piece of 'duck' architecture that advertises itself by its shape, and it was rechristened the Giant Camera [2]. NoeHill, adapting the nomination, likens it to a camera 'carelessly left behind by a giant tourist' [1]. Public support saved it when Playland closed in 1972, and when the Park Service wanted it gone during the Cliff House remodel of the early 2000s, campaigners won it a place on the National Register instead [1][2]. The nomination calls it apparently the last free-standing camera obscura in the United States that is more than fifty years old and still on its original site [1].

title: A Neighbourhood Named in the Classifieds
place: 400 block of Bright Street, Merced Heights
hook: Before 1946 nobody called this hill 'Merced Heights'. Real estate ads for compact 'Junior 5' houses gave the hill its name.
story: For most of its history the ridge between Ocean View and the Ingleside had no single name. Locals called its western summit Kite Hill or Poppy Hill. The rest was lumped in with Lakeview, Ingleside, Columbia Heights or Ocean View [1]. Some streets drawn over its crest on 19th-century maps took eighty years to become more than lines on a map [1]. Then the post-war housing rush arrived. Car ownership made steep hills practical to build on, and builders large and small bought lots [2]. In 1946 the name 'Merced Heights' began appearing in real estate ads for pre-war 'Junior 5' models, compact houses with two bedrooms, a living room and a combined kitchen and dining area [1]. Small-scale builders put up hundreds of one-storey homes over garages on standard 25-by-100-foot lots, much as builders were doing in the Sunset District [2]. Many of the 1946 ads said the owners were moving soon and wanted quick sales, a hint of the white flight that followed. Much of the new housing of the 1950s was sold to African American families [1]. The context statement uses the 400 block of Bright Street as an example [2].

title: A stool, some costumes, and Castro's first Halloween
place: Cliff's Variety (second store), 515 Castro Street
hook: Long before Castro Halloween drew huge crowds, it was a children's costume contest outside a variety store, with a stool for a stage.
story: In 1936 Hilario DeBaca, a retired merchant and schoolteacher from New Mexico, opened a small variety store at 545 Castro Street in Eureka Valley. He named it after his youngest son, Clifford [1]. It sold magazines, cigars, sewing notions, cards, toys and candy. In 1942 it moved a few doors toward 18th Street, to 515 Castro [1]. His eldest son, Ernie, was a tinkerer who had once driven his family to the 1933 Chicago World's Fair in a converted Studebaker, fixing radios along the way [1]. After a motorcycle accident crushed his ankle in 1946, Ernie set up a repair bench at the back of Cliff's. That Halloween he staged a children's costume contest on Castro Street. A stool served as the stage, and the child with the loudest applause won [1]. Over the years it grew to include a flatbed-truck stage, clowns, jugglers, an ice-cream-eating contest and a parade [1]. Wikipedia, citing the Chronicle, dates the first contest to 1948 [2]. Ernie also built chain-driven machines that carried candy bars and ribbon spools up to the ceiling and back to save counter space. One still runs in the store [1].

title: A women's club becomes a living memorial
place: Marines' Memorial Club (former Western Women's Club), 609 Sutter Street at Mason
hook: The Marine Corps wanted a 'living memorial' to its Pacific war dead. A group of Marines found one in a women's clubhouse off Union Square.
story: In 1926 Bliss & Faville, the firm that designed the Woman's Athletic Club across the street, finished a 12-storey Beaux-Arts tower on this corner for the Western Women's Club [1][2]. Its theatre carried national radio broadcasts by Bob Hope, Jack Benny and Frank Sinatra [2]. Early in 1946 the Commandant of the Marine Corps, Gen. Alexander Vandegrift, decided to create a "living memorial" to the Marines who had died in the Pacific, and to put it in San Francisco [3]. A group of Marines set out to buy a building a block off Union Square. After months of planning they found the money, and the club opened on November 10, 1946, the Marine Corps' birthday [3]. Some accounts date the purchase to 1947 [1][2]. Today membership is open to veterans of every branch [2]. The theatre went on to house the San Francisco Actor's Workshop and was the first home of the American Conservatory Theater [2]. The lobby displays the bell of the cruiser USS San Francisco, and a Tribute Wall remembers Americans killed in Iraq and Afghanistan [2].

title: Burning an island to grow a pier
place: Pier 50 (site of Mission Rock)
hook: Mission Rock was once a real island in the bay. In January 1946 the city set its old grain terminal ablaze so Pier 50 could swallow it.
story: Early maps show Mission Rock as a rocky outcrop well out in the bay, beyond the mouth of Mission Bay, and sailors used it as a navigational guide [1][2]. Over the decades it was bought and sold, built up and enlarged, and it settled into a long life as a dry dock, warehouse landing and grain terminal [1][2]. By the end of the Second World War the grain terminal was obsolete. San Francisco decided to extend Pier 50 to engulf the former island, and in January 1946 the old wharf was deliberately set on fire [1]. City photographers recorded the sequence: the terminal on January 7, the wharf going up in flames and creosote-soaked timbers burning on January 9, and an aerial view of the charred remains on January 10 [1]. Pier 50 became the farthest reach of the landfill that erased Mission Bay [2].

title: Paul Robeson sings, and the school sues
place: Presidio Hill School, 3839 Washington Street
hook: When a Presidio Heights school took Paul Robeson out to dinner and the restaurant refused to serve him, the school's board took the restaurant to court.
story:
In the late 1930s and 1940s the little progressive school on Washington Street became a place for causes. Its director Josephine Duveneck worked with the American Friends Service Committee, and the school helped refugees from Hitler's Germany settle and find work, some of them on its own staff [1][2].

When Japanese American families were sent to wartime camps, school families helped them pack their belongings and gave them food for the bus journey. The school's history calls it a centre of protest against the internment [1][2].

In 1946 sisters Rosalind and Stephanie Williams enrolled. As far as the school can tell, they were the first African American students at any independent school in San Francisco. Stephanie later sat on its board [1].

Paul Robeson sang for the school. When board members took him to Vanessi's restaurant, he was refused service. By the school's account a scandal followed, and the board sued the restaurant for discrimination [2]. As the anti-Communist hearings began, people called it the "Red Diaper Baby School." Later, blacklisted folk singer Pete Seeger came to sing for the school community with Malvina Reynolds [1][2].

title: Soap Box Speedway on Sunset Boulevard
place: Sunset Boulevard between Ulloa and Wawona streets, near Vicente
hook: Every summer after the war, a sleepy Sunset parkway turned into a racetrack for boys in homemade coasters that could cost no more than $10 to build.
story: The San Francisco Soap Box Derby moved to the Sunset in 1946. Before the war the races had run down Carolina Street on Potrero Hill, and in 1939 and 1940 down a steep ramp built on Treasure Island. There were no races from 1942 to 1945 [1]. The new course was Sunset Boulevard between Ulloa and Wawona. "Sunset Boulevard, a lovely, peaceful parkway drive in the Sunset district that is seldom used even on Sunday, was turned into a speedway," the Chronicle reported [1]. The race was sponsored by the Chronicle and Chevrolet and open to boys aged nine to fifteen. Each boy had to build his own car, and materials could cost no more than $10 [1]. A photograph from July 23, 1949, shows the twelfth annual race near Vicente Street; the winner was fourteen-year-old Paul Hodgson [2]. Most San Francisco champions actually came from out of town. In 1956 the headline read "Can It Be?—L.A. Boy San Francisco Soap Box Champ" [1]. Girls were shut out from 1935 until 1971 [1]. The Bay Area semifinals left the Sunset for Dublin in the 1960s [1].

title: The Frank Lloyd Wright House Never Built
place: 830 El Camino del Mar
hook: A downtown gift-shop owner twice hired Frank Lloyd Wright to design a house for this clifftop lot. Neither design was built, and a grocer's family moved in instead.
story: Vere C. Morris ran the gift shop at 140 Maiden Lane that Frank Lloyd Wright redesigned in 1948. Its curving interior ramp is described as a trial run for the one in the Guggenheim Museum [2]. Morris also owned a lot on the north side of El Camino del Mar, one of only ten lots on that side of the road west of China Cove [1]. A 2014 Planning Department review records that he commissioned Wright to design a residence there in 1946 and again in 1954, but the plans were never built [1]. The steep cliffs kept the lots on this side of the road empty until the late 1910s and 1920s, and many, this one included, until the 1960s [1]. The house that finally went up, in 1965–66, is a Third Bay Tradition design by the little-known architect Frants Albert, built for Edward P. and Angela Eassa. They owned the Sutro Super Market on Point Lobos Road and lived here until 1992 [1]. Planners found it too new, and too different in style, to count toward the eligible Sea Cliff historic district [1].

title: An abstract painter on capitalists' corner
place: 2520 Divisadero Street (Tudor Revival house, 1933)
hook: From a Tudor house on posh Divisadero, Nell Sinton painted cosy interiors. After she left, she became an Abstract Expressionist.
story:
Nell Walter was born in 1910 into one of San Francisco's pioneer Jewish families. Her father was president of the California School of Fine Arts, where she studied [2]. With her husband, Stanley Sinton Jr., she settled at 2520 Divisadero, one of a pair of Tudor Revival houses built in 1933, on what the architectural historians Anne and Arthur Bloomfield called "this capitalists' corner of Pacific Heights" [1].

Her first solo show came in 1947, and in 1949 the Legion of Honor gave her a museum show [2]. These early works were what the Bloomfields call "naïve and charming interiors and landscapes" [1]. In 1954 the Sintons bought a house on Russian Hill [2]. Only after selling the Divisadero house in 1955 did she begin the work she is best known for: exuberant abstract paintings in the 1960s, then figurative work, mixed-media constructions and a satirical Garden Party series [1][2]. "I find landscapes in human bodies and vice versa," she told an interviewer [1].

As head of SPUR, Stanley Sinton was at the center of the campaign for Proposition H, which in 1968 approved 2,000 units of low-cost public housing [1].

title: Bocce, Sodas and Sofas on The Road
place: San Bruno Avenue near Woolsey Street, by the Avenue Theatre
hook: Streetcar photographers caught a vanished San Bruno Avenue: Blondi's Bocci Ball, a soda fountain, a sweet shop and a coffee shop, all within sight of the Avenue's marquee.
story: Photographers who came to San Bruno Avenue for its streetcars also caught the shops around them. On 12 March 1947 one looked north near Woolsey Street at Muni H-line car #926. On the right is a business called Blondi's Bocci Ball, with the Avenue Theatre behind [1]. Around 1949 another, at Bacon Street, looked north across San Bruno to the Avenue and captured Lido Pastry and the Jolly Joan Fountain, while an H-line car went by with 'Enlist now - U.S. Coast Guard' painted on its side [2]. In May 1968 the Avenue was showing 'The Jungle Book', and a view south from near Burrows took in Leonard Supermarket, Fenech's Furniture, Hagi's Coffee Shop, Ampel Interiors, the Avenue Sweet Shop and Lido Pastry [3]. People remembered these places for a long time. In 2014, when the Breakfast at Tiffany's space sat empty, a commenter named Josie wished for a coffee shop again. She meant a real restaurant 'like Breakfast at Tiffany's or our so missed, Ave Sweet Shop', and asked who else remembered Sparta's restaurant [4].

title: Bogart climbs the Filbert Steps
place: Malloch Building, 1360 Montgomery St
hook: Hollywood picked a streamlined apartment house at the top of the Filbert Steps as Lauren Bacall's hideaway. Its real architect's name was left off the building for decades.
story: In Dark Passage (1947), Humphrey Bogart plays a man wrongly convicted of murdering his wife who escapes from San Quentin. Lauren Bacall's character, Irene Jensen, hides him in her chic apartment on Telegraph Hill, and Bogart trudges up the Filbert Steps to reach it [1]. The building was real: 1360 Montgomery, completed in 1937 and one of the city's best Streamline Moderne designs [1][2]. It was built for contractor John "Jack" Malloch and his son J. Rolph Malloch, who wanted homes with a bay view plus rental income [2]. A 1937 trade magazine feature on it never named the architect. In the early 1980s historian Gray Brechin found the designer: Irvin Goldstine, who had studied at the Ecole des Beaux-Arts but had no licence yet, so the Mallochs were listed instead [1][2]. The city said the building broke a limit of three floors above a garage. The Mallochs won, because each floor steps back up the hill [1][2]. Artist Alfred du Pont carved 40-foot figures into coloured concrete on the facade, including a worker holding a globe over the new Bay Bridge [1][2].

title: Film Noir's Favourite Clifftop Suburb
place: 25th Avenue at Sea Cliff Avenue (Nora Prentiss establishing shot, looking past 55 25th Avenue)
hook: Hollywood made Sea Cliff home to a doctor who fakes his own death, then sent a fleeing noir couple into a U-turn on El Camino del Mar.
story: In Warner Bros.' Nora Prentiss (1947), directed by Vincent Sherman and photographed by James Wong Howe, Kent Smith plays Dr. Richard Talbot, a San Francisco physician bored with his marriage [2]. He falls for Ann Sheridan's nightclub singer and fakes his own death. He puts his wedding ring on a dead patient, sets his car on fire and pushes it off a cliff [2]. The film makes the Talbots comfortable residents of Sea Cliff. Reel SF, which matches old frames to today's streets, found the establishing shot on 25th Avenue. The centre house in the frame is No. 55, with Baker Beach and the Golden Gate Bridge beyond, though the film never says which house is the doctor's [1]. The interiors were filmed on a Warner soundstage in Burbank, with the bridge view added by rear projection [1]. Three years later came The Man Who Cheated Himself (1950), with Lee J. Cobb as a homicide detective covering up a killing for Jane Wyatt's socialite [4]. Fleeing, the lovers hear a police bulletin on the radio and make a quick U-turn toward the bridge on El Camino del Mar near Sea Cliff Avenue [3]. Reel SF says the spot has "hardly changed in over 60 years" [3].

title: Grandma's Opry and a boy on Harrington Street
place: 87 Harrington Street (Garcia's grandparents' house), near Mission Street
hook: Long before the Grateful Dead, a five-year-old Jerry Garcia moved into his grandparents' house on Harrington Street. He later named a book after it.
story: Jerry Garcia was born in the Excelsior in August 1942 [1]. Until he was five he lived at 121 Amazon Avenue. Then his father drowned on a fishing trip, and Jerry moved across Alemany to his grandparents' home at 87 Harrington Street [2][3]. The house was new in 1907, when Bill and Tillie Clifford bought it, and Jerry's mother Ruth was born there in June 1910 [1]. Ruth took over her late husband's bar and worked full-time, so Jerry and his older brother Clifford ('Tiff') spent about five years with their grandparents [1]. Jerry went to Monroe Elementary, where a third-grade teacher showed him that being a creative person was 'a viable possibility in life' [1]. He remembered his grandmother listening to the Grand Ole Opry, and around then he took up the banjo, his first stringed instrument. Tiff insisted he was 'fantasizing all that': she had been to the Opry, he said, but didn't listen to it on the radio [1]. Garcia later wrote and illustrated a book called 'Harrington Street' [2]. In October 2016 a bronze plaque went into the sidewalk at Mission and Harrington. A second followed on his 75th birthday in 2017 [3]. His daughter Trixie hoped it would inspire 'a lot of working-class kids growing up here' [3].

title: The Republican window on liberal 24th Street
place: Former Twin Peaks Properties, 4072 24th Street, near Castro
hook: Harry Aleo filled his real-estate window with Nixon, Reagan and 'Looney Valley' signs. Someone shot at it. Then his racehorse became a Kentucky Derby hopeful.
story:
Harry Aleo grew up at 820 Diamond Street above his parents' fruit and vegetable store. He played ball for the Douglass Midgets, later pitched in college, and signed with the Brooklyn Dodgers until an arm injury ended it. He then fought at the Battle of the Bulge [1]. In 1947 he opened Twin Peaks Properties, and in 1958 he moved it to 4072 24th Street [1]. In 1961 Willopi Hall, condemned by the city, came up for sale. Aleo quietly gathered 19 other businesses to buy it and sell it to the city, and it became today's public parking lot [1].

Most passers-by knew him from his window. He filled it with GOP memorabilia from Ike to "Dubya" in one of the city's most liberal neighbourhoods. Vandals spat on it, scratched it, and in the Reagan years put bullet holes through the glass. In 2001 someone glued up clippings in the shape of swastikas [2]. Neighbours rallied round him. The Bay Guardian named it the "Best Place to See Startled Democrats" [2].

In 2005 his colt Lost in the Fog kept winning races and was talked about as a Kentucky Derby candidate. The horse was put down with cancer in 2006. Aleo died in 2008, and a documentary about the pair by Noe Valley native John Corey toured festivals [3].

title: The happiest boy in a streetcar wreck
place: 8th Avenue and Balboa Street
hook: A ten-year-old rail fan clipped accident reports and prayed to be in one. On July 24, 1947, his runaway streetcar granted the wish at 8th and Balboa.
story: Young Jack Tillmany lived on Anza Street, between the 31-Balboa and B-Geary lines, and collected newspaper clippings of streetcar accidents, secretly hoping to be in one. He bet on the 31, which had 'more than its share of colorful mishaps' [1]. On Thursday, July 24, 1947, he and his mother boarded car #976 at 25th and Balboa, heading downtown. On the eastbound descent the brakes apparently failed just as car #116 of the 21-Hayes line was crossing Balboa southbound on 8th Avenue. Their car sped up instead of slowing, broadsided the 21 and nearly overturned it [1]. Tillmany and his mother rolled across the floor in broken glass and dust; an elderly man with a bleeding head was hospitalised [1]. Hours later the pair's photo, taken in an ambulance, was on the front page of the San Francisco News. Each received a $25 settlement, and both cars were repaired and put back in service. His mother never rode the Balboa line again; he rode it every chance he got [1]. Two blocks away, six-year-old John Freeman heard the crash and ran to join the crowd; a schoolmate from 12th Avenue got into trouble for straying four blocks to see it [2].

title: The house the three sisters cut apart
place: 2 Hahn Street at Leland Avenue
hook: Legend says three sisters sawed their family home into pieces. One piece may have ended up on Hahn Street.
story: The Edwardian house at 2 Hahn Street, on the corner of Leland Avenue near McLaren Park, looks out of place among its midcentury neighbours [1]. Local legend says it is only one piece of a larger home that three sisters, who all loved the family house, divided between them [1][2]. Records show the lot was empty until late 1947, when the house was moved in. Its water was hooked up on October 8, 1947 [1]. Joana Louise (Rozario) Miranda was 13 when her family moved in from North Beach, the first to live there. She remembered stained glass, leaded-glass interior doors, a dining room with beveled glass, 'stairs to nowhere' and a finished attic. She walked hand in hand with her father to pay the mortgage to Mr. Harper, the man who had moved the house [1]. She had never heard the three-sisters story, though she remembered a Leland Avenue dress shop called Three Sisters [1]. After Heritage published the mystery in 2021, researcher David Gallagher suggested the house may have come from 24th and Vermont streets, displaced by Highway 101 construction, with one storey removed [1].

title: The picture house that opened twice
place: Former State / Del Mar Theater, 5825 Mission Street
hook: Outer Mission Street had more cinemas than customers. The State went dark in 1931, came back as the Del Mar in 1947, then found religion.
story: In the late 1920s, three movie houses opened within a few blocks of outer Mission Street while the area was still thinly settled. The State Theater at 5825 Mission opened around 1925. It was a medium-sized stadium-style house by architect Mark T. Jorgensen, with a sign on its roof. In September 1928 the Amazon opened a few blocks north on Geneva Avenue, and in December 1928 the Daly City Theatre opened a few blocks south. One Cinema Treasures contributor calls this "an outrageous example of over-building" [1]. Caught in the middle, the State closed in 1931 [1]. After the war it got a second chance. On December 5, 1947 it reopened as the Del Mar, with Douglas Fairbanks Jr. in 'The Corsican Brothers' [1]. The revival lasted less than three years of late-run and reissued films, and it closed for good on October 23, 1950 [1]. A religious group soon took it over as the San Francisco Revival Center. The facade and much of the interior survive, and one writer says the front is better preserved than Jorgensen's near-twin, the Parkway in Oakland [1][2]. A man who grew up nearby remembered that his sister worked as an usherette there, but he still had to pay full price [2].

title: The school the red scare shut down
place: California Labor School, 240 Golden Gate Avenue
hook: Paul Robeson and W.E.B. Du Bois lectured here, and 5,000 students took classes in a year. Then Washington branded it subversive.
story: The California Labor School started in 1942 as the Tom Mooney Labor School at Turk and Van Ness [1]. By 1944 more than 100 trade unions supported it, and 5,000 students attended that year [1]. It was accredited, so returning GIs could study there on the GI Bill [1]. In 1947 the school bought 240 Golden Gate Avenue, a 1906 labor and fraternal hall, and moved in [1][3]. It already faced charges of being "communist dominated." Within a month a witness before the House Un-American Activities Committee complained that physicist Frank Oppenheimer taught "atomic energy" there [1]. In 1948 the IRS revoked its tax exemption and California's attorney general listed it as subversive [1]. Its teachers and speakers included muralist Anton Refregier, Paul Robeson, W.E.B. Du Bois, Pete Seeger and Frank Lloyd Wright, and the basement held a mural room [1]. Enrollment and money ran out, and in 1951 the school moved to smaller quarters on Divisadero. In 1957, after the IRS seized its desks and papers, it held a last May Day party and closed [1]. A sidewalk plaque now marks 240 Golden Gate [2].

title: The shrub that died with a cemetery
place: Former Laurel Hill Cemetery, western edge near Parker Ave (exact site of the last wild patch not recorded)
hook: When bulldozers cleared Laurel Hill in 1947, a plant found only in San Francisco seemed to vanish with it. Sixty-two years later a biologist spotted one from his car.
story:
The Franciscan manzanita is a low, ground-hugging shrub that grew nowhere but San Francisco. It was adapted to the city's serpentine outcrops, sand, wind and fog [1][2]. As the city grew over those outcrops, the plant disappeared. Its last known wild patch was in the old Laurel Hill Cemetery, which was bulldozed in 1947 to make way for homes and businesses [2][3].

Just before the bulldozers arrived, the botanist James Roof saved two plants, which were kept alive at Tilden Botanic Garden in Berkeley [2]. In the wild, the species was counted as gone.

On 16 October 2009, the biologist Daniel Gluesenkamp was driving across the Golden Gate Bridge. He spotted a flowering shrub on a freshly cleared patch beside Doyle Drive in the Presidio. "It's like the unicorn of San Francisco," he said [2]. Presidio Trust biologists confirmed it was a Franciscan manzanita [2]. Because the bush stood in the way of the Doyle Drive rebuild, it was moved elsewhere in the Presidio in January 2010. In 2012, after a lawsuit by environmental groups, it was listed as endangered [3].

title: The woman who out-voted the mayor
place: Washington-Mason Cable Car Barn, 1201 Mason Street
hook: In 1947 the mayor said San Francisco should scrap its cable cars "as soon as possible." A determined Telegraph Hill resident gathered signatures, and the voters sided with her.
story: The Washington and Mason cable car barn and powerhouse, built in the 1880s, was largely destroyed in the 1906 fire and then rebuilt. After the disaster its engines were switched from steam to electric motors [1]. About fourteen barns and powerhouses once served the city's cable lines, and this is the only one left [1]. By 1947 buses were cheaper to run, and Mayor Roger Lapham declared that "the city should get rid of all cable car lines as soon as possible" [2]. When Friedel Klussmann learned that buses were being tested as replacements, she formed the Citizens' Committee to Save the Cable Cars. The committee quickly collected enough signatures to put a charter amendment, Measure 10, on the November ballot [2][3]. The fight made national news. Life magazine ran a photo spread on the gripmen, and the actress Katharine Cornell announced that she would never return to San Francisco if the cars were abandoned [2][3]. Measure 10 passed with 77 percent of the vote, requiring the city to keep the Powell Street lines running [2][3]. Klussmann couldn't stop later cuts to the system. But in 1964 the cars were declared a National Historic Landmark, and she was still defending them when she died in 1986, aged 90 [3].

title: The woman who stopped the buses
place: Friedel Klussmann Memorial Turnaround, Hyde St at Beach St
hook: The mayor wanted every cable car gone. A committee of civic-minded women took him on, and the turntable at the bottom of Hyde Street bears their leader's name.
story: In 1947, with buses cheaper to run, Mayor Roger Lapham declared that "the city should get rid of all cable car lines as soon as possible" [1]. Friedel Klussmann, a Telegraph Hill resident, pulled together a meeting of 27 women's civic groups and founded the Citizens' Committee to Save the Cable Cars [1][2]. They quickly gathered enough signatures for a charter amendment on the November ballot. Life magazine photographed gripmen, and actress Katharine Cornell vowed never to return to San Francisco if the cars disappeared [1][3]. The measure passed with 77 percent of the vote [3]. In the 1950s the city bought the California Street Cable Railroad's lines and planned to replace them with buses. Klussmann fought again, with less success. The compromise joined the Hyde Street section of one of those lines to a shortened Powell line, creating today's Powell-Hyde route down Russian Hill to the Bay [2]. "The only ones who wanted the cable cars were the people," she said [3]. When she died in 1986 the cars were draped in black, and in 1997 the city named the Hyde Street turntable after her [2].

title: Opera cakes on foggy Clement Street
place: Schubert's Bakery, 521 Clement St between 6th & 7th Aves
hook: A German immigrant's Fillmore bakery moved west in 1948 and has passed from one German baker to the next ever since, recipes and all.
story: Oswald Schubert, a German immigrant, opened the Golden West Bakery at 1014 Fillmore Street in 1913 and made his name with traditional German cakes and pastries [1]. When he retired in the 1940s he sold it to a fellow pastry enthusiast, Fred Kreye, who kept the old-world techniques but found the demand outgrowing the shop. In 1948 Kreye moved Schubert's to a larger 1910 building at 521 Clement Street, a spot easy for pedestrians and visitors to find [1]. Frank Dunnigan remembered it as a branch of an old-time bakery from the once-Jewish Western Addition, and claims you can still catch a whiff of almond paste, poppy seeds and honey in the morning air [2]. On June 1, 1969, a young German couple, Hilmar and Annie Maier, took over and stayed put as the district's population changed around them [1]. In 1995 they sold to brothers Ralph and Lutz Wenzel, the fourth generation of bakers in their family, who still turn out Neapolitan and Opera cakes whose recipes the bakery dates to 1911, alongside newer favourites like Swedish Princess cake and mango mousse [1]. The city added Schubert's to its Legacy Business Registry in 2019, listing its old wooden sign and striped awning among the features worth saving [1].

title: South of Market's Double Gold Medal Diver
place: Victoria Manalo Draves Park, Folsom and Sherman streets
hook: Born South of Market to a Filipino father, Vicki Manalo had to call herself Vicki Taylor to join a diving club. In 1948 she won two Olympic golds.
story: Victoria Manalo was born on December 31, 1924, in San Francisco's South of Market district, to Teofilo Manalo, a Filipino chef and musician, and Gertrude Taylor, who had come from England [1][2]. Money was tight, and she could not afford swimming lessons until she was ten [1]. She took up diving at 16, but facing prejudice against Filipinos, she used her mother's surname, Vicki Taylor, to be accepted at coach Phil Patterson's Fairmont Hotel club [1]. After graduating from Commerce High School in 1942 she worked in the Army Port Surgeon's office to help her family [1]. Olympic diver Sammy Lee introduced her to coach Lyle Draves, whom she married in 1946 [1]. At the 1948 London Olympics she won the springboard on August 3 and the platform on August 6, the first woman to win both diving titles and the first Asian American to win Olympic gold [1][3]. In 2006 the city named a two-acre park at Folsom and Sherman streets for her, one acre per gold medal, on the site of the Franklin Elementary School she had attended, four blocks from where she grew up [1][2].

title: Stamped "Blighted" Before the Bulldozers
place: The 1947 redevelopment study zone (Van Ness to Webster, Geary to McAllister), centred near Laguna and Eddy
hook: Years before a single Victorian fell, the city's own planners had written the Western Addition off, in language that singled out the colour of the people living there.
story: The paperwork came well before the bulldozers. In 1945 a study called Blight and Taxes, published by the San Francisco Planning and Housing Association, marked the Western Addition for urban renewal. It said the district "is not white. It is gray, brown, and an indeterminate shade of dirty black" [1]. The city's 1945 Master Plan praised the area's closeness to the financial district and its slopes for view apartments, then admitted that "only a relatively small proportion" of its "colored and foreign-born families" could be expected to live in whatever replaced their homes [2]. At the end of 1947 the City Planning Commission proposed a $52 million rebuilding of a 36-block zone enclosed by Van Ness, Webster, McAllister and Geary [3]. In 1948 the Fillmore, where 60 percent of residents were African American, was formally declared blighted [4]. Residents saw what was coming. In July 1948 a multiracial coalition met at the Buchanan Street YMCA, where Dr. Carlton B. Goodlett Jr., head of the local NAACP, warned that "scores of small businessmen would be wiped out by the plan" [2]. Demolition started eight years later.

title: The Army Came to 37th Avenue
place: Young family home, 674 37th Avenue near Balboa Street
hook: Realtors told a decorated Army officer they would not sell to "an Asiatic." So his Army buddy bought the house for him.
story:
In 1948 Lt. Col. John C. Young, a Stanford-trained engineer who had spent more than two years on the Burma front, wanted to move his family out of a crowded Chinatown flat. Realtors told him, "We cannot and will not sell to an Asiatic." His friend Lt. Col. Keith Bering bought a bungalow at 674 37th Avenue and sold it to the Youngs a month later, taking a risk under the neighbourhood's racial covenant [1].

Connie Young Yu remembered them as the first Chinese family that far out in the Avenues. A neighbour circulated a petition to force them out. In response, Young's Army Reserve comrades held their monthly unit meetings at the house, arriving in uniform with their families, until the Korean War. The petition faded [1].

Down the block, at 740 37th Avenue, stood Mei Lun Yuen, a Chinese children's home founded in 1933 by Donaldina Cameron, Dr. Bessie Yeen Jeong, Helen Wu and Chinese Presbyterian women. Gardens and fences were proposed to hide the children from white residents. Al never once saw an orphan there. Mei Lun Yuen was defunct by 1962 [1]. Al, who drag-raced his '47 Chevy on the Great Highway as a teenager, became the first Asian American world champion race car driver [2]. Connie became a historian [3].

title: The Post Office Murals Congress Tried to Erase
place: Rincon Annex Post Office, 101 Mission Street
hook: Anton Refregier painted San Francisco's history with the ugly parts left in. Congressmen called it communist propaganda and wanted it gone.
story: The streamlined Rincon Annex post office, designed by Gilbert Underwood, opened on October 26, 1940, on land once meant for a Southern Pacific station [3]. In 1943 New York artist Anton Refregier won the commission to paint the "History of San Francisco" around its lobby, the last year of federal art sponsorship; the work was not painted until after the war [1]. Instead of heroic pioneers, Refregier showed vigilantes, anti-Chinese riots, the 1934 waterfront strike, and the 1916 Preparedness Day bombing that sent Tom Mooney and Warren Billings to prison [1]. In May 1948 Refregier and CIO longshoremen carried a banner protesting the covering up of one section [1]. On May 1, 1953, at the height of the McCarthy era, the House Committee on Public Works held a day of hearings on destroying the murals. Representative Hubert Scudder of Sebastopol accused the artist of slandering the state's pioneers and pushing communism on post office patrons [2]. An American Legion spokesman complained the murals were "depressing" [1]. They survived, and the building became City Landmark #107; the murals still ring the lobby, though it is no longer a post office [1][3].

title: The city assessor who quit for ice cream
place: Swensen's Ice Cream, 1999 Hyde St at Union
hook: A Navy sailor learned to make ice cream in a hot ship's hold, left a safe city job, and built a franchise empire from one Hyde Street corner.
story: During World War II, Earle Swensen served on a Navy ship in the Pacific. To escape the heat he would slip below deck to the ice cream freezer, and he ended up making scoops for the crew [1]. Back home he took a job as a deputy assessor for the city, but found it dull. In 1948 he opened an ice cream shop at Hyde and Union, even though everyone told him he was crazy to quit [1]. It opened as See Us Freeze Ice Cream, a name still glowing in red neon, and business was slow at first. His father-in-law ran the counter by day, and Swensen worked on recipes at night [1]. In 1964 he began franchising. New franchise owners came to the little Hyde Street shop to learn the recipes from Richard Campana, who had started there part-time at about 15 and became manager at 21 [1]. By 1973 the Chronicle described a $4 million ice cream empire, but Swensen said the original shop would never be for sale. It never joined the chain, even after Swensen sold the franchise rights in the 1970s. Campana's family runs it today and still makes every batch on site [1][2].

title: The student publicist who remade the NFL
place: USF main campus, Fulton Street (Rozelle's student and staff years)
hook: Before he built the modern NFL and the Super Bowl, Pete Rozelle was a USF student writing press releases for the Dons.
story: Pete Rozelle came to the University of San Francisco in 1948 from Compton Community College, where he had been the student athletic news director and a part-time public relations assistant for the Los Angeles Rams [1]. At USF he was a student publicist for the Dons. He promoted the football team and helped win national attention for the basketball team that took the 1949 National Invitation Tournament [1][2]. He graduated in 1950 and stayed on as USF's full-time athletic news director [2]. He was the Dons' publicist in 1951, when the unbeaten football team refused an Orange Bowl invitation that would have meant leaving its Black players at home [3]. In 1952 he went back to the Rams [1]. In January 1960 the NFL's owners took 23 ballots to choose a new commissioner and settled on Rozelle, then 33 [1]. The league then had 12 teams, and their combined revenues were under $20 million a year [2]. Rozelle got the owners to share their television money, created Monday Night Football with ABC's Roone Arledge, and brought the rival AFL into one league with a single championship game [1][2]. He disliked that game's name. Lamar Hunt had coined it after his son's bouncy Super Ball, and it stuck: the Super Bowl [2].

title: Through the Ice at 'Mud Lake'
place: Pine Lake (Laguna Puerca), Pine Lake Park west of Stern Grove
hook: One winter in the late 1940s, an 11-year-old went out on frozen Pine Lake to save a drowning dog and then couldn't get out himself.
story: Pine Lake is one of the natural lakes formed when creeks running off Golden Gate Heights were dammed by sand dunes. Its old name was Laguna Puerca. 'Puerca' means pig and is used to mean dirty, and locals called it Mud Lake or Pig Lake [2]. In the late 1940s it was a muddy pond ringed by trees and steep hillsides. James Clifford, who lived on 45th Avenue, would ride his bike 25 blocks to swing out over the water on ropes tied to branches. His homemade rowboat sank the moment it was launched [1]. One winter day a small boy's dog chased a stick onto the ice and fell through. Clifford, 11, went after it and broke through too. He shoved the dog to safety and it ran off with its owner. Then, as he shouted for help and his arms slipped off the ice, a teenager in a black leather jacket threw him a rope. The teenager walked off with a curse and a warning [1]. A Mrs. Kenney in a house on the hill put him in a warm bath. Her husband later invited him to join his Boy Scout troop, Troop 108, and gave him a lesson: on ice, crawl, don't walk [1].

title: A church that crossed every line
place: Church for the Fellowship of All Peoples, 2041 Larkin St
hook: Banks called it a bad risk. In 1949 one of the nation's first interracial, interfaith congregations bought a church on Larkin Street anyway, and paid cash.
story: In December 1943 Alfred Fisk, a white Presbyterian minister and San Francisco State philosophy professor, held the first service of a new interracial church. Sixty-six people came, about a third of them Black [1]. He persuaded Howard Thurman, dean of the chapel at Howard University, who had met Gandhi in 1936, to come west as co-pastor [1][2]. Thurman arrived on July 12, 1944. At the inaugural service that October more than 400 people heard the two pastors, one Black and one white, launch what the Chronicle called the "first interracial church in the nation" [1]. Eleanor Roosevelt signed on as a member-at-large [1]. Many members were Black newcomers from Oklahoma, Texas and Arkansas working in defence industries [3]. For five years the church moved from building to building. Thurman insisted it stay outside what was fast becoming the Black neighbourhood, so it would not be seen as a mission church, and after 1944 every building it used was east of Van Ness [1]. In January 1949 the board heard of a $275 monthly deficit, then voted unanimously to buy the former St. John's Evangelical Church at 2041 Larkin for $30,000 [1]. Lenders refused, one calling it a "bad" risk. A private loan paid the cash price, and 500 people watched the mortgage burned in 1952 [1].

title: An Ocean Liner Docked at Persia Avenue
place: Clean Wash Center (former Safeway Credit Union building), 4680-4690 Mission Street at Persia Avenue
hook: Born to 1906 refugees who lived in a Presidio tent, the future Berkeley Art Museum architect designed storefronts and a credit union on Mission Street.
story: Mario Ciampi was born in San Francisco in April 1907. His Italian parents had arrived just in time for the 1906 earthquake and spent months living in an army tent in the Presidio [3]. With no money for architecture school, he apprenticed as a draftsman and took night classes, then won scholarships to Harvard, studied at the École des Beaux-Arts, and founded his own firm in 1945 [3]. Within a few years he was designing on Mission Street in the Excelsior. The Planning Department's historic context records list Ciampi work at 4463 Mission (a storefront, 1948), Cresta Auto Parts at 5050 Mission (1948) and 4680-4690 Mission (1949) [2]. That last building, on the corner of Persia Avenue, was commissioned by the Safeway Credit Union: its employees worked upstairs, and shops filled the ground floor. With its rounded corner, open ground floor and ribbon of upper windows, SF Heritage says it 'points into Mission street like a 1930s ocean liner.' Today it is the 24-hour Clean Wash Center laundromat [1]. Ciampi's Corpus Christi Church of 1952, just west of Mission, appeared in LIFE magazine in 1955 for its front wall of coloured glass panes, which were later replaced with amber glass [4]. He went on to design the Berkeley Art Museum [3].

title: Frank Lloyd Wright's Rehearsal for the Guggenheim
place: V. C. Morris Gift Shop, 140 Maiden Lane
hook: Behind a blank brick wall on a Union Square alley, Wright built a spiral ramp a decade before his famous museum.
story: San Francisco has just one building by Frank Lloyd Wright, and from Maiden Lane it barely looks like a shop: a flat wall of brick pierced by a single arched entrance [1]. Between 1948 and 1949 Wright remodelled a 1911 building as a store for the Morris family [1]. Inside, a curving ramp spirals up from the ground floor to a circular mezzanine, under a ceiling of translucent plastic discs and half-bubbles hung beneath skylights. Many critics see it as a trial run for the Guggenheim Museum's spiral a decade later [1][2]. Reviewing it in Architectural Forum in February 1950, Elizabeth Mock wrote that the ramp rose like "a wave checked in its break," and that a visitor's "transformation into a customer is accomplished with dignity and dispatch" [1]. The arch had a local ancestor: city landmark reports compare it to the Chicago-style arched entry of the Mills Building [3]. The Morrises ran the store until they died in the early 1960s; Wright associate Aaron Green restored it in 1998 [1].

title: Grace Marchant's garden on the dump
place: Grace Marchant Garden, Filbert Steps at Napier Lane
hook: The slope beside the Filbert Steps was a dump of bedsprings and broken glass. A woman in her sixties decided to turn it into a garden.
story: When Grace Marchant moved to a cottage on Napier Lane in 1949, the east slope of Telegraph Hill along the Filbert Steps was a dumping ground. People had thrown their garbage down the stairs. Marchant said it was several feet deep, and when it was burned with the city's permission, it burned for three days [2]. Columnist Margot Patterson Doss later recalled old bedsprings, legless chairs and broken glass. Marchant hauled it away herself and brought in soil, shrubs and trees, at no cost to the city [1]. Her first planting was a pot of baby tears [1]. For more than thirty years she turned the public right-of-way and the lots around her into a lush hanging garden [1][2]. She died in December 1982, aged 96, and asked her neighbour Gary Kray to carry it on [1]. The garden nearly died with her. A buyer planned to replace a 1920s cottage at 221 Filbert with a house five times the size. Neighbours, the Telegraph Hill Dwellers and the Trust for Public Land raised $320,000 in the 1980s to buy the site and protect it with conservation easements [1].

title: Lady Day's room at the Mark Twain
place: Hotel Mark Twain, 345 Taylor Street
hook: Federal agents raided Billie Holiday's Taylor Street hotel room in January 1949. She said she had been set up, and the headlines packed her shows.
story: Billie Holiday reached San Francisco in January 1949 trailing bad headlines. Two weeks earlier, at Billy Berg's club in Los Angeles, a brawl had ended with her husband and manager, John Levy, stabbing a man with a carving knife, and she was facing assault charges [1]. On January 13 she opened at Joe Tenner's Cafe Society in the Fillmore to a standing-room crowd [1]. On January 22, federal narcotics agents raided her room at the Hotel Mark Twain, 345 Taylor Street [1][2]. Wikipedia names the arresting officer as George Hunter White of the Federal Bureau of Narcotics [2]. The agents said they found a small amount of opium, worth less than fifty dollars, and a pipe. Holiday and Levy denied knowing anything about it and said they had been framed. Writer Dr. Weirde suggests the club owners may have been behind it [1]. The next day's Chronicle front page read "Billie Holiday is held on opium charge." Photographs in the Bancroft Library show her being booked at the Hall of Justice [1]. According to FoundSF, the notoriety only helped: the rest of her San Francisco run was a smash [1].

title: Laughed at, then a title shot
place: Excelsior District (Valentino's boyhood neighbourhood; the title fight itself was at the Cow Palace)
hook: Excelsior kids laughed when young Pat Valentino said he would fight for the heavyweight championship. In 1949 he did, half-blind, in front of 19,950 people.
story: 'When I was young, I told some kids I was going to fight for the heavyweight championship,' Pat Valentino remembered in 2004. 'They laughed at me' [1]. He grew up in the Excelsior [1][2], took up boxing in the Coast Guard, and had his first pro fight at 19 at the Oakland Auditorium [1]. At about 185 pounds he was small for a heavyweight. He twice fought Joey Maxim to a draw and finished his career 45-11-4 [1]. A year before his title shot he suffered a detached retina fighting Tony Bosnich, another boxer from the Excelsior [1]. On October 14, 1949, Valentino met Ezzard Charles for the world heavyweight title at the Cow Palace. It was the city's first heavyweight title fight in 40 years, before 19,950 fans, then Northern California's biggest fight crowd [1]. Valentino led on two of the three judges' cards going into the eighth round, then was knocked down and out 35 seconds into it [1]. He was due $5,000 to Charles's $40,000, but said he never saw the money and had to sue his manager to get a portion of it [1]. Two months later, blind in his right eye, he boxed an exhibition with Joe Louis, then retired. He went on to spend 22 years as the maître d' at Scoma's [1].

title: Mirror Balls at the Primalon Ballroom
place: Primalon Ballroom, 1223 Fillmore Street (site, between Turk and Eddy)
hook: A 1930s miniature golf course and roller rink on Fillmore became the ballroom where Count Basie, Lionel Hampton and Dizzy Gillespie played to dancing crowds.
story: The big indoor-outdoor lot at 1223 Fillmore Street opened in 1934 as the Woodland Dancing Hall, complete with miniature golf links [1]. After the Second World War it became the Brown Bomber Café, a beer garden with roller skating on weekdays and, on weekends, skating and dancing together under suspended mirror balls [1]. In 1949 it became the Primalon Ballroom, run by the McCoy family [1][2]. Top acts included Count Basie, Lionel Hampton and Dizzy Gillespie, alongside local blues bands such as Pee Wee Crayton's [1]. Like the Majestic up the street, which became the Fillmore Auditorium in 1952, the Primalon was one of the dance halls that shifted its bookings toward jazz, blues and R&B [2]. The Primalon closed in 1961, and the structure was torn down in 1974 [1]. Nothing of it survives today [2].

title: Miss Burke's Girls Move to the Dunes
place: Katherine Delmar Burke School, 7070 California Street at 32nd Avenue
hook: A girls' school that began with eight pupils in a Pacific Heights rental moved out to a long strip of land beside Lincoln Park.
story: Katherine Delmar Burke started tutoring for 25 cents an hour while still at Girls' High. In 1908 she opened her own class of eight girls, the "Charter Children", in a rental at Steiner and Pacific [1]. She died in Egypt in 1929. That same year, under her successor Barbara Burke, the school began acquiring land far out in Sea Cliff, at California Street and 32nd Avenue [1][2]. Its first building there opened in 1936 for the nursery school and kindergarten. In 1949 the Lower School followed [4], and the girls got a new plaid jumper to go with it [1]. The older girls stayed in Pacific Heights until 1975, when falling enrolment closed the high school and everyone moved to the Sea Cliff campus [1][2]. Traditions came along too: Pansy Day dates from 1926 and the October Festival from 1931 [1]. The site is a long, narrow three and a half acres [3]. In 2005, when the school proposed a two-story science and music building, the Lincoln Park neighbourhood groups objected. They objected to an entrance on El Camino del Mar and feared more traffic chaos on 32nd Avenue, where parents double-park at drop-off [3].

title: Paintings Nailed to a Portola Garage Wall
place: E. R. Taylor School, 423 Burrows Street, where Longfield went to grammar school (her Portola home's address is not published)
hook: In 1949 a critic ranked her among the best new abstract painters. After her death in 2013, her canvases turned up nailed to her Portola garage wall.
story:
Zoe Golovinsky was born in San Francisco in 1924, the only child of Russian émigrés. Her father had been an aviator in the Czar's military, and he died in a work accident soon after arriving in America [1]. Her mother, a seamstress, married another émigré, Maxim Dolgopoloff. In high school Zoe changed her surname to Longfield, a loose English translation of his [1]. She went to E. R. Taylor Grammar School, Portola Junior High and Balboa High, and as a teenager she skated in figure-skating exhibitions [1][2].

After Berkeley she studied at the California School of Fine Arts under Clyfford Still, Mark Rothko and Richard Diebenkorn. She was one of the few women among the first Bay Area Abstract Expressionists [1][2]. In 1949 she and eleven of Still's students opened the cooperative Metart Gallery in a former laundry on Bush Street. A Chronicle reviewer called her one of the most successful painters working in the new style [1]. In 1951 she married and set her ambitions aside. Later she lived in her childhood home in the Portola, worked as a lithographer and graphic artist, and was often seen feeding the neighbourhood's feral cats [1]. After her death in 2013, a large collection of her paintings was found unstretched and nailed to the back wall of her garage [1].

title: Soko means 'that place'
place: Soko Hardware, 1698 Post Street
hook: Closed for five years by internment, then bulldozed by redevelopment, a Post Street hardware store kept coming back and turned 100 in 2025.
story: Masayasu Ashizawa opened a hardware store at 1683 Post Street in 1925 and named it Soko, which The New Fillmore translates as "that place" [1]. During World War II the family was incarcerated and the store stayed shut for five years [2]; Masao was held at the Topaz camp in Utah [1]. In 1949, after his father died, Masao Ashizawa, then a maths graduate student at UC Berkeley, took over [1]. A few years later redevelopment arrived. Rather than leave, Masao moved Soko across the street to the north side of Post and worked with the city on the Japan Center and Peace Plaza that rose on its old site. He became founding president of the Nihonmachi Community Development Corp., which tried to keep Japantown property in Japanese American hands, and chaired the Cherry Blossom Festival in 1971 [1]. His son Philip, a biophysics major, joined in 1979 [1]. Today the shelves mix nuts and bolts with ikebana scissors, flower frogs and Japanese seeds [1]. At its centennial in 2025, the family said a fourth generation, Philip's son Daniel, was carrying on [2].

title: Television's first home was a mansion
place: Site of the Sutro mansion (La Avanzada), now the Sutro Tower grounds
hook: Before the tripod, a Sutro grandson's hilltop mansion was where ABC first broadcast television to the Bay Area.
story:
In the 1930s, Adolph G. Sutro, a grandson of the former mayor, built a mansion on the family's hilltop land. It was known as La Avanzada [1][2]. In 1948 he sold it to the American Broadcasting Company, which wanted the height for a transmitter [1]. KGO-TV went on the air on May 5, 1949. It made its programmes inside the mansion and broadcast them from a 508-foot tower beside it [1][3].

KGO was the Bay Area's second television station. KPIX had signed on five months earlier and helped its new rival by airing programmes explaining how to tune in channel 7 [3]. Soon KPIX and another station were sending their signals from the same hill. The stations later moved to real studios but kept their transmitters here [1]. In the mid-1960s viewers complained about poor reception, and the broadcasters planned a much taller tower. As part of the final deal with the city, the old tower and the Sutro mansion were torn down [1].

title: The Last Streetcar Down Mission Street
place: Mission Street at Geneva Avenue, on the old 40-line route
hook: A branch line laid in six days for the racetrack crowds, a motorman who fought in 1898, and one green-and-cream car that ended Mission Street's streetcar era.
story: Streetcars shaped the Excelsior's Mission Street early. In December 1895 the Market Street Railway extended its Mission Street electric line west along Ocean Avenue, from the corner of Excelsior Avenue to the new Ingleside Racetrack, and laid the track in just six days. That route, later the #12 Mission & Ingleside, grew into one of the longest streetcar lines in the city before it was dropped in 1948 [1]. The 40-line interurban to San Mateo, which also ran down Mission Street, lasted into 1949. On the chilly night of Saturday, January 15, 1949, crowds gathered in San Mateo to ride its last cars. Motorman August Stokes, Muni's only veteran of the Spanish-American War, told a radio reporter: 'Don't like them to take it off' [2]. Back in San Francisco the cars stopped at the Geneva barn and then headed down Mission Street toward downtown. Railfan special No. 1235 was the last streetcar ever to run on Mission Street. The line was still covering its costs, but it needed $750,000 to $1,000,000 of new track and overhead wire, and the supervisors voted to abandon it without replacement. Trolley buses took over Mission Street on January 6, 1952 [2].

title: The Taj Mahal of West Coast jazz
place: Black Hawk nightclub site, Turk and Hyde streets (200-216 Hyde)
hook: Teenagers listened from a wire cage, Billie Holiday played her last West Coast club dates, and a 19-year-old Johnny Mathis got his big break.
story: From 1949 to 1963 a small club at Turk and Hyde drew the biggest names in jazz. It was run by Guido Cacianti with Johnny and Helen Noga [1]. In 1957 TIME called the Black Hawk "the Taj Mahal of West Coast jazz, where Dave Brubeck blew himself to fame" [2]. Under a deal with Mayor George Christopher, patrons under 21 could sit in a wire-fenced "cage" where they could hear the music without drinking [1]. Billie Holiday and Lester Young played their last West Coast club dates there [1]. The Modern Jazz Quartet played its first West Coast club date there [3]. In 1955 a young sextet brought 19-year-old Johnny Mathis to a Sunday jam session. Helen Noga decided to manage him and persuaded Columbia's George Avakian to come and hear him. Avakian wired his label: "Have found phenomenal 19 year old boy who could go all the way" [3]. Miles Davis recorded a live album there in April 1961 [3]. The building is gone, and the corner is a parking lot [3].

title: The boy who saved San Francisco's streetcars
place: 24th Street at Hoffman Avenue, old terminus of the 11-line
hook: In January 1949 the last 11-line streetcar pulled away from 24th and Hoffman. A Douglass Street teenager in the doorway went on to save Muni's first car.
story: The Market Street Railway's 11-line once ran up and down 24th Street. On January 15, 1949, a photograph shows Richard Schlaich standing in the door of the last 11-line car to leave 24th and Hoffman [1]. He was 17. Schlaich was born in 1931 and spent his whole life in a Douglass Street house his parents had bought new in 1915 [1]. As a boy at Alvarado School he rode streetcars all over the city, and the 11 was his favourite [1]. In 1951 Muni began scrapping its first streetcars, including car No. 1, the first publicly owned streetcar in the United States. The 20-year-old Schlaich talked railway officials and historians into saving it, and then into saving Market Street Railway car 578 too [1]. Both cars were put back in running order in 1956. They later became the start of today's historic F-line [1]. Schlaich also helped keep the zoo's 'Little Puffer' train from being auctioned. His photographs and papers now sit in San Francisco's railway archives, where historians still credit the 'Richard Schlaich collection' [1][2]. He died at home in 2004. That May, about 40 friends rode car No. 1 along his favourite routes, past Church and 24th [1].

title: The toy king of Clement Street
place: Site of Norman's Kingdom of Toys, 645-651 Clement St near 8th Ave
hook: A Navy officer and his wife opened a tiny party-favour shop in 1949. Within five years he was 'King Norman,' crowned on Saturday-morning television.
story: Norman Rosenberg, born in Chicago in 1918, was a naval officer stationed in San Francisco near the end of World War II when a blind date introduced him to Doris Brodofsky, whose family ran the Bell Bazaar notions store on 16th Street [1]. Urged into business by his father-in-law, the couple opened a small shop at 645 Clement Street in 1949, listed in directories as 'Norman's—party favors' [1]. Toys outsold everything, and by the late 1950s it was Norman's Kingdom of Toys, spilling into 651 Clement [1]. Doris invented a hit Easter gift by wrapping Woolworth's Easter grass and candy with a little pail in cellophane [1]. From 1954 until 1961 the King, in regal robes, hosted a Saturday-morning children's show on KGO-TV, Channel 7, with Doris as his assistant, Page Joy, handing toys to children from the studio audience [1][3]. Each Halloween the royal pair led a Clement Street merchants' parade that drew children by the thousands [1]. The kingdom grew to 21 stores by 1981 before the Rosenbergs sold the remaining shops to Kay-Bee Toys in the mid-1980s [1]. Doris died in 2008; Norman died in December 2016, aged 98 [2].

title: A Navy Jet in the Playground
place: Carl G. Larsen Park, 19th to 20th Avenues between Ulloa and Wawona
hook: For years, Sunset kids clambered over real military airplanes parked in their neighborhood park, one after another. Nobody at the time found this remotely strange.
story: In 1926 Carl Larsen, a Danish immigrant who ran the Tivoli Café downtown, gave the city two blocks between 19th and 20th Avenues, Ulloa and Wawona, "for park pleasure purposes." The park even had outdoor card rooms, one for men and one for women [1]. Its best-remembered feature came later. Sunset children of the 1950s and 1960s remember the military airplanes that sat there, one at a time, for years. They were life-sized toys to climb over and sit in [1]. One photograph shows Richard Lim and his son in "the first Navy jet" in Larsen Park [1]. Historian Lorri Ungaretti says the park is best remembered for the airplane children could climb over endlessly, and for Larsen Pool [2]. That pool, a "modern" one when those same children swam in it, is now the Charlie Sava Pool. It was renamed for a beloved swimming instructor who coached the Olympic swimmer Ann Curtis [2]. A bronze bust of Larsen by Melvin Earl Cummings, who also sculpted Sather Gate in Berkeley, still stands on a boulder at 19th Avenue and Ulloa [1]. The planes are gone.

title: A Union Hall Shaped Like a Ship
place: Sailors' Union of the Pacific, First and Harrison streets
hook: The state stopped the sailors' first building site for Bay Bridge test borings. So they moved a block over and built a white ship on land.
story: The Sailors' Union of the Pacific, founded in San Francisco in 1885, had long rented space along the waterfront, including the upper floors of the Audiffred Building [1][3]. In September 1947 it broke ground for a permanent headquarters at Fremont and Harrison. By March 1948 the state had halted work with a court order: the Division of Highways wanted the site for test borings for the neighbouring Bay Bridge [1]. The union moved to the corner of First and Harrison, and the new hall opened in 1950 [1]. Architect William Gladstone Merchant designed it in white stone and concrete in the Art Moderne style, with balconies shaped like parts of a ship, porthole windows and ship models in the lobby [1]. Its heart is the Dispatch Hall, where the union still matches sailors to berths, and the union's constitution requires a library in every hall [1]. Outside stand busts of two Norwegian-born leaders: Andrew Furuseth, who fought for the Seamen's Act of 1915, and Harry Lundeberg, who led the union from the mid-1930s until his death in 1957 [1][2]. The building sits near the site of the 1934 "Battle of Rincon Hill" [1].

title: Behind the Counter at Melrose Records
place: Melrose Record Shop, 1226 Fillmore Street (site, between Turk and Eddy)
hook: Before she was famous as Maya Angelou, a young woman sold jazz and blues records on Fillmore Street, beside a Louisiana Navy veteran who would open nightclubs.
story: Not every landmark of the Harlem of the West was a nightclub. At the Melrose Record Shop, 1226 Fillmore Street, neighbors bought the latest jazz and blues, and classical records too [1]. A photograph by David Johnson shows the shopfront around 1950 [2]. In the 1950s one of the clerks was a young woman who would become Maya Angelou; in the same years she was dancing professionally at the Purple Onion in North Beach [1]. Later, in I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings, she wrote about the Fillmore's clubs and bars [1]. Working alongside her was Joseph "Bunny" Simon, born in 1928 into a family of 16 in Lake Charles, Louisiana. He had joined the Navy at 15, was badly injured at Port Chicago, and settled in San Francisco after his discharge in 1946 [3]. It was his part-time job at Melrose that made clear his passion was music. He went on to open nightclubs of his own, starting on Divisadero Street in 1961 [3]. Like most of the business district around it, the shop's building was later demolished [1].

title: Chinatown's Five-Foot-Five Basketball Star
place: Chinese Playground (now Willie "Woo Woo" Wong Playground), Sacramento Street
hook: He climbed the playground gate before school to practise alone. By 1950 he was the first Chinese American to play in Madison Square Garden.
story: Willie Wong grew up in a Chinatown flat his family shared with another family, right across the street from the Chinese Playground [1]. His first 'basketball' was a tennis ball bounced off his bedroom ceiling. In 1939 an uncle he had never met arrived from New York and offered each child a gift, and Willie chose a real basketball [1]. He climbed the playground gate early each morning to practise alone. 'I was always the last guy picked for teams,' he recalled, and the others yelled at him not to shoot [1]. At 5 ft 5 and 125 pounds, he made the 1945 All-City team, the only Chinese player to do so, and the Examiner's Bob Brachman nicknamed him 'Woo Woo' after the crowd's chant [1][2]. He led the San Francisco Saints to two Asian American national titles, and Pete Newell recruited him to USF in 1948 [1]. At the 1950 NIT in New York, hundreds of Asian fans welcomed him as the first Chinese American to play in Madison Square Garden [1]. In 2006 the city renamed his playground on Sacramento Street after him [2].

title: Guadalajara Groceries among the Pellegrinis
place: Site of Guadalajara Mexican Groceries, 4421 Mission Street
hook: Around 1950, a Mexican grocery turned up in the city directory among the Cerrutis and Mulvihills. Within twenty years, the local census tract counted two Hispanic residents for every Italian.
story: In the early 1950s the San Francisco city directory showed something new on outer Mission Street. Among the Cerrutis, Mulvihills and Pellegrinis were Guadalajara Mexican Groceries at 4421 Mission and residents such as Mary Sandoval at 4449 and Manuel Gonzales at 4789 [1]. Latino families were moving out from North Beach, South of Market and the Tenderloin, and new immigrants were arriving from Mexico and Central America [1]. The census counts for one Excelsior tract tell the story. In 1950 it had 1,006 Italians and 772 'Hispanics'. By 1960 Hispanics had pulled ahead, 1,868 to 1,779. By 1970 the Italian count had barely moved, at 1,728, while the Hispanic count had doubled to 3,714 [1]. In the 1970s researcher Phylis Martinelli interviewed old-time 'villagers'. She found that the two groups went to the same churches, shops and schools without overt discrimination, though some Italians resented the newcomers [1]. In the 1980s refugees from Central America's wars added to the neighbourhood [2]. Oscar Grande, a son of Salvadoran immigrants, has described growing up here with deep ties to the Mission [3].

title: Holloway's Corner Stores and the Suitcase Man
place: Holloway Avenue near Plymouth Avenue, Ingleside
hook: Italian grocers, then Black-owned markets and barbershops, then a man with cash offers: seventy years of change on one quiet Ingleside street.
story:
Ray Wilson remembered four little groceries in the 1950s on Holloway Avenue between City College and Ashton. The biggest was Paul Selmi's at Ashton, which stocked "everything that Safeway now would have." The smaller mom-and-pops resented it [1].

After the war, Black families moved into the Ingleside, where no racial covenants kept them out. Al Harris, who has lived at Grafton and Granada for about 50 years, remembered a Black-owned market, cleaners and café on the street [2]. Renard Monroe of Youth 1st got his hair cut at a barbershop called Kings and Queens [2]. Then, Harris said, came "the suitcase man," who put up "We buy houses" signs on telephone poles. He offered the grown children who inherited their parents' homes "$450,000 cash money," and many took it and moved to Oakland, Antioch and Pittsburg [2]. In the 1970s Harris had seven or eight Black families nearby. By 2026 there was one [2].

Holloway is still a street of small shops. Malik Rodgers runs Tailored Cuts, one of the last Black-owned businesses. Cool Guys Market at 845 Holloway had been there almost 30 years by 2024. The deli inside sells a "Rev G" sandwich, named for Ingleside Presbyterian's Rev. Roland Gordon [2][3].

title: Knights' hall becomes a Fillmore church
place: Macedonia Missionary Baptist Church (former Knights Templar hall), 2135 Sutter Street
hook: A Black congregation bought a Masonic hall full of winged knights. Martin Luther King preached there, and after Jonestown its pastor buried Peoples Temple members.
story: The Knights Templar's Golden Gate Commandery was still being built on Sutter between Steiner and Pierce when the 1906 earthquake struck. It finally opened in October 1907, trimmed with terra-cotta shields, winged knights and sculpted heads [1][2]. By mid-century fraternal orders were losing members. In 1950 the commandery moved to Van Ness and sold the building to Macedonia Baptist Church, a mostly African American congregation from the Western Addition and the Fillmore [1]. Under Rev. P. S. Ogborne it grew to 2,000 members by his death in 1957. His successor, Rev. G. L. Bedford, came from a Los Angeles church, paid off the mortgage and renamed it Macedonia Missionary Baptist Church [1]. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. preached two services there on Sunday, 26 February 1967 [1][3]. Then the congregation began to shrink. Redevelopment scattered families, and some members left for Jim Jones's Peoples Temple [1]. After the deaths in Guyana in November 1978, Rev. Bedford buried a number of Peoples Temple members [1]. The building became City Landmark No. 202 in January 1993 [1][2].

title: Sandwiches at the rectory's back door
place: St. Anthony's Dining Room (former film exchange), 121 Golden Gate Avenue, beside St. Boniface Church
hook: Next to a German church rebuilt from a fire-gutted shell, a Franciscan was tired of watching hungry people eat on street corners.
story: When the 1906 fire swept the Tenderloin, almost the only thing left inside today's historic district was the burned shell of St. Boniface Church on Golden Gate Avenue [1]. The Franciscans rebuilt it in 1906 as a Romanesque church for San Francisco's German Catholics [1]. As the neighbourhood changed, the parish turned more and more to the poor and homeless [1]. In 1950 its pastor, Father Alfred Boeddeker, began handing out sandwiches from the rectory's back door [2]. The St. Anthony Foundation says he was "frustrated to see hungry men and women forced to eat on the street corners" and wanted a place where everyone could sit down to a hot meal together [2]. That year the foundation took over a 1912 film-exchange building at 101-127 Golden Gate and turned it into a dining room [1]. The kitchen kept growing. In 1962 President John F. Kennedy sent a telegram congratulating it on six million meals [2]. Today a small park at Jones and Eddy carries the Boeddeker name [3].

title: Swapping Sandwiches at Lafayette School
place: Lafayette School, Anza Street near 37th Avenue
hook: After the war, families from North Beach, the Mission and the Fillmore met in one schoolyard, where lunch was the first thing that got traded.
story:
After World War II, one former pupil wrote, the Richmond became a "first stop melting pot" for families leaving crowded ethnic enclaves: Italians from North Beach, Irish from the Mission, Ukrainians and Russians from the Fillmore and Divisadero, Chinese from Grant Avenue. They met at Lafayette School on Anza Street [1].

Victor Berardelli swapped his mother's Italian eggplant sandwich for a friend's pastrami or another boy's empanada. In the late 1940s and early 1950s, teachers were assigned to schools in their own neighbourhoods, so a teacher might spot you misbehaving on Balboa Street and mention it at the PTA. Classmates compared fathers' war stories. One boy's father never came home. One day, when a grandmother's sweater sleeve slipped, Berardelli saw numbers tattooed on her forearm. Catholic children walked to catechism and Jewish children to Hebrew school, while Chinese children rode a bus across town to Chinese classes [1].

In 1930 voters approved a tax increase to build a branch library, and the Anza Branch was built on the site of the old Lafayette School. It opened on April 10, 1932, with 11,823 new books [2].

title: The champion who shamed tennis
place: Alice Marble Tennis Courts, Greenwich St between Hyde and Larkin
hook: The courts on top of Russian Hill are named for a San Francisco girl who became a Wimbledon champion, then used her fame to open tennis to Althea Gibson.
story: The tennis courts on the summit of Russian Hill carry the name of Alice Marble [1]. She grew up in San Francisco, played seven sports at Polytechnic High and, at 13, was the mascot of the San Francisco Seals baseball team [2]. In 1934 tuberculosis put her in the hospital, and she was told she would never play again. With her coach, Eleanor "Teach" Tennant, she fought back. She won U.S. singles titles in 1936, 1938, 1939 and 1940 and Wimbledon in 1939, and her serve-and-volley game drew sneers that she played "like a man" [2]. Her bravest shot came in 1950. In the July 1 issue of American Lawn Tennis magazine, she challenged the sport's exclusion of Althea Gibson: "If tennis is a game for ladies and gentlemen, it's also time we acted a little more like gentle-people and less like sanctimonious hypocrites." [1] Gibson, who went on to win Wimbledon and the U.S. title in 1957 and 1958, said Marble's intervention helped break tennis's color barrier. "She was my idol," Gibson said when Marble died in 1990 [2].
