title: The church that moved down the avenues
place: Park Presidio Baptist Church, 10th Ave & Cabrillo St
hook: In 1950 a 42-year-old wooden Gothic church left its corner at 9th and Anza and was hauled to a new congregation at 10th and Cabrillo.
story: Zion Lutheran Church built a wooden Gothic church in 1908 on the northwest corner of 9th Avenue and Anza Street [1]. In 1950 Zion sold the building to the Park Presidio Baptist Church, and the whole structure was moved a few blocks to its present site at 10th Avenue and Cabrillo Street [1][2]. The San Francisco Public Library holds photographs of the move in progress; a note filed with a 1964 picture of the new Zion church on the old corner records that 'in 1950 the former building on this site was moved to 10th and Cabrillo and became Park Presidio Baptist' [1][2]. Both congregations stayed woven into neighbourhood life: Rodney Jeung, growing up on 12th Avenue, was taken by his grandmother to Zion Lutheran every Sunday as a young boy, and later his brother Russell attended too [2]. The 1908 building, a Lutheran church turned Baptist, still serves its congregation at 10th and Cabrillo [1].

title: The letter that rewired Kerouac
place: 29 Russell St
hook: From a little Russian Hill alley, a railroad brakeman mailed an 18-page, unpunctuated rush of memory that Kerouac called the greatest writing he'd ever seen.
story: In December 1950, Neal Cassady was living at 29 Russell Street and working as a brakeman for the Southern Pacific railroad [1][2]. On December 17 he finished a long letter to Jack Kerouac about his wild youth in Denver and a young woman named Joan Anderson. It had few paragraph breaks and almost no punctuation. Kerouac described its style as "spontaneous bop-pros-ody" and wrote back that it was "the greatest piece of writing I ever saw." Many scholars believe it pushed him away from writing like a traditional novelist and toward Cassady's free-form, stream-of-consciousness style [1]. Then the letter vanished. Kerouac passed it to Allen Ginsberg, and Ginsberg passed it to poet Gerd Stern, who lived on a barge in Sausalito. Ginsberg later accused Stern of dropping it overboard. Stern denied it, calling Ginsberg "a mischievous son of a bitch." In May 2012 the letter turned up in the Oakland home office of the late record producer Jack Spinosa. After lawsuits from the Kerouac and Cassady estates, it was auctioned, and Emory University paid $206,250 [1][2].

title: The professor who wouldn't sign
place: Winfield Street
hook: At 23 she was SF State's youngest journalism professor. Then she refused a loyalty oath, and the FBI followed her for fifteen years.
story:
Phiz Mezey came west from New York by way of Reed College. By 23 she was the youngest journalism professor at San Francisco State, and her writing had already appeared in the New Republic, the New York Times and The Nation [1]. In 1950 a student editor of the Golden Gater, whom she had failed, told administrators she had 'Communist leanings' [1]. That year California passed the Levering Act, which required every state employee to swear an oath disavowing radical beliefs [1][2]. Mezey refused to sign. 'I will not sign the loyalty oath now because I know that hereafter no teacher can adequately be protected under the law,' she wrote to the college president. She was fired along with eight others [1].

The FBI watched her for fifteen years and cost her at least one factory job [1]. She became a freelance photographer and shot portraits of Martin Luther King Jr. and James Baldwin, and later the 1968 SF State strike [1]. The California Supreme Court struck the Levering Act down in 1967 [1][2]. SF State hired her again in 1978 and made her a full professor in 1981. She lived for years on Winfield Street, surrounded by succulents and her own photographs [1].

title: Tortillas by hand at 21st and Harrison
place: 21st and Harrison Streets
hook: 'You hardly ever heard anybody speaking English.' After the war, Latino families pushed out of other barrios made the Mission their home.
story:
Sam Rios grew up near 21st and Harrison. His family had moved to the Mission before the war, when they got the chance to own a home. His grandmother started a small tortilla factory on that corner: 'her and her comadres they used to sit around this comal and make tortillas by hand', then sold them door to door [1]. Even in the late 1930s, Rios recalled, 'I used to run up and down 24th Street. And you hardly ever heard anybody speaking English' [1].

More followed. The Bay Bridge was built through the South of Market barrio around Rincon Hill, and the Broadway Tunnel split the North Beach barrio around Guadalupe Church. Families moved south along the grid into the working-class Mission, much as Germans, Irish and Scandinavians had before them [1]. They worked in shipyards, canneries on 18th Street and factories such as the Levi Strauss plant [1]. The neighbourhood changed to match: by the 1950s the old Victoria Theatre on 16th Street was showing films in Spanish as El Teatro Victoria [2]. Between 1950 and 1970 the Spanish-surnamed share of the district's population grew from 11 percent to more than 45 percent [1].

title: Two a.m. to six at Bop City
place: Jimbo's Bop City, 1690 Post Street (original site)
hook: A dollar got you in, musicians came free, and if Jimbo didn't like your attitude, no amount of money would open the door.
story: From 1950 to 1965, Jimbo Edwards ran an after-hours jazz club at 1690 Post Street, open roughly from 2 to 6 a.m. Musicians got in free; everyone else paid a dollar [1][2]. Edwards said he put up a neon sign, befriended Billy Eckstine, "and after Billy Eckstine made it, then here come Miles. Here come Diz. And here come Charlie Parker" [1]. The city's landmark listing adds John Coltrane, Ella Fitzgerald and Billie Holiday to the roster [2]. Edwards would not tolerate racial discrimination, and white and Black players and fans mixed at a time when that was rare; one regular called it "3:00 AM" in "the early dawn of the civil rights movement" [1]. The filmmaker Harry Smith painted abstract murals on the walls [3]. By 1965 the clubs that fed it had closed, and Edwards was left "sitting with an empty club" [1]. The Victorian itself survived: in 1978 it was moved to 1712 Fillmore as the Redevelopment Agency cleared the area [2].

title: Two hilltops bulldozed into a shopping centre
place: Diamond Heights Shopping Center and Christopher Playground, Diamond Heights Boulevard (the filled saddle between Red Rock and Gold Mine hills)
hook: In 1950 the city declared cow pasture, quarries and cottages "blighted." Then it shaved the tops off two hills and pushed the dirt into the gap between.
story:
Until the 1950s, the hills above Glen Park were used for grazing and quarrying. The streets had been drawn on paper as a grid that ran straight up 20 to 35 percent grades [1]. In 1950 the San Francisco Redevelopment Agency marked out 332 acres across Red Rock, Gold Mine and Fairmount hills as "Redevelopment Area B" and named it Diamond Heights, after the street that climbed into it [1]. It counted about 450 homes, two truck yards, a radio transmitter and a single corner grocery, and it called the area one of "arrested development" [1]. A 1955 Agency description called it "a predominantly open, blighted area" [2].

Residents, mostly blue-collar workers, said there was no blight and worried they would not get a fair price for their homes [1]. The plan was approved in 1952 and then stalled for four years over land prices and legal challenges to its definition of blight. By 1959 the Agency had bought half the private land, and it condemned the rest [1]. Bulldozers levelled the summits of Red Rock and Gold Mine hills and pushed about 2 million cubic yards of dirt into the saddle between them. The Diamond Heights Shopping Center and Christopher Playground now stand on that fill. The shopping centre opened in 1965 [1].

title: A Ranch House Among the Mansions
place: 535 El Camino del Mar
hook: In 1951 a theatre architect built a low courtyard ranch house in Sea Cliff. The type is so rare in San Francisco that planners later called it historic.
story: Most of Sea Cliff was built between about 1910 and 1930, mostly in French and Mediterranean, Spanish Revival, Edwardian and Arts and Crafts–Tudor styles [1]. After the Second World War the remaining empty lots were sold, and several got modern houses that broke sharply with the older look [1][2]. One was 535 El Camino del Mar, commissioned in 1951 by Milton Meyer. Its architect, J. Lloyd Conrich, had worked for Hyman & Appleton and for Bakewell & Brown. Over his career he designed at least 31 theatres, the KPIX station on Van Ness Avenue and the Zanzibar Cocktail Lounge on Ocean Avenue [1]. The house is a single storey, U-shaped around a central courtyard, with floor-to-ceiling glass opening views to the Pacific [1]. The ranch house is rare in San Francisco, planners noted, because it uses up land that a dense, vertical city can't spare. In 2012 they found the house individually eligible for the California Register [1]. From 1960 until her death in 2009 it was home to Mariedi Anders, who ran a business managing concert musicians from the house [1]. Other modernists followed, including William Wurster at 850 El Camino del Mar in 1958 (since altered) and Joseph Esherick at No. 890 in 1963 [1].

title: A Two-by-Four Behind the Garage Door
place: Chinn family home, 539 29th Avenue
hook: A Chinese American math teacher bought a house on 29th Avenue through a go-between. The death threats that followed were kept from his children.
story:
William G. Chinn grew up in Chinatown, served as an Air Corps meteorologist in World War II and became a San Francisco public school maths teacher. He first tried to buy a house in Santa Clara and met "extreme resistance, threats" [1]. So in 1951 he used a third party to buy a single-family house at 539 29th Avenue [1].

His daughter Lenore, who was two when they moved, learned only later that there had been death threats. The real estate agent and the go-between warned her parents to wedge a two-by-four behind the garage doors. Her father refused to move [1]. She recalled "only a handful of Japanese and a sprinkling of Chinese" around her, no Hispanic or African American neighbours, and trips with her father to the de Young and the Legion of Honor [1][2].

Lenore graduated from Washington High in 1967. She became a photorealist painter whose large portraits centre queer people and people of colour, and a founder of the Queer Cultural Center [1][2][3]. His Chronicle obituary later remembered her father as a past president of the Mathematics Association of America [1].

title: A museum for kids on quarry hill
place: Randall Museum, 199 Museum Way, Corona Heights
hook: The city's recreation chief found a scarred quarry hill in 1928. Twenty-three years later it held a children's museum with live animals and sweeping views.
story: Corona Heights looks jagged because it was quarried for decades. Kilns on its slopes exploded and collapsed in the 1906 earthquake, and the quarrying stopped [1]. In 1928 Josephine Randall, San Francisco's first superintendent of recreation, visited the scarred hill. She later proposed that the city buy 'Rocky Hill' as a recreation site [1][2]. She had already started a children's nature museum. The Junior Museum opened in 1937 in the city's old jail on Ocean Avenue, and it was only the second children's museum west of the Mississippi [2][3]. In 1947 she steered a $12 million recreation bond through, which paid for a permanent home [3]. The new museum opened on the hill on September 23, 1951, and was named the Josephine D. Randall Junior Museum in her honour [1][2]. She called it a place 'in the very heart of the city where our young people could be carried away from the traffic and noise and spend a happy day in the country' [2]. It still sits on a 16-acre park [3]. Its animal room cares for injured or human-imprinted wildlife that cannot return to the wild, and admission is still free [2][3].

title: Bimbo and the girl in the fishbowl
place: Bimbo's 365 Club, 1025 Columbus Ave
hook: A Tuscan janitor renamed by a boss who couldn't say 'Agostino' built a supper club where a woman seems to swim nude behind the bar.
story: Agostino Giuntoli left Tuscany in 1922 at 19 and spent five years working his way to San Francisco, where he found a job as a janitor at the Palace Hotel. He became a cook for Monk Young, who could not pronounce his name and called him "Bimbo," Italian for boy [1]. In 1931 the two opened the 365 Club at 365 Market Street. Rita Cansino, later known as Rita Hayworth, kicked in its chorus line, and gin was served in coffee cups. The club's famous illusion was Dolfina, the Girl in the Fishbowl, who seemed to swim nude in a tank behind the bar [1]. In 1951 Bimbo's moved to Columbus Avenue at the edge of Russian Hill, fishbowl and all [1][2]. Chronicle columnist Herb Caen remembered "jugglers, dance teams, stand-up comics, crooners, chantootsies" and a band in proper uniforms [1]. The family still runs it. Bimbo's son-in-law Graziano Cerchiai and grandsons Michael and Gino Cerchiai have hosted acts from Robin Williams to Adele and Lizzo. The city has listed it on its Legacy Business Registry [1][2].

title: Christmas trays and 75-cent hamburgers
place: St. Mary's Hospital, 2200 Hayes Street, at the vanished end of Grove Street
hook: At St. Mary's on Hayes Street, a new mother kept the Nativity card from her Christmas breakfast tray, and schoolboys slipped in for cheap burgers and a cigarette machine.
story: St. Mary's Hospital settled at 2200 Hayes Street, between Shrader and Stanyan, by 1909, and it stayed there for more than six decades [1]. In late December 1918, as the influenza pandemic filled whole sections of local cemeteries, the sculptor Haig Patigian was admitted in critical condition. He did not recover until February 1919 [2]. On Christmas Day 1951 a new mother kept the small printed cardboard Nativity scene from her breakfast tray and wrote on the back: "From my breakfast tray at St. Mary's Hospital—December 25, 1951, just after Frankie was born" [3]. Frankie grew up to be the Western Neighborhoods columnist Frank Dunnigan [1][3]. That same year the hospital's nursing school graduates began receiving bachelor's degrees from the University of San Francisco next door [1]. In the 1960s, St. Ignatius boys from Stanyan Street treated the hospital cafeteria, reached from Grove Street, as their best source of cheap hot food: thick, generous hamburgers for 75 cents, and a cigarette machine out of the Jesuits' sight [4]. In 1972 a new hospital building replaced the old one and took the address 450 Stanyan Street [1]. Sometime in the 1970s the multi-storey nurses' dormitory was torn down and the last block of Grove Street was closed [4].

title: Deli, laundromat and five-and-dime at Laurel Village
place: Laurel Village shops, 3401 California Street (California St between Laurel and Spruce)
hook: A 1951 city tax photo shows a strip of butchers, bakers and a Feed Bag diner. Seventy years later only two of its shops were left.
story: In 1951 a city assessor's photographer took pictures along California Street at Laurel Village. At 3401 California they show the Feed Bag Restaurant, Hanken's Delicatessen, Joe Klein's Choice Meats and the Winfield Sage Laundromat [1]. Other storefronts ran west along California: a Danish pastry shop, dry cleaner, hardware store, furniture showroom, beauty salon, supermarket, produce store, liquor store, florist, television store and a real estate and insurance office. There was also a Standard 5 & 10 [1]. A shop called Young Man's Fancy dressed "the younger set" here in Bruce Bary clothes from the end of World War II until the turn of the millennium. The columnist who remembers it notes you don't see many little boys in navy blazers any more [2]. Harold Dobbs, a co-founder of Mel's Drive-In, also co-founded the Red Roof restaurants, one of them on California Street near Laurel Village. Dobbs was a supervisor and ran for mayor in 1963, 1967 and 1971 [3]. Tastes and rents changed. The A.G. Ferrari delicatessen here closed in 2017 [4]. By 2022, of the whole 1951 line-up, only the grocery (now CalMart) and the Standard 5 & 10, partnered with Ace Hardware, were still open [1].

title: Keeping Washington Square a green
place: Washington Square, Columbus Ave & Union St
hook: North Beach's front lawn had sheltered refugee tents in 1906. In the 1950s the neighbourhood had to fight off first a library, then a parking garage.
story: Washington Square has been North Beach's living room for more than a century. After the 1906 earthquake and fire, some 600 people lived there for a year in tents and wooden barracks [1][2]. In the 1920s it hosted Italian festivals and the Columbus Day parade, and in 1924 the Salesians celebrated the completion of Saints Peter and Paul Church across Filbert Street, a project begun in 1912 [1]. In 1951 the city planned to build the North Beach branch library in the middle of the square. Father Costanzo of Saints Peter and Paul led the fight to keep it an open green [1]. In the mid-1950s a coalition called the Committee to Beautify Washington Square commissioned a redesign. It removed the paths that crossed the park and ringed a central lawn with benches and Lombardy poplars. The design is usually credited to Lawrence Halprin and Douglas Baylis, though one account says Halprin's plan was over budget and Francis McCarthy worked with Baylis instead [1][2][3]. In 1958 a plan to dig a parking garage under the square was defeated. It kept coming back until the park was made a city landmark in 2000 [2].

title: The Booker T., Where the Stars Slept
place: Booker T. Washington Hotel, 1540 Ellis Street (site, near Fillmore)
hook: Often unwelcome in downtown hotels, Nat King Cole, Dinah Washington and W.E.B. Du Bois checked into a six-story hotel off Fillmore, where Slim Gaillard sometimes ran the kitchen.
story: The six-story, 115-room building at 1540 Ellis opened in 1910 as a rooming house. In the 1940s, as the Hotel Edison, it had a notorious reputation [1]. In August 1951 it was remodeled at a cost of $100,000 and renamed the Booker T. Washington Hotel [1]. Accounts differ over who owned what: one credits a buyer named William Bush, another says the colorful Shirley "Fats" Corlett renamed it and the promoter Charles Sullivan bought it [1][2]. What is agreed is that its lobby lounge, booked by Sullivan, became a jazz room; saxophonist Ben Webster opened it on January 31, 1952 [1]. At a time when downtown hotels often turned Black guests away, the Booker T. was where they stayed [3]. A 1953 Sun-Reporter list of guests included Louis Jordan, the Nat King Cole Trio, Dinah Washington, Joe Louis, the Harlem Globetrotters and W.E.B. Du Bois, and Slim Gaillard would take over the kitchen to cook for musicians [1]. Sullivan, the self-made "Mayor of Fillmore," was found shot dead south of Market in 1966; police called it suicide, but the coroner disagreed [2]. The hotel was torn down in 1970, and its address no longer exists [1][3].

title: They Stopped the Clock for a Library
place: Parkside Branch Library, 1200 Taraval Street at McCoppin Square
hook: When City Hall cut their library from the budget, Parkside residents stopped the clock at midnight and talked until the money came back.
story: After a 1948 library bond failed, San Francisco's library had to win money for new branches one at a time through the city budget. On the day the supervisors were to approve the budget, according to a 1952 Chronicle account, "Parkside people descended on City Hall in droves" to protest the cutting of their branch. As the deadline neared, "the people stopped the clock in City Hall at midnight and staged a filibuster till the money was put back in" [1]. Until then the Parkside's library had been a rented storefront at 1541 Taraval [1]. The new branch opened on June 21, 1951, on the edge of McCoppin Square. It was designed by Appleton & Wolfard with landscaping by Lawrence Halprin and cost $162,171 [1]. The Chronicle called it the "finest branch library in the country." Architect and Engineer compared its turquoise, yellow and natural-brick colors to "a refined night club" [2]. It had a copper-hooded fireplace, a cork floor and radiant heating, and twice as many people used it as the old storefront. City librarian Laurence Clarke said a library had to "merchandise its services" like a good bookshop [2]. It was the first of eight Appleton & Wolfard branches, and in 2023 it became a city landmark [1].

title: Undefeated, untied and uninvited
place: Burl A. Toler Hall (formerly Phelan Hall), USF
hook: USF's 1951 team went 9-0 and was offered a bowl game if it left its Black stars at home. The players refused. In 2017 a hall got a new name.
story: The 1951 USF Dons went 9-0 and were one of the great college football teams. Their two African American stars were running back Ollie Matson and linebacker Burl Toler [1][2]. The team was offered a place in the Orange Bowl on condition that it leave its Black players behind, and it said no [3]. No bowl invitation came, and USF, losing $70,000 a year on football, dropped the sport [2]. Toler, a Memphis native, was the Cleveland Browns' top draft pick, but he wrecked his knee in the College All-Star Game and never played in the NFL. He became the league's first Black on-field official and worked three Super Bowls [2]. In San Francisco he became the city's first African American secondary school principal [1], and Benjamin Franklin Middle School was renamed for him in 2006 [2]. That year the 1951 team received honorary degrees: "They sacrificed glory for honor and character" [1]. On May 9, 2017, students led by Student Senate President Shaya Kara got Phelan Hall renamed. The dorm had honoured former mayor James Phelan, whose 1920 campaign slogan was "Keep California White." It is now Burl A. Toler Hall [1].

title: Wells, septic tanks and streets on paper
place: 1300 block of Bowdoin Street, on the park's eastern edge
hook: In 1951 families were still living inside McLaren Park, drawing water from wells and driving homemade roads because the official streets were too steep to build.
story: Even after the city started buying land for McLaren Park, people were still living on it. A 1951 report to the San Francisco Redevelopment Agency found scattered homes, small farms, nurseries and greenhouses both inside and outside the park's official boundaries [1]. Subdividers from the 1860s onward had drawn a gridiron of streets straight up the hills, and many of those streets were 'no more than lines on paper'. So residents ignored them and followed gentler grades on improvised roads to reach their property [1]. No water lines or sewers had been installed in the park, and the homes there relied on wells and septic tanks. Elsewhere in the study area the planners counted a truckyard, a junk yard and a number of stables. Many families had lived on large plots for more than 50 years, and several big parcels still belonged to the 'old settlers' [1]. At the same time, builders were finishing new row houses on University, Colby and Bowdoin streets. The lots were so poorly graded that the back yards could wash away in wet weather [1]. Oral histories remember an older, rural life. After the Leotta family settled on Leland Avenue in 1917, someone from Knudson's farm, where Sunnydale and Visitacion met the future park, brought them a bucket of eggs every week or so [2].

title: A Secret Rendezvous at the Legion
place: California Palace of the Legion of Honor, 100 34th Avenue
hook: Six years before Vertigo, another thriller used the Legion for a secret meeting: two lovers who plan to murder Joan Crawford, at a Bach organ recital.
story: Six years before Hitchcock brought Vertigo here, the Legion of Honor played a part in Sudden Fear. It was a 1952 thriller directed by David Miller from a novel by Edna Sherry [1]. Joan Crawford plays Myra Hudson, a rich playwright who fires the actor Lester Blaine, played by Jack Palance, from her Broadway play. She then falls for him on the train home to San Francisco and marries him. Then his old lover Irene Neves, played by Gloria Grahame, turns up, and the two plan to kill Myra for her money [1]. In the location list compiled by Reel SF, the scene where the old flame shows up is at the Palace of the Legion of Honor [1]. Other accounts set the lovers' secret rendezvous at a Bach organ recital in the museum [2]. That organ, a 1924 Skinner, hides its 4,526 pipes in the building. Its sound comes through canvas painted to look like stucco [3]. The New York Times praised how the director used the 'steep streets and panoramic views' of San Francisco and Los Angeles [4]. Crawford and Palance were both nominated for Oscars, and François Truffaut called the film 'a masterpiece of cinema' [1].

title: A Surf Shop Where Wetsuits Began
place: Site of Jack O'Neill's first Surf Shop, Great Highway near Wawona Street
hook: Freezing at Ocean Beach, a bodysurfer started tinkering with foam and neoprene in a Great Highway garage. A friend told him he'd sell to five guys and go broke.
story: In the 1940s Jack O'Neill was one of a handful of people bodysurfing the icy water off Ocean Beach. Wetsuits didn't exist, and the only way to warm up afterwards was a bonfire [1]. O'Neill experimented with foam vests. He said the breakthrough came in 1952, when Harry Hind, a pharmacist and fellow bodysurfer, suggested neoprene [1]. His first customers bought the vests at the surf shop he had just opened on the Great Highway near Wawona Street [1], one of the first surf shops anywhere. He later trademarked the term "surf shop" but never enforced it [2]. "O'Neill, you're going to sell to five guys on the beach and you're out," fellow surfer Charlie Grimm told him. With so few surfers in San Francisco, O'Neill later admitted Grimm had a point [1]. In 1959 he moved his family and business to Santa Cruz, where the waves were friendlier and there were more surfers. The O'Neill wetsuit went on to be the world's best seller [1][3]. The origin story is disputed. Accounts of the date vary, and UC Berkeley physicist Hugh Bradner had already tested neoprene diving suits in 1950. What O'Neill added was a nylon lining that made neoprene practical for surfing [3].

title: A crowded house on 12th Avenue
place: 510 12th Ave near Anza St
hook: When a young Chinese American couple bought a $13,000 house far from Chinatown, they moved his seven siblings in too. Their son would later found Stop AAPI Hate.
story: Albert Jeung, a San Francisco native and Army veteran, married Bernice Shue in 1951, and in 1952 the couple bought 510 12th Avenue for a 'whopping $13,000' with a veteran's loan [1]. Albert's father had died, so they moved his seven siblings out of the family's Washington Street home in Chinatown; with the couple and a grandmother, the three-bedroom house with a sunroom was packed. Fittingly, a 1949 advertisement for the house had asked, 'Are you crowded in your present home?' [1]. It was a bold choice: their son Rodney recalls his mother saying there were places along California Street or Parker Avenue where Chinese people weren't allowed to buy, and on their block there was maybe one other Chinese family [1]. Dinners were hamburgers and meatloaf with rice and tea. After school Rodney was sent to Chinese classes at St. James Episcopal on California Street and then Chinese Grace Baptist at 10th and Balboa; he once padlocked his teacher to his chair [1]. His younger brother Russell, born in 1963 and spared Chinese school by busing, became a San Francisco State sociologist and in 2020 co-founded Stop AAPI Hate to track anti-Asian attacks during the pandemic [1][2]. Rodney still lives in the house, with much of the same furniture [1].

title: Balboa High invents the Bunny Hop
place: Balboa High School, Cayuga Avenue at Onondaga Avenue
hook: Before it was a wedding-reception staple, the Bunny Hop was a conga-line joke dreamed up by Balboa High teenagers in 1952.
story: In spring 1952, word reached the bandleader Ray Anthony that teenagers at San Francisco's Balboa High School had made up a new dance. Time magazine called them the school's "Coke set" [1]. It was a version of the conga line. Dancers hold the hips of the person in front, tap each foot twice, hop forward and back, then take three hops forward, over and over, while the leader snakes the line around the room [2]. Anthony saw a hit. Time wrote that he "contrived a tuneless tune", recorded it for Capitol, ordered a batch of fuzzy bunny ears as costume, and promoted the song and dance across the country [1]. By January 1953 the magazine said dance halls shook "under the thud of teen-age feet" and every verse ended "Hop! Hop! Hop!" [1]. Parents approved of it as relatively sedate, if energetic, and disc jockeys and Capitol's publicists helped turn it into "a minor teen-age mania" [1]. The craze faded, but the dance lived on long after it. It began with teenagers in the pink Spanish Colonial Revival school on Cayuga Avenue, which opened in 1928 [2][3].

title: Cabbage Fields to the Big E
place: Stonestown, 19th Avenue and Winston Drive
hook: Two brothers turned cabbage fields into the fourth-largest apartment and shopping complex in the United States, and dotted it with palm trees.
story: In July 1949 the San Francisco News reported "a small city" rising west of 19th Avenue: Stonestown, the $23 million project of builders Ellis and Henry Stoneson [1]. On 67 acres of former cabbage fields and golf links, it would hold 783 rental units for 3,000 to 3,500 people, including four ten-story apartment houses of 90 flats each [1]. The Emporium department store, with its big "E" visible from 19th Avenue, opened its branch on July 16, 1952, and the center officially opened that November [1][2]. Walgreens, Woolworth's, Gallenkamp Shoes and the Red Chimney restaurant followed [1]. The Stonesons sold the open-air mall with celebrity ribbon-cuttings, parades and fairs, and were early adopters of palm trees on a grand scale [1]. Credit for the design is muddled: the Western Neighborhoods Project lists architect Angus McSweeney, while a 1951 News caption says Welton Becket designed the entire center [1]. In 1987 architect John Field added a second level of shops, a glass atrium and marble floors, and it reopened as Stonestown Galleria [1][2].

title: Eighty-nine years to dig a tunnel
place: Broadway Tunnel west portal, Broadway near Hyde St
hook: The right to bore through Russian Hill was granted in 1863, complete with tolls on animals. Cars finally drove through almost nine decades later.
story: In 1863 the state granted Abner Doble and his partners the right to tunnel through Russian Hill along Broadway, from Mason to Hyde or Larkin, and to charge tolls on animals and vehicles [1]. Nothing happened. In 1913 a tunnel was proposed again, and one landowner called it "absolutely as unnecessary as a bridge to the moon" [1]. By 1949 the Chronicle counted "eighty-five years of false starts" before voters finally approved a $5 million bond in 1948 [2][1]. The 1948 Trafficways Plan saw the tunnel as a link between the planned Embarcadero and Central freeways [1]. Before work could start, an apartment building at 1453 Mason Street was moved to Vallejo Street. Morrison-Knudsen won the contract with a bid of $5,243,355 and began digging in May 1950 [1]. Loose rock required extra shoring, delaying the planned May 1952 finish. Mayor Elmer Robinson cut the ribbon on December 21, 1952, and the final cost was about $7.3 million [1]. The twin 1,616-foot bores still carry traffic under the hill. In 1986 the tunnel was named for city engineer Robert C. Levy [1].

title: Kerouac, brakeman on the railroad earth
place: Southern Pacific depot site, Third and Townsend
hook: Before he was King of the Beats, Jack Kerouac punched in for the Southern Pacific here, living in a $4-a-week Skid Row room.
story: In 1951 Neal Cassady, a Southern Pacific brakeman, persuaded his friend Jack Kerouac to join him in San Francisco. Kerouac started as a baggage handler and became a brakeman [1]. The railroad's main station stood at Third and Townsend, the last stop for commuter trains from San Jose and the start of long-distance runs to Los Angeles, with the company yards spreading across Mission Bay [1]. In 1952 he wrote to Allen Ginsberg about his 'fine little room in Skid Row at $4 a week', where he was 'happy for the first time in years' [1]. He also grumbled: 'The phone just called me, gotta go to work again, I'm sick and tired of it' [1]. Cassady broke his ankle on the job trying to avert a crash [1]. Out of those shifts came 'October in the Railroad Earth', a prose poem that opens among the commuters at the Southern Pacific station and that Kerouac said was meant to 'clack along all the way like a steam engine pulling a one-hundred-car-freight' [1]. It was collected in Lonesome Traveler (1960), his first openly autobiographical book [2].

title: Marching to McAllister Street
place: Third Baptist Church, 1399 McAllister Street (at Pierce)
hook: In 1952 the oldest Black Baptist congregation in the West tore down a pioneer's mansion with its own hands, and marched in to a modern church.
story: Third Baptist began in 1852 as the First Colored Baptist Church of San Francisco, the first African American Baptist congregation west of the Rockies [1]. For almost half a century after 1906 it worshipped at 1299 Hyde Street, far from the wartime Black neighborhood growing up in the Western Addition [2]. In 1950 Rev. Frederick D. Haynes Sr. led the purchase of the northwest corner of Pierce and McAllister, where Captain Charles Goodall's 1859 mansion stood [1]. A newspaper photo caption described congregation members demolishing the house themselves and planning to reuse much of its old timber in the new church [1]. William F. Gunnison designed the sanctuary, with a bell tower and bare cross visible from blocks away; the permit was approved in May 1952 and the building finished that year [1]. A 1953 account recalled how members, fresh from their centenary, "sang their last praises in the old church, and marched in a phalanx to the new." Deborah Johnson, the youngest member, cut the ribbon [1]. Only a few years later the city's other pioneer Black churches followed it west [1][2]. The city made the complex Landmark No. 275 in 2017 [3].

title: No Black family, 'regardless of qualifications'
place: North Beach Place public housing, Bay St at Taylor St
hook: The Housing Authority's own chairman testified that no Black applicant would get a flat in North Beach Place, veteran or not. Mattie Banks took the city to court and won.
story: By 1952 North Beach Place, a public housing project designed by Ernest Born with Henry Gutterson, stood ready beside the cable car turntable on Taylor Street [1][2]. Mattie Banks and James Charley Jr. applied for flats there and were turned away [1]. Behind the refusal lay the San Francisco Housing Authority's 1942 "neighborhood pattern" policy, which promised to "maintain and preserve the same racial composition which exists in the neighborhood where a project is located" [1]. In court the authority's chairman, E. N. Ayer, testified that no Black person, "whether a veteran or nonveteran, regardless of his qualifications and priorities", would be admitted to the North Beach project. Its executive officer said that on 19 September 1952 the only Black tenants in the seven existing projects lived at Westside Courts [1]. Represented by lawyers including Nathaniel Colley and Loren Miller, Banks and Charley won in the trial court. On 26 August 1953 the state Court of Appeal rejected the authority's "separate but equal" defence and affirmed the judgment declaring the policy void under the 14th Amendment [1]. After the TEL HI centre moved next door in the 1950s, it began serving more African American families from the project [3]. Born's buildings were demolished in 2001 [2], and a new North Beach Place opened in 2004 [3].

title: Ping Yuen, the 'Tranquil Garden' Towers
place: Ping Yuen, Pacific Avenue
hook: Chinatown was the most crowded place in the city, but it waited more than a decade for public housing. When it came, it arrived wearing pagoda balconies.
story: By the 1930s Chinatown had about 30,000 residents, and two of its blocks were the most densely populated in San Francisco [1]. After years of community pressure, plans were announced for a public housing project. The Second World War delayed it, and Ping Yuen, meaning 'Tranquil Garden', opened roughly a decade later, credited as the first federal housing project west of the Mississippi [1]. Architects John Bolles and J. Francis Ward wrapped a six-storey block facing Pacific Avenue in tiered, pagoda-like balcony corridors. Architectural historian Gwendolyn Wright called the style 'Chinese regionalism superimposed over a functionalist design' [2]. The complex packed 234 units onto the site at 89 units per acre, the highest density of any family housing project in the Bay Area [2]. In 1952 a model apartment showed off designs by painter James Leong, including a child's room [1]. Sources differ slightly on timing: one calls it finished in 1952 [2]. Decades later a writer noted that its reputation for calm contradicted the common view that high-rise public housing could not work for families [2].

title: Seventy Years Behind a Broad Street Chair
place: Lacy's Barbershop, Broad Street at Plymouth Avenue
hook: In 1952 a barber bought Furlough's Tonsorial Parlor on Broad Street. His godson has been cutting hair in the same shop since 1972.
story:
At the corner of Broad Street and Plymouth Avenue, in the heart of Ocean View, one old-school barbershop has weathered the pandemic, falling foot traffic and rising costs [1]. Lloyd Lacy Jr.'s godfather bought it in 1952, when it was called Furlough's Tonsorial Parlor [1]. "I've been cutting hair here since 1972, and worked here with my godfather until 1998, and I've done everything you can do with some hair," said Lacy, as he is known [1]. He took over the shop in 2010. He dreams of opening a barber college to train the next generation [1].

When the Lakeview edition of the Walk the Block series, which celebrates Black culture and resilience, came to Broad Street in July 2025, Lacy spoke to the crowd. Covid had changed the area, he said: "It's calmer now, but there's not as much foot traffic" [2]. Another speaker, Tinisch Hollins, recalled vanished businesses such as Will Reno's barbershop and a fish-fry shop [2].

In February 2026 the shop started a GoFundMe to raise $4,500 to stay open. It was applying to join the city's Legacy Business Registry. The OMI Cultural Participation Project called Lacy's "a cornerstone in our neighborhood" [1].

title: The night the cream finally floated
place: Buena Vista Cafe, 2765 Hyde St at Beach St
hook: A Chronicle columnist and a bar owner mixed Irish coffee until the columnist nearly passed out on the cable car tracks. On November 10, 1952, they got it right.
story: The Buena Vista began in 1916, when the ground floor of a boardinghouse at Hyde and Beach was turned into a saloon [1]. Its famous drink began at an airport. At Foynes, the Irish flying-boat base, chef Joe Sheridan had started lacing coffee with Irish whiskey for chilled transatlantic passengers during the war, and the drink moved with the staff to the new airport at Shannon [2][3]. Chronicle travel writer Stanton Delaplane was served one there in 1951 [3]. Back home he told Jack Koeppler, who owned the Buena Vista with George Freeberg, and they set out to copy it [3][4]. The whiskey was easy. The trick was making the cream float. After sampling dozens of failures, Delaplane nearly passed out on the cable car tracks [4]. The bar began serving Irish coffee on November 10, 1952, and Delaplane kept mentioning it in his column [1][4]. That same year Sheridan was offered a job at the Buena Vista and emigrated. He died in 1962 and is buried in Oakland [3]. By the café's own count it has since served more than 30 million [1].

title: A Home School for the Baby Boom
place: Jose Ortega Elementary School, 400 Sargent Street
hook: When new houses filled Merced Heights, the city rushed to build a small school just for its youngest children.
story: Houses filled the empty hillsides of Merced Heights in the late 1940s and 1950s, and young families came with them [1][2]. As the blocks filled, the city quickly planned a school for the new neighbourhood. The post-war baby boom had overloaded San Francisco's public schools, and the answer was 'home schools': small new campuses for children from kindergarten to third grade [1]. In the fall of 1953 the Ocean View Heights Home School opened at Sargent and Ramsell Streets, with room for 250 pupils [1]. It is now Jose Ortega Elementary School at 400 Sargent Street [1][3]. The new school sat in a neighbourhood that was changing fast. By the early 1960s the single-family houses of Merced Heights were about 65 percent African American-occupied [1]. Today Ortega runs a Mandarin immersion programme, and in 2023 the U.S. Department of Education named it a National Blue Ribbon School, its first [3].

title: Burgers and matzo balls at Miz Brown's
place: Miz Brown's, 3401 California Street, Laurel Village
hook: For half a century a no-nonsense coffee shop in Laurel Village fed Bing Crosby burgers, Herb Caen lunches and Dianne Feinstein cheeseburgers.
story:
Laurel Village is the row of shops on California Street between Spruce and Laurel [3]. Robert Overin opened Miz Brown's there, at 3401 California Street, in 1953. Harry Meharry, whose daughters were Overin's nieces, ran it for many years, and by 2002 those daughters, Collen Meharry and Marlee Meharry Simms, owned it [1][4]. At one time there were nine Miz Brown's restaurants and three bars around the Bay Area, including one on Clement Street. By 2002 only the Laurel Village coffee shop was left [1].

It was a classic American coffee shop. Breakfast was served at any hour, the hamburger meat was ground fresh daily, and there was an early-bird dinner for $9.95. Matzo ball soup was on the menu seven days a week, and on Fridays regulars had to choose between it and clam chowder in a bread bowl. The soup often ran out by 1:30 [1].

A 2002 reviewer who had eaten there since 1961 said Bing Crosby used to drop in for a burger and a milkshake, Herb Caen came in now and then, and Senator Dianne Feinstein had been seen eating a cheeseburger [1].

In 2004 the Meharry family closed Miz Brown's Feedbag, after half a century at the same spot [1][2].

title: City Lights and the Howl bust
place: City Lights Bookstore, 261 Columbus Ave
hook: America's first all-paperback bookstore sold a poem to an undercover cop in 1957. The trial that followed changed what American writers could publish.
story: In 1953, Lawrence Ferlinghetti was walking past the Artigues Building on Columbus Avenue. He saw sociology teacher Peter D. Martin hanging a sign for a "Pocket Book Shop" [1]. Martin had borrowed the name City Lights, from the Chaplin film, for a magazine. The two men each put in $500 and opened what is described as the first all-paperback bookstore in the country [1]. Clerk Shigeyoshi "Shig" Murao worked unpaid for the first weeks and became the shop's manager [1][3]. Martin sold out in 1955. That year Ferlinghetti began publishing the Pocket Poets series. In November 1956 its fourth title came out: Allen Ginsberg's Howl and Other Poems [1]. In June 1957, police bought the book from the store and arrested Murao for selling obscene material. Ferlinghetti, away in Big Sur, turned himself in [1][2]. Judge Clayton Horn heard the case from August to September 1957. He ruled that Howl was not obscene and that a work with "the slightest redeeming social importance" deserved First Amendment protection [1]. "It had four-letter words in it," Ferlinghetti said later, but he thought the real offence was the poem's attack on consumer society [2].

title: Kan's and the Birth of the Lazy Susan
place: Kan's Restaurant, 708 Grant Avenue
hook: An engineer tinkering with ball bearings in his basement built a spinning tabletop for a friend's Chinatown restaurant. Soon restaurants across America copied it.
story: In 1953 Johnny Kan opened a Cantonese restaurant on Grant Avenue at a time when Chinatown's newer restaurateurs were remaking Chinese food for American diners [1]. He wanted Kan's to feel both respectable and modern, and he had help from two brothers-in-law who had started a booming soy sauce company [1]. One of them, George Hall, was a trained engineer who liked to tinker in his basement. In the mid-1950s he rigged ball bearings and round pieces of wood into a revolving tabletop, and it became the centrepiece of Kan's new banquet room [1]. Kan's grew famous within a few years. Celebrities came, competitors across the country copied it, 'right down to its jasmine-scented napkins', and its cooks came from Hong Kong [1]. In 1959 Kan commissioned twelve paintings of Chinese American history from artist Jake Lee for his private Gum Shan, or 'Gold Mountain', dining room [2]. After Kan died in 1972 the paintings disappeared for decades. Eleven surfaced at a 2010 auction; the Chinese Historical Society bought seven, then tracked down the missing twelfth, 'Deadwood' [2].

title: Leola King's Blue Mirror
place: 935 Fillmore Street, between Fulton and McAllister (site)
hook: An Oklahoma-born barbecue cook they called Goldie opened a lounge where Louis Armstrong and Dinah Washington played, then spent decades fighting the bulldozers.
story: Leola King was born in Seminole County, Oklahoma, in 1919 and came to San Francisco in 1946 [1][2]. Friends called her Goldie. Her first hit was Oklahoma King's, a barbecue at 1601 Geary that smoked buffalo, deer and quail [1]. In 1953 she opened the Blue Mirror at 935 Fillmore, between Fulton and McAllister, among the first nightclubs in the Bay Area owned by a woman of color [1][3]. It had a circular bar, velvet festoons and molded Greek figurines [1]. Louis Armstrong, Dinah Washington, Lena Horne, Count Basie and Duke Ellington passed through, and pianist Earl Grant played Monday nights [1][3]. Touring performers slept nearby at the Manor Plaza Hotel, 930 Fillmore [4]. Redevelopment took almost everything: Oklahoma King's was taken for about $25,000, the Blue Mirror closed in the early 1960s, and a sheriff evicted her from a later bar in 1974 [1]. "The way they took everything is criminal," she said [1]. For more than half a century she lived in a 29-room house at 711 Scott Street, on Alamo Square [1]. She died in 2015, aged 96 [3].

title: Suburbia poured onto a mountainside
place: Midcrest Way, the first street of Midtown Terrace
hook: Bulldozers moved 600,000 cubic yards of Twin Peaks to fit in 800 postwar homes. Every one was built to face the view.
story:
In December 1932 dairy cows still grazed in the snow on what is now Panorama Drive [1]. Twenty years later this land, about 150 acres on the western slopes of Twin Peaks, was the biggest privately owned tract left in San Francisco. In 1953 Carl and Fred Gellert's Standard Building Company began building Midtown Terrace there [1]. Midcrest Drive, the first street, was taking shape on April 13, 1953 [1]. By March 1954 graders had moved some 600,000 cubic yards of earth to carve the hillside into seven terraces. Houses went mostly on the downhill side of each street, "to cash in on the view" [1]. Carl Gellert promised prices of $13,000 to $16,000 [1].

By February 1959, 900 of 1,000 planned homes were finished, selling for up to $29,500. Mrs. Theodore Jewell's homeowners' association had persuaded the city to lend it planner Ruth Jaffe to design greenbelts between the terraces [1]. The neighbourhood still has no shops, just houses, a school, a fire station and a church [1]. Children and teenagers make up more than twice the city's average share of residents [2].

title: The College That Kept Moving West
place: San Francisco State campus, 1600 Holloway Avenue
hook: A teachers' school burned out in 1906 and squeezed onto Haight Street finally found room to grow on the windy shore of Lake Merced.
story: San Francisco State began in 1899 as Frederic Burk's State Normal School, a teacher-training college whose first graduating class was 36 young women [1]. The 1906 fire destroyed its Powell Street home, and Burk moved it to Haight and Buchanan streets [1]. It became San Francisco State College in 1935, and with nearly 1,000 students it bought land on the Lake Merced shoreline from the Spring Valley Water Company in 1937 [1]. World War II and arguments over land use stalled construction [1]. In 1948–49, a commemorative booklet recalled, the mayor, supervisors, legislators, Chamber of Commerce and press "united to develop a master plan for nine buildings" [1]. The Administration Building was finished in 1953, and under President J. Paul Leonard the college opened on 94 acres [1]. Classes began in fall 1953 and the campus was formally dedicated in October 1954 [2]. Today it covers about 144 acres [2].

title: The High Jumper Who Chose to Sing
place: George Washington High School campus, 600 32nd Avenue
hook: Before "Chances Are," Washington High's Johnny Mathis stood 5-foot-7 and cleared six feet in the high jump. Bill Russell was his rival.
story:
Johnny Mathis was born in Gilmer, Texas, in 1935 and grew up in San Francisco, where he was a star athlete at George Washington High School: a high jumper, hurdler and basketball player [2]. He stood just 5-foot-7, yet he repeatedly cleared 6-foot-5, and his main Bay Area rival was Bill Russell, then a struggling basketball player at Oakland's McClymonds High [1].

Mathis said his jumping started in junior high, when gym teachers held a cane pole between two students and kept raising it. His "claim to fame," he said, was a Chronicle photograph of Russell sailing over his head. The paper ran a shot of the pair in May 1954, by which time Mathis was at San Francisco State. He said he beat Russell's high-jump mark once, in Nevada, "but I think that's the only time," and the two stayed friends for decades [1].

In 1956 he was invited to the Olympic trials. That same week a telegram arrived from a Columbia Records executive asking him to come to New York to record. He took the record deal, and he has been with Columbia for most of his career since [1][2]. He never learned to dunk. "You've got to be able to palm it," he said, "and I couldn't" [1].

title: The Queen of Fillmore Loses Her Crown
place: Site of the Blue Mirror, 935 Fillmore Street
hook: Redevelopment bulldozed her barbecue pit, closed her jazz club and had the sheriff carry her out of her tavern. Leola King fought the Agency for fifty years.
story: Leola King came to San Francisco in 1946 and opened Oklahoma King's, a barbecue pit at 1601 Geary that served buffalo, deer and quail. It stood inside A-1. King said she arrived one morning to find the building gone [1]. She was paid about $25,000 for the property and got nothing for the business she lost [2]. In 1953 she opened the Blue Mirror here at 935 Fillmore, a club with a circular bar and velvet festoons where Louis Armstrong and Dinah Washington performed [1][2]. The club was gone by the early 1960s. King said her liquor licence was taken after a set-up, and the Bay Guardian, which reviewed her records, reported that redevelopment reached the business and she was put out without compensation [1][2]. In 1964 she opened the Bird Cage Tavern at 1505 Fillmore. In 1974 the Agency bought that building for A-2, and the sheriff had to remove her [2]. She held two certificates of preference, and trying to redeem them turned into more than twenty years of legal fights [2]. By the late 1990s she had lost nearly everything, including her home at 711 Scott Street near Alamo Square [1]. She died in 2015, aged 96 [3].

title: The Tin Box in the Octagon's Wall
place: McElroy Octagon House, 2645 Gough Street
hook: Nobody knew who built Cow Hollow's eight-sided house until an electrician, wiring it for the first time, drilled into a wall and hit a box.
story: By the early 1950s the octagonal house on Gough Street was a puzzle. PG&E owned it and had bought the lot for a possible substation, but it had never been wired for electricity [1]. Three Riley sisters rented it for $35 a month until 1951, living like recluses by flickering gaslight. Neighbours said a ghost climbed the central stair every November 24, screamed, and fell [1]. Nobody knew who had built it. In 1952 the Colonial Dames of America stepped in and PG&E sold them the house for $1 [1]. The next year an electrician, finally bringing in power, drilled into an upstairs wall and hit a tin box [1]. Inside was a letter from William McElroy dated July 1861, about three dozen newspaper clippings mostly on the outbreak of the Civil War, and a tintype of William, Harriet and their daughter Emma. McElroy had written with pride about San Francisco's boom: 'Look which ever way you will, and you observe happiness prosperity and wealth' [1]. Built in 1861 in the octagon fad started by phrenologist Orson Fowler, the house is now San Francisco Landmark No. 17 [2].

title: The motherly psychiatrist of Delta Street
place: 150 Delta Street
hook: From a hillside house in the valley, a former surgeon turned psychiatrist challenged the 1950s belief that gay people were mentally ill.
story: In 1953, city directories place Dr. Blanche M. Baker at 150 Delta Street, a hillside house looking out over the valley [1]. A former surgeon turned psychiatrist, she treated gay and straight clients, and the 1959 Polk's directory lists her office at the same address [2]. At a time when homosexuality was widely seen as a mental illness to be cured, Baker described herself as 'a kind, friendly, motherly sort of doctor who preaches self-acceptance' [2]. In 1955 she spoke at ONE Inc.'s first Midwinter Institute in Los Angeles, reportedly the first forum in North America organised by homosexuals, for homosexuals [1][2]. In 1957 she wrote the introduction to Helen P. Branson's book Gay Bar: 'Homosexuals are human beings, too' [1][2]. The Daughters of Bilitis, who met her at ONE's Midwinter Institute that year, formed a lasting relationship with her and later set up a scholarship in her name [2]. From January 1959 she wrote an advice column, 'Toward Understanding', for ONE Magazine, cut short by her death in 1960. The ONE Library in Los Angeles was named for her in 1965 [1][2]. Artist Opal Essence, who bought the house in 1979, found a brick room, archway and fireplace hidden behind the sheetrock, and later commissioned murals on the house in Baker's honour [1].

title: The patrolman from Bosworth Street
place: Bosworth Street near Elk and Congo streets (Symons family home c.1950-1958)
hook: In late 1953 a Glen Park highway patrolman was given the Golden Gate Bridge beat. Within weeks he had watched two people jump.
story: Jack Alvan Symons was born in Holly Park in 1916 and chose "Let the world come to me" as his Balboa High School yearbook motto in 1933 [1]. He worked as a patternmaker at Bethlehem Steel, served in the Navy in the Second World War, joined the San Francisco police in 1948 and the California Highway Patrol in 1953. By 1950 he, his wife Marilyn, a nurse, and three children lived in a small house near Bosworth, Elk and Congo streets [1]. Late in 1953 he began patrolling the Golden Gate Bridge. On 30 November he saw 24-year-old Marie McCormick climb over the rail. He swung his car around and ran toward her shouting "Wait a minute!" but she jumped. On 11 December a 61-year-old San Mateo realtor stood outside the railing as Symons called out again; the man "just looked at me and stepped off" [1]. Bridge directors floated higher railings, then a barbed-wire barrier; in February 1954 a Marin newspaper photographed Symons inspecting the test section. After March the idea was dropped [1]. In April 1955 he and bystanders stopped a Navy veteran from jumping. By 1956 he was on the Bay Bridge, and in 1958 the family moved to Santa Rosa [1]. A stainless-steel suicide net along his old beat was finished in January 2024 [2].

title: A library as inviting as a bar
place: Marina Branch Library, 1890 Chestnut Street
hook: In 1951 San Francisco's head librarian complained that libraries looked like pumping stations, and said they should be as inviting as a good bar.
story: The Marina Branch opened in 1954 as the 23rd branch of the San Francisco Public Library. It cost $156,742, plus $12,926 for furnishings [1]. It was designed by Appleton & Wolfard, who between 1951 and 1966 designed eight branch libraries for the city, more than any other firm in its history [2]. The partners admired Scandinavian modernism, especially the Finnish architect Alvar Aalto [2]. The building reflected a new idea of what a library should be. In a 1951 Chronicle article, City Librarian Laurence J. Clarke argued that a library 'must merchandise its services in much the same way a successful bookshop sells its wares'. 'Unfortunately,' he went on, 'most existing public libraries look like a Water Department pumping station. Smart entrepreneurs make their cocktail lounges so attractive that you can't help but stay on for another drink. Why not libraries?' [2]. A 2007 renovation costing $3.9 million added a small addition and made the building seismically safe and accessible [1]. It is now City Landmark No. 262 [2].

title: Auden's Hundred Dollars
place: The Poetry Center, SF State Humanities Building
hook: W. H. Auden gave back half his speaking fee, and a professor turned it into one of the country's first public poetry reading series.
story: In 1954 W. H. Auden gave a talk at the brand-new San Francisco State College campus and returned half of his $200 honorarium [1][2]. English professor Ruth Witt-Diamant used the gift to found The Poetry Center, with advice from Kenneth Rexroth, Robert Duncan and Madeline Gleason, and from her late friend Dylan Thomas [1]. Its public reading series, one of the first in the United States, opened with Theodore Roethke in February 1954 [1]. Over the next years the center hosted some of the earliest recorded readings by poets of the San Francisco Renaissance, along with rare West Coast appearances by William Carlos Williams, Marianne Moore and Langston Hughes [1]. From 1955 it taped most readings, and in 1973 director Kathleen Fraser founded the American Poetry Archives to keep them [1]. The collection now holds about 5,000 hours of recordings, and the series is still running more than seventy years later [1].

title: Disneyland Employee No. 7 Came From Playland
place: Site of Playland-at-the-Beach midway, Great Highway at Balboa Street
hook: When Walt Disney planned his park, he came to Ocean Beach to study Playland. He left with the owner's son on his payroll.
story: George K. Whitney Jr. grew up as 'the boss' kid' at Ocean Beach, playing in front of the orange juice stand his mother and aunt ran at the old Chutes [2]. After wartime service in the Army Air Forces he went to work on the Playland midway, patrolling twelve-hour days that he summed up as 'walk back and forth and drink coffee' [1][2]. In the early 1950s Walt Disney, planning Disneyland, studied Playland and other amusement parks, visited, and met George Sr. [2]. The son impressed him. From 1954 to 1958 Whitney Jr. worked in Anaheim as Disneyland employee number 7, he told historian John Martini, the only person on Disney's development team with practical experience running an amusement park [1]. He organised queues for the most popular rides and reworked entrance and exit routes, adding separate exit doors to the Adventureland jungle boats [1]. He came home in 1958 when his father died, took over the family properties, and brought Disney ideas back to the beach, including the children's Fun-Tier Town [1][2]. This account rests on his own 2002 oral history, recorded shortly before his death [2].

title: Eight lanes along the Portola's edge
place: Bayshore Freeway (US 101) along the Portola's eastern edge, near Paul Avenue
hook: Silver Terrace used to be part of the Portola. Then, in the 1950s, the Bayshore Freeway came through, burying most of a street lined with greenhouses.
story: The first unit of the Bayshore Freeway inside San Francisco, 1.3 miles from Augusta Street north to 25th Street, opened on 1 June 1951. Its right of way, including clearing factories and other buildings, cost $3.4 million, almost as much as building the road itself [1]. By spring 1954 the next piece, the 1.7-mile Alemany-to-Third Street section running south past the Portola, was under construction and due to be finished early the following year [2]. Local historian Chris Ortiz writes that Silver Terrace, now counted as its own neighbourhood, was a contiguous part of the Portola until the freeway was built, and that Charter Oak Avenue, once lined on its west side with flower greenhouses, is mostly lost under it [3]. The concrete left a lasting seam. In 2022 Dee Derisse, whose Hey Neighbor Coffee sits beside the Burrows Street garden, spoke of "deep history there with the neighborhoods being split by a redline at the highway," and of her hope that shared gardens could bring the Bayview and Portola back together [4].

title: Seventh graders tear up the comics
place: Star of the Sea School, 360 9th Ave between Geary Blvd & Clement St
hook: In spring 1954, Catholic schoolchildren on 9th Avenue ripped up piles of horror comics at an assembly headlined by the police chief's daughter.
story: In the spring of 1954 the seventh grade at Star of the Sea Grammar School, the parish school founded in 1909, went to war on comic books [1][2]. The class collected comics, prepared speeches on their evils, and held an assembly for the upper grades. The keynote speaker was Elizabeth Cahill, daughter of Police Chief Thomas Cahill, and a photograph shows students in the bleachers tearing the comics apart [1]. John Freeman, who was in that class, later explained the bigger picture: a nationwide crusade driven by churches, the PTA and the comic-book industry itself. EC's rivals DC and Marvel, worried about EC Comics, maker of Tales from the Crypt, The Vault of Horror and war titles like Two-Fisted Tales, proposed a Comics Code limiting vampires, werewolves and the glory of killing, while Congress threatened legislation [1]. It was the McCarthy era, when pupils were quizzed on what they would do if a gun-waving communist burst in and asked them to choose between God and Communism [1]. 'We students at Star of the Sea were witnessing for morality,' Freeman wrote, with no idea they were also making the surviving comics rarer, and more valuable to collectors [1].

title: Skid Road: Selling South of Market's Clearance
place: Yerba Buena redevelopment area, Fourth and Howard streets
hook: In the mid-1950s, newspapers ran photos of 'winos' on South of Market sidewalks. Some of the men were posed, and a hotelier had big plans for their blocks.
story: In 1952 the city's Redevelopment Agency called South of Market "among the most severely blighted sections of the city," and in 1953 supervisors approved large parts of it for redevelopment [1]. In 1954 Ben Swig, owner of the Fairmont Hotel, unveiled a "San Francisco Prosperity Plan" with a convention center, a sports stadium and office high-rises, foreshadowing today's Yerba Buena and Moscone Center [1][3]. According to photographer and former Sixth Street resident Mark Ellinger, Swig even gave the agency money for a study to have the area declared blighted; the money was returned, but the plan moved forward [2]. Newspapers including the Chronicle and the News Call-Bulletin ran "Skid Road" stories about alcoholics and flophouses. Ellinger points to 1956 News Call-Bulletin photos in which the same men appear, posed, in more than one picture [2]. One 1954 caption admitted that a hotel in the "wino district" rented 200 rooms at 50 to 75 cents a night, "chiefly to old-age pensioners" [2]. Little was said of the workers and retirees who made up most residents. Land clearance began in earnest in 1966, and residents would fight back in court [1][2].

title: The 1954 raid on Tommy's Place
place: Tommy's Place, 529 Broadway, backing onto 12 Adler Place (now Specs')
hook: San Francisco's first out lesbian bar owner moved to Broadway, with a lesbian pick-up bar out the back. Two years later came a vice raid and a newspaper frenzy.
story: Tommy Vasu had dressed in masculine clothes since she was 12. In 1948 she opened a bar at 299 Broadway, San Francisco's first queer bar opened by an out lesbian [1]. Herb Caen called her "a gentleman among ladies", though she was also known to mix with organized crime [1]. Dick Boyd remembered her in double-breasted suits and a fedora, playing high-stakes liar's dice with the painter Walter Keane [2]. Four years later the bar moved here to 529 Broadway (KQED calls it Tommy's Joint, Boyd Tommy's Place), with live entertainment. It backed directly onto 12 Adler Place, a lively lesbian pick-up bar, also Vasu's, reached by a back staircase [1][2]. The run lasted two years. In 1954, by Boyd's dates, the vice squad closed both bars, the licence was revoked, and a bartender went to jail for allegedly serving minors [1][2]. Boyd recalled that drugs were found taped under the sink in the ladies' room, in what looked to outsiders like a set-up [2]. The Examiner called 12 Adler a "sex thrill bar", and the case was milked to stoke fears about homosexuality corrupting the young [1]. Tommy's became the Garden of Eden strip club. In 1968 Richard "Specs" Simmons opened his bar in the Adler Place room, which still has a sign reading "12 Adler Museum" [1][3].

title: The Mayor of the Fillmore's dance hall
place: Fillmore Auditorium, 1805 Geary Boulevard
hook: Before Bill Graham's psychedelic posters, a Black promoter named Charles Sullivan filled this hall with James Brown and Ike and Tina Turner, and then died mysteriously.
story: The brick hall at Geary and Fillmore opened in 1912 as the Majestic Hall and Academy of Dancing, became the Ambassador Dance Hall in 1936 and was a roller rink from 1939 to 1952 [1]. Then Charles Sullivan took the lease, named it the Fillmore Auditorium and began booking Black stars; sources mention James Brown, Ike and Tina Turner and Louis Armstrong [1][2]. Born in Alabama in 1909, Sullivan had worked his way west as a chauffeur and machinist, then built bars, a jukebox business and a promotion network, becoming known as the "Mayor of Fillmore" [2][3]. In December 1965 he let a young promoter named Bill Graham book a benefit for the San Francisco Mime Troupe here, and helped the newcomer get established [1][2]. In early August 1966, Sullivan was found shot dead south of Market with his own revolver beside him. Police leaned toward suicide; the coroner recorded "unknown circumstances," and his family believed he was murdered [2][3]. Graham then took over the lease, and the hall became famous for psychedelic rock [2].

title: The glass of beer that never emptied
place: Former Rainier and Hamm's Brewery, 1550 Bryant Street
hook: Above 15th and Bryant, a giant beer glass made of light bulbs filled up, grew a head and emptied, over and over, night after night.
story:
The brewery at 15th and Bryant has its roots in a flight from Prohibition [4]. Washington state went dry in 1916, four years before the rest of the country, so Seattle's Rainier Brewing opened a brewery in San Francisco and made Rainier beer there until 1920 [1]. A city transit photo from January 1920 was taken from the roof of the Rainier Brewing Company plant near Bryant and Alameda [2].

In 1953 Hamm's of St. Paul, Minnesota bought the brewery from Rainier and opened it in 1954 at 1550 Bryant Street [3]. On top went a 20-by-80-foot sign crowned by a 13-foot beer glass made of lights. It filled with 'beer', formed a head and emptied again, all day, every day [3][4]. Fans inside Seals Stadium, just across 16th Street, could see it from their seats [5], and it later appeared in the first Dirty Harry film [3]. The Mission's northeast corner was then full of blue-collar work: breweries, a mayonnaise factory, a cement plant and steel mills [4]. Hamm's closed in 1972. In the early 1980s punk bands took over the empty vats, and the building became famous as 'The Vats' [3][4].

title: The goddess who vanished from Mount Olympus
place: Mount Olympus, Upper Terrace (empty pedestal)
hook: For nearly seventy years a 12-foot Goddess of Liberty stood near the city's centre. In 1954 the Art Commission called her 'beyond repair.' Then she was gone.
story: On Thanksgiving Day 1887, Adolph Sutro unveiled his gift on the summit of Mount Olympus. It was a copy of a work by the Belgian artist Antoine Wiertz: a 12-foot Goddess of Liberty holding up a torch and a sword over a figure of evil, called the Triumph of Light [1]. The city climbed the hill around her, and she aged badly, losing her torch and her sword. In 1926 the ground around the statue was dedicated as a public park. Sutro's daughter, Dr. Emma Sutro Merritt, asked experts about restoring it and was told it was hopeless [1]. Charles Cushman still photographed the statue on the hilltop in March 1955 [2]. By then its end had been decided. In 1954 the city's Art Commission declared the Triumph of Light "beyond repair" and recommended taking it down. It hoped to replace it with a donated Benjamin Bufano statue called "Peace" [1]. Within a few years the goddess was removed, and nothing replaced her [1]. Annalee Newitz writes that the statue had nearly been wrecked by vandals and was removed to make way for valuable real estate. Only the stone pedestal still stands, among condominiums on Upper Terrace [2].

title: A Free School for Hands Moves West
place: Lick-Wilmerding High School, 755 Ocean Avenue
hook: Three 19th-century bequests paid for free trade schooling for San Francisco's children. In 1955 the combined school moved to Ocean Avenue, and it stayed tuition-free for twenty years more.
story:
The school at 755 Ocean Avenue grew from three 19th-century bequests. James Lick left $540,000 for the California School of Mechanical Arts, which opened in January 1895 and gave boys and girls a free education mixing academics and shop work [1]. Jellis Wilmerding left $400,000 for a boys' school of building trades and drafting. Miranda Lux left money to train girls in sewing, cooking, health, art and retailing [1]. From the post-earthquake years until 1939 the three schools shared a campus at 17th Street and Potrero Avenue, and for years one director, George Merrill, ran all three [1][2].

In the early 1950s the Lux school closed and sent its pupils to Lick, and Lick and Wilmerding merged. In 1955, by the Western Neighborhoods Project's account, the new Lick-Wilmerding High School moved to Ocean Avenue; Wikipedia gives 1956 [1][2]. It was a boys' school for 17 years, until it went co-ed again in 1972. Thanks to the old endowments it charged no tuition until the mid-1970s [1].

Lick held its entrance exam weeks before the Catholic boys' high schools held theirs. Columnist Frank Dunnigan and many of his St. Cecilia School classmates took it as "practice". On a cold Saturday in January 1966 he sat it in the gym, for a $5 fee. "For the record," he wrote, "I PASSED!" [1]

title: A Soldier's Last Sight of Home
place: Mount Davidson Cross, Mount Davidson Park
hook: A soldier bound for Korea wrote that the glowing cross was the last thing he saw of San Francisco. A church then paid to keep it lit.
story:
Since 1934 the Mount Davidson cross had been lit only during the week before Easter [1]. During the Second World War, up to 75,000 people came to the sunrise services, and CBS Radio broadcast them across the country [2].

Then came a letter. A soldier heading to the Korean War wrote that the lit cross on the hill was the last sight he had of home. The sources do not record his name. In response, in 1955, Lakeside Presbyterian Church raised money for the city to light the cross all year round [1][2]. Its twelve 1,000-watt lamps could be seen from 75 miles away [2].

The year-round lighting lasted about two decades. In 1976, during the energy crisis, the city cut it back to Easter and Christmas weeks only [1][2]. By then the park had grown to 38 acres, after its last parcel was bought in 1950 [1].

title: Blabbermouth Night at The Place
place: The Place, 1546 Grant Ave
hook: While the rest of America watched Gunsmoke, upper Grant Avenue climbed into a box and ranted, with a bottle of champagne for the best speech.
story: From 1955 to 1959 a small storefront bar at 1546 Grant Avenue was a centre of Beat San Francisco. The Place was run by two former Black Mountain College students, Knute Stiles and Leo Krikorian [1]. Its walls showed work by Jay DeFeo, Wally Hedrick and Robert LaVigne. Krikorian later said Ginsberg tried out Howl there before it was published, Kerouac was "there all the time", and a 19-year-old Richard Brautigan was a regular [1]. Once On the Road came out, hitchhikers arrived from all over with their luggage, and he let them leave it there [1]. Its most famous event was Blabbermouth Night. Each week speakers climbed into a loft called the Blabberbox and talked about anything they liked. The best got a free bottle of champagne [1]. On April 15, 1957, one speaker proposed a pipe up Coit Tower that would shoot a 1,000-foot beer geyser every hour. Another proposed passport controls to "save North Beach for the Bohemians" [1]. Italian neighbours complained about the noise. By one account, audiences started snapping their fingers instead of cheering. In 1959 the poets were thrown out anyway for making too much noise [1].

title: Fifty Cents to Fly Over Sutro Baths
place: Sky Tram route over the Sutro Baths basin, Cliff House to Point Lobos
hook: For eleven years a little cable car dangled over the surf between the Cliff House and Point Lobos. Its own family called it a big mistake.
story: George K. Whitney, the showman who a Chronicle columnist said owned 'all of San Francisco west of Sutro Park,' announced an aerial tram in 1954 [1]. It opened on 2 May 1955 and ran roughly 1,000 feet from the Cliff House across the Sutro Baths basin to Point Lobos, with the Chronicle's Joe Rosenthal, the Iwo Jima photographer, shooting opening day [1]. Fifty cents bought a seat in a car of 20, all facing west toward Seal Rock; unusually, the motor rode in the car itself rather than pulling it from a terminal [1]. An operator travelled along to calm passengers startled when spray hit the windows above the rusting wreck of the freighter Ohioan in the cove below [1]. Columnist Terence O'Flaherty called it 'a kind of funicular conspiracy to further invade the private lives of the sunbathers on Seal Rock' [1]. Whitney's son was blunter: built by the Roebling company rather than bought off the shelf, the tram was too small to carry enough riders and 'couldn't generate enough revenue to pay for itself' [2]. It stopped running in 1966, the year the baths beneath it burned [1][3].

title: Midnight shows at the Champagne Supper Club
place: New Orleans Swing Club / Champagne Supper Club site, 1849 Post Street
hook: Shows ran from midnight to five in the morning. A dancer called Lottie the Body met a Globetrotter here, and a pianist remembered Billie Holiday's first Fillmore gig.
story: In the late 1940s and early 1950s the Fillmore was known as the "Harlem of the West". Black entrepreneurs ran barber shops, record stores, barbecue joints and a string of nightclubs [1]. One of these was Louis Landry's New Orleans Swing Club at 1849 Post Street, which later became the Champagne Supper Club [1]. Lottie Claiborne had studied dance as a teenager in New York and got the stage name "Lottie the Body" while modelling. She had shared bills with Carmen McRae and Redd Foxx [2]. In the early 1950s she moved to the Bay Area and became one of the most popular dancers in the Fillmore clubs. At the Champagne Supper Club she met Harlem Globetrotter Goose Tatum, and the two became a familiar sight in the neighbourhood [2]. "The club was big and beautiful," she remembered. "Mixed. The show started at midnight. The last show was at 5 in the morning" [2]. Pianist Frank Jackson, who played the Fillmore for seven decades, said it was also where Billie Holiday first sang in the Fillmore, "probably the mid-1950s" [3]. The building is gone [1].

title: National champions with no home court
place: War Memorial Gymnasium (Sobrato Center), 2335 Golden Gate Avenue
hook: Bill Russell's Dons won two national titles without a gym of their own. They practised at the high school next door, and this gym was built only after they left.
story: In 1954-55 the University of San Francisco had no gymnasium on campus. The Dons played home games at Kezar Pavilion a few blocks away and sometimes at the Cow Palace. They usually practised at neighbouring St. Ignatius High School, or at Kezar when high school games left it free. When neither was available they squeezed into the San Francisco Boys Club's Page Street gym [1]. Coach Phil Woolpert, hired from St. Ignatius High, started three African American players: Bill Russell, K.C. Jones and Hal Perry. No major college team that went on to win a national title had done that before [1]. At the All-College Tournament in Oklahoma City, hotels refused rooms to the Black players, so the whole team camped in a college dormitory that was closed for the holidays [1]. In the 1955 NCAA final K.C. Jones held La Salle's Tom Gola to 16 points, and USF won 77-63. The team came home to a downtown parade [1]. A second title followed in 1956, and the winning streak reached 60 games [2]. Sportswriters then led a fund drive for an on-campus gym [1]. War Memorial Gymnasium opened in 1958, too late for Russell and Jones [3].

title: Penny Candy and a DiMaggio Bar on Balboa
place: Balboa Street shopping strip at 38th Avenue
hook: In the 1950s, six blocks of Balboa Street had everything a kid needed: delivery jobs, a quarter matinee and a bar owned by a DiMaggio.
story:
Victor Berardelli, who grew up near Lafayette School, described Balboa Street from 33rd to 39th Avenue as his first classroom. The strip held three food markets, where boys got their first jobs delivering groceries, plus two pharmacies, an old-fashioned pharmacy with a soda counter, a Bank of America branch, a five-and-dime, the Sugar Bowl bakery, Frosty Bossy ice cream and a Firestone store [1].

Mid-block between 37th and 38th, a man named Luke ran a penny-candy and joke shop and greeted children with a gruff "What do you vant, keeds?" Older boys learned what was hidden behind the curtain at the back. At the Balboa Theatre, a quarter bought a Saturday B-movie, a serial and cartoons, and Berardelli won his first Schwinn in a matinee drawing [1].

He also remembered that Vince DiMaggio owned a bar at 38th and Balboa, where children peeked in at the baseball memorabilia. Another bar, Hockey Haven, was owned by a former San Francisco Shamrocks player [1]. Berardelli called Vince the youngest of the clan, but he was the big brother, outshone by Joe and Dom. He left baseball in 1951 at 38 and spent years moving between jobs, from bartending to selling Fuller brushes, while his brothers prospered [2].
