title: The fight over Twin Peaks' eastern slope
place: Vista Francisco apartments, Gardenside Drive
hook: A late-night rezoning, campaign cash and a builder who boasted he'd never sold to a Black buyer. How the Peaks' east face became apartments.
story:
On October 19, 1959, San Francisco's supervisors were approving a new zoning map for the whole city. They added last-minute amendments, and one of them rezoned about 21 acres of the Gellert brothers' land on the east face of Twin Peaks for apartments. It passed 6-4 [1]. Two days later the News-Call Bulletin reported that the Gellerts' Standard Building Company had given campaign money to five of the six "yes" voters [1]. Supervisor Charles Ertola admitted taking "maybe $200" and insisted it hadn't swayed him [1].

Jack Morrison, soon a supervisor himself, called the project "the rape of Twin Peaks." He proposed that the city buy the land back for a park [1]. The parks department balked at the $6 million price. At the hearing, Carl Gellert said "Some day, these people will thank me" over a chorus of boos [1]. The Catholic Interracial Council sent the Board a letter quoting Gellert: "I have never sold a house to a Negro ... I don't think there will be any change in this policy" [1]. On December 17, 1962, the Board approved the subdivision 8-3 [1]. Today about 4,000 people live in the Vista Francisco apartments [1]. The same company had built Midtown Terrace on the other side of the hill [2].

title: The freeway Hayes Valley finally beat
place: Octavia Boulevard at Market Street
hook: Planners called the neighbourhood blighted and ran a double-decker freeway through it. After an earthquake and three ballot fights, a boulevard replaced it.
story: In the mid-1950s, city planners called Hayes Valley blighted and in need of 'social surgery'. By 1959 the elevated Central Freeway had been built through it as far as Turk Street [1]. The wealthier neighbourhoods to the north, active in the freeway revolts, blocked its extension, so the freeway emptied its traffic onto Hayes Valley's streets. By the late 1960s more than 150,000 vehicles a day came through, and by the 1970s the freeway's shadow was notorious for drug dealing and prostitution [1]. The 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake shut the freeway. The damaged stretch north of Fell Street was torn down, which opened Hayes Street to the sky and helped its shops revive [1]. Then came three ballot measures, in 1997, 1998 and 1999. In 1997, Proposition H, backed by west-side and merchant groups, passed with 53 percent to rebuild the freeway, shocking residents and City Hall alike [2]. The fight went on. The final compromise ended the freeway just south of Market Street and replaced the rest with a tree-lined boulevard along Octavia. It opened after an 11 a.m. ribbon-cutting at Octavia and Market on September 9, 2005 [3]. 'Half the city wanted the freeway restored, and half wanted it torn down,' a Caltrans spokesman said [3].

title: The homeowners who planted Midtown's greenbelts
place: Panorama Drive, Midtown Terrace (home of association president Mrs. Theodore Jewell in 1959)
hook: Nine hundred new houses climbed Twin Peaks' western slopes. An 'eager beaver' and a city planner set out to plant the banks with trees, shrubs and ice plant.
story:
By February 1959, 900 of the 1,000 houses the Standard Building Company planned on the western slopes of Twin Peaks were finished. Most sold for between $17,200 and $22,950, and 'super' models went for up to $29,500 [1]. A Muni bus looped through Midtown Terrace on weekdays, and the Midtown Terrace Home Owners Association was hoping for Sunday and holiday service too [1].

The association's president, Mrs. Theodore Jewell of 435 Panorama Way, was, the paper said, admittedly an 'eager beaver'. At the association's request, the City Planning Commission lent the association Miss Ruth Jaffe, an associate city planner and landscape architect, who drew up a plan for the whole area [1]. It would cost about $14,000, planted in three stages. Trees and tall growth would go first on the banks between the neighbourhood's seven street levels, then shrubs, then ground cover such as ivy and ice plant. The goal, Mrs. Jewell said, was 'a garden spot in the heart of the city' [1].

As of 2011 every homeowner was still a member of the association, and its 1956 bylaws, which protect the greenbelts, were still in force [1][2].

title: The painter the art histories forgot
place: Jean Halpert-Ryden studio, 778 Kansas Street
hook: She had a Legion of Honor solo show, was compared to Max Beckmann and turned up in an FBI file. Decades later her paintings turned up at an estate sale.
story:
Jean Halpert-Ryden, born in Brooklyn in 1919, came to San Francisco in the late 1940s with her husband, the printmaker and sculptor Edward Ryden. In 1958 they bought a cottage at 778 Kansas Street, which Ed rebuilt as a three-story modern home and studio [1].

Her career rose fast. In 1959 the California Palace of the Legion of Honor gave her a 35-work solo show. The first issue of Artforum reviewed her in 1962, and the critic Thomas Albright later compared her to Max Beckmann. At the Kansas Street studio she worked on a Holocaust memorial series that she had begun in 1943 and finished in 1976. In 1963 the FBI logged a talk she gave, "A Place for the Artist in a World of Crisis?", in a file on the peace movement [1]. In the 1960s the sculptor Ruth Cravath lived nearby [2].

In 1985 the Rydens moved to Israel. She died in Santa Rosa in 2011, leaving no archive. In 2022 dozens of her works turned up at a Sebastopol estate sale, and two triptychs were split between buyers. The collector who bought forty of them is now piecing her career back together [1].

title: Zen in a former synagogue
place: Bush Street Temple (Sokoji), 1881 Bush Street
hook: A Venetian-Gothic synagogue became a Japanese Zen temple, and then the place where Americans first sat zazen with Shunryu Suzuki.
story: In 1895 Congregation Ohabai Shalome, meaning "Lovers of Peace", consecrated a redwood synagogue at 1881 Bush Street. Its facade had Venetian tracery modelled on the Ca' d'Oro or the Doge's Palace [1]. As membership shrank, the building was sold in 1934 to Teruro Kasuga, one of about twenty followers of the Zen priest Hosen Isobe [1]. The Soto Mission was incorporated in 1939. During the Second World War its Japanese American congregation was sent to internment camps, and a Christian group used the building [1]. By the 1950s the Mission had grown to 250 people [1]. In 1959 Shunryu Suzuki arrived from Japan as chief priest. He had no grand plan: he sat zazen every morning in the temple, alone, until American students began to join him [3]. The former synagogue became the place where Westerners first sat with Suzuki, and the first home of the San Francisco Zen Center, until the Center bought 300 Page Street in 1969 [2]. The Redevelopment Agency bought the building in 1973, and the Soto Mission moved to Laguna Street [1]. The old temple is now part of the Kokoro assisted-living centre [1].

title: A Congregation Rebuilds on Golden Gate
place: First A.M.E. Zion Church, 2159 Golden Gate Avenue
hook: Its old church on Geary stood inside A-1. The congregation rebuilt out west for $130,000, and its pastor later sat on the Redevelopment Commission.
story: From 1912 the A.M.E. Zion congregation worshipped at 1669 Geary Street, at Webster [1]. That corner lay inside what became the A-1 project area, bounded by Post, Franklin, Eddy and O'Farrell, and Broderick [1]. The old church was torn down in the late 1950s. In 1960 the congregation rebuilt here at 2159 Golden Gate Avenue, in a building designed by the architect Robert Batchelor that cost about $130,000 [1]. The Assessor's roll still gives 1960 as its year of construction [2]. Other Black churches were making similar moves. After the war, older congregations were either full or too far from where their members now lived, and their pastors moved them to the Western Addition. Third Baptist built at 1399 McAllister in 1952, and Bethel A.M.E. settled on Laguna Street [1]. By 1960 more than a third of San Francisco's African Americans lived in the Western Addition [1]. The church also kept a voice in how the district was rebuilt. Its pastor, Parree Porter, joined the Redevelopment Commission, taking the seat of Hannibal Williams, who resigned in 1978 after calling his fellow commissioners "white liberal zookeepers" [3].

title: Fire hoses on the City Hall stairs
place: San Francisco City Hall rotunda, 1 Dr Carlton B Goodlett Pl
hook: Students sang 'We Shall Not Be Moved' outside a Red-hunting hearing. Police answered with fire hoses, and a decade of protest was born on a marble staircase.
story: In May 1960 the House Un-American Activities Committee came to City Hall to question suspected Communists, including union leaders and teachers. On Friday, May 13, it let mostly its own supporters into the hearing. Students from Bay Area campuses sat down outside the chamber, chanting and singing 'We Shall Not Be Moved' [1]. Then, without warning, police turned fire hoses on them. The protesters held on at the top of the rotunda staircase 'like trees in a hurricane', the Chronicle reported, until they were washed down the marble steps while officers swung clubs [1]. 'If you know what water and marble is like, it's like glass,' recalled Becky Jenkins, then a 23-year-old San Francisco State student [1][2]. Sixty-four people were arrested. Charges against all but one were dropped, and he was acquitted [1][2]. The next day longshoremen from the ILWU joined a much bigger crowd outside [2]. HUAC's film 'Operation Abolition' blamed Communists, but on television the soaked demonstrators looked like college kids [1]. Veterans of 'Black Friday' later said it led straight to Berkeley's Free Speech Movement [1].

title: Missiles, then a housing plan, then hang gliders
place: Fort Funston parking lot, former Nike missile site SF-59L, Skyline Boulevard
hook: The parking lot where dog walkers unload was a Nike missile site. When the Army left, City Hall drew up plans for houses on the bluffs.
story: After its big coast guns went quiet, Fort Funston took on a Cold War job. The post housed parts of the Nike missile system known as sites SF-59L and SF-61, and the SF-59L site is now the park's parking lot [1]. When the city acquired the property from the federal government in 1960, Mayor George Christopher asked the San Francisco Planning Department for a residential land use plan. Its map proposed houses, a school and shops for the windswept headland [2]. None were built. Part of the old post stayed with the Army and was lent to the California National Guard. In 1975 the city signed its portion over to the National Park Service on condition that it be kept as "open space necessary to urban environment and planning," and it became part of the Golden Gate National Recreation Area [1]. What the planners would have covered is now among the country's premier hang-gliding spots, above 200-foot bluffs. The peninsula's largest remaining dune field is here too. So is a colony of bank swallows, a state-threatened species, which dig nests in the sandstone cliffs. Fort Funston and Año Nuevo are their only known coastal nesting sites [3].

title: Osaka's Gift for a Samurai Voyage
place: Kanrin Maru Monument, El Camino del Mar at 34th Avenue
hook: A granite stone above the Golden Gate marks the arrival of the first Japanese ship to cross the Pacific. Its captain had never tasted ice cream.
story: On 17 March 1860 the Kanrin Maru sailed through the Golden Gate, the first Japanese ship ever to cross the Pacific. Japan had been closed to the outside world for more than 200 years, and only one of her crew had ever sailed out of sight of land [1]. San Franciscans stared at samurai topknots and paired swords. The visitors were amazed that the governor travelled without retainers and that men treated women as equals [1]. Captain Katsu Kaishu, later one of the architects of Japan's navy, said of the ice cream he was served: 'I have never tasted such a wonderful thing in my life' [1]. A hundred years later, on 17 May 1960, San Francisco's sister city Osaka presented this monument overlooking the Gate. It marks the centennial of diplomatic relations and a 'sincere desire to further strengthen the ties of friendship' [2]. The granite-and-bronze monument is part of the city's civic art collection [3]. It came just fifteen years after the war. As the Chronicle's Carl Nolte put it, relations 'did not live up to the early promise, as World War II proved' [1].

title: Pizza Puppies and the Red Chimney
place: Stonestown Galleria (original open-air Stonestown mall), 19th Avenue and Winston Drive
hook: Before the skylight and the marble, Stonestown was an open-air mall where teenagers learned to hang out, stores shut on Sundays, and a hot dog came wrapped in pizza.
story: Stonestown was dedicated on November 6, 1952 as San Francisco's first modern shopping center. Its stores were built with deep overhangs so shoppers could stay dry on foggy, drizzly days [1]. Frank Dunnigan's history of the mall remembers the food: the Walgreens lunch counter, Foster's Cafeteria, Blum's bakery and soda fountain, and in the supermarket Maison Gourmet, home of the "Pizza Puppy," a slice of cheese pizza wrapped around a hot dog [1]. Every store closed on Sundays until the late 1960s [1]. Shops like Portals to Music drew hundreds of high school students after school and on Saturdays, making "going to the mall" a new way of life [1]. Near the Emporium, Rickey's Red Chimney offered a fireplace and a full bar [1]. One reader remembers it in the 1970s as a music hot spot, with Bubba Lou and the Highballs and Bobby Freeman, singer of "The Swim"; the band pulled people onstage to sing, and she once sang there herself [2]. By the 1980s the outdoor mall looked run down. It was rebuilt under a glass skylight and reopened as Stonestown Galleria in October 1987. Woolworth, Walgreens and the cozy Red Chimney did not come back [1].

title: The Longshoremen's Answer: St. Francis Square
place: St. Francis Square Cooperative, Quickstep Lane (south of O'Farrell between Laguna and Buchanan)
hook: On land the bulldozers had emptied, a dockworkers' pension fund built a co-op where a three-bedroom share cost $610 and a family of any colour could buy in.
story: In 1960 the Redevelopment Agency set aside three blocks of cleared A-1 land for moderate-income garden apartments [1]. Lou Goldblatt, secretary-treasurer of the International Longshore and Warehouse Union (ILWU), wanted the union's growing pension fund put to work: "I thought there was no reason why that money shouldn't be used to build some low-cost housing" [1]. The ILWU-PMA trustees set up a Longshore Redevelopment Corporation. Architects Marquis & Stoller and landscape architect Lawrence Halprin designed 299 apartments in twelve three-story buildings arranged around shared courtyards, built in 1962–63 with a 3-1/8 percent federally subsidized mortgage [2]. A share cost $410 for a one-bedroom and $610 for a three-bedroom, and monthly payments ran from $84 to $140 [1]. The sales office advertised the Square as "open to all." In 1964 a new resident, Josephine Solomon, wrote to the Chronicle about "our marvelous, mixed-up collection of white, brown, and yellow children playing together" [3]. The co-op paid off its HUD mortgage in 2004 [2]. The city has not yet designated it a landmark, but SF Planning lists it as a proposed one [4].

title: The box Disneyland came in
place: Jack Tar Hotel (later Cathedral Hill Hotel), 1101 Van Ness Avenue at Geary
hook: It promised 'the world's most modern hotel', with a rooftop ice rink and drive-up rooms. San Franciscans called it Texas' idea of Los Angeles.
story: The Planning Commission approved it in under five minutes in 1958, and in spring 1960 the Jack Tar opened on a whole block of Van Ness between Geary and Post. Its owners hailed 'the world's most modern hotel'. It had 403 rooms, a 450-car garage and a 12-storey office block, and it was the first new hotel in the city in 30 years and the first with air conditioning [1]. Guests could drive almost to their doors, watch closed-circuit TV, swim, or skate on the roof [1]. San Franciscans hated its bright modernist skin. They called it 'the box Disneyland came in', 'the Wurlitzer Hilton' and 'Texas' idea of what Los Angeles looks like' [1]. The hotel was part of a chain named for the old slang for a sailor, and it had its moment on film in Coppola's The Conversation [1]. Renamed the Cathedral Hill Hotel in 1982, it burned the next year: two people died and 37 were hurt, and Mayor Dianne Feinstein called it 'total devastation' [1]. It was rebuilt, closed for good in 2009, and was briefly taken over by Occupy protesters before the wreckers arrived [1][2].

title: The eight-lane trench through the Fillmore
place: Geary Boulevard underpass at Fillmore Street
hook: In 1960 the city tore up Geary Boulevard and sank it into a trench. Neighbours say it became a wall between two communities.
story: Before the 1960s, Geary was an ordinary street where the Black Fillmore and Japanese American Nihonmachi met. Then the Redevelopment Agency's A-1 project arrived. Carol Cuenod writes that families and businesses were removed by eminent domain and whole blocks bulldozed, and that the first job in the cleared zone was to widen Geary into an eight-lane expressway, with tunnels under Fillmore Street and Presidio/Masonic, to rush traffic out to the Richmond [2]. Gary Kamiya dates the start to 1960, when 'Geary Boulevard was demolished and work began on the enormous Geary Expressway' [1]. For years the cleared land lay empty, and the displaced scattered [2]. Kamiya calls the result 'an ugly gash', built partly to carry shoppers to department stores on Masonic that no longer exist, and 'a Berlin Wall separating blacks and Japanese Americans' [1]. Redevelopment chief Justin Herman had warned that without housing for the poor, urban renewal would rightly be condemned as 'a land-grab for the rich' [1]. By 1967 residents had formed the Western Addition Community Organization to picket the agency and block bulldozers [1]. The dip that still carries traffic under Fillmore Street is part of that expressway [1][2].

title: A Saint's Tomb Beneath Geary Boulevard
place: Holy Virgin Cathedral (Joy of All Who Sorrow), 6210 Geary Boulevard
hook: The archbishop who led 5,000 refugees out of Shanghai built these golden domes on Geary. He now lies in the crypt as a saint.
story: When the communists took power in China in 1949, Archbishop John Maximovitch led the exodus of his Russian flock from Shanghai, helping some 5,000 refugees to a camp on the Philippine island of Tubabao while he lobbied in Washington for a change in the law to let them into the United States [1]. Assigned to the city in 1962, he found a community divided, but brought enough peace for its new cathedral, dedicated to the Joy of All Who Sorrow icon, to be finished [1]. Ground was broken on Geary Boulevard on 25 June 1961 [2]. The parish says the cathedral was completed in St. John's lifetime and consecrated in 1977; a 2010 Chronicle story gives 1974 for its completion [2][3]. He died on a visit to Seattle on 2 July 1966 and was laid to rest in a crypt chapel beneath the altar [1]. On 2 July 1994 the Russian Orthodox Church Outside Russia glorified him as a saint in this cathedral [1][2]. The domes still anchor what Carl Nolte called 'a neighborhood of Russian restaurants and shops' [3].

title: Diego Rivera's Mural Waits Twenty Years
place: Diego Rivera Theatre lobby, City College Ocean Campus
hook: Rivera painted his largest single mural for a college library that was never built. For two decades it sat in crates at the college.
story:
In 1940, during the second season of the Golden Gate International Exposition on Treasure Island, Diego Rivera painted a fresco 22 feet high and 74 feet long while fairgoers watched [1]. Its full title is "The Marriage of the Artistic Expression of the North and of the South on this Continent" [1]. It mixes Quetzalcoatl with an auto-plant stamping machine, and Chaplin's "Great Dictator" with Hitler, Stalin and Mussolini [2]. Rivera also painted three self-portraits and a portrait of Frida Kahlo into it [1].

The mural was meant for a new library at San Francisco Junior College designed by Timothy Pflueger, Rivera's patron [1]. The war stopped the library from being built, and its panels were crated and stored first on the fairgrounds and then at the college [1]. In the Red-baiting 1950s Rivera, a Communist, was shunned, and the fresco was still in storage when he died in 1957 [2]. Then Pflueger's younger brother Milton proposed putting it in the lobby of the campus theatre he was designing, and in 1961 it finally went on view [1][2]. On loan to SFMOMA until January 2024, it drew some 600,000 viewers. A dedicated Diego Rivera Performing Arts Center is now under construction on campus [3].

title: Jazz Moves West to Divisadero
place: Divisadero and McAllister streets (site of The Playpen)
hook: In the 1960s a string of small jazz rooms opened on Divisadero, where Miles Davis, Wes Montgomery and Ike and Tina Turner played.
story: In 1961 Joseph "Bunny" Simon, a former clerk at the Melrose Record Shop, opened his first club at Divisadero and McAllister. It became known as The Playpen [1]. In a neighborhood torn apart by redevelopment, it was a place where everyone in the Fillmore could gather. Neighbors lined up around the block to drink and dance to the jukebox, and teenagers were let in with chaperones on Sunday afternoons [1]. Upstairs, Redd Foxx, Miles Davis, Wes Montgomery, Sly and the Family Stone and Ike and Tina Turner performed [1]. Simon liked to tell how young Willie Brown opened a campaign office across the street in the early 1960s, and blamed losing the election partly on volunteers who spent their days in the club [1]. Others followed. The Both/And opened at 350 Divisadero in 1965, where Dexter Gordon and Archie Shepp made live records, and in 1967 Herman Warren opened the Half Note in a former coffee shop, with Thelonious Monk among its players [2]. The clubs were friendly rivals: each fielded a softball team, and the losers drank at the winners' bar [2].

title: Lenny Bruce Busted at the Jazz Workshop
place: Jazz Workshop (site), 473 Broadway
hook: Police sat in the audience waiting for one dirty word. Lenny Bruce gave them plenty, and a North Beach jury ended up defending his right to say it.
story: In early October 1961 the comedian Lenny Bruce played a two-night run at the Jazz Workshop, a North Beach club at 473 Broadway [1][3]. He arrived trailing trouble: a week earlier he had been arrested in Philadelphia on a narcotics charge, and on his first night he ridiculed the Philadelphia police. A newspaper wrote up the show, and on the second night San Francisco officers sat in the audience listening for anything they could call obscene [1][2]. Bruce obliged. He mocked the city's policing of gay bars, repeated a word no newspaper would print, and played on the double meaning of "to come." Police booked him at the end of the set [1][2]. His lawyer, the First Amendment attorney Albert Bendich, told the jury that Bruce belonged to the tradition of Aristophanes and Jonathan Swift. Jazz critics and literature professors testified, jurors listened to a tape of the whole performance, and they acquitted him [2]. The verdict widened the room for free speech on stage, but it also marked the start of Bruce's decline. Arrests followed in Los Angeles, Chicago and New York, and he died in 1966 [1][2].

title: Merced Heights Bets on Integration
place: Ramsell Street, Merced Heights
hook: Realtors told white owners to "get out while you can." One Merced Heights neighbourhood group answered with street sweeps, coffee and a bet on living together.
story: After World War II builders covered the empty Merced Heights ridge with stucco homes, and much of this new housing was sold to African-American families [1]. Unlike the residence parks nearby, the area had no racial covenants, and it became one of the few places in San Francisco where Black families could buy [2]. In 1950 African-Americans made up 5% of the Ingleside, Merced Heights and Ocean View census tracts. By 1970 they were 62% [2]. A 1961 Council for Civic Unity study called the OMI "a higher class Negro district" [1]. The change was not only natural. Genevieve Jefferson of Ramsell Street told the U.S. Commission on Civil Rights in 1967 that estate agents "swooped down on white people with offers to relocate" and urged her "to get out while you can" [1]. Jefferson belonged to the Merced Heights Neighborhood Association, formed in October 1961. Alongside cleanup days and lobbying for buses, it promoted integration. Realtor Julius T. Johnson hoped the races would "sit down over a beer or a cup of coffee and talk things out" [1]. In 1963 an assistant state labor commissioner called Merced Heights a model of integration [2]. Not every memory is so gentle. Longtime resident Ray Wilson recalled hearing that a Black newcomer was shot with buckshot [3].

title: Nine holes on the park's rough edge
place: Gleneagles Golf Course, 2100 Sunnydale Avenue
hook: The 1926 dream was 18 holes. What San Francisco got was a nine-hole course, a money-loser that was once the scene of a robbery on the third green.
story: The 1926 dream of an 18-hole course shrank to nine holes. Gleneagles was completed in 1961 on 60 acres along Sunnydale Avenue, on the park's south side [1]. By 1983 the city's master plan admitted that the course had lost money for years while its greens and fairways declined. New managers were fixing it up. If it ever became a liability, planners suggested, it could be turned into lawns for picnics and play [1]. The Chronicle later described the course as bordering the 'violence-prone' Sunnydale housing project. In 1995 three gunmen robbed three golfers on the third green [2]. In 2013 John King pointed out that Sunnydale's residents, on the park's southern slopes, could reach few of its facilities apart from the golf course, 'not the most logical fit' [3]. That same year, according to a park group's timeline, the course's operator signed a nine-year lease extension and started a pre-apprentice gardener program with Local 261 [4].

title: No slacks at the Golden Cask
place: Former Golden Cask, 1725 Haight Street
hook: A lesbian bar owner who lost her waterfront produce-district bar in 1961 moved to Haight Street and opened a bar for gay men, where women in slacks were not welcome.
story:
Before the Castro, Haight Street had its own quiet gay nightlife. Charlotte Coleman had run The Front, a lesbian bar near the old produce market, where she worked in slacks, jacket and tie. After police harassment, morals charges and the loss of her liquor licence, and with redevelopment about to demolish the building, she closed it in 1961 [1]. That same year she opened the Golden Cask on Haight Street, a bar for gay men. "I wouldn't even let women in with slacks," she later said [1].

It was not alone. Romeo's, at 1605 Haight, also opened in 1961 and drew mostly women. One of them remembered it as a "small, dirty, sleaze bar", and also as the place where she found her first female lover [1]. By 1965 there was a small cluster of gay and lesbian bars in and near the neighbourhood [1]. That year a San Francisco Examiner series called the Haight-Ashbury the city's new bohemian quarter, listing "homosexuals, lesbians" and "hippies" among its residents. The local police captain asked the bars to "be discreet and don't dance" [2]. The building at 1725 Haight still stands [1].

title: Pasta factory towers and the 40-foot line
place: Fontana Towers, 1000–1050 North Point St at Van Ness (site of the Fontana pasta factory)
hook: Two curving towers rose where a spaghetti factory had stood. The fight they set off, with Caspar Weinberger as the neighbours' lawyer, held the northern waterfront to 40 feet.
story: The brick Fontana spaghetti factory stood at North Point and Van Ness; in 1950 the army was using the old warehouse as a motor pool [1]. In the early 1960s developers proposed replacing it with curving 17-story towers [1]. In December 1960 the city's planning director, James McCarthy, had warned against a 'Chinese Wall' of skyscrapers along the waterfront like lower Manhattan's [1]. Russian Hill residents, mostly well off, organised through the Russian Hill Improvement Association. Their lawyer was Caspar Weinberger, a Republican former assemblyman who would later be Ronald Reagan's Secretary of Defense [1]. They were too late: the Fontana Towers went up in 1962 [1][2]. But the fight spread. In June 1961 the Planning Commission voted a temporary 40-foot height limit over about 100 blocks of the northern waterfront. Twenty-two neighbourhood groups, including the Telegraph Hill Dwellers, gathered 8,000 signatures, while the Real Estate Board, contractors and the Building Trades Council fought back [1]. In February 1964 the supervisors made the 40-foot limit permanent by 9 votes to 1. Weinberger argued it would preserve 'the whole relationship of the city to the Bay' [1]. Next door, talk of a similar tower on the Ghirardelli chocolate works set the stage for its rescue as Ghirardelli Square [2].

title: Polk Street becomes the gay main street
place: Former Town Squire, 1318 Polk St
hook: Before the Castro, there was Polk. A mod clothing shop and a record store opened by gay couples turned a street of candy stores into San Francisco's first gay neighbourhood.
story:
In the 1950s Polk Street below Nob Hill was lined with "mom and pop" shops: news stands, shoe repairers, candy stores. "It wasn't a magnet," recalled Randall Wallace, but it was "the cruisiest street in the city" [1]. Around 1960 a gay couple, August Territo and Terry Popek, opened the Town Squire, a trendy men's clothing store, at 1318 Polk [2]. (Sources differ on whether it opened in 1960 or 1961 [1][3].) In May 1961 Wallace and his partner opened Gramaphone Records nearby in a derelict old market, betting that society-page customers from Nob Hill and Pacific Heights would follow [1][2].

"Then the bars began," Wallace said. "It just began to multiply, and it was the place to be on the weekends and the weeknights" [1]. The city's historic context statement calls Polk San Francisco's first modern gay neighbourhood [3]. By 1966 there were at least 26 gay bars and businesses in Polk Gulch, and it was the first time the city's gay business owners formed an above-ground, upscale commercial bloc [1]. A bartender from the Suzy-Q on Polk became the first president of the Tavern Guild, the country's first gay business association, and in 1971 a gay magazine called Polk "the gayest street in San Francisco" [3].

title: Pop Warner Football Out of a Police Garage
place: Taraval Police Station, 2345 24th Avenue (across from McCoppin Square)
hook: For fifteen seasons a Sunset youth football team kept its lockers in a police station garage and practiced across the street in McCoppin Square.
story: In fall 1961 Bob Moore, John Shea and police officer Steve Spelman put together the first San Francisco Mariners, a Pop Warner youth football team, with Sully Cassou. Spelman had coached the Police Athletic League's Happy Hibernian Warriors, and Moore and Shea coached flag football at South Sunset Park [1]. The team started at 26th and Vicente. Then it moved into the garage of the Taraval Police Station, a brick-fronted 1924 building on 24th Avenue [1][2]. The boys practiced across the street at McCoppin Square and played home games on Lincoln High's field. So many came out that the club added two younger squads, the Mariner Mates and the Mariner Seaweeds [1]. They lost the 1966 championship to the San Francisco Steelers. In 1968 they won the city championship at the Junior Bantam level, beating the San Ramon Thunderbirds 14-0 in the Joe Lacy Memorial Bowl [1]. The coaches were mostly businessmen, construction workers and police officers. Their motto: 'A man never stands so tall as when he stoops to help a boy.' By 1976 the club had folded. The lockers were cleared out of the station garage, and the green-and-white jackets went into Sunset attics [1].

title: Potstickers on Polk Street
place: The Mandarin (first location), 2209 Polk St
hook: Cecilia Chiang was left holding a Polk Street lease and a lost $10,000 deposit. So she opened a restaurant that changed how Americans ate Chinese food.
story: Cecilia Chiang was born in 1920 in Wuxi, the tenth of twelve children in a wealthy family. In 1942 she and a sister walked for nearly six months to escape Japanese-occupied territory [1]. Years later, visiting a widowed sister in San Francisco, she agreed to help two friends from Tokyo lease a small space at 2209 Polk Street and wrote a $10,000 deposit. The friends backed out, the landlord kept the money, and in 1961 she opened The Mandarin herself [1][2]. It served northern Chinese dishes few Americans had tasted, on a menu of 200 or 300 items depending on the source, with five potstickers for $1 [1][2]. She could not get a liquor licence (as a foreign-born woman, says one account; as a non-resident, says another), and as a Mandarin speaker far from Chinatown she struggled to find suppliers [2]. For eighteen months she lost money. Johnny Kan, owner of Kan's in Chinatown, urged her to shorten and Americanise the menu. She refused [2]. Then Herb Caen came in (in 1963 by one account, with Trader Vic's founder Vic Bergeron by another) and certified the "hole-in-the-wall" the best Chinese food east of the Pacific [1][2]. In 1968 the Mandarin moved to Ghirardelli Square [2]. Chiang died in 2020, aged 100 [1].

title: The Hill's ladies versus the freeway
place: Pennsylvania Avenue above Interstate 280
hook: In 1961 Potrero Hill women presented the mayor with their own freeway plan while others marched outside. The freeway came anyway, and then the hillside began to slip.
story:
In April 1961 San Francisco supervisors approved a $40 million freeway to link the Southern Freeway at Evans with the Embarcadero, "nestled into the East slope of Potrero on Iowa Street" [1]. Residents remembered what the James Lick Freeway, Highway 101, had done fourteen blocks away. They fought to save the 64 properties in its path, 34 of them homes [1]. While some women presented an alternative plan to the mayor, others marched outside with anti-freeway signs. The mayor said he was impressed but had to be guided by the experts [1]. The Hill's activist women were everywhere; the press nicknamed two of them the "Gold Dust Twins" [1].

The freeway, now Interstate 280, cut off the flats to the east, which more and more people began calling Dogpatch. Residents forced out were paid well below market prices [2]. The damage outlasted construction. When the state built a big retaining wall, the ground settled under houses about 40 feet above the freeway on Pennsylvania. In May 1970 the damaged homes were auctioned off as-is. Repairs and $100 a day to bus St. Teresa's pupils were set to double the cost of the job. "This fiasco might have been avoided," the Hill's chroniclers wrote, "if they had only listened." [1]

title: The Pitcher the Wind Blew Off the Mound
place: Candlestick Park (site), Candlestick Point
hook: At the 1961 All-Star Game a gust at Candlestick made a slight Giants reliever sway. The legend that followed took on a life of its own.
story: Candlestick Park opened on 12 April 1960, built on landfill at Candlestick Point [3]. The next summer it hosted the first of two 1961 All-Star Games. The day was unusually hot and several fans collapsed, until the park's notorious wind picked up in the eighth inning [2]. Giants reliever Stu Miller threw famously slow junk pitches. He was listed at 5-foot-11, though people who stood next to him put him closer to 5-foot-8 [2]. He came in during the ninth with the National League ahead 3–2 [2]. As he set to pitch, a gust hit him. "My whole body waved," he recalled, and the umpire called a balk that moved the runners up and helped the American League tie the game [2][1]. The next day's headline read "Miller Blown Off Mound," and the tale kept growing. Don Zimmer remembered him going backward "and he just kept going" [1]. But the game wasn't televised, and the radio call, later dug up by a researcher, never mentioned the wind [1]. Miller said he had only swayed "2 or 3 inches", and he was also the winning pitcher once Willie Mays scored [1]. "I guess that's better than 'Stu Who?'" he said in 2007. "I'd rather be remembered for something." [1]

title: The Polk Street bar in Life magazine
place: Jumpin' Frog site, about 2111 Polk St
hook: In 1964 Life magazine photographed men at a Polk Street bar and called San Francisco the nation's gay capital. The bar was the Jumpin' Frog.
story: In the early 1960s Polk Street became what the city's historic context statement calls San Francisco's first modern gay neighbourhood [1]. The Jumpin' Frog opened as a gay bar in 1961 at 2111 Polk (other records give 2109 or 2123) and drew crowds to its Monday movie nights [2]. In 1962 gay bar owners and staff formed the Tavern Guild, the first gay business association in the United States, to fight police and liquor-board harassment with lawyers, bail money and a telephone alert network [1][3]. The Frog sponsored the first Beaux Arts Ball, and Daryl Glied, its manager (some accounts say owner), persuaded the guild to make it an annual fundraiser. He became the guild's third president [2][3]. From 1963 the Halloween ball was the centrepiece of the city's drag community [1]. In 1964 Life featured the Frog in a spread that dubbed San Francisco the nation's "gay capital", one of a handful of things that drew people to Polk [1][2]. A few blocks north, the owners of a slow bar at 2360 Polk turned it gay in 1962 as Cloud Seven and quadrupled their business [2]. By the late 1960s, one man recalled, customers at its numbered tables used lip-shaped phones to ask the bar for "the third guy from the end" [1].

title: The red house of the sedition trial
place: Near 24th and Kansas Streets, base of Potrero Hill
hook: When the federal sedition case against a Potrero Hill couple finally fell apart in 1961, they painted their Victorian barn red and threw a party for 150.
story:
John W. "Bill" Powell and his wife Sylvia had published the China Monthly Review in Shanghai. In April 1956, back in San Francisco, a federal grand jury indicted them and associate editor Julian Schuman for sedition. The most damaging charge was that they had reported Chinese claims that the US used germ warfare in the Korean War [1]. Shut out of newspaper work, the Powells bought, rebuilt and resold old houses, starting with one on Potrero Hill [1].

Their son Tom remembers a three-room cottage on Carolina Street under the water tower, then the "house with 47 steps" on Rhode Island Street. By 1959 they were in a corner Victorian at the foot of the hill, kitty-corner from the Dutch Boy paint factory at 24th and Kansas [2]. At the old Starr King school, Sylvia had Tom sit out A-bomb drills in the principal's office. Nobody, she said, could survive a bomb in that basement [2].

The 1959 trial ended in a mistrial, and in 1961 Attorney General Robert F. Kennedy dropped the last charges [1]. Bill finished painting the house barn red. Every wooden house then was white, Tom recalls. Sylvia threw a party for about 150 professors, lawyers, union members, journalists and artists, with drums, torches and an oak cask of red wine [2].

title: The song first sung on Nob Hill
place: Fairmont Hotel (Venetian Room), 950 Mason St
hook: A ballad two homesick New Yorkers wrote about San Francisco got its first public airing in a Fairmont supper club, and the city never let it go.
story:
In December 1961 Tony Bennett stepped onto the stage of the Venetian Room, the Fairmont Hotel's supper club, and sang "I Left My Heart in San Francisco" in public for the very first time [1][2]. Released on record the following year, the 1962 ballad became either the city's ultimate ode or its most overplayed cliché, depending on whom you ask [1].

The bond lasted six decades. When Mayor Dianne Feinstein passed the hat to save the crumbling cable cars in the early 1980s, Bennett was among the stars who lent their names [3]. In June 2018 the city renamed the block of Mason Street in front of the Fairmont "Tony Bennett Way." A stuntman dressed as the singer rappelled down the hotel's facade to open the party, and then the real Bennett, aged 91, took the stage: "It's so beautiful. The sun is out and it's San Francisco at its best right now," he said [2].

On 25 April 2020, with the city sheltering from COVID-19, residents were invited to sing the song together from windows and balconies at noon as a salute to health workers, and Bennett released a fresh rendition for them to sing along to [1].

title: Who Rolled the First Mission Burrito?
place: El Faro, 2399 Folsom St at 20th
hook: Some firemen wanted sandwiches. The grocer had none. The next day he had something else, wrapped in three overlapping tortillas.
story: Febronio Ontiveros and his wife opened a corner grocery, El Faro ("the lighthouse"), at 2399 Folsom Street on September 25, 1961 [1]. The next day, by Ontiveros's account, firemen from a station down the street came in wanting sandwiches. He had none, so he returned ready with burritos [1]. Large tortillas were not sold commercially then, so he overlapped three six-inch ones and charged a dollar [1]. The title is contested. At Mi Rancho market on 20th Street, a woman named Juanita Villalobos served burritos from around 1965; its manager conceded, "He had 'em before we did" [1]. On Valencia Street, Raul Duran of La Cumbre dates his first burrito to September 29, 1969, "because it was my wife's birthday" [2]. In 1972 he and his wife Micaela turned their meat market into a taqueria, and he says the new thing was the style of service: "Taquerias were new. No one had anything like that" [2]. By 1993, SF Weekly estimated the Mission was eating about 25,000 burritos a day [1].

title: Willie Brown Picks a Fight in Forest Knolls
place: Forest Knolls tract, Christopher Drive on the slope of Mount Sutro
hook: A 27-year-old lawyer who defended hustlers for a living took on a developer who wouldn't sell new hillside homes to Black buyers.
story:
Around 1953 crews clear-cut trees and terraced the hillside east of 8th Avenue and Lawton, below Mount Sutro, for a new subdivision called Forest Knolls [2]. In 1961 the developer was refusing to sell homes there to Black people. The Chronicle placed the tract "west of Twin Peaks" [1].

Willie Brown, 27, took him on. A Hastings law graduate who couldn't get hired by the big firms, Brown was defending pimps, prostitutes and street hustlers to make a living. His fiery, articulate protest got wide press coverage. Many white San Franciscans backed him, including Dianne Feinstein, then a little-known homemaker [1].

The Chronicle later judged that the protest failed to end housing discrimination. But it made Brown's name, and three years later he was in the State Assembly [1]. The Western Neighborhoods Project credits the community campaign with finally opening Forest Knolls to people of color [2]. Brown went on to become Assembly Speaker and mayor of San Francisco. It started on these streets below the forest.

title: A Soviet Rocket Sells Burgers on Ocean
place: Beep's Burgers, 1051 Ocean Avenue at Lee Avenue
hook: At the height of the space race, two brothers opened a drive-in on Ocean Avenue and put a Soviet Vostok rocket on the sign.
story:
In 1962 brothers Stephen and George Essaf opened a drive-in burger stand at Ocean and Lee avenues. They aimed it at students from City College and the nearby high schools [1]. Stephen had been a photographer for the Associated Press and the San Francisco Examiner, his family says. He gave that up to go into business with his brother. Even their father helped out, making sure the potatoes for the fries were fresh, peeled and cut. The stand was open seven days a week, closed only on Christmas and New Year's Day [1].

They called it Beep's after the beeping of the first satellites. The neon sign shows a spacecraft that the city's Legacy Business report identifies as the USSR's Vostok One rocket. An Ingleside Light article reprinted in the city's file calls it "no small irony" that an icon of Soviet space triumph was selling burgers and shakes to American motorists [1].

The Essafs retired in the 1970s, though the family kept the property, and a series of operators followed. For years the rocket's neon was dark [1][2]. In 2014 Samantha Wong, who had eaten there as a San Francisco State student, bought the business and had the sign restored [1][2]. In 2017 the city took up Beep's nomination for its Legacy Business Registry [1][2].

title: Fire in the tunnel under the hill
place: 19th and Arkansas Streets, above the old Western Pacific tunnel
hook: In summer 1962 a fire burned inside a railroad tunnel under Potrero Hill. As its timbers gave way, the ground sank beneath houses at 19th and Arkansas.
story:
Western Pacific trains ran through a tunnel under the north side of Potrero Hill, coming out near Mariposa and Carolina Streets [1]. At the end of June 1962 the tunnel caught fire. Photographs from June 30 and July 1 show the scene at Texas and Sierra, Missouri and Sierra, 23rd and Pennsylvania, and at the tunnel's north mouth [1]. The fire weakened the tunnel's wooden supports and it collapsed [2].

The Hill's own history records homes at Arkansas and 19th collapsing, and houses on Missouri between 20th and 22nd cracking and settling [3]. The dates don't agree. That timeline puts the Arkansas Street collapse in July 1962. Another dates it to July 1960, with a separate Missouri Street collapse in 1962 [4]. A photo caption also shows a hole at Arkansas and 19th in July 1960 [1].

The city plugged both ends of the tunnel with concrete and the railroad abandoned it. The city demanded $781,000 and settled with Western Pacific for $700,000 in 1964 [1]. The slope above stayed empty for thirty years. After a neighbourhood fight to keep it as open space, lofts were built where the tunnel had caved in [2].

title: From pharmacy to sari-sari store
place: 58 Leland Avenue
hook: Under a Space Age starburst on Leland Avenue, a druggist worried about elders and ATMs, and later a Filipino corner store moved in.
story: The 1941 building at 58 Leland Avenue is hard to miss. Its Streamline Moderne front has a centre tower that SF Heritage's Woody LaBounty calls 'both Mayan Revival and a bit Space Age', topped by a starburst finial he had never seen anywhere else in the city [1]. From 1962, Jack and Yvonne Creighton ran the Leland Pharmacy here [2]. Their ads promised 'friendly professional prescription service' and pointed out that the shop was next to the post office [3]. In November 1987 the Grapevine asked merchants what Leland Avenue needed. Jack Creighton, 58, wanted more medical services, a hardware store and another bank. He worried that Bank of America would do away with tellers and automate, which would be 'difficult and unsafe for elders and everyone else, too' [3]. The pharmacy closed in 1989 [2]. By 2001 the storefront was the Sari-Sari Food Store, named for the Filipino word for a small neighbourhood shop, and the Little Quiapo Bake Shop was working up the street at 169 Leland [4]. More recently the space has been a Mexican and Central American market [1].

title: Lowell leaves its bricks for the lake
place: Lowell High School, 1101 Eucalyptus Drive
hook: For Lowell's Class of 1962, the big news of senior year was that their school was moving to Lake Merced. Fifty years later they borrowed the old one back.
story: For almost fifty years, Lowell, the West's oldest public high school, filled a brick campus on the block bounded by Masonic, Hayes, Ashbury and Grove. It had opened there in 1913 as the school's third home [1]. Students had to be recommended for admission and came from all over the city by cable car, streetcar and trolley bus [1]. The Class of 1962 remembered that little happened that year except the biggest news of all: the school would close and move. "All year long we knew that," one graduate said [1]. That fall a new Lowell opened out by Lake Merced [1], on roughly the spot where the Ocean House roadhouse had stood until it burned in the early 1880s [2]. Before they left, the seniors' football team went 8-1 and beat St. Ignatius on Thanksgiving before 22,500 fans at Kezar. A few enterprising seniors smuggled a 20-foot sheet up Coit Tower to spell out "Lowell Champs" [1]. Students had been told the old building was seismically unsafe and would be demolished, but it never was. In May 2012 the Class of '62 borrowed it back from City College for its 50th reunion, and one of them breathed in and said it "still smells exactly the same. Polished linoleum" [1].

title: The night the Van Ness cathedral burned
place: Site of the second St. Mary's Cathedral, Van Ness Avenue at O'Farrell Street (1001 Van Ness)
hook: For 71 years a red-brick Gothic cathedral climbed steep stairs at Van Ness and O'Farrell. On a September night in 1962 it went up in flames.
story: In May 1887 Catholics laid the cornerstone of San Francisco's second cathedral at the corner of Van Ness Avenue and O'Farrell Street, and after four years of building it was dedicated in January 1891 [1]. It was a red-brick Gothic Revival church with steep front stairs and a rose window [1]. Nearly two decades later, on 18 April 1906, firefighters trying to stop the post-earthquake fire set off dynamite a block away at O'Farrell and Van Ness [3]. On the evening of 7 September 1962, a huge fire destroyed the cathedral [1][2]. Archbishop Joseph McGucken first wanted to rebuild right there, in 'a modern, contemporary design, but not what most people call modernistic' [1]. Instead the corner was judged too small. After tense negotiations and land trades, the archdiocese got a new hilltop site at Gough and Geary, and KRON-TV got the old cathedral corner for its offices and studios [1]. A 1959 photograph looking up O'Farrell from Van Ness shows the brick cathedral with St. Mark's Lutheran on the hill behind it [3]. That is one of the last views of the corner before it became a TV station.

title: The other crookedest street
place: Vermont Street curves between 20th and 22nd streets, below McKinley Square
hook: Lombard gets the tourists, but Vermont Street's fans say its curves are tighter. In 1962 its neighbours spent three weekends trying to make it famous.
story:
In the 1910s Vermont Street was a straight, unpaved road down the west slope of Potrero Hill below McKinley Square [1]. City and archive photographs of it survive from 1927 and 1930 [2]. Its serpentine switchbacks were built in the 1930s as a Works Progress Administration project [1].

The rivalry with Lombard Street goes back at least to 1962. That year Joseph Sheridan of the News Call Bulletin reported that about 40 hill residents wanted Vermont to be as famous as its cousin. They spent three weekends in a row installing sprinklers and planting 200 or more trees and shrubs, including junipers, pines, veronica and escallonia. Some were still growing in 2016 [1].

The numbers are argued over to this day. Vermont has five curves to Lombard's eight, and a 14.3 percent grade to Lombard's 18.18 percent. Its fans point to the tightness of the turns [1]. In 1977 the city made the block one-way southbound [1]. Houses line only its east side; the west side looks out over Highway 101 and San Francisco General Hospital [1]. Since 2008 it has hosted the Bring Your Own Big Wheel race, which founder Jon Brumit moved here after Lombard's residents complained [1].

title: The tower that promised beauty
place: Microwave tower, Bernal Heights summit
hook: In 1962 a newspaper called Bernal Hill ugly and promised that a phone company relay tower would make it beautiful.
story:
On May 31, 1962, the News-Call Bulletin ran the headline 'Ugly Hill to Be Beautified'. Pacific Telephone had paid $90,000 for just over an acre on the 430-foot summit of Bernal Heights. It planned a $2 million, 400-circuit microwave relay station there, one link in a nationwide chain [1]. City planner Ruth Joffe worked with the company to curve the access road and the building's roof to follow the hill. Her idea of making the antenna a free-form sculpture was 'reluctantly abandoned as not feasible'. The company promised trees, wild lilac and manzanita. It also promised to use its excavated rock to cover a scar left by 30 years of city quarrying, and it promised no fences [1].

A neighbour's history dates the finished tower to 1962, inside a minimal chain-link fence [2]. Greta Van Praag of Prospect Avenue led a campaign to plant pines that would soften its outline [2]. The neighbourhood blog Bernalwood nicknames it 'Sutrito Tower', though Sutro Tower did not exist for its first decade [1]. Some residents still wish it gone. A few, one neighbour wrote, call it Bernal's Eiffel Tower [2].

title: A ferry pier becomes a harbor of ghosts
place: Hyde Street Pier, foot of Hyde St
hook: A movie 'pirate ship' rusting in Sausalito, a museum founder with a passion for sail, and a dead ferry pier: together they made a floating museum.
story: Hyde Street Pier opened in 1922 as a car-ferry landing for Sausalito, and the last ferry left on July 25, 1938 [1]. It came back to life thanks to Karl Kortum, a maritime historian who loved the age of sail. In 1951 he founded the San Francisco Maritime Museum in the empty upper floors of the Aquatic Park Bathhouse [2]. In 1954 the museum, led by Kortum and Alma Spreckels, paid $25,000 for the Pacific Queen, a rusting square-rigger in Sausalito. She had been launched in Scotland in 1886 as Balclutha, sailed 17 times around Cape Horn, and later appeared in Mutiny on the Bounty and toured the coast as a "pirate ship." Local people gave cash, materials and labor to restore her and her original name [3]. Their efforts led to a state historical monument in September 1957. The state leased the pier in 1961, rebuilt it in 1962 and 1963, and opened the Maritime State Historical Park on October 5, 1963. In 1988 it became part of San Francisco Maritime National Historical Park, and the park still docks its historic fleet at the pier [1].

title: Every stool taken at Mel's
place: Site of Mel's Drive-In, 3355 Geary Boulevard at Beaumont Avenue
hook: Black San Franciscans could eat at this Geary drive-in but not work out front. One weekend in 1963, protesters filled every seat and waited to be arrested.
story: Mel's Drive-In at 3355 Geary was part of a chain co-owned by Mel Weiss and Supervisor Harold Dobbs, who was running for mayor in 1963 [1]. Members of the DuBois Clubs, working with Black teenagers, heard the same thing again and again: they could eat at Mel's, but they couldn't work there [2]. A student Direct Action Group found that Black employees were kept to kitchen and janitorial jobs, "always out of sight" [1]. Pickets from the Ad Hoc Committee to End Discrimination went up in October. Mario Savio, later the voice of Berkeley's Free Speech Movement, joined a Mel's picket line a couple of times [2]. On the weekend before the election, protesters picketed Dobbs's home on Saturday. That night and again on Sunday they held the first mass sit-in of the Bay Area civil rights movement, filling every empty booth and stool and refusing to order [1][2]. Police arrested 64 people the first night and 48 the next [1]. Dobbs lost to John Shelley. Within days he signed an agreement to put Black workers in "up front" jobs as waitresses, cashiers and bartenders [1][2]. Months later the same tactics came to the Sheraton-Palace Hotel [1].

title: Longshoremen build a garden in the rubble
place: St. Francis Square Cooperative, Geary to O'Farrell between Laguna and Webster
hook: Redevelopment had flattened the blocks. A dockworkers' pension fund bet it could build the West Coast's first racially integrated housing co-op there.
story: By 1960, bulldozed land around Geary had sat empty for years, while developers planned luxury towers on a hill newly renamed 'Cathedral Hill' [1]. Lou Goldblatt, secretary-treasurer of the International Longshore and Warehouse Union, had another idea. 'There was no reason why the pension funds... should just be laying around being invested in high grade securities,' he recalled, when the money could 'build some low-cost housing' [1]. Justin Herman of the Redevelopment Agency offered three blocks for moderate-income garden apartments. The ILWU-PMA pension fund, shared by the union and the shipowners' Pacific Maritime Association, sponsored the project [1]. Built in 1962 and 1963, St. Francis Square had to fit what working families could pay: a $410 to $610 share, then $84 to $140 a month, with utilities and taxes included [1]. Two streets were closed to make a superblock. Twelve three-storey buildings by Marquis & Stoller surround three shared gardens by landscape architect Lawrence Halprin, designed around Jane Jacobs' 'eyes on the street' [2]. The Cultural Landscape Foundation calls it the first racially integrated housing cooperative on the West Coast [2]. At the 1963 dedication Harry Bridges credited Goldblatt as 'the man with the imagination and drive' [1].

title: Mansell Street, the Freeway That Never Came
place: Mansell Street at San Bruno Avenue, eastern end of the 1963 parkway
hook: Mansell Street is far wider than the streets it joins. It was built as one piece of a cross-town parkway, and the rest was never built.
story:
In January 1950 the City Planning Department proposed a parkway along Mansell Street to link McLaren Park with the Bayshore Freeway, with an extension east to Bayview Park and the bay [1]. A 1951 study grew the idea into a seven-and-a-half-mile cross-town John McLaren Parkway running from Lake Merced to Bayview Park [2]. Only one piece was built: a divided four-lane road from Brazil Avenue east to San Bruno Avenue, finished in 1963 [2]. Once Interstate 280 opened, the cross-town route was no longer needed. The city's own 1983 park plan called the road 'an unneeded anachronism' that had taken the park's flattest ridgetop land and split the park in two [2]. The plan's traffic figures showed only 1,867 cars eastbound and 2,330 westbound in a day [2].

For decades, people on foot jumped guardrails to get across, a real-life game of Frogger [3]. On November 23, 2015 the city broke ground on a $6.8 million project between University Street and Brazil Avenue; the Portola blog put the total at over $7 million. It was designed to put cars on one side of the wooded median and give the other side to people walking and cycling [3][4]. The Portola stretch, from University down to San Bruno Avenue, is part of the same 1963 road [2].

title: The Castro's first gay bar
place: Missouri Mule, 2348 Market St
hook: Before rainbow flags, the Castro was an Irish-Catholic parish emptying out for the suburbs. Then a tavern on Market Street got a new owner and a piano singer.
story: In the 1950s and 1960s, Eureka Valley was a working-class, largely Irish-Catholic district whose families were leaving their Victorians for new houses in the Sunset, the Peninsula, Marin and the East Bay [1]. The empty flats and cheap rents left space for something new. In 1963 John Burgoa took over the Missouri Mule at 2348 Market Street, a tavern that had run as a straight bar under the same name for more than a decade, and it became what historians count as the Castro's first gay bar [1][2]. Burgoa ran it until 1973. Its star was a 'campy' singer called Vivacious Vivian, who played honky-tonk piano while, in one recollection, 'all order of gay men gathered round' [1]. Others soon followed: the Honey Bucket at 4146 18th Street, The Mistake at 3988 18th, and restaurants like Burke's Corner House [1]. Public historian Gerard Koskovich describes the whole area as a 'declining working-class neighborhood' that was already turning into a gay enclave. By the early 1970s, he says, it 'was becoming very clearly marked as a gay neighborhood' [2].

title: The Mayor of Butchertown Runs for Mayor
place: Sam Jordan's Bar, 4004 Third Street
hook: A Navy veteran and Golden Gloves boxer turned a Third Street tavern into Bayview's living room, then became the first African American to run for mayor of San Francisco.
story: Sam Jordan came to San Francisco from Texas after serving in the Navy in World War II. He spent about ten years as a longshoreman and boxed in the Golden Gloves, where he won as a light-heavyweight [1][2]. In 1959 he bought the old tavern at 4004–4006 Third Street, fixed it up and reopened it as Sam Jordan's Tavern [1]. It quickly became the gathering place of Bayview's Black working class, with scholarship drives, nights for local musicians, businessmen's lunches and political strategy sessions [1]. In 1963 Jordan became the first African American to run for mayor of San Francisco. He ran on equality, civil rights and workers' rights and finished fourth of eight [1][2]. Neighbours called him the "Mayor of Butchertown," after the district's old slaughterhouse trade. He wasn't sure he deserved it: "What good is it to be called a leader if you can't get people to do for themselves?" [3]. He lived at the bar until he retired in 1995 and died in 2003, and the building became City Landmark No. 263 [1]. His children kept it going through a TV makeover and heavy debt. In 2019 they announced it would close, with a last-call block party that November [2].

title: The Sun-Reporter's Upstairs Room on Turk
place: 1366 Turk Street (site of Dr. Goodlett's office and the Sun-Reporter)
hook: A doctor who won a newspaper in a poker game moved it to Turk Street, where Malcolm X, Muhammad Ali and future mayors came upstairs.
story: Dr. Carlton B. Goodlett came to San Francisco in 1945 and opened a medical practice. He soon invested with the dentist Daniel Collins in the Reporter, a Black paper founded in the Fillmore during the war [1]. The paper's longtime editor, Thomas Fleming, later told the story of how they got a second paper, the Sun: its white owner lost about $2,500 to Goodlett at poker one night and offered him the Sun for $1,500 [2]. The two papers became the Sun-Reporter, with the motto "That no good cause shall lack a champion, and that evil shall not thrive unopposed" [2]. The sources disagree on some early dates. In 1963 Goodlett moved both his medical office and the paper to his new building at 1366 Turk Street [1][2]. Its upstairs Community Room became a hub: Malcolm X, Muhammad Ali, Dick Gregory and the Black Panthers came through, and politicians from Willie Brown to George Moscone stopped by for advice [2]. Goodlett also led the local NAACP and in 1966 ran for governor, finishing third in the Democratic primary [1][2]. He died in 1997. The Turk Street building is gone [1].

title: The freeway that became a bike path
place: Mansell Street through McLaren Park
hook: Ever wondered why Mansell Street is so absurdly wide? It was meant to be a crosstown parkway that never came.
story: Mansell Street is suspiciously wide. In 1951 a redevelopment study proposed a seven-and-a-half-mile 'John McLaren Parkway' from Lake Merced to Bayview Park, running along Mansell [1]. Only one section was built, a four-lane divided road through the park from Brazil Avenue east toward San Bruno Avenue. It was finished in 1963 [1][2]. Then Interstate 280 was built and the crosstown route was dropped. The 1983 master plan bluntly called the leftover road 'an unneeded anachronism' [1]. For decades it cut the park in half. The Chronicle noted in 2004 that most San Franciscans knew the park mainly as a shortcut to Candlestick Park, and a visiting class spotted fresh skid marks from drivers using Mansell as a speedway [3]. In 2013 the Recreation and Park Commission approved a plan to close one side of the median to cars and give it to people walking and cycling. The other side would carry one lane of traffic each way, including Muni's 29-Sunset [4]. The rebuilt road reopened in February 2017 [2].

title: The night the Fox went dark
place: Site of the Fox Theatre (now Fox Plaza), 1350-1390 Market Street
hook: A 4,651-seat movie palace closed with Hollywood stars, a rising Wurlitzer and one stagehand turning off the work light. The next morning they sold the doors.
story: William Fox opened his San Francisco showplace on June 28, 1929, with the Charlie Chan picture Behind That Curtain. Designed by Thomas W. Lamb, it had 4,651 seats [1][2]. After the war, audiences shrank as television spread. In 1961 voters turned down a proposal for the city to buy the building, with 59.2 percent voting no [2]. The last night came on February 16, 1963. A searchlight swept the sky. Many of the ushers had also worked opening night in 1929. Organist Everett Nourse played the giant Wurlitzer, and the stage filled with stars including Jane Russell, Jane Wyman, Kay Starr and Hedda Hopper [1]. Hopper told the crowd she could not understand why it was happening. Herb Caen wrote that it was a wonder they hadn't torn it down sooner [1]. At the finale the cast sang Auld Lang Syne and left the stage one by one. A lone stagehand walked across, put out his cigarette and switched off the work light [1]. The next day everything was for sale: a bronze door for $250, a seat for $2.50. The theatre was demolished in 1963, and the Fox Plaza tower stands on the site. The organ now plays in Hollywood's El Capitan Theatre [1][2].

title: The pastor who took down the cross
place: Glide Memorial Church, 330 Ellis St at Taylor
hook: When Cecil Williams arrived, Glide's congregation was down to a handful. He opened the doors to addicts, sex workers and gay runaways, and it grew into a phenomenon.
story: In 1962 Glide Memorial, a well-endowed Methodist church at Ellis and Taylor, hired the Rev. Lewis Durham to rethink its mission. Durham brought in young clergy, among them Cecil Williams, the grandson of a slave from segregated San Angelo, Texas, who arrived in 1963 [1][2]. Randy Shaw, who wrote a history of the neighbourhood, says the congregation was 'almost down to the single digits' [2]. Williams rebuilt it by becoming a fierce advocate for civil rights and, most controversially then, for gay and transgender people at a time when police were arresting them in bars [2]. Glide's pastors worked with sex workers, runaways, hippies and addicts. In the early 1970s an activist said: 'You knew where the women's movement was: it was at Glide church at 7:30' [1]. Williams took the crucifix out of the sanctuary. A 1995 Chronicle profile dates this to 1965, while other accounts say 1967 [3]. Sunday services, with a gospel choir and jazz band, became joyous celebrations [2][3]. In 1980 Glide started a free meals programme serving three hot meals a day [2]. Williams stepped down as pastor in 2000 and died in 2024, aged 94 [2].

title: The spinsters' garden that became Allyne Park
place: Allyne Park, Green and Gough Streets
hook: Two sisters lived their whole lives in a Victorian house at Green and Gough. When developers came for the lot, the neighbors fought back.
story: Mary Newell Burr, daughter of the 1850s mayor Ephraim Burr, married the oil man John Winslow Allyne in 1871. They built a big house at Green and Gough, which a 1905 map shows with several small greenhouses on the grounds [1][2]. At one time the family owned all the lots from Green to Union along the west side of Gough [1]. Allyne died in 1901 and left the house to his daughters, Edith and Lucy. Neither married, and they lived there their entire lives [1][2]. With their Burr cousins they traveled the world, filling diaries and sketchbooks now at the California Historical Society, which also holds Lucy's photographs of the 1915 exposition [2]. They gave land to the Colonial Dames, who in 1952 moved the Octagon House across Gough onto it, and later a corner lot for its garden [1]. Gifts in their wills helped the California Historical Society buy the Whittier Mansion [1]. The sisters died in 1960 and 1963, though the sources disagree about which went first [1][2]. Then a developer proposed a 140-unit apartment building for the site. The Dames, neighbors, the Union Street Association and the Sherman School PTA petitioned against it. The city bought the property, tore down the house and made a park [1]. Today its lawn belongs to neighborhood dogs and hide-and-seek [1].

title: Two-pound dough at Mission and Geneva
place: Bravo Pizza, 5145 Mission Street at Geneva Avenue
hook: Bravo Pizza has been pressing two-pound deep-dish dough at the Excelsior's busiest corner since 1963. In late 2025 an Excelsior native bought it after his cousin called it a dump.
story: Bravo Pizza has been at 5145 Mission Street, on the busy corner of Mission and Geneva, since 1963 [2]. It serves deep-dish slices and Italian-American food, and Mission Local calls it the pioneer of San Francisco-style deep-dish pizza, made from a two-pound dough [1]. In the autumn of 2025 Sam Hernandez's cousin stopped in for a slice after a 49ers game. He rang Hernandez to say 'this place looks like a dump', and added that he had asked the owner whether he would sell. The owner said yes [1]. Hernandez, 43, grew up in the Excelsior and lives a few blocks away. He says he 'flew over here' to check. Then he called his best friend, Jason Yu, 34, who grew up in Chinatown. Yu had once spent $200,000 trying to open a matcha soft-serve shop in the Mission and had publicly sworn he would never open a business in the city again [1][2]. The pair bought Bravo in December 2025 and reopened it in January 2026. The chef is Jimmy Prokopos, son of a former owner, Peter Prokopos, and the dough is the same [1]. 'We may not be able to give you what your grandma gave you,' Hernandez said, 'but we'll give you something special' [1].

title: A gay rights movement planned in a basement
place: 529 Clayton Street
hook: For months in 1964, four men met in a Clayton Street basement to plan what became the largest homophile organisation in America.
story:
In 1964 four men, Bill Plath, William Beardemphl, Jim Foster and Mark Forrester, met for months in the basement of an apartment building at 529 Clayton Street. What they were planning launched in September 1964 as the Society for Individual Rights, or SIR [1]. Its statement of policy was angrier than earlier homophile groups had dared: "We find ourselves scorned, our rights as persons and citizens before the law imperiled, our individuality suppressed by a hostile social order" [1].

The founders wanted SIR to be democratic and open to "all expressions of the homosexual community" [1]. It held dances, brunches and drag shows and ran bowling leagues, bridge clubs and art classes. It also worked closely with the gay bars, and SIR-funded lawyers helped many men arrested in them [1]. In April 1966 it opened what the city's LGBTQ context statement calls the country's first gay community center, on Sixth Street, and it grew into the largest homophile organisation in the United States [1][2]. Plath already owned the D'Oak Room, an early gay bar on Divisadero [1]. Lesbian bar owner Rikki Streicher, who opened Maud's in Cole Valley, was one of SIR's leaders [2]. The Clayton Street building still stands, just along the street from 558 Clayton, where the Haight-Ashbury Free Clinic opened in 1967 [1].

title: A model-yacht pond that wanted to be marsh
place: McNab Lake, beside Louis Sutter Playground
hook: The lake was built for toy sailboats with state money. Nature, and the state's accountants, have had opinions ever since.
story: McNab Lake, in the park's northeast corner next to Louis Sutter Playground, was built in 1964 as a basin for model yachts. The State of California paid for it [1][2]. It was designed as part of the hillside's natural drainage. Water from the slope ran in through gaps in the concrete walkway around its edge, and when the lake filled, the overflow drained into pipes heading east [1]. By 1983 the city's planners admitted it went stagnant in the dry season and looked ugly whenever it was drained to clear out weeds and rushes. They suggested paving the bottom but ruled out filling it in. One reason: the state would want its construction money back [1]. In 2013 the Chronicle's John King reported that its water still regularly turned dark with algae and silt, because the reclaimed former marsh had been badly designed in the 1960s [3]. The wildlife doesn't seem to mind. That year Chronicle photographers caught a double-crested cormorant fishing and ducks swimming and foraging on the lake [3].

title: Fifty Men Lift a Dome Form
place: Palace of Fine Arts rotunda
hook: The beloved 1915 'ruin' was falling down for real. So San Francisco knocked it flat and built it again in concrete, sometimes by sheer muscle.
story: Bernard Maybeck's Palace of Fine Arts was meant to last one season. It was a wood frame covered in 'staff', a mix of plaster and burlap-like fibre [2]. In the decades after the 1915 fair it held eighteen lighted tennis courts (1934 to 1942), wartime trucks and jeeps, phone books and even a temporary fire headquarters. By the 1950s the fake ruin was a real one [2]. In 1964 it was demolished, with only the steel of the exhibit hall left standing, and rebuilt in poured-in-place concrete. A plate in the rotunda credits B.F. Modglin of MacDonald & Kahn for the work of 1964 to 1967 [2]. Construction worker Eric Johnson remembered the day his crew had to move a huge dome form that weighed many tons. No forklift could carry it safely, so fifty men in dusty white overalls lifted it by hand while their foreman, Howard, called out orders [1]. Johnson said getting it moving was like 'shoving an elephant into her stall'. For a moment they felt 'like being gods, or dreamers in unison', until the form swung wide at a doorway and nearly crushed them [1]. The steel dome was up by December 1966 [1].

title: Full carts, no sale: the Lucky shop-in
place: Former Lucky supermarket, 1201 Gough Street near Geary
hook: Demonstrators filled their carts, waited at the till, then changed their minds. After a few days of it, the supermarket agreed to hire.
story: In February 1964 the Congress of Racial Equality (CORE) put picket lines outside Lucky supermarkets. CORE had fought the chain over jobs for Black workers as far back as 1948, and an agreement the summer before had produced no new hires [1]. A week later CORE began something cleverer, the 'shop-in' [1]. A San Francisco Public Library photograph places one at the Lucky store at 1201 Gough Street, near Geary [2]. Everything the demonstrators did was legal. They piled their carts high, reached the checkout, and changed their minds, leaving cashiers with ringing registers and counters full of unwanted groceries [1]. Managers could not tell real customers from protesters, and real customers did not want to wait while every item went back on the shelves [1]. Jo Freeman, who took part in the Bay Area campaigns that year, writes that after a few days Mayor John Shelley brokered a deal: Lucky's parent company promised to hire at least sixty Black workers, and the shop-in ended [1]. The same week, pickets appeared outside the Sheraton-Palace Hotel. The 1964 season of Bay Area civil rights sit-ins had begun [1].

title: Poems and 'hippies' at the Blue Unicorn
place: Former Blue Unicorn coffeehouse, 1927 Hayes Street near Ashbury
hook: Before the Summer of Love, young poets read to strangers in a Hayes Street coffeehouse while motorcycles revved outside. A reporter found a new word there.
story: In 1964 the Blue Unicorn, on Hayes Street a couple of blocks above Masonic, was one of the few coffeehouses outside North Beach, and the base for much of the city's poetry scene [1]. Gene and Hilary Fowler ran a weekly reading series. Poets sent in poems, and two or three were chosen to read each week to audiences of twenty or thirty [1]. The poet Stephen Vincent, then a San Francisco State student, remembered it as "an extension of the street." A motorcycle might warm up outside during your first poem, or a drunk might wander in off the sidewalk [1]. He read his "495 Words for John Coltrane" there, a single long sentence written to A Love Supreme [1]. Ed Bullins and Steve Gaskin were among the others who read or dropped in to talk [1]. Vincent and his girlfriend lived nearby, "on the edge of the Haight" [2]. In September 1965 the Examiner's Michael Fallon wrote about the café and called the North Beach refugees moving into the neighbourhood "hippies," the first West Coast use of the word in print, according to Wikipedia's history of the term [3].

title: Railroad, freeway, then BART in one valley
place: I-280 cut beside Balboa Park station, Ocean to Geneva avenues
hook: The trench where BART now runs past Balboa Park began as an 1860s railroad. In 1964 engineers squeezed a freeway into it, then left room for trains.
story: The valley that runs southwest across the Outer Mission has always carried traffic. In 1964, the state's engineering magazine explained that the new Route 82 'Southern' Freeway, now I-280, followed the natural corridor of Alemany Boulevard and San Jose Avenue. For almost two-thirds of its length it used the old Southern Pacific 'Main Line' of the 1860s [1]. Sources disagree on when passenger trains stopped running: the state gave 1907, while a later account says about 1922 [1][2]. The state adopted the route in 1956. Its four miles cost $24 million to build and another $18 million to buy land [1]. The key section ran through Balboa Park and across a corner of City College. It included pedestrian ramps down from the Ocean Avenue overpass so express-bus riders on the freeway could change to local buses, and a crib wall 35 feet high and 450 feet long to keep the Cayuga Playground from eroding [1]. The engineers also worked with the new Bay Area Rapid Transit District, whose tracks would 'enter the freeway right-of-way' [1]. BART's Balboa Park station opened in November 1973 [2][3].

title: Saving the chocolate factory from a tower
place: Ghirardelli Square, 900 North Point St
hook: A high-rise had just swallowed the pasta factory next door. The chocolate works looked like the next to go, until a shipping heir intervened.
story: In the early 1960s, Ghirardelli's chocolate making moved out to San Leandro [2]. Just to the west, the Fontana Towers had gone up on the site of the old brick Fontana pasta factory, and there was talk of tearing down the chocolate works for another modernist high-rise [1]. In 1962 William M. Roth and his mother, Lurline Matson Roth, bought the property to stop it being demolished for apartments [3]. Roth hired landscape architect Lawrence Halprin and the firm Wurster, Bernardi & Emmons. They kept the old brick buildings, some dating from the 19th-century Pioneer Woolen Mill, and added new modernist elements, turning the complex into shops and restaurants [1][3]. The square opened on November 29, 1964 [2]. It is often called the first major adaptive reuse project in the United States [3]. Its owners say it became a model for places like Boston's Faneuil Hall Marketplace and Baltimore's Harborplace [2]. The idea spread quickly. A few blocks east, Leonard Martin turned the old Del Monte cannery, idle since 1937, into The Cannery [1]. In 1982 the complex was listed on the National Register of Historic Places [2].
