title: Escaping 'Juvi' into the Twin Peaks fog
place: Youth Guidance Center (juvenile hall), 375 Woodside Avenue
hook: In the Summer of Love era, runaway girls broke their cell windows and squeezed through barbed wire, bleeding and free on the slopes of Twin Peaks.
story:
In the 1940s the Juvenile Probation Department wanted to build its new detention home in Balboa Park. The Park Commission said no [1], so in 1950 the Juvenile Court and Youth Guidance Center moved from downtown to Woodside Avenue near Portola Drive. The building was first painted army green, and generations of San Francisco teens were warned to behave or be sent to 'Juvi' [2].

In 1967, the Summer of Love, running away from home was an offence only a minor could commit. Runaways who fell into the hands of the law could end up at the Youth Guidance Center [3]. The writer David Talbot called the Youth Guidance Center a 'bleak, overcrowded warehouse'. A thirteen-year-old named Deveron described steaming-hot rooms with tiny cracks for windows. One day some girls stood on their cots, broke the windows and squeezed out through barbed wire. 'They were torn and bleeding, but for the moment they were free, running through the cool mists of Twin Peaks' [3]. On June 18, 1967, the Glide Foundation opened Huckleberry House at 1 Broderick Street as an alternative [3].

In 1969 a Mission High student organizer was arrested for leafleting and held in an isolation cell in block B5 [4]. Decades later the Board of Supervisors voted to close the facility by 2021 [2].

title: Five doctors, one fire, and a burn center
place: Saint Francis Memorial Hospital (now UCSF Health Hyde Hospital), 900 Hyde Street at Bush
hook: Five doctors founded Saint Francis in 1905 and lost it to the fire a year later. Rebuilt on Nob Hill, it opened a burn center in 1967.
story: In 1905 five San Francisco doctors set out to build "the most up-to-date modern hospital west of Chicago." Despite its name, Saint Francis was never a Catholic hospital [2]. The 1906 fire burned it to the ground. For a while the hospital carried on in Dr. Redmond Payne's home [1], and in 1909 it moved into a former 30-bed hospital on Cole Street [2]. In 1911 it opened a 100-bed building at Bush and Hyde, which was full within ten days [1]. A 200-bed maternity wing followed in 1921, and in 1938 the doctors' for-profit company became a nonprofit association [1]. In 1955 the hospital set aside a four-bed ward for burn patients. After ground was broken in 1965 for a 12-story tower, the Bothin Burn Center opened in 1967 with ten acute-care beds [1], led by Dr. James Macho [2]. Saint Francis added the first hospital-based sports-medicine centre in 1979 [2]. In 2012 it began doubling the burn centre to 20 beds [1]. Since 2024 it has belonged to UCSF Health, and today it is UCSF Health Hyde Hospital [2].

title: Four Homes for the Excelsior Library
place: Excelsior Branch Library, 4400 Mission Street
hook: The Excelsior's library started in rented rooms, moved twice, and finally got a $248,000 building of its own. Decades later it went first in the city's branch rebuild.
story: The Excelsior's library had a wandering start. It was the tenth branch of the San Francisco Public Library, and it began as a 'library station' in rented rooms at 7 Bauer Street [1]. By 1925 the branch was on Ocean Avenue. Later it moved to 4465 Mission Street, where it was photographed in 1961 [1]. The neighbourhood finally got a purpose-built library at 4400 Mission Street. It was designed by the architects Appleton & Wolfard, cost $248,000 and opened on October 1, 1967 [1]. The city's survey of modern architecture lists the building under Appleton & Wolfard with a date of 1966 [2]. Nearly four decades later the Excelsior went first again. It was the first branch renovated under the city's Branch Library Improvement Program and reopened on July 8, 2005. The work made it seismically safe and fully accessible and added solar panels, a program room opening onto a patio, a new acoustical ceiling and as much natural light as the building could take [1]. Today the branch keeps a neighbourhood history file, and its collections include Filipino-interest materials in English and Tagalog as well as large Spanish- and Chinese-language sections [3].

title: Janis Lived Next Door
place: 122 Lyon Street
hook: Tour guides have pointed at four different Lyon Street houses as Janis Joplin's. Her driver's license points to just one of them.
story: During the Summer of Love, Janis Joplin lived in a small flat on Lyon Street, across from the Panhandle. The Chronicle later wrote that she walked her dog around the neighbourhood and browsed the shops on Haight Street [3]. Her exact address has been muddled ever since. In 1999 a nonprofit announced a new 20-bed rehab centre for drug-addicted mothers at 124 Lyon and said it was Joplin's old house. Media as far away as England repeated the claim. Then experts produced a copy of her 1960s driver's license, which gave her address as 122 Lyon, the house next door [1]. According to local lore, she had lived in any of four houses on the block [1]. "It just shows how mythological the whole thing is," said Country Joe McDonald, her boyfriend at the time, who had lived with her there for "three somewhat fuzzy months" [1]. Her roommate, the clothing designer Linda Gravenites, said they loved the flat but it had only one bedroom, so in 1968 they moved to Noe Street [1][2]. The confusion never quite ended. A 2009 Chronicle guide listed the apartment as 112 Lyon, No. 3 [3]. In 2014 the six-unit Queen Anne at 122 Lyon went on the market for $1.7 million [2].

title: One psychedelic month on outer Mission
place: Former Rock Garden club, 4742 Mission St
hook: In spring 1967 the Grateful Dead played a week in Jerry Garcia's old neighbourhood, and his mother came to watch.
story: In the 1950s 4742 Mission Street was an Italian bocce club [1]. In March 1967 the North Beach club owner Dave Rapkin turned it into the Rock Garden, a psychedelic venue meant to compete with the Fillmore and the Avalon [2]. It printed diamond-shaped posters, and the engineer Charlie Butten built bass speakers right into the stage [2]. The opening bill was Love with Big Brother and the Holding Company. From March 28 to April 2 the Grateful Dead played a week there, a few blocks from where Jerry Garcia grew up. His brother Tiff helped get the room ready, and their mother, who still lived nearby, saw her son perform for the first time in years [1][2]. Steve Miller and Buffalo Springfield followed. But the club served liquor, which kept out underage hippies, and it was a long ride from the Haight. Within about a month it went back to Latin dance music [2]. As 'The Ghetto' it later helped launch San Francisco Latin rock bands such as the Aliens and the Prophets, with Samoan bouncers on the door [1][2].

title: Philosophy Shelves in Grandma's Bedroom
place: Green Apple Books, 506 Clement Street at 6th Avenue
hook: A visitor walked into Green Apple Books and found the bedroom she slept in as a girl in the 1930s. It is now, probably, the philosophy section.
story: Before it held books, the building at Sixth and Clement was a family home: Hippolyte Cuneo, a foreman at the Joshua Hendy Machine Works, moved here with his wife and six children around 1895 [2]. A storefront was later pushed out in front of the house, and in the late 1940s the shopfront was shared by Ed's Togs menswear and Coliseum Furs [2]. In 1967 Richard Savoy opened Green Apple Books in a 750-square-foot space [1][3]. The store kept growing while other bookshops folded, adding a mezzanine, a second floor and its neighbour, Revolver Records [1][4]. Savoy, who ran it for almost 40 years, eventually offered the business to three employees, including Pete Mulvihill, a former temp earning $8 an hour; an owner-financed plan let them buy it over ten years, completing in 2008 [1]. In 2017, as the store turned fifty, Cuneo's granddaughter Jean Portello came back and found the bedroom she had slept in during the 1930s, upstairs in what historian Woody LaBounty believes is now the Philosophy section [2].

title: Red Power in a stucco house
place: American Indian Historical Society / Chautauqua House, 1451 Masonic Avenue
hook: From a quiet Masonic Avenue house, a Cahuilla engineer and his Cherokee wife challenged racist textbooks, and a future Alcatraz leader's committee met in its rooms.
story:
In 1967 the American Indian Historical Society moved out of the private home of its founders and into a two-story stucco house at 1451 Masonic Avenue, which they called Chautauqua House [1]. The founders were Rupert Costo, who was Cahuilla, and Jeannette Henry-Costo, who was Eastern Cherokee. Sources disagree on when they started the society: the city's 2026 landmark ordinance says 1964, while Rupert Costo's biographers give 1950 [1][2].

The house became a hub of the Red Power movement. With hundreds of members, the society challenged textbooks, testified before Congress, lobbied to protect burial grounds and held community meetings [1]. An education committee led by Richard Oakes, who was Mohawk, met there. Oakes helped create San Francisco State's first Native American Studies department and led the occupation of Alcatraz that began in November 1969 [1]. The house had a gallery for Native artists, the Museum of Indian Art, and it published The Indian Historian, a quarterly edited by Native scholars [1]. The Costos' Indian Historian Press went on to publish books such as Textbooks and the American Indian (1970) and Indian Treaties: Two Centuries of Dishonor (1977) [2]. Rupert Costo died in San Francisco in 1989 [2]. The house became a city landmark in 2026 [1].

title: Sixty Years to Close One Road
place: JFK Promenade near the Conservatory of Flowers
hook: The park's main road got its Kennedy name and its first car-free Sunday on the same day in 1967. Making it car-free for good took 55 more years.
story: On April 2, 1967, the Recreation and Park Commission shut the park's Main Drive to cars for its first 'People's Day in the Park,' and renamed it John F. Kennedy Drive that same day [1]. Chronicle columnist Ron Fimrite, cycling through the tunnels, wondered what downtown would be like without cars [1]. Sundays became a roller-skating party. In 1979 skaters formed the Golden Gate Park Skate Patrol to fight a proposed skating ban, and in 1989 the city smoothed a patch at Sixth Avenue, the 'Skatin' Place,' largely thanks to its leader David Miles Jr. [1]. For decades the de Young and the Academy of Sciences fought longer closures, saying they cost them visitors [1]. Then the pandemic arrived. In April 2020 Mayor London Breed closed the 1.5-mile stretch every day. In April 2022 supervisors voted 7-4 to keep it closed after a 12-hour meeting [1]. That November voters rejected Proposition I, which would have reopened the road, by 61 percent, and passed Proposition J to keep it car-free [2]. Renamed JFK Promenade, it has logged millions of visits since 2020 [1].

title: The Black homeowners of Page Street
place: Page Street between Shrader and Stanyan
hook: Pushed out of the Fillmore by bulldozers, Black families bought homes on Page Street and soon found themselves landlords to young white hippies.
story:
The famous version of the 1960s Haight is about white hippies. Community organiser Calvin Welch described another one. In 1960 fewer than 10 percent of the neighbourhood's residents were non-white. By 1970, 24 percent were African American [2]. The change came from next door. Urban renewal was bulldozing the Western Addition, and Black property owners there received settlements, and many moved to the Haight [1]. By 1964–65, much of Page Street just south of the Panhandle had become a Black neighbourhood. By 1967, Welch said, a simple majority of the owners of the duplexes and triplexes on Page between Baker and Stanyan were working-class Black families [1].

Then the hippies arrived, mostly as tenants. San Francisco had no rent control, and the landlord–tenant fights between Black owners and white renters threatened to turn violent. In one case, 12 units were lost in a suspicious fire [1]. The Episcopal-backed 409 House and the Free Clinic tried to find housing for young people, and a Tenants Action Group became active in late 1969 [1]. The city's LGBTQ context statement also describes the Haight of the 1950s to 1980s as a place of refuge for people pushed out by urban renewal: a mix of hippies, old-timers, gays and lesbians, and Black families from the Western Addition [3].

title: The Easygoing Parish at 5th and Irving
place: St. John of God Church, NE corner of 5th Avenue and Irving Street
hook: An old Protestant church near UCSF became a Catholic student center, and 1970s couples found a priest who allowed John Denver songs.
story:
The church on the northeast corner of 5th Avenue and Irving began as a Protestant church in the 1920s, with a classic Craftsman interior. In 1967 it became the Catholic Newman Club for students at the nearby UC medical campus, and later a parish of its own, St. John of God [1]. It is one of the Sunset's Catholic parishes, alongside St. Anne's, Holy Name and St. Gabriel [2].

For Frank Dunnigan's college friends in the 1970s, it had one big advantage. The priest was known as easier to work with than older pastors. Couples who wanted John Denver on guitar and vows they had written themselves found a welcome here, in a church much smaller and more intimate than the big neighbourhood churches, St. Anne's and St. Cecilia's [1].

It was a small sign of change on inner Irving Street. In the same decade, Dunnigan remembered, USF students crowded into the Embers bar on Irving and took first dates to the Recovery Room on Judah for tablecloths, candles and veal [1].

title: The Many Lives of 628 Divisadero
place: 628 Divisadero Street (The Independent)
hook: Jazz, punk, Nirvana, lesbian dance nights, turntablists: behind one plain red front on Divisadero, the city's music changed about every ten years.
story: "Supposedly, Thelonious Monk played here back when this was a hot jazz strip," Justice League owner Michael O'Connor told the Chronicle in 1998. He wanted to put up a plaque listing every club the room had been [2]. Accounts disagree on the 1960s name. The Bay Guardian called it the Half Note, a jazz club with a house band that included George Duke and a young Al Jarreau [1]. The Chronicle named the Both/And as a past tenant, where Janis Joplin first heard Big Mama Thornton sing "Ball and Chain" [2]. In the early 1980s it was the VIS Club, playing punk, new wave and experimental music. By the late 1980s it had become the Kennel Club, where Nirvana opened for Tad [1][2]. The DJ Page Hodel's roving club The Box drew hundreds of gay men and lesbians to monthly dances there [3]. After the short-lived Crash Palace failed, O'Connor opened the Justice League around 1997. The artist Barry McGee ("Twist") painted its murals, and the club hosted drum-and-bass, hip-hop and house nights [2]. In February 2004 it reopened as The Independent, a 500-capacity room. "The night we opened, the fire department [was] signing everything off while the band was sound-checking," recalled owner Allen Scott [1].

title: The Promise Printed on a Certificate
place: 1800 block of Ellis Street
hook: Displaced families were given a certificate promising they could come back. On this one block of Ellis Street, the city's list of affected addresses runs to 99 entries.
story: When the Agency took a house, it handed the head of household a certificate promising preference for housing built later. In 2008 an Agency spokesman admitted, "there wasn't a lot of housing built for a long time" [1]. A state law passed in 1969 made that priority a legal requirement, and the Agency's Certificate of Preference Program carried it out [2]. By 2023, the Public Press reported, city agencies had issued almost 7,000 certificates since the program began in 1967, and only 1,483 had ever been used [3]. Many of them, reporters found, were never honoured [3]. Today the city publishes the addresses of displaced households, with no names attached. The Western Addition A-2 list has 4,792 entries. The 1800 block of Ellis Street alone accounts for 99 of them, spread across 52 street numbers, and many list a flat, a floor or a basement [4]. Under a 2021 state law, descendants became eligible as well, and in January 2022 the city began issuing certificates to the children and grandchildren of people who lost their homes [3]. Investigators working with a city partner have tracked down eligible families as far away as Texas, the Carolinas and Georgia [3].

title: The Refugee Rabbi Who Talked to Germany
place: Temple Emanu-El, 2 Lake Street at Arguello
hook: He fled the Nazis as a teenager. Decades later, from Emanu-El's great domed pulpit, he asked American Jews whether it was time to speak to Germany again.
story: In 1967 Temple Emanu-El, San Francisco's largest synagogue, installed a senior rabbi with an unusual biography [1]. Joseph Asher was born in Germany into a long line of rabbis; the New York Times counted seven generations [1]. Accounts differ on when he got out: the Times said his family fled in 1936, while his son Raphael remembered his father as 'a refugee from Germany in 1938' [1][2]. His son described 'a very exciting but episodic life' in England, Australia, Cincinnati, upstate New York, Florida, Alabama and North Carolina before San Francisco [2]. In the South he became known for civil rights work [2]. On a 1964 return trip to Germany he concluded that schools were trying to instil 'a sense of atonement' but offered 'a negative and incomplete approach' [1]. At his urging, in 1966 the Union of American Hebrew Congregations sent rabbis to West Germany to teach Germans about Jews [1]. He led Emanu-El under its dome at Lake and Arguello until 1986 [1]. In 1989 West Germany awarded him the Grand Cross of Merit; he died of cancer the following year, aged 69 [1].

title: The clinic where health care was free
place: 558 Clayton Street
hook: On its first day, a second-floor flat on Clayton Street treated about 250 young people who had nowhere else to go.
story: In 1967 David Smith was a young UCSF researcher studying how drugs affect the mind. Walking home through the Haight, he kept seeing flower children in the middle of bad LSD trips [1]. The neighbourhood's established hospitals would not treat them. By one activist's account, nearby St. Mary's had a standing policy of refusing drug overdoses [2]. On June 7, 1967, Smith opened a small second-floor clinic at 558 Clayton Street [3][4]. According to his account, more than 250 patients came on the first day, including over 40 with venereal disease and 15 with hepatitis. Years later he remembered it as "like 300 people" [1][3]. His malpractice insurance was cancelled, and he said he broke the law several times a day by treating drug users without calling the police [1][3]. His motto was that health care is a right, not a privilege [1]. The clinic became the first of more than 600 free clinics opened across the US over the following decade [4]. It merged into HealthRIGHT 360 in 2011–12, and the original site closed in July 2019 after years of losses as the neighbourhood gentrified [3][4].

title: The day the Dead got busted
place: 710 Ashbury Street
hook: Police carried away a pound of pot and two Grateful Dead members. Then the band did something it would never do again: it held a political press conference.
story: In 1966–68, 710 Ashbury was the Grateful Dead's communal home. Bob Weir recalled that people came in through his front window "with fair regularity" [1][2]. On October 2, 1967, city and state narcotics officers raided the house and found about a pound of marijuana and some hashish. They arrested Weir, then 19, Ron "Pigpen" McKernan, and several friends on felony charges. The Chronicle's front page ran "The Grateful Dead: Rock Band Busted" [1]. The same day, police raided four other Haight homes [1]. The band's lawyers ran the Haight Ashbury Legal Organization from the ground floor of the same building and were not arrested [1]. Instead of keeping quiet, the Dead read out a statement at a press conference in the house attacking California's marijuana laws. Their lawyer complained that if they had lived on Russian Hill, they wouldn't have been busted [1]. In June 1968 everyone pleaded guilty to reduced misdemeanours, and most paid $100 fines [1]. It was the last time the band took a public political stand, and they soon left the Haight [1].

title: The suburban builder's tower on Russian Hill
place: The Summit, 999 Green St at Jones
hook: Joseph Eichler made his name with low, glass-walled homes in the suburbs. On Russian Hill he built a 32-story concrete tower, moved into the penthouse, and watched his company fail.
story: Joseph Eichler's company was known for low-slung, wood-framed modern houses in suburban tracts [2]. When land prices soared in the mid-1960s, Eichler turned to the city, building projects in the Western Addition and Visitacion Valley, row houses on Diamond Heights and a luxury high-rise on Russian Hill: the Summit, at 999 Green Street [1][3]. It was nothing like an Eichler home, a 32-story tower of reinforced concrete and glass. Eichler and his wife lived in the penthouse [2]. The big projects overextended the firm. By the mid-1960s Eichler Homes was in financial distress, and in 1967 it filed for bankruptcy [1]. The Eichler Network blames financial problems 'tied to urban projects like the Eichler Summit' [4]. The tower still dominates the crest. Tiny Russian Hill Place, lined with four small Mediterranean villas that Willis Polk built for Norman Livermore, ends abruptly against it [3]. The Chronicle's walking guide notes that the tall Green Street towers here were built before 40-foot height limits came to Russian Hill in the early 1970s [3]. Plenty of residents never knew the Summit was an Eichler. When the philanthropist Lorry Lokey put his unit up for sale in 2014 to fund his giving, he said he had known from the start [2].

title: When Haight Street stopped the buses
place: Haight and Ashbury Streets
hook: First the tour buses came to gawk. Then the crowds grew so thick the buses couldn't move, and the hippies decided they wanted the street for a park.
story: On April 6, 1967, Gray Line launched its "Hippie Hop" bus tour, billed as "the only foreign tour in the domestic U.S." Guides handed out a glossary of hippie slang to passengers peering through the windows [1]. It was short-lived. By mid-May the sidewalks were so jammed that buses could not get through, and Gray Line cancelled the tour [1]. The neighbourhood organiser Calvin Welch later recalled that many early hippies resented cars and buses on Haight Street. "They weren't going anywhere, they'd arrived" [2]. From 1968, he said, there were "mill-ins": thousands of people filled the street between Baker and Stanyan, skipping rope and chanting "We want a park!" until the traffic stopped [2]. Mayor Joseph Alioto answered with police. Welch described almost a month of daily clashes and said CS gas was used [2]. In his telling, the confrontation turned the Haight's long-time residents and newcomers into allies against City Hall's plans for the district. That alliance led to a later rezoning that held development to the density already there [2].

title: A pagoda from a sister city
place: Peace Pagoda, Japantown Peace Plaza, Post and Buchanan
hook: Osaka paid for a concrete pagoda as a symbol of lasting friendship. Sixty years into the sister-city pact, Osaka walked away over a statue.
story: San Francisco and Osaka became sister cities in 1957 [1]. When Japan Center opened in 1968, a five-tiered concrete stupa stood at the heart of its plaza. It was designed by Yoshiro Taniguchi, the Japanese architect who had designed the Crown Prince's palace [1][2]. Unlike the rest of the complex, the pagoda was paid for largely by donations from Osaka, and it was given to San Francisco as a symbol of friendship and peace between Japan and the United States [2]. On 8 September 2007, for the 50th anniversary of the pact, the block of Buchanan Street across Post was renamed Osaka Way [1][3]. The friendship did not last. In 2018 Osaka ended the 60-year relationship after Mayor Ed Lee accepted a memorial statue honouring the "comfort women" of World War II [1]. The pagoda still stands, and in 2025 the plaza around it was being rebuilt [3].

title: America's first real kabuki stage, then movies
place: Kabuki Theater (now AMC Kabuki), 1881 Post Street at Fillmore
hook: Japan Center's west end was built for kabuki, with a revolving stage, trap doors and dinner tables. It became a movie house and the film festival's home.
story: The concrete theatre anchoring the west end of the Japan Center was built in 1967 for kabuki. Planning's 2009 survey calls it the first authentic kabuki theatre in America. It had a low, wide proscenium, a long ramp for actors' entrances and exits, a revolving stage and trap doors [1]. The audience sat at dining tables. Under an agreement with the mall, the Kabuki Theater Restaurant could serve only Chinese and American food, so it would not compete with the Japanese restaurants next door [1]. Kunizo Matsuo, who ran the theatre, brought plays from Japan in a faster, modernised style that included actresses, who are traditionally barred from kabuki. The stage also hosted Nippon Kagekidan, a 75-woman nightclub revue, and a kabuki Madame Butterfly [1]. Sources differ on when it became a cinema: the New Fillmore says AMC bought the building in 1978 and turned the dinner theatre into a multiplex [3], while the Chronicle says it opened as an art house in 1986 [2]. The San Francisco Film Society came to hold many of its festival screenings there. Sundance Cinemas, part of Robert Redford's Sundance Group, bought it from AMC in 2006 and reopened it in December 2007 after a $6 million remodel, with reserved seats and the city's only cinema liquor licence [2].

title: Bullet Holes, Opera and Ruth Williams
place: Bayview Opera House, 4705 Third Street
hook: Police shot up Bayview's 1888 opera house during the 1966 uprising. A playwright and activist, with a young Danny Glover on its stage, helped bring it back to life.
story: The South San Francisco Opera House at Third Street and Newcomb Avenue was built in 1888 for a Masonic lodge, to a design by Henry Geilfuss [1]. By the 1960s it had been reduced to a warehouse. The Bayview Neighborhood Community Center moved in in 1965, and during the 1966 uprising police fired into the building [1]. Community leader Ruth Williams raised money to hire the Black architect Harry Overstreet to repair the damage [1]. In May 1968 Western Opera Theatre staged "The Barber of Seville" and "La Bohème" there, probably the first operas the building ever hosted [1]. That same year a young Danny Glover did improv on its stage, and longshoremen screened movies for neighbourhood kids [1]. In October 1968 it became City Landmark No. 8 [1]. Williams was a Southern University graduate who had come west with her husband and six sons. She founded the Bayview Repertory Theater Company, wrote and acted in 37 plays, and produced the first Miss Black San Francisco pageants in 1977–79 [2]. On 7 December 1995 the supervisors renamed the building the Bayview Opera House Ruth Williams Memorial Theater [3].

title: From busboy to owner at Hamburger Haven
place: Hamburger Haven, 800 Clement St at 9th Ave
hook: A student from Iran started clearing tables at a Clement Street diner in 1972. Four years later he was running it, and still serves the 1968 breakfast special.
story: Hamburger Haven opened in 1968 at 800 Clement Street, started by the owners of Mel's; Andy Saberi took it over soon after [1]. Mohammad 'Majid' Falahati arrived in San Francisco from Iran in 1970 and, while studying at the University of San Francisco, began working for his friend Andy as a busboy in 1972. He was manager by 1974 and running the place by 1976 [1]. He married Monir in 1982, and the couple ran it together. Majid's sister Nahid and her husband Tom came from Germany in the late 1980s to wait tables and cook, and after Majid's 2011 operation his son stepped in, until Majid, 'sick of retirement,' came back in 2015 [1]. The diner has kept its 1960s layout: an open kitchen behind the counter, green booths, orange tile, wood panelling and orange and yellow stained glass [1]. Being a block from Star of the Sea, it feeds priests and parishioners after Sunday Mass; supervisor candidates hold meet-and-greets in the back room, and film scouts use it for 1960s and 1970s scenes, including The Diary of a Teenage Girl [1]. It has opened at 7 a.m. every day with the same breakfast special since 1968 [1]. The city added it to the Legacy Business Registry in 2016 [2].

title: Lili Knits: Prom Dresses on Ocean Avenue
place: Lili Knits, 1500 block of Ocean Avenue
hook: An Italian dressmaker who, her daughter says, made Carol Doda's first topless swimsuit moved her business to Ocean Avenue. For decades it dressed the Bay Area's proms.
story: Rita Rivera Doyle, born Pozzi, told an interviewer in 2003 that her mother had worked in the clothing trade since she was a little girl in Italy [1]. In San Francisco her mother first worked for a manufacturer, then ran her own business on Townsend Street, and her clothes sold at I. Magnin, Saks Fifth Avenue, City of Paris and Livingston's. In Rita's telling, her mother also "made the first topless swimsuit for Carol Doda" [1]. After buying a house in the Ingleside, her mother moved the business to Ocean Avenue. Rita thought that was in 1968, though she was not sure [1]. For more than 30 years Lili Knits made prom dresses, formal wear and pep squad uniforms for customers across the Bay Area [2]. Rita remembered people warning her mother away from the neighbourhood, and a warm welcome on opening day. "As soon as African American families moved in, people moved out. What is that about?" [2]. She missed Betty's Hamburger, where truck drivers came for Tuesday meatloaf and Friday fish, and was blunt about the street's future: "It will never be West Portal" [2]. A city business registration lists Lili Knit at 1556 Ocean Avenue from 2005 [3].

title: Poly's Students March Downtown
place: Site of Polytechnic High School, 701 Frederick Street (now housing; the two gyms survive)
hook: When teachers called their school "a failure," a thousand Poly students marched downtown chanting for their Black principal. Can you dig it?
story:
By 1968 Polytechnic High on Frederick Street, across from Kezar Stadium, had 1,650 students, 51 percent of them Black and Filipino. Most white students had been assigned to Lincoln High or chose to go there. That spring Poly got its first Black principal, Nathaniel Brooks [1][2].

In October 1968, Poly teachers wrote to Superintendent Robert Jenkins that the school was "currently a failure as an educational institution." They listed drugs, violence and truancy. Students read the letter in the newspaper, and the school exploded. On October 25, backed by the Black Panthers, about 1,000 Poly students, Black, white and Filipino, marched through the Haight to the district office. One placard read "Mr. Brooks is here to stay, baby. Can you dig it" [1]. Alumna Lonetta Spears said James Brown's "Say It Loud" was their theme song [1].

The superintendent granted their demands. The number of Black teachers doubled from 8 to 16, and Black studies classes were added. But Brooks resigned in 1969, enrollment fell to 750, and in 1972 the district decided to close Poly because it was not earthquake-safe [1]. Only the old gyms were kept when the school was torn down for housing [2][3].

title: Ruth Asawa's schoolyard of clay
place: Alvarado Elementary School, 625 Douglass Street
hook: A sculptor who learned to draw in an internment camp opened an art workshop at her children's school. It became a model for 50 more.
story: Ruth Asawa learned to draw in an internment camp for Japanese Americans during the Second World War, and went on to become famous for her looped-wire sculptures [2]. In 1960 she and her husband, architect Albert Lanier, moved to Noe Valley [1]. In 1968 she started an arts programme at Alvarado Elementary, the public school her children attended [3]. She co-founded the Alvarado Arts Workshop with art historian Sally Woodbridge, and it became a model for arts programmes at 50 other San Francisco schools [1]. Her son Paul Lanier was 10 in 1968. He helped make a boy holding a red balloon for a 30-by-15-foot mosaic mural that still anchors the schoolyard [3]. Thirty years later Paul, now a ceramic artist, led the design of a second mural: 1,200 sculpted tiles forming a tree full of birds and insects. His own kindergarten daughter helped make it. Three generations of Asawa-Laniers were at its unveiling on Eureka Street in May 2000 [3]. By then Alvarado was the only public school in the city with a full-time artist-in-residence working in his own ceramics studio [3]. Asawa died at home in 2013, aged 87 [2].

title: Santana's jam sessions above Precita Park
place: 205 Mullen Ave
hook: Carlos Santana lived in a cottage on Mullen Avenue and played free Sunday concerts in the park below.
story:
The Mission District usually gets the credit for Carlos Santana, but Bernal Heights neighbours say he commuted to the Mission from their hill [1]. Longtime resident Peter Wiley pointed Bernalwood to the house: a cottage on the north side of Mullen Avenue, just east of the Franconia steps [1]. That is 205 Mullen, where Santana lived in the late 1960s and early 1970s. Later some members of Journey lived there too, a band founded by musicians who had started out with Santana [2].

Santana has called Precita Park 'where it all started' [3]. Orlando Galvez was six years old and living on Folsom Street at the time. He remembers weekend jam sessions that turned the park into an amphitheatre. 'Oye Como Va' always got the party started. Hippies, Black Panthers and neighbourhood Chicanos with their sparkling lowriders gathered around the playground. Buckets of Kentucky Fried Chicken sat among clouds of marijuana smoke [3]. In 2016 the two-bedroom house was listed at $975,000. A blog lamented that a San Francisco 'starter home' now cost nearly a million dollars [2].

title: She did the nuns' hair
place: Dalere's Beauty Salon, 660 Chenery Street
hook: Glory Dalere came from the Philippines at 19. The Chenery Street salon she opened in 1968 outlasted nearly every shop around it.
story: Glory Dalere came to the United States from the Philippines in 1956, at 19. She trained at a beauty school near Union Square, married, and worked in a friend's Mission District salon. In 1960 the family moved to Glen Park: "We had a yard, and a school right there for the kids" [1]. In 1968, at a friend's urging, she opened her own salon in the space later taken by La Corneta taqueria. In 1974, worried by rumours that the landlords would tear the building down for a mall, she bought the store at 660 Chenery and put in two stations and a row of hair dryers, which were still there in 2008 [1]. She sent her three children to St. John's school down the street, did all the nuns' hair, and worked long hours to pay the tuition: six days a week, 9 a.m. to midnight, because "back then everyone had their hair done" [1]. The Glen Park News congratulated her on 25 years in business in 1993 [2]. Her daughter Marian grew up in the salon and joined her in 1985 [1]. In 2012, when the Cheese Boutique's owners were being forced out of their shop next door, the Daleres offered to rent them part of their own building [3].

title: The Airplane's black-and-gold mansion
place: 2400 Fulton Street at Willard Street North, across from Golden Gate Park
hook: A lumberman's columned mansion facing Golden Gate Park became Jefferson Airplane's home, office and party house. The band painted it black and gold.
story: The four-story Neoclassical house at 2400 Fulton was built in 1904 for R.A. Vance, a lumber and banking magnate from Eureka, with Indian mahogany, a grand staircase and eight fireplaces [1]. A popular story says Enrico Caruso took shelter here after the 1906 earthquake, but nobody has proved it [1]. The Vance family kept the house for 64 years. In May 1968 it came on the market, and Jefferson Airplane bought it for $70,000, with every band member's name on the deed [1]. Their new manager, Bill Thompson, made it the band's office and shared home [2]. They painted it black and gold. Music writer Joel Selvin called it "a culture center for the Haight-Ashbury." At the 1968 Thanksgiving party, he recalled, Owsley Stanley wired the house and played an advance copy of "Hey Jude" over and over in every room [1]. At a welcome-home banquet, bassist Jack Casady was photographed slumped on a table with a champagne bottle. The picture became the cover of Bless Its Pointed Little Head [1]. Grace Slick wrote that she once pulled a gun on David Crosby here, thinking he was an intruder [1]. In 1987 the band named a compilation album after the address [3].

title: The Church That Built a Co-op
place: Bethel A.M.E. Church, 916 Laguna Street (corner of Golden Gate Avenue)
hook: As A-2 flattened the blocks around it, San Francisco's oldest Black congregation stayed put, built a new sanctuary, and sponsored 382 co-op homes next door.
story: Bethel A.M.E. traces its roots to a meeting house dedicated in 1852 as the pioneer Black congregation of San Francisco. By its own history, it moved to 916 Laguna Street on January 21, 1945 [1]. The church stood inside the part of A-2 that was cleared most completely. Between Ellis, Gough, Fulton and Webster, an area that had held about 2,500 Victorian-era houses was clear-cut entirely, and most of the replacement housing was two- and three-story townhouses built from the late 1960s into the early 1970s [2]. Bethel stayed and rebuilt. Under the Rev. J. Austell Hall it put up a new sanctuary and education building (1968–72 by the church's count, 1969–73 by the city's) and started a credit union in 1969 [1][2]. Hall also wanted housing, so the church sponsored Freedom West, which became the largest cooperative in the Western Addition [3]. It has 382 co-op units on about 11 acres bounded by Golden Gate, Gough, Fulton and Laguna, and the church stands at its corner [4]. Bethel went on to run Fellowship Manor for seniors, and later Prince Hall Apartments, Laurel Gardens and Thomas Paine Square [1]. A current plan, Freedom West 2.0, proposes to rebuild all 382 units [4].

title: The Longest Student Strike
place: 19th and Holloway avenues, SF State
hook: At 19th and Holloway, a linguist-turned-president climbed onto a strikers' sound truck to rip out the speaker wires, and a crowd snatched his tam o'shanter.
story: On November 6, 1968, the Black Students Union and the Third World Liberation Front called a strike at San Francisco State College, demanding a larger Black Studies program and the reinstatement of suspended instructor George Murray [1]. Their demands included Black, Asian American, American Indian and La Raza Studies departments within a College of Ethnic Studies [2]. After weeks of clashes the campus closed, and on November 26 President Robert Smith resigned [1]. English professor S. I. Hayakawa became acting president [1]. When the campus reopened on December 2, strikers parked a sound truck at the corner of 19th and Holloway. Hayakawa climbed on and tried to disconnect the speakers, and someone in the crowd pulled off his tam o'shanter [1]. In January about 350 teachers joined the picket lines [1]. An agreement on the fifteen demands was signed on March 20, 1969, and the strike ended the next day [1]. The result was the country's first College of Ethnic Studies [2].

title: The Portola Girls of St. Elizabeth's
place: Former St. Elizabeth's School (now Alta Vista School), 450 Somerset Street
hook: Ten girls met at St. Elizabeth's grammar school in 1968. Fifty years later they talked their way back into their old classroom, now a tech-founded science school.
story: In 1968 ten girls met at St. Elizabeth's Catholic grammar school, beside the church whose sidewalks run along Somerset, Wayland and Goettingen [3], and stayed friends for the next fifty years [1]. They graduated in 1975 and called themselves third-generation San Franciscans and 'Portola Girls'. On 17 November 2017 several of them came back to walk the neighbourhood. Rosanne Field, born Rosie Maffei, organised it after visiting the Sweeny Street house she grew up in, where her brother still lives [1]. Three of them grabbed a bite at Tiffany's on San Bruno, where her father's photo had once hung on the wall under the name 'Rocky'. The group took photos in front of their childhood homes, and passing E.R. Taylor they shouted for a friend who was inside teaching [1]. The school they got into had changed. In 2012 Alta Vista School, a science- and maths-focused private school founded by Abdur Chowdhury, a former chief scientist at Twitter, moved into the old St. Elizabeth's School at 450 Somerset. It took over more than 25,000 square feet [2]. The friends still 'weaseled' their way into their old classroom and told the teachers about their Catholic-school high jinks [1].

title: The Rainbow House on Steiner Street
place: 908 Steiner Street, between Fulton and McAllister
hook: A redevelopment official told Maija Peeples-Bright to paint her Victorian beige. She painted it every colour she could find instead, with a fibreglass alligator in the window.
story: Contractor P. O. Chandler built 908 Steiner in 1888 for Niels Iverson, a Danish immigrant who had sailed round Cape Horn in 1848. SF Heritage gives the builder as R. O. Chandler [1][2]. By the 1960s the house had spent years as a St. Anthony Dining Room shelter for homeless men [1]. Then the artist Maija Peeples-Bright and her husband David Zack bought it for $17,000, with $5,000 from her father [1]. When a city redevelopment agent suggested beige, she said no. "I liked color. I decided to paint it multiple colors," she recalled. She used marine enamel, and passers-by sometimes climbed the scaffold to help [1]. She added a peacock head in a gable and a 10-foot Nile alligator in an upper window [1][2]. A 1968 Chronicle story described an exterior "painted in five different psychedelic hues" [3]. The Saturday Evening Post and Progressive Architecture wrote it up too, and the house became a stop for tourists [1][2]. Artists of the Funk movement gathered there. A later owner called it the city's first "Painted Lady" [1].

title: The S.I. Store and its soda-bottle rule
place: Northwest corner of Stanyan and McAllister streets
hook: St. Ignatius seniors spent their lunch money at a corner grocery on Stanyan, where a sign threatened suspension for walking off with a soda bottle.
story: For generations of St. Ignatius boys, the most important building on Stanyan Street after the school itself was a tiny grocery on the northwest corner of Stanyan and McAllister [1][2]. Its official name, never advertised, was Acme Grocery, and everyone called it the S.I. Store [2]. Seniors had off-campus lunch privileges. In the late 1960s they crowded in to buy from Mrs. Welch and her daughter, Betty Mersich, who stocked better food than the school cafeteria at what the boys remembered as outrageous prices: 20 cents for a bottle of Coca-Cola [1][2]. A sign behind the counter warned that any S.I. student caught carrying soda bottles away from the front of the store would be suspended. It named a Jesuit administrator (the columnist recalls him as principal in one column, assistant principal in another), and a new name was pasted over the old each time the job changed hands [1][2]. Around the corner the Jesuits bought an aging Victorian at 2580 McAllister for the band, the newspaper and the yearbook. The most junior staffer was sent to Doggie Diner with orders like "11 hot dogs, 4 cheeseburgers, 6 Cokes... and 31 bags of fries" [1]. When the school left in 1969, the Stanyan-McAllister street sign went with the boys. It ended up in a friend's basement on Everglade Drive [3].

title: The World Trade Center architect's Japantown mall
place: Japan Center malls, Post Street between Laguna and Fillmore
hook: The man drawing the Twin Towers was also designing Japantown's mall at the same time, and he insisted he had no idea how to make it look Japanese.
story: The Japanese Cultural and Trade Center, bounded by Laguna, Geary, Fillmore and Post, was built from 1965 and dedicated in March 1968 [1]. It was partly funded by Japanese corporations, and Kintetsu ran its shopping centres [1][2]. Its architect was Minoru Yamasaki, working with local firm Van Bourg-Nakamura, during the same years he was designing New York's World Trade Center [1]. Yamasaki was uneasy with the brief. When Redevelopment Agency chief Justin Herman urged him to make the hotel rooms as authentically Japanese as possible, he replied: "I really do not know enough about Japanese detailing to feel adequate in this respect" [1]. The boxy buildings use concrete panels and wood meant to suggest shoji screens, and Yamasaki felt the finished project was not what he had envisioned [1]. The complex had a human cost: according to preservation architect Bridget Maley, it displaced more than 50 businesses and about 1,500 residents in a neighbourhood already emptied once by the wartime removal of its Japanese American families [1].

title: The bar with the garbled motto
place: Ribeltad Vorden, 300 Precita Avenue at Folsom
hook: Named after a misspelled Colombian flag, Bernal's liveliest bar had German shepherds upstairs, a bullet hole in the wall and a tenant with a shotgun.
story: Around 1968 Peter Cancilla, heir to Cancilla's Grocery across the street, turned a failing pinball business at 300 Precita Avenue into a bar [1]. The name came from a cloth version of the Colombian coat of arms. Its motto, Libertad y Orden, had been stitched as 'Ribeltad Vorden' [1]. In the late 1960s and early 1970s it was the place to go in Bernal [1][2]. Doyle McGowan bought it in 1971. He opened it for the Bernal Heights Association's 1973 party naming the hilltop park, and let photographer Mark Green run the Nanny Goat Hill Gallery rent-free in a tiny building behind the bar [1]. Life there was lively. A bartender's gun went off and left a hole in the wall. Upstairs lived a tenant who ran a guard-dog rental business. When the bar got too loud she cut the power at the main switch, then waited on the stairs with her dogs and a shotgun for someone to come and turn it back on [1]. McGowan sold up in 1974 [1].

title: The mermaids that beat the modernist
place: Ruth Asawa fountain, Ghirardelli Square plaza
hook: The square's famous landscape architect wanted a sleek metal shaft. Ruth Asawa gave him nursing mermaids and amphibians, and the city took her side.
story: As Ghirardelli Square neared completion, sculptor Ruth Asawa was commissioned to make a fountain for its courtyard. She made a cast-bronze fountain of mermaids and sea creatures, installed in 1968 and titled Andrea [2]. FoundSF calls it the "Mermaids" fountain [1]. Lawrence Halprin, the square's landscape architect, hated it. He attacked it as too representational and out of keeping with the plaza, and he had wanted a 15-foot metal shaft instead. The fight spilled into the San Francisco Chronicle's editorial pages, and Halprin lost [1]. Local residents, especially women, rallied to keep the sculpture [2]. Historian Alison Isenberg argues the fountain was an early skirmish of second-wave feminism, disguised as a charming piece for families. "In 1968 San Franciscans saw relatively unprecedented scenes in Ghirardelli Square," she writes: "breast-feeding, a lesbian family, an amphibian orgy, possibly mermaid vaginas." [1] In her reading, a dispute about artistic style turned into a public argument about gender, sexuality and who shapes urban space.

title: The origami family of Buchanan Street
place: Paper Tree, 1743 Buchanan Street (Buchanan Mall)
hook: Taken to Heart Mountain at eleven, he came home to find his family's belongings looted. Later he opened a Japantown shop selling paper by the six-foot sheet.
story: In spring 1942 Nobuo Mihara was eleven when soldiers took him, his nine-year-old brother Sam and his parents to join his grandparents at Heart Mountain in Wyoming [1]. His grandfather lost his sight for lack of proper treatment and died in the camp. When the family came home after the war, the belongings they had stored had been looted [1]. His father, Tokinobu Mihara, started again. The family's Japantown publishing and import business, Oriental Culture Books, put out one of the first origami books in English in the 1950s [1][2]. Nobuo and his wife Shizuko then opened Paper Tree to keep the craft going. The New Fillmore says they founded it in 1968, while the city's heritage survey, quoting the shop's own website, dates the retail store to 1978 [1][2]. It is one of a handful of family-run businesses left in Japantown [1]. Their daughters Linda Mihara and Vicky Mihara Avery became award-winning origami artists [2]. The shop sells sheets of paper up to six feet square. In 2017 the shop was displaying "Ryujin 3.2", a dragon folded by one of the world's leading paper folders [1].

title: The singing rabbi's house for holy hippies
place: Former House of Love and Prayer, 347 Arguello Boulevard (between California and Clement)
hook: For $300 a month, a Georgian house on Arguello became a commune where hundreds of young seekers came for Shabbat songs led by Shlomo Carlebach.
story: Shlomo Carlebach, known as "the Singing Rabbi," played the Berkeley Folk Festival in 1966. He invited the crowd to Shabbat that Friday, and about 800 people came [1]. He wanted a place in San Francisco where, in his words, "when you come, someone loves you; when you leave, someone misses you." In April 1968 his follower Aryae Coopersmith rented a large two-storey Georgian house at 347 Arguello Boulevard. The rent was $300 a month, plus a $50 deposit [1]. They called it the House of Love and Prayer. A few people lived there and ran it. It worked as a free hostel during the week, and hundreds came each week for Shabbat, Carlebach's melodies and his teaching [1]. The historian Yaakov Ariel describes its "Hasidic hippies" as a mixture of traditional Hasidic Judaism and the counterculture, a pairing most Jews of the time could not understand. He dates the House from 1967 to 1977 [2]. The Arguello house closed in May 1970, after the group put a down payment on a house at 1456 9th Avenue for a yeshiva. By the mid-1970s the House had become more traditionally Orthodox [1].

title: Trick-or-treat at Janis Joplin's door
place: 892 Noe Street at 22nd Street, above the laundromat
hook: The neighbourhood kids knew the psychedelic Porsche parked on Noe Street. One Halloween they rang the bell, and they were invited up to Janis Joplin's apartment.
story: Eileen Collins Spiers grew up at 913 Noe Street between 1963 and 1970, when the neighbourhood still had a strong Irish flavour and children roamed its hills freely [1]. Halloween meant the spooky Tagle Haunted House on Castro between Alvarado and 22nd, and old ladies on Hill Street handing out cold Coca-Cola and popcorn balls [1]. And one year it meant a famous neighbour. The kids knew that Janis Joplin lived in the apartment at 892 Noe, on the corner of 22nd above the coin laundry. They had seen her climb out of her 1965 Porsche with its custom psychedelic paint job, parked out front [1]. One Halloween, which Spiers thought was 1968, she and a couple of the Gallagher girls summoned all their courage and rang the bell. They were invited up into a room of exotic incense, bright fabric and beaded fringe, and Joplin was very gracious. Spiers couldn't remember whether they got any treats; they were too star-struck to care. They ran giggling down the stairs, ready to tell everyone, "Oh my God, we met Janis!" [1]. Other accounts also say Joplin lived briefly in Noe Valley, in a Noe Street apartment [2][3].

title: Twenty-Seven Prisoners Sat Down and Sang
place: Presidio stockade, Building 1213, Fort Winfield Scott
hook: A guard shot a disturbed young prisoner in the back. Three days later, 27 soldiers sat on the stockade lawn and the Army charged them with mutiny.
story: In 1968 the Presidio stockade was packed with AWOL soldiers. Peter Barnes wrote that Building 1213 held up to 120 prisoners when the Army's own limit was 88. Another account says the jail was built for 56 and held 115 [1][2]. One inmate counted 33 suicide attempts by 21 men between May and October [1]. On 11 October, Private Richard 'Rusty' Bunch, a troubled young man from Dayton, Ohio, was on a shotgun work detail. He asked his guard, 'If I run, will you shoot me?' The guard answered, 'You'll have to run to find out.' Bunch skipped away and was killed by a shotgun blast to the back. Officials called it justifiable homicide [1]. On the morning of 14 October, 27 of the 123 prisoners sat down on the grass and sang 'We Shall Overcome'. They read out demands that included an end to shotgun details, the removal of racist guards and a chance to tell the press about Bunch [1]. Firemen called in to hose them down refused [2]. The 27 were charged with mutiny, a capital offence. The first man sentenced got 15 years, but after public outcry all were released within about 18 months [2]. Sixth Army commander Stanley Larsen later explained: 'We thought the revolution was starting, and we were trying to crush it' [2].

title: Two Brothers, Two Mowers, One Chevy Truck
place: Former Bank of America Parkside Branch, Taraval Street at 20th Avenue
hook: At a Parkside bank in the late 1960s, a Spanish-speaking trainee helped newly arrived Basque brothers finance gardening businesses. Years later they were buying apartment buildings.
story: Taraval near 20th Avenue was the Parkside's banking corner. Its first two bank branches opened there in 1927, along with the district's only movie theater [2]. In the late 1960s Stephen Jordan, a Bank of America international trainee, was sent to the Parkside Branch at Taraval and 20th for credit training. The branch was, in his words, 'very Italian,' and the staff called him 'Stefano Giordiano' [1]. Manager Sam Centanni arrived at 8:30 every morning in a homburg with his overcoat over his shoulders. Operations manager Dave Dioli caught the coat, and Sam spent the day, Jordan wrote, receiving visitors 'pretty much like Vito Corleone' [1]. Jordan spoke Spanish, so he spent his days with loan officer Bob Zerrila, translating for Spanish Basques just off the boat who wanted to start as gardeners. They always came as two brothers, and they all wanted a used Chevy truck, two lawn mowers, hedge clippers and rakes. The bankers set up a $5,000 package with a local hardware store and the nearest Chevy dealer [1]. A couple of years later Zerrila told him every loan had been repaid on schedule, and the gardeners were buying apartment buildings [1].

title: Where the Bullitt chase begins
place: York Street at Peralta Avenue
hook: Movie history's most famous car chase starts at the foot of Bernal Hill, and two local kids ran into the shot.
story: The chase in 'Bullitt' (1968), often called one of the most influential in film history, begins under Highway 101 [1]. Steve McQueen's Mustang picks up the hitmen's Dodge Charger near Cesar Chavez (then Army Street) and Precita Avenue. Bernal Hill is green in the background [2]. The Charger turns off Cesar Chavez and cruises up York Street towards Peralta. At that corner, if you blink you'll miss it, two boys dash across the street [2][3]. Every car on the street was driven by a stunt driver, SF Weekly reported, yet no one stopped the Bernal kids. "He'd yell 'Cut! Cut!' But, finally, to hell with it. He left it in there," one of them, Angel Sanchez Jr., told the paper decades later. "We must have run across the street three, four times" [3]. He didn't realise he was in a movie until many years later [3]. The sequence was pieced together from locations miles apart, so the route on screen makes no geographic sense [1][2].

title: A Blacklisted Physicist's Museum of Curiosity
place: Former Exploratorium, Palace of Fine Arts exhibit hall, 3601 Lyon Street
hook: Frank Oppenheimer helped build the atomic bomb, lost his career to McCarthyism, raised cattle, then filled an empty exhibition hall with things you were told to touch.
story: Frank Oppenheimer had worked with his brother J. Robert on the Manhattan Project. After a brief youthful embrace of communism he was blacklisted from research and teaching in the McCarthy era, and ended up a cattle rancher in small-town Colorado [1]. He drifted back into teaching at a local high school. There he swapped the textbook for hands-on tools and materials, which became his trademark [1]. A National Science Foundation grant let him build about a hundred experiment models, and a 1965 Guggenheim tour of European science museums sharpened the idea [2]. In 1969, aged 57, he took over the 'cavernous, and very empty' exhibit hall behind the Palace of Fine Arts [1]. The Exploratorium opened in August 1969 [2]. Oppenheimer put the exhibit workshop in full view, believing visitors should know 'the way a shop smells when you burn the wood in a saw' [2]. He worked alongside the artists and builders who made the exhibits, and ran the museum until just before his death in 1985 [1]. The Exploratorium stayed in the Marina for more than four decades, then moved to Pier 15 on the Embarcadero in April 2013 [1][2].

title: A Killer's Cipher Mailed to Fifth and Mission
place: San Francisco Chronicle Building, 901 Mission Street at Fifth
hook: A letter in November 1969 brought 340 strange symbols to the Chronicle's newsroom. It took 51 years and three strangers on three continents to read them.
story: Since the 1920s the San Francisco Chronicle had been made at 901 Mission Street, at the corner of Fifth and Mission [1]. In the autumn of 1969 that newsroom became the killer's chosen mailbox. A letter that reached the paper in November 1969 held a cryptogram of 340 characters, and the paper ran a story on it on November 12 [2]. An earlier cipher, sent in pieces to the Chronicle, the Examiner and the Vallejo Times-Herald, had been cracked by a Salinas schoolteacher and his wife. The "340" held out for five decades [2]. In December 2020 it finally gave way to Virginia web designer David Oranchak, Australian mathematician Sam Blake and Belgian warehouse operator Jarl Van Eycke. They had tested around 650,000 ways of reading the symbols over eight months [2]. The text runs diagonally down the page and gives no name. It begins: "I hope you are having lots of fun in trying to catch me." It also says "that wasnt me on the TV show", an apparent reference to a caller on KGO's AM San Francisco in October 1969. The FBI confirmed that private citizens had solved the cipher. The case remains open [2].

title: Bethel A.M.E. Leaves Chinatown for Laguna
place: Bethel A.M.E. Church, 916 Laguna Street
hook: After most of a century on Powell Street in Chinatown, a pioneer Black congregation followed its people west, then helped house them.
story: Bethel A.M.E. was one of San Francisco's three pioneer African American churches. Since the nineteenth century it had worshipped at 1207 Powell Street in Chinatown [1]. After the war the old downtown churches were full, and far from where the city's fast-growing Black population now lived. One by one their pastors moved to the Western Addition [1]. In the late 1950s Bethel bought an old, disused church building on Laguna Street. When that grew too cramped, the congregation replaced it with a new church, which it moved into in 1969 [1][2]. Like Third Baptist and A.M.E. Zion, the new building rejected traditional church architecture in favor of strong, simple geometric shapes and plain walls [2]. Bethel then became a builder. During the Western Addition A-2 redevelopment it partnered with the Redevelopment Agency on affordable housing [2]. It sponsored Freedom West, the area's largest co-op, spread over four blocks at the church's corner, and also operates Laurel Gardens, Prince Hall Apartments, Thomas Paine Square and Fellowship Manor [3].

title: Four decades of Bell Market
place: Former Bell Market, 3950 24th Street, between Noe and Sanchez
hook: For forty years three brothers' meat-and-potatoes supermarket was the only full-size grocery in Noe Valley. Its closing on Valentine's Day 2009 alarmed a butcher and a cheesemonger.
story:
Dominick Bell and two of his brothers opened a supermarket under their own name at 3950 24th Street. They sold vegetables, meat and groceries at a time when meat and potatoes was standard fare [2]. The Voice dated the opening to February 1969 in one account and called the store a landmark since 1968 in another [1][2]. For about a decade, until the mid-1980s, the Bells ran a second branch at 1333 Castro Street, known affectionately as "Little Bell." It later became a Walgreens [1].

In the mid-1990s the grocery giant Ralphs acquired the chain. In 2005 it was reported to be seeking buyers for its Bell and Cala stores in Northern California. Bell was by then the only full-scale grocery in the neighbourhood, since the Real Food Company had shut its doors in 2003 [1]. The end came on February 14, 2009, four decades after the brothers opened. The building was to be gutted for a smaller-than-usual Whole Foods [2]. Some neighbours were thrilled. Others worried. "No matter what, we cannot compete with a big store like Whole Foods," said Charles Kung of the 24th Street Cheese Company. At Drewes on Church Street, butcher Josh Epple said, "I wish Bell were staying" [2].

title: Japan's biggest bookseller opens on Post Street
place: Kinokuniya Building, 1825 Post Street between Fillmore and Webster
hook: Since 1969 the west wing of Japan Center has held the flagship American shop of Japan's largest bookstore chain. Most of its books are in Japanese.
story: When the Japanese Cultural and Trade Center opened in 1968, Books Kinokuniya was one of its first tenants, along with Hitachi, Nissan, Mitsubishi and the Miyako Hotel [2]. It has been in its own building on Post Street between Fillmore and Webster since 1969, a building the Kinokuniya company paid for [1]. Its parent was the largest bookstore chain in Japan, and this store became the flagship of Kinokuniya's American branch. Planning's 2009 survey describes it as the third-largest Japanese bookstore in the United States. About 70 percent of its stock is in Japanese [1]. Over time the carmakers' and electronics firms' showrooms left the mall, and by the mid-1970s shops had replaced them, since American buyers no longer needed an introduction to Japanese cars and electronics [2]. The bookstore stayed. The company also became one of the largest property owners in Japantown and a sponsor of its festivals. It even owned the enclosed bridge that carries shoppers over Webster Street into the next wing [1]. The survey also notes the readings by Asian American authors the store hosts [1]. In 2009 the Kinokuniya Building still belonged to the chain's American arm [2].

title: Los Siete and the Storefront on 24th
place: Los Siete Defense Committee, 24th St near South Van Ness Ave
hook: After a police officer died on May 1, 1969, seven young Latinos from the Mission were charged with murder. Their defenders built a clinic, a breakfast programme and a newspaper.
story: On May 1, 1969, two plainclothes officers stopped a group of young men carrying a television into a house on Alvarado Street [1]. In the struggle, Officer Joe Brodnik was killed by a shot from his partner Paul McGoran's gun [1]. Police flooded the house with tear gas while helicopters circled; Francisco FloresLanda, then seventeen, watched them from Dolores Park [1][2]. Seven young men, mostly Central American and some linked to the Mission Rebels youth group, were charged with murder and defended by the lawyer Charles Garry [1]. The defence argued McGoran drew his gun and shot Brodnik in the struggle [1]. The trial began in late June 1970 and ended in acquittals; FoundSF reports six were tried and a seventh had fled [1][3]. Near 24th and South Van Ness, the Los Siete Defense Committee ran a free breakfast programme, the Basta Ya! newspaper and Centro de Salud [1]. It also ran a Valencia Street restaurant selling a Coke, hamburger and fries for a dollar [2].

title: Panther Breakfasts and an FBI Plant
place: Sacred Heart Church basement hall, 554 Fillmore Street
hook: A Catholic parish fed up to 100 children a day with the Black Panthers. Then the FBI planted hate-filled coloring books in its basement.
story: Father Eugene Boyle became pastor of Sacred Heart in 1968, having already marched with Cesar Chavez from Delano to Sacramento in 1966 [1][2]. In 1969 the Black Panther Party, which had approached most of the churches in the area, came to Sacred Heart. They 'finally came to us on a lark,' Boyle recalled [1]. The parish opened its basement hall and kitchen, and the Breakfast Program for Children began there on March 10, 1969, feeding 75 to 100 local children a day, many of them pupils at the parish school [1]. Police and the FBI took notice. That year San Francisco police told the McClellan Senate investigations committee that Boyle was letting the Panthers hand out coloring books that showed police as pigs [1]. The Panthers had printed a few but never distributed them. In 1975 the Church Committee revealed that the FBI had planted the books in the church basement as part of its campaign against the party [1]. The episode cost the program liberal support, but it carried on [1]. The parish also hosted anti-war and SF State student activists, and on September 21, 1970 Boyle said Mass there for the United Farm Workers' lettuce boycott, whose San Francisco campaign started at Sacred Heart [1][3].

title: Stripping the old school for souvenirs
place: Site of St. Ignatius High School, 222 Stanyan Street (now USF's Koret Center)
hook: When St. Ignatius left its 'fog-stained bomb shelter' on Stanyan Street in 1969, the boys pried off clocks, fountains and locker doors, even though the building had been sold.
story: St. Ignatius High School moved into 222 Stanyan Street in the fall of 1929 and stayed forty years. One alumnus reckoned nearly 9,000 boys passed through, and that from the north the building looked like "a fog-stained bomb shelter" [1]. By the 1960s the baby boom had pushed enrolment to about 1,000, and the 1929 building was bursting at the seams [2]. Students had sold candy bars and raffle tickets for years to pay for a new campus. Late in 1968 came word that it would be ready in the Sunset, at 37th Avenue, by August 1969 [3]. The last months were hard on the building. Souvenir hunters carried off drinking fountains, double-sided hallway clocks, locker doors and light fixtures. Principal Father Edward McFadden told the student body that the building had been sold to the University of San Francisco and was supposed to be handed over reasonably intact [3]. The pilfering slowed but did not stop. The wooden detention bench outside the assistant principal's office went to the new campus officially, and it is still used there [2]. USF used the old school as Loyola Hall in the 1970s. It was demolished in 1986-87 to make way for the Koret Health and Recreation Center [4][3].

title: The Family Dog Howls at Ocean Beach
place: Site of the Family Dog on the Great Highway (old Ocean Beach Pavilion), 660 Great Highway
hook: After the Summer of Love, Chet Helms took his dances to an old beachfront ballroom by Playland. The Grateful Dead once played there in disguise.
story:
By the mid-1960s the old Ocean Beach Pavilion beside Playland was known as the Surf Club [1], and by 1969 its ballroom had become a slot-car track. That summer promoter Chet Helms reopened it as the Family Dog on the Great Highway, sometimes billed "at the edge of the Western World," at 660 Great Highway, next door to Playland's old skating rink [2].

Helms brought the Summer of Love scene to the beach, with acts including Jefferson Airplane and the Grateful Dead [1]. Part of a Dead show there on February 4, 1970, was broadcast on a national educational television special [4]. On April 18, 1970, the band played a "stealth" acoustic set billed as "Mickey Hart and His Heartbeats" and "Bobby Ace and His Cards from the Bottom of the Deck," joined on some songs by members of the New Riders of the Purple Sage. Pigpen closed alone with an acoustic guitar. Nobody knew the tape existed until Carolyn "Mountain Girl" Garcia found it among Jerry Garcia's old reels; it came out in 2013 [3].

The run was short. Helms left the concert business in 1970 [2], and two years later Playland itself was demolished [1].

title: The Jesuits Build on the Biggest Dune
place: St. Ignatius College Preparatory, 2001 37th Avenue
hook: In 1969 St. Ignatius left Stanyan Street for a Sunset sand dune. Its students stripped the old school for souvenirs and hid beer in the sand.
story: Frank Dunnigan remembered the biggest dune of his Sunset childhood: 37th to 39th Avenue, Pacheco to Rivera. In 1969 St. Ignatius built its new campus on it, with the Post Office address '2001 37th Avenue' [1]. After 40 years on Stanyan Street, the Jesuit school under its president, Father Harry Carlin, moved at the end of August 1969 and took the name St. Ignatius College Preparatory [1][2]. By then about two-thirds of its roughly 1,000 students lived in the western neighborhoods [1]. Leaving was hard. The old building had been sold to USF. Students still carried off drinking fountains, hallway clocks and even the Stanyan-McAllister street sign, despite warnings from principal Father Edward McFadden [1]. Student volunteers helped load the moving vans. When the year started, only the classroom building and the Jesuit residence were ready. With no cafeteria, gym or library, the school ran a short 8:10-to-1:20 day with no lunch period, so students scouted Taraval and Noriega for food. Physics students noticed that the dunes around the campus kept beer cans cool for hours [1].

title: The Mitchell Brothers' 'Carnegie Hall'
place: Mitchell Brothers O'Farrell Theatre, 895 O'Farrell St
hook: Two film-school brothers opened a porn theatre on the Fourth of July, beat the city in court over and over, and ended in a Marin County shooting.
story: Jim and Artie Mitchell got their start in San Francisco State's film department, then opened their theatre at 895 O'Farrell Street on July 4, 1969 [1]. Police raided it again and again, but prosecutors struggled to win convictions [1]. The brothers were involved in nearly 200 obscenity lawsuits, and their wins helped set legal precedents far beyond the city [2]. In 1972 they spent $60,000 on 'Behind the Green Door'. Just before release, their star Marilyn Chambers told them her face would soon be on Ivory soap boxes nationwide. The publicity made it a smash, and it went on to earn over $50 million [1][2]. After a 1980 vice raid, the brothers put Mayor Dianne Feinstein's phone number on their marquee under 'For a Good Time Call…' [2]. Hunter S. Thompson dubbed the club the 'Carnegie Hall' of sex in America [1][2]. The story turned dark on February 27, 1991, when Jim shot Artie dead at Artie's Corte Madera home. Jim was convicted of voluntary manslaughter [1][2]. The theatre survived him but not the pandemic, closing for good in 2020 [2].

title: The Peace March Down Cabrillo Street
place: Cabrillo Street at 30th Avenue, on the 1969 march route to the Polo Field
hook: On November 15, 1969, an antiwar march filled the quiet residential blocks of Cabrillo Street on its way into Golden Gate Park.
story:
The march began at the Embarcadero and covered about 7.5 miles through business and residential streets to the Polo Field in Golden Gate Park. It was organised by the New Mobilization Committee to End the War in Vietnam, co-chaired by Terence Hallinan, as a follow-up to October's Moratorium Day. In the Richmond the crowd filled Cabrillo Street and 30th Avenue before turning into the park. Lenore Chinn, who lived nearby on 29th Avenue, remembered it passing her home [1].

Crowd estimates differ: one account says up to 100,000 marched, another more than a quarter million [1][2]. San Francisco school boards had refused to let high school students take part, calling the protest "unpatriotic"; more than half of the city's high school students skipped class the day before [2].

The Examiner noted the long hair, the blue jeans, boys walking with their arms around boys, and one man in a grey flannel suit and bow tie walking alone. At the Polo Field, former Senator Wayne Morse and the Rev. Ralph Abernathy spoke. KQED carried the rally live, including Black Panther David Hilliard's obscene remarks about President Nixon, and cast members of "Hair" performed, clothed [1].

title: The cab ride that ended on Cherry Street
place: Washington Street at Cherry Street
hook: Teenagers at a party saw a man rummaging in a taxi on a quiet Presidio Heights corner. They had just seen the Zodiac's last confirmed murder.
story:
On the night of October 11, 1969, San Francisco cab driver Paul Stine, 29, was shot dead by a passenger at Cherry and Washington streets [1]. "Kids were having a party at one of the corner houses," crime-tour guide Russell Kyle later told the Richmond ReView. "They saw the execution and called the cops" [3]. SFGATE says three teenagers at home there saw the man rummaging in the cab, and calls it the killer's closest call [2].

Then the hunt went wrong. A dispatcher broadcast a lookout for a Black suspect, and two police officers stopped a white man on a nearby street, who may have been the killer, and let him go [1].

Two days later the Chronicle received a letter with a bloodstained swatch of Stine's shirt. "I am the murderer of the taxi driver over by Washington St & Maple St last night," it began, a block off from where the cab actually stopped. It mocked the police search and threatened to "wipe out a school bus some morning" [4]. Bay Area police departments assigned officers to escort school buses [1].

Stine's is the last murder that can be definitely pinned on the Zodiac [2]. The killer was never identified.

title: The first Gap, beside the El Rey
place: 1950 Ocean Avenue at Fairfield Way (El Rey Theatre building)
hook: A couple opened a shop selling only Levi's, records and tapes in a corner of an Ocean Avenue movie palace. It became a global clothing empire.
story: In 1969 Don and Doris Fisher opened a store at 1950 Ocean Avenue, in the northwest retail corner of the El Rey Theatre building at Fairfield Way [1][2]. The idea, as the company tells it, was simple: make it easier to find a pair of jeans that fit [2]. The only things for sale were men's Levi's jeans, records and tapes [2], and the Western Neighborhoods Project describes it as a counterculture-influenced jeans and record store [1]. It was called The Gap. It shared its building with Timothy Pflueger's El Rey, a movie palace that had opened on Ocean Avenue in 1931 [3]. In 1970 a second store opened in San Jose, with half its 6,500 square feet set aside as stockroom. The chain started selling Levi's for women [2], and by the end of that year sales had passed $2 million [1]. By its third anniversary, the Gap had grown from one store to 25, and in 1976 The Gap Stores, Inc. went public at $18 a share [2]. The company later added Banana Republic and Old Navy and became one of the world's biggest clothing retailers [1].

title: The saloon that made Union Street swing
place: Perry's, 1944 Union Street
hook: A homesick New York ad man opened a saloon in a rundown contractor's office. Then Herb Caen called it a 'body exchange.'
story: In 1969 Perry Butler was a 26-year-old advertising executive who had just moved to San Francisco and missed the neighborhood saloons of New York's Upper East Side [1]. He and his then-wife, Katherine, modeled their place on Martel's, their favorite bar there. 'We lived in the Marina and a real estate guy showed us this rundown building that was a contractor's office and we said, OK, we'll take it,' Butler recalled. Union Street, he said, 'was a pretty sleepy neighborhood back then' [2]. Perry's opened pouring cocktails for 75 to 85 cents and eight-ounce glasses of jug wine for 50 cents. Butler hired career bartenders, among them Michael McCourt, brought up from Los Angeles, and Mike English, who could pour, keep three dice games going and quote the stock market all at once [2]. Then Herb Caen wrote that Perry's was a singles bar, a 'body exchange,' and 'overnight, that's what we became all throughout the '70s,' Butler said. 'It always bothered me' [2]. Chronicle critic Michael Bauer later credited Perry's with starting the 'fern bar' trend [1]. It also turned up in Armistead Maupin's Tales of the City [1]. The blue-and-white checked tablecloths and photo-crowded walls have hardly changed [1][2].

title: Where American Beauty was recorded
place: Wally Heider Studios (now Hyde Street Studios), 245 Hyde St
hook: Behind a plain door in a former film warehouse, the Grateful Dead, CSNY and Creedence cut classics. A drunk Grace Slick warned the night receptionist not to wake her.
story: In 1969 Los Angeles engineer Wally Heider leased 245 Hyde Street, a building 20th Century Fox had used to store film, and built what is generally considered the Bay Area's first high-tech recording studio [1]. Unusually, it gave musicians almost complete creative control [1]. 'It was ground zero,' engineer Stephen Barncard said. 'San Francisco for years had been waiting for a full-fledged professional studio' [2]. Here the Grateful Dead recorded 'American Beauty', Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young made 'Déjà Vu', and Creedence Clearwater Revival cut 'Cosmo's Factory' [1]. Jefferson Airplane, Santana, Van Morrison and Herbie Hancock worked here too [1][2]. In 1974 Susie Foot, 28, was the studio's gopher, guarding the front desk at night. Grace Slick wandered out of a Jefferson Starship session and told her: 'My name's Grace, and I drink a lot. If you see me passed out on the couch, don't wake me up' [1]. Foot rose to first engineer by the time Heider's closed in 1980 [1]. Under Michael Ward it reopened as Hyde Street Studios, where Tupac Shakur, Green Day and Cake recorded. A sidewalk plaque now marks the spot [1][3].
