title: "I'm Tania" at the Hibernia Bank
place: Former Hibernia Bank, Sunset branch, 1450 Noriega Street at 22nd Avenue
hook: A security camera on Noriega Street turned a kidnapped newspaper heiress into America's most wanted revolutionary. It took just a few minutes on an April morning.
story: At 9:40 on the morning of April 15, 1974, members of the Symbionese Liberation Army held up the Sunset branch of the Hibernia Bank at 1450 Noriega Street. Five went inside while four waited outside, and they got away in two cars with $10,960 [2][3]. One of the gunmen caught on the bank's surveillance cameras was Patricia Hearst, granddaughter of William Randolph Hearst. Ten weeks earlier the SLA had dragged her, then 19, from a Berkeley apartment. On April 3 a tape had announced she'd joined them and taken the name Tania [1]. When a reporter took the footage to the Berkeley School for the Deaf, students read her lips: "I'm Tania. Up, up, up against the wall" [2]. Two men were shot. The SLA's own communiqué explained that one had jumped out the front door and the other ran toward the bank [2]. The FBI launched one of the largest manhunts in its history and caught Hearst in San Francisco on September 18, 1975. Despite her brainwashing defense, a jury convicted her [1]. By the 1990s the robbery site was an ordinary Bank of America branch [3].

title: A circus with no ringmaster, no elephants
place: 400 Missouri Street, near 19th
hook: In 1974 two Mime Troupe veterans started a one-ring circus on Potrero Hill. Everyone earned the same wage, clowns ran the show, and the animals were people in gorilla suits.
story:
Larry Pisoni and Peggy Snider, veterans of the San Francisco Mime Troupe, founded the Pickle Family Circus in 1974 [1][2]. The name was made up on the spot: after they passed a TV juggling audition, someone asked what they called themselves [2]. The company kept its offices and practice space at 400 Missouri Street, and many members lived nearby [1]. The family lived at Carolina and 22nd, and the troupe rehearsed at The Church, at Missouri and 19th [3].

It was a stripped-down circus: one ring, a five-piece jazz band, no ringmaster and no animals, except performers dancing the Charleston in gorilla suits. "We're somewhat lacking in the sequins department," Pisoni said [2]. Everyone earned the same wage and shared the offstage work. Three clowns ran the show: Pisoni as Lorenzo Pickle, Bill Irwin as Willy and Geoff Hoyle as Mr. Sniff. Federal CETA jobs money paid several of them in the 1970s [1].

The couple's son Lorenzo walked into the ring at two with his own silent clown act and signed a contract at six [3]. The circus went bankrupt in 1992. In 1984 two members had founded what is now the Circus Center, and at least seven Pickle performers went on to Cirque du Soleil [1].

title: Blum's cake survives in a grocery corner
place: Yasukochi's Sweet Stop, Super Mira Market, 1790 Sutter Street
hook: San Francisco's most famous birthday cake was born at a vanished Union Square pastry shop. It lives on in the corner of a Japantown grocery.
story: Moses and Hatsy Yasukochi both spent part of their childhoods in wartime internment camps. They married in 1964 and in 1974 opened the Sweet Stop, a small bakery inside what is now Super Mira Market at Sutter and Buchanan [1][2]. Earlier they had owned a bakery in San Leandro, where a baker named Tony, who had worked at Blum's on Union Square, shared the recipe for Blum's famous Coffee Crunch Cake. Moses mastered it, and the retired Blums gave him their blessing to use the name [1]. The cake became a fixture of San Francisco birthdays, holidays and weddings. Hatsy, called the "smile of the bakery," died in 2020, early in the Covid pandemic, after an illness with cancer [2]. Their grandson Kenji Yick, trained at the French Culinary Institute, kept the shop going with longtime employee Debbie Ishida. In 2023 the tiny counter was named a James Beard Award semifinalist for Outstanding Bakery [2].

title: Eavesdropping on Union Square at Lunchtime
place: Union Square
hook: Coppola's paranoid masterpiece opens high above Union Square, listening. The only footage its fired cameraman shot that survived is that famous opening.
story: Francis Ford Coppola began writing The Conversation in 1966 and finished it in 1970 [1]. He shot it in San Francisco, on location in Union Square and at his newly formed American Zoetrope studio, one of the first major directors of his generation to base a studio outside Los Angeles [1]. Gene Hackman plays Harry Caul, a surveillance expert hired to record a young couple as they circle the crowded square at lunchtime; stitching his three imperfect tapes together, he uncovers a sentence that convinces him they are in danger [2]. The shoot was fraught. Cinematographer Haskell Wexler clashed with Coppola and was replaced within weeks by Bill Butler, and all of Wexler's footage was reshot except that technically demanding Union Square sequence, the film's most memorable [1][2]. With Coppola busy on The Godfather Part II, editor Walter Murch shaped the film, and Murch later described the opening: a God's-eye view of "the soft, billowy sounds of the city at lunchtime," suddenly cut by digital racket as you realise you are hearing through a hidden recorder [2]. Released in 1974, it turned a sunny civic square into the setting for an American nightmare about being watched.

title: Houseboaters who beat City Hall
place: Mission Creek houseboat harbor, Channel Street
hook: The Port stapled eviction notices on every houseboat on Mission Creek. Two women got on the phone and played the TV stations against each other.
story: In 1960 the state moved a houseboat community from Islais Creek to 55 berths on Channel Street [1][2]. Ruth Huffaker, an electronics worker, and her welder husband Steve built their first houseboat there in 1962; she remembered jackrabbits, foxes, cobbled streets and men living in six-foot weeds [1]. In 1974, after a fire in sheds across the channel, a Port official told her he would tear the dock down on Monday and put the boats in storage. The next day eviction notices were stapled to every boat [1]. Sharon Skolnick, who lived on a wooden-pyramid houseboat called the Azteca, had her boss Rose Farrington call one TV station, then tell another that Channel 5 was on its way; Ruth told Channel 7 that Channel 4's camera had just arrived. The coverage embarrassed the Port, which shelved the eviction and built a new float. A local paper's headline: 'It's true, you can beat City Hall!' [1]. A 1976 agreement produced a lease and new berths, and in 1977 the Mission Creek Harbor Association took over the harbor [1]. In 2001 around 20 houseboats remained, home to artists, veterans, blue-collar workers and professionals [2].

title: Indians on the balcony, Clement Street
place: 441 Clement Street (the Open Theater, now The Bitter End)
hook: In 1974 a Richmond native turned a former hummus shop into an immersive theatre. Most of its 37 actors played Indians, scaling the balcony on rope ladders.
story: 441 Clement Street was built in 1923. It held an upholsterer, a radio store that was sold off at a bankruptcy sale in 1933, a wine and liquor distributor, and from 1964 Haig's Delicacies [1]. When Haig's moved up the street in 1973, Jack Anderson moved in [1]. He grew up in the Richmond, where his family ran the Anderson Sisters School of Dance on Sixth Avenue, and he was also a radio talk-show host [1]. He took a ten-year lease and made the building the Open Theater. He wanted to use every square foot, including the balcony, the lobby and the street, and his house on Seventh Avenue became the costume shop [1]. The first production, in January 1974, was Arthur Kopit's 'Indians', a Vietnam-era allegory set in the Wild West. It was directed by Lee Sankowich, known for 'One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest' [1]. Most of the 37-member cast played Indians who kept scaling the balcony on four rope ladders [1]. Anderson called the Richmond 'one of the last cosmopolitan neighborhoods in San Francisco.' By 1975 the papers called it the Clement Cultural Center; in the 1980s it was the Open Theater & Cafe, which closed when Anderson's lease ran out. By the 1990s the building was The Bitter End bar [1].

title: Mammy Pleasant's eucalyptus trees
place: Mary Ellen Pleasant Memorial Park, SW corner of Bush and Octavia
hook: Her 30-room mansion is long gone. What remains of one of Gold Rush San Francisco's most powerful Black women is a row of old eucalyptus trees.
story: On March 21, 1974, San Francisco named a row of trees a Structure of Merit, a category the city had used only a handful of times [1]. They stand at the southwest corner of Octavia and Bush. The eucalyptus trees were planted when this was the site of Mary Ellen Pleasant's home, and a plaque in her memory stands among them [2]. Pleasant reached San Francisco around 1852, fleeing prosecution under the Fugitive Slave Law. She cooked for rich families and invested her wages, eventually owning laundries and boardinghouses and building a 30-room mansion at 1661 Octavia [3]. She is credited with giving $30,000 to John Brown before his 1859 raid on Harpers Ferry [3]. FoundSF calls her an important western terminus of the Underground Railroad in the 1850s, and says she gained quiet power by placing servants in rich households [2]. Rumours followed her: newspapers and gossip painted her as a brothel keeper and claimed there was a voodoo altar in her basement [3]. Historian Lynn Hudson told the Chronicle she was a woman who "led the Underground Railroad like Harriet Tubman, and amassed a huge fortune, but is largely unknown" [3]. The city proclaimed Mary Ellen Pleasant Day in 2005 [3].

title: Ransom paid in groceries
place: China Basin Building, 185 Berry Street
hook: To free kidnapped Patty Hearst, her father ran a giant free-food program from this old banana warehouse. The volunteers ended up remaking city politics.
story: After the Symbionese Liberation Army kidnapped Patricia Hearst in February 1974, it demanded that the Hearst Corporation feed California's poor. The first distribution, on February 22, was chaos: panicked workers threw boxes off moving trucks into huge crowds and scores were hurt. Governor Ronald Reagan quipped, 'It's just too bad we can't have an epidemic of botulism' [1]. A community coalition led by the Western Addition Project Area Committee then took over and, from February 26 to the end of March, organised six distributions: more than 100,000 bags of groceries at some 16 sites in four counties [1]. The nerve centre was the huge China Basin Building. Scores of trucks came and went every hour, with Patty's father and brother there around the clock [1]. The building, raised in the 1920s as a banana-processing plant, had been painted a rich blue by then [2]. Volunteer Calvin Welch later argued that the coalition's organisers went on to register voters for George Moscone and to win district elections, giving birth to the neighbourhood movement [1].

title: The Beatles House on Precita
place: 191 Precita Ave
hook: A junior-high girl ran out of wall space in her bedroom, so she painted the Fab Four across the front of her family's house.
story:
In 1974 Jane Weems was in junior high and had already covered her bedroom walls with Yellow Submarine and a giant Elton John album cover. So she asked her parents whether she could paint the outside of the house at 191 Precita Avenue. They said yes [1]. She sketched the Beatles freehand in pencil on the parts she could reach. Then her mother rented a scaffold so she could finish the whole front, working slowly around school [1].

One neighbour who used to stop and 'watch me paint' and talk about the Beatles was Emily Harris of the Symbionese Liberation Army. She was then living secretly in a safe house down the street [1][2]. Later Weems played drums in the teenage punk band The Maggots, and she repainted the mural in 1982 [1]. For almost two decades the 'Beatles House' was a local landmark. Strangers rang the bell, the San Francisco Bay Guardian gave it an award, and the film Living on Tokyo Time used it as a rehearsal studio [1]. Today the mural is gone without a trace [1].

title: The Day the Shipyard Went Quiet
place: Hunters Point Naval Shipyard (Crisp Road)
hook: When the Navy closed Hunters Point Naval Shipyard in 1974, over 5,000 jobs went with it. Third Street shops held closing sales where a bedroom set sold for five dollars.
story: For three decades the shipyard had driven the local economy. By the mid-1950s it employed about 8,500 civilians, many of them Black workers recruited from the South during World War II [2]. The Navy deactivated it in 1974 [2]. A 1996 community history counted 5,060 workers who lost their jobs. The Navy found other posts for most of them, often at bases in Southern California or Washington State. Many locals stayed, though, and either joined the unemployed or retired early without savings [1]. The blow hit Third Street. "The community died when the shipyard left," activist Espanola Jackson recalled. "There was nothing. Everything that was here disappeared." She remembered stores so desperate to clear their stock that she bought a bedroom set for five dollars [1]. A private firm leased the yard from 1975 to 1985, hired few locals and was fined for environmental violations [1]. Also in 1974, resident Oscar James joined the push to end naval operations and raised alarms about radioactive waste. As a boy he had heard his father's shipyard friends talk about it while he hid under a table during "Friday Night Fights". City officials dismissed him [3]. In 1989 the EPA made the yard a Superfund site [2].

title: The Sewing Aunties Who Shook Chinatown
place: Jung Sai garment factory, 646 Washington St
hook: They were called 'goats and sheep'. In 1974, 135 garment workers from an Esprit-owned factory walked out, and Chinatown's own newspaper called it earth-shattering.
story: The Jung Sai factory at 646 Washington Street was one of Chinatown's biggest sewing plants, owned by Esprit de Corps, the fashionable maker of clothes for young people [1]. In Cantonese, Jung means Chinese and Sai means West, and the English name was "Great Chinese American", a picture of happy partnership [1]. To the women at the machines it meant something else: harassment, speed-ups, no breaks and low pay [1]. In 1974, 135 workers, almost all immigrant women plus two men, went on strike [1]. They rallied in Portsmouth Square and picketed for almost a year, through sixty-four arrests and court injunctions, drawing students and activists to their side [1]. On July 27, 1974, the Chinese Times ran an editorial saying these once-obedient "sewing factory aunties", once thought of as "subservient goats and sheep", were now shouting, clapping and carrying picket signs: a "shi po tian jing", an earth-shattering and heaven-startling event [1]. Historian Harvey Dong argues the strike became a turning point for Asian American activism in the Bay Area. Afterwards, locals heard the name Jung Sai and thought of resistance [1][2].

title: The man who turned warehouses into showrooms
place: San Francisco Design Center, 2 Henry Adams Street
hook: With industry fleeing the city, one design-trade businessman went shopping for empty brick warehouses. Today the street he started on carries his name.
story: By the late 1970s this corner of the city had hit bottom. Manufacturing was moving to the suburbs and overseas, and by 1977 San Francisco kept only 12 percent of the region's manufacturing jobs [1]. Henry Adams saw something else. He was president of the Western Merchandise Mart and a leading figure in the interior design trade, which since the Second World War had clustered in Jackson Square. There, rents were rising, parking was scarce and there was no room to grow. In the early 1970s Adams went looking for old brick buildings with bigger floors, and he found them in the warehouses of the northern Potrero [1]. He bought the 1915 Dunham, Carrigan & Hayden warehouse at 2 Kansas Street and turned it into the San Francisco Design Center. In 1974 he bought two more warehouses on the next block [1][2]. By the early 1980s he or his colleagues had bought most of the neighbouring buildings. The Baker & Hamilton warehouse at Seventh and Townsend, the old Planters Peanuts factory and the Schlessinger & Bender winery at 16th and Rhode Island all became showrooms, and the district became Showplace Square [1]. The street outside his first building is now Henry Adams Street, and the building became City Landmark 283 in 2019 [1][2].

title: The merchants who wouldn't let them in
place: Castro Street between 18th and 19th
hook: The old merchants' group tried to block a licence for two gay antiques dealers. Harvey Milk answered by starting his own association and throwing a party.
story: In the early 1970s even gay men who had started their own Castro businesses were not welcome in the local Eureka Valley Merchants Association. In 1973 the association tried to block a business licence for two gay men who wanted to open an antiques store. Harvey Milk's response was to organise gay shop owners into a rival group, the Castro Village Association [1]. Milk was its first president. Working from his shop at 575 Castro, he used it to launch the first Castro Street Fair [2]. That fair drew about 5,000 people and brought a flood of dollars into local cash registers. Even the old-time merchants came round [1]. The planning department's own history gives two dates for the first fair, 1974 and 1975. The festival itself counts from October 1974 [1][3]. In 1977 fairgoers could pay to dunk Milk in a water tank outside Castro Camera, to raise money against the anti-gay Briggs Initiative [1]. The fair has become a fixture on the first Sunday in October [1].

title: The subway that wasn't, the underpass that was
place: Geary Boulevard underpass at Masonic and Presidio Avenues
hook: Planners once drew BART trains under the Richmond with a stop at Masonic. What the corner got instead was a car tunnel under Geary.
story: Geary Boulevard's fast lanes began in the Western Addition. In the early to mid 1950s the A-1 redevelopment project took homes and businesses by eminent domain and bulldozed them. Its first big job was to widen Geary into an eight-lane expressway, with tunnels under Fillmore Street and under Presidio and Masonic, to speed traffic into the Richmond District [1]. The families and businesses pushed out were scattered, and the cleared land sat empty for years [1]. In September 1961, before the 1962 vote that approved BART, an early plan showed a branch from Montgomery Street deep into the Richmond. It would have had stations at Union Square, Van Ness, Fillmore, Masonic, Arguello, 11th Avenue and 25th Avenue [2]. The branch was never built [2]. At Masonic, the city got the underpass instead. It opened in 1974. A local columnist writes that some would call it just an underpass, but with streets and sidewalks above it, it counts as a tunnel. It removed a major bottleneck between downtown and the Richmond [3].

title: Twelve Victorians Roll West
place: 33–35 Beideman Street, Beideman Place
hook: Over three stormy November weekends, a convoy of condemned Victorians crept a mile west through the Western Addition. Eight of them ended up on this narrow alley.
story: In late 1971 the new San Francisco Architectural Heritage group and the city's Landmarks Board picked out the best Victorians still standing in A-2 [1]. The Agency set aside 19 of them to sell for nominal sums, but 13 would have to be moved. Only two sold, and one was knocked down by mistake [1]. To buy time, Heritage entered minimum bids on the 12 that remained. The Agency got a $150,000 grant to cover moving costs, so a buyer needed only about $20,000 [1]. Over three weekends in November 1974 the houses moved west, most of them from the block where Opera Plaza now stands. Crews had to shift phone and power lines and Muni overhead wires along the way [1][2]. Eight of the houses ended up together along Beideman Place, the alley between Scott, Divisadero, Eddy and O'Farrell [1]. One of them, 736–738 Franklin, had been restored by 1977 and renumbered 33–35 Beideman Street [2]. The rescue was bittersweet. Some houses landed on lots where other Victorians had been demolished, and many low-income Black residents resented a rescue led, and bought into, mostly by white, upper-middle-class people [3]. About 2,500 other Victorians were demolished [3].

title: A Rock Revolutionary with an Ocean View
place: Sea Cliff (Kantner's clifftop house; exact address not published in sources)
hook: He wrote anthems about the young and poor rising up against the Empire. He wrote many of them from one of the priciest clifftops in San Francisco.
story: Paul Kantner co-founded Jefferson Airplane. Like many of the San Francisco rock crowd, he left for Marin County as the 1960s ended and spent a short time in Bolinas in the early 1970s. When the Jefferson Starship era began, he moved back to the city and settled for many years in Sea Cliff [2]. The music writer Blair Jackson interviewed him six or seven times for the Bay Area magazine BAM in the mid-1970s, and he enjoyed the contradiction. Kantner, he wrote, "lived very comfortably in a beautiful house perched over the blue Pacific in the ritzy Sea Cliff neighborhood" while writing "stirring anthems about the poor and the young rising up together in rebellion against the status quo" [1]. Jackson did not call it hypocrisy. He noted that Kantner played hundreds of benefit shows, never put on rock-star airs, and turned up regularly at punk and new wave gigs, even though that crowd dismissed him as a dinosaur [1]. He later moved to North Beach and died in 2016 [1][2].

title: A fountain of seven granite continents
place: United Nations Plaza fountain, Market Street at Leavenworth alignment
hook: Lawrence Halprin stacked Sierra granite into seven continents, with jetting-water oceans and computer-set tides. Then came decades of fights over who the plaza was for.
story: United Nations Plaza was built from January to June 1975, after Market Street was rebuilt on top of the new BART and Muni subway [1]. The plaza stands on the site of the City Hall destroyed in 1906. It was dedicated that year to the founding of the United Nations, whose charter was signed in San Francisco in 1945 [1][2]. A team led by Lawrence Halprin, John Carl Warnecke and Mario Ciampi designed it, and Halprin designed the sunken fountain with Ernest Born [1]. Its 673 granite blocks from the Sierra Nevada, stacked in asymmetric slabs, represent the seven continents. Jets of water stand for the oceans, and the water in the 100-foot basin was meant to rise and fall to imitate the tides [1][2]. It cost about $1.2 million [1]. Halprin wanted a gateway that would bring office workers, theatre-goers, transit riders and neighbours together [2]. The fountain never worked as designed and was fenced off as early as 1978 [1]. Homeless people had long gathered on the site, and in 2003 the city fenced the fountain again and shut off its water to spare crews the daily cleanup of needles and waste [1]. title: Artists race homemade cars down Shelley Drive
place: The hill on John F. Shelley Drive, near the amphitheatre
hook: In 1975 San Francisco's art museum asked artists to build cars that could only coast. One had body panels baked by a bakery.
story: The idea came from the Bay Area artist Fletcher Benton, and the San Francisco Museum of Art, today's SFMOMA, ran with it. It held its First Artists' Soap Box Derby on May 18, 1975. Director Henry Hopkins explained that McLaren Park was chosen 'not only because of its excellent curving hill but because of its good crowd facilities' [1]. The rules were short. Cars had to coast, fit within six feet by seventeen, and have 'an adequate steering and braking system.' Each artist got $100 for a car and $35 for a trophy. Sixty artists signed up to build cars and 30 more to design trophies [1]. Ceramicist Richard Shaw designed the Tuxedo Racing Pencil with Gregor Weiss and Steve Wall. Dorcas Moulton got a bakery to make the bread body panels for her 'Moulton's Edible Special', which spectators ate after the race. It won 'Most Endearing', a trophy designed by Ruth Asawa [2]. Chip Lord remembered that his brake 'was just a piece of wood that scraped against the ground' [2]. A second derby followed in 1978. Over the two races the museum commissioned cars and trophies from more than 200 artists [3]. On April 10, 2022, the derby came back to Shelley Drive's curving 800-foot hill for the first time in more than 40 years [2][3].

title: Bulldozers at the Redwood Conservatory
place: Sunnyside Conservatory, 236 Monterey Boulevard
hook: Neighbours got an inventor's Victorian plant house declared a city landmark. Then a cyclist rode past and saw heavy equipment tearing it down.
story:
In 1902 William Augustus Merralls, a British-born inventor of gold-mining machinery, built an octagonal redwood conservatory for his exotic plants on what is now Monterey Boulevard [1]. After him came Ernest Van Beckh, a con man from the "Big Five" mining-stock swindle. He bought the estate in 1919 and lived there until he died in 1951 [1].

In 1974 a new owner, Robert Anderson, began dividing up the lots with an eye to development. The newly formed Sunnyside Neighborhood Association fought back, and in 1975 the city designated the conservatory a landmark [1][2]. Anderson still managed to get a demolition permit. Neighbour Greg Gaar was cycling to City College when he saw machines at work: "I knew it was a registered historic landmark." [1] His calls to City Hall stopped the demolition, but part of the building had already been torn off and almost all the windows knocked out [1].

In 1980 the city bought the site with Open Space Fund money [1]. Neighbour Ted Kipping kept the trees alive. After Friends of Sunnyside Conservatory formed in 1999, another neighbour brought back the original rooftop spire, which he had kept in his garage for 30 years. It was too rotten to reuse, so builders copied it in copper [1].

title: Dylan, Brando and the School Budget
place: Kezar Stadium
hook: To save after-school sports, Bill Graham packed Kezar Stadium with Dylan, Neil Young, the Dead and a surprise Marlon Brando. Then the school board found the money anyway.
story: In early 1975 San Francisco's school district, short of money, planned to cut after-school sports and activities. Promoter Bill Graham read about it in a February 4 newspaper story. By February 19 he had signed up Jefferson Starship, Jerry Garcia, Carlos Santana, Joan Baez and others to play for free [1]. Herb Caen supplied the name: SNACK, Students Need Athletics, Culture and Kicks [2]. The day before the show, the school board announced it had 'found' $2.1 million through an accounting change, wiping out most of the shortfall. An angry Graham went ahead anyway [1]. On March 23 the gates of Kezar, the stadium the 49ers had left in 1971 [3], opened at 6 a.m. Seven to ten thousand fans had camped overnight on the lawn or in the park [1]. Across nine hours the crowd, put at more than 60,000, heard the Doobie Brothers, Tower of Power and the Dead, who, Graham joked, were given 30 minutes "and held themselves down to 40" [1]. Willie Mays spoke. Marlon Brando appeared unannounced. Neil Young closed the day with Bob Dylan and members of the Band [2].

title: Faeries gather above Haight and Ashbury
place: 604 Ashbury Street, near Haight
hook: In an apartment a few steps from the famous corner, an activist who fixed Volkswagens started a gay pagan circle that helped inspire the Radical Faeries.
story:
Arthur Evans had been a gay-liberation activist in New York. After two years homesteading in Washington state, he moved to San Francisco in 1974 and took an apartment at the corner of Haight and Ashbury [2]. He ran a Volkswagen repair business called the Buggery and started writing a book about how homosexuals were persecuted in the Middle Ages [2].

In the fall of 1975 he started the Faery Circle in his apartment at 604 Ashbury Street. It was a pagan-inspired group that combined, in the words of the city's LGBTQ history, "countercultural consciousness, gay sensibility, and ceremonial playfulness" [1]. It was devoted to ritual play [2]. In 1978 he published his research as Witchcraft and the Gay Counterculture [1]. The circle helped inspire the Radical Faeries, the movement Harry Hay and others started in 1979 to find a spiritual side to gay identity [1][2].

Evans never really left the corner. He lived in the same Haight-Ashbury apartment for the rest of his life and died there on September 11, 2011 [2].

title: Hoofprints in the sidewalk, a goat named Hilda
place: Goat Hill Pizza, 300 Connecticut Street at 18th
hook: Sometime around 1920, goats stepped through wet cement on Carolina Street. Their hoofprints now sit outside a pizzeria that kept goats of its own.
story:
The Potrero View tells two versions of how the prints got there. In one, some of the hill's last goats escaped their pasture around 1920 while sidewalk cement was being poured on Carolina Street [1]. In the other, a neighbour told Rosemarie Ostler the prints came from her own pet goat, which roamed the area in the 1920s [2]. In the 1990s Ostler spotted three sets by steps being rebuilt at Carolina and 19th streets, and the developer gave her one [2].

In 1975 five friends opened Goat Hill Pizza at 18th and Connecticut, named for the Italian-Americans said to have raised goats on the hill, and bought a goat from a Sonoma farm. A 1979 naming contest, won by a 10-year-old girl, made her Goat Hilda de Anchovy [2]. Hilda and her kids, Loretta and Bucky, grazed the rocky lot behind the restaurant, and Herb Caen's column made them famous citywide [1]. In 1985 the lot became a dining room and the goats went to Sonoma State Hospital as therapy animals [2].

Ostler gave her prints to the restaurant in 2011, and they were set into its sidewalk. In August 2019 a city crew began jackhammering it up. Head chef Manuel Dzib ran out and persuaded them to cut the prints out and set them back in [2].

title: Joggers arrested on Precita Avenue
place: 288 Precita Ave
hook: FBI agents in sandals and beads waited in a camper on Precita Avenue. When the couple from No. 288 came back from their run, they pounced.
story:
In 1975, during the hunt for the kidnapped heiress Patty Hearst, 288 Precita Avenue was one of two San Francisco safe houses used by the Symbionese Liberation Army [1][2]. The FBI's Charles Bates had both houses watched. Time magazine reported that four agents sat in a light green Ford LTD at the curb and three more waited in a yellow-and-white camper down the block. They wore sandals, beards and beads to blend in. Neighbours spotted the stakeout anyway, but nobody suspected the 'athletic and pleasant young couple' who had just moved in [1].

At 1:15 p.m. on a clear day in September, the couple jogged off towards Bernal Park. When they came back, agents burst out with pistols, a sawed-off shotgun and submachine guns. The woman ran and was caught within 20 feet. The man put his hands up 'like a little kid who had been caught doing something wrong' [1]. They were William and Emily Harris. Inside their flat agents found 40 pounds of black powder and a small arsenal. Less than two hours later Hearst was found at the other house, on Morse Street [1][2]. At her trial, Hearst testified that she had visited 288 Precita once [2].

title: Knock at 625 Morse Street
place: 625 Morse St
hook: The most hunted fugitive in America was hiding in a quiet Crocker-Amazon flat. An FBI agent and a city inspector climbed the stairs.
story: On September 18, 1975, the FBI was watching a postal box belonging to Kathleen Soliah. Messengers had been collecting its mail and taking it to two addresses: 288 Precita Avenue and 625 Morse Street, a concrete house with redwood facing [1]. Agents first arrested Bill and Emily Harris of the Symbionese Liberation Army on Precita. An hour and ten minutes later, FBI Special Agent Tom Padden and San Francisco Police Inspector Tim Casey climbed the stairs at Morse Street and pounded on the door [1][2]. Wendy Yoshimura opened it, and behind her stood Patty Hearst, the newspaper heiress kidnapped nineteen months earlier. 'Don't move or I'll blast your head off,' Padden said. Neither woman moved, though each had a .38 in her purse. Inside officers found a cat, dirty dishes, more guns and a two-foot marijuana plant [1]. At booking Hearst gave her occupation as 'urban guerrilla' [3]. A boy who grew up nearby later wrote that his neighbourhood was a good place to disappear [4].

title: The Corner House That Nearly Fell
place: 722 Steiner Street, at Grove
hook: The oldest and largest house on Postcard Row came through the 1906 quake and was later marked for demolition. In 1975 someone bought it for $65,000.
story: The corner house at 722 Steiner, the oldest of the Postcard Row group, was Matthew Kavanaugh's own home [1][2]. It came through the 1906 earthquake, but by the 1970s it was slated for demolition. It survived that threat too and was restored [2][3]. Michael Shannon bought it in 1975 for $65,000 [4]. By 2010 it was marketed as "The Shannon-Kavanaugh House", and it paid its way with movie and TV shoots, advertising, tours, weddings and parties [2]. It was listed that year at just under $4 million and then went through years of cuts, default and scheduled foreclosure auctions [3]. In 2014 it finally sold off-market for $3.1 million [1][4]. The new owners repainted it from its longtime spearmint green to a new palette [4]. When they listed it in 2022 at $5.75 million, the agents said it had also been home to José Sarria, the drag performer and activist who in 1961 became the first openly gay candidate for public office [1].

title: The comedy womb on Clement Street
place: Former Holy City Zoo, 408 Clement Street between 5th & 6th Aves
hook: A folk club named after a roadside zoo sign became the tiny comedy club where Robin Williams tried out new material. He called it 'the womb'.
story: The Holy City Zoo got its name from a sign advertising the zoo at Holy City, a commune that kept its own zoo. One account says the sign was stolen and turned up on Clement Street; another says it was picked up at a closing-down sale [1][2]. The room at 408 Clement began as a folk club. An impressionist first tried comedy at an open mic around 1971, other comics followed, and by the late 1970s it was a full-time comedy club [1][2]. It was tiny: the Chronicle put capacity at 85, another account at 78, on plank floors once covered in sawdust [1][2]. Robin Williams used it as his neighbourhood rehearsal space. He would sit on the bench outside and chat, which pulled a crowd in [1]. Manager John Cantu would stand on the sidewalk shouting 'Comedy! Comedy! Comedy!' at passers-by, and he sometimes slept on the stage after closing [3]. Will Durst's first set there came right after one of Williams's [3]. Sources differ on when the Zoo closed: the Chronicle says August 30, 1993, and other accounts say 1994 [1][2]. It became a karaoke bar. Williams said losing it was 'like someone pulling the life support on your aunt... The Zoo was the womb' [1].

title: The night St. Anthony's burned
place: St. Anthony's Church, 3215 Cesar Chavez Street (Army Street) at Folsom
hook: Teenagers turned up their car radio to wake the neighbourhood as the old German church went up in flames.
story: St. Anthony's began as a German parish. The Chronicle reported its birth in October 1893 [3]. It stood on Army Street at Folsom [1]. At 2:50 a.m. on a June night in 1975 (the Chronicle's front page of June 30 said 'yesterday', though Bernalwood dates the fire June 30), the church at 3215 Army Street caught fire, possibly because bungling poor-box robbers spilled an altar candle they were using for light [2]. Passing youngsters noticed the glow. They turned their car radio up to deafening volume to wake the neighbourhood and shouted to the nine priests in the rectory next door [2]. It became a four-alarm fire. Flames ran along the roof, the transept above the altar collapsed and the clock stopped at 3:12. People from what had once been an all-German neighbourhood gathered in hastily chosen clothes to watch 162 firefighters from 47 engines. Water from the hoses flooded Army Street ankle-deep from Shotwell to Harrison [2]. The church couldn't be saved, but no one was seriously hurt, and a new, smaller St. Anthony's was built [2].

title: The railroad retreats to Fourth and King
place: San Francisco Caltrain station, 700 4th Street
hook: In 1975 Southern Pacific swapped its grand Mission Revival depot for a modest commuter shed one block away, then knocked the old one down.
story: Southern Pacific's Third and Townsend depot went up in 1914-15 for the Panama-Pacific Exposition. It was meant to be temporary until a grander terminal downtown, but it lasted six decades [1]. Designed by the railroad's own architectural bureau, the reinforced-concrete, Mission Revival station was one of the city's best examples of the style, and San Francisco was 'zero mile' for the whole SP system [1]. It sent commuter trains to San Jose and long-distance trains down the Coast Line to Los Angeles [1][3]. Freeways and the loss of long-distance passenger trains doomed it. Southern Pacific built a much smaller station at Fourth and King, which opened on June 21, 1975, and the old depot was demolished in 1975-76 [1][2]. The new terminal is still the northern end of Caltrain. Muni light rail arrived in 1998, and the station is the planned first-phase terminus for California High-Speed Rail. The Portal project would eventually carry trains underground to the Salesforce Transit Center [2].

title: When the blues came to the hills
place: McLaren Park amphitheatre (now Jerry Garcia Amphitheater), off John F. Shelley Drive
hook: Before it was Jerry Garcia's, the hillside theatre hosted the country's pioneering San Francisco Blues Festival for three summers.
story: McLaren Park's Greek-style amphitheatre sits in an eastern slope, out of the afternoon wind. It was the city's bet in the early 1970s that culture could bring people to its overlooked southeast [1]. Sources disagree on the date. A park group's chronology says construction finished in 1970, while the city's 1983 master plan says 1972 [2][3]. According to that chronology, the amphitheatre opened in 1971 with 700 seats and 'excellent acoustics', and the press said it added 'a new cultural dimension to San Francisco' [2]. From 1975 to 1977 it was home to the third, fourth and fifth San Francisco Blues Festivals [2]. Tom Mazzolini had started the festival in 1973 to celebrate the blues played in San Francisco, Richmond and Oakland in the 1940s and '50s. At the time the country had only a handful of blues festivals [4]. In 1978 the festival outgrew the hillside and moved to the Golden Gate Park band shell, and later to Kezar and Fort Mason [2]. The lighting and sound system built with the amphitheatre are long gone [1].

title: 'No Soviet Domination,' Said the President
place: Palace of Fine Arts Theatre
hook: In a Marina theatre in 1976, Gerald Ford made one of the most famous slips in the history of presidential debates, and then repeated it.
story: The second Ford–Carter debate, on October 6, 1976, was held before an audience in the Palace of Fine Arts Theatre [1][2]. The theatre had opened in the rebuilt exhibit hall only six years earlier [3]. Moderator Pauline Frederick of NPR noted that San Francisco had seen the signing of the United Nations Charter 31 years before, which made it a fitting place for a debate on foreign policy. She told viewers an estimated 100 million Americans were watching [1]. (Later estimates put the audience at about 64 million [2].) Asked about the Helsinki accords, President Ford declared: 'There is no Soviet domination of Eastern Europe and there never will be under a Ford administration' [1]. Max Frankel of the New York Times, one of the panel of questioners, gave him a chance to take it back. Ford instead said he did not believe the Yugoslavians, Romanians or Poles considered themselves dominated by the Soviet Union [1]. Jimmy Carter answered with a chuckle and invited Ford to convince Polish-, Czech- and Hungarian-Americans that their homelands did not live behind the Iron Curtain [1]. The line became the debate's most infamous moment [2].

title: A butterfly clinging to the summit
place: Grassy slope inside the hairpin south of South Twin Peak
hook: On the slope below the south peak, a thumbnail-sized blue butterfly survives in one of only a handful of places on Earth.
story:
The Mission blue butterfly was listed as federally endangered in 1976. It survives in only a few places around the Bay, and Twin Peaks is one of them [1]. Its caterpillars eat nothing but lupine. They feed, sleep through winter in the roots, and emerge as adults in April and May to sip nectar from coast buckwheat [2]. Sources disagree about where the first specimens came from. The Chronicle's 2004 garden column calls Twin Peaks the "type locality", the place where the species was first collected. Wikipedia says it was first collected in the Mission District in 1937 [1][2]. The strongest patch of its food plants grows on the grassy hill inside the road's hairpin turn south of the south peak [2].

The summit nearly lost them. By around 1980 cars, hikers and off-road motorbikes had torn up the hill, and weeds were moving in [2]. In the late 1980s the city hired the San Francisco Conservation Corps. The crews built footpaths with railroad-tie steps and set massive timber barriers at the trailheads to keep motorbikes out [2]. Volunteers filled in the ruts, pulled out broom and ice plant, and replanted lupine and bunchgrass [2].

title: A school with no grades, for the over-fifties
place: Fromm Hall (former Xavier Hall), Parker Avenue side of USF's main campus
hook: A dancer who escaped a Hitler rally and reached America with $50 later founded a USF school for people over 50, with no tests and no grades.
story: Hanna Gruenbaum grew up in a prominent Jewish family in Nuremberg and trained as a dancer and choreographer [1][2]. In the mid-1930s she went to the University of Essen to pick up her diploma and found herself in the middle of a Hitler rally [2]. In 1936 she married Alfred Fromm, a fourth-generation winemaker from Kitzingen, and the couple fled Germany, sailing to the United States with $50 [1][2]. In California Alfred built a business distributing Christian Brothers wine and brandy and later took over the Paul Masson vineyards [1]. In 1976 the Fromms backed a new program at the University of San Francisco: noncredit courses for adults over 50, taught mainly by emeritus professors, with no assignments and no grades [1][2]. It started with 300 students [1]. Hanna ran it as its unpaid executive director until the last months of her life. "They may wear out," she said of her students, "but their minds will never rust out" [2]. The Fromm Institute became the model for the Osher Lifelong Learning Institutes at more than 120 colleges and universities, and it had a sister program in Jerusalem [1][2]. She died on January 2, 2003, just after turning 89 [2]. Xavier Hall, the 1959 Jesuit residence facing Parker Avenue, is now Fromm Hall [3].

title: Fire at the yacht club Christmas party
place: St. Francis Yacht Club, on the Marina jetty (99 Yacht Road)
hook: A yacht club born from a 1927 walkout lost half its clubhouse when a Christmas tree went up in flames in the middle of a party.
story: The St. Francis Yacht Club began with a walkout. In 1927 the old San Francisco Yacht Club, founded in 1869, split over whether to move from Sausalito to Belvedere. Members who wanted a club on the city waterfront left, and St. Francis was incorporated on May 6, 1927, with two-time commodore John Punnett as its first commodore [1]. They built on land left over from the 1915 exposition, beside its harbor, to a design by Willis Polk [1][3]. Polk died before the plans were finished; his office completed them [3]. On December 21, 1976, during a party at the club, a Christmas tree burst into flames. The five-alarm fire sent flames 100 feet into the air, killed at least one person and put seven more in the hospital [2]. The western half of the clubhouse was destroyed, and the members rallied to rebuild it [3]. In 1989 the Loma Prieta earthquake damaged the building badly enough that major foundation repairs were needed [3]. The club's own history says little of the original building is left [1]. Its best-known event began in 1964 with eight big yachts and was soon nicknamed the Big Boat Series; it is still sailed each September in the club's 'front yard' [1].

title: Food for People, Not for Profit, on 9th
place: 9th Avenue between Irving and Judah (Inner Sunset Community Food Store; Arizmendi Bakery, 1331 9th Ave)
hook: A volunteer-run grocery collective opened on 9th Avenue in 1976, got evicted, kept moving, and left a co-op tradition that still sells hot baguettes.
story: In May 1976 the Inner Sunset Community Food Store opened in what one member called 'a funky store front on 9th Avenue near Golden Gate Park'. It grew out of the Bay Area's People's Food System under the slogan 'Food For People, Not For Profit' [1]. Volunteers organised and staffed it at first. Later a collective ran it, barely paid, as a steward for the neighbourhood. Around 1982 a landlord's eviction forced it several blocks west along Irving, where members turned a former plumbing shop into a store. Later it moved again, to 20th Avenue [1]. In 1994 a statewide survey found it stocked more kinds of organic produce than any store in California [1]. Rent hikes and bitter internal fights closed it in 1995, and a former member wrote a scathing post-mortem [1]. The cooperative idea came back to 9th Avenue anyway. In October 2000, with help from Berkeley's Cheese Board and the Arizmendi bakery in Oakland, worker-owners opened Arizmendi Bakery at 1331 9th Avenue [2]. It is named after a Basque labour organiser, and the only job it has is worker-owner [2].

title: Last frame at Japantown Bowl
place: Japantown Bowl site (now 1600 Webster condominiums), corner of Post and Webster streets
hook: Forty lanes, 2,000 league bowlers, glow-in-the-dark midnight parties. Then its owner decided to sell, and the neighbourhood fought for its bowling alley.
story: Japantown Bowl opened in 1976 at the corner of Post and Webster. It had two storeys and 40 lanes, and by 2000 it was the largest of San Francisco's three remaining bowling alleys [1][2]. It drew 2,000 league bowlers and about 150,000 visitors a year, and turned a $500,000 annual profit [2]. Kids under 18 were its biggest group of customers, with around 325 in youth leagues run by day manager Darrell Herbert [1]. There were "Cyber Bowl" midnight parties with fog machines, lasers and glow-in-the-dark balls [1]. "This place is Japantown," Herbert said [1]. In summer 2000 the owner, Kintetsu Enterprises Co. of America, announced it would close the alley and sell. Elderly Nisei, residents and city officials protested [2]. The Japanese Cultural and Community Center offered $6.7 million to keep it open [2]. On the last day, 20 September 2000, regulars signed pins over a free buffet. Bob Tsugawa, who had bowled there twice a week since 1976, said: "It's like home to a lot of us" [1]. One bowler reminded the Chronicle that urban renewal had cleared other people's homes from the block [1]. Kintetsu rejected the offer and sold the property to a company that planned a retail complex [2]. The alley was razed in 2003, and condominiums now stand on the site [3].

title: Ruth Asawa's paper-flower fountains
place: Origami Fountains, Buchanan Mall (Osaka Way) between Post and Sutter
hook: A sculptor who spent her teens behind barbed wire gave Japantown two fountains shaped like folded paper, then had merchants' children help shape the benches.
story: Ruth Asawa was 16 in 1942 when FBI agents arrested her father and her family was forced off their farm in Norwalk and into camps [1]. She became one of the country's celebrated sculptors. When redevelopment turned a block of Buchanan Street into a pedestrian mall in 1975 and 1976, she designed its two Origami Fountains, meant to look like flowers of folded paper [1][2]. Planner Rai Okamoto designed the mall itself, with a torii-like gate at Sutter [3]. Asawa also designed the benches and got the children of the mall's merchants to help make relief panels of Japanese fairy tales and festivals, sculpted in dough and then cast in concrete [3]. The original steel fountains corroded and were removed, but after public outcry bronze replicas cast under Asawa's supervision returned in 1999 [2][3]. The water was switched off more than a decade before 2025. A 2016 estimate put repairs at $437,177, and the city planned renovation for 2026 to 2027 [2][3].

title: The Bookstore That Gave Lesbians Happy Endings
place: Old Wives Tales bookstore, 1009 Valencia St
hook: In the novels Carol Seajay grew up on, lesbians ended in suicide or conversion. So she skipped the last chapters, rode a motorcycle west and opened a bookstore.
story: Carol Seajay arrived from Michigan in December 1973, having read every lesbian novel she could find; none had a happy ending, so she simply never read the last chapter [1]. With $6,000 from a credit union and a $2,000 loan from her partner Paula Wallace's parents, the two opened Old Wives Tales on Halloween 1976 at 532 Valencia, directly below the Club for the Deaf, paying themselves $200 a month [1]. The shop later moved to larger premises at 1009 Valencia [1]. It sat in a remarkable corridor: Artemis Cafe, a women-only cafe; Osento, the city's only women's bathhouse; Amelia's dance bar, sister to Maud's in Cole Valley; and a feminist credit union lending to women-owned businesses [1][2]. Seajay also started the Feminist Bookstore News, whose first issue appeared in October 1976 [1]. "I would walk home at night and feel that it was the golden age of the world," she said [1]. Strife, debt and collective turmoil took their toll, and Old Wives Tales closed in 1995 [1][2].

title: The Cancer Gene Was Ours All Along
place: Bishop-Varmus laboratory, UCSF Parnassus campus
hook: Two UCSF virologists chasing a chicken cancer virus discovered that the gene behind it came from normal cells, including ours. Stockholm called in 1989.
story: J. Michael Bishop moved to UCSF in February 1968, turning down an East Coast offer because, he said, he would be 'genuinely needed in San Francisco' [2]. In 1970 a young physician named Harold Varmus arrived as his postdoc. The two soon worked as equals and shared lab space, staff and funding until 1984 [2][3]. Their target was src, the gene that lets Rous sarcoma virus turn chicken cells into tumour cells. Where did the virus get it? Experiments run mainly by Dominique Stehelin and Deborah Spector gave the answer [2]. In 1976 the team published a startling conclusion: src was not really a viral gene at all. It was a normal cellular gene, found across the animal kingdom, which the virus had picked up from a host and carried along [1]. Normal genes that control growth, it turned out, can become cancer genes when damaged. Researchers soon identified more than 40 of these oncogenes [1]. On 9 October 1989 Bishop and Varmus were awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine [1]. Varmus, meanwhile, had spent most of those years living in a Victorian house in the Haight [3].

title: The Corner Where Chinatown Spilled West
place: 8th Avenue and Balboa Street
hook: During the 1976 city strike, Chinese Muni drivers living at one Richmond corner quietly organised rides so elderly neighbours could still reach their doctors.
story: Steve Hong grew up at Eighth Avenue and Balboa in the 1970s, when it seemed every corner had a grocery, and three near his home were run by Chinese families [1]. Before 1965, he writes, most Chinese San Franciscans were confined to Chinatown; after immigration law changed, families moved out to the Richmond, and Clement Street became known as a 'New Chinatown' [1]. His corner held more than groceries. About 20 Chinese Muni operators worked in the whole city, and a handful lived on the south corners of Eighth and Balboa [1]. In spring 1976, city craft workers walked out and Muni drivers stopped running buses in solidarity [2]. Hong recalls that the Chinese drivers across the street organised and dispatched rides so seniors could reach their medical appointments; he believes those efforts were seeds of today's paratransit [1]. An apartment on the corner was a hangout for young Chinese activists who fought for housing and for the International Hotel, among them Fred Lau [1]. Lau had been admitted to the police academy in 1970 after Chinatown protested a height rule he missed by three-quarters of an inch; in 1996 he became the city's first Chinese American police chief [3].

title: The Cove Gets Its Name Back
place: China Beach trailhead monument, end of Sea Cliff Avenue
hook: When the federal government took over Phelan Beach, it quickly gave the cove back its older name. Five years later a family added a stone to say why.
story: In 1976 the state beach below Sea Cliff passed to the federal government and became part of the Golden Gate National Recreation Area. The Parks Conservancy says it was "promptly renamed, once again, to China Beach", dropping the name of James D. Phelan, a champion of exclusion [1]. In 1981 Henry and Diana Chung gave a monument for the trailhead near the parking area at the end of Sea Cliff Avenue [1][3]. It is a stone carved with Chinese characters. Its English text says that since gold rush times the cove was a campsite for Chinese fishermen who worked in and around the Bay, and that their efforts to supply a young city "helped establish one of the area's most important industries and traditions" [1][3]. The Conservancy points out that every visitor walking down to the sand has to pass it, and says: "This is by design" [1]. The National Park Service still directs visitors to the monument to the fishermen and early residents who camped in the cove [2].

title: The ice rink that hosted rock's farewells
place: Winterland Ballroom site, 2000 Post Street at Steiner
hook: An old skating rink at Post and Steiner saw The Band's Last Waltz, the Sex Pistols' last show and an all-night Grateful Dead goodbye.
story: Winterland began in 1928 as the New Dreamland Auditorium, an ice rink that could be turned into an event hall [1]. Bill Graham started renting it in 1966, and after closing the Fillmore West in 1971 he ran it as a full-time concert hall holding 5,400 people [1]. On 25 November 1976 The Band played its farewell concert here, The Last Waltz, filmed by Martin Scorsese, with guests including Bob Dylan, Joni Mitchell, Neil Young and Eric Clapton [1]. Van Morrison sang "Tura Lura Lural" and "Caravan" [2]. On 14 January 1978 the Sex Pistols played their last show here [1]. Photographer Bob Minkin lost his wallet and tickets on arriving for the Grateful Dead's December 1977 run, then got new tickets from Winterland's office [3]. The Dead closed the building on New Year's Eve 1978 with a show of nearly six hours, broadcast on KSAN and KQED [1]. It was razed in 1985, and apartments now occupy the corner [1][3].

title: The real Barbary Lane
place: Macondray Lane, between Jones and Taylor
hook: A hidden, tree-shaded footpath with wooden stairs became 28 Barbary Lane, home of Mrs. Madrigal and the most beloved tenants in San Francisco fiction.
story: Macondray Lane is a pedestrian path on the southeastern side of Russian Hill, running between Leavenworth and Taylor streets. At the Taylor end, wooden steps drop down to the street, and the views reach to Alcatraz [1]. It is named for Frederick W. Macondray, a merchant who came to California in the 1850s, and it feels a world away from the city below [2]. In 1976 Armistead Maupin began "Tales of the City" as a daily serial in the San Francisco Chronicle [3]. Newcomer Mary Ann Singleton rents an apartment at 28 Barbary Lane from the eccentric, marijuana-growing landlady Anna Madrigal, who is later revealed to be a transgender woman [4]. Maupin followed a group of friends and lovers, gay and straight, through the 1970s and 80s. The series became one of the earliest works of fiction to confront the AIDS epidemic [3]. Readers long suspected Barbary Lane was Macondray Lane, and Maupin confirmed it in the 2017 documentary "The Untold Tales of Armistead Maupin" [1]. The lane was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1988 [1].

title: Thirty-three years in the Streetlight bins
place: Former Streetlight Records, 3979 24th Street, near Noe
hook: It started as overflow space for a stereo shop, with sagging cardboard boxes of used records. Bobby McFerrin thanked it on his first album.
story: In 1976 Robert Fallon, whose own staff described him as an eccentric sculptor and junk collector, opened Streetlight on 24th Street as extra space for his stereo-components shop [1]. General manager Jeff Moss remembered one small sign and "saggy cardboard boxes with used records--and this was before anyone understood the concept of used records" [2]. As record sales grew, Streetlight spread to Market Street, San Jose and Santa Cruz [1]. In the 1970s and '80s collectors came from all over to dig through its bins. Bobby McFerrin, then a neighbour, was a regular and thanked the store on his first album. Tracy Chapman was spotted there too [1]. Manager Sunlight Weismehl got hired after returning a Jethro Tull album because its liner wasn't in mint condition [2]. When chains like Tower Records went under, Moss joked that Streetlight had "forgot to go out of business" [1]. But downloads, big-box discounts and the loss of foot traffic after the Real Food Company closed in 2003 took their toll [1][2]. Fallon said the store had lost money since 2001, and in 2008 he announced that 3979 24th Street would close on January 31 [2].

title: Zada Weed rings the Dolphin Club bell
place: Dolphin Swimming & Boating Club, 502 Jefferson St
hook: For 99 years the Dolphin Club was for men only. A teenage girl crashed its Golden Gate swim in 1937. In 1976 six women's lawsuit finally opened the doors.
story: Two German immigrants, John Wieland and Valentine Kehrlein, founded the Dolphin Swimming and Boating Club in August 1877. Six of their sons were among its 25 charter members [1]. It stayed a men's club for nearly a century. In 1937, the year the Golden Gate Bridge was completed, 16-year-old Zada Weed swam across the Golden Gate with the Dolphins' otherwise all-male swim, coached by the club's Charlie Sava, and stole the publicity [1][2]. "I'd ring the bell, and someone always let me in," she recalled [2]. In 1949 Anita Day Hubbard was made an honorary member, considered the club's first woman [1]. Real change came through the courts. After a successful lawsuit by six women, the rowing clubs began accepting women, and five joined the Dolphin Club in October 1976. Zada Weed Taft, by then a swim coach, was among them [1][2]. Fifty more joined the next year [1]. The first women's locker room opened in 1978, with 62 lockers and four shower heads. That same year the city evicted the neighbouring San Francisco Rowing Club for refusing to admit women and provide public access [1]. In 1980 Cynthia Ehrlich became the first woman elected to the Dolphin board [1].

title: A haunted hotel with a magic show
place: Chambers Mansion (the Mansions Hotel), 2220 Sacramento Street
hook: An adman bought a rundown Victorian with a gruesome legend, turned it into a haunted hotel with a magic show, and spent years fighting his neighbours.
story: The Chambers Mansion, a Queen Anne built in 1887, came with a gory legend. Chambers's two feuding nieces supposedly inherited it, and one was later found "cut almost in half". NoeHill notes that the story is an urban legend and that even basic facts about Chambers are hard to confirm [2]. In 1977 advertising man Bob Pritikin bought what was by then a rundown boardinghouse. He turned it into an eccentric 16-room hotel and made the most of its haunted reputation [1]. He put on a magic act, the "Pritikin Squished Eyeball Theater", and the Examiner reported that Barbra Streisand and Robin Williams stayed there for a time [3]. Chronicle photographers recorded Beniamino Bufano's grown children setting up his sculpture in 1978, and the demonologists Ed and Lorraine Warren in the billiard room in 1982 [1]. For years the hotel was also a neighbourhood polling place [1]. Not everyone was charmed. From 1979 to 1991 the Chronicle kept reporting on Pritikin's feud with the Pacific Heights Neighborhood Association [1]. The hotel was sold in 2000 and converted to housing [1].

title: A newspaper from a shelter basement
place: Hospitality House, 290 Turk Street (the paper's home by the 1990s)
hook: It began as a two-page mimeographed sheet run by shelter residents. At its peak it printed in four languages and was nominated for a Pulitzer.
story: In 1977 residents of Hospitality House's shelter began a two-page mimeographed newsletter in its basement, promising "to publish news that directly affects the residents of this area" [1]. The paper was founded by homeless people and the directors of the drop-in centre, and it printed practical guides to housing, medical and job services [2]. Under editors Rob Waters and Sara Colm, the Tenderloin Times grew into a real investigative paper. Its yearly count of homeless deaths and its reports on pedestrians killed in the neighbourhood were picked up by the mainstream press [1][2]. From 1985 it printed in English, Vietnamese, Khmer and Lao, reflecting the neighbourhood's growing Southeast Asian community [2]. According to Media Alliance's Mediafile, it was nominated for a Pulitzer Prize, and in 1989 the New York Times ran its coverage of the Loma Prieta earthquake [1]. Grants ran out in the early 1990s. The budget fell from about $300,000 to under $30,000, the remaining staff was laid off, and by the time Mediafile reported on it in 1994 a part-time crew of three residents was keeping it alive [1]. Colm left in 1991 to start the Phnom Penh Post [1].

title: An Eviction Fight Comes to El Camino
place: 740 El Camino del Mar (named in the 1977 flyer as Walter Shorenstein's home)
hook: In the month police cleared Manilatown's International Hotel, an underground group aimed its anger at a Sea Cliff address.
story: The fight over the International Hotel on Kearny Street began in 1968. The hotel then belonged to two heirs of the Milton Meyer real estate firm, and Walter Shorenstein, the firm's president and managing agent, took out a demolition permit and tried to evict the tenants, many of them elderly Filipinos [1][2]. After a fire killed three people he broke off talks. In December 1973 he sold the building to the Four Seas company, and the tenants only found out six months later, from Herb Caen's column [2]. All the tenants were evicted on August 4, 1977 [1]. That month a flyer headed "SCUMLORDS FACING EVICTION" appeared, signed by the Central Command of the New World Liberation Front. "We decided to make a parking lot at 740 El Camino Del Mar," it began, calling the house Shorenstein's home and throwing in an antisemitic insult [1]. The flyer urged readers to "plug up parking meters" and to attack supervisors' houses, cars and property [1]. It does not say what, if anything, was actually done at the house. The Manilatown Heritage Foundation, which keeps the flyer, reads it as turning the tables on the landlord [1].

title: Diana Ross Parts the Trocadero Crowd
place: Former Trocadero Transfer, 520 Fourth Street at Bryant
hook: Every week the DJ put 'Diana Ross +1' on the guest list and people laughed. Then one night she really walked in.
story: The Trocadero Transfer opened in 1977 in a 1930 warehouse at 520 Fourth Street. It was an after-hours gay disco that stayed open until 2000, when the building was remodelled into another club [1][2]. When the club won its all-night permit, DJ Steve Fabus remembers, it "ushered in a New York-style all-night party" held every weekend [3]. The room had good acoustics because television shows had once been produced there. Its lighting, run by Billy Langenheim, was taken as seriously as the music [3]. Bobby Viteritti, the main DJ in its peak years, won Billboard's national DJ of the Year award in 1979 and 1980. Dancers came from Los Angeles and Miami [3]. Viteritti used to put "Diana Ross +1" on the guest list every week as a joke. Then one night in 1978 she arrived. The crowd parted, and she climbed into the booth, kissed him and hit the turntable, silencing the sound system to huge cheers [3]. By 1982 AIDS had changed the dance floor. Local disco producer Patrick Cowley died that year aged 32, and the singer Sylvester died in 1988 [3].

title: Disco, punk and the I-Beam
place: Site of the I-Beam, 1748 Haight Street (upstairs in the old Park Masonic Hall)
hook: Upstairs in a hall where Haight merchants once met, a gay disco opened in 1977 and went on to host New Order, the Pixies and Pearl Jam.
story:
The tall windows above the storefronts at 1748 Haight once lit the Park Masonic Hall, where neighbourhood groups and the Haight Ashbury Merchants Improvement Association met [3]. On an October night in 1977, Sanford Kellman opened the I-Beam on its second floor [1]. It began as one of the city's first big gay discos [1][2]. One regular remembered that in the Haight of 1977, which shared a supervisorial district with the Castro, most of the few major businesses were gay-owned [1].

Open to everyone, the club followed the music from disco into new wave and punk, then hip-hop nights and, by the late 1980s, acid house [1]. The acts: Sylvester, the Buzzcocks, New Order (for $10), the Beastie Boys with Run-DMC, Siouxsie and the Banshees, the Pixies, Jane's Addiction, the Red Hot Chili Peppers and Pearl Jam [1]. When neighbours complained about noise to the planning commission, a supporter played a tape of Hell's Angels circling the block at 10 p.m.. The club stayed open [1]. AIDS took many staff and regulars [1]. The 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake split its ceiling; after a brief closure it reopened, and it shut for good in 1994. The site sat vacant for about ten years before the building was torn down and replaced with apartments [1][3].

title: Japantown fights its second uprooting
place: Nihonmachi (Japantown) blocks around Post and Buchanan
hook: Thirty-five years after the camps, Japantown's residents faced eviction again, and this time they occupied the buildings.
story: Before World War II, Nihonmachi covered about 20 blocks and was home to 95 percent of San Francisco's Japanese Americans [1]. By 1940 it had more than 200 Japanese American-owned businesses [2]. Many returned after the camps, only to find the neighbourhood targeted by the Redevelopment Agency's Western Addition projects, which leaders in both the Japanese American and African American communities opposed [2]. The first big change, the Japan Center, displaced more than 50 businesses and about 1,500 residents [2]. In 1977 residents formed Citizens Against Nihonmachi Eviction (C.A.N.E.) to fight the eviction of low-income tenants and small businesses [1]. The group brought thousands of people to protest at City Hall and against Kintetsu, and occupied several buildings slated for demolition, in the same spirit as the International Hotel tenants [1]. They lost. FoundSF's account says foreign-owned hotels and shops displaced hundreds of local Japanese American residents and businesses [1].

title: Leroy Looper saves the Cadillac Hotel
place: Cadillac Hotel, 380 Eddy St at Leavenworth
hook: A 180-room hotel had 40 tenants and a drug market out front. A former Harlem street kid bought it with no money down and pioneered a new kind of housing.
story: The Cadillac Hotel went up after the 1906 earthquake, a grand place where guests checked their furs at the front desk [1]. By the 1960s it was on the way down. One owner, a then-unknown Donald Fisher, before he founded the Gap, stripped much of its ornament [1]. In July 1977 it was sold, with no money down, to Leroy Looper, who ran the Reality House West drug-treatment programme [1][2]. The 180-room hotel had only 40 tenants. Looper planned to restore it and house people coming out of prison. The mostly elderly residents were wary, so he promised they could vote to end the halfway-house programme if they were unhappy. They never did [1]. The legendary manager Sarah Kearney swept the sidewalk daily and used her broom on anyone dealing drugs in front of the hotel [1]. Randy Shaw calls it the West Coast's first 'supportive housing', and its lobby became a meeting hall for neighbourhood organizing [1][2]. Reality House West was the first group to blaze the Tenderloin's nonprofit-housing trail [2]. Today the Tenderloin Museum occupies its corner at 398 Eddy [3].

title: Lightboxes Behind the Bar at the Utah
place: Hotel Utah Saloon, 500 Fourth Street at Bryant
hook: A 1908 workers' hotel beside the Bay Bridge ramps became a saloon stage for Robin Williams and Whoopi Goldberg, with lightboxes behind the bar for photographers checking their slides.
story: The Hotel Utah went up in 1908 at Fourth and Bryant as a saloon and rooms for working men. In the 1930s its bar took the name Transbay Café, after the new Bay Bridge ramps nearby. After 1945 it was Al Opatz's "Al's Trans-Bay", a blue-collar bar whose regulars included a duck-hunting club [1]. On March 18, 1977, film producer and screenwriter Paul Gaer turned Al's into the Hotel Utah Saloon [2]. He spread the bar into the two neighbouring storefronts and built a stage. Comedians and musicians including Robin Williams, Whoopi Goldberg, PJ Harvey and Guns N' Roses played there. Upstairs, rooms long used by drug dealers became homes for artists and musicians [1]. Photographers from a photo lab across the street drank there so often that the bar installed lightboxes so they could edit their work over a drink [1]. The Utah outlasted the dot-com boom too. "We saw them pull up in limos," owner Damian Samuel, who started as the doorman, said in 2007. "And we watched them drive off in U-Hauls" [2]. In 2018 the city's Historic Preservation Commission moved to make it an official landmark [1].

title: Posters pulled by hand in Japantown
place: Japantown Art & Media Workshop (JAM), Japantown near Sutter and Buchanan (exact print-shop address not recorded in sources)
hook: Sansei silkscreen artists opened a print shop that made more than 500 posters for community groups, as long as the groups helped pull the ink.
story: The Asian American movement of the late 1960s produced a set of new community groups in Japantown that Sansei founded and ran [2]. One of them was the Japantown Art & Media Workshop, known as JAM. Many of its organisers had worked with the Kearny Street Workshop in Chinatown, which was evicted in 1977. By then JAM had opened [1]. Unlike Kearny Street, JAM worked as a community print shop. Over the next decade it made more than 500 poster designs for hundreds of groups. It had one rule: each nonprofit had to send a few people to help with the printing, and often with the design [1]. In its fiscal heyday it kept up to five printmakers on full-time, low pay. In 1979 it helped East Bay artists start a sister workshop in Oakland, which folded two years later when federal CETA job money was cut [1]. Together, Kearny Street and JAM taught silkscreen to more than 2,000 people between 1972 and 1986 [1]. Urban renewal cost JAM its print shop. In 1987 the historian Michael Rossman wrote that JAM was left in "a token room without production facilities," won from Japantown's cultural authorities. JAM kept printing through other facilities, and a second generation, including Richard Tokeshi and Wes Senzaki, kept it going [1].

title: Precita Eyes paints the neighbourhood
place: Precita Eyes studio, 348 Precita Ave
hook: A mural workshop for the local library turned into one of the few community mural centres in the United States.
story:
Susan Cervantes came to San Francisco from Dallas in 1961 on a scholarship to the San Francisco Art Institute. She married the muralist Luis Cervantes, and they raised their family near Precita Park [2]. She wanted to brighten her neighbourhood. That led her to Las Mujeres Muralistas, the pioneering all-women mural collective, and to its idea of collaborative, accessible art [1][2].

Founded in 1977, the organisation grew out of a community workshop that designed and painted a mural called 'Masks of God, Soul of Man' for the Bernal Heights Library. Because it was a group effort, they signed it 'Precita Eyes Muralists', and that became the name of the organisation [1]. 'Precita' refers to Precita Valley and its old creek. The 'Eyes' are the ones we see with [1]. By its 30th anniversary in 2007, Precita Eyes had helped create more than 450 murals and was one of just five community mural groups in the nation [2]. It still runs youth and toddler classes from its studio at 348 Precita Avenue [3]. 'We pretty much stick with pencil and paper and paint,' Cervantes said [2].

title: Sami Sunchild paints the Red Vic
place: The Red Victorian, 1665 Haight Street
hook: Goldfish swam in a toilet tank, and the guest rooms had names like Flower Child. Later, a Banksy rat went up on the outside wall.
story: The building went up in 1904 as the Jefferson Hotel. In the Summer of Love it was the Jeffrey Haight, a free crash pad [1]. In 1977 the artist and activist Sami Sunchild bought it, painted the facade red and reopened it as the Red Victorian Bed, Breakfast & Art [1]. She gave the rooms themes such as the Flower Child, the Rainbow, the Redwoods and the Peacock suite. In one shared bathroom, goldfish swam in the toilet tank [1][2]. Downstairs were a Peace Cafe and a gift shop. From the 1990s she hosted Sunday-morning World Peace Conversations [1]. "The Red Vic is at the centre of the Haight, and the Haight is at the centre of the universe," she told a reporter at 81 [2]. In April 2010 Banksy sprayed a rat clutching a marker pen on the side of the building from a neighbouring roof [3]. Sunchild was about to paint over it when collector Brian Greif arranged to remove the siding, promising her he would never sell it. He later said one collector had offered him $700,000 [3]. Sunchild died in 2013, aged 87 [1].

title: The 'Radio City' of gay cinemas
place: Nob Hill Cinema, 729 Bush St
hook: Behind a plain stuccoed front on Bush Street, the old Club Hangover became a members-only gay film house with free coffee in the lobby.
story:
In the 1960s, when Nob Hill and Polk Street were centres of gay male life, the hilltop had its own after-dark geography. Police in the 1950s had already called Huntington Park "a major meeting spot," and one resident recalled hedges "taller than I am" that made it ideal for cruising [1].

Down the south slope at 729 Bush Street, the former Club Hangover became a members-only theatre and then, in the late 1960s, a gay porn cinema, the Nob Hill Cinema and Arcade [1]. In January 1977 Chronicle columnist John L. Wasserman went "trucking" there and reported a "tidy little theater" seating fewer than 100 that "serves free java in the lobby" and "has been called 'The Radio City Music Hall of gay porno theaters'" [1]. Behind it ran a dim 30-foot arcade of small rooms [1]. The city's LGBTQ context statement noted in 2015 that it was still in business [1].

The building itself hides in plain sight. It was designed by C. A. Meussdorffer to house a store, but its facade was later sheathed in stuccostone, leaving only the parapet original, so it counts as one of the few non-contributing buildings in the Lower Nob Hill Apartment Hotel District [2].

title: The Coronet's lines for Star Wars
place: Site of the Coronet Theatre, 3575 Geary Boulevard at Palm Avenue (now Institute on Aging)
hook: Fox doubted Star Wars, so a booker gave it the Coronet. Lines soon circled the block, and it became the film's top-earning theatre in America.
story: The Coronet opened on Geary on November 2, 1949 with I Was a Male War Bride. It had 1,350 loge-style seats and a room with a television set that patrons could watch for free [1]. From 1956 it was a roadshow house. Oklahoma! ran for 44 weeks, and Around the World in 80 Days for nearly two years [1]. In 1977 20th Century Fox wanted its big theatres for The Other Side of Midnight. The booker Gary Meyer put that film in the smaller Alexandria and gave Star Wars the Coronet, because "I wanted the giant screen" [2]. It opened on May 25, 1977, one of just 32 theatres in the country to do so. The lines were split in two and snaked around the block. Manager Albert Levin saw "old people, young people, children, Hare Krishna groups," with chess players and painted faces [2]. Neighbours on Jordan Avenue couldn't park, and local children sold hot dogs from wagons [2]. The Coronet took $2 million in six months, more than any other Star Wars theatre in the country [2]. It closed on March 17, 2005 and was demolished in 2007 to make way for the Institute on Aging [1][2].

title: The Fab Mab and the Pope of Punk
place: Mabuhay Gardens, 443 Broadway
hook: A Filipino supper club became the loudest room in San Francisco, run by an emcee who insulted everyone and got his nose broken seven times.
story: Mabuhay Gardens at 443 Broadway was a Filipino restaurant before it became ground zero for San Francisco punk in the late 1970s and '80s [1]. Local bands like the Avengers, Dead Kennedys and the Nuns played its basement stage, and touring acts from Devo to the Cramps came through until it closed in 1987 [1]. Running the show was Dirk Dirksen, the self-styled "pope of punk," who baited crowds and bands alike, often with his little dog, Dummy, tucked under his arm [2]. He once told an audience to "show some intelligence and sophistication and not just accept any slop that's thrown in your trough" [2]. He reckoned his nose had been broken seven times. Every year he staged a mock torture of himself for his birthday, and one year he had himself burned at the stake [2]. Robin Williams described comedy hell as "opening for the Ramones at the Mabuhay Gardens" [2]. After the club closed, the building became a dinner theatre and events hall. In 2025, after the death of owner Francesca Valdez, neighbours and investors began raising money to buy it and bring back the Mab [1].
