title: An electrician, Rosa, and 4,600 volts
place: Lake Merced pump station area, east side of South Lake (approximate)
hook: Her tester exploded on the switchgear and threw her to the floor. The engineer on duty sat with her and told her a secret, and she told him hers.
story: In 1983 Molly Martin was a temporary electrician with the San Francisco Water Department, the one responsible for the electrical equipment at the city's pump stations [1]. One day she was sent to the Lake Merced pump station, where, she wrote, the big supply pipes from Hetch Hetchy come in and 100-horsepower motors run on 4,600 volts [1]. The union hadn't let women into its apprenticeship, and she had never been trained on high voltage. When she touched her tester, rated for only 1,000 volts, to the live switchgear, it blew up with an ear-splitting bang and threw her onto the concrete [1]. The engineer on duty stayed with her while she shook. Then he told her his story: he had grown up in Mexico City, had once lived as a woman for three years, and was saving to transition [1]. She came out to him as gay [1]. In a later piece, Martin recalled a coworker telling her that her friend had announced to the Lake Merced-based engineers that she now wanted to be called Rosa. The men "looked at their hands and didn't say anything" [2]. Martin thought Rosa, finally herself, radiated serenity [2]. Spring Valley Water had built its City Pumps on South Lake's east shore in 1891; they still work today [3].

title: Peacocks, pigs and 120 horses, never built
place: John F. Shelley Drive just east of the amphitheatre (proposed model farm site)
hook: In 1983 the city planned a petting farm with cows, goats and 'ornamental' peacocks here, plus stables for 120 horses. None of it happened.
story: The 1983 master plan for McLaren Park set out to fix an old problem. The park was so short of attractions that it served mainly its own neighbourhood, and the plan called that 'a great loss to many citizens' [1]. The work had started in 1980 under landscape architects Theodore Osmundson and Associates [1]. They proposed a model farm on John F. Shelley Drive, just east of the amphitheatre and sheltered by big trees. There children could meet cows, horses, pigs, sheep, goats, chickens, ducks, geese, turkeys and, 'for ornamental purposes only', peacocks [1]. Public meetings had shown 'considerable enthusiasm' for the farm, so it was ranked as a fairly high priority [1]. The plan also sketched an equestrian centre next to Crocker Amazon Playground, with stables for 120 horses. It pointed out that people waited twenty to thirty years for a stall at the Golden Gate Park stables [1]. What most worried residents at those meetings was more basic: illegal trash dumping and a general lack of security [1]. A park group's detailed timeline of the decades that followed lists no farm and no stables [2].

title: The Grandmaster Who Never Wanted a Business
place: Korean Martial Arts Center, 1414 Ocean Avenue
hook: A probation-department employee who began formal martial arts training at a Mormon church group opened an Ocean Avenue studio in 1983. Four decades on, he still insists it's a club.
story:
Merrill Jung's parents taught kung fu, but he says his own formal training began at a Mormon church group meeting [1]. He went to city schools, including City College. He taught martial arts at clubs and recreation centres such as the Embarcadero YMCA, and he worked for the San Mateo Probation Department until he retired in 2005 [1][2].

In 1983 he founded the Korean Martial Arts Center on Ocean Avenue, with help from his student Andrew Erickson, who talked him into it. "I never wanted to do business," Jung said. "I figured that the business will hurt what I'm trying to do, my love, my sport, my martial arts" [2]. The studio teaches taekwondo, hapkido, yongmudo, judo, karate, kung fu, tai chi, Wing Chun and Filipino stick fighting, to children as young as four and to adults [1][2]. Some students have gone on to the Junior Olympics and to competitions in Korea [1].

In August 2020, 37 years in, the city's Small Business Commission voted unanimously to add KMAC to the Legacy Business Registry [1]. Jung holds high ranks in several arts, and his son, daughter and nephew help run the studio. "We're not really a 'business,'" he said in 2022. "We're more of a club" [2].

title: The Queen Dines Among the Tapestries
place: De Young Museum (then the M. H. de Young Memorial Museum)
hook: Steve Jobs, George Lucas and Joe DiMaggio dined on pheasant with Queen Elizabeth in the park, while 5,000 protesters gathered three blocks away.
story: On March 3, 1983, President Ronald Reagan and Nancy Reagan hosted Queen Elizabeth II and Prince Philip at a dinner in the de Young and the Asian Art Museum, which then stood side by side in Golden Gate Park. It was a state dinner in all but name [2]. About 260 notable guests were invited. Weeks of preparation followed: the stone lions out front were washed, the tapestries vacuumed and ornamental trees brought in from city greenhouses to line the entrance [1][2]. Reagan thanked the Queen for lending the museum Leonardo da Vinci's horse drawings from the royal library at Windsor. She opened with a joke about exporting British weather to California [1]. The menu included pheasant, caviar and lobster terrine. Among the guests were Steve Jobs, George Lucas, Gordon Getty and Joe DiMaggio, who said, "I wouldn't have missed it for the world" [1]. Not everyone was charmed. About 5,000 people gathered in the park three blocks away to protest Britain's role in Northern Ireland [1]. The building they dined in was demolished and rebuilt in 2005 [1].

title: The half-kilometre race with two beers
place: Mission Creek between the Third and Fourth Street bridges
hook: Who needs Bay to Breakers? In 1983 the Mission Creek houseboaters staged their own race: bridge to bridge, winners picked by lottery.
story: In 1983 the houseboat families of Mission Creek and their friends formed the Mission Creek Conservancy to fight for a place in the plans for the railyards around them [1]. They had fun doing it. That May, houseboater Jack Davis organised the Bridge to Bridge Run. Herb Caen described it in his column: 'Who needs Bay to Breakers? The Mission Creek Conservancy is having a “Bridge-to-Bridge” run … From the Third to the Fourth St. bridge, a grueling 0.5 kilometers, winners to be democratically determined by lottery.' The $7.50 entry fee got you a T-shirt and two beers [1]. Davis, who also ran SOMAR, a non-profit gallery and theatre, remembered the early harbour as 'like a gypsy camp'. At parties, he said, 'the one-eyed man would get in a fight with the man with one leg.' When the sinking dock went underwater at high tide, he and a friend rebuilt it themselves. Residents published a newsletter called 'Rats and Rubbers', after what the low tide revealed [2]. It wasn't all rough. On Betty Boatwright's houseboat, with its white carpet and grand piano, guests took their shoes off [1]. By 2001, a tiny wooden 'Genuine People Feeder' stood in the creekside park, where kind souls left sandwiches for hungry people [2].

title: When the police rode horses here
place: Louis Sutter Playground area, site of the former police horse stables
hook: For years McLaren Park had its own police stables, and the mounted patrol led the valley's parades. Then the horses were gone, and neighbours spent years asking for them back.
story: For years, the police in McLaren Park came on horseback. The city's 1983 master plan reported that stables and a headquarters office for the mounted patrols had been provided in the Louis Sutter Playground area 'for a number of years'. One or two mounted patrolmen were on duty every day for most of the daylight hours, and patrol cars from the neighbouring stations covered the park roads at night [1]. The riders were part of neighbourhood life. After Visitacion Valley's 1990 street fair, the Grapevine thanked the SFPD for 'the gallant mounted patrol who led the parade'. Parade awards that year went to Visitacion Valley Middle School, the elementary school drill team, the Pioneer Squares, the Herz Playground Brownies and the Woodrow Wilson Color Guard [2]. By the mid-1990s the horses were gone. In 1996 a Friends of McLaren Park planning committee listed 'Return mounted police to the park' among its maintenance recommendations [3]. Thirteen years later it still hadn't happened. Chuck Farrugia of Help McLaren Park wrote that he had been working with Officer McCarthy of the Ingleside station and the Rec and Park patrols to bring it back, and had been promised a September return. But, he added, 'promises on paper don't amount to much when dealing with our city' [4].

title: A Convention Hall Named for a Murdered Mayor
place: Moscone Center, 747 Howard Street
hook: Built underground on land cleared by a bitter redevelopment fight, Moscone Center hosted the night America's first woman vice-presidential nominee took the stage.
story: The convention centre at Howard and Fourth stands on land the Redevelopment Agency cleared of residential hotels. Tenants fought the clearance in court for years, and an estimated 4,000 people and 700 businesses were displaced [1]. After further lawsuits, the first hall opened in 1981 and carried the name of Mayor George Moscone, who had been assassinated in 1978 [1]. Three years later the Democratic Party brought its national convention here. On July 16, 1984, New York Governor Mario Cuomo gave the keynote. He answered President Reagan's "shining city on a hill" by saying the nation was more "a Tale of Two Cities" [2]. The floor was restless. Gary Hart had won more primaries and caucuses than Walter Mondale, and Jesse Jackson had taken 18 percent of the popular vote. Mondale won on the first ballot when New Jersey's delegates put him over the top [3]. On July 19 Congresswoman Geraldine Ferraro accepted the nomination for vice president: "My name is Geraldine Ferraro" [4]. Outside there were protests, and a Chronicle photo shows a protester arrested outside the Hall of Justice. In November, Mondale carried only his home state of Minnesota [3].

title: A Visual Reminder: Saving the Square
place: Alamo Square Historic District
hook: In 1984 San Francisco drew a line around Alamo Square's Victorians and declared them, officially, as much a symbol of the city as the cable cars.
story: By the time the Board of Supervisors acted in July 1984, the blocks around Alamo Square held a rare, largely intact run of houses built between 1870 and the 1920s [1][2]. The district runs from Golden Gate Avenue to Fell Street and from Webster Street to Divisadero [1]. Its styles vary, but the city found them unified by their "residential character, relatively small scale, construction type, materials (principally wood), intense ornamentation (especially at entry and cornice)" [1]. The designation called the district "a continuum of distinguished residential architecture" and "a visual reminder of how businessmen lived two to four generations ago" [2]. Most of the first owners, it noted, "were moderately successful businessmen" [1]. The city also made a bolder claim. It said the Westerfeld House and Postcard Row were "as identified worldwide with San Francisco as the cable cars and Coit Tower" [1].

title: Eleven White Figures Behind Barbed Wire
place: The Holocaust memorial by George Segal, El Camino del Mar
hook: Some San Franciscans thought George Segal's Holocaust memorial was too grim for a beauty spot. An Auschwitz survivor at the dedication said: 'Let people be upset.'
story: A cold rain was falling on 7 November 1984 when San Francisco dedicated its controversial memorial to the six million victims of the Holocaust [1]. George Segal's sculpture is a pile of life-size white-painted bronze corpses and one standing man at a barbed-wire fence, set in a grove across from the Legion of Honor [1][2]. Eddy Wyunschenk, 57, of San Bruno, had been pulled off a cattle car at Auschwitz at 16 and was the only survivor of his Dutch family. 'That's the way it was,' he told the Chronicle. Perhaps people disliked the piece because it was such a chilling reminder, he said. 'Let people be upset' [1]. The standing figure probably comes from Margaret Bourke-White's 1945 Life photograph of the liberation of Buchenwald. A Christ-like figure and a woman holding an apple point to the ties between Jews and Christians [3]. The memorial has been defaced again and again. In 2008 swastikas were drawn on it twice in two months [2]. Segal said the graffiti only proved that prejudice had not been solved [3].

title: Megahood: A Street Fair Against the Bulldozers
place: Folsom Street between Seventh and Twelfth streets (near Ninth)
hook: Today's giant leather festival began as a housing activists' plan to prove South of Market wasn't an empty shell waiting for developers.
story: In the early 1980s Kathleen Connell, a lesbian organiser, and Michael Valerio, a gay Filipino American housing developer, worked for the South of Market tenant group TODCO. Together they fought Redevelopment Agency and downtown plans that treated the district as empty land [1][2]. They won $5 million for low-cost housing from Mayor Dianne Feinstein. They also watched AIDS begin to tear through the gay men who were part of the neighbourhood's mix [2]. Supervisor Harry Britt urged them to "do what Harvey did" and use a street fair, as Harvey Milk had in the Castro, to build political muscle [2]. In 1984 they held Megahood, the first Folsom Street Fair. It ran from Seventh to Twelfth streets between Howard and Harrison, with a dance stage run by the lesbian DJ Page Hodel [1]. About 30,000 people came and the fair raised almost $20,000 for charity. Attendance reportedly doubled each year for years. What began as a show of neighbourhood strength soon became a leather and kink festival that drew visitors from around the world [1]. It is still held on the last Sunday of September [1].

title: Punks squat a laundry for the convention
place: Former Hotel Owners Laundry Company building, Fifth and Folsom streets
hook: In 1984, as the Democrats came to Moscone Center, young squatters took over an empty laundry two blocks away. They held meetings, served free meals and built a skate rink.
story: Evicted from a squat called The Vats, many young activists moved into an abandoned building near Fifth and Folsom that had belonged to the Hotel Owners Laundry Company, nicknamed HOLC, or "hole-see" [1]. From April until their eviction in October 1984 they ran a highly political squat [1]. They met twice a week and agreed two rules: no shooting drugs, and everyone had to work [1]. They held open houses with free meals, turned the ground floor into a skateboard rink and, by one account, had visits from punk bands including MDC, Reagan Youth, the Exploited and DRI [1]. A 75-year-old former merchant seaman who lived in the hotel next door helped them get the electricity going and put in a hot water tank. He told them he didn't care they were there "as long as you don't torch the place" [1]. Only a couple of blocks from Moscone Center, HOLC became a planning center for demonstrators at the 1984 Democratic National Convention [1]. At one protest, activists pushed a twelve-foot 'Trojan Donkey', which 'excreted' toy missiles and tanks, from the protest pen at Moscone down Fifth Street to the Hall of Justice on Bryant. Riot police met them there, and many protesters sat down in front of the entrance [2].

title: Sopes from Jalisco on San Bruno
place: La Placita Mexicatessen, 2531 San Bruno Avenue
hook: Juana Perez from Jalisco ran a no-frills Mexicatessen on San Bruno Avenue for nearly three decades, and it was the only place in the Portola for sopes.
story: The city's business register shows Juana R. Perez opening La Placita Mexicatessen at 2531 San Bruno Avenue on 5 May 1984 [1]. When the Portola Planet's lunch reviewers came in June 2012, she told them she was from Jalisco and had run the place on San Bruno for 29 years, a year or so more than the register shows [2]. There were no frills. The walls held pictures of Chivas, the Guadalajara football club, and photographs of Mexican towns and countryside. Mexican candies and snacks lined the counter, and the fridge had Jarritos beside harder-to-find bottles like Cuzcatlán Cola Champagne [2]. Perez said La Placita was the only place in the Portola where you could get sopes, served with crunchy radishes on top. The empanadas were fried, and goat birria was a weekend special [2]. Carl Nolte had noted in 2009 that San Bruno Avenue had 'a couple of Mexican restaurants' on a street where Chinese restaurants now filled old Italian dining rooms and the Lido Pastry had become a Central American bakery [3]. Perez's registration ends in February 2013. New owners registered the same name and address the following month [1].

title: The Zen temple that left the synagogue
place: Sokoji (Soto Zen Mission), 1691 Laguna Street near Sutter
hook: Japanese Soto Zen members had worshipped in an old Bush Street synagogue for decades. In 1984 they dedicated a Japanese-style temple of their own on Laguna.
story: In 1934 the Soto Zen Mission, Sokoji, bought a former synagogue at 1881 Bush Street (Planning's history gives the address as 1881 Post). During the war its members kept up the payments from the camps [1]. Japanese American Buddhism had borrowed Christian customs like pews. When Shunryu Suzuki began teaching zazen there to non-Japanese students, member George Hagiwara, of the family behind the Golden Gate Park tea garden, helped buy tatami mats and cushions for them [2]. Suzuki's mostly white students became the San Francisco Zen Center, and in 1969 he left to lead it on Page Street [1]. The Japanese congregation decided to build its own temple nearby [2]. In the 1970s the board weighed repairing the old synagogue against building a traditional Japanese-style temple somewhere else, and chose to build [1]. Construction began at 1691 Laguna Street in 1980, and the temple was dedicated in April 1984 [1]. Planning's context statement groups it with the Japanese Cultural and Community Center and Konko Church. All three use half-timbered walls, peaked roofs with overhanging rafters and gilded ornament, in contrast to the severe "Japanese modernism" of Japan Center [2].

title: Chained to the Federal Building door
place: Former Federal Building, 50 United Nations Plaza
hook: Two men chained themselves to a federal door over AIDS. Their vigil lasted ten years, and signs taped to the same walls inspired the AIDS Memorial Quilt.
story: On October 27, 1985, Steven Russell and Frank Bert chained themselves to the door of the Federal Building at 50 United Nations Plaza, which housed the regional office of Health and Human Services [1][2]. It has been described as the first civil disobedience against the AIDS epidemic anywhere [3]. Supporters gathered, and the protest became the ARC/AIDS Vigil, a round-the-clock camp on the plaza lawn. They demanded $500 million for AIDS research, benefits for people with AIDS-related conditions, and access to treatments available abroad [1][3]. Most of the campers were homeless or nearly homeless gay men. They cooked, slept in tents and handed out information, and doctors came daily to give free care [1]. One cold night city cleaners hosed them down. When federal officials tried to remove the vigil, a thousand supporters turned out, and the officials backed off [1]. In November 1985 Cleve Jones led a candlelight march in memory of Harvey Milk and George Moscone, and marchers taped signs naming loved ones lost to AIDS on the building's walls. The patchwork of signs gave him the idea for the NAMES Project AIDS Memorial Quilt [2]. The vigil lasted until a December storm in 1995 flattened the last tents [1][3].

title: Golden China, Ocean Avenue's Little United Nations
place: Wang Wah (opened as Golden China), 1612 Ocean Avenue
hook: When Golden China opened in 1985, it was the only Chinese restaurant on a strip of mostly Black-owned shops. Its first regulars were patient with a nervous newcomer.
story:
Bing Xu grew up in western Guangdong during the Cultural Revolution. He came to San Francisco in 1983, hauled boxes in a Chinatown grocery and took English classes after long shifts [1]. In 1985 he and a partner opened Golden China on Ocean Avenue, timed to catch foot traffic from a new Walgreens. It was the only Chinese restaurant on a corridor made up mostly of African American-owned shops, bars and restaurants [1]. When the partner left in 1987, Xu kept it, though he spoke little English.

His wife, Juan Zhou Xu, sewed and studied English before joining full time in 1991 as the restaurant's public face. She was nervous about phone orders, but her first regulars, mostly Black neighbours, were patient: "There's no rush, take your time" [1]. Muni drivers used to pull their buses up out front so she could hand them their food.

As Black homeowners moved to the East Bay and Chinese families moved in, Chinese construction crews packed the lunch hour. Xu added bone-in catfish for customers from the Sze Yup region. Now called Wang Wah, it is the Ingleside's oldest Chinese restaurant. "We are like a little United Nations," he says [1]. By 1970 the district had been about two-thirds African American (62 percent, in the city's context statement) [1][2].

title: The park that was a cage
place: Boeddeker Park, 246 Eddy St at Jones
hook: The Tenderloin fought for a park, then got one designed like a fortress, with spiked fences and sprinklers aimed at sleepers. It took three decades to get it right.
story: When refugee families with children poured into the Tenderloin, neighbourhood leaders demanded a park. Boeddeker Park, named for the founder of St. Anthony's Dining Room, opened in 1985 [1]. The Chronicle hoped it would 'welcome elderly bench-sitters and frisky children and shoo away devotees of the twist-off cap' [2]. But the design feared its neighbours: a spiked iron fence, an entrance wide enough for a police car, and sprinklers that came on at odd moments to discourage 'long-term snoozing by the sleeping-bag set' [2]. A decade later a parents' group ranked it last of 45 parks. The Project for Public Spaces called it 'an empty cage watched from outside by drug dealers' [2]. Community meetings began in 2007, and on December 10, 2014, a $9.3 million remake led by the Trust for Public Land reopened [2][3]. It had a lawn, play areas, sloped paths for disabled residents across a 16-foot drop, and a clubhouse by WRNS Studio with a zinc roof rising 31 feet [2]. From 1985 it kept a shade tree and Anthony J. Smith's bronze of 14 residents' faces [2]. About 3,500 children lived within the surrounding 40 blocks [3].

title: The supervisor who came home to hide
place: Shawnee Avenue, Outer Mission
hook: After prison, Dan White watched his son's soccer games through a knothole. He came back to the southern neighbourhoods that had elected him, and died on Shawnee Avenue.
story: When Dan White ran for supervisor in the 1970s, he walked the Excelsior and Crocker-Amazon promising to clean up City Hall. One Crocker-Amazon family remembered their mother's window poster: 'Unite and Fight with Dan White' [3]. On November 27, 1978 he shot Mayor George Moscone and Supervisor Harvey Milk in City Hall. He was convicted of manslaughter, and the verdict set off a night of rioting [1]. Released in January 1984 after five years, he served his parole in Los Angeles and then returned to the Bay Area [1]. Friends described a man in hiding. He watched his young son's soccer games from behind a fence, peering through a knothole. When he visited his family at the house he owned in the Excelsior area, he slouched down as the car pulled into the driveway so the neighbours wouldn't see him [1]. A four-month trip to Ireland, where nobody knew his face, only made coming home harder [1]. On Monday, October 21, 1985, White took his own life in his car, holding photographs of his wife and children [1]. A 2002 Chronicle portrait of the Excelsior noted that he had lived on London Street and 'committed suicide, too, right on Shawnee Avenue', then added: 'you can't blame the neighborhood' [2].

title: A failed merger creates a landlord
place: Former Southern Pacific and Santa Fe railyards, central Mission Bay
hook: Two railroads were so sure they would merge that they repainted their locomotives. Washington said no, and Mission Bay's 300 acres ended up with a land company.
story: In September 1983 the Southern Pacific and the Santa Fe announced they would merge. By December a holding company owned both. It was California's largest private landowner, and Mission Bay's old tidelands and railyards were part of the estate [1][2][3]. Confident of approval, the railroads began repainting locomotives in a joint 'SPSF' scheme [2]. Then, on a July Thursday in 1986, the Interstate Commerce Commission voted 4-1 to reject the merger. Only the ICC's chairman, Heather Gradison, voted yes. John J. Schmidt, chairman of Santa Fe Southern Pacific, called it 'a horrible mistake' and conceded, 'we are going to have to sell something' [1]. The Southern Pacific was sold in 1988 [2]. The company kept the former railroad lands, however, and put them into a new firm, Santa Fe Pacific Realty [2][3]. In 1990 it was renamed Catellus, a name that won an employee contest: CA for California, Tellus for the goddess of the land [3]. Catellus owned 300 undeveloped acres that politicians called a chance for a 'city within the City.' Houseboaters, conservationists, housing groups and neighbors spent years fighting and bargaining with it over what should be built there [3].

title: A shantytown where Dumpville once stood
place: Berry and 7th streets
hook: In 1986 Mayor Feinstein toured a squatters' village at Berry and Seventh, nearly the exact spot police had cleared of 'Dumpville' ninety years earlier.
story: In the 1870s and 1880s, Berry and Channel streets between Fifth and Seventh were the city's garbage dump. Scavengers, tramps and children picking firewood built a shantytown the San Francisco Call named 'Dumpville'. Police tore it down on the night of November 10, 1895 [1]. The corner stayed forgotten. On January 24, 1986, the Chronicle reported that city officials had declared 'the little village at Berry and Seventh Street' a health hazard and given its residents seven days to clear out. About two dozen squatters lived there in shacks patched together from wood scraps [2]. Houseboaters nearby remembered earlier generations of homeless men living unseen in the tall weeds along the channel [2]. In February 1986 Mayor Dianne Feinstein toured the encampment; photographer Greg Gaar captured the visit [1]. The site had another significance: it was her choice for a new Giants stadium, one of many proposals before the ballpark was finally built at China Basin [1]. Today apartments, a creekside promenade and even a beach volleyball court line the old Dumpville shore [1].

title: An Organ Played by the Tides
place: Wave Organ, tip of the Marina jetty
hook: At the end of a breakwater built from a demolished cemetery's headstones, 25 pipes let you put your ear to San Francisco Bay.
story: The idea came from sound artist Bill Fontana's recordings of noises coming out of a vent pipe on a floating concrete dock in Sydney, Australia [1]. Peter Richards, a senior artist at the Exploratorium, won a National Endowment for the Arts planning grant in 1980 to study the effect. A rough prototype on this jetty, shown at the New Music '81 festival, won enough support for a permanent piece [1]. Exploratorium founder Frank Oppenheimer began raising money and chasing permits, but construction started in September 1985, seven months after his death [1]. Working with sculptor and stonemason George Gonzalez, Richards finished the Wave Organ in May 1986. It was dedicated to Oppenheimer that June [1]. The jetty itself was built from a demolished cemetery, and its carved granite and marble now form terraces and benches [1][2]. Twenty-five pipes of PVC and concrete reach down to different heights so they catch the rising and falling tide. Waves slap the pipe ends and push water in and out, and the sound is faint [1][2]. As FoundSF puts it, it was 'built not for the eye, but for the ear' [2].

title: From Taipei to Buenos Aires to brie
place: 24th Street Cheese Company, 3893 24th Street
hook: A Chinese-Argentine restaurant manager who knew only three cheeses was handed an empty cheese shop by his mother. He became Noe Valley's cheese oracle.
story: Charles Kung was born in 1950. His family left mainland China for Taiwan, and in 1964 moved on to Buenos Aires, where they ran a Chinese restaurant and then a supply business for fishing boats [1]. In 1973 his sister, waiting tables at Andy's Doughnuts on Castro Street, heard the building was for sale. Their mother was on the next plane from Argentina with the money [1]. The family went on to buy several Noe Valley buildings, including the one at 3893 24th Street that housed the Cheese Company [1]. When the shop's operator left abruptly in 1984, the counter was bare. 'We can run a Chinese restaurant, but not a cheese store,' his mother protested. Still, she asked Charles to take it on [1]. He arrived in February 1986 with his new wife, and they lived upstairs. He knew Parmesan, mozzarella and provolone, 'that's it' [1]. He washed knives, watched the staff and read cheese books. Two decades later he carried 300 cheeses, and said the rising neighbourhood let him stock ones he 'wouldn't dare to carry' 15 years earlier [1]. In 2009, as Whole Foods moved in a block away, Kung told the Voice he wasn't optimistic [2].

title: The Crazy Viking of Brooks Park
place: Brooks Park entrance, Shields & Ramsell Streets
hook: Pit bull fights, dumped bodies and bullets in his garage: in 1986 Peter Vaernet moved in next to Brooks Park anyway, and decided to fight for it.
story: After the city bought the Brooks hilltop, the old house became a target. Vandals burned it, and after two more fires the city bulldozed what was left [1]. Mayor Moscone dedicated "Brooks Park" on May 20, 1978. Just a month earlier vandals had smashed the new picnic tables, so organiser Lonnie Lawson rebuilt them, helped by the three youths a judge had sentenced to the work [1]. The 1980s brought crack cocaine. At least two bodies were dumped on the hill, and by the early 1990s neighbours were finding the carcasses of dogs from night-time pit bull fights [1]. In 1986 Peter Vaernet moved to Shields Street, against estate agents' advice [2]. He watched drug deals from his window and had bullets fired into his garage. "I'm crazy, I guess. I'm a Viking," he said. "Vikings love battles" [1]. With Minnie Ward he joined Neighbors in Action [1][2]. The Friends of Brooks Park, formed in 1987, cleared glass, needles and graffiti. They also recorded dog fighters' licence plates for Animal Care & Control [3]. A $1.3 million open-space grant, approved in 1994, enlarged the park to about six and a half acres [3].

title: The First Man Burned on Baker Beach
place: Baker Beach
hook: Two friends dragged an 8-foot wooden figure onto a San Francisco beach and set it alight. Strangers came running. Burning Man had begun.
story: On the summer solstice of 1986, Larry Harvey and his friend Jerry James put together a rough wooden figure, dragged it down to Baker Beach and set it on fire [1]. Nobody gave them permission. As the 8-foot man went up, people all across the beach came running. A woman ran forward and held its burning hand, and a stranger with a guitar made up a song on the spot [2]. Harvey and James decided to come back the next year. Each year the Man got bigger. Sculptor Mike Acker joined them, and Harvey's roommate Dan Miller rigged pulleys to raise its arms. From 1989 the Cacophony Society, a network of urban pranksters, pitched in [2]. By 1990 the figure stood four storeys tall, and U.S. Park Police noticed that beach fires were limited to 3-by-3-foot campfires. After some haggling on the sand, an officer shook hands on a deal: the Man could stand, but it could not burn [2]. The crowd of hundreds, who had come for a fire, began chanting 'Burn him!' Someone grabbed Harvey by the throat. The organisers lowered the Man and carried it away. That Labor Day they took it to Nevada's Black Rock Desert [2].

title: The Grapevine, one man's 25-year newspaper
place: Visitacion Valley Community Center, 50–66 Raymond Ave
hook: For a quarter-century one volunteer wrote, edited, photographed and delivered the valley's only newspaper. Then a state budget stand-off in Sacramento stopped the presses.
story: Beginning in 1986, residents could pick up the Grapevine, a free monthly paper published by the Visitacion Valley Community Center on Raymond Avenue [1]. Its volunteer editor, Len Appiano, did almost everything: layout, editing, ad sales, writing, photography, history and delivery. He kept the paper going for more than 25 years [1]. The centre that published it was also a hub for the neighbourhood. Seniors came for lunch, hundreds of newly arrived immigrants took English classes there, and the Visitacion Valley Planning Alliance held its monthly meetings in the gym [1]. In 2010 California went more than 100 days without a state budget. Nearly 80 percent of the centre's operating money depended on the state, and the October and November 2010 issues never came out. It was the first time the valley had gone without its monthly news [1]. Appiano moved on. The paper came back in January 2011 with a small victory to report. At City Hall, Visitacion Valley had been named "Comeback Neighborhood of the Year" [1]. That same month, planning alliance chair Fran Martin was worrying aloud about what the governor's threat to abolish redevelopment could mean for the old Schlage site [2].

title: The gardener who carved a jungle
place: Cayuga Playground, Cayuga Avenue at Naglee Avenue
hook: Sent to fix a bleak park under the BART tracks, a city gardener filled it with totem poles of Barry Bonds, Herb Caen, Moses and a wooden snake.
story: Cayuga Playground is a narrow park squeezed between I-280, Alemany Boulevard and the elevated BART tracks. One branch of Islais Creek begins somewhere beneath it [1]. In 1986 the Recreation and Park Department sent gardener Demetrios Braceros to change the feel of the place, which then had a big playing field, a playground and some paths [1]. He turned it into a thick garden of trails and themed beds, filled with hundreds of carved figures and totem poles made mostly from wood he found on site, including fallen cypress trees [1]. His subjects included Barry Bonds and the columnist Herb Caen. A 'Garden of Eden' path had Moses at the burning bush and Adam and Eve under an apple tree with a big wooden snake [1]. For an elevated patio he brought a huge trunk all the way from the Presidio [1]. In 2002 a Chronicle writer found him working in a metal shipping container converted into a wood shop. He had carved handrails and steps into the slippery mud, and he had toned down some of the religious messages after his supervisors asked him to [2]. "He's turned this derelict park into a little paradise," said the artist Ann Chamberlain [2].

title: 'Valley Vision' on the library wall
place: 'Valley Vision' mural, Desmond Street side of 37–45 Leland Avenue (former branch library)
hook: In 1987 the neighbourhood shut Desmond Street to celebrate a mural that it had helped design, sketch by sketch, in the library window.
story: The 1933 building at Leland Avenue and Desmond Street long housed the valley's branch library [1]. In the summer of 1987 muralist Jo Tucker began painting its Desmond Street wall. Two summer youth workers and an adult volunteer helped her [2][4]. Tucker was born in Barberton, Ohio, and worked as a community organiser in Boston. In San Francisco she joined a project protesting the air war in Vietnam; people there were painting a mural about the war, and that set her course [3]. 'Murals have to do with community,' she said. For the library wall she held meetings with staff and residents, then posted her sketches in the library window and changed them based on what people said. An airplane was added, and a cane went into one man's hand to raise awareness of disability. Community gardens were added when their land leases became an issue [3][4]. The finished 'Valley Vision' shows the valley's plants, animals, people, industries, shops and churches from the 1770s onward, up to the era when Geneva Towers dominated the skyline [4]. On November 7, 1987, Desmond Street was closed for a celebration planned by Anne Kaartunen, who had helped Tucker win grants [3][4]. By then Tucker had also led pupils in painting a mural of valley history in the Visitacion Valley Elementary schoolyard [2].

title: A pastor for the valley's newcomers
place: Visitacion Chinese Baptist Church, 8 Desmond Street
hook: A young seminary graduate arrived to serve Chinese immigrants. Within a decade his summer camp was packed and families were pooling money to buy houses.
story: In the late 1980s and 1990s, Chinese immigrants began settling in Visitacion Valley, drawn by cheaper housing, good weather and an existing Asian community [1]. Between 1980 and 1990 the valley's Asian population rose 74 percent, from 4,551 to 7,922 [1]. The Baptist ministry noticed the change. Around 1987 it sent the Rev. Samson Wong, a young seminary graduate, to found the Visitacion Chinese Baptist Church [1]. By 2002 a neighbourhood directory listed the church at 8 Desmond Street, just off Leland Avenue [2]. In 1998 a gaggle of immigrant children jammed its summer day camp each day [1]. Wong estimated that about half the valley's immigrants owned their homes. 'They live two or three families together until they save enough money,' he said. 'Then they buy two houses, one for each family' [1]. The Li family from Guangzhou, living on Melra Street with an aunt, was saving for a home of its own. He was a cook and she worked in a sewing factory, each for under $6 an hour. 'We don't have any big goals for ourselves,' Guo Feng Li said. 'Our hope is for the children' [1]. The change also brought tension with longtime Black residents, which community groups were working to ease [1].

title: Bono Spray-Paints the Concrete Dog
place: Vaillancourt Fountain, Embarcadero Plaza
hook: In 1987 the world's biggest rock star climbed San Francisco's most hated fountain with a spray can, and the sculptor cheered him on.
story: Armand Vaillancourt's fountain opened in 1971 at the foot of Market Street as a deliberately harsh partner to the double-decker Embarcadero Freeway that loomed beside it [1]. Chronicle critic Allan Temko likened its clattering forms to "technological excrescences ... deposited by a giant concrete dog with square intestines" [2]. On November 11, 1987, U2 played a free concert in the plaza during its Joshua Tree tour, and Bono clambered onto the fountain and spray-painted a slogan on it before about 20,000 cheering fans; the Chronicle reported the words as "Stop the Traffic, Rock and Roll", though other accounts reverse the order [3]. Mayor Dianne Feinstein condemned the stunt. Vaillancourt, the fountain's own designer, defended it as art. Bono apologised, promised to pay for the cleanup, and became the 346th person cited that year in a citywide graffiti crackdown, facing a $500 fine or a stint scrubbing Muni buses [3]. KGO radio said its callers split roughly 50-50, young against old [3]. The freeway the fountain was built to answer came down in 1991. In April 2026 crews began dismantling the fountain itself, labelling the pieces so it could, in theory, be reassembled one day [4].

title: From 90-cent driver to Muni's chief
place: Curtis E. Green Light Rail Center, Geneva and San Jose avenues
hook: Muni's main rail yard is named for a Louisiana-born Marine who started as a bus driver and became the first Black head of a major US transit system.
story: Curtis E. Green was born in Louisiana in 1923 and served as a Marine sergeant in the Second World War. In 1945 he joined Muni as a bus driver earning 90 cents an hour [1][2]. He spent nearly 20 years behind the wheel, won 11 safe-driving awards and once saved a passenger from a would-be rapist [1]. He then rose through the ranks. In 1973 he became deputy general manager, and in 1974 he got the top job after a bitter fight inside the Public Utilities Commission [1]. He was the first African American to head a major US transit system [1][2]. He took over a Muni that was short of money and neglected. In 1975 he had drivers hand out buttons reading "Muni Loves You" [1]. In 1978 he sold Supervisor Harvey Milk, a friend, a Fast Pass [2]. Under Green, the Muni Metro subway opened and the budget grew from $40 million to $154 million [2]. He retired in 1982, and five years later Muni named its main rail base, beside Balboa Park station, the Curtis E. Green Light Rail Center [1][2]. His granddaughter Denise later drove trains out of the yard that bears his name [2].

title: Taking the peaks back from motorbikes
place: Footpaths to the summit of the north peak, Twin Peaks Natural Area
hook: Off-road motorcycles once tore up Twin Peaks roller-coaster-style. In the late 1980s timber barriers, new footpaths and volunteers with picks began to heal the hills.
story: Twin Peaks gives a rare idea of how San Francisco's hills looked before grazing and building: coastal scrub and grassland of coyote brush, lizard tail, pearly everlasting and lupine, with brush rabbits and coyotes [1]. It is also the "type locality", the place the defining specimens came from, for the endangered Mission blue butterfly and for Phacelia californica, a low perennial that native bees love [2]. Writer and landscape consultant Geoffrey Coffey recalled in 2004 that a quarter-century earlier the natural area was faring badly under cars and hikers "and yes, even off-road motorcycles taking those twin peaks roller-coaster-style", while invasive weeds moved in [2]. In the late 1980s the city enlisted the San Francisco Conservation Corps to build meandering footpaths to each summit, with railroad ties for steps, and massive timber barriers at the trailheads to stop the motorbikes. Local volunteers with shovels and picks erased the rutted tracks, pulled broom, cotoneaster and ice plant, and planted bunchgrass, monkeyflower, Douglas iris, silver lupine and coast buckwheat [2]. The city's Natural Areas Program took over the care. By 2004, Coffey wrote, it faced "violent opposition" from a group of dog owners; one letter to the Chronicle compared the native plant movement to Nazi Germany [2].

title: The Battleship Versus the Artists
place: Hunters Point Shipyard artist studios
hook: In 1987 the Navy wanted Hunters Point back for the battleship Missouri. In its way stood hundreds of artists, cabinetmakers and a mushroom farmer in old barracks.
story: Jacques Terzian first worked at Hunters Point at age 20, repairing warships in World War II [2]. Decades later he was a sculptor and designer being pushed out of the warehouse district that became Levi's Plaza, and he spotted a sign advertising space at the decommissioned shipyard [2]. The Navy had begun leasing the base in 1976, and Terzian sublet a building, at first for storage [2]. From 1983, with his children's help, he began rebuilding gutted barracks. He spent the better part of a year on his back reinstalling pipes. He left out a pressure-relief valve, so the building shook every time a toilet flushed [2]. By 1984 he had made about 300 studios [1]. People kept asking him "What is the point?", so he called it The Point [2]. He also hosted one of the first recorded open-studio events [1]. Then Mayor Dianne Feinstein backed plans to base the battleship USS Missouri there [2]. In 1987 the Los Angeles Times described the "ragtag army of artists, metal workers, cabinet makers" and one mushroom farmer resisting eviction. Terzian could recall only one "security breach": two artists embracing under the stars on an off-limits dock [3]. The artists stayed. Terzian died in 2016 at 94 [1].

title: The Day Walkers Flattened the Golden Gate
place: South end of the Golden Gate Bridge, by the Round House
hook: So many people crowded onto the bridge for its 50th birthday that its arched roadway sagged flat, and the mayor threw a borrowed $800 fedora into the bay.
story: For the bridge's 50th anniversary on 24 May 1987, organisers planned 'Bridgewalk '87' to recreate the Pedestrian Day of 1937. They expected a smaller crowd than the 200,000 who had walked across on opening day, because this time the roadway was open to walkers for only four hours [1]. Instead about 300,000 people poured onto the span, among them cyclists, roller skaters and a group dressed as a centipede. Another 400,000 to 500,000 packed every viewpoint nearby [1]. The weight of the crowd flattened the bridge's normally arched roadbed. District engineer Daniel Mohn later ran the numbers and confirmed the bridge had not been overstressed [1][2]. At mid-span, Mayor Dianne Feinstein was meant to throw a wreath into the water for the 11 men who died building the bridge. The wreath was stuck somewhere in the crush, so she grabbed Assembly Speaker Willie Brown's $800 fedora and sent it spinning out to sea like a Frisbee [1]. Tolls were suspended for the day. The celebrations also left something lasting near the Round House: two commemorative gardens and a walkway of personalised bricks, with 7,416 in place by March 1988 [1].

title: The Pope and Brendan, age four

hook: A block away, 2,000 protesters chanted 'Shame!' Inside, the Pope bent down to hug a four-year-old in a tiny blue suit.
story: On September 17, 1987, Pope John Paul II came to Mission Dolores Basilica. Among the congregation were people with AIDS and AIDS-related complex. The Chronicle counted 100 and the Los Angeles Times 62, along with their loved ones, some of them gay partners [1][2]. A block away, behind police barricades, about 2,000 demonstrators shouted 'Shame, shame, shame' and 'Pope go home!' The Chronicle called it the largest protest of his American tour [2]. Inside, the Pope walked slowly up the aisle and stopped to hold Brendan O'Rourke. The four-year-old had caught the virus from a blood transfusion after being born three months early. His father held him, and he wore a tiny blue suit [1]. 'God loves you all, without distinction, without limit,' the Pope said [1][2]. Afterwards Brendan's mother, Elaine, said she hoped the embrace would ease public hysteria about contact with people with AIDS [1]. Dignity, the gay Catholic group, called the visit a 'meaningless pat on the head.' Fred Powell, a 52-year-old gay man with AIDS, said: 'I will see God soon enough. But right now, the Pope will do' [1].

title: The city sues an all-male club
place: Olympic Club Lakeside clubhouse, 599 Skyline Boulevard
hook: Part of the Olympic Club's famous golf course sat on city land. San Francisco used that lease to force the doors open to women.
story: The Olympic Club's golf courses by Lake Merced include 17 acres leased from the City of San Francisco [1]. In 1987 the city sued the all-male club, demanding that it admit women and minorities or give up its lease of that city-owned land at its Lakeside course [1]. In November 1987 the city also adopted an ordinance barring discrimination against women and minorities by clubs with more than 400 members that served regular meals and accepted dues from members and expenses from nonmembers. In 1988 City Attorney Louise Renne ordered her staff to prepare a sex discrimination suit against the 128-year-old club under it, the ordinance's first legal test. She also asked the state Department of Alcoholic Beverage Control whether the club's liquor license could be revoked [1]. Club officials argued that minor changes to their dues policies exempted them [1]. In December 1990 the club, with 6,000 members, tentatively settled. It agreed to admit women within 60 days, adopt a policy of non-discrimination against women and minorities, and keep an existing court injunction against discrimination in place [2]. In exchange the city dropped the suit and gave the club an option to buy the 17 acres, part of which holds three holes of its championship course [2].

title: The drag queen who became an abbot
place: Hartford Street Zen Center, 57 Hartford St
hook: Tommy Dee was billed as 'the boy who looks like the girl next door.' Decades later, as Issan Dorsey, he opened a Zen hospice for men dying of AIDS.
story: Tommy Dorsey Jr. was thrown out of the Navy for a relationship with another sailor. He became a drag star on the road, billed as 'Tommy Dee, the boy who looks like the girl next door' [1]. By the mid-1960s years of hard drugs had put his life in danger. The temple's own history says that after watching Allen Ginsberg calm a street fight with a Zen chant, he went to Shunryu Suzuki's temple in Japantown [2]. By 1980 he was a Zen priest and helped found a Gay Buddhist Club. It soon moved to a house on Hartford Street, and a zendo opened in its basement on December 8, 1981 [2]. In 1987 the group opened the Maitri Hospice for people dying of AIDS. It is described as the first Buddhist hospice of its kind in the United States [2]. It later leased the building next door and offered nine beds [2][3]. Dorsey became abbot in 1989 under the name Issan, 'One Mountain' [1]. He died of AIDS on September 6, 1990. Some of his ashes lie under a granite boulder from Tassajara in the temple garden [2].

title: Where the AIDS Quilt was sewn
place: NAMES Project workshop, 2362 Market St
hook: A mother took a bus from West Virginia rather than mail her son's quilt panel. She had to see the place where his memory would live.
story: In November 1985 Cleve Jones was planning the yearly march for Harvey Milk and George Moscone when he learned that more than 1,000 San Franciscans had died of AIDS. He asked marchers to write the names of the dead on placards. Taped to the wall of a federal building, the placards looked to him like a patchwork quilt [1]. In 1986 he made the first panel, for his friend Marvin Feldman. In June 1987 a small group gathered in a storefront at 2362 Market Street, a former silent-movie house, to start the NAMES Project [2]. Volunteers worked at donated sewing machines on three-by-six-foot panels [1]. There were 40 panels at that June's Freedom Day parade. On October 11, 1987, there were 1,920 on the National Mall, and half a million people came to see them [2]. The storefront became an unofficial community centre where people grieved and sometimes learned that a friend had died. One often-told story is of a mother who came by bus from West Virginia with a panel she had made in secret for her son. She said she 'couldn't just put her son in an envelope' [2]. The Quilt left for Atlanta in 2001 [1][2].

title: A home for trans women on Post Street
place: Diva's (formerly Motherlode), 1081 Post St
hook: Polk Gulch's queens once owned the sidewalks in evening gowns and feather boas. One multi-storey club at Post and Larkin kept a stage for them for decades.
story:
As the Castro drew gay men away in the 1970s, and BART construction pushed sex work off Market Street, Polk Street became home to growing numbers of young male hustlers and transgender women [1]. Regina McQueen remembered the mid-1970s scene: one side of the street men "posing," the other "women dressed in evening gowns with feather boas and big hair and lots of make-up" [1]. Historian Joey Plaster describes Polk in later decades as "a home, refuge, and family" for queer runaway youth, immigrants and, increasingly in the 1990s, lower-income trans women [1][2].

At 1081 Post Street, a block off Polk, a bar called the Motherlode opened in 1988. A decade later it became Diva's, and together the two have served as a gathering place and performance venue for trans women since the 1980s [3]. The building stacked a stage on the ground floor, a dance floor on the third and a lounge at the top [3]. As Polk's other queer bars closed during the 2000s gentrification, Plaster notes, the low-income establishments that had formed the backbone of the community were largely replaced [2], and this address outlasted many of them.

title: Coming Home in the Western Addition
place: Western Addition Cultural Center, 762 Fulton Street
hook: At the height of the AIDS crisis, Black gay and lesbian San Franciscans organised in Western Addition living rooms and shared Thanksgiving dinners.
story: On May 16, 1988, Bay Area Black Lesbians and Gays held an organisational kickoff at the Western Addition Cultural Center, 762 Fulton Street. That month the group had voted to become a chapter of the National Coalition of Black Lesbians and Gays again [1]. Its San Francisco meetings took place in members' homes, including Mary Midgett's at 437 Webster Street and the AIDS activist Reggie Williams's at 630 Fillmore Street. Midgett also opened her home for a 1988 holiday party and a Thanksgiving dinner. The city's LGBTQ context statement describes these as important gatherings for people who could not always join their biological families [1]. Williams, born in Cincinnati, had settled in San Francisco in the early 1980s. He saw that AIDS prevention was not reaching Black gay and bisexual men and called a meeting that led to the AIDS task force of Black and White Men Together. That task force grew into the National Task Force on AIDS Prevention, which he ran until 1994 [2]. "My personal struggle with AIDS has forced me to demand respect and dignity from my people," he said. "Black, gay men need to be able to come home" [2]. He died in Amsterdam on February 7, 1999, aged 47 [2].

title: Piroshki on Balboa Since 1953
place: Cinderella Bakery & Cafe, 436 Balboa Street
hook: Two Russian women were running a Balboa Street bakery. Then a newcomer from the Soviet Union arrived, and they handed him the recipes.
story: Cinderella Russian Bakery, between Fifth and Sixth avenues on Balboa, has been making piroshki since 1953 [1]. It belongs to a long Russian story in the Richmond. FoundSF notes that an older Russian community once lived around Clement Street and then faded as families moved to the suburbs or assimilated [2]. A new wave followed the economic collapse of the Soviet Union, including many Russian Jews escaping state-sponsored anti-Semitism, and Russian shops, restaurants and companies spread along Geary [2]. Nearby, the Russian Orthodox Christ the Saviour Church at 12th Avenue and Anza saw enrolment in its Russian-language classes jump [2]. Mike Fishman arrived from the Soviet Union in 1988 and soon had the chance to take over Cinderella from the two Russian women who had run it [1]. They trained him and passed on their recipes [1]. In 2008 Fishman and his wife became sole owners, turned the 'dated diner' into a cosier cafe, expanded the kitchen and added outdoor tables and a parklet [1]. The menu still leans on recipes handed down through generations: piroshki, Siberian pelmeni and dark, chewy rye [1].

title: Seventy thousand voices under Sylvester's window
place: Collingwood Street, near 18th
hook: Too sick to leave his Castro flat, the 'Mighty Real' disco star heard the whole street fair chanting his name through his bedroom window.
story: Sylvester sang in a soaring falsetto and wore glitter and platform shoes. That set him apart from the Castro's crowd of look-alike moustached 'clones', and he said so [1][2]. His biographer Joshua Gamson called him the neighbourhood's 'undisputed First Lady.' He was a regular at the Elephant Walk bar and a friend of Harvey Milk [1]. On the night after the White Night riot in 1979, he sang 'You Make Me Feel (Mighty Real)' at Milk's birthday party in the street [2]. His partner Rick Cranmer died of AIDS in 1987. Sylvester, by then ill himself, moved into an apartment on Collingwood Street [1]. In June 1988 he rode in the Freedom Day parade in a wheelchair in front of the People with AIDS banner. That October's Castro Street Fair was named 'A Tribute to Sylvester' [1]. The city's LGBTQ history puts the crowd at 70,000 and dates the tribute to late 1989. That can't be right, because Sylvester died on December 16, 1988 [1][2]. He was too weak to come down, but the chants of 'We love you, Sylvester!' reached his bedroom [1][2]. He left his future royalties to AIDS charities [1].

title: Sun Ra leads a parade down Eleventh
place: Slim's, 333 Eleventh Street
hook: Boz Scaggs wanted to open the R&B club of his dreams. Six weeks after it opened, Sun Ra marched the whole crowd out the door and down the street.
story: Rock star Boz Scaggs wanted to open the R&B nightclub of his dreams. With some high-powered partners he took over a vacant South of Market restaurant called the Warehouse, threw a New Year's Eve party there, and then closed it for nine months of remodeling [1]. Slim's opened on September 16, 1988, with Katie Webster, Anson Funderburgh, Delbert McClinton and "Presidio Slim", who was Scaggs himself [1]. On October 30, Sun Ra and his Arkestra led the entire crowd on a Halloween parade out of the club and down Eleventh Street [1]. That Christmas Eve the Oakland Interfaith Gospel Choir sang the first of what became yearly concerts there [1]. The club kept a house band at first, but soon it was booking almost everything. When the power on Eleventh Street failed during a 1991 show, Mary Chapin Carpenter handed her keyboard player an accordion and the band played on from the bar. Radiohead sold out its first San Francisco show here in 1993, the year Green Day paid to replace the stage carpets it had ruined [1]. Slim's closed for good in March 2020. Scaggs said the decision had been made the year before, long before the pandemic shut the club: "Slim's did what it was here to do" [2].

title: The neighbours who took UCSF to court
place: Former UCSF Laurel Heights campus, Presidio Avenue side of 3333 California Street
hook: When UCSF planned labs using carcinogens and radioactive materials in the old Fireman's Fund building, Laurel Heights neighbours sued, and took the fight to the state Supreme Court.
story:
After the University of California bought the former Fireman's Fund building in 1985, UCSF planned to move its School of Pharmacy's basic science research units there [1]. The university's environmental impact report admitted that these labs handled possibly toxic chemicals, possible carcinogens and radioactive substances, and would vent some substances into the outside air [1].

The Laurel Heights Improvement Association went to court. The main question, the California Supreme Court said, was "whether scientific research using toxic chemicals, carcinogens, and radioactive materials is too high-risk to be conducted in a residential neighborhood" [1]. While the case went on, the court barred the Regents from bringing radioactive materials into the building [1].

On 1 December 1988 the court sided with the neighbours on the key points. UCSF could use only 100,000 square feet at first, because Caltrans leased half the building, and the report had not analysed the university's reasonably foreseeable use of the rest. An EIR, the court held, must study future expansion that is "a reasonably foreseeable consequence" of a project, and must discuss real alternatives [1]. Still, UCSF was allowed to keep its existing labs running while it prepared a new report [1]. Into the 1990s, neighbours were still bitterly contesting UC's plans for a biomedical research laboratory at the site [2].

title: When Rain Sent Sewage to the Beaches
place: Sea Cliff Avenue at 25th Avenue, above Baker Beach
hook: Under Sea Cliff's elegant streets ran sewers that overflowed in heavy rain. By one 1988 count, sewage reached nearby beaches as many as 83 times a year.
story: San Francisco's sewers are a combined system: household sewage and street runoff share the same pipes [2]. Pumping stations boosted the flow toward the main sewers, and the Department of Public Works ran two here: Sea Cliff No. 1 at Phelan (China) Beach and Sea Cliff No. 2, listed at 100 Sea Cliff Avenue [1]. Excess storm flow, the department explained, was diverted to the bay or ocean through outfalls [1]. In its report for the year ending June 1955, the department noted that Sea Cliff No. 1 had been out of service from May 8 to May 18. It took emergency work "to prevent discharge of raw sewage to Phelan Beach" [1]. In 1988 the Richmond ReView reported that winter rains sent untreated sewage and runoff onto Baker Beach, China Beach and the Lincoln Park shoreline as many as 83 times a year [2]. A 1992 federal assessment put the average at 40 overflows a year through four outfalls. It cited a state cease-and-desist order to cut them to eight a year by March 1996 [3]. The fix was the Richmond Transport, a 10,200-foot tunnel 14 feet across, which would carry the overflow to the Oceanside plant. The plan also called for eliminating all overflows at Baker Beach and demolishing its outfall [3].

title: "I Just Couldn't Leave"
place: Beach and Divisadero Streets (3701 Divisadero)
hook: As fire spread through a collapsed Marina apartment house after the 1989 quake, one firefighter refused to leave the trapped woman he had found.
story: At 5:04 p.m. on October 17, 1989, the Loma Prieta earthquake turned the Marina's fill to liquid. Two four-storey apartment buildings on opposite corners, 3701 Divisadero and 2090 Beach, collapsed and pitched over Beach Street [1]. Neighbours were first on the scene and heard voices calling for help. Captain Robert Jabs of Truck 16 went into 3701 Divisadero with firefighters and volunteers. Thomas Bailon and John Reed cut through a floor and found a man and a woman trapped below [1]. Then a strong aftershock hit, there was an explosion, and fire rolled through the wreck. The man crawled out and Jabs helped carry him across a sagging roof. Heat and smoke drove the crews back before they could reach the woman [1]. The fire's heat set 2090 Beach alight too [1]. Inside it, firefighter Jerry Shannon found another trapped woman who begged him not to go. He stayed and comforted her while others passed tools in, and colleagues hosed down the fires around them to keep him cool [2]. 'After I saw her, I just couldn't leave,' he said. After hours of work between aftershocks, he freed her [2]. Sixty Marina buildings were later destroyed [3].

title: A forest grows in Cohen Alley
place: Tenderloin National Forest, Cohen Place off Ellis St
hook: An alley full of garbage and syringes became trees, murals, a clay bread oven and a gallery cabin, rented from the city for a dollar.
story: In 1989 Darryl Smith of the Luggage Store, an artists' collective, started paying attention to the dead-end alley beside his building off Ellis Street. He remembered 'garbage…rotting out here, human excrement, syringes' [1]. He and co-director Laurie Lazer saw a place where 'fertile things could happen' [1][2]. Over the next decade they cleaned it, planted trees, vegetables, herbs and flowers, and commissioned murals on every wall [2]. In 2000 they negotiated a lease that closed the alley to traffic for a symbolic $1. The gallery says $1 a year, while a FoundSF essay says $1 a month [1][2]. Artist Kevin Leeper built a sculptured gate. A small green-roofed structure, a wood-fired clay oven and new lighting followed [2]. The alley, officially Cohen Place and about 23 feet wide by 136 feet deep, was renamed the Tenderloin National Forest in May 2009 [2]. The name came from Marco Crescenti, a San Francisco State student [2]. It has hosted concerts, bread-baking and free clothing repair in a neighbourhood with almost no green space [1].

title: Flying buttresses for an earthquake city
place: St. Dominic's Church, 2390 Bush Street
hook: Loma Prieta knocked the lantern off St. Dominic's tower. The fix came straight out of the Middle Ages.
story: After 1906 it took St. Dominic's parish more than twenty years to build a permanent home: a huge Gothic church by Beezer Brothers, dedicated on February 19, 1928, before a crowd of more than 2,500 [1]. Its tower was topped by a forty-foot octagonal "lantern" [1]. Sixty-one years later, on October 17, 1989, the Loma Prieta earthquake sent chunks of the upper tower crashing into the street [1]. Much of the painted decoration on the ceiling beams fell and was lost [2]. It wasn't certain the church would be saved. The damaged St. Rose High School building next door was demolished in what Woody LaBounty describes as an apparent compromise between the archdiocese and the city [1]. Pieces of the tower rubble were even auctioned to raise money [1]. The solution was medieval: nine flying buttresses to brace the walls, plus a rebuilt tower. The $6.6 million needed was raised by June 1991, and construction finished in July 1992 [2]. On August 1, 1992, the archbishop rededicated the church, with its new buttresses and shorter tower [1].

title: Indiana Jones flies out of Berlin
place: Administration Building (Building One), 1 Avenue of the Palms
hook: In 'The Last Crusade', Indy and his father escape Nazi Berlin through an airport draped in swastikas. The airport was Treasure Island's Building One.
story:
Building One was put up in 1938 as the terminal for an airport that was never built. It is one of the few Art Moderne buildings in San Francisco [1]. Half a century later, Hollywood cast it as exactly what it was designed to be: a 1930s air terminal.

In 'Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade' (1989), it is the Berlin airport where Indy and his father buy tickets for the zeppelin [2]. The building was still on an active Navy base, and the Nazi flags were added in post-production. 'That's the only way they would let them shoot it,' the Navy's base closure manager, Patricia McFadden, told SFGATE [2]. The city would not allow Nazi banners on the building [3].

After the base closed in 1997, the island's hangars became sound stages for films and shows such as The Matrix, The Parent Trap and Nash Bridges [3][4]. Robin Williams, who did not want to travel away from San Francisco to film, made several movies here, including 'Flubber' and 'Patch Adams' [2]. Building One also played a hotel in 'The Parent Trap' and a hospital in Netflix's 'The OA'. The security desk built for that show still stands in the lobby [2].

title: Lakeview's Hardcore Rap Pioneers
place: Randolph Street, Ocean View ("Lakeview")
hook: A young Lakeview rapper sold 1,000 tapes in a year and decided it beat "selling any kind of crack, ever."
story: In the late 1980s and 1990s Ocean View, known to many locals as "Lakeview", produced some of San Francisco's earliest hardcore rap. I.M.P., the Ill Mannered Posse, began in 1989 when DJ-producers Rob V and Stingy formed a group and brought in Rob V's cousin, the gravel-voiced rapper Cougnut [1]. Their 1989 track "Scandlous" is counted among the city's earliest rap hits. Their album Back in the Days came out in 1993 on Oakland's In-A-Minute Records, with cameos from local rappers including Cellski [1]. Cellski was visiting producer Al Eaton's studio in 1987 and 1988, when he was 13 [2]. In 1992 he sold 1,000 tapes and made $6,000: "this is better than selling any kind of crack, ever" [2]. He spoke frankly about how the drug trade cost families their homes, and how his once all-Black neighbourhood became mostly Asian [2]. Cougnut died in a car crash in 2001 [1]. Cellski kept going. In 2022 he launched Big Mafi Burger from his grandmother's recipe, with a sauce he learned at Beep's, "in Lakeview, where I grew up" [3].

title: The Fireboat That Came In at Low Tide
place: Marina Yacht Harbor, foot of Divisadero Street
hook: With the Marina's hydrants dry and a fire moving block to block, the city's only fireboat had to squeeze into a harbour almost too shallow to float it.
story: The night of the 1989 earthquake, the Marina's hydrants failed. Breaks in the high-pressure system south of Market had drained its supply, and at low tide engines could not draw water straight from the bay [1]. At 6:16 p.m. Battalion Chief Shannon called in the fireboat Phoenix from Pier 22½ [2]. Its pilot was Arvid Havneras. He was born in Norway, had handled Army tugboats and worked tugs on the Mekong River during the Vietnam War, and had joined the Fire Department in 1984 [3]. At 6:49 p.m. commanders radioed that the tide was so low the boat might not have enough water to berth in the yacht harbour [2]. Havneras brought the 89-foot boat in right beside a luxury yacht. 'He did a beautiful job of coming in there where no boat its size had ever been before,' an engineer recalled [3]. By 7 p.m. it was in place [2]. Firefighters and volunteers dragged hose from the boat to Beach and Divisadero, where seven buildings were burning [2]. The Phoenix pumped all night [3]. Former mayor Dianne Feinstein wrote that it 'unquestionably saved the Marina from a greater catastrophe' [3].

title: The Freeway That Split Hayes Valley
place: Octavia Street between Oak and Fell (former Central Freeway ramps)
hook: The 1989 quake cracked a double-decker freeway over Hayes Valley. It took ten years and four ballot measures before the city finally agreed to tear it down.
story: The double-deck Central Freeway opened in 1959. It connected western San Francisco to downtown but split Hayes Valley apart, bringing blight and crime to the blocks beneath it [3]. "The freeway was the border, and you didn't want to go under it," remembered longtime resident Madeline Behrens-Brigham. "We were called 'the bad block'... You couldn't get a pizza, you couldn't get a taxi; the police wouldn't even come here" [1]. The Loma Prieta earthquake of October 17, 1989 damaged the freeway, and key ramps had to be demolished [1][2]. What came next was a long political fight. "Half the city wanted the freeway restored, and half wanted it torn down," said a Caltrans spokesman, who kept a chunk of the old freeway in a potted plant in his office [2]. In 1997 voters approved Proposition H to rebuild the freeway to Fell Street. In 1998 Proposition E, organised by activists including Robin Levitt, repealed it in favour of a boulevard. In 1999 voters passed Proposition I, which funded the Octavia Boulevard plan, and rejected Proposition J, a compromise with elevated ramps [1]. The ramps to Fell, Oak, Franklin and Gough came down in stages, the last in 2003 [2]. "When the freeway disappeared, so did a lot of the problems," Levitt said [2].

title: The Lutherans who stayed on the hill
place: St. Mark's Lutheran Church, 1135 O'Farrell Street at Franklin
hook: Redevelopment bulldozed the Victorians around it and a new cathedral dwarfed it. Then the 1989 quake cracked the church. It took fifteen years to fix.
story: St. Mark's has stood at O'Farrell and Franklin since 1895 [1]. NoeHill calls it the oldest Lutheran church in the West [2]. It survived 1906 when buildings a block away on Van Ness were dynamited [1][2]. Then came the 1960s. Redevelopment bulldozed hundreds of Western Addition Victorians, and the round Carillon Tower apartments rose next door [2]. A 1968 photograph shows the little church almost lost amid construction on Cathedral Hill, including the huge new St. Mary's, which locals nicknamed the 'Maytag' [1]. The congregation built too. In 1964 it began Martin Luther Tower, affordable housing for low-income people over 65 [1]. The 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake badly damaged the church. According to its pastor, it took 15 years of fundraising, engineering and architecture to retrofit it and restore the interior [1]. In June 2005 the congregation moved to the Urban Life Center auditorium next door to worship, and the church reopened in December 2006 [1]. Today St. Mark's calls itself a Reconciling in Christ and Sanctuary congregation, and it shelters 50 to 60 unhoused people for three weeks each winter [1].

title: The Man in the Window on Church Street
place: 1357 Church Street, near Clipper
hook: For 18 years a retired teacher taped quotations in his window beside the J-Church stop. One sign helped a young couple decide to marry.
story:
Dean Bistline was born in Iowa in 1921. He served in the Coast Guard, then worked as a teacher and principal and later as a speechwriter in Washington. In 1989 he and his wife Susan moved into the bottom flat of his daughter's house at 1357 Church Street, beside a J-Church stop [2]. Six weeks later came the Loma Prieta earthquake, and soon after, the first Gulf War. He taped a sign to the garage: "I love my country, I fear my government." [1]

One sign grew into three. The Bistlines clipped quotations from Will Rogers, Joan Didion, Tom Stoppard and even Donald Trump and Nicole Kidman, and changed them about once a month. Eventually Susan claimed alternate months [1]. After they posted "Leap, and the net will appear," a young couple knocked with flowers. The line had helped them decide to marry. A Latina woman came by every day to copy the signs down and practise her English [1]. When Bistline died in April 2007, the last sign read, "The Man in the Window says goodbye." Within hours a memorial of orchids, lilies and notes grew on the doorstep. One came from a little girl he used to give Tootsie Rolls: "Dear Dean, I hope your second life is great." [2]

title: The car barn Muni wanted to demolish
place: Geneva Car Barn and Powerhouse, 2301 San Jose Avenue at Geneva Avenue
hook: Cracked by two earthquakes and red-tagged in 1989, a 1901 streetcar office with a turret and a 'door to nowhere' was nearly torn down for parking.
story: The red-brick building with a round corner turret at Geneva and San Jose avenues went up in 1901 as offices for the San Francisco and San Mateo Electric Railway, one of the city's first electric streetcar lines. It was designed by James and Merritt Reid, the architects of the Fairmont Hotel [1]. A second-floor 'door to nowhere' opens onto a sheer drop. It survives from the 1917 streetcar strike, when strikebreakers used a temporary stairway to sneak down to the cars [1]. Muni took over the complex in the 1944 merger. From 1957 until the late 1970s its yard was Muni's only streetcar facility [2]. The yard has kept streetcars since 1900, and in 2011 it was renamed for transit advocate Cameron Beach [4]. The 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake damaged the office and its powerhouse, and Muni abandoned them. It wanted to tear them down for parking, but neighbours worked with Mayor Willie Brown to save them [2][3]. The Recreation and Park Department bought the buildings in 2004 [2]. In March 2018 officials broke ground on a $14 million powerhouse renovation. "We were the forgotten community," said longtime advocate Linda D'Avirro [3].

title: Turntables in a Moscow Street Garage
place: Moscow Street, where DJ Qbert grew up and the Invisibl Skratch Piklz got their start
hook: A kid from Moscow Street met his rival in a school cafeteria DJ battle. Their crew got so good the world championship asked them to stop entering.
story: Richard Quitevis was born in 1969 to parents from the Philippines and grew up on Moscow Street in the Excelsior. He went to Luther Burbank Middle School and graduated from Balboa High School in 1987 [2]. He had a Fisher-Price turntable as a toddler and began playing with records at 15. In a DJ battle in the Balboa cafeteria he met Mix Master Mike, and the two became lifelong friends [2]. In 1989 he, Mix Master Mike and DJ Apollo formed a crew first called Shadow of the Prophet, which became the Invisibl Skratch Piklz [3]. According to the Chronicle, the Piklz got their start in a garage on Moscow Street [1]. Turntablism crews already existed, but the Piklz were the first to play as a band, layering drums, basslines and scratch solos [2]. As DJ Qbert, Quitevis won DMC world titles in 1992 and 1993, both times in teams with Mix Master Mike [2]. The Disco Mix Club eventually asked the Piklz to stop competing because they were discouraging other DJs from entering [3]. The group helped design DJ products for Vestax and Ortofon, developed the 'break record' that most turntablists now use, and played its last show on July 1, 2000, at Skratchcon 2000 in San Francisco [3].

title: Artists in Residence at the City Dump
place: Recology Artist in Residence studios, 501 Tunnel Avenue
hook: Since 1990 San Francisco has given artists a studio, a stipend and first pick of the dump. It was the first program of its kind in the United States.
story: In 1989 California's AB 939 required every city to keep at least half its waste out of landfills by 2000, and San Francisco's plan called for public education [1]. The artist Jo Hanson had an idea. She had become known in the 1970s for sweeping the littered sidewalk outside her Buchanan Street Victorian. That habit grew into a public art practice and a citywide anti-litter campaign, including a bus tour of illegal dumping sites [1]. In the late 1980s she suggested an artist residency at the dump itself. The programme began in 1990 at the transfer station on Tunnel Avenue, run with the San Francisco Sanitary Fill Company, now called Recology. It was the first of its kind in the United States [1]. Artists gather materials from the public disposal area and paint from the household hazardous waste facility. They talk with visiting schoolchildren and finish with a public exhibition [1]. It is less leisurely than it sounds. One 2006 resident described competing with front-end loaders for the best finds and admitted to nerves: "It is, after all, garbage" [2]. Hanson served on the programme's board until her death in 2007. More than 190 professional artists have now completed residencies [1].

title: Minnie and Lovie Ward Take Back the Park
place: Minnie & Lovie Ward Recreation Center, Ocean View Park
hook: Drug dealers riddled their house with bullets. The nurse and the linen-plant engineer living across from Sheridan School answered by holding meetings in the dealers' park.
story: Minnie Ward was born in Louisiana in 1935 and came to San Francisco with her parents during World War II. She became a registered nurse at the University of California hospital, and married Lovie Ward, a stationary engineer at Galland Linen, when she was 17 [1][2]. They raised their family in a modest house across the street from Sheridan Elementary. In the 1980s and '90s there was gunfire around Broad and Randolph streets every night, and one year there were 12 homicides near a single Ocean View intersection [1]. The Wards co-founded OMI Neighbors in Action and led the effort to take back Ocean View Park from dealers [2][3]. In retaliation gunmen shot up their house, at least ten times by one count. Accounts disagree on the year, giving 1990 or 1991 [1][2]. Lovie said he was "more determined than ever to fight on" [2]. The couple fought for a rebuilt Sheridan School and a new library, and helped bring in a dedicated police patrol [2]. Lovie died in 2003, months before the park's recreation centre was renamed for the couple. Minnie died in December 2005. Ground had been broken for a new centre that September, but she was too frail to attend [1][2].
