title: The Historic District That Lost 6 to 5
place: Scenic Way (Willis Polk houses at 9, 25 and 45 Scenic Way)
hook: In 1990 preservationists asked the city to protect five Sea Cliff houses, three of them by Willis Polk. The supervisors said no, by one vote.
story: The architect Willis Polk designed three houses at 9, 25 and 45 Scenic Way [2]. Wikipedia dates them to 1914 [3]. In 1989 the Landmarks Preservation Advisory Board recommended making them a new city historic district under Article 10 of the Planning Code, together with 60 26th Avenue and 79 25th Avenue. It was to be named the Willis Polk/Florence M. and John W. Procter Sea Cliff Historic District [1][4]. On November 9, 1989, the City Planning Commission voted against designation, and supporters appealed to the Board of Supervisors [1]. The hearing was postponed again and again. Finally, on March 12, 1990, the board heard appellants including Alice Carey and Ann Bloomfield, and respondents including Planning Director Dean Macris and Rowlin and Grace Perkins [1]. Supervisor Maher tried to save the district by leaving out 9 Scenic Way and 29 25th Avenue, but the amendment failed, 4–7. The board then upheld the commission 6–5 and tabled the ordinance [1]. Almost two decades later, city planners still cited the Polk houses as examples of the renowned architects who built Sea Cliff [2].

title: The Picnic That Made Postcard Row Famous
place: Postcard Row, 710-720 Steiner Street
hook: The Tanners never lived on Steiner Street. Fans still leave flowers there, and one woman brought a finished jigsaw of the houses all the way from Istanbul.
story: "Full House" premiered on ABC on September 22, 1987 [3]. For its first three seasons, the adult cast in the opening credits was not filmed in San Francisco. That changed with season four, which premiered in September 1990 [1][3]. From then on, the sequence ended with the cast having a picnic in Alamo Square, with the row of Painted Ladies behind them. The Tanners' house was never one of them, though many people think it was. The house used for the show's exterior was on Broderick Street [1][2]. The Chronicle has noted that the Painted Ladies, now a top-10 tourist attraction, once stood in a zone slated for demolition [4]. George Horsfall lives in the 1894 house at 712 Steiner. When actor Bob Saget died, fans left some 50 bouquets a day on his steps, along with cleaning gloves, because Saget's character was always cleaning [2]. Horsfall told them it wasn't the show's house, but they kept coming [2]. Strangers have married on his stoop. One woman rang his bell to give him a finished, glued jigsaw puzzle of the houses. When he asked where she had put it together, she said, "Istanbul" [2].

title: The Sea Lions Who Took K Dock
place: K Dock, Pier 39 marina
hook: A few sea lions flopped onto an empty marina dock in 1989. Within months there were hundreds, and the boat owners were the ones who had to leave.
story: In September 1989 a handful of California sea lions, six to ten of them, began hauling out on K dock at Pier 39's marina. The dock had just been refurbished and was briefly empty of boats [1]. The Loma Prieta earthquake hit on October 17, and many people still credit it for the move, but the animals were already there [1]. By mid-January 1990 there were about 150, and by March more than 400 [1]. Owners of the 11 boats on K dock had to step around animals weighing 100 to 1,000 pounds, and at least one Telegraph Hill resident phoned to complain about the noise [1]. Pier 39 issued a press release about the "invasion" on January 19, 1990, and the press dubbed the newcomers the "Boys of Blubber" [1]. On the Marine Mammal Center's advice, the boats were moved and the dock was given to the sea lions [1]. They became one of the city's great free shows. In May 2024, drawn by a feast of anchovies, some 1,100 to 1,200 crowded the docks, the most in 15 years [2]. In 2023 they narrowly lost a public vote for official city animal to the wild parrots [3].

title: 848: Anything Could Happen
place: 848 Divisadero Street
hook: In a windowless upstairs studio on Divisadero, a few dancers made a home for queer performance, trans art and safer-sex parties during the AIDS years.
story: In November 1991, Michael "Med-O" Whitson, Todd Eugene and the dancer Keith Hennessy took over a second-floor studio at 848 Divisadero from friends who were moving out, and kept its name [2]. The room was windowless, about 1,100 square feet, with movable risers that seated fewer than 50 people [2]. It held a weekly Contact Improvisation jam and hundreds of performances, concerts and exhibitions [2]. It quickly became a sex-radical space as well. The city's LGBTQ context statement says 848 organised and welcomed sex events partly as a way to address healing around AIDS [1]. "At 848 we bragged that anything could happen," Hennessy remembered. "For $100 a night we handed the keys to the space to almost anyone" [1]. Groups including Body Electric, Queen of Heaven, the Radical Faeries and Black Leather Wings held events there, as did the artist Annie Sprinkle [1]. In 1994 it showed Loren Cameron's transgender photography exhibit and David Harrison's performance "FTM" [2]. By Hennessy's count, it drew about 10,000 visitors a year in its later years. In 2005 its collective gave rise to CounterPULSE [2].

title: A Grove Planted Mid-Epidemic
place: National AIDS Memorial Grove, de Laveaga Dell
hook: While AIDS was still killing thousands, grieving San Franciscans hacked a forgotten, overgrown dell back to life. Congress later made it the nation's AIDS memorial.
story: In 1988 a small group of San Franciscans, living through a devastating epidemic with no place to grieve together, imagined a grove where people could remember "among the rhododendrons and redwoods" [1]. One of them was landscape designer Stephen Marcus, who died in 1989 and whose name was the first carved in the grove's Circle of Friends [2]. They chose the de Laveaga Dell. Park budget cuts had left it so overgrown that it was almost impossible to get into [1][2]. Volunteer architects and designers drew up a plan, and work began in September 1991 [1]. On monthly workdays hundreds of people came to plant, weed and dig, and by 1998 the project had raised $2.3 million, partly through $1,000 donations to carve a name in flagstone [2]. "Most memorials are built after the struggle is over," the founders wrote. "This battle rages on and we cannot wait" [1]. In October 1996 legislation led by Representative Nancy Pelosi and signed by President Clinton designated it the National AIDS Memorial Grove [1]. By 2011, about 2,000 names ringed the circle [3].

title: A medieval maze on Nob Hill
place: Grace Cathedral outdoor labyrinth, Taylor St side
hook: A canon walked a labyrinth taped to a conference floor, and Grace Cathedral ended up helping to spark a worldwide revival of an 800-year-old spiritual practice.
story:
In 1991 the Rev. Dr. Lauren Artress, a canon at Grace Cathedral and the first woman on its chapter, walked a temporary eleven-circuit labyrinth taped on a floor at a workshop led by psychologist Jean Houston. The idea of bringing one to Grace, she later wrote, "suddenly dominated her life" [1].

That autumn members of the cathedral community made a canvas copy of the labyrinth set into the nave floor of Chartres Cathedral around 1200. It was first unrolled at Grace for a 24-hour "Singing for Your Life" event on 30–31 December 1991, and from March 1992 opened twice a month, once in silence and once with singers [1]. Demand outgrew the canvas, so Artress commissioned a hand-spun rug woven with a 36.5-foot labyrinth, dedicated in April 1994. On 3 September 1995 an outdoor terrazzo labyrinth, open 24 hours a day, was dedicated "to all people from all traditions, or none at all" [1].

The cathedral's archivist lists the labyrinth project among the defining developments of Dean Alan Jones's era, which began in 1985 [2]. The cathedral's own history still credits Artress with introducing the labyrinth to Grace in 1991 [3].

title: Ex-Cons Who Built Their Own Waterfront
place: Delancey Street, 600 The Embarcadero
hook: The crew boss had poured concrete for a handball court at San Quentin. Three hundred former addicts and felons, none of them builders, raised a whole city block.
story: Delancey Street was founded in 1971 by John Maher, a former New York street hoodlum and child heroin addict, with criminologist Mimi Silbert, who has run it since 1985 [1]. Its rule is that residents, many of them former addicts and prisoners, rebuild their lives by running businesses themselves, without government money [2]. After buying a waterfront lot, Silbert put the residents in charge of building their new headquarters. "Literally, we had 300 and something people who knew nothing working on this building," she told Mother Jones. A resident who had poured concrete for the handball court at San Quentin became head of the concrete crew. Silbert took a test to become the contractor. When a wall came out crooked they tore it down and rebuilt it until it was right; "fixing your mistakes takes a lot of courage," she told them [2]. Finished in 1991, the four-storey, 370,000-square-foot complex fills a city block, with shops, a public restaurant and a café around a Mediterranean-style courtyard and housing for 500 [3]. Delancey says Pulitzer Prize-winning critic Allan Temko called it a "masterpiece of social design" [3].

title: Oasis and the White Stripes, cash only
place: Bottom of the Hill, 1233 17th Street at Missouri
hook: An Italian banquet room for warehouse workers became the tiny, all-ages club where Oasis, the White Stripes and Arcade Fire played before they were famous.
story:
The two-story Edwardian at 17th and Missouri streets was built in 1911, when the flats below Potrero Hill were home to Italian and working-class families employed at the shipyards and warehouses. It began as a saloon and eatery, the 17th Street Restaurant [2], and has been a restaurant, bar, soda fountain or speakeasy almost continuously since. For decades warehouse workers and merchant mariners ate lunch there. The Potrero View says it took the name Bottom of the Hill in 1964, advertising a "banquet room for all occasions, specializing in Italian foods" [1]; Wikipedia says the name came with its 1991 reopening [2].

Accounts of the buyer differ too: the View names realtor and punk fan Ana Lisa Belli in 1989, Wikipedia names Dave Benetti around 1990 [1][2]. On September 6, 1991, it held its first rock show, headlined by the Bird Killers. Booker Ramona Downey had a knack for new talent, and the club introduced fans to Oasis, Alanis Morissette, Pavement, Modest Mouse, the White Stripes, Arcade Fire and Death Cab for Cutie [1]. Once more than 700 people squeezed into a room licensed for 246, and for years fans slipped in free through an unlocked back door [1].

The owners' secret to surviving rising rents was simple: they own the building [1].

title: Plaid skirts on the 31-Balboa
place: Former Presentation High School, 2350 Turk Boulevard (now USF School of Education)
hook: For more than half a century the girls of Presentation High shared Turk Street, Muni buses and school dances with the St. Ignatius boys up the hill.
story: Presentation was a Catholic girls' high school with nineteenth-century roots. Columnist Frank Dunnigan's grandmother graduated in 1898 from its pre-1906 school on Powell Street [1]. From the 1930s the school stood at Turk Street and Masonic Avenue [2]. Presentation girls wore pleated plaid skirts, white blouses, navy sweaters and navy-on-white saddle shoes, and San Franciscans could tell Presentation's plaid from Mercy's at a glance. One 1970 graduate said the uniform made it easy to spot schoolmates on Muni and get to know them before and after school [3]. The boys noticed too. St. Ignatius students rode the 28-Nineteenth Avenue bus with "Pres girls", and many S.I. boys took the 31-Balboa home partly because it carried lots of Presentation girls to talk to before the next dance or football game [1][4]. The school closed in 1991, and the University of San Francisco acquired the site [2][3]. (One Dunnigan column puts the end in the 1980s [1].) The school building now houses USF's School of Education. The old convent on the corner, which Lincoln University used in the 1970s, is now USF's School of Professional Studies [1].

title: Streetcars finally come through the Bernal Cut
place: San Jose Avenue at Santa Rosa Avenue, Mission Terrace (J Church stop on the 1991 extension)
hook: A 1913 transit report called for streetcars through the Bernal Cut. The tracks down San Jose Avenue through Mission Terrace opened in 1991, 78 years later.
story: The J Church tracks down the middle of San Jose Avenue are fairly new, but the plan behind them is old. Bion J. Arnold's 1913 transit report recommended running streetcars through the Bernal Cut, and there were official proposals to extend the J through the cut to Geneva Avenue from at least 1925 [1]. Muni finally started building in January 1989, and the October 1989 earthquake slowed the work [1]. On August 31, 1991, after twelve days of testing, J and N streetcars began using the new line as they came and went from Muni's Metro yard at Geneva and San José avenues. The route gave cars quicker access to the yard and a way around a blocked Twin Peaks Tunnel [1]. Full-time J service to Balboa Park began on June 19, 1993 [1][2]. In Mission Terrace the stop at Santa Rosa Avenue is two narrow traffic islands in the middle of the avenue, and it is not accessible. A Muni project approved in October 2023 will lengthen and widen the platforms [2]. The M line had reached the same yard in 1980. Before that, M cars had to run on K tracks all the way to St. Francis Circle before starting their route [1].

title: The Freeway That Walled Off the Bay
place: Former Embarcadero Freeway, The Embarcadero near Howard St
hook: For three decades a double-decker freeway hid the Ferry Building. An earthquake, a stubborn mayor and a 6-5 vote brought it down, and cost him his job.
story: The Embarcadero Freeway opened in 1959: two thick decks of concrete that ran north along the waterfront from Folsom Street and ended abruptly at Broadway, cutting downtown off from the bay and leaving the Ferry Building stranded behind a wall of exhaust and noise [1]. The 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake damaged it. Caltrans engineers wanted to retrofit it, and Chinatown groups, the Chamber of Commerce, Fisherman's Wharf merchants and many Telegraph Hill residents wanted it back [2]. Even Herb Caen called Mayor Art Agnos's plans "disgraceful priorities" [2]. More than 22,000 people signed petitions to restore the freeway, and on the day of the vote Chinese merchants shut their shops and marched on City Hall [2]. Agnos commissioned traffic studies and went to Washington for demolition money; the Board of Supervisors backed him by a razor-thin 6-5 [2]. In a steady rain on February 27, 1991, demolition began. "It's a great day to take down a freeway," Agnos said [3]. Chinatown withheld its support when he ran for re-election that year, and he lost [2]. Chronicle critic John King later credited the teardown with reconnecting downtown to one of the most spectacular urban waterfronts on the planet [1].

title: The whale house on Delta Street
place: The 'whale house', 150 Delta Street at Tioga Avenue
hook: A huge blue whale swims across a hillside house on Delta Street. Behind the kitchen sheetrock, its owner found a brick room nobody can explain.
story: Neighbours call 150 Delta Street, at Tioga Avenue, 'the whale house'. A mural dominated by a huge blue whale covers the side most visible from the street. The front and south walls are painted too [1]. The owner, the artist Opal Essence, wanted to honour an earlier resident: Dr. Blanche M. Baker, a psychiatrist who, in the 1950s, publicly challenged the belief that homosexuality was a mental illness [1][2]. Sources disagree on when Baker moved in and when Essence arrived [1][2]. Essence invited artist friends, and they painted over a weekend. Among them were Mars-1, Damon Soule, Amanda Sage and the graffiti artist Estria, who painted a 'universal goddess' on the south side [1]. Heritage dates the whale, which it calls Geistal, to 1991 [2]. Graffiti artists, Essence explained, 'work fast before they can be chased away' [1]. The house holds a second puzzle. When Essence pulled down her kitchen sheetrock, she found a room of aged brick with an arched opening, a fireplace and hand-hewn beams [2][3]. Records date the house to 1934, and a 1914 map shows an empty lot. A 1949 insurance map marks it as the only brick house for blocks. Nobody yet knows why [2].

title: The white-haired coach of future big leaguers
place: Glen Canyon Park baseball field, near Elk Street and O'Shaughnessy Boulevard
hook: Thelma Williams took over a kids' team after her husband was tossed for arguing with the umpire. She coached in Glen Canyon for 40 years.
story: Baseball has been played in Glen Canyon since about 1907, when the Crocker Estate Company fenced the grounds and rented them out. The city bought the land in 1922, and thousands of youth, high school and semi-pro games followed [1]. For decades one of the canyon's fixtures was Thelma Williams. According to a 2000 tribute, her husband had been acting coach of the 7-to-9-year-olds until he was "tossed" for arguing with the umpire. Thelma took over, did so well that she kept the job, and spent 40 years teaching small children the rudiments, such as the fact that the second baseman does not stand on second base [2]. One neighbourhood child said she was like "Grandma, with her white hair and stooped-over body" [2]. She was named Coach of the Year by the Amateur Baseball Association, and some of her players reached the majors: Ken Reitz joined the St. Louis Cardinals and Juan Eichelberger the San Diego Padres, and a 1992 history adds Al Gallagher to the list [1][2]. In March 1991 the Glen Park News announced that she would be honoured on 6 April for her years of coaching, and the Glen Park baseball field dedicated to her [3]. She was 89 when she died [2].

title: Three hundred buildings, one cornice line
place: Hotel Commodore, 825 Sutter St (Lower Nob Hill Apartment Hotel District)
hook: Block after block, the south slope of Nob Hill marches in matching bay windows and fire escapes. In 1991 the whole ensemble became a National Register district.
story:
Walk Bush, Sutter or Post between roughly Stockton and Polk and the buildings seem to agree with each other: three to seven storeys, flat roofs under heavy galvanized-iron cornices, bay windows and fire escapes above shopfronts [1][2]. In 1991 the National Park Service listed the area as the Lower Nob Hill Apartment Hotel District. It has 296 contributing buildings, most built between 1906 and 1925, and only 35 non-contributors [1][2].

The nomination argues the district captures a moment of competition between the residential hotel, with its central meal service, and the new apartment building, made possible by kitchenettes, built-ins and the wall bed. It notes that William Murphy, of the Murphy bed, lived here in 1911 [1]. Its building list is a directory of vanished urban life: bachelors' hotels on Post Street, a Turkish bath, and the Mary Elizabeth Inn on Bush, built in 1913 by Lizzie Glide as a lodging for young working women [1].

NoeHill, adapting the nomination, calls the quantity and quality of these buildings "unequaled... anywhere in California except possibly in the Tenderloin," and "almost no new buildings" interrupt them [2].

title: A clubhouse for the boy who played here
place: Julius Kahn Playground, Pacific Avenue at Spruce Street (edge of the Presidio)
hook: When philanthropists Richard and Rhoda Goldman lost their son, they gave the playground where he had played as a child a new clubhouse.
story:
Julius Kahn Playground sits at Pacific Avenue and Spruce Street, on the edge of the Presidio. Its clubhouse dated from 1926 [1].

In November 1991 about 70 people stood in the cold for a groundbreaking. Richard Goldman dug the first shovel of dirt while his wife Rhoda and other family members looked on [1]. The couple, well-known philanthropists, had given $250,000 for a new clubhouse in memory of their son Richard Walter Goldman, who had died at 42. He had played at the park as a boy [2].

The new building had double the floor space of the old one, with a director's office, room for indoor games and reading, a kitchenette, fully accessible restrooms and tables for adults [1].

It opened in mid-July 1992 in front of about 200 people. Acting mayor Annemarie Conroy dedicated a plaque to Richard Walter Goldman [2]. The octagonal clubhouse had a metal roof and earth-toned stucco walls trimmed with wood. Windows near the ceiling let in natural light, and the playground director got a 360-degree view of the park. Fantasia Bakery made the snacks for the party, and Just Desserts the cake [2].

title: Clarion Alley: Murals Between Cops and Crack
place: Clarion Alley, between Mission and Valencia near 17th St
hook: Two painters lived in an alley with a drug market at one end and a police station at the other. In 1992 they decided to paint their way out.
story: In 1992 the painters Rigo 23 and Aaron Noble shared a studio at 47 Clarion Alley, a space that had once been the main theatre for the Cockettes [1]. The 400-foot lane between Mission and Valencia near 17th Street was a drug-dealing strip littered with needles and trash [1]. "Clarion Alley happened to be very close to a place where one could buy heroin that was I think heavily cut with baby laxative," Rigo recalled [1]. With blighted Mission Street at one end and the Valencia Street police station at the other, the pair set out to make a Balmy Alley-style gallery. Where Balmy spoke about US intervention in Central America, Clarion would address life in the Mission itself [1]. An initial six painters were soon joined by the alley's landlords, handymen and auto mechanics [1]. Rigo said the AIDS crisis made many people eager to reinvent urban life, "knowing they only had a few years to live" [1]. By its 25th anniversary in 2017, the Clarion Alley Mural Project counted more than 500 artists and 700 murals [1].

title: Whoopi's convent in disguise
place: St. Paul's Catholic Church, 221 Valley Street at Church
hook: Hollywood dumped wrecked cars and trash outside Noe Valley's granite Gothic church to make it look like a slum, just as the parish was fighting to stay open.
story: St. Paul's, with its two unequal slate spires and walls of granite from a quarry near 30th and Castro, was dedicated in 1911. It came through both the 1906 and 1989 earthquakes with mostly cosmetic damage [1]. After Loma Prieta, though, the archdiocese ordered every parish building retrofitted to new seismic standards, and the cost was so high it seriously considered closing the church [1][2]. In 1992, in the middle of that uncertainty, Hollywood arrived. The church played 'St. Katherine's' in Sister Act, starring Whoopi Goldberg as a lounge singer hiding among nuns [2][3]. The neighbourhood, by then decidedly middle class, was dressed down to look like the Tenderloin or Bayview. Crews recast shopfronts and scattered abandoned cars and trash along the streets [3]. In 1994 the new pastor, Father Mario Farana, began a campaign to save the parish. The old school at 29th and Church was knocked down and rebuilt, and the church itself was retrofitted, with a fundraising target of $7.8 million [1]. The plan worked, and St. Paul's still stands [2].

title: A Farmers Market Grows Where the Freeway Fell
place: Ferry Building and Ferry Plaza
hook: Three years after an earthquake wrecked the waterfront freeway, 10,000 people turned up to buy peaches in its shadow, and 2,122 signed a petition demanding more.
story: When the 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake buckled the double-decker freeway that had cut the city off from its waterfront and the Ferry Building, a group of restaurateurs, farmers, planners, architects and advocates saw a chance to bring a public market back to the bay [1]. On Sunday, September 12, 1992, their San Francisco Public Market Collaborative staged a one-time harvest market across from the Ferry Building: more than 50 farmers and food producers, about 15 of the city's best-known restaurants cooking street food, more than 10,000 visitors and $75,000 in sales. Some 2,122 people signed a petition demanding a permanent market [1]. On May 22, 1993, a weekly Saturday market opened in front of the Ferry Building with more than 50 farmers and 10 food vendors, and it went year-round that fall [1]. In 1994 Sibella Kraus founded CUESA, a nonprofit that would later run the market. The Collaborative pitched the long-neglected Ferry Building as the market's permanent home, and when the renovated Ferry Building Marketplace opened on March 15, 2003, several businesses that had started as market stalls moved into permanent shops. An estimated 30,000 people came when the Saturday market returned to the plaza that April [1][2].

title: Dykes take Dolores Park
place: Mission Dolores Park
hook: Pride was getting big, glossy and corporate. So on a June evening in 1993, ten thousand women gathered on the hillside and simply walked to the Castro.
story: By the early 1990s San Francisco's Pride parade had grown elaborate and commercial. Many lesbians wanted a day of their own [1]. In June 1993, on the Saturday evening before the parade, the first San Francisco Dyke March set off from Dolores Park and walked to Castro and Market. The history calls it militant, participatory and informal. It drew 10,000 people. The next year more than twice as many came: 25,000 [1]. The march still begins with a rally and cultural programme on the park's slopes, and still asks men to cheer from the sidelines [2]. Organisers describe it as a day when 'dykes can proclaim space, rights, visibility and respect,' and they say it includes trans, genderqueer and gender-fluid dykes [2]. From 2004 Dolores Park also became the starting point for the Trans March on the Friday of Pride weekend. That march heads to Turk and Taylor Streets in the Tenderloin, where the 1966 Compton's Cafeteria riot took place [1].

title: The Museum Built on a Graveyard
place: Legion of Honor courtyard and underground galleries
hook: When the Legion of Honor dug down to earthquake-proof itself, it found the poor of 19th-century San Francisco. A pipe ran inches from a skull.
story: The Legion of Honor stands on the Potter's Field of the old City Cemetery. When it was built in 1921, workers tore open about 1,500 graves. The foreman said the only thing to do was 'scrape them over and cover them up again' [1]. In 1993 the museum dug under its courtyard for a seismic retrofit and underground expansion, and the dead came back. Archaeologist Miley Holman described a 'charnel heap', probably left over from 1921. Most were elderly people buried in redwood coffins, their bones marked by fractures and arthritis [1]. Director Harry Parker complained that the delays would cost $50,000 a month [1]. The counts differ: Alta says about 900 remains went to the medical examiner, and SF Heritage lists 578 adults and 173 children reburied in Colma [1][2]. Photographer Richard Barnes had been hired to document the renovation. He photographed plumbing running inches from an exposed skull, and a gun, a comb and a shoe from the graves [3]. He called the project a meditation: 'here was part of our history that was not interesting to the curators' [3]. Thousands more still lie beneath the museum [1].

title: The giant pit at Sacramento and Maple
place: Former Marshall Hale Hospital (CPMC East Campus), 3773 Sacramento Street at Maple Street
hook: Neighbours fought a plan to bury cancer-killing linear accelerators under a hospital parking lot. The hospital won, dug the hole, then hit hard times.
story:
Marshall Hale Hospital, at Sacramento and Maple streets, had run a cancer centre on the site since 1952. In 1988 it merged with Children's Hospital next door. In 1991 the combined hospital merged with Pacific Presbyterian to form California Pacific Medical Center [2][3].

In 1992 CPMC planned a new underground cancer centre beneath the parking lot. It would house linear accelerators, the powerful machines used to kill cancer cells [1][2]. The zoning administrator had exempted it from a conditional-use permit and environmental review, as long as it did not significantly enlarge the centre's operations [1][3]. Neighbours said they were caught by surprise. The hospital said the work would take 17 months; residents worried about parking and about what would happen to the accelerators if an earthquake struck [2][3].

The appeal held up the project for eight months. Then the Board of Permit Appeals turned down about a dozen residents and let the work go ahead [3]. Crews dug a big hole and began shoring its walls [3][4].

By October 1993 financial hard times had hit. The medical centre had laid off close to 300 employees, and the project was stalled. "What to do with a giant pit?" the Richmond ReView asked. The centre's fate would be settled in a wider reorganisation [4].

title: Thirty-Fourth Floor, 101 California
place: 101 California Street
hook: A failed businessman with a grudge against one law firm turned a glass tower into a crime scene, and the grief of the survivors helped change national gun law.
story: On the afternoon of July 1, 1993, Gian Luigi Ferri, a 55-year-old failed businessman, walked into the glass tower at 101 California Street carrying two 9mm semiautomatic pistols and a .45. At the offices of the law firm Pettit & Martin he put on ear protectors and began shooting, firing more than 50 rounds; he killed eight people and wounded six before killing himself in a stairwell [1]. On his body police found a rambling four-page letter headed "LIST OF CRIMINALS, RAPISTS, RACKETEERES, LOBBYISTS," blaming evil conspiracies for his failed property deals and even railing against the FDA over MSG [1]. The dead included Jody Sposato, a young mother. Four years later her husband Steve stood outside the building with their daughter tugging at his arm and credited the tragedy with fuelling the Brady law and the 1994 federal assault weapons ban: "People once feared the NRA, (but) gun control is popular now" [2]. Pettit & Martin, already struggling, never recovered; its partners voted to dissolve the firm in March 1995, citing plummeting morale after the shootings [3].

title: A Pearl Harbor tug waits at Pier 1
place: Treasure Island Pier 1 area, south-east waterfront (approximate)
hook: On December 7, 1941, the tug Hoga pushed the burning USS Nevada aground. In 1994 she was tied up at Treasure Island, waiting to learn her fate.
story:
On December 7, 1941, the Navy harbour tug Hoga pushed the burning battleship USS Nevada onto the beach at Pearl Harbor, keeping the main channel clear, and then poured water onto her. She also fought the fires on the USS Arizona as it sank and pulled wounded sailors from the water [1].

In 1948 she was loaned to the Port of Oakland as a fireboat. Renamed Port of Oakland and later City of Oakland, she spent decades fighting fires on the waterfront [2]. In 1994 she was returned to the Navy and struck from the Naval Register [2]. In December 1994 she was tied up at Treasure Island's Pier 1. The base's historians, writing as their own station closed, described her as the last remaining ship from the attack on Pearl Harbor. A group in Honolulu was trying to buy her and take her back to the scene of her greatest day [1].

That did not happen. Hoga went into the National Defense Reserve Fleet in Suisun Bay, and in 2005 the Arkansas Inland Maritime Museum was selected to receive her [2]. For a while, though, one of Pearl Harbor's heroes sat among the old piers of a closing base, like the island itself waiting for its future [1].

title: Iguanas and Macs in Multimedia Gulch
place: Multimedia Gulch, South of Market warehouses near the Bay Bridge ramps (around 2nd St)
hook: Programmers too hip for suburbia moved into old sweatshops by the Bay Bridge ramps. The seamstresses were still working downstairs.
story: In March 1994 Fortune described a new hot spot for startups: Multimedia Gulch, a warehouse district "hard by the ramps to the Bay Bridge," where programmers "too hip to live in the banal suburbia of Silicon Valley" teamed up with artists to make CD-ROMs full of video, animation and music [1]. Residents already included Wired magazine, Tim Burton's animation studio and the software maker Macromedia [1]. One 18-person startup, Vivid Publishing, had taken over a 4,000-square-foot room once filled with immigrant Chinese women at sewing machines, paying 60 cents a square foot, about a third of downtown rents. It strung 4,000 feet of cable between its Macintoshes, put a massage table in the conference room and let an iguana named Jim roam free. The Chinese seamstresses were still working downstairs [1]. By 1999, a UC Berkeley study counted 6,000 jobs added in the district between 1994 and 1998, with some 500 digital media companies across a SoMa that was quickly all being called the Gulch [2]. "This is what has changed the San Francisco economy," said study author Ken Rosen [2].

title: Seven Women Paint the Women's Building
place: The Women's Building, 3543 18th St
hook: A feminist collective too broke to pay rent bought a whole building. Fifteen years later, seven muralists wrapped it in goddesses, scientists and anonymous heroines.
story: The San Francisco Women's Centers was formed by groups including NOW, the Daughters of Bilitis and San Francisco Women's Liberation, and it chose deliberately to support others rather than grow itself [1]. The need for a home became clear in 1975, when San Francisco State withdrew sponsorship of its conference on violence against women [2]. The drive to buy a building split the collective: an organiser named Roma led the campaign while her partner, founder Jean Crosby, opposed it [1]. The purchase on 18th Street went through at the end of the 1970s (the organisation dates it to 1978, historian Sushawn Robb to 1979), and Robb argues that owning it is what kept the group alive [1][2]. In 1994 seven artists, Juana Alicia, Miranda Bergman, Edythe Boone, Susan Kelk Cervantes, Meera Desai, Yvonne Littleton and Irene Perez, finished Maestrapeace, which covers the building after 18 months of work with dozens of volunteers [2]. It honours women activists, scientists, artists, anonymous heroines and deities [2]. The building has sponsored more than 170 organisations, including La Casa de las Madres, the city's first shelter for battered women [2].

title: Seven strangers below the crooked street
place: The Real World house, 949 Lombard St
hook: MTV put seven twentysomethings in a house at the foot of Lombard Street. One of them, an AIDS educator, changed how America saw the disease.
story: From February to June 1994, MTV filmed the cast of "The Real World: San Francisco" living at 949 Lombard Street, below the crooked block [1][2]. Among them was Pedro Zamora, 22, who had come from Cuba in the Mariel boatlift and grown up in Miami. He was an openly gay, HIV-positive AIDS educator [1][2]. On camera he fell for Sean Sasser, and the two exchanged vows in a commitment ceremony at the house. It is often described as the first same-sex commitment ceremony on television [1][3]. Viewers also watched his health decline, quickly and brutally, at a time when AIDS treatments were few [3]. Zamora died on November 11, 1994, only hours after the season's last episode aired. His roommate Judd Winick, a 24-year-old cartoonist who had joined for free rent and a shot at TV, was at his bedside [2][3]. Winick became an AIDS educator and fundraiser, and in 2000 he published a graphic memoir, "Pedro and Me." He married fellow housemate Pam Ling, who became a doctor treating AIDS patients in the city's clinics [2].

title: The Army Hands Over Its Oldest Post
place: Main Parade Ground, Main Post
hook: After two centuries under three flags, America's oldest continuously operating military base became a national park. Many people expected it to be carved up and sold.
story: When Congress created the Golden Gate National Recreation Area in 1972, it added a clause: if the military ever left the Presidio, the land would join the park [1]. It came into play in 1989, when Congress put the post on its list of bases to close [1]. The last troops sent to war from the Presidio were 200 Army engineers who left for Saudi Arabia in 1990. The first, in 1794, had been 20 Spanish horse soldiers riding out to put down an Ohlone rebellion in the Santa Cruz Mountains [2]. On 1 October 1994 the Presidio ended more than two hundred years of service to Spain, Mexico and the United States. It passed to the National Park Service as the oldest continuously operating military base in the country [1]. As it left, the Army even took the contents of the Presidio Army Museum [2]. The Army left behind crumbling barracks, run-down forts and neglected forests. As the Chronicle later recalled, many people gloomily predicted the land would be chopped up and sold to private developers [3]. Instead, Congress set up the Presidio Trust two years later to make it pay its own way [1].

title: The Sculpture San Francisco Wouldn't Take
place: Sculpture pad in the Legion of Honor forecourt
hook: Richard Serra designed a 48-foot rusting steel giant for the Legion of Honor. Public fury and a city rule sank it, and his boyhood friend's sculpture took the spot.
story: In 1994 the Fine Arts Museums announced, too early, a design by Richard Serra for the sculpture site in front of the Legion of Honor. It was a 48-foot rusting steel sculpture, and a donor had already agreed to pay for making and installing it [1]. When The Chronicle published the design, a torrent of public protest followed. What finally killed the project was city policy. The Legion's grounds belong to Recreation and Park, whose gift rules let the city move or alter a donated work. When Serra learned this, he withdrew [1]. Six years later the spot was filled by Mark di Suvero's red-painted steel Pax Jerusalem, on the 'sculpture pad' since November 1999 [1]. The two artists were native San Franciscans and boyhood pals [1]. Chief curator Steve Nash said the museum 'wanted a classic di Suvero' whose symmetry echoed the building. The Chronicle's critic Kenneth Baker called it di Suvero 'at his safest, not his best'. He also complained that its red was too close to the geraniums planted around it [1][2].

title: Two Cable Cars Hidden Upstairs
place: Carville streetcar house, Great Highway near Moraga Street (exact address withheld at owner's request)
hook: A student hunting for the last house built from old streetcars asked a stranger with a bicycle. The answer was the house next door, which happened to be for sale.
story: In the 1890s, San Francisco's transit companies sold off retired horsecars for $20, or $10 without seats. People hauled them to the dunes near the beach and turned them into homes, and the settlement became known as Carville [2]. By 1994 many locals had never heard of it. That year James L. Heisterkamp, a San Francisco State student, kept a diary of his search for Carville's "last remnant." A house on 47th Avenue turned out to have no streetcars left inside. Then, on the Great Highway, a young man pushing a bicycle pointed him to the house next door, which was for sale [1]. Upstairs, two cable cars sat side by side with their inner walls removed to make one room. The old wooden passenger benches were still built into one wall, and a horsecar, sliding panel door and all, served as the bedroom and bath [1]. Permit records showed a Mrs. Collins had the cars set on a frame in 1908; they were probably raised to two stories around 1921. Filmmaker Scott Anderson, who lived nearby, bought the house [1]. In 1999 Preservation magazine said the Sunset might be the city's "only neighborhood without a trace of apparent charm or history." Nothing on the house's plain front gives away what is inside [1].

title: A Striped Cathedral for Modern Art
place: SFMOMA, 151 Third Street
hook: The museum that gave Jackson Pollock his first show spent 60 years in rented upstairs rooms. In 1995 it got a bold brick home on old skid row.
story: The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art gave Jackson Pollock and Arshile Gorky their first shows in the 1940s, yet for some 60 years it rented cramped rooms upstairs in the War Memorial Veterans Building at Civic Center, where most of the collection had to come down whenever a temporary exhibition went up [2]. Director Jack Lane hired Swiss architect Mario Botta in 1988, along with a Third Street site opposite Yerba Buena Gardens, in a former skid row the city had marked for change, to be the cultural linchpin of the new district [2]. "We told Mario we wanted a building with some significant exterior character," Lane recalled [1]. It opened in January 1995: 225,000 square feet, costing $60 million or $62 million depending on the account, and Botta's first building in the United States [1][2]. A massive stepped brick facade, banded with black and white granite, is crowned by a striped cylindrical skylight tower; inside, visitors cross a steel bridge high under the skylight [1]. Critics were split. The Los Angeles Times loved galleries that "make the art look great and the viewer feel great," but accused the lobby of "bamboozling visitors with an extravaganza of glitz" [1]. The New York Times found it distinctive and sober, though not quite the world-class landmark it was ballyhooed as [2].

title: A silent star's first cyberspace fan club
place: Church Street at 27th (What's for Dessert cafe, 1497 Church Street, site of the 1997 exhibit)
hook: A bookseller on Church Street rented Pandora's Box, watched it twice, found no fan club for Louise Brooks, and taught himself HTML to start one.
story: One Friday night in 1991, Thomas Gladysz rented the silent film Pandora's Box from Video Wave on Castro Street. He watched it, went to bed, and watched it again the next morning, "totally wowed" by Louise Brooks [1]. He went looking for a Brooks fan club and found that none existed. So the bookseller, who worked by day at the Booksmith, taught himself HTML. In August 1995 he launched the Louise Brooks Society, which he ran from his home on Church Street and called "the world's first fan club in cyberspace" [1][2]. Within two years it had about 36,000 hits and more than 350 members in 25 countries. Fans mailed in clippings and photos from around the world; the site showed oddities such as a 1920s Chronicle ad of Brooks modelling an ankle watch. Film critic Roger Ebert told Gladysz he used the site for his University of Chicago class [1]. In September 1997 the online club came to the neighbourhood: "Louise Brooks: Portraits and Memorabilia," with 1920s photos, movie magazines and cigarette cards from his collection, went on display at What's for Dessert, the corner cafe at 1497 Church Street [1]. The society went on to be credited in reprints of Brooks's biography and her memoir, Lulu in Hollywood, and to inspire a documentary [2].

title: An acre of pink, raised in the dark
place: East face of Twin Peaks below Christmas Tree Point, facing the Castro
hook: In 1995 a few friends crept up Twin Peaks at night to pin a Nazi-era symbol to the hillside, and turned it into a Pride tradition.
story:
In 1995 architect Patrick Carney and some friends wanted to add colour to Pride weekend. "There's a big blank canvas on Twin Peaks," he remembered thinking [1]. A friend suggested a rainbow flag, but the city already had plenty. Carney chose the pink triangle instead, because many people did not know where it came from [1][2]. In Nazi concentration camps, prisoners labelled homosexual had to wear a pink triangle badge [1][3]. "We put it up in the dark of night, just to have it appear, sort of anonymously," Carney said. "We didn't expect it to continue" [1]. That first installation went up without city permission [2].

It continued. The triangle grew several times over the years and now covers about an acre, facing the Castro and downtown [2]. For the 30th display in 2025, volunteers staked out borders of pink sailcloth 240 feet long. The next morning around 800 people filled the outline with 175 pink tarps [1]. In 2020, during the pandemic, it was built from pink LED lights instead [3]. Carney calls the pink triangle and the rainbow flag "the Yin and Yang of the gay rights movement" [1].

title: From a burned church, a free farm
place: Site of St. Paulus Lutheran Church, Gough and Eddy streets (950 Gough)
hook: A Gothic wooden church seen in Vertigo burned to the ground in 1995. Fifteen years later its empty lot was giving away thousands of pounds of vegetables.
story: St. Paulus Lutheran Church, built of wood in 1893 at Gough and Eddy, was a city landmark and on the National Register. On 5 November 1995 it was destroyed by fire [1]. Readers of SocketSite still remembered that it appears in Hitchcock's Vertigo [2]. For years the corner stayed empty. Then in January 2010 the church lent a third of an acre to the Free Farm, which grew organic produce and gave it away. By September it had handed out more than 1,000 pounds [2]. Its founder, Dennis Rubenstein, known to everyone as Tree, also ran a Sunday Free Farm Stand in the Mission. He said the church had been a 'wonderful' landlord, and by late 2013 the farm had produced more than 10,000 pounds of food [3]. But 'the life of the farm was always considered temporary,' the church's pastor told Mission Local. The congregation, worshipping at a temporary site on Polk Street, planned to come back to the corner with new housing [3]. Tree went looking for a home for his 60-by-20-foot greenhouse [3]. In 2014 the church put the 950 Gough parcel on the market with plans for condos rising over a replacement church [4].

title: Keith Haring's last work
place: AIDS Interfaith Chapel, Grace Cathedral north tower
hook: Weeks before AIDS killed him, Keith Haring carved an altarpiece into wet clay without a single sketch. One casting now glows just inside Grace Cathedral's doors.
story:
Keith Haring finished The Life of Christ, a triptych drawn freehand into wet clay for casting in bronze and white gold, about two weeks before he died of AIDS in 1990. He never saw it cast [1]. In the centre panel a many-armed figure cradles the infant Jesus beneath a radiant heart; tears rain onto a jostling crowd, angels tumble at the sides [1][2].

On World AIDS Day, 1 December 1995, a casting was unveiled at Grace Cathedral as the heart of a new AIDS chapel [1]. The space, the ground floor of the north "Singing Tower," had been a storeroom, a classroom and briefly the gift shop; it was set aside in 1995 and dedicated in 2000 [2]. It sits just inside the entrance, so that people wary of the vast cathedral could come in "just a little way," as Vice Dean Frances Tornquist put it [2].

The chapel honours the 19,400 San Franciscans the archivist counted as lost to AIDS, alongside caregivers and volunteers, with symbols of many faiths on its piers and a section of the AIDS Memorial Quilt on the back wall. Quilt panels had hung here since 1992 [2]. The cathedral's own accounts credit both an anonymous donor and a group of major donors for the purchase [1][2].

title: Resoling Mother Teresa's dumpster sandals
place: Fonda's Custom Orthopedic Shoes, 1752 Church Street, near Day
hook: When Mother Teresa visited her nuns on Church Street, a local shoemaker stayed up all night rebuilding the sandals she'd found in a Calcutta dumpster.
story:
Pietro Fonda started making shoes at 13 in Pirano, a small town then in northern Italy and now part of Slovenia. A badly healed ankle break had left one leg shorter than the other, so his mother found him a trade he could do sitting down [1]. In 1957, with his village under Communist rule, a Catholic association paid to bring his family to New Orleans. He saved $150 for a bus ticket west, learned orthopedic work at Gerlach's Shoe Clinic and later went out on his own. In 1978, when his Fillmore Street rent tripled, he moved the business to 1752 Church Street near Day as Fonda's Custom Orthopedic Shoes [1]. His four children went to St. Paul's schools [1].

Mother Teresa's Missionaries of Charity had opened a novitiate for nuns at St. Paul's convent, a few blocks away, in 1982 [2]. In 1995, Fonda said, the Nobel laureate came to visit her nuns and he worked through the night on her sandals. She had found them in a dumpster in Calcutta and worn them for ten years. "I saw evidence of patch jobs done all over the world, and had to remove them all and start over." He was asked to save the old patches as possible holy relics [1].

title: Save Army Street versus Cesar Chavez
place: Cesar Chavez Street (formerly Army Street) between Sanchez and Noe
hook: When the city renamed Army Street for the farm-labour leader, orange-and-black 'Save Army Street' signs bloomed in Noe Valley windows. The ballot fight drew national attention.
story: Army Street got its name in 1851 from a developer who also named Navy and Clipper streets, apparently hoping the military would drain his swamps [1]. In January 1995 the Board of Supervisors voted unanimously to rename it for Cesar Chavez, the farm-labour leader who had died in 1993. They had first considered 24th Street, but businesses there objected to the cost [2]. Many residents of the Noe Valley stretch, a two-lane, tree-lined avenue, felt ignored by City Hall [1][2]. Mary Corbin, who had lived on the street for half a century, put two "Save Army Street" placards in her windows. "It's been Army Street for 145 years," she said [1]. Organisers gathered 18,000 signatures to put Proposition O on the November ballot. "We are the little people," said property manager DiAnne Withelder, a leader of the Yes side [1][2]. Down the hill in the Mission, people saw it differently. "It signifies we have a place here too," said grocer Maria Payan [1]. There was vandalism on both sides and even a fistfight [2]. Proposition O was losing as the votes were counted, and the street still bears Chavez's name [2][3]. In March 2026, after abuse allegations against Chavez, a supervisor and a former supervisor said the name should come down [3].

title: The Day Army Street Became Cesar Chavez
place: St. Anthony's Church, Cesar Chavez St at Folsom
hook: A gust of wind unveiled the sign before the officials could. Neighbours waved petitions to change it back. Thirty-one years later, the name is in question again.
story: On March 31, 1995, about 250 people gathered in the parking lot of St. Anthony's Church to unveil the first of 100 signs renaming Army Street after the farmworker leader Cesar Chavez [1]. "Every day you look at that street sign, you should feel great," said Supervisor Susan Leal [1]. Supervisor Tom Ammiano called it "a reclaiming, not a renaming" [1]. A gust of wind blew the burlap off the sign before the official unveiling, while some residents circulated petitions to switch the name back [1]. Opponents, largely from Noe Valley, said they felt attached to the 140-year-old name, and they put a repeal on the November ballot. With Proposition 187's anti-immigrant politics in the air, it lost by a wide margin [2]. In March 2026, after allegations that Chavez had sexually abused young girls, politicians proposed stripping his name from streets and schools. Leal suggested any new name should honour the movement, "probably Dolores Huerta" [2].

title: The Night the Glass House Shattered
place: Conservatory of Flowers
hook: Gusts of more than 100 mph tore through the park in December 1995, smashing the Victorian greenhouse's glass and shutting it for seven years.
story: The Conservatory of Flowers had already survived two fires [2]. Its worst night came in the second week of December 1995. After torrential rains, gusts of more than 100 mph were reported on December 12 and brought down an estimated 1,000 trees across Golden Gate Park [2]. The Chronicle called the Conservatory the storm's worst casualty. Its glass was smashed and much of the interior lay open to the weather [2]. Accounts of the damage differ: SFist, citing the Chronicle, reports hundreds of broken panes, while Wikipedia says 30,000 were blown out and the dome shattered [1][2]. Wikipedia also says cold air and flying glass killed about 15 percent of the plants, and that a 112-year-old philodendron was one of the hardest to save [1]. The World Monuments Fund added the building to its 1996 watch list [1]. Repairs were first estimated at about $10 million, and the final bill came to $25 million, with support from the Richard & Rhoda Goldman Fund and a public fundraising campaign [1][2]. After seven years the Conservatory reopened in 2003 [2].

title: The Night the Hillside Swallowed a Mansion
place: 125 El Camino del Mar (still an empty lot)
hook: On a December night in 1995, a century-old brick sewer burst under 24th Avenue. By morning, TV cameras were watching a three-storey house fall into a canyon.
story: The storm of December 1995 dropped close to three inches of rain on San Francisco in less than a day. Under 24th Avenue, a six-foot brick sewer about a century old gave way in the early hours of December 11 [1][2]. The water ate the dune sand like "a water hose hitting a sand pile", said city engineer Todd Cockburn [1]. Soon after dawn, the empty 85-year-old house at 125 El Camino del Mar began to tilt. When it fell into the hole, a neighbour said, "it sounded like an avalanche" [1]. The pit grew to 40 feet deep and 250 feet wide. Around two dozen homes were evacuated, among them Ansel Adams's boyhood house, which was left teetering at the edge [2]. Neighbours and state Senator Quentin Kopp blamed the city's new Richmond Transport Tunnel project. Kopp said: "I do not hesitate to say I told you so." Cockburn replied that "the evidence has all washed away" [1]. Crews filled the hole with rubble from the demolished Embarcadero Freeway [3]. In 2024 the lot was still empty [2].

title: Where a buried creek begins
place: Yosemite Marsh, north end of McLaren Park
hook: A tiny eggplant-shaped marsh shelters one of the city's rarest insects, and in 2005 it was quietly silting to death.
story: In a quiet corner at the park's north end, a creek bubbles out of the hillside and tumbles into a small freshwater marsh shaped like an eggplant [1]. This is Yosemite Marsh, the start of a creek that once flowed to the bay and is now buried under homes and streets [2]. The city named it a 'significant natural resource area' in 1995 [1][2]. Rare species live here: the San Francisco forktail damselfly, with its iridescent blue-green body, and the flowering quillwort. Red-winged blackbirds nest in the cattails, and great blue herons hunt gophers in the meadow above [1]. Writing for FoundSF, Pete Holloran calls the marsh home to one of the damselfly's last populations [3]. By 2005, silt from the creek's collapsing banks was turning the marsh into a muddy pond. The city set aside $304,000 to save it. Engineers offered competing fixes, and so did Belles Yelda, a retired civil engineer in Friends of McLaren Park. The group's president, Franco Mancini, doubted any of them would work. 'Everyone is flying blind,' he said. 'It's like designing a building with blindfolds on' [1].

title: A letter to the Grateful Dead, unanswered
place: Brazil Avenue inside McLaren Park, the stretch neighbours had gated at night
hook: Nearly ten years before the amphitheatre was named for Jerry Garcia, a neighbourhood volunteer wrote to the Grateful Dead and to his widow about the idea. Nobody wrote back.
story: The group that gave McLaren Park a voice started small. Friends of McLaren Park formed in 1994 [1]. By the summer of 1995 its president, Jo Coffey, was meeting representatives of the city's Water Department, Planning Commission and Fire Department [2]. In 1996 the Friends were already discussing an idea that would take nearly a decade: renaming the park's amphitheatre for Jerry Garcia, the Grateful Dead guitarist who had grown up in the nearby Excelsior. Coffey wrote to both the Grateful Dead organisation and Garcia's widow, but reportedly got no response [3]. The Friends worked on smaller things too. That same year they discussed children's multicultural events in the amphitheatre and drafted a letter to the police about traffic on Shelley Drive and Mansell Street [3]. A later president, Franco Mancini, called their method 'the nag tactic.' By 1999 it had persuaded Rec and Park to gate off and close at night a crime-ridden stretch of Brazil Street that was being used as an industrial dump, and to drain and clean McNab Lake [4]. The amphitheatre finally got Garcia's name in July 2005, two years after a newer neighbourhood group, Friends and Advocates of Crocker Amazon and the Excelsior, began throwing him an annual 'Jerry Day' birthday party [1].

title: Art school in a bus garage
place: California College of the Arts, 1111 Eighth Street
hook: In 1996 an Oakland art school opened a campus in the design district, in a former Greyhound bus maintenance shop. Thirty years later, a Tennessee university is buying the campus.
story: California College of the Arts was founded in 1907 and was long based in Oakland. For a decade or so before 1996 it rented spaces in San Francisco [1]. In 1996 it opened a San Francisco campus in the design district. Its main building there had been a Greyhound maintenance facility [1]. Leddy Maytum Stacy Architects converted the bus shop into 75,000 square feet of studios, workshops and galleries, with rooftop solar hot-water collectors and radiant floors that cut energy use by 60 percent [1]. The district suited it. Furniture design was based there, and the program's chair wanted students out in the galleries and showrooms [1]. After closing its historic Oakland campus, the school finished a $97.5 million San Francisco expansion in 2024 [2]. Enrollment kept falling, and its president called the tuition-driven model "not sustainable" [2]. On January 13, 2026, CCA announced it would close at the end of the 2026–27 academic year. Vanderbilt University is buying the campus as a West Coast outpost for about 1,000 students [2]. Vanderbilt's chancellor said it chose the site for its student housing and its closeness to Mission Bay's bioscience labs. The college's Wattis Institute gallery is to carry on under a 'CCA Institute' [2].

title: Evicted artists find a home above a tunnel

hook: Artists thrown out of a ramshackle Geary Street landmark spent thirteen years looking for a home, and found one on the fill of a collapsed railroad tunnel.

For decades the Goodman Building at 1117 Geary, a huge ramshackle structure from 1860, was a communal home and workspace for artists. The Potrero View counts Janis Joplin and poster designer Wes Wilson among its residents at different times. In 1983 the Redevelopment Agency evicted them [1].

The half-block at 18th and Arkansas had its own history. The south portal of a railroad tunnel came out there until the tunnel was filled after the 1962 fire and cave-in [1][2]. From 1990 to 1992 neighbours fought to keep the slope as open space, the "Potrero Commons" [2]. Anchor Brewing made a Potrero Commons Ale to raise money for the campaign [1]. In 1991 the Board of Supervisors chose housing for the displaced Goodman artists instead [1]. The deal involved Mayor Frank Jordan, the artists and developers [2].

The artists had organized as Artsdeco. In 1996 they moved into architect David Baker's new building: 30 live-work studios, a three-story atrium, a garden and a theater space, with part of the old tunnel reused as the garage [1]. Artsdeco member Martha Senger called it "the reincarnation of a grassroots cultural institution" [1].

title: From Biker Bar to Brewpub
place: Beach Chalet, 1000 Great Highway
hook: Fifty Harleys out front and chairs flying through windows under priceless WPA frescoes: the Beach Chalet had a rough middle age before a student's business plan saved it.
story: Willis Polk's Spanish-style Beach Chalet opened on May 30, 1925 [2]. In 1936 and 1937 Lucien Labaudt covered its lobby with WPA frescoes of Depression-era San Francisco [2]. After the Army used the building in the Second World War, the city leased it to the Veterans of Foreign Wars for $50 a month [1]. For a time it was a rough bikers' bar, and hurled bottles damaged the frescoes and Moorish tiles. "I remember driving past here and seeing maybe 50 Harleys parked out front and chairs flying out the window," recalled Donna Ernstson of the Friends of Recreation & Parks [1]. The VFW left in 1979 after the city raised the rent to $500. The padlocked building drew feral cats and squatters who nearly burned it down [1]. Then Gar Truppelli cycled past on his mountain bike. As a San Francisco State senior in 1993, he wrote the business plan for a brewpub there, and he and his wife Lara won the 20-year lease against four other bidders [1]. After a $6.7 million restoration, which also restored the murals, the Beach Chalet Brewery and Restaurant opened on New Year's Eve 1996 [1][2].

title: Kidnapped on Trash Day

hook: Two kidnappers cased a Sea Cliff mansion and noticed the maid took the garbage out every Tuesday at 6:30 a.m. So they came back the next Tuesday.
story: Tom Taylor, 64, chose his victim from the newspaper. He had read about a large gift that steel magnate Marshall Wais had made to the San Francisco Opera [1]. He and his partner, Michael Robison, watched the Wais house in Sea Cliff five or six times. They noticed that on Tuesdays, trash day, the housekeeper, Yung Wong, wheeled the garbage out at 6:30 a.m. [1]. On November 19, 1996, Taylor caught her in the garage [1]. The Times of London reported that the men ordered the 79-year-old out of bed [2]. Wong got to Wais's stepson, Tom Hannah, in another wing, and he called the police [1]. Wais spent nearly eight hours blindfolded and handcuffed in a van [2]. The kidnappers planned their next move over coffee in a McDonald's parking lot on Stanyan Street. They phoned Wais's finance chief from pay phones, and that afternoon they collected $500,000 from a car parked at a Thai restaurant at the end of Lincoln Way [1]. They let Wais out in Golden Gate Park and handed him $20 for a cab. Moments later, police rammed their van [1][2]. From jail, Taylor said that if it hadn't worked, Microsoft's Paul Allen would likely have been next [1].

title: Roast Duck Where Italians Once Dined
place: Wing Hing Restaurant, 2550 San Bruno Avenue
hook: By 2009 Chinese lions guarded San Bruno Avenue doorways that once led to Italian dinners. At Wing Hing, the dish missing from the English menu was ginger-garlic frog.
story: By 2009 about half of the Portola's roughly 13,000 residents were Asian, and on San Bruno Avenue, Carl Nolte wrote, 'Chinese lions guard the entrance to restaurants that once served Italian food' [1]. The city's register records the business at 2550 San Bruno from 1996 until 2022 [2][3]. At lunch the place was packed. In the evenings most orders were takeaway, phoned in and picked up by locals. Many families bought a pound of roast duck or pork from the window for under $10, had it chopped on the spot and built a home meal around it [2]. The head chef, whom Luo called Sifu, or 'master', could take a duck apart in seconds at the front of the shop. Then came the one dish, Luo said, that was unique to Wing Hing and not on the English menu: frog stir-fried with garlic and fresh ginger. Luo said it was 'very high in nutrients and often drunk with a beer' [2].

title: The Alligator of Mountain Lake

hook: In 1996 an abandoned pet alligator outwitted rangers, zookeepers, two rival newspapers and a hired Florida gator hunter for more than two months.
story: In the summer of 1996, a retired architect and birdwatcher, Dan Bushnell, 72, said he had twice seen an alligator with 'pop-up eyes' swimming in Mountain Lake [1]. It seemed to be a dumped pet, and it became a sensation. The Chronicle flew in a professional hunter from Florida. The rival Examiner sent its executive editor, Phil Bronstein, and a reporter in wetsuits to 'protect' the reptile, but police stopped them at the water's edge, citing a rule against swimming in the lake [2]. Examiner readers voted to name it 'Golden Gator', ahead of 'Van Nessie' and 'Presidio Domingo'. A Texas radio station played updates set to a rewritten 'Crocodile Rock' [2]. On 8 October, zoo associate curator John Aikin finally caught the 3-foot-2-inch male with a fishing pole and $1.47 worth of supermarket fish [2][3]. That December the zoo threw a farewell party, with a cake reading 'Best of luck', before flying him to a Louisiana preserve [3]. The gator was a sign of deeper trouble. Neighbours already complained that golf-course contaminants and litter were fouling the once-clear lake [1]. In November 2014 the Presidio Trust used a rotenone-based chemical to wipe out the invasive fish that had plagued it for years [4].

title: The Internet's Memory in an Army Building
place: Internet Archive, 116 Sheridan Avenue (Main Post)
hook: For years, the project trying to save a copy of the entire web worked out of an old Army building on the Presidio's Main Post.
story: Brewster Kahle's dream was what he called 'a Library of Alexandria for the internet'. In the 1990s he began sending out programs called crawlers to take snapshots of every page on the web [1]. The nonprofit he founded, the Internet Archive, described itself in 2002 as 'founded in 1996 and located in the Presidio of San Francisco'. Its mission was to build an 'Internet library' so that born-digital culture would not vanish into what computer scientist Danny Hillis called our 'digital dark age' [2]. It pointed out that many early films had been recycled for their silver, which captures the worry behind the whole project [2]. Its address was 116 Sheridan Avenue, a building on the Main Post of the former Army base. The Archive told visitors its Presidio facilities were open to the public on most Friday afternoons, and it recommended printing a map of the Presidio to find them [3]. Archived copies of that same contact page show the move: by 2010 the headquarters address had changed to 300 Funston Avenue, a former church in the Richmond District [3][1]. Many of the web pages the Archive saved are available to anyone through its Wayback Machine [1].

title: The district attorney's punch at Izzy's

hook: A steakhouse in the Marina's old post office became a City Hall hangout. In 1996 the new district attorney threw a punch there.
story: In 1977 Sam DuVall read about Izzy Gomez, a Portuguese immigrant and legendary Barbary Coast saloon keeper on Pacific Street, whose fans included William Saroyan. DuVall promised himself he would one day open a 'Bohemian' steakhouse in Izzy's memory [1]. He did it on February 9, 1987, at 3345 Steiner, in the building that had been the Marina's first post office. Art Deco postal eagles are still carved into its parapet [1]. Izzy's became a regular spot for judges, city attorneys and mayors [1]. In 1996, barely five months into his first term as district attorney, Terence Hallinan was heading for the door after a birthday party there attended by the city's political elite. Developer Joe O'Donoghue was furious that Hallinan had fired veteran prosecutors by leaving pink slips on their chairs while they were at lunch, and he shouted an obscene insult [2]. Hallinan, whose boyhood nickname was 'Kayo,' turned and landed a punch. Neither man was hurt [2]. One paper covered it like a prizefight, with the fighters' ages, heights, weights and reach, and David Letterman made jokes about it [2]. A few days later Mayor Willie Brown arranged a lunch where the two made up. By 1997 O'Donoghue called Hallinan 'a real nice guy personally' [2].

title: The first Salvadoran bread in the Excelsior
place: Pacita's Salvadorean Bakery, 10 Persia Avenue
hook: Maria Paz Rodriguez arrived from El Salvador in 1990, worked in someone else's bakery until she had saved enough, and opened the Excelsior's first Salvadoran bakery.
story: Maria Paz Rodriguez came to San Francisco from El Salvador in 1990. She worked in a bakery until she had saved enough money to open her own, and in 1996 she opened Pacita's just off Mission Street at 10 Persia [1]. It was the first shop in the Excelsior to sell Salvadoran bread. Until then the city's only Salvadoran bakeries were in the Mission, and with so many Salvadorans living in the Excelsior it was an instant hit [1]. For the first few years she ran it alone, until her siblings followed her from El Salvador to help [1]. The speciality is Salvadoran bread, traditionally made by hand from a bran-based recipe. The bakery also makes tamales wrapped in banana leaves, quesadillas and cakes for quinceañeras, weddings and communions [1]. Univision once featured Rodriguez as an example of someone who had benefited from Temporary Protected Status, and that brought in even more customers [1]. On September 25, 2017, Pacita's became the first Excelsior business accepted to the city's Legacy Business Registry. It was only 21 years old, but it qualified early because its building was being put up for sale [1]. Other Salvadoran businesses have since followed, including Pupuseria Metapan in the Royal Baking Company building [1][2].

title: Too Many Bars for Six Blocks
place: Inner Sunset commercial core, Lincoln Way to Kirkham, 7th to 11th Avenues
hook: State guidelines said the Inner Sunset's core should have 28 places serving liquor. It had 38, and a supervisor wanted the tap turned off.
story:
Inner Irving Street had always liked a drink. Its bars ranged from the 1893 Little Shamrock on Lincoln Way to the Embers on Irving [2]. By 1996 some neighbours thought it had too many.

In September 1996 Supervisor Mabel Teng proposed an 18-month moratorium on new liquor licenses for bars and restaurants in the area bounded by Lincoln Way, 7th Avenue, Kirkham Street and 11th Avenue. The area had 38 bars and restaurants serving alcohol, while the state Bureau of Alcoholic Beverage Control recommended 28. "This is a neighborhood and family issue," Teng said. Police said the Inner Sunset's crime rate was about 18 percent above the city average [1].

Others pushed back. Supervisor Susan Leal, author of the Mission District's ban two years earlier, said "this is a restaurant town" and argued that liquor stores and corner shops should be included. The same day the board refused a license for a new bar and restaurant on Irving Street. Only Supervisor Tom Hsieh voted for it, saying it was unfair to an owner who had already spent his money [1]. Teng was the first Chinese American elected to the board without first being appointed [3].

title: Where English Speakers Learn Cantonese
place: Alice Fong Yu Alternative School, 1541 12th Avenue
hook: In 1926 she became the city school district's first Chinese American teacher. Seventy years later, a Sunset school teaching Chinese to all children took her name.
story:
On a Saturday in January 1996, about 200 parents and students gathered at the former Columbus School in the Sunset to rename it for Alice Fong Yu. At 90 and in a wheelchair, she raised her mittened hands like a prizefighter [1]. In 1926 Yu had become the first Chinese American teacher in the San Francisco Unified School District. As the only bilingual teacher at Chinatown's Commodore Stockton School, she was also translator, social worker and go-between [1].

The new school turned her story around. It set out to teach mostly English-speaking children Chinese, spoken 50 to 80 percent of the time depending on the grade. Officials called it the first school of its kind in the nation. It capped 12 years of work by founding teacher Liana Szeto and parents; the program had run out of West Portal Elementary until September 1995. In 1996 it had 175 students in kindergarten to fifth grade, about 40 percent Chinese, 25 percent white, 20 percent Eurasian and 15 percent Black [1].

Today the school on 12th Avenue teaches Cantonese from kindergarten through eighth grade and Mandarin in the middle grades [2].

title: A Castro's house joins the gay center

hook: The founders of San Francisco's gay community center planned to demolish an 1894 Victorian. Gay preservationists fought back. The house had been built by a member of the Castro family.
story: The Victorian at Market and Octavia was built in 1894 by Carmel Fallon, born into the prominent Californio Castro family [1]. She had married Thomas Fallon, a Bear Flag Revolt veteran and later mayor of San Jose. According to the landmark account, she caught him with the maid, divorced him, and invested her settlement in San Francisco real estate [1]. Her building is the only survivor of its row on this stretch of Market. The 1906 fire took the buildings to its east, and development later took those to the west [1]. In December 1996, leaders of a proposed gay and lesbian community center bought the site. In 1997 their board voted 'not to use' the battered house after the architects estimated that renovating it would cost $1.6 to $2.6 million [2]. A coalition of gay activists and preservationists rallied to save it and collected more than 1,000 signatures [2]. The Chronicle pointed out the irony: a gay center was about to demolish a house built by a Castro, a name that had come to symbolize the gay movement around the world [2]. The house survived. It became city Landmark No. 223, and it is now part of the San Francisco LGBT Community Center, which opened in March 2002 [1][3].

title: A naval base becomes a neighbourhood
place: Former Navy housing, Avenue H area, Treasure Island
hook: When the sailors left in 1997, their houses went partly to families climbing out of homelessness. 'Everybody you see in the world, you see on the island here.'
story:
Naval Station Treasure Island officially closed on September 30, 1997 [1]. San Francisco soon let civilians move into the old Navy housing. It set aside 375 units for vulnerable people, including those with a history of homelessness [1]. An organisation founded in 1994 to plan for them, the Treasure Island Homeless Development Initiative, now One Treasure Island, still runs food pantries, job training and services [1]. In 1998 the Department of Labor opened a Job Corps centre on 35 acres, and the Life Learning Academy charter high school opened [1].

It remains one of the city's poorest ZIP codes. About half of its more than 2,000 residents live below the poverty line [1]. In 2009 Mayor Gavin Newsom agreed a deal with the Navy that could be worth more than $105 million to transfer the island and remake it as a model of sustainable development [2]. Redevelopment plans call for 8,000 homes, including 2,173 below-market-rate or affordable units [1].

In oral histories, residents describe a close community. 'Everybody you see in the world, you see on the island here,' said Atta Pilram. Ishmael Wesley and his son Jahfari were the first father and son to graduate from the construction training programme [3].

In 2005 the Filipino-American Development Foundation opened the Bayanihan Community Center on the ground floor, serving immigrant families and seniors [1][2]. title: Records where the bowling pins fell

hook: Why is the world's most famous independent record store so wide? Because it used to be a bowling alley, and the "Bowling" sign is still on the roof.

title: The City Auctions Its Tallest Cross
place: Mount Davidson Cross (0.38-acre private parcel)
hook: Courts ruled that a city-owned cross broke the separation of church and state. The fix was an auction, and Armenian Americans won it for $26,000.
story:
In 1990 the American Civil Liberties Union, Americans United for Separation of Church and State and the American Jewish Congress sued the city over its ownership of the Mount Davidson cross, arguing that a religious symbol on public land was unconstitutional [1]. The federal courts agreed, and in 1997 the Supreme Court rejected the city's appeal [1].

The settlement put the cross itself up for auction. On July 21, 1997, a 0.38-acre parcel around the cross was sold to the highest bidder, the Council of Armenian American Organizations of Northern California, for $26,000 [1][2]. On November 4 voters approved the sale by a wide margin with Proposition F [2]. The council has kept the cross as a memorial to Armenians killed under Ottoman rule, and signs on the surrounding public parkland remind visitors of the separation of church and state [1].

Two members of American Atheists argued that the city had stacked the bidding to guarantee the cross would survive. The Supreme Court declined their appeal in April 2003, ending a 13-year legal fight [1]. The council's bronze genocide plaque was stolen in 2007 [2].

title: The Peep Show That Joined a Union
place: Lusty Lady, 1033 Kearny St
hook: Tired of hidden cameras and random firings, the dancers behind the glass on Kearny Street organized, won a contract, and later bought the business.
story: At the Lusty Lady, 1033 Kearny Street, dancers performed behind glass for customers who paid by the minute [1]. In 1996 they started organising, angry about arbitrary firings, pay cuts, and one-way windows that let customers secretly photograph and film them [1][2]. Management fought back with lawyers, propaganda and a two-day lockout, but the workers voted 57 to 15 to join Service Employees International Union Local 790, forming the Exotic Dancers Union [1][2]. In April 1997 about 100 strippers, bouncers, cashiers and janitors ratified a first contract: pay of $12 to $25 an hour, grievance procedures, a sick day, and the removal of the one-way mirrors [2]. "They're tough, and they don't like injustice," said union representative Stephanie Batey, as calls poured in from dancers in Texas, Kansas and Massachusetts [2]. When the owners announced in 2003 that they would close, the workers bought the business and ran it as a cooperative [1]. It lasted another decade. After the co-op missed a rent payment, the landlord would not negotiate, and the country's only unionised, dancer-run peep show closed on September 2, 2013, which was Labor Day [3].

title: The Pigeon Lady flies home to Estonia
place: 1329 Sanchez Street, near Cesar Chavez
hook: Hundreds of pigeons lined the wires waiting for Anna Muru. A court order stopped her feeding them, but her farewell party drew more people than birds.
story: For years Anna Muru made her rounds of Noe Valley streets dropping birdseed from her coat pockets, while hundreds of pigeons waited on the wires overhead [1][2]. In the fall of 1996 a group of mostly homeowners won a restraining order barring the 84-year-old from feeding birds on the street [1]. Her supporters saw something else. One neighbour traced her compulsion to the Second World War, when she had been a homeless, parentless, starving teenager in an Estonia overrun by Nazis and Soviets [1]. That money paid for her return to Estonia, which she had not seen in 50 years [1][2]. At a sidewalk farewell party on May 10 she danced to a swing band. 'They were right too in a way,' she admitted of her critics. 'I did get carried away with the birds.' She flew home on May 19 with her cat, Zsa Zsa [1].
