title: 'We can do that': saving the egrets
place: Mission Creek Park, south bank of Mission Creek
hook: When developers planned to armour Mission Creek with broken concrete, houseboaters spent $30,000 of their own money on newspaper ads: 'Catellus must be stopped.'
story: Houseboaters and conservationists formed the Mission Creek Conservancy in 1983 and published Vanished Waters, a history of Mission Bay, in 1986 to prove the railyards were not a blank slate [1]. The 1991 development plan promised an eight-acre wetland, but it died when Catellus pulled out in 1995 [1]. In 1998 an environmental report revealed plans to line the creek's banks with rip-rap. The Conservancy bought third-page ads in the Examiner and Chronicle declaring 'Catellus must be stopped'. The $30,000 bill, its biggest expense ever, was paid by its board members [1]. Catellus's new vice president, Doug Gardner, called a meeting. Conservancy president Bob Isaacson told him they had 'charismatic shorebirds' and wanted to keep them. 'He looked me in the eye and said, “we can do that”,' Isaacson recalled, 'and for the next decade he was steadfast' [1]. Native plants were replanted along the banks. Residents now report herring runs, sea lions, bat rays, seals and even porpoises [1]. Mayor Willie Brown appointed houseboaters Jack Davis and Corinne Woods to the citizens' advisory committee [2].

title: A public school handed to a corporation
place: Edison school, 3531 22nd Street at Dolores Street
hook: Called the worst elementary school in San Francisco, Edison was given to a New York company in 1998. The fight that followed reached national news.
story: By the late 1990s, Edison Elementary at 22nd and Dolores had a longstanding reputation, repeated in the newspapers, as "the worst elementary school in San Francisco." The district had already tried "reconstitution", replacing the principal and the entire faculty [1]. Fifth-graders wrote angry letters to the press. "It looks like you were only here long enough just to take a picture," one told the Independent [1]. Then, on June 24, 1998, the Board of Education, led by Superintendent Bill Rojas, voted 5 to 2 to turn the school over to Edison Schools, Inc., a New York firm [2]. The question that followed was whether a private company should run a public school on taxpayers' money and make a profit from it. There were charges of pressure on teachers, of test scores boosted by "counseling out" struggling pupils, and of missing bilingual teaching. Many parents, though, praised the longer school day, strict discipline and new computers [2]. A new board majority elected on an anti-privatisation platform voted 6 to 1 in March 2001 to begin revoking the charter, before about 400 mostly pro-Edison parents and students [2]. By October 2002 the Edison Charter Academy was still open, boasting the highest test scores in its history [3].

title: Fifteen seconds to erase Geneva Towers
place: Former Geneva Towers site, now Kelloch and Velasco Mini Park and housing
hook: Police dodged bowling balls thrown from the balconies. Tenants held a candlelight vigil. Then 600 pounds of explosives brought the towers down.
story: By 1991 conditions at Geneva Towers were so bad that the federal housing department (HUD) took the complex over. It was the first time the agency had foreclosed on a property because it was unsafe [1]. "The post office would not deliver on site. Pizza parlors would not deliver," recalled former mayor Art Agnos [1]. Police approaching the towers braced for rocks, televisions and once a bowling ball thrown from the balconies [1]. Still, many tenants called it home. Days before the demolition, former residents held a candlelight vigil. "It was like a little, small community," said Lela Jones [1]. Marie Harrison, a former resident, argued that the towers' bad reputation was unfair to the people living there: "The stigma always fell on the tenants" [2]. At 2:30 p.m. on May 16, 1998, 600 pounds of explosives brought the two towers down in what the Chronicle called the biggest implosion California had seen [1]. Onlookers brought barbecue grills and kegs of beer [2]. HUD promised a 341-unit replacement complex [1]. Today the site holds the Kelloch and Velasco Mini Park, low-income housing and senior homes [1][3]. Former residents still gather for a reunion every Fourth of July weekend [3].

title: The almshouse that nearly closed
place: Laguna Honda Hospital's 2010 buildings, Laguna Honda campus
hook: In 1998 federal regulators threatened the money that kept 1,100 of the city's poorest patients in their beds. Tobacco-lawsuit money helped build a replacement.
story: In the summer of 1998 Laguna Honda faced closure for the first time since it opened as an almshouse 132 years earlier. Federal authorities threatened to withdraw $250,000 a day in Medi-Cal and Medicare payments over deficiencies found by inspectors, chiefly overcrowding and dining conditions. Many patients lived on wards of more than 30 beds and ate beside them. Health director Mitchell Katz acknowledged that closure would have put more than 1,100 patients into a frightening, uncertain future [1]. One of them, Michael Bergin, 54, parked his wheelchair each morning in the vast auditorium whose stage had hosted Bing Crosby and Frankie Lane, and treated it as his office [1]. That July the federal government accepted the hospital's plan of correction [1]. The lasting fix came from voters. City Attorney Louise Renne had won settlements from tobacco companies, and in 1999 Proposition A, passed with 73 percent, directed that money to a new Laguna Honda; $141 million of it went into the project [2]. The new buildings opened in 2010 as California's first green-certified hospital [2]. By December 2010 the move was complete. Residents now live in "households" of 15, among art paid for under the city's two-percent-for-art rule, by 17 artists or 18, depending on the source [2][3].

title: The last Italian bread on Leland
place: Cuneo Bakery, 96 Leland Avenue
hook: The valley's Italians left for the suburbs, but some elderly customers still drove up from Redwood City for bread.
story: Visitacion Valley was once mostly Italian and Maltese. 'The Valley was populated by mostly Maltese and Italians,' Florence Porter, whose parents and grandparents were all born there, told the Grapevine in 1987. 'We never locked our doors in the old days' [1]. By 1998 old-timers said most of their Italian neighbours had moved to the suburbs in the 1960s and '70s, and most of the Italian businesses went with them [2]. Only two were left on Leland Avenue: Armando's Shoe Repair and Cuneo Bakery [2]. Cuneo had once run four bakeries in the city. By then it was a single wholesale operation with a small retail counter out front, carried on by brothers Mario and Dominic Mallegni, whose father had started the company [2]. 'We don't have all that foot traffic like we used to,' said Wendy Mallegni, Mario's wife. 'But we still have elderly Italians who come to pick up bread. Some come all the way from Redwood City' [2]. A neighbourhood directory still listed Cuneo Bakery at 96 Leland Avenue in 2002, a few doors from the Little Quiapo Bake Shop and the Luan Fat Bakery [3].

title: Thirteen years of the disc golf wars
place: The heart of the park and its off-leash dog area, where the course was proposed
hook: A Frisbee sport split McLaren Park's neighbours twice. The second time, somebody planted 'NO DISC GOLF' posts along the fairways, and somebody else kept scraping off the 'NO'.
story: In August 1997 the San Francisco Disc Golf Club approached Rec and Park about a course in the park [2]. On February 8, 1998, more than 150 residents braved rain and flooding to be heard at a meeting. Many loudly opposed it, and Rec and Park's Marvin Yee could barely be heard. To neighbours who felt ignored by Rec and Park, disc golf was 'the final straw' [1]. On March 2 the club withdrew its proposal [2]. In 2010 it came back: Rec and Park said an 18-hole course had been approved in 2005. Opponents said it would take up at least 23 acres in the heart of the park, with 10 of the 18 holes in the off-leash dog play area. A new group, Save McLaren Park, met on April 19. At a crowded meeting the next night the club's newly elected president, Orion Sylvester, said that dog walkers who disliked the course should find another park, and 'pandemonium broke out.' He posted an apology the next day [3]. An opponent staked orange 'NO DISC GOLF' posts where the tees and baskets would go. Most soon vanished. A replacement bolted to a steel bar was bent to the ground. Someone scraped or painted out the 'NO', and someone else kept putting it back with marker pen and stickers [4].

title: World champions in the parents' dining room
place: Moscow Street, Excelsior (the Quitevis family's corner house; exact address not published)
hook: One of the world's most celebrated DJ crews ran its business from a powder-pink corner house on Moscow Street, in what had been Mom and Dad's dining room.
story: Richard Quitevis, the child of parents from the Philippines, grew up on Moscow Street in the Excelsior [3]. As a Balboa High student he hung around nearby Crocker Park, watching breakdancers and graffiti artists. He took the tag Q-Bert while hanging out with a graffiti writer [1]. In Balboa's cafeteria he battled another young DJ, Mix Master Mike [3]. The two teamed up with DJ Apollo and won the DMC world championship three years running, until they were asked to retire in 1993 because other teams were intimidated [1]. The Invisibl Skratch Piklz, the Chronicle later noted, got their start in a garage on Moscow Street [2]. In 1998 a Chronicle writer found the crew outside the powder-pink corner house that Q-Bert shared with his parents, with neighbours lining the sidewalks to watch. Rolling Stone had named them among hip-hop's 50 most influential artists. Their business office was his parents' old dining room, its walls lined with turntables, mixers and records, including a Japanese album of insect mating calls [1]. That November he released Wave Twisters on the crew's own label [1].

title: A Bridge Footing That Became a Marsh
place: Heron's Head Park (former Pier 98)
hook: Pier 98 was built from rubble for a bay crossing that never came. Shorebirds moved in first, and eventually the city gave up and made it a park.
story: In the 1970s trucks dumped fill on the Port's southern waterfront to build an industrial pier. Later it was planned as the footing for a new span across the bay [1]. Both plans fell through and years of arguing followed. Some people wanted all the fill taken out, but the port warned that removal would cost millions and leave a big hole in the shoreline [1]. Meanwhile birdwatchers noticed that as the loose fill settled, tidal pools were forming and migrating birds were arriving [1]. In 1998 crews cleared some 5,000 tons of debris and dug a winding channel to let the tides into a salt marsh. The 25-acre park, which looks like a heron's head from above, opened in 1999 [1]. Hunters Point schoolchildren planted native species, and by 2004 at least 68 native varieties grew there, next door to a working power plant and cargo pier [1]. In 2010 Literacy for Environmental Justice prepared to open its EcoCenter in the park. About 400 young people helped plan it. It was the first building in the city to run completely off the grid, and it treats its own wastewater on site [2].

title: A campus built on a patent fight
place: Genentech Hall, UCSF Mission Bay, 600 16th Street
hook: The first research building on UCSF's new Mission Bay campus was paid for partly by the company the university had sued over human growth hormone.
story: In 1990 the University of California sued Genentech, claiming the biotech pioneer's human growth hormone drug infringed a UC patent covering genetic material from UCSF labs [1][2]. A 1999 jury upheld the patent but deadlocked on infringement, and a second trial was set for January 2000 [1][2]. On November 19, 1999, the two sides settled instead. Genentech agreed to pay $150 million, plus $50 million toward the first biological sciences research building on Mission Bay, which the press release called 'a new 43-acre research and teaching campus'. The building would carry a name Genentech proposed [1]. The deal admitted no wrongdoing. Genentech chief Arthur Levinson, himself a former UCSF postdoc, said the company wanted to avoid 'another jury trial covering complex patent issues' [1]. Under UC patent policy, the three inventors and two collaborators were to share roughly $85 million [1]. The result was Genentech Hall, which was under construction by late 1999: the first building of a campus that would turn old railyards into a biomedical research district [3].

title: Craigslist Outgrows a Condo, Lands on 9th
place: Early Craigslist office on 9th Avenue, Inner Sunset (exact address not given)
hook: The website that changed newspaper classified ads forever started in a Cole Valley condo, then squeezed into an office on Ninth Avenue.
story:
Craig Newmark came to San Francisco in 1993, a programmer of about 40, hired away from IBM by Charles Schwab [1][2]. In 1995 he began emailing friends a list of arts and tech events. People kept asking to join and sending him items, until friends told him he had accidentally built a brand: "craigslist" [1].

For the first couple of years the whole operation ran out of his condo on Cole Street in Cole Valley. When he began hiring, he told the Western Neighborhoods Project, "we realized we were gonna run outta space immediately. So, we found a place on Ninth Avenue in the Sunset." He guessed that was around 1999 or 2000. He remembered the neighbourhood as "very down to earth," full of regular people and Chinese, Japanese and Thai food, Thai being his favorite. They soon outgrew that too and moved downtown [1].

Memories differ on the dates. Columnist Frank Dunnigan wrote that Craigslist was founded in 1995 "in a small 9th Avenue storefront" [3]. In 2000 Newmark stepped down as chief executive to do customer service, a job he said he was much better at [1].

title: Never trust the bushes on Jefferson Street
place: Jefferson St near Taylor St, beside the former Tarantino's
hook: A former Market Street shoeshine man hid behind eucalyptus branches for decades, leapt out at tourists yelling 'ugga bugga', and beat the district attorney in court.
story: David Johnson shined shoes on Market Street and tried dressing as a robot to drum up trade, until so many other people became robots that robots were a glut on the market [1]. Then he spotted some fallen branches. By 1999 he was the Bushman, crouched on the Jefferson Street sidewalk behind a bundle of leaves, commuting by bicycle from Hunters Point with the bush on his handlebars, and holding a city business licence that said "Bushman" [1]. When tourists strolled by he sprang up. His new partner, Gregory Jacobs, then reminded them of their moral duty to pay, plus a "$1 photo tax" [1]. A 1999 Chronicle profile made him a national curiosity [2]. Some merchants said he scared customers away, and in 2004 District Attorney Kamala Harris charged him with four public-nuisance misdemeanours. After a four-day trial with a dozen witnesses the jury acquitted him, and within an hour he was back on his perch [2][3]. Jacobs later split off to run a rival bush. When he died in 2014 the papers mourned "the Bushman", only to learn that the original was alive and still working beside Tarantino's [2][3]. Johnson kept at it until around 2019 [2].

title: Paris murders written before dawn on Alvarado
place: Alvarado Street, Noe Valley, home of mystery writer Cara Black
hook: A former preschool teacher got up at five, wrote Paris thrillers until eleven, then walked down the hill to 24th Street, which she said felt 'kind of like Europe.'
story: On a 1984 visit to Paris, Cara Black toured the Marais with a friend, who told her how her mother, a 14-year-old Jewish girl, had lost her parents to the Nazi deportations and survived the occupation alone [1]. Fifteen years later the story had become Murder in the Marais, the first novel featuring Aimée Leduc, a half-French, half-American private eye whose partner is a computer-hacking dwarf with a black belt [1]. Black, a Chicago-born former preschool teacher, lived on Alvarado Street with her husband Jun Ishimuro, a bookseller, their son, and Ishimuro's mother [1][2]. They had left the Mission and found the house by driving around on Sundays. "Go in, and look out the little window in the bathroom," Ishimuro told her. "That's what we'll have." [1] She wrote from about 5 a.m. until 11, then walked down to 24th Street, which she said "feels kind of like Europe" [1]. She thanked the Noe Valley branch librarians in her acknowledgments and held her book-signing party at Cover to Cover on 24th Street [1]. That first print run of 5,000 soon went into a second printing, and the Aimée Leduc series eventually reached 21 novels [1][2].

title: The Little House on Lake Street
place: 1725 Lake Street, between 18th and 19th Avenues
hook: A small old cottage on a block of mostly three-story homes became a test case for what San Francisco owed its small, cheap houses.
story: In 1999 a turn-of-the-century house at 1725 Lake Street stood among mostly three-story neighbours [1][3]. Developer Ernie McNabb had paid $375,000 for it and wanted to replace it with two 4,000-square-foot condominiums [1]. His lawyer argued that it was too small for anyone to buy and fix up, and that calling it affordable was "erroneous". Neighbours said it was sound housing, and that the condos would block their light and views [1]. In February 1999 the Board of Appeals deadlocked 2-2, so the denial of the demolition stood. "It would open the flood gates," said Commissioner Carole Cullum [1]. Within months the one-bedroom house sold for $500,000 [2]. Just how small it was depends on the report: 1,000, 726 or 900 square feet [1][2][3]. By 2001 its owners, Kenneth and Monique Lew, had a new plan: add two floors, taking it from 23 to 40 feet tall, so they could raise children and, following Asian tradition, eventually take in their parents. "When we first started looking for a house this is all we could afford," Lew said [3]. Larry Minnich, next door at 1727, called the plan "monstrous". Planning Commissioner Myrna Limm agreed it was too big [3].

title: The old Madison school bell rings again
place: Claire Lilienthal School, Madison campus, 3950 Sacramento Street
hook: After two decades of makeshift bungalows and a move across town, a Sacramento Street school got a new home, and its old bell rang again.
story:
The public school at 3950 Sacramento Street was once Madison School, renamed Claire Lilienthal in 1981 after a former school board president [1]. In 1973, when seismic rules were tightened, the district hurriedly put up bungalows on the site. Children were still using them more than twenty years later. "Run-down, horrible, age-old bungalows," one parent called them [1].

The school then moved to the larger old Winfield Scott school on Divisadero Street in the Marina. Its first public event there was the 1996 May Fair [1][2]. Smaller class sizes soon filled that building too, and families asked for their Sacramento Street site back [1].

The bungalows came down in late 1997. Building began in March 1998, three months late because of heavy El Niño rains. Only the old Madison Auditorium was kept. Kindergartners moved in that autumn and the first and second graders on January 19, 1999. Neighbours raised $120,000 for the library [1].

About 400 people came to the dedication in March, close to Claire Lilienthal's birthday. "It was really moving to hear that old Madison school bell again," said John Rothmann, a 1960 Madison graduate. "It brought tears to my eyes" [1].

title: What a Drag: Finocchio's Final Bow
place: Finocchio's, 506 Broadway
hook: For 63 years tourists climbed the stairs above Broadway to see men in spangled gowns. Then the rent went up.
story: For 63 years, tourists and locals climbed to Finocchio's at 506 Broadway, above what became Enrico's cafe, to watch men in spangled gowns sing, dance and crack bawdy jokes [1][2]. Joe Finocchio, who had worked in his father's Prohibition speakeasy, got the idea at his own Stockton Street speakeasy when a tipsy customer did a dead-on Sophie Tucker. He moved the show to Broadway in 1936 and was promptly raided [1][2]. The emcee Carroll Wallace opened each show with: "In New York, Mr. Ziegfeld glorified the American girl ... Here at Finocchio's, we glorify the American boy" [2]. Headliners included Lucien Phelps, a Sophie Tucker specialist for 27 years, and the 6-foot-5 Don McLean, known on stage as Lori Shannon, who played Archie Bunker's drag queen friend on All in the Family [1]. Bob Hope and Tallulah Bankhead came, and Gray Line buses unloaded crowds night after night [1]. By 1999 the buses had stopped. When the landlord raised the rent from $4,000 to $6,000 a month, Eve Finocchio, who had run the club since Joe's death in 1986, announced it would close on November 27 [1]. Lawrence Ferlinghetti's three-word eulogy: "What a drag" [1].

title: 'What happened to the ball?'
place: Willie Mays statue, 24 Willie Mays Plaza (Third and King streets)
hook: The Giants wanted to sculpt Willie Mays making his famous catch. Mays and the sculptor pointed out that his backside would greet every fan coming in.
story: At the December 1997 groundbreaking for the new ballpark, Giants president Peter Magowan surprised Willie Mays by announcing its address: 1 Willie Mays Plaza. By the following August, giving in to fans, the Giants said they would ask the city to make it 24, Mays's number [1]. That day in August 1998 Magowan also unveiled a foot-tall model of the statue at the building site. Magowan had thought of showing Mays's famous over-the-shoulder catch in the 1954 World Series. Mays and the sculptor saw a problem. 'The catch wouldn't be appropriate,' Mays said. 'The reason is you'd have to be backwards. That means you're back end is going to be sticking out coming into the ballpark' [1]. North Carolina sculptor William Behrends instead showed him dropping the bat after a swing. Mays loved it: 'I'm saying, “What happened to the ball? Where did it go?”' [1]. The nine-foot bronze was unveiled on March 31, 2000, ringed by 24 palm trees [1][2]. When Mays died on June 18, 2024, a stream of people came to it with flowers [2][3]. Max Callan remembered seeing him carted around the field at the 2007 All-Star Game when he was six. Omar Moore recalled that many white fans had booed Mays in his first San Francisco years [3].

title: A Bookstore Declared a Landmark
place: City Lights Bookstore, 261 Columbus Ave
hook: As dot-com money swept through San Francisco, the Beats' old bookstore got protection usually given to buildings, not businesses.
story: By 2000 the dot-com boom was sending rents soaring, and City Lights, the bookstore Lawrence Ferlinghetti had opened in 1953, was feeling it. Ferlinghetti said a computer company had tried to push the store out by making the building's owners a huge offer [2]. San Franciscans rallied behind the shop. In June 2000 a city advisory board unanimously backed landmark status for its 1907 building, which would make it hard to demolish [1]. The Daily Telegraph reported that this was the first time landmark status had been offered to a business rather than just a building, in recognition of its "cultural value" [2]. "Being recognized as a landmark is sort of a bulwark against the dumbing down of America," Ferlinghetti said [1]. His co-owner Nancy Peters warned, "The old San Francisco is under attack to the point where it's disappearing" [2]. It was a fitting fight for a store whose founder had been arrested in 1957 for selling Allen Ginsberg's "Howl" [1]. The city designated it Landmark No. 228 in 2001 [3]. The shop outlasted the boom, and Ferlinghetti marked his 100th birthday in March 2019 with a new novel [4].

title: A Filipino plaza inside one building
place: Mint Mall and Hall, 951-957 Mission Street
hook: A 1916 hotel became a mall where Filipinos ate, bought Tagalog books, rehearsed plays and sang karaoke. When dot-com offices began pushing them out in 2000, the community fought back.
story: The building at 951-957 Mission Street went up in 1916 as a hotel with more than 250 rooms. By the late 1940s its upper floors had become apartments [1]. The Nocon family bought it in the 1970s, and in 1981 the ground floor and basement reopened as the Mint Mall Shopping Center. Its first documented tenant was the Philipina Café [1]. Upstairs, in the Mint Hall, about 90% of residents are Filipino, most of them from Pampanga. Newcomers use the rent-controlled units as a first home, then pass the lease on to the next relative [1]. In 1998 Marie Romero moved Arkipelago Books, one of the only Filipino specialty bookstores in the United States, into the basement, and Bindlestiff Studio rehearsed in its hallways [1]. In 2000, during the dot-com boom, a Filipino theater group, a print shop and an office space were evicted to make room for internet tenants. The city cited the building's managers for illegally turning shops into offices [2]. "We need to be cognizant that we are a dying species in the South of Market area," warned the activist Bill Sorro [2]. The Mint Mall Organizing Committee fought the evictions [1]. In October 2025 the city made the Mint Mall and Hall its 321st landmark [1][3].

title: A Real Library for Ocean View
place: Ocean View Branch Library, 345 Randolph Street
hook: For years Ocean View's library was one room with a glass storefront and a toilet too small for a child. In 2000 the neighbourhood finally got a real one.
story: Ocean View's was the 15th branch of the San Francisco Public Library. The first opened in 1903 on Broad Street near Capitol Avenue [1]. Dorothy Coakley remembered the later one-room branch at Broad and Plymouth. It had a glass storefront, a kitchen that doubled as reference room and community copy centre, and "a bathroom so small that even a single child had trouble fitting into it" [2]. Classes from Sheridan and Jose Ortega elementary schools, 30 children and a teacher at a time, packed in several times a week for stories, sharing the room with seniors, teenagers and merchants. Bassim Al-Abood of Fountains's Pizza was a favourite: he could fold paper animals and hand out pizza samples [2]. The branch held its last New Year's party just before 2000 [2]. Neighbourhood leaders including Lovie and Minnie Ward had fought for a new library [3]. The two-storey branch at 345 Randolph Street, designed by the city's Bureau of Architecture, opened on June 7, 2000. It cost $2.5 million, and private funds paid for its furniture and equipment. It was the first new branch building in San Francisco since 1969 [1].

title: A ballpark on the old warehouse wharf
place: Oracle Park, 24 Willie Mays Plaza
hook: The Giants' new park was the first major-league stadium built without public money since Dodger Stadium, and its brick arches echo the warehouse it replaced.
story: Voters in San Francisco, Santa Clara and San Jose had all rejected public financing for a new Giants stadium. The team's new owner, Peter Magowan, found a way to build one privately [1]. Ground was broken at China Basin on December 11, 1997, and the $357 million ballpark opened in 2000 as Pacific Bell Park [1][2]. It was the first big-league park built without public funds since Dodger Stadium in 1962, though the city gave a $10 million tax abatement and $80 million in infrastructure, including a Muni extension and a new I-280 ramp [1][2]. Before the Giants, stevedores and switch engines worked this wharf, moving cargo between freighters in China Basin and a warehouse on the site; the right-field wall's arched openings mimic that warehouse's windows [3]. The water beyond became McCovey Cove, named for the Giants' great first baseman [2][3]. The hated Dodgers swept the first three games played there [1]. The name changed to SBC, AT&T and then Oracle Park [2].

title: A principal and the 'fourth Chinatown'
place: Visitacion Valley Elementary School, 55 Schwerin Street
hook: He used to spend Mondays counting broken windows. By 2000 the principal was predicting his valley would become San Francisco's fourth Chinatown.
story: When Vincent S. Chao became principal of Visitacion Valley Elementary School at 55 Schwerin Street around 1988, much of his time went on vandalism. 'Every Monday morning, it seemed, I would come to work to find dozens of windows broken and computers smashed,' he said [1]. Many pupils lived in Geneva Towers. 'Making home calls in those buildings was scary,' said Chao. 'The hallways were pitch dark. The elevators didn't work' [1]. By 2000 the towers were gone and the school had gone months without a break-in [1]. Its roughly 470 pupils were 45 percent Chinese, 22 percent African American, 15 percent Filipino, 11 percent Latino and 5 percent Samoan, and 63 percent had limited English [1]. The school offered Hawaiian, Samoan, Filipino and Hispanic dance classes. The advertising firm Goodby, Silverstein & Partners, creators of 'Got Milk?', helped the children paint a 'Peace' mural out back [1]. Chao predicted the valley would become San Francisco's 'fourth Chinatown', after Chinatown, Clement Street and Judah-Irving [1]. Two years earlier the school's former PTA president, Carlos Ramirez, had welcomed the newcomers: 'They're just like us - working people' [2].

title: Give Us a Brake, Said Sea Cliff
place: Lake Street at 24th Avenue
hook: Sea Cliff neighbours fed up with speeding cars and tour buses put up their own traffic signs. City Hall cut them down within days.
story: By the late 1990s Sea Cliff's biggest complaint was traffic. In 1998 the newly formed Sea Cliff Residents' Association already had committees on tour buses, parking and the neighbourhood's stone pillars. John Schiffeler of the Sea Cliff Gazette called on residents to stand together against "this onslaught by the tour bus industry" [1]. In 2000, neighbours on West Clay Street got tired of waiting for the city and put up five homemade signs on Lake Street at 22nd and 24th Avenues. They read: "Give Us A Brake. Slow Down. Children at Play." [2] Days later, city traffic engineers came out and cut them down. The acting traffic director explained that such signs were illegal and that the state no longer allowed "children at play" warnings, because it believed they encouraged children to play in the street [2]. Supervisor Gavin Newsom had pushed for lower speed limits and speed humps. "I've ended up doing exactly the opposite of what I set out to do," he said [2]. The Chronicle added that lost tourists wandered past the homes of Robin Williams and Sharon Stone [2].

title: Shot-Out Windows, Then a Family on Sargent
place: Sargent Street, Merced Heights
hook: The day escrow closed on her Merced Heights house, Elaine Ellsworth found every window shot out. Three years later she called her neighbours family.
story:
Around 2000, good friends Elaine Ellsworth and Chris Tweedie each bought a house in Merced Heights, drawn by affordable prices and big views. They later told their story to the "I am OMI" project [1][2]. Their welcomes could not have been more different. Chris's next-door neighbour, Rose Snell, greeted her "with opened arms." But on the day escrow closed on Elaine's house, she found the windows "had all been shot out by a B.B. gun." Then a neighbour's pit bull injured her dog, mysterious, likely poisoned pork chops turned up on her doorstep, and her car was keyed [1].

Then she got to know the street. An elderly Japanese woman across the way always had treats and toys for her dog, Wolfie. Elaine listed the rest: a middle-aged white gay couple, older Black families, young Black professional families who asked her to barbecues, and a backyard neighbour from the Philippines. "I thought was so San Francisco," she said [1]. Across from Chris on Sargent Street lived Juanita, who "knows everybody." The two friends helped start a tree planting with Friends of the Urban Forest, and Chris canvassed for it [1]. She had a stroke while handing out leaflets on Shields Street. Neighbours found her unconscious and got her an ambulance. "I felt like part of a family," Elaine said [1].

title: The neighbours who said no to Home Depot
place: Former Schlage Lock site, Bayshore Blvd at Leland Ave
hook: When the valley's biggest employer shut down, a big-box store wanted its land. Residents had other ideas, and they're still waiting to see them built.
story: Ingersoll-Rand, Schlage's owner, closed the Bayshore factory in 1999, ending more than 70 years of lock-making [1]. By 2000 Home Depot wanted to build a store on the empty site [1]. Neighbours fought it over traffic and other worries, and Supervisor Tom Ammiano sponsored legislation that blocked "big box" stores there [1]. Residents then drew up their own plan. A 2002 city-led community plan asked for a grocery store, open space and housing [1]. The site was polluted, though, and for years it was stuck in a lawsuit over contaminated groundwater. In 2008 Ingersoll-Rand settled and handed the 12.3 acres to the developer Universal Paragon [1]. In 2009 the factory buildings came down, all except the original office [2]. One resident noticed that, with the buildings gone, the shapes of San Bruno Mountain and McLaren Ridge could be seen again from Tunnel Avenue [2]. Building has been slow. In 2018 the site was still terraced dirt awaiting nearly 1,700 homes [3]. Russel Morine, who ran a coffee shop on Leland, had predicted in 2011: "I'm pretty sure something will happen … eventually" [4].

title: The plaza a developer nearly built on
place: Japantown Peace Plaza, between Japan Center East and West on the former Buchanan Street
hook: Japantown's central square began as private property. When a new owner wanted to build on it, the community protested until the city bought it.
story: The open space at the heart of Japan Center sits on a closed-off block of Buchanan Street [1]. It was not built as a public park. It was first owned by a private real estate company, National Braemar, which sold it to developer Sinclair Louie, whose plans to build on the open space were stopped by community protest. The City and County of San Francisco eventually bought it [1]. As first laid out, the plaza had a granite keyhole-shaped pool at the base of the pagoda, long reflecting pools on the north side, a covered walkway and a large drum tower in the middle [1]. It had drainage problems. In 2000 Kenji Murokami redesigned it and removed the covered walkway, and other original features were changed or removed [1][2]. The eternal flame, said to be 17 centuries old and brought from the Sumida Shrine in Osaka, was moved from inside the pagoda to a glass case behind the water feature [1]. Mayor Willie Brown rededicated the plaza in 2003 [1]. By 2009 it belonged to the city's Recreation and Park Department [2]. Every spring the stage around the pagoda fills for the Cherry Blossom Festival [1].

title: Under the dance floor, the 1906 fire
place: DNA Lounge, 375 Eleventh Street
hook: When a former Netscape programmer dug up his nightclub's floor in 2000 to fix the sewer, the building smelled of smoke for days. Underneath lay the burnt rubble of 1906.
story: Before 1906 this part of Eleventh Street was lined with flats. By 1893 the lot held two row houses, each with a pair of two-bedroom flats [1]. Like nearly everything around them, they burned after the earthquake [1]. Photos from 1923 appear to show Dave Lerer, who was in the truck-parts business, putting up the building that stands here now. At various times it was an auto repair shop and, reportedly, a foundry that cast manhole covers for the city [1]. In 1977, according to the club's own history, it became a leather bar called Chaps. On November 22, 1985, Jim English, Jeff Mason and Brian Raffi reopened it as DNA Lounge, a dance club [1]. In February 2000 Jamie Zawinski, a former Netscape programmer, packed a city Board of Appeals hearing with at least 150 fans while the police tried to use his purchase of the club to take away its after-hours permits [2]. That year, during a remodel, he had holes dug to repair the sewer lines [1]. Under two or three feet of sand lay four feet or more of old bricks and burned wood, the wreckage of whatever had stood here before the fire. The disturbed cinders made the whole building smell like fire for days, he wrote, "after being underground for ninety-four years" [1].

title: Where Five LaBountys Ate Thanksgiving
place: 139-141 11th Avenue near California Street
hook: A historian drove his brother past their childhood flat and found it stripped to the frame. Soon their old address no longer existed.
story: In the early 1970s Woody LaBounty's grandmother would walk him and his brother to catch the 21 Hayes at its terminus at Eighth and California, bound for the Emporium downtown [2]. Home was a basement flat at 139 11th Avenue, in a two-unit house that held nine people in 1975 [1]. In 1999 he saw the house listed for $689,000 [1]. A year or so later his brother visited from Seattle, and they drove by. The building had been stripped to its frame; they could see straight through where their apartment had been into a weedy backyard [1]. A woman got out of a car and said she owned it. 'It was a nice place to live,' LaBounty offered. 'Too small,' she replied [1]. When he returned months later, a double garage had replaced the ground-floor flat 'where five LaBountys had eaten Thanksgiving dinners' [1]. The address 139 no longer existed [1]. He guessed the rebuilt house held two or three people, with room for two cars [1]. His essay became a plea to value the ordinary Richmond and Sunset houses that no preservation society fights for [1].

title: A Banker's Free Banjo Festival
place: Hellman Hollow (formerly Speedway Meadow)
hook: A former Lehman Brothers president who took up banjo in his seventies paid for one of America's biggest music festivals and refused to let anyone sponsor it.
story: Warren Hellman had been president of Lehman Brothers at 39 and co-founded the private equity firm Hellman & Friedman [2]. On a ski trip in 2000 he told his friend Jonathan Nelson about his dream of a bluegrass festival in the park [1]. Booker Dawn Holliday warned him that if the bill featured only the music he loved, mainly Hazel Dickens and her songs about coal-mining strikes, "there will be about 13 people there" [1]. The first festival, in 2001, drew perhaps 13,000 people [1]. Hellman paid for it every year, turned down corporate sponsors and kept it free [2][3]. When Emmylou Harris played that first year with her non-bluegrass band, the name slowly shifted, and in 2004 it officially became Hardly Strictly Bluegrass [3]. Hellman got serious about the banjo after 70 and toured with his band, the Wronglers [1][2]. In 2011 more than 600,000 people came, to a meadow supervisors had just renamed for him [1]. He died that December at 77, having arranged for the festival to be funded for years after his death [1][2].

hook: A 1911 Excelsior firehouse built for horse-drawn engines became home to a Disney teenager who found out she was royalty.

Only the outside is on screen. The interior was rebuilt on a soundstage at Walt Disney Studios in Burbank, the same stage where Mary Poppins was filmed [2]. Elsewhere in the city, a cable car mishap was staged at Broadway and Taylor Streets, while the 'Baker Beach' party was really filmed at Zuma Beach in Malibu [2]. The film premiered on July 29, 2001 [2].

title: Fifteen pylons for the pink triangle
place: Pink Triangle Park, Market & 17th St
hook: A weedy scrap of city land above the Muni tunnel became America's first memorial to the gay victims of Nazi persecution.
story: Where Castro, Market and 17th Streets meet, there was once a city-owned scrap of land choked with weeds, vines and trash. In June 2001 neighbours from the Eureka Valley Promotion Association held a 'Big Dig' with a city public works crew. In October more than 20 volunteers came back to plant 40 rose bushes and 30 rosemary plants [1]. Artists Robert Bruce and Susan Martin designed the memorial. Bruce had been a founding member of STOP AIDS in 1982 [2]. It is a set of 15 granite pylons, each inlaid with a pink quartz triangle, arranged together into one larger triangle that points toward Harvey Milk Plaza [2]. The stone was cut in Minnesota. The memorial was dedicated on December 10, 2001, the anniversary of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights [1][3]. Some later accounts give its opening as 2003 [4]. It is called the first permanent, free-standing memorial in America to the gay men and lesbians persecuted by Nazi Germany [3][4]. The artists wanted visitors to remember the colours the camps assigned: pink triangles for gay men, black triangles for lesbians, yellow stars for Jews [2]. Visitors may take one quartz stone home [3].

title: From Needle Alley to Microbrew Alley
place: 500 block of Haight Street (Toronado, 547 Haight)
hook: At the turn of the millennium, the Chronicle called the Lower Haight the city's underground: beer bars, record shops, DJ nights and a dark bar lit by static.
story: "Lower Haight is to the underground what Upper Haight was 30 years ago," the Chronicle declared in 2001 [1]. The 500 block of Haight Street, once known as Needle Alley, had become Microbrew Alley. On one side was the Toronado, where owner David "Big Daddy" Keene kept a back room lined with hundreds of custom tap handles. Across the street, English fans at the Mad Dog in the Fog watched European football over pints at 6 a.m. [1]. Next door to the Toronado, Noc Noc was lit mostly by old TVs showing static [1]. The strip had five record stores, which supplied the records DJs wheeled into clubs on dollies [1]. At 460 Haight, Nickie's BBQ was one of the Bay Area's oldest destination dance clubs. It hosted Grateful Dead jams by Dark Star Dan on Mondays and Cheb I. Sabbah's global "Outer National Mix" on Tuesdays [1]. Nickie's went back to 1948, when it was Nicki's Barbecue. It was later a dancehall and a dive bar, and from 2007 an Irish sports bar [2]. In 2020 a longtime regular, Tom Mills, bought it. He said he and 20 or 30 other regulars thought of it as "the neighborhood's living room" [2].

title: Lantern on the Hill Finds a Keeper
place: Chinese Historical Society of America, former Chinatown YWCA, 965 Clay St
hook: Julia Morgan designed it with dragons on the floor and Chinese towers on the roof. After the 1989 earthquake it stood empty for years before historians moved in.
story: The Chinatown YWCA began in 1916 in an old saloon at Stockton and Sacramento [1]. For its new home on Clay Street, the YWCA hired Julia Morgan, who worked closely with a Chinese American committee [1]. Her 1932 building mixed Western and Chinese design: a courtyard with a koi pond, three Chinese-style towers, glazed tiles with Chinese motifs and a dragon painted on the corridor floor. It also kept white and Chinese American residents apart under one roof [1][2]. The 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake damaged the building, and the YWCA could not afford to retrofit it, so it sold up [1]. The Chinese Historical Society of America, founded in 1963 by Thomas W. Chinn, C.H. Kwock, Chingwah Lee, H.K. Wong and Thomas W.S. Wu, had moved from a small donated building on Adler Place to Commercial Street and Broadway [1]. With help from Supervisor Tom Hsieh and Mayor Willie Brown it bought the building in 1996, and in 2001 it opened its museum there [1]. The building had sat unused for 14 years [2]. In 2004 the restoration of the "Lantern on the Hill" won a National Preservation Honor Award from the National Trust [2].

title: Let the Dog Out!
place: Doggie Diner head, Sloat Boulevard median at 45th Avenue
hook: The last grinning fiberglass dachshund survived a developer, a two-year fight and an April Fool's Day nosedive onto Sloat Boulevard. Then it became an official city landmark.
story: Doggie Diner ran from 1948 to 1986 and grew to about 30 hot dog stands. Each had a fiberglass dachshund head in a chef's hat and bow tie, sketched by billboard designer Harold Bachman in the early 1960s [1]. The last head in San Francisco stood on a pole above a former Doggie Diner on Sloat Boulevard that had become the Carousel restaurant. When the Sloat Garden Center, which owned the property, wanted to clear the site, fans gathered thousands of signatures and held eat-ins. Bill Griffith drew the fight into his Zippy the Pinhead strip. The city took ownership of the head after two years of campaigning [1]. Then, on April Fool's Day 2001, a windstorm blew it off its rusted pole and smashed its nose [1][2]. John Law remembers Ed Lee, then head of Public Works and later mayor, sweating at the scene in the cold ocean wind [1]. Public Works recast the snout from a head lent by Burning Man co-founder John Law. The Art Commission consulted Bachman to match the original candy-apple red [2]. On June 30, 2001, about 400 devotees chanted "Let the dog out!" as a crane lifted the hood [2]. It became a city landmark in 2006 and now stands on the Sloat median at 45th Avenue [1].

title: Peeling Back an Airfield to Find a Marsh
place: Crissy Field tidal marsh
hook: In 1999 a channel was cut through the sand, and for the first time in about a century the bay's tides flowed back into Crissy Field.
story: Crissy Field sits on the site of an ancient 130-acre salt marsh where Ohlone people once gathered fish and shellfish. The Army treated it as a wasteland to be dumped on and drained, and later built an airfield on the filled land [1]. When the Park Service took over in 1994, the site was 'a derelict concrete wasteland' [1]. From 1997, crews removed almost 90,000 tons of contaminated material. Between 1998 and 2000 they rebuilt an 18-acre tidal marsh and 16 acres of dunes, digging out more than 230,000 cubic yards of dirt, sand and mud [1]. In November 1999 a channel was opened, and fresh and salt water met there for the first time in 100 years [1]. The Haas family's Haas, Jr. Fund had paid for early planning in 1986. In 1997 the fund and Colleen and Robert Haas pledged $18 million, then the largest cash gift in National Park Service history. In all, the community raised more than $34.5 million [2]. Crissy Field reopened in 2001, and the Crissy Field Center opened that May to bring in young people with little access to national parks [2][3]. Nearly 100 bird species have since been recorded using the marsh [1].

title: Six water lots become a greenway
place: Hans Schiller Plaza, Visitacion Valley Greenway, Leland Avenue at Peabody Street
hook: Six empty blocks of Water Department land ran through the valley. Neighbours and artists spent years turning them into a chain of gardens, one gate at a time.
story: Six block-long parcels spill down the hillside through the heart of the valley. They are former Water Department land, left undeveloped [1][2]. In the 1990s neighbours organised the Visitacion Valley Greenway Project to turn them into parks. Getting permission to build on what was then a Public Utilities Commission easement took five years of negotiations [2][3]. The first site finished was Hans Schiller Plaza, at Leland and Peabody, which opened in March 2001 [3]. The Columbia Foundation paid for it in memory of Hans J. Schiller, a Bay Area architect and environmental activist whom Governor Jerry Brown had appointed to the Bay Conservation and Development Commission [3]. That May the new plaza held its first big event, 'Weaving Our Roots', a Native American celebration with Sámi and Diné (Navajo) dancing and drumming and jingle-dress dancing [4]. Artists shaped the whole greenway. Sculptor Fran Martin coordinated the project from 1994 and made its tile work and weir walls. Jim Growden, a sculptor in wood and steel, forged eight of its twelve signature gates [3]. A community garden followed in 2008, and the Greenway now serves as an outdoor classroom [1].

title: The dachshund that nose-dived onto Sloat
place: Doggie Diner head, Sloat Boulevard median at 45th Avenue
hook: San Francisco's last Doggie Diner head survived a feud with the garden center next door, then a windstorm broke its nose. Four hundred fans howled at its comeback.
story: Doggie Diner began when Al Ross sold hot dogs from a stand outside Oakland's Castlemont High School in 1948 [1]. The chain's last restaurant closed in 1986 [1]. Its grinning dachshund heads, in chef's hats and bow ties, came down, but one stayed on Sloat Boulevard, where a plaque now says it "stood outside the last operating Doggie Diner restaurant" [2]. In 2000 the owners of the neighboring Sloat Garden Center announced plans to move it. After an uproar they deeded the dog to the city [3]. Then in early April 2001, gusty winds sent it nose-diving onto Sloat Boulevard [3]. The Department of Public Works molded a new snout from a head lent by John Law, who owns three, and repainted it candy-apple red; the city Art Commission consulted its original artist, Harold Bachman, to match the colors. DPW also gave the dog a new galvanized steel pole [3]. The city paid about half of the $25,000 cost, and donations covered the rest [3]. At the June 2001 unveiling, about 400 fans chanted "Let the dog out!" and Mayor Willie Brown joked, "No, that's my head!" [3]. In 2006 it became City Landmark No. 254 [1][2].

title: Waiting for the 52 Excelsior
place: Excelsior Avenue at Mission Street, site of Marta Ayala's mural
hook: A mural about waiting for the bus, a sculpture that translates the neighbourhood's Latin name, and street-sign murals on a freeway bridge: the Excelsior's open-air gallery.
story: On Excelsior Avenue at Mission Street is 'Waiting for the 52 Excelsior,' a 2001 mural by Marta Ayala [1]. It is one of many public artworks in the district. A lot of them came out of the Excelsior Action Group's mural program, which brings together students, San Francisco artists and neighbours. Their subjects include neighbourhood pride, local landmarks and buildings, multiculturalism and landscapes. There are mosaics too, among them the tiled steps in Kenny Alley [1]. On Francis Street at Mission, Delvin Kenobe Leake's 'Music is Freedom' mural, paid for by the action group and the Cucalon family, is dedicated to the Excelsior's residents and families [1]. At Geneva Avenue and Mission stands the 'Ever Upward' sculpture, which SF Heritage lists among the district's standout mosaics; the name translates the Latin word excelsior [1][3]. In 2011 members of Excelsior community groups painted murals along the sidewalks of the Mission Street bridge over I-280 and Alemany Boulevard. They show the district's 'international' street signs, such as Russia and Persia [2]. And in 2025 Tim Hon and Eric Nodora of the graffiti collective Illuminaries spent about seven hours painting a giant pool player and neon billiard balls on the side of the Billiard Palacade at Mission and Rolph streets [4].

title: A buried creek and a hubcap garden
place: Cotter Street near San Jose Avenue (neighbourhood garden lot described in 2002)
hook: Under Cayuga Avenue runs the south fork of Islais Creek. In 2002 an artist tracked it to a flooded lot full of geese, hubcaps and vegetables.
story: While researching the Balboa Park area for a city planning project, public artist and historian Ann Chamberlain found a 1926 photograph of a railroad bed with a creek running beside it. "What happened to the water?" she wondered [1]. The railroad bed turned out to be today's Alemany Boulevard. The creek was the south fork of Islais Creek, sometimes called the Cayuga River, which runs in a culvert under Cayuga Avenue [1]. Neighbours could hear it through the storm drains, and in the rainy season it squelched underfoot [1]. Its headwaters lie beneath Cayuga Park at the far end of the avenue [2]. Near Cotter Street, behind a plank fence, Chamberlain showed a Chronicle reporter a block-long vacant lot that neighbours had made into a park. It was private land but had no 'keep out' signs. There was hubcap art on the fence, a horseshoe pit, geese in a pen, and vegetable gardens around a circular path [1]. A yellow traffic sign on the fence read "FLOODED". "That's why there is this strange piece of land," she said. "It probably flooded and they couldn't build on it" [1].

title: Boy Scouts Mark the End of the Road
place: Western Terminus of the Lincoln Highway marker, Legion of Honor parking area
hook: America's first coast-to-coast highway starts in Times Square and ends beside a bus stop at the Legion of Honor. Two Boy Scout troops marked the spot, 74 years apart.
story: The Lincoln Highway, dreamed up by Carl Fisher in 1912–13, ran about 3,300 miles from Times Square to Lincoln Park, where its western terminus was dedicated in 1915 [1][2]. In 1925 the new numbered federal highways broke it into pieces [2]. As one of its last acts, the Lincoln Highway Association had Boy Scouts set roughly 2,440 concrete markers along the route on 1 September 1928. Each carried a bronze Lincoln medallion [2]. A San Francisco troop set the one reading 'Western Terminus of the Lincoln Highway' here [1]. The old highway was split among numbered routes, and Interstate 80 later followed much of it [1][2]. The association re-formed in 1992 to preserve the route [2]. On 14 June 2002 San Francisco's Boy Scout Troop 17 set a replica marker a few feet from the original spot [1]. In 2005 the association's California chapter added an interpretive sign. It tells how a young Lt. Col. Dwight Eisenhower crossed on the 1919 Army convoy, and how as president he signed the 1956 Interstate Highway Act [1]. An original 1928 marker survives nearby at 32nd Avenue and El Camino del Mar [2].

title: Collard Greens on a Dumping Ground
place: Quesada Avenue median, 1700 block
hook: In 2002 two neighbours looked at a Quesada Avenue median full of rusting appliances, needles and bottles, and decided to plant collard greens.
story: The palm-lined median down the 1700 block of Quesada Avenue, just off Third Street, had been neglected for years and was covered in rusting appliances and raw garbage [1]. One neighbour described "dead grass, weeds... beer cans, liquor bottles, needles," with drug dealing and violence on the block [2]. In early 2002 Annette Smith and Karl Paige dug up the earth and planted collard greens and flowers [1][2]. Neighbours brought plants from their own backyards. Jeffrey Betcher joined them, and after a community meeting in 2003 the group became the Quesada Gardens Initiative [2]. By 2006 the whole length of the median was a vegetable and flower garden [1], and the project grew to six community gardens, two murals and a weekly newsletter [2]. "People respond differently to everything when they're on a block where they have a sense that people know one another," Betcher said [2]. Paige died in 2007 and Smith moved off the block in 2009. The neighbours who took over still look after the garden the two of them started [1]. Photographs from August 2007 show the median in full growth [3].

title: Garcia T-shirts to rebuild Crocker Park
place: Crocker Amazon Playground, Geneva Avenue and Moscow Street
hook: While the rest of the country fretted over its 401(k)s, Excelsior neighbours raised $50,000 to fix a run-down ballpark, and a loan consultant enlisted Jerry Garcia's drawings to raise more.
story: Michael Arago remembered Crocker Park in the 1970s as 'an ill-kept ballpark more suitable for getting loaded than anything else' [3]. In 2002, while the rest of the country moaned about its 401(k)s, residents of the Excelsior and neighbouring District 11 areas put up $50,000 to help the Neighborhood Parks Council rebuild the dilapidated Crocker Amazon Playground, and kept raising more [1]. One fundraiser was launched at the Italian American Social Club on Russia Avenue. Tom Murphy, a loan consultant, unpacked a carton of Jerry Garcia T-shirts. He had spearheaded the campaign and got the Garcia estate's permission to use the guitarist's drawings of critters [1]. 'I grew up knowing world-famous Jerry Garcia grew up here, but nobody else in the city does,' Murphy said [1]. He later said he had found out in 1995 that Garcia came from the Excelsior and wondered 'how come nobody knows this?' [2] The same year Murphy founded Jerry Day, a yearly concert in McLaren Park started to raise money for a dilapidated Excelsior playground, with the Garcia estate's blessing and financial support [2][4]. In 2011 thousands turned up for what the Chronicle billed as the ninth Jerry Day [4].

title: Laughing Sal Moves to the Wharf
place: Musée Mécanique, Shed A, Pier 45
hook: Evicted from the Cliff House, a century-old arcade of fortune tellers and cackling automatons found a new home among Fisherman's Wharf fish sheds.
story: For nearly a century, coin-operated amusement machines had whirred and clicked at the Cliff House, on the city's far western edge [1]. In February 2002 came the news that the Musée Mécanique had to be out by September 10: the National Park Service was rebuilding the Cliff House, and its plans had no room for the museum [1]. "All we have to offer here," said manager Dan Zelinsky, "is a good time" [1]. The machines found a new home on the other side of the city, in Shed A on Pier 45 at Fisherman's Wharf [2][3]. The collection had begun with Zelinsky's father, who started collecting at 11 and filled the family's basement near the Presidio [3]. Today visitors feed coins to Laughing Sal, the gap-toothed cackler from Playland at the Beach, to a Ferris wheel made of toothpicks by San Quentin inmates, and to a Wurlitzer organ first installed in a Tennessee merry-go-round in 1917, which Zelinsky, gliding between machines on roller skates, oils himself [2][3]. When the pandemic shut the doors in March 2020, the museum asked the public for $250,000, "or one million quarters," to get through a year [3].

title: Ocean View Park's Promise, Ninety Years Late
place: OceanView Village, 3995 Alemany Boulevard
hook: A 1910s brochure hailed "The Gem of Subdivisions" and promised business lots. The shops finally came in 2002, and a Korean supermarket in 2021.
story: In the 1910s J.W. Wright & Co. sold lots in "Ocean View Park", which it called "The Gem of Subdivisions in San Francisco." The brochure tied the venture, somewhat mysteriously, to the 1915 Panama-Pacific Exposition, and promised that "Business streets will also develop here" [1]. They didn't. The Ocean Shore Railway cut across the plat on two diagonals, and later Brotherhood Way split it with a gully. Apart from four or five homes from the brochure's era, including two cottages on Belle Avenue near the city line, the tract was built up in the 1930s, without so much as a corner grocery [1]. By early 2002, a new housing and shopping complex, OceanView Village, was rising in the niche between Highway 280, Highway 1, the Daly City BART station and Alemany Boulevard. It promised apartments, a Rite Aid and an Albertsons [1]. In April 2021 the Korean grocery chain H Mart opened its first San Francisco store there, at 3995 Alemany Boulevard. By 2022 it had leased a neighbouring former 24 Hour Fitness to expand its food court [2].

title: Tai chi mornings on the weekend hills
place: McLaren Park's weekend lawns and paths (practice spots varied)
hook: Among the dog walkers and tennis players on weekend mornings, one group stood out: tai chi students of a master who arrived with thirty years of martial-arts training.
story: In 2004 the Chronicle noted that on weekdays McLaren Park's visitors were solitary walkers, runners and people practising tai chi [1]. In 2002 Master He XiaoDong founded the Beacon Tai Chi Group with the Visitacion Valley Community Beacon Center. She taught Yang-style tai chi to anyone 18 or older, and had practised Chinese martial arts for more than 30 years. By 2007, Tom Lee wrote in the Grapevine, a walk through the park on a Saturday or Sunday morning meant passing dog walkers, tennis players and cyclists, and 'most notably' tai chi enthusiasts 'practicing their art diligently' [2]. The group performed at community events, health expos and martial-arts tournaments, and at the retirement party of Marlene Tran, a former San Francisco Immigrant Rights Commissioner who had taught in the city's schools for more than 35 years [2]. Its fourth annual Tai Chi Festival was held in the Visitacion Valley Middle School auditorium on September 9, 2007 [2][3]. The group reflected a changing valley. In 1998 the Chronicle reported that over the previous decade Visitacion Valley had become 'a burgeoning nexus for Chinese immigrants' [4].

title: The Last Day of Shouting on Pine Street
place: Pacific Stock Exchange, 301 Pine Street
hook: For more than a century San Francisco had a trading floor where brokers shouted orders face to face. Computers ended it, and the floor became a gym.
story: Brokers had traded in San Francisco since the San Francisco Stock and Bond Exchange was founded in 1882 to handle deals tied to the Comstock Lode. In 1956 it merged with the Los Angeles Oil Exchange to form the Pacific Coast Stock Exchange, which traded from this 1915 former U.S. Treasury building, remodelled in 1930 by Miller & Pflueger with Art Deco granite figures by Ralph Stackpole [1]. Ironically, it was among the first exchanges to automate, putting computers on the floor in 1969 [1]. By 1999 the Chronicle reported that the exchange planned to abandon Pine Street, leaving the city without a central stock market for the first time in more than a century; with most trades done by computer, a floor of traders scurrying from post to post was obsolete [2]. "The floor is jazz, the adrenaline in your body," said independent floor broker Frank Gallagher. "I'm not looking forward to sitting in an office. I like my little world" [2]. The exchange sold its equities business in 2000, closed its Los Angeles floor in 2001 and its San Francisco floor in 2002 [1]. The trading hall later reopened as an Equinox fitness club [3].

title: The women's building taken back in court
place: Japanese YWCA / Issei Women's Building, 1830 Sutter Street
hook: Issei women paid for this Julia Morgan building but weren't allowed to own it. Seventy years later, their community sued to get it back.
story: In 1912, Issei women barred from key facilities of the main YWCA founded the first independent Japanese YWCA in the United States [1]. They raised money for a building at 1830 Sutter Street, designed by Julia Morgan, who donated her services and brought antiques from Hearst's San Simeon to decorate it. It opened in 1932 and even had a Noh theatre stage [2]. California's Alien Land Law barred Issei from owning property, so the women asked the San Francisco YWCA to hold the title in trust for the Japanese American community [1]. In 1996 the YWCA, short of money, put the building up for sale for $1.65 million and denied there had ever been a trust [2]. In 1997 Soko Bukai, a group of Japanese American churches, sued, inspired by the campaign for redress for the camps [1][2]. A settlement in February 2002 gave title to Nihonmachi Little Friends, a community child care centre [2]. The building was listed on the National Register in 2020 and is also a San Francisco landmark [1][3].

title: Upstairs from the funeral parlour, a college
place: Former Reilly Co./Goodwin & Scannell Funeral Home, 1598 Dolores Street at 29th
hook: For about a decade, students on the top floor of a Dolores Street funeral home learned to embalm. Many went on to become coroners. San Francisco rents buried the school.
story:
The San Francisco College of Mortuary Science opened on June 6, 1930, and graduated more than 5,000 students [1]. It started out on Post Street. In the early 1990s it moved to the top floor of the Reilly Co./Goodwin & Scannell Funeral Home, a two-storey Romanesque building at 1598 Dolores Street, on the corner of 29th [1]. Students learned on the job. The college's own chapel handled about 350 funerals a year, often for low-income families. Many graduates went on to work as coroners and deputy coroners [1].

The city's costs finished it off. Faculty couldn't afford to live in San Francisco, and students doubled and tripled up in apartments. The last class graduated on June 8, 2002, and the curriculum moved to American River College in Sacramento [1]. Since 1997 the funeral home had been owned by Steven Welch, of the Duggan-Welch family of Mission District funeral directors. Their plan to replace the 1920s mortuary with 13 condominiums led to a noisy neighbourhood fight over height and parking. At one Upper Noe Neighbors meeting, residents objected loudly to the developer's claims of local support. Supervisor Mark Leno pressed for a compromise [2].

title: Why the Tutoring Centre Sells Peg Legs
place: 826 Valencia and the Pirate Supply Store, 826 Valencia St
hook: The zoning said the storefront had to sell something. Dave Eggers decided it would sell glass eyes, beard trimmings and planks for pirates.
story: In 2002 the author Dave Eggers and teacher Nínive Calegari leased a space on Valencia Street and hung a sign: "Free Tutoring. Mops. A Pufferfish." [1] The idea was free one-on-one writing help for children, especially those whose parents worked several jobs or did not speak English [2]. The lease came with a catch: zoning required part of the space to be used for retail [2]. Eggers's answer was a pirate supply store selling drawers of glass eyes, peg legs and beard trimmings, "because not all pirates can grow their own," as the store manager said with a straight face [2]. By 2007 the shop had taken $227,000 in a year, and chapters elsewhere copied the trick with superhero, space-travel and secret-agent stores [2]. Eggers told Forbes that writing is "a craft, not thunderbolts and lightning" [2]. The organisation named after its address opened more San Francisco centres and helped launch the national 826 network in 2008 [1].

title: 'I'm taller than Willie Mays'
place: Willie McCovey statue, China Basin Park, south shore of McCovey Cove
hook: The water beyond right field got its name from two sportswriters. Its namesake got a bronze across the cove, and a one-liner about height.
story: The water beyond the ballpark's right-field wall is properly China Basin, and the nickname has never become official, the mouth of Mission Creek. The San Jose Mercury News columnist Mark Purdy proposed naming it for Willie McCovey, and his colleague Leonard Koppett of the Oakland Tribune supplied the catchier 'McCovey Cove' [1]. In May 2003 the Giants unveiled a nine-foot bronze of McCovey's left-handed swing across the cove, cast by William Behrends, who had also made the Mays statue [2][3]. Eyes stayed mostly dry through a long ceremony until former teammates Tom Haller, Hobie Landrith and Mike McCormick began to choke up. Then McCovey did too [2]. Asked why his statue was taller than Mays's, he replied: 'Haven't you ever seen us standing side by side? I'm taller than Willie Mays' [2]. McCovey played 19 of his 21 big-league seasons in San Francisco, hit 521 home runs, and died in 2018 at 80 [3]. In 2020 his statue was taken down and stored during construction of the Mission Rock neighbourhood. On March 18, 2024, it went back up in the new China Basin Park, a little west of its old spot and still in view of the ballpark [3].

title: A school named for a poet
place: June Jordan School for Equity (former Luther Burbank Middle School), 325 La Grande Avenue
hook: On the park's western edge, a campus planned in 1950 as a junior high became home to a high school designed by teachers and parents and named for a poet.
story: The school at 325 La Grande Avenue sits on the park's western edge, and the site was claimed early. In 1950 the city's plan for John McLaren Park recommended reserving 11 acres between Persia and Brazil avenues, the stretch where the campus stands, for a junior high school the Board of Education had proposed [1]. For years the campus was Luther Burbank Middle School. In March 1995 it was where volunteers were asked to gather at 9 a.m. for a big clean-up of McLaren Park [2]. Today it is home to June Jordan School for Equity [3]. The high school grew out of Small Schools for Equity, founded in 2000 by a group of San Francisco high school teachers and community members. In 2001 they teamed up with the San Francisco Organizing Project. Through one-on-one conversations and regular meetings with hundreds of families from southeast San Francisco, they designed a small school modelled on successful urban schools in New York and elsewhere [4]. It opened in fall 2003 and was named for June Jordan, the late poet, UC Berkeley professor and social activist [4]. The district describes its mission as serving working-class students from communities of color, including Latinx, Pilipinx, Black and Pacific Islander youth, and preparing them to be 'agents of positive change' [3].

title: Padlocked on Labor Day weekend
place: Former Real Food Company, 3939 24th Street
hook: Workers at a beloved health-food store asked for a living wage. Days later the doors were chained, and the building stayed dark for years.
story: Kimball and Jane Allen opened the Real Food Company on 24th Street in 1970. In 2002 they sold it to Fresh Organics, a subsidiary of the Utah supplement maker Nutraceutical [1]. In 2003 the staff began organising with the Industrial Workers of the World and asked for a living wage, better equipment and a say in running the store [1]. On Thursday, August 28, the workers on shift were told the store was closing immediately. Shoppers arrived for the Labor Day weekend to find the doors chained and padlocked, and about 30 workers lost their jobs [1][2]. The company said it was a remodel. The ex-workers called it union-busting and filed charges [1]. In 2005 a National Labor Relations Board judge ruled for them on nearly all counts, and a board panel upheld that in 2007 [2]. In 2009 a settlement awarded $371,219 in back pay and interest, but no reinstatement [2]. The building sat empty. Peter Gabel later said the company kept it closed for 15 years [3]. The anger also built something: neighbours started a farmers' market that grew into the Noe Valley Town Square [3].

title: Palm Trees for a Tired Avenue
place: Ocean Avenue at Jules Avenue
hook: Within a month of Dan Weaver moving to the Ingleside in 1978, Ocean Avenue lost its only grocery and its movie palace. He spent years helping bring it back.
story: When Dan Weaver moved to Jules Street in 1978, Ocean Avenue's only grocery store and the El Rey Theatre closed within a month. The street, he said, "looked like a place that was coming undone" [1]. It had been a busy local shopping street: the 1956 merchants' directory listed seven groceries and bakeries, four drug stores, six beauty parlours and barbers, twelve dry-goods shops and thirteen service businesses [2]. Weaver helped found the Ocean Avenue Renaissance Committee. It linked the "front-lawn neighborhoods" north of Ocean with the grid streets of the Ingleside. "We [had] a dozen trees in a mile," he said. "We needed at least a hundred more" [1]. The roadway and streetcar tracks were being rebuilt, and in the late 1990s government money was available. The plan brought better pedestrian access, blue-tinted streetlights and palm trees, which were in the ground by May 2003 [1]. There were neighbourhood battles over details, but everyone agreed something was needed [1]. In April 2005 history panels went up in 29 Ocean Avenue storefronts, from a donut shop to a hobby store, for a month-long OMI History Walk [3].

title: Refugees remake a corner as Little Saigon
place: Little Saigon, Larkin St between Eddy and O'Farrell
hook: Fleeing war and refugee camps, Southeast Asian families filled Tenderloin studios in the 1980s. Two decades later, the city made their Larkin Street official.
story: From the late 1970s thousands of refugees from Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos arrived in San Francisco, and the Tenderloin's cheap rents made it their main landing place [1]. Suddenly a neighbourhood with no playgrounds and corner stores selling 'lots of liquor but little fresh food' was home to large families squeezed into studios [1]. Community networks helped families open markets selling vegetables, meat and Asian ingredients, followed by dozens of Vietnamese, Chinese and Cambodian restaurants [1]. In September 2003 the Board of Supervisors unanimously named the two blocks of Larkin Street between Eddy and O'Farrell 'Little Saigon' [2]. About 80 percent of the businesses there were Vietnamese American-owned, from Tammy Pham's Kim Cuong Jewelry to Saigon Sandwiches, where Hang Nguyen made about 400 sandwiches a day [2]. 'Not even San Jose, with its large Vietnamese population, has a Little Saigon,' said task force member Phu Nguyen [2]. Green-and-yellow 'Sai Gon Nho' banners went up. In 2008 two pillars topped with marble ky linh, a mythical creature, rose at Larkin and Eddy as a gateway [2][3].

title: The bear that made a classroom
place: Balboa High School, 1 Balhi Court (Cayuga Avenue side)
hook: Balboa High's rivals were thrown together on camping trips. One night in Yosemite a bear raided their food, and a loner finally found her crew.
story: By the mid-1990s Balboa High drew students from some of San Francisco's poorest neighbourhoods, and ethnic rivalries ran high [1]. In 1995 two young teachers started an after-school 'Unity Club' that took students into the wilderness at weekends. They were history teacher Conrad Benedicto, who came from the Philippines at 13 and grew up near Balboa, and literature teacher Ken Gonzalez [1]. Science teacher Diana Theriault joined them. By 2000 the club had become the Wilderness Arts and Literacy Collaborative (WALC), a two-year program linking US history, literature and environmental science to trips to Mount Lassen, Joshua Tree and Lake Tahoe [1][2]. WALC students ran the school's paper recycling and spent two days a month planting and repairing McLaren Park [1]. Sierra magazine followed the class of 2003. One student, Ashley, had been moved into WALC against her will and kept to herself. On a spring trip to Yosemite she woke to heavy breathing outside her tent, but nobody believed her. The next night a mother bear and her cub raided the camp's bear box. Classmates sympathised, teachers apologised, and for the first time she felt part of the group [1].

title: Two Refugee Shacks Hiding Upstairs
place: 30 Niantic Avenue
hook: Looking for a garden shed, two historians looked up and gasped. The whole second storey of a Niantic Street house was made of 1906 earthquake shacks.
story: Cottages from the 1906 earthquake refugee camps were later moved into the OMI and reused as homes. The neighbourhood's historic context statement lists joined refugee "shacks" as a local building type and notes one at 223 Broad Street, moved from a camp after 1907 [2]. On March 23, 2003, shack expert Jane Cryan and Woody LaBounty of the Western Neighborhoods Project followed a tip from San Francisco Heritage that a shack at 30 Niantic had been turned into a garden shed [1]. Niantic is a tiny dead-end street trapped between Alemany Boulevard and the 280 freeway. There was no shed. Instead a workman on a ladder was hammering at the house's second storey, which turned out to be two "Type A" shacks joined end to end. Original park-green paint still showed where they met. Cryan hugged the owners, Tom and Maureen Ginella [1]. Instead of demolishing the shacks, the Ginellas had set them on a new foundation as their upper floor and were adding a modern level underneath. Upstairs, early walls, floorboards and cove ceilings survived. Cryan amended the city's list of surviving shacks, bringing it to 21 [1].

title: A Methodist first, in the Sunday service
place: Bethany United Methodist Church, 1270 Sanchez Street at Clipper
hook: When City Hall began marrying same-sex couples, a Noe Valley pastor wed two men during Sunday worship. Her church filed a complaint. She later became a bishop.
story: On February 12, 2004, parishioner Michael Eaton called his pastor, the Rev. Karen Oliveto of Bethany United Methodist Church, to say City Hall was issuing marriage licences to same-sex couples. He asked her to marry him and his partner, Sean Higgins [2]. She did. Over the following days she conducted seven ceremonies at City Hall, only for couples she knew as their pastor [2]. On Sunday, February 15, she married an eighth couple, Dan Johnson and Bill Hinson, in Bethany's sanctuary during regular worship. It was the first same-sex marriage held in a United Methodist sanctuary [1][2]. Four days later her district superintendent told her a complaint had been filed for 'disobedience to the order and discipline of the United Methodist Church' [1][2]. At a February 22 news conference, more than 100 Methodists stood behind her [1]. 'I am not doing a holy union,' she said. 'I am doing a legal gay marriage' [1]. She called it 'the most moving thing I've ever done in my ministry' [2]. Oliveto had led Bethany since 1992 [2]. In 2016 she was elected the first openly lesbian bishop in the United Methodist Church [3].

title: A geography class in a lonely park
place: Viewpoint near the top of Visitacion Avenue, below Mansell Street
hook: A geography professor brought his students to the city's second-biggest park and found it almost empty. From its ridge they could read a century of change.
story: 'It's empty,' said Max Kirkeberg, a San Francisco State geography professor. In spring 2004 he brought the 25 students in his 18-week 'San Francisco on Foot' class to McLaren Park. They had already explored neighbourhoods from Russian Hill to the Inner Mission [1]. Rec and Park's Jon Campo led them up a wooded trail. 'Parts of McLaren Park are very wild,' he said. 'It's the biggest grasslands left in the city' [1]. From the park's steep ridge, the Chronicle noted, you can see the city's past and future. To the east were the unfinished end of the Third Street light rail, the closed Schlage Lock factory and the site of the old Southern Pacific switching yards. To the north is the University Mound Ladies Home, a presence in one form or another since 1884. 'The Lick Old Ladies Home was its original name,' Kirkeberg said [1]. Kirkeberg, 71, remembered his first walk in the park in 1976, when it had no paved walkways, stairs, garbage cans or benches [1]. The city's 1983 master plan agrees that the park had no improved hiking trails until money came in 1977; new trails, paths and stairs followed from 1978 [2]. 'It is getting better,' he said. 'Clearly' [1].
