title: Del and Phyllis, first in line
place: San Francisco City Hall, 1 Dr Carlton B Goodlett Pl
hook: After more than fifty years together, two lesbian pioneers became the first same-sex couple married at City Hall. Then the courts voided it, and they did it again.
story: On February 12, 2004, Mayor Gavin Newsom ordered city officials to issue marriage licences to same-sex couples. The first couple married were Del Martin and Phyllis Lyon, who had moved in together on Valentine's Day 1953 and co-founded the Daughters of Bilitis, the first lesbian-rights organisation in the country, in 1955 [1][2]. About 4,000 couples followed in the next four weeks, arriving from across the country [3]. At a mass reception for 600 newlyweds on February 23, Lyon said it mattered 'for a lot of the people that got married … but also for our friends who didn't get married' [1]. The state Supreme Court stopped the weddings in March. On August 12, 2004, it declared them void [3]. Four years later the same court struck down California's marriage ban. On June 16, 2008, Martin and Lyon were first in line again, married by Newsom himself in the same mauve and turquoise suits they had worn in 2004 [1][2]. Those outfits are now in the GLBT Historical Society's collection [1]. Martin died that August, aged 87. 'We were able to enjoy the ultimate rite of love and commitment before she passed,' Lyon said [1].

title: I Am OMI: A Neighbourhood Tells Its Story
place: Ocean View Recreation Center, Lobos Street & Capitol Avenue
hook: Teen filmmakers, a stage play, a radio drama and history panels in shop windows: between 2003 and 2005 the OMI collected its memories and gave them back.
story: The name OMI is fairly new. In the 1960s residents of Ingleside Terraces made common cause with the neighbourhoods to the east and south to lobby for better services and parks, and "OMI", for Ocean View-Merced Heights-Ingleside, came into use [1]. From 2003 to 2005 the Western Neighborhoods Project ran "I am OMI", using history and shared stories to bridge ethnic, cultural and generational lines and help "an often-divided neighborhood find a unified voice" [2]. In summer 2003, twelve young people in a month-long digital video camp interviewed neighbours and filmed "then and now" shots of landmarks. About 50 people came to their screening on August 1, and each filmmaker was paid $50 [3]. The project set up tables of old photos and free history booklets at the OMI International Family Festival at the Ocean View Recreation Center, Lobos and Capitol [4]. On June 12, 2004, Arts Connection premiered an original play based on neighbourhood stories at City College's Diego Rivera Theatre [4]. In April 2005 history panels filled storefront windows along Ocean Avenue, and in June a radio drama built from the interviews aired on KPFA [2][4].

title: The Labyrinth That Keeps Coming Back
place: Lands End Labyrinth site above Mile Rock Beach
hook: An anonymous car detailer laid stones on a cliff edge at dawn to dodge park rangers. For seventeen years strangers destroyed his labyrinth and a doula kept rebuilding it.
story: On the spring equinox of 2004, Eduardo Aguilera built a seven-circuit labyrinth, in the style of Chartres, on a small plateau above the Golden Gate, using stones from the surrounding area [1]. It was a stealth project. Aguilera, who details cars for a living, spent about 16 hours laying it out at dawn and dusk so rangers wouldn't catch him. 'I wanted to be totally anonymous,' he said [2]. Vandals wrecked it soon after, and he rebuilt it. Around 2008 Colleen Yerge, a North Beach doula, became its unofficial keeper. She carried grapefruit-sized rocks up from Mile Rock Beach in a backpack [3][4]. After it was stripped in August 2015, about 50 volunteers helped her rebuild it, spacing the stones exactly 15 inches apart [2]. Aguilera had warned her not to put her whole heart into it, because it would be destroyed. She kept her compassion for whoever did it [4]. In 2020–21 it was wiped out three times, every rock apparently thrown into the sea. Because the Park Service never approved it, destroying it isn't technically a crime [3].

title: The Lake That Nearly Drained Away
place: Lake Merced boathouse, Harding Road
hook: Lake Merced was once stocked with a quarter of a million fish a year. Then golf courses and cemeteries pumped the aquifer and its boathouse went dark.
story: In the 1950s the state utilities commission gave San Francisco's Recreation and Park Department control of Lake Merced's surface. The conditions were strict: keep the drinking water potable, keep the level up, allow no swimming and no gasoline engines [1]. The city built a first-class urban fishery. At its height stocking reached 250,000 fish [1]. But heavy postwar pumping of the Westside Aquifer by golf courses, cities and cemeteries drew the lake down [1]. As the water fell, stocking all but stopped. The Boat House, once a busy restaurant and bar, closed, and fishing piers were left standing over tule-choked banks [1]. Better management of the aquifer and occasional added water helped the lake start rising again from about 1990 [2]. By 2004 angler Tony Van Houten could report a lake "on the rebound", thanks to CalTrout, the Lake Merced Task Force and the Friends of Lake Merced. There was a new fishing pier, and the state planned to plant 50,000 fish that year [1].

title: The cottage on Nanny Goat Hill
place: 111 Manchester Street
hook: A run-down Victorian cottage became the rallying point for neighbours who sued the city to stop its demolition, and won.
story: The cottage at 111 Manchester Street is about a hundred years old. It sits on Nanny Goat Hill, the steep north slope named for the goats that grazed there before World War II. Until the late 1960s the area was mostly Sicilian [2]. Its absentee owners had let it decay, and plans were drawn for a much larger home. A new buyer took them on. The Board of Permit Appeals overruled the Planning Department and approved demolition [1]. Neighbours formed Bernal Heights Preservation and sued. They argued that the city had broken its own charter and the Bernal Heights Special Use District rules, which limit demolitions [1]. On June 4, 2004, Superior Court Judge Ronald Quidachay agreed and ordered the permit voided [1][2]. "It's so important to keep this little neighborhood of humble Victorian homes intact," said neighbour Kendall Goh [2]. The owner, David Chan, called the ruling 'shocking' and said his new house would be 'conforming and modest' [2]. The judge sent the case back to the Board of Appeals, and the owner later withdrew his demolition permit [1].

title: When the Excelsior became a Filipino hub
place: Filipino Community Center, 4681 Mission St
hook: Families left a shrinking Manilatown for the Excelsior, and a local barber watched in amazement as they paid cash for their houses.
story: In the 1970 census Filipinos made up just 6 percent of the Excelsior. Within a decade it was one of San Francisco's main Filipino neighbourhoods [1]. There were two reasons. The 1965 immigration reforms ended quotas that had held the Philippines to 100 immigrants a year. Meanwhile redevelopment was wiping out Manilatown, ending with the 1977 eviction of the International Hotel [1]. In 1977 the Excelsior barber Caspare La Rosa told a reporter he was amazed to see Filipino families 'pay cash for the houses they are buying' [1]. The Apollo and Granada theatres showed Filipino films, and Filipino grocers opened along Mission and Geneva [1][2]. In the 1990s, while the archdiocese was closing parishes, the Church of the Epiphany on Vienna Street drew nearly 4,000 people a week to Mass, the most in the city. 'We survived the demographic change because of the Filipino population,' said Father Bruce Dreier [1]. In 2004 the Filipino Community Center opened at 4681 Mission Street [1]. The Excelsior is still one of the city's Filipino hubs [3].

title: A Copper Museum Paid For Privately
place: De Young Museum, 50 Hagiwara Tea Garden Drive
hook: After voters twice refused to pay for a new de Young, a fundraiser simply decided to raise $190 million herself, and a Swiss firm wrapped it in copper.
story: The 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake badly damaged the old de Young [2]. Around midnight on June 2, 1998, a second bond measure to rebuild it fell short of the two-thirds it needed by 1.7 percent. There was talk of giving up, or of moving the museum out of the park [1][2]. The next morning Dede Wilsey, who chaired the capital campaign, decided, as she put it, "I would simply raise the money myself" [1]. In January 1999 the Swiss firm Herzog & de Meuron won the commission. Critics called its twisting tower a "huge shed," an "aircraft carrier" and a "Howard Johnson's of the future," and a group called People for a New de Young sued [1]. Supervisors approved the project in January 2002 [1]. Jacques Herzog's idea for the skin came from photographs of sunlight dappling through the park's trees. The result was 7,602 individually punched and embossed panels using 950,000 pounds of copper, some of it recycled drain pipes and wiring [1]. More than 7,000 donors gave $190 million, and the museum opened on October 15, 2005 [1].

title: Broad Street Becomes a Regular Neighbourhood
place: OMI Community Service Center, 103 Broad Street
hook: Streetcars once wouldn't stop at Broad and Randolph. By 2005 the biggest complaint was sidewalk parking, and an old fish market had become a one-stop city hall.
story: The Broad-Randolph corridor, Ocean View's main street between San Jose Avenue and Junipero Serra Boulevard, was once so dominated by gangs and drug dealers that streetcars wouldn't stop there [1]. Police sergeant Michael Williams described "cycle murders": young men who had grown up together, some of whom had coached sports together, killing each other over drugs [1]. From 1996 the Taraval Neighborhood Team of eight officers and a sergeant patrolled the strip around the clock. They made more than 4,000 arrests by 2003, and also took local kids salmon fishing and camping at Camp Mather [1]. There were 12 shootings in 2004 and three in the first months of 2005 [1]. That spring the OMI Community Service Center reopened in a former fish market at 103 Broad Street, near the notorious Broad and Plymouth corner. It housed police, public works, parking, city attorney and probation staff [1]. Not everyone was comfortable: community centre director Nyree Monroe warned against harassing innocent people [1]. Old businesses had helped hold the street together, among them Furlough's Tonsorial Parlor (1955) and Reno's Barber Shop [2]. Bill Reno, the "mayor of Broad Street", found teenagers jobs and lent his back room as a community centre. The Chronicle dates his shop to 1967, a local history to 1960 [1][2].

title: From Parking Lot to Tiger's Playoff
place: Harding Park golf course, 99 Harding Road
hook: In 1998 the city's beloved public course was paved over with parked cars. Seven years later Tiger Woods won a playoff there against John Daly.
story: Harding Park opened in 1925, named for President Warren Harding, a keen golfer [2]. Byron Nelson won the Victory Open there in January 1944 and won again that December, when it had been renamed the San Francisco Open [2]. Johnny Miller learned the game there in the late 1950s. He biked over, fished in Lake Merced by the practice green and hustled middle-aged men for nickels [1]. The PGA Tour left after 1969, and budget cuts let the course decay [1][2]. It hit bottom in 1998, when it served as a parking lot for the U.S. Open at the neighboring Olympic Club [1][2]. Lawyer and former USGA president Sandy Tatum watched it "turning into a weed patch" and rallied the city and the Tour [2]. A $16 million restoration in 2002–03 followed [1][2]. In October 2005 Harding Park became the first municipal course to host a World Golf Championship [1]. Tiger Woods, who remembered it as "basically a clover field", beat John Daly on the third playoff hole [1][2].

title: George Lucas Builds an Empire at Letterman
place: Letterman Digital Arts Center, 1 Letterman Drive
hook: Where a 10-storey Army hospital once stood, the maker of Star Wars built San Francisco's biggest office project in decades and put a bronze Yoda at the door.
story: The site at the Presidio's Lombard Gate once held the 10-storey Letterman Army Hospital and a 13-acre parking lot [1]. The Presidio Trust had to make the park pay for itself by 2013, and it picked George Lucas over more conventional developers [1]. His Letterman Digital Arts Center opened in 2005, with four buildings holding 865,000 square feet. The Chronicle called it the city's largest office project since 101 California St. opened in 1982 [1]. Lucasfilm paid $5.6 million a year in rent [1]. Critic John King described the result as a 'costume drama' of brick and stucco made to look like older Army buildings. 'I'm very much an advocate of historic architecture,' Lucas said. 'I like to work in a facility that ... looks like it's been there for a period of time' [1]. Landscape architect Lawrence Halprin, then 88, laid out 17 acres of open space with 85 kinds of trees and shrubs, an artificial stream and boulders brought from a ranch near Redding [1]. It soon became a pilgrimage spot for fans, school groups and ILM staff on their breaks [2].

title: Mangoes, kabocha and chorizo on Leland Avenue

hook: The valley's main street had boarded-up shops and no fruit market. So a family from Jalisco bought a building and filled it with food for all their neighbours.
story: For years, empty storefronts lined Visitacion Valley's five-block main street [1]. Across the street, Joaquin Escobar was opening La Loma Produce #2 [1]. Business stayed hard. In 2011, 13 percent of Leland's storefronts were empty and the street closed by 8 p.m. [2]. The valley had gone about 30 years without a supermarket before a Grocery Outlet was due to open in 2014 [3]. Still, in 2015 an urban design critic enjoyed the street fair on Leland. There were "no $14 cocktails" and "no tech buses", and the crowd was local and diverse [4].

title: Mojitos versus the hustlers
place: Former Maye's Oyster House, 1233 Polk St
hook: A $6.5 million restaurant with a Spanish chandelier and a headless Apollo opened on lower Polk, and a fight broke out over who the street was for.
story:
By 2005 lower Polk was changing fast. Restaurateur Myles O'Reilly had turned the old Maye's Oyster House building between Bush and Sutter into O'Reilly's Holy Grail, a $6.5 million restaurant with imported stained glass, a headless Apollo from Rome and a 250-year-old Spanish chandelier, and remade the rundown residential motel upstairs into 14 European-style suites. "I put my life savings into making a statement on this street," he said [1].

The bars were turning over too. The Polk Gulch Saloon, known for drag queens and trans women, became the Lush Lounge; the Hemlock, full of hipsters and live bands, replaced the historic gay bar the Giraffe; Rendezvous, the last male hustler bar, had closed [1][3]. The Lower Polk Neighbors Association welcomed the "cleaning up." The radical group Gay Shame called the association a "brutal gentrification squad" and warned the street would soon be known "more for green-apple mojitos and stretch Hummers than trannies and tweakers" [1].

Historian Joey Plaster argues the clash was one of three major economic shifts on Polk since the 1950s, driven by outside market forces rather than simply homophobia: the same economics that built a gay commercial corridor in the 1960s were now dismantling it [2].

title: Patricia's Green
place: Patricia's Green, Octavia Boulevard between Fell and Hayes
hook: Where freeway ramps once came down, a small park opened in 2005. Months later it was renamed for the soft-spoken activist who fought to get it built.
story: On September 9, 2005, Octavia Boulevard opened with a ribbon-cutting at Market Street [2]. The designers, Allan Jacobs and Elizabeth Macdonald, followed the principle "No one gets everything, but everyone gets a lot" [2][3]. The boulevard has four central lanes for commuters and a slower lane on each side for local traffic [2]. It was planted with 261 trees, including evergreen elms, flowering cherries and pears, and Lombardy poplars [1]. At its northern end, between Fell and Hayes, was a new park called Hayes Green. "This is just an amazing gift for the neighborhood," said Patricia Walkup, the activist who helped lead the fight against rebuilding the freeway [1]. "In a few years, there will be people who will never know a freeway was there" [1]. Walkup, founder of the Hayes Valley Neighborhood Association, died on June 6, 2006, at 59. That August the Recreation and Park Commission voted unanimously to rename the park "Patricia's Green in Hayes Valley" [4]. "If not for Patricia, that park would not be there," said her friend Robin Levitt. "If she hadn't done that work, we would have a freeway there" [4]. In December 2006 the American Planning Association gave the project its first award for "hard-won victories" [2].

title: The National Park That Must Pay Its Bills
place: Main Post (Presidio Trust)
hook: Congress gave the Presidio an unusual order: pay for yourself. The rent from renovated Army housing, more than Star Wars money, is what kept it going.
story: Two years after the Army left, Congress created the Presidio Trust. In 1998 it took charge of the park's non-coastal lands with an unusual order: become financially self-sufficient by 2013 [1]. The Trust decided to lease out old buildings and use the rent to run the park, with tenants paying to renovate [2]. It was George Lucas's campus that got the headlines, but the Chronicle reported that more than half of the operating budget came from homes [2]. Starting with the Baker Beach Apartments in 1999, the Trust restored barracks and officers' quarters. Rents ran from $1,675 for a spartan two-bedroom to $11,000 for a 7,000-square-foot general's house [2]. 'Residential saved us,' said former real-estate director Paul Osmundson, remembering the dot-com crash of 2001 [2]. In 2004 the Trust earned $43.2 million, spent $40.5 million, and made money for the first time [2]. Critics objected. 'What we've got is over-development,' said John Rizzo of the Sierra Club. Director Craig Middleton replied: 'What is sustainable if you can't pay the bills?' [2] Two decades later the model faced a new challenge. In 2025 a presidential executive order targeted the Trust's 'non-statutory components', and the Trust insisted that all of its activities are based in law [3].

title: "Huh? What's NoPa?"
place: Nopa, 560 Divisadero Street (at Hayes)
hook: Realtors get the blame for the name NoPa. It actually came from a neighbourhood newsletter, and a restaurant in an old bank made it stick.
story: The North of the Panhandle Neighborhood Association was founded in 1991, as neighbours organised against drug-related crime [2]. At some point in the 1990s the group's newsletter briefly changed its name from "North Panhandle News" to "NoPa News." The name didn't stick, according to longtime board member James Cowan. He had also heard that someone proposed "Parc North" and residents vetoed it [1]. In 2000 the writer Mat Honan used "NoPa" in the Bay Guardian, which may be the first time it appeared in print. He described a neighbourhood "struggling to define itself as gentrification takes hold" [1]. The name only caught on after April 11, 2006. That night Jeff Hanak and Allyson and Laurence Jossel opened a restaurant in a grand old bank building at Divisadero and Hayes [3]. When they were choosing a name, a friend pointed out that the address was in NoPa. "We were like, 'Huh? What's NoPa?'" Allyson recalled [3]. At the time, only a few restaurants stood on that stretch of Divisadero. On opening night the kitchen ran low on food, and a customer brought in chicken from the Popeyes across the street [3]. As restaurants such as Bi-Rite, Bar Crudo, Ragazza and the Mill opened nearby, a name that needed constant explaining became the neighbourhood's own [1][3].

title: Cappuccino, Opera and The Godfather
place: Caffe Trieste, 601 Vallejo St at Grant Ave
hook: A window washer who dreamed of opera taught North Beach to drink cappuccino, and Francis Ford Coppola wrote a masterpiece at a back table.
story: On April 1, 2006, Caffe Trieste at Grant and Vallejo turned 50. To celebrate, it sold cappuccinos for 30 cents and espressos for 25, its 1956 prices [1]. The founder, Giovanni "Papa Gianni" Giotta, then 85, had been a poor fisherman who studied opera in Trieste. He emigrated, washed windows, and opened the cafe, which his family says was the first espresso bar on the West Coast [1][2]. "It was all Italian people," he remembered. "But I got the American people to like cappuccino" [1]. Before long the Beat writers outnumbered the Italians, with Ferlinghetti, Ginsberg and Kerouac among the regulars [1][2]. Along the back wall is the table where a young Francis Ford Coppola spent months working on the screenplay for The Godfather, and a photo above the jukebox shows him typing there [1][2]. On Saturday afternoons the family sang: Papa Gianni with his sons Fabio and Gianfranco [2]. Off stage, the harmony faded. After Papa Gianni died in January 2016 at 96, a long-running family feud ended up in court in 2017, when Fabio sued to dissolve the company that ran the cafe [2].

title: Chained to the Gates of a Power Plant
place: Former PG&E Hunters Point power plant, India Basin shoreline
hook: For decades one of San Francisco's biggest air polluters stood on India Basin. Mothers from Hunters View and a grandmother in chains finally shut it down in 2006.
story: PG&E's Hunters Point power plant stood on the India Basin shoreline for decades. A 2004 essay called it the state's oldest and most polluting power plant. The same essay cited a 1995 city health department study that found four times as many toxins in Bayview–Hunters Point as in any other neighbourhood [2]. Residents blamed the plant for headaches, asthma and skin disease. In December 2004 Marie Harrison joined neighbours protesting outside it [3]. Harrison came from Kansas City, had sold clothing at Nordstrom and Macy's, and loved singing gospel. She worked for the group Greenaction for two decades [3]. In 2006 she chained herself to the front of the plant [3]. That year Greenaction and the Huntersview Mothers Committee won their fight and the plant was shut down. By 2009 it had been demolished [1]. Tests on the 38-acre site found PCBs, arsenic, lead, hexavalent chromium and asbestos in the soil and groundwater. The mothers then got PG&E to stop sending the PCB waste to Kettleman City, a farmworker town already suffering high rates of birth defects [1]. Harrison later chained herself to the shipyard fence too. She died at 71 of chronic lung disease while still organizing a walk for a cleaner southeast [3].

title: Two Acres for Two Gold Medals
place: Victoria Manalo Draves Park, Folsom and Sherman streets
hook: A diving coach once told a South of Market girl she could join his club only if she dropped her Filipino surname. Her old schoolyard now carries her full name.
story: Victoria Manalo was born in South of Market on December 31, 1924. Her father, Teofilo, was a Filipino musician and chef, and her mother, Gertrude Taylor, came from England [1]. She went to Franklin Elementary School, which was later renamed for its principal, Bessie Carmichael. When she wanted to join the Fairmont Hotel's diving club, the coach told her bluntly that as a Filipino she could not. He suggested she dive under her mother's name, and for a time she became "Vicki Taylor" [1]. Later, competing as Vicki Manalo, she was barred from a contest at the same club. Her coach, Lyle Draves, left for Los Angeles in disgust. She followed and married him there in 1946 [1]. At the 1948 London Olympics she won gold in both springboard and platform diving [1][2]. Decades later neighbours pushed the school district and Recreation and Park Department to turn the old Bessie Carmichael school site into open space named after her. Sources date the naming to 2005 or 2006. She visited the site and remembered her school days there [1][2]. Draves died in 2010 [1].

title: Volunteers Find a Lost Trail on Mount Sutro
place: Rotary Meadow, Mount Sutro summit, UCSF Mount Sutro Open Space Reserve
hook: Surveying Mount Sutro for a new trail in 2005, volunteers found an old one instead, and then spent 5,000 hours bringing it back.
story: Mount Sutro's dense eucalyptus forest, planted by Adolph Sutro, fills 61 acres above UCSF's Parnassus campus. At the urging of neighbours, in 1998 UCSF began a management plan. Public meetings in 2000 produced a plan to protect native plants, improve the forest's health and open up access [1]. The Rotary Club of San Francisco gave $100,000 for Rotary Meadow, a native plant garden at the summit on the site of a former Nike installation. The Stewards date the gift to 2003; another account says 2004 [1][2]. In 2005, surveying for a proposed new trail, workers found a very old trail instead, which the Stewards believe was built in the 1880s [1]. In September 2006 local volunteers proposed a stewardship programme to UCSF, and the Mount Sutro Stewards were formed [1]. In the first twelve months volunteers put in more than 5,000 hours, restoring the Historic Trail and freeing rare native plants from ivy and blackberry. They won a San Francisco Beautiful award in 2007 [1]. Fog drip from the tall trees supplies 30 to 40 percent of the forest's moisture [2].

title: Woo Woo's Home Court
place: Willie "Woo Woo" Wong Playground, 830 Sacramento St
hook: He was 5-foot-5, the last kid picked on the Chinatown court across from his flat. Crowds chanted 'Woo Woo' every time he scored. Now the playground bears his name.
story: Willie Wong was the third of seven children of a poor immigrant couple, and the family's flat faced Chinese Playground. That is where he learned basketball [2]. "I used to stand and watch, and I was always the last guy picked for teams," he recalled. "When I got to play, they always yelled at me not to shoot, because I couldn't" [2]. He grew into a dead-eye shooter, 5-foot-5 and 125 pounds. He was the only Chinese American on the 1945 All-City prep team, and Examiner writer Bob Brachman named him "Woo Woo" after what crowds chanted when he scored [2][1]. Pete Newell recruited him to USF in 1948. "He was a god in San Francisco's Chinatown," Newell said [2]. Wong died in September 2005, aged 79 [2]. In January 2006 the Recreation and Park Commission renamed the playground on Sacramento Street, between Stockton and Grant, the Willie "Woo Woo" Wong Playground [1]. After a $14.5 million renovation that kept it closed for more than two years, it reopened in February 2021, in time for Lunar New Year, with new courts, a clubhouse and play areas [3].

title: 756, and the asterisk ball
place: Oracle Park right-center bleachers
hook: At 8:51 p.m. on August 7, 2007, Barry Bonds passed Hank Aaron. The ball went to a Mets fan, then to a designer, then to a vote.
story: Boats and kayaks crowd McCovey Cove on game days hoping for a 'splash hit', and Bonds landed 35 of them there in his career [2]. At 8:51 p.m. Pacific time, with one out in the fifth inning, he hit a full-count pitch from Washington's Mike Bacsik 435 feet into the right-center bleachers. It was his 756th, breaking Hank Aaron's career record [1]. His son Nikolai, the Giants' batboy, met him at home plate, and even the Nationals applauded [1]. Bacsik's father had pitched to Aaron in 1976, after Aaron's last home run [1]. The ball was grabbed by Matt Murphy, a Mets fan from Queens passing through on his way to Australia [1][3]. He sold it for more than $750,000 to fashion designer Marc Ecko, who let the public decide its fate: give it to the Hall of Fame, brand it with an asterisk first, or launch it into space. With 47 percent of more than 10 million votes, the asterisk won [3]. That verdict on the steroid era was itself controversial. Bonds vowed to boycott any Hall display of it, and in 2008 the Hall balked when the gift became a loan [3].

title: A backyard oak joins the city's landmarks

hook: You can't see it from the street, but a century-old coast live oak on 23rd Street became Noe Valley's first official landmark tree after a trench nearly cut its roots.
story: When Robert and Susan Call moved into 4124 23rd Street in the late 1980s, they found a giant in the back yard. It was a coast live oak, a species native to California, standing 35 to 40 feet tall. Its 50-foot crown covered their yard and a third of the neighbour's [1][2]. The tree was thought to be about 100 years old. It can't be seen from the front of the house, but its canopy is visible from 23rd and Castro [1]. The family hung chandeliers in it for birthday parties, and three crows came to yell at the cats [1]. In mid-2006 the Calls came home to find a trench being dug across the neighbour's yard for an addition, one that would have cut the roots under half the tree. Robert Call persuaded the neighbour to stop, then hurried to City Hall. Supervisor Bevan Dufty's nomination protected the oak for 180 days, but that ran out before a decision, so Call applied himself [1]. On November 13, 2007 the Board of Supervisors made it the first landmark tree in Noe Valley, alongside 12 other individual trees and the Dolores Street palms. It can now come down only if it becomes a hazard [1].

title: Christmas night, a tiger clears the moat
place: Tiger grotto by the Lion House, San Francisco Zoo
hook: Minutes after closing on Christmas Day, a Siberian tiger got out of her grotto. Afterward the zoo measured its moat wall and found it far shorter than its records said.
story: Tatiana, a Siberian tiger, had mauled a zookeeper during a public feeding in December 2006. The state ruled the zoo responsible because of the unsafe configuration of the cages [1]. On Christmas Day 2007, shortly after the zoo's 5 p.m. closing, she escaped [1]. She killed 17-year-old Carlos Sousa Jr. and seriously injured two of his friends, brothers Paul and Kulbir Dhaliwal, all from San Jose [2]. The attack was reported at 5:17 p.m., and the tiger was shot dead by police while attacking a visitor near a cafe on the zoo's east end [1]. Shotgun-carrying officers gathered at the south gate while firefighters shone flashlights through the eucalyptus from tall ladders [1]. How had she got out? Earlier that week zoo officials had said the moat wall was at least 20 feet high. When they measured it themselves, it was 12 1/2 feet, about four feet below the national standard recommended by big-cat experts, although the 33-foot-wide moat met standards [2]. "How she jumped that high is beyond me," said director Manuel Mollinedo [2]. With no video cameras watching the animals, investigators had to piece the night together without them [2].

title: Dinner in a 1930 auto barn
place: Spruce, 3640 Sacramento Street
hook: Presidio Heights waited more than two years for its big restaurant. It opened inside a 1930 garage, with a farm truck that ran on its used cooking oil.
story:
At the start of August 2007, more than two years after its planned debut, Spruce opened at 3640 Sacramento, near Spruce Street. It was built inside a 1930 auto barn converted to a 5,000-square-foot restaurant [1].

It came from the Bacchus Management Group, the team behind Woodside's Village Pub. Tim Stannard was owner, Mark Sullivan chef-partner and Andrew Green wine director. Designer Stephen Brady filled the old garage with mohair banquettes, saddle-leather chairs and a small takeout cafe by the door. The wine list had nearly 1,000 choices [1].

Most of the produce came from the restaurant's partner farm, SMIP Ranch in Woodside. The farm's delivery truck ran on biodiesel made from Spruce's used cooking oil [1]. The opening bar menu had a Niman Ranch burger [1].

By 2025 Eater said Spruce had the only burger in town "rumored to induce labor." It was served only at the bar, where you had better arrive when the doors opened. The dining room still had valet parking and white tablecloths [2].

title: Don't Feed the Parrots
place: Telegraph Hill east slope
hook: A homeless man befriended a flock of escaped pet conures, a film made them famous, and then City Hall had to step in.
story: The wild parrots linked with Telegraph Hill are cherry-headed conures, a species native to a small area of Ecuador and Peru. Their ancestors were most likely pets from the exotic-bird trade that escaped or were set free [2]. Their best-known friend was Mark Bittner, who had arrived in San Francisco homeless and began feeding the birds and naming them. "The parrots got me off the street," he said [3]. Judy Irving's 2003 documentary The Wild Parrots of Telegraph Hill made the flock famous [3]. Fame brought fans with sunflower seeds. In June 2007 the Board of Supervisors voted 10 to 1 to ban feeding the birds in city parks, with fines of up to $100 [1]. Board President Aaron Peskin compared it to not feeding Yosemite's grizzlies. Bittner backed the ban, while neighbours of Ferry Park, where the birds fed in the evenings, planned one last feeding [1]. The flock grew from dozens in the 1990s to an estimated 250 to 300 birds [3]. In 2023 the parrots were voted San Francisco's official animal, beating the Pier 39 sea lions with 51.3 percent [4]. Bittner still says the name is wrong: "Telegraph Hill is a misnomer" [2].

title: Ichiro and the wall's strange bounce
place: Right-center field wall, Oracle Park (then AT&T Park)
hook: The ballpark's quirky right-field wall produced something no All-Star Game had ever seen: an inside-the-park home run.
story: San Francisco hosted the All-Star Game on July 10, 2007. Before the first pitch the crowd honoured Willie Mays, who threw the ceremonial pitch to the Mets' José Reyes [1]. The National League led 1-0 in the fifth inning when Baltimore's Brian Roberts walked. Seattle's Ichiro Suzuki, leading off for the American League, drove Chris Young's first pitch deep to right-center [1][2]. Ken Griffey Jr. seemed well placed to play it off the padded wall. But the ball took a strange bounce off a sign and ricocheted to his right [1][2]. By the time Griffey chased it down and threw it in, and nobody cut it off, Ichiro had scored standing up, with Roberts crossing the plate just ahead of him [2]. It was the first inside-the-park home run in All-Star history and the first of Ichiro's seven-year major-league career [2]. It gave the American League a 2-1 lead. The AL won 5-4, and Ichiro was named Most Valuable Player [1].

title: The firefighter who wouldn't give up
place: Louis Sutter Playground and Roundhouse, University Street side of the park
hook: As a boy he found a body in the park. As a man he helped win it $12 million, after the city's parks bond left it out entirely.
story: Chuck Farrugia grew up in the Portola, next to a park that felt like wilderness. 'You could climb a tree, ride bikes on the trails, capture snakes - it was like a forest,' he told the Chronicle [1]. He also remembered walking his dog as a boy and finding a dead body, and seeing burned-out cars [1]. A 1981 Examiner headline summed up those years: 'McLaren Park: great potential, much trash.' The previous year's crime figures included two murders, six rapes and 18 stolen cars [1]. Farrugia grew up to be a firefighter and bought a home near his parents. As friends left for the suburbs, he became an activist. When neighbours saw that the next city parks bond included nothing for San Francisco's second-largest park, they founded Help McLaren Park in 2007 [1]. The next parks bond, in 2012, included $12 million for McLaren [1]. The group raised money with yearly pancake breakfasts in the Louis Sutter Roundhouse [2]. 'For this corner of the city, it's our Golden Gate Park,' said neighbour Linda Litehiser [1].

title: The school that learned to be still
place: Visitacion Valley Middle School, 450 Raymond Avenue
hook: The principal of a school surrounded by gunfire tried something radical: twice a day, everyone stops and sits in silence.
story: Visitacion Valley Middle School sits on the park's southeastern slope. In the mid-2000s, violence pressed in on it. In 2004 two students found the body of a 19-year-old stabbing victim. Later that year a gunman stormed into the school and robbed two employees [1]. 'Everybody in this school was either related to somebody who has been shot, who did the shooting, or who saw a shooting,' said the principal, Jim Dierke [1]. In spring 2007 he tried something unusual called Quiet Time. Twice a day the whole school meditated or simply sat still, for 12 or 15 minutes depending on the account. The program was paid for mostly by the David Lynch Foundation and run with the San Francisco-based Center for Wellness and Achievement in Education [1][2]. All but two teachers voted in favour, and nearly every family signed the permission slip [3]. Critics called it 'stealth religion.' The school superintendent, Carlos Garcia, called it 'thoroughly secular' [1][3]. The school said suspensions fell from 85 in 2005-06 to 10 in 2009-10 [1]. Dierke put daily attendance at more than 98 percent [2].

title: A Museum Under a Hill of Wildflowers
place: California Academy of Sciences, 55 Music Concourse Drive
hook: Renzo Piano lifted a piece of the park, slid a natural history museum underneath, and planted the roof with native wildflowers.
story: By the 2000s the California Academy of Sciences was working out of 12 worn, earthquake-damaged buildings [2]. Renzo Piano replaced them with one. "Renzo wanted to lift up the landscape and slide a museum underneath it," botany curator Frank Almeda explained [1]. The result was a 2.5-acre living roof planted with native wildflowers, including wild strawberries, which captures about 3.6 million gallons of rainwater a year and gives local wildlife somewhere to live [1]. The walls are insulated with old blue jeans. Skylight portholes open to let cool Pacific air flow through the central piazza instead of air conditioning [1]. Two exterior walls of the old African Hall were kept as the building's northeastern corner [2]. Moving back in meant packing up 20 million research specimens and 38,000 live animals [2]. The $488 million building opened to the public on September 27, 2008, and earned LEED Platinum ratings [1][2]. Because its footprint is smaller than the old buildings', it also gave an acre of open space back to Golden Gate Park [2].

title: A Spire Made From a Dying Forest
place: Andy Goldsworthy's Spire, Bay Area Ridge Trail near Arguello Gate
hook: A British artist bound 37 felled cypress trunks into a nearly 100-foot spire, knowing the young forest planted around it would one day hide it.
story: The Army began planting the Presidio's forest in the 1880s. More than a century later, many of its cypress and pines were dying [1][2]. In 2006 the British artist Andy Goldsworthy visited and learned about the Presidio Trust's replanting programme [1]. He came back in October 2008 and worked with the Trust's forestry crew to choose 37 Monterey cypress trunks felled at the site. They were fastened together into a spire nearly 100 feet tall on a 15-foot base [1]. Young cypress were planted around it. In the Trust's words, it is 'the old forest welcoming the new', and as the new trees grow they will slowly swallow the sculpture [1][2]. Goldsworthy said it recalled one of his earliest works, a 1984 group of tree spires in England's Grizedale Forest: 'I have not found another great location for this type of work until now' [2]. Spire was the first of four Presidio works. Next came Wood Line (2011), a 1,200-foot line of eucalyptus branches off Lovers' Lane; Tree Fall (2013), inside a Civil War-era powder magazine; and Earth Wall at the Officers' Club [3]. Together they make up the largest collection of his work on public view in North America [3].

title: Cheyenne's half hour at Tyger's
place: Chenery Street at Lippard Avenue (Loftin home from 1957)
hook: For 27 years a Wyoming-born cowboy in boots and a Levi's jacket sat at the round table by Tyger's door every morning, for exactly half an hour.
story: Henry "Cheyenne" Loftin was born in Buffalo, Wyoming, on 18 November 1910 [1]. He lived on Chenery Street from 1957, in a house at the corner of Lippard, for more than half a century [1][2]. Every morning he walked down to Tyger's, arriving at 6:40 for oatmeal "laden with vast amounts of sugar." For 27 years he sat at the round table near the door, sipping coffee for exactly half an hour [1]. He had spent many years working with cattle, and neighbourhood lore said he had driven cattle for Gene Autry [1][3]. He told a fellow regular he was half Irish and half American Indian and had lived in a teepee for his first 13 years. Another Wyoming native remembered him saying, "Ernie, you would be surprised at how many men in San Francisco couldn't handle a team of horses" [1]. Each year he gave waitress Sandy Kim $20 for her birthday. In 2006 he modelled the Friends of Glen Canyon Park T-shirt outside Glen Park Hardware, and in 2007 the store put out a card for his 97th birthday [2][3]. He died on 14 May 2008, a few months short of 98, having outlived Winnie, his wife of 70 years, by nearly a decade [1].

title: Halloween Central at the Williams House
place: Sea Cliff (the Williams family home; address not given in sources)
hook: Robin Williams's Sea Cliff house hosted big-ticket fundraisers. For local kids it was something better: the best stop on the Halloween route.
story: Robin Williams married Marsha Garces in April 1989. She had first come into his life as a nanny for his son Zachary, then became his assistant. Their daughter Zelda was born that July and their son Cody in 1991 [1]. The couple worked as a team. In 1991 they founded Blue Wolf Productions, and Garces produced Mrs. Doubtfire and Patch Adams. Through their Windfall Foundation they gave to education, health, the environment and the arts [1]. Home was Sea Cliff [1]. By 2000, lost tourists looking for the 49-Mile Drive or the beaches were wandering past the houses of Williams and Sharon Stone [2]. When Garces filed for divorce in March 2008, the Chronicle's Leah Garchik remembered what the house had meant to the street. It had been the scene of "big-ticket fundraising dinners and cocktail parties, but also Halloween central for neighborhood trick-or-treaters" [1]. By then Williams was reportedly living in Marin, though he still surprised Bay Area audiences with unannounced drop-ins at comedy clubs [1].

title: Mistaken identity on Congdon Street
place: Congdon Street at Maynard Street
hook: Tony Bologna backed up his Honda to let another car turn on a narrow Excelsior street. The gunman inside thought he and his sons were rival gang members.
story: On Sunday afternoon, June 22, 2008, Tony Bologna was driving his sons home from a family barbecue in Fairfield. He wanted some sleep before his night shift at Draeger's market in San Mateo [1]. On narrow Congdon Street his Honda Civic met a car trying to turn onto Congdon from Maynard Street. Bologna reversed to let it through, and the driver pulled alongside and opened fire [1]. Bologna, 49, and his son Michael, 20, a former Lincoln High athlete, died at the scene. His son Matthew, 16, died two days later [1][3]. Another son, Andrew, later identified the gunman; accounts differ on whether he was in the car [2][3]. At first the Chronicle reported it as road rage [1][3]. It turned out that Edwin Ramos, an MS-13 member, had mistaken the family for rival gang members [2][3]. Ramos, who was in the country illegally despite earlier arrests, was never referred for deportation, and the killings became a rallying point for critics of San Francisco's sanctuary policy [2][3]. He received three consecutive life sentences. In 2015 a second man, who had been in the car, was sentenced to ten years [2]. Tony had coached youth baseball and basketball for years. 'There are 12 little guys... who are without him,' said a police lieutenant who had coached alongside him [1].

title: Steam-clean the sidewalk, or else
place: 1600 Webster Street condominiums, beside the Nihonmachi Street Fair route at Post and Webster
hook: New condo owners called Japantown's street fair schlocky and threatened to fight its permit. The community answered with 2,800 signatures and a reminder of 1942.
story: The Nihonmachi Street Fair has filled Japantown's streets with taiko drums and teriyaki smoke every August since 1974 [2]. In 2008 it got a threat from its newest neighbours. David Zisser, president of the homeowners' association at the new 1600 Webster condominiums, emailed organisers complaining about "schlocky souvenirs, mediocre food stands" and filthy sidewalks [1]. He and the developer, John McInerney, demanded that the fair steam-clean the pavement outside their building. Otherwise, they said, they would protest its next city permit [1]. "It is not a negotiation," McInerney wrote [1]. Co-chair Grace Horikiri replied that steam cleaning was beyond the budget, but volunteers would sweep and "physically scrub" the street [1]. Paul Osaki of the Japanese Cultural and Community Center started a petition. He wrote: "First it was us, then our homes and businesses, our property. Next our festivals?" [1]. It collected 2,800 signatures over the fair's two days [1]. The fair survived. In 2024 the city named it a Legacy Business, the first festival producer to get that status [2].

title: The George W. Bush Sewage Plant?
place: Oceanside Water Pollution Control Plant, 3500 Great Highway
hook: Beside the zoo sits a sewage plant most people never notice. In 2008 a group of pranksters put a president's name for it on the city ballot.
story: Most people pass the Oceanside Water Pollution Control Plant without noticing it. Owned by the Public Utilities Commission and tucked beside the San Francisco Zoo, it treats sewage and storm water from the city's west side and sends the treated water out into the Pacific [4]. In 2008 a handful of friends who had dreamed up the idea over beers, calling themselves the Presidential Memorial Commission of San Francisco, set out to rename it the George W. Bush Sewage Plant. They also wanted supporters to join a "synchronized flush" at the next inauguration [1]. Toting flags and blaring patriotic music, one of them sometimes dressed as Uncle Sam, they said by June they had 8,500 signatures; at least 7,168 valid ones were needed to reach the ballot [1]. A reporter asked about it at a White House briefing, and press secretary Dana Perino replied, "I just don't think it dignifies a response" [2]. The idea did make the November ballot as Proposition R, which would have changed the name when the next president was inaugurated [4]. On November 4, 2008, it lost, 233,733 votes to 101,376 [3].

title: The curb that couldn't spell Visitacion
place: Visitacion Ave at Desmond St
hook: A city crew stamped the neighbourhood's name into fresh concrete, and got it wrong. A local history buff wasn't having it.
story: The valley's name comes from Spanish, not English. According to legend, Franciscan missionaries lost in the fog found themselves here on July 2, 1777, the feast of the Visitation of Mary to her cousin Elizabeth, and "Visitacion" with the Spanish spelling stuck [1]. Outsiders write "Visitation" all the time. In 2008 the city made the same mistake. A crew poured four new curbs at Visitacion Avenue and Desmond Street, and on the southwest and northeast corners the street name was spelled the English way [2]. Russel Morine emailed the Chronicle's ChronicleWatch column to complain [2]. Morine was part of a group of residents who had spent years recording the valley's history and had worked on a 2005 book about it [3]. Within hours, the Department of Public Works sent another crew to redo the concrete. "We regret this mistake, and we worked fast to fix it," said spokeswoman Christine Falvey [2]. For a neighbourhood so often ignored, the spelling mattered. "We want to make sure this ends up in history," Morine said in 2005 [3].

title: The mayor's home court on Chestnut Street
place: Moscone Recreation Center, Chestnut and Buchanan Streets
hook: The Marina rec center's gym has always been too narrow for a regulation court. George Moscone played there anyway, and his wife watched from the balcony.
story: When the city reopened the Moscone Recreation Center at Chestnut and Buchanan in July 2008, after an 18-month, $8 million makeover, a brass band played 'Bye Bye Blackbird' and other songs that were popular when the building opened in the 1920s [1]. One thing the money couldn't buy was a wider basketball court. 'The sides of the court are too close to the wall,' said 23-year-old Anthony Harrison. 'You bump into them... It's still a great place to play' [1]. George Moscone knew that court well. He was an all-city basketball star at St. Ignatius [2], and the Chronicle wrote that the future mayor used to put up 'his patented jump shots' here [1]. At the reopening his widow, Gina, stood beside a giant red 'M' on the new floor and remembered sitting in the balcony bleachers watching him play. Their daughter Jennifer remembered him walking her to the rec center and the park and buying her popcorn from a vendor on the corner [1]. The park, which runs between Chestnut and Bay and between Laguna and Webster, is named for Moscone, who was assassinated in City Hall in November 1978 [3][1]. 'There's a lot of sports things to play with,' seven-year-old Brigid Maher said [1].

title: A Burning Man tower on the dog field
place: The big field off John F. Shelley Drive
hook: Dog walkers gather on the big field off Shelley Drive. One Saturday in 2009 it held something else: a tower and dome being test-built for Burning Man.
story: The big field off John F. Shelley Drive is a favourite starting point for McLaren Park's dog walkers and their group walks [1]. Dog owners had fought for their place in the park. When a disc golf course was proposed in 2010, opponents pointed out that the park's off-leash dog play area had been created by Rec and Park only 'as the conclusion to a long struggle led by dog enthusiasts' [2]. Park regulars turn up in the record. In 2004 a Chronicle photographer caught Sulpicio Mariano tossing a disc for his dog, Jet, in the nearby amphitheatre [3]. One Saturday in 2009, the Grapevine's park columnist Betty Parshall found something new on the field. A small group had built a tower and was working to fit a circular piece on top. It was, she learned, a test run for building a tower with a geodesic dome for the Burning Man festival. She filed the item under 'Another Use for the Big Field' [1]. The same column reported that volunteers from Volunteers for Outdoor California spent a weekend building and repairing trails in the park, including a gentle switchback down to McNab Lake, and many brought tents and camped in the park [1].

title: A Library of Alexandria in a Church
place: 300 Funston Avenue at Clement Street (Internet Archive)
hook: Inside a 1923 Christian Science church, where the pews still face the altar, servers blink every time someone somewhere opens an old webpage.
story: Carl Werner designed the Fourth Church of Christ, Scientist at Funston and Clement, and it was finished in 1923 with Corinthian columns across its front [3]. By 2009 its congregation had dwindled, and the 23,000-square-foot building went to a buyer nobody in 1923 could have imagined: the Internet Archive, the nonprofit founded in 1996 to keep the web from vanishing, then based in the Presidio [1]. Market sources put the price at about $4.5 million [1]. Founder Brewster Kahle said plainly why they chose it: 'We bought this building because it matched our logo,' a Greek temple [2]. His idea, he told visitors, was 'to build the library of Alexandria, version two' [2]. Rather than flattening the sloped sanctuary floor into a library, the Archive decided to 'take it slow' and let the building adapt [2]. The pews stayed. In a niche where you might expect a saint stand towers of servers whose blue lights blink with each upload or download [2]. From that old church the Wayback Machine keeps crawling the web, preserving pages that have otherwise disappeared [2].

title: A library that lends seeds
place: Portola Branch Library, 380 Bacon Street
hook: After eight decades in rented storefronts, including one eviction, the Portola got its own library in 2009, and started lending chard and radish seeds.
story: The Portola's library began in 1927 as a deposit station, the 14th branch in the city system, and spent the next eight decades in leased sites on San Bruno Avenue [1], at one point evicted, as a later branch manager put it, by "the paradigmatic crotchety landlord" [2]. On 28 February 2009 it opened in its own building at 380 Bacon Street at Goettingen: 6,300 square feet by Stoner Meek/Noll and Tam, with skylights, a north-facing view garden and a glass-shutter artwork by Dana Zed [1]. The Portola Garden Tour had begun as a way to pay for its books and play spaces [2]. Branch manager Nicole Termini Germain, in the system since 1993, fought to open the garden door, kept locked because thieves might use it for quick getaways ("We had this whole Blu-ray thief ring for a while"). With $700 in city money, a teacher from the nearby Alta Vista School and parents with construction know-how, she planted fruit trees, strawberries and a pumpkin patch [2]. Her seed library, one of only two in the city in 2017, lets anyone take seeds home, no library card needed [2][3]. Borrowers who never bring seeds back are forgiven: "I don't send them to library jail" [2].

title: Coit Tower Becomes a Movie Screen
place: Coit Tower, 1 Telegraph Hill Blvd
hook: On Thanksgiving eve, the white tower atop Telegraph Hill lit up with films of the Native American occupation of Alcatraz, visible for miles.
story: On the eve of Thanksgiving 2009, Coit Tower became a movie screen. The artists Ben Wood and David Mark put three projectors on neighbourhood rooftops, each one covering 120 degrees of the 210-foot fluted tower, and used new software to correct for its grooved surface [1]. On two nights, from about 7 p.m. until dawn, the tower showed films about the Native American occupation of Alcatraz, which had begun 40 years earlier. The soundtrack went out on KPOO 89.5 FM, and organisers said the images could be seen from three miles away [1]. The occupation began on November 20, 1969, when a group calling itself Indians of All Tribes, many of them young urban college students, took the island. It lasted until June 11, 1971 [2]. The screenings also honoured the Ohlone, whose territory ran from San Francisco to Big Sur. Ann-Marie Sayers of Indian Canyon, a consortium of Ohlone tribes, worked on the project. "This serves as an awareness," she said, "that as a people we are still here" [1]. Wood had once imagined the white tower as a totem pole. Rec and Park and the Telegraph Hill Dwellers approved the show [1].

title: From 'seedy' to the National Register
place: Central YMCA Hotel, 351 Turk St, in the Uptown Tenderloin Historic District
hook: For decades the papers called it 'seedy'. In 2009 its hotels and apartment blocks became one of the largest residential historic districts in the nation.
story: Almost everything in the Tenderloin was built between the 1906 earthquake and the early 1940s. After the fire, the city required fire-resistant construction, which helps define the district: mostly three- to seven-storey hotels, boarding houses and apartments in Tudor, Spanish Colonial and Renaissance Revival dress, with a few Moderne towers [1]. A survey in 1983 proposed a historic district, but residents rejected it. They feared it would bring gentrification before their protective rezoning was secured [2]. The idea was then forgotten for two decades, until the Tenderloin Housing Clinic won a grant for a new survey in 2006 [2]. On July 25, 2008, the State Historical Resources Commission voted unanimously for the nomination. Its buildings include what Randy Shaw called the world's largest collection of historic single-room-occupancy hotels, plus landmarks like the Central YMCA, the Hibernia Bank and the Alcazar Theater [2]. The Uptown Tenderloin Historic District joined the National Register on February 5, 2009 [1]. Beyond Chron counted 470 buildings, while the Register lists 408 contributing ones [1][2]. Seventy-three plaques now mark buildings across the blocks [1].

title: Mai tais to the rescue
place: Tonga Room, Fairmont Hotel (California & Powell side)
hook: When the Fairmont planned to rip out its tiki bar for condos and a ballroom, fans fought back the most San Francisco way possible: by drinking there.
story:
The Tonga Room occupies what was the Fairmont's 1929 indoor swimming pool, the Terrace Plunge. In 1945 MGM set director Mel Melvin turned the pool into a lagoon with a floating stage [2][1]. Today it has a dance floor of lumber-schooner planks and a fake thunderstorm every half-hour [2].

In 2009 the hotel's owners unveiled a renovation built around condominiums that would have removed it [2]. The plan also called for demolishing the hotel tower and moving the grand ballroom into the Tonga's space. The developers' adviser argued the bar was "so inconsistent" with a Beaux-Arts hotel going upscale [1]. But the city's draft environmental report, informed by architectural historian Christopher VerPlanck, declared the Tonga a "historical resource," calling it "one of the best examples of 'high-style' Tiki bar/restaurant in San Francisco" [1].

Meanwhile fans simply showed up. "They had a line out of the door every single night of the week for months," said tiki enthusiast Otto von Stroheim [2]. A Save the Tonga Room Facebook group peaked at 4,000 members, and the spike in sales made management reconsider [2]. The Tonga survived, though the National Trust noted in 2014 that it was not protected in perpetuity [2].

title: Maltese on 'The Road,' and POR-da-lah
place: San Bruno Avenue commercial strip ('The Road')
hook: Sam Spade hunted the Maltese Falcon downtown. But in 2009 the Maltese consulate was on San Bruno Avenue, the Portola's main street.
story: Immigrants from the Mediterranean island of Malta began arriving in the 1920s and formed a small ethnic island around San Bruno Avenue, which locals called "The Road," opening grocery stores and small businesses [1][2]. Barbara Fenech, who grew up there, told Chronicle columnist Carl Nolte that at one time about half the families in or near the Portola were Maltese, and that the district was "a city within a city": two furniture stores, clothing stores, cleaners, bakeries and a big movie theatre [1]. By 2009 the Maltese consulate was still on San Bruno Avenue, but Lido Pastry, famous for its St. Honoré cake, had become a Central American bakery selling pan salvadoreño, and about half the Portola's roughly 13,000 people were Asian [1]. "Like any other place, things change," Fenech said [1]. The old settlers left their mark on the name itself. Longtime residents insist it is "POR-da-lah," not "por-TOE-la," and SF Weekly traced that stress to the Italian and Maltese immigrants of the 1920s [3]. The argument is older than the neighbourhood's name: before the 1909 Portola Festival, committee member James Rolph consulted scholars, who agreed it "should be a crescendo, ending with a crash on the 'LA'" [3].

title: Ninety saints dancing, Malcolm X among them
place: St. Gregory of Nyssa Episcopal Church, 500 De Haro Street
hook: Above a congregation that dances around its altar, a twelve-foot Christ leads ninety saints, including Anne Frank, Lady Godiva, Shakespeare and Julia Morgan.
story:
St. Gregory of Nyssa Episcopal Church went up at 500 De Haro Street in 1995. Its architecture mixes Russian Orthodox, Japanese Shinto and Craftsman styles, and light comes in through windows ringing its dome [1][2]. It is named for a fourth-century bishop who defended music and movement in worship at a time when many thought dancing dangerously sensual. So the congregation dances around the altar during services [1].

Above them, circling the rotunda, is a giant icon of ninety larger-than-life dancing saints, led by a twelve-foot Christ in jewel colours and gold leaf. Some are traditional, like St. Teresa and St. Francis. Others are surprises: Malcolm X, Anne Frank, Margaret Mead, Sojourner Truth, Lady Godiva with her horse, Queen Elizabeth I, Shakespeare, Bacchus, and the architect Julia Morgan, whose Potrero Hill Neighborhood House stands farther up De Haro Street [1][4].

The painter Mark Dukes, a deacon of the St. John Coltrane African Orthodox Church, first came to St. Gregory's through its soup kitchen, and the church eventually became his studio. He spent ten years on the icon and finished it in 2009 [1][3]. "It's about love," he said [1].

title: The Carnegie Branch Made Quake-Safe
place: Richmond/Senator Milton Marks Branch Library, 351 9th Avenue
hook: San Francisco's first Carnegie library kept its shelves nearly unchanged for forty years. Then the Richmond's readers doubled them, and a bond rebuilt the whole thing.
story: The Richmond Branch on Ninth Avenue was the first San Francisco library built with Andrew Carnegie's money, dedicated in 1914 in an Italianate design by Bliss and Faville [1][2]. Its later history is quieter but telling. Sometime in the early 1930s the growing children's collection moved downstairs, into a room whose 'Lecture Hall' lettering still marks the 10th Avenue entrance [2]. From the 1930s to the 1970s the book collection barely grew, filling only the original wall shelves; after that, the librarians wrote, the reading, listening and viewing demands of Richmond residents doubled the shelving and brought books, tapes, videos and CDs in several languages [2]. In December 2000 the Landmarks Board nominated the building as a city landmark [1]; it became Landmark No. 247 [3]. With a city bond and $6 million in state Proposition 14 funds, the library was renovated to be seismically safe, accessible and wired, and reopened on 16 May 2009 [1]. Today it carries the name of the Richmond/Senator Milton Marks Branch [1].

title: The Ingleside Library Finally Gets a Home
place: Ingleside Branch Library, 1298 Ocean Avenue
hook: For 76 years the Ingleside branch made do in a rented storefront, for a long time the second-smallest in the city. In 2009 it got a building of its own.
story: The Women's Club of Ingleside asked for a branch library building about eight years before it opened, but the money, Carnegie grant included, had run out [2]. So the Ingleside branch, the city's 11th, opened in 1925 in a storefront leased for $40 a month [1][2]. That storefront, on side-street Ashton Avenue, had just 1,237 square feet, and for many years it was the second-smallest branch in San Francisco. Its floor plan was designed for retail, which made children's storytimes almost impossible. Yet it was one of the busiest branches in the 26-branch system [2]. On May 30, 2001, the library moved into a leased former Bank of America building at 1649 Ocean Avenue, near Faxon. Almost four times larger, it had full disability access, computers and internet access, and a place on the main street [1][2]. Neighbours wanted more. In 2003, community leader Al Harris said he was "really pleased that we're getting a brand-new library on Ocean Avenue" [3]. The long-awaited new branch building opened in 2009 at 1298 Ocean Avenue, at Plymouth [1].

title: Walt Disney's Story Moves Into a Barracks
place: Walt Disney Family Museum, 104 Montgomery Street
hook: Walt Disney's daughter turned an empty 1897 Army barracks into a museum of her father's life, and builders found a WWII soldier's secret letters in the walls.
story: The red-brick barracks at 104 Montgomery Street went up in 1897, one of a row built to house soldiers on the Main Post [1]. By the time the Army left, the building's historic interior walls, ceilings and finishes were gone. John King reported it was stripped for structural work in 1995 [1][2]. Walt Disney's daughter, Diane Disney Miller, founded a museum about her father here, and it opened in October 2009 [1][2]. The whole project cost $110 million, including $52 million for construction. The brick front and porch look much as they always did, but seismic concrete now hides behind the white walls. The old courtyard has been filled with a 31-foot-tall glass-walled gallery by the theatre designer David Rockwell [2]. Visitors walk in past 248 awards. A former gym next door, built in 1908 with bowling alleys, became offices, and the museum's mechanical systems were tucked into an old machine-gun shed [1][2]. The rehab turned up something unexpected. Behind a wall, workers found a stack of handwritten letters in Italian. They came from an Italian soldier held here as a prisoner of war, who stayed on as a soldier after Italy switched sides in World War II [3].

title: A Farm Where the On-Ramps Were
place: Laguna Street between Oak and Fell (Hayes Valley Farm, 450 Laguna)
hook: For three years, vacant lots left by the demolished freeway ramps grew fava beans and fruit trees, until the condos arrived as planned.
story: After the Central Freeway's on-ramps came down, the land on Laguna Street between Oak and Fell stood empty [1][2]. In 2010 Mayor Gavin Newsom's Office of Economic and Workforce Development proposed an interim use and put up a $50,000 first-year grant, paid for with parking revenue from Octavia Boulevard [1]. Volunteers built Hayes Valley Farm on the lots. The soil was tested at 64 points, and only one exceeded federal lead standards [1]. "Our main yield is education," said director Chris Burley [1]. The farm grew a permaculture garden by sheet-mulching cardboard, horse manure and mulch straight onto the old freeway land, and planted fava beans to put nitrogen back into the soil [2]. "It doesn't take a lot of time, funding, or resources to create biodiversity spaces loved by communities," said co-founder Jay Rosenberg [2]. The farm was always meant to be temporary, with the lots set aside for mixed affordable and market-rate housing [1]. By the farm's own count, tens of thousands of visitors took part [3]. It moved off its Oak Street side on March 1, 2013, and its final day was May 31, 2013 [3]. Volunteers went on to start a string of new urban-farming projects around the city [2].

title: A Library Named for History's Rescuer
place: Chinatown Branch Library (Him Mark Lai Branch), 1135 Powell St
hook: As a boy he escaped an 8-by-10-foot family home through books from the Chinatown library. The library now carries his name.
story: Him Mark Lai was born in Chinatown on November 1, 1925 [2]. He grew up in his immigrant family's 8-by-10-foot home and escaped through books borrowed from the Chinatown branch library [1]. He went on to rescue a history that others had ignored. He wrote ten books and more than 100 essays in English and Chinese on Chinese American life, and with a colleague he taught the country's first Chinese American history course, at San Francisco State [1][2]. Scholars called him the "Dean of Chinese American History" [2]. He died of bladder cancer in May 2009 [2]. In November 2010 the Library Commission voted unanimously to add his name to the Chinatown branch. It was only the fifth city library named after a person, and the first since 2003 [1]. "Him Mark Lai single-handedly helped us recover our voice, our history," said Sue Lee of the Chinese Historical Society of America. Vincent Pan of Chinese for Affirmative Action noted that Chinatown's streets are named for Jackson, Washington, Stockton and Powell: "It's obvious Him Mark Lai's name needs to be there" [1].

title: Mary on a Donkey, Seeking Room
place: Saints Peter and Paul Church, 666 Filbert St
hook: A parishioner and a homeless dog walker invented a North Beach Christmas procession about people with nowhere to stay.
story: In 2006 Marc Bruno, a parishioner at Saints Peter and Paul, and Vincent Depasqua, then homeless, came up with a North Beach version of Las Posadas, the Mexican Christmas re-enactment of Mary and Joseph's search for room at the inn [1]. Depasqua, a well-loved neighbourhood figure and dog walker, built many of the props, including the huge lanterns, and brought other homeless people to walk in the procession [1]. On December 23 it set off from the National Shrine of St. Francis of Assisi on Vallejo Street, stopped at four street corners to pray for the less fortunate, and ended on the steps of Saints Peter and Paul on Washington Square. There "Joseph" asked for room, and the church doors opened [1]. American Conservatory Theater lent biblical-looking costumes, and a mariachi band played [1]. In 2010 Mary was played by Michelle Lambert, a Berklee music student and former parishioner, who rode a donkey in silence [1][2]. Depasqua was not there that year. He had died in March of an alcohol overdose [1]. "We have a place and we think about those who don't," Bruno said [1]. The church, once the heart of Italian North Beach, now also holds Masses in Cantonese [2].

title: Parking meters sprouting like wheat
place: 'Street Life' sculpture, Leland Avenue at Bayshore Boulevard
hook: The gateway to 'downtown' Visitacion Valley is a grove of surplus city parking meters, painted orange and raised on tall, arching poles.
story: In 2009, as the city redesigned Leland Avenue's streetscape, it set aside money for public art [1]. A panel of neighbours and arts professionals picked a proposal by Matthew Passmore and his artist group Rebar. Their plan was twenty poles topped with recycled parking meters, donated by the Municipal Transportation Agency [1]. The community saw the design at the branch library in September 2009, and the Arts Commission approved it on November 2 [2]. Among the panel's requests: make the meters more orange-red, so they wouldn't look like giant matchsticks [1]. According to the Arts Commission, the meters were meant to look as if they had grown to 'a whimsically tall height', like swaying grain. That nods to the valley's farming past and to the nearby Greenway [1][2]. The work, called 'Street Life', was slated for the corner of Leland and Bayshore, in front of the Shun Lee Market, and was standing there by 2011 [2][3]. Its budget was $35,000 in the planning documents; one later account put it at $38,000 [1][3]. 'The street furnishings of today may well be the art supplies of tomorrow,' Passmore said [3].

title: Seven seasons of greens on Cotter Street
place: 203 Cotter Street (former Little City Gardens farm)
hook: For almost seven years, two young farmers tried to make a living selling greens and flowers grown on a three-quarter-acre lot in the Outer Mission.
story: In spring 2010 Brooke Budner and Caitlyn Galloway moved their farm onto an overgrown lot at 203 Cotter Street. Little City Gardens set out to test whether a small commercial urban farm could pay its way. It sold greens, herbs and vegetables to restaurants and neighbours, and later mixed bouquets, dahlias among them, to Bi-Rite [1]. Their hold on the land was always shaky. The owner, squeezed by rising property taxes, put the lot up for sale, and in February 2011 it went to a developer [1]. That March the farmers testified as a Board of Supervisors committee passed new zoning for urban agriculture, which co-sponsor David Chiu said would put the city 'at the forefront of urban agriculture policies nationwide' [1]. In 2014 the three-quarter-acre parcel went up for sale again, and Golden Bridges School bought it [1][2]. On September 29, 2016, after more than three hours and close to a hundred public comments, the Planning Commission voted 7-0 to allow a 200-student school [1]. Neighbours showed photographs of their flooded homes on this former creek bed [1]. The farm packed up by December 15. Its perennials went to Alemany Farm, the Botanical Garden and other farms [1]. The school settled into its long-term home in the Portola in 2020 [2].

title: The sidewalk law born on Haight Street
place: Haight Street at Ashbury
hook: A new mayor pushing a stroller down Haight Street saw a man smoking crack. The ordinance that followed made sitting on San Francisco sidewalks by day a citable offence.
story: Haight residents and storekeepers had long complained about transients blocking the sidewalks and aggressive panhandling [2]. Kent Uyehara, who ran skate and snowboard shops on the street, said he and other merchants took the idea of a ban to police that autumn [1]. Mayor Gavin Newsom had recently moved his family to the neighbourhood. He said that while strolling Haight Street with his infant daughter he saw a man smoking crack, and in March 2010 he and Police Chief George Gascón proposed banning sitting or lying on city sidewalks from 7 a.m. to 11 p.m. [1][2]. Opponents, campaigning as "Sidewalks Are for People" and "Stand Against Sit/Lie", argued it targeted the homeless and day labourers [2][3]. A vice-president of the Haight Ashbury Neighborhood Council, the group born in the 1960s freeway fight, questioned whether voters understood what they had approved [2]. Voters approved it as Proposition L on November 2, 2010 [2][3]. Enforcement peaked at 1,011 citations in 2013 and fell to 114 by 2017 as police changed tactics [4].

title: A Filipino Stage in a Sixth Street Basement
place: Bindlestiff Studio, 185 Sixth Street
hook: When redevelopment took their theater, Filipino American artists refused to disappear. They came back to the same address, one floor down.
story: Bindlestiff Studio was founded in 1989 by Chrystene Ells, Chris Brophy and a group of local theatre artists as an experimental space in the Plaza Hotel at Sixth and Howard [1][2]. In the late 1990s Filipino artists took it over. The studio's own history credits Allan S. Manalo of the company "tongue in A mood", who became artistic director in 1997. Community historians date the Filipino management to 1998, the year the PinoisePop music festival was held there [1][2]. It became known as the centre of Filipino American performing arts in the Bay Area [1][2]. Then the Redevelopment Agency bought the Plaza Hotel for low-cost housing. The accounts give 2000 and 2003 for different stages of the takeover, and the theatre was lost [1][2]. After a public outcry the agency agreed to build the shell of a new 99-seat black-box theatre in the basement of the rebuilt housing. After delays and negotiations the new Bindlestiff opened on September 15, 2011, back at 185 Sixth Street. In its first three months it staged four full productions for more than 2,100 people [1]. It calls itself the nation's only permanent community-based venue dedicated to Filipino American performers [1].

title: From a box of books to a branch
place: Visitacion Valley Branch Library, 201 Leland Ave
hook: The valley's library began in 1934 as a small deposit of books. It took 77 years for the neighbourhood to get a library building of its own.
story: San Francisco Public Library came to the valley in 1934, not as a building but as a "deposit collection", a small stock of books placed in the neighbourhood. It was the system's 18th branch [1]. It later became a full-service branch, housed in a leased storefront at 45 Leland Avenue [1]. Residents wanted more. In 2005 the neighbourhood historians writing a book about the valley hoped to keep their oral histories and local stories at a new branch library that was "yet to be built, pending funding" [2]. The new library opened on July 30, 2011, on the corner of Leland Avenue and Rutland Street [1]. It was one of several city investments, along with a Muni streetcar extension and new street improvements, meant to work together with the planned redevelopment of the old Schlage Lock site [3]. The library quickly became part of neighbourhood life. At the 2015 Leland Avenue street fair, its staff ran a prize wheel where a four-year-old won a picture book [4].

title: Occupying the Sidewalk at the Fed
place: Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, 101 Market Street
hook: For three months in 2011 protesters camped outside the Federal Reserve. Police cleared them again and again. Each time, they came back.
story: In autumn 2011, as Occupy Wall Street spread, San Francisco's version took root on the sidewalk outside the Federal Reserve Bank at 101 Market Street, the original Occupy protest site, established in early October [1]. A second tent city grew up in mid-October in Justin Herman Plaza a block away, protesting bank bailouts and economic injustice [2]. At about 1 a.m. on December 7, police surrounded the plaza camp, gave protesters five minutes to leave and arrested 70 people; crews power-washed the ground afterwards. "I lost everything I owned," said 51-year-old camper Jack Martin. Asked what he would do next, he answered: "Occupy, occupy, occupy, occupy" [2]. Within a day the campers had returned to the Fed sidewalk. After hourly warnings, officers moved in at 4 a.m. on Sunday, December 11 and arrested 55 more for illegal lodging [1]. Nick Shaw, 32, said police struck him with batons as he tried to grab his duffel bag, which held his medication, birth certificate and coat; police said protesters spat on officers. By afternoon many were back with sleeping bags and signs. "I'm undeterred," said protester James Cartmill [1].

title: Public radio in a high school

hook: One of the West Coast's earliest FM stations belongs to the San Francisco school district, and broadcasts from a makeshift studio on a Portola campus.
story: KALW 91.7 FM is technically owned by the San Francisco Unified School District [1]. Its origin story comes in two versions. The Chronicle reported that it first broadcast at the 1939 World's Fair on Treasure Island and was donated to the district in 1941 to train students in radio; federal records cited on Wikipedia show the district applying for an educational FM station in May 1940, with test transmissions from Samuel Gompers Trades School on 10 March 1941, making it the first FM station on the West Coast [1][2]. The station cut financial ties with the schools in 1992 but kept a free home at Burton High School on Mansell Street [1]. In January 2011, 70 years on, it was about $120,000 in the hole on a $1.4 million budget, and the school board voted unanimously to lend it up to $200,000, a line of credit equal to about two teachers' salaries [1]. "This is a bridge loan for an entity that provides a lot to this community," general manager Matt Martin said, as reporters worked out of the station's makeshift studio [1]. Two years earlier Carl Nolte had counted KALW, "tucked away in a corner of the neighborhood," among the Portola's secrets [3].
