title: Switching off the city's last fossil-fuel plant
place: Former Potrero Power Plant, 23rd and Illinois Streets
hook: For decades a power plant at Potrero Point pumped heated water into the bay and pollution into the southeast. In 2011, after a generation of fighting, it went dark.
story:
The site at Potrero Point is where San Francisco Gas Light built a small generator around 1890, the first power plant of the company that became PG&E [1]. Its big boiler, Unit 3, went up in 1965, and three diesel generators for peak demand followed in 1976 [1]. At full power the plant drew about 226 million gallons of bay water a day through its condensers and sent it back about 10°C warmer [1].

Many southeast residents suffer unusually high rates of cancer, asthma and other illness, and some fought for more than a decade to close the plant [2]. In 2006 the state Public Utilities Commission rejected owner Mirant's expansion plans [1]. City Hall split over whether to replace it with cleaner gas plants, a fight that contributed to the 2008 firing of the city utilities chief, Susan Leal [2]. In the late 1990s the Potrero Boosters had also faced a plan for a 570-megawatt plant at 23rd and Illinois [3].

Closure finally came once new transmission lines, including a transbay cable in November 2010, could carry enough power into the city [2]. "People have waited a generation for this," said Mayor Gavin Newsom [2]. The plant shut down in January 2011 [1]. "It's closed down," said Supervisor Sophie Maxwell, whose district included it. "That's the bottom line." [2]

title: The Furniture Mart That Became Twitter
place: Market Square (former San Francisco Mart), 1355 Market Street
hook: Twitter threatened to leave town. San Francisco answered with a payroll-tax break drawn around a nearly empty Art Deco furniture showroom on Market Street.
story: In 2011 Twitter had about 400 employees, a home on Folsom Street and plans to grow to as many as 3,000. It told the city it might move to the Peninsula to escape San Francisco's payroll tax [1][2]. City leaders saw a chance to revive Mid-Market, where nearly one in three storefronts stood empty [2]. Their answer was a six-year break on payroll taxes for new jobs at companies that moved into the Central Market and Tenderloin area. Three days after the Board of Supervisors approved it, Twitter signed a lease on the old furniture mart at 1355 Market Street [1]. "We were ready to go," Twitter's policy chief Colin Crowell later told TIME. "Did not want to go" [2]. Mayor Ed Lee said he was "absolutely convinced" Twitter would otherwise have left. He pointed to new cafés and apartments along a corridor that had been "vacant and dark" [2]. Critics called it the "Twitter tax break". "Twitter held San Francisco hostage," said one housing advocate. By 2014 union members were chanting outside the headquarters, and some residents had nicknamed the area the "Twitterloin" [2].

title: 27 up, 27 down

hook: In 130 years no Giant had thrown a perfect game. On a June night in 2012 Matt Cain did it, thanks partly to a belly-flop on the warning track.
story: Before the game on June 13, 2012, Matt Cain and golfer Dustin Johnson hit golf balls from home plate into McCovey Cove [1]. Then Cain retired all 27 Houston Astros he faced, striking out 14, as the Giants won 10-0 in front of 42,298 people [1][2]. It was the first perfect game in the franchise's 130 years. None of Mathewson, Hubbell, Marichal, Perry or Lincecum had managed it [2]. It needed help. Melky Cabrera made running catches in left [1][2]. In the seventh, Jordan Schafer drove a ball to right-center that looked like extra bases. Gregor Blanco, whom coaches had told to shade toward center, dived and landed belly-first on the warning track in front of the Visa sign with the ball in his glove [2]. Back in the dugout, Cain hugged him [2]. In the last three innings, Cain said, there was so much adrenaline he had trouble seeing Buster Posey's signs [2]. Pinch-hitter Jason Castro bounced the 125th pitch to third. Joaquín Arias backed up and threw across to Brandon Belt, and the Giants poured out to mob Cain [1][2]. He was, as it happens, the only pitcher ever to score a run in his own perfect game [1].

title: A Chinatown Kid's Courage, Named in Concrete
place: Betty Ann Ong Chinese Recreation Center, Mason & Washington
hook: She learned basketball at the rec center on Mason Street. On September 11, 2001, flight attendant Betty Ong calmly stayed on the phone for 23 minutes aboard Flight 11.
story: Betty Ann Ong grew up in Chinatown and played basketball at the neighbourhood rec center at Mason and Washington [1][2]. On September 11, 2001, she was a flight attendant on American Airlines Flight 11. Her call to the airline began: "The cockpit is not answering the phone and there's somebody stabbed in business class" [3]. For 23 minutes she calmly passed on what she learned from crew and passengers; the call ended two minutes before the plane hit the World Trade Center's North Tower [3][2]. In October 2011, after a petition with more than 3,700 signatures, the Recreation Commission voted unanimously to name the center after her. "The legacy of Betty and other 9/11 heroes will be remembered forever," said her brother Harry [2]. The old 1951 three-storey concrete building was rebuilt with 2008 parks bond money, and on July 14, 2012, Mayor Ed Lee opened the new Betty Ann Ong Chinese Recreation Center [4]. Her childhood friend Rev. Norman Fong, who pushed for the name, listens to her recording every year. "Maybe sometimes, we don't appreciate that an average Chinatown kid could be a national hero," he said [1].

title: A Nobel for rewinding cells
place: Gladstone Institutes, 1650 Owens Street
hook: In a lab on reclaimed railyard in Mission Bay, a Japanese doctor turned stem-cell pioneer keeps working on the discovery that won him the Nobel.
story: Shinya Yamanaka trained as a doctor in Japan, including a residency at National Osaka Hospital, then came to San Francisco as a postdoctoral fellow at the Gladstone Institute of Cardiovascular Disease from 1993 to 1995 [1]. Back in Japan in 2006, he showed that ordinary adult cells could be reprogrammed into an embryonic-like state by delivering a handful of transcription factors. These 'induced pluripotent stem' (iPS) cells can in principle become any cell in the body [1][2]. In 2007 he returned to Gladstone as a senior investigator, while also leading Kyoto University's iPS center [1]. Gladstone, founded in 1979 at San Francisco General Hospital, had moved to Owens Street beside UCSF's new Mission Bay campus [3]. On October 8, 2012, the Nobel Assembly awarded the Prize in Physiology or Medicine jointly to Yamanaka and John Gurdon, who had shown in 1962 that a frog cell's specialisation could be reversed [2]. The Nobel committee said their discoveries had 'revolutionised our understanding of how cells and organisms develop' [2]. Gladstone lists him as a senior investigator and UCSF professor of anatomy [1].

title: Goats, Parrots and a Hawk on Woolsey Hill
place: Woolsey Street side of University Mound Reservoir's South Basin
hook: One August morning in 2012 a truck unloaded 275 goats onto the reservoir slopes. They were there to eat the brush and cut the fire risk.
story:
On the morning of August 2, 2012, a truck unloaded 275 goats onto the Woolsey Street side of University Mound Reservoir's South Basin [1]. The mixed herd of Angora, Pygmy, Alpine and Spanish goats came from a company called Goats R Us. With a goatherd and a dog, they were to spend a few days eating the brush on the steep slopes to reduce the fire risk, as part of the water department's integrated pest management program [1]. Jerilyn Downing, the department's landscape manager, said the goats were hired once a year for sites across the city: about 300 more were at Twin Peaks, and roughly 1,000 were working citywide [1]. Two weeks later a flock turned up at College Hill Reservoir in Bernal Heights. A new neighbour there worked out that they belonged to the same SF Water brush-clearance project that had 'recently devoured the tall grasses of the Portola District' [2].

The hill has wilder residents too. In 2017 neighbours reported a flock of wild parrots, apparently cherry-headed conures, living in the trees between Woolsey Street and the north end of Burton High School. Neighbours said the birds flew off toward downtown in the morning and came back in the late afternoon. A block away, near Goettingen and Dwight streets, a hawk had built a nest [3].

title: Last Call at the Rudest Waiter's Noodle House
place: Sam Wo Restaurant (original site), 813 Washington St
hook: You walked through the kitchen and climbed to the dining room, and your food came up by dumbwaiter. In 2012, a century of Chinatown late nights ended.
story: To eat at Sam Wo, you walked in through the cramped street-level kitchen and climbed a narrow staircase to tiny second- and third-floor dining rooms, and your food came up by dumbwaiter [1][2]. Nobody agrees on its age: some say it opened after the 1906 earthquake, others say earlier [2]. It stayed open until 3 a.m., and Beat poets hung out there in the 1950s [2]. Its legend was Edsel Ford Fung (often spelled Fong), "the world's rudest waiter", who insulted customers, criticised their orders and slammed down plates. Armistead Maupin put him in Tales of the City and Herb Caen wrote about him often [1][2]. Fung died in 1984, but the house-rules sign lived on: "No Booze, No B.S., No Jive, No Coffee, Milk, Soft Drinks, Fortune Cookies" [1]. In April 2012, after a meeting with the city's health and fire departments, owner David Ho, who had run it for three decades, said he could not afford the repairs. "Too old. Everything's too old," he said [1][2]. On its final Friday, fans lined up for one last bowl of chow fun, jook and barbecue pork rolls [2].

Paul Leonard and Sutro Library [2]. It won the 2012 Project of the Year award from the Design-Build Institute of America's Western Pacific Region [2]. title: The College Told to Prepare for Closure

hook: In 2012 accreditors threatened to shut the city's biggest public school. Students, teachers and City Hall spent five years fighting to keep it open.

The crisis hit in 2012 [1]. In July 2013 the Accrediting Commission for Community and Junior Colleges decided to revoke the accreditation of City College of San Francisco, the largest public school in California. The decision was put on hold after a legal challenge [2]. The commission, the Chronicle noted, had "never found wrongdoing or substandard instruction." Its complaints were about governance, finances and reporting [2].

The crisis came to feel like a fight over the city's future. Students and teachers rallied downtown in July 2013. A state-appointed special trustee cancelled a voter-approved performing arts centre, and some campus land came under development pressure [1]. "City College is a mirror for what is happening in the city," organiser Kevine Boggess said [1].

In January 2015 the commission granted a two-year reprieve, though it still found the college out of compliance in 32 areas [2]. In February 2017 Mayor Ed Lee and Supervisor Jane Kim announced Free City College: San Francisco would pay $5.4 million a year to cover the $46-a-credit fee for city residents [3].

title: The Gardener Who Kept a Promise
place: Grace Marchant Garden, Filbert Steps at Napier Lane
hook: As a boy he met the woman gardening a former dump on the Filbert Steps. He spent the next 33 years keeping her garden alive, unpaid.
story: As a boy in the 1950s, exploring the city alone by streetcar and on foot, Gary Kray wandered up the Filbert Steps and met the woman tending a garden there [1]. She was Grace Marchant, who had moved to Napier Lane in 1949, when the steps ran through an informal garbage dump. The city let her burn the trash, and the story goes that the fire burned for three days [2]. In 1975, with her help, Kray moved into the 1855 cottage next door at 10 Napier Lane. From 1979 he did the pruning and weeding she could no longer manage [1]. Before she died in 1982 at 96, she asked him to carry on her work [1]. He did, without pay, for 33 years, as long as she had worked there, adding palms, Italian cypresses, tree ferns and dozens of roses [1]. He drove a night taxi to keep his days free. When development threatened the garden in the 1980s, neighbours formed Friends of the Garden and, with the Trust for Public Land, protected it for good [1][2]. His Halloween jack-o'-lanterns grew to more than 300 glowing faces, until the crowds forced him to stop [1]. Kray died at home on Napier Lane on September 7, 2012, aged 70 [1].

title: The Windmill That Turned Again

hook: For decades the world's largest windmill of its kind stood sail-less at the edge of Ocean Beach. A Dutch millwright rebuilt it, labelling every piece of timber.
story: Banker Samuel G. Murphy gave $20,000 for the park's second windmill, and it first turned its sails on April 11, 1908 [2]. It pumped well water for irrigation and was said to be the largest windmill in the world. But electric pumps soon made it obsolete [2]. In 1944 one spar was so rotten it threatened to bring the whole structure down, and it was removed [2]. The windmill may have spent more decades without its sails than with them [2]. A community group, the Campaign to Save the Golden Gate Park Windmills, helped raise money, and restoration finally began in 2002. Private donations, state grants and city funds added up to about $4 million [1]. Fourth-generation Dutch millwright Lucas Verbij took charge, and a new 68-ton cap went on in 2011 [1]. "When we took the building apart, we labeled every piece of timber and wood," said Recreation and Park project manager Dan Mauer. Only the concrete base and about a third of the materials were original [1]. On April 28, 2012, its sails turned for the city's Queen's Day festival, alongside the Dutch Windmill to the north [1].

title: The battle over the library's walls

story:
The Bernal Heights branch library at 500 Cortland Avenue was designed by Frederick H. Meyer, built with WPA funds, and dedicated in 1940 [1]. It closed for nearly two years for renovation and reopened in January 2010 [1]. What to do about the mural covering its outside walls turned into a long, heated fight. Some people wanted the old mural restored, some wanted new art, and some wanted bare walls. The Arts and Library commissions were unsure how to proceed. Supervisor David Campos and neighbours brought in a Bernal mediator, Beth Roy, and a community group met week after week until it reached a consensus [2].

Opponents caused more delays. Finally, on October 4, 2012, the old mural was painted over [3]. The comments poured in, ranging from 'Today is the BEST DAY EVER!' to grief over losing 'a piece of Bernal Heights culture' [3]. Artist Ruben Rude painted the Moultrie Street side, and Precita Eyes made the Cortland facade in hand-painted tile [3]. In January 2015 the branch celebrated the finished murals with salsa music from longtime resident Michael Govea [4].

On Tomaso Court, Amy Hung, 30, came back with her baby to the house she had lived in for 25 years and found the garage full of mud. 'All my stuff is in that garage,' she said. 'My books. My camera. title: The doctor who called it God's Hotel
place: Laguna Honda Hospital campus, site of the demolished Clarendon Hall
hook: A machine 'like a praying mantis made out of metal' ate the old ward building one bite at a time. The doctor watching it wrote a book.
story:
Clarendon Hall opened at Laguna Honda in 1910. It was the first building put up specifically for long-term medical care [2]. For decades the hospital's patients lay in long, open 'Florence Nightingale' wards [2]. Dr. Victoria Sweet worked there for decades [3], and in 2012 published God's Hotel, her account of the old almshouse-hospital [1].

In it she describes the demolition of Clarendon Hall. Workmen first stripped out windows, faucets and sinks, 'the way termites take things apart'. Then 'a machine that looked like a praying mantis made out of metal' bit off pieces of the tiled roof, one after another, until by the end of the day the century-old building was rubble [1]. Two weeks later Sister Miriam resigned. She wrote a newspaper article about the 'beautiful spirit of Clarendon' and warned that the hospital was being cut back quietly: its patient numbers down by a third, the hospice chaplain laid off [1]. When a marketing plan proposed taking 'Hospital' out of Laguna Honda's name, the doctors asked who, then, were all the sick, frail patients they cared for every day.

The two towers that replaced it were finished in December 2010 [2]. 'Hospital' stayed in the name [1]. Sweet described Laguna Honda's people as those who 'fall through the safety nets of the safety nets' [3].

title: What the Navy left in the soil
place: Northeast corner of Treasure Island, former USS Pandemonium training site
hook: Residents were told to grow their plants in pots. In 2012 the Navy finally admitted what the island had really been used for.
story:
Cold War training left marks on the island. From 1946 the Navy ran radiological safety training here [1]. Around 1959 the Damage Control School staged a 'Mock A-Bomb' with TNT, smoke grenades and hundreds of gallons of napalm, while 150 Marines acted out radiation injuries [1]. Students practised decontamination on the USS Pandemonium, a full-size mock ship built from salvaged parts that sat at the island's northeast corner [1].

In August 2012, a draft Navy report acknowledged fully for the first time that the island had also repaired and scrapped material from Pacific Fleet ships exposed to atomic tests [2]. Other possible sources of radiation included the training ship, which had been deliberately doused with radioactive material, and glow-in-the-dark buttons handed out at the 1939-40 fair [2]. A state health official wrote that Navy contractors had removed 16,000 cubic yards of dirt, some of it 400 times the EPA's exposure limit for topsoil. The Navy and state toxics regulators said the remaining levels were too low to harm people [2].

Resident Emily Rapaport had long grown her plants in above-ground pots, as island rules required. 'They should have been more open and upfront,' she said [2].

title: 148 Steps and 600 Donors on 16th Avenue
place: Hidden Garden Steps, 16th Ave between Kirkham & Lawton Sts
hook: Inspired by the famous tiled steps up the hill, neighbours spent four years turning a neglected concrete stairway into a garden sanctuary covered in mosaic.
story: The 16th Avenue Tiled Steps drew visitors from all over the world, and neighbours a few blocks north wanted the same for their stairway. For four years volunteers worked, in one organiser's words, 'setting aside differences' and giving hundreds of hours to transform 'a small, neglected piece of San Francisco' on 16th Avenue between Kirkham and Lawton [1]. They brought back the same artists, Colette Crutcher and Aileen Barr, whose earlier staircase had inspired the project [1][2]. Their design covers 148 steps in ceramic tile, and KZ Tile installed it. More than 600 donors paid for it, and it was dedicated on 7 December 2013 [1]. The gardens came next. Until the COVID-19 shutdown in 2020, volunteers met on the second Saturday of every month to sweep the steps and plant succulents, California natives and clivias on the slopes on either side [1]. A neighbour writing a decade later described what they had made as 'an almost sacred space'. Scrub jays, mourning doves, hawks and ravens share it with visitors [1].

title: A $21 million park and a doomed windmill
place: Palega Recreation Center and Playground, Felton Street
hook: The Portola's biggest park got a $21 million rebuild. Its showpiece, a giant twirling sculpture, was no match for the neighbourhood's wind.
story: Palega, the big park and recreation centre in the middle of the lower Portola, won about $21.1 million from the city's 2008 Clean Parks Bond [1]. Ground was broken on 7 March 2012. The plan gutted and renovated the gym and offices, added a 3,200-square-foot steel-framed wing with floor-to-ceiling glass and a new entrance on Felton Street, and replaced fields, courts, playground and planting, aiming for LEED Silver [1]. It was meant to take about 14 months; by August 2013 new grass was going down and completion had slipped to the end of September [2]. Not every neighbour felt sure the new building would be for them: artists Kate Connell and Oscar Melara drew a lotería card, "The Hoops," after residents worried that young African American men would be less welcome after the remodel, to stake a claim for returning players [3]. The rebuilt park also got a twirling kinetic sculpture called "Zephyros." It was in and out of the repair shop almost from the start, while neighbour Jackie Morri phoned the Arts Commission monthly for updates; in March 2019 the city gave up on fixing it safely and proposed a replacement from its collection, which the Portola Planet hoped would be "completely static" [4].

title: A Buried Creek Beneath Wayland Street
place: Wayland Street near University Street, along the proposed Upper Yosemite Creek daylighting route
hook: A creek rises in McLaren Park and runs to the bay, mostly in a pipe under Portola streets. In 2013 the city began planning to bring part back above ground.
story:
Yosemite Creek rises from a spring in McLaren Park and once ran downhill all the way to the bay [1][2]. Today most of it flows through a covered pipe under the Portola's streets and into the city's combined sewer system. On a dry day that system treats about 80 million gallons of water; in a heavy rain it can be 575 million [1]. An early Portola resident, in oral histories gathered by Chris Ortiz, recalled a creek by his house near Mansell Street, 'probably Yosemite Cr.' [3].

In the autumn of 2013 the Public Utilities Commission led a packed crowd of neighbours along the route of its Upper Yosemite Creek Daylighting project, a plan to bring part of the creek back to the surface along McLaren Park's border with the Portola [1]. One idea was to move back the reservoir fence and let the creek wind down beside the basin through a new public space [1]. Project manager Raphael Garcia said that if it succeeded it would be the city's first daylighting project of its kind. Asked for money to take it further, he said: 'the funds I have, are the funds I have' [1]. In March 2017 the final design, with the creek drawn along Wayland Street, was shown at a church hall on Woolsey Street [2].

title: A neighbourhood lotería on the freeway fence
place: Alemany Island panels, north entrance to San Bruno Avenue
hook: Two artists asked neighbours what the Portola looked like, turned the answers into a bingo game, then hung it at the neighbourhood's front door.
story: Artists Kate Connell and Oscar Melara came of age in the Mission's Latino and Chicano arts movement; Melara co-founded La Raza Silkscreen Center [1]. When they moved to the Portola they started collecting its stories, first by offering their garage as a polling place [1]. They distilled what they heard into Porto-Lotería, a version of Mexican picture bingo with 54 cards: "The Recycler," a Chinese neighbour carrying cans and bottles on a shoulder pole; "The Parol," the Filipino star lanterns lit in December windows; "The Herbalist," the trilingual Chinese-Nicaraguan businessman and acupuncturist Sergio Lee. Neighbours vetted it with gusto: "more Italians!" and "no 'possoms, put skunks" [1]. Opening day at the Portola Branch Library drew more than 800 people, playing in Chinese, Spanish and English [1]. When the Portola Neighborhood Association wanted a mural, board member Lia Smith proposed the lotería, and more than forty households, whole classrooms and one fire station painted panels [1]. One October morning in 2013 volunteers hung 38 of them on a new Caltrans fence at the entrance to San Bruno Avenue, with more to come; best viewed, the Portola Planet advised, while walking to the Alemany Market [2]. Connell counts 48 panels in the finished Alemany Island [1].

title: A trail built for thinking
place: Philosopher's Way trailhead, parking lot southwest of Mansell Street and Visitacion Avenue
hook: Money for a water-tank upgrade paid for 14 granite 'musing stations', including one of Martin Luther King Jr. looking toward the Cow Palace.
story: The money came from a water tank. When the Public Utilities Commission gave La Grande Tank a seismic upgrade, the project's public-art funds paid $146,000 for a 2.7-mile loop trail around the park. The Arts Commission coordinated the work [1][2]. Artists Peter Richards and Susan Schwartzenberg designed it. Stonemason George Gonzalez, who had built the Wave Organ near the Exploratorium with Richards, made its 14 'musing stations' [1]. One black granite marker faces the Cow Palace and carries an etched image of Martin Luther King Jr., who spoke there in 1964 [1][3]. Others describe native grasses and the history of the neighbourhoods, and one shows a 1935 aerial photograph alongside a Visitacion Valley resident's memories [1][4]. At the dedication on January 5, 2013, neighbours and politicians talked about a part of the city they felt had been ignored. 'It's symbolic of the overall neglect of the southeast,' said Portola resident Barbara Gersh. 'It's about time we get our fair share,' said Supervisor Malia Cohen [1].

title: An artist builds his own tomb of sky
place: San Francisco Columbarium, 1 Loraine Court
hook: Facing death in the AIDS years, painter Ed Aulerich-Sugai designed his own niche at the Columbarium: marble, clouds and an empty blue sky.
story: In the 1970s the writer Robert Glück and the Asian American artist Ed Aulerich-Sugai were lovers, both in their twenties [1]. Years later, facing death, Ed decided he wanted his ashes to go in the Columbarium. Glück drove him out "on a bright blue and white day" to look the place over, and when Ed looked up at the tiers of niches he nearly fainted [1]. Glück remembered the building as a "magnificent ruin" and called it a "lovely wedding cake" [1]. Ed and his partner Daniel bought a niche, and Ed made the tomb himself. It is a diorama with a ground of polished viridian marble under a robin's-egg sky of drifting white clouds, and his ashes are in a ceramic vase. He had been painting clouds for two decades [1]. He chose long-lasting pigment and a Plexiglas liner so the canvas would not touch damp cement. He also asked Glück to join him in the niche someday [1]. In 2013 SFMOMA published this chapter from Glück's AIDS memoir-novel About Ed, alongside an art project at the Columbarium and talks there on arts, AIDS and activism [1]. Staff speak of the Columbarium's longstanding embrace of the queer community [2].

title: Jazz finally gets a home
place: SFJAZZ Center, 201 Franklin Street
hook: After thirty years of trucking pianos to borrowed stages, SFJAZZ opened a hall of its own, billed as the first freestanding building in the West made for jazz.
story: SFJAZZ has produced the San Francisco Jazz Festival since 1983 [2]. For three decades it rented trucks to deliver pianos and drums to gigs at other people's venues [1]. In January 2013 it opened a home of its own at Fell and Franklin, billed as the first freestanding building in the West built for jazz performance and education. More than $60 million had been raised over more than a decade to build it [1]. McCoy Tyner, Chick Corea and Esperanza Spalding played the opening gala on a rainy night, with Tom Waits and Amy Tan in the audience [1]. Architect Mark Cavagnero's $64 million building has a see-through glass ground floor. Above it, bands of clear and translucent glass deliberately fail to line up from one floor to the next, an 'off-center syncopation', in the words of Chronicle critic John King [3]. Inside, the 700-seat auditorium wraps seats all the way around the stage. 'I didn't want anything axial, where you feel like you should be in the middle,' Cavagnero said [3]. News coverage of the opening linked the hall to the Fillmore a few blocks north. The Fillmore was once nicknamed 'Harlem of the West', and many of its jazz clubs were destroyed by urban renewal [1].

title: Linda's House on Third Street
place: Bayview Linda Brooks-Burton Branch Library, 5075 Third Street
hook: For generations of Bayview kids, walking into the library felt like walking into "Linda's House." When the new branch opened, it soon took her name.
story: Bayview's library started as a storefront in 1927. In 1969 a red-brick branch went up at Third Street and Revere Avenue, paid for with a $185,700 bequest from Anna E. Waden, a city clerical worker [1]. Linda Brooks-Burton was born and raised in the neighbourhood. She ran the branch from 1995 until 2011, when she was promoted to oversee the southeast libraries [2]. Generations of residents said walking in felt like walking into "Linda's House" [2]. She co-founded the Bayview History Preservation Project in 2007 to record the migration of Black workers to shipyard jobs and the culture they built [2]. The SF Bay View remembered her excitement at finding decades-old community newspapers, one of which she lent them to reprint accounts of the 1966 uprising [3]. Library officials called her the quiet champion behind the push for a new branch [2], which opened on 23 February 2013 [1]. Seven months later, on 19 September 2013, she died suddenly of a heart attack. She was 49 [2][3]. Residents campaigned to honour her, and in March 2015 the library was renamed the Bayview Linda Brooks-Burton Branch [2].

title: Shakespeare comes to the southeast
place: Stage of the Jerry Garcia Amphitheater
hook: San Francisco's free summer Shakespeare began at a Golden Gate Park picnic table. Thirty years on, the company added a second city stage: a hillside bowl in McLaren Park.
story: San Francisco Shakespeare Festival started in the summer of 1983, 'on or around a picnic table in Golden Gate Park', with a production of The Tempest. Its mission was to make Shakespeare accessible to everyone, and it has staged Free Shakespeare in the Park every year since [1]. Its 30th season came in 2012. The company's own history lists 2013 as the year it added 'a second San Francisco Free Shakes venue' in McLaren Park [1]. A park group's chronology puts the first shows in the amphitheatre a year later: five performances of The Taming of the Shrew in 2014. Then came Romeo and Juliet, The Winter's Tale, Hamlet, A Midsummer Night's Dream and As You Like It [2]. In 2018 the amphitheatre also held a sing-along Grease screening [2]. When the venue reopened in September 2021 after a $1.45 million renovation, the company was on stage right after the ribbon-cutting, starting its season with Pericles, Prince of Tyre. 'Like the character Pericles experiences, today is a joyful reunion,' said resident artist Carla Pantoja [3]. The upgrade paid for room for food trucks, better access, bike racks and more backstage storage [3].

title: The Morning Protesters Boarded the Google Bus
place: Valencia St at 24th St
hook: Protesters surrounded a double-decker shuttle bound for Mountain View and climbed aboard. A city's argument about tech had found its symbol.
story: On the morning of December 9, 2013, activists from a group called Heart of the City boarded and blocked a double-decker Google shuttle at Valencia and 24th Streets [1][2]. For about half an hour the protesters chanted "San Francisco, not for sale" and "Stop evictions now," while Google workers waited inside and tweeted [1]. "My shuttle came under siege this morning," wrote one [1]. A man who screamed at organiser Erin McElroy, 31, turned out to be a union worker only pretending to be an angry Google employee [1]. The buses, McElroy said, had "become very symbolic of what's happening to the city in terms of gentrification" [1]. Reuters noted that evictions had risen 25 percent, to 1,716, in the year to February 2013 [1]. The group also handed out a mock ordinance setting out how the tech industry should pay for displacement [2]. The action drew coverage from over a hundred outlets, and Supervisor Eric Mar called for a hearing and an analysis of the shuttles' impact [2].

title: The Museum That Moved Onto the Bay
place: Exploratorium, Pier 15 (Embarcadero at Green St)
hook: A blacklisted physicist, brother of the atomic bomb's father, started a hands-on science museum in 1969. In 2013 it moved out onto a pier and made the bay its exhibit.
story: Frank Oppenheimer had worked beside his brother J. Robert Oppenheimer on the Manhattan Project. After a youthful flirtation with communism he was blacklisted from research and teaching in the McCarthy era, became a cattle rancher in small-town Colorado, then drifted back into teaching at a local high school, where he threw out the textbook in favour of hands-on tools [1]. In 1969 he opened the Exploratorium in the cavernous, nearly empty Palace of Fine Arts, and ran it until just before his death in 1985 [1]. In April 2013 the museum moved to Pier 15 on the Embarcadero [1]. The $300 million new home opened with 600 exhibits, a glass-walled bayside observatory and 1.5 acres of free public space on the pier's plazas and walkways [2]. It turned its setting into the show: the tides, the bay water and its organisms became exhibits, and even the shadows and reflected sunlight from the Financial District towers across the Embarcadero were put to work demonstrating optics. "The location forced us to figure out how to make the whole of the city and the bay hands-on," said director Dennis Bartels [2].

title: Tire Beach, Toxic Beach, Warm Water Cove
place: Warm Water Cove, foot of 24th Street
hook: At the foot of 24th Street, an old sewage outlet beside a power plant became a punk driving range, a graffiti gallery, then a scrappy park neighbours refused to abandon.
story:
Warm Water Cove sits at the foot of 24th Street, just south of the old Potrero power plant [1][2]. People have also called it Tire Beach and Toxic Beach [1]. Next door, the plant sent its cooling water back into the bay about 10°C warmer than it came out [3]. For a long time the cove was a sewage outlet [1][2].

Then, as Chris Carlsson tells it, came a decade as the "toxic golf course". Punks and other "underground culture vultures" hit golf balls into the bay from the abandoned shore, while a remarkable graffiti gallery grew on the surrounding walls over about ten years [1]. Abandoned, graffiti-covered Muni streetcars sat on the neighbouring docks [1].

Then came the clean-up. The city and local property owners held a painting party to cover the graffiti, the old streetcars were finally hauled away, and a native plant garden was started. In January 2013 Carlsson photographed pelicans and coots feeding on herring off the cove [1]. In 2016, as the Port and Planning Department drew up plans to nearly double the park, a city planner praised "a dedicated community around Warm Water Cove of longtime residents" who had hauled out trash and turned it into "the asset it is today" [2].

title: Twenty-Five Thousand Lights on the Bay Bridge
place: Rincon Park and the Embarcadero beneath the Bay Bridge's western span
hook: A publicist wanted the Bay Bridge out of the Golden Gate's shadow. A Burning Man artist gave it 25,000 LEDs and called it a digital campfire.
story: On March 5, 2013, 25,000 white LEDs flickered to life along 1.8 miles of the vertical cables on the Bay Bridge's western span, rising 500 feet above the water just off the Embarcadero [1]. The Bay Lights, by New York artist Leo Villareal, was the brainchild of Ben Davis, founder of the nonprofit Illuminate [1]. The $8 million privately funded piece glittered in abstract patterns for about seven hours a night, invisible to drivers on the bridge; Mayor Ed Lee predicted 50 million people would eventually see it [2]. It was meant to last two years, and in 2015 it went dark. Villareal, a Burning Man veteran used to seeing art consumed by fire, was at peace with that. But so many people begged for its return that Illuminate raised $4 million to reinstall a sturdier set of lights, relit on January 30, 2016 [1][3]. "It's a digital campfire that brings everyone together," Villareal said [3]. Wind, fog, salt air, lightning and constant vibration took their toll, and in early 2023 Davis said the LEDs were failing faster than they could be repaired [4]. They went dark that March, and returned in March 2026 [1].

title: A burrito on the hill, then 59 shots
place: Bernal Heights Park
hook: Alex Nieto grew up on Bernal Hill. One March evening, eating dinner in the park before work, he became the target of a 911 call.
story:
Alejandro 'Alex' Nieto was born in Bernal Heights in 1986 to Mexican immigrants, Refugio and Elvira Nieto [1][2]. As a teenager he worked as a youth counsellor at the Bernal Heights Neighborhood Center. He studied criminal justice and hoped to become a probation officer [2]. He worked as a nightclub bouncer and carried a Taser for the job [1][2].

Just after 7pm on March 21, 2014, he was eating a burrito and chips in Bernal Heights Park, wearing a red 49ers jacket. A newcomer's off-leash dog went after his food. Soon afterwards another passer-by called 911 about a man with a gun [1][2]. Four officers arrived and fired 59 shots. They said Nieto had pointed the Taser at them and that they mistook it for a pistol [1][3]. The district attorney declined to file charges in 2015 [3]. In March 2016 a federal jury cleared the officers in the family's civil suit. Protests followed, and so did debate about policing and the gentrification of the Mission and Bernal [1][2]. In 2016 his father was still visiting a memorial on the hillside road at least once a day [2].

title: A dumping-ground dead end becomes a garden
place: Burrows Pocket Park, east end of Burrows Street by San Bruno Avenue
hook: At the end of Burrows Street, Caltrans land full of dumped washing machines became a terraced garden, shaded by grapevines sprouted from old restaurant scraps.
story: The dead end where Burrows Street meets the Highway 101 embankment was a dumping ground and occasional encampment when, in early 2012, the Portola Neighborhood Steering Committee began working with Caltrans and Public Works to reclaim it, with volunteer designers from Architecture for Humanity [1]. The plan included a bioswale to clean runoff from the street and freeway, a footbridge and stone seats; every Friday lunchtime a "Brown Bag Brigade" turned up to weed [1]. Organisers also wanted a coffeehouse as an anchor, and Four Barrel Coffee opened beside the park in late 2013; SF Weekly dates the park itself to 2014 [2]. In the pandemic it grew far beyond the original lot. Volunteers hauled out old washing machines and plumbing, built an amphitheatre and a propagation station, and Angie Matt built 110 feet of retaining wall from scrap license plates, chains and tools [3]. Co-director Paul Alaga learned that the feral grapevines overhead had grown from food scraps thrown out by old restaurants [3]. title: Care for life, until the money ran out
place: Former University Mound Ladies Home, 350 University Street
hook: In 1884, $300 bought a woman lifelong care on University Mound. In 2014 the endowment was gone, and 27 elderly residents were fighting eviction.
story: James Lick's fortune founded the University Mound Ladies Home in 1884, after Mary Staples persuaded him to double his gift to $100,000 for a home for unsupported women [1]. Admission once meant a single $300 payment for care for the rest of one's life; by 1939 it was $50 a month or $3,000 for good. In 1932 Martin J. Rist redid the wooden building with the red-brick facade that still crowns the hill [1]. The endowment ran out in 2008 [2]. On 8 May 2014 the board announced the home would close; about 50 residents moved out, while 27 hung on, hoping it could be saved [1][2]. "We should have known something when they were having a chili cook-off," said Sandra Parker, whose mother Alice lived there [2]. Anna Stratton's mother had lived in nearby Bernal Heights for 50 years; the only room Stratton could find was in Hayward [2]. The board agreed to sell to the Alta Vista School, a private elementary school a few blocks away, but AgeSong, a for-profit operator that had sued claiming a right of first refusal, was allowed to match the offer and took over on 15 August 2014 [1][2]. Since 2018 CiminoCare has run a care home there called Portola Gardens [1].

title: Crated Masterpieces in a Pink Mansion's Garage
place: 224 Sea Cliff Avenue
hook: Sixteen de Koonings, Picasso etchings and a supposed Degas arrived by truck at a Sea Cliff mansion. The buyer had them left in the garage and never paid.
story: The salmon-pink house at 224 Sea Cliff Avenue was built in 1925 and looks out over Baker Beach [1]. In April 2014 crates of art were delivered there. Its owner, the real estate investor Luke Brugnara, had agreed to pay $7.3 million for 16 Willem de Kooning paintings. He had also agreed to $3 million for a sculpture sold as a Degas, plus works by George Luks, Joan Miró and Picasso [2]. He told the dealer he was opening a museum, first in San Francisco and then in Las Vegas. He had the crates left in his garage. The dealer came into the house and found it empty except for two chairs [2]. Brugnara never paid. He told his lawyer the art had been a gift [2]. The FBI raided the house. Brugnara slipped away from the federal courthouse while awaiting trial and was caught a week later in Los Gatos. He was then sentenced to seven years [1][3]. The Degas has never been found [1]. In 2024 the house sold for $6.5 million, and the new owner planned to tear out its zigzag pink staircase down to the rocks [1].

title: Flowers for Mrs. Doubtfire
place: The 'Mrs. Doubtfire' house, Steiner Street at Broadway
hook: When Robin Williams died, hundreds of San Franciscans didn't go to his home or a theatre. They went to a Pacific Heights doorstep from a 1993 comedy.
story: In Mrs. Doubtfire (1993), Robin Williams plays a father who disguises himself as an elderly nanny to stay close to his children [1]. The family's home in the film is a Victorian house at Steiner Street and Broadway, and both credited screenwriters had Bay Area ties [2]. On August 11, 2014, Williams was found dead at his home in Tiburon. In the days that followed, hundreds of fans came to the Doubtfire house and left flowers, photographs and letters on its steps [1][2]. "There was really no other place for me to pay my respects," 31-year-old Mike Orlick told the Chronicle. "This was the first thing I knew to be comedy" [2]. The house's real owner, plastic surgeon Douglas Ousterhout, told reporters he didn't mind the growing tribute. The Los Angeles Times noted the coincidence that his own work involved surgery for transgender patients, in a house made famous by a man in disguise as a woman [1]. The next night the Giants held a moment of silence for Williams, a regular at their games [1]. For a few days a private front stoop became the city's shrine to him.

title: Peeling Back Four Eras at the Officers' Club
place: Presidio Officers' Club, 50 Moraga Avenue
hook: Under 1970s Army drywall, 1930s fabric and 1880s woodwork, restorers found the adobe walls of Spanish San Francisco.
story: The Presidio Officers' Club is the park's oldest building and the second-oldest in San Francisco. Parts of it belonged to the Spanish presidio of the late 1700s [1]. For years it sat dormant. Then the Presidio Trust spent three years and $30 million restoring it, and reopened it in October 2014 to mark 20 years since the Army post became a park [2]. The hardest part was working out what was actually old. The 36,895-square-foot building had been added to so many times that the Chronicle compared it to the Winchester Mystery House [2]. In the Mesa Room, once a Spanish soldier's family home, the walls held four eras: adobe from the 1790s, an 1880s fireplace and woodwork, 1930s fabric meant to look Spanish Colonial, and 1970s Army drywall over the lot [2]. Restorers peeled them back layer by layer and fitted sliding glass panels so visitors can uncover the history themselves [2]. The new heritage gallery needed an international hunt for artifacts, because every departing army had taken what it could carry [2]. Under glass sits an Ohlone basket that looks like the oldest thing in the room. It is actually the newest: Linda Yamane was commissioned to weave it, and it took her 1,000 hours [2].

title: The Dragon Head Who Courted City Hall

story: In February 2006, Allen Leung, the 56-year-old "dragon head" of the Chee Kung Tong, was shot dead by a masked gunman in his import-export office on Jackson Street while his wife watched. Leung also sat on a city economic task force [1]. Within months Raymond "Shrimp Boy" Chow, released from prison in 2003, took over the tong [2][4]. Chow presented himself as a reformed man, collected certificates from local politicians and got a photo with Mayor Gavin Newsom. "We never bought his schtick," said a Newsom aide [3]. The FBI didn't buy it either. After a five-year undercover probe, Chow was arrested in March 2014 with 28 others. The case brought down state Senator Leland Yee, accused of trading a Senate proclamation honouring Chow's tong for a bribe [2][3]. At trial, prosecutors said Chow had called himself the "sun of the underworld" [5]. A jury convicted him of ordering Leung's murder, a charge carrying a mandatory life sentence, plus racketeering conspiracy and 154 counts of money laundering; an appeals court upheld the verdicts in 2019 [4].

title: 'No More Chinese' Became 'Love More Chinese'

hook: One September morning the Portola woke to racist graffiti on homes and shops. Within hours neighbours had painted hearts over the hate.

Public Works crews answered 311 calls and cleaned the walls quickly, and Captain Vaswani of the Bayview police station opened a hate-crime investigation [2]. The Portola Neighborhood Association called a community meeting at Palega Park for that Thursday evening, and neighbours were urged to knock on doors and bring the people next door [2]. A few days later a large, mixed crowd rallied at one of the graffiti sites. It was led by Supervisor David Campos and the association's president Chris Waddling, an immigrant gay man whose husband is Chinese American [1]. The vandal turned out to be a long-time resident. He was prosecuted and convicted of multiple counts of vandalism and hate crimes, and by 2017 there had been no repeat [1].

title: An Olympian's gun shop on Mission
place: High Bridge Arms, 3185 Mission St
hook: San Francisco's last gun store was opened by a Chinese American pistol shooter who went to the 1948 London Olympics.
story:
For decades a faded 'GUNS' sign hung over 3185 Mission Street. High Bridge Arms dates back to the 1950s, when Bob Chow opened it [1]. Chow was born in 1911 to Chinese immigrant parents. He was a ham radio pioneer and a Navy Reserve non-commissioned officer, which was rare for an Asian American at the time. According to a biography quoted by Bernalwood, he was the first Chinese American to compete in Olympic pistol shooting [1]. At the 1948 London Games he finished 13th in the rapid-fire pistol, with all 60 shots on target [2]. He also worked as a movie extra and is said to have taught John Wayne and Roy Rogers to shoot straighter [1].

Chow died in 2003, but the shop kept going under new owners. By 2015 it was the last gun shop in San Francisco. That September its managers announced it would close at the end of October. They blamed a proposed city rule that would have required video of every sale and weekly reports of customer data to police [1]. Many neighbours were glad to see it go. Others missed the old sign as a link to a lost Bernal [1].

title: Fifty Thousand Mirrors Over Kearny Street

hook: A forgotten concrete footbridge from a hotel to Chinatown's 'living room' was covered in 50,000 mirrors, glued down by the aunties who dance in the square.
story: A concrete footbridge crosses Kearny Street from the Hilton, home of the Chinese Culture Center, to Portsmouth Square. Most days it held a few sunbathers and a skateboarder [1][2]. On sunny days, visitors were told to bring sunglasses [1]. The biggest group of volunteers came from Chinatown's "Dancing Aunties", women who dance to 1950s and '60s Chinese pop in Portsmouth Square every morning and evening, and they laid the mirrors in what turned out to be the hottest week [1]. Curator Abby Chen said the aim was to highlight open space in the country's second-densest neighbourhood, where "seniors and the children are really kind of trapped in their SROs" [1]. That December, plans were unveiled to turn the 270-foot bridge into a mini-park with planters, benches and a mosaic called Sunrise by Mik Gaspay [2]. "Our alleys and our sidewalks are our front and back yards," planner Roy Chan said. "Portsmouth Square is our living room" [2].

title: Forty households told to leave the hill
place: Former Navy housing, Forest Road area, Yerba Buena Island
hook: Residents who had keys to each other's homes were offered about $5,000 to leave Yerba Buena Island. Some came to City Hall in hazmat suits.
story:
After the Navy handed Yerba Buena Island to San Francisco in 2007, a small community grew up in the old Navy housing on the hill [1]. By 2015 it was about 40 households, roughly 100 people. That summer the city told them to leave to make way for the long-planned redevelopment. They could take roughly $5,000 and move off the island, or move into an apartment on Treasure Island, and they had until September to choose [1].

Residents protested at City Hall. Betty Mackey, who had lived on the island for 11 years, said neighbours were so close that many had keys to each other's homes. She said their community would be torn down for "exclusive luxury homes for the ultra-rich" [1]. Some protesters wore white hazmat suits to show what they thought moving onto Treasure Island's contaminated soil would take. Their signs read "No Luxury Island For The Rich" and "Public Land for Public Hands" [1].

The evictions went ahead. About a third of the households took the payment and left; about two-thirds moved to Treasure Island [2]. In June 2019 the developer Wilson Meany began building 266 condominiums on Yerba Buena Island, only 14 of them below market rate [2].

story: The Veterans Administration hospital opened on Fort Miley's old parade ground in 1934. Over the decades it took on specialist work: an Epilepsy Center of Excellence, a centre for the surgical treatment of Parkinson's disease and other movement disorders, a 3D imaging laboratory, and a clinic for veterans of the wars in Afghanistan and Iraq [1]. It has been affiliated with the UCSF School of Medicine for more than 50 years, and every physician is recruited jointly by the hospital and UCSF [2]. The Northern California Institute for Research and Education, an independent nonprofit, is based on the grounds [2]. By 2015 the San Francisco VA had the largest funded research program in the Veterans Health Administration, with $90.2 million in research spending. It also held national centres of excellence in epilepsy, cardiac surgery, post-traumatic stress disorder, HIV and renal dialysis [2]. Around the modern wards, the concrete of the old gun batteries still edges the hospital grounds [3].

hook: It went from movie palace to futon showroom, rave venue and pigeon roost. Then its 70-foot marquee lit up again for Star Wars.

After that it was a furniture showroom with futons in the auditorium, then a rave venue, then a home for pigeons [2]. Alamo spent four years planning and rebuilding. Both were parents at the Katherine Delmar Burke School right next to the stairs, which was looking for a way to mark its 100th anniversary [1][2]. Barr's first tiled bench was finished in 2010. Rec and Park put in a $180,000 grant for structural repairs, on condition that the friends raised at least $250,000 privately for the tiles [1]. title: Two cameras on 'Forever Upward'

hook: Excelsior means 'ever upward'. Two photographers, ten years apart, borrowed the motto for projects on the neighbourhood that the rest of San Francisco rarely looks at.

Jensen suspected it was the first time anyone had asked to take his picture [1]. His friend and subject Rasta Dave once told him, on the corner of Excelsior and Mission, that five years earlier he would have been standing there with a pistol in his pants: 'Now I'm out here with a camera' [1]. A decade later Jeff Murray, a San Francisco native who moved to the Excelsior in 2018, was shooting on film for his own series, 'Ever Upward', his capstone at City College [2]. At Excelsior Playground a man named John offered to step out of the way of the mural Murray was photographing. Murray asked him to stay where he was, and that became the portrait [2].

title: Coming home at 55 Laguna
place: Openhouse at 55 Laguna Street (former Richardson Hall)
hook: An old teachers' college campus became the nation's largest LGBTQ+-welcoming affordable housing for seniors.
story: Richardson Hall was built at 55 Laguna in 1925 as the Kindergarten Training Building of the San Francisco State Teachers College. It is one of three city landmarks on a campus listed on the National Register [1]. After the college left, the University of California Extension used the site until the mid-2000s [2]. More than 20 years before that, two women had begun worrying about where the city's LGBTQ+ elders would live. They were Dr. Marcy Adelman and Jeanette Gurevitch, the founders of Openhouse [3]. Working with Mercy Housing, Openhouse won a landmark decision from the Planning Commission in 2012 for what it describes as the nation's largest LGBTQ+-welcoming low-income housing project [3]. Residents began moving into the renovated 55 Laguna in December 2016. That same year Openhouse opened San Francisco's first LGBTQ+ senior center next door at 65 Laguna [3]. In 2019 residents moved into a new building at 95 Laguna, named for the two founders [3]. Of the 117 apartments, 14 are reserved for formerly homeless people through the federal Housing Opportunities for Persons with AIDS program. Historic murals are preserved throughout the buildings [3].

title: Drag Queens Buy the Oldest Queer Bar
place: The Stud (1987-2020), 399 Ninth Street at Harrison
hook: Facing a doubled rent and a condo tower next door, San Francisco's oldest queer bar was saved by a co-op of drag queens, DJs and nightlife people.
story: The Stud opened in 1966 on Folsom Street and moved in 1987 to 399 Ninth Street, a kitsch-cluttered room at Ninth and Harrison [1][2]. It welcomed people other gay bars turned away. "Hair fairies, leather daddies - everyone was there on the dance floor," co-owner Honey Mahogany said. Sylvester, Patrick Cowley and Lady Gaga all passed through [2][1]. In 2016 a new landlord raised the rent to $9,000 a month, more than double what owner Michael McElhaney had paid. A huge condo complex was rising next door, and McElhaney planned to sell [3]. Drag performer VivvyAnne ForeverMore (Mica Sigourney) sent out a call to nightlife leaders. A 15-member co-op formed, including Honey Mahogany, DJ Siobhan Aluvalot and promoter Kelly Lovemonster, and raised the money to buy the business [3]. The co-op survived the rent but not the pandemic. In May 2020, with bars shut by COVID-19, it announced it would leave Ninth Street and planned a virtual "drag funeral" [1][2]. "It survived the AIDS epidemic," ForeverMore said, "and now it's the COVID pandemic that's forcing us to close" [2].

title: From gas station to town square
place: Noe Valley Town Square, 3861 24th Street
hook: In 1979 drivers queued three blocks for gas here. Later it was a car park, then a protest farmers' market, and now it's the city's only neighbourhood town square.
story: The square sits on the site of a former gas station [4]. During the 1979 oil crisis, Noe Valley's only service station, Dan's Shell at 3865 24th Street, drew queues from 6 a.m. The line of cars ran up 24th Street and three blocks down Sanchez, and most afternoons the pumps ran dry [1]. The station site later became a parking lot [4]. Then the Real Food Company closed without warning in 2003. Neighbours including Leslie Crawford and Peter Gabel decided to grow their own alternative [2][4]. On December 6, 2003, the Noe Valley Farmers' Market opened in the lot between Vicksburg and Sanchez. More than 2,000 people came the first day, and a live band played every Saturday [2]. Not everyone was pleased: a florist complained that the farmers sold flowers below wholesale [2]. In June 2013 the Recreation and Park Department bought the quarter-acre site. After more than four years of work with a residents' group and Supervisor Scott Wiener's office, Noe Valley Town Square opened in October 2016 [3]. 'There's a utopian dimension to it that I really like,' Gabel said [4].

title: Half the figure eight goes car-free
place: Eastern half of the Twin Peaks Boulevard 'figure 8'
hook: For decades cars circled the summit on a looping figure eight. In 2016 the city handed half of it to walkers.
story:
Twin Peaks Boulevard wraps around both summits in a loop shaped like a figure eight. For decades both halves carried cars [1][2]. In July 2016 the SFMTA and the Recreation and Park Department tried an experiment. The western half became a two-way road, and the eastern half was closed to cars and opened to people walking and cycling, marked off with paint and concrete barriers [1][2]. The results were striking. The number of drivers going over the 30 mph limit fell by 77 per cent. More than 58 per cent of people in a year-long survey wanted the change made permanent [1]. It was, in June 2020 [1].

The summit is 64 acres of open space with three trails, including one named for the Mission blue butterfly [1]. The Chronicle reported that construction was due to start in 2025 on rebuilding the car-free side as a wide promenade, after improvements to the Noe Peak trail and the path down to Crestline Drive [2].

title: Irene Crescio's Lilies on San Bruno Avenue
place: San Bruno Avenue commercial corridor, near Bacon Street
hook: A lifelong Portolan and 38-year phone-company worker walked San Bruno Avenue almost daily, tending its lilies, reporting graffiti and pushing the city for street-tree lights.
story: Irene Crescio spent her whole life in the Portola. She was the daughter of Mario and Elide Crescio and worked for 38 years at Pac Bell [1][2]. Into her eighties she sat on the board of the Portola Neighborhood Association, and she took San Bruno Avenue as her own project [1]. She worked with the city to bury the street's power lines and plant trees along it. She also lobbied for electrical outlets on the streetlights, which were later used for the decorative tree lighting she had imagined [1]. Her funeral Mass was at St. Elizabeth Church, Somerset at Wayland [1][2]. Her family asked that, instead of flowers, people give to the neighbourhood association or to the Good Shepherd Gracenter on Bacon Street [1]. Later that year her memorial fund helped pay for a new multimedia mural in the neighbourhood [1].

title: No High-Pressure Hydrants for the Portola
place: Silver Avenue at University Street, on the proposed route of a high-pressure fire main to University Mound Reservoir
hook: After 1906 San Francisco built an emergency firefighting water network that never reached the Portola. By 2016 the proposed substitute was fifteen miles of hose.
story:
After the 1906 disaster, a city committee called for a separate high-pressure fire main system supplied with water pumped from the bay. It was meant only for the 'congested value district' downtown [2]. The resulting Auxiliary Water Supply System was finished by 1913 and never reached many outer neighbourhoods, the Portola among them [1].

Between 2010 and 2012, Public Utilities Commission maps showed an extension running along Geneva and Silver avenues to University Mound Reservoir, the Portola's 140-million-gallon hilltop basin [1]. The agency's later plans dropped it. Instead it floated a 'Flexible Water Supply System': about 15 miles of 12-inch hose stored at the Sunset and University Mound reservoirs, which volunteers from the Neighborhood Emergency Response Team would lay out after an earthquake. Critics warned of debris-blocked, pitch-dark streets, and the plan was abandoned [1]. On April 6, 2016, firefighters' union president Thomas O'Connor wrote to Supervisor Aaron Peskin that the union was 'greatly disturbed' that the Silver Avenue extension and others were being dropped. At a hearing on March 15, 2017, Peskin wondered aloud whether the city should 'bite the bullet' on a half-billion-dollar investment [1]. By then only University Mound's North Basin had been seismically upgraded, in 2010 [1].

title: Soccer's windy home in Balboa Park
place: Boxer Stadium, 166 Havelock Street, Balboa Park
hook: San Francisco's soccer stadium in Balboa Park is a grass pitch with 3,500 seats and no lights. A pro rugby team found it too windy.
story: Off Havelock Street, at the north edge of Balboa Park, is Boxer Stadium, a full-size grass pitch with room for 3,500 and no lights [1]. It is named for Matthew J. Boxer, whom the Chronicle listed among the figures behind the city's century-old soccer legacy [2]. The San Francisco Soccer Football League began in 1902, as the California Football Association, with five teams, including the Albion Rovers, Thistle F.C. and the Vampires. The Vampires wore a bat on their jerseys, and Bela Lugosi once donated a cup for a match between San Francisco and Los Angeles sides [2]. In 1976 the league's San Francisco Italian Athletic Club became the first non-college team from the city to win a national championship, the National Open Cup [2]. City planners have listed the stadium, with the park's pool and other pre-1955 buildings, as part of a potential Balboa Park historic district [3]. It is not a grand venue. In 2016 the new professional league PRO Rugby played its San Francisco Rush here. In December it folded the team. The owner, Doug Schoninger, wrote that they 'could not return to Boxer due to its substandard facilities, fan experience and wind conditions' [4]. The Chronicle's verdict from 2002 still holds: the city has never had enough fields for all its players [2].

title: The Hospital That Serves Warm Water
place: Chinese Hospital, 845 Jackson St
hook: Chinatown built its own hospital because other hospitals turned Chinese patients away. Bruce Lee was born there. In 2016 it opened a new eight-storey tower.
story: In an era when other San Francisco hospitals turned away or discriminated against Chinese patients, Chinatown looked after its own [3][2]. In 1899 the Tung Wah Dispensary began seeing patients, staffed by Western-trained doctors and Chinese herbalists. In 1925 the community-built Chinese Hospital opened on Jackson Street [1]. Bruce Lee was born there in 1940 [3]. The kitchen serves jook, and macaroni soup with diced ham, and around Lunar New Year grateful patients drop off tea, oranges and mooncakes [3]. NBC News called it the only Chinese-operated and -governed independent hospital in North America [3]. The 1925 building was later judged seismically unsafe. It was pulled down in 2012 to make way for a new tower [1][2]. On April 18, 2016, the hospital opened the eight-storey, $180 million Patient Tower, with hand-painted cherry blossoms in nearly every room [1][2]. "We have the food, we have the language, we know the culture," said CEO Brenda Yee. "Other hospitals give you cold water. We know to provide warm water" [2].

title: The Leaning Tower of Mission Street
place: Millennium Tower, 301 Mission Street
hook: Residents of San Francisco's most glamorous condo tower were summoned to a secret meeting, IDs checked at the door, and told their building was sinking.
story: The 58-story Millennium Tower opened as a home for professional athletes and venture capitalists. Its plans forecast it might settle as much as six inches; by late 2016 it had sunk 16 inches and was tilting, an estimated two to four inches at the base and 14 at the top [1]. A paper trail of concern dated back to early 2009, but most residents knew nothing until they were summoned in May 2016 to a private meeting in a club-level lounge, where identification was checked at the door and they were told what they heard must stay secret [1]. The story broke on the Chronicle's front page that August. In November, City Attorney Dennis Herrera sued the developer, saying it knew the building "had sunk more than it was supposed to" before selling a single condo and didn't tell buyers [1]. After years of litigation, a $100 million foundation fix began in 2020, with the building occupied throughout. In June 2023 crews finished transferring its load onto 18 new piles driven to bedrock; the engineer reported the settlement had been arrested and the tower had risen slightly, undoing some of the 30 inches of tilt to the northwest it had gathered over 15 years [2].

title: The Soil Samples That Weren't
place: Hunters Point Shipyard, Parcel A homes (Innes Court)
hook: The Navy's contractor was supposed to show the old shipyard was safe for thousands of new homes. Instead, regulators found, some of its soil samples had come from somewhere else.
story: From 1946 to 1969 the Naval Radiological Defense Laboratory worked at Hunters Point, cleaning ships contaminated by the Bikini atomic tests and studying fallout. In 1956 alone, 980 tons of radioactive waste were dumped at sea [1]. Decades later, cleaning up the Superfund site was the precondition for turning the yard into a neighbourhood of more than 12,000 homes [2]. Tetra Tech, the contractor hired to measure radionuclides and other contaminants, had been testing soil there since at least the mid-1990s [2]. Whistleblowers inside the firm began speaking out around 2012. The Nuclear Regulatory Commission confirmed that the company had taken dirt from an area known to be clean and passed it off as coming from another area, where housing was planned [2]. In July 2016 the Navy admitted to Greenaction that it had found 386 "anomalous" samples out of more than 25,000. On 13 September the EPA wrote to the Navy, and land transfers to the developer FivePoint were put on hold [2]. Critics argued that the bigger problem was how much of the shipyard had never been tested at all [3]. By then the first 88 townhomes, built on land handed over years earlier, had already sold out [2].

title: The Year the Famous View Closed
place: Alamo Square Park (Hayes and Steiner streets)
hook: For a year, chain-link fences surrounded the city's most photographed lawn. When the park reopened, its planners wanted it to become the view itself.
story: In May 2016 the 12.7-acre Alamo Square Park closed for a $5.3 million renovation. The work was supposed to take seven months, but it took a year because of a wet winter and extra work that wasn't in the original plan [1][2]. Crews rebuilt the irrigation system, which is controlled by a small device on a nearby flagpole that monitors temperature and rainfall. The park was expected to save more than 2.5 million gallons of water a year, about a third of its use [2]. They repaved the paths, added an all-gender accessible restroom, and planted a rain garden and native plants, using the tennis court as a temporary nursery [1][2]. Neighbours paid for 45 new trees [1]. "Everyone loves the views out of the park," said Recreation and Park project manager Brett Desmarais. "But we want the park to become the view itself" [2]. On the last quiet morning before it reopened, the sidewalk by the Painted Ladies, normally crowded, was empty except for a woman in a bathrobe handing her husband a mug of coffee as he set off on his bike [2]. The ribbon was cut on May 24, 2017, and Board of Supervisors President London Breed called the park "one of the jewels of our city" [1].

title: The art school that swallowed apartments
place: 1055 Pine St
hook: A for-profit art school quietly bought up some 40 buildings, many of them homes. The reckoning turned two Nob Hill properties into housing for low-income seniors.
story:
Over more than a decade, the for-profit Academy of Art University and a web of affiliated companies bought or leased some 40 San Francisco properties, including a cluster on Nob Hill's Bush, Sutter and Pine streets [1][2]. A March 2016 Planning Department memo found at least 33 violated zoning, permit or preservation rules. The city said about 160 affordable homes had been illegally converted into student housing and another 140 units removed from rent control [1].

On 6 May 2016 City Attorney Dennis Herrera sued, calling the academy "one of San Francisco's most egregious land use scofflaws." His complaint targeted properties including 1055 Pine, 1080 and 1153 Bush, and 860 Sutter [2].

That December Herrera announced a settlement valued at over $60 million, then the largest in a city code-enforcement case: $20 million in cash, including $7 million to help low-income tenants stay housed, and at least 160 affordable units [1]. The housing would come from two Pine Street buildings. Students living at 1055 Pine would be moved out and the building renovated, while a new building would rise at 1069 Pine, both for low-income seniors for 66 years [1]. The deal was guaranteed personally by academy president Elisa Stephens, granddaughter of its founder [1].

title: The fire mains that never reached Geneva
place: Geneva Avenue between San Jose Avenue and Mission Street (route of the abandoned AWSS extension)
hook: After 1906 the city built quake-proof water mains just for fighting fires. In the south they stop at Ocean Avenue, and a plan to extend them down Geneva was dropped.
story: After the 1906 fire, San Francisco built the Auxiliary Water Supply System (AWSS). It is a separate, heavily braced network of mains and hydrants that can draw reservoir water or seawater after a great earthquake [1]. Finished by 1913, it was never extended to some fifteen outlying neighbourhoods, among them Mission Terrace, the Outer Mission, the Excelsior and Ocean View [1]. A 1986 bond brought a loop along Ocean Avenue up to Mission Street, at the edge of this district [1]. After a mid-1990s study, archaeologists monitored work on an AWSS connection along Ocean Avenue between Onondaga Avenue and San Fernando Way. The only thing they found was a redwood utility pipe 2.5 feet down near Ocean and Plymouth [2]. Between 2010 and 2012 the Public Utilities Commission's maps showed new mains running from Ocean Avenue to Alemany Boulevard and along Geneva and Silver avenues to University Mound Reservoir [1]. Then the maps changed. In April 2016 the president of Fire Fighters Local 798 complained of plans to 'abandon' the Alemany, Geneva and Silver extensions [1]. By late 2017 a reporter found no plans for AWSS-style pipelines in the city's southernmost neighbourhoods. The city's bonds were paying for more cisterns instead, and a cistern, once empty, is useless and needs a fire engine to pump it [1].

title: The girl beneath the garage floor
place: Former Odd Fellows Cemetery grounds, near Rossi Avenue (exact house not published)
hook: In 2016 a remodelling crew's shovels hit a tiny bronze coffin with glass windows. Inside was a little girl, a rose still in her hand.
story: On May 9, 2016, workers remodelling a house in the Lone Mountain neighbourhood struck something beneath the concrete garage floor: a small lead-and-bronze coffin with two glass viewing windows [1]. Inside lay a girl of about three in a long white dress, a rose in her right hand and lavender woven into her curly blond hair [1]. She had been left behind when the Odd Fellows Cemetery, which once covered these blocks, was emptied to Colma [1][2]. The medical examiner's office said that because the coffin was on private property, it was the homeowner's problem. Ericka Karner, whose family had lived there since 1976, was quoted $7,000 by one undertaker [1]. The Garden of Innocence charity stepped in, the Odd Fellows paid, and the girl, provisionally named Miranda, was reburied at Greenlawn Memorial Park in Colma on June 4, 2016, with about 140 people attending [2]. In 2017 researchers matched old plot records and obituaries, confirmed by DNA from a descendant of her brother, and gave her back her name: Edith Howard Cook, who died on October 13, 1876, six weeks short of her third birthday [2]. Her father, Horatio Nelson Cook, ran a leather-belting business [3].

title: The sidewalk that keeps sinking
place: 1200 block of Fourth Street, south of Mission Creek
hook: The buildings stay put. The sidewalks beside them sit on old swamp and bay fill, and on one Mission Bay block they keep dropping away.
story: On the 1200 block of Fourth Street, the sidewalk has been pulling away from the buildings beside it. NBC reported in 2016 that it had sunk as much as six inches. The city's chief of street use, Jerry Sanguinetti, said it was not up to standard because it was separating from the building [1]. A temporary fix and wheelchair ramps followed in 2017, and permits for permanent work that December. Yet photos in January 2019 showed the gaps getting deeper [1]. The reason is underground. The neighborhood sits on artificial fill over land once known as Mission Swamp, and a shallow bay teeming with marsh life [1][2]. From about 1860 to 1910, steam shovels dumped sand hills into Mission Bay. Garbage dumps near Seventh and Eighth streets added more, and finally rubble from 1906 [2]. A longtime houseboater once described building here as pile-driving down through unconsolidated fill toward bedrock [3]. The sidewalks, laid on the fill itself, have not stayed put [1]. Historical geographer Gray Brechin noted that scientists have known Mission Bay's land was sinking for well over a century. The U.S. Geological Survey warns that such soil can liquefy in an earthquake and makes shaking worse [1].

title: Bringing a buried creek back to daylight
place: Yosemite Creek route between Yosemite Marsh and Louis Sutter Playground
hook: Yosemite Creek has run through pipes for generations. The city now plans to dig it up and let it flow in the open again.
story: Much of Yosemite Creek, which starts at Yosemite Marsh on McLaren Park's northern edge, now runs underground in pipes. The Recreation and Park Department and the Public Utilities Commission now plan to bring about 1,700 feet of it back to the surface. The open channel will run from Yosemite Marsh, near Bacon and Oxford streets, past Wayland and University streets to the Louis Sutter ballfield [1]. Another 400 feet will stay underground beneath one block of Wayland Street, making 2,100 feet of new creek in all. Along the way, bioretention basins will let stormwater soak into the soil instead of overloading the combined sewer [1]. A gathering place called Yosemite Creek Station, near Wayland and Princeton streets, will teach visitors about the city's hidden watersheds. Stormwater stored in underground tanks will water the Louis Sutter soccer field in a five-year pilot that the city calls its first [1][2]. An open house for neighbours was held in March 2017. By 2021 the budget was about $13.7 million, paid by the PUC's sewer improvement program [2]. Construction is scheduled for late 2026 or early 2027, and opening for late 2029 [1]. It is the last of eight early projects in the PUC's multi-billion-dollar programme to upgrade the city's ageing sewers [1].

title: From 'no bicycles' to a pump track
place: McLaren Bike Park, Sunnydale Avenue
hook: In 1983 the city's planners ruled McLaren too steep for bikes. Thirty-four years later, volunteers opened a dirt pump track on its slopes.
story: McLaren Park has a longer cycling history than its master plans suggest. SF Urban Riders say the Recreation and Park Department built a BMX race track here in the 1970s and held races every year [1]. The 1983 master plan mentions 'the present bike area', but it also blamed motorbikes for bare, eroding soil, and its view on bicycles was flat. The park's topography 'does not lend itself' to bike trails, it said, so 'bicycle trails are not recommended for the park' [2]. Riders did not accept that. SF Urban Riders held Take A Kid Mountain Biking Day here from 2009 to 2011, and the SF Mountain Bike Festival in 2013 and 2014 [1]. The first festival, on September 7, 2013, drew more than 300 participants [3]. The group started the bike park project in 2011 and handed it to a volunteer group, the McLaren Bike Park Founders [1]. Construction started in April 2017. The park opened on October 21, 2017, with a youth BMX and mountain-bike dirt pump track, a beginner skills loop with ramps, and a toolshed. Its construction budget was about $650,000, from bond money, other public funds and private donations [4].

title: Julius' Castle Fights Its Way Back
place: Julius' Castle, 302 Greenwich St / 1541 Montgomery St
hook: A turreted 1920s restaurant under Coit Tower went dark in 2008. Reviving it took lawsuits, a sliding hillside, a fire and 14 years.
story: On the cliff below Coit Tower, Julius' Castle was built between 1923 and 1928 by the Italian restaurateur Julius Roz and the architect Luigi Mastropasqua. It paid tribute to Layman's Castle, a hilltop folly that fire destroyed in 1903 [1]. Inside, the panelling came from the 1915 Panama-Pacific Exposition [2]. For generations it was where San Franciscans got engaged and celebrated [2][3]. The whole cast of The Empire Strikes Back once came to dinner. Another night the guests were weathered mountaineers, some missing fingers, gathered to honour Sir Edmund Hillary [1]. It closed in January 2008 [3]. In 2012 the attorney Paul Scott bought it in a bankruptcy sale, outbidding someone who wanted to turn it into condos [3]. Neighbours warned of idling Ubers and drunken revellers, but in July 2017 the Planning Commission voted 7 to 0 to let it reopen. "That is city life," said Commissioner Kathrin Moore. "We are not living in the suburbs" [2]. Then came a building found to sit over the property line, a sliding hillside, and a fire that destroyed a turret [3]. In July 2026 Scott said a chef had been hired and the castle would reopen that September [3].
